Tuesday, 9th March, 1926.
The Second Session of the Second Parliament of Northern Ireland, appointed to meet
9th March, 1926, in the Sixteenth year of the
Reign of King George V, was opened by the
Governor (His Grace the Duke of Abercorn,
K.P.) in person.
The House met at Ten minutes before
Twelve of the Clock, Mr. SPEAKER (Right
Hon. Hugh O'Neill, D.L., M.P.) in the
Chair.
Local Bill.
Mr. SPEAKER laid upon the Table
Report from the Examiner of Petitions for
Local Bills, that he has certified that the
Standing Orders have been complied with
on the following case:
Carrickfergus Harbour.
Divorce Bill.
Mr. SPEAKER laid upon the Table Report
from the Examiner of Petitions for Local
Bills, that he certified that Standing Orders
have been complied with on the following
case:-
McCaldin's Divorce Bill.
MEMBER SWORN.
The following Member took the Oath and
signed the Roll:
Patrick O'Neill, Esquire, County of Down,
The Gentleman Usher of the Black Rod
(Major T. Dalby Hackett, D.S.0.) was
announced.
Addressing Mr. Speaker, the Gentleman
Usher said:
His Grace the Governor of Northern
Ireland commands this Honourable House
to attend immediately in the Senate.
The House went, and having returned,
The Sitting was suspended until Three of
the Clock, and then resumed.

The following Papers were presented
during the Recess and delivered to the
Librarian of the House of Commons during
the Recess, pursuant to Standing Order No.

SESSIONAL ORDERS.
ELECTIONS.
Ordered, That all Members, who are returned for two or more places in any part of
Northern Ireland do make their Election for
which of the places they will serve, within
one week after it shall appear that there is
no question upon the Return for that place;
and if anything shall come in question
touching the Return or Election of any
Member, he is to withdraw during the time
the matter is in debate; and that all Members returned upon double Returns do withdraw till the Returns are determined.
Resolved: That if it shall appear that any
person hath been elected or returned a Meinber of this House or endeavoured so to be,
by Bribery, or any other corrupt practices,
this House will proceed with the utmost
severity against all such persons as shall
have been wilfully concerned in such Bribery
or other corrupt practices.
WITNESSES.
any
Resolved: That if it shall appear that any
person hath been tampering with
Witness in respect of his evidence to be
given to this House, or any Committee
thereof, or directly or indirectly hath endeavoured to deter or hinder any person
from appearing or giving evidence, the same
is declared to be a high crime or misdemeanour; and this House will proceed
with the utmost severity against such
offender.
Resolved: That if it shall appear that
any person hath given false evidence in any
case before this House, or any Committee
thereof, this House will proceed with the
utmost severity against such offender.
ROYAL ULSTER CONSTABULARY.
Ordered: That the Commissioner of the
Royal Ulster Constabulary do take care that,
during the Session of Parliament, the passages through the streets leading to this
House be kept free and open, and that no
obstruction be permitted to hinder the passage of Members to and from this House,
and that no disorder be allowed in the precincts of or in the passages leading to this
House, during the Sitting of Parliament,
and that there be no annoyance therein, or
thereabouts; and that the Serjeant at Arms
attending this House do communicate this
Order to the Commissioner of the Royal
Ulster Constabulary aforesaid.
VOTES, PROCEEDINGS, AND RECORDS.
Ordered: That the Votes, Proceedings and
Records of this House be printed, being first
perused by Mr. Speaker; and that he do
appoint the printing thereof; and that no
person but such as he shall appoint do presume to print the same.
PRIVILEGES.
Ordered That a Committee of Privileges
be appointed.
OUTLAWRIES BILL,
"for
the more effectual preventing
Clandestine Outlawries" read the First time
and ordered to be read a Second time.
KING'S SPEECH.
Mr. SPEAKER: I have to report to the
House that the House has this day attended
in the Senate to hear the Speech of his
Grace, the Governor, on behalf of the
Crown, to both Houses of Parliament; of
which I have for greater accuracy obtained
a copy. The Speech is as follows:-
Members of the Senate and of the
House of Commons:
I am deeply gratified at the satisfactory
arrangement reached with the British
Government in regard to the future of the
Unemployment Insurance Fund. Following
upon the procedure in the Imperial Parliament a Bill will be laid before you to give
full effect to the agreement at an early
date.
9 MARCH 1926
King's Speech.
King's Speech.
arisen in the interpretation and administration of the Intoxicating Liquor Act,
and Measures for the provision of better
accommodation for Juvenile Offenders and
for the Protection of Animal and Bird Life
will be laid before you.
It is a matter of profound regret that I
am not yet able to comment more favourably on the question of Unemployment,
though I am glad to note that there have
recently appeared some slight indications
of an improvement in the volume of work
generally, and I learn with pleasure that
advantage continues to be taken of facilities
afforded under the Loans Guarantee Acts.
Every practicable step will be adopted to
assist industry by means of these Acts and
by Grants to Local Authorities and Public
Bodies in necessitous areas to carry out works
of permanent public utility. The measures
which my Government are taking in cooperation with the trade to stimulate a
demand for linen goods will necessarily
require time to achieve their full object.
Bills will be submitted to you dealing
with National Health and Unemployment
Insurance and for the purpose of securing
authority to extend for a further period
of one year the provisions of the Loans
Guarantee Acts.
was
It is gratifying to record that the great
measure of social reform-the Widows',
Orphans' and Old A ge Contributory
Pensions Act-which
passed last
Session, has been brought into operation
so speedily and smoothly, and to learn
that no fewer than 3,350 widows and 8,300
dependent children and orphans
already receiving benefits under the Act.
are
As it was not found possible to complete
the necessary arrangements to admit of
Measures for the purpose of amending the
provisions of the existing Juries Acts, and
the improvement of Mining facilities being
dealt with during last Session, I trust that
the Bills which are now to be laid before
you will receive your earnest consideration.
A Measure for the Preservation of
Ancient Monuments was duly introduced
in the Senate last Session and circulated.
A Bill relating to this matter will be laid
before you and proceeded with this
Session.
Proposals will be laid before you to
secure the more effective control of motor
traffic on public roads in order to minimise
the risks of accident to persons and property-particular regard being had to those
vehicles carrying passengers for hire.
Your assent will be invited to the
extension for another year of the Housing
Acts which have proved so useful in encouraging the activities of Local Authorities and private builders in the erection of
houses for the working classes.
Legislation will be submitted to you
dealing with minor difficulties which have
I am glad to observe that the Marketing
of Eggs Act, which came into operation at
the beginning of last year, has already had
a beneficial effect on this important industry. Some revision is necessary, and
accordingly appropriate legislation will be
introduced during the Session.
It is gratifying to learn that the results
which have attended the first Season's work
of the Society formed last year to promote
the cultivation of pedigree flax seed
throughout the Empire, towards which you
have afforded and still continue to afford
financial assistance, are encouraging, and
that a sufficient stock of seed has now been
accumulated in Somersetshire to permit of
the allocation of appreciable guaranteed
quantities to Northern Ireland, Kenya,
Canada, and other parts of the Empire.
There are also numerous and important
problems relating to animal nutrition
which await solution. Having regard to
the special conditions which prevail in
Northern Ireland, the time has arrived
when the investigation of such problems
should be undertaken, and with this object
in view you will be asked to make provision for the establishment of a Research
Experimental Farm, which will be conducted by a Board of Trustees.
Other Bills will be laid before you dealing with the following matters:-
The finance of Teachers' Pensions and
the increase of low-rated pensions of
certain state and local authorities'
pensioners.
Members of the House of Commons:
Estimates for the Public Services will be
laid before you in due course. Every
effort is being made by my Ministers to
to
reduce expenditure
the minimum
amount consistent with efficiency.

Debate on the Address.
Mr. COOPER (in morning dress): I beg
to move:
"That an humble address be presented
to His Grace the Governor of Northern Ireland, as followeth :-
Your Grace,
We, His Majesty's most dutiful and loyal
subjects, the Commons of Northern Ireland,
in Parliament assembled, beg leave to offer
our humble thanks to Your Grace for the
Speech which Your Grace has addressed to
both Houses of Parliament."
The House will observe from the King's
Speech that a very considerable programme
is to be put before us in the coming Session.
The programme deals with every section of
the community. First of all, and most
important, I think, is the Bill to confirm
the arrangement made with the British
Government in regard to the future of the
Unemployment Fund
us
Most of the Members
connever
of this House have often listened with very
great apprehension to the statements made
showing the ever-increasing volume of debt
created by the provision for unemployment.
In the rural districts of Ulster, the people
have found great difficulty in understanding
this expenditure, and some of us have on
many occasions been pressed by our
stituents to protest against it. The people
who asked to protest really
thoroughly understood the subject, because
they never thoroughly understood that there
were perhaps 50,000 people in Northern Ireland who were altogether unable to obtain
employment. When the wives and children
of those persons are added, the number of
people who are affected by unemployment is
very large indeed. As I have said, we were
asked on many occasions to protest, but
when
this
the rural representatives in
House realised the large number of people
affected they refrained all through from giving what might have been unhelpful
criticism.
I think the whole House has understood
the very difficult task which the Minister
of Labour has had to carry out, and none
of us desire, in any way, to criticise him in
his part. Now that an arrangement has
been reached, I think it is a matter for congratulation that a problem of such complexity, so far as can be judged at present,
has been so satisfactorily settled from the
(Hon.
point of view of Northern Ireland.
Members: Hear, hear.) Though our troubles
are not yet over, troubles which are entirely
due to the war, I think there is no doubt
on this
whatever that the great strain
Province has been eased. It has been considerably eased, and it will enable the
Government to continue to give relief where

A Bill which may cause some amusement to

think it is time the Government took over

Mr. T. W. MCMULLAN (in morning dress):
I rise to second the Address so ably moved
by my hon. Friend (Mr. Cooper). I would
thank the Members of the Cabinet for their
kindness and confidence in selecting me for
this honourable task. I take their decision
as a compliment to the county which I have
the privilege to represent; a county in
which loyalty to the King and cordial
support of this Government have been
abundantly manifested. (Hon. Members:
Hear, hear.) I would ask the indulgence
of right hon. and hon. Gentlemen for
my shortcomings to-day. I am very
conscious that in anything I shall say I
shall fall very much below that
high standard that has been set
by previous speakers to this Motion-a high
standard that has been delightfully maintained by my hon. Friend and Colleague.
We are met to-day in an atmosphere of
political peace. The tension due to the
Boundary difficulty having been relaxed, we
welcome the gestures of good-will, and
desire for mutual understanding which have
passed between our Government and that of
the Free State. In this House we can now
settle down, free from outside distraction,
to the discussion and solution of our Own
domestic problems. We shall welcome
amongst us those Nationalist Colleagues
who propose to take their seats, and we
shall, I am confident, find them able and
willing to co-operate in those matters of
common interest. (Hon. Members: Hear,
hear.) For them and for us may there be
one goal and one goal only-the happiness
and prosperity of our people.
It is very regrettable that year by year
in his Speech from the Throne his Grace
the Governor has to call attention to the
spectre of unemployment. We had hoped to
speed this unwelcome guest in the year that
is past, but our hopes have not been fulfilled. There are, however, indications of
better times ahead. Trade, I believe, in
Great Britain has taken a distinct turn
for the better, and the number of unemployed has been very considerably reduced.
I am hopeful that we shall soon participate
in this prosperity on the other side. Good
trade and bad trade, prosperity and adversity are not poles asunder. They lie on
either side of an ill-defined boundary line.
A change of sentiment, a general confidence
that the worst is past, and demand will spring
up again, and the line will be crossed. If
employers and employed will pull together,
every man cheerfuly pulling his weight, we
shall soon find ourselves over the divide,
in that pleasant land of prosperity where we
desire to be.
I would join with my hon. Friend in congratulating the Prime Minister and the
Minister of Finance and the Minister of
Labour on the success of their negotiations
with the Imperial Government as to the Unemployment Insurance Fund. (Hon. Members: Hear, hear.) As a result serious
financial conditions will be alleviated and
once for all the principle established that in
social services Northern Ireland must be enabled to keep step by step with Great
Britain. (Hon. Members: Hear, hear.)
Unwilling as struggling taxpayers are to
shoulder fresh burdens, all hon. Members
will agree with me that the Widows',
Orphans' and Old Age Contributory Pensions
Act was a noble public acceptance of a
Christian duty. Many thousands of the
fatherless and widows amongst us have been
relieved from anxiety and distress, and today can thank God and take courage for the
future.
The programme of legislation foreshadowed
in the King's Speech is a lengthy one, and
the time does not permit me more than a
hurried reference. I welcome the Bill for
Amending the Juries Acts, a belated and
very necessary Measure. I am glad to see
that the Loans Guarantee Acts are to be
extended for another year. They have been
of great service to our shipbuilders in these
difficult times. I trust that our public
authorities will continue to make full and
patriotic use of the Government grants in
employing labour on works of public utility.
I congratulate the Government on its wise
decision to help our linen trade financially
in its united advertising campaign, which 1
am confident will do much in helping to
restore prosperity to that important industry, so giving increased employment to
our working classes.
In many ways, I am glad to see from the
King's Speech, our Government will continue
to use every means within its resources to
help the revival of industry and the relief
of unemployment.

There is an appeal to national sentiment in

shone have in too many cases crumbled into

I regret exceedingly that our farmers
during the past few years have met with so
much ill-fortune. Excessive rain was their
enemy during two seasons. Last year's sunshine should have helped them, but the fine
weather was so widespread that world-crops
were heavy and unremunerative markets
were the result. May our farmers in the
coming season have a happier experience.
(Hon. Members: Hear, hear.)
I congratulate the Minister of Ariculture

The work of the Linen Research Association at Lambeg I am glad to know promises
good results for our farmers in the growing
of flax and for our spinners in the securing
of fine and reliable material for the spinning
of their yarns.
I would impress on the Minister of Agriculture the urgent necessity of working hand
in hand with this Association. Our linen
trade cannot prosper unless an adequate
supply of flax, its raw material, is available.
This should be obtainable through our own
farming industry with its market at its door.
The quality of Irish flax if scientifically
grown and treated would be equal to, if not
superior to, any other growth. Our linens
made from such flax would regain and hold
their ascendancy throughout the world. To
secure the growing of flax on an extensive
scale it will be necessary to convince the
farmer that flax growing can be really remunerative. To this end he must be educated in the latest scientific processes in
cultivation and after treatment, in saving
the seed and using its products for which
there are good markets The great linen industry depends for its prosperity to-day
largely on the capacity and enthusiasm of
the Ministry of Agriculture.
There are other interesting matters referred to in the King's Speech but I fear
that I have wearied honourable Members
(hon. Members: No, no) and I conclude with
earnest hope that in the session begun to-day
we in this House may be enabled to do useful work for Ulster and with the prayer that
the dark clouds of bad trade and unemployment, which for so long have hung over our
land, may soon be dispelled by the rising
sun of prosperity. I beg to second.

HOUSE OF COMMONS
[The Prime Minister]
I wish to express on behalf of all sections
of the House our relief and thankfulness
that the Governor was able to deliver the
gracious Speech in person owing to the
splendid recovery of the Duchess after her
serious illness and operation. We earnestly
hope that she will soon be again in our
midst, thoroughly restored to her old health
and vigour.
non-
The programme outlined in his Grace's
markedly
Speech is
modest and
contentious. My Colleagues and I feel very
strongly that what Ulster requires above
all else is a period of quietude and rest to
enable the people to concentrate on recovering agricultural prosperity and lost trade,
unhampered by acute political controversy,
and helped and encouraged in every practical
way by the Government. Our difficulties
during the past five years have been of three
separate and distinct categories. First:
Vis-a-vis Southern Ireland. We are now on
a satisfactory, or, at all events, a friendly
footing, and in a position I hope to discuss
amicably any outstanding matters that lie
between us. Secondly: Vis-a-vis successive
British Governments. It is gratifying to me
to be in a position to announce that, one by
one, matters of paramount concern have
been surmounted, culminating in the agreement over Unemployment. (Hon. Members:
Hear, hear.) Anything remaining to be
cleared up is of comparative triviality, and
should occasion but little difficulty. Thirdly:
Regarding our Own internal difficulties--
they have disappeared I hope and believe for
good and ever. (Hon. Members: Hear, hear.)
Broadly speaking, I am happy to say with
regard to all three that we are now in a
position to rule the books, and with a
balanced Budget and a clean slate to face
with Ulster grit and determination whatever
fate holds for us in the future.
Before metaphorically burying the past, I
would like to pay a warm tribute to those
branches of our Special Constabulary which,
owing to the settled state of the country,
and to the limitations of our financial resources, had to be disbanded. We are largehearted enough and broad-minded enough to
efface from our memory the one single lapse
-a regrettable lapse of a certain section of
the "A's" at the termination of their engagement. We are fully alive to the fact
and will never forget that for over five years
they were instrumental in bringing the
country to the peaceful state in which we
And it to-day. On behalf of all our citizens
I tender hearty thanks for the duty they so
nobly performed through anxious and
indeed dangerous times. (Hon. Members:
Hear, hear.) We had in the "C1's"
splendidly disciplined and effective body of
men. To them, too, officers and men alike,
a
I pay a similar tribute, and I will always
look back with pride upon the picture of
both forces when on parade, and on whatever other more arduous and effective duty
circumstances demanded.
It may be appropriate for me at this juneture to state the Government's intentions
regarding the "B's." The House may
remember that in my speech of the 9th
December last I indicated that the same
amount of duty would not be required from
them in future. We are, accordingly, putting into force an arrangement which has
been sanctioned for some time past, which
should fully meet the requirements of our
Province in times of peace. The Government feel that it would be against the best
interests of everyone concerned to interfere
unduly with what is practically a voluntary
body of men, who have so materially and
so gallantly contributed to the pacification of
the Province, and who continue to enjoy
and inspire that confidence amongst the
people, without which it would be impossible
to settle down in comfort and security to
face the problems of the future.
Since we last met the Government and
the Senate have sustained a heavy loss in
the retirement of Lord Londonderry. (Hon.
Members: Hear, hear.) His courage and
wise counsel, his powerful individuality and
initiative were all characteristics of inestimable value to Ulster. I can truthfully say that one occupying the responsible position of leader could have had
a more loyal and lovable colleague and
comrade. There will be no change in the
Government's educational policy; the Act
bearing his honoured name-that charter of
our children's future-will be administered
by his successor in the same broad spirit
and in the same happy co-operation with
the Regional Committees, to the end that
the youth of Ulster may be provided with
every reasonable facility for meeting the
competition of life in every sphere. (Hon.
Members: Hear, hear.)
Turning our thoughts to the immediate
future, it will be observed that the gracious
Speech makes early reference to the question
of unemployment. The live register on 4th
January last was 64,448 and on first March
61,594, showing a decrease of 2,854, or a fail
in unemployment of 1.1 per cent. since the
beginning of the year. The position to-day
is really better than these figures indicate
owing to the fact that 1st March fell in a
week during which the majority of workers
on systematic short time systems were off
work.
The continued uncertainty in the linen
and shipbuilding industry makes it unwise,
indeed impossible, to speculate as to what
the present year has in store for us, but I
can reiterate with emphasis the determi-

nation of the Government to assist in every

Members for the able manner in which they

Members: Hear, hear.) It was admirably

Through their brilliant advocacy it was

The PRIME MINISTER: Events
demonstrated that the Fund in Great Britain
had been placed upon an unfairly favourable
basis as compared to ourselves. That is now
rectified and not a day too soon. I refrain
from commenting further upon the scheme
at the moment. It will be fully explained
by my two right hon. Friends when the
necessary legislation is introduced. I have
to admit quite frankly that the solution of
this crucial question has materially eased
the anxiety of the Government. It was a
dreadful thought to carry always with one,
that Ulster having emerged from the other
many difficulties which surrounded her, and
having vindicated her determination to remain part and parcel of Great Britain and
the Empire, might find herself so hampered
financially that she could not carry on as a
definite subordinate unit. In that connection
the Ulster people must have listened to or
read with particular interest the recent statement by Mr. Winston Churchill, whom we
may accept as a typical though particularly
brilliant British Cabinet Minister.
Mr. DEVLIN: Oh.
Mr. KYLE: Since 1912.
The PRIME MINISTER: These are his
words, all the more significant but quite

Churchill's recantation?
The PRIME MINISTER: My hon. Friend
who is so adroit at Parliamentary tactics will
have the chance of reading the whole of
Hansard. At all events, I think it very

I have declared again and again-
I am going to emphasise particularly what I
think is of such importance coming from the
British Government and a Cabinet Minister
speaking on behalf of the British Governmentthat neither by threats of violence nor
by intrigue, nor yet by unfair economic
pressurethese are the points I wish particularly to
emphasise to-day--
shall the people of Ulster be compelled

We have always fought for that position and
now having won it let us nerve ourselves to
make the very best of our circumstances in
the future.
In accordance with the recent agreement
(subsequently to be embodied in correlative
Acts of Parliament) between the Imperial
Government and the Governments of
Northern Ireland and of the Irish Free
State, the administration of the Diseases of

April next, and the work will be placed

am glad to announce that some important
economies will be effected thereby. The
powers and duties of the Council in regard
to transit of animals and agricultural produce will also from the date mentioned be
assigned to the Ministry of Agriculture.
The operation of the Marketing of Eggs Act
(N.I.), 1924, has effected a marked improveruent in the manner in which our eggs are
placed on the British market. Experience,
however, has shown that some revision of
the Act is necessary, and the authority of
Parliament for the purpose will be sought
at an early date.
Some slight amendments in the Horse
Breeding Act, 1918, are also needed, and a
Bill for the purpose will be submitted in
due course.
In order to protect and extend our important trade in potatoes, the Ministry of
Agriculture also intends to require that
potatoes for sale or export shall be inspected
and properly graded. The Ministry is at
present in consultation with both growers
and merchants in the matter, and hopes at

an early date to introduce the necessary

It will be observed that I am confining
myself to-day particularly to matters of
outstanding importance. Criticisms, however, from whatever quarter they come,
will, of course, be met in the ordinary way.
I class amongst very important and urgent
matters the vital one of economy. The
Estimates will shortly be in your hands,
and I venture to predict that they will cause
satisfaction. During the past consistent,
vigorous efforts have been made to effect
economy without impairing efficiency in our
public service. It has to be borne in mind
that our Governmental departments were
originally established on an after-the-war
economic basis, and, therefore, there has
been and still is but a limited field in which
to search for even a moderate cutting down,
but, as one instance of what has been done,
let me point to the great achievement of
the Ministry of Labour; it has established
and carried through the Widows', Orphans'
and Old Age Contributory Pensions Act
with the addition of only three permanent
boy clerks and some twenty temporary
juniors, and it continues to administer the
Act, involving no fewer than 3,350 widows
and 8,300 children and orphans with this
negligible addition of staff. I trust the
House will give generous credit to my right
hon. Friend, the Minister of Labour, and to
his able advisers for this most creditable
accomplishment. (Hon. Members: Hear,
hear.)
over
In considering the subject of economy, it
is well for hon. Members to bear in mind
that our administrative
expenses only
amount to slightly over 3 per cent of the
total expenditure on those services
which we ourselves have complete control;
consequently any cutting down which it may
be found possible to effect in administration
will have but a small result if spread over
the whole of our expenditure upon Unemployment, Old Age and Contributory
Pensions, Education, Police, Land Purchase,
and numerous other social services. And it
must further be remembered when the question of administrative economy is discussed
that for almost two whole years that great
arbitration tribunal, the Colwyn Committee,
directed its investigation to the question of
whether any superfluity of departments or
excess of staff existed in Northern Ireland.
It can readily be understood that this quesor
tion necessarily entered into the very heart
of the problem which they had to solve.
What was the outcome? Our arrangements
on this head were confirmed in every respect, and not only so, the head of the British
Treasury-the protagonist of British interests-had to admit that our departmental
organisation could not be questioned, as no
evidence of extravagance could be found.
You will readily recognise that if any confirmatory evidence was needed of our case in
respect of this important matter, nothing
more definite or effective could be found than
British Treasury approval. Had the Colwyn
Committee found that one Minister, or even
one Under-Secretary or Inspector of a department was superfluous, the saving thereby
effected would have gone to swell our contribution to Britain, and the money would have
left Northern Ireland, and, consequently,
could not under any circumstances be intercepted by us to become available for grants
in aid of local rates, agriculture or any other
social service, no matter how urgent
desirable. I need hardly say that this in
no way relieves us of the obligation to continue to enforce the strictest economy in
every particular. (Hon. Members: Hear,
hear.) Our honour is bound up in this
question as well as our interest as taxpayers
of the United Kingdon. However, in order
to satisfy the people of Ulster, I hope once
and for all, and to circumvent unwarranted,
uninformed, and, I fear, sometimes malicious
criticism, on so important a matter, my right
hon. Friend, the Minister of Finance, has
obtained permission from the British
Government-which, I have pointed out, is
more involved than ourselves-to have the
services of Sir Russell Scott, the distinguished Chier Establishment Officer of the
British Government, to thoroughly overhaul
the whole of our administration, and to report as to the staffing of our departments
and the rates of pay of our Civil Service.
The report will be communicated to the
House in due course, and I sincerely trust,
as I have said, that it will allay for ever
those wild, ill-informed and malicious charges
that the Ulster Government is wasting
public money, or spending public money in
a way that it should not be spent. It is
indeed regrettable that anyone should lend
himself to spreading about reports for which
there is not the slightest foundation, and
it is also, I think, unfair to the Province
of Ulster, now that we have got settled down
in peace and quietness, that some people
should start again this annual bogey, as I
may call it, for the purpose of creating a
wrong impression amongst those whom it is
impossible to reach and to coach as to the
exact facts of the case.
In conclusion, I would like to say-it is
only emphasising what I have already stated
-that what the Government are most

anxious to do this year is to keep clear of
all matters which might arouse anything in
the nature of trouble in our midst, to endeavour to cut away controversial, political
topics, and not only for the coming year,
but for the remainder of the Parliamentary
life of this Ministry, to have as the slogan
of Ulster, "Less talk, and more work."
(Hon. Members: Hear, hear.)
After all, I think most of us have laboured
very hard for the past twenty years through
difficulties, upheavals, small and great
troubles, and now I am delighted to say we
have emerged into smoother water. In that
smooth water I hope it may be possible for
agriculture and trade to recover, and I do
earnestly pray that nothing may crop up
to prevent the Ulster people making the
most of their opportunity when the recovery
comes. What is it that we should all be
working for above everything else? To pick
up every man and woman who is unemployed
off the street, to so help and encourage industry-we have limited resources,
have large hearts-that there may be in the
future years a steady decrease in the figures
supplied by my right hon. Friend (Mr.
Andrews), so that at last we may be able
to say that Ulster has regained her old
proud position, when unemployment was
quite unknown, and when the labouring
classes lived, perhaps, in greater harmony
and greater peace than the labouring classes
of any other part of the country. (Hon.
Members: Hear, hear.)

Mr. KYLE: I want, if I may, to congratulate the mover and seconder of the
Address. I think the Prime Minister has
well described the King's Speech as modest
and unpretentious. I think I may parody
that by describing the Government as
mediocre, and its mind as moribund. Those
of us who sit on the Front Opposition Bench
were glad that the Prime Minister and the
Government have stressed the point regarding unemployment, because it is the one
thing that is paramount. It is the one thing
that is a nightmare to us, and I am sure to
the right hon. and hon. Gentlemen opposite.
(Hon. Members: Hear, hear.) When one
reckons that there are 61,000 people unemployed here, and adds the wives and children,
as suggested by the mover of the Address,
it will be seen that they comprise a very
considerable part of the entire population
of the Six Counties. The amount of suffering, the amount of anxiety that those people
must endure can better be imagined than
described. We want to say that we welcome
the return of some of the money that the
Government have given to Great Britain.
We welcome the return of that money. All
we say is that none of it should
go until
Own people are attended to 61,000
people. We are getting a grant, I underour
stand-this is a matter which probably would
be better left to be debated when the
Measure comes before the House-of £650,000
for this year and £850,000 for next year
and the following year, and then we are
told from the Government Benches that we
pay at least £3,000,000 per annum as an
Imperial contribution, while we are leaving
61,000 of our own people more or less in
starvation.
our
The number of unemployed has increased
since last we had the pleasure of hearing
the Gracious Speech from the Throne. The
regulations under which Unemployment
Insurance is administered have been tightened since that, and one fears that the
British Government, in giving this £650,000
this year and £850,000 for the following two
years, are going to depress the position of
unemployed brethren still further.
Some one may say that we will get this
grant if we administer our Unemployment
Insurance on the same basis as that on which
it is administered in Great Britain, but there
are other things which I have no doubt the
Imperial Treasury will take into account.
They will take into account the relief which
the unemployed people get in Great Britain
from the Poor Law Guardians in contradistinction to the want of relief that our
unemployed get in Northern Ireland. I am
sure the Government will watch this particular phase of the agreement that they have
arrived at with the Imperial Government
regarding the Unemployment Fund.
I would like further to say that it is a
pity that, with the very welcome good relations with Southern Ireland, and now
that the feeling is very good both on this
side and on the other side, there should not
have been some attempt on behalf of our
Government to make those good relations
more secure. I would suggest again in this
House that one way of attempting to do that
is by having a reciprocal arrangement with
the Free State Ministry of Labour in regard
to the payment of unemployment benefit for
contributions paid on either side of the
border. Let no one make the cheap criticism
that in the Free State unemployed
persons are paid a different rate of
benefit to what they are paid here.
Let no one make the cheap criticism
that they do not pay extended benefit on the
other side of the Border. I do not desire to
enter into a mere quibble about this matter.
I do desire, however, that the best relationship possible should exist between the
North and South. (Hon. Members: Hear,
hear.) You have people working in Northern
Ireland and living in the Free State-you
can take it in Derry or you can take it in
Belleek. I daresay it happens in other parts
but these are two that have been brought to
my notice these people are working in our

There is another matter which I consider
to be of grave importance to the people of
the Six Counties-I do not know how it
affects the country districts as well as I
know how it affects the town-and that is
that there ought to be some amendment of the
Rent and Mortgage Interest Restriction Act
which was passed last Session. What is now
happening in Belfast is what we on these
Benches said would happen. People
leaving a house and the landlord of that
house is charging the incoming tenant whatever rent he likes to charge. I will give one
instance. In a street in North Belfast there
is a house that was let at 10s 5d per week.
The people went to America and the landlord is to-day charging the new tenant 258
per week with impunity, and getting it. I
think something to amend the harshness of
that particular Act ought to have been
mentioned to-day.
In regard to the housing, or the additional
year that is being granted for the building
of houses, or rather for the Government

Six Counties has ceased to build houses. One

they were going to follow the lead of the

establishing the Scottish National Housing

Sir ROBERT ANDERSON: Steel houses.
Mr. KYLE: I am not talking about steel

Mr. KYLE: If my hon. Friend (Sir Robert
Anderson) wants to talk about the breaking

Hear, hear)-in our own town. Still the

the only other people to put it up to are
cur own Government, and we put it up to

keep in step. Surely it is not asking too

There is another matter with which the
Imperial Government have attempted to
deal but with which there has been no
apparent attempt to deal here, and which I
think is just as ripe to be dealt with here
as it was on the other side, and that is the

Britain. Now I want to deny that. I want
to say that that is wrong. So far as our agreements with employers are concerned
accept the "Ministry of Labour Gazette" cost
of living figures for Northern Ireland, which
are based on statistics gathered in Great
Britain. Now the Free State have a Board
of Trade "Gazette"-I do not know exactly
what they call it, but it is on a par with
our "Gazette"-and there the cost of living
is proved to be some thirteen or fifteen points
higher than it is in Great Britain. I want
to say that, though we may not be exactly
fifteen points above Great Britain here, we
are at least ten points above Great Britain
in regard to the cost of living, and I think
the Government would be well advised to
establish some sort of inquiry, some sort of
committee, or some sort of a council to follow
the lead given some time ago by the
Imperial Government in this particular connection. Our people here are the more hard
hit because the wages of the operatives,
speaking in the main, are less than the
wages paid even in Great Britain.

When I came into this House I was toldat least, I told myself-that one of the things

to see it in the midst of their universal
poverty. That is my first objection to this
Parliament.
My second objection to this Parliament

that the only branch I know of is the one

The PRIME MINISTER: Perhaps I may

House for Northern Ireland. There is no

building will cover the whole of the Civil
Service, or practically so, and the two
Chambers, the Senate and the Commons.
The obligation rests upon the British
Government to supply these buildings, at no

The PRIME MINISTER: There will be

Secondly, I do not think that is the place

Let me say in conclusion that this is a
very interesting day. As I have said, I think
it is historical. It has created a precedent
in the history of Parliament in that we had
three speeches instead of one. We had an
appeal from the Prime Minister, an appeal
that I think will be responded to. So far as
we are concerned we will pursue our course.
I can only speak for myself, but, as far as
I am concerned, we will pursue the course
we have pursued of legitimate, and, as a rule,
fair criticism. We will make suggestions,

will be adopted. In the midst of these appeals let me finally say to the right hon.
Gentleman (Sir James Craig) that he ought
also to be responsive to the suggestions that
we make from this side. We are different
from most Oppositions. In the first place
there are three or four parties on these
Benches. We are not a composite Opposition at all. We, perhaps, do not hold the
same opinions upon everything, but one
thing that stands out clearly in the history
of this Parliament is the possibility of the
right hon. Gentleman and his friends continuing to remain in office in his day and
mine. That consideration ought to make it
easier, and it certainly would be more magnanimous, and a finer form of gesture, if
the right hon. Gentleman would consider,
and consider carefully, those considerations
which we have ventured to put before him.
We are all Ulstermen and proud to be
Ulstermen. (Hon. Members: Hear, hear.)
We want to further the welfare of our
Province. We are all Irishmen and want to
see North and South working harmoniously
together. The causes that divided them have
largely disappeared. We rejoice at that, because we do not believe that unity can ever
spring out of conflict. We believe that
unity can only come out of common consideration of the well-being, not of one, but of
both. I think we ought to remember that
the perils are grave, and that they imperiously demand immediate consideration.

Mr. PATRICK O'NEILL: I am told it is
not unusual to allow certain latitude, that
is not otherwise permitted, in the case of
a Member addressing the House for the first
time, and if, in the few brief observations
that I have to make, I drift outside the
general scope of the discussion, I hope that
you, Sir, will grant me that forbearance

I have been a Member of this House for
almost five years, but this is the first occasion on which I have had the pleasure of
addressing it, due to the fact that I represent
a section of the people of Down, a large
majority of whom did not expect to be anything more than temporarily under the jurisdiction of this House, and consequently did
not desire to be represented in it But, with
a decision on the Boundary question having
been arrived at, when their opinions were
ignored and their wishes unattended to, they
have now decided to accept the situation as
it is, and to endeavour to make the best of
it. I think, however, it would not be fair
either to those people or to this House if I
did not say that, if not in active hostility,
they are in strong opposition to this Parliament. They and I believe that there is no
necessity for two Parliaments in Ireland, and
that so long as we have partition here the
contentment and prosperity that we should
all like to see will not obtain. How long or to
what extent this hostility may last in my
opinion depends on the Government themselves. If your laws are just and fairly administered, you may allay this hostility, and
even gain the confidence of these people;
but in that case your laws require to be different from those which already have been
passed, and these in some instances will have
to be materially altered.
Take, for instance, the system of representation in local government areas. There
you have abolished what, I think, must be
admitted is the fairest system of representation, and in its place you have instituted a
plan by which the majority of the whole area
are only a minority in the governing bodies.
I think, if there is any honesty or sincerity
in the oft-repeated promises of the Prime
Minister, this is one of the things that should
be remedied, and the fairest system of
representation-Proportional Representation
--restored.
The new Education Act, to which the Prime
Minister yesterday gave a special blessing,
also requires to be amended. It has already
been amended to suit the needs of one class
of schools, and I think that it should be
amended in such a way as to suit the needs
of another, so that they should not have to
contribute their proportion to the equipment
and upkeep of those schools without getting
a proportional grant for similar needs of
their own.
In regard to the administration of the law,
there is the question of the few remaining
political prisoners who did not get released in
the general amnesty when the British Government reviewed their cases, and I think that
the Government, merely from a merciful
point of view, should order at once the
liberation of those men, because in my
opinion their offences are not any worse than
were committed by some of those who have
been granted their liberty. There is in my
opinion one case of mal-administration of
the law, and that is in the case of a number of
men not charged with any offence, who are not
permitted to live in their homes, and as a
matter of fact
are being prosecuted and
jailed for doing so. That, in my judgment,
is a thing that should not obtain or receive
countenance in any civilised community, and
I hope that before it is necessary to raise the
question again these men will be permitted
to return to their homes on approbation.
Now my last complaint is in regard to the
hastily-considered and hurriedly-enacted
Licensing Act. I think I am entitled
to describe it in that way because
it is mentioned in the King's Speech as
requiring further amendment. I think it
should be amended in such a way that it
would be fair, not alone to those engaged in
the trade, but also to the public generally,
who have not been considered in this matter.

Debate on Address.

Unemployment.
But humbly regret that no proposals have
been made in the gracious Speech to ensure
that all those who are willing to work
should get work to do, or failing that,
should be provided with maintenance by
the State.
(Hon. Members: Hear, hear.) There is no
doubt that this question is one in which
there is a terrible lot of dishonesty. Even
yesterday while my Friend, the hon. Member,
the Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Kyle), was
making his speech here, he nearly got into
hysterics over the fact of this thing being
mentioned in the King's Speech. He seemed
to be under the impression that there was a
possibility, as he said himself, of the "pubs"
being opened on Sunday. I do not know
whether he considered this in itself to be
such a great iniquity, or whether he probably
thought that if such did occur he might lose
the love of his audience at the Custom House
steps.
But that is not the only thing we have
heard mentioned with regard to the Licensing
Act. Only yesterday in this House one of the
Ministers told me that the Government had
accepted a lease of this building in which we
are sitting, with a special stipulation clause
that no alcoholic liquors could be consumed
in it under any conceivable circumstances,
and that even if we were to drink the health
of the King, it must be done in ginger pop.
Now, was there ever such hypocrisy or dishonesty known? Do you ask us to believe
that all the Members of this House are teetotallers? If that is so I suggest that many
of them could take an action against their
countenances for libel and obtain very heavy
damages. I hope that in the new lease for
the building of the Parliament at Stormont
no such clause is inserted, because if there is
I can foresee very great difficulty and even
trouble. We were told by the Minister of
Finance yesterday that this "Home of Rest"
in the country would be inhabited by 700
Government officials. If that is so I am sure
these men are very likely to complain that
they are unable to obtain reasonable refreshments there while the other 400 who live in
the city will be able to go to the licensed
houses.
I think it is about time the Government
looked on this matter in a more straightforward and more honest way and were determined
not to be led or directed or dictated to by a

I regret that I have to stand up to move
this Amendment. I would have much preferred that an Amendment of this kind was
not necessary, because in that case the list of
unemployed would be reduced to a negligible
and infinitesimal number. The situation,
however, being what it is we are reluctantly
compelled to move an Amendment of this
character notwithstanding the fact that there
was one in similar terms proposed twelve
months ago. I do not propose to-day to go
into detail in connection with this matter
as I did on the previous occasion. I regret
that the Government have not given greater
attention to this problem than they appear to
have done up to the moment. Yesterday
reference was made to the Boundary controversy having been settled and that this in
some measure would warrant the Government
giving much more consideration to this question than was previously given. I can understand that if this portion of the country was
in the throes of sectarian trouble it would
not be possible for the Government to give
undivided attention to any social or economic
matter, but fortunately that is not the
position in which we find ourselves at the
present time. These sectarian troubles are
settled, and it is a very gratifying and
fortunate thing that the recent political
controversy between Great Britain and the
Free State has been settled. For that reason
the Government should give undivided attention from now onwards to social and
economic questions.
If we are to judge by the King's Speech
that has not been done, and for that reason
I think the Government are entitled to a
considerable degree of censure. As was to
be expected the Prime Minister attempted
to put the best face he could on the economic
situation. He tried to handle the figures
very adroitly. He endeavoured to show the
population of Northern Ireland that the unemployment problem was in a fair way to
solution and that the situation was much
better than at the beginning of the year.
I deny that that state of affairs exists.
suggest that the comparison was not fair.

of unemployment further than to point out

I stated more than once in this House that I

that would mitigate to a considerable extent
the unemployment problem as it confronts us

One suggestion I remember putting forward was that the Minister of Labour should
take steps to ascertain the number of youths
engaged in industry, and also the number
of people over 65 years of age engaged in
industry. The view of the Government-it
is only a passing phrase-is that we are

Last year I attempted to show what effect
machine production would have on
problem, and I was told by a number

the Stone Age. I have not the slightest
objection to the introduction of improved
machinery. I hold that machinery should
be utilised for the purpose of lightening the
burden of people, but not penalising the
people. I regret that any improvement in
machinery is used for the purpose of making
the position of the people worse. I pointed
out the effect of the conversion of ships
from coal burning to oil fuel. We have
gone a stage beyond that. We have now
introduced the Diesel engine which has
resulted in the disemployment of a large
number of people. The only way to solve
the problem is to tackle it on orthodox lines
or otherwise. We are simply to go on and
continue paying thousands of pounds each
week by way of unemployment benefit without getting any nearer to the solution than
at the present time.
Now, I may may be told that it is very
difficult for this Government to grapple
with the problem in the way I suggest inasmuch as the Government has not really got
the power. I will probably be told that in

I regret to say we have not got those

We are told that the figures have been
reduced, that while we had 64,000 in January
we have only 61,000 unemployed at
the present time. I suggest that
these numbers have not been reduced
as a result of an improvement in
trade or as a result of numbers of people
obtaining work. I suggest the way these
numbers have been reduced has been by
disallowing benefit to a large number of
people who were receiving it. We have got
a most extraordinary state of affairs. We
have the Parliamentary Secretary (Mr.
Gordon) going to the Shankill Road and
making a speech, in which he says it is a
slander on the working classes to say they
are not genuinely seeking work, while his
own Department are disqualifying people on
these grounds. We cannot accept both statements. If one is right the other is wrong.
Perhaps the hon. Member next time he intends to make speeches will make speeches
that are really true and are a reflex of the
activities of the Department he represents.
I want to suggest that that speech was not.
A large number of people have been disallowed benefit. That is how the figures
have been reduced.
I come to the main point of the Amendment. I will probably be told it is an outlandish idea that could only originate in
the brains of the three people who occupy the
front Opposition Bench-that no other people
of loyal Ulster would be able to conceive
such an outlandish idea as this. We ask
that work should be provided for them, or
that the State should maintain the people.
I have no doubt the hon. Member (Dr.
Morrison) who represents the University
will suggest this is an outlandish idea-that
it is wild, extravagant, and fantastic, and
could only come from an irresponsible
person like myself. But we find that larger
and larger numbers of people who do not
accept our full point of view are being forced
to the conclusion that if the employing
class of the country cannot provide employment the State should give them some sort
of maintenance. I happen to have a letter
to-day from a fairly unexpected quartera quarter that formerly was looked upon
as a citadel of Unionism and Protestantism
-from the people of the Shankill Road. One
of these people asked that the Government
of Northern Ireland should reinstate all
contributors to the Unemployment Fund
who have been signed off the register within
the last twelve months. I suggest that is
tantamount to the plea I am putting forward. If they are restored to the unemployment register it is the duty of the
Government to provide some sort of maintenance for these people who have been
struck off the unemployment register.
Does any right hon. or hon. Gentleman contemplate the position a person unemployed
is placed in? Did anyone for a moment ever
stop or hesitate to think about the awful
suspense people are in who are in receipt
of unemployment benefit at the present time?
I am daily in contact with these people. I
am at the Labour Exchange practically every
day in the week. I know the fears and
apprehensions of these people, coming before
the courts and committees, very often unsympathetic, where it is a crime to be idle
for two years, and where it is becoming a
greater crime. Can you imagine the harrowing suspense and inental agony of waiting
day after day for the whole source of income
to be cut off, and for them and their families
to be forced to go to the poorhouse? I suggest it is a desperate state of affairs
altogether.
The Minister of Labour has a heavy
responsibility on his shoulders, a responsibility that some of us would not care to
undertake an exceptionally heavy responsibility, and from his own point of view he
may be attempting to discharge that responsibility as satisfactorily as he possibly can.
But I do say with all the emphasis I can
command it is unsatisfactory that simply
because a person is unemployed for two
years it should be looked upon as a crime,
and that these people as a consequence
should have their income cut off, and their
only fault is they are unemployed for two
years.
I do not want to weary the House. I
have explained our point of view very fully
before. In attempting to do it again it is
only a recapitulation of things I have stated
on former occasions. (Hon. Members: Hear,
hear.) I may point out that unless a change
has taken place in the mentality of the
people who occupy the Front Benches their
reply will be a rehash of old replies and
shibboleths that we have got from the Front
Bench since we came into this House. I
hold that until such time as production is

for use instead of for profit there is absolutely no solution to the question of unemployment. You may attempt to dispute
that. You may say it is very far fetched.
I challenge you to suggest any other remedy

that production should be for use instead of
for profit.
If I wanted to examine the thing closely
I might point out that scarcely a commodity
produced at the present time is produced
for use. All commodities are produced for
the purpose of making a profit. Foodstuffs
are not grown for the purpose of satisfying
the pangs of hunger of the people. Foodstuffs are produced for the purpose of making
a profit. We have seen in this country when
there has been an abundant crop of potatoes
or an abundant crop of corn, and at the
same time we have seen many people in
Belfast going hungry. If these foodstuffs
were produced for the purpose of satisfying
the natural appetites of the people they
would be utilised for that purpose.
But
they are being produced for the purpose of
providing a profit. As long as that is being
done we hold it is absolutely impossible to
find a solution of this problem. Well, I
do not expect the Government will look upon
it from our point of view, or that they will
attempt to tackle the economic interests of
their supporters, who are really standing
between the people and this problem. We
say it is a serious enough matter for the
Government taking a different point of view.
It is no longer a question of an employer
having a right over the management of his
own affairs. Up to the time that our economic troubles became acute it might be
argued that the employer could be allowed
to manage his industry in exactly the way
he liked. I would point out that the situation
is radically different at the present time.
We, as ratepayers, have got to bear the
burden as a result of the mismanagement
on the part of the employer class in this
country. If the shipyards and linen
merchants and those responsible do not
attempt to bring the management of their
industries up to date it probably means that
we are incapable of competing in many respects with employers in different other
countries throughout the world. The inevitable consequence is that large numbers of
people are unemployed. With employment being denied we ratepayers have got
to come to the assistance of the Unemployment Fund, and if we have got to pay the
piper we have a right to call the tune.
Inasmuch as we are paying or will have got
to pay to a very considerable extent
should be allowed a voice so far as this question is concerned.

I suggest that some practical help should
be given to the Minister of Labour in trying
to solve this question of unemployment. It
is not a question that is going to be solved
by one section of the House or by one party,
but by the united efforts of everyone in the
House. Personally, for five years I have
made suggestions here with regard to unemployment, and even at the risk of wearying
the House I will repeat them. I have said
the present is a most suitable time for the
Government to take over the principal roads
in the country and re-make them. In the
memory of even the youngest of us a revolution has come
Whether
over transport.
people like it or whether they do not the

We know that the majority of our roads are
absolutely unsuited to the heavy traffic they
have to carry.
Sooner or later the Government will be called upon to take on the task
of re-making all these principal roads. Could
there be any more suitable time for doing
that work than the present? Why, nearly
every one at least of the men folk who are
unemployed-could with very little training
be utilised for making these roads so that
they could carry the heaviest traffic. History
teaches us and our own experience teaches us
that good roads lead to prosperity in every
country where good roads have been introduced. Then there is another point. This
Province of ours suffers from flooding, and
there is an enormous amount of work that
will have to be undertaken by public bodies
because private bodies cannot do it.

normal. My hon. Friend (Mr. Devlin)

The question is what have we done? The
hon. Member's curiosity is quite laudable and
quite justifiable. I should like to satisfy
him. We passed the Measure last year to
which the hon. Member (Mr. Devlin) has
referred. That Measure imposed on public
authorities the responsibility of supervising
the condition of the land under their control
and the enforcement of certain work upon
the farmers themselves so that watercourses
and drains that were clogged and various
other difficulties should be removed prior to
any preparation for the relief which it is
hoped will be received for the promotion of
main drainage in the Six Counties. That
brings me to the Bann, which is the outlet of
practically the whole eastern part of the Six
Counties. I gave an undertaking when the
Measure was submitted that is now an Act of
Parliament from last Session that we would
prosecute scientific investigation of the
conditions of the Bann in order that it
might be discovered whether modern
scientific and engineering knowledge could
solve the problem that for a period of 150
years has been attempted and was discovered
or thought to be insoluble. Our engineers
have been working from that time to this
moment on this subject assiduously and I can
give the assurance to the House that within
a few days, perhaps, or at any rate within
two or three weeks, we shall have the full
report and recommendations of these
engineers as to how the Bann problem can
be tackled.
Any conferences or conversations I have had
with the engineers on the subject rather point
to the fact that in their opinion the problem
is not insoluble, that, at any rate, it can
be greatly ameliorated, if not absolutely and
thoroughly cured to the extent that perhaps
some of us wish it to be cured; but, at any

be undertaken on the Bann, and I am living

means. Beyond that I cannot go, and I hope

to any country where timber and wood are
always a necessity.
These are the points I wish definitely to
reply to. I hope what I have said will

Belfast (Mr. W. McMullen) will be dealt
with effectively, I am sure, by the right hon.
Member (Mr. Andrews) beside me when the

helped our employers and our workers to

In addition to that through our Loans

would otherwise have been idle, and

ferred to the question of roads. Well, since

Again, someone has referred to the question of artificial silk, and suggested that the
machinery of our mills which could not be
employed in spinning flax might be used for
the purpose of producing artificial silk. In
the first place the situation of our linen
mills in very rare instances is suitable for
silk factories, because of the enormous
quantity of water required in the manufacture of artificial silk, and in the second
place because the machinery which is entirely suitable for flax spinning would be
totally unsuitable for silk manufacture.
Mr. DEVLIN: Would the right hon.
Gentleman say how it is that an English

Mr. ANDREWS: The answer to that question is this. The firm that came over from
England, and which we welcome, has gone

where there is plenty of water, and they
are there establishing entirely suitable

is actually, through the Loans Guarantee

are also giving help to them to the extent

And then again we have done what we

upon which he with so much public spirit

My own Department has also done what it

(Mr. Devlin) referred to those young people

And then it should not be forgotten that

The PRIME MINISTER: Hear, hear.
Mr. ANDREWS: There is nothing I detest

I have said before in this House, and I

struggle for these five years has been to keep

May I say in conclusion that I am rather

Conference should be held, and it was held.
The personnel of that Conference has never
been criticised. It was composed of employers, it was composed of workers' representatives, it was composed of hon. Members
opposite as well as those behind me, and
included the hon. Member for West Belfast
himself. That Conference very earnestly
tackled the whole problem. We formed ourselves into various committees. There was a
Shipbuilding Committee, a Linen Trade
Committee, a Building Trade Committee, and
a General Purposes Committee, and my hon.
Friend (Mr. Devlin) was actually the vicechairman of the General Purposes Committee. Those committees all worked. The
Parliamentary Secretary (Mr. Gordon) and
myself attended every meeting of the main
Conference. It is true we did not attend the

that we felt it was right that we should
leave the committees untrammelled in any
way to explore the problem from their
standpoint and from the fact that they were
experts in connection with the particular
matter into which they were asked to
inquire.
Those committees reported to the main
Conference, and their reports were earnestly
considered and were published. I have never
heard those reports criticised. I have heard
them favourably commented on in many
directions. If those reports did not unearth
anything very new, at any rate they proved

anything beyond what the Government had

tragic difficulty that we have faced all these

The Development Commission is also still
sitting. It is exploring various problems
with which we are faced. It has considered,
Mr. BEATTIE: I rise to support the
Amendment, and I do SO because of
the necessity of such an Amendment
being put into operation immediately.
I was rather surprised at the innocence
the Minister of Labour has shown
in regard to what it really means. I am
sure that with the knowledge at his command he has got a greater conception of the
interpretation of the Amendment than he
allows this House to understand. Several
points in his remarks were worth noting.
He gave us three ideals-peace, stability, and
security. The last is the most important to
the class I represent here, because I claim,
and rightly claim, it is the lack of security
that is the cause of so much discontent and
grumbling and differences of opinion. If the
Government can give security to the workers
that is all they ask. They ask for security
of a kind that will give them the same treatment and the same social standard whilst .
out of employment as they would enjoy when
in employment.
I would like to draw the Minister's attention to this. Sometimes I have been very
severe in regard to the Ministry, not to the
Minister as a person. When the Minister
has had as close contact with the masses of
the people who have no security whatsoever
as I have had perhaps the attitude he adopts
to-day will be discarded. Here is the case of
a man who claimed to get security in the
Six Counties:
Dear Sir-I am writing to ask you if you
could get me a job on the relief work, as
the wife and I and family are on the verge
of starvation. I have tried everywhere to
get a job, but no use, and if I cannot get
unemployment money I must get something. For God's sake do your best and
do something for me.
That is a man who was constantly in employment up to the year 1921. Owing to the
upheaval at that particular time he was
thrown out of employment. He was never
able to return to employment, he never had
the opportunity. The Government of
Northern Ireland never provided work for
him although he is quite willing to work
to-day. He is struck off unemployment
benefit because he has not fulfilled the conditions in the past two years.
Here is the case of a widow who has two
sons, and who, owing to the insecurity, has

HOUSE OF COMMONS
[Mr. Beattie]
had to turn out and get a job in the Belfast
Ropework Company to support her two ablebodied sons. They are willing to work but
cannot get it, and owing to the tightening
up of the new regulations in regard to extended benefit are denied the right to benefit,
and the widow, who is up in years, has had
to turn to the Belfast Ropework Company
and take employment. That is security of a
kind I am not inclined to agree with.
There is another man, the father of six
children, who lives in Kilroot. He happens
to have the same name as the hon. Member
for County Down (Mr. Patrick O'Neill), who
made his maiden speech to-day. He was in
constant employment in the shipbuilding industry up to August, 1920, when he was
compelled through circumstances to leave.
He was working in Govan shipyards till
1922. He drew unemployment benefit from
1922 to January, 1923, when he joined up in
the Free State army. He came back in
April, 1924, and after he had been restored
to benefit his case was brought under review, and he was finally turned down as not
meeting the conditions set out by the
Ministry. He has six children, and his wife
and he are now on the verge of starvation.
If that is security I am rather surprised.
The masses, so far as I can see by past legislation have no security whatever. They
have free access to the roads, but I read in
a story recently that the reason the masses
were allowed to use the roads to go to their
work was that if they did not get them free
they would not go over them, and the
employing classes would have to go and do
the work themselves.
We have 61,000 unemployed workers in the
Six Counties. This number is ever increasing. It is not decreasing, because, while you
show a decrease this month against the
month of January, I want to challenge the
Minister and tell him to-day that we stand
at a higher figure of unemployment than we
did in January. Not on his register, quite
naturally, because he has made a provision
that he is going to reduce the register under
his control. Then the regulations, against
which I protested in this House on the last
occasion, have been the means of turning off
thousands of heads of families, and young
men and young women who have no provision for their upkeep other than their
parents. I heard the hon. Member for the
University (Dr. Morrison) say he would put
a test.
We have already challenged the
Minister to give us a test, a test for work.
All you have got to do is to offer a job to
any man and you will find out whether you
will be disappointed by his refusal. I do
not say they are all of the one brand. There
are black sheep in every squad, but the
majority of these 61,000 are genuine seekers
for work. I am sorry the hon. Member for
the University (Dr. Morrison) is not here.
Mr. WILLIAM MCMULLEN: He is.
Mr. BEATTIE: I did not see him behind
me. I am glad to see him on this side of
the House because I believe that the day is
not far distant when he will be sitting along
with me and my two colleagues. I know of
a case in which the test was put to an applicant for work. He got instructions from the
Bridge End Exchange to go out to a farmer
named Henry, away out at Craigantlet, a distance of about six miles from the city. He took
the position and walked the six miles out to
the farm in the morning. When he arrived
the farmer told him he had got to work about
nine hours a day and the wages would be
twelve shillings a week with three meals a
day. That was a married man with a family.
He took the challenge and followed that employment for three weeks, doing the six
miles in the morning and six at night, living
on twelve shillings a week with three meals
a day and keeping his wife and family. That
is one of the men whom the Minister has
now turned down from extended benefit.
We have also hundreds of other genuine
cases, cases that I personally took up and
brought to the Ministry only to find that
there was no redress from the decisions
arrived at. I have been told that Local
Employment Committees have been set up
and that representatives of the workers are
on those committees. If you will bear with
me for a moment or two I will tell you how
those committees act. I happen to be a
member of one. The members that now act
on the Rota Committees, in regard to
extended benefit, have no more power than
the ordinary individual who walks the
streets of Belfast. They can give a decision,
but that decision is not taken into account
when it goes into the scrutineers' quarters.
The scrutineers' quarters are in the various
Exchanges. There is no claim passed through
the Rota Committee now which is allowed
direct. It passes through the manager's
hands, and another new thing that has been
introduced—one of the methods of tightening
up the regulations-is that when you are
overdrawn to the extent of, I think, 120 or
125 stamps--a man who reaches the age of
say twenty or twenty-two-if you are overdrawn these stamps by that amount the axe
goes on the table. For people from twentytwo upwards I believe another margin of the
overdrawn account is allowed. I believe
there are about three scales, and if they have
overdrawn their accounts to those extents I
hear-I only take it from hearsay the
decision of the officials in the Department is
to disallow any claims presented to them.

Mr. ANDREWS indicated dissent.
Mr. BEATTIE: If I am wrong I got the
information from a member of your committee. I prided myself on having got the
age of self-dependent persons reduced from
twenty-five to twenty-two during the last
Session, but I have now received a circular
