twenty-two to twenty-five. I regret this
increase in the age. It means that a man
who has a son of twenty-five years of age,
and who has £2 8s per week, is going to have
to keep his son and his wife on that amount,
because his son will be denied the 18s of
extended benefit. 38s for the man and
woman, with 10s for the son is 48s. That is
the maximum, and anything over that would
prevent him from receiving benefit. I regret
that that provision has been added.
I would also like to refer to one more of
the Minister's remarks. He said that the
Government were assisting Sir Samuel Kelly
in the development of the coal industry. I
personally would have been more satisfied if
he had said that they were going to restore
the Bill discarded by the last Government,
namely the Bill for the development of the
hydro-electrical scheme. Electricity is the
coming force, and we should have an eye to
that condition of affairs, so that we may be
in a position to take up electrical development when the time arrives. I believe that
the sooner the Government restores that Bill
the better it will be for Northern Ireland.
The Minister referred to several schemes
to which I was going to refer, but seeing
that they have been dealt with already, I
do not intend to say anything about them
at the present moment. I would just like
to tell the Minister that we are drifting
every day towards a state of affairs which,
once it matures, will be very hard to check.
You claim that you want to work on parallel
lines with Great Britain. We claim the
same, but if your conditions for extended
benefit are going to be on parallel lines with
those in Great Britain, you are doing a
grave injustice to the working-class people
of Northern Ireland, because you must remember that the regulations drawn up in
Great Britain have been drawn up knowing
that if they cut off benefit from a particular
class of applicant, then he is provided for
under the Poor Law. That does not prevail
here, and I say that if you should relax the
regulations and allow people either to have
extended benefit, or else bring pressure to
bear on your comrades in the Government
to compel the Guardians to do as the various
Boards in Great Britain do, grant outdoor
relief to all those who are denied the right
to extended benefit. Something has got to
be done. I live right in the heart of my
constituency, and I seem to be the only representative here who has the whole cares
and worries of that division on his shoulders.
Perhaps my hon. Friend (Mr. Gyle) on my
left will not allow me to say that, but I
come in close contact with these people. I
meet them at my own door, morning, noon,
and night, and their hardships are unbearable. I can assure the House that I feel it
myself when I take up a case, write to the
Ministry, find that I am denied the right to
reconsideration, and then have to inform
the claimant of the result. I can assure
you that it is small wonder that they seem
ready for an explosion almost at any time.
I would appeal to the Minister to consider
fairly and justly the relaxation of the regulations. That would be maintenance in a
way. It would not be maintenance in the
sense of the Amendment, but it would be
maintenance in a way, and it would be such
as would give some little comfort in the
homes of these people. It will not give all
that is needed or required, but it would be
a palliative, and we on these Benches are
prepared to take a palliative, knowing perfectly well that that is about all we will
get. I would ask the Minister to put the
full facts before a committee, and I believe
that if the conditions of affairs in England
and Scotland were placed before that committee, and also the condition of affairs in
Northern Ireland, they would ask to have the
regulations relaxed. Your auditor-or whoever it may be that is coming over-will
surely consider the position of the
Guardians in refusing out-door relief. I desire to support the Amendment in its entirety, but at the same time I would ask the
Minister to give what I have said in regard
to securing equal treatment under the new
regulations his sympathetic consideration.
Mr. KYLE: I want to support the
Amendment which has been so eloquently put
forward by my colleague, the hon. Member
for West Belfast (Mr. William McMullen).
This Amendment states specificially the
Socialist demand on behalf of the working
classes. That is that the State should provide work, or, failing work, that the State
should provide maintenance for the people.
That in a nutshell is the position which the
Socialist Party in Northern Ireland, or the
Socialist Party in any part of Great Britain
and Ireland, will put forward to the upholders of the capitalist system to-day. We
have heard very eloquent speeches this
afternoon from the hon. Member for West
Belfast (Sir Robert Lynn) who sits behind
us, and from the Minister of Labour (Mr.
Andrews). Both these speeches were admirable, but neither of them attempted to deal
with the fundamentals of this particular
Unemployment.

Debate on Address-
HOUSE OF COMMONS
[Mr. Kyle]
Amendment. It is all very well to say that
we should have the roads mended. Undoubtedly we should have the roads mended
and kept in repair. It is all very well to say
that we should have inquiries made into the
possibility of developing the sugar beet industry. That is very necessary and very
useful. It is all very well for the Minister
of Labour to say that he has supplied the
community of the Six Counties with something round about 9,000 houses. That may
be very necessary and very useful. It is all
very well to have inquiries made into why
there is this volume of unemployment. All
these inquiries are useful and necessary.
I would say to the Minister, in reply to
the question which he asked of these Benches,
as to how we were to determine what that
maintenance should be, that he should here
and now declare his willingness to set up a
Commission in Northern Ireland consisting
of representatives of all parties in this House
to inquire fully into what would be necessary to keep a man, his wife, and three
children, so that that Commission might
determine accurately the amount of money
that it would take to buy the necessaries of
life for the ordinary or normal family, and
that then that should be the standard of
maintenance that he, as Minister of Labour,
should give to the people for whom the State
cannot provide work.
My colleague, the hon. Member for East
Belfast (Mr. Beattie) has dealt with the
problem of security. I would like to add a
word or two to what he has stated in regard
to the problem. If there is one thing more
than another that we of the working classes
need and desire, it is security, and the State
has recognised that up to a point. Within
the last twenty years there has been a tremendous development of the social services,
development along the lines of National
Health Insurance, Unemployment Insurance,
and in various other ways. The State is
endeavouring in its own way to get security
for the great mass of the working people. We
want to see that further extended. We want
still further to increase the security which
we of the working classes have. That
security to the huge number of the unemployed at the present day in the Six Counties
may seem a myth, yet it is more than there
was twenty years ago, more than there was
ten years ago.
The Socialist party want that security developed, because after all it is the working
classes who produce all the wealth of the
community. It is not that the workers cannot produce enough to keep the people fed,
clothed and housed. The workers
can
produce the food, the workers can produce
the clothes, the workers can produce the
machines, and they can produce the goods
with the machines. It is because, as the
Member for West Belfast (Mr. William
McMullen), stated, that the primary object
of industry to-day is to enable people to make
a profit, instead of to supply the people
with the things that they require, that the
State should be organised, and so provide the
people who are the community, with the
necessaries of life. I have yet to hear that
denied. It is the State's duty to look after the
people whom it governs. Surely that is one
of the first things that the State should conceive to be its duty, namely, to see that the
inhabitants of the State are fed, clothed and
housed. Those are three essential things. It
is for that reason that I support this Amendment.
The acceptance of this Amendment would
mean a fundamental change in society.
There is no doubt about that. It would mean
an entirely different outlook. It would mean
the acecptance of that principle which the
hon. Member for West Belfast (Mr. William
McMullen) laid down, that things should be
produced primarily not for profit. The passing of this Amendment would mean a
tremendous change, because we see from the
Press that the interests which supply capital
to the various industries have made more
profits during the past three years than they
did in the three previous years when industry was good. The banks are paying 18,
20 and 25 per cent. interest to their shareholders, in the last three years of the most
unexampled depression. The putting into
operation of this Amendment would mean
the alteration of all that. It is not, as I
have stated, that the workers cannot produce
the goods, because we have it on the
evidence of some of our leading scientists
that one man with machinery can produce
enough woollen goods to do 300 people for one
year. One man with machinery can produce
enough cotton goods to do 250 people for a
year. Five men with the aid of machinery
can produce enough out of the ground to
supply 1,000 people with food for a year. It
is because of this capitalist system, which
is a curse, not only to the working people,
but a curse to many of the employers, and
it is because of this outlook of the employing
class, speaking generally, that we are in this
impasse, and that we are in the deplorable
position in which we find ourselves to-day.
Make no mistake about it, capitalism itself
is breaking up. The hon. Member for West
Belfast (Sir Robert Lynn) is away. I am
sorry for that, because he is rather keen on
this particular question. In fact, he brought
in the name of Karl Marx. Karl Marx was
not always right, but he was not very far

wrong in his magnificent work on Capital,
which the hon. Member for the University
(Dr. Morrison) has doubtless seen used as
a text-book in Queen's University. He outlined, in that magnificent work, the breakup of the capitalist system. As I have said,

and the Minister of Finance telling us that
we are actually supplying something round

in the shipyards. We are using State credit
to bolster up private enterprise all along the
line, instead of using our State capital to
build up our own industries, run by the
nation for the benefit of the people of the
nation. We should not allow people to run
industries to make profit, but to supply
clothes to people, because people in this
climate of ours need clothes to wear-
Mr. SPEAKER: I am afraid the hon.
Member is going beyond the scope of the
Amendment. It can hardly lead to a
general discussion on Socialism, which, of
course, could form the subject of a separate
Amendment. I think this Amendment
should be strictly confined to unemployment.
Mr. KYLE: I bow to your ruling, but I
was trying to point out the implication of
this Amendment. We have come to find out
that if we are ever going to tackle this problem of unemployment we must ensure that
all those who are willing to work should get
work to do or should be provided with
maintenance by the State. The issue is
really between the Socialist party and the
non-Socialist parties. This is a living issue in
the modern world to-day, and we want the
Northern Government to face this problem,

Position of Leaseholders.
Mr. McALLISTER: I beg to move as an
Amendment to the Address, at end to add
the words:-
But humbly regret that no mention in
the gracious Speech of intention to initiate
legislation to enable leaseholders, during
the currency of their leases, to have their
leases renewed, or to purchase the landlord's interest on just and equitable terms.
In rising to propose this Amendment I
feel I am moving an Amendment which will
commend itself to 95 per cent. of the people
of Northern Ireland and that it is in the
form of a highly constructive Amendment,
and, if accepted by the Government, it will
promote the collective and individual
interests of all the people in Northern
Ireland. Shortly stated the position of a
leaseholder in Northern Ireland up to the
present time is this: He takes a lease at a
stated ground rent, and he is compelled at
high cost to build a house or other building
on that land, and at the expiration of that
lease if he is in the hands of an extortionate
or unconscionable landlord-a landlord
without any sense of moral responsibility in
his business dealings, he is entirely at his
mercy. He has to accept his terms or surrender and allow his property to be confiscated.
About twenty years ago the Irish
Nationalist Party in the Imperial House of
Commons introduced a measure which would
have remedied the grievance which I propose
should now be remedied and the measure was
of such a meritorious character that it was
adopted by the English Government of the
day. It passed through the British House of
Commons, but by ingenious manoeuvring the
Tory landlord party in the English House of
Lords secured the insertion of an ingenious
amendment making it inapplicable to
building leases and the whole intention and
the whole benefit of that beneficent legislation was destroyed.

We all know, particularly those who are
coming into daily contact with these leases,
that 95 per sent. of the leases granted in
Northern Ireland are what are termed building leases. The House of Lords introduced
an Amendment to the Bill as it then stood
excluding these building leases, that is, leases
with a covenant to build, from the scope of
that Measure. They realised at that time
what they were doing, because Lord
Lansdowne rather gave the show away by
stating that every lease of any value in
Ireland was in the nature of a building lease.
Therefore, this Act was of no material effect.
The official Unionist Party from Ulster
impeded and opposed and stopped by every
means in their power the passage of that
beneficent legislation.

I wish to point out a few concrete cases
which have come to my personal knowledge

HOUSE OF COMMONS

after only a few minutes' inquiry. I know
of one man who holds two houses in a town
in Northern Ireland. The present rent of
those two houses is £4 19s 6d.
Mr. POLLOCK: Ground rent?
Mr. MCALLISTER: Ground rent. His
lease is about to expire. I should say the
houses were built entirely by him and his
predecesors in title. The landlord did not
contribute a brick, did not pay for an inch
of cement in the entire structures, and his
demand now is that he should receive a fine
of £200 and a rent of £20 before he will renew the lease. I know of another instance
under the same landlord. I may say that
landlords own whole towns in Northern Ireland, and in many instances are ruining the
towns. I do not speak in regard to all landlords, because there are just landlords in
Northern Ireland as well as unjust. This
particular landlord in a case which came
under my personal notice let land whereon
six houses were built. The rent for the
whole six houses was £7 15s. The lease was
about to expire, and an offer he made, along
with several alternative offers, was that he
would let one of these six houses at a fine of
£200 and a new rent of £15 for the one house,
where the original rent for the whole six
houses was £7 15s. Not only so, but he gave
the tenant seven days to accept or refuse that
offer. Further, there was a covenant in his
lease whereby the tenant was bound to keep
the premises in repair. He said to the tenant, "If you do not accept my terms at the
end of the lease I will confiscate your property and I will sue you for £1,000 damages
for failure to keep the property which you
built yourself in order." That is a case
which has come under my own personal
notice.
I know another case in another town, and
this is a town in which I suppose I did not
get ten votes at the last election. Leases are
about to expire practically throughout the
whole town, and one landlord holds in his
hand the prosperity or the absolute ruin of
that town. In one instance brought before
my notice the only terms upon which the
landlord will renew his lease is at thirty
times the present poor-law valuation. Within the last few years the tenant has spent
£1,500 in creating and erecting and renovating the place. There are many more instances like that, but I have only a few moments
to quote these few concrete cases. Men like
myself engaged in my profession are coming
across these cases continually and daily, and
are in a position to realize the great injustice of this wholesale confiscation that some
of the landlords are guilty of at the present
time.
I came into this Parliament with the intention of offering constructive criticism, and
if this is not constructive criticism I do not
know what constructive criticism is. This is
an Amendment which if accepted will improve the collective and individual interests
of the people. Take the case of a thrifty
artisan who denies himself throughout his
whole life every luxury, only spending his
money on the necessaries of life. He expends
his whole funded income on building a house,
say, at £400 and the lease expires at the end
of ten years and the landlord puts a pistol
to his head and says, "Instead of £4 rent you
now pay £20." I suggest this is a state of
affairs that in a civilized community at this
hour of the day a just Government with the
interests of the people at heart cannot allow
to continue for another moment.

The ATTORNEY-GENERAL (Mr. Babington): This Amendment, which has been so
clearly moved and seconded, is an Amendment which goes a great deal further than
the House has been led to believe, either by
the hon. Member for Antrim (Mr. McAllister)
or the hon. Member for Derry (Mr. McGuckin) who has spoken in support of it. If
the Government were to accept this Amendment to the Address it would cut right across
all the law of the land as it at present
exists. As the House is probably aware, the
relations between landlord and tenant, at
any rate so far as holdings other than agricultural are concerned, have been governed
for centuries by the law of contract. That
law has left both landlord and tenant perfectly free to contract with each other upon
Debate on Address-
Position of Leaseholders.
HOUSE OF COMMONS
[Mr. Babington]
any terms that they may think fit. If this
Amendment were accepted it would necessitate the passing of legislation, first of all,
on the lines of the Land Act of 1881, by
which fair rents were fixed in the interests
of agricultural tenants, and also on the same
footing as the Land l'urchase Acts, which
provided the machinery and financial assistance to enable agricultural tenants to purchase their holdings from their landlords,
and when the House considers that those
provisions would necessarily have to apply
not only to urban holders in every small
town and village in the Six-County area, but
also to every tenant or every business man
or merchant in the City of Belfast or in the
City of Londonderry, or in Ballymena or in
Portadown, who holds business premises at
an annual rent, the House will immediately
see that this question is one which goes to
the root, not only of the relationship between
landlord and tenant, but also to the root of
all business in Northern Ireland.
Therefore, I might point out to the House
in the first place that this question which
has been raised in this method, by way of
an Amendment to the Address, is one of
supreme importance when you come to consider the ultimate bearing that it has on
the life of the community. As I have said,
the relationship between landlord and tenant
has been governed for centuries by our law
of contract, and one would think to listen
to some of the remarks that have been made
in the introduction of this Amendment that
this grievance, which is now being voiced.
is one which is peculiar to Ulster. But
that is not So. The law of Northern
Ireland with reference to the relationship of
landlord and tenant, allowing for some small
differences, is exactly the same as the law
of Great Britain as a whole, or Great Britain
and Northern Ireland as it is now, and the
tenant in England or Scotland or Wales,
who holds business premises or urban
premises, or indeed any premises--for they
have not got the relief given in this country
by our Land Acts-is on exactly the same
footing as the tenants in this country, and
any difference that may arise, and any injustice that may be done, is an injustice
which arises from individual cases between
individual landlords and individual tenants.
Many Members of this House who have
seen that most fascinating play of Mr. George
Bernard Shaw's "John Bull's Other Island,"
will remember the protest of the motor
driver when the Irish tenant was complaining that the land that he had torn from the
hillside with his own hands had been taken
from him by his landlord. He replied that
his father had set up in a drapery business
in London, had expended a large sum of
money in developing that business, and had
produced a very valuable business indeed,
and after he had reached the summit of
success he was turned out in the street by
a harsh landlord without a penny of compensation, and had no redress at law. Therefore this proposition is one that is not
peculiar to our country. It is peculiar to
the law of contract as it applies all over the
United Kingdom of Great Britain and Northern Ireland, and it is most necessary that
this House should look into the matter very
carefully before they allow themselves to be
committed to anything in the nature of
legislation, which goes so deep into the roots
of the commercial life of this country. I am
rather surprised that this point has been
raised now, though I know that all who have
been engaged as I have been, just as the
proposer of the Amendment (Mr. McAllister)
and the hon. Member for Londonderry (Mr.
McGuckin) have been engaged all their lives
in the practice of the law, are aware of the
injustice that is undoubtedly done in individual cases as between landlord and tenant.
But individual injustice is done in almost
every branch of life as between individual
members of the community, whether it be
between landlord or tenant or whether it be
between two commercial men who contract
together in respect of any commodity,
whether it be houses or whether it be land.
Therefore it is not a wise thing to be
stampeded upon a general proposition of this
sort, because unfortunately in the weakness
of human nature a certain amount of
injustice may be done as between individual
landlords and individual tenants. I cannot
help thinking that the mainspring of this
Amendment must be narrowed down to a
very small field, because in my experience I
have never come across a very strong demand
among householders in the commercial
community for legislation of this description.
Fortunately I am able to say that most of
the people in our country are able to
adjust their differences between themselves
having regard to the position of the premises
without either recourse to the courts or
clamouring for legislation. But, as I have
said, I do not understand why this proposition should be raised at this particular
moment. I remember that for a great
number of years there was a solid block of
Nationalist Members in the British House
of Commons and no legislation was brought
in then at their instigation for the purpose
of remedying this evil.
Mr. McALLISTER: I am sorry to interrupt the right hon. Gentleman, but I
distinctly stated in moving the Amendment
that in 1906 the Town Tenants' Bill was
introduced by the Nationalist Party and it
was adopted by the Government of the day.

Mr. BABINGTON: My recollection of the
Town Tenants Act was this, that it only
gives the tenant a right to compensation for

were used for business purposes, or a right
to compensation for improvements where
those improvements were made before the
passing of the Act. It goes on further to
give a right to compensation for improvements after the passing of the Act in cases
where those improvements were made with
the knowledge of the landlord, and there are
provisions in the Act enabling questions of
dispute as to whether the improvements
were to be made or not to be decided by the
County Court Judge. But I submit those
provisions of this Act are not on the same
footing as the Amendment now before the
House, because this is an Amendment to
give absolute security and tenure and also to
give them the right, or perhaps it may be in
the alternative to purchase out their premises
and become the owners of the premises which
they formerly had as tenants.
May I point this out to the House? That
as a general proposition a tenant who takes

which only gives him a tenure of say from

to 60 years, which was the common

Northern Ireland, did so with his eyes open.
He knew what he was doing. Conditions of

with this difficulty in Northern Ireland,
namely, that a lot of these tenants have built

Thursday, 11th March, 1926.
The House met at Three of the Clock, Mr.
SPEAKER in the Chair.
Oral Answer to Question.
CASE OF MR. THOMAS O'DOHERTY,
SCHOOL TEACHER.
1. Mr. DEVLIN asked the Minister of Home
Affairs whether Thomas O'Doherty, a public
elementary school teacher, presently undergoing a third year's course at Queen's University, was arrested on the 23rd January,
1926, at the Donegall Pass Barracks, Belfast,
on the charge of stealing a bicycle from the
Students' Union, on the 19th January;
whether on the 25th and 26th of the same
month the police in charge of the case received written and oral statements from Mr.
R. N. Greer, a fellow student; Mr. William
Parr, Registrar of Stranmillis Training
College, and Professor Lloyd, M.A., of the
same college, proving conclusively that Mr.
O'Doherty was at the training college at the
time at which the bicycle was supposed to
have been stolen, and at the time he was
supposed to have been seen riding the cycle
in the University grounds; whether the
police suppressed this evidence, and whether
Mr. O'Doherty, after being twice before the
Magistrate at the Belfast Police Court, was
committed for trial on 1st February on the
charge; whether at the Commission on the
24th February Lord Justice Andrews, after
hearing only part of the evidence for the defence, stopped the case, and instructed the
jury to return a verdict of not guilty;
whether the Minister can say what action
he proposes to take against the police connected with the case, and what compensation
he is prepared to offer Mr. O'Doherty for the
treatment he was subjected to.
The ATTORNEY-GENERAL (Mr. Babington): As this matter relates to prosecutions
for which I am responsible, I have been
asked to reply to the question. The reply
is as follows:-
In this case Mr. Thomas O'Doherty was
returned for trial on the evidence of three
witnesses, one of whom identified him as the
man who removed the bicycle; the other two
identified him as the man who subsequently
disposed of it in their shop.
There was nothing irregular in the proceedings or in the conduct of the police, and
no evidence was suppressed.
Under these circumstances no claim for
compensation can be entertained.
Mr. DEVLIN: Can the right hon. and
learned Gentleman say whether the magistrate who tried this case stopped the case
and said there was no evidence against this
man upon which he could be convicted? Is
the right hon. and learned Gentleman aware
that three distinguished members of the
Teachers' Training College came forward
and gave evidence that it was impossible for
this man to have committed the offence as
he was in the college at the time it was
committed?
Mr. BABINGTON: The facts with reference to the action of the learned judge who
tried the case are as follow: The witnesses
for the Crown were produced and maintained
their evidence as to the identification of the
accused. The Crown case proceeded to a
close, and was not stopped by the learned
judge and, therefore, it must be taken that
on the case, as presented by the Crown, there
was, at any rate, a charge which had to be
answered. After the Crown case had closed
five witnesses were called on behalf of the
defence, and at the end of the evidence of
the last of these five witnesses the learned
judge stated that having regard to the
standing of these witnesses and the volume
of evidence for the defence it would not be
safe for the jury to convict, as there might
have been a mistake, and, accordingly, he
directed the jury to find a verdict of not
guilty. The case was not stopped; it was
allowed to proceed until a sufficient volume
of evidence had been called by the defence
to warrant the learned judge in saying that
the matter was in doubt, and that, therefore,
the accused was entitled to be discharged.
Mr. DEVLIN: Is it not a fact that the
police were in possession of the statement
of these three distinguished men, and that
the police kept this evidence of these men
back when the trial took place in the police
court? I should like to ask the Attorney-
General, as, I take it, he directs prosecutions, or at least controls them, whether
this information was put in his possession
before he sent the case to the assizes.
Mr. BABINGTON: The supplementary
question which the hon. Member has just
asked me is based on a misapprehension as
to the way in which criminal prosecutions
are carried out under our law. When the
accused is brought before a magistrate on
an indictable offence the magistrate has no
jurisdiction to try the case. His only
jurisdiction is to say whether or not there
is a prima facie case on the evidence of the
Crown against the accused, and, though
that evidence may be contradicted by
evidence upon the other side, if he is satisfied that a prima facie case stands and
Oral Answer.
11 MARCH 1926
Debate on Address.
Mr. SPEAKER: Order, order.
requires investigation he is bound to return
it for trial. The matter then comes before
the law officers upon the evidence of the
Crown witnesses, and again if there is a
prima facie case a prosecution is directed.
It then comes before the grand jury, and
again if a prima facie case is established a
true bill is found. It then comes before a
petty jury and a judge for the purpose of
trying the issue that has been raised between
the respective parties.
In this particular case the police behaved
with perfect propriety. They had the
positive identification of the accused by a
messenger, who was attached to the
University, and who swore that he saw the
accused riding this particular bicycle out of
the University on 19th January, at some
time after three o'clock. They had also the
evidence of Mr. Andrews, junior, who said
that at 4-30 on that afternoon the accused
presented the bicycle to him for sale, and
they had the evidence of Mr. Andrews,
senior, the last witness's father, who said
he purchased the bicycle from the accused
at some time about 5-30, and upon that
evidence the police charged the accused before the magistrate. The police had in their
possession when the accused was brought
before the justice a copy of the statement
by Mr. Greer, who, I think, is also in the
University, accounting, or purporting to
account, for the movements of the accused
at some of the material times. The police
with perfect propriety produced that
document to the magistrate, but were told
that as there was a prima facie case that
document should be preserved for use, if
necessary, when the matter was investigated
by the petty jury.
The accused was represented by counsel
and a solicitor, and his counsel, who
has very considerable experience in these
matters, could if he had so wished, or if he
thought he could displace the prima facie
case, have produced not only this Mr. Greer
but the two other witnesses whose names are
mentioned in the question. They were not
produced, and accordingly the prima facie
case stood. There was absolutely no alternative but for the matter to come before a
petty jury for investigation.
Mr. SPEAKER: I am afraid this is really
developing into a debate. I certainly should
not have allowed it but for the fact that
there is only one question on the Paper.
Mr. DEVLIN: Arising out of that may I
point out that in the course of the somewhat
elaborate reply of the right hon. and
learned Gentleman he has made statements
of clear and distinct evidence of identification ? From my reading of the case the
witnesses were not distinctly clear-
Mr. DEVLIN: Therefore I wish to
announce that I shall raise this question on
the adjournment.

Which Amendment was at end, to add

Position of Leaseholders.
Mr. BABINGTON: When our proceedings
were interrupted last night under Standing
Orders I had almost concluded what I had
to say with reference to this Amendment.
I think I had pointed out to the House that
so far as this Amendment is concerned it
raises issues of very great magnitude, indeed
a great deal more serious and fundamental
than was suggested by the proposer of the
Amendment.
This question as to the renewal of leases
by landlords is one which has always been
D
Position of Leaseholders. 100
Debate on Address--
HOUSE OF COMMONS
[Mr. Babington]
carried out under the ordinary law of contract. Of course, it is quite obvious that
renewals are made upon reasonable terms
by landlords, or terms which are considered
reasonable by tenants. In other cases unreasonable demands are made, and the
reasonableness or otherwise of those demands
must be defined by the value of the premises
at the fall of the lease. We are all perfectly
well aware of the fact that in a big number
of cases the value of the premises has appreciated to a very great extent during the
currency of the term, and when the lease
falls in the reasonableness or otherwise of
the demands of the landlord must be determined by the value of the premises in the
open market, whether that value be determined by reference to rent or whether it be
determined by reference to the capital value
of the premises.
It happens every day, and it is not very
long since I had a case of this sort before
me in the City of Belfast in one of the main
thoroughfares. The tenant had held premises at a rent of £600 per annum, and
when the lease fell in the demand his landlord made from him, and which the landlord
was able to get in the open market, was a
rent of £2,500 per annum, so greatly had the
value of premises in the central part of the city
increased during the currency of that lease.
The House will readily understand that if
the interests of the tenants, and it is impossible to distinguish between them, are converted into perpetuity, either by giving them
perpetual tenure or by some system of purchase by which the interest of the landlord
is transferred to the tenant, the whole basis
on which dealing and trafficking in houses
and house property is carried on will be
completely done away with, and a new system
will have to be evolved in its place.
It can easily be seen that there is a very
great distinction between the case of land
and the case of houses and house property,
because in the case of land the tenants are
cccupying tenants, and such a thing as a
lease of agricultural land in this country is
very rare, indeed. Therefore, when the
tenants were converted into peasant proprietors the lands continued to be dealt with
on the basis of an absolute interest from that
time on, but in the case of houses that
cannot be so, because there are a great
number of people who set up in business
who require terms. They do not know
whether their business is going to succeed
or not, they have not the financial backing
behind them to take perpetuity or to purchase the absolute interest in the premises,
and they have to go into the market and
lease premises. In the same way
great number of householders are not in a
position to purchase the fee-simple of their
a
dwellings, and they have to take them on
lease.
If any interference such as this Amendment suggests was to be sanctioned by Parliament the only effect of it would be that
those persons who became perpetuity holders
under any Act that might be passed to that
effect would in their turn become landlords
of other tenants. It is impossible to devise
any new form of tenure by which the
business instincts of the people could be
satisfied without upsetting the whole of the
commercial relations of the community.
Therefore, I suggest that so far as this
Amendment is concerned it has not been
properly thought out. It has been dictated
by the fact that there are, unfortunately, in
some cases landlords who are unreasonable,
but it does not necessarily follow that because some landlords are unreasonable the
whole system of land tenure is one that
ought to be done away with and scrapped.

There is no country in the world, so far
as I am aware, that has ever been able to
devise a satisfactory system for the tenure
of land other than the one based upon freedom of contract in the open market.
same rules, with slight modifications, apply
in the great communities in America, and
also on the Continent, and until some better
system is devised it is quite impossible for
the Government to undertake to interfere
with landlord tenure and to destroy the
basis upon which all commercial contracts

hundred years. I have nothing more to say

reform of this sort upon the very short and

susceptible of explanation.

He will surround or cover with legal camouflage the real and vital questions which are

He gave us an elaborate disquisition upon

Governments. There was a contract between

the simple proposition that my hon. Friend

My own view is that these increased values
should go neither to the tenant nor to the

that interest. I am supporting this Amendment

what the hon. Member for Antrim (Mr.

After all, the tenant who takes a piece of
land from a landlord and erects a house on
it is making a bargain with his landlord.
He may make a good bargain or he may make
a bad bargain. He may make an exceptionally bad bargain, and then everybody says
he has been badly treated. We are all liable
to make bad bargains. I do not suppose
there is a single Member of this House who
has not made a bad bargain.
It should be said that Parliament has
always been in favour of protecting men who
are put in a position which an unconscionably bad bargain has forced upon them. Innumerable Acts have been passed by various
legislatures to protect borrowers from money
lenders, and I do not see why the Government
should not consider the question of protecting
the tenant from a landlord who is trying
through an unconscionably bad bargain to
extort from him a perfectly extortionate
rent for the land which he has to give up
at the end of his term of tenancy. He has
taken his tenancy for 10, 15, 20, 50, 99 or 999
years in the expectation that he was going to
make something out of the tenancy, otherwise he did not deserve to be in business
at all. But there should be a limit to the
extortion which his landlord is able to exercise over him at the end of that tenancy. The
same procedure has been recognised in a
number of other cases. It has been recognised in connection with the carrying on of
business. A man must get reasonable compensation for the amount of business he is losing.
At the present time you have passed laws
which prevent the ordinary landlord of an
ordinary house from getting an extortionate
rent out of his tenant, and I do not see why
the Government should not consider the question of setting up a Committee as has been
suggested to consider in what way the tenant
could be protected from being treated in an
extortionate way by the landlord.
The PRIME MINISTER (Sir James Craig):
I suppose there is no Member of the House
who has learned more during the debate

brought to our notice yesterday by the hon.

occasions. All I can say is that it is one of
the most difficult problems that any person
can undertake, because the moment you touch
the sanctity of contract, whether that contract is entered into between one rich man
and another rich man or between two poor
men-the moment the State steps in and says
under certain circumstances the sanctity of
that particular contract is not to hold good
then you do really strike in my opinion a
very heavy blow at the stability and credit
of the community.

see

tenant. The Act allows that to go on, and
from that point of view we say that the Act
is unfair. It is a grave injustice to the working-class people. These are ways and means
to give the landlord the right to increase
the value of his house during the time when
you should not be asking for an increase.
Then as to the 15 per cent. for repairs
which this Government graciously granted to

I asked, there has been no better results

to-day in several houses I have been in, to

carry out repairs. He does not distinctly
tell people he will not do it, but putting off

One very important matter in regard to
which the Minister of Home Affairs should
take action is the estate agents or landlords
who are holding up at the present time anything from 300 to 500 houses. They get the
tenants out whether they want the houses
or not and they put the houses up for sale.
Some action should be taken by the Minister
of Home Affairs to compel these people after
a certain period to let their houses. Under
the Act of Parliament what happens? They
have a house built forty or fifty years ago.
They get the tenant out and put the house
up for sale. It was built forty or fifty years
ago for £90. I know some of these houses
on the Lisburn Road. The agents put a
lurid advertisement in the papers stating
that the purchaser will be assisted under the
Small Dwellings Acquisition Act, and they
sell the house for £500 or £600.
It is the duty of the Minister of Home
Affairs, who is responsible for the housing
of the people, to put a stop to anyone ex-

sincerely hope and trust the. Minister of

stand the whole of the provisions passed in

We find after the Act has been on the Statute

the provisions of that last Act passed in this

I will probably be told that responsibility

Mr. LEEKE: Portrush?
Mr. W. McMULLEN: Portrush is not so

That, perhaps it will be argued, is not absolutely relevant to the matter under discussion.
To go back to the reasons why an Amendment should be made to the recent Rent
Restriction Act, great hardship has been inflicted on people where the valuation of their
houses is more than £20. Rents have been
enormously increased and people who occupy

Act.
Mr. HANNA: I quite agree with the hon.
Member (Mr. W. McMullen) that a good deal
of misunderstanding exists with regard to
this Act of Parliament. I think that has
been very fully exemplified by the speeches
of those who have spoken on the other side
of the House and particularly by the speech
of the hon. Member for North Belfast (Mr.
T. Henderson). It is idle to suggest that any
man who says he is the owner of a house,
and it is the only house he holds, can go
right off to the county court judge and demand possession of that house. That is not
the law. What he would have to do would
be to serve a six months' notice on the
tenant that he required the house for himself, and only those single house owners who
purchased their houses before 1st May, 1923,
could possibly claim the benefit of this Section. Then he must prove to the satisfaction
of the judge that he requires the house for
himself, and if he makes false representation
to the judge, and if he succeeds in getting
a decree, and if afterwards he proposes to let
the house at an exorbitant rent or sell it
he is subject to the penalties of the law provided in the Act.
If, on the other hand, he wants the house
for his mother-in-law whom he likes-if
there is such a thing in the world-he has
got to determine the tenancy in the ordinary
way and he has got to prove that he requires
the house for himself or for some of his
friends for a residence, and he must at the
same time be prepared to offer alternative
accommodation to that tenant. He must find
another house for the tenant reasonably
equivalent to the house he wants possession
of in all respects as to situation, rent and
accommodation. When hon. Gentlemen in
this House suggest that the law is that a man
can go down and get his house at once, is it
any wonder that people in Newry are mystified as to the meaning of the Act?

taken place.

Mr. LEEKE: I feel disappointed that
greater provision has not been made for
agriculture. This, as we all know, is one of
the most important industries in Northern
Ireland, and the only thing that I can see
is the foreshadowing of legislation for the
inspection of the potato crop, which will be
exported. That is a very questionable
method of assisting agriculture, because it
has been tried in the past, and has not been
a success. However, on this occasion it may
improve, and if so it will certainly facilitate
the trade of Ulster.
As the House knows, the farmers presently
are faced with pre-war prices for their produce and with war expenses for carrying out
their business, and a grant should be made in
order to enable them to carry on their
business in a manner that would help unemployment in this country. There has recently been passed-at least within the lifetime of the last Parliament-an Education
Act, part of the expense of which was thrown
upon the farmers. This is the first time the
farmers have been asked to shoulder
burden like that, and I do not think it
is fair. I hold that that should have been,
as it has always been in the past, a completely national charge, and not added to
the burden of taxation, which is retarding
and handicapping the development of the
agricultural industry in this country.

I would like to back the hon. Member's

for the farming industry. The farmers are
not insured against ill health. They have no

better than that of artisans, and they have

only necessary to employ an additional three
boy clerks permanently. That, I think, goes
to show that that Department must have
been considerably overstaffed.
Mr. ANDREWS indicated dissent.
Mr. GYLE: It is quite evident that the
work cannot have been of very great importance. There are something like 5,000
widows, and I do not know how many
orphans to be looked after, and if that was
done by three boy clerks and twenty temporary clerks I think it goes to show that
the Ministry of Labour must have been considerably overstaffed. I am rather inclined
to think that all the departments in the
Northern Government are very considerably
overstaffed, and I suggest to the Government
that, when they bring this eminent gentleman
over, instead of asking him to go into the
matter himself, they should appoint a committee of this House, or at any rate of business
gentlemen in Belfast, to sit along with him,
so that when his report is presented to the
House we will know that the matter has been
thoroughly investigated. I am perfectly sure
that the Government are as anxious as we
are to have the affairs of the Government
conducted for as reasonable an amount as is
possible. At the same time there is a feeling
right throughout the whole of Ulster that
this Government is wasting money continuously. If they are not, why are they afraid
to have a committee set up in order to
investigate the matter thoroughly?
I am exceedingly pleased to see that at
long last the Government have recognised
that they made a fatal mistake when they
brought in the Intoxicating Liquor Act of
1923. That Bill was rushed through this
House. It was forced through this House
by men who had nothing else in their mind
but an attempt to ruin the liquor trade.
That was at the bottom of the whole agitation. As I have said on the platform and
in this House, there was no demand for that
Act. Not only was there no demand for it,
but there was actually an agreement made
between the two sides-the Temperance Party
and the Anti-Prohibition Party-that there
was to be no temperance legislation introduced during the lifetime of the last Parliament.
But in spite of the Prime Minister's desire
to have a Royal Commission, that Act was
forced on to the Statute Book, and now we
have it stated in the King's Speech that
there must be an Amending Bill. I hope
that the Government will not make the same
grave mistake this time. I hope that they
will take into consultation the hotel proprietors and the wholesale and retail trade,
and that in this Amending Bill we will get
something really worth while. I know perfectly well that some portions of the Act
are practically unworkable, simply because
it was put through in such a hasty manner,
and because the Government did not take
into consideration so many phases of the
matter. I am not going to say anything
about the new Bill until I see it; I reserve
to myself the right to criticise it.

I would like to remind my hon. Friend,
the Member for Antrim (Mr. Crawford), that
since I entered this House I have always
paid attention when the grievances of the
farmers were being discussed. I have at all
times raised my voice on their behalf.
was not asleep when he was speaking about
the farmers, and awake when he spoke of
the liquor trade. I have at all times done
my best for the farmer, just as in the future
I will continue to do my best for the trade
I belong to. I did not enter this House
under any false colours. I made my position
perfectly clear to the electorate. I made it
perfectly clear to them that my first business,
when I came here, would be to try to get
the 1923 Act amended. If I do not succeed
it will not be my fault. I congratulate the
hon. Member for Derry Mr. Leeke) upon
bis maiden speech, and I also congratulate

The hon. Member for Derry referred to

of Ireland for many years. I happen to
have been connected with the hotel and

the reason why we had such enormous tourist
traffic in Northern Ireland last year. But
what did the tourists tell us when they were
going away? They told us we had a beautiful
place, magnificent scenery, and a hospitable
people, who were anxious to give them the
best of everything, but there was one blot
in Northern Ireland, and they were not
coming back. That is the unfortunate
position. We want the tourists to come this
year, and to come with their friends next
year. In connection with the tourist traffic.
I would suggest to the Prime Minister that
residents in hotels should have the same
rights as they enjoy at home, or in an hotel
in another place. The tourists coming to
Northern Ireland should have the same
rights and privileges as if they were in

that before this Bill is drafted the Prime
Minister will invite all sections of the trade
to meet him in conference, so that we may
get something of real value to the people of
Ulster.
Mr. MCALLISTER rose.
Mr. DEPUTY SPEAKER (Mr. Moles): I
take it that the hon. Member has not previously spoken on the main question?
Mr. MCALLISTER: No. As a Nationalist
representative I would be false to my
position, to those whom I represent, and to
this House, if I did not enter my protest
against the fact that no cogent proof, no
tangible promise, is included in the King's
Speech that the disadvantages and injustices
under which we labour are about to be readjusted. We appreciate and we reciprocate
the expressions of goodwill and concord that
have been so frequently uttered by the Prime
Minister, and his hopes that a better spirit
and more cordial relations will prevail between the different sections of the community. But I would suggest to him that
if those hopes are to fructify, if they are
not mere picturesque phrases, he should take
immediate steps to transform them into
practical shape. Let us see that we are
entitled to draw natural and logical inferences from those expressions of opinion. I
would suggest to him that he should take
immediate steps to show that those gestures
of goodwill are not gestures made by Ministers with empty hands, but gestures made
by Ministers equipped and ready to deliver
the goods to us in the shape of fair and
equitable and just treatment to the minority,
equal status in the State, equal representation in public and local boards, and in all
the Departments of the State.

We seek no favours. We are only here
for the rights which our population of onethird of this State entitles us to, and I
suggest to the Government as a business
proposition that if the industries of Ulster
are to prosper, if they wish to develop the
full resources of the area, they can only
do that by the co-operation of the whole
community, and not by the efforts of twothirds alone. If you do not deal out to the
minority equal rights of citizenship, which
is the price of their co-operation, you cannot
develop the full resources of the State.
know that you are spending £10,000 in advertising the linen industry in America.
hope that that will bear fruit, and that it
will be repaid to you manifold, but in all

the best propaganda they could have in

a justly governed and satisfied minority.
That you can have in overflowing measure if

must realise that, if we are not to receive
equal rights of citizenship, human nature
forbids us contributing our full quota, and
our full co-operation to restore the prosperity

develop that point any more. We are reluctant to raise this issue, but if we are to
perform useful service here we must insist
on having some tangible proof that we are
going to receive justice from the Government
of this country.
I do not want to take up the time of the
House, but there is another item that I
would like to mention. One thing that has
struck me, particularly since I came into
this House, is the unaccountable haste with
which legislation is introduced and passed
through all its stages, without giving the
Members an opportunity of considering the
probable results and consequences of that
legislation, without giving Members an opportunity of obtaining the opinion of the electorate upon it, and without giving the
electorate an opportunity of investigating
how that legislation is going to affect them
and without giving them an opportunity of
voicing their opinion on the proposed legislation. Now I suggest that the Government
take into consideration the relative position
of Members of the Government and private
Members who sit on these benches. When
you introduce legislation here you come fully
equipped with all the relevant data handed
to you in tabloid form by an efficient staff of

In conclusion before I sit down I must say
I am disappointed that no comprehensive
practical scheme is forecasted for restoring
the decaying industry of agriculture in this
country. Now, as long as countries like
Denmark and several other countries with
less natural resources and admittedly of less
fertile soil can make this a lucrative and
paying proposition I refuse-until every
avenue is explored and every field exhausted
-I refuse to believe that what is done in
Denmark cannot also be done here.

it is a very serious thing for Ulster when

I believe the Government should encourage

start deepening the channel and extending

I am not sure that my hon. Friend or the
hon. Member for Antrim (Mr. Crawford) who
exhibits such concern for the farmers, can
really put forward anything that will urge
the Government or that is necessary
urge the Government to care for that very
important industry. This I can say, that so
far as the interests of that body are concerned there is no country in the world, I
believe, where the Government has shown
such concern for the interests of those who
have suffered hardships undoubtedly in the
past two or three years Not only has
relief of rates been given to a very great
extent, but we have lent money at such rates
of interest as to be practically negligible for
the purpose of replacing stock lost through
disease, and also, which is equally important,
in my judgment almost more important,
there has been the provision of seed potatoes
at about half the natural commercial value
of this article.
It must be remembered that potatoes have
suffered greatly in the North of Ireland from
a disease known as the scab, and it must be
obvious to anyone who has discussed this
subject that this disease is developed by
impure and improper seed. The Department
has arranged for immune varieties of seed
to be provided to farmers at, as I say, very
low cost in order that the whole country may
be relieved of this pest. It must be clearly
understood that our great market for the
surplus of our potato crop is Great Britain
and Great Britain will not accept the
potatoes coming from the North of Ireland
under the conditions under which we have
been raising them. All these things are being
taken into account by the Ministry of Agriculture. I repeat there is no country that I
am aware of which has shown more concern
for the interests of that industry than
Northern Ireland.
My hon. Friend (Mr. Crawford) behind me
put forward the rather empirical suggestion
that the period of extension of the land
annuities should be largely increased, and
the rate consequently lowered, alleging as he
did that a parallel case was that of the
licensed trade. There is no parallel between
the two cases. In the case of the licensed
trade the doubling of the term of repayment
by the publicans costs the Government or the
country nothing, but if the period of 68
years which is accorded to the farmers
for the redemption of the cost of their farms
were extended in the sense suggested by my
hon. Friend it would mean an enormously
heavy charge upon the Province and would
automatically reduce our revenue So
seriously that the money thus lost would not
be available for the ordinary services of the
country. Therefore, a suggestion of that
kind, I am afraid, cannot be received
favourably by the Government. If there
was no other difficulty in the way, this is a
reserved service, and anything of that kind,
even if it was conceivable, would have to be
introduced by the Imperial Government.
We ourselves have no authority to deal with
the provisions of the Land Act, and
particularly with the provisions of the
previous Land Acts which were entirely
carried out by the Imperial Government.
The hon. Member for Derry (Mr. Leeke)
referred to education as a national charge.
Education in Northern Ireland is at present
a national charge. The extremely simple and
negligible rate which the county authorities
have imposed and which the Government
have indeed supplemented cannot bear with
any hardship on the farmers, and if the
education of the children of the farmers is
not a subject about which they are SO
greatly concerned that they cannot afford
twopence or threepence additional on the
rates imposed by the county councils, they
have very little concern for the interests of
their children. Let me make a comparison.
We speak of the burdens we have to bear
already, and they are great no doubt at the
present time. Our taxation is on the same

Mr. POLLOCK: This Resolution, as the
Committee is aware, is the preliminary to a
Bill which will be submitted to this House
early in the coming week. I do not propose
to enter in great detail into the questions
that are involved, preferring to leave the
main discussion on the question until the
Bill itself is introduced. But I may, perhaps,
briefly outline something of the history of
the conditions under which we find ourselves
in relation to this great subject.
It is common knowledge that our Unemployment Insurance Fund had reached a condition when it was necessary that we should
take some radical steps to bring it into a
condition of re-solvency. This position or
condition developed from circumstances over
which we here in Northern Ireland had no
control. When the discussion over the
Government of Ireland Bill of 1920 took place
the White Paper made no provision whatever for the service-as it turned out one of
the most important services of the countryfor dealing with the probability or possibility of labour unemployment. The result of
Insurance Agreement-
Committee.
HOUSE OF COMMONS
[Mr. Pollock]
that was that the White Paper, on which the
financial proposals of the Bill were framed,
did not deal with that subject or make any
provision for the liability that would possibly ensue in respect of that subject, and we
were entirely ignorant ourselves of the whole
thing. Labour matters were transferred to
Northern Ireland, and the liability consequent upon that fell on the Northern Government.
This Measure, having become a transferred
service, the Treasury, in dealing with the
subject, not only admitted that there was
no fund in existence-no surplus in existence
in order that we might start our operations
in regard to this insurance matter, but as
a matter of fact the British Fund having
been at the time in the condition of a deficit
to the extent of some millions we were
charged with a proportionate amount, which
on calculation came to £160,000. We, therefore, started an insurance enterprise, not
with any capital behind it, not with a surplus that had been derived from the previous
operation of the Fund, but actually there
was a deficit of £160,000. That amount has
been paid by Northern Ireland to the Unemployment Fund of Great Britain.
Following that, we were met with a very
unexampled condition of depression and consequent increase of unemployment, so that
this deficit of £160,000 began to creep up and
creep up until at the end of the last financial
year it amounted to two and a half million
pounds approximately. It was at this point
that it was quite obvious that the situation
rendered it necessary that the Government should take some steps to resolve our liability, and indeed by statute the
responsibility was laid upon my shoulders
so long as I occupied the position of Minister
of Finance to take such steps as would bring
the Fund into a condition of solvency.
matter was then taken up with the British
Government, and the grievances under which
we laboured were presented to the Government on the other side. Discussions began
between the two bodies the British
Government and ourselves-with the result
that a Departmental Committee was appointed, under the chairmanship of Sir John
Anderson, to examine the whole question.
The
was
This Committee reported to a Cabinet
Committee appointed by the British Cabinet,
of which the Lord Chancellor was chairman,
and out of its negotiations and as a result
of its deliberations an agreement
reached, which is embodied in the White
Parer, which I have had circulated to hon-
Members, and which, I hope, has been read.
On the assumption that it has been read
I need not enter into all the details beyond
stating a bare outline. It provides that as
from the 1st October, 1925, the responsibility
for the maintenance of the Unemployment
Insurance Fund in a condition of solvency
shall be undertaken as to 75 per cent.
liability on the part of the Imperial Government, with 25 per cent. left upon Our
own shoulders. That, in essence, is the
nature of the arrangement that has been
made. The details and method of calculation are of a somewhat complex character
such as it would be difficult for me to enter
into and explain fully. The White Paper
contains the whole of the Agreement that has
been made between the Chancellor of the Exchequer and myself officially and it also very
clearly sets out by way of memorandum the
whole of the conditions under which that
Agreement was reached and the results that
are expected to accrue. It shows that for
the six months from the 1st October until
the end of our financial year it is estimated
that the responsibility of the British Government will be a certain sum, £600,000 odd, and
our liability will be proportionately £300,000
odd.
British
Under the Agreement also the
Government undertakes to pay fully 75 per
cent. of the deficit that has accrued on the
1st October; that is to say, assuming that the
liability on that date is £3,600,000 it must be
carried by the provision of yearly interest,
and the British Government is undertaking
to provide 75 per cent. of that interest-that
is to say upon the accumulated deficit. 1
do not pretend that this is an arrangement
that I in my position of Finance Minister
would have preferred. I thought, and I still
think, that under the conditions in which
the transference of an autonomous authority
was made to us that the merging of the two
funds into a General National Fund would
and should have been the natural and proper
solution of this matter. I am glad to see
that reference was made in the Imperial
Parliament only yesterday to this fact, and
the opinion was offered that possibly that
might have been the best solution of the
problem. But be that as it may, we were
very glad indeed to be able to arrive at this
solution because it relieved the Northern
Parliament, the Northern Government, and
the people of Northern Ireland, of a burden
which it was quite impossible for them with
their limited area to bear. Under these circumstances, therefore, I think the House
will agree that the arrangement that has
been made is the best that could be made,
the Bill when it is presented will probably
receive the approval of the whole House. I
beg to move.

CASE OF MR. THOMAS O'DOHERTY,

Mr. DEVLIN: I must apologise to the
House for raising a question that perhaps
may be regarded by most Members as of
very little importance, but I think it would
be well even in the midst of the tremendously
important issues which have been discussed
during the last few days if we should sometimes remember that the jealous guardianship
of the spirit of justice is one of the first
functions of a constitutional assembly. I
ventured to put a question to the Minister
of Home Affairs to-day with reference to a
recent event that took place in our city and
I think the best and simplest way for me
to deal with this question is to recite the
facts briefly as they were stated in the Press.
School-teacher's Case. 152
School-teacher's Case.
HOUSE OF COMMONS
[Mr. Devlin]
an
On 19th January a bicycle was stolen from
the basement of the Students' Union at
Queen's University. On the 23rd of the same
month two detectives called at the house
where Mr. O'Doherty, a teacher, lodged and
questioned him about some stolen property.
He denied that he knew anything about such
property and was asked to go to Donegall
Pass Police Barracks to take part in an
identification parade. He did so. The parade
was held, and I understand from information
conveyed to me that that parade was
absolute farce. Two of the men who were
called-I think it was two men-Mr. Andrews
and his son, stated they thought they saw
this man before. Mr. O'Doherty was arrested
and charged with the larceny of the bicycle
and removed to the police headquarters where
he remained until the following Monday,
when he was brought before the magistrates.
He was remanded until the subsequent Monday, when he was committed for trial to the
Commission. The Resident Magistrate said a
prima facie case had been made out.
On Wednesday, as I have said already, the
trial of Mr. O'Doherty started at the Commission, and before it was finished the judge
directed the jury to acquit this young man.
His Lordship stated a message boy who was
the chief witness for the Crown had made an
honest mistake. The only direct evidence
against Mr. O'Doherty was the evidence of
this message boy. There was no doubt two
other men were brought in to identify this
man but they were very circumspect and they
were not at all sure, and thev certainly were
not very distinct that that was the man.
Under these circumstances one might not
have any reason to complain if it were not
for the subsequent facts. And what are the
facts? It was stated that at the time this
larceny took place Mr. O'Doherty was in the
company of Mr. William Parr, registrar of
Stranmillis Training College, and Mr. R. N.
Greer, a student of the College, half a mile
from the scene of the larceny of the bicycle.
and that at twenty minutes past three
Professor Lloyd, M.A., entered the room of
the College and found them there.
My ailegation against the Government, or
against whoever is responsible for the conduct of these prosecutions, is that all these
statements were in the hands of the police
and that this evidence was suppressed. I
want to know whether counsel or whoever
appeared for the prosecution had the evidence
of these three honoured members of the community and eminent men in the College that
Mr. O'Doherty was in their company at the
time this larceny took place and that it was
impossible for him to have stolen the bicycle,
and why the police suppressed this evidence
and did not bring it before the magistrates.
What I think ought to have been done is that
the police themselves should have consulted
the Attorney-General, or whoever authorises
these prosecutions, and told him they had
this evidence in their possession, and have
the case instantly dismissed instead of keeping this young fellow in prison having a
stigma put upon him on the eve of a great
career of public usefulness in a position of
responsibility where a charge of this character was destined materially to damage his
prospects. At the same time the charge was
allowed to hang over his head and the only
evidence was the evidence of these people.
The case went on, and, as I have said,
the judge, Lord Justice Andrews, ordered it
to be stopped and said there was no evidence
against him except the evidence of this boy.
and clearly that was a mistake. No doubt
a small matter of this sort may seem of
very little importance, but the character and
the position of a young student in a Teachers'
College is of some importance to the community. What would have happened if this
Mr. O'Doherty at the time he was engaged
in conversation with these professors and
representative men in the College had gone
out to take a long walk and had been away
at the time this incident occurred? Nothing
would have saved him from a conviction and
the ruin of a life-long stigma enduringly
placed upon his character. Yet all that evidence was withheld by the police and never
produced in the lower court. It was not
brought forward although they had it in their
possession until the case came before the
Commission.
Mr. O'Doherty had been freed by the action
of the judge and jury from the stigma or
crime, and I think that considering his posi
tion and the wrong that has been done him
and the torture to which he has been subjected by this curiously tortuous policy by
which he was prosecuted he is entitled to
a public apology and compensation at the
hands of the Government. Therefore I think
it my duty to raise it here. It may have no
effect, but I take it that it will make the
police and those in charge of the administration of justice more careful in the future
before they bring citizens before a Police
Court. force them into an Assize Court, and
have a charge of this character levelled
against them. Although a man may be subsequently declared innocent one knows that
when these charges are made and carried so
far as in this case they are very often a
stigma for life. I have, therefore, felt it my
duty, in view of what I regard as the unsatisfactory answer of the Attorney-General,
to bring this matter before the House.

they appeared in the Press but as they appeared in the court. I can assure the hon.

most necessary, of course, in a case where
there is any suggestion of unfair practice or
maladministration that that should be investigated at the earliest possible moment.
I investigated the procedure in this case
as soon as this question was tabled in the

are brought before the court are not
acquitted. But that does not entitle them
to anything in the way of apology either from
the Law Officers of the Crown or to compensation from the Government. It may be
unfortunate in any one particular case. It
may be more unfortunate in one particular
case than in another that a charge which
is ultimately disproved is brought against
that particular individual, because he may
be in such a position that a suggestion of anything in the nature of dishonesty may do
him incalculable harm. But that, unfortunately, cannot be avoided, and that, 1
would suggest to the House, has got nothing
to say to the matter that is being debated
here. The question is was this prosecution
properly conducted or was it not. Was there
maladministration on the part of the police
or was there not? I unhesitatingly say that
there was not; that in this particular case the
evidence was clear so far as the prosecution
was concerned, and it was not until it was
displaced, or, at any rate, until there was
a doubt thrown upon it by the evidence for
the defence that the accused was entitled
to be acquitted.
The hon. Member (Mr. Devlin) who has
raised this question has said, in the first
place, that the parade was a farce. I have
investigated that, and I can assure the House
that that is not so. The parade was carried
Now, what statements were in the hands
of the police? They had the evidence of
these three witnesses. They had the bicycle
which had been stolen. They had also a
statement from a Mr. Greer, which was taken
by the police, I understand, at the instigation of the accused, and which threw some
doubt upon this question of identification.
But that was not a matter which the police
had any authority or right to try. That was
a matter for the magistrate alone in the
first instance, and the statement was not
suppressed, but was produced to the magistrate in court. As I said before, the accused
was represented by very able counsel, who
elected, in the accused's interests, I take
it, not to call these three witnesses, and
some other witnesses who afterwards appeared when the matter was tried at the
Commission, but kept that evidence until
the case was tried finally before a jury. If
there is any cause for complaint in the fact
that these witnesses were not produced when
the matter was before the magistrates, who
returned the accused for trial, the blame
for that rests with the accused's Own
advisers, who, I assume, as in any of these
cases, were acting in consultation with the
accused, and giving the best advice they
could, according to the circumstances of the
case.
Mr. DEVLIN: Did the counsel say to the
magistrates that he had these witnesses
ready?
Mr. BABINGTON: It makes no difference,
according to the procedure of our courts,
whether the counsel for an accused person
makes a statement that he has other
witnesses or has
He knows
perfectly well that
has a right
not.
he
to call them, and can call them, and in this
case he could have called them. They were
not called, and, therefore, the prima facie
case stood. When a case comes before the
Law Officers, and is submitted to me, it is
School-teacher's Case.
Adjournment.
HOUSE OF COMMONS
[Mr. Babington]
submitted upon the evidence upon which the
prima facie case is established. The accused
was then returned for trial in the ordinary
way.
It is suggested here that, so far as the
Attorney-General is concerned, the statement
for the defence should have been submitted
along with all the other statements, and
that then I should have said there should
be no prosecution. I would like to inform
the House that, so far as this prosecution
is concerned, and so far as my duty as
Attorney-General is concerned, it would have
made no difference to the question as to
whether a prosecution should go on or should
not go on if all this evidence which was
ultimately produced had been submitted to
me. If there is a clear statement by competent witnesses, unshaken upon their own
testimony, but only contradicted by other
witnesses, I have to direct a prosecution,
because that is a question of evidence, which
has to be submitted to a petty jury, who
have to believe one side or the other, according as the witnesses present themselves to
the jury in court. Therefore, this prosecution could not have been stayed, no matter
what evidence had been laid before me, and
the case rightly went to trial, and was duly
disposed of by the learned judge before whom
it came.
As I said before-and I want to emphasise
this point, because a lot of importance seems
to have been attached to this particular case
-when the case came before the learned
judge and petty jury, it is quite plain that
the evidence of the three Crown witnesses
stood, because if there had been a flaw in
it, or if it had broken down in crossexamination, the learned judge would have
withdrawn the case from the jury before the
defence was gone into; but that was not done.
It was not until four or five witnesses had
been called for the defence that the learned
judge saw that there was such a conflict of
evidence as between the witnesses for the
prosecution and the witnesses for the defence
that there might possibly have been some
mistake.
Mr. DEVLIN: That is a scandalous way
in which to present the situation. The right
hon. and learned Gentleman has no right
whatever to say that in the mind of the judge
there was conflicting evidence, because the
judge distinctly stated that there might have
been a doubt in the case. The right hon.
Gentleman is acting as a further Crown
prosecutor in this case.
Mr. BABINGTON: I am not acting as a
further Crown prosecutor. If anything
arises out of this it is not due to any action
upon my part. The hon. Member who raised
this question said that the learned judge
said there was clearly a mistake. The
learned judge did not say that. What the
learned judge said was that having regard.
to the evidence for the defence there
might have been a mistake, and, therefore,
there was a doubt in the case, and it would
not be safe for the jury to convict upon that
evidence. That is the way the matter stood.
The learned judge directed the jury that
under the circumstances of the case it was
safer for them to return a verdict of not
guilty, and accordingly that was done.
I do not know whether any wrong has been
done. The accused has now been acquitted.
He is in no different position from any other
accused brought before the Court on insufficient evidence and acquitted. The only
really serious matter in this case which I
wish now to contradict in the clearest and
most emphatic manner-the only thing which
distinguishes it from the case of any other
accused person acquitted on a criminal
charge is the fact that there has been an
allegation made against the police of, first
of all, having held a parade which was a
farce, and, secondly, of having suppressed
evidence which was in their hands. I say
to the House that in neither of these charges
is there any degree of substance whatever,
and that this particular prosecution was
conducted with perfect propriety.
