COLERAINE INQUIRY - ARBITRATOR'S
FEES.
1. Sir ROBERT ANDERSON asked the
Minister of Finance whether it is a fact
that, in connection with an inquiry at
Coleraine into the price of land for the
erection of 48 labourers' cottages, the
arbitrator's fees amounted to £72 9s 0d, and
if so what action he proposes to take in the
matter.
(Mr.
The MINISTER OF FINANCE
Pollock): The amount of the fees is correctly cited by the hon. Member; they are
collected by the arbitrator, not for himself,
but on behalf of the Ministry of Finance,
and are paid into the Exchequer as Stamp
Duty on the award.
The Stamp Duty is fixed so as to approximate closely in its yield to the amount
which the Ministry has itself to pay to the
arbitrator. In deference to views put forward to the Ministry by a local authority
last year the scale was revised as recently
as 21st August, 1925, in a manner which
appeared to be more equitable, both to the
local authorities and the State. The Order
embodying the scale will be found amongst
the published Statutory Rules and Orders,
and I am sending a copy to the hon.
Member. I see no grounds for revising the
Order afresh. It must be borne in mind
that up to the year 1919 Rural Councils were
frequently put to the expense of High Court
appeals against the amount of compensation
assessed, whereas now there is no appeal,
save on matters of law. This represents a
very considerable saving.
The arbitrator's personal fees, which are
payable by the Ministry of Finance, will
amount to slightly less than the figure
quoted. The basis on which they are paid
was fixed after prolonged discussion between
my Ministry and the Surveyors' Institution,
and is lower than the corresponding scale
in force in Great Britain.

DISSOLUTION OF LOCAL AUTHORITIES.
4. Dr. MORRISON (for Mr. MILLER)
asked the Minister of Home Affairs if he will
state how many public boards or councils
have been superseded during the past five
years, and what, in the view of the Ministry,
was the result as regards economy, efficiency,
co-ordinance with the Ministry, efficacy of
appointments, and matters in general.
The MINISTER OF HOME AFFAIRS (Sir
Dawson Bates): In the latter end of the year
1921, and the beginning of the year 1922, the
Ministry dissolved 21 local authorities in
Northern Ireland, including 1 County Council, 4 Urban District Councils, 1 Town Commissioner, 7 Boards of Guardians, and 8
Rural District Councils.
The urban authorities in question were reconstituted in January, 1923, and the rural
and county authorities in May, 1924.
As the hon. Member is aware, the circumstances under which it was found necessary
to dissolve these local authorities and to
appoint Commissioners to discharge their
duties were of an exceptional character, and
the period of dissolution was too short to
enable the Ministry to constitute a comparison of a reliable character.
At the same time, the Ministry is satisfied
that during the short period of office the Commissioners on the whole discharged their
duties with economy and efficiency, and in
due accord with the Statutes and Regulations
governing the services for which they were
responsible.

These men are subject to no public opinion
at all; is not that why they are so satisfactory?

CASE OF JAMES MOORE, LABOURER.
8. Sir ROBERT ANDERSON (for Mr.
COOPER) asked the Minister of Labour if
James Moore, who lived at Dramleagues Big,
Ballindaugh, Co. Fermanagh, was at the date
of his death an ordinary labourer unable to
work owing to having contracted consumption, and if he is aware that his widow and
children have been refused the benefits of the
Widows' Pensions Act; and if so, why.
The MINISTER OF LABOUR (Mr.
Andrews): An application for a widow's
pension was received from the widow of Mr.
Moore, but on the facts shown it has not
been possible to admit the claim.
Under the conditions laid down in the
Widows,' Orphans', and Old Age Contributory Pensions Act it is necessary for the
applicant to show that the late Mr. Moore
was either an insured person with certain
contributions to his credit or that he was
at the date of his death normally occupied
in employment in respect of which contributions would have been payable if the Widows'
Pensions Act had been then in force.
Mr. Moore does not appear to have ever
been an insured person and the evidence submitted does not, in the opinion of the
Ministry, prove that his normal occupation
was insurable. The statements show that for
some years he had been in delicate health
and when he was able to work he was self
employed in his own garden.

KING'S SPEECH.
The Governor's Answer to the
Address.
The PRIME MINISTER (at the Bar) reported the Answer to the Address from His
Grace the Governor of Northern Ireland as
followeth :-
I have received with great satisfaction the
expression of your thanks for the Speech
with which I opened the present Session of
Parliament.
165 Insurance Agreement Bill-

16 MARCH 1926
Second Reading.
ORDERS OF THE DAY.
Unemployment Insurance (Agreement) Bill.
Order for Second Reading read,
Motion made and Question proposed: "That
the Bill be now read a Second time."
Mr. ANDREWS: The Bill which I have
the honour to ask the House to give a Second
Reading to to-day is in my opinion one of
the most important measures which this
House has ever been asked to consider.
After all, it is a Bill to ratify an Agreement
entered into between His Majesty's Imperial
Government and our Government for the
purposes of establishing a mutual re-insurance scheme in order to ensure that insured
persons throughout Great Britain and Northern Ireland shall receive for equal contributions equal benefits.
It has been suggested in this House and
outside it that this Government should never
have accepted any responsibility for dealing
with unemployment insurance. I would like
to make it perfectly clear that we had no
option, that it was laid down in the Act of
1920 that this insurance matter as well as
other labour matters would be a transferred
service. Hon. Members are aware of the fact
that our Parliament was opened by His
Majesty in June, 1921. As early as September
of the same year I brought the position as
regards unemployment insurance before my
colleagues and notwithstanding the fact that
we did not take over our powers until
January of the following year my colleagues
and I made frequent representations to the
appropriate Departments in Great Britain,
laying before them the injustice which had,
unintentionally no doubt, been done to us
through the White Paper which in setting
out the financial relations between Great
Britain and Northern Ireland had not made
any allowance for the probable liability we
would be faced with as regards this Fund.
Owing to the persistent exertions and the
influence of our Prime Minister early in
that year we received a sum of approximately
£477,000 in order to meet the transferred
deficit from the British Fund of £160,000 plus
the increased debt which we incurred up to
the end of the financial year. I may say that
we never accepted that payment as a final
solution of the problem, and since then we
have with considerable persistency and
carnestness been pressing successive British
Governments to right this wrong. It was not
until August last that we were able to arrive
at a settlement of the matter as set out in
the Schedule to this Bill. I do not feel that
it is necessary that I should take up the time
of the House to-day in going through, clause
by clause, the various provisions in the Bill
itself or in the Agreement in the Schedule
to which I have referred. I think it will
suffice if I make a general statement which
would put hon. Members in possession of
the real effect of the Agreement to which I
have referred.
The debit balance on our Fund at the 30th
September last, viz., £3,614,000, less the sum
of £183,000, which is the proportionate part
for Northern Ireland of the British Fund's
deficit of £7,935,000, calculated on an insured
population basis, shall be placed to a suspense account-that is the first part of the
Agreement-while the parity figure of
£183,000 shall be placed to the debit side of
the current account-that is the second part
of the Agreement.
It is proposed that the Unemployment
Fund of Great Britain and the Unemployment Fund of Northern Ireland will be
maintained in a state of parity in respect of
the period from the 1st October, 1925, to the
31st March, 1926, and for the four succeeding
years. This state of parity will be maintained by the payment of additional Exchequer grants, called the equalisation payments,
from Northern Ireland revenues to the
Northern Ireland current account of the
Unemployment Fund.

The burden so placed upon the Northern
Ireland Exchequer will be relieved by a payment from the Imperial Exchequer amounting to approximately 75 per cent. of the sum
required to equalise the respective burdens
upon a population basis. The remainder of
the equalisation payment will remain a net
charge on the Exchequer of Northern Ireland. I may add, however, that if at any
time the liability of the Imperial Exchequer
exceeds £1,000,000 in any one year the Imperial Government will be free, without
breach of agreement, to re-open the question on its merits. It is estimated that
the payment from the Impe
chequer will be this year, calculated in the
manner prescribed by Article 3 of the
Agreement, about £680,000, leaving about
£335,000 to be found by the Northern Ireland
Government beyond its normal contribution.
Now, hon. Members may ask what is to become of the £3,431,000 placed to the Suspense
Account. The interest will be dealt with and
borne by the two Exchequers in exactly the
same way as the equalisation payment, and
only the future can disclose what will be
the fate of the capital debt. Hon. Members
will fully appreciate the great advantage
that this Agreement is to us--
The PRIME MINISTER: Hear, hear.
Mr. ANDREWS--when I say that the
debt per insured person with us was £14, and
when measured in exactly the same way the
167 Insurance Agreement Bill— HOUSE OF COMMONS
Second Reading. 168
[Mr. Andrews]
redebt was only 15s per head of the population
of Great Britain. It will be interesting for
the House to know that three proposals were
made for dealing with this important
natter. The first was our proposal, namely,
that the two Funds should be
amalgamated. For the time being,
at any rate, that proposal was not
acceptable to His Majesty's Government,
and the Agreement which is contained in the
Schedule attached to the Bill itself was
arrived at after prolonged negotiations and
very earnest efforts on both sides. It is perfectly evident to prominent statesmen in
Great Britain, I think, that if the burden
which this Agreement imposes upon us is
beyond our capacity to bear the only solution
of the problem will be that of re-amalgamation.
A third proposal was, however, put forward
by the Socialist Party in Westminster, and
I think I am stating it quite fairly when
I say that that proposal was that we should
continue to borrow to the full extent of our
capability to do so, and when we had exhausted our own strength that the British
Treasury would come to our aid as moneylenders to allow us to get further into debt,
the dead-weight of which would in the end
have submerged us.
The PRIME MINISTER: Hear, hear.
Mr. ANDREWS: That was a proposal
which, of course, under no circumstances we
could have agreed to. The hon. Labour Member for West Belfast (Mr. W. McMullen)
has put forward the view that after all the
Socialist Party in Westminster were simply
acting in the interests of their own constituents. They may have thought so, but
I doubt it very much, taking the long view.
But even supposing for argument's sake that
I grant that, what would have been the
position if the Unionists at Westminster had
taken the same short-sighted, selfish,
parochial line? (Hon. Members: Hear, hear.)
We would not have to-day been considering
this Measure, which will undoubtedly confer
such great advantages upon our industrial
classes in Northern Ireland. On the contrary, we would have been left in the very
serious position in which we were placed
prior to this Agreement having been entered
into. I cannot help thinking that Mr.
Churchill described very fittingly the action
of the Labour Party when he quoted the
words:
Willing to wound, and yet afraid to strike,
Just hint a fault and hesitate dislike.
I think our Labour friends in this House
would be justified in saying, "Save us, oh,
save us from our so-called friends," because,
after all, I venture to say that the first duty
of a Labour Party is to see that equal social
standards are maintained unimpaired
throughout the whole of the United Kingdom.
Mr. KYLE: The Labour Party did not
oppose.
Mr. ANDREWS: My hon. Friend (Mr.
Kyle) says the Labour Party did not oppose
it. I have already shown that the Labour
Party's proposals would have made it impossible to continue to give effect to that
policy. But there is another matter which
I want to make perfectly clear to-day. This
is an honourable Agreement, honourably
entered into, and it must be honourably
carried out-
The PRIME MINISTER: Hear, hear.
Mr. ANDREWS- -as if it were not it
would crumble to pieces, and would become
a mere scrap of paper. What does it mean?
It means similar legislation in this Parliament to the legislation carried as regards
unemployment insurance at Westminster.
Mr. KYLE: Agricultural Wages Boards?
Mr. ANDREWS: That has nothing to do
with the subject. Further, it means equal
administration, and it means similar legislation. Very frequently appeals have been
nade to me and my colleagues to depart from
parallel legislation with the Imperial Par
liament. I am often appealed to to relax
regulations, and very painful it often was
that I could not comply with these requests,
but I said that some day I expected to be
in a position to prove that by keeping in
step with Great Britain the Government
here was doing the best it possibly could to
safeguard the position of our industrial
classes, and to ensure the greatest good to
the greatest number. This Agreement is the
proof of the truth of the words which I
very frequently had to utter in this connection, because I am justified in saying that
if it had not been for the fact that we do
keep in step with Great Britain in all matters this Agreement would not have been
possible.
The PRIME MINISTER: Hear, hear.
Mr. ANDREWS: We would consequently
have violated our right to ask Great Britain
to help us to deal with the matter, and to
deal with it on similar lines to them. May
I say in conclusion that our Insurance Acts
cannot be strained to bear a burden which
they never were designed or intended to bear?
Our Insurance Acts provide that under certain prescribed circumstances benefit will be
payable, and under other circumstances
benefit will not be payable, and being respon-
169 Insurance Agreement Bill-

16 MARCH 1926
Second Reading.
sible for the administration of these Acts,
which is a very difficult and thankless task,
I have no power to go beyond the provisions
of the Acts themselves. I feel that we are
deeply and I say it in no party sense-indebted to Mr. Churchill, for he was
prominent among British statesmen in
coming to recognise that we were too small
an area to be a safe insurance risk, and
that the safeguarding of our industrial classes
in Northern Ireland in this connection was
through close association with Great Britain.
He also recognised the fact that an injustice
had been done to us through the White Paper
to which I have already referred, and,
further, that men here in the same trade
unions as their brother trade unionists in
Great Britain had a right to expect for equal
contributions equal benefits. That is a policy
which this Government has stood for before
there was any official Opposition in this
House.
Then, again, I feel our thanks are due to
Lord Cave, who was Chairman of the Sub-
Committee of the Cabinet which investigated
this matter, and which took the utmost pains
to arrive at an agreement which was felt to
be, for the time, at any rate, a workable
one. We are also indebted to the British
Prime Minister and to all his colleagues for
the public-spirited way in which they have
viewed this problem; and last, but not least,
I wish to express my personal gratitude to
Sir John Anderson and to the staffs of the
Treasury, the Home Office, and the Ministry
of Labour for the courtesy which they displayed and for the exertions which they put
forward in order to extricate us from a
position in which we never should have been
placed. By so doing they have lifted a burden
from the Prime Minister's shoulders, from
ny other colleagues' shoulders, and from
myself, which was becoming almost unbearable, and they have conferred a security and
advantages upon our industrial classes in
Northern Ireland beyond words to express.
I beg to move.
Mr. BEATTIE: I rise to welcome the
Bill. I would have welcomed it more heartily
if there had not been such a thing as limitation in it. The limitation in the Bill is
something that I think should have been
wiped off. It is limiting us to the amount
from the Imperial Exchequer of a million
per year. That is a lesser amount than the
British Government imposed upon our funds
when they opened them to the textile and
other classes of workers by their Bill of 1929.
Therefore when they made the Bill of wider
scope the British fund should have assisted
to bear the brunt of those people being
brought in. I would prefer to have complete
amalgamation to what is in the Bill, because
the time is not far distant when that amalgamation will have to take place. Whether
it is with the whole of Ireland or with Great
Britain it matters not.
Mr. ANDREWS: Oh!
Mr. BEATTIE: I say with the whole of
Ireland or with Great Britain, because your
Fund, as it stands to-day, is uneconomic.
Your insured population is too small to carry
on, and I think the best interests of the
workers would be served by complete amalgamation rather than by this Agreement as
drawn up and agreed to by the British
Minister of Labour and our own Minister of
Labour of Northern Ireland. We have
11,642,000 people insured in Great Britain
with a lesser percentage of these people unemployed than we have in Northern Ireland.
I think it is about 11.1 per cent. against 24
per cent. in Northern Ireland out of an
insured population of 250,000. Now that
being so and in view of the 24 per cent, unemployed out of 250,000-if that is going to
continue any length of time, paying out
£53,000 per week-you will exceed the million
that Great Britain is limiting you to in the
first year, because the remainder will not
allow you to meet your liabilities on a percentage of 24 per cent being unemployed for
the incoming twelve months.
I would support the Agreement in the hope
that the best intentions will be applied to the
details we are asked to accept along with the
Agreement-that is we have got to walk step
by step with Great Britain. (Hon. Members:
Hear, hear.) Now step by step means something to the people of Northern Ireland and
especially to the unemployed workers. (Hon.
Members: Hear, hear.) If the Government
are prepared to see that we keep step by step
with regard to the unemployed workers in
Northern Ireland with what is being done
across the Channel I am with them. But remember your duty extends to more than unemployed benefit only. Your duty extends
also to compulsion being brought to bear on
the various boards of guardians operating in
Northern Ireland to see that they fulfil their
duty also to the unemployed workers.
There are several cases I would like to
quote in regard to deficiencies in Northern
Ireland compared with what is prevailing in
Great Britain. Unemployed workers in
Great Britain are subject to certain regulations laid down and some of these regulations
are stringent while others are very lenientmore lenient than what they are in Northern
Ireland. One of the lenient ones in Great
Britain is the scale of family income, better
known throughout Great Britain as the hardship rule. In Northern Ireland we have the
hardship. We allow a husband 21s to exist
on, and we allow the wife 10s. We allow a
maximum of 30s plus 16s for the wife, that is
36s, and the total for man and wife is 38s 6d.
Insurance Agreement Bill-
Second Reading.
HOUSE OF COMMONS
[Mr. Beattie]
For a child under 16 you allow 4s, that is
42s 6d for man, wife and child under 16.
That is the maximum we allow in Northern
Ireland, but the maximum allowed to the unemployed in Glasgow and industrial centres
similar to our own where the cost of living
is 10 points lower than it is in Northern
Ireland is 50s for man, wife and child
against 42s 6d.
That is one of the questions that are creating hardship in various homes at the present
time. Northern Ireland allows 54s 6d for
four of a family; Glasgow allows 60s. Northern Ireland allows 58s 6d for five against
Glasgow's 658. For six Glasgow allows
70s against Northern Ireland's 62s. For
seven of a family Glasgow allows 75s against
Northern Ireland's 66s 6d. For eight of a
family Glasgow allows 82s 6d against
Northern Ireland's 70s 6d. For nine of a
family the maximum amount allowed is 90s
against Northern Ireland's 74s 6d. In view
of the cost of living in Belfast being higher
than the cost of living in Glasgow I think
immediate attention is required to this scale
of family income as set out by the Minister
of Labour in Northern Ireland.
I would like also to draw attention to
another section of the hardship rule, that
is, in regard to the age of a self-dependent
person. Last November the L.E.C., the local
unemployment committee, drew up a new
scale of family income and in that scale
they set out a reduction of the self-dependent
age. Prior to that we had 25 years of age
up to which your father was expected to keep
you. When the committee drew up that I
complimented the Minister in this House for
reducing the age to 22. But on the 8th of
March, 1926, I got a circular setting out that
the age of 25 is to be reverted to, that is, increasing the age again on March 8th from 22
to 25 years of age. That is a hardship.
Mr. ANDREWS: It is the same in Great
Britain.
Mr. BEATTIE: There is no age limit laid
down in Great Britain as far as family
income goes. I have looked over the codes of
regulations and instructions in Great Britain
and I cannot see the age stated. I say here
that we in the Six Counties have not reasonable opportunities. In Great Britain the men
have reasonable opportunities. Our area is
too small. Our unemployed have not the
scope or the big field of industry to seek
after work that they have in Great Britain.
That is never taken into account when the
point of not genuinely seeking work is put
against a man's claim. In Great Britain
you can tramp from the South of England to
the North of Scotland and you have fields of
industry throughout the whole tramp. In
Northern Ireland where do you go to look for
employment other than in about three of the
principal towns? Now when a man is
genuinely seeking employment I think that
point of view should be kept in mind-the
scope the man has for seeking employment.
Now as to the ten points in cost of living I
might be making it too definite. I know it
is anything from 8 to 10 points higher here
than in Great Britain. I would like that also
to be kept in view when drawing up a scale
of family income, and I hope you will set
yourself to that immediately.
Another movement that is taking place in
our city is the movement of the young men
and young women-the minority movement
which demands the right to live, the right to
be maintained by the State. Perhaps you
may smile, but do you know it is the duty
of the State to see that no person starves
whether he is married or single. You have
the young manhood of Northern Ireland with
the sentiment of pauperism and the taint of
the workhouse combined together. They are
off unemployment benefit and are willing to
work but cannot get it. What is their alternative? Their parents say they cannot afford
to maintain them. They, in fact, have only
sufficient to provide for those in the home.
Their object will have to be the workhouse.
Mr. SPEAKER: May I interrupt the hon.

The policy of the Government, which has
been consistently followed and which has
been embodied in the various Acts passed by
this House, has been to encourage private
enterprise as much as possible; to reduce
unnecessary hampering restrictions, and at
the same time to work in the closest cooperation and harmony with the local
authorities, offering them the same inducements as we hold out to private builders.

I would like to take this opportunity of
paying a tribute to the whole-hearted support
which the Government has received from the
various local authorities. They have given
grants ranging from £25 to £40, and in a
very large number of cases they have
arranged to remit rates for a period ranging
from 5 years to 10 years.
Representations have been made to me by
some of the Urban Authorities, advocating
the extension of the maximum limit from
950 superficial feet to 1,400 superficial feet,
The Government, after careful consideration, have been unable to accede to this
request. They feel that if the maximum
limit was extended, it would act as an encouragement to private builders to confine
their attention to houses of the villa type,
a type which always commands a ready scale,
and by this means the policy of the Government to provide houses which would be
within the resources of the working classes
would be neutralised and defeated.

EMPLOYMENT OF EX-SERVICEMEN.
Colonel WOODS: I beg to move:
in the opinion of this House, it is the duty
of the Government in all Government contracts to make provision for the employment
to the fullest possible extent of disabled. .ex-
Servicemen, and to this end to confine such
contracts to employers enrolled on the King's
National Roll."
This Motion, I know, will meet with the
sympathy of every Member of this House.
It contains nothing new. It is only brought
up for the purpose of showing public bodies
what their duty in this matter really is. 1
will not take up the time of the House by
enlarging upon the subject. It is one well
known to every Member. I am simply asking
for the unanimous vote of the House on this
Motion. There may be someone who may
object to the wording or phrasing of the
Motion, but it is surely one that has more
decision about it than the one passed two
years ago in this House, that really meant
nothing at all. If such a Motion as this is
passed it will strenghen the hands of the
Government in dealing with contracts.
Major SHILLINGTON: I would like to
second the Motion moved by the hon. Member
for West Belfast (Colonel Woods). I think
that the time has come now when the
Government should put down its foot and
not receive contracts from any firm unless
that firm is on the King's National Roll of
Honour. There was a resolution passed two
years ago, to which my attention has been
drawn, but I do not think it goes quite far
enough. I understand this matter was under
discussion quite recently in the Imperial
House, and a resolution was passed there
something on the lines now suggested. I know
arguments will be put forward by the Government that they do not see their way to accept
the resolution, and that the resolution
already passed has resulted in large numbers
of firms being added to the National Roll.
I quite admit that during the last few years
the number of firms enrolled on the Roll
has tremendously increased, but that is
largely accounted for by the fact that up to
1921 and 1922 we had no local Employment
Committees here, and the Roll was not prominently brought before the public. It
was worked by a sub-committee of the
Selection Committee of the Appointments and
Training Branch of the Ministry of Labour.
Since the local Employment Committees and
Roll Committees were set up the matter has
been working satisfactorily, and the Ministry
of Labour has been able to bring the Roll
under the notice of employers.
The number of firms enrolled has increased
from 100 or 200 to 900. Unfortunately, while
that is true, it is also quite true that the
numbers of disabled ex-Servicemen now unemployed are considerably greater than years
ago. I understand that throughout the North
of Ireland we have some 1,800 or 1,900 disabled
ex-Servicemen, and of that number 1,200 or
1,300 are in the city of Belfast. I think,
seeing that it is seven years and more since
the Armistice, it is really necessary that
there should be some benefit shown to firms
to induce them to employ a certain percentage of disabled ex-Servicemen. The giving of
contracts should be considerably tightened.
They should only be given to firms on the
National Roll, and I hope the Government
will see their way to accept this Resolution
proposed by the hon. Member for West
Belfast (Colonel Woods).
There
Mr. POLLOCK: Some two years ago a
Motion in character exactly similar was introduced by a Member in this House and a
very exhaustive discussion ensued.
was no difference of opinion whatever between the Government and those Members
who discussed the question then, nor do I
apprehend is there any difference of opinion
at this moment. The whole object of the
Resolution is intended to ensure that all
contracts will be given to those firms on the
King's Roll. I am here to say to-day that
the Resolution as then passed by the House
and which has been in operation for that
time has been most fruitful in its results.
I will read the Resolution which was then
passed by this House unanimously:-
Government Contracts HOUSE OF COMMONS. Employment of Ex-Servicemen. 164
[Mr. Pollock]
That in the opinion of this House all
contracts made by the Government Departments, and for the services of all local
authorities should give preference all
other things being equal to firms on the
King's National Roll of Honour.
As I understand the Resolution which has
been proposed by the hon. and gallant
Member (Col. Woods) the only difference
between it and that which I have just read
is the omission of the words, "All other
things being equal."
Now let me discuss for a few minutes if
I may the results that have ensued from
that Resolution which I have read.
Incidentally, I had almost a feeling of resentment as I listened to my hon, and gallant
Friend (Major Shillington) who hoped that
the work of giving contracts would be
tightened up, because that rather implies the
suggestion that there has not been that
particularity in regard to the issue of contracts that should have existed. Therefore,
I say that I felt something in the nature
of resentment, if I may say so without any
disrespect to the hon. and gallant Member,
that there should have been such a suspicion
in his mind or in that of any Member of the
House.
Preference is always given in the giving of
contracts to those firms who are on the King's
Roll--I wish to state that most emphatically
--unless there are some circumstances which
call for adopting a different course, and
when I proceed for a few minutes with the
figures that I propose to submit to the House
I think it will be agreed that it was very
seldom that any such qualification had to be
introduced. When this subject was discussed
I gave an instance of a type of contract
which was of such an exceptional character
that the custom had to be departed from,
and it is because that things will happen,
that circumstances will result at times, all
absolutely rigid rules cannot be adhered to.
The instance I gave then may well be repeated because it is so typical of something
that may possibly arise that hon. Members
should be fully seized of the nature of it.
It was a case where ex-Servicemen's
houses were being built in Londonderry.
Tenders were taken out with the object of
proceeding with that work. It was found
that there were tenders from those who were
on the King's Roll and one tender from a
firm who were outside that category, but the
difference between the two lowest-the one
firm on the King's Roll and the other outside the King's Roll-was so great that it
enabled 13 additional ex-Servicemen's houses
to be built. Would any Member of this
House suggest for a moment that the rules
which we have laid down in cases like that
should be adhered to. It is very seldom that
cases like that turn up, but there are instances where there are exceptional circumstances, and these exceptional circumstances
are provided for in the British Resolution.
The wording in the British Resolution is
"Except under exceptional circumstances."
Our wording is "all other things being
equal." I cannot myself see that there is
any great difference between the two,
and I think that my hon. Friend (Major
Shillington) is meticulously careful particularly in view of the exceptionally successful working of the Resolution which was
passed by this House two years ago.
If we take an analysis of the contracts
of over £500 in value which were entered
into by the Ministry of Finance from the
beginning of the year 1924 to August 1925,
out of a total of £159,000 of money value
in contracts approximately £135,000 were
given to firms on the King's Roll. The
balance of £24,000 arose from circumstances
of such an exceptional character that it was
not possible to adhere to the principle which
I have outlined. My hon. Friend (Major
Shillington) has dealt with the increase in
the numbers of those firms who are on the
King's Roll, and who have come under the
aegis of the King's Roll, and he has endeavoured to explain that the operation of the
Resolution passed has not been successful,
because there is a greater number of unemployed to-day than there was two years ago.
In 1922 there were 105 on the King's Roll;
in 1924 when that Resolution was passed
to which I have referred, there were 573, and
to-day there are 943 firms in Northern
Ireland enrolled in that category.
The inference I draw from that is that the
rigidity of the application of the Resolution
passed by this House is so great that manufacturers, merchants, and others have found
it absolutely necessary to come within the
ambit of the King's Roll in order that they
may get any contracts. I think that the
figures which I have now given afford the
most irrefragable evidence of the effect of
the Resolution that was passed. As I said,
I am not very particular as to the exact
language that is used-whether it should be
in the wording of the English Resolution
or in our language. I am not at all
particular, because the object in view is the
same. It would require a very careful
analysis to see any difference in the phraseology. Therefore, if it is the wish of the
House that the wording on the English
Resolution should be adopted I have not the
slightest objection.
It will have the same result in the end.
It will not help to get any further tenderers

Mr. SPEAKER: We must first dispose of

Sir ROBERT ANDERSON: Then I am in
order in speaking to the Motion and Amendment at present before the House. What I
feel about this Motion, and what I think will
be felt by every other Member of the House,
is that as far as possible in the case of
Government Departments, local authorities
and private firms preference should be given
to those on the King's National Roll of
Honour, and in this way they should help
those who have helped their country so much.
But I would like to point out the real danger
there is in accepting a Motion such as has
been proposed by the hon. and gallant
Member for West Belfast. To leave it without a saving clause is extremely dangerous.
You simply compel the Government in their
contracts to accept a tender notwithstanding
what the price may be, and if there is a
margin of hundreds of pounds I hardly think
a Government would be acting in harmony
with the wishes of the House in paying that
money, because there is danger of certain
things being done in connection with contracts and matters being left open to abuse.
an
Then the moment the Government
accepted the principle laid down by the hon.
and gallant Member for West Belfast they
must allow all the local authorities to do
the same thing. In that way, I am afraid,
it would open up the way to certain abuses
that might take place in regard to the fixing
up of contracts which would not be in the

give preference to certain firms and certain

Seeing the Resolution adopted by the House
two years ago has worked in such
eminently satisfactory way it ought to be
allowed to continue. With the saving clause,
"all other things being equal," I see no

British Resolution, but if it is more in

in the Imperial House then I am at one with

should be inserted that would prevent abuses

Mr. KYLE: I rise to support this
Motion proposed by the hon. and gallant
Member for West Belfast (Colonel Woods)
in its entirety. I have listened to the argument submitted by the hon. Member for
Derry (Sir Robert Anderson) with amazement, because what he is doing now is, he is
actually indicting his fellow employers and
particularly those employers who have
joined up in the King's National Roll of
Honour, that is to say, those who employ a
certain percentage of employees who are ex-
Servicemen. What the hon. Member for
Derry is saying is that these men will employ
a few ex-Servicemen, or a sufficient percentage to enable them to get on the King's
National Roll of Honour, and then they will
defraud the Government by putting in extortionate figures. We on these Benches up
to now have not made such a wild, and I
would like to say unfounded, charge against
employers, speaking in general, as the hon.
Member for Derry has just done. The hon.
and gallant Member (Major Shillington) who
seconded the Motion has stated, and stated
quite truthfully, that the number of unemployed ex-Servicemen in Belfast is between
1,200 and 1,300. I think it is a disgrace to
the employers of the City of Belfast that
1,200 ex-Servicemen--
Major SHILLINGTON: Disabled.
Mr. KYLE-disabled ex-Servicemen have
not found employment, particularly in view
of the fact that hon. and right hon. Gentlemen opposite during the period from 1914 to
1918 made promises to these men such as,
"A grateful country will never forget you."
That being the case, it seems to me they
are doing their best to forget them to-day
to the extent that there are so many idle in
Belfast and a larger number in the Six
Counties. It is a desirable thing that employers who have not done this thing
voluntarily should be compelled to do it. I
take it that is the purpose of the Motion
that has been put down by the hon. and
gallant Member for West Belfast, and as
such I will support it in its entirety..
One can understand the arguments that
might be put up by the right hon. Gentleman, the Minister of Finance, and one can
understand, of course, how Governments
always want to have saving clauses. They
want to protect themselves against every
possible eventuality, but in protecting themselves they are leaving themselves open to the
charge I am making against them this afternoon of making it easy for employers to
forget their promises to the ex-Servicemen.
I happen to be in the position that I have
never made a promise to ex-Servicemen, and
either here or in another place I have always
tried to compel people who did make
promises to keep them. We are perfectly
justified this afternoon in making it as difficult as we possibly can for the Government
to refuse to do justice to the disabled ex-
Servicemen. For these reasons I will support
the Motion.
Mr. THOMAS HENDERSON: I rise to

Woods). I think it would be a regrettable

This is a Motion which should be accepted

Mr. GYLE: I support the Motion proposed

Sir DAWSON BATES: When the debate
was suspended I was giving the reasons that
led the Government to refuse to accede to
the request of certain of the local authorities that the maximum should be increased.
I think it is well to point out in this connection that during the last month the Belfast Corporation arrived at the conclusion
that it would be desirable in connection with
their future housing schemes to embark on
a somewhat smaller and cheaper house than
those hitherto erected, in order to meet the
requirements of the comparatively poorly
paid workers.
I have already had a conference with the
representatives of the Corporation with a
view to arriving at an arrangement which
would involve the erecting of a certain
number of houses with a minimum of 550
superficial feet. Since that time I have
observed a good deal of unfounded criticism
in regard to the erection of this type of house.
It has been suggested, if one can believe all
one sees, that the Government's policy really
is to create slums instead of do away with
them. I emphatically deny that. What we
aim at is a cheap, self-contained, well-built,
and healthy house even though it may be
small.

Sir DAWSON BATES: Yes, two bedrooms.
I hope the House will pass this Measure so

Mr. KYLE: One would have liked to have
been able to welcome this Measure.
Personally and for my party we would have
done so had it not been for the concluding

Dawson Bates) when he stated that he is
prepared apparently to give this subsidy of
£80 per house for the erection of houses of
550 superficial feet with only two bedrooms
and no bath. Surely it has come to a pretty
pass when the Government of Northern Ireland are prepared to grant a subsidy of £80
for the erection of buildings which are not
any better, which are not any larger, which
have no more accommodation than the
houses that were erected in Belfast in 1898
or thereabouts. I stated the other day that
we are going to go back a generation practically if we permit these houses to be erected
in Belfast. It is all very well for the right
hon. Gentleman (Sir Dawson Bates) to say it
is in order that these houses can be let at a
rent which the workman can pay. We have
pointed out time after time that the way
the workman can pay is not by reducing the
rent for the house but by giving him decent

wages, and obviously that is a much fairer

I am sure there is not in Belfast or out of
it a public man, or a party, or any people
who are interested at all in housing but will
condemn the proposal to erect these small
houses. I had thought we had got to a
higher standard. I had thought that the
Government had realised that it was the
proper thing that the working classes should
be housed in better houses than they were a

the Minister of Home Affairs does not think
fit to reconsider the decision at which he has
apparently arrived, that is to grant a subsidy of £80 a house to houses of the nature
which the Belfast Corporation are talking
about building-and I did not catch in its
entirety his remark as to whether or not he
had determined to give this subsidy of £80
per house to the Belfast Corporation for
these buildings that they propose to put up.
I call them buildings for you could not call
them houses. There are several associations
of women who are interested in housing in
Belfast. There is one-the Women's Advisory Council-which I understand is not a
party organisation. I think the Minister of
Labour (Mr. Andrews) addressed a meeting
of it one day, so that if that is the case it is
hardly to be looked upon as a blood red
revolutionary party. They have, I understand, condemned in no uncertain measure,
the proposal which the Belfast Corporation
has before it to erect these houses.
The right hon. Gentleman (Sir Dawson
Bates) might have said that he hoped or
believed that in another year we are going
to have a sufficiency of houses, that the
housing grant will be no longer given after
this year for which he proposes to extend
the Housing Act. We know quite well, and
he knows quite well, that next year he will
be met again with the request to extend
these Housing Acts for a further period, to
extend the subsidy for a further period, because he knows as well as the head is on
his body that it is not possible to get all the
houses that are required built inside one
year. Further than that, it should be the
Government's aim, when the Corporation of
Belfast has failed to house adequately the
people of Belfast, to be responsible as a
Government for the erection of houses. We
have a precedent for that, and Conservatives
always dearly love a precedent. We want
them to accept the precedent of the Conservative Government on the other side,
namely, to build the houses themselves, so
that the people may be housed in a more
adequate way than they have been housed
hitherto.
Sir DAWSON BATES: May I interrupt

Mr. T. W. McMULLAN: I had not the
advantage of seeing this chart to which the
right hon. Gentleman (Sir Dawson Bates)
has drawn attention, but I congratulate
him on the statistics he has been able to
give us this afternoon as to the great success
which has attended the administration of
the Housing Act. I see, however, that there
has been a difficulty, a real obstacle to the
full success of this Act in the fact that the
houses do not, in every case, go into the
occupation of the men for whom they are
intended. Artisans do not get these
houses. The difficulty has arisen from the
fact that houses to rent are not obtainable.
If a man owns a house to-day, or builds a
house to-day he wants to sell it, and people
of limited means, who cannot afford to buy,
scramble for these subsidised houses, and the
artisan is met by keen competition from
quite a number of classes of people in our
community. Even civil servants have been
known to occupy houses which are built for
artisans, and people of limited means in
every direction are keenly fighting to get
nominated-for it comes to nomination-for
the occupation of one of these subsidised
houses.
I think that beyond that suggestion which
the Minister has turned down--for very
adequate reasons I am sure as he sees them
-that the limit should be increased beyond
950 feet, say up to 1,200 feet. I have the
feeling that if houses could be built with an
accommodation of 1,200 superficial feet the
class which is competing for workmen's
houses would automatically be taken away
from that competition, and be able to
occupy this other class of house. I have
talked this matter over with the surveyor
for a local authority, and he tells me that
a house of 1,200 feet could be built for about
£750, and that it could be let at a rent of,
say, £45 a year. If such houses could be
produced and be let-not sold, but let-at a
rent of £45 a year by public authorities it
would really help in the end the working
men very greatly, because it would take
away this competition for workingmen's
houses which at present exists. Of course,
I quite see the arguments against it. It is
a big question, but it might be worth the
reconsideration of the Government.
Another point that occurred to me was
that this is Government money, this is taxpayers' money, which goes into the subsidising of these houses. I am told that a great
deal of the material used in the houses
which are built under these subsidies is not
home production. I am told that French
slates, French cement, and many other
things are introduced in these building contracts. They may not be in the houses that
are built by public authorities, but they
certainly are in a great many houses that
are built by private enterprise. I think the
Government should have the power, seeing
that they are giving away the taxpayers'
money, to have inserted in the contracts a
proviso that British manufactured goods
should be used in the entire construction of
these houses.
I thought I would like to say a few words
on the Housing Acts. I know my own constituents in Bangor, County Down, would
like to see the 1,200 superficial feet introduced into the Act, and, looking at it with
whatever intelligence I have got, I can see
a great deal of reason for the raising of that
limit, in taking away the keen competition
which exists at present for those houses
which are supposed to be built for working
men, but which are practically open to
competition amongst all classes of the
community.
Mr. THOMAS HENDERSON: I am
pleased to know that the Government is

I was strongly opposed in the Belfast
Corporation to the introduction once again

were twenty-one. How in the name of goodness could you accommodate a family like

you that there are families of labouring

There are labouring people with nine, ten,
and thirteen of a family.

Sir DAWSON BATES: These houses are

As one who has worked in the shipyard, I

There is one other matter in which I think
the Minister of Home Affairs is to blame.
Quite recently we had a housing scandal in

that this scandal was going on?

means that
who lives
a working man
there, and who works in the centre

You have heard of the cost of these houses,

thing of
kind will be done to
improve the conditions under which

Mr. DEVLIN: I cannot quite follow the
point of the observations of the hon. Member
(Mrs. Chichester) who has just sat down.
She was rather critical of the protest made
by the hon. Member (Mr. Wm, McMullen)
who objected to this matter of compelling
working people to live in two-roomed
houses.
Mrs. CHICHESTER : I did not question it.
Mr. DEVLIN: She did not tell us whether
that was an admirable housing condition or
not. She stated that she spoke on behalf of
rural Ireland. The hon. Member (Mrs.
Chichester) must know that if there is one
section of the community more than another
that ought to value decent housing conditions it is the people who live in rural
Ireland. I myself am very proud to belong
to a party which forced a Labourers'
Housing Act through Parliament-an Act
which was responsible for the creation of
some 60,000 labourers' cottages. It seems a
curious reflection, but I remember that that
Act was passed in spite of the protest and
votes of those who support the hon. Lady
(Mrs. Chichester) in this House. Then as
now those who constitute what I call the
reactionary classes in this country, thought
any place good enough for the working
classes to live in, but, fortunately, the social
conscience of the toiling masses of the people
has been so roused that they are not prepared to accept with the placidity of the
hon. Member the conditions that previously
prevailed.
In my judgment next to the question of
unemployment the most pressing of all problems and the most human of all problems is
the question of housing. (Hon. Members:
Hear, hear.) A proper adjustment of our
housing question means the adjustment of
countless other questions-health, comfort,
ease of mind. All these things are dependent upon the occupation of decent
sanitary dwellings for the workers, and
when we consider that people spend about
three-fourths of their lives in their homes it
is vital that these homes should be made as
attractive as possible for those who inhabit
them. What sort of life do you expect
people to live who occupy a house with two
bedrooms and a kitchen? My hon. Friend
(Mr. William McMullen) referred to some of
the houses he has seen in the ward which he
represents, and which constituted for many
years part of my constituency. I was round
those districts, and I went into some of these
houses. I found that it is almost impossible
for an ordinary adult to crush himself into
the bedrooms of these houses-and these are
Corporation houses built before the war.
They were most discreditable, and now instead of trying to improve these conditions
you are going to spend public money in perpetuation of these evils. That is what you
are doing.
For my own part I would not give a farthing of a subsidy to any builder unless a
builder who is erecting decent healthy houses
at a rent which the people can pay. We
know ourselves that most of the houses being
built now are, as the hon. Member for Down
has said, mostly built not for the class
whom the State intended the houses for, but
are built for what is known as the better
class. Nearly all these houses for which
subsidies have been granted are houses
which we know are not for letting but for
sale. You are actually subsidising commercial enterprise. You are giving people
Government money to make money out of it
for themselves. That is what you are really
doing. It was never intended by those who
approved the subsidy for houses that that
class should benefit by that step. It was intended, as I understand it, that since
economic conditions made it impossible to
build houses at rents which the people could
pay that the subsidy would be given to
enable them to let houses to the working
classes at rents which they could pay. That,
I think, is in the minds of many hon. Members. I wonder is it in the minds of the
Government? Was that the Government's
intention? Or is it a general proposition
that you are to give subsidies to everybody
who builds houses? If that is so it is opposed
to all sound economics.
I am sure no one is prouder than the hon.
Member for Derry (Mrs. Chichester) to see
labourers' cottages scattered all over the
Province and all over Ireland, but let me
point out to the House that the same spirit
of mentality prevails here as prevailed in
the days when these labourers' cottages were
being built. I remember-and I do not
think the right hon. Gentleman, the Prime
Minister can contradict me-that a certain
proportion of the funds for building these
cottages was given to the whole of Ireland, and the Unionist and the Tory
Councils in Ulster would not use the
money. It was used in the South of Ireland
with the result that they had a larger proportion of houses in the South than you have
in Northern Ireland, and that was simply
because you have a strange mentality, as I
said before. You cannot understand why
there should be an uplifting ambition
amongst the working classes to live a cleaner
and healthier life.

The MINISTER OF COMMERCE (Mr.
Barbour): Hon. Members will see that the
net amount of this Estimate is £32,185, and
is made up of the items amounting to
£33,315 included under the first five Subheads which hon. Members will see on page
3 of the little pamphlet of Supplementary
Estimates less the Section 2 Receipts of
£1,130 which are brought to account under
Sub-head S.-Receipts Appropriated in Aid.
The gross expenditure provided in Section 3
represents additional services carried out on
repayment terms on behalf of Northern
Ireland Departments and this sum, namely,
£5,980, is off-set by receipts which are paid
in from the various Departmental Votes.
sum
Dealing with Section 1, there is provided
a sum of £29,500, which represents expenditure incurred this year over and above the
work
originally provided for
at
Stormont. This points to a welcome acceleration in the carrying out of the works.
I should remind hon. Members that, al-.
though under the accounting arrangements
which govern the service it is necessary for
this money to be voted by the Parliament
of Northern Ireland in the first instance,
recoupment is subsequently effected from the
Imperial Government under whose control
the works are being carried out, but under
the procedure prescribed by the Act recoupment is not made directly through this Vote
but payment is made direct to the Exchequer
of Northern Ireland.
Turning to Section 2, the first item of
£700 will interest hon. Members as this provides for the expenses of surveying the River
Bann in connection with the drainage investigation. The actual work of survey has
now been completed, and it is hoped that the
Report of the engineers will be in the hands
of the Government in the course of a very
few days. The second item provides for
payment of rates for Hillsborough Castle,
which is a liability of the Northern Government. The Imperial Government undertook
the purchase and initial renovation expenses
in consideration of the Government
Northern Ireland assuming liability for
maintenance, and of course the Government
of Northern Ireland is liable for the rates.
of
The third item of £1,100 for insurance
represents, as explained in the note, arrears
of premiums payable in respect of the year
1924-25.
Section 3 provides for three new services.
The purchase of Hampton House is for use as
a Men's Hostel in connection with the Stranmillis Training College Scheme. When the
Supplementary Estimates. 214
Supply-
16 MARCH 1926
original estimate for the current year was
presented, a sum was provided for the erection of a new hostel, but it is now proposed
to adopt Hampton House for this purpose on
grounds of economy. The building will provide living accommodation, it is estimated,
for a maximum of 80 students. Their instruction will, of course, be carried out at
the Training College itself. The temporary
hostel at present in existence is a hired
building and only accommodates a portion of
the male students, the remaining living in
lodgings or their homes. It will be given
up as soon as the adaptation of the new building has been completed. This charge of
£4,850 will be finally met from what we know
as the Colwyn or Imperial grant of £400,000.
Subhead "N" provides for two new services: An unemployment relief scheme at
Ardglass Harbour, which contemplates the
reclamation of a plot of ground to be subsequently leased to herring curers. This estimate provides merely for the cost of the
requisite material, and provision for wages,
estimated at £420, in connecton with the
work has been included in the Supplementary Estimate for Harbour and Commercial Services. The total cost of this reclamation, therefore, amounts to £840.
As regards the additional laboratory at
Stormont, this is for veterinary research,
and hon. Members will see that a token
vote of £10 only is asked for in this connection. It is in order that Parliamentary
approval may be given for this work, the
expenditure on which will not mature for
payment until the coming financial year.
The necessity for the laboratory arises from
the transfer as from 1st April next to
Northern Ireland of the veterinary services
formerly carried out as a Council of Ireland
Service by an Imperial Department. The
work has so far been carried out in a
laboratory in Queen's University, but it is
considered desirable that the entire work of
animal research should be concentrated at
Stormont now that the Northern Government will shortly have control over the entire field of operations and a small laboratory
at present exists at Stormont.
The next three items in Subheads P, Q,
and R provide for works expenditure in
consequence of the taking of the census.
The items included in the credit Subhead
are self-explanatory and require no further

House to rise-to have all these very important matters raised here. It is an extraordinary thing that when a very disagreeable
duty of this sort has to be performed it is
always given to the right hon. Gentleman
(Mr. Barbour).
The CHAIRMAN:
I am sure the hon.
Member (Mr. Devlin) will realise that I have
no control over that.
Mr. DEVLIN: I am not questioning your
conduct. It only shows the shrewdness of
the Government that when they have a very
disagreeable job they always put up the
right hon. Gentleman (Mr. Barbour), who
smiles us all away. (Laughter). As I say
I object altogether. I object on principle
and as a method of procedure to this method
of dealing with these sums of money. After
all, although the amounts are comparatively
small, the Committee ought to be given a
full opportunity of discussing them at a
normal Parliamentary time. It is not that
we have not time to do it. This Parliament
only meets about three months in the year
and there ought to be adequate time given,
especially now that there is such a cry for
economy. I read in the Unionist Press that
the extravagance and the lack of economy
that are shown by the Government is one of
the most indefensible transactions of which
the Government are guilty. If that is the
view held by the Government organs surely
they ought not to plav into the hands of
their enemies by trying to sneak these things
through Parliament at a time when we are
tired and the followers of the Government
are somnolent. These things ought not to
be introduced under these circumstances.
I want first of all to ask what is the meaning of this item of £29,500 for Stormont, for
new works, alterations, and additions. I was
told repeatedly-at least as far as I could
drag it from right hon. Gentlemen opposite
-that we have nothing whatever to do with
the Government Buildings at Stormont.
Mr. POLLOCK: That is so.
Mr. DEVLIN: Then what is this Vote
down here for?
Mr. POLLOCK: That is the agency for
paying the money.
Mr. DEVLIN: But have you no arrangement whereby the British Government pays
for this without it being put here? Are we
merely voting as agents for something for
which we are not responsible? Who ever
heard of a Vote being put down for an estimated sum not to pay what was due but for
what was due back to ourselves by somebody
else? I must say I shall go to a division on
this question. I am very anxious to hear
where we really stand in relation to these
Parliamentary buildings, what is to be the
cost of them, who is going to pay for them,
and what are the terms and conditions under
which they are being erected at Stormont.
It is a very big question. As I have said
I am fundamentally opposed to the whole
transaction. No one could defend the building of a Parliament House five miles away
from the city, and what is still worse the
building of Government offices five miles
away from the city where it would be impossible for business people to do their business if they have to go out to No Man's Land
to do it.
The Prime Minister was, no doubt, very
amusing the other day. Of course it would
take well with his supine followers, but his
explanation did not affect me in the least
degree. He said "Look what they are doing
in Australia." I forget the place where they
are building, but it is a long way from any
centre of population. What is really the
fact? That this is a Federal Parliament
they are building out in Australia. There
are four State Parliaments and there is a
Federal Parliament, and the real reason
why this Federal Parliament House is being
built is this-because I know Australia well,
and I remember following the controversy
that took place in regard to the new capital
-that, Melbourne being jealous of Sydney
and Sydney jealous of Melbourne, neither of
the two would consent to the other being
made the capital, and, therefore, they decided to build the Federal Parliament House
in some neutral place. There is no analogy
whatever between this case and the case of
Northern Ireland. This Parliament covers
an area almost as small as a county in
Australia, and yet we are building a Parliament House away out five miles from the
city, a most unbusiness-like transaction from
a purely business point of view and a most
inconvenient arrangement from a Parliamentary point of view.
This House has never been consulted about
it. We have never been told how far this
enterprise has developed, or who is building,
or what it is going to cost, or who is responsible for it. The first opportunity we
have for securing information is when
quietly, now fifteen minutes after the normal
time for the adjournment, we get this paper
with £29,500 placed upon it. 1 will take a
division upon that, first of all as a protest
against it being raised here at all at this
stage of our proceedings, and, secondly,
against the Government having deliberately
refused to give us any information upon this
point.

CLASS V. No. 2.
AGRICULTURAL SERVICES.
Motion made, and Question proposed:
"That a supplementary sum not exceeding
£10 be granted to His Majesty for the services
of the year ending 31st March, 1926, to defray
the expenses of the Ministry of Agriculture
in respect of Agricultural Education and Research, Improvement of Live Stock, Agricultural Development, Agricultural Statistics
and Afforestation, including sundry Grants
in Aid and certain capital expenditure under
14 and 15 Geo. V., c. 13, s. 1 (N.I.)."
The MINISTER OF AGRICULTURE (Mr.
Archdale): This Supplementary Estimate is
to bring to the notice of Parliament certain
sums which could not have been foreseen
when the 1925-26 Estimates were introduced.
We have been able to find the amount required from savings on our main Estimate,
so that the Supplementary Estimate simply
provides for a token figure of £10. A1 refers
to Agricultural Research and Faculty of
Agriculture. As mentioned by the Minister
of Commerce (Mr. Barbour), we found it
necessary since we have to take over the administration of veterinary diseases on the
1st April, to erect a laboratory at Stormont.
We have one there already, but we want
this new one so that we can carry on necessary post-mortem work, and deal with milk
samples submitted in connection with the
Bovine Tuberculosis Order.
The next item is Agricultural Education.
Following on the provisions of the Education
Act a Superannuation Scheme has been
framed, applicable to agricultural teachers
in Northern Ireland. Under this scheme
contributions to the Technical Teachers'
Superannuation Fund, Northern Ireland, are
to be made by the employers of agricultural
teachers. The next item is the building
grant to the Royal Ulster Agricultural
Society. For the last number of years the
Royal Ulster Agricultural Society has given
us a large space in the Londonderry Hall at
Balmoral in order to show the Ministry's
exhibit. They did not charge any rent for
it, and they were most helpful to us. Owing,
however, to the increasing exhibits in cattle,
poultry, etc., they find it is impossible for
us to continue exhibiting in that hall. They
have, therefore, arranged to erect a building
on a prominent site in their grounds for
our exhibits. It has been found that nothing
so much interests the farmers at these shows
as the Ministry's exhibit. They have been
crowded from morning till night. We have
found also in the Ministry that there is
nothing better to educate the farmers than
this exhibit, where they can see the effect
of all research work before their eyes.
As I have said, the society is erecting a
large shed for our permanent use. It will
cost about £5,000. We will pay £2,000
towards it, as the society's finances would
not enable them to pay the whole cost. We
think it will prove a tremendous benefit to
those engaged in farming to have this big
shed at Balmoral for continual use, and I
think it is very generous of the Royal Ulster
Society to pay their large proportion (£3,000)
as they have arranged to do. (Hon. Members:
Hear, hear.)
As to G2 (Seed Supply Schemes), the first
two items, A1 and A2, were before the
Committee last year, and were agreed to. As
there are two new schemes adopted (B1 and
B2), we thought it advisable to bring them
here, so that the Committee would know
exactly how much money was spent on these
subjects. Owing to a big outbreak of black
scab amongst potatoes in the Londonderry
area a considerable area had to be scheduled.
The farmers had been in the habit of growing non-immune varieties of potatoes for the
Belfast and Dublin markets. On the scheduling of the district the sale of these
varieties was immediately stopped. Owing to
the low prices obtained for what they did
grow, their sale in the ordinary market being
stopped, we provided a considerable quantity
of immune seed, which we wanted to get
grown in these districts, and sold it to them
at the price of their own seed. That involved
a loss of £3 10s per ton to provide the
farmers in that scheduled area with immune

varieties, which they had not been able to
get before. They only grew skerries before,
and they were in great demand in Belfast
and Dublin.
B (2) refers to the great want there is
in the country for a white immune potato
to replace the varieties that have been grown

figures are only up to 31st March, and in

original Estimates-that is the technical

The PARLIAMENTARY SECRETARY OF
THE MINISTRY OF EDUCATION (Mr.
Robb): The Committee will find details of
this Estimate on page 11 of the Supplementary Estimates. It arises in this way:
Although the sums already voted by Parliament for Educational Services in the current
financial year will be sufficient to cover all
expenditure which will become chargeable to
that year, it is considered necessary to present this " token" Supplementary Estimate
in order that the specific authority of Parliament may be obtained for certain payments
for which no express provision was made in

have the money in hands, but we have not
got Parliamentary authority to pay it out.
The first item is the provision of Hampton
House. That, of course, has been bought by
the Government for the purpose of a men's
hostel in connection with the Training
College at Stranmillis. The present hostel
for men students-a rented house at Royal
Terrace has accommodation for only 27
students, with the result that 45 students
are obliged to live either at home or in
lodgings; those not provided with hostel
accommodation receiving an allowance in lieu
of board and lodging. This arrangement is
not satisfactory, and it is very desirable
that all the men students should live in the
hostel.
The other two items are contributions to
be paid by the State to two.teachers' pensions
funds-one for secondary and the other for
technical teachers. The statutory orders
under which those payments fall to be made
come into operation at 1st April this year,
so that those two sums could not be provided
for in the original Estimate. The orders
have not come into operation during the year,
and these are sums which under those orders
will receive sanction during the current
financial year. I beg to move.

Motion made and Question proposed:
That it is expedient to amend the Loans
Guarantee Acts (Northern Ireland), 1922-
1925-
I. By increasing from six million pounds to
seven million pounds the limit on the aggregate capital amount of the loans, the prinpal or interest of which may be guaranteed
by the Ministry of Finance thereunder; and
by extending to the 31st day of March, 1927,
the period within which guarantees may
Loans Guarantee-
Committee.
16 MARCH 1926
be given under the Loans Guarantee Act
(Northern Ireland), 1922; and to charge on
the Consolidated Fund of Northern Ireland
any moneys required for fulfilling any such
guarantees.
II. By authorising the Ministry of
Finance, in any case where the principal or
interest of a loan has been guaranteed by
the said Ministry to pay an amount not exceeding one-tenth of the interest payable in
respect of so much of the loan as is proposed
to be raised for expenditure in Northern
Ireland, or, alternatively to pay a capital
sum, not in excess of the value of such
interest payment; and to charge on moneys
provided by Parliament any sums required
for the said purpose. (Governor's Recommendation signified)-(Mr. Pollock.)
Mr. POLLOCK: This Money Resolution
which I am now about to submit to the
Committee is the foundation of a Bill which
will be presented in due course, probably in
a day or two. As the Committee is no doubt
aware, Parliamentary sanction was given up
to a limit of £6,000,000, empowering the
Ministry of Finance to guarantee certain
sums on behalf of those who undertook to
make capital expenditure in Northern Ireland.
Up to the present, of that £6,000,000
we have exhausted a sum of something over
£4,000,000, leaving approximately a balance
of £2,000,000 unexhausted. For reasons I
will explain in a minute or two I think it is
necessary we should come to ask for an additional £1,000,000 in order that the money at
our disposal, or rather that the guarantees
which will be at our disposal, will amount
to a sum of £3,000,000.
In asking the Committee to increase the
existing margin to £3,000,000 the Government
have taken into account the possibility of a
greater demand on the part of ship-owning
interests for tonnage during the coming year.
I am in hopes that that expectation will be
realised, and there are indications at the
present time that ship-owners are beginning
more and more to discover the necessity for
keeping pace with modern development in
regard to shipbuilding. For this reason 1
feel that it is necessary we should have this
amount of £3,000,000 to enable us to guaran,
tee up to that extent should the necessity
arise. Undoubtedly, the provision of these
guarantees has had a very substantial bearing upon the provision of labour in Northern
Ireland. At the present moment there are
something like 8,000 men who are employed
in work being carried on under these guarantees, and I think I am not going too far in
stating that the probability is that if such
Government encouragement had not been in
existence a number of these men would to.
day be unemployed.
The second part of the Resolution which
appears on the Paper deals with a different
department of the same subject. Up to the
present, as I have informed the Committee,
we have guaranteed ship-owners and shipbuilders up to approximately £4,000,000.
This money has been advanced by lenders
of various kinds, bankers and others, at the
same rate as the British Government's Guarantees, working under the Trades Facilities
Act, have been able to secure. But in case
some exceptional circumstances might arise
when the Government may find it necessary
to bridge any small difference that might
accrue by reason of the Northern Ireland
guarantee not being exactly of the same
standard as the British guarantee we think
it necessary that some provision of this kind
should be made.
Undoubtedly, British security stands at
the top of the world, and whether the
Northern Ireland security, good as we know
it to be, will be able to secure continuously
the same rate as the British Government
is something I am not prepared at the present moment to argue, because it may be
possible that owing to some exceptional
circumstances, where we may probably desire
to guarantee some operation, we might have
to pay some small trifle under the rate of
the British guarantee. The difference cannot
be very great, but I think it is right that
the Ministry of Finance should have the
power to negotiate on these lines if the
contingency should arise.
The Committee is fully aware of the present depression in shipbuilding, and of the
necessity that exists, especially in Northern
Ireland, to provide labour for those men,
who, unfortunately, are walking about the
streets through no fault of their own, and
it is because of this that I am asking the
Committee now to give the Ministry of
Finance the necessary authority to negotiate
under the conditions I have just outlined.
I beg to move.
Question put, and agreed to.
Resolution reported, and agreed to.
Bill ordered to be brought in by the

EX-SERVICEMEN IN CIVIL SERVICE.
2. Colonel WOODS asked the Minister of
Finance whether he contemplates allowing
temporary civil servants to qualify by
examination for permanent positions in the
Civil Service as has been done in Great
Britain.
Mr. POLLOCK: The position in regard
to the employment of ex-Servicemen in the
Northern Ireland
Civil Service in
is
materially different from that which exists
in Great Britain. On the constitution of
our various Departments a large number
of ex-Servicemen were employed as temporary clerks, and approximately 65 per
cent. of the clerical appointments made
have been filled by ex-Servicemen, who were
admitted to established posts without
examination. The treatment accorded to
ex-Servicemen in the Northern Ireland
Civil Service will bear favourable comparison with that extended to them in the
Imperial Civil Service, and, indeed, it is
believed with any other Government
Service in the world.
Further, all temporary appointments of
a clerical and subordinate character are
reserved for qualified and suitable ex-
Service candidates, and it has been
arranged that a percentage of future
clerical vacancies in each Department will
be reserved for ex-Service temporary clerks.

6. Mr. WILLIAM MCMULLEN asked the
Minister of Home Affairs whether he is
aware that at a meeting of the Belfast City
and District Water Commissioners, held on
the 11th March, 1926, the Finance Committee
reported that during the month of February
2,481 streets were inspected; that it was
ascertained that 357 dwelling-houses were
vacant, and whether he would state if he
conceives it to be in the public interest to
have dwelling-houses vacant while so many
citizens urgently require houses, and what
steps he proposes to take to remedy this
state of affairs.
Sir DAWSON BATES: I am aware that
according to the report furnished to the
Finance Committee of the Belfast City and
District Water Commissioners on the date
in question 2,481 streets had been inspected
during the month of February by the Inspectors of the Commissioners, and that it
was ascertained that 357 dwelling-houses
were vacant at the time.
I also understand that from the corresponding report made to the Commissioners
in December last, the number of vacant
dwelling-houses was 400, while from the report made in July last the number was 475,
and also that the number in April last was
487.
It will thus be observed that according to
the official records of the Water Commissioners there has been a substantial decrease during the last year or so of the
number of vacant houses in the city.
Further, it should be borne in mind that
new houses are being completed in Belfast
at a rate of, approximately, 100 a month,
and it is only natural that in these cases
there may be some delay in the occupation
of them.
Accordingly, the circumstances do not
appear to me to warrant any action on the
part of the Government, even if it were
possible to take such action usefully.
