MONEY FOR ERECTION OF PARLIA-
MENT BUILDINGS.
9. Mr. DEVLIN asked the Prime Minister
whether he is prepared to appoint a deputation, consisting of representatives of all
parties in the House, to interview Mr.
Churchill, and ask him to consent to the
diversion of half the cost of the new Parliament buildings at Stormont Castle to the
erection of workers' houses in Belfast and
other parts of Northern Ireland, where the
shortage of dwellings is most acute.
The PRIME MINISTER (Sir James Craig):
No, Sir. The British Government have no
statutory power to divert any of the money
destined to the erection of Parliamentary
buildings. The Joint Exchequer Board only
approve of such a scale of expenditure as is
deemed necessary to meet the Imperial
statutory obligation under the Act of 1920 to
provide Northern Ireland with her Parliamentary and administrative buildings, together with the necessary equipment, and I
am satisfied that the expenditure proposed
has been reduced to the minimum. Further,
I would point out that the building of
houses is a matter primarily for local
authorities and private enterprise, to which,
however, this House is voting contributions
from time to time which compare favourably
with grants by the Imperial Government to
local authorities in Great Britain. The
British Government could not be reasonably
asked or expected to give an additional
grant towards housing in Northern Ireland
which they are not in a position to make
towards housing in Great Britain. In this
regard we are already assured under the
Colwyn Committee of sufficient money to
provide equal subsidies and to maintain
equal conditions with Great Britain.
man
Mr. DEVLIN: Does the right hon. Gentlenot think that, if a request of the
character indicated in my question were put
to the Chancellor of the Exchequer, Parlinment would sanction a change in the
arrangement so as to enable Parliament to
have a smaller House and the poor people
larger ones?
The PRIME MINISTER: As a matter of
fact, I do not think the House to be erected
at Stormont would be considered by anybody
as larger than is absolutely necessary for the
purposes for which it is intended.
CIVIL SERVICE. SIR R. SCOTT'S
INQUIRY.
10. Mr. DEVLIN asked the Prime Minister
the precise task which Sir Russell Scott has
been asked to undertake; whether he will
confine his investigation and inquiries to
inside Civil Service, or whether he will receive statements in writing or verbally from
members of the House; whether he will investigate the present method of appointment and promotion; and, further, whether
the Prime Minister will arrange with the
Minister of Finance to postpone the introduction of the full Estimates for the Civil
Services until such time as Sir Russell Scott
has reported.
Mr. POLLOCK: The Prime Minister has
asked me to answer this question, and I
think it best to inform the House of the
terms of reference which have been agreed
upon for Sir Russell Scott's inquiry. They
are as follows:-
"Taking into account the desirability of
maintaining in Northern Ireland the
traditions of the British Civil Service, but
making allowance for any difference in
conditions which may exist, to inquire into
the present establishment of the Civil Service in Northern Ireland, the standard of
remuneration, and the conditions of service; to report-
Oral Answers.
Oral Answers.
HOUSE OF COMMONS
[Mr. Pollock]
(a) whether the general organisation is
on sound lines;
(b) whether there is a redundancy of
staff;
(c) whether the standards of remuneration and conditions of service are
reasonable;
and to make recommendations."
The Government think it best to give Sir
Russell Scott the greatest possible latitude
in conducting his inquiry, so that it will be
left to him to decide what evidence he will
take and the procedure which he will adopt.
In regard to the last portion of the hon.
Member's question, it would not be possible
to postpone the introduction of the Estimates
until Sir Russell Scott has reported, but this
procedure will, in any case, cause no delay in
giving effect to any recommendations which
Sir Russell Scott may put forward. Members
will, therefore, have an opportunity, when
the Estimates are introduced, of making any
suggestions in regard to possible economies.
Mr. DEVLIN: Will the right hon. Gentleman answer that portion of the Question
which asks whether Sir Russell Scott will
investigate the present method of appointment and promotion? Will that be included
in the terms of reference?
Mr. POLLOCK: Yes, I presume that all
relevant circumstances connected with the
conditions of the Civil Service in Northern
Ireland will be taken into account. That is
contemplated.
Mr. DEVLIN: What form will this inquiry take? Will Sir Russell Scott sit and
receive evidence from outsiders?
Mr. POLLOCK: It is entirely within the
province of Sir Russell Scott to determine
the best method of arriving at what the
Government has in view. It is not for us to
dictate to him where he will sit or how he
will occupy his time. That is entirely a
matter of his own volition.
NEW ROADWAY AT STORMONT.
11. Mr. BEATTIE asked the Prime
Minister whether he can state the reason
for the delay in starting to make the new
roadway from the new Parliament House
to the main road,
Mr. POLLOCK: I propose to take this
Question. At the end of January last the
Joint Exchequer Board approved the proposal of the Northern Ireland Government
that the cost of construction of this road
should be met from Imperial Funds under
Section 34 of the Government of Ireland Act,
1920.
The necessary surveys were put in hand
forthwith and cross and longitudinal sections
prepared and transmitted to H.M. Office of
Works.
The Imperial Government gave an undertaking that advertisements for tenders would
be issued as soon as the specifications and
Bills of Quantities had been prepared, and
I anticipate that these advertisements will
be issued shortly.
Continual representations are being made
to the Imperial Government as to the necessity for an early commencement of the work,
which will give much needed employment
to many unskilled labourers.
Mr. BEATTIE: In view of the abnormal
distress that is being caused by unemployment and the simplicity of the work is the
Minister not prepared to proceed at once
with the making of this new roadway so as
to relieve the distress in the city?
Mr. POLLOCK: It is not within our
province to undertake this work, but constant pressure is being brought to bear on the
British authorities in regard to the matter.
It cannot be expedited any more than it is
being carried out at the present time.
ERECTION OF NEW PARLIAMENT
HOUSE.
12. Mr. BEATTIE asked the Prime
Minister whether he can state what date
building operations are going to commence on
the erection of Parliament House.
Mr. POLLOCK: I have been asked to
reply to this Question. The hon. Member
will no doubt recollect that the plans which
were originally decided upon for the new
Parliament and Departmental buildings at
Stormont were, for reasons of economy,
amended to a very considerable extent. This
has resulted in unavoidable delay, but work
under the foundations contract is approaching completion and a contract has already
been made for the supply and delivery on the
site of the stone and granite required to
bring the building to the first floor level.
The development of the drawings and details for the complete super-structure is
being proceeded with at present, and strong
representations have been made to the Office
of Works as to the necessity for pressing on
with the work with the utmost possible expedition.

MIDLAND RAILWAY-EXPELLED
WORKERS.
13. Mr. McMULLEN asked the Prime
Minister whether he is aware that a number
of men were expelled from their employment
in the Midland Railway during the recent
sectarian troubles in the city on account of
their religion, some of whom had given up
a life-time service to the Company, and had
almost qualified for pensions, and whether
now that we are enjoying uninterrupted
peace he will use his good offices to have
these men restored to their former positions.
The MINISTER OF LABOUR (Mr.
Andrews): I have been asked by my right
hon. Friend, the Prime Minister, to reply.
This is a matter, I am informed, which
was not brought about by any action of the
Company, and it can only be settled between
the Company and their employees; it is not
one in which the Government is in a position
to interfere.
I understand that the question is a particularly difficult one at the present time,
having regard to the regrettable retrenchments which the Company is forced to make
owing to the continuous fall in its receipts.
Mr. W. McMULLEN: I would like to inquire whether a move of this character
would not do more to promote peace throughout the Province than any number of
speeches from right hon. Gentlemen opposite?
Sir DAWSON BATES: It is expected that
the Report in question will be issued in the
course of the next few days.
Mr. W. McMULLEN: Would the right hon.
Gentleman be prepared to put a date-week
or month?
Sir DAWSON BATES: I have already said
the next few days.
Mr. W. McMULLEN: Your days are somewhat long. I want to find out the length of
them.
SCALE OF FAMILY INCOME.
15. Mr. BEATTIE asked the Minister of
Labour, in view of the abnormal distress
caused by the introduction of the Hardship
Rule on family income, whether he is prepared to reconsider the whole question, and
reduce the self-dependent age to 21 years.
Mr. ANDREWS: The direction by my
Department to Local Employment Committees on this subject is to the effect that
extended benefit will ordinarily be withheld
from single persons who are not more than
25 years of age if a Rota Committee is satisfied that there are relatives to whom the
claimant can reasonably look for support,
and that the family incomings are such that
hardship would not result if a grant of extended benefit were not made.
This direction is to the same effect as the
direction of the Imperial Ministry to Committees in Great Britain, and, having regard
to the Government's policy of parallel
administration, I cannot agree to alter it.
Mr. BEATTIE: As to the last part of the
answer, is the Minister prepared now to
appoint a Committee to reconsider the question of the scale of family income, and have
it on parallel lines with Great Britain?
Mr. ANDREWS: I am of opinion that the
scale of family income taken as a whole is
about in step with the scale in Great Britain.
If the hon. Member can produce evidence to
the contrary I am prepared to consider the
matter.
Mr. BEATTIE: In view of the evidence I
have produced, and as the cost of living is
ten points higher here than in Great Britain,
is the Minister still determined to keep the
family income at the starvation rate he has
now said?

ROMAN CATHOLIC EX-SERVICEMEN IN
ASSISTED SCHEMES.
19. Colonel WOODS asked the Minister of
Labour whether he can state what steps
have been, or are being, taken by the
Government to protect the interests of
Roman Catholic ex-Servicemen in Government assisted schemes, and to ensure that in
such schemes they will receive equal treatment to that given to Protestant ex-Servicemen, and also to increase the percentage of
all ex-Servicemen to be employed upon all
Government assisted schemes.
Mr. ANDREWS: I can assure the hon. and
gallant Member that steps are taken by the
Government to protect the interests of both
Protestant and Roman Catholic ex-Servicemen on Government assisted schemes. Outside Belfast preference is given to ex-Servicemen irrespective of their religion, and inside
Belfast, where employment is given to
Roman Catholics in the proportion of onethird, the question is being carefully
watched by the Belfast Local Employment
Committee. I may add that the priority conditions at present in force in Belfast were
drawn up at the outset by a Committee upon
which all sections of the community were represented including representatives of ex-
Servicemen.
Colonel WOODS: May I ask the right hon.
Gentleman if he intends to increase the percentage of ex-Servicemen employed on
Government assisted schemes, as in England,
it is 75 per cent., and in Ulster it is somewhat less than 60 per cent?
Mr. ANDREWS: The position in Great
Britain and here is different because there
I am glad to say it has not been found
necessary to discriminate as between Protestant and Catholic. At the time these
relief schemes were started it was considered
by a Committee representative of all classes
and creeds in the community that there
should be a discrimination, and on the whole
it has worked satisfactorily. As I have said
the Local Employment Committee is keeping
watch on the position as it may change from
time to time.

HANDLING GOODS AT THE DOCKS,
21. Mr. W. McMULLEN asked the Minister
of Labour whether he has recently framed new
regulations under the Factory and Workshop
Act, 1901, for the processes of loading, unloading, and handling goods at the docks
and wharfs of Northern Ireland, and if so,
will he state when it is intended to introduce
such regulations.
Mr. ANDREWS: The answer to the first
part of the question is in the affirmative.
New draft regulations, similar to those recently adopted in Great Britain, have been
published in Northern Ireland and certain
minor objections have been lodged.

Department and can, I think, be satisfactorily met without formal inquiry. As

MARKETING AND EXPORT OF EGGS.
22. Mr. W. McMULLEN asked the Minister
of Agriculture whether he is aware
that British public opinion is not informed
as to the improved way in which Irish eggs
are now marketed and exported, and whether,
in conjunction with the Minister of Agriculture for the Irish Free State, he will take
steps to inform the British public of these
improvements.
The MINISTER OF AGRICULTURE (Mr.
Archdale): Every effort has been made by the
Ministry, since the passing of the Marketing
of Eggs Act, to inform the trading community and the general public in Great
Britain as to the provisions of the Act. To
this end the daily Press and the appropriate
trade journals have been freely used. Explanatory matter has been furnished to
various associations of traders in Great
Britain and to individual merchants, and
the Ministry's principal marketing inspector
has been in constant touch with British
merchants interested in egg distribution.

Where feasible I shall be happy to cooperate with the Minister of Agriculture for
the Irish Free State in promoting the general
interests of the Irish poultry industry.

18 MARCH 1926
Adjournment of the House.
Motion made, and Question proposed:
That this House, at its rising this day, do
adjourn until Tuesday next.-(Captain
Dixon.)
Mr. DEVLIN: I rise for the purpose of
entering a protest against the methods by
which the business of this House is carried
on. We are suffering in this Parliament
from the impatience of Ministers to rush
Bills through the House. We are in the
habit of getting the Second Reading of a
Bill one day and a day or two after the
Committee stage is announced; in fact, the
Committee Stage of the Housing Bill is on
the Paper for to-day and the Second Reading was only passed on Tuesday. Yesterday
was a holiday for the Ministers, but not
for everybody.
Mr. POLLOCK: No.
Mr. DEVLIN. It was not a holiday for
some of the Ministers, because I see they
were making St. Patrick's Day speeches too.
Mr. POLLOCK: And others.
Mr. DEVLIN: Yes, I said others, some of
them good and some of them bad St.
Patrick's Day speeches. It is easy for the
Ministers to be ready for the Committee
Stages of these Bills, because they have very
efficient Civil Servants and they have legal
advisers. They can get all their Committee
work done for them, whereas those of us
who have no Civil Servants behind us and
are not able to secure any legal Parliamentary assistance from draughtsmen or
others have to sit down and study these
Bills. First of all we have got to study the
Bills themselves and then we have to draft
the Amendments, and very often we get
only a day or two in which to do the work.
The result of this hurried legislation is
that we have already had to introduce other
Bills to improve the Bills already passed
owing to the imperfections contained in
them due to the hurried way in which they
were passed. I do not know whether it is
-I see you are getting impatient, Mr.
Speaker.
Mr. SPEAKER: It occurred to me that
the hon. Gentleman's arguments are rather
directed towards the delay of business which
this Motion proposes, because it proposes the
House shall not sit again until Tuesday
next.
Mr. DEVLIN: I was only taking advantage of it. I thought the proper time
to have done it, as the hon. Member for
North Belfast (Mr. Kyle) proposed to do it,
was upon the previous Motion, but you
ruled that would not be in order.
Mr. SPEAKER: It was not in order.
Mr. DEVLIN: Therefore, we could not
discuss it then, and I thought on the present
Motion would be a good time to raise it.
I do put it to the Prime Minister that this
is not an overworked assembly. We only
work here about three months in the year,
and, as I have already stated, three days
in the week and three hours in the day.
Yet these Bills are flung at us. In fact,
last night one of the Bills was flung after
me as I went out-someone flung a Bill at me
and that was the first I knew about it.
That is a most unsatisfactory way of carry.
ing on the business of a Parliament, and it
is especially indefensible since nearly all
the Members of the Government are business men. I hope the reason we have so much
industrial depression and that our com.
mercial condition is in such an unfortunately
tragic and pathetic position to-day is not
that the business men are controlling their
businesses by
the same methods as
they are now conducting their Parliamentary affairs. I put it to the Prime
Minister that when a Bill passes its Second
Reading we ought to get at least a week before it is put down for the Committee Stage,
in order that we should understand the
character of the proposed legislation and also
the best methods by which we can amend
that legislation if it is possible to do so.
The PRIME MINISTER: I am afraid I
will be just as much out of order as the hon.
Member (Mr. Devlin), but it may shorten
discussion at a future time if I explain the
Bills to which the hon. Member referred. If
I take them as they are on the Order Paper
he will follow me. The Unemployment Insurance Bill is a Bill with which everybody has
been thoroughly familiar for some time past.
As he knows, it is merely confirming the
Agreement entered into and to which it
would be impossible to allow any Amendment whatever. We must carry out the
Agreement or throw it over, and, of course,
it is in the interests of the working classes,
and all classes, in Ulster that this Bill
should go through. The other one is the
Housing Bill, which is merely a continuing
Bill and which has proved so useful to the
community here. The same remark applies
to the Loans Guarantee Bill, which is a Bill
merely continuing the present practice which
has helped our industries so much.

Loans Guarantee Bill.
Order for Second Reading read.
Motion made, and Question proposed:
"That the Bill be now read a Second time."
Mr. POLLOCK: This Bill, of which I propose to move the Second Reading, is really
in effect a continuation Bill also. It has
been so often moved by me in this House
that those who have been Members for some
time are perfectly familiar with the subject,
but, in view of the fact that we have some
new Members who have recently taken their
seats. I think that courtesy demands perhaps,
that I should give a little more extended examination of the proposals of the Bill.
I had thought that perhaps it might
expedite matters and suit the convenience
of the House if I read a few lines of the
statement which I made when the original
Measure, or principal Act as it is called, was
before this House. On that occasion I fully
explained not only the aims and objects of
the Measure, but also the method of procedure. Let me state again that
It is a Measure intended to authorise the
Government to guarantee loans to public
bodies, to corporations, and to other persons, provided that there is sufficient
security behind the borrowers to warrant
the Government in undertaking the liability of guaranteeing the lenders against
any possible loss.
There is a clear difference, it must be remembered, between lending money and
guaranteeing the payment of money, and the
Bill, of which I am now moving the Second
Reading, is intended simply to guarantee
and not to lend. In regard to the procedure
under the Measure, it may be as well to repeat that a small advisory Committee has
been established of three persons of financial
experience, intelligence and independence,
whose duty it is to determine on the evidence
which is submitted to them whether the conditions or circumstances of the applicants
conform to the intentions of the Act.
The two primary considerations involved
are, first, that the security offered is sufficient to warrant the Government in undertaking the liability, and, second, that the
amount of employment provided under the
scheme is commensurate with the Government guarantee.
This Committee, of which I have spoken,
will have the assistance of technical persons,
such as accountants and professional men of
knowledge and experience, to advise them
on the matter, while, of course, the veto of
the Ministry of Finance is always retained.
One of the very important objects in connection with the Government guarantee is to
enable those who propose to expend money
on capital enterprises to secure that money
at a lower rate of interest than would be
possible under their own personal securities.
Of course the main concern of our Government in prosecuting the Measures under this
Bill is that unemployment may be relieved,
and that labour may be provided for numbers
of those who otherwise would not be engaged
in work, and I am sure I may state that any
sacrifice which the Government and Parliament may undertake in regard to this is
fully justified. A leaflet has been circulated,
I believe, giving the particulars of those
guarantees into which the Government has
entered, and it will be found that we have
utilised the Measure to the extent of
slightly over four million pounds. Assuming
that the British Government have given
guarantees to something like the same extent,
and that the owners themselves have provided considerable capital in connection with
these undertakings, it is not an unfair as
sumption that there has been provided
through the machinery of this Act work of
the value of ten million pounds. It is also
not unfair to assume that if these guarantees
had not been provided a great part, if not
the whole of the work that I have just now
mentioned, would not have been undertaken,
and therefore the conditions of unemployment would have been much more acute than
they are to-day. From that point of view
alone, I am sure hon. Members on both sides
of the House will admit that the Act which
we passed as early as 1922 has been fully
justified in its operation.
The Act of last year gave Parliamentary
authority to the Government to issue
guarantees to the extent of six millions, and
one of the objects of the present Bill is to
increase that amount by one million. That
is to say, that the Government in the aggregate should be empowered to give guarantees
to those persons who are desirous of borrow.
ing money under the circumstances that I
have outlined up to a maximum of seven
million pounds. That will leave a margin of
three million pounds to be operated upon in
case of necessity. I think I am justified in
asking the House to take the precaution of
adding this additional million to the surplus
which I have indicated, because there are
some signs, not perhaps very definite or
very manifest, of an improvement in trade,
and we have ourselves tentative indications
of shipowners in Great Britain undertaking
a programme in regard to the provision of
additional tonnage. For that reason therefore, I think it is necessary to provide that
three million pounds should be at the disposal of the Government for the purpose of
giving guarantees up to that amount, if
necessary.
The second clause in the Bill, which I may
touch upon very lightly, introduces another

guarantee is better than anything else in the

Northern Ireland guarantee is just as good
as anything going. (Hon. Members: 1[ear,
Hear.) But at the same time should such a

a firm borrowing or attempting to borrow in
future under the Ulster guarantee should be
compelled to pay a higher rate than it would
under the British guarantee, I ask that
liberty should be given to the Ministry of
Finance to meet that contingency by bridging
the gap, if I may say so. Of course, if hon.
Members will consult the Clause in the Bill
they will notice that that power is strictly
limited to a very fractional difference. In
Clause 2 of the Bill, the first paragraph
states
(1) Where the principal or interest of
any loan to which this section applies has
been guaranteed by the Ministry of Finance
under Section one of the principal Act, the
said Ministry may undertake to pay to the
lender-
(a) such proportion, not exceeding onetenth, of any interest payable during
the currency of the loan as may be
prescribed by the said Ministry; or
This will, therefore, let the House understand that the limit imposed upon the
Government, or the Ministry of Finance, in
regard to these guarantees is that any gap
which may be filled shall not exceed one-tenth
of the amount of the interest. I have stated
that such a contingency may not arise, but
as the amounts have now become very considerable it is in my judgment, and in the
judgment of the Government, better to provide for such a contingency, if it should come
to pass, and as the limitation is very rigid
in regard to the amount of liability that
would arise under the circumstances I feel
that the House would be justified in passing
the Measure in that form. I beg to move.

The PARLIAMENTARY SECRETARY
OF THE MINISTRY OF LABOUR (Mr.
Gordon): It is difficult with any degree of
accuracy to estimate the real expenditure
by a Department, more especially a Department such as the Ministry of Labour. This
Supplementary Estimate is a result of the
prolonged and unprecedented unemployment,
and also of the social legislation that has
been brought in during the past twelve
months. I think it only right that I should
explain as briefly as possible to the Committee the necessity for introducing this
Supplementary Estimate. If hon. Members
will look at A (Salaries, Wages and Allowances) on page 8 of the Estimates they will
observe that there is £18,000 down for the
purpose of the employment of additional
temporary clerks. When we introduced the
Widows', Orphans', and Old Age Contributory Pensions Act we had to take on some
temporary officers, and at the same time we
had to employ a certain proportion of the
headquarters' staff for the purpose of carrying out the preliminary work in connection
with that Act. Those two things represent
a sum of £18,000.
D1 (Printing), £1,300, also reflects the
heavy unemployment obtaining. There has
also been some very heavy printing in connection with the introduction of the new
Contributory Pensions Scheme. In order
that reduced rates might be obtained it was
necessary to secure as large quantities of
stocks as possible, but a corresponding reduction in the Vote for 1926-27 will be
effected. As to postage, telegrams and telephones (£1,500), this is largely the result of
work in connection with the Widows',
Orphans', and Old Age Contributory lensions Act. It will be remembered that some
of my hon. Friends on the Opposition side
suggested that the Ministry of Labour should
endeavour to make it as easy as possible for widows claiming widows' and
orphans' pensions by obtaining certificates of birth and marriage, and other
matters connected with the claim.
As a
result of the Ministry of Labour undertaking this responsibility we estimate for
£165. You will see that on page 9 £1,200 is
required as payment to officers in respect
of cost of administration of unemployment
insurance.
Some of the trade unions have been unable
to pay the unemployment benefit out of
their own funds for some considerable period,
and as a result could not enter into a contract with the Ministry of Labour whereby
they would use the funds of the Ministry
for the purpose of paying unemployment
benefit to their members through their trade
unions. These are known as association
claims. Consequently, some of these societies
are in a better position to-day than they
were formerly, and have made an arrangement
with us whereby they are paying unemployment benefit to their members through their
trade unions and not directly through the
local employment exchanges. This means
extra cost on the Department, and we are
asking the Committee to vote £1,200.
Then there is the sum of £1,000 for the
manufacture of health, pensions, and unenployment insurance stamps and other
matters. There is also the audit of approved
societies and insurance committees. I might
let the Committee know that the National
Health Insurance Audit Department charged
this Ministry to 31st March, 1925, on the basis
of 289,000 insured persons, of which 90,000
were members of international societies
whose accounts were audited in Great Britain.
The Audit Department since then has discovered that these provisional figures should
have been 344,000 and 120,000 respectively.
This Supplementary Estimate is therefore on
account of the increased cost of the Audit
Department, which is an agency service
carrying out work in connection with our
Health Insurance Department.

Case of Mrs Whan.

Case of Mrs Whan.
The case goes back to the year 1922 when
this woman was arrested on the charge of
sending poisoned chocolates to a Mr. Walker,
who resides in the Braniel, Castlereagh.
That case was disposed of, and immediately
following that this woman was again
arrested along with her son on a charge of
assaulting Mrs. Walker, despite the fact that
her son had never seen Mrs. Walker in his
life before. Following on that this woman
was again arrested and charged with assaulting Mrs. Walker in High Street, Belfast.
and, despite the fact that there was no independent witness to give evidence, she was
again brought to book for this alleged
offence.
take too gloomy a view of the situation, and
one who is responsible for estimating has got

In addition to that we have had a great deal

months due to the Widows', Orphans' and
Old Age Contributory Pensions Act. My
hon. Friend asked the question why, if we
had made up our minds to introduce a
Measure following on the lines of the British
Measure, did we not in our Estimates include the sum which would be necessary to
finance that Measure. Of course we are not
entitled to anticipate the views of Parliament
or to assume that, because we as a Government have made up our minds to introduce
a Measure, Parliament is necessarily going
to pass that Measure. It is only when
Parliament has passed the Measure that we
are justified in coming to Parliament to vote
the money that is necessary in order to give

that explanation is perfectly clear, and I
hope my hon. Friend will be satisfied with it.

Motion made and Question proposed :

-(Captain Dixon.)
Mr. KYLE: As we have ended our work a
little early I want to draw the attention of
the House to a question I had on the Paper
asking the Minister of Home Affairs (Sir
Dawson Bates) if he is prepared to issue a
synopsis of the report that was given by
District-Inspector Allen in regard to the
Whan versus Walker
case. I have endeavoured on two or three occasions to get
this report from the right hon. Gentleman.
To-day I have asked for a synopsis of the
report as I believe that if this report was
either acted upon by the Home Office or
made known to the people who are interested
in the case of this Mrs. Whan it would be
sufficient to prove that this woman is innocent, and that she has been the victim of
circumstances unparalleled in this city or in
the Six Counties.
It seems to me that there is a conspiracy
against this woman, and it is in the interests
of justice that we ask for the publication
of this District-Inspector's Report. This
District-Inspector was in the Imperial Secret
Service for a long period-about twenty
years I understand-and he was put on by
the responsible authorities to investigate
this case.
In the course of his investigations a pocket book, which was supposed
to have dropped from the pocket of a son or
son-in-law of Mrs. Whan was discovered. He
investigated the source from which that
pocket book came, and we understand that
that source is marked in the report which
we are asking should be published.
Out of that pocket book there were two
letters taken. One of these letters was supposed to have come from Mrs. Whan's sonin-law, a young man named James Ferguson
Courtney. It purported to have been delivered through the usual post channels and
bore evidence of having passed through the
General Post Office at Belfast. But, as it
transpired afterwards, it was never posted
in the usual course of posting, nor was it
ever delivered by a postman or anyone else
to Mr. James Ferguson Courtney, nor to anyone at his address or elsewhere. The second
one purported to be a reply from the same
gentleman to Mrs. Whan. It was duly
stamped and ready for posting but not
closed.
Sir DAWSON BATES: Might I ask my
hon. Friend what he is reading from?
Mr. KYLE: I am reading from the affidavit of Mrs. Whan. If there is any other
information the right hon. Gentleman wants
I will be pleased to give it to him. If he is
going to issue this report and so clear his
Department from the charge which I am
trying to level at them now, of deliberately
withholding this report to cover up their own
incapacity, to cover up a scandal connected
with the administration of his Department,
if I can assist him in any way I will do so
with pleasure. This District-Inspector Allen

Gentleman for the publication of this report.
Sir DAWSON BATES: The whole question
is whether or not the police report, made
as a result of the investigation of an alleged
crime, is to be published. In my opinion
nothing would be more disastrous to the
proper administration of the law than that
a police report, which has been sent in to
the authorities, should be published. Now
in this case the facts appear to be, shortly,
as follow:-
In April, 1922, Mrs. Whan was charged, as
a result of a private prosecution, with sending
chocolates to Mr. Walker. Informations
were refused. In the following month a
further private prosecution was brought by
Mr. Walker, alleging an assault. As a result of the investigation of the Court on
that occasion Mrs. Whan received sentence
of two months' imprisonment.
On August 23 following proceedings were
again taken-by the public prosecutoragainst Mrs. Whan for sending threatening
letters. That case
was returned to the
Assizes after due investigation by the
Attorney-General, and the case came before
the late Lord Chief Justice and a jury, and,
as a result, Mrs. Whan received sentence of
six months' imprisonment. Further charges
were subsequently made in 1923 in regard
to further threatening letters, and, as a
result, District-Inspector Allen was autho
rised to make a report in regard to that
case and the other cases that had gone before.
That report was duly received. It was
submitted to the former Attorney-General,
and, having investigated the whole facts of
the case, the Attorney-General decided that
there was no case to bring criminal proceedings against either Mrs. Whan or against
Walker. That was in 1923.
At the end of two years Mrs. Whan
appears to have arrived at the conclusion
that she had been badly treated in respect
of the matters on which she had been found
guilty by a competent Court and jury.
Accordingly she brought an action against
Mrs. Walker, claiming damages for false
imprisonment. The case came before the
Court, and on an application on the part
of the defendant that the case should be
remitted to the county court judge the Court
went into the whole case and granted the
application, and the case was remitted to
the county court judge. That was in 1925. I
understand that since that time Mrs. Whan
has abandoned her case.
These are the facts, which I have gone into
very fully. I think nothing would be more
disastrous than that private reports should
be published. Any individuals who think
that they have been wrongfully treated by
anybody have got a remedy in the High
Court. Mrs. Whan took that remedy and
subsequently abandoned her case. While I
say it would be quite improper and a very
wrong thing to publish the report, any individual I can point out this, and I am
sure Mrs. Whan received this advice also
from her advisers-if they think any police
officer can throw any light upon the case
it is open to them to apply to the Court
to issue a subpoena to that officer, and, of
course, he will give evidence in due course.
Colonel WOODS: I would just like to ask
the right hon. Gentleman if he thinks it is
quite fair that nothing more definite should

23 MARCH 1926
HOUSE OF COMMONS.

Tuesday, 23rd March, 1926.
The House met at Three of the Clock, Mr.
SPEAKER in the Chair.
Oral Answers to Questions.
COST OF LIVING IN NORTHERN
IRELAND.
1. Mr. KYLE (for Mr. Beattie) asked the
Minister of Labour whether in view of the
statement made by him that he does not
consider the cost of living higher in Northern Ireland than in England, and as this is
in direct conflict with the prevailing opinion
in Northern Ireland, he would be prepared
to set up a committee to consider the
question of the cost of living in Northern
Ireland.
The MINISTER OF LABOUR (Mr.
Andrews): A committee under the chairmanship of my hon, and learned Friend,
the Parliamentary Secretary of the Ministry
of Education (Mr. Robb) investigated this
whole question, and, after exhaustive
evidence had been taken, reported in
September, 1923, that they had no reason to
think that there was any large difference
between the cost of living in Northern
Ireland as compared with that in Great
Britain.
Since this report was presented my
Department has kept in close touch with
the course of prices in this area, and, while
there are variations in the prices of particular commodities-some being cheaper
and some dearer-all the evidence points to
the fact that the cost of living is not
greater here than in Great Britain. I am
of opinion, therefore, that no useful purpose
would be served in incurring the expense of
setting up another committee to consider the
question.
Mr. KYLE: In view of the fact that
bread, milk, and coal-three very essential
things to working-class life—are all dearer
here than they are in England, would the
Minister not see his way to reconsider that
statement, especially in view of what has
taken place since that inquiry, and that
these prices are higher to-day than they
were then?
Mr. ANDREWS: I have really nothing
to add to what I have already stated.
SALE OF IMPORTED BUTTER.
2. Mr. McBRIDE asked the Minister of
Agriculture whether he is aware that
foreign butter is sold in shops wrapped with
Irish creamery labels, and will he make
inquiry if such is the case.
The MINISTER OF AGRICULTURE
(Mr. Archdale): For some time past very
close attention has been given by the
Ministry to the question of the descriptions
applied to butter sold in Northern Ireland.
In consultation with the Ministry, the
Ulster Agricultural Organisation Society
convened a committee representative of the
Ulster creameries (some of whom during the
scarce season import butter to supplement
their own manufacture and thus keep up
their trade connection with their regular
customers). The recommendations of that
committee in which the Ministry concurred
were to the effect that in order to secure
uniform observance of the terms of the
Merchandise Marks Acts, creameries should
arrange to show on wrappers containing
imported butter the following description-
"Finest Imported Creamery Butter,
Empire Produce;"
or
"Finest Imported Creamery Butter,
Foreign Produce."
Following the issue of a circular to the
creameries intimating that the Ministry
would be satisfied with an arrangement of
this kind, public notice was given by the
Ministry through the medium of the Press
to all persons dealing in imported butter
of their legal obligations in the matter of
descriptions under the Merchandise Marks
Acts, and advising merchants and retailers
to safeguard themselves by having wrappers
containing imported butter conspicuously
marked on the lines set out in the intimation to the creameries.
The Ministry is satisfied that the action
taken has been productive of good results,
and inquiries are at present being pursued
on behalf of the Ministry in connection with
complaints as to non-observance. The Ministry
will not hesitate to take legal action in any
case where the facts warrant such a course,
especially as every section of the butter
trade must now be aware that, under the
Merchandise Marks Act, 1887, the application of a false trade description to goods
renders the person concerned liable to
prosecution.

as technical considerations and finance, and
in the circumstances I can see no object in
continuing the Bill beyond 1927 unless the
situation should necessitate such a step.
Question put, "That the words proposed to
be left out stand part of the Question.'
The Committee divided. Ayes, 20; Noes, 5.

listen too attentively to the remarks made by

Now, I would like just to put a few of the
facts concerning the country before the House.
This Bill is framed for the purpose of relieving the housing shortage. That housing
shortage is very acute in rural areas, especially as to the sort of houses that could be or
would be occupied by the agricultural
labourer. I believe that this Bill has as it
stands, or as it has stood up to now, to a
certain extent-perhaps indirectly-helped
the housing shortage, and I believe that
gradually it might relieve the housing shortage in the country still further. But, unfortunately, the tendency at the present
moment is to erect houses averaging perhaps
roughly 700 feet and upwards. Well, now, it
is quite obvious that houses of that size, even
in the country where perhaps it is
possible to erect them at slightly less cost
than in towns-could not be built at a cost
which would make it possible for the agricultural labourer to inhabit them. It is
quite impossible for the builders to erect
them at a cost which would make it possible
for rents to be charged which the average
rural worker could pay. At the present
moment in my district the utmost that any
agricultural worker could pay would be 4s a
week, and I believe that that is the rent
which is being paid for the ex-Servicemen's
cottages, and I know that they are finding it
very hard to be able to find the money for
their weekly rent. Three shillings I should
say would be really the highest amount that
ought to be charged. The average is a rent
of 1s 6d to 2s. Now, it is quite obvious
that it would be impossible to build
houses of these larger sizes which could
be let at those rents. And I know
that I certainly would be glad and thankful
that a great many houses of 550 square
feet could be erected in my rural area,
and I know that the agricultural labourers
would be glad and thankful if houses of this

labourers' houses.
that boast can be justified, but I do know

HOUSE OF COMMONS

That is the condition at the present moment
in some of the cottages because of the housing shortage.
It is impossible to order that these houses
be repaired, because they are beyond repair.
If a sanitary order were taken out and enforced it would simply mean that the cottage
would be closed and the worker would have
nowhere to go. I would like to ask the hon.
Gentleman opposite if he would care to try
living in that for twelve months, and if at
the end of that time he would come back to
this House he would not then say he would
prefer to go into a small house of 550 feet
with two bedrooms and living room, clean,
healthy and decent. I believe if he were
to try that I know what he would say.
And it is because I know what these conditions are I am so anxious to see these smaller
houses built, because the building of larger
houses is not going to remove the present terrible condition of affairs at any rate
and for a long time. It is because I am so
anxious to see these small houses built that
I move this Amendment.
I want to see small houses in which the
agricultural labourer can live and be happy,
and then possibly some day larger houses
may be built for him at less money, and
perhaps they will be let at rents which the
ural worker can afford. Perhaps by that
time trade unions may relax their rules and
it may cost less to erect these houses. Consequently, the rural worker may then be
able to have all the advantages he should
have, cleanliness, healthiness, airiness, and
a larger space. but until that day comes I
am perfectly convinced that the agricultural
worker would welcome these small houses.
I do hope the right hon. Gentleman (Sir
Dawson Bates) will consider whether it
would not be possible to accept this Amendment because, as I said at the beginning, in
the country this type of house is required.
The Government are anxious to see this
type of houses, and there would be great
benefit to the people of the Northern
districts. I beg to move.

HOUSE OF COMMONS
[Mr. Devlin]
kitchen. But what is still more important
is that these two-roomed houses will be
mainly in crowded centres with all the limitations that crowded centres have in regard
to health and sanitation, but these
labourers' cottages are built in the country,
and in addition to the cottage there is in
nearly every case half an acre of land, and
in many cases there is an acre of land
attached. There is no comparison so far as
health is concerned between the living conditions of the labourer in the rural parts of
the country and the worker coming home to
a crowded street in a big city like Belfast.
These houses to which I refer are mostly let
at 1s a week. In many parts of Ireland they
are only 10d. I do not know whether they
have been increased since, but I believe some
of the Northern boards have increased them.
There certainly has been no universal increase in the rents.
Why do some of us feel so intensely upon
this housing question? I myself never pass
by these labourers' cottages without venturing to look into them, to watch those who
inhabit them, and to try to understand what
is the effect of these improved housing conditions in rural Ireland. I find it
mirrored in the faces of the people
-a finer sense of civic responsibility and
a larger desire to work upon the part of
the men; a more cheerful look on the faces
of the mothers, and I would almost say
laughter dancing in the faces of the little
children who inhabit these houses. Viewing
it purely from the point of view of the State
and the Government, apart altogether from
that of the happiness, contentment, and
health of those who inhabit them, I say there
never was a greater contribution to the
welfare of the State than the building of
these houses. But what do you propose to
do here? You propose to duplicate the slum
system. No doubt they will be cleaner
slums; that makes them less unattractive,
but they will ultimately become slums. What
is the greatest possible weapon you could use
for the prevention of drunkenness and
crime? It is good housing. Give a man
a decent house to come home to, after a hard
day's work, and he will find less attractions
in the public-house and at the street corner.
But what you propose to do is to encourage
the building of these two-roomed houses, in
which there will be five or six children.
The mother will be doing the housework,
and the whole conduct of the domestic affairs
will be carried on in such a way as to make
home life repellent to the working man when
he comes home.

the Government to give an additional subsidy to those who build these working-class

The PRIME MINISTER: The whole
housing question must be dealt with apart
altogether from the question of whether it
is popular for the Government to do certain
things or not. The whole argument on a
previous occasion and to-day seems to me to
have got completely out of the practical
sphere. What has happened? If you ask
any workingman in Belfast, he will tell you
he finds that the rents for the larger type
of houses are beyond his means. He finds
that he has to go and take a room in some
other house, belonging to somebody else, and
to pay for that room almost as much as the
rent he would have to pay for one of these
small houses.
Mr. POLLOCK: And more.
The PRIME MINISTER: And sometimes,
as my right hon. Friend says, more. But
whether it is more or whether it is less,
surely everybody in this House, on either
side, would like to see these poor people of
very limited means being provided with a
front door with a key, so that when they get
inside the house, no matter how humble or
small it is, they will be able to feel that at
all events it is their own, that they have
control of it, that they pay the rent of it,
and that it is their castle as much as the
rich man's residence is his castle. I really
do not understand some of the arguments
that have been used. There is no compulsion upon any person, there is no compu!-
sion upon
a husband and wife with five
children, to take such a small house. They
would obviously take a larger one, but when
a working man's son gets married he wants
to start economically and low down in the
scale. He looks about to get a small house,
as he has no children, no encumbrances. He
wants a kitchen, he wants perhaps two bedrooms.
I was very much struck with the plans of
these houses, and a certain number of people
in the Belfast Corporation spoke to me on
the subject very feelingly indeed. They said
they thought it would be a good thing to
build a certain number of these houses.
They are not going to substitute these houses
for the larger houses. They will be built
pari passu. The richer people among the
working classes can take the larger houses;
the married people with four, five, six or
seven children can go for the larger houses.
But do let us consider those who are poorer
and who have no children, and who cannot
afford anything but an odd room here and
there, and that with great difficulty, at the
present time. I would like to see all the
inhabitants of the Six Counties properly
housed. My right hon. Friend (Sir Dawson
Bates) has got certain latitude in the matter,
and he is able to say, "Yes, I think that for
a certain part of the town, or for a certain
part of the country, the superficial area can
be reduced," and thus permit a few of these
houses to be erected. That is all it means.
We are not going to thrust these houses on
the local authorities; they will be able to
judge whether they will provide such houses
or not. The local authorities are not going
to make married people with families live
in these houses. There is no compulsion the
whole way through. Supposing after
year's time it was found that people were
not taking these houses, naturally no builders
would build them. If they found such houses
an uneconomic proposition they would stop
building them and would build a larger type
of house. In the meantime, what the Government are most anxious to do is to meet the
requirements of the working people, whether
they are very poor or moderately rich.

This principle has, I think, been debated,
not only in Great Britain and South Africa,
but in many countries. Where Government
money is being used in the interests of
private companies there should be a representative on the board of directors. I want

to me that it is getting back to the old
principle of no taxation without representation.

Mr. KYLE: A few moments ago in Committee I was endeavouring to make clear a
point of principle in regard to this Bill, and
I am not at all satisfied with the Government's attitude on this very important question. Clause 2 of the Bill says:
(1) Where the principal or interest of
any loan to which this section applies has
been guaranteed by the Ministry of
Finance under section one of the principal
Act, the said Ministry may undertake to
pay to the lender-
I proposed to put in there :—
That the Government shall have the right
to appoint a director on a company receiving a loan whose duty it will be to see that
the employees of that company are paid
a reasonable wage.
I endeavoured to point out that it seems to
me a reprehensible practice that the Government should loan money or credits to any
company without having representation on
the board of directors of that company. If
we give credit to a company for £1,000,000
or £100,000 I hold we are entitled to have a
representative on the board of directors.
This is not a harum scarum idea. I want to
point out that just last week this principle
was adopted by the Government of South
Africa. I want the Government to accept
that principle. I have been ruled out of
order on some technical points in regard to
the title of the Bill. It seems to me that
when the Government is responsible for
credits to the tune of seven millions without
having any say as to how those credits will
be used, I should have the support of every
fair-minded person, unless it is the intention
of the Government to deliberately use State
credits to bolster up private enterprise.
That is what is being done. I am not asking
you to refrain from bolstering it up. All I
ask is that in that private enterprise there
shall be a representative of the Government
to see that the credits are administered in
the way they ought to be, and principally
along the lines that the employees will be
reasonably paid.
The MINISTER OF FINANCE (Mr.
Pollock): I would like by way of reply to
ask the hon. Member a question. Does he
propose to stop all enterprise in respect of
shipbuilding, for example, in the City of
Belfast?

question. I do not. All I say is that if we
give credits to Messrs. Harland & Wolff or

used and see how much money is spent.

should give guarantees to Messrs.

Mr. POLLOCK: On the front page of this
Bill will be found a short statement setting
out in simple language the purport of this
315 Administrative Provisions Bill- HOUSE OF COMMONS
Second Reading. 316
[Mr. Pollock]
Measure. But I think it would be convenient
if even at the risk of taking up the time of
the House for a few minutes, that I should
enter at some greater detail into the circumstances which led up to the Measure which
I am now presenting to the House.
Those who carry their minds back to the
period when the Government of Ireland Bill
was under consideration and became
an Act of Parliament will recall that provision was made for the establishment of a
body which was described as the Council of
Ireland. The function of that body, as described in the Measure, was to administer the
services common to both areas, that is,
Northern and Southern Ireland. It was contemplated of course at that time that
Southern Ireland would conform to
the terms of that Measure, as we
have done here
in the North, and
if that had happened the establishment
of the Council of Ireland would, no doubt,
have been of very considerable service. But
as Southern Ireland refused to accept the
terms of that Measure, it became necessary
for the Imperial Government to substitute
some administration that would take the
place of the Council of Ireland so far as
Northern Ireland was concerned.
The services to which the Council of Ireland
had to direct its attention, presuming it had
come into existence, were diseases of animals,
fisheries, and railways. The Imperial
Government then took over SO far as
Northern Ireland was concerned the
functions which it was intended the Council
of Ireland should carry out, and appointed
an Imperial officer in Belfast, with a staff, to
administer the services to which I have referred. We had the advantage here of the
presence of a gentleman of long experience
in administrative work, of great military record, and altogether a most efficient servant.
(Hon. Members: Hear, hear.) And I should
like to express not only as a personal matter,
but on behalf of the Government our great
appreciation of the attitude of Mr. Tallents
towards all the matters with which he was
brought into contact. Not only did he do his
duty as an Imperial servant, watching
Imperial interests, but he entered sympathetically into any matters concerned with
our difficulties here in Northern Ireland with
a sympathy which I am bound to recognise.
Following the operation to which I have
referred, and which was to have have had
existence for five years, the Boundary question intervened. When a settlement of that
matter was reached there was embodied
therein an arrangement by which the powers
of the Imperial Parliament in respect of
the old Council of Ireland services should
bo transferred to us here. The wording of
that part of the Agreement which followed
upon that arrangement was a provision as
follows:-
The Governments of the Irish Free State
and of Northern Ireland shall meet together
as and when necessary for the purpose of
considering matters of common interest
arising out of or connected with the exercise and administration of such powers.
I have no doubt that this provision will be
of considerable value both to Northern Ireland and to Southern Ireland, assuming that
Southern Ireland approaches the different
subjects in the same spirit as we desire to
do on our own part. Up to the present, of
course. there has been no definite gesture
made from one side or the other in respect
of these matters.
In the meantime it is necessary that we
ourselves here in this Parliament should by
the Measure which I am now introducing
take or give the necessary powers to administer the services that formerly came
under the control of the Imperial Government--the services known as the Council of
Ireland services. It probably would have
been possible that His Majesty's Privy Council by Order in Council could have transferred these services without the necessity
for legislation in this Parliament. But in
view of the fact that we have been legislating
in local matters for some years, the feeling
was that we were in a position to deal with
these things more satisfactorily than by
Order in Council or by adaptation of the
law. It was thought right that the Measure
I am now submitting should be presented to
this Parliament, and that is being done with
the full accord of the British Government.
so that there is no difference of opinion
in respect of the procedure as regards that.
But some of the provisions of the Bill
go further than mere adaptation. These are
necessary in order that the financial provisions of the existing Acts may be brought
into line with the changes of law that have
already been made in this House. I am referring at the present moment to the method
of financing services under the Government
Loans Fund which was passed here some
time ago. Provision was made for the supply
of money to the different objects which come
within the ambit of that Act, and power is
therefore taken in the present Bill to enable
loans, for example, for fishery purposes to
be made from that fund instead of from the
Endowment Fund of the Department of
Agriculture or from voted money as the
case may be.
Similarly the whole section of the Bill
headed Contagious Diseases of Animals presents in a clear and easily understood form
the financial provisions of the various
Diseases of Animals Acts. Briefly, it may
be stated that these diseases fall into two
categories, and these categories correspond to
two separate accounts within the Cattle
Diseases Fund. One class of disease is that

relating to cattle, pleuro-pneumonia, foot and

There is, however, one disease which recent

is met from State funds or moneys voted

The only other matter in the Bill to which
I think I should call attention is the allocation of these services in respect of fisheries
and railways. It is intended that our
Ministry of Commerce should have control of

some of the inland fishing districts which

re-arranged by agreement between the Irish
Free State and the British Government, in
order that each Board of Conservators may
be completely within the jurisdiction of one
Government. Full effect has not yet been

This is the general purport of the Measure

Mr. KYLE: I see the right hon. Gentleman
the Minister of Home Affairs, has mentioned
the sum of £2,130, being, I suppose, the
Government's share of the expenses of the
Housing Inquiry which sat for a considerable
period in the City Hall. I found out the
number of sittings which this Inquiry held.
There was
a preliminary sitting on 15th
September, and there were subsequent meetings which began
October and
ended on
18th January. There was a
total of 35 sittings, that is, if you take the
preliminary sitting as one, so that the cost
to the Parliament of Northern Ireland is £60
per sitting. We have not yet been favoured
with the report of the Housing Commissioner,
so, I suppose, we cannot very well go into
that particular question, but I was afraid we
might not have an opportunity at any other
stage of going into this Housing Inquiry
report, so far as we are responsible for it.
It is because I feared we might not at a later
stage get an opportunity of discussing the
proceedings of the Inquiry, which we partly
pay for, that I have taken this opportunity
to-day.
I think everybody will agree that the
Housing Inquiry was necessary, and, therefore, there is no question of our quarrelling
with the Government over the establishment
of the Commission, but we do think that the
cost to the Government and Parliament of
Northern Ireland is excessive, in that we
should pay to one or two people who were
responsible no less a sum than £60 for each
sitting. This sum of £2,130, which we are
asked to vote this afternoon, I expect, will
only be about one-third or one-quarter of
the total expenses of this inquiry. It goes
to show how expensive it is to have
tremely capable Commissioners appointed.
Nevertheless, it seems to me to be an exorbitant sum of money to be demanded for
their services without knowing to what
detail they had to go or the amount of their
work. All we do know is that the sittings
covered a period of four months, and that
we vote the sum of £2,130 for those services.

If it had been bricklayers who asked for

As I said a moment or so ago, the Housing
Inquiry was necessary, because I think, reading the reports that appeared in the Press,
it has been clearly demonstrated that so far
as private enterprise is concerned in regard
to the building of houses they have deliberately and with malice aforethought robbed
the community. There is one firm in particular who, according to the evidence submitted at the Housing Inquiry, deliberately
robbed the public, robbed the citizens of
Belfast. I say that deliberately. And that
is in the name of private enterprise. That
is all being used by some strange twist of
people's minds into an argument against
direct labour for housing, because the Corporation of Belfast and the Housing Committee of the Belfast Corporation are
composed of business men. There is only
one Labour representative out of fifteen on
that Housing Committee. All these business
men, who are out to serve the interests of
the community, forsooth, could not stop
private companies from robbing the Belfast
Corporation, and thereby robbing the people,
both by supplying rotten material in regard
to timber and in regard to slates. In all
these regards this Inquiry, to my mind, has
been an indictment of private enterprise and
an indictment of the morality of private
enterprise.
Where it has been possible, through the
slack administration of the Belfast Corporation to rob the public of an extra £100,
these business men never thought twice
about doing it, and it is, I think, nothing
short of a scandal that the people who are
responsible for this deliberate defrauding
should be able to hold up their heads in the
City of Belfast to-day. I do want to say
that this sum of £2,130, representing £60
a sitting, is, in my opinion, too much for

NATIONAL HEALTH INSURANCE.
That a supplementary sum not exceeding
Five Thousand Pounds be granted to His
Majesty for the service of the year ending
31st March, 1926, to defray the grant in aid
of the cost of Benefits and Expenses of
Administration under the National Health
Insurance Acts, 1911-1924.
The PARLIAMENTARY SECRETARY
OF THE MINISTRY OF LABOUR (Mr.
Gordon): I would like to make perfectly
plain to the Committee the reasons for introducing this Vote. The amount of sickness
was greater than was anticipated and
budgeted for in the original Estimates, and
consequently the increased unemployment
meant that great numbers who were not entitled to benefit were retained in insurance
under the Prolongation of Insurance Act,
1921, as extended by the Expiring Laws Continuance Act. As a result of the prolonged
unemployment, the physical standard of
these people was considerably lowered, and
undoubtedly many of them have been thrown
upon the funds of the Health Insurance
Societies. May I explain what the amount
is required for? As Members of this Committee are aware, the State gives a statutory
grant of two-ninths of sickness, disablement,
maternity benefit and administrative
penses, and it has been found that the sickness exceeded our former Estimate, and
consequently we are called upon by the
Approved Societies to make good our statutory grant of two-ninths of all benefits.
Accordingly I beg to move.

STATEMENT BY MINISTER OF

Motion made, and Question Proposed:
"That a sum not exceeding Two Million
Five Thousand Five Hundred Pounds be
granted to His Majesty, on account, or towards defraying the charges of the several
services for which a Vote on Account is
required, for the period ending 31st March,
1927."
Mr. POLLOCK: The majority of hon.
Members of this Committee are familiar
with the procedure in respect of the Vote
which I am about to present. It was my
custom, in the earlier days of the Parliarent, to enter into this matter with some
considerable detail, but as time proceeded,
and as the White Paper which is issued conveys
full information in regard to the different
items of the Vote, I curtailed my remarks
last year, and the year before, to a simple
explanation of the salient features of the
Vote. It is, of course, intended to provide
for the continuity of the services until hon.
Members have had an opportunity of entering into and criticising as much as they
think just, the different Estimates, when they
will be submitted. Towards that end, therefore, this White Paper has been issued,
showing that we require £2,005,500 for presumably three months' expenditure upon the
different services of the Province.
I think, perhaps, it would be convenient if
I bring out some of the prominent features,
by taking the classes of the Estimates categorically. Class I, which deals with the
Houses of Parliament, Cabinet Offices, and so
on, shows an increase of £657. This is a
comparatively small increase and arises because of the addition of Senators' expenses,
and also a reduction in the returns from
Private Bills which we expect will accrue.
It does not require any further comment, I
think, than this explanation of the small
increase.
When I come to Class II, the Ministry of
Finance, of course, I am on larger ground.
I think I should explain that the small increase in the Ministry of Finance itselfthat is, in the Department-of £6,000 odd,
results from the decision to take a census in
the coming year. We estimate that the expenses of the census will be anything from
£5,000 to £7,000. Public Works and Buildings show an increase of £25,000 or thereabouts, but that has not very much interest
to us as a Parliament, because that money
is repaid by the Imperial authorities. Old
Age Pensions show an increase of about
£150,000, and hon. Members will realise the
cause for that increase. It is due, not only
to the removal of the thrift disqualification,
but also to the estimate made of the additional cost arising from the Widows,'
Orphans' and Old Age Contributory Pensions
Act, which was recently passed in this House.
I come now to the Ministry of Home
Affairs, in which there is a very happy decrease in all departments. The Royal Irish
Constabulary, it will be noticed, is down
some £35,000.
Mr. KYLE: Ulster.
Mr. POLLOCK: The Royal Ulster Constabulary, thank you. I was so long accustomed
to the old form that it is hard to get away
from it. There is £35,000 of a decrease in
the Royal Ulster Constabulary. In the
Special Constabulary there is a very dramatic decrease from £1,220,000 to £164,000.
Hon. Members will realise without any difficulty the explanation of that very large decrease, namely, the disbandment of the Special
Constabulary and the winding up of all
matters connected with that great body.
The other items do not call for any comment.
Prisons are down £16,000, which I am sure

a total decrease of £1,153,000 odd on the

The Ministry of Labour shows
welcome decrease in the net cost of the
Department, but under National Health
Insurance there is an increase of approximately £30,000, which is estimated to provide
for the state contribution towards the
additional benefits which will become payable next year. I touch now upon the
question of Unemployment Insurance, under
the heading of the Ministry of Labour. This
includes provision for a full year's equalisation payment, that is to say the amount that
will be necessary to equalise the Unemployment Insurance Fund, and to provide for any
deficit that may arise in the working of it.
Hon. Members will appreciate the burden
which this equalisation payment imposes
upon our Exchequer when I remind them
that of the full sum of £1,365,000 included on
account of the equalisation payment, the net
liability on Northern Ireland funds for the
year is estimated at £490,000. It may be even
greater. It depends entirely on the amount
of unemployment we have to face.
I come now to Class V. The Educational
Services show a reduction of over £100,000,
and this is largely the result of the reduction
in teachers' salaries which took place in
January. The increase in Class VT (Agriculture) is due to the provision for the first
time in respect of Diseases of Animals
administration. The Committee will under
stand that although this is a charge brought
into our Estimate it is simply a transfer from
that which was provided by the Imperial
Authorities and deducted from our residuary
share, that is to say, instead of the Imperial
Authorities paying it we ourselves deal with
the matter direct. There is also an
additional sum of about £20,000 provided in
order to establish a Research Station and
Experimental Farm at Hillsborough.
Class VII (Ministry of Commerce)
shows a reduction on the Estimates in the
amount of the subvention in aid of wages in
the coal mining industry, which will not,
presumably, apply to the coming year, and
also to reduced expenditure on flax development and other services. Therefore, the
Ministry of Commerce estimate is reduced by
£11,358.
The net result of the two parallel columns
is that there is a reduction in the expenditure
of £667,732. I think, considering the
circumstances with which we have been
faced in the past, these estimates are not
at all discreditable to those who have control of the administration of the various Departments. I am sure I express the hope of
the Committee that when the year 1927 comes
to be reckoned with this time next year we
shall be able to emerge from it with decreased expenditure arising from the
economies which I trust will be made in all
Departments. I beg to move.

suppose we would not be in order in dealing

The CHAIRMAN: The Vote on Account is
in part a presentation of the general Estimate,
but the procedure usually followed is, that
when the Estimate proper is introduced in
full detail on the Budget statement, the
whole field of discussion is then thrown open
at that particular stage. It is obvious that a
Vote on Account, while it allows a certain
measure of latitude, does not give the wide
field that the Estimates proper present for
discussion.

The MINISTER OF COMMERCE (Mr.
Barbour): The object of the first of these
financial resolutions is to enable the Ministry
of Commerce with the approval of the
Ministry of Finance to place on the annual
Estimates any sums necessary for the purpose of assisting any light railways, either
by means of a capital sum or by an annual
payment. Similar provision is contained in
the Light Railways (Ireland) Act, but it is
necessary to re-enact this, being a financial
provision in the present Bill. So far as can
be foreseen the section will never operate in
connection with any new undertaking, but it
is necessary to make provision to continue
the grants which were agreed by the
Imperial Treasury at the inception of the
Clogher Valley Light Railway. The annual
provision to be made is in respect of a sum
not exceeding 2 per cent. of the dividends
guaranteed by the local authority on the
capital locally subscribed at the time that
that railway was laid down.
The second financial resolution which I beg
to move will enable the Ministry of Commerce to make grants from voted money for
the purpose of assisting fisheries. This power
was previously inherent in the Department
335 Administrative Provisions (Money). HOUSE OF COMMONS Administrative Provisions Bill. 336
[Mr. Barbour]
of Agriculture and Technical Instruction,
and generally speaking the grants were confined to grants in aid of the fund of boards
of conservators of inland fisheries. These
grants were to assist them in the protection
of such fisheries which are a valuable asset
to Northern Ireland, not only from the point
of view of its export trade, but also by reason
of the attraction that well stocked fisheries
prove to the more sporting class of visitors
to this area.
The third resolution which I beg to move
relates to payment out of voted money in
respect of cattle slaughtered in the case of
the existence or suspected existence of
tuberculosis. Until last year the compensation paid for cattle slaughtered by
local authorities on these grounds was as
respects one half borne directly on the rates
and as respects the other half payment was
made from the general account of the Cattle
Diseases Fund. This fund is built up from
a cattle diseases rate struck by county and
borough councils, the proceeds of which were
paid over to this State fund. In the year
1925, however, the Imperial Government considered that this was placing an undue
burden on local authorities. more parti-
Icularly in view of the national interest involved in the suppression of tuberculosis,
which, as hon. Members are aware, is at
times occasioned by germs being carried from
the cow. Accordingly an Act was passed
which extended both to Great Britain and
Northern Ireland by which the local
authority was relieved from any direct liability, one-fourth was charged to the central
fund and the remaining three-fourths was
provided from moneys voted by Parliament.
The present resolution proposes to continue
this system, which I am sure will have the
support of all hon. Members.
The fourth and last of the financial resolutions which I beg to move deals with the
State grant on account of compensation to
be paid by reason of the slaughter of animals
suffering from certain diseases. In moving
the preceding resolution I touched on the
finance of the general account of the Cattle
Diseases Fund, which in the main is provided
from a rate struck by the local authorities
themselves. There is, however, a special
account of the fund for which the State
accepts almost total liability. This account
provides for the payment of compensation in
the case of cattle slaughtered by the State
on account of pleuro-pneumonia, foot and
mouth disease or swine fever. The suppression of these diseases is regarded as a matter
of such national concern that the entire responsibility is undertaken by the State. This
resolution proposes that there shall be voted
annually to finance this special account a
sum of money not exceeding £8,000 in any
one year. This maximum is Northern Ireland's proportion of the maximum in the
Diseases of Animals Act, 1894, for all Ireland
of £20,000, I need hardly say that the
amount voted each year within this maximum is usually based on the experience of
former years. If any outbreak of these
diseases on a large scale took place in Northern Ireland it would, of course, be necessary
to seek the sanction of the House to provide
a sum in excess of the statutory maximum
proposed to be fixed by this resolution.
beg to move.
