The MINISTER OF HOME AFFAIRS (Sir
Dawson Bates): The Bill before the House is
intended to amend the Act which was passed
last year in two small but at the same time
important details. The last section of the
Act makes provision for the fixing of an
appointed day to bring into operation those
parts of the Act which deal with examinations and the issue of annual licences. These
licences, according to certain provisions of
the Act, had to be issued on or before the 1st
of January. In consequence, it was necessary
to fix the appointed day before that date so
that there might be legal authority for
collecting licence fees.
When this appointed day was fixed, all the
Act came at once into operation, including,
of course, the sections which deal with the
holding of examinations. This empowered
our Pharmaceutical Society to set up their
own examinations, but it also debarred them
from recognising those of the Southern
Society.
I had hoped that the first meeting of the
Council of the new Society could have been
held during the summer, shortly after the
passing of the Act, but owing to difficulties
which a new Society such as this had to face.
that was found quite impossible. The result
was that since the appointed day there have
been no means by which students could take
the examination and qualify for membership of the Society, and the Bill now provides for the recognition of the examinations
of the Southern Society up to 30th September
of the present year. I think to do anything
else would impose a hardship during the
interregnum between the formation of our new
Society and the setting up of the examinations under the Society. Of course, hon.
Members realise that that only lasts to 30th
September of the present year.
Another connection in which we propose to
amend the present Act is under Section 19,
sub-Section 2 of the Act, which provides for
the executors of a deceased chemist who was
registered under the Act carrying on the
business, subject to the usual control and
having a proper manager, but unfortunately
no provision was made in the case of a
business being carried on by the executors of
or
a chemist who died prior to the passing of
the Act, and therefore would not be a
registered chemist. We propose to rectify this
by providing for the business of a
chemist or druggist who dies before
within nine months of the passing of
this Act being carried on, provided
they have a qualified manager. Hon. Members will appreciate that it would be very
hard in certain cases if the executors through
a technical fault could not carry on the
business on behalf of the relatives of a deceased chemist. Those are really the only
two points in the Bill. I beg to move.
Mr. WILLIAM MCMULLEN: The way in
which measures relating to the Pharmacy
Bill have been dealt with by the right hon.
Gentleman would seem to me to be fairly
extraordinary. In May last year a Bill was
introduced which he described then as a
piece of perfect legislation. We have become used to the right hon. Gentleman and
his Parliamentary Secretary refusing to
alter even a comma in any Bill introduced
in this House. During the passage of this
Measure through the House the right hon.
Gentleman moved Amendments which occupy
about twenty columns of Hansard, and now
before the ink is properly dry on the Act
passed in May last we are asked to pass
further Amendments. I am of the opinion that
even if this amended legislation is passed
this afternoon it will be necessary before
very long to come to the House again and
ask for further legislation. I do not recollect
that the right hon. Gentleman and others
who spoke from the Government benches
made any attempt to tell us exactly how
pharmaceutical chemists. in Northern Ireland were placed under this new arrangement. I understand they are placed in a
very disadvantageous position, and that there
are no reciprocal arrangements between the
Pharmaceutical Societies in Great Britain
and the Free State with that in Northern
Ireland, so that the activities and the operations of pharmaceutical chemists who
qualify in Northern Ireland are very much
circumscribed.
It is not possible, I understand, for a pharmaceutical chemist who qualifies in Northern
Ireland to obtain employment in the Free
State. I understand a similar state of affairs
exists in Great Britain, so far as anyone who
qualifies in Northern Ireland is concerned.
I am told on exceptionally reliable authority
those are the circumstances, and if that is
so it is not a satisfactory arrangement at all.
The Government should have taken this
aspect of the matter into consideration before now. I do not think it could be argued
that a person who qualifies in Northern Ireland is not as satisfactory a pharmaceutical
chemist as anyone who qualifies either in
the Irish Free State or in Great Britain,
Pharmacy Bill----

because the examination is exceptionally difficult, at least it is as difficult as that in any
other part of the world I have any information from. The right hon. Gentleman when
speaking to some of the Amendments in May
last stated:
This will ensure that in future those who
wish to sell poisons by retail or dispense
prescriptions will have to undergo a
lengthy practical training and pass the
severe examination required for the certificate of pharmaceutical chemist.
The point is this, if that statement is correct
how is it a person who qualifies as a pharmaceutical chemist in Northern Ireland when
he goes to Great Britain before his membership is recognised has to serve 4,000 hours?
Sir DAWSON BATES: We hope he will
be.
Mr. W. McMULLEN: Your hopes are one
thing, but the actual facts are another.
That, person at the moment is expected to
serve 4,000 hours, or two years, before he is
allowed to qualify and serve as a pharmaceutical chemist in Great Britain. Why that
should operate against a person who qualifies
in Northern Ireland is somewhat difficult to
understand as I am told a person who comes
from New Zealand will be allowed to practise
as a pharmaceutical chemist in Great Britain
on payment of a fee of fifteen guineas. It
seems a remarkable thing that a person who
qualifies in Northern Ireland should be discriminated against. Those are the points I
would like the right hon. Gentleman to take
into consideration, because it leaves a person
who qualifies in Northern Ireland in an unsatisfactory position. It means that under
the present arrangement if he becomes unemployed he has no possibilities or opportunities of obtaining employment either in
the Free State or in Great Britain, and that
is not a very satisfactory state of affairs for
a person who has passed a very stiff examination in Northern Ireland.
I think we have got the right to request
that before legislation of this kind is introduced in Northern Ireland some regard
should be had to these matters. The right
hon. Gentleman assured us on the last occasion that as a result of consultations with
members of the Pharmaceutical Chemists'
body he succeeded in having perfect legislation, and now he comes and asks us to
amend that legislation. I suggest he should
go and have consultations with those peorle
again and give them amended legislation
along the lines I have suggested. If he does
so, as far a the occupants of these benches
are concerned, we will facilitate him.
The PARLIAMENTARY SECRETARY OF
THE MINISTRY OF HOME AFFAIRS (Mr.
Hanna): I do not know if the hon. Gentleman (Mr. William McMullen) is complaining
that the Government have taken steps to set
up a Council here to secure that only people
who are properly qualified to deal in pharmaceutical matters should be allowed to do so,
or if he is complaining of the length of
service we expect or the amount of skill they
must have. It is the intention of the Government in conjunction with representatives of
the Society that those people who served
their apprenticeships here and passed their
examinations should be able to take their
place in any part of the world as skilled
pharmacists. It would be impossible for this
House, as the hon. Gentleman must know, to
pass a law that England and the Free State
should recognise our chemists immediately
they have passed their examination.
This amending Measure has been brought
in not without consultation with the members of the Northern Pharmacy Council,
but at their express request, and in strict
conjunction with them. They are anxious
for it. I understand an old arrangement
existed between the Pharmaceutical Society
in Ireland with the similar Society in
England that chemists in the one country
were recognised in the other, and we are not
without hopes that having secured that only
fit and proper person are admitted with
the passing of this amending Bill reciprocal
arrangements will again be made between
the Councils so that the chemists of the one
country will be recognised in the other.
Mr. DEVLIN: It seems to me in the
midst of this somewhat slipshod method of

McMullen has stated, with first of all a

are introduced, the ill-digested information
on which they are based, the bad draughtsmanship due to the ill-considered methods
of the Ministers, put this House to tremendous inconvenience and trouble in considering these matters. There would be a cry of

work smoothly in connection with this Bill,
which was passed during the last Session
of Parliament. The Bill before the House
is a very simple one. It is to remedy something that could not have been foreseenthat is my reading of it--when the legislation was passed last year, and I do not
think the severe criticisms that have been
passed upon those responsible for bringing
this Measure in to-day are really deserved.
As I understand the point raised by the
hon. Member for West Belfast (Mr. Devlin),
who has just sat down, in regard to having reciprocal arrangements with the authorities
in Great Britain, it is impossible for reciprocal arrangements to be made with a body
that has not been created. The Council in
connection with pharmaceutical matters in
Northern Ireland has only been brought into existence, and when it has been completed
is the time to start to have reciprocal
arrangements with the larger body in
Great Britain. I do not think there is
any point in what the hon. Member has just
said. I hope this short Bill will be placed
upon the Statue Book in a very short time
to remedy the grievances, which I am glad
to say, my right hon. Friend undertook to
remedy at the first opportunity.

Municipal Corporations Bill.
Order for Second Reading read.
Motion made, and Question proposed:
That the Bill be now read a Second time."
Sir DAWSON BATES: The object of this
Bill is to amend the law relating to the
granting of charters of incorporation as
boroughs to urban districts so as to bring
it into line with existing conditions. At the
present time, if the inhabitants of one of
the large urban districts desire that their
urban district should be constituted into a
borough with all the rights and privileges
attaching to that status, the procedure is
somewhat complicated and indefinite. Prior
to the transfer of the services under the
Government of Ireland Act, 1920, a petition
for incorporation had to be presented to
His Majesty, in whom was vested the authority to grant a charter, acting, of course,
on the advice of the Privy Council. It is
understood that the functions of His Majesty
in this respect have become delegated to the
Governor of Northern Ireland, but it appears
that there is some doubt as to whether the
Governor should act on the advice of the
Privy Council of Northern Ireland or the
Privy Council of Great Britain.
We propose under this Bill to regularise
the situation and to establish the position
of the Northern Ireland Privy Council as
the body on whose advice the Governor will
act, following any petition which his Grace
may receive from any urban authority asking
for a charter of incorporation. Under this
Bill we propose to amend Section 14 of the
Municipal Corporations (Ireland) Act, 1840.
by repealing that section and substituting
a new section enabling his Grace the
Governor, acting on the advice of the Privy
Municipal Corporations Bill-
Second Reading.
24 MARCH 1926
Council of Northern Ireland, to grant a
charter of incorporation to the inhabitants
of any urban district with a population of
not less than 10,000 inhabitants. We also
propose to preserve the rights which still
existed in the old boroughs prior to the 1920
Act, whereby they can petition, notwithstanding the fact that their population is
not up to 10,000.
I might point out that the fact of becoming
a borough, beyond the enhanced dignity
which it confers, does not confer any
additional power on the authority. Of
course one of the privileges will be that the
chairman, instead of being chairman of the
urban district council, will become Mayor,
while a certain number of the councillors
will become aldermen. In addition to that,
such a borough would be entitled to a grant
of arms, which, of course, an urban district
does not have. I beg to move.
Mr. KYLE: I want to welcome this Bill
with certain reservations. It is a good thing
that our various urban districts should be
granted charters if and when their populations warrant it, and if and when those
urban districts want to be made into municipalities, but I think that in Clause 1 of
the Bill somewhat drastic action is being
taken by the Minister before the council of
such an urban district can have a charter
granted to them. It says in the Bill that
the application for the petition must be
signed by at least one-fourth of the local
government electors within the urban district. It seems to me that that is a very
drastic barrier to put between an urban
district and the charter which it is desirable
that it should have. It would mean that
roughly 2,500 signatures would have to be
put to the petition, and any one who has
any experience of dealing with matters of
that character will know quite well that,
though it may be easy to get the signatures
put down on a piece of paper, to get 2,500
people interested out of an urban population
of 10,000 is a big proposition.
There is another thing I would like to see in
this Bill which is not in it at the present
time. That is that the Bill should empower
municipalities to carry on any work save that
which they are expressly forbidden to do by
statute. There is a reason for that.
Ministers opposite look amazed or bewildered,
but I will endeavour to make more clear the
point I want to get at. I want any municipality to have power to carry on any work
other than that which they are expressly
forbidden to do. This would enable the
municipality to have a 'bus service if they
want it, say, in Belfast, or, if Lisburn becomes a municipality, they could have a 'bus
service if they want it without having the
trouble of putting a Bill through this House;
or if the Belfast Corporation want to sell coal
direct to the people, instead of through pipes
as they do now in the form of coal gas, they
should have power to sell that coal to the
people of Belfast. If the Corporation of Belfast, or any of these villages or urban dis
tricts that are going to be made into towns,
desire to have power to have a milk supply,
they are compelled to come to this House
to seek powers to have that milk supply
established and run by the corporation of
their town. If we put in a clause in this Bill
which will empower municipalities to do anything other than that which they are
expressly forbidden to do, I think it would be
a step in the right direction. One can see,
one saw recently-
Mr. SPEAKER: I have sent for the
Municipal Corporations (Ireland) Act, 1840,
but before I get an opportunity of looking at
it perhaps the right hon. Gentleman (Sir
Dawson Bates) in charge of the Bill would
tell me whether such an Amendment as the
hon. Member for North Belfast (Mr. Kyle) is
suggesting, giving large powers to municipalities, would be an Amendment which
could be made to Section 14 of the Act of
1840, which is the section with which this
Bill deals.
Mr. WILLIAM MCMULLEN: Before the
right hon. Gentleman replies to that, would
he give an explanation of what Section 14 of
the Municipal Corporations (Ireland) Act of
1840, the section he proposes to repeal,
means? He must be aware of the fact that
we have not got all those old Acts at our disposal in order to ascertain what the purport
of these particular sections is. I think he
should give some explanation of what that
section really is.
Mr. SPEAKER: Legislation is very constantly now legislation by reference, and of
course hon. Members are supposed to go to
the Library and look up all these Acts.
Could the right hon. Gentleman (Sir Dawson
Bates) answer my question?
Sir DAWSON BATES: The suggestion
made by the hon. Member for North Belfast
(Mr. Kyle) is entirely outside the scope of
this Bill. All we really propose to do, as I
explained in my opening remarks, is to substitute the Privy Council of Northern Ireland
for the Privy Council of Great Britain. It
is simply amending the old section, and
setting up machinery for the granting of a
petition, if presented to His Grace the
Governor, asking that a local authority
should be turned into a corporation. The
suggestion is entirely outside the scope of
the Bill.
Mr. DEVLIN: In view of the discussion
that has taken place, I would like to move
that we report progress for the purpose of
having further time to consider this Bill.

Mr. DEVLIN: I beg to move to leave out

I do so for the purpose of once again, in

(Mr. Kyle) is quite right in saying that most

dealing with measures already passed. As
I said before, these Bills are flung at us.
Most hon. Members of this House are inexperienced in Parliamentary work. Other
hon. Members of the House have no time in
which to study the Bills to which these refer,
and the whole task is a very difficult one.
I think I can prove how difficult it is when

staff. not only of Civil Servants but of

we have been considering-and introduce

of this sort at hon. Members of the House

HOUSE OF COMMONS.

Thursday, 25th March, 1926.
The House met at Three of the Clock, Mr.
SPEAKER in the Chair.
Oral Answers to Questions.
EX-SERGT. P. DONOHOE'S GRATUITY.
1. Mr. KYLE asked the Minister of Home
Affairs if he would expedite the payment of
a gratuity to Mr. P. Donohoe, Ex-Sergeant,
R.U. (S.)C., who was rendered unfit for
further service by an injury received while
on duty on the 30th May, 1925.
The MINISTER OF HOME AFFAIRS
Sir Dawson Bates): The delay which has
taken place in the settlement of this case
has arisen from the fact that my Department was not aware until quite recently
that Mr. Donohoe was in receipt of a
pension as an ex-member of the Royal Irish
Constabulary. Under the Special Constabulary Pensions Amending Order, 1924, the
amount of such pension or gratuity may be
taken into consideration in the assessment
of any pension, allowance, or gratuity payable to Mr. Donohoe in respect of his
service in the Special Constabulary, and the
extent to which this factor will be taken
into account, is at present receiving my
sympathetic consideration.
I hope that the matter will be settled
within the next few days, and I regret the
delay which has unavoidably arisen.
Mr. W. MCMULLEN: I would like to
ask the right hon. Gentleman whether it is
legal to disburse outdoor relief by way of
money in Northern Ireland.
Sir DAWSON BATES:
follow.
I do not quite
Mr. W. MCMULLEN: Is it legal to give
outdoor relief in money instead of goods?
Sir DAWSON BATES: I am not aware
of anything against it. I think what has
taken place is perfectly legal.
Mr. BEATTIE: I think a clearer explanation is necessary. I would like to know
from the Minister is it the practice in
Northern Ireland in the case of the majority of Guardians to give outdoor relief in
money instead of in kind.
Sir DAWSON BATES: The hon. Member
is a Guardian himself, and is familiar with
the practice. It sometimes happens that
relief is given in money. It is usually
given in kind.
Mr. KYLE: I can give the right hon.
Gentleman an example in connection with
what has taken place at Antrim Poor-Law
Guardians where a person, who is receiving
outdoor relief, has to go to the shop of a
member of the County Council.
Sir DAWSON BATES: Unless the member of the County Council is also a member
of the Board of Guardians I am not aware
that he is doing anything illegal. I think
it is unusual but not illegal.
OUTDOOR RELIEF IN ANTRIM.
2. Mr. KYLE asked the Minister of Home
Affairs whether he is aware that the Antrim
Poor-Law Guardians in giving outdoor
relief insist that applicants for relief are
compelled to make their purchases at a
shop which is owned by a member of the
County Council.
Sir DAWSON BATES: So far as the
Ministry of Home Affairs is aware, poor
relief as dispensed by Antrim Board of
Guardians is generally paid in money, but
sometimes in kind.
No stipulation of any kind is made or
could be made by the Guardians as to where
the recipients shall spend the money or obtain the goods.
It may be added for the hon. Member's
information that a County Councillor, as
such, has no connection with a Board of
Guardians, unless he should also happen to
have been elected as a Guardian.
LABOURERS' COTTAGES IN BALLYMENA
RURAL DISTRICT.
3. Mr. KYLE asked the Minister of Home
Affairs whether any application has been
made by the Ballymena Rural District
Council to his Department for the erection
of labourers' cottages in that area; whether
any of these houses have been erected, and
whether it is a fact that no choice is
given to the applicants as to the suitability
of the sites.
Sir DAWSON BATES: The Ballymena
Rural District Council have formulated a
scheme under the Labourers Acts, providing
for the erection of 175 cottages, and a local
Inquiry in connection with the scheme is
being held on the 15th proximo.
None of the houses have yet been erected,
and cannot be started until the Ministry's
confirming Order has been issued as a result
of the Inquiry.
It is not a fact that no choice is given
to the applicants as to the suitability of the
sites. The rural district councils in Northern
Oral Answers.

HOUSE OF COMMONS
[Sir Dawson Bates]
Ireland generally endeavour to meet the
wishes of the applicants in this respect as
far as possible. In the event of any applicant being dissatisfied with the action of the
rural district council it is open to him to

INSPECTION OF MEAT.
4. Mr. KYLE asked the Minister of Home
Affairs whether he is aware that in the
Urban District of Ballymena provision has
been made for the inspection of all meat
intended to be sold within the urban area
for human consumption, and for prohibiting
the sale of meat except after inspection,
while in the adjoining rural district no such
provision exists, and if he will consider the
advisability of introducing a Bill to confer
legislative powers on rural district councils
similar to those already conferred on the
urban district councils, so as to bring about
a state of uniformity in both town and
country in the matter of ensuring for the
public a sound and wholesome meat supply.
Sir DAWSON BATES: Suitable arrangements exist already under which rural district councils can be invested with powers
enabling them to exercise control over
slaughter houses and meat supply generally
in their districts.
These powers have not been generally
availed of by rural district councils, and the
whole question of ensuring uniformity of
inspection in connection with food and milk
supplies is at present, I understand, engaging
the attention of the Local Government Commission.
Pending the receipt and consideration of
that Report, I am not at present in a position
to give any undertaking in regard to the
introduction of new legislation on the subject.
Mr. KYLE: May I ask the right hon.
Gentleman whether he would expedite the
work in that connection in view of the recent
outbreak of disease in the country areas in
particular? It is thought that this, perhaps,
has something to do with it. Would he
expedite the Local Government Inquiry, and
would he see that the rural districts put
these by-laws into force?
Sir DAWSON BATES: I can assure my
hon. Friend that the Local Government Commission, which is presided over by the hon.
Member of the University, is fully alive to
this matter.

in Parliament, which, in passing the Bill,
decided that greater hardship would be imposed by depriving the one house owner of
the right to obtain their houses for their own
occupation.

Mr. DEVLIN: In the discussion that took
place on the Address, some of us on these
Benches ventured to raise a number of
matters which we deemed to be of sufficient
public importance to bring before the
Government. I was somewhat surprised that
we really got no reply from the Government
Benches to many of the questions which
we raised on that occasion. Therefore, this
is the opportunity which presents itself for
Members like myself to, in some cases, repeat the statements we made, and in others
to bring before the House other aspects of
the question dealt with by us at the time.
Now, in the first place, I desire to register
my protest against the seeming neglect of
the Government in regard to the problem
of unemployment. It is quite true that the
right hon. Gentleman, the Minister of Labour
(Mr. Andrews) has repeatedly told us about
the work he was doing for the unemployed,
and the methods by which he was dealing
with unemployment grants, and
we have
always said, at least I have, that in that
matter he has displayed considerable sympathy, though I do not admit, nor am I
prepared to admit now, that he is free, or
that his Department is free from that
criticism which I propose to apply to the
administration of the unemployment grants.
One of the claims that have been made
repeatedly in this House, and outside this
House, by the Prime Minister, is that the
treatment of unemployed in Northern Ireland is carried out precisely on the same
lines and in the same spirit of justice and
generosity as that which exists in Great
Britain. I desire to say that that is not so.
(Hon. Members: Hear, hear.) When we consider what we regard as a very satisfactory bargain that the Government has
arrived at with the Imperial Government
in relation to the finances of unemployment
we are entitled, speaking here for the poorest
and lowliest of the population, to make a
claim for treatment at least equal to the
treatment meted out to the unemployed in
Great Britain.
It may be perfectly true that the amount
of the unemployment allowance given by the
Government is similar to that which is paid
to the unemployed in Great Britain, but
there has always been an attempt made here,
not so much by a policy of rhetorical obscurantism but rather by a complete and absolute
silence on the part of the Government to
keep this aspect of the situation entirely
away from the public, and that is that the
unemployed in Great Britain have their unemployment grant considerably augmented
by contributions from Boards of Guardians.
In the financial adjustments I therefore say
that Northern Ireland does not pay the same
amount to the unemployed as they do in
Great Britain, and that the ratepayers in
Northern Ireland have not to bear similar
burdens.
What is the reason why unemployment has
been so deeply and profoundly felt in
Northern Ireland? It is because an in-

dustrial blow has been struck at our two

blow has been struck.
Govan,
I will give you a case in point.
which is a comparatively small community,
at least small compared with Belfast, depends
entirely on shipbuilding, and their case is

Govan Parish Council, which is a body

paid out in 1925 £237,295 more in outdoor

about Poplar; I am talking about Govan.
The Belfast Guardians in 1925 only paid out
in outdoor relief £14,178, or about £7,000
more than in 1922.
I think the Minister of Finance would be
able to adjust for himself these figures and
to see what a tremendous contribution a
community like the community in Govan
must have paid in order to enable the poor
to bear the burden imposed on them by

If that generosity, if we choose to put it
that way, has been shown where only one
industry has been struck, then how much
more limited or how much more penurious
has been the spirit shown towards the unemployed here, where you have the linen industry struck as well? When we contemplate
the number of women who have been out of
employment in consequence of depression in

that
I want to come to the question of the
Ministry of Labour. The Ministry of Labour
in stopping extended benefit to so many men
and women have acted, in my judgment, in
an indefensible way. You say to these people
they must get a spell of work and stamp
their cards a certain number of weeks before
they get benefit. The Minister knows from
his own official statistics that it is impossible
for these people to get a spell of work. I
should like to ask him how many people have
been deprived of benefit on the ground that
they were not looking for work, because, as
the right hon. Gentleman knows, and as he
has often complained to me, I have showered
his Department with communications which
I have received from persons who have been
denied unemployment benefit, and the ground
on which the unemployment benefit has been
refused to them is that they were not looking
for work. Who decides that they are not
looking for work? What is the test that is
applied? I know myself that this test could
not have been effectively applied in many cases
that have come to my own personal knowledge. I have one case in my mind of one
of the decentest and most respectable men in
Belfast, who has haunted my own door-he
is only one of many but I take an interest
in them all-and who had trudged for months
in the search for work and could not get it.
Only the other day through the kindness of
an hon. Member of this House I got him
employment, and that man is moved by
almost inexpressible gratitude to the person
who secured him employment. That was one
of the men who was turned down because he
was not looking for employment. I say that
there must be some clearer explanation
given by the right hon. Gentleman (Mr.
Andrews) in regard to the methods and the
tests that are applied when these people are
refused benefit, and of the grounds upon
which they are refused, before we can regard
the present system of administration
satisfactory.

I come now to another question which I
raised here on the Address, and to which I
draw the attention of the Prime Minister,
because this is a matter about which I feel
most profoundly and one to which I think
he will give most sympathetic consideration.
That is the question of the position of the
boys and girls leaving our primary schools.
The question is: What is to become of the
adolescent population who are coming out
into the world after they have completed
such education as they have got? I understand that 12,000 boys and girls leave our
primary schools every year in Northern
Ireland, 6,000 in Belfast and 6,000 in the remainder of the Six Counties. I live quite
close to the Technical Institute here and
some evenings I watch the pupils going into
and coming out of that Institute. I watch
their ingress and egress with pride, because I am very happy to see so many of
our young men and women taking advantage of that magnificent institution.
But has it ever struck Ministers or those
who are responsible for the strength and
stability of the State and its future
what is to become, first of all, of the boys
and girls when they leave school, and,
secondly, of those more efficiently equipped
youths when they come from our great
Technical Institute? I have got no answer
to that. I think it is more than an
economic or industrial question. It is a
State question, it is a human question to

which attention must be given. I asked for

The worst of this Government is that
they have the mentality of the old politicians. They are thinking in the past.
They think that if you say a word against
the present Government you shake and destroy the glory of the Empire. That is the
attitude they take up, with the result that
every suggestion that comes from these
Benches is turned down. If it comes from
me, according to the Attorney-General (Mr.

an enemy of Ulster. I understand that is
how he stigmatised me in St. Jude's Church
the other night. I hope he will so stigmatise me here in the Presbyterian General
Assembly, because the stigmatisation is the
more sacrosanct the more sacred the institution in which it is delivered. If it comes
from me it comes from an enemy of Ulster.
If it comes from any of the hon. Gentlemen

I think the Government ought to approach

source they come from and see on their
merits how far they ought to receive the
the consideration of the Government.
Let me go further. I have in this regard, and in many other regards, to protest
against the mentality of the Government in
relation to all other parties but their own
in this House. For all practical purposes
you might as well write your decrees in
Stormont Castle, call them Bills, bring
them down here, and get them sanctioned,
if not approved, so far as our opinion in
legislation or administration is concerned.
I do not believe since we came into this
House you have ever accepted a single suggestion we made. I do not believe you have
ever accepted an Amendment we proposed.
We may be very ignorant-and no doubt we
bear the brand of our cult-but at the
same time it is quite possible that even the
most ignorant may make a suggestion
worthy of consideration, but we have never
made any. I must point out to the right
hon. Gentleman (Sir James Craig) that
when he invites us into this House and
makes what he calls, and what others call,
a generous gesture, I would like to know
what we are invited into this House for.
You could just get on the same way without us for all the influence we have been
able to exercise since we came in. I could
understand that attitude if you were dealing with politics or with matters of
sectarian concern, but not on questions of
industry, on questions of humanity, on
questions like shipbuilding, questions like
the linen industry, or housing. On
questions like unemployment and the treatment of those who are unemployed we are
far more competent to form a judgment and
to give advice than anyone on the Government Benches, because we live amongst the
people and the people are constantly coming to us. The Government in my judgment suffer from one defect. They are too
much detached from the people, and do not
know what the people are thinking or what
they are doing. Therefore, I trust that 'in
what I have said I have been able to give
you some free information which will be much
more useful to you than the legal advice
given by many of the somnolent guides and
officials whom you have.
I come now to the question of housing.
That is another matter on which we have
been treated with absolute contempt. We
have raised in this House, and out of it,
the vital importance of building houses for
the class of the community who want houses,
that is the working class. The Prime
Minister the other day, when dealing with
this matter, said-I must confess it was a
very innocent observation for him to make-
"Oh these two-roomed houses"-because I
still prefer to call them two-roomed houses
-"are only occupied by a man and his wife
without children; those who have children
can get larger houses." The right hon.
Gentleman (Sir James Craig) with his knowledge of Belfast must be well aware that
the people who go to these two-roomed
houses are the people who are worst paid,
that the men with large families are very
often the worst paid. If there is only a
man and his wife they are very often
better able to pay for a costly house than
the poor man who is badly paid with a
large family. In this regard I am glad to
see that there was a more public spirit in
the Senate than in this House, and that one
of the supporters of the Government took
up the same attitude as we did and made a
very strong appeal to the Government to do
something to give better and cheaper houses
for the badly paid working classes.
Two rooms! Why not give a larger grant
to the builders of the houses to build an
additional room and a bath room for the
poor people instead of, as I said the other
day, giving these large grants to exploiters
who build the houses and then sell them
after they are built at a profit? For the
last two or three years in passing round the
different parts of the Province, especially
where there has been increasing building
done, or in reading the housing advertisements you will see that the greater number
of the notices in the windows and of the

Dr. MORRISON: I should like to say a
word or two in reply to what has fallen from
the hon. Member for West Belfast (Mr.
Devlin). To begin, I may say I listened to
him with great interest, and with a number
of his remarks and a great many of the aims
he has in his public life I am entirely in
sympathy. He touches no subject that he
does not bring humour into and he touches,
if I might say so, no subject that he does
not adorn. Notwithstanding this similarity
of view he has raised points on which I
totally disagree with him. It may be that I
have not the vision that he has, but I understand that for the greater part of his public
life he has been trying to help the poor.
I am sure that is so, and I know he has
done very valuable work in this respect, with
a great deal of which I agree, but I, too;
in my small way have been doing a little
with the same object in view, and I am sure
he would agree with a great many of the
things I have helped.
But in this matter of unemployment insurance I believe there is room for a considerable difference of opinion. I congratulated
the hon. Member in the lobby this morning.
When coming to the House to-day I travelled
with some people from County Antrim and
we had a very interesting conversation as
to the meeting at Armoy addressed by the
hon. Member. I said I thought it was a
very nice and sensible thing that in loyal
County Antrim the Nationalists could have a
demonstration without intervention from
people who differed from them, and I hoped
that state of affairs would continue in all
parts of Northern Ireland. "Yes," said the
man, "and the curious thing is that a large
number of our people went to hear Mr.
Devlin." Said I, "I think that is not to be
wondered at, because he is a most interesting
speaker, and I am sure you would enjoy him,
but while he tells you a story that seems very
nice I could tell you a story that is different.
He tells you what he has done for pensions
and how much money he has got for the
deserving poor, and there is a considerable
amount of truth in what he says, but he does
not tell you that he wants to supplement unemployment insurance by striking rates you
farmers will have to pay." He said, "If
that is so, we have no use for Mr. Devlin.
We may as well give him the land at once
and have done with it." And the woman
who was sitting beside him told me her son
had found farming so unprofitable that
he had sold his place and gone to the
States rather than work for nothing. That
shows the point of view the agricultural
worker has towards this suggestion of the
hon. Member for supplementing unemployment insurance out of the rates.
The chief objection to the hon. Member's
proposition is this: Why should unemployment insurance be treated differently from
other subjects for which provision is made
by the Imperial Parliament and by general
agreement amongst all politicians? Why, for
instance, should unemployment insurance be
treated differently from workmen's accident

The hon. Member also referred to certain

turned down because of a complaint that

thought it unfair that he should be struck off
the dole. There was one thing in his story
that he did not venture to tell me about,
and it was that last year he was for six

said he had been turned down through an
anonymous complaint. I said that that was
a very unreasonable thing, and that I would
go to the Ministry about it. I went to the
Ministry and I found out the whole story.
They had all the files before them. The case
had been looked into very particularly, and
the decision of the Ministry with all this
evidence before them was that the man was
instructed to go before the Employment Committee and tell his story. The Ministry said,
"Here you have a Committee appointed to
deal with these things. It takes it out of the
hands of the Ministry, and if the Committee
say such a man is entitled to unemployment
benefit they will not over-rule the decision
of the Committee." The man went to the
Committee. I do not know what evidence
they had, but I know it was composed of men
of all sections, and they decided the man was
not entitled to the dole and that he had made
no genuine effort to obtain work.
I was
talking over this matter with a business man,

Remember, there is no absence of work.

-"the men are not allowed to work at that

With regard to this question of two-roomed
houses, of which I have heard so much, I am
entirely in agreement with the views put
forward by the Prime Minister when this
subject was under discussion in the House.
I have been engaged all my lifetime working
for the poor, and doing what I could for
them. I think nobody has done more as a
dispensary doctor than I did for the district
over which I was medical officer. I got the
forms and had them filled up, I condemned
the houses in which they were living, and
I had new houses built. We have double the
number of houses in that dispensary district
than are to be found in any other dispensary
district in the Coleraine Union. I speak
therefore, with authority on this matter,
with more authority, perhaps, than that
of the hon. Member for West Belfast (Mr.
Devlin). He spoke of the great improvement
in the social position of the workers who
Occupy these houses. I agree with him,
wholly agree with him. He spoke of the
bright houses, and the healthy, cheerful
children. Again I agree with him. I could
have told him how we, in our own district,
got up an association and offered prizes for
the way in which these cottages were kept.
We had rambler roses climbing up the sides
of the houses, as a result of the prizes offered
to encourage the workers to beautify their
houses and set an example to the others. It
is beyond all question that that has done
an immense amount of good. If you house a
man well, you alter his whole social position.
If we had in the country what you call here
two-roomed houses-houses with good kitchens
and two bedrooms-many of the labourers
who are compelled to live in the old cottages
would be glad and delighted. They would be
thankful to God that they had places where
they could sit under their own vine and
under their own fig tree, none daring to make
them afraid. They would not be under the
farmer; they would be sitting there free of
the farmer. They could sell their labour in
the best market, as many of them do, and
they could hold up their heads in the same
way as the farmers are now able to hold
up their heads when they meet the landlords.
I take advantage of this occasion to appeal
to the Minister of Home Affairs to see that
every facility will be given in the country
for the erection of these houses, and I could
easily understand that in Belfast it would
be an immense advantage to people to have
such cheap houses rather than to go on
living in some of the slums in which they
are compelled to reside. I had no intention
of speaking to-day, but these are subjects
that affect me very deeply, and in which I
am deeply interested. My viewpoint is
different from that of some of the Members
opposite, and I hope I am right. At any
rate, I can easily understand that people
may differ from me, and that both of us may
have the same object in view.

What happens when a claim is submitted?
The hon. Member for the University (Dr.
Morrison) said a few moments ago that

benefit is generally granted. I want to
asure him as well as other hon. Members

Claims are being submitted to the Local
Employment Committees. The Committee
hear the case. So that hon. Members may
know, let me explain that the Committee
which decides these cases is composed of an
employer, a worker and a clerk. The employer and worker, at least, decide the cases,
and the clerk registers the decision of the
Committee. The employer and worker after
having heard the applicant before them go

applicant is entitled to be recommended for
a further period of benefit. They are aware

or occupation that the applicant was seeking

the Ministry of Labour are turning down
these applicants for benefit. This is happening in numerous instances to-day. I had
just one with me before I came to the

weeks benefit. If the Minister is taking

take the word of the employer and worker

worse in the country. What happens in the

bring along a statement from the employer
the committee will not see their way to
accept it.

Mr. LEEKE: I was intending to point out
generally a field of employment, and it was
with a view to its effect on unemployment
that I had intended to discuss it.
In regard to fisheries, in the past it has
always been the habit of the Government,
through their Fishery Boards, to grant to
the Irish fishermen along our coasts money
to purchase trawlers and to purchase gear.
This in the past was largely availed of,
and in a great manner reduced unemployment around our coasts. When the system
of Government in Ireland was changed the
Fishery Boards became a reserved service,
so far as Northern Ireland was concerned,
and the Southern Government have now a
separate Fishery Board. In Northern Ireland these grants were stopped, and not
allowed to be given any more, for what
reason I cannot say, but it was a great
handicap, and to my mind the chief reason
for the unemployment which is existing
round our coast to-day. Had these grants
been continued the fishermen could have
renewed their gear and purchased boats, and
you would have found our fisheries to-day
one of the most profitable sources of employment in Northern Ireland. I hope the new
Board, whatever means by which the Government intend to carry on their fishery administration, will deal effectively with this
business.
Then there is the question of piers and
harbours. I come from County Derry, which
has one of the finest fishing grounds in
Northern Ireland washing its shores, and
which is within twenty-five miles of the
finest herring fishery, I should say possibly,
in the world. Yet, for want of harbourage,
not one local trawler can engage in the
herring industry. One of the cases to which
I should like to point is that of Portstewart.
A great deal of work has been done, grants
have been given, and little pieces added to
this pier from time to time, but there has
been no advantage, and unless a substantial
amount is given and the matter dealt with
in an effective manner, the giving of small
doles will not solve this problem. Again, in
Coleraine, we have one of the finest waterways in the country but for the fact that a
very serious sandbank lies outside the mouth
of the river. Had a grant been given for
dredging and clearing the mouth of the
river you would have had one of the greatest
commercial towns in Northern Ireland.

The hon. Member for the University (Dr.

rates and taxes it naturally follows that

of hands. It is only by keeping expenses

their industry, and at the same time employ
and give the agricultural labourer the
standard of subsistence to which he is
entitled, or give him those facilities which
are essential to his life and comfort and
which make him an effective workman.
If the Government could see their way to
carry out my idea in regard to the fisheries
I would suggest that they should appoint a
small Committee to go into the matter of
the whole fishing industry in Northern Ireland, and to accept suggestions from people
who are interested in it regarding the manner in which it should be governed and developed in the future. I respectfully submit
to the House that this should be promptly
and effectively dealt with, as I hold it would
be one of the first ways in which unemployment could be reduced in the Northern area.
I know that there are fishermen at present
anxiously awaiting some move by the
Government by which they will be able to
purchase new boats and new gear in order
to engage in this attractive industry which
lies off our coasts, and which is at present

should be set up to go into that and see how

not been developed to the extent that they
should, and lesser still have the deep sea

miles of fisheries lying without a harbour or

which would attract customers. I hope the

industry developed to its utmost limits and

What policy has the Government to deal
with the problem of unemployment? They
have no policy at all. They have no conception of the way in which they should deal
with the problem. Suggestion after suggestion has been made by Members sitting in
these Benches-I think we could fairly claim
a monopoly of suggestions as far as this
House is concerned-that some attempt
should be made to find the number of youths
and juveniles in our industries at the present time and also the number of people of
65 years of age in them. There should be
some attempt made at one end of the scale
to give juveniles and youths a better education than they get at the present time, and
there should be an attempt to take our aged
of 65 and over 70 out of industry, in order
to give our young and middle-aged, male
and female, population an opportunity of
performing useful service. I will be told
that will cost money. I have been told
before that it would cost money, but I believe it would be a much better alternative
than paying approximately £53,000 per week
in unemployment benefit indiscriminately.
We may temporarily relieve the situation
until such time as the Government may be
able to prepare even some partial solution

There are a great many proposals that

our imports are paid for by our exports, and
I find that last year our imports exceeded
our exports.
Mr. POLLOCK: By how much?
Mr. W. MCMULLEN: I do not know

He was a member of the Conference which

and myself, so that we might explore this

was actually the Vice-Chairman of one of

Purposes Committee. We established sub-committees of that Conference of men engaged in
the different industries-shipbuilding, linen,
and the building trade-and they investigated
their own particular side of the problem
Reports were presented by them and the

anything new that the Government could
do in order to deal with this problem, in

proved the truth of what I have frequently
said in this House, that this problem cannot be solved by any Government. It can
only be solved when trade gets going again
through its natural channels and when the
state of Europe permits that being an
accomplished fact. No Government can
compel people to order ships who do not
require ships or to order linen who do not

that I say this Government has done to the

doing everything possible to help our unemployed. I deplore the fact that Members
of the Opposition should come here and
raise these debates with the greatest of
frequency, and at the same time not be able
to make a single practical suggestion towards the solution of the problem.

Members of the Opposition pursue which,

to take into consideration some statutory

The hon. Member for West Belfast (Mr.
Devlin) went over ground I intended to travel
myself, and I would agree with him in
several of the remarks he has made. He
quoted the case of Govan in regard to the
assistance that unemployed were getting
from the relief committees in that area. I
myself on a previous occasion quoted Partick
in regard to the scale of family income
adopted there, and pointed out that it was
sufficient to maintain a family of three. The
scale here is 42s 6d for three persons, and
is much lower. I have made inquiries, and
find that in every industrial city, such as
Govan, Partick, Glasgow, Birmingham, Manchester, London, Southampton, and Cardiff,
the scale of family income is on a higher
percentage than obtains in the City of
Belfast. I have repeatedly condemned that
scale and how it was based.
I have shown by argument that the cost
of living is higher here than in Great
Britain. The Minister of Labour has repudiated that, and takes the report of the
Committee on the Cost of Living that was
set up in Northern Ireland as his authority.
I want to tell the Minister that the report
of that Committee did not convey to the
minds of the general public the real position
as to the cost of living in Northern Ireland.
Although it was argued that the cost of
living was higher here at that particular
time there were other reasons brought in
by the Committee-no separate index figures
were set out. At that time it was recognised
that the cost of living was higher here than
in Great Britain, and I based my arguments
on that point of view.
I believe that the Government has room
for improvement in this connection without
violating any of the conditions attached to
the Uemployment Insurance Agreement
with Great Britain. There is room for improvement in regard to the period within
two years, owing to the small scope of our
area and the few industries at the command
of the unemployed workers of the Six
Counties. I referred previously to the poorlaw. The Minister says it is the duty of
Boards of Guardians to give outdoor relief.
The Minister and his colleagues have, I am
sure, repeatedly read about my colleague
(Mr. W. McMullen) and myself being politely
put outside meetings of the Guardians. What
for? For asking them to do their duty as
public representatives to the unemployed
workers of Belfast, and give them assistance
on parallel lines with that given across the
water. I ask the Government to bring pressure to bear on the Boards of Guardians.
A controversy arose between the Minister of
Home Affairs (Sir Dawson Bates) and the
Board of Guardians. He claimed that the
Guardians had all sufficient powers to do
what was necessary, while the Guardians
declared that they had no such power. I
want the Government to step into that breach
and tell the Guardians and the public gener-
Consolidated Fund Bill-
Second Reading.
HOUSE OF COMMONS
[Mr. Beattie]
ally that Section 13 of the 1898 Act is
workable in Northern Ireland in the same
way as it is worked across the Channel.
The Minister of Labour (Mr. Andrews)
referred to the relief committee that was
formed last year, and of which the hon.
Member for West Belfast (Mr. Devlin), who
sits behind me, was vice-Chairman. He says
that after the reports of that committee had
been issued nothing new came forward. It
was not the fault of the Committee. It was
the fault of the agenda to which they were
tied down and the scope to which their
activities were confined.
Mr. ANDREWS: On a point of order, I
really must correct my hon. Friend (Mr.
Beattie). I am sorry to interrupt, but it is
necessary that I should let the public know
what the position is. In no way were the
Committee tied down. The Committee had
power to go over as wide an area as ever
they liked, and to cover the whole field of
unemployment from every standpoint.
Mr. BEATTIE: I accept the statement of
the Minister. I took it from the various
statements made of ways and means whereby
the problem of unemployment could have
been attacked. I think the hon. Member for
West Belfast (Mr. Devlin) put other points
of view before the Government, but the
Government refused to accept them in the
light in which he presented them. It was
from that point of view that I made the
statement. I wanted to say that the Committee had at its command representatives
of all classes, and several schemes of relief
could have been brought about which the
Minister's own Committee had also been discussing. These schemes were not brought
forth, why I do not know, but perhaps whoever replies for the Government may be able
to tell us.
One of the schemes was the widening of
the Upper Newtownards Road, to make the
footpath safe for travellers who have to use
it against the heavy motor traffic that goes
along that road. That was one of the suggestions put forward at the Minister's Committee. It was stated that both the Belmont
and Knock Roads were unsafe for people to
walk on the footpath, and that actually one
part of the road had no footpath at all.
That would have employed from three to
four hundred men and would have been at
least a palliative. If the Minister had
accepted the suggestion from the Committee
it would have given a short spell of employment to some of the unfortunate people who
are so long out of employment, and who are
denied the right to unemployment benefit.
The next point to which I would like to
draw the Minister's attention is the adminis
tration of the regulations. I suppose I am
one of the Members who just knows sufficient to warrant him in attacking the
Minister of Labour's Department on occasions when I think fit. The Minister states
that three per cent. have been turned down
as against the statement of the hon. Member
for North Belfast (Mr. Kyle) of fifty per cent.
I do not believe that they eventually went as
far as fifty per cent-(hon. Members: Hear,
hear)--but if they have only gone the length
of three per cent. then that three per cent.
must have come to my door, without at all
taking into consideration the number of
claims to which hon. Members sitting alongside and behind me attend. I believe I must
have attended to three per cent, of the claims
turned down. Therefore. I feel justified in
saying that a very large percentage of the
claims that are recommended by the Rota
Committees are disallowed when they go to
headquarters on the grounds, as set out in
the regulations, either of family income, or
of not having sufficient employment within
the past two years, or of not genuinely seeking work.
I know from my personal experience that
the hon. Member for West Belfast (Mr.
William McMullen), who sits beside me, is
right when he states that the 6,000 people
who are off the register have not really found
employment. Some may have found employment, but the 6,000 have not, and I do not
believe that the Parliamentary Secretary to
the Ministry of Labour (Mr. Gordon) has
any authority for saying that 6,000 persons
have found employment within the last three
months. My contention, so far as the reduction of the register is concerned, is that
1,600 Specials had to come on to unemployment insurance, and so the regulations were
put into operation and the rod was laid on
fast and furious for a period of two months,
weeding out all the applicants it was possible
to weed out and throwing them on the streets
with the idea that these 1,600 men were to
come on to the register on the 1st March.
Perhaps the Minister may say that that is a
wild idea, but it is my opinion, and I am
right in holding the opinion that the
Ministry made the regulations more severe
in the first two months of this year than was
necessary, with the result that a lot of
people are in semi-starvation at the present
time and living on charity from one day to
the other.
The next thing to which I would like to
draw the attention of the Government is
housing and their failure to tackle the question in a reasonable way. Housing has been
under discussion by the Government, and,
while from their speeches they seem to be
anxious to solve it, they have never made
a real effort to solve the housing problem.
If the Government were serious about the
problem at all they would have set up a
Second Reading.

Consolidated Fund Bill-
25 MARCH 1926
committee with the object of building themselves the houses necessary to house the
people. It is part of the Government's duty
to see the people fed, and I think they were
neglectful as representatives of the people in
not setting up a housing scheme of their
own and in getting the labour put into
operation with so many people unemployed.
The Minister of Home Affairs (Sir Dawson
Bates) spoke about a bath. I would like to
tell the Government that working-class
people require to be washed just the same
as the Government. There is only one difference, namely that the working-class people
would not require any whitewashing the
same as the Government. We may be gross
and crude, but the hon. Member for West
Belfast (Mr. William McMullen), I think,
expressed it when he said it is a grand little
class to belong to.
I want to say quite candidly that the lack
of sincerity on the part of the Government
since I became a Member of this House in
regard to the requirements of the working
classes of the Six Counties has been deplorable. I regret that they have not tried to
put their house in order and to establish
themselves as a Government to which the
people would look up and of whom they could
say, "They have done their best for us."
All I can say is that if this is the best
the Government now in office can do for the
people of the Six Counties, then the sooner
the people realise that and say "You are unfit to hold office in the Six Counties. We will
have to displace you and put the Members
of the Opposition in your place," the better,
because, even if we did not put all we would
like to into practice, we would have the sincerity. You were sincere enough in your
talk, but when it came to putting it into
practical operation it did not materialise,
and the people had to suffer because the
Government were thinking more of economy
than of the peoples' needs.
Before sitting down I would like to say
that I endorse all the remarks passed by my
hon. Friends on the Front Bench and behind
me. The sooner the Government realise their
fault in neglecting the wants of the people
and drop their policy of coming here one
day, and no sooner are they here than they
are thinking about what time they can get
away, the sooner they get into good practical
working order the better for them and for
the people. I endorse all the remarks that
have been made from this side of the House.
Mr. THOMAS HENDERSON: I have listened with a good deal of attention to the
speeches delivered from both sides of the
House to-day regarding many important
questions concerning the lives of the people
of Ulster. I am satisfied after listening to
the speeches from this side of the Houseand with a great many of them I quite
agree that had the Government any plans
for solving the unemployment problem they
would readily put them into operation. I
regret, along with many other hon. Members
on this side of the House, the absence of
the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Archdale)
this afternoon. I think his presence was
most important in view of the statements
that have been made from the Government
Benches regarding emigration. If the
Canadian Government and the Australian
Government can bring people from this
country, place them on the land out there,
give them the land, give them implements
to till the land, give them homes to go into,
surely to goodness the question of adopting
some regulations so that the Ulster people
might be put on the land here instead of
being obliged to go to foreign lands is worthy
of consideration by the Government. I think
the Minister of Agriculture should have been
here to let hon. Members know whether
emigration is a good thing or a bad thing
for Ulster. Personally, I believe that, with
hundreds of thousands of acres lying undeveloped in Ulster, emigration is a bad thing
for Ulster, and that if this Ulster land were
developed it would be a good thing for Ulster.
Regarding the road construction schemes,
about which many of us on the Opposition
Benches have spoken, report has it that the
London Omnibus Company have purchased
many of our local firms here. If that is so,
the people from London will make you hurry
up and give employment in the reconstruction of your roads. Going out on one of
the country roads, I found that the Ulster
Government apparently has no control over
the urban districts. I think the time has
arrived now when the Minister of Home
Affairs should have a frontage line on all
our main arterial roads, that is for the
future development of Ulster. Motor
omnibuses and other motor vehicles have
come to stay, and it is absolutely necessary
that the Minister of Home Affairs should be
the responsible authority in the reconstruction of the roads for future development.
Many of our main roads are a disgrace.
Belfast is the capital of Ulster now, and it is
essential that the main roads throughout
the length and breadth of the Province
should be made 60 feet wide and should be
constructed in such a way as to be able to
carry the heavy traffic of the future. The
Minister of Home Affairs should get in touch
with the various urban districts and the
authorities in the small towns and get them
to arrange to have a frontage line. If you
go along any of these roads you will find
new houses are being built, and they are
making the roads so narrow that when
Ulster develops in the future these people
will have to be paid heavy compensation
in order that the roads should be widened.

HOUSE OF COMMONS
[Mr. Thomas Henderson]
The hon. Member for East Belfast (Mr.
Beattie) spoke about the widening of the
Belmont Road and the Knock Road. What
has happened there? It is necessary for the
Corporation time and again to negotiate
with the people who Own the ground.
They will not part with their ground except
they get an exorbitant price.
Mr. BEATTIE: Take it from them.
Mr. T. HENDERSON: I would not like
to say that. If some individual was coming
along the street with no coat and took the
coat off the back of the hon. Member for
East Belfast he would not be well pleased.
These people have got the ground, and the
responsible people have let them build out
on the frontage so near to the road that it
is essential should now be widened. The
people were quite right in getting the best
bargain they could for their ground. The
time has arrived when the Minister of Home
Affairs will have to take drastic action in
regard to the frontage line on all the main
roads throughout Ulster. I have spoken
and other hon. Members have spoken on
various schemes for the relief of unemployment. One that I referred to was the reclaiming of the foreshores. The land could
be utilised for the benefit of the Ulster
people in the future. I also spoke abɔut
extending our docks. It is the duty of the
Government to extend the docks.
Mr. ANDREWS: No, no.
Mr. T. HENDERSON: It is to the
Government the people will have to look to
in future to make Ulster the Ulster we want
to see it. The small urban councils will
not develop the docks and arrange for the
berthing of Atlantic steamers, therefore, it
is up to the Government to step in and
make the docks. It is absolutely essential
that the Government should adopt other
methods of solving this very important
question, as apparently the old methods are
no good. It is necessary
now for the
Government if they want to try to solve
this question, to throw some of the responsibility on the Opposition side by setting up
a Commission and inviting Members of the
Opposition to sit on it. It is also most
essential that the principals who were responsible for the unemployment should also
sit on that Conference, that is the captains
of industry who made huge fortunes in the
past.
Mr. T. W. McMULLAN: And lost them.
Mr. T. HENDERSON: Very few of them
lost them. Many of them are enjoying
them in foreign lands. I would suggest
that these captains of industry should be
compelled to go there and explain why
they have not come to the Government's
assistance in trying to relieve this very important question of unemployment. I have
very little respect for the captains of the
linen industry. They have let it lapse in
such a way that it will never recover. It
does not matter whether this Government
gives grants to the linen industry. It is
my honest belief the linen industry will
never come back to Ulster. What is at the
back of it? I may be wrong, but my
opinion is that the reason there is so much
unemployment is the action of people in a
certain position trying to get the wages
of the industrial and agricultural workers
in Ulster reduced. I think it is the duty
of the Government to punish those people
as they are really responsible for the starvation that exists in our midst.
I have often sent hundreds of people to
the Minister of Labour, and numbers of
those people have been turned down. Some
of them to my mind were unjustly turned
down and very harshly treated. Of course,
I do not know all the facts, but I believe
that in some cases some of the applicants
for unemployment insurance were harshly
treated and were entitled to get the money.
If there is a better way of treating those
people who are unemployed in the future
than there has been in the past I for one
will be delighted to see it, and I am certain
every Member of the Opposition will agree
that the Minister of Labour should try to
bring about that result which will bring
happiness to the homes of those people.
I would suggest to the Government now
that they should hurry on with the building
of the Parliament House at Stormont. Surely
to goodness there are some parts of the plans
ready which would enable a very large
number of men to be employed. The Minister
of Labour has said there is going to be
an avenue constructed to the Parliament
House at a cost of £50,000. The weather has
taken up now, and since the time the
Minister spoke about it a considerable
number of men could have been almost
started there.
Mr. ANDREWS: So there are.
Mr. T. HENDERSON: Are they started?
Mr. ANDREWS: Almost.
Mr. T. HENDERSON: I am very glad the
work has started, and that some of these
people will be able to eat their Easter eggs.
Mr. WILLIAM MCMULLEN: Almost
started.
Mr. T. HENDERSON: I hope they will be
started before Easter. I would suggest to
the Government that they should get on with
the law courts. What is holding them up
there? There is no one working on the law
courts now, yet the ground was acquired

Mr. DEVLIN: On a point of order. We

Mr. T. HENDERSON: My reason for bringing forward that question about bobbed hair
was that a very eminent specialist says that
the ladies of the future if they are not careful

House they have given very useful advice

heard the Minister of Labour criticising the

Mr. T. HENDERSON: I admit the Government have done a few things that have relieved unemployment, but something more
drastic will have to be done for the unemployed of Ulster. Seeing the Prime Minister
is here, I would say that it is time this
emigration stunt was stopped. The Government should try to keep the Ulster people
at home. In regard to the suggestion of the
hon. Member for West Belfast (Mr. W.
McMullen), that the land should be taken
from the people, it is easy for the Government to acquire it from the people and compensate them for it. They could put them
on the land instead of sending them to
foreign places. Ulstermen and women do not
want to leave these shores. They want to
stay at home. I hope the Government will
come back after Easter with new ideas
Mr. DEVLIN: Hear, hear.
Mr. T. HENDERSON: The old ideas, to
my mind, have failed them. They need new
ideas, and the only way to get them is by

because, after all, trade-union leaders are

Things have reached the stage that the
Government cannot solve the unemployment
problem, and no matter how we may blackguard the Government from this side of the
House it is not going to do any good. It is

Mr. MCALLISTER: I was rather tickled
at the introductory 1eferences of the

very admirable
Measure which was passed here, the Small
Dwellings Acquisition Act. As the House is

This Act has been passed, but for some
reason or other it has been pigeon-holed,

authorities. I had a question on the Paper
to-day on this subject, and I was astonished
to find that there are only six local bodies

District of Belfast, that have made application to make this Act operative. In the

Belfast, there have been only 140 applications

picturesque legislation. I do know of one

not even treated with the decency and

Another circumstance which tends to retard the progress of provincial towns in

Mr. SPEAKER: I thought that, from

The hon. Member was good enough to give

I have looked into the matter. I cannot do
better than read to the House what the rule
is. On page 365 of Erskine May's book, it is
stated:-
407 Municipal Corporations Bill- HOUSE OF COMMONS

Committee
[Mr. Speaker]
The amendments which an instruction
proposes to sanction must be such as
would further the general purpose and
intention of the House in the appointment
of the Committee. The object of an
instruction is, therefore, to endow a Committee with power whereby the Committee
can perfect and complete the legislation
defined by the contents of the Bill, or
extend the provisions of a Bill to cognate
subjects; and an attempt to engraft novel
principles into a Bill, which would be
irrelevant, foreign or contradictory to the
decision of the House taken on the introduction and Second Reading of the Bill,
is not within the due province of an
instruction.
I am afraid that a sweeping amendment
such as the hon. Member desires to propose
would be an attempt to engraft novel principles into this Bill. Therefore, even if it
were possible for him to move an instruction-which it is not without notice-I do
not think an instruction would be in order.
Considered in Committee.

Oral Answers to Questions.
APPOINTMENTS TO STAFF OF CROWN
AND PEACE, BELFAST.
1. Mrs. CHICHESTER asked the Minister
of Finance whether any appointments have
been made to the staff of the Clerk of the
Crown and Peace, Belfast, since the passing
of the County Officers and Courts Act
(Northern Ireland), 1925; if so, whether such
appointments were made in accordance with
the terms of that Act, and whether the persons appointed were ex-Servicemen,
The MINISTER OF COMMERCE (Mr.
Barbour): My right hon. Friend (Mr. Pollock)
has asked me to take this question for him.
per-
No definite appointments have been made
to the staff of the Clerk of the Crown and
Peace, Belfast, since the passing of the
County Officers and Courts Act (Northern
Ireland), 1925, save of those officers who,
under the terms of the Act, were entitled
to permanent establishment. Some
manent posts are still unfilled, and under
Regulations shortly to be issued will be
staffed by candidates recruited by examination. In the meantime, in order not to
hamper the work of the office, it was found
necessary to make temporary appointments
to these posts, and assent was given to the
transfer from the personal staff employed
by the Clerk of the Crown and Peace, in his
capacity as Registration Officer of Voters'
Lists of two officers who were not ex-Servicemen. The last two temporary appointees
have, however, been ex-Servicemen candidates.
As stated, however, these appointments are
purely temporary, pending examination
candidates becoming available.
CONVICTIONS AGAINST LICENSED
TRADERS.
2. Mr. CRAWFORD asked the Minister of
Home Affairs whether he will state the
number of convictions against licensed
traders for the years 1924 and 1925 respectively, and also the number of cases in which
their licences were endorsed.
The MINISTER OF HOME AFFAIRS (Sir
Dawson Bates): The number of convictions
in 1924 was 234, as against 196 in 1925.
Licences were endorsed in 27 cases in 1924,
and in 14 cases in 1925.
NEWTOWNARDS CAMP.
3. Major SHILLINGTON asked the Minister
of Home Affairs under what terms the camp
at Newtownards is in the occupation of the
Northern Government; also, how many men
are quartered there at the present time.
Sir DAWSON BATES: The camp at Newtownards is held by the Ministry under a
yearly agreement dated 30th November, 1925,
from the War Department at an annual
rent of £1,080, subject to six months' notice
on either side.
The Ministry has to pay all rates and taxes,
to insure the premises, and to keep them in
good condition and repair.
The number of men quartered at Newtownards camp at present is 143 of all ranks,
including 20 members of the Special Constabulary.
