ORDERS OF THE DAY.
Mines (Working Facilities, Support
etc.) Bill.
Order for Second Reading read.
Motion made and Question proposed:
"That the Bill be now read a Second Time."
The MINISTER OF COMMERCE (Mr.
Barbour): The primary object of this
Bill is to enable rights to work
minerals to be granted in cases where
there is a likelihood that they may
be left permanently unworked, either
through legal disability, or through the concurrence of two or more persons being required and not being obtainable, or, further,
by reason of the minerals being owned in
such small parcels that they cannot be
properly or conveniently worked by themselves. In order further to facilitate the
working of minerals power is also taken in
the Bill to grant ancillary rights, such as
way leaves and the right to a water supply.
A surface owner may claim protection for
his interests in respect of damage to any
buildings or works belonging to him by
reason of the working of minerals under his
land, or compensation in the event of its
being held that the importance of the getting
of minerals is paramount.
The power to grant rights to work minerals
or ancillary rights, or to impose restrictions
upon the working of minerals is vested in
the Ministry of Commerce acting upon the
findings of a tribunal which is set up by
Clause 11 of the Bill. With respect to the
personnel of this tribunal I should explain
that in Great Britain, where a similar Bill
received legislative sanction in the year 1923,
the Railway and Canal Commissioners constitute the tribunal. Their services are not,
however, available for this particular duty
in Northern Ireland, and it becomes
necessary, therefore, to set up a new body in
Northern Ireland.
The members of the tribunal in Northern
Ireland will number three, one being a
practising barrister of at least ten years'
standing, one a member of the Panel of
Official Arbitrators, and one an officer of the
Ministry of Commerce. In cases where there
may be dissatisfaction with the findings of
the tribunal as to the amount of compensation, provision is made for an appeal to the
County Court; and it is provided that in
hearing such appeals the County Court shall
have the assistance of a specially qualified
assessor.
Hon. Members may remember that the
Commission on the Natural and Industrial
Resources of Northern Ireland recommended
the application to Northern Ireland of a
Measure on the lines of that now before the
House. Other representations to the same
effect have been made to my Ministry, and,
while I do not desire to suggest that undue
obstruction to the development of minerals
has occurred in the past, I do think that the
existence of the powers outlined in Part 1 of
this Bill will tend to foster the development
of the mineral resources of our Province.
Part II of the Bill concerns coal mining
only, and repeals two sections of the Mining
Industry Act, 1920. The first is Section 4,
which required the Board of Trade to appoint
Pit and District Committees and Regional
and National Boards. As hon. Members will
appreciate, local conditions in Northern Ireland render a provision of this kind unnecessary in our Province. Section 20 of
that Act established a Fund, for the
improvement of social conditions of colliery
workers, to be administered by a Committee
and a body of Assessors officially appointed.
Mines Bill-
Second Reading.
HOUSE OF COMMONS
[Mr. Barbour]
The income of this Fund is derived from a
levy upon the coal owners of one penny per
ton of the output of coal mines. The life of
the Fund was limited by the Act of 1920
to five years, which period expired in
March, 1926. While such a Fund may be
desirable and of value to the workers in Great
Britain where the coal mining industry has
attained very large proportions, there
appeared to be little justification for putting
it into operation in Northern Ireland during the past two years. We have only one
coal mine, and during the past two years
it had not fully emerged from the development stage. A levy of one penny per ton
upon the output would not have produced a
sum sufficiently large to make a contribution of any effective value to the welfare of
the workers. We, therefore, propose through
a slight amendment, which I shall move on
the Committee stage, to ask the authority
of the House for the view that Section 20
is not applicable to the circumstances obtaining in Northern Ireland. I beg to move.

Mr. BARBOUR: With the permission of

under the Bill is to provide facilities which
do not exist at the present time, and that
is what I tried to make clear. Any rights
that have existed in the past are not intended to be interfered with under this Bill
provided these rights are not exercised in
the obstruction of the development of such
mineral resources as might have existed.
This Bill is entirely to provide or to secure
the granting of rights where it is really in
the interest of the community that minerals
should be worked, but where those rights
cannot be obtained for various reasons. One
may be due to the owners of the property
where the minerals are situated not being in
a position to grant sufficient legal title to the
working of the minerals. Another case may
be where the minerals would have to be
worked under two or more separate properties and where the consent of two
three separate owners would be required in
order to make it a satisfactory proposition.
The Bill is not designed to include quarries
as minerals in quarries will never be permanently lasting in the same
way that

HOUSE OF COMMONS
Sir DAWSON BATES: This Estimate
possesses at all events one satisfactory
feature, that is, it represents a saving of
over £15,000 as compared with last year.
Last year the Estimate was for £70,365,
while this year it is £54,863.
This decrease is due to a variety of reasons.
It is partly due to the fact that we have
fewer convicts and fewer prisoners. That
everyone in this House will agree is satisfactory. Last year owing to there being no
accommodation for convicts in Northern Ireland we had to maintain a considerable
number of convicts in English and Scottish
prisons at very considerable expense. Since
that time we have been able to fit up part of
Belfast gaol as a convict prison, and we have
been able to bring back all our convicts who
were formerly in England and Scotland, and
following the reduction of prisoners we have
been able to make certain re-arrangements with a view to further economy.
have reduced Derry Prison to the status of
a local prison or bridewell now, and instead
of having a governor there we have a
warder in charge. This enabled us to transfer the Governor of Derry Prison to Armagh,
to take the place of the Superintendent who
had resigned. This, of course, effected
considerable economy.
We
a
This new arrangement has also enabled us
to transfer a number of warders to Belfast
Prison, and the result is we have been able
to deal with these new prisoners from
England and Scotland practically without
any increase to the general staff.
Hon. Members will observe in looking
through the Estimate that in addition we
have been able to make a considerable reduction in the total number of our staff.

Now with regard to food, the Committee

in the food of the prisoners.
duction is mainly due to perhaps better contracts and reduced prices. I would like to

We have made arrangements for the erection of 16 houses for the use of married
warders within the Belfast Prison grounds,
but of course outside the prison walls. It
will be very much more satisfactory to have
these warders close at hand, and in addition
it will enable us to effect a considerable
saving in the allowances for these warders
for quarters when they had to find them.
With regard to motor transport last year
a system of motor transport for the conveyance of female prisoners to Armagh from
Belfast was instituted by means of a prison
van. The system proved both economical and
satisfactory as it saved escort, and it is
undesirable to have these women taken by
train. Now to meet an objection that was
raised we have decided to have this van running daily, so as to enable us to discharge
these female prisoners in Belfast rather
than Armagh, where they have to find their
own way home by train.
I think hon. Members will agree that
while the main object of imprisonment is
that it will act as a deterrent, at the same
time, where possible, we should do something on the reformative side of prison
treatment, I feel that this applies particularly in the case of first offenders and
youthful criminals, and every effort is made
to keep this aspect of the question before
our prison officials, and I am glad to say
that they entered into the spirit of it and
are fully alive to the necessity of helping.
I would like to refer to the activities of
the Prisoners' Aid Societies operating in
Northern Ireland, which are run entirely
as voluntary institutions. A small grant
is made to them out of Government funds
towards the expenses, and the gratuities,
which are earned by prisoners, are paid to
the prisoners through these societies.

think the greatest possible affliction that can

In the first place, I wish to protest against
the outrageous conduct of the hon. Gentleraan in raising religious questions in this
House. When we raise any question about
the rights of minorities you are always
howling about our introducing sectarianism,
and here is an hon. Gentleman, a pious,
glorious, and immortal, one of the high elect
of Christianity in County Antrim, a model
for the people down there, and he comes
here and not only introduces sectarianism
but introduces it in a grossly offensive and
inaccurate fashion.
He has stated that the salary of the
Catholic chaplain is greater than the salary
of the Protestant chaplain. Now, there are
two Protestant chaplains at £320, and one
Catholic chaplain at £260. The opinion
the hon. Member expressed and wanted
to give to the public was that there were

paid to the Catholic chaplain on that
account. I think that was an absolutely
indecent and outrageous statement for the
hon. Member to make. The fact of the

way about.
I am sorry this matter has been raised,
but I am not going to sit in this House
and hear a statement of this character made
by one of a party who constantly complain
about our introducing sectarianism if we
raise a question here about the way the
minority is treated, and I want to contradict his statement.
Mr. CRAWFORD: I challenge the hon.
Member for West Belfast (Mr. Devlin), or

Sir DAWSON BATES: In regard to the

With regard to the question raised by the

prisoners are allowed to associate under

With reference to the pay of the chaplains,
which has been raised by several hon.
Members, I did not have the privilege of
fixing these salaries. These chaplains were
existing officers when we took over the
Prison service and their salaries were fixed

of prisoners belonging to the different denominations which the chaplains represented.
So far as I am concerned, if it comes to the

Government cannot alter the salaries or

conditions under which these chaplains were

With regard to the question raised by the
Member for Antrim (Mr. Crawford), I am
afraid he does not give the Government
credit for very much. I think he has added
everything together, divided the total cost
by the number of prisoners, and says the
result is the cost per head. I would prefer
to think that the hon. Member has not taken
the trouble to analyse the figures and work
out the actual cost, rather than that he was
trying to mislead the House, because a great
deal of this expenditure is for structural
alterations, the cost of the erection of these
houses at the Crumlin Road Gaol, and so on.
He will find that the cost works out at £103
per annum. We paid £126 to the Scottish
Prisons' Board for the maintenance of our
convicts, and I think hon. Members will
agree, therefore, that this is on the whole
a reasonable figure.
It has been suggested that the cost of
Derry Prison is unreasonable. Hon. Members realise, of course, that the smaller the
number of prisoners the greater are the overhead charges, and I cannot see my way at
the present time to close down Derry Prison.
If Derry Prison were closed down, we might
be able to effect some economies all round,
but as matters stand now I canot see my way
to close that Prison. We maintain it as a
sort of local Prison.
Then, again, I am told that the cost of
escorts is too high, but if Derry Prison were
closed down, there would be an enormous
addition to the cost of escorts, because
prisoners sentenced to a fortnight's or a
month's imprisonment would have to be
brought to Belfast. I would ask hon.
Members to go into the figures more carefully. I take credit for the fact that we have
made enormous economies during the past
year, and I hope that we will be able to
effect greater economies during the present
year. We must, however, have efficiency in
our Prison Service.

Industrial Assurance.

13 APRIL 1926
Industrial Assurance.
The following Notice of Motion stood on
the Paper in the name of Dr. Morrison:-
"That, in the opinion of this House, the
Industrial Assurance (Northern Ireland) Act,
1924, has not been instrumental in abolishing or effectually controlling the abuses
which existed previous to the passing of that
Act; and this House calls upon the Government to appoint a Select Committee to investigate and report upon the whole question
of Industrial Assurance in Northern
Ireland."
Mr. SPEAKER: Before the hon. Member
proceeds, I take it that he has got a seconder
for the Motion?
Mr. DEVLIN: If nobody else seconds the
Motion, I will do so.
Dr. MORRISON: I beg to move. This
matter, so far as I know, is non-controversial. Every Member of this House has
the same object in view as I have, and whatever decision we come to will be a decision
to try to secure that justice shall prevail
in Northern Ireland. The Second Reading
of our Industrial Assurance Act took place
on 8th October, 1924, and those who turn
up the Official Report, Volume 4, No. 15,
will find that the Minister of Agriculture
on that occasion informed the House that
the average of the sums assured was about
£10, and that the payments made were
about 2 d. per week. The total amount contributed under this system in the United
Kingdom was £37,000,000 a year. Then he
made what was, to me, a striking statement, that for every shilling paid by these
people, sevenpence was returned to them, and
fivepence went to the Companies. In ten
years 9,000,000 policies were issued by one
company, and of that number 6,400,000
lapsed.
Mr. KYLE: For the purposes of accuracy,
would the hon. Gentleman enlighten me by
repeating those figures. We understood him
to say that for every shilling paid ninepence went to the contributor.
Dr. MORRISON: Fivepence was collared
by the companies, and sevenpence went to
the people who were paying their 21d. a
week. In the case of one company, 6,400,000
policies lapsed out of a total of 9,300,000.
In ten companies 5,000,000 policies lapsed in
1913, and 4,000,000 of those were effected in
1912 and 1913. These facts are taken from
Lord Parmoor's Commission which was instituted by the British Government, and its
report on this matter was unanimous.
Now the Industrial Assurance Act was
passed in the British House in 1923, and it
was passed in this House in 1924. The second
Section of the Act provides that the Minister
of Commerce shall appoint an officer who is
called the Industrial Assurance Commissioner for Northern Ireland, and I think
he also acts as Registrar of Friendly
Societies. Section 44 enacts that the Commissioner shall make a report to the Minister
with comments on the valuations of these
societies, their returns, or on other matters
brought before him, and that this report is
to be laid before the Parliament of Northern
Ireland by the Minister. That is what I
want to comment on in this case. I want all
these tables submitted in some form whereby
we can analyse them and see whether or not
justice has been done.
The most remarkable thing I have noticed
in connection with industrial assurance is
the growth of these societies. Twenty-five
years ago these societies were practically nonexistent, or at least they did a very small
business, and now the turnover that they
have is something amazing. I have the report here of one of these societies issued in
the local Press in my neighbourhood. It has
total funds of £38,000,000, an increase of
5,000,000 for the year, and it has twelve
officers in Coleraine. If you multiply those
twelve officers by five or six other societies
you have in every district in Ulster this band
of men running into the houses of the poor
and inducing these people to insure, and,
therefore, it is our policy to see that justice
is done to them.
I have here a report taken from the "Whig"
of another of these societies. Of new policies
issued in 1925 there were 723,873 assuring a
sum of £12,745,440. The premium revenue on
existing policies was £3,945,035. The increase of revenue over the previous year was
£199,636. The income from investments
after Income Tax had been paid was
£444,659. I do not know what amount of
total wealth that represents, but there must
be a huge capital sum invested when they
have an income of almost half a million
annually. The number of policies in force in
this society is 5,762,579, and the sum assured
represents the vast figure of £73,321,250. Now
that does not refer to general insurance at
all. It is described in the report of that
society as the "industrial branch," that is
for sums of £10.
In the report of that annual meeting the
Chairman said:

Quite a lot has recently been heard
about the Locarno spirit. We had our
Locarno some years ago, and I am proud
to say that the best I can wish for the
new Locarnos is that they will produce
results as beneficial to all concerned as
have the efforts of our company and its
staff in this direction,"
Industrial Assurance.
Industrial Assurance.
HOUSE OF COMMONS

[Dr. Morrison]
We do not often hear high moral principles
enunciated at business, annual, or general
meetings. That is the sort of stuff that we
hear occasionally coming across the Atlantic
from Washington. This high-toned morality
is familiar to us, and this unctuous rectitude
is fortunately not very common here.
would like to point out in this connection
that the chairman of this company, who
takes such a high moral tone, is, if this
report of Lord Parmoor's Commission is
correct, at the head of a
company whose
officials are putting their hands into the
pockets of 5,762,579 poor people every year
and taking from them £3,954,035. It works
out that they are taking 80,000,000 shillings
from these poor people, and for every shilling, as I stated at the beginning, all they
are paying back to these people is 7d, they
themselves retaining 5d.
Now, I am able to allege from my own
experience and that is the experience of a
dispensary doctor, whose work in his neighbourhood lies amongst the poor, and who
knows the conditions probably better, or as
well as anybody in this House-that in connection with these industrial assurance
societies there is a very large amount of
fraud and of exploiting of the poor. The
poor who join the assurance societies belong
to what I call the "submerged tenth." They
are the most helpless and, I maintain, the
most deserving people in the community.
They are down and out, and in many cases
-indeed in practically all cases-they suffer
from sickness or some other visitation of
Providence. They are not in any trade
union, and so have no trade union leaders
to defend them. They are not able to defend
themselves, and they are at the mercy of
anybody who comes round telling a plausible
story and offering them something that will
erable them to provide for the burial of
their relatives or of themselves.
I once heard a Labour Member of this
House raising this question of where the
poor died. I think he could not have raised
a more important question. Some of my
people, after the flax mills were done scutching, used to go across to Scotland. Some of
them, as frequently happened, took ill and
died, and then their friends had to face a
very serious problem, and that was how
were they to bury their dead in a strange
place like that; either that or bring the
body home. The question was not an easy
one. They had no money, and I suppose
the friends and relatives raised what they
could. I am told-and this is speaking of
pre-war days-that it cost from £7 to £10
to bury a dead person in Glasgow, and that
was a matter of very serious moment to
these people. I myself had to bury an aged
servant, and the cost to me was £11 for a
modest funeral. I put it to the House that
there should be some provision by which
people who die after coming from a strange
place into an industrial centre such as this
for a moderate sum, such as can be had
in the country, would be able to get a place
to bury their dead. The very last time I
came to this House I saw a motor hearse
coming down Donegall Place and turning
into Royal Avenue. There were four people
carrying the coffin. They were taking the
coffin away, and, as a last tribute of respect,
they were carrying it. They stopped in
Royal Avenue to put the coffin into the
hearse to take it away, perhaps, to some
remote portion of County Derry.
It contained, probably, some person who had come
into Belfast, and had died there. We have
plenty of privileges in the country, but I
am afraid it is impossible for a poor person
to get buried here, and naturally all poor
people, who know that death is coming with
sure and certain steps, know that provision
must be made to get a coffin and a grave,
and that leaves them at the mercy of these
people who go about.
What I maintain happens is that the agent
gets the applicant to sign a form. That was
the old system in operation in my day.
These people put their names to the bottom
of a form and undertake to pay 2d or 3d
per week, and then the agent fills in the
rest of the paper. One of the peculiarities
of these societies is that the agent makes a
weekly report. He must have new business,
and that forces him, perhaps, to do things
for the sake of retaining his position that
otherwise he would not do. Now, when the
name is signed and the report filled in, when
the state of health is filled in, and all these
things are done for the people, and death
takes place, the society repudiate the age
or they repudiate the state of health. I
know that the agent in many cases would
be willing that the policy should be paid in
full, but when death occurs these reports
and all particulars have to be sent to the
head office, inquiries are made, and then
it is found that the age is inaccurate. The
man in the head office asks for the length of
the disease. The agent knows that the
patient may have been suffering for twenty
years from that disease, but the head office
raises the question, and the result is that
difficulties like this are raised, and that
hundreds of these cases are paid a reduced
sum, while hundreds of them never get a
penny.
On the Third Reading of this Bill I said
that three things were necessary to protect
the poor. Unfortunately those recommendations could not be added to the Bill at that
particular stage, but I said that three things
were essential to protect the poor. The
first was that for every lapsed policy there
Industrial Assurance.

should be returned to the insured person
half of the premiums that he had paid.
Then, with regard to the age, my recommendation was that if the age is accepted at the
time the policy is issued no powers should
be allowed to these people to raise the
question of age when the policy matures.
I stated further that when the agent accepted
the age of the insured without a certificate
he should be barred from raising that question when the policy matures. It is very
easy for the agent to get the age. You can
get a certificate which costs 3s 7d. This
House could make it easier than that because
it has already provided a means in another
direction of getting a certificate at a cost of
sixpence. That power could be extended to
these people for the purpose of life assurance.
None of these suggestions of mine were accepted, and the Bill went through.

This Commissioner who has been appointed
will be paid by this House. It is his business to make a report of some nature.
think it is the desire of a great number of
people in this House that we should have a
detailed report from the Commissioner as to
four particular things. I would like to know
how many policies have lapsed during 1925?
How many matured policies were paid short
and how much were they paid short? How
many were disputed on the ground of fraud
as to health and age? As the Act provides
for the policy holder getting protection in
the Recorder's Court or free of cost under
the Insurance Commission how many have
sought protection at these tribunals and
with what result? I think that if the Commissioner would secure from these societies
a return covering these points we would be
able to judge whether or not these poor
people are being treated fairly, decently and
honestly. What I maintain is that very few
of these cases come into court. These people
are helpless. In many cases they have no
means of fighting their claims. They.may
have become insured for £10, and they will
take £3 or £5 in settlement. I maintain
that that is unjust, and seriously unjust,'
and that this House should set its face
against it and stamp it out, and see that
justice is done to these poor people.
One of the recommendations made with
regard to benefiting the position of these
people was that they should get a free paid
up policy, and it was stated that if the
details on the application forms were not
filled in by the individual but by the agent
the forms were not valid. Who is to prove
all this? I maintain that if you create difficulties like that the injustice will go on and
on. As I have said, very few of these cases
ever appear, but I have clipped one out of
the paper.
It is the report of a trial that
took place in Co. Tyrone last year. It is
typical of the way these people are induced
to sign some form that is not correct; in fact,
a form that can be legally described as a
fraud. By means of that fraud, however, a
rich company is able to get rid of its liability
and pocket the premiums that have been
paid by these poor people. This is the case:
Before Judge Linehan, at Dungannon
Quarter Sessions, Catherine Quinn, Creenagh, Dungannon, brought an action against
the Britannic Assurance Company, Ltd.,
for the amount of a policy on the life of her
mother, Sarah Quinn, deceased. Her sister,
Susan Quinn, brought a similar action
against the same Company on foot of
another policy. The respective amounts
were £9 and £9.
Mr. Corr appeared for plaintiffs, and
Mr. Skeffington for defendants.
Catherine Quinn said she insured her
mother about fifteen months before her
death. She paid the premiums till her
mother's death when the defendants refused to pay. After the insurance a nice
gentleman (laughter)-came round and
looked at her mother, and said she looked
well. There was no objection till her
mother died.
Before the policy was effected or completed
the inspector had to come round and inquire
into it. He came round and saw this woman
and said her mother looked very nice. He
was quite pleasant and amiable, and no difficulties were raised until the mother died, and
then they objected to the policy on the
ground that it was granted under fraudulent
misrepresentation. It appeared that the
mother was 13 years older than they had
stated. When she died the company refused to pay. So far as I can see they
pocketed the fifteen months of contributions in both cases and refused to pay. Mr.
Corr, an honest man, probably thought that
as other societies settled these cases and gave
a trifle to close people's mouths, if he took
them into court they might be ashamed of
themselves and settle with the parties. I
know that when you have written your name
to a fraudulent statement it cannot be expected to hold in law, but my point is that
these people were enticed to do this thing.
The insurance agent induced them to do it
and they put their names to this document,
which stated the facts wrongly, at his request. He assured them that they would
make it all right. Mr. Corr thought to
shame this company into making payment,
but Mr. Skeffington took a high line. He
said:
The defendants closed down part of
their business in certain parts of Tyrone
owing to the frauds being perpetrated on
them. There was wholesale fraud, dishonesty, and misrepresentation in in-

surance in certain districts which the company were determined to put down, hence

I maintain that this wholesale fraud of
which this gentleman speaks is brought about
not by the poor people direct, but by the
agent of the society who induces them to
put their names to these documents and then
fills them in. At any rate serious injustice
is done on a vast and huge scale to I think
the most deserving of our community. It is
the duty of this House to see that a correct
and full report is given of everything that
is carried on in Northern Ireland under our
Insurance Commission.
I do not intend to move that a Committee
should be appointed. My only object was to
ventilate this question and let the people
know what is going on. I consider, and my
experience during a somewhat lengthened
life has taught me, that the best solvent
for abuses is public opinion. If you get the
attention of the public concentrated on any
abuse you will find that it will be shifted
by the force of public opinion. I maintain
that this injustice has been going on and that
it is time, now that we in Northern Ireland
have got the control of this matter in our
own hands, we should insist on a detailed
report on these matters being put before us
so that the House would be in a position
to criticise them, and direct public attention
to them with the object of having the abuses
abolished. I beg to move.

Twenty and thirty per cent. are not unusual.
It means that a great many people pay into

for some reason or another their policies

I think that the hon. Member (Dr.
Morrison) has made a good case for the
appointment of a Select Committee. We of
the working class know what takes place.
An agent comes along and asks you to insure
either yourself or those dependent on you in
order that they may be buried decently.
Most of us desire that to take place. The
result is that we become insured and pay the
premiums, and then the breadwinner gets out
of work. He may be out of work for a considerable period, with the result that the
premiums go behind. Though he may have
been a member for a considerable number
of years, yet when his contributions get behind a certain amount or a certain length
of time the insurance company lapse the
policy, and all the money paid on behalf of
the man's wife and children and himself is
lost.
The hon. Member (Dr. Morrison) only
wants a Select Committee to report on this
question. If the Government see fit to agree
to this Committee and to its reporting on the
question I think this House will perhaps take
more definite steps towards ending this particular scandal than even the hon. Member
who proposed this very laudable Motion
might care to support. It seems to me that
the only logical outcome of any Committee or
of any report that may be submitted will be
the adoption of some national scheme of
assurance. No doubt there is a tremendous
field open for the Government to take up the
question of industrial assurance. It would
mean that the people would have the security
of the State behind them. If there was a
national scheme the people who pay in would
get some recompense for their money if they
happened to be out of work and were not able
to pay the premiums. It is for these reasons
that I want to support the hon. Member for
the University on this question. I think
he said quite truthfully that the growth of
these societies during the last 20 years has
been phenomenal. In my own lifetime they
have increased out of all knowing.
Dr. MORRISON: It is a gold mine.
Mr. KYLE: It is a perfect gold mine for
the shareholders of these societies. There
is no doubt about it, it is a tremendous hardship to ordinary people to pay in without
much knowledge of the policies they sign.
They have probably the best intentions in

The amount of profits made by various

are made principally on the pennies and twopences of working-class members whose.
policies have lapsed. I do think it is a great

What led up to the passing of our Act was
the result of an inquiry which, as the hon.
Member for the University has said, was
conducted by Lord Parmoor. He made a
report on the general condition of this
industrial insurance business as carried on
at that time. In that report he warns

insurance must in no way be confused with
ordinary life assurance business. It consists
in the assurance of small sums payable for
the most part on the death of the life assured
in consideration of the payment of weekly
premiums. The average premium on all
policies would hardly exceed 21d. per week-
I think my hon. Friend said, and the average

give some idea of the magnitude of the business after all the magnitude of the business
must be accepted to some extent as an indication of the popularity of the scheme and
the measure of confidence which the public

in the United Kingdom exceeded £25,000,000
sterling, and at the end of that year there
were about 51,000,000 policies of this type in
existence, affecting about 35,000,000 people.

assurance although they say it was

As to the first, that is transfer to the

to the Committee that the State can properly undertake its administration.
That probably is the reason why no legislation was attempted in that direction at that
time as regards the method of carrying on
the business prior to the passing of these
Acts on both sides of the Channel.
There is no doubt that at that time many
Companies and Societies of repute were conducting their business fairly and with a
reasonable regard to the interests of their
policy holders. There is no doubt, however,
that side by side with this there was a great
volume of business conducted without any
real desire to safeguard the interests of the
policy holders. The public conscience was so
stirred in the matter that in May, 1919, the
Board of Trade set up a representative Committee under the Chairmanship of Lord
Parmoor to inquire into the whole business.
The Committee found that the employment
of these men, this army of collectors, was a
very costly business, and that in the majority
of cases they enjoyed quite extravagant remuneration as considered in relation to the
premium income of the companies.
business was, and is, conducted by Joint

as much as 30 per cent., while on the average

Hon. Members will understand that the
position of the collector was one for which
there was considerable competition, and that
the privilege of making a particular collection was readily marketable. The Committee found that as much as £200 to £300
would be paid for the privilege of collecting
£10 per week, and of that £10 so collected
it was not unusual for the agent to receive

continually carried on. Mothers were

to pay

in the City of Belfast see that the money
spent on this Inquiry was well spent, and
that the duties of the Commissioner were
duly carried out. I think the Government
should devote more consideration to this
question than they have already given to it.
Mr. POLLOCK: In the answer which I
gave to the hon. Member's question I stated

curtail the printing of any further copies of

the business of the taxpayers of the whole of
Northern Ireland-(hon. Members: Hear,
hear) to pay for the publication of Reports
that are directed to the alleged purification
of the morals of the Belfast Corporation.
But apart altogether from that there were
two pages and a half of that Report published in the newspapers of Belfast, and for
the modest sum of a penny or three-halfpence at the very outside any ratepayer concerned in matters under the purview of the
Commissioner could put himself in possession
of all the material facts which were adduced
by the Commissioner in his very voluminous
Report.
I have only to repeat that, but it is a very
remarkable thing that when the question of
the cost of this Inquiry came up for consideration in this House my hon. Friends on
the other side entered a protest, and as a
Mr. BEATTIE: Hear, hear.
Mr. POLLOCK: I do not think it is the

Mr. KYLE: I did not intend to take part

on the occasion of the introduction of the

One is glad to welcome the advent of

to spend £600 on a cheaper issue of this

the City Council and of the Government,
By getting this Report for 6d they may take

there is a tremendous interest being taken
in this Report, and a very considerable

number of people who cannot afford to pay.
5s can afford to pay 6d. I suggest, therefore,

Mr. DEVLIN: The Government have regarded this whole business as a very important matter. They so regarded it when they
appointed a Special Commissioner, as I
understand, at the request of the City Corporation. The result of it has been a very
costly inquiry. A tremendous sum has been
spent on legal expenses, partly by the
Northern Government, partly by the City
Corporation, and partly by persons interested
in the explorations of the Commission.
Having regard to that tremendous expense--
I think £3,000 odd it cost the Government
and the City Council-£100 a day-and also
to the cost of the Inquiry to the individuals
concerned, I cannot for the life of me understand why the Government want to confine
the knowledge of the result of the Inquiry to
a very limited number of people.
This Inquiry was of the greatest possible
interest and concern to the working classes
of the community. We have been discussing
here almost day after day the question of
housing. It is the biggest and most vital
concern of the common people, and therefore I think it is all-important, if we are to
have sound and honest civic administration,
that the report of this Commissioner should
reach the home of nearly everyone who is
interested in housing, and that is practically
every citizen in the community. What
workingman can afford to buy a copy of this
report at 5/-? I do not see why the Government, when they were not making it a document easily accessible to the masses of the
people, should have gone to any expense at
all, because the people who pay 5/- for a
document of that sort could easily have paid
£1 for it. They could have allowed anyone
who liked to print it, and anyone who was
very much interested to go and buy it at £1.
If the purpose of publishing it at all is to
allow the findings to pierce their way into
the homes of the people, who are preeminently the parties concerned, then it
ought to be published at a price that would
make it easily accessible to all these people.
The right hon. Gentleman (Mr. Pollock)
says, why should the taxpayers of our
Northern Province pay for this report when
it does not concern them? It does concern
them. An hon. Gentleman suggested that
the cost of the report should be 3d. I would
suggest that it should be sold for a penny in
the country, for the benefit of the people of
Limavady. No doubt they will have a report
of their own, and I would like to know how
many people in County Derry will buy that
report if you are going to charge the same
price for it. Then the right hon. Gentleman
says you can read the report in the newspapers. A great many people do not read
newspapers at all. At all events, when you
buy a newspaper you put it to one side
if you are busy, and you do not see it
again, but when a report is published in a
Blue Book or in pamphlet form you put
it to the one side-that is, if you
have any civic pride-and after you have
ceased to be shocked and you want to settle
down into a condition of mental inquiry,
you lift the document again. Therefore, 1
do not think there is any point at all in the
assertion of the right hon. Gentleman that
if anyone wanted to read this Report he
could do so in the newspapers. The newspaper report is an abbreviated report, although it is a very long report. The papers
gave very considerable space to it. Notwithstanding that, I do not think the people
would be satisfied with having it in that
form; they would want to have it in
pamphlet form, such as has been published
here at a cost of 5s.
I press this matter from the point of
view that the Government regarded it as
so important that they spent £3,000 upon
the Inquiry; secondly, that if they thought
it worth while to publish the Report at any
price they ought to have published it at a
price that would make it accessible to the
people; and, finally, it is all-important that
when an inquiry of this sort takes place
the people should have in some substantial
and permanent form a record of the deliberations of the Inquiry, and the judgment
of Mr. Megaw who conducted the Inquiry.

As I say, the matter is very important. I
believe that many of our constitutional institutions are hanging in the balance. There
is a tendency to suppress municipal authorities, not only in Ireland, but elsewhere. I
an all the time for the maintenance of whatever democratic principles in the constitution we have. I do not believe in
autocracies, and I do not believe in handing
over to autocrats control of the people's
affairs. I think the only way to prevent
Bolshevism or Mussolini-ism is to preserve
the purity of our civic administration, to
exercise a keen watchfulness on the part of
ali concerned in our civic and public administration, and to give every encouragement
to the common people to take a practical and
continuous interest in the manner in which
their vital affairs are carried on.
Therefore I would again say to
the right hon. Gentleman that since
sound governmental

it equally sound economics-because it is

common
people the knowledge of what has been done
under the administration of the City Council in relation to housing matters.
The housing question, as I have said, is
one of the biggest and most vital of all our
public concerns. I do not want to repeat
what I have said so often in this House and
elsewhere, that I believe bad housing is the
cause of nearly all our vices and our
miseries, that if you have decent, clean and
sanitary houses and comfortable homes for
the people, you have the best safeguard
against criminality and disease and all the
evils incidental to bad housing conditions.
But if you are going to let the people feel
that their housing interests are to be played
fast and loose with, either by elected representatives or any other authorities, then I
am afraid that you will cause such a spirit
of mistrust amongst the people themselves
that they will cease to have faith in public
men or in democratic and constitutional
government. As one who believes in every
safeguard for the preservation of our constitutional rights, I think the more a document
of that sort is scattered widespread amongst
the people the better it will be in the public
interests.
Mr. WILLIAM MCMULLEN: The Government have attempted to make great play out
of the fact that the Press of Belfast have
given considerable space to this Report. I
know a large number of people have come
to borrow the copy of the Report that I was
fortunate enough to get from the Belfast
Corporation who have absolutely no faith in
the Belfast Press giving them the truth of
the whole matter. (A laugh.) The right
hon. Gentleman (Mr. Pollock) laughs. I do
distinctly remember that one of the most
important points in connection with the
whole inquiry was suppressed by one of the
leading papers in Belfast. I refer to the aspect of the matter in which the late Mr.
Crotty of Messrs. Crotty & Aicken, was
acting in a dual capacity as valuer for the
Corporation and agent for the vendors. As
a matter of fact, on returning from a visit
to Dublin, I bought two Belfast papers, one
an evening paper, and one a morning paper.
One of those papers made no mention of the
fact that Mr. Crotty had acted in a dual
capacity. As a result, I have heard that
matter discussed in many parts of Belfast,
and there has also been comment on the
attitude that the Belfast Press have adopted
since the Report was issued. I have heard
it stated repeatedly that, with the exception
of one paper, no lead has been given in the
Press of Belfast to the public as to what
should be done to the people who have been
adjudged guilty of mal-practices and maladministration in the Corporation.
I should point out, as has been pointed out
before, that there is a great desire on the
part of the people to have the full Report,
so that the salient features and important
points in the Report should not be kept
back from the people. There is a great
suspicion in the minds of the people that
the Press of Belfast is not giving them the
whole truth, and the people are anxious to
ascertain the full findings of the Commission
that was appointed. In view of the many
things that will come up in the Estimates
as we go along, I do not think it is a strong
argument for the Government to say it
would not be good economy, on their part,
to publish this Report, even at a loss of £600.
because, after all, it would not be a loss. I
hold that money spent in educating the
public is not lost at all. As we go through
the Estimates, we will probably be able to
point out to the Government that larger
sums are being spent for a much less useful
purpose, than the amount it would cost the
Government to issue this Report at a nominal
price. For these reasons, I would like the
Government to reconsider this matter. They
are possibly adopting this attitude out of
consideration for the people who have been
impeached. I cannot understand any other
reason for their attitude. The argument of
economy does not strike me as being sound
at all. There may be a desire on the part
of the Government to save the people impugned in the Report. Powerful influences
are being brought to bear at the moment
with the object of trying to save some of the
people who have been adjudged culpable up
to the moment. If the Government cannot
give us a more satisfactory reason for refus-

ing to publish the report at a nominal figure,

Mr. McBRIDE: Seeing that I do not make

Mr. KYLE: Could the Prime Minister tell

Stationery and Printing will be taken, and
on Thursday, the 15th inst., Houses of Parliament, Cabinet Offices, Widows', Orphans',

Record Office.

Mr. LEEKE: In rising to support this

there is really no evidence such as excessive
motor speeds or breaking the licensing lawsshould bring defendants before the Courts,
and then if the case goes against the police
it turns out that the defendant has to pay

is ridiculous and that where a case goes
against the police the Crown should pay the
expenses and not the defendant. It is most
unfair that there should be any encouragement given by the Government to public
officials, who are anxious in most cases to
bring themselves before the authorities in
order to get promotion, to chance their arm,
as I said, and place themselves before their
superiors by some case in which they are
beaten. If they are beaten then I hold that
the Crown should pay the costs. It is ridiculous, and it encourages officials to bring cases
for which there are not substantial grounds,
and it is a waste of public money caused by
the action of public officials. I hold that
every discouragement should be shown by the
Government in order to check that practice
and to save public money, and where judges
and magistrates think it necessary they
should be able to give a decision against the
costs being paid by the defendants, and the
costs should be charged to the Crown. That
would discourage officials from bringing
ridiculous cases.

As to the basis of cost of publications that
entered a good deal into the discussion
carried on yesterday it is the desire of the
Government in the matter of Government
publications that great regard should be given
to the ability of the persons interested in that
publication to pay the price demanded for
its issue. The cost of issuing any Government publication is borne by the Department
from which it originates, but then the
Stationery Department takes over the supply
at what is fixed as the market or sale price,
and any loss-the difference between the cost
of producing the publication and the amount
which we hope to realise eventually by the
sale or disposal-has to be borne by the Department from which the publication originates. I may say for the information of
hon. Members that even a publication of this
sort, the Estimates, costs about 10s. to produce, but as hon. Members will see the sale
price of this to the ordinary public is 4s.,
it being considered desirable and a justifiable
thing in the public interest that the Government should bear that difference in the cost
of the publication. This is a matter of
very great public interest throughout the
whole Six Counties.

that we did get competitive tenders for all
the printing work. We are always particularly anxious to receive competitive bids
from stationers and printers throughout the
Six Counties. Being a representative of a
county myself I can assure him I am particularly jealous on that point, to see that no
one should be at a disadvantage in tendering
for public work by reason of the distance
which separates him from the seat of
Government in Belfast.
In the matter of the typewriters raised by
the hon. Member for North Belfast (Mr. T.
Henderson), I would remind him that this
has already been the subject of a question
in this House. When setting up the Government offices we were not altogether free
agents. I cannot say whether if we had been
free agents the present position would have
been materially different. As a matter of
fact, we received our stock of typewriters in
use in the different Government Departments
out of the surplus stores carried by the
Imperial Government owing to the great
contraction of Government activities consequent on the termination of the war, so that
if we come to renew the typewriters when
that surplus stock of typewriters in the
hands of the Imperial Government is disposed of I can assure him we will be only
too glad to give preference to typewriters of
British manufacture. I hope British manufacturers will be able to supply us by that
time with machines comparable to or superior
to those with which we are equipped at
present.
I can assure hon. Members that every care
is given to cut down expense of these items
to the least possible point. I am glad to see
that even those hon. Members who have
criticised them have not overlooked the fact
that a reduction of £7,000 has been made this
year as compared with last year in the gross
amount of the Estimate.

Mr. BARBOUR: Hon. Members will
realise that the amount asked for under
this Estimate is to provide the sums
of money which the beneficiaries under
the different Acts are entitled to receive.
The administrative expenditure incurred
by the Imperial Departments acting as our
agents, namely, the Customs and Excise
Department and the Post Office, and by the
Local Pensions Committees, which last year
Supply-
Committee.
14 APRIL 1926
formed part of the Old Age Pensions
Estimate, has now been transferred to the
administrative Vote responsible for this
Service, i.e., the Ministry of Finance Vote,
Class II, No. 1, page 19, which will come up
for consideration and discussion when the
other Votes for the Ministry of Finance are
submitted to the Committee.
Secondly, the Estimate now provides for
the first time for the cost of Old Age
Pensions which are payable by virtue of the
Widows', Orphans' and Old Age Contributory Pensions Act of 1925. This new expenditure is shown separately in Sub-head
B, page 38, from the normal Pension charge
under Sub-head A.
The net increase of £153,000 in the Estimate is a consequence of the passing of
legislation in this House during last year.
Of the total increase, £114,000 is due to the
Old Age Pensions Act (Northern Ireland),
1925, and £39,000 to the Widows', Orphans'
and Old Age Contributory Pensions Act
(Northern Ireland), 1925. In point of fact,
the increased charge under the Old Age
Pension Act of 1925 is greater by about
£127,000, but owing to the facts that the
amount provided for the payment of pensions
in the past year was somewhat overestimated, and that a certain number of
pensioners, estimated at 500, who receive
pensions at less than the maximum rates
will have their pensions increased to the
maximum rates under the Widows',
Orphans' and Old Age Contributory Pension
Act and transferred to Sub-head B, the
actual increased charge in the Estimate
under Sub-head A is reduced to the figure
mentioned above, namely, £114,000.
Hon. Members will remember that it was
stated in the White Paper issued when the
Bill for the modification of the statutory
condition as to means was introduced last
Session that
an addition is expected of
approximately 5,500 pensioners-some at
modified rates-through the operation of that
Measure, while it is probable that the
majority of the 3,500 persons who, prior to
1st April this year, were in receipt of reduced pensions only, will now have their
pensions increased to the maximum rate.
Sub-head B.-Pensions (Insured Persons)-
provides for a nine months' charge only as
the Service begins on 2nd July, 1926, in respect of Old Age Pensions payable under
the Contributory Old Age Pensions Scheme.
I should, perhaps, remind hon. Members
that Contributory Pensions are paid to
persons over 70 from voted moneys irrespective of the statutory conditions as to
means, residence or nationality of the
pensioners under the Old Age Pensions Acts
-otherwise the provisions of the Old Age
Pensions Acts apply to these pensioners.
It is estimated that as from the commencing date, 1,500 new pensioners will draw
pensions under the Act, and, in addition,
500 persons who, under the ordinary Old Age
Pensions Acts (Sub-head A) draw pensions
at less than the 10s rate, will now be transferred to Sub-head B, and will have their
pensions brought up to the maximum rate
of 10s a week.
The cost of administering the Contributory
Old Age Pensions Scheme is a liability of the
Ministry of Labour and consequently the
administrative costs, including the payments
made to Imperial Agent Departments, are defrayed from the Vote for the administrative
expenses of the Ministry of Labour. Such
costs are finally chargeable against the
Pensions Account, and a payment is, therefore, made from the Pensions Account to the
credit of the Ministry of Labour Vote. That,
of course, refers to pensions paid to insured
persons, because the responsibility for administration under the ordinary Old Age
Pension Act rests with the Ministry of
Finance. I beg to move.

Mr. CRAWFORD: I am not sure whether
or not it is permissible to raise the question
on which I desire to seek information. It is
with regard to the method by which the income of an applicant is calculated under the
thrift Disqualification Clause. The idea has
got abroad in the country that £39 of unearned income is not taken into consideration in granting an Old Age Pension,
but a misapprehension exists as to the
method adopted by the authorities in arriving at the unearned income. For instance, if
a person, say with £1,200 invests it at 4
per cent. he would have £48 in interest. He
is of the opinion that £39 should be deducted
from that and a pension granted on the £9,
but the statutory method adopted by the
officials in arriving at the income of such a
person is to take the £400 first, deduct £25
from that, on which they charge nothing,
and count 5 per cent. interest on the remaining £375, which amounts to £18 15s. Od.
They then take the remaining £800 and
charge 10 per cent. on it. That comes to £80,
and added to the £18 15s. Od. it makes
£98 15s. Od. From this they deduct the £39,
leaving the person's income £59 15s. 0d., and
they accordingly give him no pension.
I would like it made clear that that is the
way these thrift qualifications are dealt with
and that if persons have that amount of
money, namely £59 15s. Od., they do not get
a pension at all.

Mr. KYLE: An entrance fee.

In regard to the £500 grant in aid to the
Inn of Court, this is following also a practice that has existed from time immemorial.
A considerable sum of money was granted
by the Imperial Government to the Inns of
Court in Dublin, and when the separation
took place and an Inn of Court was established here it was only following the practice
that had been adopted. It must be borne
in mind that the purpose of this £500, which
is spoken of here as a grant in aid, is not
necessarily for barristers. It is for the
judges and all members of the Court in
order that they may have their law reports,
their reference books, and all kinds of
literature for the purpose of assisting in
the administration of the law. Therefore,
this £500, which is called a grant in aid,
is not really a grant in aid for barristers
at the Bar, but a grant for the purpose of
assisting in the administration of the
general law of the land in the different
Courts.

of Court. I would like to know whether that

The ATTORNEY-GENERAL: This question is one which agitated the legal profession
in Northern Ireland for a considerable time
before a solution was found for it. As the
Committee are aware, prior to the Act of
1920 the legal profession in Ireland was one
and undivided and all the members of the
profession graduated in the King's Inns in
Dublin. That had not always been so, because in more remote times members of the
legal profession in Ireland had to eat their
dinners and take their terms out in London;
but from the time the jurisdiction was conferred upon the King's Inns we trained our
own lawyers at home. The King's Inns
Library when it was set up was one of the
libraries which originally had the privilege
of getting a copy of every book that was
published, and consequently they had a
magnificent library. That privilege was afterwards compounded, and a sum of money was
paid each year by the Imperial Government
to the King's Inns for the purpose of maintaining their library. That was done as a
public matter. It was not done as a private
matter, and the library that was bought out
of those funds was not a private library.
One of the hon. Members opposite has said
why do not the lawyers out of their large
fees pay for their own libraries. I may inform the Committee that they do. There is
no lawyer in Northern Ireland in decent
practice who has not got a library of his own
-in most cases a great deal more valuable
than the amount of money that is to be found
in this Estimate-because, unfortunately, the
law has now reached such a stage of complication that a library for even private use
runs into somewhere about £1,000. But in
addition to that there must of necessity be
some public library, to which students have
access and to which young members of the
profession have access in order to consult
authorities which they are not able to purchase for themselves. That is done in order
to keep up the profession of the law,
and to keep up the knowledge of the
community in law, and the benefit
of that is reflected in public matters,
because when a member of the public hires a
barrister he expects to get somebody who
knows what he is talking about, and unless
some proper library is established where
people can learn their business and where
they can have access to the authorities it is
quite impossible that the knowledge of the
law should be at all adequate.
I think the Committee will realise that
nowadays this question of the law is one of
the largest and most important matters in
the State. If the Committee will only think
it over they will realise that there is hardly
an action that a man takes from the time he
gets up in the morning until he goes to bed
at night which is not governed by law. His
house is ruled by law; he is protected in his
bed by the criminal law; he is protected,
again, as he walks to his business in the
morning by the criminal law; he is protected
also by the law of negligence; if he is a workman, when he gets into the workshop in the
morning to do his work he is protected by
the Factory Acts and by the Workmen's
Compensation Acts, and if anything goes
wrong with him during the course of his business he has the Pension Acts, which have
to be construed, and to which he is entitled
to resort for compensation. In the same way
his employer is governed by law from morning till night. He has the company laws
with which he has to comply, and a hundred
and one other statutes which rule his conduct of his life and business from the time
he goes into business until the day he leaves
it.
If some hon. Members of the Committee
would only devote a little time to finding out

us to place at the disposal of our students
some means of making themselves acquainted
with these matters of law and legal decision
and statute law, which it is necessary they
should become familiar with before they are
fitted to transact any business before the
Courts. Accordingly, I submit to the Committee with some confidence that this is, after
all, a public matter, one which is absolutely
necessary not only in the interests of the
profession but in the interests of the public,
and that it is most reasonable and proper expenditure to be made by the Government in
regard to the position in which the profession
finds itself.
It has been suggested here-it is not the
first time I have heard it suggested that we
voluntarily severed our connection with the
King's Inns in Dublin, The way in which that
occurred was this: It was perfectly obvious
that originally we could not set up any form of
body which could adequately deal with legal
education in Northern Ireland. The root of
the jurisdiction and the right of the barrister
to practise depends originally upon the
authority of his Majesty's judges, who say
who is to practise in their Courts. The right
of audience depends upon the authority of the
judges, and as it depended upon the authority
of the judges from time to time they delegated that power to the Inn of Court across
the water. That precedent was followed in
this country, and they then said that any
student whose credentials had been inquired
into, who had partaken the necessary terms,
who had passed the necessary examination,
and who had been certified by the Benchers
as being fit to have audience in Court-they
then said they would grant audience to those
members. But if you will think over it for a
moment you will see that it is quite obvious
that that could not obtain in Northern Ireland so long as the jurisdiction to authorise
the members of the profession to practise was
in the hands of the King's Inns in Dublin,
because, while the authority to certify a
barrister as having passed the necessary
examination would be vested in the body in
Dublin, the authority to say whether that
individual should practise or not would
remain with our judges here, and they would
have no power or control over the body in
Dublin which certified the individual as
having the right to practise.
Consequently it was absolutely essential
that we should set up some body in Northern
Ireland which should undertake the legal
education here and which should be subject
to the authority of the judges of our own
Courts and not subject to the authority of
the judges of the Free State. It became abso-

There is another aspect-I am sure it will

As to the suggestion made by the hon.

As to law reporting, the hon. Member for
West Belfast (Mr. McMullen) referred to
the grant in aid of the expenses of the
Northern Ireland Council of Law Reporting
for the year ending 30th June. This is a recurrent grant which is made yearly. As the
hon. Member will be aware the administration of our law to a very great extent is
governed by precedent, and consequently,
each case as it is tried may form the basis
of the decision of some case of an analogous
character which may crop up in the near
future. Therefore, it is of great importance
that a careful record should be made and a
proper digest of the different cases of importance should be prepared and kept, in
order to insure uniform justice and afford a
proper guide for the decision of similar
cases in the future.
As regards the general criticism of the
amount expended in salaries, I notice that
reference has been made to the amount expended in the year 1924-25. I may say for
the information of hon. Members that any
comparison made between these figures
would be on an entirely different basis.
Since the year 1924-25 a complete change has
taken place in the officers whose salaries are
the subject of this Estimate. In those days
they were part time officers employed partly
on Imperial business, and partly in con
nection with the administration of the law
in the Six Counties. The allowance made by
the Government of Northern Ireland for the
discharge of these duties was what might be
called a lump sum allowance. The officials
really suffered a great deal of disadvantage
and I think even an amount of injustice.
To such an extent was this appreciated by
this House that legislation was actually introduced in order to define their position
and to establish the conditions of their service, and it is in accordance with
that Act of our own that this Esti.
mate has been drawn. I should like to draw

the amount of the increase in salaries. No

expenditure for 1924-25 with the Estimate

think even after granting a certain measure
of justice to these officials whose lot this House
consdered it only right to improve and put
on a more satisfactory basis, the actual increase in the amount of charge under salaries
would not amount to more than about £800
a year. I trust that will be satisfactory to
the hon. Member.

UNEMPLOYMENT GRANTS.
Motion made, and Question proposed:
"That a sum not exceeding £120,000 be
granted to His Majesty to complete the sum
necessary to defray the charge which will
come in course of payment during the year
ending on the 31st March, 1927, for Grants
to Local Authorities, etc., in Northern
Ireland for assistance in carrying out
approved schemes to relieve unemployment."
-(Note.-£40,000 has been voted on account.)
The MINISTER OF LABOUR (Mr.
Andrews): This Estimate will be found on
page 99. It contains one item of £160,000,
but the Ministry has received £40,000 on
account, so that the actual sum sought on
this occasion is £120,000 for the purpose of
carrying out schemes of public utility in
conjunction with the local authorities, and
of providing as much employment as possible
for those who are unfortunately unemployed

at the present time. This Estimate is a
reduction of £40,000 on last year's Estimate
of £200,000, but it allows for an increased
expenditure of £32,000 on the amount
expended last year.
Members of the Committee may regret that
the whole £200,000 is not being voted this
year, the same as last year, but I may point
out that it would be quite wrong to over
estimate in a matter of this kind, just as it
would be wrong to under estimate, and this
sum is based upon the expenditure which it
is considered will likely be incurred in this
connection during the present financial year.
No doubt hon. Members appreciate that the
number and the magnitude of these schemes
which the Government subsidize is entirely
decided by the local authorities. All that
the Government can do is to influence and
encourage in every way they possibly can the
local authorities to promote schemes of the
kind.
I think it will interest the Committee to
know how the money was expended during
the past year. We had in Belfast 38 schemes;

135 schemes in

of the schemes in Belfast was

The grants actually paid were £89,000 in Belfast: £39,000 outside Belfast, a total of
£128,000. It will be seen, therefore, that the
£160,000 which will be available will be
ample to carry out as many schemes of this
kind as were carried out during the
last financial year. If more money is
required for these all-important purposes, I
have an understanding with the Minister of
Finance that I will be permitted to introduce
a supplementary estimate.
It may interest the Committee to know that
by means of these schemes 7,000 men obtained
employment for various periods, varying
about three months, during the past financial
year. I beg to move.
Mr. PATRICK O'NEILL: I am sorry that
the amount asked for in this particular case
is not larger. In the other instances I had
occasion to regret that the amounts were not
smaller, and here, if I took up the Minister
of Labour rightly, the right hon. Gentleman
thought the amount should be larger. However, I regret that it is not larger, because
the smaller the amount of these grants to
local authorities, the larger the amount that
will have to be paid in unemployment benefit,
without work of public utility being carried
out in return. As a matter of fact, I think
it is a great mistake not to compel local
authorities to undertake works of public
utility, in the present state of unemployment.
There are many schemes the work on which
would be very useful to the community, and
I do not know whether I would be in order
in mentioning some of the schemes of public
utility that I have in mind.
Take, for instance, the neighbourhood of
Newry and Carlingford Lough. For many
years a deep water scheme from the town
of Newry to Carlingford Lough, a distance
of five or six miles, has been under contemplation. That, undoubtedly, would be of
immense advantage to the neighbourhood,
and it is one that I think this Government
should assist in developing.
Then it has occured to me that there has
been great difficulty with regard to the mail
service between Belfast and England, and you
have only to look at a map to see that the
most direct route from Belfast to London,
passing through the Six Counties, is via
Carlingford Lough. With comparatively
little expenditure, that Lough could be made
available for any size of boat that crosses
the Channel, and you could have a direct mail
service between Belfast and London, just as
near and as convenient as the Kingstown-
Holyhead route.
I understand that at the present time the
London, Midland and Scottish Railway Company have many millions to spend on developing their services, and that it would
not be opposed to considering the question of
a harbour scheme in Carlingford Lough.
Therefore, I think that the Minister of
Labour, or whichever Minister is in charge
of such affairs, should consider this question.
It would be much better to employ labour in
a work of such public utility, and one that
would be of such advantage to the whole of
the Six Counties, than to spend it simply on
unemployment benefit from which you get
no return. I make the suggestion in all
sincerity to the Minister in charge of this
Estimate, and also to the Minister of Finance,
who, I notice, is taking some interest in what
I am saying.
Mr. BEATTIE: I rise to support this Estimate, and I regret that the amount shows a
reduction on the figures of last year. I do
so on the ground that last year's Vote was
insufficient for the needs and requirements
of the unemployed that we have in our midst.
I quite agree that under present conditions
it would be impossible for the Minister to
get more schemes adopted, but if this
Government had brought compulsion to bear
on the urban councils throughout the Six
Counties, and forced them to go on with
schemes of public utility, I think the
Minister would have been very pleased, as
that course would have enabled him to give
support to a larger number of unemployed
in 1925 than was actually the case. When
you remember that the number of the unemployed has risen from 38,000 to 61,000, you
must realise that the schemes promoted by
the local authorities were insufficient to deal
with the existing unemployment. The
amount for this purpose is less than appears
on paper, inasmuch as £40,000 has been
expended. Our register of unemployed is
very high in the Six Counties.
I believe Londonderry has started on a
drainage scheme for which a grant will be
available. Bad drainage is a menace to the
population of any town, and owing to the increasing population of towns in Northern
Ireland the existing arrangements are insufficient to take away the sewage. One
drain in Holywood has been blocked on
several occasions. I believe the Holywood
Urban Council is going to take action to deal
with the difficulty. The Minister of Labour
should have power to approach these urban
councils to induce them to look after these
matters and to improve the roads, so that
they could have a grant and provide work
for the unemployed. I feel that the unemployment fund regulations are too
stringent, but this is one of the ways in
which we can reduce the claims on the fund,

by providing schemes of work for the persons

Mr. ANDREWS: I would like to say that

One suggestion was made that I would like
briefly to refer to. It was that we, as a
Government, should compel the local authorities to carry out work of this kind. I
venture to suggest that that would not be a
very democratic procedure. After all, the
local authorities are the elected representatives of the ratepayers, and as such, powers
and responsibilities are imposed upon them
of considering what work they can undertake

already said, on behalf of the Government
I will do what I can to encourage the local

existing conditions.

Thursday, 15th April, 1926.
The House met at Three of the Clock, Mr.
SPEAKER in the Chair.
Oral Answers to Questions.
THE LAND ACT-APPOINTED,DAY.
1. Mr. DEVLIN asked the Minister of
Finance whether he will represent to the
Imperial Government the necessity of expediting the appointed day under the Northern Ireland Land Act, so that it may be
fixed generally not later than the first day
of May.
The MINISTER OF FINANCE (Mr. Pollock): I assume that the hon. Member is
referring to the fixing of appointed days for
the vesting of estates in the Land Purchase
Commission. It will be realised that it
would be impossible without an inordinate increase of staff for dates to be arranged
instanter.
I am satisfied that the Commission are
proceeding with the administration of the
Act as rapidly as possible, and in these
circumstances I do not consider it necessary
to make representation to the Imperial
Government in the sense suggested by the
hon. Member.
TENANTS ATTENDING RECORD COURT.
2. Mr. KYLE asked the Minister of Home
Affairs whether he will state when the Bill
amending the law in respect of the necessity
of tenants attending the Record Court will
be introduced, according to his statement in
December last.
The MINISTER OF HOME AFFAIRS
(Sir Dawson Bates): This matter is under
consideration in connection with other
points relating to summary jurisdiction.
There are many points to be investigated,
and the hon. Member will readily understand
that great care has to be exercised in dealing
with matters of this kind.
I am afraid it will be some time before I
am in a position to introduce a Bill.
Mr. DEVLIN: Is the right hon. Gentleman aware that the Recorder made a very
important statement upon this matter as far
back as three months ago? Has the Home
Office not been considering representations
made by the Recorder since then?
Sir DAWSON BATES: As I pointed out
to the hon. Member, the question of increasing the jurisdiction of the Summary Courts
in regard to such cases is only one of many
other points that have to be dealt with in
this matter.
ALLEGED ASSAULT ON EX-SERVICE
MAN.
3. Mr. KYLE asked the Minister of Home
Affairs whether he is aware that a brutal
assault, necessitating medical attention, was
made recently on a young ex-Service man
who was holding a trade union meeting in
Garvagh; whether the police are entitled to
decide who is to be permitted to hold such
meetings; whether he has received any report from the police on the subject; and
will he take steps to prevent a recurrence of
such incidents in future.
Sir DAWSON BATES: The facts regarding
the incident are as follows:-
On the 27th ultimo a meeting to establish
a Branch of the Transport Workers' Union
was held in Garvagh. It was addressed by
Mr. George Simpson, District Representative
of the Union, whose remarks met with
frequent interruptions from the audience.
In consequence, the police on patrol kept
Simpson under observation after the meeting to prevent him being molested. A
potato, thrown by one of a crowd, struck
Simpson on the eye, but the police did not
see it thrown. The injury appeared to be
trivial, and as far as is known, Simpson was
not medically attended. The police did not
in any way interfere with the holding of the
meeting.
Mr. BEATTIE: Will the Minister give
this House an assurance that in future duly
appointed representatives of trade unions
when they are sent on duty such as this will
get the same protection as Cabinet Ministers
get when they go outside. (Laughter).
Sir DAWSON BATES: Every citizen who
obeys the law is entitled to the protection of
the law, and the Government will give them
that protection.
Mr. KYLE: If I give the right hon.
Gentleman the fact that the police-I was
going to use a dangerous word, and it would
not be very far from the truth-the police
encouraged the molestation of this young
man, would he be prepared to take action?
I would like the right hon. Gentleman to
correct the answer he has given. It was not
a meeting of the Transport Workers' Union
that this young man was speaking at. In
view of the fact that this young man went
out and fought for his country while some of
his molesters stayed at home, will he not see
that in future such discreditable incidents
do not occur.
Oral Answers.
Oral Answers.

Sir DAWSON BATES: I am not prepared
to admit for one moment that the police permitted this young man to be molested.

DEPORTATION ORDERS.
5. Mr. O'NEILL asked the Minister of
Home Affairs whether he will state the
number of persons on whom he has served
deportation orders in Northern Ireland, and
when he proposes to withdraw these orders.
Sir DAWSON BATES: Fifteen Orders
under Regulation 23A made under the Civil
Authorities (Special Powers) Act (Northern
Ireland), 1922, prohibiting entry to or
residence in certain specified areas in
Northern Ireland, have been served which
are still in force.
Of the fifteen persons affected by these
Orders, 6 are not ordinarily resident in any
part of Northern Ireland.
These Orders are kept constantly under
review, and are withdrawn when their
continuance is no longer considered
necessary. It is not possible to state when
withdrawal can be made in any particular
case.
Mr. DEVLIN: Was the withdrawal of
this order part of the negotiations carried
on yesterday at Stormont Castle between the
Governments of Northern Ireland and
Southern Ireland?
Sir DAWSON BATES: I do not know
what my hon. Friend refers to. I am not
aware of any discussion.
Mr. DEVLIN: The right hon. Gentleman
must be aware that there were negotiations
yesterday, at Stormont Castle, between the
Prime Minister and the representative of
Southern Government. I want to know is the
withdrawal of the deportation orders part
of the negotiations that were carried on.
Sir DAWSON BATES: I may point out
that I have not withdrawn the deportations.
Mr. DEVLIN: I know you have not or
I would not be asking. Not having withdrawn the order is the withdrawal part of
the negotiations?
Sir DAWSON BATES: I am not aware of
any negotiations.
The PRIME MINISTER: Perhaps I can
clear the matter up. There was no question
of these deportees yesterday at all. It was
never mentioned.
Mr. DEVLIN: That is what I wanted to
know.
