The FINANCIAL SECRETARY (Mr.
Barbour): This Estimate appears on Page 1
of the book and offers very little scope for
observation, as the various charges for which
it provides have become more or less stereotyped. There is, however, a net increase in
the total Estimate, which is referable to an
under-estimate for the previous year for the
expenses of members of the Senate. The
numbers of the sittings of the Senate were
more numerous than was anticipated. On
page 2 it will be seen that £940 is provided
for the payment of Senators as against £400
in the preceding year, and on page 4 the
sum of £200 is provided in respect of their
travelling expenses as against £100 in the
previous year.
Another increase is in the amount of
printing costs under sub-head E1. Here again
the Estimate in the previous year was under
the mark and we have to provide for a
greater output. One other item which contributes towards the net increase charged
on the Estimate is the reduction under subhead I of fees for the promotion of Private
Bills. It may be of interest to point out
that the previous classification of salaries
under the three sub-heads has been abolished
and the salaries of the officers of the House
are now included under one sub-head. I beg
to move.
Mr. BEATTIE: I beg to move a reduction
of £1,000 in this Estimate for the Houses of
Parliament. I do so owing to the abnormal
increase in this Department. When I first
came into this House and had the pleasure
of listening to the Estimates being gone over
a very old Parliamentarian placed upon the
Paper a Notice of Motion, asking that a
Commission should be set up to inquire into
the claims which were set out here in regard
to the upkeep of our Houses of Parliament.
I regret that he is absent to-day. I would
have preferred to have seen him in his seat
doing his duty the same as the other
hon. Members who are sent here.
The first item we come to is salaries and
allowances. Mr. Moles, Sir, you come under
the hammer under that head, but I know
that, no matter what I may say, my remarks
will not be taken personally. I believe that,
while you fulfil your duties with all the
efficient ways and manners that any Chairman of Ways and Means could do, £1,500 is
too high a figure for the salary of the Chairman of Ways and Means for the Six Counties.
We have been told in the past that the
working-class people had to go step by step
with Great Britain. If we are going to ask
the under-dog to go step by step with Great
Britain we are bound to ask the heads and
officials of the House also to consider the
people whom they govern and for whom they
legislate. We are legislating for a million
and a quarter people, and, while I recognise
that it is just as easy to legislate for five
millions as for a million and a quarter, still
the million and a quarter are not so able
to bear the expense as the five millions are.
Therefore, under that head I think £1,500
is really too much for the Chairman of Ways
and Means.
The next point I come to is in regard to
the Members of the Senate. We are asked
to vote a sum of £940 this year as against
£400 last year, plus an addition on page 4,
of £100. I do not object to the Senators,
who are not being paid, being given railway
fares, but I would ask the Minister what
class fares are given. Is it first class, or
second class, or third class. This seems an
enormous amount for all the meetings the
Senate holds.
We come down to the Members of the
House of Commons and we find here a reduction. I presume that is on account of
one of the Members on the Government
Benches having been elevated to a higher
position with, I expect, attached to it a
salary of £1,200 or £1,500.
Then we come to "B" (Salaries, wages and
allowances). We find there that there has
been an increase all over, and that there
has been a reduction of the staff. You will
notice from the figures that although we
have got rid of one superfluous member of
the staff, in the person of a messenger at 258
a week, we have instituted instead a second
clerk assistant to the House of Commons at
a salary of £684. That is, we have taken
away one messenger at 25s a week, and we
have substituted a second clerk assistant to
the House at £684. You carried on for four
years, I understand, without this second
clerk assistant, and if you carried on during
those trying years, which you contend were
the hardest, in the life of your Government
then I say you should this year be able to
Supply-
Committee.
15 APRIL 1926
carry on without that extra appointment.
For that reason, I think this appointment
should be reconsidered, thus saving the
amount of money allocated to this particular office.
Other items of the Estimate are in reference to the Sergeant-at-Arms and Black
Rod. While, perhaps, one does not like to
reiterate the opinions expressed by the Opposition time and again, and by some Members
of the Government who had the courage of
their convictions that these positions are too
highly paid, we do believe that one man
should be capable of carrying out the
duties. The Government should be prepared
to economise as much as possible in the upkeep of this Parliament, because economy is
called for by the people of the Six Counties,
and a Commission has been called for by
Members of this House, although the
Government defeated the aims and objects
of the mover of that Amendment. If you do
not economise I believe the continuation of
your Parliament of Northern Ireland will be
shorter than you expect, because I am fully
satisfied that the economic conditions of
the Six Counties will not warrant your
spending money on the Houses of Parliament to the extent set out in this Estimate
which we are asked to pass to-day. If you
are to retain your Parliament intact for the
term of your life and for generations to
come you have got to cut down your Estimate for the Houses of Parliament.
Minister who set out this Estimate has, I
say, increased every Department and to-day
there is a net increase of £1,269 on last year's
figure. I claim that this is uncalled for. No
increase in work has been put on the staff,
and surely no extra calls have been made on
this House. I believe the calls in the past
were the heaviest and that future calls will
be less, and so less money should be spent
on the Houses of Parliament. Therefore, I
move that a reduction of £1,000 should be
made in this Estimate.

The first subject I want to discuss is the cost

Mr. DEVLIN: I want to make sure. You
might not regard it as proper when we

The CHAIRMAN: Sufficient unto the day

Mr. DEVLIN: I am giving away my right
which I am entitled to now on the Estimates
for rates and taxes on the building. What

Mr. DEVLIN: Then I am, satisfied with
that. I rise for the purpose of protesting
against any sum of money being voted by
Parliament for the expenses of the Senate.
I am here as one of those who represent
35 per cent, of the population of Northern
Ireland, and that population has not a single
representative in the Senate I do not think
there is a more deplorable condition of
affairs in any part of the world than to
find that the Senate, one of the Houses of
Parliament, has not a single representative
of the religion of those who constitute over
35 per cent. of the population. One would
have imagined that when we had arrived at
the era of peace and goodwill, and when in
public generous gestures were made to the
minority to come into this Parliament, and
take their seats, and to associate themselves
with the conduct of Governmental affairs,
that that gesture would have meant more
merely than eye-wash and rhetorical camouflage for the purpose of the promotion of
political ends.
One would have thought that the first
thing would have been to give representation
Supply-
Committee.
HOUSE OF COMMONS
[Mr. Devlin]
to the Catholic minority whom you invited
here. Through constitutional circumstances
we were able to take a vote for Members
of the Senate some months ago, and we
voted, and for reasons for which we were
admittedly not to blame we lost the representation of one individual in the Senate. I
am not going into the merits of this question now, because you have got nothing to
do with that. Shortly afterwards a vacancy
occurred in the Senate, and it was within
the power of the Senate to co-opt a Member,
and to give to the 35 per cent of the population some representation on that Senate.
And what was done? You refused to co-opt
a Catholic. So brazen has been the bigotry
of the Government in these matters of giving
us no say whatever in the conduct of our
affairs that they would not even trust one
Catholic in the Senate-
The PRIME MINISTER: Perhaps the hon.
Member is not aware that the Senate do
not co-opt if there is a vacancy. This House
elects. I understand there was no one put
up for election last time on behalf of the
hon. Member's party.
Mr. DEVLIN: That does not meet the
case of the right hon. Gentleman, because
this House is controlled by the right hon.
Gentleman. If he stated to his followers
that he thought it was desirable in the public
interest and in order to give a very powerful
element of the community not decent representation, not adequate representation, but
merely some form of representation-
The PRIME MINISTER: I merely wanted
to point out that if there is any blame in
the matter it is not the fault of the Senate.
If the hon. Member likes to put the blame
on my broad shoulders I am quite prepared
to carry it.
Mr. DEVLIN: With me it is not a question of who is to blame. The question is
that I decline as a representative of 35 per
cent. of the population to give my vote
here to pay the expenses or cost of the
Senate in which not a single Member of my
faith is allowed to enter. That is my case.
I am now giving my reasons. After the
death of one of the Members of the Senate
this Parliament was entitled to select a
successor, and all the right hon. Gentleman
and the Government had to do was to say
to their followers, as would be said in any
country where there was the slightest spark
of decency-all they would require to have
said was, "Well, this looks very bad"-I am
putting it from your own point of view-"that
there is not a single Catholic in the Senate."
The candidate was a man against whom nothing could be said. He was not a wild
politician. He was not a politician
at all. We selected a leading merchant
honoured by all members of the
community in order that he might be
acceptable. He was turned down and one of
the camp followers of the political party of
which the right hon. Gentleman is the leader
was appointed. A more indefensible action I
never knew of, a more intolerant performance I have never heard of, and in the interests of the Government themselves in
order to protect themselves from attacks of
bigotry it ought to have been their duty to
elect one of the minority. This action is, I
know, only part and parcel of the whole
system and mentality of the Government.
We have no place in the administration of
the Province whose laws we are supposed to
accept and whose laws we do accept. I
believe and I believe I can prove it with
statistics-that by a gradual process you are
driving out all the Catholics who were employed in the administrative offices of the
city.
Mr. POLLOCK: No.
Mr. DEVLIN: I can give the right hon.
Gentleman some startling statistics which he
can have if he wants. No doubt it may be
said, "Why raise these sectarian questions ?"
I have heard that repeated often and often
before. It is not comfortable for you to hear
these things, and, I must confess, it is not
pleasant for me to talk about them, because
I should like nothing better if it were
possible to avoid the discussion of them and
particularly because I do not think that any
representations we make have the slightest
possible effect. But if we live under the
system, if we are governed by certain laws,
and if these laws are administered, we claim
the right to have some say in the administration of them. We have not a single
Catholic on the Bench, not a single Judge
in Ulster-
Mr. POLLOCK: Yes, you have.
Mr. DEVLIN-though we constitute 35 per
cent. of the total population. We have not a
single Catholic in the Senate, we have not a
single Catholic in the Privy Council, we have
not a single Catholic in any department you
can keep them out of, not one, and yet,
strange to say, the right hon. Gentleman,
the Prime Minister, the other day boasted
that he had got a Parliament and that he
would never give it up. There can be a
meeting of the party afterwards. These are
points I want to bring before the Prime
Minister primarily. The Prime Minister the
other day boasted that he would never revert to the old system; that he had got a
Parliament and would keep it. I am very
glad that he has now become so solid a
Home Ruler, that he has so much faith in
the capacity of the people to govern themselves in their own country, and I would be
the very last not to rejoice in that new spirit
and mentality in the right hon. Gentleman.

He
But why did he get a Parliament?
never would have had this Ulster Parliament
unless he had made a deep and profound
impression in the propaganda of himself and
his party in England that you were
a Protestant minority and you could not subject yourselves to the Catholic majority
because you would get no justice from these
people. Upon that plea you got this Parliament, and how have you conducted yourselves?
The CHAIRMAN: Perhaps the hon.
Member will help me in a little difficulty.
I fully appreciate the line of argument he
is forced to follow. His objection to the
payment of the Senate at all is that his
party is not represented in the Senate.
Obviously a good deal must be allowed by
way of analogy and illustration, but it is
equally obvious that we must not permit
the specific question before us to drift into
something that is only remotely related to
it.
Mr. DEVLIN: In Southern Ireland,
against whose Government on religious
grounds you made so violent a protest that
you got a Parliament of your own, they
proceeded to give nearly half the seats in
the Senate to Protestants. I rejoice at that
and I am very glad to be able to do it,
because a generous act of toleration cannot
be overdone. The result is that the
Protestants were won over, and the Southern
Government have secured the support of the
overwhelming mass of the Protestant population in the South of Ireland. We did not
ask for half the Senate. We did not ask for
a third of the Senate. All we asked for in
the first instance was one Member and you
refused to give it. Therefore, from the point
of view of voting any money for the Senate
I could not conscientiously do so.
I hate to introduce these matters in the
House, but I must remember that I am here
as one of the representatives of the Catholic
minority, and I would be unworthy of my
position and lacking in courage if I did not
come here, no matter whom it pleased or
whom it displeased, and say what I have to
say. You will always have these sectarian
questions raised until you realise that we are
something more than the blacks in South
America. In South America the blacks have
no rights; they have to obey the laws.
They are told that they are allowed to live,
and that is precisely what we are allowed
to do. The only function we are allowed to
discharge is to come here and represent the
people who sent us and try, although we
never succeed, to redress the people's
grievances.
I understand a compliment was paid to the
right hon. Gentleman, the Prime Minister,
for the gesture of good-will he made towards
the Southern Parliament. Would he make
a gesture of good-will towards the North?
It is not the Southern people who have to
live under this regime; it is the Northerners.
The Southern people have to bear no responsibility, but we have. We have to obey the
laws and we are subject to their administration. We have to bear civic and public
responsibilities, and we are entitled, not
merely to fair play, but to some slight mead
of justice and tolerant treatment at the hands
of the Government. Therefore I say that
every time a Vote of this character is proposed in this House when I can discuss it.
and protest against the treatment we receive
I will take the opportunity of doing so.
With regard to the general question of
economy I am sorry the Member for West
Belfast (Sir Robert Lynn) is not here to
discuss the retrenchment part of these Estimates. It is really a pity that Members of
Parliament will not come to the House and
try to practice what they preach, because
this is the place to do it. I do not go to
the house-tops to attack the Government or
do it in the newspapers. I come here and
attack them face to face, where they can
meet my impeachments if they can, and
where they can deal face to face with the
questions we put forward and the protests
we make. I think it would be desirable
that other Members having other views
should come to the House and discuss them.
I can only say that the carrying on of this
Government is a very costly experiment.
According to the speech of the Prime
Minister it is going to be a permanent and
enduring factor in the life of the community,
and I quite agree that if the masses of the
people are to be asked to make retrenchments they ought to be shown an example
by the Government itself. I do not, therefore. propose to enter into any of the subjects raised by the hon. Member for East
Belfast (Mr. Beattie), but I take advantage
of the opportunity to make the protest I
have just made.
The PRIME MINISTER: As the hon.
Member (Mr. Devlin) has confined himself
to the political constitution of the Senate I
think it might be appropriate if I recalled
to his memory and to the memory of Members
of this Committee what are the real facts of
the case. There was a General Election in
1921 and there were twelve Roman Catholics
returned to this Parliament. Those twelve
representatives had the power in their own
hands, without an ad misericordiam appeal
to Members on this side of the House, to
return, I think three certain, and possibly
four Members to the Senate. (Hon. Members:
Hear, hear.) Those twelve Roman Catholics-

for West Belfast (Mr. Devlin) has introduced

HOUSE OF COMMONS
[The Prime Minister]
this religious side of the question, and not
of my own volition or desire-
Mr. DEVLIN: You cannot discuss this
without mentioning it.
The PRIME MINISTER: As long as the
hon. Member is satisfied I am satisfied to
stand up for the Protestant point of view,
if he puts it that way. Those twelve Members
repudiated this Parliament, they stayed out
of it, they insulted it, they said this Parliament was not here to stay, and it was not
a proper thing to have a Parliament. These
are the gentlemen who have been fighting
for Home Rule all their lives.
Mr. DEVLIN: For all Ireland.
The PRIME MINISTER: There is Home
Rulo for all Ireland. Nobody denies it. It
is true there are two Parliaments instead of
one, but it is we on this side of the House
who are endeavouring to carry on Home
Rule largely because these twelve Roman
Catholic Members kept out of the House and
refused to do their duty as representatives of
the people. Now, forsooth, the Leader of
that Party (Mr. Devlin) comes here to-day
and complains that we do not do what they
themselves would not do when they had the
opportunity. That is my first point.
There was another election to this House
last year, and again twelve Roman Catholics
were returned-I am speaking from memory.
Again only a minority of them have come
here to represent their own views. Whose
fault is that? It is not the fault of the
Senate and it is not the fault of hon.
Members sitting on this side of the House,
but it is a repetition of the fault for which
the Roman Catholics were responsible in
1921, that they did not come here and take
full advantage of their voting strength and
put into the Senate those representatives
they desired. Such a travesty of argument
I have never heard before, even from the
hon. Member.
Mr. DEVLIN: Will the right hon. Gentleman tell me how it was that when the
Southern Protestants had not the power to
secure any seats in the Senate the Southern
Government gave them half the seats.
The PRIME MINISTER: I can answer
that very satisfactorily, indeed. Ulstermen
in the South of Ireland, like loyal men, threw
themselves into the task of helping the
Government of the day to govern the country.
They entered heartily into every branch of
civic life. Throughout the length and
breadth of Southern Ireland they said,
"There is a Government in power. It is our
duty to support and sustain that Government,
and make it workable." The hon. Member's
followers throughout Northern Ireland did
nothing of the kind. They repudiated and insulted this Parliament, and then, having
changed their tactics--and I am delighted
they have done so and come in here to do
their duty-they blame our party for the
faults they themselves have committed. I do
not think it would be fair of me to transgress
any longer on the patience of the House, but
I can only say that I am prepared to meet
the hon. Member at any time on any platform to justify the action this Government
has taken since its establishment.
Mr. MCALLISTER: I think that in the
whole history of politics there was
never a Government that turned its back on
the past as this Government has done. You
sit on those Benches by reason of the cry
you raised from the house-tops as to the fate
of the minority at the hands of those who
differed from you, and at the first opportunity, and throughout your entire history,
you have never made one generous gesture
by action to promote the confidence of the
minority. The hon. Member for West Belfast
(Mr. Devlin) has referred to one isolated
case in connection with the Senate, over
which you had complete control, and you
have tried to side-track his argument by
covering the whole history of the last four
years with regard to the Senate.
We did everything that was in our power
to secure the election of one Member to that
Senate, and through no fault on our part we
did not succeed. It was open to you, as the
Leader of the Unionist party in Northern
Ireland, by the slightest suggestion to your
followers, to make good the defect that deprived us, through the action of this Parliament and its officials, of the representation of
one of our party in the Senate. The Prime
Minister has complained that the rest of
those elected to represent the minority in
the Six Counties have not taken their seats
in this Parliament.
Mr. DEVLIN: They see how we were
treated.
Mr. McALLISTER: Why, judging by the
history of the past four years, they had absolutely no hope that they would receive
justice or their fair and equitable representation in the administration of the country.
Can we, after our experience here on other
occasions, prove to them any act to show
that we are justified in coming here in the
hope of obtaining fair and equitable representation in the administration of the country?
We are here with the best of motives, anxious
to assist by constructive criticism and in
every other way, but we are bound, when we
feel justified, to enter our most emphatic
protest against the treatment we and those
we represent have received from the Government during the last four years, and particularly since we came into this House. It is

CLASS I. No. 2.
CABINET OFFICES.
Motion made, and Question proposed:
"That a sum not exceeding £9,196 be granted
to His Majesty to complete the sum necessary to defray the charge which will come
in course of payment during the year ending
on the 31st March, 1927, to defray the
salaries of the Department of the
Prime Minister, the salaries of the
Cabinet and of the Cabinet Secretariat, and
other expenses in connection therewith, including the expenses of the Privy Council
Office (15 and 16 Geo. V., c. 3, s. 4 (N.I.) ).”
(Note. £3,000 has been voted on account.)
The PRIME MINISTER: I have availed
myself of the opportunity each year of introducing the Estimates attached to the
office over which I have the pleasure to preside, and I will be very glad to elucidate
any points that seem to be difficult to understand, though I think that the way in which
the Estimates are prepared is so clear there
is really very little to be said. There is a
slight saving this year, I think of £112 as
will appear on page 6. So far as the
personnel is concerned, it is exactly the
same as last year. Of course it is
difficult in such an office to foretell
accurately from year to year exactly
what the amount will eventually be, but I
am glad to say that from the start we have
been able to make a slight saving each year,
without exception. It was somewhat heavier
before, but now we are getting accustomed
to accurate forecasting of the year's requirements. Of course, it is not to be expected
that we will be able to continue making a
saving of any very great amount.
The principal officer who is associated with
me is the Secretary to the Cabinet. He fills
three positions Secretary to the Cabinet,
Clerk to the Privy Council, and Private
Secretary to myself. He is paid an overhead salary for the three offices, each of
which he is quite fit to carry on, and in
each of which I do not think we could have
a better person for doing the work.
With regard to the other staff, it is exactly the same as last year, as far as I recollect. I may repeat what I said at the
start, if any hon. Member desires to put a
particular question regarding any item on
the Paper I will be glad to reply to it. Of
course hon. Members will realise that the
Cabinet Ministers' £2,500 is placed upon this
particular Estimate, because the Cabinet
Offices are under discussion.
Mr. DEVLIN: May I ask the right hon.
Gentleman whether the salary of the Prime
Minister includes the sum of £200 paid to
Members of Parliament?
The PRIME MINISTER: No. The £200
is not paid to anyone in receipt of this. The
amount named here does not refer to myself,
but to the other Members of the Cabinet.
Mr. BEATTIE: I rise to move a reduction
of £1,000 in this Estimate for Cabinet
Offices. You ask me to vote in favour of an
additional £500 to the Cabinet Ministers,
who have already £1,500. What do we find
outside of the Parliament House? We find
Cabinet Ministers on every occasion going
out to tell the common people, to whom I
belong, that I am a danger and a menace
to the Six Counties. We have seen it in the
Press. We have seen it everywhere. The
three Labour Members who sit on the
Opposition side of the House are referred to
as the Red Peril. We find Cabinet Ministers
going into the constituencies that we represent and making these foul statements. They
make statements that they cannot defend,
such as that we are a disgrace to the people
of the Six Counties. Then you come along
and ask us to vote a sum of money to people
of this type. I say that on this occasion I have
no intention of voting £500 to each of the
Cabinet Ministers, and I have no intention
of voting for the salaries of the three
officers, the Parliamentary Secretary, the
Permanent Secretary, and the Principal.
Those are three positions with very decent
salaries attached to them, and their duties
are confined to dealing with six Cabinet
Ministers.

I say that the Cabinet of Northern Ireland
should be paid on similar lines to the district
committee of a trade union. I say that advisedly, because the Members of the Cabinet
have no
more duties to fulfil than the
district committee of a trade union. I cannot see how you can claim £500 for such
duties. You have attached fairly decent
salaries to the offices you held in the various
Ministries. Why do you come along and
have the audacity to hold out your
hand for another £500? It is ridiculous and
scandalous in the present state of trade depression and unemployment. I hope that
when this Division is being taken, the
Government back benchers will come out
with us. It is not argument or criticism
that is going to effect any change in the
Government Front Bench. They know as
well as they are sitting on that bench that,
no matter what argument is brought up
against the Estimate, no matter what fair
criticism is levelled at it, they can rely on
their supporters behind trooping into the
lobby with them. I am prepared to
go into any constituency in the Six Counties
to seek a vote against the Government on
this Estimate. I know that if the people
had to deal with these matters, the Government would not get the Estimates carried as
they are compiled by the Departments.
There are various items in this Estimate
to which exception can be taken. My
special objection is to the Cabinet positions.
I do not think Cabinet Ministers are entitled to receive any money. I believe that,
if they are Ulstermen at all, if they have
the welfare of Ulster at heart, they should
give their services free. They should hold
their offices in an honorary way. From that
point of view, I strongly protest against the
inclusion of the £2,500 in this Estimate. The
Ministers are quite well paid with £1,500 a
year, without expenses of this kind. For
that reason, I move a reduction of £1,000.
Mr. DEVLIN: I rise to support the Motion
for reduction made by the hon. Gentleman
(Mr. Beattie). I do so because, after the
speech of the Prime Minister, I have no
other course open to me than to support any
proposal that will constitute a vote of censure upon him. One would have expected
that, after the speech I delivered-in my
judgment constituting an irresistible case for
fair play for the people I represent-he
would have risen in his place to receive the
suggestions I made in the spirit in which
they were offered; but, instead of that, he
stood precisely where he did in 1886. He has
not advanced one single inch beyond that
position. My own belief is that he regards
us as an inferior race, and thinks we ought
to be so treated.
In the course of his speech he said that the
whole responsibility for the refusal to give
us our legitimate rights and our ordinary
place in the citizenship of the community is
ours, because we did not come into this
Parliament five years ago. The right hon.
Gentleman, if he had any sense of fair play,
would know perfectly well why we did not
come in. He knows as well as I do that we
were in the midst of a political cataclysm
at the time. He knows that both on his
side and on other sides there was such
passion and hatred aroused in the community that it was impossible for a vast
mass of people to take any sane line. He
says we waged war upon the Northern
Parliament. Who waged war upon the
Northern Parliament? The right hon.
Gentleman ought to be very explicit. I
speak for myself, and I say that during the
four years that I was an elected representative in this Assembly and did not
attend, I do not believe I made any speeches
or took part in political associations of any
kind, and I can say the same for my colleagues. But the right hon. Gentleman went
from platform to platform, and from city
to city making eloquent and touching
appeals to us to come into this Parliament,
and stating that if we came in and associated
ourselves with the life of the community and
occupied our legitimate positions in the conduct of the Parliamentary institution, we
would get fair play. We have not got fair
play.

religious denomination?

Mr. MCALLISTER. It did.
Mr. DEVLIN: The right hon. Gentleman

The PRIME MINISTER: I am only telling

of the Senate. It is only because you do not

place in the magistracy. It is not because

Gentleman is not so simple as to think that

Of course it would be splendid if those
of us who are their representatives here,
and who have come here on trust, sat silent
and never uttered a single word of protest
against it. We came in, I say, in response
to the appeals of the right hon. Gentleman,
but we might as well not be here at all. The
right hon. Gentleman says he is glad we

right hon. Gentleman's word, but I confess
that I do not think he likes us here with
enthusiasm. What is the good in our coming
here? What function do we discharge? In
what way do we justify our Parliamentary
existence, but by securing concessions and
rights for the people we represent? We get
none of them whatever, not one. The right
hon. Gentleman will no doubt say, "Do you
not get the old-age pensions for the old-age
pensioners?" I read of some funny story
like that having been told at a pompous
oration at a Unionist meeting some time ago.
"Do you not get the unemployment allowance?" You cannot deny us that. Probably that would be taken from us if you
could, but you cannot deny us the unenployment allowance, and you cannot prevent
us securing the old-age pensions.
ceive them by law. Anything we have, we

We re-
This is my point. We are a big element
in the community. You have stated over
and over again that the bringing about of
peace was contributed to largely by the
spirit which the Catholic people in Ulster
had shown. Therefore we contributed that
But what encouragement is it to those who
remain outside if those of us who have come
in are treated this way. We are not looking
for anything for ourselves. We would take
no privileges or personal advantages. We
are merely here for the public good and to
defend those people to whom I have referred,
but we might as well not be here as far as
the sum total of our achievement is concerned. That is the point. During the four
years that we did not come in we got
nothing; during the twelve months that we
have been in we have got less. Yes; practically less. (Laughter.) I am glad I say
something to interest hon. Gentlemen
opposite. I am glad I roused their sense
of humour-the only sense they have-when
it is roused by me. But this is an unhappy
admission to have to make for a public
representative who wants other people to
come into this Parliament to have to makethat he might as well not be here at all
except for this, that I have always made a
point in public life that if the people I represent are to be ill treated or maltreated
at least I will have the advantage of exposing
it. (Hon. Members: Hear, hear.) I do not
want to expose it if you do the right thing.
And the right hon. Gentleman and his
Friends need not think that he will carry
on negotiations with other parts of Ireland
and suppose that we must be as if we did
not exist at all-regard us as pariahs and
outcasts and, as I said before, that we must
be treated like the blacks of South America.
No doubt you do not murder us; you do
not take away our property. You do not
do any of these things. You allow us to
exist. That is practically what it amounts
to. I claim as a citizen of a country constitutionally governed that we have some
right to something further than mere existence. That is all I want to say on the
general question.
I want to say this further, in my judgment
if this Parliament is to be run on its present
lines this is entirely an indefensible expenditure. This Parliament is a voting machine,
not a free deliberative assembly. Your
ukases are prepared elsewhere and are
brought down here to be sanctioned by us.
A deliberative assembly is an assembly where
the Government stands for main principles
and defends them. In the freedom of discussion there is some come and go, some give
and take. There has never been any here.
I venture to say that no Government has
been freer from criticism than this Government either outside or inside. None. There
has been practically no passion, no violence.
That there has been strong, vigorous and
intelligent criticism I admit.
But you
should not complain about that, because it
gives you the right to reply and to justify
yourselves. There have been no scenes.
On the whole, this Parliament as an
assembly has been an exceedingly creditable
one. The only form of criticism that we
have been engaged in has been largely criticism of social legislation. We never said
that you did not feel for the people. At
least I never said it. But some of us feel
more intensely for the people, because as
you are in the Government you cannot feel
as intensely as those of us who are outside
and in touch with the people. Therefore we
have criticised your social legislation. We
have pointed out its flaws. We have argued
in favour of how it could be developed on
more humane lines. Do you mean to say
if we choose to apply ourselves to violent

Never once on the Widows' Pensions, upon

for the motion of the hon. Member for East

The PRIME MINISTER: It is rather
difficult to know where to begin. If my hon.
Friend (Mr. Devlin) will allow me I will
answer the hon. Member for East Belfast
(Mr. Beattie), who moved the reduction, first
of all. I would like to point out with regard
to the salaries of Ministers that these salaries
were all fixed by a free Committee of this
House outside any Government control whatever. It was appointed very early on, and
the whole question was placed in their hands
and they settled these salaries and the
Government decided to accept whatever they
recommended. That has held ever since, so
that the Government cannot be involved in
any way in the uqestion whether the salaries
are too high or too low,
I can assure the House of this at all events
that there is not a single one of my colleagues, when we come to lay down our office
in due course, who will not lay it down a
very much poorer man than when he took on
the onerous job of endeavouring to govern
Ulster. (Hon. Members: Hear, hear.) So
that hon. Members may make themselves
quite easy upon that. If the salaries are big
they go into Ulster, and more than that,
in order that Ministers may carry on as they
think fit in the interests of the Ulster people.
Then I come to the charge made by the
hon. Member for West Belfast (Mr. Devlin).
One would think to hear him he had never
been in opposition in his life before.
Mr. DEVLIN: I always was and always
will be. (Hon. Members: Hear, hear).
The PRIME MINISTER: Because, after
all, the minority in any House is there to
criticise the Government, but it is not there
to govern. It is not here to govern, or to
claim any rights or privileges over
majority.
Mr. DEVLIN: We never asked that.

The PRIME MINISTER: You never asked
that? The hon. Member goes on to point out
all the disabilities under which he and his
particular followers labour in Ulster. There
never was a more unfounded charge. This
Parliament carried on for some four years
without the presence of the hon. Member or
any of his colleagues. And I will say on
behalf of these Members who from the start
in spite of the turmoil, in spite of the difficulties, came here day by day, that those
Members took no action whatever in order
to penalise in any way the Roman Catholics
in our midst. (Hon. Members: Hear, hear.)
The fact that the hon. Member and some of
his colleagues whom, I repeat, we are
delighted to see taking part in our discussions
and show up whatever is wrong-I think the
very fact that they have come here to join
in our deliberations and have not been able
to bring before the Government or the House
one single case so far as I know of what the
hon. Member called ill treatment or maltreatment of his fellow Roman Catholics-
Mr. DEVLIN: Surely the right hon.
Gentleman is not serious in making a statement like that. I told him distinctly we had
no representation on the Bench, no representation in the Senate. We have practically no representation in the magistry
(Hon. Members: Oh.) No, unless what the

The PRIME MINISTER: If I may take
the last illustration the hon. Member mentioned. I am speaking entirely from
memory. He says "We have not a single
representative in the police.”
Mr. DEVLIN: We have practically none.
The PRIME MINISTER: That is entirely
the fault of the hon. Member's own fellow
Roman Catholics. A Committee of this
House was set up. I think if I remember
aright, every staunch Orangeman on this
side of the House was put on that Committee in order to devise what they considered a proper police force for Northern
Ireland. It is to the credit of that Committee that they recommended two-thirds
Protestants and one-third Roman Catholics
on that force. Is it fair that the Government and Members on this side of the House
are to bear all the blame, because Roman
Catholics would not come forward and fill
the thousand places left at their disposal?
These are the sort of wild charges that
are thrown across the floor here. As the
hon. Member says, of course, it gives us the
opportunity of correcting them. I personally
would far sooner that the criticism were fair
and that there was no necessity for correction. I think in this small community
of ours it would be far better if there was
less acrimony and every person would try
to live in peace and harmony together, than
that this religious question should be raised
in this House. It would be far better. If
the hon. Member goes on and begins to talk
about what is forbidden to Roman Catholics
it makes it very difficult indeed. I am not
going to be drawn into saying one provocative thing. Ulster has got on so quietly.
I do not think when one considers all we
have gone through during these past five
years anyone can cavil at the small Estimate put forward by the Head of the Government that is what it comes to-having a
daily watch over the whole affairs of Ulster,
keeping in close touch not only with
Great Britain and the British Government
of which we are the channel of communication, but generally carrying on the
Government of the country. I do not think
anyone can possibly say these Estimates
are otherwise than very moderate and very
fair.
Mr. MCALLISTER: With reference to the
remark of the Prime Minister that he deprecates raising the sectarian question in
this House no one in this House knows
better than the Prime Minister that it lies
in his power at any time he wishes to cause
all these questions to cease to be raised in
this House. If he is prepared to mete out
justice to the people we represent I guarantee he will never hear the question of
sectarianism raised in this House.
The hon. Member for Antrim has referred
to the fact that his co-religionists in Ballymena were praised on a recent occasion. It
was my privilege to contribute to that praise.
But let me point out to the hon. Member
that we on these Benches believe we have a
right to differentiate between the public representatives and their co-religionists in
Northern Ireland. If we did not feel some
confidence in the people they represent, we
would not be here. But we realise the fact
that this Government is living in the middle
ages, and that the people are living in 1926.
That is proved by the result of the last
election when the official representatives of
the Government were at the bottom of the
poll. It was not the representatives of the
people but the people generally who were
praised, and it was my privilege to associate
myself with that praise.
The hon. Member for Antrim (Mr.
Crawford) does not represent Ballymena. He
was not referred to. As his colleagues know
he was elected for Antrim to the exclusion
of Mr. Megaw, and I must say with regard
to Mr. Megaw-and no two men could differ
further in political beliefs than he and Ithat he was always an educated gentleman
in every act, or word, or deed. (Hon.
Members: Hear, hear.) I do say that the
hon. Member for Antrim (Mr. Crawford) has
no right to associate himself with any praise
that was contributed because, as his colleagues know, when he was on the look out
for number one votes he made a special
mission to Lisburn to seek those votes.

Mr. T. W. McMULLAN: I just wanted to
say a few words with reference to one item
of this Vote, and that is the salary of the
Prime Minister. The Prime Minister has
just told us that when it comes to the day
or which he and his colleagues lay down
their offices-and I trust that that day is
far distant--(hon. Members: Hear, hear)-
they will leave their offices poorer men than
when they took them up. I believe that
statement is fairly justified. I am just as
much out for economy as anyone on the
opposite side of this Committee, but I think
economy should be fair to the individual,
and I do not think that under present circumstances the salary of the Prime Minister
is adequate for the position which he has
to maintain.
I am a little diffident of speaking on this
matter with the Prime Minister present, but
I think it is but right that I should say
what I feel. When this salary was fixedand I was one of the Committee which fixed
it-we had no idea that a great establishment like that at Stormont would have to
be maintained by the Prime Minister. Now
I look upon that salary of £3,200, and I would
suggest to hon. Members that they should
look at it as having Income Tax and Super
Tax deducted from it. It seems to me that
the net result to the Prime Minister is somewhere about £1,700 or £1,800 a year, and I
would imagine that that would scarcely be
sufficient to pay for the actual service of
that huge establishment at Stormont.
But beyond that our Prime Minister has
to support his family. He has many private
expenses and then he has a great many public
expenses. He has got a big and a generous
heart-(hon. Members: Hear, hear)-and he
is always ready to help every cause in Ulster
and to entertain deputations. I may say
that deputations within the last four or five
years have proved very much more willing
to go to see the Prime Minister at Stormont
Castle than to see other Ministers at their
offices (Laughter)-and I can quite understand it, because they are certainly entertained in a most hospitable way. I feel that
the Prime Minister incurs a great burden
of expense for the sake of Ulster, to help
to keep us happy and peaceful and contented.
He is always trying to do something for us,
and this salary seems to me in no way
adequate for the position he has to maintain.
If the Prime Minister, at that distant day
of which he speaks, had resigned office I
cannot see how anyone without enormous
means could undertake the upkeep of Stormont Castle and the dignity which must be
kept up in connection with it, and show the
lavish hospitality which the Prime Minister
has been showing. To do that a man would
require to have very large private means,
and it would mean that the position of Prime
Minister would be confined to a very few
of our leading people in Ulster. It seems
to me that it might be a suggestion to the
Minister of Finance (Mr. Pollock)-and I
hope I have got his sympathy-that some
allowance should be made for the maintenance of this establishment at Stormont
Castle, because I feel that it is not fair to
our Prime Minister to ask him to do it on
the present salary.
Mr. KYLE: I did not intend to take any
part in this debate except to raise a point
which I raised this time last year. The
point is that the practice established by Mr.
Gladstone. I think as far back as 1867, should
be established in Northern Ireland, and that
when a Cabinet Minister takes office he
should resign all directorates. That is as
much in the Minister's own interests as it
is in the interests of the community itself.
I do not think it is right or proper that right
hon. Gentlemen should be members of the
Cabinet, directing responsible Departments
of the State, and at the same time be in
control-direct control-of various huge
concerns as directors. I think it was an
admirable principle which was laid down in
Great Britain and which has been carried
out ever since, and, seeing that there is so
much talk about moving on parallel lines
with Great Britain and going forward step
by step with Great Britain-those blessed
phrases! at least there might be some
attempt to carry it into effect in this very
important matter, for it is an important
matter.
Gentlemen occupying positions as directors
in various concerns ought not to be members
of the Government, ought not to be in the
Cabinet. I want to say that the reason
why I am very strenuous about this is that
I think it is as much in the interests of the
Cabinet themselves as of the general community. What trust, what confidence can the
people have if they know, for example, that
a member of the Cabinet is a director of one
of the big works in Belfast? What confidence
have the working people or the general body
of citizens that these people will not allow

CLASS IV. No. 5.
WIDOWS', ORPHANS' AND OLD AGE
CONTRIBUTORY PENSIONS.
Motion made, and Question proposed:
"That a sum not exceeding £145,000 be
granted to His Majesty for the Services of
the year ending 31st March, 1927, to provide
the sum payable to the Ministry of Finance
Pensions Account in accordance with the
provisions of the Widows', Orphans' and Old
Age Contributory Pensions Act (Northern
Ireland), 1925."

have the honour to submit to the Committee
is for the sum of £145,000. It represents the
State contribution under the Widows',
Orphans' and Old Age Contributory Pensions
Act which was passed in October last, and
which became operative, so far as the
Widows' and Orphans' Penisons portion of it
is concerned, on 4th January last. I think it
will interest the Committee to know that the
number of pre-Act widows' pensions which
have been paid amounts to 3,245.
Mr. DEVLIN: For what period?
Mr. ANDREWS: Those have been paid
since 4th January last. The number of dependent children in respect of whom mothers,

Shillington, Major David Graham

When this Measure of social reform was
passed in this House we had great hopes and
aims, and I am very glad to be in a position
to say that those hopes and aims have all
been realised. It was a great Measure of
social reform. It has brought brightness,
consolation, and hope into the homes of
many of our people where previously there
was little but despair and distress. It has
been said that this Parliament of ours is
extravagant, that the Government has really
not justified its existence, because it has done
nothing for our industrial classes. This Act
was passed by this House, and personally I
feel that if we had done nothing else since
our Parliament was established but pass this
great Measure, considering the advantages

which it confers upon SO many of our

in the way we would like if it had been a

hon. Gentleman in administering such an

productive expenditure. All money spent in
this way comes back to all the classes involved in the State. They get it. None of
the widows' pensions, orphans' pensions, unemployed benefit or old age pensions is put
into the bank. It is all spent. It
comes back to every element in
the material life of the community.
Therefore, I wish to congratulate the right
hon. Gentleman, and I am sure he is proud
to be associated with legislation of this
character.
Colonel WOODS: I would like to associate
myself entirely with the observations of the
last speaker (Mr. Devlin), and I would like to
emphasise what the hon. Member for North
Belfast (Mr. Kyle) has said about infusing a
little more sympathy into the administrative
staff. For instance, last summer when I was
at Wembley I heard of a case in Belfast
where a man who was 84 years of age could
not find his birth certificate. No one could
find it for him. The administrative staff insisted on having a witness of this man's
birth. The man was 84 years of age, and I
leave it to you whether it would be possible
to secure evidence of the birth of a man after
all those years. However, after a few weeks
the Minister of Labour was informed of the
circumstances and the matter was adjusted
and the man is now in receipt of benefit.
This always reminds me how easy it is to
misjudge appearances. I have heard of a
Member of a Government who found that a
member of his family was being taught the
tango, and threw the partner out on the
street simply because he was deaf and could
not hear the gramophone. I hope that the
Minister of Labour will see that the
members of his staff show a little more of the
mercy and tact that he exhibits himself, and
he will deserve the support of every right
thinking man.
Supply-
Committee.
HOUSE OF COMMONS.
Mr. MILLER: I would like to put a
conundrum to the right hon. Gentleman (Mr.
Andrews), and it is: "When is an orphan
not an orphan?" A case was brought to my
notice some time ago and I thought the
party was very badly treated. The case was
that of a widow whose husband had been a
delicate man. He died and left the widow
and two small children. The widow remarried in August last. She put in a claim
for pension for the children but not for herself, because she could not get it. The pension
was refused, and the matter was brought to
my notice. I went to the Ministry about
it, and I was told that if she had not been
married until after the 4th January she
would have been entitled to a pension of
18s a week, but that immediately on her
marriage she would lose the 10s, while the
pensions for the children would continue. But
as she had married before January the
children were left out in the cold. That is
the way the matter stands at present. The
man she married is a soldier, serving his
King and country in Egypt, and she is doubly
a widow, or rather a grass widow. There are
probably many cases of that sort, and I
would ask the right hon. Gentleman to give
them his earnest consideration.
Mr. BEATTIE: I wish to take this opportunity to call attention to exceptional circumstances that have come under my notice.
Our Act as it stands requires further legislation in order to make the whole of it
operative. Section 44 is lying dormant at
the present time; it cannot become operative
until this House passes a Legitimising Bill.
I may be wrong, but I have received replies
from the authorities to that effect. Section
44 applies to illegitimate children. A husband
dying leaves a woman with a child, which
is called an illegitimate child. That widow
is not qualified for the pension. I had one
case brought under my notice of a naval
man, who was the father of a child. He
went to sea, and coming home at the end
of twelve months he married the girl. But
he died four months after the marriage. The
widow applied for a widow's and orphan's
pension, but owing to Section 44 not being
rendered operative by a further Legitimising
Bill her application was refused.
I would also like to bring before the notice
of the Minister the case of widows who
claimed the pension prior to the 4th January,
1926. A widow who became a widow prior
to the 4th of January, 1926, will be in receipt
of the pension until her youngest child
attains the age of 14, or, if the child is
attending a continuation school, the age of
16. But her pension will cease when the
child reaches the age of 14 years and 6
months, and she will not be entitled to any
further pension until she becomes 65 years
of age. A lady whose husband died on the
4th January, 1926, or afterwards, and who
is left in a similar position, receives the
pension throughout her life if she does not
re-marry. Is there any way of remedying
that great hardship, which is causing a
good deal of dissatisfaction? I have had
cases brought to my notice in which one
husband died last year and another husband
this year. One has the pension for a limited
period only, and the other has continuity
of pension. I do not know whether it would
be possible to make the Act retrospective in
order to cover those who have been left
widows since 1922, when the depression in
trade set in. In Scotland a widow who ha
had a child previous to her marriage could
obtain the pension for the child. but in
Northern Ireland she could not do that
owing to the absence of a Legitimising Bill.
It has been contended by some Members of
the Government that we are opposing the
Estimates for political reasons. I want to
repudiate that statement.
The CHAIRMAN: I think the hon.
Member had better defer his statement of
the reasons for reducing an Estimate until
he reaches an Estimate on which he makes
such a proposal. I understand he is not
doing that in this case.
Mr. BEATTIE: I would like to increase
the amount of money mentioned in this
Estimate. This is a Vote on which I think
we could not expend too much money. If
we tried to make the whole Act workable,
and to remove the anomalies, some of which
I have indicated, more money would be required.
Another case that I want to bring to the
notice of the Minister is that of the insured
contributor who had 52 stamps to his credit.
His normal occupation was that of a cobbler.
A cobbler is a person employed by shoemakers. who takes the cobbling work home.
I understand that in past years the big warehouses that carried on boot repairing gave
out cobblers' work, but did not class the
cobblers as employees of the firm,
and took no responsibility for paying
health insurance stamps. Α cobbler
is now classified as a master shoemaker, and owing to that fact his widow is
not entitled to a widow's pension. The case
I want to refer to is that of a cobbler who
had 52 stamps to his credit, and who was
two years on the sick list before he died.
His widow has been denied the right to a
pension, and she has five little "kiddies" depending upon her. At the present moment
she is carrying on the cobbling business
herself. I called in to see her, and told her
that if it had been possible for me to bring
her in I certainly would have done so, but,
unfortunately, the Advisory Committee ruled
against me, because the normal occupation
Supply-
Committee.
15 APRIL 1926
of her husband was described as master shoemaker, and he could not be classified as an
insured contributor. I would be pleased if
anything could be done in that exceptionally
hard case. I am sure some ways and means
could be devised for securing the desired
object. I am pleased to support this Estimate, and I would be more pleased if all
widows were brought under the Act irrespective of whether their husbands had been
insured or not.
Mr. ANDREWS: Notwithstanding the fact
that the Amendments put forward from the
Opposition Benches were not accepted by the
Government, I am very glad to feel, using
his own words, that the Member for West
Belfast (Mr. Devlin) considers that the Act has
brought happiness, peace and security into
thousands of homes in our midst. The hon.
Member for West Belfast, however, went on
to claim that he was really the father of the
Measure, and in support of that contention
he put forward the argument that the
Government had not included the Bill in
the King's Speech. I may point out, however, that the Minister of Finance in his
Budget statement in May a year ago referred
to the fact that it was the intention of the
Government to bring in this Measure and to
follow Great Britain in this connection, as
we have always done-whether there was an
Opposition here or not-with those social
services which my Department is charged
with the responsibility of administering.
Hon. Members have referred to certain
administrative matters. I do not propose to
deal with them in detail, but if hon. Gentleman will furnish me with the names of the
widows I will have each case carefully reconsidered. Speaking generally, however, I
am entitled to say that, keeping within the
four walls of the Measure, which I am bound
to do, the administration is as sympathetic
as it can be, and I would like to say that
I think this Committee, as well as the
Government, are deeply indebted to my staff
for their splendid and unselfish efforts in
order to bring this Measure into being at
a very moderate expense and in a very expeditious and able way.
May I just add in conclusion that it is
quite true that "existing widows," as they
are called, that is women who became widows
prior to the 4th January last do not
receive the same benefits under the provisions of the Act as those who have become
widows since the 4th January, the reason
being that although the husbands of the pre-
Act widows contributed to health insurance
benefits they did not contribute to the

reach of those who became widows after the
4th January.
Question put, and agreed to.
CLASS II. No. 9.
RECORD OFFICE.
Motion made, and Question proposed:
"That a sum not exceeding £1,946 be granted
to His Majesty to complete the sum necessary
to defray the charge that will come in course
of payment during the year ending the 31st
March, 1927, to pay the salaries and expenses
of the Public Record Office of Northern
Ireland."
Mr. BARBOUR: I would ask hon. Members
to turn to page 46 of the book of Estimates.
In this Estimate there is an increase of £74,
and a re-arrangement of the charges for
staff. The salary of the Deputy Keeper is
now entirely borne on this Estimate, as
owing to the increase of work in the office
his time has been more and more occupied
on Record Office work, and he has been relieved to a corresponding extent of some of
his duties in the Ministry of Finance. It
has also been necessary to advance the status
of one of the clerks who acts as substitute
for the Deputy Keeper. The senior clerk,
instead of receiving a salary on a scale of
£60-£250, plus an allowance of £50 a year,
is placed on the scale of £300, rising by £15
to £400.
There is no other expenditure item to
which attention may be called in the Estimate, but in general it may be stated that
the Office continues to stimulate public
attention, as is evidenced in the collection
and recovery of various types of Ulster records and in a number of very valuable
donations which have been received and
made available for public consultation.
It is so rarely it is possible to draw the
attention either of Members of this House
or even of the public generally to the nature
of the work that is carried on by the Record
Office, that I should appreciate it very much
if hon. Members would bear with me just a
few minutes while I illustrate in an interesting manner one feature of the work done
by this Office.
In order to gather in papers of historical
interest to the Province inquiries were
addressed to persons likely to be in possession of historical family papers, and, as a
result the Marquess of Downshire, Viscount
Massereene and Ferrard, and the Earl of
Antrim have either presented papers to the
Department, or allowed extracts of interesting matter to be made. Amongst other
original documents relating to Ulster which
have been received by the Record Office may
be mentioned maps, deeds, rentals, yeomanry
papers, vestry books.
It may be of interest to hon. Members to
mention a curious discovery made as a result
of the deposit by Major Dobbs, of the wellknown family of Carrickfergus, of a collec-
Mines Facilities [Money]-
Committee.
HOUSE OF COMMONS
[Mr. Barbour]
tion of family papers. These related in the
main to Carrickfergus, but included among
them, however, were three journals dealing
with exploration of the North-West Passage.
It appears that a member of the family--
Arthur Dobbs-was Governor of North
Carolina between 1754 and 1765, and had
collected information relative to exploration
to discover the North-West Passage into the
Pacific from the Arctic Ocean. The earliest
of these documents was the journal of Henry
Kelsey, covering the period between 1683 and
1722. Kelsey had spent a whole life in
exploration, and was probably the first
Englishman to penetrate from the Hudson
Bay coast to the prairie country of Western
Canada. It was not known that a copy of
this journal was in existence, and the Hudson
Bay Company, in London, as soon as they
heard, sent over members of their staff to
copy the journal in extenso. In addition,
inquiries have been received from Canada
as to the possibility of making manuscript
or printed copies for use in the Dominion.
It may also be mentioned that the Dobbs'
papers include an account of the Quebec
campaign of 1757, evidently by an eye-witness.
This, by the way, gives a different version
of the death scene of General Wolffe from
that which appears in the histories.
Mr. KYLE: Tell us about it.
Mr. BARBOUR: It is available in the
Record Office.
Coming to that part of the Department's work which deals with the replacement of destroyed records-it may be
n:entioned that about 1,400 papers of this
kind have SO far been received. So in
addition to the mere receiving and recording
of the less interesting legal papers it is
hoped that this may be the means of building matters of considerable historical and
sentimental interest relating to the historical
life of our Province. I beg to move.
Mr. BEATTIE: I am not going to move a
reduction, because I believe the Office is
necessary. But I would like to know, seeing
it is a Record Office Vote, can we in that
Office in any way get at the assets of the
Northern Government. Do you keep a
record of the buildings purchased either by
Imperial money or Northern Ireland money?
Can we get at what the assets of the Northern
Government are?
Question put, and agreed to.
Resolution to be reported on Tuesday.
The Committee to sit again on Tuesday.
Mines (Working Facilities,
Support, &c.) Money.
Considered in Committee under Standing
Order No. 65.
Motion made, and Question proposed:
"That for the purpose of any Act of the
present Session to make provision for facilitating the working of minerals, and for
imposing restrictions on the working of
minerals required for the support of buildings and works, and to amend the law with
respect to Mines, and for purposes connected
therewith, it is expedient to authorise the payment out of moneys provided by Parliament,
subject to Rules made under any such Act,
of the salaries or remuneration and the expenses of the Tribunal appointed to hold
inquiries and determine compensation, and
of the Assessors appointed to sit with the
County Court when hearing appeals, for the
purposes of any such Act."-(Governor's
Recommendation signified.)-(Mr. Barbour.)
Mr. BARBOUR: This is the Mines (Working Facilities, Support, etc.) Money Resolution. The Bill provides for the establishment
of a tribunal consisting of a practising
barrister, a member of the Panel of Official
Arbitrators appointed under the Acquisition
of Lands (Assessment of Compensation) Act,
1919, and one officer of the Ministry of Commerce. The rate of remuneration to be paid
to these members, and generally the incidental expenses which may be incurred in
connection with any sittings of the tribunal,
will be laid down in accordance with the
provisions of the Bill by Rules to be made by
the Ministry of Commerce with the approval
of the Ministry of Finance. The officer of
the Ministry of Commerce to serve on this
tribunal will be an existing officer of the
Ministry, and consequently no additional
expense will be incurred under this head.
We are, therefore. concerned only with the
fees which may be payable to a barrister and
to a member of the Panel of Official Arbitrators, together with any small incidental
expenses which may arise, and a possible expense in the event of appeals from the
tribunal's awards being made to the County
Court. The Bill in this case provides that
when hearing an appeal under this section
the County Court shall have the assistance
of a specially qualified assessor, who will be
selected from a list of persons of experience
in mining matters to be framed by the
Ministry of Commerce.
I am sure hon. Members will appreciate
that this Bill must be a provisional Measure
to a very great extent. We think it right
that the Government of Northern Ireland
should be in a position of readiness should
the desire originate on the part of anyone to
prosecute the development of minerals within
our borders and it would be a great pity if
any barrier should be found to exist for
which legislative provision had not been
made. The meetings of this tribunal will
only be called very rarely, but it is not
possible to give any idea of what expense may
be involved in providing for this tribunal,
but in any case it is bound to be very light
indeed. I beg to move.
Supply.
Adjournment.

CASE OF MRS. WHAN.
2. Mr. KYLE asked the Minister of Home
Affairs whether it is a fact that the case of
Mrs. Whan has now been taken out of the
hands of District-Inspector Allen and put
into the hands of the Detective Department,
and whether it is a fact that Mrs. Whan's
son was brought to the police station on
Sunday, 11th April, and directed to give a
sample of his writing.
Sir DAWSON BATES: The answer to the
first part of the question is in the negative.
The police investigations requiring the

Mr. Allen, which were recently the subject

CONSTABULARY.

Sir DAWSON BATES: Number of paid

Written Answers.
BALLINAMALLARD POLICE BARRACK.
Mr. COOPER asked the Minister of Home
Affairs whether he can state the cause of the
delay in building a police barrack in Ballinamallard, and if he is aware that many complaints have been made owing to the village
being left so long without police protection.
Sir DAWSON BATES: I regret to say
that the scheme for the reconstruction of
police barracks and for the erection of new
barracks, including one proposed to be bullt
in Ballinamallard, has been delayed for
some months mainly on account of the fact
that if the scheme had been carried out in
its entirety the cost, it is now ascertained,
would have been very much in excess of the
original Estimates.
It has been found necessary, therefore, to
revise the various plans of reconstruction
and erection so as to bring the total cost
within the financial resources at the Government's disposal.
With regard to the latter part of the hon.
Member's question, I may point out that
Ballinamallard is constantly visited by
police from Irvinestown, and I am not aware
of any complaints having been made in the
manner suggested.
The whole question of the reconstruction
and building programme is at present receiving my earnest attention, and I hope
that operations will be resumed at a very
early date.

AND TYRONE.

how many widows' pensions have been
granted in the counties of Fermanagh and
Tyrone respectively.
The MINISTER OF LABOUR (Mr.
Andrews): The total number of claims to
widows' pensions granted up to the 15th
instant in respect of County Fermanagh is
56 and in respect of County Tyrone 181.
Pensions Bill-
Second Reading.
20 APRIL 1926
ORDERS OF THE DAY.
Pensions (Increase) Bill.
Order for Second Reading read.
Motion made, and Question proposed:
"That the Bill be now read a Second time."
The MINISTER OF FINANCE (Mr. Pollock): I rise to move the Second Reading of
this comparatively small Measure consisting
of five Clauses. Although in itself not so
very important, still I think it will be necessary that I should offer some explanation
of its incidence and of the interests which it
affects. In order that this may be
thoroughly understood I would remind the
House that the Imperial Parliament passed
two separate Acts in connection with the
increase of pensions to the different Services.
Both these Acts deal with pensioners whose
pensions were in force prior to August, 1914.
It will be realised that the pensions were on
a very low scale in the period prior to the war
because of the low rates of remuneration
which were generally accorded in comparison
with those of later dates. Accordingly, in
order that grievances might be removed and
justice done to those poor pensioners the
British Government passed an Act in the
year 1920, granting certain increases to the
pensions then in existence, but as time went
on it was found that this increase did not
conform fully with the rise in the cost of
living, and in 1924 an amending Act was
passed directed to increasing further the
pensions to which I have referred.
The pensioners affected include on the one
hand Civil Service and police pensioners and
other pensioners paid from State funds, or
quasi-State funds, and, on the other hand,
pensioners of local authorities.
The pensions paid by the last-named, that is, the
local authorities, were only to be increased
by consultation with the Treasury, and although decisions were reached between the
Treasury and the local authorities these pensions were not mandatory, and it was left
to the local authorities to use their own judgment in regard to the standard of pensions
they gave to those who had been in their
employment. The amending Act of 1924, as
I have said, brought into operation larger
increases than the 1920 Act, and if hon.
Members will consult the Bill itself they will
see that they conform with the increases
mentioned in the sub-section of Clause 2.
Turning for a moment to the relationship
between these two Acts passed by the
Imperial Government to ourselves, I need
hardly remind hon. Members that the Act
of 1920 was passed before the transfer to
Northern Ireland of any of the functions
under the Government of Ireland Act, and
they, therefore, applied to such pensions as
were at that date being paid from Imperial
T
funds to Royal Irish Constabulary pensioners
and the Civil Service pensioners retired
from Irish Departments. A proportion of
the pensions belonging to Northern Ireland
were collected, and are being collected from
us through a deduction from our residuary
share of taxes.
When the 1924 Act was passed the situation was a little different because at that
time this Parliament was functioning, and
the situation arose that some of these
pensioners became legally entitled to claim
upon the British Government for the increases that were granted in that Act, but
our Ministry of Finance established the
position with the British Treasury that it
was not competent for the British Government, without consultation with this
Government, to impose any additional
burden upon the Government of Northern
Ireland through the machinery of this Act.
Therefore, when it came to us we agreed that
while in equity and in justice it was quite
right that we should bear our portion of that
burden we established the position with the
British Treasury that it was not competent,
as I have said, for the British Parliament to
pass any Measure of that kind without our
concurrence, and it is to conform with the
arrangement that this Bill is required. In
other words it regularises, if I may put it in
that way, the arrangement as between the
British Government and ourselves. I need
only say now that the main increase will
take place in connection with the Royal
Irish Constabulary pensioners. It will add
about £6,000 per annum, which, of course,
will be gradually diminishing as the
pensioners disappear from Northern
Ireland expenditure.
Clause 2 of the Bill makes corresponding
provision for those pensioners whose
pensions are directly paid from Northern Ire
land funds or revenues-namely, National
School Teachers and Petty Sessions Clerks.
The Government feel that as we have kept
pace with British social legislation and
have conceded the propriety of a charge in
connection with the R.I.C. and other
pensioners to whom I have already alluded,
it would be inequitable and illogical not to
treat similarly the pensioned teachers and
Petty Sessions clerks. It is, therefore, proposed that further increases be made on the
same basis as is provided in sub-Sections A,
B, and C of the second Clause of the
Measure. If reference is made to this particular part of the Clause hon. Members will
be able to understand the exact character of
the increases that are suggested.
The first sub-section to the proviso to
Clause 2 is somewhat involved, and perhaps
requires a little explanation to make it
simple, but it is both simple and equitable
when it is understood. It insures that no
Supply.

Pensions Bill-
HOUSE OF COMMONS.
[Mr. Pollock]
pension shall be increased beyond the
pension that would be awarded to a
pensioner retiring to-day with a similar
length of service, who has cost of living
bonus reckoned as a pensionable emolument.
An example will explain. Suppose a prewar pensioner retiring on a salary of £140
receives a pension of £70.
Under the proposals embodied in the Bill he will, if otherwise qualified, receive a total pension of
£105, that is to say, £70 and 50 per cent.
added, making it £105. If, however, a Petty
Sessions Clerk who retired on the 1st April
of this year on a similar salary, but with
cost of living bonus added only receives a
pension of £100, the pre-war pensioner will
get not £105 but £100. I am sure that the
House will agree that it would be wrong
that anyone should be in receipt of a larger
sum under the new arrangement than a
clerk retiring at the present time under
identical conditions.
The second sub-Section to the proviso deals
with a different matter. Under Clause 70,
sub-Section 3, of our own Education Act it
provides that the Ministry of Finance may
grant to any then existing pensioned teacher
such increase beyond that authorised by the
Pensions (Increase) Act of 1920 as would
bring his pension to an annual sum not exceeding £50. The object of this sub-section
is that the provision made in our own
Education Act of 1923 for the pensions of
retiring teachers will not be prejudiced; in
fact, that the bargain, if you like to put it
that way, that was then made with the
teachers shall be maintained. That is, in
short, the object of the sub-Section.
Now I come to Clause 3, which is very
simple, and I am sure that it will be held
by hon. Members to be very equitable; that
is to say, there was a provision which was
made originally that pensioners must reside
within the area of the British Isles, otherwise the pensioner would forfeit his pension.
Under this Clause that embargo is removed,
because, as we can readily realise, it may
happen that the relatives of the pensioner
may have gone abroad, and it is an unfair
thing to refuse to pay a man his legitimate
pension simply because he desires to reside
with his family at a distance.
Clause 4 of the Bill, which is really the
last Clause, gives the Ministry of Finance
power to apply the provisions respecting
increased pension percentages to the
pensions payable by local authorities.
Power is given to local authorities stil!
to preserve the right of these authorities
to regulate the terms and amounts
of the pensions given to their retiring
servants. I can only say in regard
to that that it seems to be only fair.
Those who have close and intimate knowledge of all the circumstances of their
servants and the question of whether they
have or have not earned a particular pension
-it seems only reasonable to assume-really
understand these matters to a greater degree
than the central authority. Therefore, instead of making this provision mandatory
with local authorities, it is a permissive
increase, and is left to their own judgment
to decide. These are the main features of
the Bill, and I beg to move.
Question put, and agreed to.
Bill committed to a Committee of the
Whole House for to-morrow.
