CLASS VI. No. 1.
MINISTRY OF AGRICULTURE.
Motion made, and Question proposed:
"That a sum not exceeding £51,448 be
granted to His Majesty to complete the sum
necessary to defray the charge that will come
in course of payment during the year ending
on the 31st of March, 1927, for salaries and
expenses of the Ministry of Agriculture."
(Note.-£13,000 has been voted on account).
Mr. ARCHDALE: Of the total increase
of £14,972, which this Estimate shows, page
112, £13,313 is due to the transfer to the
Ministry as from the 1st April last of the
administration of the Diseases of Animals
Acts. This Service was previously administered by the Imperial Government. The
inclusion of provision in the Northern Ireland Estimates for the Service does not, however, imply a new charge on our revenue.
Under the old arrangement we were still
liable for the cost of the Service, which was
recovered from us in the form of a deduction
from the Northern Ireland residuary share
of reserved taxes. In future we will adminster the Service ourselves and meet the
cost direct.
The real increase, therefore, is only
£1,559, which is entirely due to automatic
increments of salary to staff and to certain
additions of personnel necessary by the progressive extension of the Ministry's activities.
Sub-head A-Salaries, Wages and Allowances-This has been divided into eight Sections so as to give a clearer idea of the salary
cost of the various branches in which the
head-quarters establishment is grouped.
The total increase of £13,990 in the salaries
Estimate is to the extent of £11,376 due to the
transfer to the Ministry of the staff previously employed in the Imperial Secretary's
Department for Diseases of Animals work.
The total staff taken over numbers 43, including 13 veterinary inspectors engaged at
ports or on general duties, 21 ship inspectors,
cattle brander, disinfector, and an outdoor
clerical staff of 7 persons. With the exception
of one veterinary inspector, who has been
allocated to the Animals' Diseases Station at
Stormont for the purpose of research work,
and whose salary is included in the Agricultural Services Estimate, the salaries of all the
staff transferred are shown on this Estimate.
The real increase in salary costs is represented by a sum of £2,515, partly due to
automatic increments of salary and partly to
a slight increase of staff to keep pace with
the expansion of the Ministry's work, particularly with regard to the marketing of
eggs, live stock schemes and the suppression
of black scab in potatoes.
Sub-head B-Travelling and Subsistence
Expenses--provides for the travelling
expenses of administrative staff and headquarters' inspection staff, and would have
shown a reduction but for the necessity of
providing for the travelling expenses of the
newly-transferred
staff of Veterinary
Inspectors.
Sub-heads C1, C2, C3, and C4 would have
shown a material decrease of £265 in the
aggregate but for the new responsibility devolving on the Ministry for maintenance of
the Headquarter and Portal Inspection
Offices taken over in connection with the
Diseases of Animals work which necessitated
an additional provision of some £400.
Sub-heads D1 and D2-Printing and
Stationery-the decrease under these heads
would have been still larger but for the inclusion of provision in respect of Diseases
of Animals Services, which really is what
makes an increase altogether on this Vote.
In connection with Sub-head D3-Stationery
Office Publications-the increase on this subhead is due to inclusion of provision for
publication of a Register of non-pedigree
cattle and for the issue of a Report on the
Census of Agricultural Production.
In the case of Sub-heads E, F, and G-Law
Charges, Postage, Telegrams and Telephones, and Incidental Expenses-the increase in each of these Sub-heads is, as
before entirely due to the inclusion of provision in respect of Diseases of Animals
Services. I beg to move.
Mr. KYLE: I beg to move that this Estimate be reduced by £500. I do so to call
attention to the fact that this Estimate has
been increased by over £1,500, and I think the
Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Archdale) should
have raid more attention to the criticism
that has been going on in the country than
is apparent from the Estimate. I do so for
the other reason that the Minister of Agriculture seems to be living about fifty years
ago, before the names of trade unions were
ever heard of, or before there was any idea
of Agricultural Wages Boards being set up in
the counties. He seems to me to pay all his
attention to gentlemen whom he desires to
serve on his committees and one thing and
another, but he never pays any attention at
all to the interests and desires of the people
who produce all the wealth of the community,
namely, the agricultural labourers and the
tenant farmers. It is all very well for him to
ask us to vote a sum of £64,000, a net increase
of £14,972. He explains that away by saying
that £11,376 is due to the Diseases of Animals
Branch being transferred to Northern Ireland, leaving a total of £1,559 in excess of his
former estimate. One cannot see that the
Ministry of Agriculture is doing such valuable work in the Six Counties as to warrant
this huge expenditure, and, therefore, I beg
to move the reduction of this Vote by £500,
Supply-
Committee.
HOUSE OF COMMONS
Mr. P. O'NEILL: I beg to second the
Amendment proposed by the Leader of the
Opposition (Mr. Kyle). I think the agricultural service is not at all worth the amount
of this Vote. As a matter of fact, I think
the service has been a complete failure, and
we have only to look at the state of agriculture in the Six Counties to-day to bear out
what I say. In the matter of the planting
and growing of potatoes, one of the most important industries in the Six Counties-as a
matter of fact the principal industry for the
farmer-the farmers in some parts of the Six
Counties, in County Down particularly, have
been asked by the Ministry to plant a certain
class of potato. As a matter of fact, I think
it has been almost compulsory to plant this
class of potato. The farmers did so, and
they produced fine crops. But what has been
the net result? There is no market for
these potatoes to-day, and they cannot even
give them away.
Mr. ARCHDALE: May I just correct my
hon. Friend on one point as I do not want
him to be speaking under any misapprehension? He intimates that we induced the
men in County Down to plant Lochar potatoes. As a matter of fact ever since we came
into office we have been trying to get them
not to plant Lochar.
Mr. P. O'NEILL: Might I ask who it was
who induced the farmers to plant Lochar?
(An hon. Member: No one.) Did I hear
someone say "No one?" Did they do this off
their own bat? Were they not prevented
from planting another class of potato? Have
there not been areas scheduled under the
Black Scab Order and have not the farmers
in those areas been compelled to plant immune varieties? Was Lochar not one of the
immune varieties? Was Lochar not among
the varieties provided by the Department
and sent out to the farmers? It is so, and if
that were all it would not be so bad, but
you ask them this year to plant an immune
variety, and you supply them with an immune variety, a very good potato, I admit,
but still one which they cannot market,
and for which there is no demand across the
Channel, and there will be the same result
next year. That is why I say the Department are altogether wrong in their ideas
with regard to potatoes. As a matter of
fact they have made a complete failure and
have absolutely ruined the farmers of
County Down.
Potatoes are not the only thing. Take the
case of flax. You have advised them to grow
flax, and if there is one industry on farming
lines that should pay it is flax. But still
it is not an economic proposition at all, as
the farmer knows. Why, I cannot understand. The linen industry has practically
a monopoly, but still the growing of flax has
not been a paying proposition to the farmer.
I do not see why you should advise them to
grow flax, because I daresay that in seventy,
eighty, or ninety per cent, of cases there has
been a loss on it. I think it is a great
mistake, yet that is how you expect the
farmers to live. How do you justify the
service at all? Would you get the farmers
to say that the Ministry of Agriculture
could not be done without? If you ask the
farmers ninety per cent. of them will tell you
that it has not been of the slightest service
to them, and 100 per cent. in some districts
will say that it has been an absolute disservice to them, and particularly in the
county I represent-the County of Downwhere there are so many areas scheduled
under the Black Scab Order that they really
do not know what to turn their hands to.
Thousands of tons of potatoes to-day in Down
could be got for the taking of them away.
I do not see how under these circumstances
the Ministry can at all justify its existence,
and I certainly believe that I am quite
justified in seconding the reduction of this
Vote by the amount stated by the Leader
of the Opposition (Mr. Kyle).
Mr. LEEKE: In supporting the Amendment for the reduction of this Estimate 1
would like to know something about this
Marketing of Produce and Agricultural Education Branch. According to the Minister's
reply to the previous speaker (Mr. P.
O'Neill) his Department did not recommend
the farmers to grow Lochar or to grow flax.
What is the use of the expenditure of this
huge sum of money if the Department,
which was established primarily for the
development of agriculture, will not give the
farmers any advice on two of their most important crops? In South Derry there has
been a very big area scheduled because black
scab was discovered in it. It is a much
wider area, I think, than was necessary, due
to the action of the Department. They sent
their inspectors and officials down there to
market the produce of the farmers in this
district as they would not allow it to be
marketed in Belfast. It was the first thing,
fortunately, that they did, and it was a very
good idea, and I congratulate the Department on the fact that they did make some
effort to market the produce when they
scheduled the district. I praise them for
that part of their efficiency, and for the fact
that they grappled with the situation. But
the sellers, or those responsible for the
machinery that was established, were selling
these potatoes at fifteen shillings a ton below
the price at which the ordinary merchants
were selling the same variety, and the result
was that that caused the first real fall in
the English market for Irish potatoes, and
I largely attribute the poor market for Irish
potatoes to-day to the effects of that indiscreet
action. The English merchants, naturally
enough, saw the advantage to them, and,
Supply-
Committee.
20 APRIL 1926
instead of entering into the market where
there was competitive selling, took their
potatoes from this area. The result was that
the market went down and has never gone
up. It is possible to sell certain varieties

.
I think the Minister will agree that there
should have been more consultation with the
merchants with regard to this potato before

Another thing is that when the Department
is advising the farmers to grow an immune

Mr. WILLIAM MCMULLEN: I think it

Mr. ARCHDALE: That will arise on the
next Estimate.
Mr. WILLIAM MCMULLEN: If that will

may be quite a trifling sum, but still I

In view of the fact that I shall have an

Mr. DEVLIN: I think the Committee is
under an obligation to my two hon. Friends
for having raised the very important matters
which they have brought before the Committee in connection with this Vote. I
rather think it would have been preferable if
the Minister of Agriculture instead of confining himself to a mere recital of the
figures, had given us a real statement as to
what the agricultural policy of the Government is. Considering the present depressed
condition of agriculture in Northern Ireland, and indeed all over Ireland, it seems
to me rather contemptuous to treat one of
the most vital interests in the Province in
the manner in which it has been treated by
the right hon. Gentleman. I do not think
on an occasion of this sort we should confine ourselves purely to discussion of the

ought to be taken into the confidence of the
Minister as to what precisely the Government propose to do in order to relieve and

Mr. ARCHDALE: I am sorry to interrupt the hon. Member, but these potatoes

a free
grew these potatoes but had not

The Government gave a grant to the agricultural industry, and I am in favour of
helping the agricultural industry as much
as possible, but in my judgment a portion
of that grant ought to have been given to
these poor farmers to compensate them for
the loss brought upon them in consequence
of the action of the Government in narrowing the markets in which these potatoes
could be sold. If Parliament votes a large
sum of money such as Parliament has done
for the relief of agriculture, surely those
engaged in agriculture, who have been
vitally struck at, apart altogether from the
general depression, by a peculiar series of
circumstances for which they have no responsibility at all, are the people who should
be pre-eminently entitled to favourable consideration at the hands of the Ministry of
Agriculture.
I understand that the growers of these
potatoes waited upon the right hon. Gentleman and put their case before him. I would
be glad if, when the Minister replies, he
would give the Committee the reasons why
he has not given grants to these poor people.
It was no fault of their own that they
suffered from the general depression, and,
therefore, they should get the advantage of
the general grant. They should be regarded
as a special case and they should receive
special consideration because of the peculiar
circumstances in which they have been
robbed of their property and robbed of the
fruits of their industry.
I come now to another question, and that
is the question of sugar beet. There has
been a Commission set up for the purpose
of considering this and other germane
matters. This Commission has been sitting
for three years and we have had no recommendation from it on this subject. It seems
to me that there is a paralysis of initiative
in every branch of the Government service.
We have not a single fruitful suggestion
from the Government as to how we are to
grapple with either our industrial or economic difficulties, and what this Commission
is sitting on I do not know, for it has
brought forth nothing. If it has we have
not seen it on the Table of the House. This
Commission has been sitting and we do not
know what its recommendations are with
regard to the growing of sugar beet. When
potatoes are no longer a source productive of
revenue for the farmers, many people think
sugar beet would be a profitable substitute.
The experiment has been tried in England
and in Southern Ireland, and grants of Government money have been given for the
growing of sugar beet in the South of Ireland and also, I think, in England, and I
would like to know why the Government of
Northern Ireland has done nothing in regard to the growing of sugar beet here.
Not very long ago the Ulster Farmers'
Union passed a resolution accepting the
Land Purchase Bill. The Government said
this Farmers' Union was the only representative body of its kind in Ulster. Well,
when the Ulster Farmers' Union was making representations in favour of the Land
Purchase Act, which was most unfavourable
to the unbought farmers of Northern Ireland, it was a most wonderful organization.
Has the right hon. Gentleman, the Minister
of Agriculture, paid any attention to the
recommendations of the Ulster Farmers'
Union in regard to sugar beet? In case
he does not know what the Farmers' Union
recommend perhaps I will have the permission of the House to inform him. They
say :-
It was with much regret that the Executive Committeeand this is a rather important thing because
they refer to this potato question with which
my hon. Friends and myself are dealing-
It was with much regret that the Executive Committee had seen the inability
of many farmers to sell their potato crop
at any price.
That is perfectly true, because I think it is
a moderate expression to say that thousands
of tons of potatoes were destroyed in County
Down, in the Killough district, in the district of Portaferry, and in the surrounding
districts.
Through the Ministry of Agriculture an

where for a considerable period potatoes

failed. It was the considered opinion of
the Executive Committee that, generally
speaking, it had now become a necessity
to find at least a partially alternative
crop to potatoes. They were, therefore,
awaiting with interest the report of the
Development Commission on the subject
of sugar beet growing.

They were awaiting with interest the report

some of us awaiting with fervid intensity
the report of that Commission, and as far

The apparently successful development of

Free State, apart from the many years' experience of Continental countries, would
seem to indicate that by the establishment
on similar lines of sugar beet growing in
this country at least a partial solution for
the increasing difficulties in potato production and sale might be found.
I understand it would require a subsidy

But even if that subsidy was granted the

ways. If the Free State Government granted
a subsidy for the growing of sugar beet,

not know why a similar experiment should

are, and we ought to know what the intentions of the Government are. I will

their list of immune varieties Lochars are

I have grown Lochar potatoes. I remember
one occasion in 1921 when I had eighty to
a hundred tons of these potatoes left on my
hands, and I need not say that I have never
grown them since. I made the best use of
them I could by using them for feeding
purposes. This year, like many other
farmers, I am a sufferer through having a
large quantity of potatoes left on my hands.
It is impossible to get rid of them at a
remunerative price, but how the Ministry
of Agriculture is to blame is beyond my
comprehension. I had a visit from a buyer,
who offered me 30s a ton. I said, "Thank
you, very much, but I cannot get anything
cheaper for use on my farm." I have kept
those potatoes, and will use them.
We can save in many ways by using them
for the feeding of horses and pigs.
The County Down farmers know they are
in a Black Scab area, and therefore that
they have a limited market for any variety
that they grow, because their potatoes can
be exported only to certain areas in Great

In regard to the question of sugar beet

West Belfast (Mr. Devlin), if it means
progress I would like to see it adopted. We
want every new industry that we can get
in Northern Ireland, but I read somewhere

money to support the sugar beet industry

that any advocate of the scheme boasts
that it would make millionaires of the
farmers. If we had a clear coast and a good
market for potatoes, I would prefer potato
growing to sugar beet, although if the sugar
beet industry should be started in Northern
Ireland I would recommend the farmers to
give it every support, in order to ensure its
success, if that is possible. I do not feel
competent to say it would be successful;
there are others much better able to judge
of that matter than I am. We have to be
guided by our experts. I am sure the
Government will meet this demand in the
sympathetic way that they meet every demand, if it is found possible to make a
success of the sugar beet industry in this
country.
It is strange to hear some of the criticisms that have been levelled against the
Minister in this Committee. I have been
keeping in very close touch with his actions
in regard to horse breeding and cattle
breeding, flax growing and potato growing,
and also eggs, and I know that we will
never have a more sympathetic Minister
of Agriculture in Northern Ireland than wo
have at present. (Hon. Members: Hear,
hear.) He is at all times willing and ready
to be advised by those who know the subject, and he takes every means of ventilating among the agricultural community what
he intends to do before he does it, of finding
out the pros and cons of the case, and
whether it will be for the benefit of the
farmers that something should take place.
He acts with caution and sympathy. I find
that he does not rush to prosecute farmers
who have inadvertently overstepped the
regulations. He gives them fair and reasonable notice that they are doing wrong before he launches a prosecution.
The farming community to-day are on perfectly good terms with the Ministry of Agriculture. I think my hon. Friend, the
Member for Derry (Mr. Leeke), is bound to
admit that. If he thinks of the spirit that
existed amongst the farmers of the County
Down when the old Department of Agriculture held sway, and of the friendly spirit
that exists between the Ministry of Agriculture and its officials and the farmers today, he will find that a very different state
of affairs now exists. (Hon. Members: Hear,
hear.) I know that the farmers have been
very badly hit. I know that the efforts made
to get assistance for the farmers were sympathetically considered by the Minister of
Finance and the Minister of Agriculture, and
I am sure they are prepared to adopt

Opposition or on this side of the Committee

regard to the potato crop. I would recommend the farmers of County Down to grow
a variety of potatoes that they can get a
market for, and not Lochar. They have
known for years that they can get no market
for Lochar, but if they do plant Lochar they
have this advantge they get double the crop,
and they are as well off in the long run as if
they grow another variety.
I think the Minister is perfectly right in
making compulsory the growing of immune
varieties. If they find fault with the Minister
because they are not allowed to grow nonimmune varieties I think they would have
something worse to say of him if he allowed
them to do so. I have great pleasure in
supporting the Minister in connection with
this Estimate.

A
I come next to the Chemical and Animal
Nutrition Division. Experiments in feeding
minerals to pigs, poultry, milch cows and
calves are being carried out with
interesting results, and in some cases
with practical and economic benefits.
series of experiments with balanced rations
is in operation. Most of the loss and mortality
in livestock is due to malnutrition and
through this cause farmers are annually
losing thousands of pounds.
As to the Seed Testing and Plant Disease
Division, let me give figures to show the
increase. In 1925, 2,703 samples of seeds
were tested, an increase of 30 per cent. on
the previous year, and five times the number
received in the 1923 seed testing year-the
year we began.
The Committee will be interested to know
that Northern Ireland produces annually
about 30,000 tons of rye grass seed. Our
Province is the chief world centre for rye
grass seed production, and exports 20,000 to
25,000 tons annually. The Division is paying a good deal of attention to the investigation of potato diseases and diseases of
fruit trees.
The egg laying competitions conducted by
the Poultry Division continue to be popular
and every year entries have to be turned
down. At present 71 pens of six pullets
each are complete. I would like to call the
attention of the Committee to the fact that
in England the average number of eggs per
pullet of the National Utility Poultry
Society is 161.55; United States, 164.4;
Canada, 172.2; and Northern Ireland, 181.86.
(Hon. Members: Hear, hear.) Our egg laying competitions are doing some good.
The Animal Diseases Division has only
been functioning for a comparatively short
period, but already 1,000 cases chiefly of an
advisory character have been dealt with.
The laboratory at Queen's University has
been given up since 1st April, and all investigations are now made at the Stormont
laboratory. At present the Division is cona
Plant breeding is still being pursued, and
we have now quite a number of new promising varieties of flax, oats, etc., but it
will be some time before we have these in
bulk for distribution.
The Animal and Crop Husbandry
Division is a new feature of the Ministry's
work and will centre largely at the Hillsborough Research Station.
As to the building grant to Queen's
University (A2), the erection of the building
which provides lecture rooms and laboratories for the purpose of the Agricultural
Faculty at the Queen's University is now
proceeding apace, and its completion before
the end of the current financial year is expected. Provision is made for payment to
the University of £30,000 as the balance of
the total grant in aid of £34,500 allocated
by the Government in accordance with the
Government Loans and Exchequer Provisions (Northern Ireland) Act, 1925. This
expenditure will, as heretofore, be repaid
from the special grant of £400,000 awarded
by the Imperial Government. The Estimate
of £30,000 includes a re-vote of the unexpended portion of last year's provision of
£18,000.
As to the Hillsborough Research Station
and Experimental Farm (A3), it is proposed
to establish an Animal Nutrition, &c., Research and Experimental Station under the
control and management of a Board of
Trustees representing the Ulster Farmer's
Union, the Ulster Agricultural Organisation
Society, the Ministry of Agriculture and the
Faculty of Agriculture of Queen's University. The Board will act in co-operation
with the Ministry and with the Agricultural
Faculty at Queen's.
To finance such a station a total sum of
£100,000 will be needed, viz., £40,000 for
capital, and £60,000 as an endowment, to
produce an income of £3,000 per annum,
which is calculated to be the annual cost
of running the institution when fully
established.
As to the capital required, the Government
agreed to give a direct State contribution of
£20,000 in the form of £10,000 cash together
with lands and buildings at Hillsborough,

When the Government decided recently to
reduce by 25 per cent. the amount of the
supplemental grant in relief of agricultural
rates an assurance was given, not only that
this action would not interfere with the
establishment of the proposed Research
Station, but that, in addition to the State
contribution of £10,000, cash and the lands
and buildings at Hillsborough, the Government would, on behalf of the farmers, make
good the balance of the £40,000 for capital,
together with the £60,000 for endowment.
During the financial year which has just
begun it is expected that the expenditure
on this project will amount to £20,300, and
provision to that extent has, accordingly,
been made in the Estimates.
As to Agricultural Education, this subhead shows a decrease of £6,300 as compared
with last year, when it was necessary to
provide for considerable capital expenditure
on the erection of farm buildings and cottages at the North-West Institute, Strabane.
This work as well as the works of extension
and improvement at Greenmount Agricultural College, Antrim, is now practically
completed, a few outstanding charges only
remaining to be met. Provision for upkeep
of the Ulster Dairy School is slightly higher
in view of the progressive increase in the
number of pupils in residence. There are
now 47 pupils in residence-it is full-and
there were only 32 in 1922-23. The upkeep
of the North-West Institute is also estimated
at a higher figure to allow for development
of operations following the completion of the
new farm buildings. That Institute is also
full. There are now 20 pupils, and there
were only 10 in 1922-23. At Greenmount
we have got 36 pupils. We hope that the
number will gradually reach 50.
re-
The Estimate for the improvement of live
stock (C1) shows an increase of £400 over the
Estimate for last year. This increase is,
however, more than counter-balanced by a
corresponding increase in the Estimate of
departmental receipts accruing from
sales of stud animals. Additional provision is made for grants to milk recording
associations to cope with the rapid increase
in the number of associations. The extra
funds are provided out of the special Development Grant of £54,000. It may interest the Committee if I give the figures of
the various years:-In 1921, there were six
associations, and 1,244 cows under test; in
1926, there are 53 associations and 10,360
cows under test.
In conection with the Live Stock Breeding Acts (C2), the increase of £50 for cost
of special inspectors for licences is due to
the large number of special inspections
of bulls required. The expenditure included under this heal is more than
covered by receipts which may be estimated
at about £1,000 a year. We have now 6,639
licensed bulls in Northern Ireland. When
we began this work a great many were complaining that we would not have bulls in the
country. As a matter of fact the number is
practically the same as in 1923-24.
The Estimate for the Animal Quarantine
Station remains at the same figure (£500)
as the original Estimate for last year. Two
consignments of valuable breeding animals
were recently brought in from Scotland
through this station. Unfortunately, the
prevalence of foot-and-mouth disease in
England and Wales renders it necessary to
continue to prohibit importations of cattle
in the ordinary way. Grants are included
under the head of Diseases of Animals
(grant in aid), which was heretofore under
the Imperial Government, as follows:--
(a) £750 for payment of compensation
and other expenses in connection with
pigs slaughtered on account of Swine
Fever.
(b) £3,500 for grants to Local Authorities in respect of compensation, etc., for
cattle slaughtered under Bovine Tuberculosis Order.
In the poultry industry, it has been
possible to effect a reduction of £100 in the
provision for this service,, and as to the
Marketing of Eggs, experience has shown
that a slight increase in the Vote is necessary to cover expenditure on this Service.
In the dairying industry there is a small
reduction of £60. The fuller development of
this Service must await the completion of
the buildings at Queen's University intended for the Agricultural Faculty and in
which accommodation for courses of instruction in creamery management is proposed to be provided.
As to grants to County Committees, it has
been possible to effect a slight reduction
this year in the Temporary Grant for Agricultural Development. This
Temporary
Grant is portion of the sum of £54,000
which was to be spread over a period of not
less than four years, so that any savings in
one year are available in future years. We
have now 106 black-faced rams which we
are putting into the poorer parts of the
country.
There is a reduction of £275 under the
head Grants to Agricultural Societies.
Grants are proposed to be made to the
Ulster Farmers' Union and the Ulster Agricultural Organisation Society in order to enable
these bodies to carry on their educational
and organisation work. The Ministry feels

Mr. DEVLIN: Please explain about the
Weeds Act. Give us some elucidation of it.
Mr. ARCHDALE: There are certain weeds
scheduled as noxious. Inspectors were sent

noxious weeds. It was left over for some

increase of £1,100, due to the taking over
of additional areas for afforestation purposes.
In November of this year 300 acres will be
taken over, so that we will have a total area
of 5,106 acres. We are trying to get land,
not to buy it out altogether, but taking it
on lease, so as to leave something for our
families to pay for.
My hon. Friend talked about large
families. We thought it was as well to leave
them something to do, and not let us pay

time. If we can get land at a very low rent
it is better for the country than to pay it
all at once.
Mr. DEVLIN: Is the right hon. Gentleman undertaking forestry schemes on land
he has leased?

years.
Mr. DEVLIN: That will satisfy us. He

Mr. ARCHDALE: I have already spoken

With regard to the census of agricultural

The CHAIRMAN: No; I have very carefully indeed considered the point put by
the hon. Member. I have considered what
position we would be in if I yielded to the
argument of the hon. Member. It would
open to the Opposition at any time to quit
the House, and on that ground to suspend
the business. Equally if the hon. Member
were pressing some point of paramount importance it would be open for the whole of
the Members on the Government Benches
to quit the House, and that that should be
advanced as a reason for the suspension of
public business. That is an argument that
could not be held.
Mr. DEVLIN: I do not want to contest
your ruling in the matter. I would like you
to read the Standing Order which prevents
a Member of the House from reporting progress.
The CHAIRMAN: "If Mr. Speaker or
the Chairman of a committee of the whole
House, shall be of opinion that a motion
for the adjournment of a debate, or of the
House, during any debate, or that the
Chairman do report progress, or do leave
the Chair, is an abuse of the rules of the
House, he may forthwith put the question
thereupon from the Chair, or he may decline to propose the question thereupon to
the House."
It is the latter course I have taken.
Mr. BEATTIE: My point here the lack
of interest displayed-is a very important
one, because we in the Opposition, have
claimed since we came into this House that
the Minister of Agriculture and the Minister
of Labour are the two persons who are responsible for the unemployment question.
Now the absence of the Minister of Labour
or any of his deputies during the Estimate
for agriculture, I say, shows their lack of
interest and that there is no sincerity shown
by other Departments in regard to the
question of unemployment. I still maintain
with all respect to your ruling that the
Government have not shown the interest
that might have been expected from them
in this question.
The CHAIRMAN: I am sure the hon.
Member understands that I cannot enter
into a discussion as to whether the action

question is whether upon the point of procedure I ought to exercise my judgment in
favour of the hon. Member's motion. I
think I have adduced reasons why I should
not.
Mr. W. McMULLEN: I desire to move a
reduction in this Estimate of £1,000. I do
so for the purpose of asking the right hon.
Gentleman who has just spoken, whether
there is such an animal in Northern Ireland
as an agricultural labourer. I have heard
animals of all classes discussed on this and
the previous Estimate, but he appears to be
oblivious of the fact that such people as
agricultural labourers exist in Northern
Ireland.
I am at loss to understand on an occasion
of this character, when two very important
Estimates have been submitted to the
House, why no effort has been made by the
right hon. Gentleman to discuss the problem of unemployment. I had occasion previously to call the Government's attention
to this aspect of the matter. You were
absent in Dublin, I understand, on that day
for a purpose which you oelieved to be of
more importance than the question discussed before the House on that occasion.
Of course it is for yourself to determine
whether the business which took you to
Dublin. But, as I say, I cannot understand
question we were discussing. I have come
to the conclusion that the subject under discussion was of tremendously greater importance than the object of your visit to
Dublin. But, as I say, I cannot understand
how it is that you have not attempted to
deal with the problem of unemployment.
I have observed in reading the Press that
a large number of people are unemployed in
all our small provincial towns throughout
the North of Ireland. Most of these people
are in receipt of unemployment benefit. We
have repeatedly stated from these Benches
that it is not a satisfactory state of affairs
by any means to have people continually
drawing benefit week after week without
any attempt being made to deal with the
problem of unemployment. The hon.
Member for North Belfast mentioned what
appears to me to be very important, the
large number of people who are leaving
week after week for Canada and the United
States of America. You were inclined to
laugh and to treat the whole matter in a
very jocular way. It may appear to you to
be a matter for mirth. To other people it
is quite a serious problem. Two or three
days ago I observed a family of seven, the
father and mother and five children who
were emigrating to the United States of
America. Now it appears to me to be absolutely a tragic thing. I attempt to put
myself into the position of that father who
is forced to take his family from Northern
Ireland away to seek a home in the wilds
and prairies of Canada, and if it is possible
for the Government by any means, even at
the risk or expense of making in roads upon
the vested interests of Northern Ireland, it
is the duty of this Government to try to
establish more people on the land than there
are on it at the present time.

Now some people may be inclined to
criticise this idea and to suggest that an
attempt was being made on our part to
establish a number of industrial workers on
the soil who have got no previous knowledge
of agriculture. It is not a question of that
kind at all, because, that would be a state
of affairs not too satisfactory-(hon.
Members: Hear, hear)-although perhaps
these people were turned into almost anything during the course of the late war.
They have been made machine-gun men and
airmen. They were trained and equipped
for any particular purpose for carrying on
the war. When the purpose is peace and a
suggestion is made of any kind at all then
it is impossible to do it. If you want men
of Northern Ireland to take the life of a
German or an Austrian lack of knowledge
is no drawback and money is no obstacle.
But when it becomes a question of trying
to solve the problem of unemployment the
difficulties are insuperable and the Government are not capable of dealing with them.

Does the right hon. Gentleman ever take
any thought of the problem I have mentioned. Hundreds of people in Banbridge
and Portadown-take County Antrim.
large number of people are drawing unemployment benefit week after week, and you
do not even imagine that any such a person
as an agricultural labourer exists in
Northern Ireland. We know your attitude
towards the wages boards. You have repeatedly taken up a hostile attitude
towards the question of the wages boards.
We have been told we are proceeding on
parallel lines with Great Britain, and we
point out that wages boards are in operation
in Great Britain while you refuse
to put them in operation in Northern
Ireland for the purpose of giving
the agricultural labourer a livelihood.
The rate of wages paid in Northern Ireland is absolutely scandalous, and it is a
disgrace to any civilised community
that people should be expected to exist on
the wages paid. I have heard that repeatedly from people.
Of course I do not know as much about
agriculture as possibly the hon. Member for
the University (Dr. Morrison), or the hon.
Member for County Down (Mr. O'Neill),
who appears to know so much about the
problem of agriculture. It appears to me
not so difficult a question at all, provided
you are prepared to tackle it in the right
spirit. I made a remark on the question of
agriculture one day previously which caused
much merriment.
Mr. MARK: You are always amusing.
Mr. W. McMULLEN: I am very glad I
serve some purpose, even if it is only to
amuse. Even that is a legitimate purpose to
serve. Some people are even less useful than
to be amusing. Even if I only amuse I
serve some function. But I am speaking of
the number of people settled on the soil
here in comparison with other countries. 1
think the Government publication gives the
figures as 239 people to the square mile as
compared with about 618 for Great Britain.
I suggest that this is a very serious state of
affairs that there should be only 239 per
square mile in Northern Ireland as against
638 in Great Britain. That should give the
right hon. Gentleman some food for thought.
I think you have got 41 per cent. of the land
of Northern Ireland under hay, and you
have 12 per cent. of the land under grass.
Now can some development not take place
there? Can some attempt not be made for
the purpose of planting a large number of
people on the soil of Northern Ireland. If
you did that by taking the very large holdings you have in Northern Ireland and
possibly starting on them without encroaching on the land preserved by the supporters
of the Government-if you attempted to induce these people with their large estates
to employ more labour than they employ
at the present time, you probably would be
able to absorb a very considerable percentage of the unemployed in Northern Ireland
at the present moment.
You have got, further, to take into consideration the purchasing power you would
give to these people. Their purchasing
powers at the present time are very, very
low. In most of the towns it is only for a
very short period they are allowed to draw
unemployment benefit. At a later stage I am
hoping to give the Parliamentary Secretary
to the Ministry of Labour (Mr. Gordon)
some information on that subject as to how
unemployed workers in these small urban
areas and in the country districts are being
treated. Their purchasing power is exceptionally low, and if it were possible to
place these people in employment, to give
them more purchasing power than they have
at the present time, you would relieve probably the unemployment in the cities to a
very considerable extent. Would not that be
a much more satisfactory state of affairs? It
might cause the right hon. Gentleman (Mr.
Archdale) to think. After all, that is not
a terribly difficult process, and if any remarks I can make will induce the right hon.
Gentleman to think, and to think along
those lines because I should probably point
out that in a great many of the things the
right hon. Gentleman has tackled he has
proved very progressive and some of the things
he has done mark a tremendous amount of
progress as compared with the state of agriculture in Northern Ireland ten years ago.
But while the right hon. Gentleman (Mr.
Archdale) is quite prepared to think in terms
of hens, of cows, of horses, and of cattle of

HOUSE OF COMMONS
[Mr. W. McMullen]
all kinds, he cannot give any consideration
to or understand the problem of the agricultural labourer. I notice that the farmers
who are behind the right hon. Gentleman
always give him unflinching support. I am
forced to the conclusion that he is satisfactory from the farmers' point of view, but,
without offence, allow me to tell the right
hon. Gentleman that he is extremely unsatisfactory from the point of view of the
farm labourer. I do not know any gentleman who is more unpopular with the farm
labourers throughout Northern Ireland than
is the Minister of Agriculture. I know he
is very popular with the farmers, but after
all the farm labourers should count as much
as the farmers do, and I would suggest to
him that he should give some thought to
those things about which I am attempting
to speak. From that point of view your
Estimates are entirely unsatisfactory, and
you may expect nothing but opposition in
relation to agricultural matters from the
people who occupy these benches until you
are prepared to give some consideration to
the agricultural labourer and to make some
attempt to put these people on the land.
The countryside is being depopulated. J
pointed out on the last occasion on which
I spoke on this subject that the population
of Northern Ireland from 1841 up to the
present time had decreased in round figures
about 370,000, and that during the same
years the population of Belfast has increased
from about 70,000 to about 470,000. Nearly
every urban area in Northern Ireland has
increased its population too, while the
countryside is depopulated. Some steps
should be taken for the purpose of keeping
the agricultural labourers in the countryside instead of allowing them to flood into
the cities to overcrowd an already overcrowded market, and some attempt should
be made also to stem the tide of emigration.
The life blood of Northern Ireland is being
drained. What you are losing Canada,
Australia, and other countries are gaining.
I hope that in future when the right hon.
Gentleman (Mr. Archdale) comes to this
Committee he will at least have developed
so far that we will get some mention from
him of the agricultural labourer.
Dr. MORRISON: I will not waste the
time of the Committee by a lengthy speech.
I have listened to the denunciation of and
the complaints about the Minister of Agriculture more or less with amazement. So far
as I can judge from going through the

Members of the Government. (Hon.
Members: Hear, hear).
Mr. WILLIAM MCMULLEN: With the
farmers.
Dr. MORRISON: The hon. Member for

Dr. MORRISON: In any event, may
I be allowed to say that I think this
is one of the lapses, one of those

and seeing the mortalities that Occur
amongst cows from milk fever, amongst
horses from lockjaw, in every sphere and
amongst every type of animal death upon
death, to the great loss and detriment of
the farmer and to the detriment of the
State in general. Early in the formation of
this Parliament I went to the Ministry and

man, who had first-hand knowledge of what

which has been developed in connection with

Last year I got from the Ministry of
Agriculture a list, a rough estimate of all
the animals that had died in Ireland, of
horses, cattle, and sheep, from operations
and other causes, and the steps that were
being taken to prevent such losses. If I
would be inclined to say anything about the
Ministry it would be that, instead of lacking

his principal clerks have, even for me,

to get up to talk about was this grant to the

Union and the Agricultural Organisation
Society. The Agricultural Organisation
Society has very strong claims. As I understand it, there is £1,000 given, and of this
£700 goes to the Ulster Farmers' Union for
the educational work carried on by them,
and the Organisation Society gets £300 out
of the £1,000. Now that is not enough; it
is not a fair division, and I would suggest
to the Minister that it should be divided
in the proportion of £500 to each. Originally
the Organisation Society got £1,200 in
1923-1924. The Farmers' Union have got
three grants of £1,000 each, and now, of
this grant of £1,000, £700 goes to the
Farmers' Union and only £300 to the

Committee.
20 APRIL 1926
I am told that it is impossible to keep
an organiser on the road for the sum of
£300, and, while the farmers themselves
through this Organisation give £600 to help
to educate their brethren living and working
on the land, they cannot keep their
organisers going about lecturing and trying
to educate the farmer unless they get a
little extension of their grant. I would like
to point out that it is a co-operative society,
which I know will meet with the approval
of hon. Members on the opposite side of the
Committee. It stands for co-operation, for
self-help, for enabling a man to make an
effort for his own benefit and for the benefit
of those who are going about begging and
craving for work; it is to make two blades
of grass grow where only one grew before.
That is exactly what this Organisation is
doing, and, therefore, I think the limit
should be increased in this matter.
With regard to emigration and this
subject which the hon. Member for West
Belfast (Mr. William McMullen) brings up
so frequently, I think that in discussing
agricultural questions it is rather out of
place. We know that agricultural labourers
are excluded from unemployment benefit,
and it is a bad thing. It is a bad thing
for a man to be an agricultural labourer,
but the reason for that is, as hon. Members
on the opposite side of the Committee know,
because there is no outlook for them by
reason of the fact that the Labour Party,
of which hon. Members opposite are such
distinguished members, have kept their
brethren in agricultural Ulster and in the
country badly fed, badly paid, and badly
clad in order that in the cities they might
have plenty.
Living in the country as a dispensary
doctor I have come in contact with a large
number of people, and I have recommended
them to emigrate. I said, "There is no
chance for a working man or for a farmer
here. Go to the Colonies, not to the United
States. Keep under your own flag." I got
in touch with the Commissioners of different
countries like Australia and New Zealand,
and I know to-day hundreds of men who
followed my advice, with whom I have kept
in touch ever since, and who are grateful
for the advice I gave them. What we want
in this country is not the limiting of
emigration and the congregating of the
people in slums in Belfast and other
places, but the encouraging of our people
to go out to free countries where they have
a chance, and where their arrival will be
good for the nation and for the countries to
which they go as it will be a help to this
country.

When on the previous Vote I referred to

that in the present Vote a matter of £3,000
has been allowed for the supply of seed
potatoes to those potato planters in Black
Scab areas. I presume that means about
1,000 tons of potatoes. If I am correctly
informed they are the Arran Victory and
Kerr's Pink varieties, for neither of which
there is any greater demand in the English
market than there is for Lochars. Therefore these farmers will be in exactly the
same position next year as they are in this

potatoes but they will be unable to find a
market for them. If that is so, that 1,000 tons
of seed will not in any way be compensation
for the loss farmers have sustained this year.
When the Minister replies I would like to
know the area this £3,000 worth of seed
potatoes is to be sent to, the conditions under
which it is given, and if all the applicants
who applied for these potatoes have received
them. I may say that I think this was a very
foolish arrangement, because there was no
difficulty in getting these very same potatoes
in the neighbourhood without the Government supplying them. As a matter of fact
I know that at the present time farmers can

CHICHESTER: I feel bound to

The farmers of Co. Down have already had

greatest gratitude. However, if that is not
possible I would ask if some further concession might be made on their behalf.
Their condition is really a calamitous one.
The rates in our part of the county are
higher than in any other part of county
Derry. These men have looked upon the
potato crop as their most important crop,
and this year has perhaps been the worst
since 1846.

Regarding the £1,000 voted to the Ulster
Farmers' Union Education Committee and
to the Ulster Agricultural Organisation
Society, it seems to me to be a reprehensible
thing to grant £1,000 to the Ulster Farmers'
Union. The Ulster Farmers' Union is no
better than a workers' union.
Mr. BEATTIE: Hear, hear.
Mr. KYLE: It is neither better nor
worse; it is just the same. It is a union of
men to promote their own interests, to get
prices for their crops. They hold meetings
for the purpose of educating their members
in regard to the best use of their land and
the best use of the labour on the land.
The workers' union is exactly the same. It
is a body of men who want to get the best
terms for their labour, and who want to
render faithful and efficient service.
think the right hon. Gentleman should be
chary about putting down £1,000 for the
Ulster Farmers' Union. He would not have
dreamt of asking the Government for a
grant of £1,000 to enable us to help the
agricultural labourers. I assure the right
hon. Gentleman that the agricultural
labourers need organisation as much, if not
more, than the Farmers' Union. They need
education. I think it is very strange that
the Government should back up the enemy
of the agricultural labourer, and subsidise
them with £1,000.
Agricultural wages is a tremendously important matter. According to the figures
supplied by the right hon. Gentleman, some
of these agricultural labourers are getting
only 22s 6d a week. It is no wonder trade
is depressed, for at such a rate of remuneration these people cannot buy things. The
agricultural labourers are just as important
as the farmers, and, therefore, they should
be considered, educated and subsidised,

but, apparently, as I said a few moments

Mr. THOMAS HENDERSON: I would
like to ask the Minister of Home Affairs
when he is likely to have the report of the
recent inquiry that was held in the Lisburn
Road Union Infirmary into a case concerning a coloured man named Ross. This man
was abused in some way, and as one of the
people interested in the case I am most
anxious to know exactly what the findings
of the inquiry are. I cannot compliment
the Minister of Home Affairs on the officer
he appointed to conduct the inquiry. Mr.
Beattie, who is a King's Counsel, tried to
make little of me in drawing attention to
the fact that this man received very serious
injuries. Mr. Beattie is a man who is most
anxious for Parliamentary honours, and
after his conduct at that inquiry there is
one thing I am convinced of, and that is
that he will not be a useful asset to this
House.
I am anxious, as I say,
to know
what are the findings of the inquiry.
I believe this man was very seriously
abused. It was stated at the inquiry that
I was overstepping my duty, but I
want to say that I went to this particular
mental hospital as an ordinary citizen. It
was just human sympathy that attracted my
attention to this man lying there with his
arm injured. I do not want to interfere with
any official. My only idea is to draw the
Minister's attention to this particular case.
If there is anything being done in this
hospital that should not be done I hope the
Minister will see that the abuses are stopped.
I believe it should be the duty of the
625 Union Infirmary Inquiry.

Barbour): I beg to move in Clause 6, page

thereto ") at the end to add :
"Provided that in case such compensation
is payable in respect of a holding subject
to a land purchase annuity, the tribunal or
county court shall determine whether the
security for the payment of the annuity
is prejudicially affected, and, if so, what
amount of the annuity ought to be redeemed in view of the prejudice to the
security, and thereupon the applicant shall
cause the amount of the annuity so determined to be redeemed, and the redemption
price until paid shall be a charge on the
compensation to be paid by him."
Hon. Members will be aware that under
the Land Purchase Act the minerals were
vested in the Land Commission, and, consequently, this clause has been inserted in
order to protect their position under this
Act. It is in order to provide that any
security for the payment of the annuity
should not be prejudiced by the granting of
any right to work minerals or any diversion
of them. The amendment has been agreed
to by the Ministry of Finance.
Mr. KYLE: I think I would like the
Minister to explain how this would affect
farmers who hold the land or are buying out
the land. Does this mean that tenant farmers themselves will not have any right to
the minerals, but that they will be vested in
the Land Commission?
Mr. BARBOUR: Hon. Members should
remember in considering this Bill that it
is only to provide means for working
minerals where satisfactory arrangements
cannot be arrived at between any parties who
may be interested in working the minerals.
It is intended to facilitate and encourage the
working of minerals. Consequently, the
farmer who owns the surface and wishes to
work the minerals will have to satisfy the
Land Commission that the security for the
annuity is not prejudiced in any way. Any
application from the farmer will receive
most favourable consideration.
Amendment agreed to.
Clause, as amended, ordered to stand part
of the Bill.

Sections four and twenty of the Mining
Industry Act, 1920, are hereby repealed.
Mr. BARBOUR: I beg to move in Clause
18, page 13, line 31, to leave out "are hereby
repealed" and insert "shall be deemed never
to have applied in Northern Ireland."
This is an Amendment of which I gave
notice when moving the Second Reading of
the Bill. It will enable hon. Members to
understand the reason for seeking the insertion of these words when I remind them that
the coal mining industry in Great Britain
is an industry of immense importance and
the number of men employed is very great,
and any sum raised by the levy proposed at
that time, of a penny a ton, represented such
a sum as would enable many schemes of
social welfare, research, and education to be
carried out which might be of very great
interest to the industry. At that time coal
mining was practically unknown in Ireland.
It was before the passing of the 1920 Act and
the provision made for the administration of
this fund was a scheme, which if applied to
Northern Ireland, would be altogether of a
too grandiose character. In fact Northern
Ireland would not be represented in any way
on the personnel of the committee which
managed this scheme.
As a matter of fact the Act in which these
clauses were included expired in March of
this year, but I believe the provisions have
been subsequently re-enacted. Our only coal
mining in Northern Ireland, as hon.
Members will be aware, is only just about
emerging from the stage of installation and
development, and it of itself would not be
sufficient to justify the setting up of
machinery of the character provided in the
Act to which I have referred. I think it
would be more convenient if we were to leave
any move of this kind to stand over until
such time as we are better able to judge as
to the extent of the requirements of the
mining industry of Northern Ireland. I,
therefore, beg to move the Amendment as on
the Paper.
Mr. KYLE: On the Second Reading of this
Measure I endeavoured to get the right hon.
Gentleman to promise that he would insert
in some way in this Measure the principle
that for miners who mine coal there should
be a certain sum set aside for welfare work
in the mining industry. One appreciates, as the right hon. Gentleman (Mr. Barbour) has stated, that our
mining industry is not large, and that,
therefore, if the penny a ton which is set
aside in Great Britain were set aside here
for all the coal that is being raised at the
present time, or has been raised over the
past few years, it would not be sufficient to
give the miners here the benefits of the
social welfare which miners can get on the
other side of the water.
I understand from what the right hon.
Gentleman has stated that, in consequence
of the fact that mining here is in a very
embryonic stage, he does not intend to insert
this principle. Well, I want to protest cn
behalf of the miners who are presently employed, and who may be employed, in
Northern Ireland against the right hon.
Gentleman's action in not allowing the

Great Britain had a tremendous task before
they got this right conceded to them by legislation. Though one may hope, one cannot
see that it is at all possible under any contingencies that the mining industry in
Northern Ireland will be tremendously extended, yet the interests and rights of the
miners who work, or who may work, the coal
in Northern Ireland should be protected by
the right hon. Gentleman in a measure such

Mr. BARBOUR: The effect of this Amendment and what the Government desires to receive is absolution for not having applied to
whatever extent might have been necessary
the Clauses of this Act. I could really

Mining Industry Act of 1920 provided that
the Advisory Committee on coal and the
coal industry should consist of a chairman
and twenty-four other persons, of whom
four should be representative of owners of
coal mines; four should be representative
of workers in or about coal mines; three
should be representative of employers in
other industries; three should be representative of workers in other industries; one
should be a mining engineer; two should be
agents or managers or under-managers of
coal mines, holding first-class certificates;
one should be a coal exporter; one should
be a coal factor or coal merchant; one
should be a person with experience of commerce other than the production or distribution of coal; one should be a person with
experience in co-operative trading; and three
should be persons with expert knowledge of
medical or other science. To apply that
Act as it stood would have been almost impossible, but, so far as the future is concerned, I think the hon. Member for North
Belfast (Mr. Kyle) may regard us as sympathetic to the coal miners. At the present
stage when the coal mining is in such a very
early state of development we should have
liked, anyway, to have consulted the views
of the owner of the mine before entering
into any commitments. I would respectfully
suggest that this is a matter which might
stand over until we know how best the
interests of the people who work in the coal
mines can be protected, and until we have
gathered knowledge of the extent of the
industry and the likelihood of coal, or other
mining, in Northern Ireland progressing.
Mr. KYLE: Would the right hon. Gentleman (Mr. Barbour) consent then to postpone
the Committee Stage of this Bill until he
prepares a form of words that would meet
our requirements?
The PRIME MINISTER (Sir James Craig):
I think my right hon. Friend (Mr. Barbour)
has interpreted the desire of the Government
that we should carefully keep watch upon
this matter, and if the development of coal
mining in Northern Ireland is such as to
involve a very large number of persons we
I will see to it when the time comes that the
miners in Northern Ireland are placed in a
somewhat analagous position to those in
England or in Scotland. In this Bill, which
is of a different character, it is not proposed

Member (Mr. Kyle) refers, but he can rest

mining industry in Northern Ireland, and,
if that industry develops to any large extent,
my right hon. Friend (Mr. Barbour) will
bring in a short Bill to establish the principle of which the hon. Member (Mr. Kyle)
is speaking to-day.
Mr. DEVLIN: I would suggest that we
should allow this Bill to pass. I am very
glad to know that the representations made
by the hon. Member for North Belfast (Mr.
Kyle) have had the desired effect. He did
not, as far as I gathered, put forward any
suggestion that the elaborate machinery recited by the right hon. Gentleman (Mr.
Barbour) should be set up here. What he
simply asked was that precisely similar
labour conditions should exist in Northern
Ireland to what exist in the mining districts
of Great Britain. I am very glad that the
Prime Minister has given that promise-a

OF

THE MINISTRY OF FINANCE (Mr.
(Barbour): In moving this Vote I think
that the Committee will expect that I shall
say a few words in regard to the recent
sudden death of Northern Ireland's first
Comptroller and Auditor-General, Mr.
Huggett--an officer whose position has necessarily brought him into close touch
with those Members of this Committee who
have served on the Committee of Public
Accounts. The Comptroller and Auditor-
General is, in fact, the arbiter who indicates
to that Committee whether the money
voted by this Committee for supply
services is properly and economically spent,
and who suggests to them possible lines of
criticism in dealing with the annual
Appropriation Accounts. Coming to us at
the close of a long and distinguished career
in the Army Audit Department, Mr.
Huggett brought to hear on the accounts
of our Public Departments ripe experience,
indefatigable zeal, and wide knowledge of
the technique of accounting not only in
the region of Government finance, but also
of commercial procedure. He has reported
on the accounts of our Department for the
first four financial years his last report,
that on the accounts for the year 1924-25,
having been completed but a few weeks
before his death at a time when he was
struggling against that illnesss which
suddenly carried him away. He was indeed a faithful servant of the public and
of this House. (Hon. Members: Hear,
hear.)
The Estimate is to be founl on page 23,
and as the items of which it is composed
show little if any variation from last year's
provision there is little necessity for any
comment or explanation. There is, however,
one new provision, and that is the £400 for
additional audit assistance, which is to be
found at the top of page 24. As explained in
the note to this item, the details have not
yet been worked out, but the Ministry of
Finance is satisfied that some reorganisation
of the staff is necessary, and accordingly this
lump sum is inserted to meet any additional
charges arising therefrom. I beg to move.

fully with what the right non. Gentleman
has said in regard to the Comptroller and

in this Estimate of £300.

Sir ROBERT ANDERSON: Before touching upon the subject of the Amendment which
has been submitted to the Committee by the
hon. Member (Mr. Kyle), may I be permitted
as one who was associated with the late Mr.
Huggett as Chairman of the Public Accounts
Committee, just to say a word in regard to
the splendid services he rendered to this
Government during the period he was associated with it. I do not think I ever had
to do with a higher-minded public servant
that the late Mr. Huggett. He was a man
of the greatest courage, a man who had in
the very fibre of his being all the best
traditions of the Civil Service, who in whatever work he did did it with the greatest
efficiency, the greatest ability and with a
single eye to promote the interests of the
Government he was associated with. Mr.
Huggett came to his duties at a very difficult
period in the history of this Government,
just when the foundations were about to be
laid, and I think no Government and no
country could have been better served at
that particular stage than by the late Mr.
Huggett. I am sure I am only voicing the
feelings of every Member of the Committee
when I say we all deeply regret his passing
hence, but we are glad-some of us-that we
had the proud privilege to be associated with
him in the work of the Department that he
carried on with such conspicuous ability.
(Hon. Members: Hear, hear.)
Now in regard to the Amendment before
the Committee I think my hon. Friend (Mr.
Kyle) was especially dealing with this particular Department that has to do with audit
matters and the Comptroller and Auditor-
General's work. I know from personal knowledge that the late Comptroller and Auditor-
General worked night and day in order to
get through the work he had to perform,
and on several occasions he mentioned to me
that the work of the staff, that he had available, while possessed of the greatest efficiency,
could be more efficiently and better carried
on if extra assistance could be given to it.
I think it is one of the Departments in
connection with the work of the Government
with which we should not deal with a parsimonious hand. Anyone who has studied
those very admirable reports that the Comptroller and Auditor-General has submitted
to the House from time to time will see the
great importance of the work that has got
to be done. They deal with every Department of the Government's work, they go into
every detail down to the expenditure of every
penny of public money. I think we should
for the sake of a few hundred pounds extra
see that there is a proper staff to do this
work, and do it well. It would be money
that would be spent to the advantage of
Parliament and the country as a whole.
Mr. DEVLIN: I am sorry I have to
disagree with my hon. Friend (Mr. Kyle), who
moved a reduction of this Vote, because, in
my judgment, the expenditure is perfectly
justified. (Hon. Members: Hear, hear.) I
take this opportunity of associating myself
with the generous eulogy which has been
delivered by the right hon. Gentleman the
Minister of Commerce (Mr. Barbour), and
the touching and eloquent references made
by the hon. Member for Derry (Sir Robert
Anderson) in relation to the late Mr. Huggett.
I desire to associate myself with these
tributes to the memory of a great, fearless,
and competent public servant. I have not
much direct experience or intimate association with Civil Servants, though I try, as
a public representative, to observe the
methods by which they perform their duties,
but I must say this, that a more faithful
watchdog of the public interests and a more
competent official in the discharge of the
exceedingly delicate duties he had to perform I never met. (Hon. Members: Hear,
hear.) The hon. Member for Derry (Sir Robert
Anderson) has spoken of him as a Government servant. He regarded himself as more
than a Government servant. He was a great
defender of the public interests, and I
confess that my relationship with him was
of this character, that his one great passion
was to inspire Members of Parliament with
a spirit of watchfulness over public accounts
and public expenditure. He sought their
co-operation that there might be a close and
watchful interest manifested in all that concerns the workings of our financial system.
He was a simple, modest man, of great
personal charm in addition to his fine
qualities as a public servant, and I am sure
Ulster and the public service are poorer by
his death. I desire to join with those who
have spoken in paying this tribute to his
memory, and extending to his relatives our
profound sympathy.
Mr. BEATTIE: I would like to associate
myself with the remarks made by the
Minister of Commerce, the Chairman of the
Public Accounts Committee, and the last
speaker, regarding the late Mr. Huggett. I

Barbour) and other hon. Members in regard
to the loss that Northern Ireland has sus-

CLASS III. No. 2.
ROYAL ULSTER CONSTABULARY.
Motion made, and Question proposed:
"That a sum not exceeding £603,736 be
granted to His Majesty to complete the sum
necessary to defray the charge which will
come in course of payment during the year
ending on the 31st day of March, 1927, to
defray the salaries and expenses of the Royal
Ulster Constabulary, including Police
Women (12 and 13 Geo. V., c. 8 (N.I.)); and
certain capital expenditure under 14 and 15
Geo. V., c. 13, s. 1 (N.I.)." (Note.-£200,000
has been voted on account.)
The MINISTER OF HOME AFFAIRS
(Sir Dawson Bates): In submitting this Estimate, I think it is due to the officers and
men of the Royal Ulster Constabulary, that
Morrison, Hugh Smith
Mulholland, Captain The Hon. Henry
George Hill

TELLER FOR THE NOES-
Capt. Dixon.
I should, at the outset, express the appreciation of the Government for the valuable
services they have rendered during the past
year. One of the most important adjuncts
to a State is the existence of an efficient
Police Force, and one in which all classes
of the community have reposed their confidence. I venture to say, and I am sure hon.
Members, even on the Opposition Benches
will admit, that in the Royal Ulster Constabulary we have a Force which commands
the respect of all classes of the community.
If you want an efficient Police Force, you
must, first of all, have men whose character
will bear the closest investigation; men of
educational attainments; men of good
physique; and men with the proper temper
and tact to deal suitably with the people
with whom they come in contact. The fact
that we have such an efficient Force to-day
is due to the great care that has been taken
in the selection of the men. The Govern-
641'

Supply-
Committee.
21 APRIL 1926
ment are most anxious to attract to the
Force the best type of man, and we offer
every encouragement to the best type to come
forward. I would remind hon. Members
that 50 per cent. of the promotions to the
commissioned ranks are given to the rank
and file, so that it is open to any constable
who joins the Police Force to look forward
to the time when he may become a District-
Inspector, or a County Inspector, or possibly
the Inspector-General himself.
Turning to the Estimate itself, one of the
most satisfactory features about it is that it
represents a saving of £35,000. Whether or
not my hon. Friend, who sits opposite (Mr.
Kyle) will use the converse argument he
used on the occasion of the last Vote, and
offer no opposition to this Vote on account
of the fact that it shows a decrease I cannot
say, but I suggest that he should. Dealing
with some of the most important Sub-heads,
hon. Members will find under the Sub-head
of "Pay" that there is an increase of £11,000.
This is due partly to the fact that last year
the pay was slightly under-estimated, and
secondly it is due to the normal operation of
increments. Hon. Members will apperciate
that the longer the man remains in a Police
Force the bigger the amount of his pay up
to a certain period. In connection with this
Sub-head hon. Members will see that in
accordance with the undertaking which I
gave this House, the temporary service of
Weights and Measures which was rendered
necessary at the time of the disbandment of
the old Royal Irish Constabulary has been
discontinued, these temporary Inspectors'
places being taken by members of the Royal
Ulster Constabulary, seventeen of whom, I
am glad to say, have passed a very stiff examination which is provided for the purpose
by the Board of Trade. The Inspector-
General, by a re-arrangement of the districts,
has been enabled to reduce the number of
men employed on this particular duty to 12,
and I am in hopes that it may be possible to
continue the number employed at that
number.
With regard to Rent Allowances, hon.
Members will see that there is a slight increase in regard to that, but here again this
arises from the fact that there are more men
qualified to get these allowances because they
are married. With regard to Clothing, hon.
Members will see that we have been able to
effect a saving of no less a sum than
£13,500. That is due to the fact that last
year, in order to give more employment, and
in order that we should have a reserve stock
of clothing, we placed larger orders than
were absolutely necessary for the Force,
and this year we only provided for
15,000 yards. As regards Transport, here
again we have been able to effect a reduction
of 50 per cent. in the amount for Transport.
Ι
Dealing with Appropriations in Aid, hon.
Members will observe an Appropriation in
Aid for the first time of £6,000. This represents the cost of the police service in the
administration of the Road Acts. The
advent of motor cars has of course placed a
considerable additional burden on the police.
For instance, they have to look after the
control of motor traffic, and make sure
motorists pay the licences, and we feel it
only right that this sum should be paid out
of the Road Fund.
With regard to the Appropriation in Aid
for the use of extra police, hon. Members
will see that it is more than last year. This
is due to the fact that we had the "A"
Special Constabulary and our own Royal
Ulster Constabulary was not up to full
strength, and the local authorities concerned
got those extra police free.
My hon: Friend the Member for West
Belfast (Mr. Wm. McMullen) raised the
question the other day of the accommodation for prisoners while under arrest in
the police court. Hé complained that the
washing accommodation is not such as it'
should be. I have gone into this matter
personally, and there is a great deal in his
complaint. I am taking this matter up,
and I hope I may be able to arrive at a
satisfactory solution as I agree with him
that prisoners awaiting, trial should, at all
events, have the opportunity of making
themselves as respectable as they can in
appearance. Reverting to the Sub-head
dealing with Rents, I might point out that
we have not yet been able to arrange for
the establishment of a depot, but in the
meantime we are carrying on with the
camp at Newtownards which we rent from
the military authorities. A sum of money
has been appropriated to provide a depot,
but we thought it would be better to wait
until things became more stabilised when
we might be able to build more cheaply
than at present, and we considered that
the present arrangement, which enables
the police to come to Newtownards for
their refresher courses was the most satisfactory for the present.
With regard to barracks, considerable
progress has been made both in the reconstruction and erection of barracks, but
we have had a great many difficulties to
meet in regard to sites. However, I hope
that during the course of the present year
considerably more progress will be made
as the Government is most anxious that
the members of the Royal Ulster Constabulary should be properly housed. Hon.
Members know that the condition of the
barracks was simply deplorable when we
took them over and we are doing our best
to rectify them. I think these are the main
points of the Estimate, but I shall be very

When this Estimate was brought fully
under the notice of the Public Accounts
Committee, and after investigating the past
extravagance of the Constabulary, I, as a
member of that Committee, felt it was my
duty to draw the attention of this Committee
to that extravagance. Each and every
Member who has read that report will now
realise the significance of the previous Vote.
The Department which that Vote concerned
was the department that has brought about
the exposure of the extravagance of the
Department to which the present Estimate
refers. Under the heading of travelling expenses there is an amount asked for of
£3.800. It does not say whether that refers
to travelling by rail, by motor, or by foot.
Sir DAWSON BATES: May I point out
that the Estimate says "Car hire, cycling
allowance, and railway fare."
Mr. BEATTIE: That is a very handsome
sum to give for that. In my judgment the
amount asked for for that purpose exceeds
the sum required. The cost of hiring cars
in the country districts is less than it is in
the city. I am not in possession of the
cost per mile for cars, but I would like to
know what class of work these cars were
hired for, because it is very important to
know what we are paying car fares for. I
understand that the officers of the force have
a personal allowance for using their own
cars up to a distance of fifty miles, and that
over that distance they have the use of an
official car. It has been suggested to me that
the official car is used from the beginning,
and that they do not use their own car.
There is a case of a two-seater Ford car in
respect of which a personal allowance of
£150 a year has been given. I understand
that the car is three years' old and that the
price of such a car is £125, so that if you
calculate £150 for each of the three years
that the car has been in use you will find
that the hiring and using of cars for work
of this description is a money-making business.
I would also like to draw the Minister's
attention to cases in which cars are used for
other than official purposes. I suppose the
Minister will make a statement to the effect
that under his survey nothing of the sort
has happened, and, therefore, may I ask this
personal question. How does the Minister
come to use a Government car during his
private journeys in and out of the country?
I do not think he himself is entitled to use
a car any more that I am, and, therefore,
I think the time is overdue for the Minister
himself to set an example to those in his
Department in regard to the use of cars.
Perhaps by his example other persons under
his control will cease using official cars for
purposes other than official duties.
We now come to the sub-head, Maintenance
and Repairs. I understand that refers to
police barracks. The maintenance and
repair of police barracks cost us some money
during the past year and it is going to cost
us some more money during the coming year.
