Mr. KYLE: I want to support the motion
for the reduction of this Estimate by £1,000.
I do so because, worked out, the total Estimate that is being asked for is roughly
13s. 4d. per head of the population of
Northern Ireland, that is, it takes £803,736
to police a population of 1,250,000 in the Six
Counties, men, women and children. So we
have got to console ourselves that in
these days of peace in these days when
everybody lives in harmony with everybody else, and there is no real need for
such a large police force-we have to face
up to this proposition that we have got to
pay 13s. 4d. for every man, woman and child
in the community of Northern Ireland. This
is something he asks us to receive with
equanimity. The amount is £3 6s. 8d. for
the mythical, normal family of five, the
man, wife, and three children.
I think it would only be one in a hundred
or perhaps one in a thousand of the people
in the Six Counties who require the useful
advice and restraint of the Royal Ulster
Constabulary at any time. Surely the
question that has been asked by the hon.
Member for Down (Mr. O'Neill) should give
the Minister furiously to think-as to when
we are to expect in the North of Ireland a
reasonable police charge and a reasonable
Estimate for the police. We are not saying
any one word about the calibre of the men
or even about their wages. We believe that
when we employ men in the Royal Ulster
Constabulary they should be paid properly.
Everybody agrees with that. We do say it
seems a tremendous sum to have to pay for
a small area relatively speaking such as ours
is-to have to pay 13s. 4d. per head of the
population for police. It is a burden on
industry. It is a burden on the people
which it seems to me the people are rather
foolish in having to carry, because we have
during the past two years entered into a
blissful state of peace for which a good deal
is due to the Royal Ulster Constabulary.
(Hon. Members: Hear, hear.) But now
that we have entered into that haven it
seems to me that the Minister should cut
down very considerably the expense of policing the Six Counties.
The hon. Member for East Belfast (Mr.
Beattie) referred to the item for whitewashing the barracks. I notice here that in
connection with the various messages sent to
the various barracks telephone calls amount
to £5,100. That seems to me to be inordinate
and telegrams £500. I suppose they were
all spent in making inquiries about one
thing or another. I do agree with the hon.
Member for East Belfast that these amounts
are out of all proportion to the volume,
quantity, and value of the work done.
The right hon. Gentleman in making his
opening statement says because there was a
reduction in the total amount we on these
Benches should refrain from moving a still
further reduction. Well, I think we are
justified when we state that we in the Six

heavily for police than any other part of
the world-13s. 4d. per head. I want to try
to get every Member on the opposite Benches
to realise what that means. I know it is a
bit difficult to get right hon. Gentlemen on
those Benches to realise what that means.
I do not think it would take so much
trouble to get the hon. Member for Antrim
(Mr. Crawford) or even the hon. Member
for the University (Dr. Morrison) to realise
what that 13s. 4d. per head means. For
every person, including every unemployed person, 13s 4d has got to be paid for the police

sum of £1,000.

the cost has been reduced to £6,235, in spite

I do hope that there is not a tremendous

the telephone or a telegram is not used for

There is another thing I wish to draw the

I venture to say he thinks 3,001 people in

I should like to see this reduced, and more
women employed. I believe women can discharge duties which men cannot discharge so
well. In the interests of the morals of the
community we should have at least twenty to
assist in carrying out that duty.
On the whole it is a satisfactory thing to

that next year there will be a greater
reduction. I am astonished that the hon.
Member for North Belfast, who said he would

Then there is the question of travelling
expenses, transport charges, and subsistence
allowances. Under these three headings
there is room still, I think, for considerable
saving to be effected. During the difficult
and trying times through which the Constabulary passed undoubtedly they had to
use transport very freely. They had to use
the best possible means of locomotion irrespective of expense, and one could not
criticise them for so doing because they were
effectively dealing with law breakers, trying
to restore order throughout the country, and
to secure peace and good government.
now that we have reached a state of comparative quietude it would be well for the heads
of the Constabulary in association with the
responsible officers of the Ministry to see that
the most rigid rules are laid down by which
these transport charges could be reduced and
subsistence allowances and things of that
kind brought down to a minimum. I see by
the Comptroller's recent report, which the
Public Accounts Committee have yet to consider, and to which I presume it would not
be in order to refer to-day, that these matters
are again dealt with, so that we may take it
that there is still room for improvement in
these directions.
I must say I can only corroborate what

irrespective of creed, class, or religion. I
think they have behind them, and no work
Colonel WOODS: I wish to associate myself
with the remarks of previous speakers who
have expressed their admiration of the Royal
Ulster Constabulary, but I would like to
see the time come when we can get back again
to the strength of the police force which we
had pre-war in Ulster, when we will have

are one or two items to which I would like

The clothing is not supplied by Northern

Mr. POLLOCK: I am afraid you are wrong

Colonel WOODS: I hope so. I will be

HOUSE OF COMMONS
[Colonel Woods]
The other item to which I wish to refer
is that of £1,250 for accoutrements. There,
again, I would ask the attention of the right
hon. Gentleman (Sir Dawson Bates) to the
pointsmen who are still carrying revolversor holsters, at least-batons, and ammunition
pouches without any shoulder support. These
when they get their overcoats on constitute
a considerable weight. The right hon.
Gentleman checked me once when I said
that the weight was somewhere about
thirteen pounds, but I think it is somewhere
between nine and thirteen, and when the
coat gets wet the strain of this heavy weight
on their waists all the time the men are
moving their arms about is very fatiguing
and uncomfortable, and, in my opinion, it
is quite unnecessary. It only requires a
little thought or consideration from the right
hon. Gentleman to correct that particular
complaint.
Some attention has been directed to locomotion and boot allowances. I find after
comparison of these two items that there
are thirteen men in the force who have got
neither boot nor motor-car allowance. I
should like to know who these gentlemen
are, and why there are only thirteen of
them who have no need of one or other of
these allowances. Do they go about in their
bare feet? The other matters on which I
would have liked to touch have been very
thoroughly dealt with by previous speakers.
The hon. Member for Antrim (Mr. Crawford), who found fault with the charges for
postage and telephones, suggested that the
telephones should not be used when postage
would do. Local telephone calls only cost
1d, while a postage stamp costs 1d.
Sir ROBERT ANDERSON: Long distance
calls cost more.
Colonel WOODS: Yes, of course, but I take
it that most of these telephone calls are
local. I would like to see a reduction of this
force, and the time will come when it will
not be necessary to keep up such an enormous force as we have now, when you take
into consideration that we have a splendid
volunteer force as well. It is strange to think
that where one policeman was sufficient once
there are about four now. I hope the time
will soon come when it will be possible to
reduce this force to normal dimensions.
Major SHILLINGTON: I should like to
congratulate the Ministry on the fact of
their being able to introduce an Estimate
which shows a small reduction as compared
with that of the previous year, and also to
join in the compliments that have been
paid by previous speakers to the members
of the Royal Ulster Constabulary. There is
one of the points which the Minister
mentioned in introducing the Estimate on
which I would like to join issue with him
to a certain extent. He spoke of the fact
that we are getting the pick of the men of
Northern Ireland into the Constabulary. I
admit that we are getting a good class of
man, but I do not admit we are getting
as good a class a man as we might get.
I am given to understand that at the present time applicants for enrolment in the
Royal Ulster Constabulary have to pass an
examination in general knowledge, and that
after that they are segregated into two
classes solely and only in relation to their
height, that men of five feet eleven inches
and upwards are put into class one, and
that if a man does not reach five feet eleven
-if he is, say, only 5 feet 10 inches-he
is put into class two. My contention is that
you would be just as likely, and much more
likely in some cases, to get a more efficient
man of 5 feet 10 inches than you would be
if the man were 5 feet 11 inches, and
height should not be the only question
to be taken into consideration. (Hon.
Members: Hear, hear.)
The Minister referred to the promotions to
commissioned rank in the Force, and I think
he said that fifty per cent. of those promotions go to men who rise from the ranks.
I would like to know what arrangements
are being made in regard to the filling of
vacancies in respect of the other fifty per
cent. Have the Government any scheme for
the training of cadets, or any system
whereby some of our promising young
Ulstermen who have done well, say, at the
University can get into the Royal Ulster
Constabulary? I do not know of any such
arrangement at the moment, but I would be
glad to hear if anything of that sort is
contemplated.
I would like again to refer to the question
of the camp at Newtownards. The Minister
very kindly answered a question which I
put to him a few weeks ago and gave me
to understand that that camp is costing the
Government £1,080 a year altogether, and
that the Government have to pay the rates
and taxes on that camp and insure it.
They have to pay that for what is really
a camp of sufficient size to accommodate
two military battalions. I understand that
there are two camps, but now that there are
never likely to be more than 200 men of the
Royal Ulster Constabulary there at the
present time there are only something like
150-would not it be possible to get the

In connection with Sub-head D-Travelling
Expenses I would very much like to know
whether the Royal Ulster Constabulary are
still carrying out the same old arrangement
which held good in the Royal Irish Constabulary under which a constable who produced a
bicycle to his superior officer was
mediately put down for a cycling allowance
of so much a month, so much a quarter, or
so much a year as the case might be. I
understand that that man's superior officer
never had any authority to inspect that
bieycle from time to time, and it might
have done duty for any number of constables in the same barracks. I think it
would be much better if the Government
would provide so many bicycles for each
barracks at their own expense and do away
with that allowance altogether, and I would
like to know what proportion of this
£3,800 for travelling expenses is really due
to this cycling allowance.
I would like also to emphasise the points
that have been raised already by hon.
Members who are Members of the Committee
on Public Accounts in regard to the questions that were referred to them. I think
there is room for great saving yet in regard
to telegrams, postage, and telephones. It
seems to me that the expenditure under that
head has been reckless in the past. I hope
that the matter is receiving the attention
of the responsible officials. I would also
like to say that I think it would be desirable,
as regards those motors that are used on
Government service, that a record should
be kept, so that some responsible official
would see that the uses to which these motorcars are put are proper uses.
Dr. MORRISON: There is only one point
in the Estimate to which I would like to
refer. We hear complaints against the
Government for lavish expenditure. The
point to which I wish to refer is a matter
within the control of the people themselves.
It is this sum of £35,000 for extra police. So
far as I know that expenditure is incurred
largely for attending political organisations
and also elections. The elections do not
come very often, and, therefore, I think the
bulk is due for police attendance and the
preservation of the peace at political demonstrations. Surely we have reached this stage
in Northern Ireland when we can have our
political demonstrations without interference
from those who differ from us. I have
witnessed processions of all classes of Irishmen in Dublin and in Cork, and I have
enjoyed them. They can do the thing more
artistically in Dublin than in Belfast.
have now in this Parliament amongst the
private Members representatives of both
sections, and I do not see why we should
not be able to suggest to those who look to
us as political leaders for guidance that
these demonstrations should be arranged in
such a way and in such territory that it
would not irritate anybody, and where no
interference would take place, and where the
presence of police would be unnecessary.

The hon. Member (Sir Robert Anderson)
is a man who is working hard for economy.
He has done good work on the Public
Accounts Committee. He could bring about
this reform, and he could save, perhaps, a

particular parts of the city. In South

Mr. BLACK: There is one matter not
touched on in this Estimate which seems to
me very striking, and that is the archaic
manner in which remuneration to bath
officers and men is set out here. The first
we have under Sub-head A-pay, and the
second under Sub-head B--allowances. If
the allowances were only allowances to
special officers and men for special duties on
special occasions one could understand that
they may be set out separately. Take the
men. You have boot allowance for 2,930 men
at £3 18s. each, and medical allowance for
2,950 officers and men at £1 7s. Or look at
the officers. You will find that the Inspector-
General, the Commissioners, the County
Inspectors and the District-Inspectors are
given rent allowance. The Deputy Inspector-General the County Inspectors, and
the District Inspectors are also given locomotion allowances. These form really part
of the salary or remuneration. Instead of
setting them out separately surely it would
be more satisfactory if boot allowance,
medical allowance and other allowances
were added on to the pay of the men so that
they would get a certain fixed amount equal
to the additional perquisites. If the rent
allowance, locomotion allowance and other
things were added to the ordinary salaries
of the superior officers we would be able to
see at a glance the real remuneration of the
sergeant or constable and also the real remuneration of the Inspector-General, County
Inspectors, and District Inspectors, per
annum. As it is now one has to go through
quite a number of things to try to find out
what the salary is or what wages are being
paid to the members of the Constabulary.
I know in no other Estimates, so far as I
have been able to see, is there this splitting
or setting out as allowances what is in
reality pay. In other services they do not
allow for a certain amount of salary and a
certain amount of medical allowances. Give
a man his salary and let him find his own
doctor and his own boots and his own locomotion. It would be more satisfactory and
businesslike than the present arrangement.
We would see what we were voting as remuneration both to officers and men.
There is one other matter I would like to
mention, and that is just to rub in what has
been stated already by the Member for
Derry (Sir Robert Anderson). The Public
Accounts Committee were startled and
shocked by some things they came across
in the Constabulary accounts. I see that the
Estimate for telephones is £1,500. That is
a decrease from the Estimate of last year,
which was £5,100. That is some decrease,
but I would like to have an assurance from
the Minister that the greatest vigilance will
be observed in regard to this matter which is
one of the things we had occasion to look
into at the Public Accounts Committee.
When we come to next year's Estimate we
hope to see a still further decrease. I can
assure the Minister that the Public
Accounts Committee-and I can say certainly the Auditor-General whoever may be
appointed-will keep a very vigilant eye on
these matters. As well as the matter of
telephones there is the use of motor cars.
With regard to that item; I see a very
striking and surprising thing in this Estimate. At the end of Sub-head B there is
set out a number of drivers to whom it is
proposed to pay an allowance of 2s. per day.
That is, I presume, because they have
qualified themselves as drivers. The item
sets out the number of drivers who got
this allowance in 1925-26 and the number
estimated for in 1926-27. The curious thing
is that there were only 40 in 1925-26, while
the estimate shows that 55 are to be paid
for in 1926-27. Are we to infer from that
that there is an increase in the use of motor
cars instead of a decrease? That is a
matter that demands the attention of the
Minister.
One other thing I would like an explanation in regard to. Under sub-head A it is
stated that one county inspector, two district
inspectors at headquarters and one district
inspector in general are redundant. That is
a very serious thing to come before the Committee at a time when all sections are most
eagerly demanding that the greatest economy
be shown. Does that in reality mean what
it appears to mean on the face of it that we
have four officers in high position whose services are redundant? Are there any other
people for whom we are asked to vote in this
Estimate whose services are redundant? I
am glad that this police Estimate has been
reduced this year. I hope the greatest
vigilance will be observed so that we may
have a further reduction, possibly next year.
I hope that there will be an assurance from
the Minister that the greatest vigilance and
the greatest care will be shown throughout
the year in regard to this Estimate, whi..

when acting as Chairman of the Committee

Mr. HANNA: I do not think that the

I would like to say this. If I do not fully

perhaps hon. Members can give me an opportunity at another time, in another place, and
I will be very glad to explain more fully than
I can now the meaning of the allowances provided for in this Estimate.
The hon. Member for East Belfast (Mr.
Beattie) asked some questions about the subsistence allowance. That allowance is provided for where any member of the Force is
absent from the station on duty, and a
special scale is set out of the amounts that
are paid. If they are away for eight hours,
and under twelve hours, constables and sergeants are allowed 3s 6d, head constables 4s,
and officers 5s, and if they are away for
twelve hours and over, they are allowed 5s,
68 and 7s respectively. Then there are a
number of regulations which are all set out
in the Statutory Rules and Orders of Northern Ireland under the Constabulary Act.
Those matters are provided for, and that
scale is rigidly enforced. Vouchers must
always be supplied by any members of the
Force applying for subsistence allowance,
and all travelling expenses require to be
audited.
The hon. Member (Mr. Beattie) pointed out
that he had reason to believe that in connection with the motor cars belonging to
certain officers the men were engaged in
doing repairs to those private cars. If that
is so, we have no knowledge of it. It is
improper and not right, and we would be
very glad of any information which would
help to put a stop to anything of that kind.
Let me, at this stage, say in connection
with the report of the Public Accounts Committee that every word of it has been carefully studied, not only by the Minister of
Home Affairs, and by those associated with
him, but by all the officers in charge of the
Constabulary, and that the greatest regard
will be paid to every recommendation the
Committee have made. We want to take the
fullest advantage of their most careful deliberations to see that there will be no abuses
of any kind in connection with the Constabulary.

Mr. THOMAS HENDERSON: At yesterday's sitting of the House, I said I would
ask the Minister of Home Affairs, at the
adjournment of the House to-day, a question
regarding the result of the Inquiry that took
place recently in the Union Infirmary. I
may say that I have seen the result of the
Inquiry, and that I am quite satisfied.
only want to take this opportunity of thanking the Minister of Home Affairs for the
very prompt manner in which he took up
this matter. I am quite satisfied that, as a
result of the Inquiry, proper attention will
be given in future to patients who are in
the unfortunate position of having to be
taken to the Mental Hospital. I believe that
good has been done as a result of the Inquiry,
and I wish to compliment the Minister and
the gentleman who conducted the Inquiry.
But I cannot allow this occasion to pass
without referring to a statement made by Mr.
Beattie, K.C., who represented the Poor-law
Guardians at the Inquiry. He said that I
had told falsehoods and made mis-statements,
and that I had not the courtesy to attend
the Inquiry and prove my statements. The
statement that I gave to the Minister of
Home Affairs was the statement given to
me by the deceased gentleman, who was an
inmate of Purdysburn Mental Hospital.
Therefore, I only took down the statement
of the patient, and handed it to the Minister
of Home Affairs. The Superintendent, or the
head of the Purdysburn Mental Hospital, I
understand, had previously sent a letter to
the Minister of Home Affairs, so that I was
not the first one to call attention to the
injury that this poor man had received. I
want to take exception to the methods
adopted by a member of the Bar in attacking
me and in trying to intimidate Members of
this House.
Mr. SPEAKER: I understand the hon.
Member is making a personal explanation
in connection with some adverse comments
upon his actions, but he is not entitled in
this House to go further than that, and to
make reflections upon members of outside
bodies such as the Bar.
Mr. T. HENDERSON: I will content myself, then, with sincerely thanking the
Minister of Home Affairs for the great
improvements that will be brought about as
a result of the Inquiry.

Thursday, 22nd April, 1926.
The House met at Three of the Clock, Mr.
SPEAKER in the Chair.
Oral Answers to Questions.
BALLYMENA ARTIFICIAL SILK
}
FACTORY.
1. Mr. DEVLIN asked the Minister of
Commerce whether his attention has been
called to the statement in the Imperial
House of Commons by the President of the
Board of Trade, to the effect that ten artificial silk factories have been started in
England since the 1st of July, 1925; whether
he can say when the factory near Ballymena
will start production; whether other factories are to be established in Northern
Ireland; and what steps, if any, the heads of
the linen industry are taking to adapt some
of the linen factories to the production of
the new material.
"
The MINISTER OF COMMERCE (Mr.
Barbour): The answer to the first part of
the question is in the affirmative. With regard to the factory established near Ballymena, the Company issued their prospectus
in February this year, in which it was
stated that the property, works and water
rights had been acquired, the machinery was
in course of manufacture, and that the
Company expected to be in a position to
commence delivery to customers during the
month of September. So far as my information goes, no concrete proposals for the
establishment of other factories in Northern
Ireland have hitherto been made, although
I am aware that negotiations towards this
end are proceeding. While I have no doubt
that the linen industry is carefully watching
the development of the uses of this new
textile, I have no information which would
suggest that steps have been taken by any
linen manufacturer to adapt an existing
linen factory to the production of artificial
silk.
Mr. DEVLIN: Is the right hon. Gentleman aware that within the last few days the
President of the Board of Trade has made
further statements in the Imperial Parliament to the effect that the value of artificial
silk manufactured in the United Kingdom
and exported during the first quarter of 1926
has increased by 82 per cent., and does the
right hon. Gentleman not think this new
industry offers a magnificent opportunity to
the heads of the linen trade to open up a new
branch and find an outlet for their own
enterprise and work for their operatives?
Mr. BARBOUR: I have noted the reference that has been made to the wonderful
development that has taken place in this
new fibre. My personal opinion is that there
would be considerable difficulty in adapting
the linen machinery in any way to the preparation of this fibre, but I am sure the
heads of the linen industry are watching the
course of these developments, and if they
can see that it can with advantage be adapted
to any of the fabrics which, they make at
present, they will not neglect such an opportunity.
Colonel WOODS: Is the right hon. Gentleman aware that in Dunfermline the linen
machinery has been adapted to the manufacture of artificial silk fibre?
Mr. BARBOUR: I am not aware of it.
Mr. DEVLIN: I have a number of other
supplementary questions. Shall I send them
to the right hon. Gentleman?
Mr. BARBOUR: I shall be glad to receive
them.
CHAIRMAN OF NORTH ANTRIM
REGIONAL EDUCATION COMMITTEE.
2. Mr. BEATTIE asked the Parliamentary
Secretary to the Ministry of Education
whether the Chairman of the North Antrim
Regional Education Committee holds the
offices of sanitary sub-officer under the Ballymoney Rural District Council, relieving
officer under the Ballymoney Board of
Guardians, and Infant Life Protection
officer; whether it is legal for him to hold
these offices, and, if not, why he is permitted
to do so.
The PARLIAMENTARY SECRETARY OF
THE MINISTRY OF EDUCATION (Mr.
Robb): The Ministry has been informed
that Mr. Hanna, who has been appointed.
Chairman of the North Antrim Regional
Education Committee, holds the other offices
to which reference is made in the hon. Member's question.
The attention of the Antrim County
Council as the education authority for the
county, the Regional Education Committee,
the Ballymoney Urban Council, and the
Ballymoney Rural Council was called to the
matter in order that these bodies might
have an opportunity of considering it, and
in the event of their being advised that an
irregularity had occurred, of taking such
action as might be competent for them.
Oral Answers.
Oral Answers.
•
22 APRIL 1926
The Ministry also communicated with Mr.
Hanna, but that gentleman has informed the
Ministry that he had been advised that his
position is unassailable.
In these circumstances the Ministry did
not consider that it developed upon it to interfere any further in this matter as it was
not in any way responsible for the appointment of Mr. Hanna as a member of this
Regional Education Committee.
LOCAL GOVERNMENT OFFICERS ON
REGIONAL COMMITTEES.
3. Mr. BEATTIE asked the Parliamentary
Secretary to the Ministry of Education
whether he can state what Local Government
officers were appointed members of Regional
Education Committees in Northern Ireland,
and were then required to resign; and
whether other Local Government Officers
were appointed members of Regional Education Committees in Northern Ireland and not
required to resign, and for what reason was
this distinction made.
Mr. ROBB: The only case which has come
under the notice of the Ministry of Education where a member of a Regional Education
Committee when appointed to that position
held an office of profit under a local Council
or Board in the area under the control of
the Committee is that of Mr. Hanna, member of the North Antrim Regional Education
Committee referred to in the preceding
Question.
A member of the Ballymena Regional
Education Committee was appointed by that
Committee as its solicitor on condition that
he resigned his membership of the Regional
Committee, and he duly complied with this
condition.
The Ministry has no knowledge of any
other cases of this kind.
ULSTER OFFICERS IN "B" SPECIAL
CONSTABULARY.
4. Colonel WOODS asked the Minister of
Home Affairs whether he will consider the
advisabality of augmenting the number of
Ulster officers and Ulster non-commissioned
officers, clerks, and instructors employed in
the "B" Special Constabulary, which is recruited and regarded as essentially territorial in its constitution.
The MINISTER OF HOME AFFAIRS
(Sir Dawson Bates): As I pointed out to the
hon, and gallant Member in reply to a
question put by him on the 20th instant, out
of the total staff attached to the Force of
"B" Special Constabulary over 90 per cent.
are Ulstermen.
In selecting the full-time personnel of the
reorganised "B" Force, preference is given
to members of the Special Constabulary and,
other things being equal, to those who are
Ulstermen.
SIR RUSSELL SCOTT'S INVESTIGATION.
5. Mr. DEVLIN asked the Prime Minister
whether Sir Russell Scott had started his
investigation into the Northern Ireland
Civil Service, and, if so, why no public
announcement was made to this effect:
whether he will state what method Sir
Russell Scott has adopted to get at the facts,
and whether Members of this House will be
given an opportunity to place their views
before him.
The MINISTER OF FINANCE (Mr.
Pollock): I have been asked to take this
reply.
Sir Russell Scott assisted by two other
Treasury officials, started his inquiry in Belfast on the 7th April, and concluded his
examination of the work of the various Departments on the 13th instant. The method
he adopted was to begin with a personal
investigation on the spot into the work and
staff of each department, and he is now coordinating the results thus obtained with
additional statistics and reports which are
being supplied at his request. The conduct
of his investigations was left entirely to the
discretion of Sir Russell Scott, who
apparently did not consider it necessary to
make any public announcement of his
inquiry.
Mr. DEVLIN: Does the right hon. Gentleman think that this method of inquiry will
satisfy the public, and did he convey to Sir
Russell Scott that representations had been
made in this House that the inquiry should
be of a public character and that all persons
interested in his investigations should have
an opportunity of taking part in them?
Mr. POLLOCK: Yes. Sir Russell Scott
was informed that reference had been made
in this House in something like the terms
the hon. Gentleman has now suggested, but
the gentleman in question did not think it
necessary to do other than conduct the investigations in regard to the matters which
he was called upon to undertake without
consulting any outside authority.
Mr. DEVLIN: Does the right hon. Gentleman not think it a scandalous performance
on the part of this English official to come
over here and investigate the accounts of the
Ulster Government and the Ulster Province
without giving a single member of the
public an opportunity of taking part in his
investigations or appearing before him?
Y

Mr. SPEAKER: Order. The hon. Gentleman (Mr. Devlin) can talk about the
scandalous conduct of the Ulster Government,
but I do not think he is entitled to talk about
the scandalous conduct of an official of
another Government, who undertook a duty
without restrictive terms of reference and to
whom complete liberty of action was allowed.
Mr. DEVLIN: With all respect, this man
comes over here to interfere in our business.
Mr. POLLOCK: No.
Mr. DEVLIN: Yes, he does.
Sir
Mr. POLLOCK: Might I intervene?
Russell Scott was invited to come here by the

Mr. SPEAKER: The position is, as I understand it, that this British Civil Servant was
invited to come here, and so far as his actions
are concerned I do not think it falls to the
lot of this House to depreciate them, though,

Mr. DEVLIN: Again with all respect, the
Minister has stated that this man came over
here and interfered in our business, that he
set up his own court, carried on his own
inquiry, pursued his own explorations and
treated with contempt the citizens of Ulster
and all those who were interested in-
Mr. SPEAKER: Order, order.
Mr. DEVLIN: I will discuss the matter in
a minute or two. When we come to the
Economy Bill I will say more about the whole
performance.
Mr. SPEAKER: The hon. Member is entirely outside the purview of what comes
within the province of this House in what
he says.
He can criticise the Government
for having adopted this way of bringing
about economies, but he is not entitled to
cast aspersions on the gentleman whom they
asked to come here, and who is the servant

Mr. DEVLIN: I would like to know what

has to come here and interfere in our business and then to be immune from the criticism of this House. It is the most extraordinary position I ever heard of.
Mr. SPEAKER: As I say, that is a matter

NORTHERN IRELAND CIVIL SERVICE.
6. Mr. DEVLIN asked the Prime Minister
whether he is prepared to appoint a Select
Committee, consisting of representatives of
every section in the House of Commons, to
inquire into the method of appointment to
and promotion in the Northern Ireland Civil
Service, the number of officials dismissed
during the past six months, and the reason
assigned for their dismissal, and the number
appointed during the same period.
Mr. POLLOCK: I have been asked to reply
to this question. The reply is in the negative.
I may say, however, for the hon. Member's
information, that the only officials whose
services have been dispensed with are those
who had been engaged in a purely temporary
capacity, and whose employment has been
terminated because their services were no
longer required.
Mr. DEVLIN: In order to remove more
than a suspicion-a sound fundamental belief
on the part of a large number of the public
that these appointments are made for purely
political reasons and given to camp followers
of his as against the appointment of efficient
officials, and to avert and prevent a continuance of this form of criticism, will the
right hon. Gentleman agree to the appointment of a Select Committee of the House
to investigate the matter?
Mr. POLLOCK: I am not prepared to concede the statement of the hon. Member, and
I cannot agree to the suggestion he has made
that a Select Committee should be appointed

Economy Bill-
Second Reading.
22 APRIL 1926
Bill Presented.
JURY LAWS AMENDMENT BILL,
"to amend the Laws relating to Juries in
Northern Ireland," presented by Sir Dawson
Bates; supported by Mr. Hanna; to be read
a Second time upon Thursday, and to be
printed. (Bill 9.)
ORDERS OF THE DAY.
Economy (Exchequer Relief) Bill.
Order for Second Reading read.
Mr. POLLOCK: I rise to move the Second
Reading of the Economy (Exchequer Relief)
Bill. I have caused to be circulated a
memorandum explaining the provisions of
the Bill, which will, I hope, serve to remove
any obscurities which the inevitable legislation by reference necessarily entails.
This is a very important Measure, not
alone because of the material issues involved,
but because it seeks by its provisions to
emphasise the fundamental truth that the
financial stability of the State transcends
every other consideration. It is the foundation of all progress, all prosperity. The
State differs in no respect from the individual; once destroy a man's financial credit
and catastrophe ensues. So it is with the
State. Many States, great and small, in
their departure from this law have brought
upon themselves calamitous results.
It is, therefore, to maintain the traditional
unimpeachable structure of British credit
that the Chancellor of the Exchequer some
weeks ago submitted the Economy Bill, which
has been the subject of so much discussion
at Westminster. In two of the most important features of this Measure we are very
directly interested for very definite and
cogent reasons. First, under our present
constitutional arrangements our whole financial system is so interwoven with that of
Britain it would pass the wit of man to keep
them separate. Second, our own financial
necessities are so great, I am searching in
every quarter and in every Department of
our national machinery for any saving that
can be effected.
The provisions of the Bill fall naturally
into two main divisions; firstly, the amendment of the law in regard to the State's
contribution to the Contributory Insurance
Schemes, and secondly, the readjustment to
a small extent of the State's financial relations with local authorities. I propose to
place before the House, as briefly and concisely as possible, the main principles
underlying the Bill, and to explain at the
same time the motives which have led the
Government to contemplate the various
changes which are now proposed. I would
ask Members in raising any points to recollect that detailed explanation will be given
on each clause in Committee, and an opportunity will then arise of that close scrutiny
of detail which is not appropriate to a
Second Reading.
I turn now to the clauses dealing with the
two Contributory Insurance Schemes, and
in order to explain them fully it is necessary
for me to ask the House to carry their
thoughts to what is commonly termed the
Colwyn Award, with which this matter is
so closely interwoven. The House will recollect that in devising a formula for the
determination of our contribution towards
Imperial services, the Colywn Committee
first constructed a standard year-1923-1924and then proceeded to enunciate principles
for the guidance of the Joint Exchequer
Board in determining the manner in which
any deviations from the expenditure and revenue in that standard year were to be dealt
with. Stated in broad outline, and without
certain necessary correctives, if Great
Britain increased her local expenditure-in
the main, expenditure on social servicesabove the expenditure of the standard year,
Northern Ireland was to be allowed a corresponding increase, if warranted by the
circumstances. On the other hand, if Great
Britain's local expenditure actually decreased, the Joint Exchequer Board are to
presume that a corresponding decrease in
our local expenditure is called for, and if
such does not take place the costs of maintaining the service at the old level must be
found by Northern Ireland from her own
resources.
It immediately follows, therefore, that if
the Imperial Government takes steps, which
result in a diminution of their local expenditure, and we, for our part, decide to maintain the particular services involved at the
old standard we have to bear the excess
cost ourselves. These considerations have,
as the House will at once realise, a most important bearing on our whole financial situation and policy, and unless we are in such
affluent circumstances that we can afford to
disregard the effects of the Colwyn Report,
and to bear entirely unaided the cost of maintaining local services here at a higher level
than in Great Britain it follows that we
must, of necessity, carry into effect here any
reductions in expenditure which are made
across the water.
This, therefore, is the position which has
confronted the Government since it became
known that the Imperial Government had
decided to make certain reductions in its
State contributions toward the contributory
insurance schemes. The first eight clauses
of this Bill provide for changes in the
administration of these services in Northern
Ireland, which are identical with those now
Economy Bill-
Second Reading.
HOUSE OF COMMONS
[Mr. Pollock]
being carried into effect in Great Britain,
and if Members will refer to the last page of
the White Paper which has been circulated
with the Bill they will notice that the total
savings which it is estimated will result
from these clauses amount to nearly £170,000.
Suppose that we had decided not to reduce
the State Grant toward National Health Insurance or the Exchequer contribution toward
Unemployment Insurance, we would have
been required to find that £170,000 entirely
out of our own resources; it would not have
entered in any way at all into the calculation of the contribution, and under the
arrangement we would have received no
allowance for it whatever. I do not need to
emphasise the fact that we cannot afford to
pay this £170,000, and it follows, therefore,
without argument, that we have no choice in
the matter, but must of necessity legislate
on parallel lines with Great Britain.
a
That is the financial effect viewed in the
light of the Colwyn Award. But we can
view it from less material standpoint.
Take Health Insurance for example. The
whole scheme in Northern Ireland is absolutely interlocked with the British Scheme;
we have large societies operating in both
areas, and both providing similar benefits,
and we have a Joint Central Committee on
which we are represented, controlling
common Central Funds. It would, therefore, be wholly impracticable to dissociate
ourselves from, and to do anything else
but follow suit with Great Britain.
Then take Unemployment Insurance. There
is here too a reason why it is incumbent
upon us to follow Great Britain in regard
to the changes which are now being made.
The terms of what is generally known to us
as the Cave Award are no doubt still fresh
in the minds of every hon. Member of this
House. They are embodied in the agreement
made between the Chancellor of the Exchequer and myself and ratified by this
House in the early part of the Session, and
the full scope of that agreement, with its
consequential substantial contribution by the
British Exchequer to our Unemployment
Relief Fund, can only be obtained if we continue to follow any measures taken by the
Imperial Government. We are, therefore,
from a common-sense point of view bound to
reduce our State contribution to the Fund
to the extent of the reduction made in
Great Britain. Of the general effect of this
reduction 1 will deal at greater length when
I come to consider the clauses of the Bill.
I think I have now been able to show the
necessity of following Great Britain in regard
to these Insurance Services, but at the same
time it is desirable that I should show that
in so doing we are not acting inequitably
toward the insured population of Northern
Ireland, a very important factor in the discussion of this Measure. Ever since its inception in 1911 the National Health Insurance Scheme has been attended by the most
remarkable and phenomenal measure of
success; approved Societies have been able
to build up large reserve Funds, and one
factor which has assisted them in so doing
has been the rise in the rate of interest
which can be earned. I do not propose to
enter into this factor, but I may mention
that the present accumulated funds of these
Societies are the tremendous sum of
£65,000,000. One of the first factors or causes
of the exceptional success in respect of the
accumulation of these reserves is that when
the Insurance Fund was started in 1911 the
rate of interest on investments was only calculated at something like 3 per cent, or 3
per cent., while from the financial development that ensued the value of money increased so much that these Societies were
enabled to invest their money at from 44 per
cent. to 5 per cent.. and we have the Chancellor of the Exchequer's authority for
stating that this one factor alone increased
the volume of their surplus by £2,000,000 a
year.
Moreover, the Widows' and Orphans' Contributory Pensions Act of last year has, in
addition to placing a very considerable new
charge on the State, provided a large
measure of relief to Approved Societies inasmuch as from January, 1928, additional
sickness and disablement benefits will not
have to be provided for insured persons between the ages of 65 and 70. We have, therefore, at the present time a very remarkable
contrast between the financial position of the
State and the financial position of these approved societies. Here we see these great
societies rolling in-I do not want to use extravagant adjectives, but I think ordinarily
we would describe them as almost colossally
wealthy.
On the one hand there is undoubted
stringency, and continual examination and
re-examination of expenditure in order to see
whether reductions can be effected; while on
the other hand we have a very satisfactory
condition of wealth and prosperity. I maintain that the time has now come when the
State should make some small reduction in
the annual sums granted to approved
Societies, which are based on the benefits distributed by such Societies, and provision on
this behalf is accordingly made in the Bill.
There is nothing inequitable in this. That
is the whole issue. It will not affect contributors in any way whatever, and the sole
effect which it will have will be to
slow up to some extent the rate at
which approved societies are accum
lating surpluses. And if we did not
make this reduction what would be the
Economy Bill-
Second Reading.
22 APRIL 1926
result? The formula of the Colwyn Award
would relentlessly operate, as I have already
explained, and we would be forced to find
the money from our already too depleted
pockets.
I have already touched upon the provisions
in the Bill affecting the Unemployment
Fund, namely, a reduction in the Exchequer
contribution from 8d. to 6d. If we stood
alone and discussed our Unemployment Insurance Fund purely from our own point of
view I have not any doubt at all that if we
attempted to reduce the contribution from
8d. to 6d. we would bring our fund into a
very parlous condition, but in discussing this
matter we have to recall the whole circumstances under which the Fund is at present
operating. Let me say at once that this proposal-the reduction from 8d. to 6d.-does
not affect in the slightest degree the position
of our Unemployment Fund vis-a-vis the
corresponding British Fund. Under the Unemployment Insurance Agreement the
finances of our Unemployment Fund here are
definitely linked up with those of the British
Unemployment Fund, and to a very considerable degree have become associated with our
Exchequer, obtaining large issues therefrom,
not by way of repayable loan as in the past,
but by direct out and out payments.
Let me in a few words attempt to explain
the position. It is of such an involved
character-the calculation between the two
Governments-that I think it may be said
in the words of the Chancellor of the Exchequer that it is expressed in language only
intelligible to those who are masters of this
intricate and highly specialised subject.
Therefore, the explanation that I propose to
offer will be made as clear as I am able to
do in the simple language that I would
naturally employ. The two Funds are to be
maintained on a parity-at present a parity
deficit-proportionate to our insured populations. To achieve this parity, we under
present conditions must make large
additional contribution from our Exchequer,
termed the Equalisation Payment-this is
over and above the normal State contribution
-which goes on unchanged-made to the
Fund. Of this equalisation payment the
British Government recoups us something
less than three-fourths-75 per cent.
a
Now see how this operates under the
change proposed in the British Bill and reproduced here. Britain reduces her normal
State contribution to her own Fund; we do
likewise the state of parity between the
Funds is not disturbed, for the loss is an
identical loss to both. What would happen
if we did not reduce our normal State contribution? The formula of the Colwyn
Award would again operate, and we would
have to find from our Own pockets the
£75,000 referred to in the summary of the
White Paper. That is to say we avoid a
loss of this sum, but in fact we secure also
substantial gain-the second sum of
£41,000 referred to in the summary of the
White Paper. The saving of £41,000 arises
from the conjunction of the terms of the
Cave Award and the Final Colwyn Report.
a
Sir ROBERT ANDERSON: May I ask the
Minister has he in this calculation taken into
consideration the lessened contribution that
we receive towards unemployment insurance?
Mr. POLLOCK: Yes, that has been taken
into the calculation in making up this result
which I have just mentioned. I can see that
my hon. Friend understands this subject
rather more than I expected, but I can
assure him that this was taken into consideration. Under the Cave Award N.I. is
deemed to subscribe her total population proportion of all expenditure on Unemployment
Insurance, which includes the State Grant.
But, under the Colwyn Report she is only
allowed in cash her actual expenditure on
State grant, with the result that she has
to make up the difference between this expenditure and the amount she is deemed to
spend under the Cave Award. Naturally,
the more the figures of each item are
reduced proportionately, the more the
difference diminishes. In this case the net
effect is £41,000 on the latest Estimates.
This is a real immediate saving to the Exchequer, which, if the 8d. contribution stocd
would have had to be found from our own
pockets. I almost despair of making myself
clear on this point-it is one for mathematicians rather than for debate, but I can
assure the House that the facts are as I have
stated them.
I have dealt sufficiently with two important parts of the Bill which relate to
our relations as between Great Britain and
ourselves. I now come to the second main
division of the Bill, namely, that part from
Clause 9 onwards, which touches upon the
fringe of the subject of our financial relations with local authorities. When assistance was first given to local authorities,
chiefly for the relief of rates, it was by way
of the assignment of some definite source of
revenue for that purpose. This system has
since undergone very considerable modifications, and for a number of years the
tendency has been to replace it by some
system of definite grants, Accordingly,
Parliament has on numerous occasions provided by statute for the payment of grants
to local authorities for a great variety of
purposes, amongst which of course we have
Housing, then grants for various purposes
connected with Public Health; and more recently grants for educational services. There
still exist, however, one or two relics of the
early system, and I think it is clear that
Economy Bill-
Second Reading.
HOUSE OF COMMONS
[Mr. Pollock]
the equities of the case-certainly the simplicities of the case-demand at the present
time some re-adjustment of these financial
relations. (Hon. Members: Hear, hear.)
I think my point can best be illustrated
by reference to some of the specific provisions of the Bill. Take Clause 9, for instance. Existing legislation provides that
after certain of the expenses of collecting
Dogs Licence Duty have been met, and
an appropriate transfer made to the Petty
Sessions Fund, the balance of the proceeds
of the duty is to be handed over to local
authorities in relief of local rates. Since
this was originally enacted years ago many
other forms of State assistance to local
authorities have been created, and the
Government feels that to a very large extent,
if not indeed entirely, the purposes for
which the proceeds of this Licence Duty were
originally handed over to local authorities
are now met by grants from the Exchequer
in aid of particular services. It is proposed
therefore, that first of all
recognise as a legitimate charge on the
Dogs' Fund the expenses of the Royal Ulster
Constabulary in connection with the collection of the Duty, as well as the other
expenses already charged thereto, and that
after allowing for these expenses one-third of
the surplus should be paid into the Exchequer, leaving two-thirds to be handed .
over to the local authority. While logically
under the circumstances I have mentioned
the Exchequer might have appropriated the
whole sum, it was felt that it would be unfair
to local authorities to require them to forego
the full amount immediately. I have suggested, therefore, that they should receive
two-thirds.
we
should
Now I come to a clause that has been
the subject of some discussion and takes us
back to a somewhat remote past, this is
Clause 10 It has always been recognised that
the Valuation Department performs a dual
service. It not only carries out valuations
which govern the collection of local rates,
but it is also an important piece of machinery
in connection with the assessment of Income
Tax and Licence Duty. Some 50 years ago
it was agreed in principle that local authorities should contribute toward the cost of
the Valuation Office, and their payments
were fixed at a sum which then amounted to
one half of the cost of the Department. Now
it must be remembered that this arrangement was made very shortly after the great
valuation of Ireland made by Griffiths, and
consequently there was at that time very
little real work carried out by the Valuation
Department. It followed then that the cost
was on a very low basis and the local authorities, having agreed to pay half or rather to
pay an amount which then represented half,
escaped with practically a nominal sum.
Since then conditions in this Department as
well as in every other department of life
have changed very materially. The costs
have increased to a very large extent relatively in the last ten years. There has
been a very large increase in salaries and
travelling expenses.
We feel, therefore, that the time has now
come-in fact I am of opinion that it was
reached many years ago--when we should
make some adjustments in the annual payments. The Bill proposes, therefore, to amend
the contributions of counties and county
boroughs in order to bring the total annual
payment up to approximately one-half of the
present cost of the service. That is simply
on the same principle that has been adopted
50 years ago, when the amount was originally
settled.
Licence
It is interesting to note that the income
which local authorities obtain as a result of
valuation approximates to the sum of
£2,500,000 per annum, whilst the Exchequer in Income Tax and
Duty receives something less than £300,000.
That is to say, the Valuation Office is maintained as to nine-tenths for the local authorities practically, and one-tenth for the State.
As I have, therefore, been hunting around-I
quite frankly admit it-(laughter)-for something that could relieve the pressure, I did
think it was fair that the local authorities
should bear a proportion-not necessarily the
proportion involved in the relative
importance of the work carried out for them,
but that they should at any rate bear the
proportion that was originally arranged 50
years ago, that is to say, one-half. The arguments are overwhelmingly in favour so far
as the equities are concerned. I do not think
if it were submitted to any tribunal that
there would be any difficulty in coming to
that decision.
Since this Bill was introduced I have received various representations from various
parts of the country through our representatives-not that this is an unfair claim, I do
not think anyone has made such a contention
-but that in view of the very heavy burden
on the local authorities at the present time,
it would be an additional burden upon them
-although the cost would not be very heavy,
but it would be an additional burden upon
the rates if the Government carried out the
intentions of the clause I have been discussing. The Government sympathises with
the argument, although still contending for
the propriety of the claim that has been
made, and the Government, having concern
for the interests of the ratepayers equally
with their concern for the State, have
arranged, in deference to the representations,
to amend this clause in such a way as will
meet the views of the local authorities at the
present time.

amount of pains he must have taken to get

Clause 11 of the Bill does not require any
great explanation. At the present time we
are bound by statute to pay annually the sum
of £42,881 to Road Authorities in aid of expenditure on roads and bridges. This grant
dates from a period long before the establishment of the Road Fund, which is now specifically earmarked for the purpose of constructing and maintaining the roads, and is, under
present circumstances, an anomaly.
Members will no doubt agree that this expenditure should now fall on the same plane
as other expenditure of the same nature,

authorities, and the clause proposes to make

Summing up the effects of Parts 3, 4 and 5
of the Bill, if we deduct £5,000 surrendered

amply justified, for the credit of a State
transcends every other consideration. May
I cite a parallel? Government property is
exempt from rating, but Government pay a
bounty in lieu of rates which closely approximates to the ordinary rating. The Government has not stereotyped its contribution. As
the rates have increased of recent years, so
the contribution has increased. The Government has automatically increased its contribution, therefore applying the same argu-
Inent we did not think it was unfair-that
the local authorities should recognise the

Fund.
The additional burden which will be imposed as a result of this legislation is
negligible, and though it will not be welcomed, I would remind local authorities that
they escape here many burdens wihch corresponding bodies in Great Britain have to
shoulder.
I have now explained generally the reasons

Mr. KYLE: I propose to leave out all the
words after now," and to insert "this day
six months." I want first of all to congratulate the right hon. Gentleman upon the

The right hon. Gentleman has stated that
the stability of the State is above all else.
One readily agrees with a general statement

State is based on the common people's belief

Mr. KYLE: That is the interpretation I
put on the right hon. Gentleman's statement
here to-day. While we may let you have the

Where is the economy, except at the expense

that no body of employers could have had
the unblushing audacity to bring a Measure

Britain. If Britain does a foolish thing, and
proposes to rob its insurance societies, I do
not think it is right that Northern Ireland
should do the same, and I think that the
public of the Six Counties should be and will
be bitterly opposed to the proposals in this
Measure.
The right hon. Gentleman has made a very
plausible case. He gave as one of the reasons
why these societies should be robbed the fact
that the interest on some of the funds has
increased since the time the money was invested. Surely that applies to practically
every investment that has been made. If
you are going to take into account the fact
that the rate of interest has changed from
the time the money was invested, you should
also take into account the same fact when
it applies to other things. When people lent
money to the State during the war money
was not worth as much as it is now, with the
result that people to-day are getting more

money to the State. If it is right to

valuable point about the Measure. I beg to

I think this is a very good occasion for me

here to inquire into the charges of extravagance made against the Administration. We
asked for a Select Committee of the House.
That was a very natural method by which

Government in the world. I think that was
the charge made either by the hon. Member
or by one of his colleagues who are supporters
of the Government. But instead of appointing a Select Committee of the House, to determine the financial affairs of its own household, you introduce a stranger here, a gentleman from London; and one would have
expected, if any respect was to be given to

Mr. DEVLIN: But in order to maintain

to be brought about. Supporters of the

Committee for the purpose of inquiring into
the question as to whether there was any

instead, as a substitute, they invited over Sir
Russell Scott to do the work which
thought should have been done by a Committee of the House of Commons. Now, we
cannot know what the economies are until
we have Sir Russell Scott's report, but before
we get Sir Russell Scott's report what we
want to know is what are the methods that
he adopted. He came over here and he
consulted nobody. As far as I can hear he
walked through the Government offices and
said "Is there anybody extravagant here?"
And the answer was "No, sir." Then he
passed from that Government office into
another Government office and he looked
around and he said "Are you extravagant?"
and the person addressed said "No, sir."
Then he pursued his itinerary all round the
Government offices, and obtained the answer
from all the persons who were supposed to
be extravagant that they were not extravagant. Then he went home. There never was
so ludicrous a performance in the history
of government or of finance as that method
of inquiring into a matter of this character.
This is a stranger brought in to inquire into
the household affairs of this Parliament
which cannot be inquired into by hon.
Members of this House themselves. All I

they have the most complete contempt for

Economy Bill—

to the rigid and pure administration of
their funds, and having spent years and
years in building up these funds-which,
when they were built up, and when large
surpluses had accrued, would have enabled
them to get additional benefits, because that
is what these surpluses were for-you come
along and, instead of having the courage to
put on fresh taxation and to meet the
criticism which is incidental to fresh taxation, you go to these, the poorest and most
helpless classes of the community, and rob
them of the rights to which they are entitled.
That is your measure in a nutshell, and it
does not require a very intricate knowledge
of finance or a very clear exposition of an
Act of Parliament to see that that is simply
and solely the purpose of this Measure. I
must say I will be very much surprised if
the masses of the people do not rise in indignation in this country, as they are rising
in indignation in England, against the
infamy of a proceeding of this character.
You were in a great hurry with this Bill.
You want to go step by step with England,
but you were not in such a hurry in connection with the question of the removal of
the Old Age Pensions thrift disqualification.
You waited eighteen months until you got
into the step by step arrangement there,
and you robbed the old-age pensioners of
£356,000 by the delay which occurred. But
you rush this Bill here without Members of
Parliament getting time practically to read

to consider it-a Bill which the right
hon. Gentleman (Mr. Pollock) has repeatedly
declared it is almost impossible for him,

It is an
indication that if they manage their affairs

penalised for it when the exigencies of
Government finance demand it. I, therefore,
second the rejection of this Bill, and I hope
it will not be passed by the House.

effect to-day? Through circumstances that
nobody could foresee the National Health Insurance Societies have a huge surplus of
something like £60,000,000. It was never contemplated by Parliament they should build
up such a huge surplus, and that surplus is
steadily on the increase. This Measure
which was brought in and passed by the
Imperial Parliament, and which we now
follow, does not propose to do what the hon.
Member for West Belfast (Mr. Devlin) has
indicated. It does not propose to take one
penny piece of that surplus that already
exists in connection with these Societies. It
is theirs for them to appropriate in whatever
way they like, but the State steps in now and
says that in view of this huge accumulated
surplus they have got it is not necessary
for the State to give them such large contribution as hitherto.
There is nothing unreasonable in a proposal of that kind, especially when we bear
in mind the difficult financial position which
the country is in and is likely to pass through
during the coming years. Further, why have
these Health Societies accumulated such a
great surplus? It has not always been through
frugal management. I am sure a great deal
could be attributed to that, but from information that sometimes comes to me I think
these Societies should have been a little more
generous and should have given to their
members greater assistance and help than
they have been doing. If that had taken
place then the surplus would not have been
as large as it is to-day.
The same argument that I have used in
regard to national health applies with equal
force and strength to the question of unemployment insurance. Here, again, there is
a modification proposed and neither the
actuaries nor those who have criticised the
proposals submitted to the British House or
to this Parliament have made the statement
that the withdrawal or reduction of the contribution provided from Parliament would
make any of the societies bankrupt or would
lessen the benefits they would confer upon
the insured persons or upon the unemployed.
They have never made that argument, and,
bearing those facts in mind, Parliament is
now proceeding to review them in the light
of fresh facts and in the light of
ascertained knowledge, and I think that a
change can take place without doing any

preventing additional taxation, both direct

Mines (Working Facilities,

As amended, considered.
Motion made, and Question proposed:
"That the Bill be now read the Third time."
-(Mr. Barbour.)
Mr. O'NEILL: I am sorry I was late for
the discussion on this Bill yesterday. There
was some information I should like to have
had from the right hon. Gentleman opposite
(Mr. Barbour). What I would like to know
is this. Where are these minerals that are
unlikely to be worked? I understand from
the speech delivered by the right hon. Gentleman on the Second Reading that the only
reference to Coal Mines was with regard to
the portion of the Act that was repealed, or
rather put out of operation yesterday, so that
the Bill in itself evidently does not apply to
Coal Mines. Neither is it connected with
Quarries. The Minister of Commerce told us
that, I think on the First Reading of the
Bill. What then, is the mineral that is unlikely to be worked? He says this Bill has
been promoted at the instigation of the Commission on the Natural and Industrial Resources of Northern Ireland, and that it was
suggested by someone else that a Bill of this
nature should be introduced. I should like
to know who the someone else is, what is
the nature of the minerals, and where we are
likely to find them. Is there lead in Slieve
Gullion or gold in Slieve Gallion, because
many of us in this House would like to stake
our claim wherever these precious minerals
are.
In regard to Clause 9 of the Bill which
annuls that part of the Act dealing with
coal, I think it was a mistake to annul that
part of the Act. It provided for a levy for
welfare purposes, and I understand the
reason it has been annulled is that on
account of the small proportion of coal that
is being raised at present they could not
afford to pay a levy. I hope that what the
Minister said as to the possibility of much
larger quantities of coal being raised in the
future will turn out to be true, and that the
gentleman who had the courage to undertake
the development of an industry such as
Sir Samuel Kelly has undertaken to develop
at Coalisland will be successful in his efforts,
because I think he deserves every credit for
having the courage to start these mines. If
they are a success I do not see why this
little levy for welfare purposes should not
have been retained, but if the undertaking is
a failure I am sure that no one in this House
would claim that the levy should be put into
operation. Therefore, I hope that the
Minister in charge of the Bill will give us
at this stage when the Measure is about to
leave the House more information with regard to this particular mineral which the
Bill itself says is not likely to be worked.
Who are the individuals who are anxious
that the Bill should be introduced? I think
that information should be made known
to us.
Mr. BARBOUR: I explained at one stage
of this Bill that it was an entirely provisional thing, and in order to facilitate any
person who desired to work minerals and was
finding difficulty in getting the proper legal
right or access to such minerals as he might
discover. In the promotion of this Bill there
was no particular mineral in view. I think
the Bill is very explanatory. The particular
clause referring to coal which is in part 2reads: "Shall be deemed never to have
applied in Northern Ireland." I told the
House in moving this that this Bill was only
a temporary measure when passed, and as a
matter of fact this clause expired in March
last. It was simply to regularise what has
in fact taken place. The clauses of that Bill
were not put into operation during its
currency, owing to the reason that at the
time of the passing of the Act there was no
coal mining in Northern Ireland, and for the
whole provision of the working of these
clauses there was no representative of Ireland included on the Committee. Consequently, in reading over the provisions of
the Mining Industry Act, 1920, it was perfectly obvious that in that form they had
never been designed with regard to being
carried out in Ireland. If the hon. Member
for Down (Mr. O'Neill) had been here yesterday he would have heard an assurance from
the Prime Minister that we were anxious to
protect and safeguard the interests of the
miners in Northern Ireland, and should the
mining industry develop the Government certainly would bring forward some measure to
give analogous benefits to the miners in
Northern Ireland.
Mr. O'NEILL: May I say that the right
hon. Gentleman in introducing the Bill or
on the Second Reading stated:
Hon. Members may remember that the
Commission on the Natural and Industrial
Resources of Northern Ireland recommended the application to Northern Ireland
of a Measure on the lines of that now
before the House. Other representations
to the same effect have been made to my
Ministry.
May I ask what the other representations
were or from whom did they come?

were simply to the effect that in order to

LOCAL BILLS-STANDING ORDERS.
The CHAIRMAN OF WAYS AND
MEANS (Mr. Moles): I beg to move the
Amendments to the Standing Orders
lative to Local Bills, which stand in my
name upon the Order Paper. Standing
Order No. 38 enumerates the places in
London at which the promoters of Local
Bills are required to deposit copies of those
Bills, and the effect of the first of the proposed Amendments is to take out the Irish
Office, which no longer exists, and to add to
the list the War Office. It also requires the
promoters to lodge a copy with the Home
Office in place of the copy which was previously deposited with the Imperial Secretary, that office now no longer existing. A
new Order which appears on the Paper together with an Appendix is to require more
detailed information from local authorities
and joint boards where permanent works
are intended to be undertaken by them.
The information which these Estimates will
give is essential to the Ministry under
whose authority it may be necessary to
raise the desired loan. I may add for the
information of the House that this Standing
Order has been included in the Standing
Orders reecntly passed at Westminster, and
it is merely keeping our Standing Orders
in line with those of Great Britain. With
the permission of the House there are a few
corrections I desire to make in the new
Standing Order as set out on the Paper.
In line 2, after "(C)" it is necessary to insert the words "proposed to be carried
out," and in the last line but one of the
third paragraph, after the word "statement," the word should be "of" instead of
"for," this being a purely typographical
error. Then in the Appendix at the top of
page 3 the word "wire" should be " ware."
I beg to move.
ORDER No. 38 (Deposit of Bills at
Public Departments).
On or before the twenty-first day of
December a printed copy shall be deposited:
(1) of every Local Bill at the Ministries of Finance, Home Affairs, Labour,
Education, Agriculture, and Commerce
in Belfast.
Local Bills-Standing Orders. 706
(2) of every Local Bill at the Office of
His Majesty's Treasury, at the General
Post Office, at the Home Office, at the
Irish Office, so long as it shall continue
to exist, and at the Office of Woods in
London.
(3) of every Local Bill affecting any
dock, harbour navigation, pier or port,
foreshore or tidal lands, at the Office of
the Board of Trade in London.
(4) of every Local Bill affecting any
railway at the Ministry of Transport in
London.

Questions for Oral Answers.
CANDIDATES FOR ROYAL ULSTER
CONSTABULARY.
1. Major SHILLINGTON asked the
Minister of Home Affairs whether he can
state how many candidates are at present
on the waiting list, in the different grades,
for the Royal Ulster Constabulary, and
whether in the grading of these applicants
preference is given to men with Army service or services in the Special Constabulary.
and what is the average height required in
each grade.
27 APRIL 1926
Oral Answers.

Oral Answers.
Sir DAWSON BATES: I wish my hon.
Friend had been more precise in stating what
he is asking for, but so far as possible the
quota will be kept up.
The MINISTER OF HOME AFFAIRS (Sir
Dawson Bates): With reference to the first
part of the hon. and gallant Member's
question, the number of candidates at present
on the waiting list for the Royal Ulster
Constabulary is 159. They are graded as
follows:-
1st Class
2nd Class
3rd Class


The reply to the second part of the question in the affirmative.
With regard to the last part of the question, the height standard for the 1st Class
list is 5 ft. 11 in., for the 2nd Class list
5 ft. 10 in., and candidates of a lower height
standard are placed in the third category,
but this arrangement is subject in all cases
to the proviso that a man who possesses
special educational or other qualifications
may be graded to a category above that for
which he would be qualified on the ground
of height alone.
Mr. PATRICK O'NEILL: Arising out of
that question may I ask the right hon.
Gentleman if in the further recruitment of
this force the undertaking or agreement
made by the Prime Minister as to the
religious basis of the force will be carried
out fairly?
Sir DAWSON BATES: I may remind my
hon. Friend that the recommendation of the
Police Committee was that one-third of the
force should be Roman Catholics. The
Government have so far as possible tried to
carry that into effect, but, unfortunately,
the Roman Catholics did not come forward
and the police force had to be filled up.
Mr. DEVLIN: But will the arrangement
be carried out in case applications are made
by them?
Sir DAWSON BATES: The whole question is whether or not the candidate is suitable for the police force and has the necessary qualifications.
Mr. PATRICK O'NEILL: But if they are
suitable will the quota of Roman Catholics
be kept up?
Sir DAWSON BATES: As far as possible, but I would remind the hon. Gentleman that the police force originally had to
be filled up owing to the fact that the Roman
Catholics did not come forward.
Mr. DEVLIN: Now that the force is
filled up and that the Catholics have not
got the numbers which, according to the
arrangement, they were entitled to, will the
right hon. Gentleman consider the advisability of trying to meet that situation by
giving favourable consideration to those
applicants who may now apply?
Colonel WOODS: Might I ask the right
hon. Gentleman are there any vacancies
existing at present, and if so how many?
Sir DAWSON BATES: I really could not
tell. There may be about three or four, but
not more.
Mr. McBRIDE: Might I ask the Minister
of Home Affairs has the height required for
the Royal Ulster Constabulary been increased
from 5 feet 8 inches to 5 feet 11 inches since
the disbandment of the Special Constabulary
in December last, and if it is a fact that a
candidate who has passed all the examinations but is just below 5 feet 11 inches is
only graded in the second class while an
applicant with little or no distinction is
graded first class if he is over 5 feet 11 inches
in height?
Sir DAWSON BATES: I am afraid my
hon. Friend could not have been listening
to the answer I gave earlier. 1 have explained that the men are all graded, and
those who are 5 feet 11 inches are placed in
the first category, and until that list is exhausted no appointments are made out of
the second category. Of course I would remind my hon. Friend that height is not
the main thing. The main question that
arises is whether or not a man is likely to
become a suitable policeman and possesses
the necessary qualifications.
BANN DRAINAGE.-ENGINEER'S
REPORT.
Major SHILLINGTON asked the Minister
of Finance whether he has received the report
from the engineers who have been investigating the flooding of the Lough Neagh and
River Bann areas; whether this report, when
ready, will be made public, and whether the
Government have considered what action
they will take in connection with this matter.
(Mr.
The MINISTER OF FINANCE
Pollock): I have received the report. Having
regard to the importance and difficulty of
the question, my hon. and gallant Friend
will appreciate that the Report needs careful
consideration, and this it is receiving. It is
not in a form suitable for publication in its
entirety, but, without making any promise
at the moment, the Government will consider how far, consistently with the public
interest, it would be possible to make public
later the more important parts of the Report.
Mr. COOPER: Arising out of that question, may I ask the Minister of Finance if
anything has been done about the drainage
of Upper Lough Erne?
711 Economy (Exchequer Relief)---

HOUSE OF COMMONS
Committee.
Mr. POLLOCK: No, sir. The position in
regard to Lough Erne is somewhat different.
As my hon. Friend (Mr. Cooper) knows, both
sides of the country are concerned in that
very difficult problem, and until a solution
is found in respect of that difficulty nothing
has or can be done.
POSSESSION OF ARMS BY "C" FORCE.
Major SHILLINGTON (by private notice)
asked the Attorney-General if he can inform
the House whether any provision is being
made with reference to arms in the possession
of members of the "C" Force consequent
on their disbandment.
The ATTORNEY-GENERAL (Mr. Babington): The Government proposes to deal with
the matter under the existing Firearms Act,
and for that purpose to amend the Act, so
as to allow two forms of permit to be granted
-one to have arms, and another to have
and carry arms. These permits will be
granted by the County Inspector as heretofore, but the Government propose to give a
right of appeal from any decision of a
County Inspector refusing a permit to a
Resident Magistrate. All ex-members of the
"C" Special Constabulary will be eligible to
apply like other civilians.
