Economy (Exchequer Relief) [Money]
Considered in Committee under Standing
Order No. 65.
(Mr. MOLES in the Chair.)
Motion made, and Question proposed:
"That for the purpose of any Act of the
present Session to make provision for re
ducing in respect of certain Services the
charges on Public Funds, and for increasing, by means of a payment into the Exchequer of Northern Ireland of certain
sums and otherwise, the funds available for
meeting such charges, and to amend accordingly the law relating to National Health
Insurance and certain other matters, and
for purposes related or incidental thereto,
it is expedient to authorise payment out of
moneys provided by Parliament, as a contribution towards any additional benefits
payable out of the Navy, Army and Air
Force Insurance Fund by virtue of any Act
passed in the present Session of the Parliament of the United Kingdom, such sums
as the National Health Insurance Joint
Committee may periodically ascertain to be
required for such contribution, having regard to the number of persons entitled to
benefits out of the said Fund, and actually
resident in Northern Ireland." (Governor's
Recommendation signified.-Mr. Barbour.)
The FINANCIAL SECRETARY (Mr.
Barbour): I think it will be the wish of
the Committee that I should explain the
exact effect of the Resolution, which is now
under consideration. This Government has
already accepted the principle that any
benefits which may be given by legislation
of the Imperial Parliament to British members of the armed forces of the Crown
should also be extended (where corresponding legislation comes within our powers) to
those soldiers, sailors and air men who enlist from our Province. I might refer in
passing to the provisions of Section 9 of our
Finance Act of 1924, in which we extended
to serving Ulstermen certain concessions
which had been made by the British Parliament in regard to Death Duties. The proposals in the Resolution now before the Committee seek to give to those of our men who
have served in the Forces, and who are
subsequently discharged, the same benefits
which men from other parts of the United
Kingdom will receive under the new
British legislation in regard to National
Health Insurance.
In order to explain the Resolution I must
outline briefly the existing conditions under
which men of the Forces receive benefits
under the National Health Insurance
Acts. These men pay no contributions
whatever to this scheme. Contributions are
paid on their behalf from the Service Votes,
and after provision has been made for the
necessary credits to approved societies in
the small number of cases where the Service
man belongs to such a society the residue is
transferred to the Navy, Army and Air
Force Insurance Fund. During the period
of service no benefits are payable out of this
Fund except maternity benefit, because in
the ordinary way these men, while in the
service, receive hospital treatment, etc., according to the terms of their engagement.
A value is, however, placed on these entitlements, and the usual State contributions

The CHAIRMAN: I am afraid we are
entering upon a Second Reading debate the
second time-(hon. Members: Hear, hear)-
whereas the simple question before the Committee is whether or not the Resolution we
are now asked to pass ought to be or ought
not to be accepted by the Committee. That
somewhat narrows, though it still leaves a
wide field.
Mr. DEVLIN: I do not know within what
limits the Committee are to discuss this
matter, but for my own part I think it is
our business, profoundly and vitally opposed
as we are to this Measure, that we should
take every advantage of expressing our views
and pointing out to the public and those
interested the grave wrong that is being done
to the working classes of the community.
Now, what is really being done in connection with this Measure. The Government,
as my hoa. Friend (Mr. Kyle) has said, are
pledged in honour to make certain contributions to the National Health Fund.
The employees are pledged in honour and
law and so are the employers. This is not a
Bill to readjust the payment. It is not a
Bill to estimate fairly what reductions ought
to be made by each party concerned in the
transactions, but you come forward now still
to place the burden upon the shoulders of
the employers and employed, and to sneak
out of your own responsibility in regard to
a matter so much concerning the health and
welfare of the toiling masses of the people.
Apart altogether from the broad opposition which I have to this Measure, I have
particular reasons for objecting to it in
Ulster. We have no medical benefits in
Ulster. The medical service is not available
for the insured persons in the Six Counties,
and while it is quite true that in England at
the instigation of the Chancellor of the Exchequer compulsorily insured persons are to
be deprived of £2,800,000 a year in addition
to the charge placed upon them of £1,900,000
per annum in respect of medical benefit, the
insured persons there have medical benefit,
and the sickness experience, I am told,
though increasing there is nothing like so
heavy as it is in Northern Ireland. The net
result of the legislation in England will be to
place many societies in deficiency, and in
Northern Ireland, if this Bill is placed on
the Statute Book it will mean that the contributions will not be able to maintain the
sickness experience. I, therefore, think that
legislation of this character is to be
seriously deprecated, apart altogether from
the question of economy.
The Government, as I have said, have come
along here and they propose to lessen the contribution they are to pay at a time when
there is a clamant demand on the part of the
people of Northern Ireland for medical benefits. These benefits have been denied to
Ulster and, consequently, proportionately
you are taking away more from the working
classes of this country than is being taken
away from the working classes of Great
Britain, because the State makes a certain
contribution to medical benefits in England,
and it makes no contribution to medical
benefits here in Northern Ireland.
The CHAIRMAN: I am very reluctant, as
my hon. Friend appreciates, to intervene, but
I am afraid we are getting away from the
specific question. Also, the aspect of the case
he is now discussing is not to be found in the
Bill, the Committee Stage of which will be
taken an order or two down the Paper.
Mr. DEVLIN: I will not be here to-morrow
and I want to say what I have to say to-day.
The CHAIRMAN: If my hon. Friend can
get it within this Resolution that is all I am
concerned with. I am not in the least objecting to his saying it, except as a matter of
order.
Mr. DEVLIN: I want to warn the Government that they are doing a grave injustice
to the people of Northern Ireland. They
are not moving step by step with Great
Britain, they are moving a step forward
against the people just as they did in the
case of the old-age pensions. For that
reason I oppose this Money Resolution and
will vote against it.
Mr. ANDREWS: Mr. Moles, in accordance
with your ruling, with which I am in entire

to the Money Resolution set out on the
Parliamentary Paper. I would like to remove some wrong impressions that are held
by hon. Members opposite. This Money Resolution simply gives the Government power
to put a charge upon the State which the
State has not borne up to the present. Those
persons who remain, owing to their having
certain disabilities, upon this Army, Navy
and Air Force Fund have up to the present
been denied the advantage of extended
benefits. It is now proposed to place those
insured
persons in exactly the same
position if after their period of service they
remain insured persons, as other insured persons associated with our various approved
societies. Therefore, I cannot see how hon.
Members opposite are holding the view that

robbing the insured persons, the approved

from Government funds both as regards the

other occasions upon which I shall probably
have opportunities of putting my views before
the Committee as regards the general charges

Member can enter the Lobby to vote. At
any time before that--two minutes are given
--any hon. Member is entitled to go into

before it-it does not matter-he can record

cannot do so.

passed to a better world by that time perhaps, we are not concerned with it. We are
concerned with our own convenience. Posterity can look after itself.

it is proposed simply to take them from
them without any reason whatever, and I
have a most decided objection to that.

requires all the money it can get for purposes
with which hon. Members are very familiar.

the local authorities do not do any act in

Government deliberately increased the Dog
Tax, and the stamp duty on the licence in

might be larger. The local authorities are
getting more money than they have got in
the past, and the £8,000 which will be going

27 APRIL 1926
SUPPLY.
Estimates, 1926-1927.
Considered in Committee.
(Mr. MOLES in the Chair).
CLASS III. No. 1.
MINISTRY OF HOME AFFAIRS.
Motion made, and Question proposed:
"That a sum not exceeding £43,605 be
granted to His Majesty to complete the sum
necessary to defray the charge which will
come in course of payment during the year
ending on the 31st March, 1927, to defray
the salaries and expenses of the Ministry of
Home Affairs (15 and 16 Geo. V., c. 3, s. 4
(N.I.) )."--(Note- £16,000 has been voted on
Account.)
Sir DAWSON BATES: The Estimate
which I have the honour to submit for the
consideration of the Committee shows a
saving of £5,719 over that of last year.
The Committee will observe that with regard to inspectors there is an increase of
four. Two of these inspectors are appointed to deal with the increased work under
the Housing of the Working Classes Act.
When it is realised that houses are increasing and being completed at something
like 200 a month, and having regard to the
increase in the number of labourers' cottages, I think hon. Members will agree that
it is a right measure that these inspectors
should be appointed.
The Committee will also observe that provision is made for the appointment of a
pharmacy inspector. The duty of this
officer is to see that the terms of the Act
are fully complied with. The officer appointed is an ex-Service man with very high
qualifications. I should explain that this
item will not be a permanent burden on
this Vote. Hon. Members will recollect that
under the Pharmacy and Poisons Act, 1925.
it is provided that during the working of
the Act for the first two years the entire
amount of the fees collected for licences
should be handed over to the Society so as
to enable that Society, which had not funds
of its own, to get thoroughly on its legs.
At the end of the first two years the Government can claim half of the fees which,
having regard to the amount collected, would
amount to something like £480, which will
in future go to appropriation-in-aid.
Then it will become necessary to appoint
an assistant temporary inspector to keep upto-date investigations in connection with oldage pension appeal cases. I may point out
that for the year ended 31st March, 1925, we
had no less than 2,460 cases to deal with,
while for the year ending 31st March, 1926,
there were 2,688 cases decided. There were
arrears to the extent of over 500. I think
it is obvious to hon. Members that it is very
unfair and undesirable that poor people who
are claiming pensions should have their
claims held up owing to the fact that it is
impossible to get through the work. The
inspectors are part time men and are paid
a fixed fee for each day employed.
With regard to the administrative staff
we have been able to effect considerable
savings. I think before the end of the year
we will be able to effect still further savings
having regard to the disbandment of the
Special Constabulary.
I think it would be interesting, in view
of the charge which is sometimes made
against the Government that we are not fully
alive to the claims of the ex-Servicemen,
if I was to point out that out of a total of
84 new appointments-i.e., by new appointments I mean those other than transferred
officials-no fewer than 78 are ex-Servicemen,
and of the balance of 6, four were too young
to serve, and two were over age.
With a view to further economy, while it
became necessary for the appointment of a
medical officer to inspect school children
under the Education Authority, we have
been able to make an arrangement under
which one of our medical officers, who has
had less work to do owing to the disbandment
of the Special Constabulary, will be employed
on this particular work. It was first thought
that it was necessary to appoint an additional
inspector, but we have been able to make this
very satisfactory arrangement. These are
the only particular items which I think
necessary to explain to the House. I need
not point out that I shall only be too glad
to answer any point that may be raised by
hon. Members.
Mr. BEATTIE: I beg to move a reduction
in the Vote of £1,000. In doing so, I believe
if any Estimate within the confines of the
two covers of this book requires particular
attention and the strictest investigation it
is the Estimate of the Ministry of Home
Affairs. We have one or two Services run
and controlled by the Minister of Home
Affairs, and, after the wilful extravagance
we have found under other headings, I am
sure you will admit we are warranted in
drawing attention to what we call wilful
extravagance under the Minister himself.
We will start right from the head of the
house downwards. We will start with the
Minister himself, who has £1,500 a year.
The CHAIRMAN: I may point out that
under the head of Cabinet Salaries we have
discussed and disposed of that particular
item. Can the hon. Member show me the
Minister's salary under this?

carried on in the future than in the past.

Mr. BEATTIE: I looked at the Estimate

Sir DAWSON BATES: On a point of
order. May I point out that this matter has

The CHAIRMAN: I would ask the hon.

the Estimates he links up this matter with.

Only the other Sunday a lady came here
from Dublin having taken advantage of a
cheap excursion to Belfast. She was
arrested, and taken to the police barracks.
She sent for me because she knew I would
always come to the aid of persons in difficulty whether guilty or not. There was no
charge against her. She simply had her
name upon this list. As a matter of fact
the police treated her with great courtesy.
I raise no objection to the manner in which
she was treated, and neither did she. She
was kept there two or three hours, and I had
to sit the whole time there myself. I was
asked to be responsible for her for the rest
of the day. Of course, I accepted the responsibility under duress. No sooner did I
do that than they let her free, and then she
went her way and I went mine. She went to
the station that evening and took the train
back to Dublin.
What is the meaning of all that senseless
proceeding? I cannot understand it at all.
At any rate, I do not care who the people
are, guilty or guiltless, if their liberty is to
be taken from them they ought to be told
the reason why. If they are criminals they
ought to be indicted for their crimes. If
they are not criminals they ought to be
allowed to be free to discharge their functions
of citizenship without being arrested any
time they come within the sacred precincts
of the Six Counties. Therefore, I hope we
will get a promise from the hon. and learned
Gentleman (Mr. Hanna) that they will stop
these deportations, and that they will erase
from the list the names of respectable
citizens and put an end to this senseless
procedure.

761 Labour Situation in Derry.
Labour Situation in Derry. 762
27 APRIL 1926
Adjournment.
LABOUR SITUATION IN DERRY.
Motion made and Question proposed:
"That this House do now adjourn."-
(Captain Dixon).
Mr. LEEKE: I wish to draw the attention
of the House to the position of the
unemployed in Derry City. They are at
present going through a very bad time owing
to being deprived of the unemployment
grant. Hon. Members will have seen from
the Press that a huge procession marched
through Derry recently on a deputation to
the Board of Guardians, with a view to
getting some subsistence, which would place
them and their families in a position that
they would not starve. It is a very serious
situation in which they are left owing to
some legal technicality which deprives them
of the right to draw unemployment benefit.
I would appeal to the Minister of Labour to
take into consideration the case of these unfortunate people, and establish some machinery or some method so that possibly something will be done to relieve them from the
serious plight in which they are placed at
the moment. I recognise how difficult it is
at times for the Minister of Labour to deal
with cases such as this, but I think of all
the cases at present existing in Northern
Ireland this is the most extreme.
The
The local ratepayers are, I know, groaning under excessive taxation, and it is very
difficult for the Guardians to immediately
hand out sufficient money to meet these
deserving and necessitous cases. I think
it is the Government's duty to see that no
one starves, and it would be a slur on this
Government if it happens that in Derry
City anyone dies from starvation.
Minister of Labour presides over the Department of the Government which is
primarily charged with the duty of seeing
that the unemployed are paid benefit. I
pay this tribute to him--I recognise how
sympathetic he is towards Labour in Ulster,
and I know if it is possible for him to do so
he would immediately and promptly take
some effective measure that would help
these unfortunate people in the position in
which they are placed to-day. There are,
I understand, 700 of them altogether.
think that surely some temporary measure of
relief could be passed through this House.
I am not sufficiently acquainted with the
legislative machinery to know how quickly
it could be done. I think it could be done
in a day-bave a temporary measure passed
that would deal with these cases and I
think it is the duty of the Government to
take immediate steps to have it carried out.
I
I see where a local contribution was
given by Lady Anderson in Derry-a very
prompt action for which I think a tribute
should be paid her. In the meantime, the
Government must feel it is their duty to
have these cases dealt with immediately. 1
think the Minister of Labour will surely
take some steps to co-operate at least with
the local authorities with a view to having
these cases met. There is a real danger in
allowing people to march in procession
through the streets hungry. That is what
breeds Bolshevism and all other revolutions,
which, we believe, are so dangerous to the

area.

that nothing is done which will cause any

to the Minister of Labour here to-day to
take the Derry case immediately, and deal
with it promptly and effectively, and to relieve the present existing distress in that

into the various industries which are presently languishing in Derry City, and to see

who are

Right hon. Gentlemen-I do not know

I came to the House this morning of, at

tions of the right hon. Gentleman have become more stringent recently. I want to
submit this for the consideration of the
House. Do hon. Gentlemen opposite suggest

I know men who have walked the boots off
their feet in making an earnest effort to
obtain employment, and they cannot possibly
get it. When they have been unemployed for
two years their benefit is discontinued.
Perhaps the most pitiable cases are those
who are single. I have seen cases of spinsters
advanced in years, absolutely friendless and
moneyless, and those decent respectable
people, who have spent all their lives in
industry, cannot get employment and cannot get unemployment benefit; and under
your obsolete poor-law they are not supposed
to exist. The poor-law has no knowledge of
a person who is single. Perhaps the Prime
Minister is not aware of that. I submit this
to the Prime Minister and ask for an impartial decision and judgment upon it;
is it fair that a person who has lived
an honourable life in industry until
he has become 50 years of age, and
who cannot get employment or unemployment
benefit, should be offered the hospitality of
the Union Workhouse? It appears to me to
be a scandalous state of affairs altogether.
I appeal to the right hon. Gentleman, not
in any party spirit, but in the interests of
the people of Ulster, to reconsider the whole
thing. I know that the Prime Minister has
got great influence with the British Government, and surely it is not beyond his power
to point out to them that the situation here
is entirely different to the situation in Great
Britain. We have two main industries, and
if there is a slump in those two main industries what opportunity is there for the
people to obtain employment? In Great
Britain many other opportunities offer; the
industries there are numerous and diverse.
Here we are limited, circumscribed, to about
two industries, and then the poor unfortunate
people who have been unemployed for two
years are denied their unemployment benefit.
There is this benefit. Our Unemployment
Fund is in a better position than it was six

not want to approach this question in an
embittered way at all,

Motion made, and Question proposed,

add to the number of societies that will
be deficient, and decrease the number of
societies that have surpluses. I find that

Sir ROBERT ANDERSON: In discussing
this particular Clause it is well for us to
bear in mind at the outset one great principle
which I think we are sometimes liable to
forget when discussing matters of this
character in this Committee. We in
Northern Ireland have not got the skill or
the financial independence so that we are in
a different position entirely when discussing
a matter of this kind from what the Members
of the Imperial Parliament are, and if we
concentrate our thoughts upon that particular
point I think a good deal of unnecessary
discussion will be avoided.
To me the question in connection with this
matter at the moment is a financial one.
There has been no reply to the argument
that has been advanced by the Minister of
Finance (Mr. Pollock), and others as to where
the £117,000 is to come from to meet the
deficiency that will arise as far as we are
concerned if we do not adopt exactly similar
measures to those which have been adopted
by the Imperial Parliament. (Hon. Members:
Hear, hear.) That really is the crux of the
whole position. We have in connection with
a matter of this kind to consider ways and
means most carefully. The £117,000 stands,
according to the financial basis on which we
are working at the moment, until four years
hence when the Exchequer Board under the
Act of 1920 may reconsider the whole position.
In the meantime we have no alternative but
to move step by step in matters of this kind
with the legislation of the Imperial Parliament. Otherwise we will find ourselves up
against the greatest possible difficulty. I
asked a question on the Second Reading, and
I repeat it here to-day. Will our hon.
Friends opposite tell us where the Northern
Exchequer is to find this money?

Mr. ANDREWS: Thank you. The point I
was making was that this Royal Commission
composed of high authorities, very impartial
and disinterested admittedly, came to this
conclusion:
We cannot take the view that we are
limited by the necessity of adhering to any
particular principles on which the scheme
was originally set up or by any statement
which was made at the time of the inception
of the scheme, or any explanation, or any
defence of the provisions contained in the
original Bill. On the contrary we hold
that the National Health Insurance scheme
was in the nature of a great, novel
experiment in the field of social welfare,
And it must now be open to Parliament,
untrammelled and unfettered, to review the
whole scheme in the light of thirteen years'
experience of its working, and to make
such changes, however drastic, as that
experience may have shown to be desirable.
Therefore, I take it that the Royal Commission came to the conclusion that there
is no breach of any pledge when the Government of the day, whether here or in Westminster, came to the conclusion that it is
desirable, owing to altered conditions, or for
other reasons, to depart from the original
scheme.
In this connection I would like to point
out that this is not the first time that the
original Act has been departed from. The
benefits have been changed, the contributions have been changed, and on a previous
occasion the statutory contribution has been
changed by the father of the Act himself,
Mr. Lloyd George. In the first instance, the
statutory contribution for men was twoninths, and for women, one-fourth. In 1920,
Mr. George was responsible for changing
the fourth to two-ninths, so there is no
foundation, in my opinion, for saying that
there was a pledge given so definite, so distinct, and so clear that it fettered and trammelled future Governments to such an extent
that under no circumstances could they
depart therefrom.

necessary that I should say any more than

on every occasion when economy is suggested
they are opposed to it.

is going to be the position it would be far

That is an extremely unsatisfactory state

and telling him he is a decent fellow.

The MINISTER OF COMMERCE (Mr.
Barbour): After the debate which followed
the moving of the Money Resolution yesterday, and the few remarks made on this
Clause, I cannot help coming to the conclusion that hon. Members do not altogether
understand the object of this Clause. I am

This Clause is provided for those men who
have gone out and taken part in the armed
forces of the Crown, and have come back
crippled in health, and on account of the
disability which they have derived from the
War, will not be accepted as an insurable
risk by any Approved Society, and, therefore.
are obliged to fall back on such benefits as
are afforded by this Navy, Army, and Air
Force Insurance Fund. When this Fund
was started no provision was made for any
additional benefits being extended, but now,
when so many of the Approved Societies are
enabled to give additional benefits to those
first contemplated under the National Health
Insurance Act, it was felt that it was only
justice that this one fund to which these men
could turn, in their crippled state of health,
should be able to give as generous benefits
as the Approved Societies.
Therefore, this is one of the few Clauses
in the Bill in respect of which the Government is prepared to accept an extra charge
on its Exchequer. We have 500 men in
Northern Ireland whom the Clause may
benefit, and the extra charge amounts to
about £100 a year. I am sure if hon, Members appreciated the position they will most
gladly support the Clause.

HOUSE OF COMMONS.

Thursday, 29th April, 1926.
The House met at Three of the Clock, Mr.
SPEAKER in the Chair.
McCaldin's Divorce Bill.
The following Report was made by the
Joint Committee on Divorce Bills:-
That they had considered McCaldin's
Divorce Bill, and that the averments in
the Preamble had been proved to their
satisfaction, and that they had gone
through the Bill and reported same without Amendment to the House.
NEW SCHOOL AT LISBELLAW.
3. Mr. MILLER (for Mr. Cooper) asked the
Parliamentary Secretary to the Ministry of
Education whether he can state what is the
delay in building the new school at Lisbellaw.
The MINISTER OF FINANCE (Mr. Pollock): I propose to reply to this question.
I understand that the delay in completing
the school in question has been caused by the
difficulty experienced by the manager and
his contractor in getting delivery of bricks up
to the standard which had been agreed between the manager, his contractor and the
Government architect. Efforts are being
made, with the assistance of my Ministry, to
find a way out of the difficulty.
Oral Answers to Questions.
MEMBERS OF PARLIAMENT IN
AMERICA.
1. Colonel WOODS asked the Minister of
Commerce whether any Member of this
House is employed by the Northern Government in America; if so, in what capacity;
and whether the whole or any part of his
remuneration is chargeable against public
funds.
The MINISTER OF COMMERCE (Mr.
Barbour): The answer to the first part of
the question is in the negative. The remainder of the question, therefore, does not
arise.
NORTH ANTRIM REGIONAL EDUCATION
COMMITTEE.
2. Mr. KYLE asked the Parliamentary
Secretary to the Ministry of Education
whether he would state if the North Antrim
Regional Education Committee has purchased
a garden in which to erect huts for school
purposes; what price was paid for the garden;
and what was done with the bulbs, flowers
and vegetables in the garden.
The
PARLIAMENTARY SECRETARY
TO THE MINISTRY OF EDUCATION (Mr.
Robb): The North Antrim Regional Education Committee recently bought a plot for
the erection of temporary huts to relieve
existing congestion in the Ballymoney Model
Schools; the price paid was £300. The
Ministry has no information as to what was
done with the bulbs, flowers and vegetables
in the plot.
Mr. KYLE: Is the Ministry satisfied that
the plot they bought is worth £300?
Mr. ROBB: Yes, Sir.
HOURS OF TEMPORARY CIVIL
SERVANTS.
4. Colonel WOODS asked the Minister of
Finance whether he proposes to make the
working hours of the temporary civil servants uniform with those of the transferred
civil servants employed by the Northern
Government.
Mr. POLLOCK: Under the conditions of
their engagements the working hours of
temporary civil servants are 44 a week
(inclusive of luncheon interval) or 8 hours
a day on ordinary week-days and an attendance of 4 hours on Saturdays. It is not
proposed to modify this arrangement, which
is also in force, as regards new entrants appointed to established posts since this Government was established. Transferred officers
came here with certain rights; amongst
others their terms of service in most cases
comprised a 42-hour week, the same as is still
in force in the Imperial Service. I am happy
to say, however, that almost without exception they have voluntarily, and, in some
cases, continuously, much exceeded this
limit without any increased cost to the Exchequer. The few anomalies that have occurred owing to the different conditions of
service of the two classes are of trifling importance, and I fear, inevitable in the
circumstances, and they will automatically
disappear in course of time.
HOUSING IN BALLYMONEY.
5. Mr. KYLE asked the Minister of Home
Affairs whether he can state if the Ballymoney Urban District Council purchased a
field wherein to erect houses; what is the
area, and what was the price paid for the
field: from whom was it bought; what did the
levelling of the ground cost; what did the
building of the houses cost; how many houses
were built, and what is the rent of each?
Oral Answers.

Oral Answers.
29 APRIL 1926
The MINISTER OF HOME AFFAIRS (Sir
Dawson Bates): The Ballymoney Urban District Council purchased a field some years
ago, for the purpose of a housing scheme,
from Lord Antrim. The area of the field in
question is 6.74 acres, and the purchase price
was £500, together with a sum of £50 paid by
way of compensation for disturbance.
The estimated cost of the development of
the land, i.e., for the provision of roads,
sewers, etc., was £719 14s 6d.
Twenty-two houses in all were built on the
site of three types of varying sizes and
character.
The contract price for the erection of the
houses was £9,530, or on the average £433 per
house.
The houses are at present let at rents of
10s, 11s 6d, and 12s 6d a week, respectively,
according to the class.
POLICE BARRACKS AT BALLYMONEY.
6. Mr. BEATTIE asked the Minister of
Home Affairs whether he can state the cost
of the Police Barracks at Ballymoney, the
total cost of lighting the same, and the total
number of Royal Ulster Constabulary living
in the barracks.
Sir DAWSON BATES: The R.U.C. Barracks at Ballymoney are the property of the
Government.
The premises were reconstructed last year,
and the cost of adaptations and alterations
amounted to £5,210, exclusive of the cost of
lighting. The cost of lighting the premises,
including the provision of generating plant,
switchboard and batteries was £332.
The fixed strength of the Station is:-
1 District-Inspector,
1 Head-Constable,
2 Sergeants, and
9 Constables.
Of these, 1 head-constable, 2 sergeants, and
5 constables reside in the barracks. The
head-constable occupies the only married
quarters provided.

down a Question, the Minister of Finance
will give him all the information he asks for.
Mr. BEATTIE: The accuracy of my statement will be confirmed by the Ballymoney
Lighting Company.
CLOGHER VALLEY RAILWAY
COMPANY.
7. Mr. MILLER (for Mr. Cooper) asked
the Prime Minister whether the Government
has received representations from the Clogher
Valley Railway Company asking for financial
assistance, and, if so, what action the
Government propose to take in the matter.
Mr. BARBOUR: I have been asked by my
right hon. Friend to deal with this Question.
The reply to the first part of the Question
is in the affirmative. As to the second point,
the Government liability in respect of the
working of the Clogher Valley Railway for
the financial year 1926-27 will not, it is estimated, fall much short of £5,000. In these
circumstances and having regard to the
present financial stringency, the hon. Member
will appreciate the Government's difficulty
in acceding to the request of the Company
for further financial assistance.

Economy (Exchequer Relief) Bill.
Considered in Committee. (Progress, 28th
April).
(Mr. MOLES in the Chair).
CLAUSE 8 (Amendment of s. 3 of Unemployment Insurance Act (Northern Ireland),
1925).
Debate resumed on Question, "That the
Clause stand part of the Bill."
Question again proposed.
Mr. BEATTIE: In continuation of the debate on this Clause, I may say I think the
Committee has reason to understand the
position so far as this Clause is concerned, as
it affects one of the most important issues in
the Six Counties at the present time, that is,
the Unemployment Fund. I know the
Minister of Finance is desirous of seeing
financial stability. I would also be desirous
of seeing it, but I would not be prepared to
make the sacrifice the Minister of Finance
is prepared to make. The sacrifice for stability in my opinion is too great to make on
this occasion. The reduction of the State
contribution to the Unemployment Fund
means perhaps more than some hon. Members opposite realise. I maintain that any
reduction of the contribution means a further
extension of disallowances.
We have an arrangement here brought into
operation between Great Britain and
Northern Ireland. That arrangement, I presume from the Minister's reply to questions
put from these benches, means step by step,
and that failing that we are going to lose our
arrangement with the British Exchequer.
We can lose money, which is very valuable,
I know, to the Government of Northern Ireland at the present moment, but there is
nothing more valuable to any State than
human life. I believe the existence of human
life is at stake in regard to this Clause because of the percentage of unemployed we
have in Northern Ireland. If it was decreasing I would be hopeful, but I think that on
the whole, if anything, it is increasing.
Economy Bill-
Committee.
29 APRIL 1926
Mr. ANDREWS indicated dissent.
Mr. BEATTIE: I believe a decrease has
taken place on the register of unemployed
according to the figures of the Minister of
Labour, but is the decrease any intimation to
hon. Members that all the persons who are
not signing the register for unemployment
benefit are really in employment? I maintain that those persons who have been disallowed benefit under this agreement with
Great Britain have not all really found
employment. The majority who were struck
off the register are walking about the streets
of Belfast in starvation. It may be argued
that our fund will not be any the worse off
or any the poorer, and that the insured contributors will not suffer through this Clause.
Mr. POLLOCK: Hear, hear.
Mr. BEATTIE: If it can be argued that
though this is going to take place the Fund
will stand in the same position as it previously did when 6d was paid, I certainly
will be an attentive listener to the propounder of that argument.
Mr. POLLOCK: What about the million
and a half?
Mr. BEATTIE: I will say this that while
you are making for security you are going
into a state of bankruptcy. You are making
no security under this Clause for the people
whom it most affects. You say you are
walking side by side with Great Britain in
all things of importance to this Government,
but, we, on this side of the Committee, know
that step by step is not being kept in all
things. In this thing, which is a most important thing to the Government at the
present moment, I think that a deviation
should also take place. You grant certain
powers to the Minister owing to your arrangement with Great Britain. Great
Britain reduced the contribution, and the
Minister of Finance for Northern Ireland
also comes along to reduce the contribution.
In my opinion the reduction of this contribution means the throwing off the register
of anything from 5,000 to 10,000 people.
The Minister is declaring his line of action
without hiding behind a bushel, and without
undue reservation as to what the circumstances of the present case are, and he
is using his iron rod and declaring in
fact of all opposition that the arrangement made between Great Britain and
ourselves must be adhered to. Men,
women and children are suffering to-day
owing to that arrangement, because if a
man in the Six Counties to-day cannot show
more than eight weeks' work in the past two
years the Minister of Labour is determined
he shall receive no more extended benefit.
Mr. ANDREWS: That is not so.
Mr. BEATTIE: When you make a statement in repudiation it seems quite natural
that it is not so, but as one who has had large
experience, and is intimate with the work,
I say it is correct. As to the point made last
night by my colleague, and the point made
by the hon. Member for North Belfast, I
will not retract or retrace them because I
might be subject to severe criticism elsewhere, but it is very hard at the moment to
think out the lines best suited to meet the
Government in their very simple arguments.
If 6d was paid and if they give 6d now to
take its place I cannot see how this reduction
in the State's contribution is going to make
the Fund any better for the unemployed
worker, but I would say that, as hon. Gentlemen opposite are aware, when pledges are
given, no matter whether they are verbal or
in writing, they should be kept. Pledges by
the State to contribute so much to this Fund
were given, but the State is coming now at
this late hour of the day and asking this
Fund to sacrifice to the State a certain
amount. They are not asking the employer
or employee to reduce his contribution.
I would be more inclined to accept a reduction from the employer and the worker than
from the State, because I believe the State
has broad shoulders.
This Clause really means to take from the
weakest and give to the strongest. A sum of
£117,000 is involved. It could be very easily
saved, I believe, in this Northern Parlia
ment, and is not such a large amount when
you consider the amounts that have been
spent in the past. I believe if the Government want to save £117,000 they can save it
from other Services, which are not so important as the Service I am speaking of now.
This reduction will do a serious injury to
the working-class people of the Six Counties,
by depriving them of the right to live under
State assistance through the Unemployment
Fund. I protest against the reduction, and
will oppose it on a division.

Pollock) has proposed to withdraw.

Mr. DEVLIN: I am delighted always to

cautious-in criticising the Government along

those things, because I can assure the Committee that it is in the best interests of these
local authorities, of the Government, and of
the whole of Ulster, that we should be able

both education and the police.
Therefore, I do hope that hon. Members
will give my right hon. Friend (Mr. Pollock)
due credit that when he brought in a Bill to
show the British Government that we were
out for economy, as they are, and somewhat
along the lines of their own Bill, in order to
enable him to introduce his Budget this week-
I hope they will give him due credit for

Government would have said "How is it that

Bill in connection with economy, and that
you in Ulster are making no attempt at all

that, though this House is small and there

to the debates here by the people outside,
every word said in this House is scrutinised
by the British Treasury, and when my right
hon. Friend has to go and stick up for

he is faced with these debates of ours. They
are handed over to him, with the words
"You will observe here and there and else
where violent criticisms against the Government." I think it is only right, as head of
the Government, to ask for the fullest
possible protection of my right hon. Friend
in his endeavours to produce a balanced
Budget. After five years of very dificult
government he has produced not only a
balanced Budget, but, what I think no other
country in the world has done, a balance on
the right side. I say do let hon. Members
bear that in mind. Give him full credit
for it, and back him up in his endeavour,
so that in future years he will be able to
do some remarkable accomplishment.

here is a charge upon a central fund. It is
not so on the other side. I think that onehalf of all the charges for Primary Education has to be borne by the local authorities
in Great Britain. There is another matter,
and it is a rather delicate one for me to
mention here. I am not at all sure that the
local authorities have not got the best part
of the bargain, if we consider the basis of
valuation in Northern Ireland compared
with the basis of valuation as it exists in
Great Britain.
The CHAIRMAN: Perhaps the hon. Member will allow me to point out that he is
travelling a little from the clause before the
Committee. I think I must remind the
Committee that, whilst this clause is a
clause of great importance and raises very
large issues, I have allowed a great deal
of latitude and have permitted the discussion
to drift a good deal when I might have enforced a more rigid interpretation of the
Rules. That, I think, was in the general
public interest, but I wish it to be understood that the indulgence granted on this
occasion must not be taken as a precedent.
Sir ROBERT ANDERSON: May I take it
that that is an admonition, that whilst
others who have proceeded me have transgressed I am not to be allowed to continue?
The CHAIRMAN: I allowed the hon.
Member to travel over every foot of ground
anybody else has travelled over, but when
he proceeds to deal with the question of
valuation he is going outside the scope of
the clause.
Sir ROBERT ANDERSON: I quite appreciate your position, and I do not intend
to open up this fresh subject. If I want
to deal with valuation matters I can have
my fling on the next clause without any
difficulty. On the general principle I have
laid down I am going to support this clause,
although it is going to put a little additional
burden on the local rates. Still, I think
the local authorities will have to recognise
the position this Government stands in in
regard to future developments, and realise
that, after all, the cheapest policy either
for the Government as a whole or for the
local taxayer is that little economies of this
character should be made if they enable
the Government not to go into debt again,
because, eventually, the taxpayer in
Northern Ireland has got to make the
money good, as it cannot be made good from
any other source.
Question put, "That the clause stand part
of the Bill."
The Committee divided: Ayes, 25; Noes, 9.

Mr. POLLOCK: I beg to move on page 8,
line 30, to leave out Clause 10.
I must take responsibility for the inclusion
of this clause in the Bill, and, equally, I
have to take responsibility for its withdrawal. I think it is entirely due to the
Government and to myself that I should
reiterate the circumstances under which the
clause was included in the Bill, and the
circumstances under which I agreed to its
withdrawal. For many years a definite sum
had been contributed in respect of the valuation of premises by the local authorities,
but, as I reminded hon. Members before, an
arrangement was made under circumstances
of a very exceptional nature some fifty or
sixty years ago, when the Valuation Department was a very small affair, because the
whole of the Province had been valued a
very short time before this arrangement was
made. The small sum then spent upon valuation, it was agreed, should be divided in two;
one-half to be borne by the State, and onehalf by the local authorities; but it was a
definite amount which was not flexible or
elastic, and necessarily at that time the
amount was very small.
In the course of time as valuations on new
property became necessary, and as the area
of valuation necessarily enlarged the maintenance of the establishment cost considerably more money. Up to now no claim has
been made upon the local authorities to bear
any part of that cost over and above the
small amount originally arranged. When it
is realised, as I explained when the matter
was discussed on the Second Reading, that
this Valuation Department is maintained in
the interests of the local authorities to the
extent of 90 per cent. of its cost, it will be
realised that conditions have changed so
materially-the county councils are the
agents for levying on the ratepayers--when
it is realised, as I say, that the machinery
of the Valuation Department is almost entirely maintained in their interests, it did
seem to me that it was only suitable that
those who received the benefit of the estab-

Imperial matters. If we follow the British

authorities to bear the whole of the charge
of the Valuation Department, or, rather, to
take the whole of it over, which would have
been the same thing, but in order that the

with a clearer recognition in our minds that
the burden of rating is, or appears, to be

It did not seem very unreasonable, and, as
I frankly said to the House what the Committee and hon. Members must know, there
is great necessity at the present time for

the great burden of unemployment insurance
may be met. It did not seem an unnatural
thing in looking round and raking over the
cupboard in the whole of the Six Counties,
that I should have asked that a Service that
was maintained in the interests of the ratepayers and in the interest especially of the
county councils, who levy on the ratepayers,
should be borne in the proportion of fifty
cent. by the local authorities. I
have nothing to charge myself with in
regard to the insertion of the clause.
I feel it was a fair thing to do, and I think
the county councils would have only shown
an appreciation of the treatment which they
have universally received from this Government if they had accepted it, and admitted
that it was a fair share of the burden to
bear. But, apparently, they have forgotten
a great many things this Government has
done, and has tried to do for them. Some
of the things were recounted to-day, not only
by my right hon. Friend the Prime Minister,
but also by the Member for Derry (Sir
per

29 APRIL 1926
Robert Anderson), who very fairly and
generously and courageously championed the
Government in respect of what they have
done in regard to these matters.
As I mentioned when the subject was discussed before, we did receive representations
in general from the county councils. I am
bound to admit there are county councils
who have been appreciative of what has been
done. I did receive representations from
several hon. Members here, who were concerned for the opinions of the county councils
in the counties which they represent, and,
as I explained, the Government had no particular reason for burdening the county
councils with charges that involved an increase on the rates, because whether a man
pays money out of his right pocket or his
left pocket, whether he pays it directly in
rating or in taxation, he naturally resents it.
Therefore, for that reason, when representation was made to me, I agreed that we
should delete the Clause entirely. This is
my explanation and justification for the
appearance of the Clause in the Bill, and it
is also the explanation of the circumstances
under which I move that it be deleted from
the Measure.
Sir ROBERT ANDERSON: I have no
desire, seeing the Clause has been withdrawn,
to enter into any controversy with the
Minister of Finance on the particular matters
involved in this Clause or on the arguments
he has used that induced him originally to
make this demand upon the county councils.
On the Second Reading of the Bill I expressed
appreciation of the fact that he recognised
that the burden of the local rates was more
than the ordinary ratepayer could bear, and
that it was steadily increasing.
Mr. POLLOCK: On a low valuation.
Sir ROBERT ANDERSON: It may have
been a low valuation, but they had it for
the last fifty years, and so there is no argument to be grounded on that, for other circumstances that exist to-day have existed
for the last half century. The fact remains
that the burden of taxation from the central
Government has been steadily mounting up
and the burden of local taxation has also
been steadily mounting up. Between the two
the unfortunate taxpayer and the unfortunate ratepayer have SO many demands
made upon them they are naturally critical,
and rightly so, in regard to anything that
would involve an increased charge upon their
purse. I am sorry in one sense the Minister
of Finance has re-argued this question, because I think it only right that another viewpoint should be placed before the Committee
in justification of the action of some who
opposed this Clause, and of some of the local
authorities who were critical of it. This
charge was fixed, as the Minister of Finance
states, some forty or fifty years ago, and it
has not varied or changed since. I would
like to point out to the Committee that the
fixed Government grants in aid made forty
or fifty years ago to local authorities have
never changed. They are just as small to-day
as they were fifty years ago.
Mr. POLLOCK: For certain services.
Sir ROBERT ANDERSON: For certain
services-main services. Take the maintenance of lunatics, take the grants towards
the salaries of sanitary officers, and take the
union and medical charges. In regard to
these local authorities have made appeals, and
I have been associated with some of them.
For the last twenty years we have never
been able to induce any Government to increase their grant in aid to local authorities
for these services. It was, I think, after all
natural for the people to be somewhat critical
in regard to a matter of this kind, and they
naturally reason in this way. The other
question evidently has worked out on the
wrong side as far as the Government is concerned, and they want to remedy that right
away, but the answer of the local authorities
on that point is that the fixed grant in respect of those other things has worked out to
their disadvantage, and, therefore, if the
Government were going to get the advantage
on one side the local authorities claimed it
on the other.
That is really the position summarised, and
I think the local authorities who were critical
and some hon. Members of this Committee
who gave the Minister of Finance, perhaps,
some little annoyance and trouble had so'ne
ground to work upon in connection with a
matter of this kind. But I am glad the
Minister of Finance has recognised, and recognised in the most generous way possible,
that the burden of local rates is so heavy that
he has no desire if he can possibly avoid it to
have that increase. On these grounds he has
withdrawn this Clause, and I am sure all
interests concerned will fully appreciate the
kindly and generous action he has taken.
Question put, and agreed to.

Mr. CRAWFORD: It is somewhat unfortunate that anything at all in the nature
of criticism should be levelled at the Minister
of Finance, and that local bodies should be
ungrateful for the favours they received in
the past. My reason for moving this Amend-
Iment that the words unconditionally as at
present" be inserted after the word "district is very simple, and will not cause
very much trouble, I am sure, to the Minister
of Finance. I will tell the Committee the
circumstances. The Exchequer intended
seizing £43,000, which had hitherto been paid
to local authorities out of money raised. It
is promised that the local authorities are not
going to lose anything by the transaction.
I cannot see that the county councils are
going to suffer from it except in this way.
The Exchequer mean to hand us that £43,000
deducted from the Motor Taxation Fund, and
we agreed to accept. We would get that £43,000
and hold the Motor Taxation Fund as well.
This fund is financed entirely from the
motor vehicle duties. I have never heard the
Minister suggesting that he is going to pay
into the fund from any other source an
amount equal to what he is taking out this
time. The council expected that the grants
they received hitherto and they have received them from 1868-would be continued,
and this motor taxation, which is of more
recent occurrence, they expected also to be
continued. I think I heard responsible
Ministers in this House saying that every
penny received from motor taxation would
go to the roads. I know the Minister of
Finance is an exceedingly clever man; in
fact, he is most uncanny in the way he
defends his position. No doubt he will say
that every penny is going to the roads. The
mysterious thing is that the £43,000 that is
going to be used on the roads came hitherto
from another source. I think the most uninitiated person in arithmetic will easily
understand that if you take £43,000 from the
Motor Taxation Fund you will not have so
much to divide at the end of the time as if
you had left it there. There may be conditions attaching to this thing, because when
getting grants out of the Road Fund you
get a 60 per cent. grant on expenditure on
first class roads, a 30 per cent. grant on
second class roads, and a 15 per cent. grant
on some third class roads. I want it to be
distinctly understood, and if possible have
it inserted in the Bill, that no conditions
will be attached to this grant of £43,000
that is coming to us out of the Road Fund.
I do not think I am asking anything unreasonable, and I hope the Minister will he
able to grant that concession. I ought to
say that I have reason to find fault that
no intimation was given to the county
councils in regard to this matter. It would
have been much easier, and much more
pleasing, if the Minister when telling us
about the charges he was going to put on
the county councils for revaluation purposes
had also told us what the other changes,
would be, and so enabled us to face the whole
thing at once. I hope the Minister will give
us an assurance that these grants out of the
Road Fund will be made without any conditions attaching to them.
Mrs. CHICHESTER: I would like to
support what has been said by the hon.
Member for Antrim (Mr. Crawford). At
the same time I wish to point out that I
do not intend to vote against the Government in this instance. I want to make that
plain at the start, because I feel that we

authorities have felt that this particular
pocket was one to which they could claim a

monopoly. The Government, of course, are

In making my protest in support of what

at any rate of the Six Counties. I would like
to speak of the district I know best. The
roads in that district are probably the worst
in the whole of the Six Counties. The problem is a terrible one for the ratepayers.
We are a very poor part of the country. Our
rates at the present moment are 10s. 4d. in

obvious to hon. Members and right hon.
Members that we in that part of the country
take a very particular interest in the Road

consider this to be the worst winter on record, and a great many are faced with

roads are a burden and a nightmare which
never leave them.
I think right hon. Gentlemen could
allay the feeling of anxiety to a great extent
if they would make clear the exact position
with regard to the Road Fund. Perhaps the
Minister would possibly accept the word
"unconditional." I do want to impress upon

country. The fact that the local authorities
will be very grateful indeed for the concession which has been granted, prohibits
me from saying as much as I otherwise

Member for Derry (Sir Robert Anderson).
Everything he said with reference to the last

The ATTORNEY-GENERAL (Mr. Babington): I might explain to the Committee the
way in which this matter stands from the
point of view of draftsmanship of the
Bill, because I think when the Committee
understand the frame of the Bill they will
see that the fears that have been expressed
are groundless, so far as this clause is
concerned. At the present time there are
two funds out of which the local authorities
draw money for road purposes. The first
one is the fund drawn from what is called
the Probate Duties Grant, and that fund
is paid unconditionally to county councils.
Under the Roads Act, 1920, there are certain
sums paid to the county councils
out of the fund which was established
by that Act. In the first place, there
are paid to them under Section 3
certain costs of administering the fund and
certain overhead charges for management,
and these are paid unconditionally and are
a first charge on the Road Fund. They then
are entitled to a portion of certain sums
out of the money that remains after the
payment of these sums which are paid unconditionally, and those funds that are paid
to them for the maintenance of roads are
undoubtedly subject to conditions.
What this Bill is intended to do is this,
and what it does do is that it transfors
the grant in aid of roads and bridges, known
as the Probate Duties Grant, and it makes
it a charge upon the Road Fund under the
Roads Act, 1920, but it does not make it
subject to the conditions which are applicable to the portion of that Fund which is
paid in respect of roads. It is placed as
an Amendment to the section, and the
transfer of this fund, known as the Probate
Duties Grant, is to be on the same footing
as the payments made under the Act of
1920, which are subject to no conditions.
And, consequently, if the Committee accept
this Clause 11 in the form in which it is,
that Amendment of the Act of 1920, which
is set out in this clause, will have the effect
of making the fund, which was formerly
payable out of the Probate Duties Grant, now
be paid out of the Road Fund, but it will
be paid unconditionally and not condition-

ally. (Hon. Members: Hear, hear.) That

be carried on in the future.
Mrs. CHICHESTER: The right hon.
Gentleman has not answered one of my questions. There was an announcement or a

Sir DAWSON BATES: I think the whole

Sir ROBERT ANDERSON: I am very glad
of that. That clears away any doubt I had
in my mind in regard to a matter of that
kind. Every penny in the Road Fund here has
been spent up to the present moment, and it
has not been sufficient to put the roads in
first-class order. That is unquestioned.
very much regret that the necessities of our
financial position have made it necessary for
the Minister of Finance on this occasion to
impose this £35,000 upon the revenues of the
Road Fund. I hope it will be the last raid
that will be made for some time to come,
although let me say here that as the roads
are built up in Northern Ireland and when
they are brought into first-class conditionthat will take some time, but I can forsee the
time when all the money received from the
motor taxation may not be required for the
upkeep of the roads-it will be a long time,
I grant you, but it is as well for us to face
the problem. Eventually, this Government
may find it necessary to divert part of it to
some other purpose. However, the whole of
the Road Fund matters will be in the melting
pot probably within the next two or three
years.
From what the Imperial Chancellor has
indicated in the British House we may see
a customs duty upon petrol and the other
duties done away with altogether. Although
it may not perhaps be germane to the discussion, may I be permitted to say I shall
welcome the introduction of a Measure of
that character, believing that it is the most
equitable form of taxation in connection
with the whole motor question. (Hon.
Members: Hear, hear.) When it does arise
of course our position is a peculiar one. We
have nothing to do with customs. It will
be a question then what policy our Government will pursue when the British Government will impose a customs duty upon petrol.
I am sorry that the Chancellor has seen
fit to take the course he has done. I know
he has only taken it because he saw no other
way open in the peculiar circumstances he
finds himself in. I do regret it, yet I am
going to support the Government in the
peculiar circumstances in which they find
themselves.

Mr. PATRICK O'NEILL: I desire to
move the deletion of this Clause altogether,
and I believe I am justified in doing so by
the speeches which I have heard from the
opposite side this afternoon. One of the

future time should become more in credit
than it is this Clause of the Bill, or a Bill
similar to this, may be passed, but doubts
have been expressed as to this fund increasing to any more than it is by the Minister of
Finance, and I think some of the other
Ministers as well. Therefore, if this Road
Fund is not to increase in amount there
certainly does not seem to be any justification at present for robbing it of this amount
of £43,000 annually.
We have heard from the different rating
authorities protests-I have had some of
them myself from the county which I represent, from some of the officials in any case –
stating that it is a mistake, and that they
think it is quite wrong that the ratepayers
of the county should be saddled in the
interests of the Exchequer. The Road Fund
was established and financed, I believe, from
the Excise licence duties paid on motors in
Northern Ireland, and we know that the
purpose of establishing this Fund was for
the sole and simple reason of the upkeep
of the roads. Anyone who has travelled
over the roads knows that their condition
at the present time, while greatly improved
from what they were some two or three
years ago, is still short-very much shortof the requirements needed at the present
time, and in my opinion to take any part
of the Fund that was specially designed and
adapted and established for that purpose is
a mistake on the part of any Government,
and is not justified on any ground. It is
for that reason that 1 have risen for the
purpose of moving the total rejection of this
Clause, and I do so now.
Mr. GEORGE HENDERSON: I beg to

your own expenses, or saving your own expenses, is economy, but when, as this Clause
as I apprehend it proposes to do, you put
your hand in some other body's pocket and
call that economy, I cannot agree.
I am

The sum of £300 is provided for the Consultant to the Electricity Commissioners for
Northern Ireland. This Consultant advises

which come before them for consideration.
Among these may be mentioned:-
Applications for consent to the erection

A sum of £300 has been provided for fees

As the Committee is aware my Department

The balance of £100 in this Estimate is

contingencies in which it may be necessary
for my Department to employ expert consultants, and in particular for the necessary service of inspection at the Coalisland mine,
which is carried out periodically by qualified
inspectors of the Mines Department of Great
Britain, under an agency arrangement with
my Ministry. The inspection of coal mines
is specialised work, and subject to special
statutory requirements. It follows that a
coal mines' inspector must be properly qualified for the purpose of exercising these special
duties, which do not fall within the scope
of the duties of an inspector of mines and
quarries. Amongst the technical contingencies to which I have above referred might
be mentioned such fortuitous circumstances
as boiler explosions, in connection with enquiries into which it may be necessary to
summon expert assistance.

With regard to the housing grants, the first
of these is A1. Hon. Members will recollect
that under the Act of 1919, the Government
undertook to pay an annual sum of 25s for
every 20s of rent collected. That Act was
availed of to a very small extent owing to
the high cost of building materials, and of
course, has long since expired.
With regard to A3, hon. Members will recollect that two years ago an arrangement
was entered into between the Government
and the Belfast Corporation in respect of
houses which they built under the 1919 Act.
459 houses were built, and the Corporation
were entitled to get a grant of 25s in respect
of every collected, and accordingly the
Government decided to commute that sum
for a cash payment of £127,500, and the
sum appears under A3, represents the interest
on that amount. I might point out that this
arrangement was subsequently embodied in
an Act of Parliament of this House.
A4 and A5 deal with the subsidies to local
authorities and private owners, and I might
point out that in connection with the houses
erected under our Housing Acts, a grant is
made of £60, subsequently increased to £80.
I find that as regards the houses erected by
local authorities that up to date, no fewer
than 1,936 houses had been approved for

877 houses have been completed up to date,
and grants have been paid in respect of 348.

I think it is an audacious thing for the
Government to reduce this grant in aid of
rates on agricultural land, because they are
doing it at a time when the rates are a
crushing burden. The people think after this
that the Government might cease making
promises, or at least leading the people to
believe that they think agriculture is
the most important industry. It seems
to me no matter what other
gain, if there is to be a loss it is
agriculture that has to bear it. I oppose
in the strongest measure any diminution
in the grant in aid of rates on
agricultural land. The Minister of Home
Affairs said that they had to do that under
the Colwyn Commission and on the basis of
population. What is the basis of population in Northern Ireland compared with
Great Britain? The basis we have tried to
obtain is much more fair. I got a question
put by Mr. D. D. Reid, Chairman of the
Ulster Unionist Party, in the Imperial
House last year on this matter. He asked
to what extent the rates on agricultural
land were relieved in England, and the
Department replied that the rates were
relieved to the extent of 75 per cent. I put a
similar question to the Minister of Home
Affairs in this House and he said that the
rates on agricultural land were relieved to
the extent of 52 per cent. I say that the
Government of Northern Ireland, if they
have the power-and if they have not the
power they should get it-should refuse to
pay the Imperial contribution until the
rates on agricultural land here are relieved
to the same extent as in England. The
Government say they are keeping in step
with Great Britain. They are doing so in
regard to unemployment, but not in regard
to agriculture. Agriculture is not recognised in this House, and agriculture deserves
all the kicks it gets. Until it sends people
here to represent it it will get more kicks.
Agriculture, or any other business only
exercises an influence on Governments in
accordance with its representation in Parliament.
I want to know what has been done with
the money that has been taken. To what
purpose has it been diverted? This is
money that went in the relief of rates on
agriculture last year. To what purpose
has it been put? I hold there is no relief as
equitable to the farmers of Northern Ireland as the relief that goes to reduce the
rates, because a great many of the schemes
of the Government that go to improve
agriculture do not to any great extent
affect the majority of the poorer farmers.
It is really the poorer farmers on the small
holdings that have no capital left to carry
out the improvement schemes suggested by
the Government in some directions. It is
the poorer farmers who are being hit by
taking away this money that was an
equivalent to the grant in aid of the rates
on agricultural land in England. It is a
breach of faith on the part of the Government to take away this grant. It is a most
audacious attempt to filch money out of the
pockets of agriculturists to balance the
Budget. I object to that strongly. I am
sorry I am not in a position to move that
this grant be increased to the same extent
as last year. I know it would not be in
order. The Minister may say in palliation

the agriculturists in the Six Counties.
certainly agree that it is the duty of a

premier industry in Northern Ireland. The
farmers are groaning under the burden of

Those from agricultural districts know that
the Ulster farmer finds it impossible to meet
the big demands for rates, rents and wages,
and everything else. They are getting low
prices for produce, and yet the Government
who have expressed sympathy, and who
should be supposed to support the farmers

It is the method of dealing with these Estimates against which I venture to protest.
We should have had a whole day for the discussion of this-probably two days-and, as
the hon. Gentleman (Mr. William McMullen)
below me has said, why should these things
be rushed? This is not a very busy Parliament. We, as he has stated, only meet about
three months in the year, and we ought to
find time for the consideration of these
matters. It would be a very useful pursuit for
the Members of Parliament to find time to
come here to consider and discuss these Votes

rather unsatisfactory discussion-in a
practically empty House, with all the heads of
the Government gone away-I think a Member of the Government peeped in just now,
but when the most of the Members of the
Government have gone, all their agricultural
supporters gone, and no one left here but the
Minister of Home Affairs (Sir Dawson Bates),
his assistant, and the despised Opposition. If
it were not for this Oppostion we would never
know anything about the mystery of this
proposal to take away a grant of £32,00 at a
serious time for agriculture.
Here, let me say that at a time when the
linen industry is in a bad way, and when the
shipbuilding industry is in a bad way, and
when the possibilities are that our people
must go back to the land-because after all,
however industries may disappear, the grass
will continue to grow, and we must ultimately fall back upon agriculture-it is at
this moment, when everything should be done
to cultivate and foster our agricultural
strength, and to assist the farmers in the
difficult tasks they have to perform, that the
Government, at eight o'clock at night, proceed to rob them of £32,000, just as you were
robbing the workers in the earlier part of the
day by this Economy Bill. It has been a good
day's work, and I put the Government in the
political dock for their criminal conduct towards these two great interests, the interests
of the working classes, who were robbed by
the Economy Bill, and the interests of the
agriculturists who are being robbed by this
Vote.

Oral Answers to Questions.
RETIRED PUBLIC ELEMENTARY
TEACHERS.
1. Mr. GEORGE HENDERSON asked the
Minister of Finance whether he can state
how many of the Public Elementary Teachers
of Northern Ireland, who retired before the
31st March, 1901, are still alive, and whether
he will state the amount of the pension
granted to each on the occasion of retirement, and the increase in each case allowed
under the Pension (Increase) Act, 1920.
The MINISTER OF FINANCE (Mr.
Pollock): The number of Public Elementary
School Teachers who retired from schools in
Northern Ireland on or before 31st March,
1901, and are still alive is 32. It is,
obviously, outside the scope of an oral reply
to give the figures relating to each case, but
I may state that the total of the original
pensions amounted to £832 Os 8d. The total
of pensions now in force is £1,403 19s 8d, an
increase of £571 19s 0d, or 69 per cent. on the
original pensions. Of this increase £314
15s 4d was directly due to the Pensions (Increase) Act, 1920, and £189 12s 8d to the
amendment of that Act by the Education
Act (Northern Ireland), 1923. In conclusion,
I might point out that under the Pensions
(Increase) Bill, which has been before this
House, an additional increase is given, which
will take effect from 1st April, 1926.
I am sending to the hon. Member a detailed statement showing the particulars in
connection with each case.
2. Mr. GEORGE HENDERSON
Colonel Woods) asked the Minister of Home
Affairs whether he will state the number and
rank of the officers and non-commissioned
officers employed at the Royal Ulster Constabulary Depot at Newtownards; what their
duties are; whether any of these officers are
in receipt of locomotion allowance, and if so,
why this allowance is considered necessary;
and whether he can give the number of constables in training at the Depot on the 28th
instant.
The MINISTER OF HOME AFFAIRS (Sir
Dawson Bates): As my reply to the hon.
and gallant Member's question is a lengthy
