Sir DAWSON BATES: In moving the
Second Reading of this Bill, I fear I shall
have to trespass for some time upon the
patience of the House, as the subject is
both difficult and complicated, and as a result there appears to be a great deal of misunderstanding as to the effect of this Bill.
Jury Laws Bill-
Second Reading.
HOUSE OF COMMONS
[Sir Dawson Bates]
At the outset, I propose to explain some of
the reasons which have led the Government
to bring in this Measure. The Jury Law has
remained unaltered since the Act of 1876,
with the important exception of the Sex
Disqualification Act which was passed in
1919. The 1876 Act under which we are working at the present time, dealt with the qualification of Jurors, and provided a procedure
for summoning them, but I need hardly
point out to this House that the conditions
to-day are very different to those prevailing
fifty years ago, and as a result the Act has
become, to a large extent, obsolete and outof-date, and I think this will appear clear
to the House when I come to deal with the
details of the Measure.
For many years past there has been a
growing discontent with the burden of the
jury service. This discontent is, I believe,
largely due to the inequalities which prevail
at the moment. These inequalities partly
arise owing to change of conditions, notably
the passing of the Land Acts under which
tenant farmers become the owners of the
freehold, and this I will refer to afterwards,
but it is also very largely due to the difficulties in procedure prescribed under the present law. As
a result, many people are
escaping jury service who are in a much
better position to bear the loss of time and
the expense involved than others who are
called upon to serve. For example, a person
whose name appears on the list may be never
called upon to serve, while his neighbour,
who may own a farm of a very much smaller
valuation, and be in a very much poorer
financial position, may be called at frequent
intervals, and this anomaly may, and does,
result from the mere accident of the initial
letters of their names.
But there is another reason. I am sorry
to say that there are a large number of
cases of evasion of this important duty of
citizenship, with the result that an increased
burden is thrown upon those who are prepared faithfully to discharge their duty.
In the country, the existing qualifications
produce an unnecessarily large number of
jurors, while in the city, the reverse is the
case. In the country, as the result of the
present qualifications, many people
called upon to serve who can ill afford the
time and the expense, when, as a matter of
fact, there is really no necessity for them
to be summoned.
are
In the cities the number of jurors is too
small and, consequently, they have to be
summoned at frequent intervals, and the
burden there is very severely felt, and as regards Belfast this condition of affairs is more
acutely felt since the transfer of the
Judiciary to Northern Ireland, where the
jurors of Belfast are called upon to serve
in cases which come from all over the Six
Counties.
a
The Government, since they came into
being, have been urged to undertake
Measure of Jury Reform, but, knowing the
difficulties surrounding the question, they decided before embarking on legislation, to explore the matter thoroughly from all angles,
as they felt that even if there should be delay
it would tend towards having a more satisfactory Measure, and accordingly, the
Government appointed a Commission, with
Lord Justice Andrews as Chairman, to inquire into the whole matter. That Committee was very representative, not alone of
the legal profession but also of the laymen,
and while I refer to this matter, I would
like to take this opportunity of expressing
the thanks of the Government to Lord Justice
Andrews and his Committee for the very
exhaustive and valuable report, which forms
the basis of the present Measure now before
the House. The Committee made a large
number of recommendations, some of which
we could not see our way to adopt for
reasons which I will explain hereafter, but
I think it will be agreed that we have included in the Bill most of the important
recommendations.
There is one matter which I wish to make
clear, before going into a detailed explanation of the Bill. Hon. Members are aware
that under the Government of Ireland Act,
1920, matters relating to the Supreme Court
are reserved, and the Committee made recommendations which fall into three categories namely:-
(1) Those which were clearly outside the
competence of this Parliament;
(2) Those which were clearly within our
competence; and
(3) Those about which there is some
doubt as to whether they are within our
competence or not.
We have, therefore, excluded those falling
within the first category, from the Bill, but
I shall refer to them later on, and we are
now dealing with the second and third
classes, so far as we have been able to
accept the recommendations. We have
adopted this course after consultation with
the Imperial Home Secretary.
Coming now to the provisions of the Bill, I
think it would be convenient if I was, first,
to state shortly the existing law, governing
the qualification for jury service, and then
to indicate the changes which we propose
making; afterwards I will deal with the rules
of procedure which we propose to make.
The qualifications for jury service are
contained in Section 2 of the Act of 1876, and
that Section provides that every man between
917 Jury Laws Bill-

4 MAY 1926
Second Reading.
21 and 65 residing in any county, and having
the necessary qualifications, is liable to serve
on all juries, whether civil or criminal, and
the qualifications are:-
(1) he should have a clear annual income
of £10 from freehold lands;
(2) that he should have a clear annual
income of £20 from leasehold lands;
(3) that he should either in his own
name, or a member of a firm, be rated-
(a) in respect of lands and tenements
of a net annual valuation of £40;
or
(b) £10 in respect of a dwelling-house,
except in the case of Belfast and Derry,
where the vaulation should be £20.
(4) that he should be a director of any
Incorporated Company.
(5) that he should be a member of a
Board of Harbour Commissioners.
Now, with regard to the first two qualifications, namely, a clear annual income of £10
free from freehold lands, or an annual income of £20 from leasehold lands, it will be
obvious to hon. Members how difficult it is
to ascertain how much a man derives as
annual income from either freehold or leasehold land. Some registration authorities, I
understand, assume that because a valuation
is of £10, the individual must necessarily
have an income of £10 out of it. Others have
not accepted this view, and I think that it is
unsatisfactory that there is no certain measure of qualification, but apart altogether
from this disadvantage, the tenure of land in
Northern Ireland has altered very materially
since the Act of 1876 was passed. In the old
days a £10 freeholder was very often a man
of substance, and a man well able to bear
the burden of jury service, but by the
operation of the Land Purchase Acts, the
number of freeholders has increased enormously, and, at the present moment, a
farmer who has bought out his farm with a
£10 valuation may be called upon to leave his
farm with nobody in charge, and go and serve
on a jury, while his neighbour, who may be
a judicial tenant, with a valuation up to
£40, and who is in a very much better
financial position, escapes altogether.
With regard to urban areas other than
the county boroughs of Belfast and Derry,
as I said before, the rating qualification is
£10. Fifty years ago that amount brought
in a fairly substantial class of householder,
but since that time the standard of valuation has risen, and the result is that this
valuation captures many men to whom jury
service is a real hardship.
As I have already stated, the number of
jurors produced under the existing Jury Acts
is, apart from the county boroughs, excessive, and our object is to simplify the qualification, and to fix it at such a figure as
will produce the required number of jurors,
and, at the same time, not impose a hardship upon those least able to hear it. Lord
Justice Andrews' Committee recommended
the abolition of the freeholder, and the leaseholder qualification, and the substitution of
a simple rating qualification, and in this Bill
At
we have adopted this recommendation.
the same time, and having regard to the
fuller statistics at our disposal than were
available for the Committee, we have come
to the conclusion that the rating qualifications which were recommended by Lord Justice Andrews' Committee, would be too high
to produce sufficient jurors, and, accordingly,
we have decided that the qualifications should
remain as at present in county boroughs,
namely. £20; that in the case of counties it
should be fixed at £20 for urban districts
and towns; and at £16 for other parts of
the counties, and hon. Members will find
these particulars set out in the First
Schedule at page 14.
I believe the adoption of these qualifications will produce a sufficient number of
jurors, and, at the same time, relieve the
man of small means, especially those dependent upon their daily wages, or others, such
as farmers and shopkeepers, who have no
assistants to work for them in their absence.
I might point out here that under Section
2 of the 1876 Act, it is provided that if a
person is qualified within the Borough but
lives within 12 miles of the Borough Courthouse in the county, he is to serve in the
Borough and not in the County. Unfortunately, the Section is somewhat obscure.
It is doubtful whether this Section applies
to all jurors, or only those who are qualified
by reasons of being a Director of a Company
or Harbour Commissioners. In practice, a
narrow interpretation is put upon this
Section with the result that the present
Section is not of very much use. I think
this might be regarded as another example
of how modern conditions have rendered the
old Acts obsolete. The great growth of
travelling facilities has caused an increasing
number of business men to reside outside
the city, and, as a result, their services are
lost to the city, and I think hon. Members
will agree that it is only right that those
men, whose interests are mainly bound up
in the city, should bear their share of jury
service in the Borough. On the recommendation of the Jury Commission, we propose
to extend the distance from 12 miles to 25
miles, and we propose to make it quite clear
that this will apply to all jurors qualified
in the city who reside outside the city within that area.
There is just one other matter in this Clause
to which I would like to draw the attention of

HOUSE OF COMMONS
[Sir Dawson Bates]
this House. It has been found that there
has been a considerable evasion of jury
service by the practice whereby persons who
own property, and who would otherwise be
qualified, transfer the rated property into
the names of their wives.
Mr. DEVLIN: Could the right hon.
Gentleman give us a case of that?
Sir DAWSON BATES: My hon. Friend
is very innocent, but I am certain that if
he will put a question down later on he will
receive full information.
Mr. DEVLIN: Does the right hon. Gentleman ask a body of sensible men to believe
that any man would transfer his property

Sir DAWSON BATES: My hon. Friend is
a bachelor, and I do not think he
appreciates it. (Laughter.) We propose
in this Bill, in order to stop what
We regard as a very unfair evasion,
that the husband in such cases is to be

The second Clause of the Bill deals with
the preparation of the lists of special juries,
and makes very little change in the existing
law, save that it reduces the qualification
for a special juror in some of the counties.
We propose to fix it at the figures set out
in the Second Schedule, page 14. I might
point out that special jurors are required
for the trial of actions in which the parties
require a special jury, and they are also
required for the purpose of forming grand
juries at quarter sessions, and we have found
that, as a result of the present qualifications,
we have got an insufficient number of special
jurors in certain of the counties. The changes
we propose follow the recommendation of
Lord Justice Andrews' Committee.
Now we come to the very important question-the question of exemptions-and these
are dealt with in Clause 3, and if hon.
Members will turn to the Third Schedule on
page 15 they will find the exemptions. In
putting forward these exemptions I have been
mainly guided by this principle that no
citizen is entitled as a matter of privilege
to claim exemption-(hon. Members: Hear,
hear) and that there should only be exemption in order to meet the convenience of the
public, or in the interests of the State, and
for no other reason can exemption be justified. The First Schedule to the old Act
of 1876 contains a list of exemptions, and we
propose to re-enact this list with some very
important exceptions. In this matter we
have followed the recommendations of the
Committee, and we propose to abolish the
exemption that has hitherto been given to
civil engineers and pharmaceutical chemists,
with this important exception that in the
case of a "one-owner" shop, who has no
qualified assistants, he should be exempt.
I think you will agree with me that it is in
the public interest that shops of this kind
should be left in the hands of qualified
individuals.
But I come now to what is a more farreaching change. Under the Act of 1876,
all persons holding any public office under
His Majesty's Government or in any public
Department, or any local authority, and
paid from rates or taxes, are exempt from
jury service. That is the present law.
Mr. DEVLIN: Why?
Sir DAWSON BATES: My hon. Friend
will get ample opportunity later on to explain what a good Measure this Bill is.
Mr. DEVLIN: But the right hon. Gentleman is explaining this Bill-and it is his
Bill, not mine-and I would like him to
explain why these exemptions were granted
in the past.
Sir DAWSON BATES: If my hon.
Friend will only have patience I will
matters
try to explain these
to him.
Lord Justice Andrews' Committee recommended that this exception should be entirely
abolished. There is no such general
exemption in England, and generally speaking civil servants and officials of local
authorities have to take their share in jury
service, and we think that the reasons for
the exemption given in 1876 do not exist today. I think in the absence of cogent
reasons why these officials should be exempt,
the public naturally resent that these
officials should escape the burden of jury
service, and thereby throw a greater burden
on others. The Committee do not recommend any exceptions, but we have found it
necessary to insert certain exceptions from
the general rule. We have tried to make
these exceptions as few as possible, having
regard to the principle which I have laid
down, but there are certain classes which we
consider should be exempt, such as officers
of the Army, the Navy, the Air Force, members of the Constabulary and Prison Officials.
These are exempt in England and we propose
to exempt them here. So far as regards our
own Civil Service, we have only exempted
from jury service the permanent Head and
Deputy of each Ministry, and hon. Members
will appreciate that they can only mean
three at the most in each Ministry. We have
921 Jury Laws Bill-

Second Reading.
also exempted the Comptroller and Auditor
General, but, apart from these cases, the
only exemption in the whole Civil Service, is
in respect of a few officials in the Ministry
of Home Affairs, and I will tell you why.
These officials-they are very few in
number-deal with the administration of
the criminal law, and I think it would be
manifestly unfair to persons on their trial,
whose cases may previously have been
investigated by these officials, that they
should have at their trial these officials on
the jury.
With regard to Inperial Departments in
Northern Ireland, we have thought it right
to exempt the heads of these Departments
who may be in charge of the Head Office in
Northern Ireland. We also exempt officers
of the Post Office, and officers in the
employment of the Commissioners of
Customs and Inland Revenue, and, with
regard to these categories, we might, point
out that they are already exempt by Imperial Statutes, and the reason why we have
reinserted their names in this Bill is for the
purpose of having a comprehensive Schedule
which will be easy of reference. I think hon.
Members will agree that there is an overwhelming case for exempting these officials
on the grounds of public convenience, as
hon. Members will realize the enormous
inconvenience that might be caused to
the public by the taking away of a
postmaster or postmistress, and apart altogether from this, a great deal of expense will be caused to the public service
in having to send down substitutes for these
officials, many of whom carry on duty singly.
With regard to officers of local authorities,
we propose to exempt, for obvious reasons,
all officials who have statutory duties to
perform in connection with the preparation
of jurors' lists, and this would exempt such
officials as town clerks, county secretaries,
and rate collectors.
Clause 4 provides that grand jurors should
be selected in Belfast in the same way as
grand jurors are selected in the counties.
I confess that I approach the explanation
of the next Clause of the Bill with a certain
amount of diffidence, and I fear that it will
be difficult to explain this very technical
matter clearly. It deals with the method
to be adopted by the sheriff in selecting the
names for his panel, and I will try to explain how the selection takes place at
present, and how we propose to alter it in
the future, because, as I said before. it is
very largely due to the existing procedure
that so
many inequalities exist in the
present system.
I shall assume that the sheriff is starting
his book for the first time, as we provide
that he should do in the first lists prepared
under this Act. The names are arranged in
alphabetical order on the same principle as
our words are arranged in a dictionary.
The sheriff begins at the letter "A," and
takes the first name. He then goes to the
letter "B" and takes the first name, and so
on through the letters of the alphabet, coming back to the letter "A" and taking the
second name there, and so on through the
letters of the alphabet, he proceeds in this
way until he has obtained a sufficient
number of names. When he comes to strike
his second panel he goes to the letter next
after the letter from which the last name
on the previous panel was taken, and he
proceeds as before.
Now, hon. Members are probably saying
that there is very little difficulty about that,
but the difficulty now comes in when the
sheriff starts a subsequent panel, and it acts
in different ways in towns and county, and
I will tell the House how it arises. Section
19 of the Jury Act of 1871, which prescribes
the rotation in which the sheriff is to summon
the jurors, had the object in view that no
one was to serve more than once in three
years, and, accordingly, this Act, in order
to ensure this condition of affairs, laid it
down that in making up subsequent panels
after the first, the sheriff should proceed in
like manner as before, "taking the names
of the persons not already summoned during
the current or next two preceding years,
so far as may be necessary until the entire
book has been exhausted, and then he is to
start again.
Coming back to the book, no difficulty probably arises in regard to the second panel,
and if the book contained sufficient names for
the panels for three years without repetition
and no more, no difficulty would arise at
subsequent panels. In the cities, however,
the lists do not contain the requisite number,
with the result that when the book becomes
exhausted in any year, the Sheriff, on account
of the words I have emphasised, cannot go
to the name of a person who served at the
remotest date, but must go to the first name
on the list, with the result that the persons
whose names come early in the letters of
the alphabet, such as the names beginning
with letters "AB" or "MA" are summoned
much more frequently than those beginning
with "AO" and "MO." The people whose
names come under the short letters, such as
"I" or "U" are at a great disadvantage as
compared with those down in the long letters
such as "A," "G," or "M."
In the counties it operates somewhat
differently. It does not cause anyone to be
summoned more than once in three years,
but it prevents the people low down in the
long letters ever being called at all. I am
afraid that this system can only be clearly
understood by seeing the system in actual
Jury Laws Bill-
Second Reading.
HOUSE OF COMMONS
[Sir Dawson Bates]
operation on the Jurors' List, and if any
Members desire to see the process, I would
have no difficulty in arranging a demonstration.
After hearing evidence of those with
practical knowledge of the system, the Committee recommend that the words:-
Taking the names of the persons not
already summoned during the current or
next two preceding years
should be repealed. This will mean that the
sheriff, instead of going back to the beginning of the book after three years, will go
right through it from beginning to end, and
thus every person on the list will take his
share of service. Where the book contains
less than a three years' supply, the names will
be gone through, and the Sheriff can take
in those who have failed to serve before going
to those who have already served.
"
The next Clause-Clause 6-makes improvements in the machinery for the revision of
the lists. Under the provisions of this
Clause, on the first list prepared by the local
officers after the passing of the Act the name
of every person who appears to be qualified,
apart from any question of exemption, will
be included, and each case will be ruled on
by the County Court Judge or Revising
Barrister revising the list. Where a claim
for exemption is proved to his satisfaction,
either on the grounds of Statute, ill-health,
or for any other cause, he will strike the
name off the list, and he will mark it
"permanent," or "temporary," as the case
may be. If marked permanent the
name will not appear on future lists, but if
marked "temporary" it will appear again as
soon as there is reason to believe that the
temporary disqualification, say on the ground
of ill-health, has disappeared, notice being
given to the person concerned of the intention to re-insert his name on the list.
This system should prevent the list being
cumbered with persons who are really
exempt, and should prevent a great deal of
inconvenience and annoyance to the public.
I fear that the task of revising the first list
will be a rather lengthy process for the Revising Barrister, but, at the same time, I am
convinced that a great deal of the success
of the Act will depend upon the thoroughness
with which the list is revised, and, as regards future lists, this will give less trouble
to the Revising Barristers in the future.
With regard to Clause 7, this Clause speaks
for itself. In the cities,, the jurors' lists
were prepared by wards, but this has really
served no practical purpose, and indeed has
caused inconvenience, and accordingly, we
have provided that in the future, there will
be one general jury list for the whole city.
As regards counties, the unit hitherto has
been baronies, but this is entirely obsolete,
and we propose that the list should be, in
the future, prepared according to the Local
Government areas now in existence.
Clause 8 also speaks for itself, and I would
like to draw the attention of the House to
the fact that for administrative convenience,
we propose to divide the letter "M" into
two-names beginning with "Mac" or any
abbreviation being treated as a separate
letter.
Clause 9 removes a small anomaly which
was created by the Local Government Act
of 1898, in connection with the expense of
preparing the lists. Hon. Members will remember that the lists are prepared by the
Secretaries of County Councils, and by the
Clerks of Unions, where the Clerk is an
existing officer. The Act of 1898, to which I
have referred, provides that the expenses incurred by the county council in the preparation of the lists should be borne as a
county-at-large charge. On the other hand
the urban district councils have to pay for
the expense of preparing the lists so far as
the urban district councils are concerned,
and the result is that the urban district
councils have both to pay their own expense,
and also their share of the county-at-large
charge. This Clause will exempt urban
authorities from any county-at-large charge
so far as regards their own area.
Clause 10 provides for the payment of the
officials who undertake their work, on the
average of the previous three years, and this
is in accordance with the recommendation of
the Lord Justice Andrews' Committee.
Clause 11 gives power to the Presiding Judge
to divide the panel into two or more sections,
and will enable him to excuse from attendance on any specified days during the
sittings of the Court, the names of the jurors
whose names appear in any one or more of
these sections into which the panel may
have been divided. This provision is one entirely in the interests of the jurors, and will
meet a long-felt want.
The second part of Clause 11 confers
powers on judges similar to those which they
have in England, under which a judge, after
a very heavy trial-for example, a murder
trial-will be empowered to excuse the jurors
who have served, from further service for
a period of years, and I cannot but think
that this should appeal to the House as an
eminently fair provision.
The third Sub-Clause of Clause 11 provides
machinery for the judge to deal with cases
where incapacity to serve has either escaped
the notice of the Revising Barrister, or has
arisen since the revision. At the present
time if a man who is otherwise disqualified
Jury Laws Bill-
Second Reading.
4 MAY 1926
appears on the jury panel, while the judge
may on that occasion excuse him from attendance at a particular Assize, he has no
power to strike his name off the jury panel,
with the result that he will be called on the
following Assizes. We propose to give the
judge power to direct the sheriff to pass over
such name during the curreny of the list,
and we provide machinery that the circumstance will be brought before the notice of
the Revising Barrister at the next revision.
With regard to the fourth Sub-Clause of
Clause 11, this deals with the question of
medical certificates. At the present time I
do not think there can be any doubt, but
that sometimes medical certificates are given
to jurors on very slight grounds, and with
comparatively little cause, and the result
is the judges are placed sometimes in a very
difficult position when the panel is called.
Under this Sub-Clause we provide that a
juror is only to be excused on the ground of
ill-health on the production of a proper
medical certificate, the form of which is set
out in the schedule. It is quite true that
Lord Justice Andrews' Committee recommend that the medical doctor should provide
an affidavit. We fear, however, that this
would impose a hardship on the jurors, and
we cannot but think that the matter will be
rectified by the proposals in the present Bill.
Clause 12 has for its object the tightening
of the machinery for the imposition of fines
on defaulting jurors, and we propose that the
fine should be imposed by the judge unless
some reasonable cause is shown for the nonattendance, and that immediately after a fine
has been imposed that notice shall be immediately given to the defaulter, and subseqeuntly enforced, unless the fine is remitted by the judge for cause shown. We think
that if this Clause is strictly enforced it will
do away with an abuse which has been undoubtedly a legitimate cause for grievance on
the part of jurors in their endeavour to do
their duty.
Clause 13 only applies to juries in civil
cases. It has been customary up to the present to pay a common jury £1 1s 0d-that is
for the whole jury-and we propose that in
lieu of that, each member of the jury shall
receive a sum of 5s. This remuneration, of
course, will be borne by the litigants.
As regards special juries, it is provided by
an old Irish Act that each juryman in the
special jury was to receive £1 1s 0d, but it
is also customary to pay this only where a
jury had found a verdict, or where the action
had been settled after the jury had been
sworn, and the effect of this Measure will be
to make the custom legal. It is also proposed that in the case of a new jury that
each juryman shall receive an additional
sum of £1 18 0d. These amounts, of course,
as I have said before, will be paid by the
litigants.
Clause 14 provides that the judge trying
a civil case, may direct that the jury ought
not to disperse during the luncheon interval,
and he may order that lunch should be pro-
Ivided for the jury at the expense of the litigants. This will save the time of the Court
and the time of the jurymen, and will also
save expense.
We provide under Clause 15 that unless
a Coroner deems it necessary, it should not
be essential in the interests of justice for a
Coroner's jury to view the body.
Clause 12.-The provision giving the
Government power to bring the different
parts of the Act into force at different
dates will enable us to put in force the
portions of it which are essential for the
preparation of next year's lists on the new
basis, even though the arrangements, about
which I am in correspondence with the
Imperial Home Secretary, may not have
matured by that date, as there is no doubt
as to our competence to deal with these particular matters.
I fear I have made considerable demands
on the patience of this House, but before
sitting down I would like to refer briefly to
the recommendations which were made, and
which we have not been able to deal with.
These recommendations fall into two
categories:-
(1) Those matters which are within our
competence to deal with;
(2) Those which partly come within our
competence and partly outside it.
Now, with regard to the first of these categories, i.e., those which are within our competence, the proposals are five in number :-
(1) The abolition of grand juries at quarter
sessions;
(2) The payment of the expenses of certain
jurors in crime cases;
(3) The payment of certain expenses of the
sub-sheriff;
(4) The exemption of women jurors;
(5) The enactment of an income qualification by persons who are not rated.
With regard to the abolition of Grand
Juries, I might point out that the Committee
recommended that the Grand Juries at Assizes
and at the Belfast City Commission should
remain, partly on the ground that some of
the cases that are tried at these tribunals
are more serious than those tried at Quarter
Sessions, and partly that it is desirable that
every precaution should be taken to see that
prisoners were not put on their trial without
adequate justification, but I would point out
to this House that serious criminal cases are
Second Reading.

Jury Laws Bill—
HOUSE OF COMMONS
SO
[Sir Dawson Bates]
also dealt with at the Quarter Sessions, and
the view of the Government is that it is
equally important that a prisoner should not
be put upon his trial at Quarter Sessions unless there are substantial grounds for
doing, and it does not, therefore, seem logical
to abolish the protection to the prisoner at
Quarter Sessions, and to retain it at the
Assizes and the Commissions. I might point
out that this matter was very fully debated
in the Imperial House of Commons, and the
proposal was there rejected, and after very
careful consideration the Government have
come to the conclusion that we should not
bring about this change.
The Committee also recommended the payment of expenses in criminal cases where the
juror was brought over a distance of 10 miles.
It is suggested by the Committee that these
expenses should be paid out of the fines on
jurors. It is quite clear, however, that the
fines on jurors would not provide sufficient
funds to anything like meet such an expense;
indeed, in some counties, there might be no
fines at all. But apart altogether from this
aspect of the question, this proposal would
introduce an entirely new principle of farreaching effect. Jury service, especially in
criminal cases, has from the very earliest
time been regarded as a duty of citizenship,
which ought to be discharged by the citizen
without payment. After all, while citizenship
has its privileges, it has also got its duties,
but the criminal law is designed, not merely
for the punishment of criminals, but also for
the protection of law-abiding citizens, so that
they may pursue their daily avocations in
peace and have security of life and property.
The duty of jury service is a part of the
return which they make for this security.
Under the proposals contained in this Bill
jury service should approximate to a maximum of once in 3 years, and in some counties,
the interval of service may be even 4 or 5 or
possibly 6 years, and it does not seem to me
that it would be a great hardship if a man
should be called upon to attend at Quarter
Sessions, or at Assizes, once in 3 years or
sometimes even less, but apart altogether
from this, the provisions of the Bill will
exempt from jury service a great many individuals who are at present on the lists, and
who are less able to bear the cost of
attending.
This recommendation of the Committee
would not apply to Belfast, and I would remind
this House that the additional power which
we have given the Courts to divide the
panel into sections will in itself lessen the
actual time in which a juror will have to
attend. We have considered the whole
question very carefully, and we are strongly
of opinion that it would introduce a principle
that has never been hitherto adopted in
Great Britain and that is opposed to the
whole theory of jury service.
With regard to the recommendation that
under sheriffs should be relieved of the
expense of printing jury panels, jury summonses, and ballot cards, the Government
feel that all these matters were taken into
consideration when the salaries of the
sheriffs were fixed in 1920. The position of
these officers was enormously improved by
the Sheriffs Act of 1920, and the Government
do not see that there is any case for an
alteration in the existing system.
The Committee recommended that the law
should be amended so as to enable women to
be excused from service without the necessity of having to give a special reason for
their application for exemption, but we are
unable to accept this recommendation, which
appears to be wholly opposed to the principle
of the Sex Disqualification Removal Act of
1919. After all, women who are qualified to
serve as jurors have received the full rights
of citizenship, and I cannot but think that
they must also undertake the duties and
responsibilities attaching to their citizenship.
Now we come to a recommendation of the
Committee where it is recommended that persons in receipt of an income of £250 a year
and upwards, who are not rated, should be
liable for jury service. The Government
agree that there is much to be said for the
equity of such a proposal, but I think on reflection it will be seen that the administrative difficulties would make it impossible for
the Government to accept the proposal. Hon.
Members have only to reflect on the inquisitorial attitude of the income tax people in
regard to this, in order to see the undesirability of having a similar body inquiring as
to whether they are financially qualified to
serve on a jury. Apart altogether from this
point of view, the expense involved in setting
up such machinery renders the proposal unacceptable.
Now we come to the second class of recommendations which are partly within our
province, and partly without it, and they
are:-
(1) The reduction in the number of common jurors in civil cases from 12
to 6.
(2) The reduction in the number of
challenges where persons are jointly
charged.
(3) The alteration in the form of oath.
These matters, no doubt, are within our competence, so far as they relate to trials at
Quarter Sessions, but they are clearly outside our competence so far as they relate to
High Court trials. Trials of civil cases at

Quarter Sessions with juries are of extremely

consider legislation on these lines, and
the same remark applies to legislation
with regard to the right of challenge
and a form of oath. I might explain that
with regard to the right of challenge where
prisoners are jointly charged with felony,
each prisoner is entitled to 20 challenges, and
the Committee recommended that in noncapital cases the right of challenge should be
limited to 20 among all prisoners jointly
charged with an offence, unless the judge
otherwise ordered. It will, of course, be
obvious to hon. Members that where there
are a number of prisoners jointly charged at
an Assizes, the Sheriff must necessarily
summon a large number of jurors in case
all the challenges are exercised, but I think
we have met this point to some extent by the
provision in Clause 11 which enables the
Judge to divide the panel into sections, and
to require the attendance only of those jurors
who are required at the moment. I regret
that we cannot go further than this, but we
are precluded by the decision of the Imperial
Government.
Mr. DEVLIN: What about challenges for
the Crown? Is that continued?

Sir DAWSON BATES: That was not the
subject of a recommendation by the Committee. That is a matter entirely for the Imperial Government and not for this Government. The Committee also made an important
recommendation with regard to the trial of
actions by a judge without a jury, a matter
which is outside our competence.
based their recommendation on certain provisions of the Administration of Justice Act
of 1920, which was in force in England at the
time the Commission sat, but we find on inquiry these sections did not work satisfactorily, and they have been actually repealed by an Act passed in the Imperial
House last year. We are, however, discussing the matter with the Imperial Home
Secretary, and I hope it will be possible to
arrange for å provision being inserted in an
English Bill, whereby complicated civil cases
which depend on the prolonged examination
of expert witnesses, and documents or
accounts should be tried by a judge without
a jury, but this, however, is a matter outside
our competence, and can only be carried by
arrangement with the Imperial Government.
I have thought it right, even at the risk of
wearying this House to explain this Bill at
considerable length, because, as I said earlier
in my remarks, the subject is a somewhat
difficult one, and I also hope that by going
into the Bill at considerable length, I would
remove a good deal of misunderstandings
that appear to exist in regard to the contents
of the Bill, and perhaps save a certain
amount of unnecessary discussion. We have
endeavoured, so far as possible, to make the
Bill self-contained, and to avoid legislation by
reference. It was impossible to have a complete codification of the existing Acts, but I
think the Bill, as it now stands, will be a
fairly complete guide to the Jury Law as we
propose it shall be in its amended form.
We have dealt very fully with the two most
important recommendations made by the
Committee, viz:-
The alteration in the qualification of
jurors; and the inequality of the incidence
of jury service.
We have attempted to stop evasion, and
we have, I am glad to say, immensely improved the administrative precedure of the
preparation of the jury lists, and I have no
doubt as time goes on, it will be found that,
as a result of this Bill, the whole system of
jury service will have been immensely improved, and the burdens, which have hitherto
pressed sorely upon a large body of people
will have been removed. I beg to move.

has taken place since this Measure was first

Committee recommended the abolition of

[Mr. T. W. McMullan]
very serious affair for him. If he is in the
employment of a firm in Belfast it is a very
serious affair for the firm, and I think, considering the advantages that accrue from
the service of commercial travellers, the
Minister of Home Affairs should take
seriously into consideration the exemption
of these gentlemen from service.
Another class for whom restrictions are
suggested in the Bill are pharmaceutical
chemists. Pharmaceutical chemists have
heretofore been exempted, but now the suggestion is that those only will be exempted
who are duly registered, who are the proprietors of a business and have in their
employ no duly qualified person or persons
to assist them. Under recent legislation in
connection with the Dangerous Drugs Act the
proprietor of a pharmacy has serious responsibilities. He is responsible for the safe
custody of all drugs coming within the
Dangerous Drugs Act, and he is responsible
under heavy penalty. Certain potent drugs
are only used in emergency cases, and by
Act of Parliament the proprietor must keep
in his possession the key of the poisons lock.
I would submit that, even though a pharmaceutical chemist should have a qualified
assistant, he is not permitted by law to delegate his authority on potent drugs to any
assistant, whether qualified or otherwise.
In a case of life and death it might be a very
serious thing if the head of the firm, the
responsible proprietor who must carry the
key, should be absent from his business, and
I would appeal to the Minister to take this
matter into his serious consideration.
Chemists and druggists and registered
druggists are not exempted, and yet they
come under the same restriction in the
Dangerous Drugs Act. In quite a number of
towns in the North of Ireland there are no
pharmacies, and as a rule in those little
towns, poisons are distributed through the
only registered druggist. The registered
druggist cannot have a qualified assistant, so
under circumstances of that sort he is the
only one who can supply poisons or medicines
containing poisons. One of the poisons used
most frequently in these country places is
laudanum, and that is used in connection
with sicknesses of horses. I can quite
imagine that a farmer coming a very considerable distance into one of these small
towns to get medicine for a horse that was
in a dangerous condition would be very much
upset if, owing to the absence of the druggist
on jury service, it was impossible for him to
get relief for that animal on that day, or,
perhaps, two or three days subsequently. In
the meantime he might lose his horse. I
would appeal to the Minister that chemists
and druggists and registered druggists should
be treated in the same way as pharmaceutical
chemists.
In a short time these bodies will be one.
We have a new Pharmaceutical Society, and
it is only a question of a year or two until
they all amalgamate as pharmaceutical
chemists. I think it would be a matter of
anticipatory courtesy, apart from this
question I have raised, that the same treatment should be meted out to chemists and
druggists and registered druggists as is meted
out to pharmacists.
Mr. GEORGE HENDERSON: I would like
to join in congratulating the Minister of
Home Affairs, on the very full explanation

areas. I gathered that from him.

ing laws.

There is one other matter I want to refer

in the High Courts in the City of Belfast to

Sir DAWSON BATES indicated assent.
Mr. G. HENDERSON: I think that radius
is much too wide, but this is really more a
Committee point than a Second Reading
point. It is a great injustice to bring men
a distance of twenty-five miles to serve on
juries in the High Courts. I understand
that sometimes these courts will last as long
as six weeks. It is a great hardship to bring
a man twenty-five miles. It is all very well
to talk about the service jurors do in the
city. The city man can get a tram and go
to the Courthouse, and if he is not called he
can go home and attend to his business, but
if you bring a man twenty-five miles to serve
in the High Courts in the City of Belfast he
cannot go home in the next half hour and
start his work again. I think the area should
not be enlarged, or if it is enlarged it should
be a very much smaller area than is proposed.
The other point I want to touch upon is
this. It is certainly a pity the Government.
in this Bill have not seen their way to adopt
the recommendation of Lord Justice Andrews'
Committee, and to pay jurors who travel
over ten miles at least their out-of-pocket
expenses. The Home Minister in justifying
the Government in not adopting that recommendation said it would clearly be a new
principle. I think after fifty years it would
not be an unpardonable sin if one new principle was introduced into this Bill to do
away with an injustice that has prevailed for
fifty years. Of course, the right hon. Gentleman put this on a very high level and
wanted to talk about the privileges of citizenship, but when you summon, at a distance of
25 miles, to serve as a juryman a small farmer
who has not the money to pay his expenses,
it is very hard for him to raise his patriotism
to that pitch. I do hope that before this Bill
goes through this House the Government will
see its way to change its attitude in this
one respect, and will pay jurors who are
summoned a distance of over ten miles at
least their out-of-pocket expenses.
I have known of my own experience and
I suppose I am not the oldest man in this
House, although I am creeping up-men summoned to serve on juries in the City of
Belfast, and because they had not the money
to pay their railway fares they tramped
seventeen or eighteen miles to the Court and
back again at night. If you try that you
will find your patriotism evaporates before
you get to the end of the thirty-four miles.
Therefore, I do appeal to the Government to
introduce at least one new feature into this
thing, which has not been revised for fifty
years, and pay these men at least their outof-pocket expenses.
Dr. MORRISON: One or two suggestions
have been made in regard to changes and
alterations that I would like to comment
upon. The first is the proposal to abolish
the grand jury. I have always thought it was a
wise thing that the person placed in the dock
should have the protection of a jury, and it
is a further benefit for him to have the protection of a grand jury. I can easily understand a case happening where there was a
prejudice against a particular man or
against his religion, or his principles, that
may influence a decision, and the decision
would be injurious to him. Therefore, I
think that the more protection a man can get
the greater is the advantage. I do not believe
that substituting a judge for the grand jury
would meet the case. My experience of
judges, and I speak with a certain amount
of trepidation as there are prospective judges
in this House-
Mr. DEVLIN: They are in the smokeroom.
Dr. MORRISON: My experience of judges
is rather unfortunate, because I think that
everyone in connection with the Crown, from
the Crown prosecutor up to the judge, when
he sees a man in the dock at the instance
of the Crown assumes that he is guilty. It
is a principle of British law that until a
man is proved guilty he is assumed to be
innocent, and the Crown, in my opinion, is
biased by force of habit in the other
direction. On that ground, therefore, I
would object to the abolition of the grand
juries.
•
Secondly, the grand jury is a very old
institution. It discharges not only its
functions for finding bills, but also social
functions. It brings people together. It
enables me, for instance, as I happen to be
a grand juror, to meet my hon. Friend, the
Jury Laws Bill-
Second Reading.
HOUSE OF COMMONS
[Dr. Morrison]
Member for Derry (Mr. Leeke), and round
the social board to shake hands and spread
the friendship and common feelings of
citizenship that should animate us all. I
agree with the sentiment expressed by Goldsmith when he said:
I love everything that's old: old friends,
old times, old manners, old books, old wine.
The grand juror thinks it an honour to be a
member of that august and influential body,
and I think the same spirit should animate
the common juror. He is performing very
important duties, and he should feel it is a
privilege for him to occupy that position.
The injustice that was done-and in my
opinion it was a very serious injustice-to
the small farmer will be remedied by this
Measure, notwithstanding the fact that since
land purchase became practically uniform
over Northern Ireland, indeed over all Ireland, and since the farmer became the
owner in fee, it was his duty to serve as a
juror if he was summoned. Some men who
could not afford to bear the expense were
summoned at very serious inconvenience, as
I know from very small farmers in my own
district. That, I think, will be abolished by
this Bill.
Then there is the question which I think
is a vital one, namely payment of jurors. I
remember ten years ago trying to start a
party to bring about reforms in connection
with injustices and grievances that were common to the whole country, and to do it by a
non-political body. One of the things that I
had down in the programme was the payment
of jurors. We had a big meeting in Coleraine, the whole question was discussed, and
subsequently I had conversations with men
occupying high positions on the Bench, and
they told me of the enormous diffculties that
presented themselves the moment you attempted to alter the jury law. They told me
that to pay jurors in Ireland would involve
an expenditure of something like £17,000 a
year.
This is an age of economy, and, seeing that
we have set free the small farmers, to whom
an injustice had been done, and upon whom a
heavy task had been laid, is it a wise thing
for us to adopt this principle of the payment
of jurors? You have, for instance, in the
County Insurance Committee, dealing with
the question of tuberculosis, members paid
for their services. If you extend that
principle to jurors, you have also the same
right to extend it to members of boards of
guardians and to members of rural district
councils. You are extending a principle that,
I think, will certainly involve the country
in extra expense and in extra taxation. I
think that the principle is a bad one, and
that it should not be adopted by us.
Economy, in my opinion, is the first and most
important lesson that we have to learn in
Northern Ireland to-day, and if we violate
this principle in the matter of the payment
of jurors I think we will be making a mistake.
Mr. DEVLIN: I would like to start by
congratulating the right hon. Gentleman, the
Minister of Home Affairs, on his remarkably
lengthy, and, as far as he went, extremely
lucid speech, because for length I have not
heard anything like it since Gladstone introduced his Home Rule Bill in 1886. In fact,
the next greatest speech I ever heard before
this one was the speech of Mr. Lloyd George
introducing his famous Budget. Then the
Imperial Parliament had to adjourn for two
hours to give him a rest, and I was thinking,
having regard to the length of the right hon.
Gentleman's speech, in all consideration and
humanity, of suggesting a rest for him. The
lucidity of the speech was remarkable in this,
that it was not made so much for the purpose
of making clear what was in the Bill, as trying to obscure what was not in the Bill.
That is the only justification that I can
understand for the rally which the hon.
Member for the University (Dr. Morrison)
has made to the assistance of the Government. He has delivered a fine old Tory
speech worthy of half a century ago. He has
told us about "old friends, old times, old
manners, old books, old wine," and he wants
to show us that the only safety for existence
rests in the preservation of antique institutions. The hon. Gentleman who has just
sat down has asked why should a juror not
discharge the duty he is called upon to discharge without payment, just as a member
of a rural district council. My answer to
that is this, that in the one case it is compulsory, and that in the other case it is not.
A man can serve upon a rural council when
the meeting place is very near his own home
if he likes, but in this case a man is compelled to come a long distance, very often
under not very attractive conditions, and to
give his time and his attention to public
work without being paid for it.
But I do not understand the principle
the hon. Gentleman has laid down, that there
should be no payment for public service.
Has he not accepted it as a Member of Parliament? Is it not accepted by the Ministers?
Is it not the rule and law in the matter that
judges are paid, and if you pay Cabinet
Ministers and pay Members of Parliament
and pay judges, and pay lawyers to prosecute,
and pay lawyers to defend, simply because
you are using their professional capacity and
their time, what justification have you for
denying payment to a juror, who is in an
infinitely worse position to give his time and

his services, and who, as in the case of my

All these things are things that the ordinary juror has to do, but he is the one class
of citizen less capable of doing it than any
other, and then the hon. Gentleman answers
it by saying there is nothing in the world
so fine as good old wine. The hon. Gentleman attacked the judges in his usual style
and charm. He almost went as far as I ever
went in his references to judges and Crown
prosecutors and other permanent and enduring corner-stones of the State. He told us he
did not like to speak frankly, as he was in
the midst of potential judges. He was not
in anything of the sort; all the potential
judges were in the smokeroom, and my own
view is that the hon. Gentleman took an
unfair advantage of his legal colleagues in
the Government party by making that sweeping declaration against the sacrosanctity of
those whom he calls prospective judges.
This Jury Bill was proclaimed as one of
the chief marks of the excellence of the
present Government.. It was to be one of
their star Measures, and it must have been
so regarded by the Home Secretary when, as
I have said, he gave so much of his own time
and study, and occupied so much of ours, in
explaining it. What single abuse does it remove? In what way does it simplify the jury
system? In the first place, you would hardly
ever have heard of the necessity for changing
the jury laws if it had not been for the
elamant demand of those who are legally
jurors for payment for their services. That
is really what caused so much controversy in
the newspapers, the injustice that is done to
jurors in this way. You are going to add to
the number of jurors, but you would not
have had to do so to such an extent if you
had accepted the recommendation of Lord
Justice Andrews' Committee to make a jury
of six instead of twelve. You are extending
the distance which jurors must travel to
25 miles of the City of Belfast. The right
hon. Gentleman may just contradict me as I
go along, because I want to meet anything
he has to say.
But of all the extraordinary things I ever
heard in order to justify this Measure-and
this was the argument about which he got
so intensely indignant when I ventured most
modestly and moderately to interrupt him-
I never heard anything to equal the proposed
change in the law to prevent men transferring their property to their wives if they
otherwise would be compelled to act on a
jury. Was there ever such a preposterous
statement made, not only by any Minister,
but by any sensible man, that because I am
not a juror at present I am transferring all
my property to my wife in order to prevent
my being put upon the jurors' list? Surely
the right hon. Gentleman was not serious
when he put forward that proposition.
I suppose that on this matter I disagree
with everybody, but I am going to state my
point of view. Lord Justice Andrews' Committee recommended the abolition of grand
juries in the case of Quarter Sessions. For
my part, I am in favour of the abolition of
grand juries everywhere. I do not believe
in them at all. I did not know what their
functions were until I heard it described by
my honourable, humorous, and delightfully
frank Friend who sits opposite. (Dr.
Morrison). He told us what the function of
the grand jury was. I thought he was describing not a trial, but a social saturnalia,
from the description he gave. He said that
the grand jury was a gathering of good old
Tories, assembled not in a Court of Justice
but round the festive board in which they
drank their wine and paid mutual compliments. They shook each other by the hand,
and roused old memories; they fostered good
feeling and developed old friendships, and
concluded by singing "Auld Lang Syne." I
think that is not an exaggerated description
of the grand jury given by the hon. Gentleman. But was there ever such a farce as to
preserve an institution for the purpose so recited by the hon. Gentleman?
I know what the grand juries were for. They
were political institutions in the old daysa collection of seasoned Tories brought into
Court to be addressed by a Tory judge who
was an ex-politician, and who, having no
further opportunities of making political
speeches, used to make them to the grand
juries. That was the grand jury, as I understand it, of the old days; that is what my
hon. Friend wants to perpetuate still. I
am opposed to that altogether. I agree with
Lord Justice Andrews' Report that they
should be abolished at the Quarter Sessions.
I go further, and say they should be abolished
altogether. In the first place, they take up
the people's time. Here were litigants, common jurors, busy lawyers, all sitting in court
until the grand jurors marched forth from
the festive board, after the High Sheriff had
proposed the toast of the judges and told
them what magnificent men they were. They
replied, and told the High Sheriff what a
grand character he was, and then further
speeches were delivered by civic and Ulster
statesmen upon what grand administrators
they were, and meantime the scales of justice
were unmoved.
These affairs went on in a practical community like Ulster, where we are supposed
to do our business on business lines. I say,
therefore, that the grand jury should have

Mr. CRAWFORD: I think in regard to
this Bill it will, to a considerable extent, help
the poorer people in the Six-County area.
The raising of the qualification will exempt
them from attending the Courts, and will
help them in some measure. I do not quite
follow the hon. Member for West Belfast
(Mr. Devlin) regarding the 25 miles radius.
If I understood the right hon. Gentleman
(Sir Dawson Bates) aright, this refers only
to city people living within 25 miles of

Mr. DEVLIN: If I might interrupt the
hon. Member, I do not object to that. I
think it was quite right to make these
people serve on juries, but my point was

Mr. CRAWFORD: I think it would be a
wise thing if the Government, before the
Committee or Report Stage, could see their
way to do what they ought to do, and that
is that jurors who are summoned from a
considerable distance to the place where
justice is being administered, should receive
their out-of-pocket expenses. Just imagine
five juries being sworn-sixty jurors. The
jurymen fortunate enough to act in one case
would get 5s each, but the other forty-eight
jurors, who were not called on would have
to go home and pay their own expenses. I
really think something ought to be done, and
that they should be paid their out-of-pocket
expenses. I believe that would be favourably received in the country. Such remuneration has always been demanded by
those who served on juries in the past. I
agree with the hon. Member for Down (Mr. T..
W. McMullan) that commercial travellers
ought to be exempt, and a case might be
made also for the managers of business
houses, who are called away from their
business, which is thus disarranged in their
absence.
I do not see why teachers should be
exempted. If a teacher is taken out of a
school, arrangements can be made to do his
work in his absence. The same thing applies
to any business. If one class of person
claims exemption any other class would have
an equal right to make that claim. I think
the officials of the Court could easily ascertain
whether or not any cases were to be tried
at Quarter Sessions. Little trouble or expense would be entailed by sending the
jurors notice and saving them coming to
Court when perhaps there was only one case
--and perhaps no case at all-to be tried.
Clergymen come within the exemptions, but
I do not see why they should be exempted at
all. Another class of person who is exempt,
as described on page 16, is a person who
cannot read or write. How is the Minister
of Home Affairs, or his able Secretary, to
know whether they can read or write?
There are other persons, who, from lunacy,
imbecility of mind, deafness, blindness, or
other permanent infirmity, are unfit to
serve as jurors. I think that is a peculiar
expression, and I wonder who is to be the
judge of these things?
On the whole I would be in favour of
voting for the Second Reading of this Bill.
But I earnestly hope that the Government
will see their way to make some concessions
in the Committee Stage. The most important
one, so far as my opinion is concerned,
would be that jurors should be paid, at least,
their out-of-pocket expenses. I would not
like, however, that this should be put on
the county councils, and that they would
put the cost on the rates. I would not like
the Government to walk along that line. I
am all for economy. (Laughter.) Members
may laugh, but economy is not cheese paring.
Economy is good management. The thing
could be managed so that the poorer section
would receive some help. Why should they
have to do service without being paid? Go
to a Court of Law and you will find the
lawyers are paid, win or lose. Everybody is
paid except the poor jurors, who can
hardly afford the expense of travelling from
their homes. I suggest that the Government
would be doing a good service to themselves
and a good service to the community in
arranging that the out-of-pocket expenses of
these jurors would be paid.
Mr. MILLER: There is one point I
would like to make in answer to the Minister of Home Affairs. The right hon. Gentleman has given us a great lecture on the
duties of citizenship, and I quite agree with
him, but it should be equal citizenship. At

Mr. GYLE: As one who has served on both
common and grand juries, I feel that the
grand jury system is one that should be
abolished. I was sorry, indeed, to find that
the grand jury system was not abolished in
this Bill. Those of us who have served on
grand juries know that it is nothing but a
farce from beginning to end. We go upstairs
with the various Bills, and when you get upstairs you find that there is scarcely a grand
juryman who knows what the first procedure is. Then you ask someone who has
happened to be there before to take the
chair. A general conversation ensues around
the table, and the Bills are passed down and
marked "True Bill." That has been my experience, and I have served on grand juries
on several occasions.
With regard to the commercial travellers,
I quite agree that there is a considerable
amount of hardship existing regarding them.
Often and often we know that the traveller
makes up his journeys perhaps for a month
or even six weeks ahead. I would suggest
that if you cannot see your way to exempt
the commercial traveller that at least he
should get six months' notice before he is
going to be called on for service. He only
receives 21 days' notice at the present time.
I suggest he should get six months'
notice. He would then be in a position to
go down to the Sub-Sheriff and arrange with
him whether it would be convenient for him
to attend at the particular time he was summoned for, or whether an arrangement could
be made whereby he could attend a subsequent time. These are little things, but
they are important to many men who have
to find time to attend on juries.
There is another thing in connection with
the juries. I think there should only be
a sufficient number of men summoned to
take up the likely business for one week
at a time. I have found myself summoned
on a jury and have often had to attend
every day for three weeks, and yet was never
called on to serve on a single jury. Over
and over again that has occurred. Why it
has occurred I do not know, but I do find
that on many occasions a juryman has been
summoned say on Monday. He goes away
after being discharged on Tuesday, and when
he came back on Wednesday he was again
summoned to serve, and so on right through
the whole time the Court was sitting. Ι
think some arrangement should be come to
whereby alternate weeks could be taken, and
the matter so arranged that we would not be
summoned to attend for three weeks in succession when perhaps only one week was
necessary.
I hope that there will be some amendments put forward in connection with this
Bill. I am sure it would be competent for
this House to arrange for six jurymen instead
of twelve. We all know the old saying, that
the best committee of any is a committee of
three and two do not attend. That is
usually the best committee you will find to
do work. When you have twelve men acting
on a jury you find one or two dominating
the others. The other ten men are not
thinking anything about the case. They are
rather wondering how soon the verdict is
going to be brought in so that they can get
off to attend to their business. I do hope
that if it is not competent to do this
in this Bill the Government will impress on

are quite competent to deal with all cases
except those cases where men are brought up

men are, I think, quite competent to deal
with them. As I say, I hope that this
Government, if it is not competent to carry
out this reform, will impress on the Imperial Government that in the very near
future something of that sort will be done.
Mr. LEEKE: I would like to join with
those members who expressed the view in
favour of the payment of jurors. All jurors
should at least get their expenses. Consider
the position of the small farmer who is
probably fifty miles from the Court in which
the Assizes or Quarter Sessions are held.
He is summoned there and has to remain
perhaps for three or four days' time, which
is very valuable to him. He may or he may
not be called on to serve, but he has to remain there in any case, otherwise he will be
seriously fined. That fine will be imposed
on a man whose finances are unable to stand
the strain at the present time.
I would also like to join with the Member
for Antrim (Mr. Crawford) when he says
that this should not be a local charge. The
local rates can bear no further financial
strain. I think it is the duty of the Government to make this a national charge. The
Government has shown a weakness recently
to push all possible charges on the local
rates. They are throwing the duty, which

has always been the duty of a Government,
on to the people responsible for the finances

I found that the consideration shown to common and special jurors was the worst I
have ever seen. Judges were received with
all the pomp and ceremony associated with
the Courts; officials were specially attended,
and even the police had special provision
supplied; but the jurors were kicked about
and ordered about. Not the slightest consideration was shown to them either by
judge, officials or anyone else. I think it is
the Government's duty to see that in future
special consideration is shown to these men,
who are largely composed of agriculturists.
They are not treated in the way that men
who are performing the highest duties of
citizenship should be treated.

I have always noticed the treatment which

whenever they were wanted. They
never told when the Court would adjourn, or

again expressed. I think it is not the intention to abolish the ornamental system of
Grand Juries at Assizes; it is only as regards

Mr. HANNA: In rising, as I hope, to

What they complain of are some matters in

Mr. HANNA: It does not necessarily follow

The debate has resolved itself, as I have

One thing that is opposed is the fact that
we have retained Grand Juries. I have never
listened and I say it with great respect —
to a greater travesty of the functions of a

describe the functions of a Grand Jury.
than I have listened to to-day. The hon.

West Belfast, in this regard, said that he
did not know until the hon. Member for the

what the functions of a Grand Jury were,
and, having flippantly dealt with the observations of the hon. Member (Dr. Morrison),
he proceeded to tell us all he thought a

listening to an ex-political judge making

However, it is perfectly clear that the

As has already been indicated in the House
this matter was left a few months ago to

a free vote in the Imperial House, and that

The next matter raised was the question
of reducing the number of the jury. That
is not within our province at all. We must
not, and we cannot deal with that. Then
another matter was the payment of jurors.
The hon. Member for Down (Mr. T. W.
McMullan) who sits behind me was, I think,
perfectly frank about the matter. He said
that it would be a popular thing. There is
nothing that makes more for popularity than
to get control of money, whether it be your

give it out for anything. It is a very popular thing, and I am sure that any hon. Member of this honourable House, who on every
possible occasion votes for the handing out
of money, will rank amongst our most popular Members. But is it a right and a proper
thing to pay jurors? The answer to that
must be a distinct "No." On the question
of principle the answer to it is a distinct
"No." What can be done to make jury
service reasonable, and fair, and proper,
those were the matters to which the Government had to apply their minds, and the Bill
. indicates what they propose to do in that
regard.
May I just indicate in a word some of those
things? It is true that a great number of
jurors have in the past been summoned to
attend at Court-by reason of the state of the
law as it stands to-day, great panels had got
to be summoned-and it is true that when they
arrived there was not a great deal of work
for them to do, but that is practically
finished now, because it will be within the
competence of the judge presiding in the
Court to divide his panel into one, two, three,
or more sections, so that he will only make
such demands upon the attendance of jurors
as are absolutely necessary to have the work
of his Court carried out. That is one thing
that has been done.
The hon. Member (Mr. Leeke) opposite says
that the jurors have been subjected to very
bad treatment both by judges and by officials,
and the hon. Member for Tyrene and Fermanagh (Mr. Miller) says that they are
herded about like cattle. I venture to
suggest to those hon. Members that they
should be very careful in regard to statements of that kind. I have had twenty-five
years' experience in constant practice, both as
a solicitor and as a barrister, and I have never
known any juror to be subjected to any
indignity or to be put to any inconvenience
that any judge or any official of the Court
could have avoided. But even if there were
any justification for the extravagant
language of the hon. Members in this regard,
the Bill in one of its sections proposes to
provide meals for jurors if the judge requires
their attendance in Court. We have, then,
made provision that the panel can be divided,
we have made provision that the jurors will
be accommodated, and everything that could
be thought of within the power of the
Government has been done for their convenience.
The hon. Member for the University (Dr.
Morrison) made one observation which I am
sure must have escaped him without due
thought, but it would not be right that it
should go without some comment by way of
contradiction. In making his case for the
continued existence of the Grand Jury, he
indicated that the Grand Jurors were the
only people in court who had not already
condemned a prisoner. In giving expression
to that thought the hon. Member said that,
from the humble officials of the Court up,
they had all, when they saw the man in the
dock, made up their minds that he was guilty
already. It is my privilege as well as my
duty to offer an immediate contradiction of
that statement. I am bound to say, and 1
think it must be the experience of us all who
have ever taken part in any Criminal Court
in any capacity, that our judges are particularly hard to persuade of the guilt of a prisoner
-(hon. Members: Hear, hear)-and I do not
think it would be right that that statement
should go without contradiction.
The hon. Member (Mr. McAllister) who
shares with me the honour of representing
County Antrim, and who sits opposite, raised
the point that the Government have dealt
unfairly with the Clerks of the Crown and
Peace in connection with their remuneration.
As this is a very technical matter, perhaps
the House will bear with me if I stick very
closely to my note in connection with it.
The hon. Member's suggestion was that we
were making an onslaught upon the emoluments paid hitherto to the Clerks of the
Crown and Peace. We do no such thing.
The Clerks of the Crown and Peace will be
paid under this Bill all that they were entitled to be paid, and the amount that they
have always been paid. Under the Jury
Acts, 1871 to 1876, the Lord Lieutenant was
empowered to fix scales of remuneration for
the officers who had duties under the Jury
Acts, including Clerks of the Peace. At
Jury Laws Bill--
Second Reading.
HOUSE OF COMMONS
[Mr. Hanna]
that time Clerks of the Peace and Clerks of
the Crown were paid mainly by fees, but by
the County Officers and Courts (Ireland) Act,
1877, the offices of Clerks of the Crown and
Peace were amalgamated so far as new
entrants were concerned. These amalgamations took place as vacancies occurred, and
were completed in all counties in Northern
Ireland many years ago.
The Act provided that, after the union of
offices, the Clerks of the Crown and Peace
were to receive a consolidated salary payable
by the Treasury, and Section 21 provided
that all fees, which were then payable in respect of their duties to Clerks of the Crown
and Peace, should be paid into the Treasury,
but that they should be allowed to keep such
part of the fees as would cover their actual
out-of-pocket expenses of doing the work.
The revision of Jurors' Lists is specially referred to. The intention of the Act is clear
that Clerks of the Crown and Peace were to
receive no personal profit other than their
salaries. The remuneration of Clerks of the
Crown and Peace, that is, as between the
Clerk of the Crown and Peace and the
County Council, has been fixed by various
Orders in Council, the last of which are
dated 26th November, 1919, and 5th November, 1920. The scale is £20 up to 500 names
on the general list of jurors, and 8d for every
additional name, and £5 up to 500 names, and
2d for each additional name, for all names
appearing on the Special Jurors' Book.
An Order in Council dated 2nd February,
1920, provides that this remuneration, which
is collected by the Clerk of the Crown and
Peace from the County Council, is to be
divided into two moieties-one, representing
the profit, is to be paid into the Treasury,
and the other, representing the amount of
the out-of-pocket expenses incurred in the
preparation of the lists, is to be retained by
the Clerk of the Grown and Peace. This
Order in Council merely continues an arrangement which has been in force for many
years, and is based on the assumption that
it actually cost the Clerk of the Crown and
Peace one-half of the remuneration in outof-pocket expenses.
The Clerk of the Crown and Peace does not
require assistance throughout the year for
the purpose of the Jury Lists. His work
thereon does not begin until he receives the
lists from the county secretaries on the 1st
August, and is completed as soon as he sends
the lists to the Sheriff some time in December.
So far as the present Bill is concerned the
amount received by the Clerk of the Crown
and Peace for expenses will be increased for
the first year at any rate in Belfast, but will
probably decrease after that; it will only decrease in so far as the number of names is
reduced, and in the case of the Clerk of the
Crown and Peace, as distinct from that of
the county secretaries and the rate collectors,
his work will decrease in arithmetical proportion to the number of names. It is,
therefore, obvious that he will not require
the same amount of clerical assistance in
future as in the past, and that, therefore,
he ought not to receive the same amount for
expenses.
If the Clerk of the Crown and Peace argues
that he is losing any profit to himself, the
answer is that he should never have received
such profit, and that it was never intended
that he should do so. If, on the other hand,
he argues that 50 per cent. of the remuneration, which he receives from the county
council, will not cover his expenses, he will
have an overwhelming case for obtaining a
revision of the 50 per cent. basis in his
favour, provided he proves his case by the
production of proper vouchers.
The hon. Member for County Antrim (Mr
George Henderson) was rather confused when
he suggested that the Bill extended the area
from which jurors were chosen. The twentyfive miles referred to in the Clause of the
Bill which was then in his mind is the area
within which those members of the public,
who have a rated valuation in the City of
Belfast, may be brought to serve in the City
of Belfast.
I do not know that there is really any
other matter I should mention, except to
point out, as I might have done earlier, but
will do now, that the hardships that were
inflicted in the old days on people in very
humble circumstances will all disappear now.
It will now be impossible for a juror's summons to be served upon any man who would
not have the means to pay his train fare or
'bus fare to the court, because no man whose
valuation is less than £16 will be called upon
to perform any service as a juror. It is the
sincere hope of the Government that many
reliefs will be experienced by the general body
of jurors in the country, and I respectfully
take this opportunity of stating to the House
that in my humble belief they have made
great progress along the road to that desired
end.
