here. That is not true. The State is paying
for the dispensary system in connection with
the poor-law. Therefore, the statement made
by the hon. Member for West Belfast is not
in accordance with the facts. This is a matter, not for a particular class, but for the
State, and the safety of the State. Any man
who has given any thought to this question
will recognise that the safety of the State
comes first, and that if the State gets into
debt it will ultimately crumble to pieces, and
the whole fabric of our social system in
Northern Ireland will disappear.
I regret that the hon. Member for West
Belfast is not here to listen to this discussion of the way in which the poor are
neglected in this House by men who so often
champion their interests, but who, when
matters like this are being discussed at a
critical point, are absent and neglecting
their duty. It is clear that the hon. Member
for West Belfast appreciates this point, because when the State was in danger he patriotically I am glad to admit it-led a recruiting crusade to enable the Army to fight
against the threatening invader. He recognised that it was the duty of the individual
to sacrifice not only his contribution, but to
sacrifice his property and his life, if necessary, in a state of emergency.
I think that, notwithstanding all the
severe things he said about us, we can
proudly look back upon our record of helping
the poor and the distressed, and that none
of those reckless charges that have been
made will be believed by the people who know
the record that we have behind us since this
Parliament was opened. I think the Government have met those of us who are defending
the ratepayers in a legitimate way by withdrawing this Clause in regard to the expenses
of revision of valuation. I recognise that
this Bill may be in some respects unpleasant. It is not a very pleasant thing for
any of us to have to reduce our expenses and
to economise, but it is a wise thing, and if
the Government have had to carry out this
unpleasant duty, I think they have made a
praiseworthy effort, and they should have
the support of every reasonable Member in
this House. I claim to be one such, and,
therefore, I approve of the Bill.
Economy Bill—
Third Reading.

Mr. GEORGE HENDERSON: In view of
Part IV and part of Clause 3 of this Bill, I
am left no option at all but to vote for the
rejection of the Measure. I agree entirely
with the "Irish News" when they call the
name of the Bill an entire misnomer. The
hon. Member for the University (Dr. Morrison) in his speech congratulated the Government on economising, but I do not know
where in this Bill the Government are showing economy except by putting their hands
into other people's purses. Take Part III,
with regard to the Dog Tax; up to the present that went, with the exception of the
charges for administration, to the relief of
local rates. Now the Government are taking
one-third of that. That means about £4,000
that the Government are taking of money
that went in relief of local rates in Northern
Ireland.
Then take Part V of the Bill-grants in aid
of local expenditure. In this part of the
Bill the Government are taking not £4,000
but £43,000 from the county councils of
Northern Ireland. That is a grant in relief
of rates which they have enjoyed since the
year 1888, and then the Government have the
audacity to say that they are compensating
the county councils by paying them an equal
sum from the Road Fund. That whole Road
Fund, according to pledges given in this
House, belongs to the county councils. Now
you are taking a grant of £43,000 that was
used in relief of rates, and out of the county
councils' own money, according to Government pledges, you are recouping that. It
would have been far more honest to have
done what the Chancellor of the Exchequer
did in the Imperial Parliament, namely, to
go direct and raid the Road Fund. This is
only an indirect way of doing the same thing.
This is done at a time when the Prime
Minister has stated in this House that the
Government are anxious to keep down rates
to their lowest level. It is done but a short
time after a very heavy additional burden
has been placed upon the agricultural industry by the Widows', Orphans' and Old
Age Pensions scheme passed last year. I am
not going into the merits or demerits of that,
because I believe it is a fine scheme in a
great many directions, but what is the
effect of it? I say that at the very lowest
estimate that Act put an additional burden
upon the agricultural industry of from
£170,000 to £180,000 a year. And yet, at this
time, the Government have seen fit to come
and take a grant that has been used up to the
present time in relief of local rates in order
to balance their Budget. And they call that
economy. I think it is deplorable, with the
rates as they are at present, crushing down
men who cannot afford to pay them, that the
Government should put such a proposal before this House and ask us to pass it.
Then, again, they come here and tell us
that they want to relieve agriculture, which
is our chief industry and the very basis of
all our prosperity, and yet, instead of giving
agriculture a little more relief, in order to
balance their Budget they are putting additional burdens on the industry. And that is
done at a time when they are taking from
the direct grant in relief of rates on agricultural land the sum of £32,000. I said in
this House last year, when the Widows,'
Orphans' and Old Age Contributory Pensions
Bill was before the House, that in my
opinion, considering the good health that
agricultural labourers enjoy as a rule, the
Government would be justified in saying we
had a perfectly fair claim in asking that on
that account the subscriptions asked for
from the employers and employees in the
agricultural industry should be reduced. I
think the figures now before the House
justify my contention then, and I do say
that if the Government feel that they are in
a position to reduce their contribution to
Health Insurance I think the fair and the
honourable way to have done it was to say
they would make a pro rata reduction in the
contributions of the employers and employees. I have no other course open to me
under these circumstances but to vote
against the Third Reading of this Measure.

succeeded to his own satisfaction, but I
think it was only to his own satisfaction, because I do not believe any right hon. or hon.
Member in the House feels that the hon.
Member for the University made a damaging case against the people who occupy these
benches.
I have come to the conclusion that there
should be a new orientation of policy so far
as this Government is concerned. We are
told it is absolutely impossible to afford this
thing, that owing to the Colwyn Committee
arrangement if we do not agree to these
proposals made in the British Parliament
our taxpayers are going to suffer. What
about the £2,500,000 that we paid into the
British Exchequer last year? I hold that
there is absolutely no justification for a
penny piece being paid into the Imperial
Exchequer as long as there is one hungry
man, woman or child in Northern Ireland.
You have no money for unemployment benefit. You have no money to give but a
guaranteed minimum benefit 80 far as
National Health Insurance benefits are concerned, but you can devote £2,500,000 of the
North of Ireland taxpayers' money for the
purposes of the upkeep of the Army, Navy,
and Air Force. I do not know how the
right hon. Gentleman views that question,
but the view I take of the matter is that
we should satisfy the needs of the community before we start to indulge in such
luxuries as an Army, Navy, and Air Force.
I am pleased to know, Mr. Speaker, that
you are associated with an organization
which is attempting to bring about a state
of affairs when an Army, Navy, or Air Force
will not be necessary. I think if the Government attempted to pursue a policy of that
kind we would not then have such ridiculous
proposals put before the House as we have
in this Economy Bill. The right hon.
Gentlemen have searched in every possible
direction to effect economies, and they can
only effect these economies at the expense of
the poor by reducing the State contribution,
in face of a solemn pledge and obligation
which the State undertook to fulfil between
three parties. Without consultation with
the other parties to the arrangement, the
State break through their bargain, and simply because this Measure has been put
through the Imperial Parliament, we are
asked to accept this arrangement in this
Parliament as being satisfactory. Having
listened with care and attention, and with
an open, unbiassed and impartial mind to
the case stated by the right hon. Gentleman
opposite, I am still unconvinced and I am
still very unrepentant of the attitude I
have taken up so far as this Measure is concerned.
Mr. ANDREWS: I feel it is necessary at
this stage that I should say a few words in
Third Reading.
Economy Bill—

HOUSE OF COMMONS
[Mr. Andrews]
reply to the hon. Member for West Belfast
(Mr. W. McMullen), because if I did not a
quite wrong impression would be created
throughout Northern Ireland. I understood
him to say that because of the arrangement
we had made as regards re-insurance in connection with the Unemployment Fund we
had really adopted a course which had been
a great disadvantage to the unemployed in
Northern Ireland. Nothing is farther from
the truth. I would remind the hon. Member
that before this agreement was made we
were receiving in contributions £17,000 a
week and we were paying out in benefits
approximately £53,000 a week, or, in other
words, something between £35,000 and £36,000
per week more than we were receiving, and
that we took the responsibility as a Government of going into debt to the extent of
about £4,000,000 in order that we might keep
in step with Great Britain in connection
with this all-important social service.
Now, it is perfectly obvious to those who
desire to know the truth that that could not
go on, that we had to consider whether we
would increase the contributions here or make
an arrangement with Great Britain which
would ensure for four years at any rate, and
probably for all time, that our unemployed
would be kept in exactly the same position
as the unemployed in Great Britain are.
After a great deal of difficulty we were able
to get this arrangement brought about, and
I think I can remember that when this reinsurance scheme was before this House it
was blessed by hon. Members opposite.
The PRIME MINISTER: Hear, hear.
Mr. ANDREWS: And yet now they turn
round and they say-
Mr. WILLIAM MCMULLEN: I regret to
interrupt the right hon. Gentleman, but if
he would consult Hansard he will find I
made a speech in which I analysed the figures
and pointed out that the arrangement with
the British Government could not possibly be
satisfactory. I said that the British Government were going to pay to the extent of a
million, and that under the parity arrangement our figure would be round about
£250,000. I pointed out that unless economies
were going to be effected that was
sufficient money to maintain the Fund for
twelve months. I put it to the right hon.
Gentleman as to whether economies would be
effected, and he said "No," and he repeated
that a moment or two afterwards. If he consults Hansard on that question he will find
that I pointed out that what was taking
place could not possibly be successful.

Mr. ANDREWS: Really, Sir, hon. Members cannot have it both ways. They must
either condemn this re-insurance arrangement and accept the consequences for what
will follow, or else they must agree that this
re-insurance scheme was a great benefit to
the workers of Northern Ireland who are
unemployed-which it, undoubtedly, is-and
then recognise the fact that we cannot give a
preference to the workers here over the
workers in Great Britain. You cannot have
it both ways.
Other charges were made against the
Government in reference to this Economy
Bill, and I think I ought to refer to them.
There was the charge that by it we are robbing the unemployed. We are doing nothing
of the kind. We are not taking a penny from
the unemployed through this Economy Bill,
because owing to our re-insurance scheme the
matter is adjusted by the equalisation payment, so that really it is quite wrong to
create the impression that we here on these
Benches have taken a course in reference to
this matter, which has re-acted against the
interests of our unemployed. Hon. Members,
if they have really studied the Agreement,
and understand it, must be aware of the
fact that it has been an enormous and incalculable benefit to them.
Then, as regards the charge that we have
robbed the contributors to the National
Health Insurance Fund, the insured persons,
and the approved societies. Again I maintain
that we have not broken a bargain. What
was the bargain that was entered into that
the approved societies would get the advantage of their efficient administration. The
Economy Bill does not interfere with that at
all. What the Economy Bill really does is
this. The approved societies got a great
many unexpected windfalls, and to some extent those windfalls are being taken from
them.
Again, hon. Members accused us of breaking a bargain; because it is now proposed
to reduce the State contribution. As a matter of fact this is not the first time the State
contribution has been reduced. Mr. Lloyd
George, who is the father of the 1911 Act, in
1920 came along and reduced the contribution
paid by the State for women from one-fourth
to two-ninths.
Further, it is suggested by hon. Members
opposite that because of some bargain which
they say was made, but which never was
inade, Health Insurance is never to be interfered with. I would point out to hon. Members opposite that there have been ning
Amending Acts in connection with Health
Insurance, and that, if the original bargain
was to be adhered to, if there was such a
bargain, it would have to be adhered to right
along the line.
Hon. Members opposite know as well as I
do that in the 1911 Act there was only 10s
of benefit paid to men for a contribution
here of 3d. At the present time there is a
minimum statutory benefit being paid of 15s,

and only a half-peany more of contribution
was asked from the workers. Practically
every approved society, in addition to the
statutory benefit payable, is paying
additional benefits, and, what is more, notwithstanding the payment of these additional
benefits, the accumulations, the reserves
associated with Health Insurance are
increasing, and increasing rapidly. After
the first valuation there was £1 per head of
insured persons. After the second valuation
there was £3 per head of insured persons.
Now, the most that this Bill does is that
to some extent it reduces the rate of increasing those reserves. Having regard to the
existing state of affairs, and to the fact that
the taxpayers ought to be considered, surely
it is not unreasonable to say as the Health
Insurance Funds are in such an extraordinarily sound condition, that for the time
being at any rate the State should not be
asked to give quite so much towards the
building up of the reserves which are really
not required under existing conditions.
The hon. Member for Antrim talked about
the Widows and Orphans Act. I accept a
large measure of responsibility for that Act,
and I am proud of the fact.

ORDERS OF THE DAY.
Emergency Powers Bill.
Order for Second Reading read.
Motion made and Question proposed: That
the Bill be now read a Second time.
Mr. BARBOUR: Hon. Members will recollect that in the course of an answer to a
question by the hon. Member for North
Belfast on the subject of coal supplies, I
announced the Government's intention of
seeking powers to protect the interests of the
community, especially of those who, through
lack of financial means, are least able to face
the hardships which an upheaval, such as is
occurring across the Channel, brings in its
train. The peculiar feature of the present
position is that the difficulties which face us
do not arise through any industrial dispute
or disagreement within our own borders,
where, I am glad to say, amicable relations
continue. Unfortunately, however, our
sources of supply of coal and certain imported foodstuffs have, for the time being, been
seriously interrupted, and although the
general public throughout Northern Ireland
has taken the position calmly and risen to
the occasion, there has been a tendency on
the part of some to endeavour to secure as
large stocks of supplies as possible, regardless
of the interests of the general community.
There are in our midst a number whose
means of subsistence are not such as to enable
them to take thought for the morrow by
laying in adequate stocks of fuel and food
while these were freely available. These less
fortunate members of the community must
be protected, not only against any difficulty
in securing their daily needs, which would
be likely to arise from panic purchases on an
unnecessarily large scale by those who can
afford to do so, but also so far as this is
practicable by means of regulation against
any unwarranted increase in prices of
essential commodities.
Now, turning to the Bill, which is in the
hands of hon. Members, I need make no
apology for the brief time given for consideration. If action on the lines I have
indicated is to be taken, it must be taken
now. (Hon. Members: Hear, hear.) It is
axiomatic that only the existence of very
exceptional circumstances would justify the
Government asking for powers to intervene
in the general commercial life of the community.
In 1920 the Imperial Parliament enacted a
Measure entitled the Emergency Powers Act,
to deal with a situation somewhat similar
to that which faces us to-day. That Act we
have adapted to local conditions. Stated
briefly, the Bill empowers the Governor,
when satisfied that a state of emergency has
arisen, to issue a proclamation that such
emergency exists, and, thereafter, to make
regulations for securing the essentials of
life to the community and for regulating the
supply and distribution of food and other
necessities.
Emergency Powers Bill-
Second Reading.
HOUSE OF COMMONS
[Mr. Barbour]
Before sitting down I should like to take
advantage of this opportunity of appealing to
the people of Ulster to take to heart the plea of
the Prime Minister of Great Britain, that the
community at large should bear with fortitude and resolution any inconveniences
which they may be called upon to face, and
so facilitate and support the efforts that the
Government is making to safeguard the
supply of the essentials of life for all classes
of the community. I beg to move.
Mr. KYLE: This Measure has been introduced in much haste, and even the right hon.
Gentleman himself says that the Bill under
the circumstances is not required for
Northern Ireland, that is to say the conditions here are normal. We all hope and
trust that they may remain normal in the
industrial field. (Hon. Members: Hear,
hear.) The right hon. Gentleman has
stated that the Bill is based on the Emergency Powers Act, 1920. It is because he has
left out two of the most important Clauses
in the Emergency Powers Act, 1920, that I
took the step I did a few moments ago, in
giving my opinion and the opinion of the
Opposition that this Measure should not be
rushed through this House this afternoon.
In the Emergency Powers Act, 1920, there
are two provisions which are not mentioned
at all in this Bill, and unless the right hon.
Gentleman is prepared to put these two provisions in, I shall give this Bill all the
opposition I possibly can. These are two
vital provisions. One of them is:
Provided that nothing in this Act shall
be construed to authorise the making of
any regulations imposing any form of compulsory military service or industrial conscription.
The other proviso, which is more important
than that is:
Provided that no such regulation shall
make it an offence for any person or persons to take part in a strike or peacefully
persuade any other person or persons to
take part in a strike.
These two Clauses are in the Emergency
Powers Act, 1920, which was passed by the
Imperial Parliament, and on which the
right hon. Gentleman is basing this Bill.
If the right hon. Gentleman can get up in
his place and say he is prepared to put these
two provisions in, it may modify considerably
the amount of opposition which will come
from these Benches. It is desirable that the
people of the Six Counties should remain
calm. It is also desirable that the Government should have control of the essential
foodstuffs. It is essential that they should
have control of the coal supplies. I am not
wanting to minimise in any way the importance of any of these factors in the
general situation. All I am concerned about
is that if the occasion arises, which heaven
forbid, we in the trade union movement in
Northern Ireland have got to take our stand
along with our comrades and brethren in
Great Britain in this huge industrial strike.
Now I want to see that the interests of the
trade unionists in Northern Ireland are
protected. We would be very much indebted
if some Member of the Government can say
whether or not they are prepared to put in
these two provisos. Limp and all as they
are, they do maintain some of the liberties
of the subject, and it is because I believe
that these two provisos should be in this
Bill that I want an assurance from the
Government that they are prepared to accept
Amendments along these lines. I have stated
that we are not opposed to the Government
getting control of the food supplies,
or the coal supplies, or anything
that would help to see that the people
are given the essentials of life. It is
essential at the present time with any
Government in power, to see after the supply
and distribution of food and water, and fuel
and light amongst the common people. It is
in order solely to see that the interests of
the trades unionists are protected that I am
offering this opposition to the Emergency
Powers Bill.
The PRIME MINISTER: The intention of
the Government in introducing this Bill was
to limit it as far as possible to the points
actually mentioned in the Measure. It was
not intended to go further afield for all sorts
of restrictions or references to other Acts
or anything of that sort. So far as the first
point referred to by the hon. Member is concerned, we have no power, even if we desired, to conscript in any way under the
Act of 1920. Therefore, it would not have
been within our ambit or powers to include
any section dealing with enlistment as suggested by the hon. Member. With regard to
the other point, of course, that is somewhat
different. There are slightly different conditions in Great Britain to what there are
here. I am as hopeful as anybody can be
that no untoward difficulties will arise in
Northern Ireland. Our sole object in this
Bill is to have the necessary powers in our
hands to prevent any panic or greed, or anything of that sort interfering with the
general public-large masses of the public,
and especially poor people, being deprived of
their fair share of food, coal and the other
amenities of life. I think that the hon.
Member will see that it is impossible for
us to cover everything or all exceptions, and
I do not think he need have any fear that
there is any ulterior motive behind the Bill.
except what appears on the face of it.

CLAUSE 2 (Emergency Regulations).
(1) Where a proclamation of emergency
has been made, and so long as the proclamation is in force, it shall be lawful
for the said Governor, by Order in the
Privy Council of Northern Ireland, to
make regulations for securing the essentials
of life to the community, and those regulations may confer or impose on any Minister
or Ministry of Northern Ireland, officer of
the Government of Northern Ireland (including any police officer or constable),
local authority, or other person acting on
behalf of the said Government, such powers
and duties as the said Governor may deem
necessary for the preservation of the peace,
for securing and regulating the supply and
distribution of food, water, fuel, light, and
other necessties, for maintaining the means
of transit or locomotion, and for any other
purposes essential to the public safety and
the life of the community, and may make
such provisons incidental to the powers
aforesaid, as may appear to the said Governor to be required for making the exercise
of those powers effective.

the Government of Northern Ireland on

The expenditure on national monuments is
expected to be greater by £400 than last year,
but much of this is for the purpose of overtaking arrears of maintenance, some of them
having been allowed to get into bad repair.
Section III summarises the main works
activities carried out by the Ministry of
Finance on behalf of other Departments of
our own Government. They are really
domestic works services. Each item will be
found charged in the appropriate Departmental Vote, so that hon. Members will probably be familiar with them. In this
connection, I should explain, for the benefit
of those Members who are not familiar with
our Estimates system, why a second opportunity is afforded to hon. Members to express
their views upon this expenditure. There is
a dual responsibility in connection with
work services.
(1) The responsibility of the requisitioning
Department for its requisition; and
(2) The responsibility of the Ministry of
Finance for the technical performance
of the work.
Our object in adopting this formula is to
ensure that our system does place responsibility for these Services upon the proper
shoulders, even though it entails the submission to Parliament on two separate occasions
of each item of expenditure. Sub-head "M"
shows in tabular form the various schemes of
new works, their total cost, the rate of progress expected, and the amount which it is
expected will be required for each in the
current year.
I am sorry to report that more rapid progress has not been made with the new
Central Employment Exchange in Corporation Street. This is due to a variety of
causes, but the Ministry is taking all possible
steps to expedite the construction of the
building, and we hope it will not be long be-
As regards new works generally, I should
mention that last year there were considerable under-spendings, owing to a variety of
unforeseeable obstacles which delayed the
commencement of building operations.
These difficulties are not unique or unusual,
as most of us who are familiar with architects and building contractors know.
The provision for Grants for the building,
etc., of Public Elementary Schools, which
will be found as the last item in the tabular
statement on page 30, is intended to cover
expenditure on building grants already
authorised by the Ministry of Education
where, for various reasons progress with
the works has been slower than we anticipated. The provision for this Grant Service
will disappear in due course, when the buildings are finished, as the responsibility for
the provision of schools now rests with the
various local school authorities in Belfast
and the Province.
The works required in connection with the
provison and equipment of the Training
College, a most important building at Stranmillis, and also the Hostel, are progressing
steadily, and the Ministry has recently
issued advertisements inviting tenders for
the erection of the new Lecture Block. It
is anticipated that the work at Stranmillis
will be commenced at a very early date.
Plans are being prepared for the adaptation
of Hampton House as a Hostel for the men
students, and work thereon will be almost
immediately commenced. Arrangements have
been made to take over an existing school at
Stranmillis, and to adapt it as a Practising
School, in order that pupils at the Training
College can obtain instruction in the practice of teaching. This is a very necessary
adjunct to the training college, and will practically complete the whole of the machinery
for the training of teachers for our Public
Elementary Schools. All this expenditure is
being recouped by the Grant of £400,000
given under the Colwyn Committee's award
for the purpose of making provision for these
large institutions, so that there is no cost
entailed on the Northern Government under
these heads.
The remaining sub-heads do not require
much explanation or criticism, as they include merely the sums necessary for the
upkeep of our offices and buildings. I should
state, however, in passing that every effort
has been made by the Ministry to reduce
the expenditure to the lowest degree compatible with the keeping of the buildings in
proper order and repair.

CLASS III. No. 3.
SPECIAL CONSTABULARY.
Motion made, and Question proposed:
"That a sum not exceeding £64,281 be
granted to His Majesty to complete the sum
necessary to defray the charge which will
come in course of payment during the year
ending on the 31st day of March, 1927, to
defray the Salaries and Expenses of the
Special Constabulary (12 and 13 Geo. V., c 8.
(N.I.)). (Note.-£100,000 has been voted on
account.)
Sir DAWSON BATES: I may point out
that following the settlement of the Boundary question and the final arrangement
arrived at, with the British Government
giving their assent to the sum of £1,200,000
to cover the cost of the Special Constabulary
to the end of the financial year and also the
cost of disbandment, we proceeded at once
to take steps to reduce the number of
Special Constabulary. The first two forces
dealt with were the "A" Special Force and
the "C 1" Special Force. The terms of disbandment were that each was to receive two
months' pay and allowance as a bonus.
Since December there has been a steady
process of disbandment, but hon. Members
will appreciate that a Force of this size cannot be disbanded all at once. Barracks had
to be evacuated, and the stores brought into
the depot and checked, and during that process, until each barrack is actually evacuated, there must be a certain number of men
in charge. The operations have, I am glad
to say, proceeded with great smoothness
during the past few months, with the result
that out of a total in Class "A" of 3,600,
only a little over 400 remained at the beginning of the current year.
Hon. Members will appreciate that in
dealing with the personnel of Class "A" it
is necessary to have men at Sprucefield,
where we have very valuable stores, which
have to be arranged with a view to their
sale at a subsequent date. The same remark
applies to Princes' Dock where the bulk of
the motor cars are being stored prior to their
sale. Many of these cars have been sold,
and we hope to be able to evacuate Princes'
Dock early in June. Then, again, we have to
keep a number of Special Constabulary at
Rosscor, looking after the ferry until the
bridge there is completed, but I hope that
the road and the bridge will be completed
by June.
Mr. BEATTIE: What about Ballyvarley?
Sir DAWSON BATES: My hon. Friend will
get an opportunity of discussing this Vote
afterwards.
Mr. BEATTIE: I wanted to know about
Ballyvarley Bridge.
Sir DAWSON BATES: Perhaps my hon.
Friend has discovered where it is.

we have a "B" Force?
Mr. DEVLIN: Hear, hear.
Sir DAWSON BATES: My answer is that
there is nothing that tends to the peace of
the community more than the fact that you
have a number of trained men ready to
answer a call if it should come. If at any
time, in any district, a disturbance should
break out we are now in a position to call
out whatever number of men is necessary.
Hon. Members will realise that we work with
a minimum of regular police, and so have
not a big reserve. If these "B" men are
called out for whole-time work they will
receive the ordinary pay of the "A" Special
Constabulary. They will also receive the
indemnity which every policeman has in
respect of injuries which he may receive, and,
in the case of death, the relatives will have
that indemnity. Hon. Members will observe
that there is a cash provision for a bonus of
£80,000 to the "B" Force. I might point out
that this comprises a bonus for the March
Quarter of last year, at £10, which is estimated at £45,000. The balance of £35,000 is,
roughly, three-quarters of the full annual
We are still going to retain Special Constabulary of the "A" class at a strength of
250 for the year. On 1st April, we had 374,
and we are asked to estimate for a strength
of 250 for the whole year. Of course, that
number includes 60 "A" Specials who are
doing duty under the Customs regulations
and their cost is recovered from the Imperial
Government. I understand these 60 men
might be necessary to assist the customs,
but it cannot be stated that 250 are necessary
for the year. If it is going to be implied
that 250 men are necessary as a guard for the
valuable materials that we have stored in
our depots, I think we are going to have a
very costly guard. When the winding-up
took place the Government should have
wound the Force up completely, and no
estimate should have been brought in this
year for a force which has now become nonexistent except for 250 men.
I understand that in the reduction of the
Force, those who were left over have been
very unfairly dealt with. I understand
that men with long experience, and officers
with families depending upon them, are being
dispensed with, and that younger men who
have only the experience they gained during
their term in the Specials are being retained.
I know for a fact that that has actually
happened in platoon offices. I believe that
in other offices preference will similarly be
given where influence is used. If it is going
to be a question of retaining a position in
the remaining 250 by influence, I am opposed
to any number being retained. I think at
this late hour of the day we should abolish
the 250, with the exception of the 60 men
required for Customs work.
In regard to the "B" Force, I do not
think that any case has been put up for
retaining it. Some hon. Members suggested
to put them on the dole. These men are
already on the dole. The only thing they
have been useful for in the past twelve
months has been guarding the homes of some
of the Members of the Government at night.

his duties, and there was never at any time
any suggestion of complaint against him as
to unfitness. But, suddenly, the right hon.
Gentleman's Department found that this man
was inefficient, after he had been four years
in the position, and they put forward
that lame excuse in order to avoid paying him
what he was entitled to. I think that course
would rightly be regarded as an insult to any
individual. The right hon. Gentleman did
not take the opportunity that he got in
March last to remedy this injustice, and I
think this Committee ought to express its
opinion of the Minister who is responsible for
the action of his subordinates in allowing
this man to suffer this injustice. I support
the motion to reduce this Estimate.
Mr. DEVLIN: In the previous discussion
that took place on the police Vote I did not
intervene, because I quite recognise that the
first duty of the State is to have an adequate
Police Force, and a Police Force that is not
only adequate in the public interest and for
the service of the State, but a Police Force
that would be decently and even generously
treated by the Government. But I rise to
oppose this Vote on principle. On the last
occasion on which I discussed the "B"
Specials, I objected to them upon this fundamental ground. I objected to policemen who
are not policemen. It is not a Police Force;
it is a class apart. They are private individuals given a bonus by the State for the
purpose of having some superior rights over
other members of the State. You may take
a street or road in which there are fifty
people living, and two or three individuals
in that street or road are specially selected
to have some superior right over the rest of
the community. I, as a democrat, object
entirely to the setting up of a class section
amongst the members of the community.
This Committee has not withheld from the
Government any claim the Government may
make for adequate financial support for the
maintenance of an ordinary Police Force.
There is no such Force in England. There
is no such Force in Southern Ireland. There
is no such Force in any democratically
organised community that I know of in
Europe. And why it should exist in Northern Ireland I do not know. I am sorry the
right hon. Gentleman, when submitting this
Estimate did not give the Committee some
reasons for its existence. My hon. Friend,
the Member for North Belfast (Mr. Kyle),
has stated that this is merely giving a grant
to your own political supporters. I think
that is the general view held by everybody.
Why should you select any particular and
specific members of the community, and give
them authority as policemen without being
policemen ? That is what you have done.
What is really the fact? You have in this
most extraordinary Force, 500 officers and 40
Who was the genius who conceived
that system-500 officers and 40 men? The
40 men were the wise men in the Unionist
Clubs, and the 500 officers were the English
garrison brought over to Ulster. I believe
these 500 officers are nearly all Englishmen,
and they were brought over here to rule 40
Irishmen. That is the explanation. It shows
once again the advantages that England can
always have over even Northern Ireland.
men.
Now, perhaps the right hon. Gentleman
(Sir Dawson Bates) will tell us why this
entirely useless expenditure is continued.
First of all, let him deal with the principle
involved, namely, that there should be no
policemen in the State unless they are policemen. You have been given all the financial
power you need to employ an adequate police
force. The right hon. Gentleman, the Prime

and out of it, that there is now peace in the
North of Ireland. We all agree that there

is peace. No one can question it. No doubt

The right hon. Gentleman, the Home Secretary, is in a difficulty about explaining that,
because he could not, but the hon. and

I have no doubt that what has not been

Vote for a reduction of this Estimate. One

Mr. T. W. MCMULLAN: I rise to support

We are glad that peace now reigns. We are

Mr. P. O'NEILL This Vote is for £164,281,
and I think if the Government are in earnest

I think it is quite unnecessary, and there is
no justification for it.
In speaking on the R.U.C. Vote, I said I
understood that the cost per head of the
population in the Six Counties was roughly
10s. In that Estimate I was out by a considerable amount, because I believe it would
come to 13s 4d. With the addition of the

Therefore, I think the time has arrived when

B men out at night in very bad times I do

Mr. WILLIAM MCMULLEN: I want to

Vote. The hon. Member (Mr. Cooper) who

class and others-and I say that, apart from

That appears to me to be a ridiculous proposition altogether. I do not agree with the
right hon. Gentleman that this force will perform the function he suggests, because if he
is right I think the way to keep absolute and
perfect peace would be to enrol every
citizen as a special constable. Pay us all £3
and then you will have a safe and absolute

sound why not extend it? You are confining
your principle to 15,000 people. If your
argument is sound that it is a proper way to

hope to be loyal citizens of Ulster-be enrolled as special constables, and then you
will be guaranteed that perfect peace which
the whole of us very much desire.
My strong objection to this is based, first
of all, on the fact that I do not consider this

to afford it. As the hon. Member for West

as far as this force is concerned. It appears

Under another item in this Estimate you

That is another item of £10,210 which is quite

and to spend an additional amount of £10,210.
Of course, it does not serve much purpose to

absurd, and the details are quite as absurd
as having 500 officers and forty men.
whole thing is perfectly ridiculous.

Mr. BEATTIE: What about the ex-

Mrs. CHICHESTER: I believe that, in
spite of the fact that some of those men feel

Perhaps we are too occupied at times in making gestures of friendship-of a friendship
which is not always reciprocated but I
would like to feel that we here send out from
this Committee a message to those men, which
will allay some of their feelings, and, perhaps, do a little towards wiping out some of
the grievances which they think, at the present moment, are theirs. We are to-day
closing the book, or rather nearly closing
the book, on the final chapter of a period
which brought forth everything that was
vilest and worst in our Province, but it was
a period which was illumined in its darkness
by the self-sacrifice of these men. That
should never be forgotten. They showed us
another side of the picture, and they were
instrumental in bringing about everything
that was best and noblest in Ulster to fight
and destroy the evil that was in our midst.
I do not think any words would really be
adequate to say what I think about these
men's deeds, or what I think of hon. Member's opposite, who can stand there and
decry what was accomplished by them.
Everyone knows-it would be only a platitude to say it-that prevention is better than
cure, and I think the best answer that can
be given to the hon. Member (Mr. W.
McMullen) opposite, who last spoke as to
the necessity for these men, is that if we
at the outset of our troubles had had a Force
like that ready and prepared and drilled,
our troubles might never have risen to the
height they did in this province, and that
the best way we can secure peace in the
future is to se that there is a Force of that
nature ready to our hand. I know quite
well our finances and our resources are not
unlimited, but I believe there are very few
in this province of loyal men, women and
children who would, at this particular time,
have grudged extra taxation if that were
necessary, to bring to the minds of these men
the fact that we realise and are grateful for
what they did for us during our troubled
years. I have very much pleasure in supporting the Estimate.
The PARLIAMENTARY SECRETARY OF
THE MINISTRY OF HOME AFFAIRS (Mr.

Moles, with your high sense of humour, must

many occasions outside, the Prime Minister
has stated that while he remained Prime
Minister the "B" Force would be continued.
There is no alteration in the terms in connection with the "B" Force-the £3 bonus
when peace has been restored--as was indi-
Supply-
Committee.
HOUSE OF COMMONS
[Mr. Hanna]
cated in the document that they had then.
There was no want of sincerity in the
expression of gratitude to the "B" men of
any Member who spoke from this side of the
Committee. We are all exceedingly grateful
to them for what they have done, and I
think it will be generally recognised and
appreciated that in making provision for
keeping 15,000 of these men we are acting
very wisely indeed. The hon. Member who
opened the debate could only discover 250
men.
Mr. BEATTIE: "A's."
Mr. HANNA: Then the hon. Member for
West Belfast discovered 500 officers and 32
men, but he did not turn over the page, and
of course he was very wise in that when he
wanted to make the point that he did make.
But his colleague turned over the page, and
he discovered that there was provision for
the bonus for 15,000 men. That accounts for
the necessity for so many officers as there are.
A great number of those officers-district
commandants-and sub-district commandants
-are only part-time men.
The hon. Member for Down (Mr. P.
O'Neill) said that no word had been spoken
to justify this Vote. I think every word that
has been spoken on this side has tended to
justify the Vote, but what does justify it
more than any words that can be spoken by
any hon. Member of this House are the deeds
done by the police in the performance of
their duty.
Mr. WILLIAM MCMULLEN: Why do you
not pension them?
Mr. HANNA: They do not want pensions.
They have not asked for pensions.
Mr. WILLIAM MCMULLEN: May I be
allowed to interrupt the hon. Member? Is
not the whole case of the Government that
owing to the meritorious service rendered by
these men consideration should be given to
them. I want to suggest to the hon. Member
that the best way to compensate these people,
if they have done something for the Province,
is to pension them, but the hon. Member,
after so eloquently praising the services that
these men rendered to the Province, now suggests that they are not desirous of pensions.
Was there ever anything more ridiculous-
The CHAIRMAN: I am afraid we cannot
discuss the subject of pensions since no such
item appears in the Estimates.
Mr. HANNA: The hon. Gentleman (Mr.
William McMullen) always mystifies me. I
could understand him asking pensions for
people who had come to the end of their service, but this is making provision for the
continued service of 15,000 men.
Mr. WILLIAM MCMULLEN : Had the
hon. Gentleman made that point I would
have been in perfect agreement with him.
If there is one point that has been made from
the Government Benches, it is that the men
have rendered splendid service to the Province, and as a result of that they should be
given consideration. All I am suggesting is
that, if they have given this great service to
the Province, why do you not do the obvious
thing and pension them? Our contention is
that a Force of that kind is quite unnecessary
and superfluous.
The CHAIRMAN: The hon. Gentleman
has made that identical point, that you could
not pension them and at the same time continue them in your service.
Mr. HANNA: Apparently, the hon.
Member thinks the only people who should
get anything are the people who do nothing
for anybody. He has told the Committee
that we cannot get any money for essential
services. I am perfectly sure he does not
forget that we find upwards of a million and
a half per year for the people in whom he
professes to be most particularly interested.
I think I have detained the Committee long
enough. I hope I have dealt with all the
general criticisms that have been offered.
I want to say, in conclusion, that I join very
heartily with the hon. Member for Derry
(Mrs. Chichester) when she gave expression
to the desire that this debate would do something to allay the feelings of any Members
of the "B" Force who may consider that they
are not being fairly treated, or treated with
absolute justice. I would like to say that the
Government is grateful for the services that
have been rendered, and hopes, in accordance
with what the Prime Minister has repeatedly
stated, that the "B" Force will continue as a
voluntary force. We do not suggest-it never
has been suggested-that anything they have
got in the shape of money has been a sufficient
reward; it was more in the nature of a token
payment to them. There will be no difficulty
in making arrangements as to the number of
drills they will have to perform; that is a
very minor matter. We are anxious to retain the services, loyalty and help of every
law-abiding citizen.
Question put: "That a reduced sum, not
exceeding £63,281, be granted to His Majesty
for the said purpose."
The Committee divided: Ayes, 6; Noes, 21.

HOUSE OF COMMONS.

Thursday, 6th May, 1926.
The House met at Three of the Clock,
Mr. SPEAKER in the Chair.
Oral Answers to Questions.
RETIREMENT OF POST OFFICE
OFFICIALS.
1. Mr. DEVLIN asked the Minister of Commerce whether it is a fact that retirement
in the Civil Service generally is fixed at 60
years, and that during the past four years
practically every Post Office official in Northern Ireland, who attained 60 years of age,
has been retained for additional periods of
from one to two years; whether he can state
the number of (a) head postmasters, (b)
salaried officials, and (c) other ranks (indoor
and outdoor) who are at present serving or
who have been granted periods of extension
beyond the age limit of 60; and whether he
will undertake to make representations to
the British Postmaster-General to have all
Post Office officials compulsorily retired at 60
years of age with a view to reducing the
number of unemployed in Northern Ireland.
The MINISTER OF COMMERCE (Mr.
Barbour): As the hon. Member is aware
the Post Office is a reserved service, the
establishment regulations of which are
common throughout the United Kingdom. It
will accordingly be readily appreciated that
it is not within my province to interfere in
these arrangements which are a purely
domestic matter of the Service concerned.
I, therefore, regret that I am unable to give
the undertaking referred to in the last part
of the question.
Mr. DEVLIN: Is it a rule of the Northern
Government that they do not interfere in any
degree with the administration of the Post
Office? Have the Northern Government
nothing whatever to do with the Post Office?
Mr. BARBOUR: We are consulted in
certain matters entirely at the discretion of
the Post Office, in which case, of course, we
express any opinion that seems to us desirable.
Mr. DEVLIN: The right hon. Gentleman
could not see his way to make representations on the lines I suggest in the question?
Mr. BARBOUR: No, Sir. As I have stated,
I think it would be an interference on my
part with the internal administration of the
Department.
LOWER BANN DRAINAGE RATE.
2. Mrs. CHICHESTER asked the Minister
of Finance whether he will state what
Authority is at the present responsible for
the drainage of the Lower Bann, and if that
Authority is the Lough Neagh Drainage
Board; whether the Trustees are bound to
apply the maintenance rates which they levy
to the drainage of the area subject to these
rates; and, if this is not the case, whether
he will state specifically the works in the
Lower Bann which they are bound to maintain, and on which the Drainage Rate is at
present expended.
The MINISTER OF FINANCE (Mr.
Pollock): Since the passing of the Drainage
Act of 1925-that is our Drainage Act-each
County Council is the Authority responsible
for the drainage of lands within its area.
The Lough Neagh Drainage Trustees are,
however, responsible for the maintenance of
certain portions of the channel of the
Lower Bann as well as certain other
works and watercourses in and surrounding Lough Neagh and the Lower Bann,
which are specified in the Award of
the Commissioners of Public Works dated
the 4th day of April, 1859, and of which I
have lent the hon. Member a copy. The
Trustees cannot apply the maintenance rates
levied by them to general drainage purposes
within the area subject to these rates, but
only to the maintenance of the works, etc.,
specified in the Award of the Commissioners
of Public Works which I have mentioned.
Mrs. CHICHESTER: Arising out of that,
is the right hon. Gentleman aware that in
a recent test case in regard to this Drainage
Rate the solicitor for the Lough Neagh Drainage Trustees definitely stated, with regard
particularly to the question of the Glenstall
River, which is mentioned in the Award to
which the right hon. Gentleman has referred,
that the Lower Bann Navigation Trustees
had no jurisdiction over that area, and in
fact had no control over that area at all
quite apart from the one to which I have referred?
Mr. POLLOCK: I am not cognisant of the
particular case to which my hon. Friend be
hind me has referred, but it would appear
to me that it is not competent either for
me or for the Government to interpret an
Act of Parliament. That lies within the
domain of the Courts, and if the person who
is aggrieved in this case will present it to
the Courts in the ordinary way, I have no
doubt that a legal interpretation of the
Award of the Commissioners of Public Works
will be given. I cannot go any further than
that, I think.
Oral Answers.
Bill Presented.
6 MAY 1926
BELFAST UNION-BOOT CONTRACT.
3. Mr. BEATTIE asked the Minister of
Home Affairs whether it is the fact that he
has refused to sanction a local boot manufacturer's estimate for supplying boots and
shoes for the ensuing twelve months to the
Belfast Board of Guardians.
The MINISTER OF HOME AFFAIRS (Sir
Dawson Bates): The Belfast Board of Guardians at their meeting on the 23rd ult., resolved to accept a tender for the supply of
boots, shoes and clogs from Messrs. Williamson, of Belfast, although the tender in question was not the lowest tender received by
them.
The action of the Guardians in this respect
is not subject to the sanction of the Ministry,
The Ministry has no power at this stage to
intervene in the matter.
The Guardians have been, accordingly, informed to this effect, and also that it is a
case in which the Guardians should act on
their own responsibility and be prepared to
justify their action to the Auditor in the
event of any question being raised.
Mr. BEATTIE: In view of the state of
unemployment among boot and shoe operatives in this city, and the danger that the
Guardians see ahead of a surcharge being
made, could the Minister not give instructions to the Board that the conditions they
have set forth and their reasons for giving
the contract to a local employer are such that
he in his wisdom should sanction the contract as agreed upon by the majority of the
Belfast Board of Guardians?
Sir DAWSON BATES: I am not satisfied
that the granting of this contract to Messrs.
Williamson would relieve unemployment,
but I would like to point out that the hon.
Member (Mr. Beattie) does not quite appre-
The
ciate the position of the auditor.
auditor is there for the purpose of protecting
the ratepayers against improper or imprudent contracts, and it is a matter entirely for
the Guardians to justify the granting of such
a contract when the matter comes before the
auditor at the annual audit.
Mr. WILLIAM MCMULLEN: Is the right
hon. Gentleman aware that the reason that
determined the Guardians to give the contract locally was that they received a letter
from the local branch of the National Boot
and Shoe Operatives indicating that unless
the work was placed locally it would mean
that about twelve men would be unemployed
after a period of about three months?
Sir DAWSON BATES: From the information at my disposal I am absolutely satisfied
that the information which my hon. Friend
(Mr. William McMullen) has is entirely incorrect.
COAL PRICES IN BELFAST.
Mr. BEATTIE (by Private Notice) asked
the Minister of Commerce whether he is
aware that, despite the definite assurance of
the Coal Merchants' Association that coal
prices had not been advanced in Belfast,
there have been instances where merchants
have in the present week charged bellmen
prices in excess of those charged in the preceding week; whether he is aware that such
advances in price range between 1s. 4d. and
6s. per ton; and what steps he proposes to
take in the matter.
Mr. BARBOUR: It has been intimated to
my Department that in certain cases merchants have advanced the prices at which
coal is charged to bellmen. From inquiries
made, however, I am satisfied that such cases
are exceptional, and that the great majority
of the transactions have been carried through
at the regulated prices. As regards the last
part of the question, I would inform the hon.
Member that I propose to issue immediately
a direction definitely restricting coal deliveries, and fixing maximum prices at which coal
may be sold by merchants.

Motion made, and Question proposed:

Mr. BARBOUR: In introducing the Estimate for Fisheries, Harbours, Railways, and
Commercial Services, I am glad to be able
to inform the Committee that a reduction is
made in the amount asked for for the current year.
This year the cessation or restriction of a number of Services included
in last year's Estimates, or introduced in the
Supplementary Estimates during the year,
has more than counterbalanced the introduction of the new expenditure following the
transfer of Fisheries and Railways.
Before dealing with the details embodied
in this Estimate, I should like to make a
brief reference to the new Services formerly
referred to as Council of Ireland Services
which, on 1st instant, came under the
jurisdiction of my Ministry. These are
Services connected with Fisheries and Railways.
Although the local Fishery industry is not
operated on an extensive scale, it is I believe
capable of development. We have no drifters
locally owned, and a great part of the industry is of necessity in the hands of cross-
Channel fishermen or curers. I am glad to
say, however, that last year was a most
successful one in the herring industry, the
6 MAY 1926

Committee.
by this House last year. £350 has been included in respect of the cost of remodelling
and furnishing an existing potato store
building as a fish market and offices, and I
may mention in passing that a steady and
not inconsiderable revenue is expected to
accrue as a result of the changes proposed.
Prospective works and repairs in connection
with damage to the outer sea slope at Ardglass account for £500 of the Estimate, and
the dredging of portions of Ardglass Harbour
and the protection by horizontal walling of
Ardglass Quay, costing in all £340, bring the
total of the new works to £1,420. It has in
addition been necessary slightly to increase
the provision for maintenance and repairs at
these two harbours.
total exports from Ardglass being approximately 20,000 barrels. The administrative
arrangements resulting from the agreement
between Great Britain, Northern Ireland and
the Irish Free State, have had the satisfactory effect of centralising in one Department the administration of Harbour and
Fishery Services. As hon. Members will observe when we come to an examination of the
detailed items in the Estimate, we are endeavouring to improve the harbour at Ardglass. At the same time, however, we are
awaiting a report on Killough Harbour with
a view to ascertaining which of these two
Harbours is likely to prove the most satisfactory from the fishery standpoint. While
dealing with Fishery Service arrangements I
may mention, as a point of interest, that we
have already had a visit in Belfast from the
Captain of the Imperial Fishery Flotilla, who
has courteously assured us that we can count
on every assistance from him in the matter
of the protection of fisheries within our
Coastal waters.
Turning now to the inland fisheries we are
faced with a number of problems, perhaps
the most urgent of which is a demand from
several sources for legislation dealing with
the pollution of fishery waters by flax water.
Hon. Members may know that a Committee
appointed by the Secretary of State for Home
Affairs, and my right hon. Friend, the
Minister of Agriculture, recently investigated
this question and made several recommendations for legislative changes. The report of
that Committee has still to be acted upon.
In order that fishery interests may have an
opportunity of keeping in touch with the
legislative or other contemplated changes, I
propose to establish a small Advisory Council
representative of such interests.
In regard to the administration of railways, hon. Members will, I am sure, appreciate that this is a most complicated matter.
If I may cite an example-each railway company in Northern Ireland is under obligation to furnish to my Ministry, as successors
to the Ministry of Transport, very detailed
statistics, and representations have been
made that a curtailment of such statistics
might be made with advantage, not only to
the railway companies but to the community
in general. This point I am having very
carefully investigated.
If hon. Members will now turn to the details of the Estimate they will note that the
first Sub-head in which a change occurs is
A2, Works Services. Practically the whole
increase, which amounts to £994, is in respect
of new works or works of special maintenance at Ardglass Harbour. These include
the completion of the work of cleaning and
repairing the old dock purchased in 1925-6.
The amount, £230, included for this item is
the balance of the provision already approved
Hon. Members will, no doubt, recollect
that a Supplementary Estimate was presented
last month in respect of certain unemployment relief work at Ardglass. The half of
the cost relating to materials, etc., was included in last year's figures for this Subhead, the balance, consisting of wages cost,
being accounted for under a separate Subhead A3, which is now, of course, deleted.
In Sub-head B is included the last instalment of the grant of £9,000 to Kilkeel Harbour, authorised in 1923-24. The work has
now been completed at a somewhat smaller
cost than originally anticipated, and the
amount shown, £1,441, represents the Ministry's share of the final liability of 20 per
cent. of the contract price, which, in accordance with custom, has been retained for
twelve months after the completion of the
work. In the same Sub-head the item of £10
included in respect of reconstruction works
at Coleraine Harbour refers to a service in
which my Ministry is co-operating with the
Ministry of Labour. The works are expected
to cost upwards of £60,000, and the Ministry
of Labour has consented to make, from the
Unemployment Grants Vote, a grant amounting to 75 per cent. of the wages expended in
respect of unemployment workmen specially
engaged for the work in accordance with the
usual conditions governing Relief Scheme
Grants. The Ministry of Labour grant is
limited to a maximum of £20,000, but should
the assistance given by way of unemployment
grant be less than £20,000, the Ministry of
Commerce has undertaken to contribute
either the difference between that sum and
the amount advanced by the Unemployment
Relief Grant or a sum of £3,000, whichever
is the less. The Ministry of Commerce will
not become liable for its share of the grant,
if any, until the work is completed, probably
next year, and, therefore only an Estimate
is now included.
The next Sub-head in which there is any
notable change is Sub-head D. The utilisation of mechanical devices for the tabulation

HOUSE OF COMMONS
[Mr. Barbour]
of trade statistics made it possible to include
an item of £105 in respect of payments to
local collectors of fishery statistics without
increasing the total for the Sub-head by more
than £63.
The situation with regard to the Census of
Production is already familiar to this Committee, and I need only mention that the
figure of £700 included under this Sub-head
is that supplied by the Board of Trade, who
are acting as the Ministry's agents in taking
the Census.
Notwithstanding the substantial amounts
involved I need not detain the Committee by
an extended explanation of Sub-heads G1,
G2, and G3. These Sub-heads formed the subject of portions of last year's Estimates and
Supplementary Estimates, at which time they
were very fully explained. Hon. Members
will be able to note the explanation given
in the Estimates. It sets forth the object of
these grants in connection with the bulking
of flax seed and also the grant in connection
with the linen publicity campaign.
Very careful consideration has been given
to the results secured by the Ulster Tourist
Development Association, and to the tangible
and intangible return obtained for the grant
made last year towards the funds of the Association. So satisfactory do these results
appear that it has been decided to contribute
a further sum of £500 in aid of the Association's work.
I now come to an entirely new Sub-head
which up to the present has been borne on
the Northern Ireland Services Vote of the
Imperial Government, viz., Fisheries Grants
and Allied Payments. I shall deal first with
the last four items covered by this Sub-head
by saying that the grants to hatcheries,
grants in respect of marine motor engineering classes, special inquiries and experiments
and miscellaneous expenses are provided for
to the same or to a smaller extent as in
last year's Imperial Estimates, and that, in
the opinion of the late Imperial Secretary,
who has heretofore administered these Services, the provision made is adequate and
reasonable.
The other item, namely, Contributions to
Conservators, calls for fuller explanation as
it exceeds by £415 the corresponding Imperial
Estimate last year. As the Committee is no
doubt aware, the inland fisheries of Northern
Ireland are at present supervised by four
Boards of Conservators, three of which have
been accustomed to receive necessary financial assistance from the Government. Without this financial assistance they would not
be able to carry on their work and the inland
fisheries would suffer severely. In recent
years there have been several important
changes in the area and an increasing need
for vigilance; consequently the expenses of
some of the Boards have been very greatly
increased. Recognising this, the Imperial
Government has granted considerably increased sums to these Boards, and as a result
of territorial changes which took place during
the last financial year, further increases and
changes in amounts of financial assistance
were under consideration. In view of the
pending transfer of the Fisheries Services no
decisions upon these grant questions were
made by the Imperial Government. The
sums, therefore, included in the Estimate
before the House are those recommended by
the transferring Department.
Sub-head L and M may require some explanation, relating as they do to Services
which have not formerly appeared on this
Vote. Sub-head L was formerly borne on
the Vote of the Ministry of Home Affairs,
but now it appears on the Vote under consideration, as it was felt desirable to include
in one Vote all railway expenditure from
public funds. The Government is under a
statutory liability to pay to the County
Councils of Tyrone and Fermanagh a certain
proportion of the rates raised in those two
counties in respect of the baronial guarantee
to the Clogher Valley Railway Company.
Sub-head M is transferred from the Imperial Estimates. Under the Clogher Valley
Railway Act a baronial guarantee was given
of 5 per cent. on the paid-up ordinary capital
of the Company. The Government guaranteed a repayment to the County Councils
of part of any payments under the baronial
guarantee up to a maximum of 2 per cent.
on the capital. The Clogher Valley Railway
Company has never been able to pay its own
dividends, and the Government has each year
been called upon to pay the full amount of
its guarantee, viz., £2,467.
The final expense Sub-head with which I
must deal is that relating to the Ulster Publicity Branch. The Committee are doubtless
familiar with the valuable work which has
been carried on during the last four years
by the Ulster Association. That Association
is being wound up on 30th instant, and the
Government feel that the very valuable
machinery created by the Ulster Association
for the dissemination of commercial and agricultural information should not be allowed
to disappear. As hon. Members are aware, it
is the practice for overseas parts of the
Empire to maintain offices in London where
information relative to the respective
Dominion can be readily obtained. While
there is no proposal to set up any elaborate
Government Office in London, the Government, having regard to the fact that during
the past two years many inquiries relative
to Ulster have been dealt with by the London
Office of the Ulster Association, think it
would be of service to Northern Ireland

With regard to the Revenue Sub-head O,
I need make no observations beyond remarking that the receipts in 1925-6 were very much
greater than anticipated, owing almost entirely to the substantial development during
the year of the Ardglass Herring Industry,
which resulted in increased harbour dues
and an increased revenue from the letting of
curing plots. It is hoped and anticipated
that last year's good season will be repeated
and improved upon, not only in 1926-7, but
also progressively in future years, and that
it will be possible to draw correspondingly
increased relief from this Sub-head. In this
connection I would direct the Committee's
attention to the item "Branding Receipts,
£80." This is the first occasion on which this
item has appeared in respect of Northern
Ireland, either in the Imperial Estimates
or in these Estimates, and is an indication of
the extent to which herring curers appreciate
and take advantage of the new Crown Brand
for Northern Ireland. I beg to move.

Another matter I would like to mention
is the question of the herring industry. This
has been a very neglected industry in
Northern Ireland. I think that along the
Ulster coast are to be found the best fishing
beds; at least, they are as good as any along
the English or Scotch coasts or other parts
of Ireland. These are largely fished and
exploited by Englishmen and Scotsmen.
make no objection to English capitalists
coming here and investing money, but it is
a pity that the same thing could not be done
by Ulster firms instead of English and Scotch.
firms. I do not see any reason why they

Uister should not be able to encourage its
own workers and develop the fishing industry themselves. These English and
Scotch firms come here, and then take the
fish direct to English and Scotch ports, where
they are handled. As a matter of fact, they
are then shipped back to Belfast, and to the
Belfast people-fish actually caught at their
own doors.
There are about 500 tons of fish caught and
sold locally, and about 4,000 tons imported,
so far as I can gather from the figures I
have obtained. That is a state of affairs
that should not exist, and it is clearly the
duty of the Minister of Commerce to look
into it. I am sure that this Advisory Council
will take steps to make Ulster a very important fishing centre. One of the greatest
disadvantages we labour under at present is
the matter of harbour accommodation. Right
round the coast of Ulster are many useless
harbours, owing to the fact that they are
silted up or have not been properly attended
to within the last few years. I do not see
why the Government, at little expense, could
not engage a dredger to have these harbours
cleaned out. Besides being useful for
fishing purposes, they would be effective
in the development of commerce, and bringing supplies to the small towns round
Ulster.
There is a type of pier I would like to
draw attention to, namely, the fishing pier.
A special class of fishing pier is largely used
about the Hebrides, in the North of Scotland. These piers could be erected in small
villages, and they would largely assist in
the development of the fishing industry,

There are also along the coast several small

There is one other matter with regard to

there, a man who has been engaged all his

now a man considerably over 80 years of age
for that matter. But during the war times
one of his boats-if not more than one-was
sunk by a German submarine. That was in
the year 1918, and in the following year he
got from the Fishery Department of the Local
Government Board in Dublin a loan towards
the equipping of some boats. That loan was
secured by some of his neighbours and
friends, and it was repayable at a certain
amount each year over a certain number of
years. For the first year or two he was able
to pay his instalments of this loan, but as
you can see by the report of the Industrial
Commission here, fishing became worse in
the following year or two. As a matter of
fact, it became very bad. He was unable to
pay his instalment of the loan and he has
not paid any since.
But now when the work of that Department in Dublin has been taken over by this
Government they are pursuing this man for

fallen on evil days. We want to find markets for the stuff that we produce. I think
if we are to judge the Ministry on its record
this year in finding markets for potatoes and
linen they have not done their job too well.
However, I know perfectly well that the
Minister of Commerce (Mr. Barbour) cannot
do impossibilities, but I do think that, perhaps, he might introduce a little more
initiative and a little more originality in
trying to find markets for the stuff produced
in Ulster. We can produce in this community along our own special lines the best
stuff in the world. (Hon. Members: Hear,
hear.) I do not want to enumerate them, but
along certain lines, where we specialise, and
where Nature has provided us with special
facilities for making linen and other things,
we can beat the world, and I think that, with
proper initiative in our Government Departments, and a little more aggressive policy and
more originality, we might find markets for
this stuff that we produce. Of course, I am
perfectly well aware that the Minister of
Commerce, at the head of this Department,
is a successful business man, and I am sure
he is giving his very best energies to it, but
I do feel, rightly or wrongly, that with the
qualities I have mentioned introduced into
this Ministry they might-to use a hackneyed
expression-make things hum a little bit
better for the industries of our country.
I would like if the Minister could give us
any further information with regard to the
development of pedigree flax seed, or tell us
how far we have got in that direction towards
producing sufficient seed to meet the needs of
Ulster. If this flax seed is to give the results
we were led to believe it would give in the
earlier stages the sooner we get it into the
hands of the Ulster farmers the better, because, with present prices and the present
yield, flax is not a successful crop for the
farmer. Of course, I admit that probably
during the past two or three years the seasons
have been against us in this matter. We
have had cold springs and hardly sufficient
sunshine. Though last year we could not
complain that we had not sufficient sunshine,
we had a very cold spring in its early stages,
and whenever that occurs it is very seldom
that the flax crop is what it should be.
Therefore, our yields have been reduced, and
with reduced yields, reduced prices, and the
still comparatively high cost of production
flax is not an economic crop for the farmer
at the present time. Therefore, if this
pedigree flax seed is likely to increase the
yield and to improve the quality of the flax
the sooner we get it into the hands of the
Ulster farmers the better for both the farming industry and the linen industry. Except there is some encouragement for the
farmers and, of course, though the farmers
are not generally supposed to be good business men, in the long run what appeals to
the farmer, even as it does to the business
man, is "Is there going to be any £ s. d. in
this for me? If I put my money and my
labour into it am I going to get back not
only what I spend on it but a little bit of
profit" It is very essential, not only to the
farming industry-because our farming industry in the past has got a good deal of
money out of flax-but to our linen industry,
that every encouragement should be given to
the farmers to sow flax, and to produce as
much as possible in our own area.
On looking over these Estimates-I am not
now confining myself entirely to this Estimate
-one is a little bit disquieted, because we feel
that rents are paid for buildings and salaries
are paid to officials that we might not like to
see paid in our private capacities. I think
we, as guardians of the public, should be as
careful of spending public money as we would
be of spending our own money. If only for
a minute I may be pardoned for being disorderly I pride myself on being a very
orderly man-(hon. Members: Hear, hear)-
and if you do not blow your own horn nobody
else will-

Mr. DEVLIN: I desire once more to utler
a protest against the method by which these
Estimates are presented to the Committee.
We are accustomed to the Minister rising up
here and reciting a series of figures, and giving us a sort of alphabetical statement of
what these figures are, with here and there a
word of explanation. I do not conceive that
that is the proper function of the Minister.
He ought to give to the Committee and to
the people of Ulster a clear and definite
statement covering all the services which are
affected by this expenditure. The only
practical issues that have been touched here
to-day have been touched by hon. Members
who have criticised these Estimates. We
have really been told nothing as to what is
the result of the expenditure on advertising
Irish linen in America. We have been told
nothing as to what the Government propose
to do in regard to the fishing industry, whether they propose to spend
any money on the development and preservation of our harbours. Nothing has
been told to us in this Committee to-day,
nor, indeed, is anything ever told to us, as
to what the industrial and agricultural policy
of the Government is.
We hear in speeches, mostly by the
Minister of Labour (Mr. Andrews), constant
eulogies of their own magnificent service,
and when you get down and dissect and examine the precise character of their service,
what does it amount to? That they pay so
much every week, or every month, or every
year, in unemployment allowance. I have
never thought that was a matter to boast a
great deal about. Any Government, even
the most extreme Socialist Government,
would not only pay what the right hon.
Gentleman (Mr. Andrews) is paying, but far
more, so that, whatever value there may be
in that boast, it could be made with a much
greater spirit of boastfulness by a more extreme Administration. As I say, we never
have from the Government any intimation as
to how we stand in industry, what the prospects of an improvement in industry are.
what we are doing to revive old industries, or
to create new ones. After all, these are matters that come within the purview of the
Minister of Commerce. He is not an
ignorant Minister. No one is more qualified,
both by training, by experience, and by success-I think I can say that to speak on all
these questions. But the Minister, so
respectable as he is, has got into the usual
Ministerial rut of treating Members of
Parliament and the Province with contempt,
instead of giving a clear and lucid statement
to the Committee and to the Province, as to
what the relationship of the Government is
to the general prosperity of the Province.
That is my first point. Secondly, you have
several times set up Commissions, although
when I suggest anything of that sort they
are despised in the most eloquent manner by
my right hon. Friend (Mr. Andrews). You
have set up Commissions from time to time
to deal with questions which you have
neither the patience, nor the knowledge, nor

the recommendations of your own Commissions, although they are your personal
friends and political associates, because I
have never known anyone from this side of
the House to be asked to co-operate on any
of these questions. This is the only Parliament in the world where the Opposition are
never invited to co-operate in anything that
concerns the common welfare. (Hon. Members: Oh, oh.) Never. At least, if there is
any instance of it I would like to hear it.
We are never invited, as the Opposition always is in any well-regulated and constitutionally-governed country, to give the benefit
of our advice and our experience in dealing
with these matters.

Like myself, he has a good deal of experience

is restricted to the particular Estimate that
inay be under review. Here, because we are

adhered to the line of action of allowing a

would be tolerated at all on the other side,

There are two Votes which have been
slightly touched upon by my hon. Friends,
both in front of me and beside me. One

what is called the Publicity Association.
Frankly, I want to say to the Committee that
I am opposed to governmental subsidies
for any purpose whatever, unless there is
full governmental control, or at least partial
governmental control. I object altogether
to this policy of giving to private associations
and organisations the money of the taxpayers.
Mr. GEORGE HENDERSON: Hear, hear.
Mr. DEVLIN: We have no control over
it at all. What is this Publicity Association? It has nothing in its favour except
the somewhat questionable heritage left to it

Association was a mystic body that poured
