The principal thing that I want to speak
about is on page 19, under the heading of
old-age pensions. I want to draw the attention of the Minister of Finance to a peculiar
arrangement which I mentioned here before,
and regarding which no explanation was
offered. A peculiar arrangement exists in
regard to calculating the means of applicants
for old-age pensions. I want to cite one
particular case. It is that of a person who
had £1,200 cash which was invested at four
per cent. That brought in £48 interest. It
is publicly broadcast that £39 unearned
income will not be counted. An ordinary
person thus has only £48 coming in, and £39
is allowed. You substract the £39 from the
£48 and give a pension on £9 of an income.
Instead of the pension committees being
allowed to make it up in that way the
statutory arrangement is that they take
£400 less £25 of that £1,200 and calculate
that at five per cent., which would be £18 15s.
They then take the remaining £800 and
calculate it at 10 per cent. They get a sum
of £98 15s and substract £79 from it, and
declare the person has no pension.
It is a peculiarly tortuous method of discovering a person's income, and it is considered by a great many people to work
exceedingly unfairly. They think they are
entitled to deduct £39 from unearned income
and get a pension on that basis. Although it
is a statutory thing I think that some
arrangement should be made whereby it
would be known that the Government insist
on calculating the pension as follows: the
first £500 at five per cent. and the remainder
at ten per cent no matter what interest the
person gets. If they invest that sum the
right hon. Gentleman will not allow them
more than four per cent. I do not advocate
a person having £1,200 in cash getting a
pension and being allowed to leave the money
behind to relatives. They have a right to use
some of the money in addition to the pension.
I say this is not a fair way to have the oldage pension calculated.

On page 16 there is the question of rent

With regard to the receipts appropriated

There is another item in connection with the

As I said at the beginning of the few remarks I have had to make in connection

Mr. POLLOCK: Although I can hardly
say that my hon. Friend's inquiry is germane to this Vote, at the same time, out of
courtesy, I am bound to answer her. The
amount of £8,000 which appears in this
Estimate, as against £11,000 last year,
exactly relates to the nature and character
of the services that have been rendered.
We rendered £11,000 of services last year,
and we expect to render £8,000 of services
this year. That is the only answer I can
give to the question in regard to the
difference between the £8,000 and the
£11,000.
As regards the number of houses which are
built, there is no change in the number,
1,069, speaking from memory. These are
being built now in different parts of the
country, and the services we render to the
Imperial Government as an agency involve
all the secretarial or clerking arrangements
in connection with the collection of the rents
of those houses that have been built, the
supervision and carrying out of the estimates
for building, and the various matters that
are concerned with the construction of the
houses. That is why we expect to receive the
sum of £8,000 for those services, and the fact
that the amount estimated this year is less
than that of last year arises from this, that
the houses are gradually nearing completion,
and therefore the services are not of exactly
the same value as they were before.
There are some other matters that I should
like to touch upon, leaving the details to my
right hon. Friend (Mr. Barbour), who is
naturally much better acquainted with them,
and who can deal more effectively with the
definite questions that have been asked than
I can.
It is usual for Members in this House
to speak of the Ministry of Finance as if it
were a small water-tight compartment concerned solely with the question of receiving
money and giving out money, and because
there is an estimate of £192,000, it is assumed
that there must be gross extravagance.
course there must, because it is £192,000!
But what does the Ministry of Finance
imply? I wonder if hon. Members have
taken the trouble to read the names of the
fifteen departments of the Ministry of
Finance, each one of which would be enougn
under ordinary conditions for the head of a
Department on the other side of the Channel.
Of
You have here under the head of the
Ministry of Finance all the revenue services.
That is the collection of the revenue that we
control, and also the supervision to some
extent indirectly of all the revenue of the
State. You have the Valuation Department,
which is a very considerable Department.
You have Registration. You have the Loans
Services-all the loans that are given to the
various public authorities throughout the
country, and not alone to them, but to every
one who gets a loan from the Government, or
who is in correspondence with the Ministry
in regard to loans.
Then there is the vast Department of
Public Works, which comprises not only the
works that we have to do ourselves in connection with matters under our own control,
such as the Constabulary, but also the
Reserved Services, Post Office, etcetera,
Imperial Government matters that are delegated to this Department by the Imperial
Government. That in itself is an immensely
large Service.
Then there are the Charity Funds; that is
not a very small matter. Those funds have
to be dealt with by a special staff, and they
must be dealt with by persons who have
specialised in the work. The Stationery
Office is not so heavy, but still it means
keeping all the accounts for all the different
Departments in connection with the supply
of stationery. Teachers' pensions. That
may appear a very small thing, but it really
is a very large matter, and it involves the
services of a very large staff. There is a
sum of £150,000 a year concerned with this
work, and the infinite amount of calculation
that has to be made requires a very large
staff. I am going through these items, because there is apparently a misapprehension
on the part of hon. Members as to what the
Ministry of Finance implies.
There is also the Civil Service Commission,
which deals with the supervision and control
of all the officers of the Departments. Then
there are the Ulster Savings Certificates, not
Supply Committee-

a very large matter in itself, but the time
and attention of five, six, or seven officers
are taken up in dealing with that rather
important work. The Loans Guarantee Act
comes under the Ministry, and there is some
work in connection with it; not very large,
but still it requires separate officers for that
particular work. Then there is the big
service involving the collection of Land Purchase Annuities and Tithe Charges. There
are 120,000 farmers in the country, not all
concerned with the Commission, of course,
but still there is a very large number of
people concerned with Land Purchase
Annuities. All these have got to be collected, and that requires a very large staff.
Mr. GEORGE HENDERSON: Do the
farmers not pay these into the banks?
Mr. POLLOCK : They are paid everywhere, the Post Office, the banks, wherever
is the most convenient. All the accounts
have got to be kept, and all must come
through the central department. All these
matters are mixed up with the Estimate that
we have here, and all are concerned with
what is called the Ministry of Finance. I
want to remove from the minds of hon. Members any idea that because the aggregate is
large the items are excessive.
Regarding the visit of this gentleman
whose name has been mentioned by several
Members, it was exactly with the idea of
seeing whether in all these Services there
could be any reduction of the staff that he
was asked to come over here. He has performed that work, and we are waiting his
report.
In answer to the hon. Member for West
Belfast (Mr. Devlin), who was concerned
about the housing of the officers of the
Government in the different buildings, at the
present time it requires sixteen different
buildings for the housing of the Departments
in Belfast. The rents of those buildings are
paid by the Imperial Government, and the
rates which appear here, and which have
been criticised, are the rates upon
the
buildings which we must pay, not the Imperial Government. When the arrangements
have all been completed, the officers of the
Government will be housed in two buildings,
not in sixteen. One set will be housed in
the Parliament Buildings at Stormont, that
is, those servants who do not come into daily
contact with the people, and whom it is not
necessary to keep next door to the commercial people of Belfast. The other set will be
housed in the Law Buildings, which, as hon.
Members of the House are
aware, will
shortly be started, and which will be a very
large building.
Mr. DEVLIN: Where?
Mr. POLLOCK: At the Markets. In the
lower part of May Street. When that
amalgamation or consolidation takes place,
all these inquiries in regard to housing will
be unnecessary, because the staff will be
arranged to suit the convenience of all
sections of the community in Belfast. That
is the answer I make to the statements that
have been made here to-day.
My hon. Friend, the Member for Antrim
(Mr. Crawford)—I am sorry he has gonemade inquiry with regard to teachers' pensions, and I have had my memory refreshed
on the question. The pensions of the older
teachers have been, by a recent Act, increased exactly by the same percentage as
those in Great Britain, so that that is a
complete and perfect answer to the point
in the mind of the hon. Member.
With regard to the complaint that was
made, also by my hon. Friend, as to the
method of calculating the income of a
claimant for an old-age pension, who had
£1,200 of a capital sum, I wish to tell the
Committee, and perhaps it may be of interest to those who are concerned with oldage pensions, that in such a case the income derivable from a capital sum of £1,200
is calculated on an annuity basis, and not
upon the year's interest derivable from investment of the money. Of course, when
the calculation is based on the annuity
principle, the income of the recipient is
greatly increased. It is because of that
that he was ruled out of his claim for an
old-age pension.
My hon. Friend, the Member for Antrim
(Mr. George Henderson), was greatly exercised in respect of the present charges on
Land Annuities, and not for the first time,
he suggested that the period of repayment
should be extended. Of course that would
mean a very considerable loss to the revenue
of Northern Ireland. In the first place, we
have no power to legislate, so far as I know,
in respect of anything in connection with
the Land Commission, and although we collect and we receive and have the benefit
of the £650,000, or thereabouts derivable
from Land Annuities, we have no power, so
far as I know, either to increase or to
diminish the rates, or to influence them in
any way. What we can do with farmers is,
we can make allocations and independent
grants, but once we impinge upon what is
called a Reserved Service, we are then up
against the Imperial authorities, and our
action is ultra vires. Therefore, when I say
we cannot extend it I hope he will understand that it is not within the compass of
our power to do it. But even the benefit
of extending it for a few years to these
people would be infinitesimal, and it is
hardly worth while discussing.

HOUSE OF COMMONS.
[Mr. Barbour]
In reply to the hon. Member for Derry
(Mrs. Chichester), I am glad to be able to
give a little further information. She might
be interested to hear that within two or three
miles of this place there are a large number
of sailors' and soldiers' houses being erected
quite close to Finaghy. The Ministry acts as
agent in connection with the acquisition of
sites for these cottages, also the construction
and maintenance of the cottages after
erection. I may remind hon. Members that
1,046 of these houses were allocated to
Northern Ireland, and of these 867 have been
built, or are in course of construction, and
arrangements are being made for the building
of the remainder with the least possible
delay.
In addition to work of this character we
are carrying out some work to improve the
standard of accommodation at the Board of
Trade Coastguard Stations in Northern Ireland. This is an agency service also, and involves the maintenance of these buildings and
the furniture therein, payments of rent, provision of fuel and light, etc., for the coastguards. The maintenance of the buildings
occupied by the Mercantile Marine, Ministry
of Pensions, and the Government Instructional Factory is also performed by the
Ministry of Finance Works Service.
Then in regard to Reserved Services similar
duties are performed, which comprise Inland
Revenue, Customs and Excise, Temporary
Law Courts, Registry of Deeds, Land Registry and Probate Registry. Among the works
in hand at the present moment are the erection of a garage and workshop in connection
with the General Post Office in Belfast and
the erection of a new Post Office in Strabane.
Another special work in which I am sure
hon. Members will be interested is the reconditioning work required at the Belfast
Custom House. As hon. Members will doubtless have noticed, the condition of the foundations at the Custom House has given rise
to a good deal of anxiety for the safety of the
building. It was considered desirable, as a
measure of precaution, to remove the staff
and records from about two-thirds of the
building. The walls have been shored up
and preliminary investigations are being
made as to what measures are necessary and
what facilities are available to preserve the
building and make it safe for occupation.
The problem presented to our technical
officers is a very difficult one as ordinary
piling work is not practicable owing to the
lack of head room inside the building, and
in any case such operations might be
attended with risk to the fabric. A system
of piling has, however, been brought to our
notice which can be carried out without the
risks referred to, and experiments are proceeding with a view to using this system. I
merely mention these so as to further inform
hon. Members as to the very varied character
of the work being done by our officers.
Two or three references have been made
to the cost of the acquisition of site for certain houses in the neighbourhood of Coleraine. I should like, as two or three questions have been asked, to give particulars as
to the exact nature of the costs incurred in
that connection. When a rural district requires land and the matter of price comes
into dispute, an arbitrator is selected from
what is known as the Land Values Referees
Committee. The panel is selected by the
Lord Chief Justice and the President of the
Surveyors' Institute. There are about eight
persons on the panel, each of the highest
standing in the profession. This is necessary
inasmuch as their assessment is without
appeal save on matters of law.
The account of the arbitrator has now been
received, and amounts as has been stated
here to £66 7s 10d, and the amount of fees collected by way of stamp duty amounted to
£72 9s, leaving a difference of £6 to the
Government's credit, which is not unreasonable seeing that in addition to the arbitrator's expenses the Government is put to
certain expenses in connection with the Land
Values Committee and the expense of the
stamp-accounting branches. The arbitrator's
personal account when dissected is as follows:
The actual hearing of the case occupied
seven hours, for which he charged 12 guineas;
viewing the sites, eleven hours, 11 guineas;
time spent travelling, four hours, £4 18s;
travelling expenses and subsistence, £7 11s 10d;
correspondence and interviews, £19 12s, which
is made up at the regular rate of a guinea
per hour; making up the award, £10 3s.
When, therefore, it was stated in the previous
discussion that the total time spent was 23
hours, it was assumed that nothing more was
done by the arbitrator in the case after
hearing the case and viewing the sites, I may
say that there were no fewer than twelve
solicitors and agents in all to be dealt with,
and there were many parcels of land involved
under different ownership, so that the acquisition of that particular site was not an easy
one.
As regards the rearrangement of offices
which will be possible when Stormont is
available, the Departments will be housed
in two separate buildings as against about
sixteen separate buildings at the present
time. I think I have covered the different
points raised.
Question put, That a reduced sum not exceeding £146,745 be granted to His Majesty
for the said purpose.

Oral Answers to Questions.
ADVERTISEMENTS IN STATE-AIDED
SCHOOLS.
1. Mr. BEATTIE asked the Parliamentary
Secretary of the Ministry of Education
whether he would say if each manager and
each principal teacher of a public elementary school has received in the same envelope
a circular condemning the utilisation of
teachers in State-aided schools for purposes
of the advertisement of the commodities of
business firms, and a catalogue of books
which teachers of elementary schools are recommended to procure, what the various
publishers of the books advertised by this
catalogue pay for these advertisements, and
what is the cost of its publication.
The PARLIAMENTARY SECRETARY OF
THE MINISTRY OF EDUCATION (Mr.
Robb): The facts are as stated by the hon.
Member in the first part of his Question.
The catalogue of books to which he refers is
not, however, regarded by the Ministry as
being an advertisement, but is a carefully
selected list of educational works suitable
for the use of teachers, and is intended to
be used by them as a guide in the selection
of their reading.
No payment in this respect was made to
the Ministry by the firms whose names appear in the list. The cost of printing the
list, which may be purchased from H.M.
Stationery Office, or through any bookseller
for 3d, was £18 10s Od.
With a view to economy, circulars and
other documents issued to the teachers are
often distributed in the same cover.
CANDIDATE TEACHERS AT QUEEN'S
UNIVERSITY.
2. Mr. BEATTIE asked the Parliamentary
Secretary to the Ministry of Education
whether he would state if the professor of
English in the Queen's University, Belfast,
in addressing his class of English this
session, referred to the section of it which
consists of candidates for the teaching profession as not the real Queen's students but
persons who are enjoying the hospitality of
the University, and what steps he proposes
to take to have these candidates protected
from offensive observations of this character.
Mr. ROBB: No complaint in regard to
the statement referred to in the hon. Member's Question has reached the Ministry.
But, on inquiry, I am informed that the
words "not the real Queen's students" were
not used. The candidates for the teaching
profession referred to are not taking the
same courses as full-time students of the
University, and the words "enjoying the
hospitality of the University," which neither
bear. nor were intended to bear an offensive
sense, allude to this.
In reply to the second part of the Question,
the Ministry is assured that, so far from
needing protection, the students in question
are welcome at the University.
Mr. DEVLIN: Would it not be well that
these University professors should be instructed to be very careful about the expressions used towards teachers? They may
be regarded as humiliating and offensive.
Mr. ROBB: I do not think there is any
necessity to discuss the matter further.

UNEMPLOYMENT
STAMPS.

collected from his employees for the past two

stamps, but did not stamp any cards for
them; if, in consequence, these men when unemployed are refused unemployment benefit;
if this action of his was reported to the
Ministry, and why he has not been
prosecuted,
The PARLIAMENTARY SECRETARY OF
THE MINISTRY OF LABOUR (Mr.
Gordon): The Ministry has at present under
consideration a case of alleged noncompliance under the Unemployment Insurance Acts in which the facts appear to be
approximately as stated by the hon. Member.
In this case legal proceedings were taken in
1923 for an offence similar to that now
alleged, and a conviction was secured; in
view of complaints which have recently been
received further investigations are being
made by the Ministry.
Mr. BEATTIE: I would like to ask the

against with a view, perhaps, to joint action
being taken in the other cases mentioned by
me?
Mr. GORDON: As the case the hon. Gentleman has before his mind may be different to
the case we are proceeding in at the moment,
I do not think it would be right that I should

give the name. If the hon. Gentleman would

RURAL DISTRICT OFFICIAL AS
GUARDIAN.
4. Mr. BEATTIE asked the Minister of Home
Affairs whether it is legal for a paid officer
in the employment of the County Antrim
Rural District Council to occupy a seat
on the Belfast Board of Guardians, seeing
that the Board administers the Poor Law
Acts for the County Antrim Rural Council,
and what action he is prepared to take in the
matter.
The MINISTER OF HOME AFFAIRS (Sir
Dawson Bates): So far as 1 am aware, an
officer of the Antrim Rural District Council
would not be disqualified for being a member
of the Belfast Board of Guardians, merely
on the ground that he held a paid office in
the employment of the Antrim Rural District Council.
In any event the Ministry of Home Affairs
has no jurisdiction to determine questions as
to the qualification or disqualification of
individual members of local authorities, but
it is open to any person who has reason to
doubt the validity of the qualification of
any much member to have the matter contested before the competent Court.
Mr. BEATTIE: In view of the recent
decision in another public board and this
officer acting in the administrative affairs
of the board by which he is paid, is it
not within the purview of the Minister to
give a decision to this House by which the
interests he represents may be protected.
Sir DAWSON BATES: I am not here to
give an opinion on a legal point. As I have
already pointed out to the hon. Member, he
has a
course open to him if he wishes to
take it.
Mr. W. McMULLEN: I would like to
inquire of the right hon. Gentleman is it
not his function if an alleged irregularity is
reported or takes place to inquire into the
matter; whether if it is an irregularity some
steps should then be taken by the Ministry
rather than to ask persons who are extremely poor like myself to enter upon litigation.
Sir DAWSON BATES: I am not aware
that an irregularity has been reported.
Mr. W. McMULLEN: Would the right
Gentleman make inquiries into the matter?
If he has not, as he apparently has not, will

Mr. DEVLIN: Would the right hon. Gentleman not consider the advisability of getting
a "B" Special to stand outside and keep out

Mr. BEATTIE: Are we not going to get
some finality on this question? It is a very
important one from our point of view. I
would like if the Home Secretary would be

position of the gentleman concerned in this
matter.
Sir DAWSON BATES: With the permission
of the House I would like to repeat the
answer I gave a short time ago:-
So far as I am aware an officer of the
Antrim Rural District Council would not
be disqualified for being a member of the
Belfast Board of Guardians merely on the
ground that he held a paid office in the employment of Antrim Rural District Council.
Mr. SPEAKER: I suggest that as it is a
legal question the hon. Member might repeat

PRISONERS' PRIVILEGES IN NORTHERN
IRELAND AND GREAT BRITAIN.
5. Mr. BEATTIE asked the Minister of
Home Affairs whether he is prepared to grant
the same privileges to the prisoners in
Northern Ireland Prisons as in those in
Great Britain.
Sir DAWSON BATES: As a result of the
establishment of a Convict Prison at Belfast,
and the transfer of the convicts hitherto confined in prisons in Great Britain to Belfast,
among other matters, the question of the extension of privileges corresponding to those
in Great Britain to the prisoners now in our
custody has been receiving very careful and
I may say sympathetic consideration, and I
hope it will shortly be found practicable to
permit a number of relaxations to be given
without impairing the discipline of the
prison.
Mr. BEATTIE: In view of the immediate
attention that my question requires is the

which is now in general practice in Great

Sir DAWSON BATES: I am not aware that
it is the general practice in English prisons
to allow smoking.
Mr. BEATTIE: I am only taking the
answer the Minister gave to me in a letter
which I have in my possession.

CLASS V. No. I.
MINISTRY OF EDUCATION.
Motion made and Question proposed:
"That a sum not exceeding £53,671 be granted
to His Majesty to complete the sum necessary to defray the charge which will come
in course of payment during the year ending
31st March, 1927, to defray the salaries and
expenses of the Ministry of Education (15
and 16 Geo. V., c. 3, s. 4 (N.I.))." (Note-
£18,000 has been voted on account).
The PARLIAMENTARY SECRETARY OF
THE MINISTRY OF EDUCATION (Mr.
Robb): With the leave of the Committee I
shall endeavour to cover the whole field of
educational administration on this first Vote
of the Ministry of Education--the Estimate
for the administrative expenses of the Min-
1221 Supply Committee-
Education Estimates. 1222
13 MAY 1926
istry during the coming year. So far as I
am able I shall endeavour to sketch the aims
and activities of the Ministry and review our
educational policy. Of course, later on I
shall be glad to answer any question that
may be asked as to details of the expenditure
and as to any sub-head of either Vote, but
I trust I shall carry the Committee with me
in suggesting that we have our general
debate upon the first Vote which includes
Ministerial salaries.
Before touching the Estimates for the
coming year, I think I should refer to the
change which the past year has seen in the
Ministry of Education, by reason of the resignation of Lord Londonderry. Everyone in
Northern Ireland recognises the earnestness
and ability which Lord Londonderry brought
to the task which had been entrusted to
him, the task of reorganising the system of
education in this Province. His name will
always be remembered in honour by the
generations which come after us, and which
will enjoy the fruits of his labours. Those
of us who were privileged to be associated
with him will remember him, not only with
honour, but with affection. We all in Ulster
regret the severance of his official ties; but
we are glad to know that he will still be
with us in actual fact, and always with
us in spirit, and that he will ever be ready
to give us of his ripe experience. We know
that only the imperative call of duty led him
to give up the work he did so well, and loved
so much. We know the good heart and conciliatory spirit he brings to the solution of
the difficulties in the great industry with
which he is so intimately connected in England, and we are certain he has much
wise counsel to give. What is our loss is
the gain of others. Lord Charlemont has
taken up the work Lord Londonderry has laid
down, and already the most cordial good feeling exists between our new Minister and his
official staff.
To proceed then. I feel that my first duty
is to draw the attention of the Committee
simply to the sum total of our estimated educational expenditure. Taking the amount of
the two Votes together, we anticipate that,
for the financial year 1926-27, we shall be
called upon to spend, out of moneys voted
by Parliament alone, and without taking into
consideration moneys raised by local rating,
no less a sum than £1,874,645. That figure,
it is true, is a smaller figure than appeared
in last year's Estimates, and I shall be glad
to explain the decrease to the Committee in
due course.
But, for the moment, I am
content to dwell rather upon the magnitude
of the total, than upon the diminution,
which we have been able to secure-a diminution, let me add, which we have secured
without we hope, any corresponding loss of
efficiency in the service. This figure,
£1,874,645, though less than the figure for
last year, is still more than one-seventh of the
total revenue of this Province. It is, in
itself, a very considerable figure, but I
venture to think it is made even more remarkable, when it is compared, as I have
just compared it very roughly, with our total
tax revenue.
Whatever cry against contraction of
educational expenditure may be raised elsewhere, we, here in the Parliament of
Northern Ireland, cannot justly be accused
of stinting the services of education. These
are, it is true, days when the cry for economy
is loudly heard, and very properly so heard,
through the land. But economy does not
mean the starvation of essential services. It
means, to my mind, and to the mind of the
Government, the proper expenditure of public
money, in the maintenance of essential
services, and the cutting of expenditure upon
those services which are non-essential. It
implies no relaxation of the determination of
the Government to raise the general standard
of life amongst all classes. We in this House
understand that, at any rate, so far as the
services of education are concerned, economy
is not to be translated into parsimony, and
that, whatever sacrifices the older members
of the community are to be called upon to
undergo in the name of entrenchment, those
services which are of such vital import to the future of our children, are
essential services, and, as such, are not to
be reduced, either in their efficiency or in
their progressive development.
I am not seeking to defend these figuresthese Votes by the simple assertion that
they are a good round sum and a very
proper amount to spend upon the services
of education. Far from it. I only mean
to call the attention of the Committee to
the fact that the sum proposed to be spent
is a very large one, in order to prove to
this House and to that great body of my
countrymen outside, who are determined
that no rash hand shall be laid upon the
future welfare of the children, under the
guise of economy-I say, in order to prove
to them that we are not disposed to be
miserly towards the services of education,
in which their interests are peculiarly
centred; and, if those services are inadequate, that is not because they are suffering
from any financial starvation.
I will now pass to a general review of the
activities of the Ministry, to establish, if I can,
to the satisfaction of the Committee that the
Province is obtaining a full measure of
value for this great expenditure. At the
same time I shall be glad, if by statement
I am able to arouse helpful criticism from
all quarters of the Committee in the course
of the debate. The policy, which the
Government have in view is the establish-
Education Estimates. 1224
Supply Committee-
HOUSE OF COMMONS.
[Mr. Robb]
ment of a sound public system of education
on progressive lines; and I do not stand
here to-day to attempt to make party capital
or to score mere debating points. I shail
endeavour to unfold the educational policy
of the Government, to gain support for our
aims, and to win the assistance of the
Members of all parties in carrying out our
intentions. We believe that one good result of the controversy over the Education
Act has been to lift the question of education out of the arena of party politics. I
think I may say, without fear of any contradiction, that we are all determined, whatever our party, to unite in building up a
sound system of public education in Ulster,
with the single aim before us of the good of
the children and the youth of the Province,
and without any consideration of personal
political advantage or party profit.
The object of our policy, the policy expressed in the Education Act of 1923, is to
ensure that every child shall have at least
an elementary education; and, for that purpose, to make his parent responsible under
penalties for his attendance at some school
supported at the public expense where such
education is afforded, unless the parent is
willing and able himself to provide other
efficient instruction for his child. After the
elementary stage we seek to secure that
every child of ability, despite the poverty
of his parents, shall be enabled by scholarship or other similar form of State
assistance suited to his means, to proceed
with his education at a secondary school,
from which place he may win further
scholarships which will open the
way for
him to the University; or, on the other
hand, if his circumstances and the necessities
of his future career do not permit of this
course, we desire to make it easy for
him, by attendance at continuation schools
or technical schools, to acquire a liberal
education at a time when, without such
opportunities for intellectual development, all
his energies would be devoted to the acquisition of the mere mechanism of his craft,
and the whole of his leisure might be
frittered away in idle self-amusement.
as-
That, in the very broadest terms, is the
policy of the Ministry of Education as expressed in the Education Act. All else in
the Act is directed to the fulfilment of that
policy and subservient to that aim. In the
achievement of that policy we have
sociated with ourselves the councils of the
counties and of the county boroughs, and
we have sought to employ, under their
supervision, for the good of the children
the energy and experience of the men and
women generally in the local direction of
education throughout the Province. Of the
work of the new local authorities and the
various local committees I shall speak later
on.
But to return to the general question, our
problem is, of course, widest in the field of
elementary education, which is compulsory
for every child between the ages of 6 and
14. Now, where we make education compulsory, it follows that we must be ready to
provide, at the expense of the State, elementary school accommodation and teaching for
every child in the Province between the age
of 6, when he is first obliged by law to attend
school, and the age of 14, by which time the
elementary stage of education, at any rate,
normally comes to an end, and the law no
longer compels the parent to send his child
to school.
Our school-going population between 6 and
14, during the school year just closed, was
167,404. In addition there were the younger
children, in the infants' departments, between 3 and 6, making a total school population of 201,969. It may be of interest to
hon. Members to learn that the average
attendance of children of all ages has been
164,541 or 81.5 per cent. of the public elementary school population. But that figure
is improved upon when we leave out of consideration the children between 3 and 6 years
of age whose attendance is not compulsory,
and who, in addition, are naturally less
regular in their attendance, as weather conditions bear more heavily upon those of
such tender years. Taking the attendance
of the children of the age of compulsory
attendance, from 6 to 14 years alone, the
figure is now 140,823 or 84.1 per cent. of the
total public elementary school population
of the age of compulsory attendance. Unfortunately, we have no separate figures for
1924-25 showing the numbers of pupils of the
age of compulsory attendance and the percentage of their average attendance. But the
figure I have mentioned is nearly six points
higher than the percentage for the attendance of children of all ages for the year
1924-25, which was 78.4. But although we
have attained to 84.1 per cent. we are still
a long way behind the English figures, which
are over 89 per cent.
These figures mean that the Education Act
is really at work and effective. They prove
that compulsory education is fast becoming a
real thing in Northern Ireland, instead of
the mere legal fiction that once it threatened
to be. The figures are the more satisfactory in
that the school year has been practically extended, because the attendance of a child
between the ages of 6 and 14 is now compulsory on every day on which his school is
open. Not only are we maintaining the
schools to accommodate the children, but the
children are actually using the opportunities
which we provide.
The public elementary schools in connection with the Ministry number 2,006, and the
teachers employed therein number no less
Supply Committee-
Education Estimates.
13 MAY 1926
than 4,995. The number of teachers is increasing with the increase in the school
population and the advance in the average
daily attendance of the pupils. By far the
largest single liability incurred by the Ministry of Education is that for the salaries of
these teachers. For salaries alone, the charge
for the coming year is estimated at £1,403,000;
and this huge figure marks a decrease of
£80,000 when compared with the figure in the
Estimates last year. That saving has been
affected by a reduction in the salary rates.
The new scales of salaries were adopted by
the Ministry after a long and painstaking
inquiry by a Departmental Committee representative of the Ministry, of the teachers,
and of the public. I, myself, in succession
to the late Mr. McKeown, was its Chairman
in the later stages of the inquiry, and I
can say from my own experience that that
Committee had a very difficult task. I should
like here to make public acknowledgement
of the gratitude of the Government to the
ladies and gentlemen who gave their time
and their services so willingly in performing
a difficult and, in some ways, an invidious
public duty. The new scales became effective
on the 1st of January last.
It is at all times an ungrateful task for a
department to reduce the rewards of those employed in the service which it administers,
but the Ministry was of opinion—and I think
I may say, with the Ministry, the general
mass of the public-that, in these days of
nearly universal hardship and financial difficulty, it had become necessary to lower a
scale of salaries which had been fixed at a
time when the cost of living was at its peak.
It was felt that salary scales, whether they
had a sliding element or no, whether they
were what is called "temporary," or whether
they had no such expedient for keeping them
in touch with realities and were called "permanent," must be examined in order that
they might be brought to figures more in
conformity with existing conditions.
We cannot expect any class of public
servants, or any other body of men for that
matter, to accept lowered rates of salary
without reluctance, much less with rejoicing.
And so it has been with the teachers. We
have been charged with ill-faith; but in
answer to that I should like to ask a single
question: Had we adopted a policy of financial inflation, and had the purchasing power
of money fallen and prices risen accordingly,
would not the teachers have cried, and justly
cried, for an upward variation of their salary
scales? And would we not have been bound,
on our side, to accede to their demands on the
plain grounds of elementary justice? I
would venture to say, too, that, in spite of
the resolutions recorded almost habitually
at annual congresses, the general body of
the teachers does not feel that we have acted
so very harshly; and, when one of their
leaders appears to threaten the Government
with disloyalty on the part of the teachers I
believe that they regard it themselves, as
we regard it in the Ministry, as a form of
procedure which, in actual practice, they
would never adopt themselves nor countenance in others.
At all events, speaking for the Ministry
and for myself, I believe that the country
can always count upon the loyal co-operation
of the teachers in carrying on the work of
the schools; and that, whatever differences
of a more or less domestic character may
arise in the future, or may have arisen, between the Ministry of Education and the
general body of the teachers, whether over
the rewards of the teachers for their services
or any other matter, those questions will not
be allowed to stand between any individual
teacher and the faithful discharge of his
duties.
In addition to the annual charge of the
salaries of elementary school teachers, the
Vote of the Ministry is called upon to bear
a very large share of the expense of their
training. In this connection, when we are
accused of parsimony in our treatment of
these teachers, I am anxious that the Committee, and the general public outside this
House, should realise what the Government
actually does for these teachers, or at least
for the vast majority of them.
It educates them from their earliest years
without charge. Many of them, as pupil
teachers or monitors, it takes early for
special training, and pays them a smal!
salary in that capacity while it educates
them. Then, when they have come to the
training college, the State bears at least
three-quarters of the cost of their maintenance and training. Finally, on leaving the
training college, the young teacher is able to
command a good commencing salary, with
fixed yearly increments for satisfactory service, and with pension rights at the close of
his professional career. It seems to me that
the mere recital of these facts is a full and
sufficient answer to the charge.
This year we are spending on training
colleges the sum of £26,130. At present we
are training 340 students-103 men and 237
women. Owing to the increase in our school
population we anticipate raising the numbers
of the teachers in training to 375 in the
immediate future-115 men and 260 women.
Hampton House, which was purchased last
year for the purposes of a hostel for men
students in connection with our college at
Stranmillis, will be opened in due course,
when the necessary alterations have been
made, and that will enable us to give up the
present quarters in Royal Terrace which
have never afforded satisfactory or sufficient
accommodation.
1227 Supply Committee-
Education Estimates. 1228
HOUSE OF COMMONS.
[Mr. Robb]
In addition, we are seeking to secure the
Stranmillis Public Elementary School, at the
gates of the College, as a practising school
for the use of the students there. The Committee will notice that only part of the
total expenditure on this head falls upon the
present Estimates, and as against this there
will be an appropriation from the sum of
£200,000 in respect of Training College buildings out of the Colwyn Award.
While I am speaking of elementary education, I may, perhaps, be allowed to say a
few words on the programme of instruction
in our elementary schools. It is repeatedly
charged that this programme is overloaded
Mr. DEVLIN: Hear, hear.
Mr. ROBB and that the Ministry is too
rigid in its insistence upon close adherence
to it by the teachers.
So far as the charge of rigidity is concerned, I may say that, in our anxiety to
avoid cramping the teachers, we have not
only divided the subjects into categories of
"obligatory" and "optional," but we have
also actually asked managers and teachers to
submit alternative programmes, modified to
suit the special circumstances of their
schools, if the prescribed programme appears
unsuitable. To this invitation the response
has been very meagre. As was stated in the
Report of the Ministry last year, over ninetysix per cent. of the schools adopted the programme without modification. In spite of
our invitation to accept an alternative programme the cry that we are too rigid
persists, and it is very difficult to see what
further steps we should take.
The arrangement of a satisfactory
programme is no easy problem. We
are dealing not with machines, but with
flesh and blood; with children, who, with all
the budding intelligence of grown men and
women, already share with them many of
their aspirations. For them we shall need
something more than mere instruction-far
more than that. We shall require an education laid down upon liberal lines.
There is, I know, a certain school of
thought an influential school to-day-which
weighs everything in the balance of practical
utility. It is a school of thought to which
these hard times certainly add numbers, and
to whose arguments they appear to add
strength. "What," they ask, " is the use of
singing, of drawing, of physical training, of
nature study, of Algebra, or Geometry, to
the pupil at the elementary school?" "It is
all a waste of time," they say. In reply, I
in my turn, would propound a question:
:-
"What, in point of actual fact, is the prac
tical utility of the total sum of knowledge,
which children can acquire up to the age of
11?" "What," to bring it to the touchstone
by which these people appear to judge all
things, "what is its commercial value?" It
is very little. How can it be otherwise? The
truth is, that what matters, in elementary
schooling, is not so much what the children
learn, what facts they acquire, what dates
they know, how they can cipher, but how far
their capacity for knowledge, for learning,
has been developed, how their intelligence
has been fostered, how their humanity has
been evoked.
The three "R's, it is quite true, are the
very alphabet of all learning, the prerequisite of all development, and upon them
our programme has been based. Beyond the
mere mechanical acquirement of the arts of
reading, and writing, and ciphering, which
are pre-supposed, there is to be sought the
development of the faculties and of the intelligence, which will make use of these
faculties as a means of self-expression. To
this end we desire to make learning attractive. Singing is the natural expression of
childish joy; drawing is the first use to which
a child will attempt to put his pencil;
physical training is merely the proper direction of the natural impulse in children for
healthy exercise; nature study will bring
the child, sooner than any other course, to
the knowledge of God's Providence, and to
habits of kindness and gentleness to the
brute creation. How can any reasonable
man or woman object to the presence of these
aids to natural development in our elementary school programme?
I will not detain the Committee any longer
on this subject. I think I have said enough
to show that it is not so simple as those who
cry out against our programme for elementary schools would lead us to expect. I pass
now to deal with the secondary school system,
though, of course, I do not pretend to have
covered the whole ground in what I have
said regarding elementary education.
The numbers, either of pupils, of schools,
or of teachers, with which we have to deal
in the department of secondary education are
naturally very much smaller than those concerned with elementary education, which we
have just been considering. There we had
to deal with more than 200,000 pupils, with
over 2,000 schools, and with a body of 5,000
teachers. Here we have some 9,000 pupils
only, some 70 schools, and some 600 or 700
teachers, of whom 500 are holding full-time
engagements.
These may not seem great numbers. But
we have an eye to the future, and it does not
need any great power of vision to foresee
that before long we shall need greatly increased facilities for secondary education.
To give a comparison-in the year 1923-24,
the first comparable year for this purpose,
there were 6,206 pupils in the secondary
schools of Northern Ireland recognised by

the Ministry. In the year 1925-26, the year
just closed, there were 9,357, including some
1,600 in preparatory departments not previously included.
In this field of secondary education we have
made great changes, changes which I think
the Committee will agree are for the benefit of the children, for whom the schools
exist. We have been faced with what has
amounted practically to the re-organisation
of secondary education in Ulster. Thanks to
the co-operation of all concerned the new
system is laid, and we are now ready for expansion upon what we consider are the right
lines.
In the first place we have laid it down that,
in order to qualify for recognition, in order
to establish a claim for State assistance, all
possibility of private profit must be eliminated from the working of a school. To secure
this a board of governors must be set up to
manage the school, and by them all profitthough I fear not many secondary schools in
Ulster are yet making a profit-must be
devoted to the improvement of the educational facilities afforded by the school. The
work of converting the whole of the
secondary schools from private ownership
and management to public ownership and
public management has been completed.
There have been found everywhere, I am
glad to say, men and women in sufficient
numbers with public spirit to induce them
to undertake the onerous but by no means
irresponsible duties attached to a seat on a
board of governors.
In the second place, we have directed cur
attention to the well-being of the teachers in
our secondary schools and their preparatory
departments. Hitherto they have been for
the most part drawing very meagre salaries.
State assistance has been small. For years
they had been leading a difficult and precarious existence. The rise in the cost of
living, owing to the war, had only intensified
their difficulties.
I do not pretend that we have done for the
teachers all that they asked us to do. I do
not pretend even that we have been able to
do for them all that we should have liked
to do. We have not been able, I know, to
give them that full recognition of their past
service which they have demanded. But the
cost of that concession was too great to be
borne, and we are in agreement with the
Minister of Finance in that reply to the
claims of the teachers. My right hon.
Friend, the Minister of Finance, is well able
to defend himself, and I am not seeking to
defend him now. But I desire to take this
opportunity of making public acknowledgement, on behalf of the Ministry of Education, of the sympathy and understanding
with which the right hon. Gentleman has
always regarded every case for financial
assistance which we have brought before him
in the interests of the teaching profession.
To return to the teachers, we have established salary scales for them in preparatory
and secondary schools which ensure that they
shall, at least, be adequately rewarded, while
we have left the door open for their more
liberal treatment by the governing bodies
for whom they work.
Our method has been to divide the salary
into two distinct portions; the one, a certain
basic amount which is the minimum commencing salary of the teacher, and which is
provided for by the governing body; the
other, an incremental part which, within
limits, is variable according to the length of
the teacher's service, and is the sum of the
fixed annual increases in his salary. For
this latter portion the Ministry is responsible, paying over to the governors the
amount due to each teacher in respect of
increments.
When a teacher is seeking an engagement
his previous experience, which is infinitely
valuable educationally, is not gathered up
against him before the eyes of prospective
employers in the shape of a formidable
array of increments. Whatever the experience, the years of service of the teacher,
the responsibility of the board of governors
is limited to the amount of his
basic salary, the salary which a teacher
receives in the first year of his
service. Their financial liability will be
the same, whoever they select. They are
therefore, able to choose the applicant best
qualified for the vacant post without regard
to his salary.
In addition, the Ministry is responsible
for a special grant, known as the Principal's
Grant, which is made as an additional reward to teachers in positions of special
responsibility in the conduct of their schools.
In consultation with the Ministry of Education, the Ministry of Finance has lately
laid before Parliament, for the statutory
period, regulations establishing a scheme of
superannuation for the teachers in secondary schools from August 1st, 1922, and for
teachers in the preparatory departments of
these schools from August 1st, 1923. Those
regulations, and the conditions of superannuation, are sufficiently in the minds of hon.
Members. Here again financial stringency
has prevented our yielding to the claims of
those teachers for full recognition of past
non-contributory service. What I have said
regarding this claim, in the matter of salary,
applies equally to superannuation.
Seeing that we have assumed so great a
financial liability in respect of these schools

[Mr. Robb]
and the teachers employed in them, for, in
addition to grants for the incremental
portion of the teachers' salaries and the
principals' grants, we also pay to the schools
grants on the basis of attendance of the
pupils-in view, I say, of this great financial
responsibility we have laid down regulations
which govern the staffing of the schools, the
professional qualifications required for the
teachers, and the length of working hours
necessary to establish a claim for full-time
employment. Henceforth we require that a
teacher shall be properly qualified in a subject before the State undertakes any liability
for his teaching in it, or for the school in
which he teaches. These are new considerations, and I believe that we have already
raised not only the status of the teachers
but also the general standard of education
in the schools.
There is a further important change to
which I feel bound to allude, because it will
have what we hope will be a considerable
effect upon the manner in which secondary
education is imparted by our schools. We
have, to all intents and purposes, abolished
the pernicious system of payment of grants
according to the results of the Ministry's
examinations. We have reduced the numbers
of examinations by doing away altogether
with the Middle Grade Intermediate Examination. In place of the old Junior and
Senior Intermediate Examinations, we have
now two School Certificate Examinations,
one for the Junior Certificate at the close of
a three-years Intermediate course for pupils
of 15 and 16; and the second for the Senior
Certificate, which marks the close of the
school career after a full five years' course
of secondary education.
I am happy to say that there are not wanting signs all over the Province of an increasing demand for secondary education. As I
have already indicated, we must be prepared
to meet that demand. The one great danger
at present threatening secondary education
in Ulster is the insufficiency of the supply
of schools, and the inadequacy of the accommodation afforded in many existing schools.
The position is further complicated by the
unsatisfactory financial position of many of
our schools. Very few of them do more than
just make ends meet. Most of them have no
money for upkeep, much less for expansion.
In 1922-23 our Estimate for secondary education on the old basis was £60,000. To-day,
for 1926-27, we are debating an Estimate of
£114,170 without including the charge for
pensions. I do not think after what I have
just told the Committee that I need argue
that the Treasury is already doing its fair
share. The Ministry hopes that local education authorities will give sympathetic attention to the appeals which they may receive from secondary schools under properly
constituted governing bodies, who may be
faced with problems of renewal or expansion,
which in many cases threaten the necessity
of complete reconstruction in order to meet
the public demand. Neither the Ministry nor
the general public has forgotten the services
rendered by these schools, which from their
very inception have, many of them, had a
hard struggle for existence.
In addition there is to be considered the
cry for secondary education which is becoming more and more insistent in our remoter
country districts, and we look to the local
authorities to do their best to help to meet
that demand.
There is one form of the activities of local
education authorities from which our
secondary schools are already deriving an
indirect benefit. It is not the duty of these
authorities to provide secondary education
free to all in the same way as it is to provide
elementary education. But it is their duty
to see that there are reasonable opportunities
for all children in their district to obtain
this form of education, and, further, to assist
to place promising children of poor parents
in secondary schools.
Even though our authorities in the
counties, at any rate, have only been in
enjoyment of their full powers for twelve
months, there has been a very fair supply
of scholarships from the edementary schools
to the secondary schools and thence to the
university.
The county boroughs, it is true, have had
two years in which to organise their scholarship scheme. Belfast, with fifty secondary
school scholarships of £30 each, and
four university scholarships of £40
each, has certainly made an excellent beginning, for the rates can be
put to no more fruitful purpose than this.
From the city of Londonderry the report is
not so good; but, we are all aware, the education committee there has had peculiar
difficulties. In future years we feel sure
that they, too, will be able to offer secondary
school scholarships on a correspondingly
liberal scale.
Of the counties, where, as I have just said,
the regional education committees have
really only just got to work, I can speak most
encouragingly. They have, between the:n,
offered 84 secondary school scholarships, of
an average value of £20 each, and 18 university scholarships, ranging from £40 to £60
each. That is what we can say of the year
1925-26.
But the problem of the construction and
administration of a scheme of scholarships
is a formidable one. Lord Londonderry,
under whom I had the honour to serve, and
whose services to education will never be for

I must apologise to the Committee for the
length of time which I am occupying this
afternoon. I have important matters yet to
refer to, which deal with technical instruction and our local administration generally.
I will speak first of technical instruction,
under which I shall include continuation
schools and classes of various kinds.
Seeing then that our elementary school
population, between the ages of 6 and 14, is
no fewer than 167,000, while our secondary
school population, including 1,600 children
between 6 and 12 years of age, though rising
steadily, is no more at present than 9,400, it
is evident that the great majority of our
children do not pursue an intermediate or
secondary school course after leaving the
elementary school. This, I may say, is also
true of the great majority of the children
in other parts of the United Kingdom. So
far as we can judge, the children and young
persons available for further instruction
from 14 to 19 number about 100,000. We find
when we deduct the population of our
secondary schools that some 90,000 remain to
be dealt with.
What, then, are we doing for this important body of the population, these adolescents,
who will so soon enter upon the full responsibility of citizenship?
This field of the activities of the Ministry is
a very wide one. It embraces courses in the
various subjects of technical instruction, at
fixed centres in our cities and our larger
towns; it includes shorter courses, under
itinerant instructors, whom we encourage
the various local authorities to send periodically into our smaller towns and our more
thinly populated rural districts. In whatever way we can, and whereever we can, we
seek to assist the establishment of classes
giving instruction which has, or ought to
have, a particular appeal to the local inhabitants. If it is a fishing centre we try to
establish classes in navigation, marine motor
engineering, and so on. Where some cottage
industry is strong, we set up classes of instruction in it-lace-making, crocheting, and
the like. The Ulster housewife, wherever
she is, is always willing to send her daughters
to a course of domestic economy if she can.
We are endeavouring here, by means of
these classes, not only to convey instruction
where it will in itself be actually of practical

value, but to foster, by the study of at least
one subject, the habit of study generally.
I must add that in this work we are greatly
assisted by the Ministry of Agriculture, with
its classes in agricultural subjects.
I must not forget to mention that under
the head of technical instruction come the
subjects taught in our day commercial
schools, in our junior technical schools, in
classes for the unemployed, classes for ex-
Service men, classes to enable our elementary
school teachers to include domestic economy,
manual instruction, and drawing in their
curriculum.
The local control of technical instruction,
which was given to our local authorities
under the Agricultural and Technical
Instruction Act of 1899, was the
nursery in which they first qualified
for the wider task of the general
administration of education in their areas,
which has been entrusted to them by the
Education Act of 1923. It was their success
here, in the field of technical instruction,
that emboldened the Ministry to enlarge
their educational responsibility and to look
forward with confidence to their further
success.
Under their guidance the facilities for
technical instruction have been eagerly
grasped and have become immensely and increasingly popular in Ireland-not least in
Ulster. The Belfast College of Technology is
second to none in the whole Empire, and our
technical schools in urban areas generally
compare well with those similarly situated
in other parts of the United Kingdom.
In my view, one of the most encouraging
signs of the times is the overcrowding of
our evening classes. It affords a complete
reply to the pessimists, who tell us that the
young generation wants nothing and does
nothing beyond dancing and going to the
pictures. Not so! Our local authorities,
backed to the fullest extent by the
Ministry of Agriculture and the Ministry
for which I have the honour to speak, are
doing everything in their power to encourage
and to foster what seems an almost natural
bent in our young people for the acquisition
of useful knowledge.
The one danger, and it is a very real
danger to my mind, is lest the cry for useful
instruction may deafen our ears to the call
for liberal education-lest the longing to do
something, or to make something, deaden us
to all recognition of the need for the simultaneous development of the reasoning capacity and the intelligence.
Great though the success of technical
instruction had already been when the
Ministry of Education first came into existence, there has been a continuous increase,
not only in the number of individual students
but also in the number of classes taken.

The spread of technical instruction has

technical instruction; and, of these, two

The position of the teachers in our

responsibilities. They certainly had the

With the sanction of the Ministry of

of
Before I leave the subject of technical
instruction, I should like just to say one
word upon
the direction in which the
Ministry is moving in this field.
We recognise the vital importance, not only to the
future welfare of technical instruction, but
to the welfare of our skilled industries, that
there should be a lively and intimate connection between our technical schools and
our industries.
Lord Londonderry, in a Presidental
Address to the Association of Technical Institutions at its meeting in London, early
in March last, urged upon the Association
the necessity of establishing a satisfactory
system of apprenticeship in skilled industries in order to ensure the proper recruitment of the ranks of our skilled
workers. He pointed out the way in which
technical schools could assist this work.
"What profit," he asked, "is there in a
scheme of technical education, however perfect, which is not generally recognised as an
integral part of our industrial training."
With that view the Ministry and, I have
no doubt, the country at large are in full
agreement. To this end, we have been giving
a certain number of trade scholarships
eighty annually, to be precise-which are
awarded to apprentices in certain skilled
trades at the conclusion of the second year
of their apprenticeship. They are tenable
at the Belfast College of Technology, where
the scholars pass through a specially trained
course in their particular trade, a course
which is a blend of theoretical and practical
instruction. I am happy to be able to report that employers have welcomed the institution of these scholarships, and that
generally they recognise the scholarship
period as part of an apprentice's years of
indenture. The expenditure on these
scholarships will be found under Sub-head
D2, of Vote II, which announced to £3,000.
Before I pass to our
local education
authorities I ought, I feel, to say something
of the Queen's University, to which we make
annual payment of thirty-six thousand
pounds under statute. It is true the University is a self-governing body, in the
guidance of which the State can exact no
share as a condition of this expenditure.
That is a good thing educationally, and one
which we do not, in the least, wish to see
changed. But we are always glad to assist
the University, which, in its turn, has shown
itself very ready to assist the Ministry in its
difficulties, particularly in the matter of our
arrangements for the training of teachers.
The Committee will remember that a short
Act was passed recently, enabling local
authorities to contribute from the rates to
the funds of the University. We are aware
that a beginning has been made, and that
some of these authorities are now taking
advantage of their powers under this Act.
It requires no word from me to commend
the services of the University to the community, and I feel I shall not be alone in
expressing the hope that the University may
receive a really adequate measure of assistance from these local bodies.
I have left as my last topic what is, probably, of most interest, namely, the progress of the local administration of education in the counties and the county boroughs.
The Education Act of 1923 is now in full
operation everywhere. The Education Committees of Belfast and Londonderry are at
the close of the second year of their existence. In the counties, the Regional Education Committees have been in charge of their
areas for the past twelve months. We are
already able to speak of the working of the
new system, though naturally we shall be
able to say more about it in another year
or so.

I think we may claim to have revived, if
not actually to have created, a healthy public
interest in education in Northern Ireland. In
the days of a highly centralised system, when
the public voice had so narrow a channel
for expression, public interest was naturally
never very widespread, and, in any event,
could never be very vocal.
From the
But that has all been changed.
day when the proposals of the Government
first appeared, when it was seen that educational administration would be shared between the Ministry of Education and the
organs of local government, the columns of
our newspapers have been full of the topic
of Education.
Now that the Act of 1923 is in operation,
the doings and sayings of the various local
authorities are fully reported and are eagerly
read. The Press has done much to encourage
this healthy interest, and to it much of the
credit belongs. But the Press itself is largely
a reflection of public opinion-
Mr. DEVLIN: I do not know.
Mr. ROBB and the extent of public
interest may be fairly measured by the
amount of space devoted to a subject in the
newspapers. We welcome this activity, and
in spite of the fact that the Ministry is often
a subject of criticism, we regard that as a
sign of health in the body politic. We had
far rather be criticised than forgotten.
As hon. Members are no doubt aware, three
of the counties are divided into several
regional areas; the County of Antrim has
five; the County of Londonderry has three,
and the County of Tyrone has five. Each
region is under its committee, responsible to
the county council-the education authority
in all the counties, whether divided or notfor general educational administration within
the area allotted to it.
Three counties, the Counties of Armagh,
Down, and Fermanagh, are being administered
as a single region each. That is to say, there
is one regional committee in each of these
counties which, under a scheme approved by
the Ministry, administers the whole county
the area allotted to it.
The difference between these two kinds of
local administration is really one of form,
rather than of substance, because, in order
to secure the full local representation and
control required by the Act, the schemes
under which the three single-region counties,
if I may call them so, are operating, all provide for the appointment of various local
sub-committees, upon which devolves the performance of the duties of administration in
the locality which they represent.
There is, of
course, this important
difference, that, whereas in the single county
areas the regional education rate is a flat
rate over the whole county, in the other
counties, the counties divided into several
regions, the rate is struck for that part of the
county only which is comprised within each
region. Finance, of course, must play a very
important part in every scheme of administration; and we shall watch closely the
operation of the system in each county, in
order to secure the most economical-under
which head I include the most efficientmethod of working. The Ministry has an
open mind in regard to the mode of applying
the Act in particular counties, a mind which
is governed chiefly by the two considerations
which I have just named.
Of all the problems confronting our local
education authorities there are five, which,
in my opinion, overshadow the rest; first,
there is the problem of securing efficient elementary school accommodation; second, is
that of enforcing school attendance; third,
comes the provision of opportunities for
further education, whether at secondary
schools or at continuation and technical
schools; fourth, the establishment of an
effective system of medical inspection and
treatment; and last, we have that bugbear of
all administrations, the problem of finance.
That there are other problems I know too
well; but they are either minor problems by
comparison, or problems which have an
interest more or less peculiar to one or two
areas or localities within areas. But the five
which I have mentioned are of universal
application, though they do not, of course,
exert an equal pressure over all. I propose
to do no more than touch upon these to-day.
In Belfast the problem of elementary
school accommodation stands by itself. It is
a problem, not of to-day, nor of yesterday,
but of many years' standing, and it is a
problem which has arisen largely owing to
the rapid rate of the growth of the population. Schools, not so long ago ample enough
and within the reach of green fields, are now
overbuilt, cramped and overcrowded. There
are, I know, old schools, schools long out of
date, which in a normal state of things
would require replacement or reconstruction.
That is the case everywhere, and we must
always be prepared for a policy of systematic
and periodic rebuilding.
But the trouble in Belfast is that even our
newest schools, those of comparatively recent
date, which are otherwise quite admirable
school buildings, are in a great number of
cases planned on altogether too small a
scale.
I cannot speak too highly of the way in
which the local education authority in Belfast has faced its difficulties and taken the

In the City of Londonderry, and in the
