are
Single-teacher schools are, in the nature of
things, the least economical form of school
accommodation, and educationally the least
efficient. While we recognize that these
schools must always persist in sparsely populated and remote rural districts, we
aware that there are many such small schools
now which, by judicious amalgamation or
by a well-placed new building, could be
superseded, to the benefit of pupils and
teachers and to the advantage of the public
purse.
In pursuing a policy of amalgamating
schools wherever possible, local education
authorities may rest assured that they will
receive the full support of the Ministry.
They will, doubtless, be confronted with
obstacles with which the Ministry itself has
long been familiar, but, armed with an intimate knowledge of local conditions and with
the added weight which their representative
capacity gives them, they will probably find
themselves better able to deal with these
difficulties than any central authority could
hope to do. In any event, their battle is the
battle of the Ministry, as indeed it is that of
the taxpayer at large, and, as I say, they can
rely upon our assistance.
Before any general line of action can be
taken by the local authorities it will be necessary for them to formulate schemes, after a full
review of existing facilities. Such a course
has hitherto been rendered difficult, if not
actually impossible, owing to the delay of
transfers, pending the settlement of doubts
as to the effect of transfer upon the facilities
for religious instruction. These doubts have
now been removed, and conditions satisfactory to all parties appear to have been decided upon. The Ministry knows that the
detail arangements are liable to make the
actual transfer a long proceeding, but we
hope, now that the path seems clear, managers will without delay intimate to the
authorities everywhere in what relation they
desire their schools to stand as part of the
local school supply.
I have already spoken of school attendance.
The figures I gave make it clear that this
part of the Act is being everywhere effectively administered. I have also alluded to
local responsibility regarding secondary education and continuation and technical
schools and classes. On that I will say no
more now.
Medical inspection and treatment of elementary school children has, I am glad to
say, been recognized by all our local authorities as a matter of first importance. Belfast
already has a very complete scheme in course
of operation. The other authorities have
taken preliminary steps and are all at one
stage or other of the establishment of a form
of medical service under the Education Act.
There is no doubt that ultimately the whole
of our elementary school population will be
brought under proper medical supervision.
Here, perhaps, more than in any other part
of their activities, local authorities will be
breaking new ground in Northern Ireland.
Progress undoubtedly depends upon the measure of co-operation which the parents
accord them in this work, and the Ministry
feels sure that the authorities will not look
in vain to the public for sympathy in their
efforts to secure for the Province the full
benefits which will be derived from a school
medical service organized upon a sound and
economical basis. I may say, in the same
connection, that the Belfast Education
Authority has already had a scheme in operation for the feeding of necessitous children.
The Estimates of the Ministry show that
out of a total contemplated expenditure of
£1,942,145 we are looking to the local education authorities to raise £67,500 from the
rates. Hon. Members will get this last
figure from the sum of £135,000, which they
will find under Sub-head F of Vote II, that
amount representing the Ministry's grant to
local education authorities of two pounds for
every pound raised by the education rates.
We know that there is an outcry against
the burden of the rates, but this cannot be
based upon the burden imposed by educational expenditure. Let me make a brief
comparison of the incidence of this expenditure upon the common purse and upon the
local rates. A penny rate in the pound is
estimated roughly to produce £20,000 over
the whole Province. Expressed in terms of
rating, therefore,
total educational
expenditure comes to just over the equivalent
of a rate of eight shillings and a penny. Of
this, the State finds seven and ninepence
three farthings, while the local authorities
find the rest-say, threepence farthing.
our
Supply Committee-
Education Estimates.
13 MAY
That is the position to-day. My right hon.
Friend, the Minister of Finance, has no
Fortunatus's purse of limitless capacity. He
has, as a matter of fact, already warned us
that the very limit of aid to local expenditure which he can contemplate is the
equivalent of an eightpenny rate, namely,
one hundred and sixty thousand pounds. As I
have pointed out, that limit has been nearly
reached. It will be attained if and when
the State grant reaches another twenty-five
thousand pounds.
We are, undoubtedly, faced by an expansion of our educational services. We have
economised to the utmost to assist in meeting
that expansion. This year shows a net decrease in the Ministry's Estimates of one
hundred and nine thousand, four hundred
and nineteen pounds. I find it difficult to
suggest any direction in which the Ministry's
Estimates can be further reduced if we are
adequately to perform the task given us, and
it seems to follow that the cost of expansion
must be met locally. Before the Act of 1923,
local authorities used to rate for technical
instruction, up to a maximum of twopence
in the pound. There was, perhaps, an
average rate struck, throughout the Province, of a penny farthing. As I showed,
the average local rate comes to threepence
farthing, and that means that the local
authorities have, so far, only paid twopence
of new money for the benefits which they
receive under the Act.
By the Education Act, in the words of
Canning, “We call the new world into existence to redress the balance of the old."
We created local education authorities to
assist the State in the supreme task of
assuring the future of our children. I refuse to believe that these authorities will
answer us with words which were also used
by the great Canning, though in quite
another connection-" I give thee sixpence !
I will see thee damned first!" I beg to
move.
Mr. O'NEILL : In the first instance I
think I am bound to compliment the hon.
and learned Gentleman on the lengthy and
rather lucid case he has presented for his
Ministry. I regret that I am not in agreement with all he has said on this matter.
The Committee might think from the statement of the case he has made that all the
schools in this Province were satisfied under
the recently-passed Education Act, but, unfortunately, it is true that the schools,
which 35 per cent. of the school-going children attend, have been put to a very serious
disadvantage by the recent Education Act.
They are in a much worse position now than
they were under the old National Board.
There they were provided with two-thirds of
the cost of the erection and equipment of
the schools, but under the present educa-

tional system in the North they have not any
grant except one small amount for the cleaning of the schools. That, in my opinion, and
I think the Committee will agree with me,
is a very serious injustice to more than onethird of the population of this area.
I would suggest to the hon. and learned
Gentleman and also to the Members of the
Cabinet that they might consider inserting
even a further Amendment in the Act in
order to do the people for whom I speak
fair justice in the matter. I believe I can
state with a fair amount of authority that
the transference of the schools belonging to
the body which I represent will not take
place, and that they will hold the schools as
they are. I think I am also correct in saying
that many of the schools which do not belong to the party I represent have not been
transferred, and that there is a possibility
that they will not be transferred.
Under the Act of 1923 there seem to be
two classes of schools-in fact there are two
classes of schools, A and B. There are the
private schools which the Ministry provide
for and equip, and there are the transferred
schools which seem to belong to the same
class. There are also the voluntary schools
and they also seem to have two classes. They
appoint a committee to manage the school
and then the Ministry are prepared to grant
half the cost of the upkeep and equipment
of the schools, but in cases where there are
only single managers-which applies to the
schools belonging to the faith I am associated
with--then no grant of any sort is made except, as I said before, a small grant for
cleaning which only amounts to a few pounds
in the year. In my opinion that is a
serious injustice to these people, and I hope
the Government will take a note of it, and
perhaps in the near future they may consider
the advisability of doing justice to these
people. I should like to know from the hon.
and learned Gentleman if the Annual Report
of the Ministry of Education has yet been
published?
Mr. ROBB: No.
Mr. O'NEILL: I am sorry it has not been
published. I think it should be published,
if possible, before the Vote is taken. If that
were done it would be much easier for Members who would have time to consider the
thing more fully than they have been able
to do. I hope the hon. and learned Gentleman will take a note of that. The first item
I have to make reference to is with regard
to the grant of £36,000 to the Queen's University, Belfast.

Mr. DEVLIN: I should like to congratulate
the hon. and learned Gentleman on the very
fine and illuminating speech which he has
delivered in introducing this Estimate.
Although some people might complain that
it was a very lengthened statement, I think
those of us who remained in the House to
listen to it will quite recognise that he
amply justified the time which he occupied in
the delivery of a most impressive and interesting statement. (Hon. Members: Hear,
hear.) I rise to join with my hon, Friend (Mr.
O'Neill) in a protest against the manner in
which the voluntary schools are treated.
We understood that when the Act of 1920
was passed-that is the Act which established
this Parliament-no religious denomination
would suffer thereby.
Now the Catholics of Northern Ireland do
suffer by the operation of this Measure, because they are in a worse position now under
this Parliament than they were under the
Imperial regime. Under the old system they
were entitled to a grant of two-thirds for
their schools-for Catholic schools-as indeed
a two-thirds grant was given to all schools
under the national system in those days.
Under the new arrangement they are not entitled to any grant towards the building of
schools, and, considering the financial difficulties to which the hon. and learned Gentleman (Mr. Robb) referred, it seems to me
rather an indefensible policy that, while you
are finding it difficult to raise money to build
schools, you refuse to assist those who are
ready to raise a substantial portion of the
building fund themselves. That has always
been done in the case of Catholic schools.
They have raised one-third of the building
fund themselves, and the State has given
them a two-thirds grant.
Now it may be said that under this new
system, since there is a rate in aid, the
public are entitled to representation in the
government of the schools, but what do you
get out of the rates? I was quite astonished
to hear the figures read by the hon. and
learned Gentleman (Mr. Robb). He said that
if there was a rate struck for education it
would amount to 8s 1d in the pound. But of
the total amount spent on education 7s 93d is
paid by the State. In other words about
3ld is voted by the local authorities, and
yet because of the introduction of this principle of making the local authorities partly
responsible for the building of schools, you
take away two-thirds of the grant from the
voluntary schools.
This Act was passed in 1923. There was an
Amending Act passed in 1925 to meet the
objections raised, not by the Catholic school
managers or the Catholic authorities, but by
the Presbyterians, who are always a most
militant body when they are looking for
anything, as the hon. Member for Antrim
(Mr. Crawford) well knows. (Laughter.)
They raised a row and they got an Amending
Bill, but I want to know how many of the
schools have been transferred in the intermediate period between the passage of that
Amending Act and now. I should also like
to know how many schools have been transferred altogether-Catholic and Protestant
schools--because I take it that an Education
Act when it is passed is for the purpose of
creating, if not perfection, at least an improved system, something that will appeal
in a more widespread way to the general desires of the people.
I would like to know whether all this talk
about these educational reforms and the
passage of these two Measures have justified
themselves in what has occurred from then
till now. For my part I think it would be a
far wiser policy for the Government to give
to voluntary schools the grant of two-thirds
for building which was formerly given under
the National Board. If you want the public
satisfied, and if you want to maintain the
position which our schools occupied before
this Act was passed, then you ought to do
that. Probably if we had been as vocal as
the Presbyterians were we might have got
our wrongs righted long since. In my judg
ment there ought to be great consideration
shown to the Catholic body in Ulster, which
constitutes thirty-five per cent. of the population, on the fact that, although holding so
strongly on these questions, although holding
very deeply and profoundly conscientious
convictions, they have given no trouble to
the Government in relation to education,
neither in relation to the education nor in
the administration of that Act. I think that
will be admitted by the hon. and learned
Gentleman opposite and by his staff.
And this I must say in regard to his staffand I must say it in regard to Lord London-

derry, who was the Minister of Education for
so many years-that, although I have the
profoundest objection to his method and to
his educational solution, for broad-mindedness, for a desire to conciliate, for a

spirit. (Hon. Members: Hear, hear.) For
my part, for that reason-and indeed for
other reasons as an Ulsterman-I deeply regret the disappearance of Lord Londonderry
from our public life, and I would have been
one of those who would have gladly joined,
if I had not thought some political purpose
was at work, in paying any tribute to the
splendid public service and to the genuinely
unselfish spirit which inspired Lord Londonderry in his association with this Province.
(Hon. Members: Hear, hear).
Now, as I said, you passed an Amending
Act to please a certain section of the community. It did not please them and it did
not satisfy them. I do not say they are insatiable, although once a notorious-I will
not say a notorious, but a well-known judge,
who is one of themselves, asked a witness
what his religion was, and he said "I am
a Presbyterian," and the judge said "That
is not a religion; it is an appetite."
(Laughter.) I believe that, notwithstanding
what that judge said, they were not insatiable, but, although you have made these concessions to them, they are unsatisfied still.
And yet you have never made the slightest
concession to the Catholic minority. One
would have imagined that when you got all
the power into your own hands-because, as I
have before stated in this House, you went
to England and told them that you were a
minority and did not want to put yourselves
under the heel of a Catholic majority-and
that is how you got your Parliament-and
when, on the strength of your being a
minority, a very vocal minority, a very
violent minority, and a very revolutionary
minority, and as a result of your violence
you got this Parliament, one would have
thought that, in the light of your
experience of your propaganda, and of
your success both as propagandists and
as revolutionaries, you would have given some
consideration to the rights of the minority—
larger in Ulster than you were in the whole
of Ireland-in respect of educational matters.
I trust, however, that the new Minister
(Viscount Charlemont), who, I hope, comes
with a virgin mind, free from all the fetid
atmosphere of these religious and bitter
controversies, will apply himself to the task
of devising some scheme whereby justice may
be done to the Catholic voluntary schools.
Before I deal with one or two other matters I want to come to the question of the
Irish language. I was very glad that the
hon. and learned Gentleman (Mr. Robb)--
who, one would think, was a model
utilitarian from the method in which he
delivered his speech-denounced what he
called the fetish of practical utility, and that
he also told us that he did not regard as
sacrosanct the commercial value of education.
I was delighted to hear so idealistic a
sentiment secretively issuing from the mass
of oratory with which he dealt with the
Estimate. Therefore, I trust that I will find
a sympathetic listener in the hon. and
learned Gentleman. I think it was wrong to
attempt to take away the privileges, very
much enjoyed by the pupils, by the parents,
and by the teachers, that were given in our
elementary schools in regard to the teaching
of the Irish language. No teacher has been
compelled to teach Irish. The work has been
done voluntarily. Therefore, I think that
where the pupil wanted to learn Irish, where
the parents wanted their children taught
Irish, and where the teachers were willing
to teach Irish, they should have had an opportunity of doing so. After all, although you
are Ulstermen, you must have some respect
for the language which is regarded as the
native language of Ireland-I was going to
say of your native land, but it is also the
language of a considerable portion of your
native Ulster. It is spoken in Donegal, in
the Glens of Antrim, and in many other parts
of Ulster, but even so, as a mere matter of
sentiment, if the people want to learn the
Irish language or have their children
taught the Irish language they ought to have
the privilege of having it taught in the
schools.
Mr. ROBB: So they have, and we pay for
it.
Mr. DEVLIN: Yes, but you have changed
the programme. According to the programme formerly the Irish language was
taught from the third standard up. Now it
is only to be taught from the fifth standard
up, and the revised programme in Irish is
so difficult that it is almost impossible to
teach it efficiently. Under the Commissioners of National Education in Dublin
Irish might be taught as an optional subject
in all standards in primary schools. That is
not done now. As I have said you have
raised it from the third standard to the fifth
standard. If you permit the Irish language
to be taught at all you ought to permit it to
be taught to children from the third standard up. At any rate I want to point out to
the hon. and learned Gentleman (Mr. Robb)
that the Irish language, even to those of us
who are Irishmen, and who do not hold extreme views, is a thing that is deeply appreciated. It is regarded as the vocal sentiment
of our people. You may not like it. We
may be fools. It may be thought that it is
of no commercial value. I need not argue

I want to subscribe most heartily to the
doctrine of the widest possible education for
all, and when I say widest I mean widest.
I do not mean that the elementary school
should be used only for turning out a good
shipyard worker or a good textile worker. I

be used only for the purpose of turning out
a good technician. They are all useful and
necessary, but we of the working classes want
what has been called here a liberal education.
We want to be able to use our reason and
our intelligence. It is because I believe that
the Parliamentary Secretary is interested in
that liberal education that I do subscribe
most heartily to the doctrine of the widest
possible education for us all.

I do not know whether the hon. and

take very little interest in education, and

taught. It is only when they approximate
to the age of 20 that boys who are bright and
intelligent come to appreciate the value of
education. That gives a period of from 14

Ministry of Education in conjunction with

was fixed by the Committee appointed
by the House, shortly after the formation of
our Parliament, was proving to be inadequate. The Prime Minister's colleagues have
for some time past, realised this. They have
had experience of the very heavy demands
that are made on the Prime Minister's hospitality, and have also recognised the appropriateness of such hospitality as the Prime
Minister extends to those people who call on
him so repeatedly. Consequently, they were
only too ready to take advantage of the
suggestion that was made to them. They also
took the trouble of ascertaining whether it
would receive a sufficient measure of support
throughout the House to justify a Supplemental Estimate being brought forward.
are
We have, of course, the Hospitality Vote,
which was passed yesterday. That was a
fund which was started very shortly after
the establishment of this Parliament, and
was designed to meet the entertainment of
those visitors or deputations who
obviously suitable for the Province, at
large, to entertain. That, however does not
meet the expenditure of the classes which
this Estimate is intended to provide for. It
is an addition to the Vote under Cabinet
Offices, and is a contribution towards the
expenses which we consider are necessarily
incurred by the Prime Minister in the discharge of the duties which have been imposed
on him. The amount especially devoted to
this purpose is £1,750. There is a further
item of £250, which relates principally to the
heating and lighting of that part of Stormont House which is set apart specially for
the accommodation of the Cabinet. It has
always been a matter of rather troublesome
accounting between the Ministry of Finance
and the Secretary to the Prime Minister as
to the apportionment of the total charges and
expenses of heating Stormont, and so it
has been felt that equitable arrangements
would be made if the Government were to
contribute towards the fuel and light, and
this sum of £250 is towards that. I beg to
move.
Mr. BEATTIE: I desire to move the rejection of this Estimate, or at least to vote
against it. I do so on the ground that this
is a very inopportune time to put forward
an increase of salary to any official of this
Parliament. I claim that this is an increase of salary under another heading. We
have a Hospitality Fund at our command.
We had £1,000 voted last year for it, and we
only used £500, and I cannot see why now,
under the title of Cabinet Offices, we should
be asked to vote this additional money for
hospitality, or the incidental expenses that
the Prime Minister is committed to by
deputations, and one party or another which
go out to Stormont. I want to say quite
candidly-and I will say it either outside or
inside that the offices attached to the Northern Government are far too highly paid. 1
am not saying anything in depreciation of
the value of the services of the men we have
at the head of the various Departments. I
agree that we have competent men, but I do
not agree that the services should be run
with a salary to the head of each Department of £1,500 plus £500 as a Cabinet
Minister.
We had a Select Committee of this House
set up, when no Opposition was here, and
this Committee set out a salary of £3,200 for
the Prime Minister. Now at that time
things were higher, the cost of living and
everything else were higher than now, and
I presume that they took all these things
into account and set the wage accordingly.
Let us study the workers' point of view.
The working classes had high wages at one
time, but when things began to come down
a bit they were asked to reduce the price of
their labour, no matter about the increased
liabilities that had cropped up through their
high wages. Remember that when the
workers had high wages there was an increased financial liability which they took
upon themselves during that time, but when
times were getting back to the normal state
they were asked to accept a reduction of
wages, and still they had to keep up the
higher expenses that had occurred during
the period of high wages.
The Prime Minister has stated himself
that he is a poorer man now than he was
when he came into this House. I would accept that statement. I am a poorer man myself now than I was when I came into this
House. (An hon. Member: Question.) There
is no earnest, straightforward representative
who has the interests of Ulster at heart who
will come into this House to make a profit
out of it. I believe he should give his labour
to the Government at a fee, but not at a fee
which any person could say was profiteering
or that there was a profit in it, and I believe
the fees allocated to the various Ministers
as heads of Departments-I am speaking now
of those fixed by the Select Committee-were
exaggerated in value, exaggerated to the
extent, I should say, of £500 per head. I will
suggest a value for them now, and I would
say that £1,000 would be quite sufficient in
respect of their departmental duties and the
labour attached thereto.
I would be failing in my duty if I allowed
this to go through without protesting against
an increase of this description. The unem-

Mr. T. W. McMULLAN: On the Estimate
for Cabinet Offices there was some criticism

to protest and to defend as well as I could
the salary of the Prime Minister. At that

colleagues who were available, and I am
glad to say that they see eye to eye with me

been put forward this afternoon.
There has been some suggestion that that
Select Committee arranged the salaries of the
Ministers with all the facts before them.
That Committee was set up immediately
after the inception of this Parliament, and
they had very little data to go on. They
approached the subject matter of the
salaries with a view which has been
expressed very often by my hon. Friend
the Member for West Belfast (Mr. Devlin).
They thought adequate salaries should be
paid to the gentlemen who were assuming
heavy responsibilities. They had in their
minds another point, which I think is also
in the mind of my hon. Friend the Member
for East Belfast (Mr. Beattie), and that was
that they must go slowly, and that they must
be as economical in the apportionment of
those salaries as possible. Their judgment as
to what they should do was entirely free and
unfettered. They had no instructions as to
how the salaries were to be given, nor had
any Minister, with one exception, approached
them on the matter at all. The only
recommendation they got was that exception,
and that came from the Prime Minister himself, and the suggestion of the Prime Minister
was a very characteristic one-and it is a
suggestion to which men in receipt of salaries
are not often prone-and it was that his
salary should be made as low as possible as
he did not want a burden on the finances of
our young Parliament.
In settling the salary of the Prime Minister
we had to keep this wish to some extent before us, and I think I am speaking the minds
of my colleagues on that Committee when I
say that, though we settled the salary of the
Prime Minister at £3.200, we did not think it

HOUSE OF COMMONS

represented his value to Ulster. We put that

I am satisfied, and I think most hon. Members of this Committee will feel satisfied that
we were wrong in our conclusions as to this
salary and the allowance which should be

proved that hospitalities have been forced
upon him far beyond what the payment given
would be sufficient to meet. I think the

Sir ROBERT ANDERSON: I do not look
upon the proposal now before the Committee
as a proposal for an increase of salary at all.
Mr. POLLOCK: Hear, hear.
Sir ROBERT ANDERSON: I do not think
it is fair to put it in that category.
Mr. POLLOCK: Hear, hear.
Sir ROBERT ANDERSON: I was hoping
that a proposal of this character, considering
the facts, which must be known to all hon.
Members of this Committee, would have gone
through without any opposition and practically unanimously. I do not intend to labour
the many points referred to by some of the
previous speakers, but I think we must all
be familiar with the very heavy outlay that
must exist in connection with the Prime
Minister's residence. It is a very delicate
matter to refer to, and I was hoping that in
the most generous and magnanimous manner
possible this amount would be voted here today. My hon. Friends in the Opposition, I
am sure, are looking forward to the time
when they will sit on this side of the House.
I am sure the Leader of the Opposition (Mr.
Kyle) will look forward to the time when he
will be in occupation of Stormont. I think
it is fair and reasonable to fix some figure
that will be a precedent for the time when a
very poor man who has ability, character,
standing, and efficiency, may occupy the
supreme position in Ulster. We would be
all glad to put him in a position to maintain the good name of Ulster, and to be able
to extend generous hospitality-to all who
called with him. I think if we look upon the
question in that broad, generous way we
would not refuse to allow this small sum
that is proposed to-day to go through. We
are not voting this sum to the man at all.
We are really voting the money to whoever
may be the occupant of the position of Prime
Minister in connection with our Parliament
here. We may have a man who may not require it, or we may have the other type of
man I have indicated, and then assistance of
this character will be needed.
I am sure that no matter on which side of
the Committee we sit we will all have sufficient pride in our Province to see to it that
even the man without any money will be
in a position to maintain the good name and
hospitality of the Province over which he
may be called upon to preside. On those
grounds I support the proposal now before
the Committee, and I sincerely trust it will
go through without any controversy, and
that our Opposition Friends will see that
after all on this occasion the money is not
going into the pocket of the Prime Minister,
but to the office. I am sure that we on this
side, and those who are on the Opposition,
consider that he has adorned the position,
and has rendered splendid service to the
whole country, irrespective of creed or class.

My namesake, the hon. Member for Down

If they are going to reconsider the situation

We possibly would not offer any hostility

have regard to the times. Surely, hon, and

those circumstances are we justified in voting

The whole of the sum might be spent on the

I do not accept the standpoint of the hon.
or right hon. Gentlemen opposite. To me the
problem seems to be this. I confine my
attention to the speeches of hon. Gentlemen
opposite. We are told we are a community,
the community of Ulster that Ulster counts.
I have mentioned before that Ulster to me
means men, women and children. We are being
repeatedly told that our finances are limited.
If the Ulster loaf is only a certain size, and
everyone requires to get a slice of that loaf,
the larger the slice the Prime Minister gets
the smaller the slice someone at the opposite
end of the scale gets. If the Prime Minister
is going to be the big brother of Ulster, he
will surely have some concern for the smaller
members of the family. In ordinary circumstances if there is a weak member of a
family the collective love and care of the
other members of the family would be bestowed upon the member of the family who
is weak. It should not be a question of the
person who is the big brother usurping or
abusing his position for the purpose of doing
injury to the person who is at the bottom of
the social scale. That is precisely what is
happening here.
I am sure my hon. Friend (Sir Robert

Committee yesterday. I took the opportunity of bringing before the Committee a matter which was entirely germane to the matter of that Vote. Now, I wish to remove some
apprehensions that appear to be in the mind

I stated that as a result of my observations
from this time last year when the Hospitality Vote was presented by my right hon.

that I had considerable uneasiness that the

bear in mind what the hon. Member for
Derry (Sir Robert Anderson) has emphasised

people, not people of our own Province alone,
but individuals coming from the other side,
entirely in the interests of the Province.
The hon. Member who has just addressed
the Committee used some fantastic figures in
saying the Prime Minister had £80 a week.
That is fantastic nonsense. If you take the
Prime Minister's salary as it appears in the
Estimate book at £3,200 and deduct incometax and super-tax, I question if his income
from it is £30 a week, and to speak of £30 a
week as sufficient to maintain the position
he does in the interest of the Province is
quite absurd.
Comparisons have been made by hon. Members between salaries on the other side of the
water and those obtaining here. I am not
now discussing the general question of
salaries, but I am adhering to the particular
case under discussion. It is on record that
Mr. Clynes, Minister without portfolio in the

11 Downing Street. It is perfectly ridiculous
and fantastic to compare the expenditure in

necessary in our Province by one in the

What I want to put before the Committee
is this: Are our Cabinet Offices at the present time not costing as much as this Province can afford? I do not wish to repeat
the figures that have been already put before
the Committee, but I find that the Free
State has a President and six Cabinet
Ministers costing £12,700. In the Six
Counties the Prime Minister and five Cabinet
Ministers cost £13,200, even without this
Supplementary Estimate. I, for one, find it
impossible to support this Supplementary
Estimate, because we are making a precedent.
Whoever occupies the position of Prime
Minister is in receipt of other emoluments
as well as the salary of £3,200. I find here
that rent and rates are estimated £330. A
private person has to pay his own rent and
rates. Therefore whoever occupies the
position of Prime Minister has an emolument
of £330 for rent and rates, besides the sum

Mr. DEVLIN: I only intend to occupy

that brings with it many costly encumbrances. And that is borne out by the fact
that the right hon. Gentleman, the Chancellor of the Exchequer, has said that Mr.
Clynes recently stated that it was impossible for him to live in Downing Street on
£5,000 a year. But I confess I think it most
unwise proceeding to introduce a matter
of this sort at this stage. The question as
to whether the Prime Minister is sufficiently
compensated for his work, or whether he
has no adequate grants towards hospitality,
is one that I think might have been left
over until a better time. When you consider the great amount of unemployment
and privation amongst the people, the depression that exists in trade, I think it is
an unwise thing to bring forward this proposal at this time. The real fact of the
matter is we are permanently establishing
a position at over £5,000 a year, and it is
all very good for people to say: "No matter,
some day someone else will be Prime Minister," and all that sort of thing. That
does not draw me. (Laughter). I mean
that does not matter to me. It may draw my

(Mr. Kyle). But the fact is you are permanently in power. The present Prime
Minister is there as long as he chooses to
remain. You have so regulated the affairs of
the Province of Ulster that there is no
chance of any of the Opposition ever occupying the seats of the mighty.

(Northern Ireland) established for the purpose of the National School Teachers'
(Ireland) Act, 1879, and certain other funds

Mr. BARBOUR: This Resolution has reference to the paragraph printed in italics
on page 4 of the Teachers' Superannuation
Bill. In plain language it simply means that
in future the bulk of the money required
for teachers' superannuation purposes will
be drawn from direct Votes of the House. Instead of attempting to build up any superannuation fund to meet these pensions, the
burden of it will be on the direct Votes of
the House. In order to explain the
machinery by which this will be carried out
I may say that the Teachers' Superannuation
Fund established under the Bill will be made
up of three items, namely:-
The capital handed over from the old
fund;
The contributions made by the Teachers
of every grade;
The contributions made by Local Education and School Authorities in respect of
Secondary, Preparatory, Technical and
Agricultural Teachers employed by them.
These various contributions will be added
to the income derived from the capital, the
capital itself being left intact, and that
amount will be available to meet the superannuation benefits payable to pensioned
teachers. It is anticipated that for the
current financial year this amount will be
sufficient to meet all the charges, but
beginning with 1st April, 1927, the growing

pension charge will
commence to exceed

It is very difficult to estimate what the ultimate charge on the Exchequer will be under
the Bill. On the best information available,
however, it will rise from £7,000 in the year
1926-27 to about £95,000 in the year 1939.
Hitherto, under the old system of financing

per annum. The proposals of the present
Bill lighten the immediate charge but, while

Pollock) yesterday, affect our general
financial position adversely owing to the way
in which the Final Report of the Colwyn
Committee operates. I beg to move.

Sir DAWSON BATES: I beg to move in

(2) Save as aforesaid an indictment presented in pursuance of this section shall
be presented and shall be proceeded with

been presented and proceeded with before

all enactments and rules of law relating

subject only to such modifications as are

(3) An indictment against any person presented to a court of quarter sessions in

addition to the counts for the offences

any further counts founded on facts or
evidence disclosed in any examination
or deposition taken before a justice in the
presence of the accused.
A court of quarter sessions may in any
case direct any such further counts as
aforesaid to be added to any indictment
presented to the court."

Sir DAWSON BATES: The first paragraph of the Amendment is merely for the

moved by the hon. Member for North Belfast
(Mr. Lloyd Campbell), and to make it clear
that the county court judge will have power

is dissatisfied that a prima facie case is
made out against the prisoner. The county
court judge will be able to prevent a prisoner
being put on trial unless he is satisfied a
prima facie case is made out against him.
The second sub-clause is purely formal and
observes the existing procedure except so
far as it is modified by the abolition of the
grand jury.
The third sub-clause is really consequential.
When the grand jury was in existence a Bill
was sent up dealing with the charge on
which the prisoner was returned. At the
same time it was open to the Crown to send
forward a lesser Bill if the Crown so desired.
The Amendment is to make it perfectly clear
that there will be the same right vested in

Mr. CRAWFORD: A few words will serve
to indicate the purpose I had in my mind
when I put down these three Amendments.
In page 3, lines 1, 2, and 3, it says that certain
people, though they are not actually resident

The PARLIAMENTARY SECRETARY OF
THE MINISTRY OF HOME AFFAIRS (Mr.
Hanna): No. They will have to serve in

Mr. CRAWFORD: Then again, the Bill says
that this twenty-five miles is to be measured
from the courthouse in the city. So far as I
know miles on the road are not measured from
the courthouse, but from somewhere in the
centre of the city, and that being so makes
the thing a little more difficult. I do not see,
unless you take a pair of compasses and
measure all round from the courthouse how
you are going to arrive at this distance.
The words in the Clause are
"being resident within twenty-five statute
miles of the courthouse thereof,"
and I suggest that we should strike out these
words and so allow any person who has property in the city of Belfast, and who lives
even thirty miles away from the city to
serve. I do not think it would do any harm.
Then, again, I think it would be a great
advantage it it could be arranged in any
way that not so many jurors are summoned
to Quarter Sessions. I have myself seen
sixty men summoned and some of them
brought from as far as thirty or thirty-five
miles, and when they arrived they found that
there was only one small case to be tried. I
think it would be a wise thing if the number
of jurors summoned to Quarter Sessions
could be limited to some number, even say
fifty-two, so that, even if you had two
prisoners and all the rights of challenge were
exercised, there would still be a sufficient
number of jurors to try the cases. I see the
Parliamentary Secretary to the Ministry of
Home Affairs (Mr. Hanna) shakes his head
as much as to say that that could not be
done, but time and again I have seen jurors
submitted to the greatest injustice by being
hauled up to Quarter Sessions when there
was practically no business to be transacted.
These men had to pay their own railway
fares backwards and forwards and lose their
day, and sometimes, just to suit the convenience of some highly paid official, who
could have been there earlier in the day,
they had to wait for some considerable time
before they could get away. The result was
that they missed the train that would take
them home and had to spend an evening in
Ballymena. I think if the number summoned was limited to some number like
fifty-two it would enable jurors not to be
summoned so frequently. It would do no
harm in the cause of justice, but would be
an immense advantage all round.
Another thing I would like to see is that
if it is discovered, say, three days before
the Court was held that the cases are very
few in number, or that the prisoners could
be remanded to a later Court without any
injustice being done, the jurors should be
notified of the fact, and not brought in
there on a wild-goose chase. I am suggesting
these things in the interests of jurors and
of common sense, and I do hope that the

Oral Answers to Questions.
COTTIER
HOUSES IN
BALLYMONEY
RURAL DISTRICT.
1. Mr. KYLE asked the Minister of Home
Affairs whether he will state in how many
cottier houses in Ballymoney Rural District
there is only one bedroom; how many of
these cottier houses were condemned as
insanitary by the Medical Officer of Health,
and how many cottages does the Council propose to build.
2. Mr. KYLE asked the Minister of Home
Affairs whether he will state how many
cottier houses in Ballymoney Rural District
have no chimneys, the smoke coming out by
the door; has the sanitary sub-officer
reported on them, and what action the
Council took in the matter.
3. Mr. KYLE asked the Minister of Home
Affairs whether he will state if in the hamlet
of Balnamore, in Ballymoney Rural District,
the sanitary accommodation consists of one
out-office for each street; if each street has a
public cess-pool in front of five residences;
how many reports on the sanitary state of
the hamlet were made to the Rural District
Council by their sanitary officer during the
six years ended the 31st March, 1926; and
what action the Ministry proposes to take in
view of the danger to the public health in
that district.
The MINISTER OF HOME AFFAIRS
(Sir Dawson Bates): I propose to embody
in one reply the answers to the three
questions put down by the hon. Member on
the subject of the housing conditions in the
Ballymoney Rural District.
The information at the disposal of the
Ministry in this connection does not indicate
the number of rural labourers' houses with
only one bedroom or without chimneys, but in
this connection I think it well to state that
the Ballymoney Rural District Council have
formulated a new scheme for the erection of
96 labourers' cottages, which in addition to
the 379 cottages already provided in this
district, will make a total of 475 cottages
provided for rural workers in the Ballymoney Rural District.
A public inquiry will be held at Ballymoney
by the Ministry's Inspector on the 26th
instant, into the Council's scheme, and the
Inquiry will deal generally with the housing
conditions in the district.
It may, however, be added that it is the
duty of the Council's Sanitary Officer to
report to the Council any unsanitary housing
conditions that come under his notice, and
the Ministry notes that during the last 44
years no fewer than 61 such reports were
submitted to and considered by the Council.
The Ministry has no definite information
as to whether these reports specifically relate
to the classes of houses referred to by the
hon. Member, and it can only be presumed,
pending the holuing of the local inquiry referred to, that the scheme now pending is to
a considerable extent the result of the Council's consideration of these reports.
As regards the case of the village of Balnamore, the Ministry notes that an adverse report was made to the Council in February
last by the local Medical Officer of Health as
to the sanitary condition of certain houses
in the village, and that the Council has taken
appropriate steps to have remedied the insanitary conditions referred to.
The Ministry's functions do not arise in
such cases unless and until formal complaint
is made as to default on the part of the
local authority concerned.

financial.

ESTIMATES, 1926-1927.
Considered in Committee.
(Captain MULHOLLAND in the Chair.)
CLASS IV. No. 1.
MINISTRY OF LABOUR.
Motion made, and Question proposed:
That a sum not exceeding £103,278 be
granted to His Majesty to complete the sum
necessary to defray the charge which will
come in course of payment during the year
ending 31st March, 1927, to defray the
salaries and certain expenses of the Ministry
of Labour under the Administrative Provisions Act (N.I.), 1925; the National Health
Insurance Acts (Northern Ireland), 1911 to
1924; the Unemployment Insurance Acts
(Northern Ireland), 1920 to 1925; the
Widows', Orphans' and Old Age Contributory Pensions Act (Northern Ireland), 1925;
for advances to workpeople for fares under
the Labour Exchanges Act, 1909; fees and expenses of members of Trade Boards under
the Trade Boards Act (Northern Ireland),
1923; fees and expenses of arbitration under
the Industrial Courts Act, 1919; fees and expenses of medical referees under the Workmen's Compensation Acts (Northern Ireland), 1906 to 1923, and fees to certifying
surgeons under the Factory and Workshop
Acts, 1901 to 1920." (Note-£30,000 has been
voted on account).
The PARLIAMENTARY SECRETARY
OF THE MINISTRY OF LABOUR (Mr.
Ministry of Labour. 1302
Supply Committee-
17 MAY 1926
Gordon): I think it will be more convenient
in introducing the annual Estimate of the
administrative expenses of the Ministry of
Labour to give a general view of the extensive activities of the Department which are
performed in Great Britain by the Home
Office and the Ministry of Health as well as
by the British Ministry of Labour. To facilitate the performance of these duties the
work of the Ministry here is organised, as
you will observe from the Estimate, in four
Departments, and I should like to explain
briefly the scope of each in order to show
that they are run on economic lines, performing good work and giving a good return for
the expenditure involved.
The first department with which I propose
to deal is called Industrial Relations, which
will be found on page 88 of the Estimates.
The foundation for all our economic wellbeing is the promotion and maintenance of
industrial peace by fostering cordial relations
between employers and their workers. I am
glad to say that our record of good relations
between employer and employee continues
unimpaired, and at no time was it more in
evidence than during the general strike when
both sides showed anxiety and earnestness to
do nothing which would imperil those relations.
In 1925 there were only 52 disputes involving a stoppage of work, and the number
of working days lost in consequence was the
lowest on record since this Government was
established, only 3,900 workpeople being
affected as compared with 14,800 in 1924. It
is our earnest hope that this record will continue throughout the ensuing year.
This Department is also responsible for the
administration of the Trade Board system,
which covers 4,800 firms. About 6,900 factories and workshops are subject to the provisions of the Factory and Workshop Code
and the Truck Acts. These firms, employing,
roughly, 250,000 workpeople, are inspected periodically. 2,800 premises were
inspected during the year, and active
steps taken to secure the protection
of those engaged in industry, and although
we show an increase in the number of
officials, this has been caused by an internal
reorganisation of the Department which will,
I trust, assist still further the working
of the Trade Board system and will concentrate in this Department the supervision of
compliance with the whole body of statutes
administered by the Ministry.
The Employment and Insurance Department of the Ministry administers the three
great insurance schemes-National Health,
under which 340,000 persons are insured;
Unemployment Insurance, covering 266,000
insured persons, and Contributory Pensions
covering 347.000. The National Health Insurance Vote has already been taken, so that I
need not detain the Committee further on the
subject. The Contributory Pensions Act, as
hon. Members are aware, came into operation
on the 4th January last and pensions and
allowances have already been awarded to
approximately 3,500 widows and over 9,500 dependent children. Applications are still
being received at the rate of about 40 per
week, and as from the 2nd July next old-age
pensions at the age of 70 will become payable
to insured persons without the fulfilment of
tests as to means, etc., and we have strengthened this section to deal with these new
claims, as will be seen from the Estimates.
The Unemployment Insurance administration has been fully debated on Vote 3 of
the Ministry, and I should like on this
occasion to refer to some of the other
activities of the Ministry in this connection.
The work of the Employment Exchanges, of
which there are 20, with 22 branches, contiues to receive the greatest assistance from
those public-spirited gentlemen and ladies
who give freely of their time to serve on the
Local Employment Committees and their subcommittees. There are 17 Local Employment
Committees at work and 57 sub-committees.
Their help is extended in many directions,
but I will just mention a few.
Last year
26,247 vacancies were filled through the
operation of the Employment Exchanges.
This is a record and compares with a figure
of 14,727 for 1922, the year when we first assumed control.
The King's National Roll in connection
with the employment of disabled ex-Servicemen has grown from 124 firms employing
1,371 disabled men in January, 1923, to 950
firms employing 4,984 disabled men. The
Committees have also assisted the Department
greatly in the organisation of instructional
classes for unemployed women and juveniles.
With the valuable and generous co-operation
of the local Technical Education authorities
44 classes for unemployed women have been
completed at several centres throughout
Northern Ireland, and 19 are now in progress. Over 1,000 women have been covered
by this scheme of training.
As regards unemployed juveniles, educational classes for 542 have been held last
winter in Belfast and for 243 in Londonderry,
while manual instruction has been given in
9 centres to about 230 juveniles. The
Ministry is greatly indebted to the Local Employment Committees and Technical Education authorities for their assistance in this
promising movement, and it is hoped that it
will be developed further this year.
The total capital value of the Relief
Schemes that have been approved to date is
just over £4,250,000, in respect of which the
Department has sanctioned grants amounting to £1,070,000. By this means 685 under-
Supply Committee-
Ministry of Labour.
HOUSE OF COMMONS
[Mr. Gordon]
takings of permanent public utility have been
put in hand, which have provided almost
23,000 spells of work for our unemployed. At
the present moment 88 schemes are in hand,
on which about 2,000 men are receiving
direct employment, in addition to the persons
who are indirectly engaged in providing the
necessary materials.
The last two Departments of the Ministry
to which I wish to refer briefly are the Inspectorate and Finance Departments. As the
Committee is no doubt aware, instead of having separate staffs of inspectors to secure
compliance with each code of statutes as was
the practice heretofore, and is still the case
in Great Britain, we have placed all the inspection duties imposed on the Ministry by
Parliament in the hands of a combined inspectorate, so that as far as possible when
any premises are inspected in connection with
one code of legislation the inspector sees at
the same time how compliance stands as regards all the other statutes for which the
Ministry is responsible. This is obviously
as convenient as it is an economical arrangement, and I am glad to say that the extent
of compliance with the standards laid down
by Parliament is steadily improving.
The Finance Department of the Ministry
is naturally a very important one, as it is responsible, in addition to general financial and
establishment duties, for all the accounting
arrangements in connection with the disbursement of an annual sum of approximately
£4,000,000, of which by far the greater part
is paid in small amounts. In addition, a considerable proportion of the income of the Department is received in the form of individual contributions under the Insurance
Schemes, which have all to be credited
directly or indirectly to individual accounts.
For instance, under the Health and Unemployment Insurance schemes about 950,000 insurance books and cards have to be examined
each year in order to allocate the credits between the various approved societies and insured persons. In connection with both these
schemes our financial relations are so interwoven with those of the corresponding
schemes in Great Britain that our system of
accounting must be uniform in the interests
of our own insured contributors.
A sum of £14,589 is included in the Estimate
for the Finance Department for the cost of
such services as registry, typing staff,
messengers, cleaners and establishment
services generally, which are common to the
whole Ministry. Eliminating this figure,
and also the cost of the agency
service- £1,058-in connection with the
re-establishment in civil life of disabled ex-Servicemen, for which the Imperial
Ministry of Labour pay us, the estimated cost
of the financial and accounting work of the
Department for the current year is £25,719,
or no more than slightly over one-half pe
cent. of the sum to be disbursed.
I have thought it desirable to give this
general review of the work of the Department because its very wide ramifications
may not be generally appreciated. The Estimate for this year provides for the first time
for the administration for a full year of the
new contributory pensions scheme, and the
administration of any new social service, of
course, necessarily involves additional cost.
It has been our constant endeavour, however,
to see that strict economy in administrative
expense is observed, and Sub-head A of this
Estimate, which is for the cost of the staff,
and includes the principle administrative
cost, shows a decrease of £3,322 over last
year's Estimate.
The Estimate provides for a gross administrative expenditure in 1926-27 of £252,433, but
this figure includes a sum of £20,150 for
capital expenditure on the new Belfast Employment Exchange. The net expenditure
figure, before credit is taken for the receipts
appropriated-in-aid under Sub-head V, is
£232,283, and this is no more than 5.8 per cent.
of the sum for the disbursement of which
it is estimated the Department will be responsible during the current year. In my
view, this is a very reasonable administration
charge for the many wide-reaching social services administered by this Department. The
receipts from the various funds and other
sources, however, which will be appropriated
in reduction of the administrative expenses
are shown to be £119,155, so that the net
amount which Parliament is being asked to
vote this year is £133,278, or £12,592 less than
last year.
I trust that this explanation of the farreaching duties of the Ministry will give hon.
Members an indication of its important services to the community. With the generous
co-operation of every section of the public,
and of members of Local Employment Committees in particular, the Ministry exists to
serve and promote the well-being of the whole
community, and to enable the Ministry to
carry on this work, I have the honour to beg
to move.
Mr. KYLE: I want to move the reduction
of this Vote by £1,000 to call attention
to the attitude of the right hon. Gentleman,
the Minister. The Under Secretary in introducing this Estimate laid great stress on the
fact that under the heading of Industrial
Relations Department there were only 52 disputes during the year, involving 3,900 workpeople. And yet we see under the heading
Industrial Relations Department an increase
in the Vote of £1,400. Anybody who knows
Northern Ireland and who knows the relationships that do exist between employer
and employee in the North of Ireland would
naturally wonder at that, particularly in
view of the statement of the hon. Member
who has just sat down that we have reached

a record last year in only having 52 disputes,
involving 3,900 workpeople. And yet he is
coming here, as suave as ever, asking for
£1,400 extra for this Department. I think
the hon. Gentleman will require a great deal

to be able to explain away why this Industrial Relations Committee should be seeking for £1,400 extra this year in view of the
fact that he himself has stated we had so few
disputes last year.
I would like also to ask the hon. Member
if he could state how many applications he
had received for pensions for widows who
have been turned down by his Department.
He says 3,500 widows have got widows' pensions paid to them. How many widows are
there in Northern Ireland who have made
application and who have not received the

There is also another matter I would like
to mention. The hon. Member went out of
his way, I think, to thank the members of
the local employment committees who have
served in the Six Counties.
Mr. ANDREWS: Hear, hear.
Mr. KYLE: And yet the other day in this
House his chief, the Minister of Labour,
stated that on 1,700 occasions he, the Minister

these local employment committee members.
These local employment committees which
the hon. Member has thanked so much, I
think, would have appreciated it much more
if on these 1,700 occasions-which some of us

I would like also to ask the hon. Member
in regard to the industrial relations branch
has he received any communication or has
he taken any further steps in regard to good
relations with the Free State, so far as administration of unemployment insurance
benefits is concerned. This matter has been
put before this House on a good few occasions, and the right hon. Gentleman, the
Minister of Labour, has stated that he wants
to see good relations between the North and
the South.
Mr. ANDREWS: Hear, hear.
Mr. KYLE: We, too, want to see good relations. We want to see more than the giving
of lip-service to good relations. We want to
see that these workpeople on the Border who
work in Northern Ireland and live in the
Free State shall be able to draw unemployment insurance benefit at least to the
value of the stamps that they have been
asked for in Northern Ireland. It is not
outside the wit of man to devise a scheme
whereby the Free State and the Ministry of
Labour of Northern Ireland might be able
to exchange these benefits. I do not want
to be told in this matter that as the Free
State does not pay extended benefits that
would be an insuperable barrier. There is
no barrier insuperable in this connection.
I am not asking that the impossible should
be attempted. I am only asking that under
the head of these good relations an arangement should be made between the Free
State and the Northern Parliament to have
benefits paid in every part of the country.
I am not sure by the reply of Mr. McGilligan
in the Free State Parliament this matter
will receive very sympathetic treatment.
This question has been raised I understand
not only in the Free State Parliament but
in the Imperial Parliament, and apparently
the Minister of Labour does not think it of
sufficient importance to devote his attention
and energy to getting something accomplished in this direction. I would like to ask
him if he would in his reply state what he
is prepared to do in this connection in view
of the fact that in the Dail Debates of
9th April, 1926, Mr. McGilligan says that
the Minister of the Northern Government
seems to indicate that there is every likelihood of a decent reciprocal arrangement
being made.
That was some little time ago. I want to
know how far these arrangements have developed so that this reciprocity may be to
the advantage of a considerable number of
workpeople.
There is another matter which the Parliamentary Secretary was interested in a few
years ago and which I think he mentioned
when he was speaking under the heading of
the educational activities of the Ministry of
Labour, a thing which I am sure everybody
in this House of any party welcomes-the fact
that the Ministry is seeing that the young
people get a chance of developing their minds.
The Parliamentary Secretary a few years
ago was interested in the question of a
summer camp at Carrickfergus where a
number of boys and young men got the advantage of the open-air life they have down
there. They also had some lectures by some
people of Belfast. It has a distinct educational advantage as well as a physical advantage. I would like to know from the
Minister has he considered the possibility
of the development of that particular scheme
or of some scheme in that connection.
It seems to me that when the Parliamentary Secretary was dealing with the
question of the inspectorate and telling us
that under the Ministry of Labour the inspectors dealt with every statute that was
on the statute book and dealt with
ever

other matters-it seemed to me to be an

In regard to the number of schemes which
the hon. Member has stated are in operation
now, he said there are some 88 schemes employing 2,000 men. He knows as well as I
do, perhaps better than anybody in this
House, that the numbers of unemployed instead of decreasing in the way he himself
would like to see, are unfortunately increasing in this way that in Frederick
Street Exchange it is nearly impossible for
any man unless he has been out of employment for three or four years to get a chance
of a job on the rota as it is called. That is
to say, there is a list put down for men to
get work in their turn, and these men have
to be unemployed for three or four years
before they are eligible to get work. The
Minister of Labour in unemployment insurance schemes turns these people down if
they had not had work inside the last two
years, particularly if they had been employed in shipyard trades. I know some exceptions are made in some instances, but we
can see by the figures which we get from
time to time in the Belfast Committee that
although there are fluctuations there is a
very considerable number of men unemployed who, it seems to me, have no hope
of ever going to work again. What does
the right hon. Gentleman the responsible
Minister mean to do in this connection?
The only other item in these Estimates I
want to speak about is again a question
under the heading industrial relations department in connection with the trade boards.
These trade boards are very important and
i want to ask the right hon. Gentleman is
he satisfied with the chairman of the trade
boards whom he has working for him or
acting in that capacity. The duties under
the Trade Boards Act, as passed by the
Northern Government some years ago, are
much more responsible than ever they were
in this way: that to-day they act as independent chairmen more in the position of
an arbitrator than ever they have been before. Prior to the Northern Government
Act in this matter there were three chairmen, two appointed persons, and that
always led the workpeople to assume that at
least there was some chance of some one of
the three persons appointed to preside that
might be able to put up a particular point
of view. But now that there is only one
person the importance of the office is such
that it would require the Minister of Labour
to be extremely careful as to whom he
appoints.
I want to ask him categorically the
question: Is the Chairman of the Rope, Twine
and Network Board a man that should be
able to carry out the duties of chairman of
this Trade Board? I want to put that definitely, because I have had experience in
this trade board for a considerable number
of years. In my opinion, and I have a fair
industrial knowledge of trade boards and
relationship between employers and employees covering a period of over ten years,
that man is not capable. He does not take
the trouble. Now it is a very serious thing
I am saying. I want it to be taken seriously.
I hold that the man does not take sufficient
pains to understand or to attempt to understand these intricate problems of industry.
He is a lawyer, a very clever lawyer, I
believe. I believe he knows the law, but he
does not take any pains at all to find out
anything at all about the industry in which
he is such an important factor.
Only within this past few months has this
gentleman gone out of his way to read a
lecture to myself as a member of that board
for acting in my capacity as workers' representative. I resented it very much because he was in a privileged position just
as I am to-day. He was in the privileged
position of chairman with nothing before
the meeting, and read me a curtain lecture.
I am doing my best to read him a curtain
lecture now. (Laughter.)
I do not want hon. Members to think this
is a mere matter of spite or spleen. It was
a matter of 3,000 workers in the Ropeworks
being denied a shilling per week owing to
the ineptitude, stupidity, and inability of
the Chairman to understand the Regulations
and the Minutes he signed as Chairman of
the meeting. I want to ask the Minister of
Labour if he is satisfied that this gentleman
who is serving him is a fit and proper person
to carry on the work in view of the fact that
the duties are more important to-day than
they were when there were three independent members on the Trade Boards. Now
this man is in the position of being ก
dictator and saying that the men to whom
I have referred shall starve for over a month
to satisfy him.
Mr. BEATTIE: This is an Estimate in
which I can faithfully say the Opposition

I want to deal with the question of the
new Labour Exchange that has been referred
to by the Parliamentary Secretary. 1
claimed here on a previous occasion that
East Belfast was entitled to a separate Exchange for that particular part of the city.
Some Members of the Government scoffed at
the idea of my advocating economy and then
asking for an Exchange to be built in East
Belfast. I believe that last week 20,000 male
workers were paid off in the shipbuilding
and engineering trades, and a big pay-off
also took place in female industries. 1
happened to go to the Exchange one day and

Last year Parliament voted £20,000 for the
new Exchange, and this year the Minister
asks for £18,000.
We are
We want to know what the Minister is
going to do with this money. I know the
Exchange is being built and that workmen
are being employed on it, but is the money
being spent in a proper manner.
building an Exchange to accommodate about
12 per cent. of the insured population of the
city. We require a good building, we require
good light, and we require everything in
perfect order. We do not desire anything
to go wrong, because if it does the whole
machinery will break down. I would like
to ask the Minister of Labour if he is satisfied that the building is being erected
according to specification and with materials
of the class that are necessary for a building
that is to cost what this Exchange will eventually cost. I want to refer to one particular
thing that is being put into that building,
and it is a thing that I, from my experience,
would not put into it. I am sure hon. Members will remember the great fiasco of the
Portrush Clubhouse that was taken over by
the Government. A certain gentleman estimated for the work at that place and the
whole thing broke down, and he departed
very quickly and left the Government to reconstruct the place at the expense of the
people. I want to avoid a similar thing in
the case of the new Labour Exchange.
The Minister is in receipt of an estimate
from a contractor to carry out the lighting
of this new Exchange for £10 10s. Fer
thousand yards with Hackbridge cable. Five
estimates were put in, and the other estimates were up to specification and quoted
for C.M.A. cable, one estimate specifying
outside C.M.A. cable. That is a guarantee
that it will last a lifetime, while Hackbridge cable carries only a guarantee of
eighteen months. If defective cable is put
in and anything goes wrong the Minister
will have made a very bad bargain. He is
only throwing money away on that class of

this matter and see if it is not possible to

I want now to refer to the King's National
Roll of Honour. I heard the Parliamentary
Secretary say there were so many employers
on the King's National Roll and that it had
been such a huge success since 1923, and as
far as the employers were concerned, that
it was here to stay. He did not tell us how
many situations had been found for disabled ex-Servicemen, for whose aid it was
established.
Mr. GORDON: I did.
Mr. BEATTIE: I did not hear you.
When the King's National Roll was estabfished there were between 900 and 1,000 disabled ex-Servicemen unemployed, and to-day
there are between 1,300 and 1,400 unemployed,
an increase of between 300 and 400. I do
not agree that the money spent on this
King's National Roll is well spent. It is
ill-spent money, and no good object is served
by the continued existence of this departnent, and I would suggest to the Minister
that he should do away with it as soon as
possible. The Minister is now not only compelled to find work for disabled ex-Servicemen, but he has to find employment for men
of the Ulster Special Constabulary. The

privilege that was formerly only extended

stating that applications for temporary

positions in the Labour Exchanges have been

by reason of these appointments being taken

E.I.401, and I think the Minister will have

Mr. GORDON: There is no spice.
Mr. BEATTIE: There is spice for those
who are holding these positions and are
drawing the salaries. We find a juggling
match taking place, and I want to know
how this juggling is going to end. It is
all right when you are one of the jugglers,
but when one is the ball thrown in between
the two jugglers there is generally a squeal.
That is the position of the poorer class of
the people of the Six Counties. I refer to
those who are thrown out of employment
through no fault of their own, and after a
lapse of a few years are thrown off extended benefit and left on the streets to
starve and die.
We have called upon the Minister upon
occasion after occasion to give a definite decision on the Regulations which are in
force in Northern Ireland, and which are
imposing great hardships upon the people,
and he has always given us the reply that
owing to the agreement with Great Britain
it is necessary to walk step by step with
Great Britain. Taking that as a definite decision of the Minister, my colleague (Mr.
William McMullen) and I, who are Members
of the Board of Guardians, pursued another course. We tried to get the Guardians
to assume the responsibility, but we failed
miserably, because the Guardians would not
do so. The Guardians are friends of the
Government. I cannot give you their
speeches word for word, but their effect is
that if you do not meet your responsibilities
they will put you out of office. That is
from the Belfast Board of Guardians. Here
is the decision of the Guardians:--
The responsibility for providing for the
genuinely unemployed is a national obligation, and has been so recognised by the
legislation of recent years, which has
made provision for this purpose, and a
huge staff of officials has been brought
into existence under the direct control of
the State.
That is to say, you have all the machinery
for providing for the genuinely unemployed.
The Minister of Labour limits the meaning
of "genuinely unemployed." You may be
genuinely unemployed for two years, but
when that period has elapsed the Minister
tells you it is a crime to be unemployed.
If you have not had a reasonable period
of employment within the two years, off you
go; you have really committed a crime under
the regulations that exist. The Poor-law
people say that
the Poor-law Acts were never intended to
provide for the compulsorily unemployed
under existing circumstances, and to
attempt to do so even in part would ne
cessitate a large additional staff, which,
with the increased cost of relief, would inflict upon the ratepayers of Belfast a
burden which would be unfair to the working classes, and disastrous to the industries
and businesses of the city, and would only
result in further unemployment.
In justice to the bona-fide workers of this
city we protest against the present system,
which results in transferring in rapidly
increasing numbers unemployed insured
persons from State benefit, and putting the
responsibility on outdoor relief, which is
unfair and demoralising to those desiring
work and unable to find it, and inflicts
upon the Guardians an unreasonable
burden and an impossible responsibility.
We, therefore, call upon the Government,
with their specially organised State Department, to make arrangements, and if
necessary further provisions, so that all respectable deserving citizens who are insured persons, honestly endeavouring and
genuinely seeking employment and unable
to find it, will not be driven to seek Poorlaw relief.
In face of that unanimous decision of the
Board of Guardians, you must face the fact
that they are throwing the onus on to the
Minister of Labour. They charge the
Minister of Labour with pauperising the decent industrial classes of the city and Six
Counties. He is charged with putting the
taint of pauperism on those who are out of
work through no fault of their own after a
period of two years. The Guardians also say
that the Poor-law Acts were never intended
to provide outdoor relief under existing conditions. That is where I say the juggling
comes in, and the poor fellow who is thrown
in the air from one party to another is
dropped between the two, with the result
that life has become intolerable to him.
Then you have the Derry Board of Guardians.

What do they say? I think my colleague
the Member for West Belfast (Mr. William
McMullen) has dealt with that. They say
likewise.
We want some final decision on this
matter. Who is going to handle the situation?
It is all right talking about Estimates, it is
all right talking about economy, it is all
right talking about the great services that
the Government have established on behalf
of the people. I have not yet seen one
service for the people for which the Government is paying. Is the Minister prepared
to shoulder the responsibility of providing
for the unemployed workers of the Six
Counties until such times as he can provide
work for them, or failing work, maintenance?
He has got to give us a definite decision.
He has got to say definitely what the responsibilities and duties of the public boards are,
and he must show them that the law is in
accordance with what he states. I am giving
him this opportunity to reply. My colleague
and I have made speeches, similar to those
we listened to last Tuesday, with the
object of incurring the censure of the House
for the language we used. We want the rights
of these people given to them. We do not
want sympathy; we do not want charity, because the working classes are not charitable
objects. These people want their rights as
citizens, whether under unemployment insurance or some other Act.
There is another matter which I wish to
raise. I am bombarded week in, week out,
about the way people obtain Government
positions, especially in the Ministry of
Labour. I am asked what influence is at
the back of any person who gets a salaried
position for which he is not qualified, and
to which he has no right? I have asked
the Minister repeatedly, are there two ways
of getting a job in his Ministry? He has
replied "No, there is only one door, the front
door." But I have discovered that there is
a back door, and I want that back door
elosed against all who are not competent to
enter in by the front door, whether they
are the sons and daughters of Members of
Parliament or not. If my son is not qualifiied to go in by the front door, I do not
want him to get in by the back door.
The back door is badly abused, and I hope
to see it barred right and tight. If a girl
is not qualified to pass the entrance examination, she can be put in as a temporary
clerk into one of the Exchanges. She may
only remain there for one week, and may
then be transferred to the Minister's Department without undergoing an examination.
When she gets into the Minister's Department she may get a permanent position over
the heads of highly qualified girls who cannot obtain the position because of the way
priority is given. They should be admitted
on merit, but the appointments are not made
on merit. That back door must be closed.
You must give consideration to merit, and
to merit alone, and not have these inferior
people going in to abuse the unemployed,
people who are not competent to administer
the regulations.
This is a grand opportunity to place all
these matters before the Minister. Hundreds
of people who are turned off the register go
up to sign, but they are told, "There is no
use of you coming here to sign, because your
benefit is stopped, and you will not be on

wrong instruction. They should be told, definitely told,

the Exchange, and was highly qualified to

fellow was quietly transferred to Frederick
Street. A D.I., whose name is Hickson, and
who was demobilised from the Specials, was
notified to appear at the Shankill Exchange,
and he got a job as a sort of supervisor over
a department on the 19th February. That
man was drawing two months' pay from the

Then we find another case of a man who
actually had his return ticket for America
in his pocket, but because he had influence
he got into the Exchange and an ex-Service

That man was established, and I say he had
no qualifications, because he was tested and
he proved a failure.

I suggest that that is tantamount to a person

down, due to the attachment of this

person's policy. The whole thing is
complete travesty. I would not take part on
these Courts, because it is an insult to the

the Minister of Labour to function on a
local committee, and then when you have
exercised your judgment to the best of your
ability and you make a decision, having had
the whole facts before you, the clerk in the
employment of the Ministry of Labour is
asked to veto the decision that we may have
arrived at or call the judgment in question.
It is a complete farce to expect employers or
workmen's representatives to come there and
waste their time. It is doing no more than
