Now in regard to this Entertainment Tax, I
only want to say a word or two. It is unfair to continue this tax because it is putting
a burden upon the people of Northern Ireland which is not put upon the people of
England of similar character. That is my
first objection. My second objection to it is
if it was desirable to make cheaper entrances
to places of amusement for the poorer section
of the community in England the same ought
to have been done for a similar class in this
Northern Province. And then in Southern
Ireland there is no tax upon outdoor sports
at all-none whatever. I think the right
hon. Gentleman would have been well advised-I advised him in private. I brought
a deputation to him. We made strong
speeches. We made an irresistible case.
That is why he is not listening to me now.
(Laughter.) We made an irresistible case for
the abolition of the tax on outdoor sports.
I think the amount is so small that the right
hon. Gentleman might very well have made
that concession. I think what he gets from
football matches is something like £4,000.
Mr. POLLOCK: No, no.
Mr. DEVLIN: How much?
Mr. POLLOCK: Between ten and twenty
thousand.
Mr. DEVLIN: Not so much as that. I
am talking about ordinary football-"soccer."
It would be infinitesimal if it were equalised
with the tax in England. Everybody knows
that there is not a single football club in
Belfast paying at the present time.
Mr. POLLOCK: Why?
Mr. DEVLIN: Because they cannot get
the money to keep them up the way clubs
in England are kept up, by some of the best
Irish players, who have to be sold to English football associations owing to the Entertainment Tax. The right hon. Gentleman
need not put any questions to me, because he
put all these questions to the deputation
that we had, and he had no answers to the
answers he got. (Laughter). None whatever.
Therefore, I can say I congratulate myself
on having compelled you to reduce the expenditure on the police, upon removing the
thrift disqualification for old-age pensions,
upon the passing of the Widows' Pensions
Act, and I condemn myself for not being
successful in securing other reforms adumbrated in my speech of twelve months ago. But
we are getting on. The Government that got
so violently resentful as they were last year
when suggestions were made to them and that
gave way, may give way on the similar
things which I have ventured to put before
the Committee this afternoon.
Now, I was interested to hear the analysis
the right hon. Gentleman gave of the amount
of drink consumed in this country and in
England and Scotland. I was glad to hear
these figures, because I trust it brings to an
end the allegation made against the Irish
as being a race of drunkards. It never was
a justifiable charge to make against them.
Now, I am glad to see that in Ireland-I take
it we are still in Ireland though in Ulsterwe drink half the quantity of whisky that
Scotsmen do, and that Englishmen drink
three times the amount of beer that Irishmen do. I think that is a very satisfactory
vindication of the national character. It
shows at all events that in this competition
of thirst we take a very back place.
I should be glad to go into many other
matters, but this I will say that in my judgment an expenditure of £11,000,000 upon the
Government of a population of 1,200,000 is
1399 The Budget-
General Debate. 1400
HOUSE OF COMMONS.
[Mr. Devlin]
rather extravagant, to say the least of it.
If we had a Government of ourselves by ourselves for ourselves with the right to impose
taxes and to collect them, the right to
manage our own internal affairs, which is a
mere negation so long as we are denied any
control over our own affairs, then we might
economise. But what do we find? We find
that every time economy is suggested in this
House by anyone from these Benches we are
asked: What is the good of it to Northern
Ireland? England would only get the advantage of it. Well, what I would suggest is
this, that you really ought to make an
arrangement with England and find out
what you are entitled to pay. I think
£1,900,000 was paid as an Imperial contribution this year.
Mr. POLLOCK: And we got £600,000 back.
Mr. DEVLIN: That was £2,000,000. Would
it not be well to have your contribution
standardised?
Mr. POLLOCK : We have got it
standardised.
Mr. DEVLIN: If it is standardised why
is it changed from year to year? You
accepted the Act of 1920, and it imposed on
you the responsibility at that time of paying
to the Imperial Exchequer £8,000,000 a year.
Mr. POLLOCK indicated dissent.
Mr. DEVLIN: Yes, it did; you cannot
deny that. And then by the policy of
financial hokey-pokey you have gone on
chopping and changing until now, and we
do not know really where we stand on this
question. That was one of the great assets
the Government had in having the right
hon. Gentleman, the Minister of Finance.
(Hon. Members: Hear, hear.) Whenever we
wanted to find out anything about this he
had a magnificent capacity for throwing dust
in our eyes, and he has succeeded, because
really up to this moment we do not know
how we stand financially. While the whole
of Ireland in 1912 did not cost more than
£12,000,000-that covered the whole nationwe are spending a sum of £11,000,000.
Mr. POLLOCK: We are not spending anything like that.
Mr. DEVLIN: What are you spending?
Mr. POLLOCK: We have paid £2,000,000
to the Imperial Government, and it reduces
that.
Mr. DEVLIN: We are spending £11,000,000.
That is what the cost of government is, I
do not care how you make it out.
Mr. POLLOCK: We pay our debts.
Mr. DEVLIN: If I throw sovereigns by
the handful out on the public street I am
spending it. That is the amount of money
the people have to pay-over £11,000,000, and
it does not make any odds to me what you
do with it. All I can say is that this £11,000,000
is taken out of the pockets of the taxpayers
of Northern Ireland, and, if you give
£2,000,000 to England, that is no concern of
mine for the purpose of my argument. What
I say is that that is too heavy a burden to
bear. Consider the income tax the people
have to pay. Remember this, that in connection with the adjustment of these taxes
you will have to visualise the future. How
long will you continue to make much upon
the income tax. You are already losing your
Corporation tax. The E.P.D. has disappeared altogether. These were moneys that
you had received for a number of years. All
these disappeared, and, of course, the
capacity of the people to pay these taxes
depends upon the value of their trade. If
trade disappears, of course, income tax
disappears. If the workers are out of employment they have not as much to spend.
Take the taxes upon tea, upon tobacco, upon
drink. The most of these taxes comes from
the working classes. Of course, as the
working classes are depressed by bad trade,
just like the manufacturers in regard to
income tax-if the working classes cannot
find employment-if they are living upon
something like one-third of what they
formerly earned, they cannot buy tea, they
cannot buy sugar, at least, in such large
quantities; they cannot buy tobacco, and
they cannot purchase drink. These are the
main sources of your revenue.
Therefore, I think all these things are very
vital trade considerations which ought to be
taken in conjunction with the general fiscal
question. That is all I have to say about
it. Now that the Session is coming to a close
and as this Parliament will not meet for
three or four months, I do venture to make
a fresh appeal to the Government to endeavour to bring together men of all parties
who can contribute anything, either by experience or knowledge, to the solution of
this tremendously important trade problem.
The brains and the experience of every man
in the Province who can profitably offer suggestions or assistance should be given to
endeavour to do something to resuscitate
trade in Northern Ireland and to make fresh
suggestions as to how trade can be improved.
I think the Government could have done
more. I quite admit the Government cannot
do everything in regard to trade, but I have
always thought that this Parliament was
wrongly fashioned in spirit. It was tco
much like a big tremendous legislative &ssembly. It ought to be a working body of
representative men, who should come close
together for the purpose of consultation,
each giving his contribution to the common
reservoir of wisdom and experience and help
on the Province, and not sit in picturesque

attitudes looking at each other and arguing

Mr. GYLE: I wish to join with the
various Members of this House in congratulating the right hon. Gentleman on the very
I am
lucid explanation that he gave us.
exceedingly sorry that once more we have
been told that we are not going to get rid
of the Entertainment Tax. That is a thing
that is creating widespread dissatisfaction
amongst a considerable section of the community. I had occasion to introduce a deputation of the cinema proprietors to the
Minister of Finance some time ago, and of
course we were told that it was an absolute
impossibility on account of the great sums
that had to be paid for unemployment and
other things. The Minister was assured at
that time that the tax would be passed on
immediately to the people. The same thing
applies to the football public. Last year
when I was speaking on this matter I was
questioned very seriously by some Members
on the opposite side as to whether the tax
would be passed on. I have made inquiries
since, and I found out from all parts that if
this tax is remitted the benefit will be passed
on to the people. I hope that the Chancellor
of the Exchequer will try to see his way
to remit this tax, because, as I said at the
beginning of my remarks, it is causing great
dissatisfaction amongst the people. We have
been told over and over again that we are
keeping step by step with England, but here
is a matter where we are not keeping step
by step with England at all.
I want to know the reason why the betting tax is not being imposed by this Government. Surely they know that in the city of
Belfast more betting goes on than in any
other city in the United Kingdom. Here
we have an opportunity of tapping a new
source of revenue and they deliberately and
absolutely refuse to take advantage of it.
Why is this refused? Of course, I know
perfectly well that the way it is going to be
applied will never be a success. We all
know that. I am surprised that the Chancellor of the Exchequer in England, Mr.
Churchill, does not recognise the fact that
the basis of his taxation is absolutely wrong.
How could one possibly apply a five per
cent, tax on the turn over? It is absolutely
wrong.
I can tell the Chancellor of the
Exchequer how easy it would be to get a
very substantial revenue in Northern Ireland from this very tax. I do not know
whether we would be allowed to do it in
our own way.
Mr. POLLOCK: Certainly.
Mr. GYLE: It is very simple. All you
have to do is to issue to every man who
wants to make a bet an annual licence at
£1 per annum. If he requires to go to the
rings make him take out another licence
at £3 per annum. That will cover an enormous amount of money. It will get you
over all your difficulties. You will make
the bookmaker responsible in that he will
only bet with those people who have got
their licence. You can also tax the bookmaker. I do not care whether you make it
£10, £20 or £100. That is a matter for the
Chancellor. There is no doubt about it that
bookmaking is going on in every street and
entry in the centre of this city. It is going
on in the outlying districts too. Why are
we closing our eyes to the fact? Why do
we not apply this tax? That is what I
want to know, and I cannot get any answer.
I have been amongst the people and talking
to them and I know that the people would
welcome a tax of this description. The
bookmakers would rather be an honourable
profession than be hunted by the police and
dragged before the police magistrates, and
be fined in sums which they would prefer
to pay as licence duty. Then why are these
private motor-cars not taxed? How does
that come?
Mr. POLLOCK: May I intervene? The
private motor-cars are taxed. No change is
made in the taxation of private motor-cars
in Britain. The only difference is that the
Treasury or the Chancellor raided the Road
Fund to the extent of the luxury tax which
he claimed as part of the present revenue
derived from private motor-cars. The tax
itself is not changed.
Mr. GYLE: At any rate I pass from that
point. I understood from the Chancellor's
speech that he had absolutely refused to put
on the tax in connection with private motorcars.
Mr. POLLOCK: It means raiding the
Road Fund.
Mr. GYLE: The hon. Member for Antrim
(Mr. Crawford) very kindly indeed said
that so far as gentlemen like himself were
concerned they did not offer any opposition
to the amount of the compensation levy that
was made here last year, and that that was
an arranged matter between the Government and the members of the trade. I wish
to point out to him that the trade is paying
full interest on the amount of the loan and
they are prepared to pay back for everything that was got including the interest on
it. I have no objection at all to the Government trying to do something similar for the
farmers. If the Government can see their
way to increase the number of years for the
repayment of the money the farmers have to

this Entertainment Tax would only be in
keeping with what has been done in England.
It certainly is a step they could not take

Colonel WOODS: I wish to say a few words
on exactly the same point as was raised by
the last speaker, that is, the Entertainment
Tax. I asked the Minister of Finance about

consider the remission of this tax, and he
said, in reply, surely I would not expect
him to anticipate his Budget statement. i
took it from that that he had under consideration at least the question of giving
relief to outdoor entertainments. That
would not cost such a very big sum. I am
more concerned with outdoor sports, because
they are of more benefit to the nation in the
way of health and exercise.
The hon. Member for West Belfast (Mr.
Devlin) spoke the truth when he said that
players of "Soccer" were being actually sold
to English clubs in order that the local clubs
might be able to pay the Entertainment Tax.
That is quite so. On various occasions in
London last summer I have actually seen
them being sold like white slaves to the
football clubs of England. It is very hard
that the best players and the best sportsmen
we can find in Northern Ireland have to be
sold out of the country like that, simply to
pay the Entertainment Tax. It is a small
item that could be got over quite easily,
especially when we are missing such other
things as motor taxation.
In order to make up for the relief that
the remission of this tax would give to outdoor sports, I would suggest to the Minister
that he might encourage the sale of beer, in
some way best known to himself.
If we
drank, say, half as much beer as they do
in England, that would make up the difference caused by the remission of the tax in
respect of outdoor sports.
Mr. POLLOCK: How would it do that?
Mr. P. O'NEILL: Greater consumption
and less duty.
Colonel WOODS: I would appeal to the
right hon. Gentleman to consider this question of the Entertainment Tax seriously,
and to consider what the various deputations
have put before him as to the benefits that

Surely, the Minister can find some means of

Can he not go to the dogs again? I would

Mr. POLLOCK: With the permission of
the House, Mr. Speaker, I should like to
reply very briefly to one or two of the points
that have been made by hon. Gentlemen on
both sides of the House. On the other side,
controversy seems to have ranged around the
question of the Entertainment Tax. What I
did state to the deputations that were re-

ceived in February was that if the financial
conditions of the Province warranted we
would certainly consider very sympathetically a change that would relieve them from
the imposition of the tax, or from that part
of the tax to which they objected, and to
bring the position into harmony with the

But while I make that statement I must
take exception to the arguments that are
used, because, in the first place, I do not
believe I could pass that in the House. For
although I have received deputations on the
subject, making protests in respect of the
imposition of the tax and the great advantage that would be reached by the relaxation of the tax, I have on every hand and
on every side had protests from people who
object to any relaxation of the Entertainment duty, regarding it as they do as the
fairest tax that we could impose. They held
that people who propose to amuse themselves
are entitled to pay some trifle to the Stateit is a very small trifle indeed.
In regard to the arguments used by my
hon. Friend, the Member for West Belfast
(Mr. Devlin), as to the position of professional footballers, surely he does not suggest,
in order to prevent the buying and selling,
as he describes it, of professionals in sport,
that the Government should change its fiscal
or financial policy? I can understand the
arguments in the direction of the advantage
of making provision for the relief of outdoor
sports, but I cannot understand the argument that, because people come across here
from Great Britain to buy professionals, the
Government should, therefore, change its
financial policy.
I question very much whether on the
equities of the case, although I do not urge
that very much, there is any ground for the
suggestion that this is a burdensome tax,
because, as I am advised, if you take the
great mass of the people who attend these
professional football matches they are young
fellows who can smoke cigarettes, and apparently can go to any form of entertainment
without any difficulty. They seem to have
money for all these things. It is well known
that those who are receiving unemployment
insurance benefit are to be found in these
places in large numbers. Can it be argued,
therefore, that Government money, provided
--as it is being provided-for those in distress,
should be used for the purpose of securing
entrance to football matches? If I were
arguing the case on the merits, I should
certainly stress that point. I think those
engaged in amateur sports or football
matches have a greater right to be considered
than those who simply go to watch a number
of professional players who are paid very
large sums of money for their exhibition.
But apart even from the football claims, we
cannot relax the tax in respect of the entrance to football matches without extending
the same concession to picture shows and
other forms of amusement. If we did that
we should certainly deprive the State of a
very large amount of revenue which in the
conditions in which we find ourselves is
necessary for the payment of our obligations.
Mr. P. O'NEILL: That would be only the
British Exchequer.
Mr. POLLOCK: In regard to these taxes
over which we have control, there is no obligation upon us to make them larger or
smaller. We can impose any tax within our
powers that we please, so that that point
does not arise. I have already informed the
House in my statement that last year we
would have been immensely behind if it had
not been for the large amount of money we
received from the British Government by
way of a grant to the Unemployment Insurance Fund. We will receive this year a very
large grant also. But our own burden is so
heavy, amounting to half a million of money
-between £500,000 and £600,000-that if I let
go any source of revenue, no matter what it
may be, the accounts will not balance, and
they must balance.
I am bound to get the money from some
source, and no matter what particular interest I touch-it does not matter whether it
is a football club or a place of entertainment
-there are objections raised. In fact, everybody objects to taxation. All the different
classes of people complain that this tax is
a burden. All taxes are a burden, but still
we must provide for these services. The
hon. Member for West Belfast( Mr. Devlin)
seems to think that these things can just
be relaxed at the will of the Government,
and that economy should be effected. I
want to ask the House seriously where does
economy begin? We have had many attacks
made upon the administration. We have
raked the administration to see where any
economy could be effected, but even if we
were to take 10 per cent. off the cost of administration what would it amount
to?
Are
Are we to reduce old-age pensions?
we to reduce the education services? We
would have some of my hon. Friends up in
arms if we proposed to reduce the education
services. And so I could go over the whole
gamut. Unemployment insurance, all these
things, have to be provided for.
If I spoke of economy in regard to those
services I would have the whole House, one
side or the other, up in arms. Therefore, I
want to know how the money is going to be
provided for the services of the State. It
must be provided by taxation and revenue,

permit us to relax some of the heavy obligations we have towards these services, I
do not really see how any of these taxes can

HOUSE OF COMMONS.
Mr. O'NEILL: Would the right hon.
Gentleman tell us how his position would
be any worsened if he remitted the Entertainment Tax completely and deducted that
amount from the contribution to the
Imperial Exchequer each year.
Mr. POLLOCK: We are under an obligation to the Imperial authority to pay what
is regarded as our fair share of the great
Imperial services of the Kingdom. We are
not the arbiters of that. An independent
tribunal, which I regarded as a fair
tribunal, has the determining of what we
can really pay in proportion to our taxable
capacity. Therefore for the hon. Member
to suggest that we can relax this tax and
deduct such an amount is simply begging
the question altogether, because we have no
power and no right to do so, and I do not
think that from the point of view of our
equitable obligations to Great Britain we
should do that.
We started with an obligation to pay
£8,000,000 a year, or rather it was imposed
upon us. It is now down to £1,700,000. I
do not know what it may reach if taxation
is reduced further. If the Income Tax is
reduced 1s in the £ it would be £800,000 a
year less, so that from year to year it must
vary in accordance with the taxation
imposed upon the people. I do not regard
the awards of the Joint Exchequer Board
during the three or four years it has
functioned as being unjust or inequitable.
Question put, and agreed to.
Resolved: "That this House approves the
proposals of the Government for meeting
the financial requirements of the year."
Land Purchase.
Mr. GEORGE HENDERSON: I beg to
move:-
That this House is of opinion that the
subject matter of the Acts relating to Land
Purchase should be under the control of the
Parliament and Government of Northern
Ireland, and that the said Government
should make representations to this effect
to the Imperial Government.
I wish to say that I am compelled to put
down this Motion and bring this question
before the notice of the House owing to the
numerous inquiries I have had from
farmers all over Northern Ireland with regard to what is being done with the
Northern Ireland Land Act of 1925. They
ask why what seems to them unnecessary
delays and postponements have taken place
in putting the Act into operation, and why
they are not in receipt of the benefits that
should come to them under the provisions
of the Act. I thought it my duty to bring
under the notice of the Government and of
this House the disappointment that exists,
because there is acute disappointment among
these men that this Act has not been put
into operation, and there is a growing
impatience and discontent which is beginning to find expression.
I would draw the attention of the Govern
ment to a resolution that was passed by the
Antrim branch of the Ulster Farmers'
Union about a week ago, deploring this
delay, and stating that in their opinion,
farmers would be quite justified in only
paying 75 per cent. of rents until this Act
was put into operation.
Mr. SPEAKER: I must interrupt the hon.
Member. He knows that this is a Reserved
Service, and he must be careful to
differentiate his argument in favour of its
ceasing to be a Reserved Service, and must not
combine that with criticism of the conduct
of the Land Commission, for which this
Government is not at present responsible,
and in respect of which they cannot give a
reply.
Mr. GEORGE HENDERSON: I wanted
first of all to show the Government that
there was discontent under the present
administration. The present administration
is under the auspices of the Imperial Parliament and I want to show that there is discontent and dissatisfaction with the present
administration. Then I want to go on to
show that, in my opinion, rightly or wrongly,
the only way this question can be adequately
dealt with is by having it transferred to the
Northern Government. I think the House
will agree that it would be in the interests
of this country and in the interests of the
people that this Act should be put into
operation immediately and universally, and
in my opinion the only way that can be
accomplished is by the transfer of the Land
Purchase service from the Imperial Parliament to the Northern Parliament.
I have said in this House before, that it
was a great pity this Act was not made
operative from the gale day before the passing of the Act, and in my opinion that could
have been done with the co-operation of this
Government, because the Government of
Northern Ireland have accepted the responsibility of financing the Act of 1925. They
have estimated that it will mean a charge of
£45,000 on the finances of Northern Ireland.
These unbought farmers were the first men
in our agricultural community who had a.
special claim on the Government and on
Government money, and if the Northern
Government had paid this £45,000 into the
Land Commission these men could have been
in receipt of the benefits of this Act
immediately it was passed. That is one of
the reasons why I suggest that this service

because in 1918 we had a scheme of Land
Purchase proposed, and at that time the
Government gave a pledge to carry it out.
That is eight years ago. Last year we had a
compulsory Land Act passed and how many
tenants have benefited by the operation of
that Act? I would like to know how many
tenants have been dealt with under that
Act since it was passed a year ago, and how

rate of progress.
Another thing that has produced this discontent is the delay that has occurred since
the Government were aware that the Act
had been passed in May of last year. The
Land Commission, acting under the jurisdiction of London, issued an order that ail
landowners should have the necessary maps
and documents lodged with the Land Commission before the 31st October. I gather
that at that time the Land Commission must
have thought that a sufficient time for these
landowners to comply with that order.
Then, apparently without consulting this
Government or giving any reason, they extended the time from 31st October to 1st
January. I am giving these dates from
memory, and they may not be the exact
dates, although they are very near it. I am
informed that some landowners had not
lodged their maps and documents up to April
last.
This order was issued by the Land Commission with a warning that if landlords
did not fulfil the order they would forfeit
the bonus. We do not want landlords to be
penalised in this way. We all want to live
in a state of harmony and goodwill. We have
nothing but the best wishes for landlords,
especially those who live amongst us, and
identify themselves with the life of the community. We do not want them to be victimised, but we think it is unfair that the
tenant should be victimised through a landlord failing to lodge these papers and thus
holding the scheme back for several years.
In my opinion the only way that can be
remedied is by this Government getting this
service transferred and making the necessary
financial arrangements for universally put
ting the Bill into operation at an early date.

of the Imperial Government. It was urged

if the Imperial Parliament proposed to
transfer this service to the Government of

there will be absolutely no objection on their

Ireland.

The PRIME MINISTER (Sir James Craig):
Before I proceed to answer to the best of
my ability the arguments put forward by the
mover and seconder of this Motion, I would
like to call the attention of the House to the
years about 1900 when the Wyndham Act was
first mooted in Ireland for the complete purchase of the landlords' interests by tenants,
and to trace the various steps from then
down to to-day. I cannot quite understand
how the hon. Member (Mr. G. Henderson)
can put forward this plea to-day to block
once more land purchase, because that is
really what it amounts to. In my opinion if
we carried out the suggestions he has made
to the House we would be delaying land pur-

The PRIME MINISTER: I am going to
Ideal with that. There were certain landlords whom the hon. Member now blames

We who have stood for County Down or for

know well that a section got up-
Mr. G. HENDERSON: Name them.
The PRIME MINISTER- -who said, "Do
not buy under the Wyndham Act." Alongside the cry, "Do not buy under the Wyndham Act," was a cry for a Compulsory Land
Purchase Act. All through the years since
1906 there was an agitation in favour of a
Compulsory Land Purchase Act. Well, we
have got a Land Purchase Act of a compulsory nature to-day. It is on the Statute Book.
And now the hon. Member comes along saying
that it is a bad Act, just as he used to
say before, that the 1903 Act was bad and we
should get a better. These constant irritating discussions or speeches about the
iniquities of land purchase-
Mr. G. HENDERSON: I did not use any such
words. I want the Prime Minister to say
when I advised people not to take advantage
of this Act or any of the other Acts.
Let us
be fair.
The PRIME MINISTER: I am only saying
that if the hon. Member would use his whole
endeavour to get the tenants throughout
Ulster to take advantage of this magnificent
Act he would be doing far better service than
coming to this House and ventilating socalled grievances which this House has not
got the power to remedy, because under the
cloak of asking us to take over the administration of the Land Acts he has brought out
matters that no one, either in this Government or in this Parliament, has any right to
interfere with in the slightest degree. The
Act is a British Act. It is on the British
Statute Book and has been carried out in the
same way as the Wyndham Act of 1903 was
carried out.
Let me point out the futility of the whole
argument. If we had in our own hands the
power of carrying out this Act, could we
devise better machinery for doing so than
under the Land Commissioners that at present
exist? How could we devise a better
system? The hon. Member talks about
giving the administration over to one
of the Departments of the Government,
but what Government Department here
could deal with all the intricacies
of land purchase with anything like the same
skill and rapidity that the Land Commission
are carrying on at the present time? It is
absolutely absurd to think that the Ministry
of Finance, or of Education, or of Agriculture could suddenly cope with all the legal
and technical difficulties and take over that
Department. It would mean that you would
have to continue the present system of the
Land Commission dealing impartially with
this whole thing. Therefore, no great saving
would be effected so far as this is concerned.
The hon. Member has suggested that we as
a Government should approach His Majesty's
Government in Great Britain and ask them
to do what? Pass legislation in their House
to alter, not only the 1925 Act or to scrap it,
but actually to alter the whole charter of
our own existence here, which is the Government of Ireland Act of 1920. Of course, the
whole thing is absurd. He himself says
that when he interviewed the Home Secretary in London he turned him away and
pointed out that they had some, I think he
said fifty, Acts to deal with in the Imperial
Parliament, and consequently they could
not give time to do anything of this kind.
Does the hon. Member realise that the
British Government might take two years,
and it might be a much longer period than
two years, before they could make a Bill of this
kind fit into their Parliamentary programme?
Consequently he would be putting still
farther off the desirable day when the
tenants of Ulster would come in under the
new Land Act. It was a foolish suggestion.
May I point out that the British Government is under a solemn obligation to the
landlords of Ireland, and especially to the
landlords of Ulster, to see that this land
purchase is carried through? I remember
quite well, prior to the Government of Ireland Act of 1920 going through the House,
the British Government-and I rather fancy
it was not only one, but two or three
British Governments--gave a definite pledge
to the people of Ireland that pari passu with
the Government of Ireland Act, they would
facilitate through both Houses a Land Purchase Act, along the lines of the Wyndham
Act of 1903, and along the lines of the
agreement which was reached at the time
of the Irish Convention. That was a
pledge given by the British Government on
behalf of the British people, and it would
be futile and foolish of us to go and ask them
to break it.

It is impossible for me to go into the

point out that in any big scheme of the

It takes time in the first instance to get

call preliminaries. But once those preliminaries have been got over then things
ought to go on rapidly, which I hope will
satisfy those tenants who are keen on
availing themselves of this Act; in other
words, although there may seem to be no
outward appearance of speedy working at
the moment, I have no doubt that, as the
months go by and as the Department gets
into its full swing and into full working
order, there will be much greater rapidity
of action, which ought to satisfy those who
are looking forward to purchasing outright.
The hon. Member for Down (Mr. P. O'Neill)
mentioned that the Free State was given a
better Act than our Act. That, of course,
is an old bone of contention, and one that
I cannot agree with at all. There appears
to me to be a great flaw in the Free State
Act, and that is the right of pre-emption
by the Government, which does not apply
to our Act here in Ulster. There is a certainty of tenure for Ulster farmers in this
Act of 1925, that nobody but the most pronounced pessimist like the hon. Member
for Antrim (Mr. G. Henderson) could take
exception to. Therefore our Act is a better
Act. I think it would be foolish, in the
interest of the tenantry, to ask the British
Government to tear this Act up and give
another one when they were able to legislate
in the Imperial Parliament. I believe, as
time goes on, the Land Commission will be
able to turn out the work a great deal more
rapidly.
Then there is another point, and a very
important one. The British Government
have given Ulster, and Ulster farmers,
terms under this 1925 Act which have not
been granted to Great Britain; in other
words they have treated us infinitely better
than the farmers in Great Britain. In my
opinion it is perfectly marvellous to think
that, in time, the tenants of Ulster will be
the owners of their own plots of ground,
of their own 100 acres, or 70 acres, or 30
acres, or 10 acres or, even. 5 acres, as the
case may be, and that when 68 years, or
whatever the term is-I think it is something like that--under the Wyndham Act of
1903 go by, instead of the annuities amounting to a sum of £628,000 a year being paid
in here, or, as was the case before, being
taken in the form of rent, very often out
This Act is a great Act. It is one for
which Ulstermen should have pleasure in
thanking the British Government who have
displayed generosity and kindness in carrying it out in the way they have done, thus
helping this great work. They have
guaranteed the stock which is issued in order
to complete the land purchase, while we meet
the administrative costs and the cost of the
bonus. We are helping by foregoing half a
year's rent in order to bring the landlords
and tenants to a harmonious settlement. I
say that all that shows the great interest
that this Government has in seeing the Act
made a success. It also shows that Great
Britain, whatever else she may do, is loyal
in carrying out her obligations both to the
landlords and to the tenants of Ulster.
I may say, in conclusion, that it was a great
day when the Ulster Farmers' Union shook
hands with the Northern Government and
said that this was a good Act, and that it
should go on and be placed on the Statute
Book. It was to the credit of that body of
men, who really represent far more than the
hon. Member pretends to represent in connection with land purchase in Ulster, when
they told us they were thoroughly satisfied
that this would be a good Act and would
clean the whole thing up. I say the Government were justified and have been justified
since in clinching the bargain with the three
parties concerned, the British Government,
the tenantry of Ulster, and the landlords of
Ulster, and in having put their hands to
that solemn pledge. I believe it will be
found in time that the British Government
were justified in the optimism with which
they passed that Act.

Ancient Monuments (Money).
Considered in Committee under Standing
Order No. 65.
(Mr. MULHOLLAND in the Chair.)
Motion made, and Question proposed:
"That for the purpose of any Act of the
present Session to amend and extend the
law relating to ancient monuments, and to
make provision for the preservation of
objects of archæological interest, and for
other purposes in connection therewith, it is
expedient to authorise the payment out of
moneys provided by Parliament of such
expenses as may be incurred by the Ministry
of Finance in the exercise of its powers in
connection with-
(a) the inspection and maintenance of
ancient monuments, whether vested in the
Ministry of Finance or of which that
Ministry is guardian;
(b) the purchase by agreement of any
ancient monument;
(c) the payment of compensation for acts
done under this Act involving interference
with private rights of property; and
(d) the purchase or assistance towards
the purchase of archæological objects of
which the finding has been reported to the
Ancient Monuments Advisory Committee,
appointed in accordance with the provisions of any such Act;
and also such expenses of the Ancient
Monuments Advisory Committee as may be
sanctioned by the Ministry of Finance."
(Governor's Recommendation signified-Mr.
Barbour).

Captain Dixon
needs little explanation. It is intended to
provide for the necessary expenses likely
to be incurred in the administration of the
Ancient Monuments Bill, the principle of
which, I am pleased to note, has been
approved by unanimous Vote of this House.
The sources of expense in this connection
are indicated in the terms of the Resolution. It will be understood that inspection
and maintenance will cause a certain amount
of outlay, while there will possibly be,
from time to time, charges for the purchase
of an ancient monument, or for compensation to an owner whose monument is taken
over in the public interest. A charge may
conceivably arise for the expenses of the
Advisory Committee which will be set up
under the Bill, but as it will be an honorary
body, the expense can hardly be material.
Finally, expenditure may be incurred for
the purchase or assistance towards the purchase of archæological objects found in
Northern Ireland, provided that the finding
is duly reported to the Advisory Committee.
I may recall to hon. Members that the provision in this year's Estimates for the maintenance of twenty-four monuments, which we already have, and which include such celebrated
remains as Greyabbey, the Giant's Ring,
Devenish Abbey and Round Tower on
Lough Erne and Arboe High Cross, on
Lough Neagh, amounts to £600, and, of
course, any expenditure likely to arise as
the result of this Bill would have to be
voted by the House. We do not expect to
make any extensive additions to the list in
our charge, but we may, perhaps, if the
book-buying public seems likely to support
the project, follow in the steps of sister
countries by preparing and publishing
illustrated accounts of the antiquities of the
Province generally. Of course, any outlay

to misuse them. If there is the slightest
chance of the Government being able to get
control by this Bill or by any other Act it
would be all to the benefit of the country.
The argument used by the hon. Member
for East Belfast (Mr. Gyle) with reference to
bombs is not a very good one, because if a
man is out to do harm he is not relying upon
the possession of a revolver or a bomb. He
always has those missiles which used to be
called Irish confetti and which can be dug
up from the streets. I know of a considerable number of men who have had arms
from Germany and various other places
captured during the war. It would be a
great pity if those men had to give them up.
They have no idea of using them either now
or at any time. There is one man I know,
an ex-officer. Someone under the present
regulations gave information that he was in
possession of a revolver without a permit.

It was an old dud Mauser pistol, and I do

Mr. KYLE: You know the place that is

not be quite so safe. If someone had intentions against a man who had something

a chance of keeping his own. That would
not be for the peace of the country. That
is my point of view on the subject. I think
this Bill could possibly be improved, but the
intentions of the Government are quite good.

Mr. BEATTIE: Thank you for your ruling. Seeing that I failed in the first Amendment to get the first permit amount changed,
I desire that the holder of a firearms permit,

Clause I ordered to stand part of the Bill.
CLAUSE 2 (Appeals to Minister of Home
Affairs in certain cases).
(1) Any person aggrieved by a refusal of
a chief officer of police to grant to him, or
to vary or renew, a firearm certificate under
the principal Act or a firearm permit, or
by the revocation of any such certificate or
permit, may appeal, in accordance with
such rules as may be prescribed, to the
Minister of Home Affairs; and the said
Minister shall have power to make such
order on the appeal as he thinks fit, and an
order so made shall be final and not subject to appeal to any court.
(2) Sub-section (9) of section eighteen of
the principal Act shall not be construed as
referring to any appeal for which provision
is made by this section.
Mr. BEATTIE: I beg to move in page 2,
line 38, leave out the words "the Minister of
Home Affairs" ("to the Minister of Home
Affairs") and insert "a Court presided over
by two Resident Magistrates."
I want to say that we have gone away
altogether from the custom adopted in Great
Britain. Under the principal Act of 1920 an
aggrieved person has the right of appeal to a
court. It was stated that this also applied to
Northern Ireland, but I discovered to my disappointment that it does not apply. The
principal Act provides:
Any person aggrieved by the refusal of the
chief officer of police to grant a form of
certificate or to vary such certificate may
appeal in accordance with the rules made
by the Lord Chancellor to a Court of
Summary Jurisdiction acting for the petty
sessions division in which the appellant
resides.
I do not go that distance, but I ask you to
insert after the words described "to a court
presided over by two resident magistrates."
That is taking away from the Minister of
Home Affairs the right of being the final
authority to grant permits or not grant them.
TELLER FOR THE NOES-
Mr. Beattie.
We would be well advised to accept this
Amendment. The more publicity there is in
the granting of these permits throughout the
Six Counties the better for all concerned. I
am prepared to say here that if this
authority is given to the Home Office we
would be as far back in 1926 as we were in
1922. Many people would be applying to the
Home Office and getting these permits
although they had been refused by the police
officer of the area in which these people
reside. I think that the English law is
much more in favour of the public than the
present Bill is. I think, also, in the interests of the whole citizens of the Six
Counties, a person who desires to keep a
revolver in his home should not be ashamed
to go before a court presided over by two
magistrates and there make application for
a permit. The public would thus get to
know the persons who were applying for
permits. I know certain individuals in my
district have been turned down by the chief
police officer, and I am not sure that they
would be turned down by the Home Secretary. I make that statement very deliberately, knowing what history has taught me
for the past three or four years. I know
that arms were given out to irresponsible
people in the Six County area. If the law
was administered in that way in the past
there is no guarantee that the administration
is going to change in the future. I am prepared to press this Amendment to a division,
believing that it should be made as hard as
possible for every individual to be in
possession of firearms in his home.

has a wife and a family of three. His claim
was allowed last Wednesday by the Rota
Committee, but on Saturday morning that
form was sent to him informing him that
he was disallowed under the regulations,
as he had not a reasonable period of employment within the past two years.
The Minister certainly did repudiate my
statement yesterday that that was in operation. Here is a man in the enjoyment of
a good industrial history, a willing worker
who cannot get work. I can personally recommend him, and other Members of the
House could recommend him. I am sure
that the Parliamentary Secretary (Mr.
Gordon) could recommend him too if he
only knew the man of whom I am speaking.
I ask the Minister candidly has there been
a reasonable opportunity in the engineering,
textile, shipbuilding, or any industry that
caters for the engineering class for this man
to show any better return than he has done
on the record I have given. I take this
opportunity of asking that that claim be
reconsidered and the condition of employment taken into consideration and a restoration of benefit granted to this man.
Mr. ANDREWS: I regret that it is not
possible for me to withdraw this form. It
is quite necessary to have a form of this
kind in order to make claimants aware of
the reasons why they are turned down. It
is only reasonable that those persons who
are turned down should be told the reason
why, as I am sure the hon. Member (Mr.
Beattie) will admit. But what I am prepared to say is that if the hon. Member will
furnish me with this name, and all the facts,
I will have the claim very carefully investigated. I will look into it myself, and
if the law will permit of the man obtaining
benefit it will be a great pleasure to me to
see that he gets it. But when I say that, it
is right that I should also add that, of
course, if the man is not entitled to benefit
it will not be in my power within the four
walls of the Act to give it to him. I hope,
however, that the hon. Member will accept
my assurance that I will have the matter
very carefully inquired into.
Mr. BEATTIE: I accept the Minister's
assurance, of course. The name is on the
back of that form. I recognise the right of
the Minister to issue to each applicant an
intimation as to why his claim is disallowed,
but I say again that that Clause should not
be applied to men in the engineering, shipbuilding, or textile industries. That is my
point.
Mr. THOMAS HENDERSON: Could the
Minister of Labour let us know if there is
any likelihood of a decrease in unemployment in Ulster. Many schemes, I think, are
being held up by people who own land,
refusing to part with it except at an exorbitant price. I do not know whether the information I have received is right or not,
but I am almost certain that it is. I want
to compliment the Minister of Labour on
being most anxious to get another section
of the Great Western Road carried out. I
understand, from information I received the
other day, that he was in the City Hall on
Saturday, or some day during the week,
trying to get this Great Western Road
started again. I believe what is keeping
that work back is the fact that certain
people who are interested in the land refuse
to give it up except at an exorbitant figure.
I think the Minister of Labour should try
to get this Parliament to pass a special Act
immediately, because people are holding up
the land while there are thousands and
thousands of people starving-
Of
The TEMPORARY CHAIRMAN:
course, the hon. Member fully understands

Mr. T. HENDERSON: I want to support
the Clause, but if there was more work

Committee.

there would be no necessity for this Clause.

at no distant date. I understand that the
hold-up has not been due to the fact that

Ancient Monuments Bill.
Considered in Committee.
(Mr. MULHOLLAND in the Chair).
CLAUSES 1 (Appointment of Ministry of
Finance as guardian of ancient monuments),
2 (Effect of guardianship), 3 (Purchase of
ancient monuments by agreement), 4 (Gift,
devise or bequest of ancient monuments to
Ministry of Finance), 5 (Notice to be given
by owners of certain monuments), 6 (Orders
placing ancient monuments under protection
of Ministry of Finance), 7 (Effect of Preservation Orders), 8 (Penalty for injuring ancient
monuments), 9 (Compensation for infringement of private rights), 10 (Power to receive
voluntary contributions for maintenance of
ancient monuments), and 11 (Powers of
county councils with respect to ancient
monuments) ordered to stand part of the
Bill.
CLAUSE 12 (Public access to monuments).
The public shall have access to any monument which is vested in the Ministry of
Finance or a county council, or of which
that Ministry or a county council is
guardian, at such times and under such
conditions as may from time to time be prescribed by regulations of that Ministry or
such county council respectively:
Provided that-
(i) this section shall not apply to any
monument of which the Ministry of
Finance or a county council has been appointed or constituted the guardian before
the commencement of this Act, except in
cases where the consent of the owner has
been given to the public having access to
the monument, either by the deed appointing or constituting that Ministry or such
county council the guardian, or where a
right of access has arisen through the
acquiescence of the owner or otherwise;
and
(ii) Where the deed appointing the
Ministry of Finance, or a county council,
the guardian of the monument is executed
after the commencement of this Act, if the
deed so provides, the public shall not have
access to the monument without the consent of the owner of the monument.
Mr. W. McMULLEN: I beg to move in
Clause 12, page 7, line 30, to leave out all the
words after "respectively," that is, to leave
out provisos i and ii. I think there is no
justification for these two sub-sections. The
first deals with monuments that have been
entrusted to the Ministry before the passing
of this Act. It would appear to prevent
people getting access to these monuments if
no stipulations have been made by the person who formerly owned the monument. I
think there is no justification for that at all.
And in connection with the second subsection I think it is a direct encouragement
to people who may be inclined to entrust a
monument to deny access. If a monument
has been entrusted to the Ministry, why
should the public be denied access. And in
connection with the second sub-section it
would be a direct inducement to anyone who
contemplates in future to entrust a building
or historical monument to provide that
people should not have access to it.
To me that seems a ridiculous state of
affairs altogether. I do not think you should
encourage people to make stipulations of that
1449 Ancient Monuments Bill—

18 MAY 1926
Committee.
character when entrusting the guardianship
of a historical monument of any kind to the
Ministry. I presume it will be necessary in
the event of a monument being entrusted to
the Minister that some of the taxpayers'
money should be spent in keeping the monument in a state of preservation. Is it fair,
then, that public money should be spent for
the purpose of keeping a monument and that
the public who are paying should be denied
access to it? It seems to me to be an unfair
proposal that the public should be asked to
keep a monument in a state of preservation
without having access to it. If a person
wants to entrust the Minister with a
monument, and a stipulation is made
that it should be private, what is the sense
of it? Why does not that person retain the
monument in his own hands and keep it
private? He could decide himself whether
people are going to have access to it or not.
There does not seem to be any sense in entrusting a thing to the Minister and asking
the taxpayers' money to be spent in keeping
it in a state of preservation, and then decide
that the public should not have access to it.
Is there any justification for it? To me there
appears to be none, and therefore I move the
deletion of these two sub-clauses.
Mr. BARBOUR: Of course, the object of
this, as explained by the hon. Member (Mr.
William McMullen), will be practically to
provide public access to the monument in
question. The whole object of this Bill, as
hon. Members will see by the title of it, is to
make provision for the preservation of
ancient monuments. The idea underlying the
Bill is that it is of the greatest public interest
that these monuments should be preserved
irrespective of their ownership. It is the
historical association connected with them
and the scientific interest that attaches to
them. Only such monuments as are considered by the Advisory Committee to
be of
public interest would be taken
over by the Ministry of Finance, and
in the framing of this Bill we have desired
to secure the goodwill of the owner of the
property on which the monument is situated.
The Ministry would be very pleased if the
owner could be sufficiently aroused to undertake the preservation of the monument, and
it is only in such cases where he will not
undertake that work himself that the
Ministry is enabled, should they consider the
monument of such public interest, to go to
the expense of ensuring that the monument
should be preserved. I am sure the hon.
Member (Mr. Wm. McMullen) will have in his
mind many monuments which possibly
might be deemed of sufficient interest to be
preserved.
I can remember many monuments consisting of cromlechs which are available from
the public road but which are in the middle
of a field which could, and very probably
would, be used for ordinary agricultural
purposes, and consequently it would not be
right for this House to grant rights to the
public to use for purposes of access to such
monuments the property of individuals over
which this House has no legitimate claim.
If this House is to provide public access
to these monuments it would obviously have
to acquire the necessary property and pay,
as provided by the Bill, suitable compensation to the owner from whom such property
was acquired. If the Ministry should deem
it advisable to acquire certain monuments
I am sure they will provide as far as they
can suitable public access to them, but they
have to be guarded in the power which they
take here, and to take into regard the
necessary cost that would be incurred in
order to secure the surrounding property.
It is hoped if these monuments are provided
the owner of the surrounding property will
be public-spirited enough to grant reasonable access to them, but that would be a
matter entirely within his own right.
Mr. KYLE: The right hon. Gentleman
has mentioned the camp stones in County
Down. They are at the side of a field about
100 yards from the road, but there is a
right-of-way to them, although the field
that the camp stones are in is very often
under cultivation. There is a right-of-way
to any of the ancient monuments that are in
the middle of the field that the right hon.
Gentleman was speaking about. What is the
use of the Ministry acquiring a monument
and paying for it if the public who provide
the money cannot get access to it? It seems
to me to cut across the whole principle which
you have outlined in this Bill if you are
going to draw up deeds which will in fact
provide that the public shall not have access
to the monument without the consent of the
owner of the monument. If you own a monument, and the Government comes along and
acquires it by right under this Measure, I
cannot see why the owner should have the
right, after it has been purchased by the
Ministry of Finance, to say that the public
shall not have access to it.
Mr. THOMAS HENDERSON: I want to
tell the Minister of Commerce that I am
delighted with the fact that the Government
have taken this matter up. As one who is
interested in ancient places, I want to draw
the Minister's attention to one particular
place that is very sadly neglected. Every
Member of this House is aware that King
William landed at Carrickfergus. The spot
on which King William landed is in a deplorable state. In England and we should have
more love for King William than the English
people there is a monument in his honour
at Torquay. If the English people have
erected a monument and put railings round

is not a point of order.
No, it
Mr. BEATTIE: Then the Government is
responsible.
Mr. BARBOUR: I think that hon. Members in raising this question have forgotten
that it is entirely within the judgment of
the Ministry of Finance whether they undertake the preservation of an ancient monument or not. Consequently, they would be
influenced in their decision as to what
ancient monuments they should undertake to

was reasonable public access to it.
I think hon. Members will be aware that
some of these ancient monuments, which, it
is obviously desirable for their historic interest to maintain and preserve, are situated
in private property and in some cases so very
near the dwelling place of the owner that it
would not be fair to allow uncontrolled
public access to such a monument situated
in a private demesne. So long as these monuments are in existence and are preserved the
possibility of their eventually coming into
the public possession remains, whether it is
in our day or not. Once an ancient monument is destroyed it is an irreplaceable relic
of the past and of course is gone for all time,
so even although the people of our day may
not get that unrestricted access, the opportunity to preserve such interesting monuments for the future should not be neglected.
I feel it would be an unwarrantable intrusion of public rights if we were to strike
out these protective Clauses which have been
inserted in the Bill. Therefore I cannot
agree to the Amendment.
Mr. THOMAS HENDERSON: Will the
Minister of Commerce give us an undertaking that the spot where King William landed
at Carrickfergus will be preserved?
Mr. WILLIAM MCMULLEN: In view of
the fact that the right hon. Gentleman thinks
the Ministry have got power under the Bill to
exercise their discretion in the case of monuments in respect of which there is any restrictive Clause, we do not propose to press
the Amendment.
Amendment, by leave, withdrawn.

HOUSE OF COMMONS.

Wednesday, 19th May, 1926.
The House met at Three of the Clock, Mr.
SPEAKER in the Chair.
Oral Answers to Questions.
"B" SPECIAL CONSTABULARY
INSTRUCTORS.
1. Colonel WOODS asked the Minister of
Home Affairs whether he can state the
number of paid Instructors of the "B" Special
Constabulary who are employed in Fermanagh and Tyrone; and how many of these
Instructors are Ulstermen.
(Sir
of
MINISTER OF HOME AFFAIRS
Dawson Bates): The total strength
Sergeant Instructors of the "B" Force is 59.
Of this number 32 are Ulstermen, 4 are from
other parts of Ireland, 22 are Englishmen,
and 1 is a Scotsman.
In the Counties of Fermanagh and Tyrone
the total number is 18. Of this number 1 is an
Ulsterman, 3 are from other parts of Ireland,
and 14 are Englishmen.
Mr. BEATTIE: In view of the answer of
the Minister will he state to this House his
reasons for dismissing Ulstermen and retaining the services of English officers?
Sir DAWSON BATES: I may point out to
my hon. Friend that these appointments are
made on the recommendation of the County
Commandants, and both the County Commandants of these counties are Ulstermen.
Mr. MILLER: Will the right hon. Gentleman confirm or deny the report going about
that of the "B" Specials, that is the full-time
men, a very large proportion are not Ulstermen at all?
Sir DAWSON BATES: No. The total
number of "B" Constabulary Officers is 468,
of which 428 are Ulstermen.
Colonel WOODS: Might I ask are the more
highly paid appointments held by Englishmen?
Sir DAWSON BATES: No; out of all the
County Commandants only one is an Englishman. The rest are all Ulstermen.
DISTRICT COUNCIL OFFICIAL AS
GUARDIAN.
2. Mr. BEATTIE asked the Minister of
Home Affairs whether he is aware that Mr.
J. Wilson, a Poor Law Guardian, representing Duncairn Ward, in the city of Belfast, is
also a paid official of the Antrim Rural
District Council, and will his Ministry take
steps to have this illegal practice discontinued.
Sir DAWSON BATES: I am not aware that
the member of the Belfast Board of Guardians
referred to is a paid official of the Antrim
Rural District Council.
I am aware that he is a Rate Collector in
the service of the Antrim County Council.
As regards the second part of the question
I can only repeat my answer given to the
hon. Member for North Belfast on the 13th
instant, when I said that the Ministry for
Home Affairs has no jurisdiction to determine
questions as to the qualification or disqualification of individual members of local
authorities.

follows:-
Generating Plant
Switch Board
Batteries
...
Sundry materials, including wiring,
cables, switches, tubing, lamps, etc.

DISCHARGED RAILWAYMEN AND UN-
EMPLOYMENT BENEFIT.
4. Mr. BEATTIE (for Mr. W. McMullen)
asked the Minister of Labour whether he is
aware that a considerable number of railwaymen have recently been discharged from
the services of the various railway companies
operating in Northern Ireland owing to depression in trade; whether it is a fact that
these men were exempt from the payment of
unemployment contributions on the understanding of the various companies that employment was to be permanent, and if, having regard to the fact that employment has
Oral Answers.

HOUSE OF COMMONS.
[Mr. Beattie]
not been permanent, he will take very practicable steps to enable these men to quality
for unemployment benefit; and whether any
steps have been taken to enable railwaymen
at present in employment to qualify for
benefit.
The MINISTER OF LABOUR (Mr.
Andrews): Under arrangements to which
the Trade Unions concerned have agreed,
certificates of exception from insurance under
the Unemployment Insurance Acts are issued
in respect of certain classes of railway employment under conditions laid down in the
Acts.
Contributions are not paid by or in respect
of men in any of these employments, and on
their becoming unemployed I very much regret that as they are not insured persons it
is not possible to pay them benefit.
Mr. W. MCMULLEN: I would like to
inquire of the right hon. Gentleman as to
whether the railwaymen were not exempted
owing to the undertaking given by the
directors of the railway companies that the
men would be permanently employed. If that
is so is it now fair to deprive these men of
unemployment benefit as the result of an
undertaking given by the railway companies
and not fulfilled?
Mr. ANDREWS : I am not aware that
the hon. Member's suggestion is correct. I
will inquire into the matter, and on some
future occasion, if he puts the question, I
will be able to answer.
Mr. W. McMULLEN: Might I be permitted to inquire as to what steps he proposes to take in regard to railwaymen at
present employed and who may soon become
unemployed owing to the depression in trade?
Is it proposed to exempt them still from
contributions, or is it proposed to bring them
under the Act?
Mr. ANDREWS: I think that is a matter
that the trade union leaders might move in
in the first instance. It was they who agreed to
the arrangement being made which excepted
these men from insurance.
DISTRESS IN DERRY.
5. Mr. W. McMULLEN asked the Minister
of Labour whether he is aware that great
distress exists in Derry in consequence of
acute industrial depression and the disqualification of many recipients of extended benefit; whether he will state what steps have
been taken to provide employment; and
whether extended benefit will be restored to
all insured workers unable to obtain employment.
Mr. ANDREWS: The percentage of unemployment in Londonderry is lower than
the general average for Northern Ireland,
and, prior to the reactions of the industrial
dispute in Great Britain, unemployment in
the staple industry of Londonderry was as
low as 7.9 per cent. I understand prospects
in this trade are favourable.
The Unemployment Insurance Acts are
being administered no less sympathetically
in Londonderry than elsewhere, and I have
no power to continue grants of extended
benefit to persons who are unable to satisfy
the prescribed conditions.
The Government has already approved 35
relief schemes in and near the city. At the
moment 8 schemes are in operation on which
115 men are employed, and it is expected
that this number will shortly be considerably
increased.
Mr. W. McMULLEN: Can the right hon.
Gentleman give us any idea of the approximate number of people disallowed benefit
within recent weeks, so that we might have
an understanding of the acuteness of distress
there?
Mr. MARK: Might I ask the right hon.
Gentleman before he replies to that, can he
give the House the average unemployment
figures for all Northern Ireland.
Mr. ANDREWS: The percentage of unemployment for Northern Ireland was 22.3
and for Londonderry 20.2. The number of
persons who were deprived of benefit
during the last three months in Londonderry
city, speaking from memory, was about 450.
Mr. W. MCMULLEN: Is the right hon.
Gentleman aware that the Derry Guardians
have refused to any considerable extent to
come to the relief of the people who are in
distress or are destitute in Derry, and,
having regard to that state of affairs, can
the right hon. Gentleman, on behalf of the
Government, tell us whether the Government
propose to take any steps to mitigate the
hardship that exists owing to the acute state
of unemployment in Derry?
Mr. ANDREWS: As I stated in the House
the other day, I do not hold either the
Guardians' conscience or their purse in my
possession. I would remind the hon. Member
that I feel that, so far as it is possible to do
so, the best way of dealing with this problem in Londonderry, as elsewhere, is through
the medium of relief schemes, and in the
answer which I gave to the hon. Member a
few moments ago I stated that already in
Londonderry 115 men were employed on these
schemes, and eight more schemes have been
undertaken, and it is expected the number
would shortly be considerably increased.
Mr. MARK: May I ask the right hon.
Gentleman if these further schemes referred
to in his answer come before him is he prepared to give them his immediate and sympathetic consideration so that there may be
no delay?
Mr. ANDREWS: The schemes referred to
in my answer have already been approved.
Oral Answers.
Oral Answers.
19 MAY 1926
I may say, in regard to my hon. Friend's
question, that if further schemes are brought
before my notice on behalf of the Government I will give them sympathetic consideration.
ULSTER PUBLICITY BRANCH
OFFICIALS.
6. Colonel WOODS asked the Minister of
Commerce whether he can state what is the
birth place of the officer in charge in Belfast
of Ulster Publicity Branch; whether he is an
ex-Serviceman; whether the typist employed
in the London office of the Ulster Publicity
Branch is an Ulster woman, and whether the
messenger employed at the same office is an
Ulster man or an ex-Serviceman.
The MINISTER OF COMMERCE (Mr.
Barbour): The officer in charge of the Belfast
office of the Publicity Branch was born in
Galloway. He served with the Royal Naval
Volunteer Reserve from May, 1915, to
February, 1919. Neither the typist nor the
messenger employed in the London office of
the branch was born in Ulster. The latter is
an ex-Sergeant of His Majesty's Regular Army
in which he completed 22 years' service, including service with the Colours during the
South African War, and in Gallipoli and
France during the Great War.
Mr. DEVLIN: Will the right hon. Gentleman consider the desirability of abolishing
this Publicity Organisation? Or would he
tell us what good it does?
Mr. SPEAKER: I am afraid that does not
arise out of this question.
THE ULSTER CENSUS.
Sir ROBERT ANDERSON (by Private
Notice) asked the Minister of Finance
whether he is yet in a position to make a
statement on the subject of the recent Census
of Northern Ireland.
Mr. POLLOCK: The numbers of persons
recorded on the night of April the 18th have
been summarised by each enumerator, and
these summaries show that there were
1,255,881 persons present in Northern Ireland
on Census night. This number represents an
increase of 5,350 persons over the number recorded in the same area at the Census taken
in April, 1911.
The population as recorded for Belfast
County Borough numbers 414,844 persons.
A statement showing the numbers recorded for each County and County Borough,
with separate figures for Males and Females,
in comparison with similar figures for 1911
and 1901, will be circulated with the Official
Report.
The hon. Member will doubtless appreciate
that it is inadvisable to attempt to give results in greater detail until all the Census
material is available, when a Preliminary
Report will be prepared and issued. It is
hoped that this Report, which must be prepared with due deliberation, will be available
in two or three months' time.

Prime Minister whether he can inform the
House of the legislative proposals of the
Government for the autumn.
The PRIME MINISTER (Sir James Craig):
I have been considering how best to afford
to hon. Members and the public the longest
possible time for studying the legislative
proposals which the Government intend to
put forward in the Autumn Session. It
seems to me that the best plan is that we

-(Mr. Barbour.)
:
Dr. MORRISON (who was received with
cheers) I would like to say a word or two in
regard to this Bill. It has been my misfortune to be absent from the House and not to
have an opportunity of intervening in the
discussion on it, a circumstance which I very
much regretted. I read a summary of the
speech of the hon. Member for West Belfast
(Mr. William McMullen) in yesterday's
paper, and, while it was very short, I have no
doubt that there were a good deal of
his suggestions with which I agree and also
many matters with which I would have disagreed had I been present. He made reference to Goldsmith, and I am sure he deplored what I consider is to the shame of
Ireland, that this most distinguished literary
man has had no recognition from his fellowcountrymen-practically no recognition. I
know that there is a statute to his memory
in front of Trinity College, and that that
ancient seat of learning took advantage of the
fact that he had been studying medicine there
for one or two years to claim him as one of
their students. It is a fact, however, that his
home is being used as a cattle shed, and that
there is no lasting memorial to the work of
this distinguished Irishman, who was associated with some of the ablest men of his day
in the literary clubs in London. He was an
associate of Burke, of Sir Joshua Reynolds, of
Dr. Johnson, and of Boswell, the most select
club probably in the world, and the most distinguished men, perhaps, in the British
Empire at that time, and the fact that he
lies now in an unknown grave in London is
a terrible calamity for the credit of this
island of ours. I think no better purpose
could be served if this Bill would allow the
right hon. Gentleman (Mr. Pollock) who is
Minister of Finance, and who has in future
to deal with these questions, to make arrangements with the Free State by which some
national memorial could be erected
memory of this distinguished Irishman.
in
1469 Ancient Monuments Bill-

19 MAY 1926
Third Reading.
Mr. POLLOCK: Where?
Dr. MORRISON: That is a matter for discussion and agreement. He is an honour to
Ireland North and South, and every rightthinking man would claim to have the privilege of perpetuating his memory. The hon.
Member (Mr. William McMullen) referred to
modern history-in fact the hon. Gentleman
is a modernist. I think he referred to the
monuments to Dr. Cooke and Dr. Hanna.
This Bill is intended to deal with ancient
monuments, and I would like to refer briefly
not to the memories and monuments of men
whom some of us remember-because I myself
remember Dr. Hugh Hanna-but to events
that took place probably 1,500 years ago. It
is those things which I think this Bill is intended to look after and to perpetuate. I
have the privilege of living in the Bann
Valley, which in my opinion, and in the
opinion of others well qualified to judge, is
the garden of Ulster. Through the Bann
Valley runs the River Bann.
Mr. DEVLIN: Hear, hear. (Laughter.)
Dr. MORRISON: I am glad to think that
the hon. Member for West Belfast (Mr.
Devlin) has improved his geography, because
when the Drainage Bill was under discussion it seemed to me that he wanted
a lesson or two.
Be that as it may, the Bann was formerly
the main avenue by which the enemies of
Ulster found access to the heart of the
Province. Anything that was worth raiding
on the banks of the Bann, and from the
Lough, they raided. In my own dispensary
district there was an abbey at the southern
end of the Bann-the abbey of Agivey. This
was raided by the Norsemen in the tenth
century, and in order to protect many valuables from these marauders a gold cup was
carried away by one of the monks and
buried in a field. In 1833 this valuable cup
was discovered, and it appears that it was
manufactured in the fifth century-1,500 years
ago. It is now preserved and kept for safety
in the safe of the parish church. I think
that that cup should be kept in the National
Museum of Ireland or in the Ulster National
Museum.
Further north was the monastery or abbey
of Macosquin. There is an ancient burying
ground there, and it was used by Protestants
as a burying-ground until it ceased to function. It is a very old ground, and the
Protestants of Ulster buried there since 1620
-the date of the Plantation. I have been in
it frequently. It was the site of an old abbey
-the abbey of Macosquin. A remarkable
thing in connection with the abbey or graveyard is a beautiful Celtic cross, which was
probably produced in the eighth century. It
was used as a pillar attached to the gate leading into the graveyard, The humiliating
position in which it was placed was recognised, and a voluntary effort on the part of
those who were interested in relics like that
enabled sufficient money to be produced to
take it from that dishonourable position in
which it was placed and erect it in the centre
of the graveyard, where it is now admired
and will be preserved by coming generations.
In a corner of that graveyard there is an
old baptismal font, probably 1,500 years old,
and there is an old pathway to it by which
members of the faith to which this
monument originally belonged go to
respect it and to treat it with the
reverence which they customarily show to
anything associated with their religion. This
graveyard is now in the hands of the district
council, and while they take care of it I think
it should be a national duty to preserve
things like that that are priceless and perpetuate them for the use of coming generations. (Hon. Members: Hear, hear). You
have the Tourists' Association, of which I
have heard something during the discussions
on some of the Estimates. When people
come from Portrush and Portstewart they
drive to the Salmon Leap, the Cutts at Castleroe, but if these things were properly advertised they would go along past Castleroe to
this old abbey at Agivey, and the abbey or
graveyard of Macosquin. These are old
historic places with scenery equal to any
scenery that can be seen in County Wicklow,
where you have such delightful places as the
Vale of Avoca, Glendalough, and the Powerscourt demesne.
If these things were placed before the
public in a handbook they would find them
more interesting than anything they could
find in Scotland or England. If we preserved
the valuable things we possess in Ireland we
would have not only beautiful landscapes
but most interesting relics which we could
inspect and admire at our leisure when we
are on holidays. In connection with ancient
monuments I should like to refer to Dunluce
Castle. The history of Dunluce is interesting
to those who have read it. It is especially
interesting to me, because the district in
which I live on the opposite border from
Dunluce-was perpetually raided by the
McQuillans, who had already occupied the
Route territory. The McQuillans and
O'Cahans were constantly cattle-raiding and
burning, but ultimately the McDonalds
superseded the McQuillans. I do not know
anything more interesting than the story of
Sorley Boy McDonald, who was then head
of the clan. He was sitting in this ancient
castle of Dunluce when an envoy from Queen
Elizabeth came to him with a document in which she recognised and
confirmed him in his estates. When
his secretary read this document to
him Sorley Boy McDonald asked for the
document and pushed it on the point of his

sword into the fire, at the same time saying

That was the independent

It is a most interesting thing to look back
on the crumbling ruins of that castle and to
think that this Bill may be the means of

know who originated this Bill. I see associated with it the name of a noble Lord from
the other House. I think if he has had any

for he has done, in my opinion, a national

am quite certain that nothing could have
