from Parliament during that most prolific
period, if it were not for the fact that in
the solitude of his home on the banks of
the Bann, he was engaged in the archæological, historical and antiquarian studies, of
which he has given us SO complete and
masterly a result in the speech which he
has just delivered.
He has told us of the need for a monument
to Oliver Goldsmith in Ulster. I thought
he had forgotten, but he did not-the hon.
Member never forgets any real historical
fact that there is a monument to Oliver
Goldsmith in front of Trinity College, in
Dublin, and, therefore, the only point of
his reference to Oliver Goldsmith was that
we ought to erect a monument to him here
in Ulster. If the hon. Gentleman introduces
a Bill to carry that suggestion into effect
I will gladly join with him in carrying it
through this House, and, of course, after
what he has said about the Senate, there
will be no difficulty there.
Now, I was delighted to hear this high
and splendid note of patriotism sounded by
the hon. Gentleman. It is a fitting thing,
I think, that in Ulster there ought to be
some tribute to the many fine and conspicuous and brilliant figures in the life
of this nation. Oliver Goldsmith was not
only a poet of great charm, but he was also
to some extent a great social figure. I am
not quite sure whether the hon. Gentleman
(Dr. Morrison) agreed with him in his
dealings with social questions. I do not
know if he remembers one of the poems of
Oliver Goldsmith, in which he said-
Princes and lords may flourish and may
fade,
A breath can make them as a breath has
made,
But a bold peasantry their country's pride
When once destroyed can never be supplied.
I think that is as appropriate to our present
conditions as it was when these words were
written over a century ago.
I would like to see a monument raised in
this city to Wolfe Tone. We are now all
making our suggestions. He was the first of
the great revolutionaries. From the Cave
Hill he proclaimed the eternal principle of
independence and of equality and fraternity,
and I take it that we owe our Parliament to
the declaration of the principles of Wolfe
Tone, and that if we are comparatively free
to-day we owe that to that great Protestant
revolutionary. Of course it took a century
of education and a series of political vicissi
tudes to get us to emulate Wolfe Tone. He
tried to rouse the people in a spirit of revolution. He did not succeed. The only successful revolutionary I know is the present
Lord Carson. He was able by the organisation of a revolution to secure
this Parliament. Although he did not
secure
us
us the liberty which Wolfe
Tone fought for at all events he secured us
such a measure of liberty as we have got, and
it would be in the nature of things considering it was revolutionary methods that won
our Parliament that there ought to be erected
in Belfast on the Cave Hill a great monument to Wolfe Tone who was the first of the
revolutionaries.
I am glad that this Bill proposes also to
maintain and to keep perfect as far as possible
Greyabbey. Greyabbey is to us known as the
place in which was born the Rev. Mr. Porter,
the great Presbyterian Minister. He fought
in 1798 against foreign aggression, and his
name has been immortalised for the courage
and self-sacrifice with which he went out to
fight against the imposition of foreign rule.
All these monuments have been associated
or less with recurrent risings or
revolutions in
support of the great
principle of the right of the people
to control the destinies of their native
land. I am
very glad that this Bill
has been proposed, because in addition to the
preservation of these historic monuments
it shows the birth of a spirit of genuine
patriotism upon the part of the Government

a real day's work.
These young men they are not really
young men; most of them are merely boys
from the age of 16 on-even if they have to
attend a technical class for an hour or two
during the day, are not learning habits of
regularity and unremitting industry at the
most important time of their lives, and at a
time when it is vitally necessary that they
should acquire those habits.
No man or nation is of very much good to
the world unless he or it has acquired habits
of regular hard work. The time to acquire
those habits is when the boy is becoming a
man. If he does not acquire those habits
at that time, if he is taught that he is going
to receive a few shillings a week, just suffi-
Icient to keep him above the borders of starvation, and that there is no necessity for
him to work to receive that money, he is
never going to turn into a useful citizen.
We have heard over and over again from
the Minister of Labour that we are moving
step by step with England. In this matter
we are not moving step by step with England. The Minister of Labour and the Minister of Finance know perfectly well-better
than I do the conditions in England. They
know that in England these boys, instead of
receiving unemployment benefit, are being
put into training schools where they are acquiring training in a large number of useful
arts and crafts, with a view to their being
sent to the Colonies, where they will have a
chance of becoming good citizens of the
Empire.
I know the Minister of Labour and the
Minister of Finance are both taking a very
great interest in this matter, and I rise in
the hope that I may get some assurance from
them that similar advantages will be given
to the unemployed boys and young men of
Northern Ireland.

When the "A" Force was disbanded I do

Mr. LEEKE: I should like to take this
opportunity of drawing the attention of the
House to the unemployment that exists in
Derry City. If you carry your minds back
a
few months you will remember the
strenuous efforts which were made by the
Government to retain Derry City under the
flag of Northern Ireland. (Hon. Members:
Hear, hear.) Evidence was given then by
the leading people in the city, who were supporters of the Government, that Derry City's
economic life depended upon their remaining
in Northern Ireland. They have managed
to retain it, and the result to-day is that
Derry City is seething with unemployment
and its industries are lying paralysed. 1
would like to read to this House a letter 1
received this forenoon. It is from the Unemployed Workers' Council, and is as
follows:
We have decided to organise a march of
the unemployed of Derry to Belfast to interview the Minister of Labour with a view to
having a rate of outdoor relief struck at
once.
For this purpose we intend to set out on
Monday, May 24th, hoping to arrive in
Belfast on the 26th.
We earnestly desire that you arrange
with your colleagues representing Derry
City and County to meet us in Belfast on
above date, also that you arrange a meeting
with the Minister and our deputation, and
that you act as spokesman on our behalf
along with Mr. Sam Kyle, M.P.
Thanking you in anticipation, and sincerely trusting the above arrangements will
not cause any inconvenience. I hope to
hear from you at your earliest.
I am, yours faithfully,
Patrick McCauley.
I think that unless people were on the verge
of starvation they would not start on such a
desperate journey as marching from Derry
City to Belfast under existing circumstances.
While a great deal has been done-I must
say to a certain extent there has been some
effort to assist the large industries of Belfast, Derry City has been surely and steadily
ignored. I do not see why this should be.
After all, Derry City and County represent a
part of Northern Ireland, and they should
receive the same consideration as other parts
of Ireland, the same, at any rate, as Belfast
City. Even some of the provincial towns
have received some assistance, but there is
none for this area. I think Derry City at
the present time is in a worse position with
regard to unemployment than any other part
of Northern Ireland. You must remember
that this serious condition of affairs affects not
only the unemployed, the workers, but
equally affects the capitalists of the City of
Derry. If they are not getting some encouragement and assistance the same as other
areas like the City of Belfast and other
merchants, they cannot be expected to compete in industry, and 80 the Government
should take some serious steps to deal and
grapple with this problem.
These people have approached the Derry
Board of Guardians, who have said that they
do not feel that they could at the present
time accept the responsibility of granting
outdoor relief to these people. Financially
they say they are unable to do it. The
Government say that they have no legal
standing to do it. Therefore, what is everybody's business is nobody's business, and
these people are allowed to starve between
these two bodies. That, after all, is surely a
serious refusal on the part of the Government to do its duty. They should at least-I
appeal to the Minister of Labour (Mr.
Andrews)-get into consultation with the
Derry local authorities to see if they cannot
give some grant, and if the local authorities
cannot give some grant something should be
done to deal with this problem.
I do not know what reply I shall get from
my Unionist colleagues from Derry City and
County as to whether they are prepared to
meet this deputation or not, or whether they
are sympathetic enough to meet and deal
with this problem when the deputation arrives. I shall consult with one of them
later, but at any rate, I should like to know
from the Minister of Labour now if any
practical steps have been taken to deal with
the problem of unemployment in this area.

I should like to point out to the Minister
of Commerce (Mr. Barbour) that he has had
in his hands for six weeks now some of the
reserved services, which were previously retained by the British Government, such as
harbours. Has nothing been done yet which
would, to a certain extent, absorb some of
these people who are presently unemployed
in Derry City? There are many improvements surely which could be made around
that area in regard to harbours which would
be work on which some of these people could
be usefully employed and which would remove them from their present position.
Surely, after all, it is a stigma on the Ulster
Government to see the people on the verge
of starvation, and, although I know that one
cannot expect financial miracles, even from
so clever a financier as the Minister of
Finance (Mr. Pollock), I think he should
surely have some funds which he could use
to deal with the present situation existing in
that area.
There is also the question of agriculture.
There is surely a method here, if the
Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Archdale)
would take it up, by which something could
be done to relieve the position in Derry
City. The time of employment in the agricultural area round Derry is now coming on,
and surely some steps should be taken to
inquire as to what are the prospects for
employment in the rural areas for the people
who are unemployed in Derry City. I ask
on behalf of these people that something
should be done, particularly in the case of
Derry City. As I say, it has been in the past
steadily ignored, and it is the duty of the
Government now to see that nobody starves
in the area over which they have control.
When you consider the Departments the
Government have under their control they
should surely be able to inquire and to make
careful research into the economic and commercial possibilities of the country. They
can surely grasp and devise some method to
deal with this problem. I admit freely that
we have no more sympathetic Minister than
the Minister of Labour (Mr. Andrews). I
know that he is dealing with a very difficult
problem, a problem which is baffling not
only him but the Labour Ministers in every
other country in the world; but in the area
I speak of there is more distress, there is
more unemployment, there is more starvation than in any other part of the world.
From the information we have received,
unemployment here can be proved to be
higher here than in any other area. I say
that something should be done, and done
immediately, to stop this present serious
condition of affairs. With the knowledge the
Government have at their command of the
economic conditions of Derry City they can
surely make some suggestion to the Derry
Board of Guardians and to the Derry Corporation so that some method may be found
to alleviate the present distressing conditions existing in that area.
Mr. MARK: I would just like to say a
word or two on the matter of unemployment
in Derry City. If the hon. Member (Mr.
Leeke) who has just sat down had been in
the House earlier to-day he would have
heard from the Minister of Labour (Mr.
Andrews) a statement giving the figures of
unemployment in Derry as compared with
the average of unemployment throughout the
rest of the Six Counties. I was glad to learn
from the right hon. Gentleman that Derry
City compares very favourably, in fact,
to-day, Derry City is from two to three per
cent. under the average for the rest of the
country. Notwithstanding that, I know that
there is a certain amount of unemployment
in Derry City. Everything has been done up
to the present, I think, that could reasonably
be required from the Corporation of Derry.
One-third of the members of that body are
elected to represent Labour, and do represent
Labour very efficiently and well.
I had from the Minister of Labour to-day
a pledge that any further schemes that may
be submitted by the Corporation of Derry
will be immediately and most sympathetically considered. I have had interviews
with the Minister in the past-not this year,
but during the last Parliament-over various
schemes for Derry City. I always found the
Minister of Labour most sympathetic, and
he has met any request ever made to him,
as far as Derry is concerned, in a most
reasonable spirit. I am quite satisfied that
if any scheme is placed before him he will
give it every consideration, and I will be
pleased to assist as far as I can every effort
by the unemployed in Derry to get work.
But we know what the problem is in Belfast
and elsewhere throughout the Six Counties.
There are great difficulties to be overcome,
and if the hon. Member (Mr. Leeke), or any
other person, can put any reasonable
suggestion before the Minister of Labour 1
will be very pleased to back him up, and
I am certain that my colleagues on this side
of the House, who sit for Derry City and
county, will also give any assistance they
can.
Mr. POLLOCK: I do not propose to deal with

to do so this year, in order that the trade

Mr. LEEKE: On a point of order, might
I ask the right hon. Gentleman has one
single penny been granted to the shirt industry or any other industry in Derry? The
grant for the bridge does not count.
Mr. POLLOCK: No, Sir, not specially.
The shirt and collar industry of Derry, 1
presume, is part of that great general trade
which we are accustomed to call the linen
trade, but which in fact is not the linen
trade. There has been considerable assistance given to the trade as a whole, but it
is not limited to Belfast. The grants that
have been made to the linen trade have not
been limited to Belfast, but extend to the
whole of the Six Counties where operations
are carried on either in the direct manufacture of linen itself or in subsidiary enterprises of a similar or allied character. To
that extent, therefore the presumption is
that the cotton, or linen as the case may
be, industries of Derry must benefit. That
trade is indirectly benefitting, but it
is not necessarily located in Belfast.
These are matters that should be
approached in a very broad spirit, and
to give publicity to the charge that the
City of Derry has laboured under any discrimination-against it I mean- is simply
something that I think deserves, at any
rate, to be contradicted as quickly as possible after the statement has been made.
That is all I have to say on that subject,
leaving to my right hon. Friend (Mr.
Andrews) the task of dealing with the other
charges levelled against his Department in
connection with unemployment.

have done so. We have, in the first place, a

The hon. Member went on to refer to the
desirability of having a reciprocity arrangement with the Free State in reference to
those workers who were working in one
and who happened to live in the
other area. I really do not think I can add

was quite anxious that an arrangement of
the kind should be made if it were possible.
The hon. Member for North Belfast (Mr.
Kyle) said that he would not ask that extended benefit should be given to these persons, but that they should receive benefits
to which their stamp contributions entitle
them. That is quite a reasonable proposal
for him to make, but again there is a very
big difference; that is the value of the
stamps in Northern Ireland is very
different from what it is in the Free State.
Benefit in Northern Ireland is paid at the
rate of 18s for men, while in the Free State
it is 15s. The benefit for women in Northern
Ireland is 15s, while in the Free State, speaking from memory, it is I think 12s. Again
we here give 2s per child, while in the Free
State-again speaking from memory-I think
I am right in saying it is only 1s. The difficulty is not to place Northern Ireland
workers under any arrangement of the kind
at a disadvantage as compared with Free
Staters. That is the problem which has got
to be investigated, and it cannot be settled
without a great deal of research work being
done.

As regards the question of having another

ally, I must say that I cannot see any

Mr. LEEKE: What scheme is that.
Mr. ANDREWS: The Banagher scheme.
Mr. LEEKE: It is held up.
Mr. ANDREWS: I am afraid it is a bit

I am very glad to say that at the present

In it the percentage of unemployment is only
7.6; in other words, about one-third of what

Nothing would grieve me more than that

other country in the world is expected to

The hon. and gallant Gentlemen then suggested in connection with disbandment that
it was the policy of the Government to down
every Ulsterman who had not got any influence. That is not the fact. I am informed
and believe that the system of disbandment
has been that when a branch is disbanded
all ranks go, but that when a branch is cut
down volunteers under the new terms who
are recommended for detention get the first
chance, and that the selection is made regardless of any question of nationality. I
am further informed that all have suffered
equally in this regard.
In regard to the matter which the hon.
and gallant Gentleman raised in his speech
as well as in the question asked in the
House as to the number of sergeant
instructors in the counties of Tyrone and
Fermanagh, I can only repeat what the
right hon. Gentleman the Minister of Home
Affairs said in that regard. These sergeant
instructors were appointed on the recommendation of the County Commandants in
those two counties. Both Commandants are
Ulstermen and are local men. I would not
attempt to try to inform the hon. and gallant Member on a matter of which he has
had great experience, but I do understandand I think perhaps he will agree with methat every man who has been a soldier is
not qualified to be an instructor. I understand an instructor requires to have particular skill and aptitude for the work he
has got to perform. I have no doubt the
County Commandants were greatly influenced by the requirements necessary
on
that occasion, and I have no doubt they
consulted and considered that sentiment
that suggests an Ulsterman should get
preference. I think that as far as the Government is concerned no complaints have
been made by either the officers or the men
themselves in regard to those instructors.
Indeed, we have evidence from time to time
that the most cordial and happy relations
exist amongst them.

HOUSE OF COMMONS.

Thursday, 20th May, 1926.
The House met at Three of the Clock, Mr.
SPEAKER in the Chair.
Oral Answers to Questions.
NUMBER OF WINE LICENCES
GRANTED.
1. Mr. CRAWFORD asked the Minister of
Home Affairs whether he will state the
number of Wine Licences granted by the
Excise Authorities in Northern Ireland
since the Intoxicating Liquor Act of 1923
came into operation.
The MINISTER OF FINANCE (Mr.
Pollock): I propose to take this question on
behalf of my right hon. Friend. Since the
passing of the Intoxicating Liquor Act, 1923,
10 new licences for the sale of wine for offconsumption have been issued by the
Customs and Excise Department, of which 8
are at present in force.
CONVICTIONS FOR ILLICIT
DISTILLATION.
2. Mr. CRAWFORD asked the Minister of
Home Affairs whether he can state the
number of convictions for illicit distillation
during the last three years, and also the
number of persons sent to prison during the
same period for this offence.
The MINISTER OF HOME AFFAIRS (Sir
Dawson Bates): In answer to the question
of the hon. Member, I beg to state that the
number of convictions for illicit distillation
during the last three years is 195, and the
number of persons sent to prison during the
same period for this offence is 63.
Mr. DEVLIN: Is not the cause of all this
illicit distillation the high duty on whisky?
RURAL AND COUNTY COUNCIL
WORKERS' HOURS OF LABOUR.
3. Mr. KYLE asked the Prime Minister
whether he will state when the Government
intends to introduce a Bill to regulate the
hours of labour of workers employed by
rural district councils and county councils.
The following question also stood in the
name of Mr. Kyle:
WHITLEY JOINT INDUSTRIAL COUNCIL.
4. Mr. KYLE to ask the Prime Minister
whether it is the intention of the Government to set up a Whitley Joint Industrial
Council to govern the conditions of employment of workers employed in the nontrading departments of the rural district
councils and county councils.
Sir DAWSON BATES: I have been asked
by the Prime Minister to reply. I propose
to embody in the one reply the answers to
the two questions put down by the hon.
Member.
The establishment of the councils is a
matter for consultation and decision as
between the local authorities and their employees, and the same consideration applies
to the question of the hours of labour of
workers employed by the local authorities.
Mr. KYLE: Is the right hon. Gentleman
aware that the time of the working week of
these workers is 56 hours, whereas in the
shipyards and textile trades the hours are
47 and 48? In view of that fact is he not
prepared to ask the county councils to set
up this Whitley Council to regulate the hours
of the workers who work for the county
councils?
Sir DAWSON BATES: The principle of
the Whitley Council is an entirely voluntary
one. It is a matter between the employers
and the employees.
Mr. KYLE: I am quite aware that the
Whitley Councils are voluntary associations.
It is because I know that that I am asking
the right hon. Gentleman to ask the county
councils and rural councils to be so good as
to volunteer to set up the Whitley Council
to regulate the wages and hours of their
employees.
Sir DAWSON BATES: I am afraid my
hon. Friend does not understand the
position that I occupy in relation to the
local authorities. It is a matter entirely in
their own discretion. I do not propose to
interfere with it.
Mr. KYLE: The right hon. Gentleman
seems to think that I do not understand
his position. Well, it is quite obvious that
no one in this House can understand his
position as well as himself. I do understand
the position of the road workers and the
other workers who are employed by the
county councils and rural councils. I merely
asked the right hon. Gentleman if he would
be so good as to ask the county councils to
set up the Whitley Council, and he says no.

ORDERS OF THE DAY.
Queen's University Bill [S.]
Motion made, and Question proposed:
"That the Bill be now read the Third time."
Dr. MORRISON: I have not had an opportunity until to-day of speaking on this
Measure, and I would like to say a word or
two with regard to it. There have been some
letters complaining of the fact that the
library and the museum were not available
for the public. So far as I know, the Senate
and everybody connected with the University
would be keenly desirous of creating an
interest in the University amongst the people
of Belfast and the Six Counties, and if any
plan could be devised that would secure that
object it would be welcomed by the governing
body of the University. Some Amendments
were put down to the Bill by the Labour
Party and they were ruled out of order. I
think that was due to a misunderstanding as
to the powers of the University. We are
protected in the University in this way that
no legislation can take place without the
sanction of Convocation. We should clearly
1509 Queen's University Bill—
20 MAY 1926

Third Reading.
of
understand that Convocation consists
every graduate of the University who has
entered his form and paid his fee. It is the
broadest constitution in the world; nothing
can be broader than it.
Mr. KYLE: It is, within limits.
Dr. MORRISON: Every member has the
right to vote on this important question.
After Convocation has decided the changes
that were necessary to give representation to
the county councils nothing further could be
introduced into the Bill without a further
meeting of Convocation. I think that if
Labour desires to be represented in the University nobody would take serious objection
to it. I have heard a Member of the Labour
Party say in this House that he thought the
time was coming when his party would cross
the floor and the Government would disappear.
Mr. KYLE: Merely change, not disappear.
Dr. MORRISON: The Government would
retire to the other side into the cold shades
of the Opposition.
Mr. KYLE: That is better.
Dr. MORRISON: I think there is a possibility, but not a probability, that that might
happen, and if it did happen I imagine the
University would confer an honorary degree
upon the leader of the Labour Party.
The MINISTER OF LABOUR (Mr.
Andrews): Hear, hear.
Dr. MORRISON: I quite imagine that my
hon. Friend (Mr. Kyle) opposite would be
introduced by me and that the noble Marquess, who is Chancellor of the University,
would robe him. But, on the other hand,
there is the possibility that he or his party
may never cross the floor of the House. Indeed, when he was making his speech I
thought of the celebrated answer which the
second Charles gave to his brother James
when he told him, "James, there is no possibility of the British people ever killing me
to make you king."
What we have done is that we want to give
representation to the county councils, and
we want the county councils to recognise the
great fact that the University is their own.
It is for the education of their boys and girls.
It is a thing everybody in Ulster should be
proud of, and we should look upon it as a
privilege and not a duty to contribute. In
my days in the University I think I paid
more attention to sport than to study, but,
be that as it may, I was in the first Rugby
fifteen. (Hon. Members: Hear, hear). The
House is only beginning to discover the versatility of my attainments. (Laughter).
Probably as a result of that the Secretary
of the University, the late Mr. Finnegan,
whose unexpected death produced such depression and regret amongst all sections in
Belfast, asked me to go out to see the football
field and the cricket field.
We used to play in the grounds of the University, but those grounds were exhausted by
being built upon to provide further accom
modation for the students. I went out to
see this field, which is remote from the
University, on the Ravenhill Road. It was a
splendid field but there was no pavilion. I
put it to the Labour representatives across
the House that Labour is able to have
splendid pavilions in the football clubs with
which they are associated. They have legitimate and proper accommodation for their
players in their clubs, but here you have
boys and girls who are going to have control
of very serious matters in Ulster, and they
have a cricket field and a football field, but
no pavilion. I think that is in itself a matter
greatly to be deplored, and if they had ample
funds in the University a grant would be
made to meet that end. I come to this question of the contribution to the University.
It is admitted, I think, by everyone who has
studied the facts that Queen's gets a smaller
contribution from public bodies than any
other university in Great Britain.
Mr. KYLE: Look at the county council, a
representative of which is sitting beside you.
Dr. MORRISON: I will deal with that.
When the congestion, and the numbers, and
the expense of running the University came
before the Senate they looked around for
help, and they naturally followed the example of the older universities in England
and went to the county councils. Now this
Bill is simply for the purpose of giving the
county councils representation on the Senate,
a fit and proper proposal which meets with
the approval of not only Dr. Livingstone,
the Vice-Chancellor, but of all the Senate
and of all the University members. I regret
to find that in two counties-one of them I
am ashamed to say is my own-no grant was
made. I represent not the University
specially. I represent the country graduates
of the University, and what I say on this
matter I say on behalf of the country graduates, the men who occupy in the remote
districts of Ulster very important positions
and help to run the social services, and who
are doing good in their various capacities for
the community amongst whom they live.
These people to my knowledge regret that
this step has been taken, but I am not without hope, and I think it is no breach of confidence for me to say that to-day I was
cheered by an interview I had with the
Chairman of the Down County Council. He
is a broad-minded man, and he said he would
not be content with a contribution of 4d,
but that next year he hoped the Down County
Council would give d.

Dr. MORRISON: I told my hon. Friend

In regard to County Derry, County Derry

Dr. MORRISON: I did not get an opportunity of speaking on this Bill until to-day.
I hope as Member for the University I have

would irritate. Such was not my intention. 1
was told that if I spoke we would have a

Mr. BEATTIE: I rise to move the rejection
of this Bill. I do so because, as Members
of the Opposition and as Members of this
Parliament, we have no right to amend the
Bill as presented. Actually we have no
authority whatever over the Bill, other than
to accept it or to reject it. If we accept
the Bill we accept a liability of £36,000.
The PRIME MINISTER indicated dissent.
Mr. BEATTIE: Am I wrong? At any rate,
leaving it at that point, we do accept a
financial responsibility. Now, when this
financial responsibility is accepted by us,
I contend that we should have the right to
put into the Bill as it passes through this
House what we think is in the best interests
of the whole community. We in the
Opposition put down two Amendments. One
was to secure Labour representation on the
Senate. We were told that the Amendments
could not be accepted on the ground that
some body outside this House had already
agreed on the Bill, and it was not within
the purview of this House to add anything
to or delete anything from the Bill as it
was presented.
Now, we have heard the hon. and learned
Member for the University (Dr. Morrison)
make the statement that this Bill is really
to extend and to add representation from
the county councils. You are going to invite
representation from the county councils, the
people who absolutely refused to impose a
tax for the upkeep of the University. I
know the hon. Member for Antrim (Mr.
Crawford), who is the high priest of the
temple of reaction, will, perhaps, some day
next year come back and assist the hon. and
learned Member for the University to get
a tax imposed in the county to which he
belongs. We on the Labour side agreed to
the principle, not being aware that when the
opportune time came for the Labour section
of the Six Counties to ask for representation
on that august body we would be absolutely
refused representation of the kind we sought.
It has been recognised by all leading men
that there are as able advocates of educational ideals amongst the ranks of Labour
as in any other section of the community.
In Great Britain universities and other
similar bodies have invited the co-operation
of gentlemen from the Labour Party. But
we are told here to-day that only when we
become the party that has the power to grant
the assistance which the University gets will
we be invited to take a seat on that elaborate
body called the Senate. I quite agree that
we may not be all that is desired by the
heads of the University, but I am sure it
will be agreed that very useful work could
be done on that board by Labour representation from the point of view of education.
The refusal to accept our Amendment in
Committee left me no option but to move
the rejection of the Bill at this particular
stage, and I am now doing so on behalf of
the Opposition.

Mr. JOHNSTONE: Before the House proceeds to vote on this matter I should like
to say a few words in regard to this Bill.
I possess, I think, the unique distinction
in this House of being a member of those
three bodies whose actions have been so
much discussed in connection with this
Measure. I am a member of the Senate, I
am also a member of the Academic Council,
and I am a member of Convocation, and I
was present at the meetings when this Bill
was considered, and at the meetings when
this Bill was accepted. A great many criticisms of this Bill have been offered since it
came before the Senate and before this
House. There is only one of those criticisms
which was offered when it was passing
through one of those three bodies of which
I have just spoken, and which alone, I may
say, has the right to say what the changes
in the constitution are going to be.
I should like to clear the air a little in
regard to what I think are misconceptions
regarding the relative positions of Queen's
University and this Parliament. This Parlia-
Inent has absolutely no power whatever to
interfere with Queen's University, except on
the original proposition of the University
itself. The University has to make up its
mind what changes it wishes, and then it
must have them passed in a Bill by this
House and by the Senate. It is open for
the House of Commons and the Senate, or
for either, to refuse to pass that Bill, in
which case the position reverts to what it
was before.
This is not a Bill to give Queen's University
£36,000, because that £36,000 is part of the
deed under which this Parliament sits, and
this Parliament could not refuse that £36,000
to Queen's University. If it refuses that
£36,000 it breaks the Act by which it sits.
So let there be no misconception or misunderstanding. That £36,000 is not a grant
from this Parliament, and, as a matter of
fact, I should like to take this opportunity
of saying that £36,000 is not even a fair
estimate of the amount that comes to the
funds of Northern Ireland's University. The
exact grant towards Queen's University is
£26,000. The £10,000 which makes up the
£36,000 is something over which this Parliament or this Government have no control
whatever, because it is part of the residuary
estate of the old Royal University, which
comes to Queen's University automatically,
and which the Government have no power
whatever to divert from that object. The
£10,000 is handed to the Government of
Northern Ireland, and they in turn hand
it over to the University, and if the
University were not to get that £10,000 it
would not come into the funds of Northern
Ireland. Therefore, I would like the
positions of the University and this Parliament to be perfectly clear.
Having said so much in regard to the
power of the University, I would also like
to make the position of the three bodies,
which I represent here, again perfectly clear.
The principal criticism offered against this
Bill is that we propose to give representation to the county councils who are not
giving us money, or at least some of whom
are not giving us money. Now we are very
anxious for money-it is, perhaps, the most
pressing need of the University at the present time-but we are not giving this
representation for the purpose of getting
money from any single county council, and
if, at the end of the next financial year,
every single county council in Northern
Ireland refused to give us even the farthing
in the pound, which some are giving at
present, we would not come back and ask
this House to withdraw that representation.
The object with which this representation is
being given is that of extending, as far as
we possibly can, the interest in the University, of extending, widening, and deepening
interest in the University, and of making
the people of Northern Ireland feel that
Queen's University is the University of
Northern Ireland-(hon. Members: Hear,
hear) is the University which Northern
Ireland ought to support, and to which the
sons of Northern Ireland ought to come for
their education. (Hon. Members: Hear,
hear.)
That is the principle which was advanced
when the Bill was being put before these
three bodies I speak of. When I say that
is the principal object with which this Bill
is being put forward-in order to broaden,
widen, and popularise interest in the
University-I think I will to a very large
extent have disarmed the criticism that is
offered, because I am perfectly certain that
no body which has such a desire and such
an aim in front of it can afford to disregard
the claims of Labour to any reasonable
representation that they ask for. May I
say one thing? We have been accused-and
I do not say that the accusations are illfounded-that we have been in the past, perhaps shall I say?-sectarian in the University of Belfast. I do not know how that
could have been altogether avoided owing
to circumstances into which I do not at
present wish to enter. But, this morning,
you, Mr. Speaker, and myself were present
when we were laying to rest one who was
the last Vice-Chancellor of the Queen's
University. He was a great Vice-Chancellor.
He found Queen's College a very small and
rather insignificant seat of learning. He left
it a University, which is great and which is
glorious, and which, I hope, will be a credit
to the whole of Northern Ireland in the
future. (Hon. Members: Hear, hear.)
1515 Queen's University Bill-

HOUSE OF COMMONS
Third Reading.
[Mr. Johnstone]
When that Vice-Chancellor retired owing
to the weight of years Queen's University
had then to look round for
a new Vice-
Chancellor. Now we did not select any of
the eminent men of any sect, or of any
party, or of any pursuasian in Northern
Ireland. We went-and I think it is the
best sign that those who wish for the University to be broad and wide in its aims
could ask for-we went across to one of the
oldest, one of the most famous, and one of
the most distinguished of the Universities
in England-the University of Oxford-and
we brought over here a man who had only
one claim on the Vice-Chancellorship, and
that was that he was a man of wide and
deep learning, a man vitally interested in
education, and especially in University education. (Hon. Members: Hear, hear.) I do
not think there is a single Member of this
House who has even remotely come in contact with our present Vice-Chancellor who
will not agree that we made an exceedingly
wise choice. (Hon. Members: Hear, hear.)
I do not think there is a single man who
has ever come into contact with him who
could feel that he is in the slightest degree
narrow, or bigoted, or that he wishes in any
way to restrict the University to being the
University of any particular class, or the
University of any particular creed, or the
University of any particular sect. I feel
sure that we must all agree with the Vice-
Chancellor when he wishes the University
to be in the broadest sense a University for
the whole of Northern Ireland, and that
there shall be no single person, be he high
or low, who will not benefit from having the
University here. I know nothing would please
the Vice-Chancellor better than that this
Bill should go through, and I would beg my
hon. Friends on the Front Opposition Bench
to withdraw their opposition to this Measure,
and to allow that spirit, which is in the
University at present, to take care that
Labour will receive whatever representation
it will be necessary for them to have.
They must remember that, after all, the
Senate of the University is only to a very
small extent the body which is responsible
for the running of the University. It is
the board of directors of the University.
The people who really carry out the work
of the University are its Professors and its
teachers, and the people who must in the
long run support the University are the
great body of graduates, and it is to them
that the success of the University will be
very much more largely due than to the
Senate. A single representative, or two representatives of Labour, will influence to a
very small extent the policy of the University, but they can influence very largely
the policy of the University by their influence on public opinion, as I am perfectly
certain that in the future as in the past,
the running of Queen's University will be
very largely guided by public opinion in the
Province. (Hon. Members: Hear, hear.)
Mr. DEVLIN: I am sure that everyone who
has listened to the speech of the hon. Gentleman must be deeply impressed with its sincerity and spirit of good will. (Hon. Members: Hear, hear.) Of course, I am sure it
will be admitted that those of us who belong
to the Province of Ulster are most anxious
for the development of our great University
and for its progress and for its growth and
for all the great purposes which it seeks to
attain. I should be glad if it were possible
that this Bill which has been submitted
should pass through the House unanimously,
because I think it ought to be our duty to
encourage the University authorities to feel
that not only do we recognise that the University itself is discharging a public function
but that it has the moral and financial support of every section of citizens. But I
should like to say this; that if we owe that
obligation to the University the University
also is under an obligation to the citizens,
and it ought to make an effort, partly on
selfish grounds, to win the goodwill and cooperation of every section of the community
by recognising the right of every section of
the community to influence the life of the
University.
The purpose of this Measure is, as I understand, to give representation to the county
councils. Well, the democratic principle is
that representation and responsibility go
hand in hand. In this case, however, some of
the county councils have not agreed to make
the contribution which it was thought they
would make, and which would have some
influence with the University when they propose to give these councils representation;
and it does seem rather curious that while
you are willing to give representation to
these county councils who decline some of
them to assist you, you are not disposed to
give representation to those who represent
the masses of the people. Speaking for my
own co-religionists, I do not think we have
a right to be satisfied with our representation. Out of a little over one thousand
students there are 200 Catholics.
In the University Act we secured a representation of five and that representation has
been cut down to two. I am quite certain
that the University authorities and the Government will recognise that they ought to
make our position no worse. That is not a
very large demand. On the University
governing body there are some 42. We had
five, and it has been reduced to two. The least
we can expect is to occupy no worse position
under the new regime than we occupied when
the University Act was passed in the British
Parliament.
1517 Queen's University Bill-
Appropriation Bill- 1518
20 MAY 1926
May I say that I think the University
authorities ought also to consider the desirability of giving Labour representation.
Everyone who follows the development of our
modern life and the development of modern
culture is well aware that the passion for
learning exists as largely amongst the working classes as amongst any other section of
the community. We cannot all divorce ourselves from prejudice. Nobody knows that
better than I do. And really there ought to
be a desire upon the part of the University
authorities to allay the spirit of suspicion
that exists that the powerful intellectual
forces in a place like Ulster are not inclined
to allow for these prejudices, natural passions, and ambitions which exist in the mind
of the working classes in regard to the principle of higher education. There are many
working men and many representatives of
Labour who are men of culture.
I have been reading some of the speeches
at great intellectual assemblies, and I do
not know any speeches more instinct with
culture and great intellectual power than the
speeches of Mr. Ramsey McDonald. There
are other speakers who are ornaments to
those assemblies and who enrich the discussions with the powerful contributions they
make to the culture and progress of English
public life. That, perhaps, may not be very
manifest in the narrower area over here, out
it ought to be the function of the University
to encourage intellectual development and to
give opportunity in intellectual life for those
who have those qualities and opportunity to
manifest them in our public life. And therefore without attempting in any way to lecture
the University authorities I venture to submit to them that apart altogether from the
fundamental right of Labour and the citizen
right of those for whom I speak, from the
purely selfish aspect of it, it would be good
for the University and good for the Province
that all sections should get legitimate representation and be allowed to take an interest
in the purposes for which the University
exists.
I, therefore, appeal to my hon. Friend, in
view of what was said by the hon. Gentleman opposite (Mr. Johnstone), to withdraw
his opposition and allow the Bill to pass.
Mr. KYLE: I think after the speech of
the hon. Member for the University (Mr.
Johnstone) those of us who sit on the Labour
benches are put in a rather difficult position.
We feel we have achieved what we set out

attention to the question with which I am
so familiar that is the question of unemployment. It may be boring-I am sure it
is-to some Members of the Government,
but I can assure them that the boredom
they have got to suffer by my speaking here
is nothing like the pangs of hunger the
unemployed workers have to suffer owing
to the depressed conditions of labour and
their being denied benefit under the Unemployment Insurance Act. We have been
told, even in this House we have been told
repeatedly, that the Opposition repeat
their speeches.
There is only one way of
presenting the unemployment question, and
that is by telling the facts in regard to the
regulations. I have endeavoured on several
occasions to make that perfectly understandable to every Member of the House, but I
have not been able to get the Minister and
his colleagues to make any alteration.
There is the case of a man, one of my constituents, who a fortnight ago was allowed
twelve weeks' benefit by a Rota Committee.
That committee was composed of representatives of the employers, of the workers,
and of the Ministry. But the headquarters
of the Ministry were not quite satisfied with
the man's history, they were not quite satisfied with the decision of that composite
body, and they sent the man's case to another court, with a footnote of so damning
a character on the application that the com-
Imittee had no option but to disallow the
claim. There is a case in which one court
allowed the man twelve weeks' benefit, and
the other court disallowed his claim owing
to the request of the headquarters of the
Ministry of Labour.
We have heard it stated here that only
2.7 of the claims that pass through the Rota
Committees are disallowed. If I did not
know the Minister as well as I do, I would
take it that his figures were wrong. But I
would like to know how those figures are
compiled. I would be prepared to challenge
that figure of 2.7 owing to the number of cases
that have come under my own observation
of claims being disallowed by headquarters
after being passed by the Rota Committees.
I am quite satisfied in my own mind that in
every case in which a Rota Committee
grants the application of a man who has
been more than two years out of employment, as soon as the headquarters receive
the claim they either disallow it or refer it
to another committee within twelve days
from the date of the decision of the first
committee. That is quite clear, and that is
a fact.
The regulation in regard to the two years
is hitting the unemployed so hardly that
I take the opportunity presented by the
Third Reading of this Bill to present their
case once again to the Minister. It is all
very well endeavouring to keep a fund in a
state of solvency, but the sacrifice is rather
great, because there are 10,000 people who
have no income whatever. You have the
Boards of Guardians all over the Six
Counties refusing to meet their obligations,
and the Government are condoning the
offence by standing idly by and allowing
them to adjudicate in the manner to which
I have referred.
It has been repeatedly stated that the
poor-law does not give sufficient power to
that authority to administer outdoor relief
on the same scale or conditions as prevail
in Great Britain. If that is so, I ask the
Government, who have got legal advice at
their command, to make a definite statement defining the duties of the Guardians,
and how far the Guardians can go under
Section 13 of the Poor-law Act of 1898. If
they make that statement adverse to the administration of the poor-law guardians, I
will say they have acted in the manner I
have expected, that is, if they tell the
Guardians in a direct fashion that they have
sufficient law to see that no man, woman
or child is allowed to starve, owing to the
state of unemployment and the refusal to
pay unemployment benefit.
I would also like to refer to the Widows',
Orphans' and Old
Age Contributory
Pensions Act. Great hardships have been
created under the Act which was placed on
the Statute Book at so recent a date. I
pleaded once before that the date should be
made retrospective, but of course
Minister of Finance told us that a money
resolution would be required to meet the
liability. Last night three widows came to
me. Their husbands had died between
Christmas and the New Year.
They have

Mr. BEATTIE: I hope the great hardships

We have another matter that is hitting
hard a certain class of the community at

who have been out of industry for a period
of years, and who have no opportunity of
ever again being placed in industry. I refer
to the older shipbuilding and engineering

was due to the strike, according to the
Belfast Press, but orders were given that
30 per cent. of the total number of men
employed and 50 per cent. of the staff were
to be paid off. I understand that those were
the instructions.
Mr. POLLOCK: That was due to the
strike.
Mr. BEATTIE: It was not due to any
strike; it was due to the want of work.
Certain people were paid off who were 35
or 40 years in the industry, and as soon as
their 156 contributions are exhausted the
Minister of Labour will turn them off the
unemployment benefit. I want the Minister
to consider that class of person. I want the
question of age to be abolished, because, if
you do not, you are imposing a great hardship upon people who are walking the streets
through no fault of their own. One way of
remedying the grievance that exists would
be not to take age into consideration until
such time as the man becomes entitled to
the old-age pension at 65.
I hope the principal question that I rose
to speak about will not be overlooked by

the Government before they leave this
building. If they do overlook it I, being a
constitutionalist, will proceed on constitutional lines; but we can follow what took
place across the water. There is a sufficient
number of people in the Six Counties who
are prepared to go into the workhouse and
to remain there for a term, so as to compel
the authorities to keep them at a higher
rate than it would cost to maintain them
outside.
That is one way of defeating the drastic
decision of the Guardians of Northern Ireland not to give outdoor relief to any person
who has been turned off unemployment
benefit. That really is the decision in a
crude way, and I ask the Government to
make a statement what they are prepared
to do for the unemployed during the period
in which this House will be adjourned. I
hope the Prime Minister will state what
the Government are going to do.
The PRIME MINISTER: My right hon.
Friend, the Minister of Labour, has dealt
in detail with the whole subject of unemployment insurance and other matters so
frequently throughout the Session that I
feel, as this will be our last day for discussion for some little time to come, it
might not be out of place if I myself replied
on this occasion to the hon. Member. I
sometimes think that his speeches in this
House create a false impression outside, and
if they remained unanswered the public
might feel that Northern Ireland, as exemplified by this Parliament, and by this
Government, was not doing all that was
humanly possible to help the unemployed in
our midst.
The hon. Member raised individual cases,
which are always very difficult for a Minister
to deal with without having specific notice
beforehand that they are going to be raised.
A specific case of hardship in a population
of a million and a quarter or more is bound
to crop up. The worst of it is that these
isolated cases, when they are given the prominence of discussion in this House, rather
create a false impression outside. I am
quite sure that there is not a single case
of real hardship in Northern Ireland that
cannot be met by the proper authority.
I would have all the Ulster people know
that my right hon. Friend here (Mr.
Andrews) is limited by statute as to what
he can do and what he cannot do. I wish
to make that perfectly clear. The second
point that I would like to make is that if
my right hon. Friend was to take the easy
road towards popularity it would be possible
for him to endear himself to the hearts of
all who are unemployed to-day, but
on the other hand he would gravely
prejudice the unemployed of the future.

be a workman or any other person inside the

to aid the unemployed and the poor in our

of

dammed up. I mention these matters because it seems to me that some of them
might be dealt with now, and so relieve the
people whose lands are flooded in this particular area. I am also told that the fishery
cribs at Castleroe are of great assistance to
the discharge of floods, and in this connection I would like to read what has been
written to me by one of the farmers who
live in that neighbourhood, and who suffer
greatly from the floods. It seems that the
lessees of the salmon fishing board up these
cribs until the season opens for taking
salmon, which is sometime about the first
of May. He goes on to say-
66 You can imagine what this means
during two of the principal spring months
when miles and miles of land are covered
with water as at present."
He goes on to ask if I could find out, either
by question in this House or otherwise, if

indeed in all countries. I remember attending in America a great Arbour day celebration which was the first initiated by

I read with some interest the report of
the Commission, which has just sat, on the
subject of introducing beet growing into
Northern Ireland. While they did not seem
to be convinced that this could be introduced
at the present time without some further

chance of success. I want to suggest to the

there are three other lines of our

to-day to the question of the dairying industry. For some reason or other that industry has not been the success it should
have been, and I want to say in this connection that with modern conditions and modern
markets the only way in which we can hope
to make this dairying industry of ours a success is along co-operative lines.
Modern market conditions at the present
time demand that we should be able to
supply butter and other milk products with
some uniformity, and if every farmer is
making his own little bit of butter that
uniformity cannot be secured. Up to the
present time it will be admitted that co-operation has not been the success it should have
been in that respect, and I think the two
main reasons for that are, that we had not an
adequate supply of milk, and that the milk
supply was not stable. The great difficulty
of our creamery system is that we have been
throwing in too much milk into the creameries in the summer time when there could
not be a market for the butter, and that in
the winter time we have been giving them no
milk practically when there would have been
a fine market for the butter. I say that the
efforts of the Government in encouraging the
dairying industry should be directed to stabilising the supply, and I am going to make a
suggestion as to how that could be done.
It has been stated in public again
and again that in the summer we have this
big flush of milk owing to the cows all being
brought out in the spring months before the
grazing time, when our creamery managers
cannot get a market for the butter, and then
in the winter time our supply is negligible,
and it has been said that, in order to hold
their customers, creamery managers have
forced to buy butter from abroad, take it to
their creameries, re-churn it, and sell it for
Irish butter. I say that if our creameries
were in a position to go to their customers
here, or in England or Scotland, and say "We
will supply you with such and such a quantity of nice, fresh, Irish creamery butter in
the month of May and an equal quantity
in the month of December, that would put
our creamery industry and our dairying industry in a position to demand prices that
would ensure success.
Now how is that to be done? The only way
is to compel or may be I should say induce
-the farmers to produce winter milk. The
Co-operative Society in Belfast have produced
a plan whereby their suppliers are compelled
to produce winter milk, and I would suggest
to the Government that it would be worth
while trying to compel these people by inducement to produce winter milk. It would
be in the interests of the country and of the
the
dairying industry that
Government
should grant a subsidy for every cow that is
producing winter milk in the month of
October or November. The only hope that I
see of giving our dairying industry a
chance is by stabilising the supply.

I recognise that good work has been done
by the Department in connection with the
Milk Recording Association in the way of
grading up our cows so that the individual
cows would produce a greater amount of
milk. That is good as far as it goes, but I
think it will be admitted by this House, or
by anybody who has any knowledge of the
dairying industry, that it has suffered considerably in the past by too much attention
being paid to breeds mainly built for producing beef. There has been a charge made
against the Department-rightly or wrongly
I do not know that they have discouraged
the introduction into this country of a
breed
of cattle that is pre-eminently a milking
breed. I think it is generally admitted that
all progressive countries at the present time-
Canada, the United States, New Zealand, and
all the others that are famous for the production of milk-are introducing this breed
more and more, and no Ulsterman could help
but be proud that in this small community
of ours we have two cows that beat the whole
world's record, one that gave inside twelve
months 3,000 gallons of milk, and another
two-year-old heifer that gave 2,000 gallons of
milk. I do not say that is normal, but 1
do say that a breed that is capable of producing results like that, even under abnormal
circumstances, deserves the consideration of
our Department and of this community.
I have been informed-rightly or wronglythat the Department have refused to grant
permission for the introduction of this breed
from Holland, I suppose on account of the
danger of foot and mouth disease. I am
told that the best specimens of this breed are
to be found in Holland, and that the prices
paid there are not nearly so big as those
which you are forced to pay for inferior
animals in England. I think that difficulty
should be easy to get over. They have a
quarantine station in Belfast, and could not
they keep these cattle in quarantine for a
sufficient time to make sure that there is no
infection brought into this country.
Now I do enter a complaint that in the inspection of bulls for registration purposes
this year there was a pure bred Friesian bull
turned down by one of the Department's inspectors. I do not say a Friesian bull should
be registered because it is a Friesian, but this
bull was of particularly good ancestry as regards milk production, both sire and dam.
The inspector said, according to my information, he never took that into consideration
in registering a bull. It should be taken into
consideration as one main factor, because the
production of milk is one of the main sources
of wealth for the agricultural community,
and it should be one of the main objects of
our Department of Agriculture to help in
every way the production of milk by grading
the present cows and by the introduction of
this breed which, as far as we can gather,
would be likely to help milk production.
I do think the time has arrived when
the Department in conjunction with the
Ulster Organisation Society should be prompt
to consider the organisation of the whole
dairy industry of this Province, with a view to
co-ordinating our dairy system and establishing central factories in suitable places that
would turn out large quantities of fresh
butter, and also with a view to stabilising
supplies so that you could send butter sweet
to customers every day in the year. In the
agricultural industry you cannot produce a
revolution, and this thing will take time.
But I would appeal to Parliament to take the
long view and to have a courageous policy,
and I do believe with proper education and
proper encouragement and reorganisation of
the dairy industry we can make the industry
one of the biggest successes in Northern Ireland.
I would have liked to say something on the
other two heads, pork producing and poultry,
but at this time of the evening, and I understand other Members want to speak, I do
not wish to trespass on the time of the House
very much longer. I think good work is done
under the Inspection of Eggs Bill, but there

was not built in a day, and probably the full
effects of this Bill are not yet apparent, and
that eventually its efficacy will be shown in
increased price and the enhanced value will
get to the farmer and help him in his financial difficulty.
The MINISTER OF AGRICULTURE (Mr.
Archdale): My hon. Friend the Member for
West Belfast asked me about forestry and the
reason we did not employ more labour in
forestry at the present time. A little more
than two years ago we saw the necessity
would begin to arise for more forestry in the
country, and we started increasing our nurseries of young trees, because no forestry
work can be begun until the trees are about
three years old. You cannot start forestry
until the trees are ready to plant. We foresaw the necessity and we increased our nurseries. Unfortunately last year a bug of
some sort got into the young plants, and we
lost considerably over a million trees. But
we have already increased this year our men
working on special forestry stations. They
are a great deal more than double last year.
We are increasing that as rapidly as possible,
but you cannot get trees from England except
at prohibitive prices. Our nurseries
are

My hon. Friend the Member for Antrim
(Mr. George Henderson) was talking about
dairying, and I am entirely in agreement
with him. Our great object has been to
stabilise the milk industry as much as we
possibly can by milk recording. I did not
know he was going to make a point of milk,
but I happened to take down some particulars I discovered the other day which I
thought were extraordinary. Perhaps the
House would like to hear them. We started
milk recording societies in 1921 with six
societies and 1,200 cows. In 1926 there were
53 societies with 10,360 cows, and owing to
the milk recording societies and the value of
milk feeding which has been discovered by
Dr. Robertson at our research station the
average yield of milk per cow has been enormously increased. So much so that in 25
creameries we got the figures for the
yield during the four months December,
January, February, and March, in 1924-25,
and the same this year, and the returns
were so extraordinary that we went over
them again, but we got them the same,
and also got them the same from the
creameries. These returns show that the
milk yield in 1925-26 increased 70 per cent.
over the returns for the same months of
1924-25, for a cow population, decreased 7 per
cent. That is, for fewer cows during the
last four months we got 70 per cent more
milk. It just proves that milk recording
societies are the only way of making some
farmers in Northern Ireland know how much
their cows give. It is utterly impossible for
a man to tell outside a milk-recording
society. Also the demonstration has enormous effect in showing on what rations cows
produce more milk. I am hoping certainly
in a short time to have creameries with cows
calving in the autumn. At present it is
almost impossible. I have been president of
a creamery for about twenty years. It was
one of the first established, and all that
time we have been trying to get milk during
the autumn and winter, and we have not
Leen able to do so. As the Member for
Antrim (Mr. George Henderson) says, a short
time ago the creameries were buying New
Zealand butter, which comes here during the
New Zealand summer and our winter, and
they have been making it up and issuing it
as Irish butter. We hope to put a stop to
that. We do not mind them selling it as
imported Colonial butter, but it must not
be marked as Irish creamery butter. That
is a thing we have been trying to stop. The
poultry industry has also been greatly improved.

us. Other sums we have expended are:---
Collection of Agricultural Statistics, £2,160,
Dairying Industry, £2,134, Subsidies to Shows,
£1,529, Miscellaneous Agricultural Services,
£918, Ordnance and Geological Surveys,
£8,529, and General Expenses, £37,636. In
addition to that there was a sum of £54,000
voted in 1923 which was to be expended over
four or five years. Over £14,000 of that sum
has been used this year, and of the remainder
part has been utilised for providing stallions
and helping livestock schemes and milk recording societies.
During the last four years the Ministry
has purchased and placed 12 thoroughbred
Appropriation Bill-
Third Reading.
HOUSE OF COMMONS.
[Mr. Archdale]
stallions, 9 clydesdale stallions, 1 Irish
draught, and 1 half-bred, and 5 Welsh cobs
have been placed in the mountain districts
of County Antrim where they have never had
any chance of having cobs or ponies of that
stamp before. In 1921-25 we spent altogether
over £49,000 on agricultural education, including capital expenditure, and this covered
the cost of the upkeep of the Ulster Dairy
School at Cookstown, the North-West Agricultural School at Strabane, and a grant to
the Greenmount College, County Antrim.
The winter agricultural classes have been a
very great success and the attendance has
increased. This year we had 382 pupils
attending, compared with 288 in the year before, an increase of nearly 100.
In connection with research work, we have
established five research stations. They are
all working well, and a tremendous amount
of interest is taken in them by the farmers
of the Six Counties. Every week brings an
increased number of requests for examination
and report in connection with animal and
plant diseases. We are always willing to
consider any advice that is tendered to us,
although I do not say that we will always
follow it. With regard to Friesian stock,
complaint was made about a Friesian bull
that was not licensed and was turned down.
You cannot give a licence to a bull because
it has a swagger name. We try to be as fair
as we can but we do not license beef bulls
any more than dairy bulls; in fact during
the past year we have been bringing in so
many more dairy bulls than beef bulls that
different people have been getting rather
annoyed, and this year we brought in three
or four beef bulls to keep up the standard
of the country.
As regards the use of Friesians, at the present time fat cattle of about 9 cwt. fetch top
value. The big, fat, old bullocks of 11 cwt.
they used to have several years ago will not
get within 3s. or 4s. a cwt. of the price of
the fat bullock of about 9 cwt. We do not
want to breed cattle that will not fetch the
top price, and we do not want big heavy
beasts that are not very good for any man
to get his teeth in. I do not know that there
is anything else I have to say.
Mr. THOMAS HENDERSON: You might
give us a few words about turkeys.
Mr. ARCHDALE: I wonder that the hon.
Member does not want to talk about goats.
Turkeys are most useful birds, but it requires a good year to rear them. If you have
a lot of turkeys in a wet year you will not
bring many of them up. They do bring up
geese in some parts of the country, especially
in the mountain districts, and I have seen
big flocks of them from our part of the
country being sent over to Liverpool and
Manchester.

Mr. THOMAS HENDERSON: I intended
to attack the Minister of Finance, but he is
so tactful that I am afraid to attack him.
I could not help smiling when I heard the
hon. Member for Derry (Mrs. Chichester) attacking him. The right hon. Gentleman gol
up and stroked her back, with the result that
the hon. Member went away smiling and she
knew as much about what was happening
as did the Members of the Opposition. The
Minister of Finance is always preaching
economy in this House, and we on this side
of the House are most anxious for economy,
but I want to know what is the cause of all
the delay that is taking place in the erection
of public buildings under the control of the
Ministry of Finance.
In connection with the building of the
Parliament House and the Law Courts, which
would give a great deal of employment, very
little has been done. When those buildings
are completed, other buildings now occupied
by the Government will have to be given up
and the country will be saved the rents and
other expenses of these buildings. I would
urge the Minister of Finance to speed up the
work on the Houses of Parliament and the
Law Courts, and thus provide work for our
unemployed. I must compliment the Minister of Labour for many things he is doing
to provide work for the unemployed, but I
think there should be more co-ordination of
the work of the Ministry of Labour and the
Ministry of Home Affairs, and for this
reason. The Ministry of Home Affairs is responsible for the roads, and the Ministry
of Labour is responsible for giving employment to the unemployed.
Let anyone take a motor car on any of
the roads leading from Belfast to any part
of the Province, and what would he find?
Half of them are nothing less than death
traps and they are not able to take the
heavy traffic that uses them. If the Minister of Home Affairs and the Minister of
Labour called a conference and invited representatives of the urban districts to attend to
discuss the question of the improvement of
the roads and the abolition of dangerous
corners, I believe useful work could be found
for the unemployed, and when the work was
completed it would be of great benefit to
the Province. Hon. Members who are
familiar with the road to Bangor must be
acquainted with one very dangerous corner,
and as one who has previously drawn attention to this particular corner I shall hold
the Government responsible if any lives are
lost there.
The Government is aware of these dangerous corners on the Bangor Road, and it knows
that it is utterly impossible for two of those
heavy buses that carry from 32 to 40 passengers to pass each other at those

I am not at all satisfied with the part
this Government has played in regard to

Take Belfast for instance. There building is at a standstill, notwithstanding
the fact that every public representative
knows that in Belfast there are thousands

I want to compliment the Government on

shall do what the Belfast education authority

in connection with the provision of meals

Province there are many hungry children.
They have also got powers to provide the

the children with food, clothing or books. I

The unfortunate part of it is that many

Tuesday, 1st June, 1926.

Oral Answer to Question.
EX-SERVICE COLONY AT GLEN-
GORMLEY.
Mr. GEORGE HENDERSON asked the
Minister of Finance whether rents on the
ex-Service colony at Glengormley are being
increased to new tenants from five to eight
shillings per week; and if the facts are as
stated, why is this increase being imposed,
and who is responsible for it.
The MINISTER OF FINANCE (Mr. Pollock): I understand the facts are as stated
by the hon. Member; but as I have previously
explained to the House the Sailors' and
Soldiers' Land Trust is an Imperial Service,
and questions touching on the policy of the
Irish Land Trust should, therefore, be addressed to the appropriate Minister in the
Imperial Parliament. My Department in
its capacity as agent is responsible merely
for giving effect to the decisions of the Trust.
Colonel WOODS: Might I ask the right
hon. Gentleman if this Trust is not being
administered from his Department by an
official of the Northern Government?
Mr. POLLOCK: Yes, sir, as an agent. As
I explained in the latter part of my answer,
my Department does act as agent for the
Irish Land Trust, and carries out the
arrangements, whatever they may be, which
are made by the Trust.
Mr. BEATTIE: I would like to ask the
Minister if it would not be possible for him
as agent to approach the Land Trust with a
view to getting a reduction in the rents of
these houses owing to the large amount of
unemployment which exists amongst the
tenants, who at the present moment feel it
very hard to meet their obligations as far
as rents are concerned. If there could be
any effort made by the Minister in that direction I believe it would be very serviceable.
Mr. SPEAKER: I am afraid if I had
realised what this question was it might not
have been allowed in this form. I did not
realise that the fixing of the rents was also
an Imperial service, though I knew that the
construction of the houses was.
