Oral Answers to Questions.
EFFECT OF COAL STRIKE.
a
Mr. DEVLIN (by private notice) asked
the Minister of Commerce whether he can
make statement explaining the exact
position of Northern Ireland, especially Belfast, in respect of stocks of coal; whether it
is true, as reported, that at present there are
not more than one thousand tons of coal in
Belfast, and that a large industrial concern
is going to close down in consequence of the
shortage; and what steps the Ministry has
taken to keep up supplies and distribute
them to the best advantage.
The MINISTER OF COMMERCE (Mr.
Barbour): The notice I have had of this
question is very brief, and I am sure the
hon. Member will not expect me to give a
very definite reply to the question, which is
of such importance to the community. I may
say
the position in Northern Ireland
generally is that supplies of coal are very
short, and unfortunately the situation has
been a good deal aggravated by the very
severe weather of the last few days which
has delayed the arrival of steamers which in
in the ordinary course would have been here
two or three days ago. Some of the acuteness
of the situation would not have been
experienced but for this fact. As to the
amount of coal actually in Belfast at the
moment, the situation varies almost from hour
to hour. I have just received information
that a steamer is coming up the Lough with
about 3,000 tons of coal on board. That will
be very welcome. It is true that a large industrial firm has had to close, but I am
confidently informed that they are expected
to resume work to-morrow. The Government have been watching the situation very
closely and are making such arrangements as
they hope may enable the more urgent wants
of the community to be provided for.
But
the condition of affairs is one in which I do
not believe we are suffering to the same extent as the people across the water, where a
very strict system of rationing and restriction of supply has been necessitated for
some months past.
Mr. DEVLIN: Arising out of that answer,
when will the Minister be able to make a
statement giving complete details as to the
method and the machinery which the
Government have brought into operation
during the last few months of the coal
strike? The Government appointed a Coal
Controller and, if I am not mistaken, also a
number of subordinate Coal Controllers in
different parts of Ulster, and I should like
to have a clear, definite, and detailed statement as to what the operations of these
Coal Controllers were and the results.
Mr. GRANT: Arising out of the reply of
the Minister of Commerce, I would like to
ask the right hon. Gentleman if his Department is aware of the fact that even with the
short supply of coal we have in Belfast there
is a great deal of profiteering, and if it is
the intention of his Department to take any
action in the matter.
Mr. DEVLIN: Would the right hon. Gentleman in the course of his detailed statement,
which I hope he will make at the earliest
possible moment, include an answer to the
hon. Member's question?
Mr. BARBOUR: Yes. I think that in view
of the importance of this matter the
Government will endeavour, as soon as they
are in a position to do so, to make a statement as to the position.
BANN DRAINAGE SCHEME.
Mrs. CHICHESTER (by private notice)
asked the Minister of Finance whether he
will state when the Government are prepared
to give a day for the discussion of the Bann
Drainage.
The MINISTER OF FINANCE (Mr.
Pollock): This question only came into
my hands a few minutes ago, and
therefore the hon. Member must be
content with an extempore and brief
answer to her question. The report on
the Bann Drainage question has been circulated to hon. Members and has been made
public through the columns of the newspapers. Following that, the Government
purpose to get into touch with the local authorities who are largely concerned in this
important matter and endeavour to make
such arrangements as will help towards the
prosecution of some scheme that will make
for the amelioration of the trouble. On behalf of the Government I am prepared to
give facilities for the fullest possible discussion in this House with regard to the entire
question.
1567 Marketing of Eggs Bill-

HOUSE OF COMMONS
Second Reading.
ORDERS OF THE DAY.
Marketing of Eggs (Amendment) Bill.
Order for Second Reading read.
The MINISTER OF AGRICULTURE (Mr.
Archdale): The Bill of which I now move the
Second Reading is one which has been found
necessary by reason of several small omissions, I might call them, from the previous
Measure, and it also embodies improvements
in that Act which in practice we have found
to be desirable.
Th main provisions of the present Bill relate to breaches of the Rules, purchase by
weight and the sale of stale and dirty eggs.
Under the present Act the suspension or
revocation of licences is the only remedy for
breaches of the Rules. This is obviously a
drastic course, and in practice is adopted
only where there has been a persistent contravention of the Regulations, as the Ministry
is, naturally, reluctant to put any wholesale
dealer out of the trade, even temporarily.
My proposal is that there should be the
alternative of a prosecution in the Courts
for such offences. The effect would be that
the withdrawal of a licence would take place
only in cases of continued and persistent noncompliance.
The second proposal is concerned with
quality and cleanliness. The 1,900 odd licensed
wholesale dealers are prohibited from including stale and dirty eggs in consignments. They
have serious difficulties in inducing producers of eggs to market them in a clean
condition. Very real assistance has been
given by the great majority of wholesale
dealers in improving the appearance and
quality of Northern Ireland eggs on the
market, and, for further headway, we must
look to the producer. There is seldom any
justification for the dirty condition of eggs.
I have heard many remarks about the
countryside to the effect that we are ordering
producers to go about with cloths and wipe
the hens legs when they step into the nests.
We do not go as far as that, but we do want
clean nests and clean yards, and then there
will be no dirty eggs, because I do not believe
any Member of this House has ever seen a
hen lay a dirty egg-in fact, I think the hen
that would lay a dirty egg would be worthy
of a medal. Simple precautions to ensure
cleanliness have been repeatedly brought to
the notice of poultry-keepers, but general
improvement will come only as a result of
making such precautions mandatory.
Again, while we have redress against the
merchant, who holds eggs for a rise in price,
there is none against that large number of
persons from whom he draws his supplies.
The time has now come for the producer and
the trader to share the responsibility for the
fresh condition of the eggs.
The last important proposal is purchase by
weight. There is no doubt that this is the
only fair basis of exchange, and it will encourage the marketing and production of
larger eggs.
Mr. CRAWFORD: Perhaps the right hon.
Gentleman will speak a little more loudly.
Those who are sitting behind cannot hear
him.
Mr. ARCHDALE: I must apologise to the
hon. Member, but it is very hard to speak
behind your back. There is a general desire
for purchase by weight, as areas where the
system has been tried are conspicuous for the
size of the eggs produced. This change is
most desirable since grading has now been
brought to a high state of perʼection, and the
lower grades do not command such a ready
sale. Close grading has done as much as
any other feature of the regulations to
popularise Ulster eggs, but more of the
heavier grades are wanted.
It is interesting to record that for the
twelve months ended May last, the number
of great hundreds of eggs exported from
Northern ports was 2,554,252 as compared
with 2,451,123 great hundreds for the previous
year; that is, 100,000 great hundreds more
eggs in the last year. There are 120 to the
great hundred. Since 1921, I am sorry to
say, the export of eggs gradually dropped
until last year, but this year an increase has
begun, and I hope it will continue steadily.
Not only has the number of eggs increased,
but the hens and chickens within our
borders in 1926 show an increase of more
than a million over the 1925 figures. The
actual numbers are: 1925, 5,741,784; 1926,
6,768,361. I think with over a million more
hens and chickens in Northern Ireland we
can safely count on the increase in the export
of eggs being continued. I beg to move.
Mr. ELLIOTT: I want to speak on this
Bill.
Mr. SPEAKER: The hon. Member should
get up.
Mr. ELLIOTT: I was led to believe I could
not be on my feet at the same time as you.
Mr. SPEAKER: Yes, certainly, on a point
of that kind. I looked round the House and
I thought nobody wished to speak, but as the
Question has not been fully put the hon.
Member may proceed.
Mr. ELLIOTT: I believe it is necessary we
should have an Amending Bill to the Marketing of Eggs Act, because the present Act has
proved a failure. I am sorry I cannot agree
with the Bill brought into this House to-day.
because instead of making the Marketing of
Eggs Act a better one it will practically
drive what in my opinion is a decaying and
dying industry out of Northern Ireland. I
1569 Marketing of Eggs Bill—

12 OCTOBER 1926
Second Reading.
am rather at a disadvantage in replying to
some of the arguments of the right hon.
Gentleman because I could not catch them.
I did, however, catch the argument that there
was a considerable number more hens in
Ulster to-day than ever before. Naturally
one would expect an increase in hens to mean
an increase in eggs; that is the logical conclusion anyone would draw.
The Marketing of Eggs Act, in my opinion,
has done a great deal to deteriorate the
marketing of Ulster eggs, as is proved by the
figures supplied by the Ministry of Agriculture themselves. Last year our export of
eggs from Northern Ireland was 144 great
hundreds less than the previous year. I find,
according to the figures supplied by the
Ministry of Agriculture, that eggs from
Northern Ireland when the Marketing of
Eggs Act was in full swing were 13s 4d per
120; a year before the Act came in eggs were
14s 2d per 120 in the month of July. In
1926, when the Act had been more than
twelve months in operation, eggs were only
10s per 120 in the month of July. Instead of
prices increasing under the Marketing of
Eggs Act they have been steadily going down.
That is according to the figures that have
been supplied to me by the officials of the
Department over which the right hon.
Gentleman presides.
What is the cause of the decrease in the
export of eggs from Northern Ireland? I
hold in my hand to-day letters from important merchants in Liverpool. I do not want
to delay the House by reading them, but I
am prepared to read them to show that the
eggs we are putting on the market are not
in the condition in which the Liverpool
merchants want them to be. The Minister
of Agriculture has a Marketing of Eggs Committee, and one would naturally expect that
when this Committee was set up due heed
would be given to the claims of all Northern
Ireland. But I am afraid it is very hard,
even for the Minister of Agriculture, to look
past the great City of Belfast. I find the
City of Belfast has got a very large representation on this Committee, but the County
of Tyrone, which is part of the right hon.
Gentleman's constituency, seems not to have
anyone capable of giving any advice whatever in regard to the marketing of eggs.
There were two members from County
Fermanagh. One is from Enniskillen. I do
not object to that, but another gentleman,
who was on the Committee from the County
of Fermanagh, had his own egg licence revoked some time ago, and, consequently, was
unseated from this Committee. After all,
we might have got a man, even in County
Tyrone, who knew quite as much about eggs
as the County Fermanagh gentleman, who
was unseated, and whose licence was
revoked.
The Department's officials have been and
are going about the country, and up to the
present time have compelled egg shippers to
put their eggs up in a particular way. No
one seems to want the eggs put up in the
way that these officials want them except the
officials themselves. The merchants on the
other side do not want it to be done at all,
and it is only the officials who want the eggs
put up in a particular way. Not only that,
but they are going about the country recommending the No. 2 Baker Egg Grader. This
is an egg grader manufactured in Southern
Ireland. I do not object to that, but I find
that the Government of Southern Ireland
in their wisdom would have nothing to do
with it. One of the Gentlemen on the
Advisory Committee for Northern Ireland
happens to be the agent for this No. 2 Baker
Egg Grader, and, consequently, the officials
and those gentlemen are very anxious that
these egg graders should be used solely in
Northern Ireland. And so
our egg merchants are told, and repeatedly told, they
must have this No. 2 Baker Egg Grader,
otherwise their eggs would not be properly
selected and graded, and their licences would
be revoked.
I have heard over and over again from the
officials of the Ministry of Agriculture that
the Marketing of Egs Act has brought into
the country some hundreds of thousands of
pounds. I naturally look round to see how
this money has all gone because I am always on the hunt for money. I go to the egg
producer and I ask him, "Have you got any
of this money that is coming into Northern
Ireland through the Marketing of Eggs Act,
which has been introduced here?" The facts
I have been supplied with show that the producer is getting less than before the Act was
introduced. I go to the egg dealer. I ask
him, "Have you got any of this money?" and
he informs me he never was making less
money in eggs in his lifetime. I go
to the shipper. He tells me he cannot
get the cost price out of eggs, because
there is SO much expense put on in
grading and packing them and re-packing
them and testing them. I think that would
be a conundrum that perhaps the Research
Department of the right hon. Gentleman
might solve. They might find out exactly
where this money has all gone. Could it be
possible it has gone into the usual channel
of officialdom in the right hon. Gentleman's
Department, and that the only people
who have got any money out of the increased
income from the export of eggs are the egg
inspectors?
Naturally one would ask oneself what
other good points there are in connection
with this Act. Up to the present I
have discovered that the only good points
about the Act of 1924 are that the eggs
marketed must be clean and fresh and in a

proper condition. There is no one in Northern Ireland who would dispute the fact that

over-dose of inspectors who are practically

constituency as the right hon. Gentleman

make egg boxes out of local home-grown

enough straw to pack all the eggs in the Six

to home-grown timber, we have got an
Afforestation branch in connection with the
right hon. Gentleman's Department. What
is it for? Growing timber, I suppose, to
beautify Northern Ireland. I hold there is
no use in planting timber if it is not fit to
make egg boxes.
Therefore, I want to tell the right hon.
Gentleman that if he proceeds with the Bill
introduced to-day he is going to kill the
marketing of Ulster eggs entirely. I was in
the city of Derry a few days ago and I saw a
consignment of eggs being sent from the
Irish Free State through Derry port to a
firm in Glasgow. Those eggs were put up in
a case which would not at all please the
Minister or the officials in Northern Ireland,
but they were put in a case quite good
enough for the merchants in Glasgow and
quite good enough for the merchants in the
Irish Free State. They were packed in good,
clean Irish straw-not good enough, of
course, for the officials of Northern Ireland,
but good enough for the merchants of Southern Ireland and the merchants of Glasgow.
And here to-day instead of having our export of eggs increased we are having it
decreased, and it will be further decreased
if this Bill passes its Second Reading and is
eventually placed on the Statute Book of
Northern Ireland. We want the eggs put on
the market, as I said before, to be clean eggs;
we want fresh eggs put on the market, and
we want them put on in a marketable condition, and we want them put on in the way
that those who would buy our eggs want
them to be put on.
May I read a letter dated 2nd September,
1926, from S. M'Cain and Co., Liverpool?
They say:
Many thanks for wire received yesterday.
We did not reply, as we are not in the
market for eggs at the moment. Trade
was never worse, and we have large stocks
on hand. The Irishmen, we are sorry to
say, have completely killed the demand
owing to the rotten stuff that has been
shipped for the last two months. It is a
disgrace to Ireland, and the complaints
have been more numerous this year than
ever.
Mr. ARCHDALE: Where are they from?
Mr. ELLIOTT: From Northern Ireland.
Mr. ARCHDALE: Are you positive?

I am writing you with regard to the grading of Irish eggs, and have to inform you
that having experienced grading by the

For instance we find it very difficult to

That is from another egg merchant in

We must apologise for not replying

the disadvantages of Irish eggs being

Book as part of an Act of Parliament--that
a man who comes along and buys premises

"No." That is in the Bill. In other
says
words a minor official of the Department
can come along in Northern Ireland and

I am speaking about something I know
something about. A few days ago in a town
in my constituency one of these Department
officials, an egg inspector, came round. This
was not an ordinary Ulsterman. This was a
superhuman man, an English inspector, of
which the Government is so fond. As I said
before, he was not an ordinary Ulsterman.
He came round to this egg store after the
opening of the store, and the first question
he asked was: "Is this a concrete floor or
is this a cement floor?" (Laughter.) I am
no expert either on concrete or cement, but
I always was led to believe that a cement
floor was a concrete floor, and vice versa a
concrete floor was a cement floor. Are the
people who carry on the marketing of eggs
to be handed over to officials of that description, men who know simply nothing about
the job they are in? Are they to have the

is not right. I do not know whether it is
concrete or cement, but one thing I know
you are not going to have a licence?"
The thing to me is absurd. I wonder at
the Minister and the Department of the
right hon. Gentleman asking this House to

of Northern Ireland hundreds of people who

any Department was set up, and who are

Mr. GEORGE HENDERSON: This is not

it dealt largely with the revoking of licences.

Then again the Department ask for powers,
I think, under Section 4. The Ministry may,
by rules made under the principal Act. provide that persons purchasing eggs for resale
by retail shall comply with conditions which
are the same as, or similar to, the conditions
from time to time prescribed in relation to

That is another provision, as I read it,
giving the Department power to enforce all
the regulations that are in existence in regard to wholesale shippers on grocers and
other merchants going to local markets to
buy eggs for retail purposes. That is another
point where I think too much power is
given into the hands of the Department, because these conditions, applied to men who
are buying these eggs for retail in the home
market, would add considerably to the expense
of handling them and might, of course, put a

in competition with shippers out of the

buying. I think the Department, when the
eggs are shipped to other markets, should see

not ask for these further powers with regard
to eggs put into retail in our own home
markets.
With regard to the other provision, that is,
making compulsory the selling of eggs by
weight, that does seem on the face of it the
ideal way of selling eggs. I am not here to
say that, if it can be enforced generally, it
will not be an improvement, but I do say
that at the present time where it has been
tried I am informed it has not been an improvement. Those men who do and have
bought eggs by weight do not get the supply
of eggs. There is just this I want to put
before the Department. Trade is a rather
sensitive thing. I have known in my own
experience, for example, that if you change
even a fair from one place to another you
kill it. You cannot tell why it is. I have in
my mind's eye at the present time a case
where there was a good fair and it was
changed to a fair on the street and in a
short time the fair was killed. I do think
the Department should be careful before entirely scrapping the method which has been
in existence for a long time. I am not
standing up for selling eggs by number.
That is the custom that has prevailed for a
great number of years. If we do any of
these things we do not know how it would
affect the trade.

would either have to weigh his eggs at home

There have been complaints that there are

that three grades are quite sufficient, and

point. I think it is really worth putting,

and it is this-Take the smaller retailer.
cannot afford to buy four or five cases of eggs

Now, with regard to the production of
clean eggs, the Minister said there was
seldom any justification for the marketing of
dirty eggs. I agree with him up to a point.
It is very essential that our eggs should be
clean, but I do not go the whole way with
this Bill and say that a dirty egg, or an egg
with a small stain on it should not be
allowed. I say it would be infinitely preferable to the washing of eggs that goes on
at present. I do not think I overstate the
case when I say that under the present regulations seventy-five per cent. of Irish eggs
have been washed. I do not know whether
the Minister of Agriculture will agree or not,
but I do feel that I am not overstating the
case when I state that seventy-five per cent.
of Irish eggs for export have been washed,
and there is no doubt at all that these eggs
deteriorate far more quickly, because I am
informed that a hen in laying an egg puts
some sort of sealing process over it that
keeps out microbes, as it were, and protects
it, and if you wash it you do away with
that protection and the egg will not keep to
the same extent.
Another thing is that we have got to
visualise if we can the conditions under
which a great many of these eggs are produced in Northern Ireland. We in Northern
Ireland are largely a community of small
holders, on the average of probably fifteen
acres, and on a big percentage of these holdings there are no proper hen runs or proper
hen houses. The hens lay in byres, and
stables, and a great many other places. Now
it is very casy to preach the doctrine of
cleanliness to these people, but it is very
hard to carry it out, and it may hamper
production. I think the best thing the Department could do would be to say to these
farmers, if they say they must produce clean
eggs and that is essential for our export
trade, and it is essential for our own home
trade, because I certainly would rather buy
a dozen clean eggs than a dozen dirty ones--
Mr. ARCHDALE: Hear, hear.
Mr. GEORGE HENDERSON: I think the
Department should say "If you are not able
from your own financial resources to put up
proper hen houses and proper hen runs to
produce the best quality of eggs then we will
lend you on easy terms the capital to put up
these hen houses and hen runs, so that you
will be in a position to produce clean eggs
and to sell fresh eggs."
There seems to be, I admit, a great divergence of opinion with regard to this Bill. I
have received letters from shippers asking me
to support this Bill, and I have received
letters from shippers even more urgently
asking me to oppose it. I have received

body of shippers, but there has been a body

It is to their interests surely that they should

My chief objection to the Bill is that it
gives too much power into the hands of the

too much with bureaucracy; instead of putting the provisions with regard to various
matters into the Bills, where they should be

with the hon. Member for Fermanagh and
Tyrone (Mr. Elliott) in appealing to the
Government not to rush this Bill through,

further consultation.
Like the hon. Member (Mr. Elliott) I find

handed over to the Department with regard

to sell and to buy. When the eggs are
graded average weight they do not pack
so well in the case. There are different
grades in the same case.
I do not understand what the objection of
the hon. Member (Mr. Elliott) was to the
case, because our cases are just the same as
the Free State cases except that we pack
rather more perhaps in the small cases than
in the big divisible cases. As to rules for

making any further rule, and we are not

means about the increased price obtained in

As regards the straw and the home-grown

home-grown timber. We want seasoned
timber for our eggs. We certainly will not
allow, nor will any respectable egg merchant
buy unseasoned timber for his eggs. You
must have seasoned soft timber, and that is
what we wish to have. When the Egg Bill
came into operation three years ago we found

damp wood nearly double the weight of
proper egg boxes. The damp wood damped
the straw and when the eggs arrived at their

bad smell so much as a fresh egg. Everyone
in England has agreed that our Orders have
had a good effect on the value of our eggs.
The hon. Member (Mr. George Henderson)
said that the price of eggs was less now.
What has the price of eggs in Ulster got to
do with this? What we want is to have our
Irish eggs higher in price than other eggs.

Mr. CRAWFORD: May I, as a represen
tative of a country constituency, say two or
three words on this Bill that is before the
House at present. I would like to commence

the Bill was going to inflict hardship on
small farmers I would vote dead against it.
Judging, however, from what I have been
able to glean from studying the Bill I am
of opinion that it will not inflict any great
hardship, and that any hardship it may
inflict will be well repaid in the long run
by the better prices the producers will receive for the eggs if they carry out the
intentions in this Bill. I am not sure that
the opposition to it does not come from the
dealers (hon. Members: Hear, hear)—and
perhaps they are dealers, if one may say it,
of the baser sort, if there is such a thing
as that. I have consulted two or three of

the largest shippers in County Antrim, and

objection to the Bill. When I heard that
I asked myself the question if these dealers

mean that he will get a bigger price next

out.
It is a temptation for a farmer if the
market is rising-and they need all the
money they can get-to hold over his three
or four dozen of eggs from one week to
another. They are held back for two or
three weeks and the dealer then buys them.
He sends them to the shipper and it takes
two or three days to get them packed and
ready for going away. It takes two or three
days for them to go to their destination, and
there will be a few more days before the retailer can sell to the customer. By the
time the eggs get to the customer they are
bad. I hold it would be better in the long
run that we should take a long vision and not
a short one and that farmers should take a
little trouble in this matter. I do not believe
that the farmers of Northern Ireland are
dirtier than those in other countries. If they
sell their eggs once a week and use a damp
cloth to remove any stains on them and not
wash them, I understand they would enable
dealers to ship them and put them on the
market in the proper way. Taking as I do
on this occasion a long view and believing
that it is better for us to act so that the
good name of the Province may be maintained I feel it my duty in the interests of
the farmers to support this Bill.

The MINISTER OF HOME AFFAIRS (Sir
Dawson Bates): I would ask the indulgence
of this House if, in moving the Second Reading of this Measure, I go into the details
somewhat closely, but I consider, and I am
sure hon. Members will consider, that too
much time cannot be given to a Measure
which must have such far-reaching effects.
The object of the Measure is to institute
a better, a safer, and more comprehensive
system for the control of motor traffic, with
a view to reducing the number of accidents,
and obviating, so far as possible, the risk
to lives of persons and to property due to
motor traffic. I offer no excuse, therefore,
for the introduction of the Measure, and if I
did, I would ask hon. Members to look at the
pubiic Press. Hardly a day passes without
someone being injured, or, worse still, killed
-as a result, I am sorry to say, in very many
cases, of gross carelessness on the part of
certain individuals who drive motor vehicles.
A record has been kept of accidents which
have occurred in Northern Ireland for the
year ending 31st June, 1926. I find that no
fewer than 1,300 accidents have occurred in
which motor vehicles were either directly or
indirectly concerned. These accidents involved loss of life in no fewer than 59 cases,
and in 759 other cases resulted in serious
injury to the persons. In other words, at
the present time, the number of motor accidents which take place in our community
amounts to an average of not less than 25 per
week. For the year 1925, on the railways, six
people were killed and 189 injured.
May I say at once that this Measure is not
introduced by the Government as a vindictive
Measure against motor users. So far from
this being the case it is introduced for the
purpose, not alone of protecting the public
against the reckless and the thoughtless
ariver, but for the purpose of protecting the
careful and the thoughtful drivers-who, I
am glad to say, form the large majority of
the motoring public-against the recklessness
and the gross carelessness of their fellow
motorists.
If the House will bear with me for a
moment, I would like to refer shortly to the
existing legislation bearing on this subject.
The first of these Acts is the Locomotives
Act of 1861, which was the first attempt to
deal with traffic other than horse traffic. At
that time the motor vehicle was never
thought of. Following on that came the
Locomotives Act of 1865, which prescribed a
maximum speed limit of 4 miles an hour and
required the vehicle to have a man with a red
flag walking in front. Some hon. Members
will recollect the hostility that was shown by
the public to the removal of that restriction,
which took place under the Locomotives on
Highways Act of 1896. That Act may be described as the "Charter of Liberty" to motor
vehicles, because it recognised that motor
Second Reading. 1586
Motor Vehicles Bill-
12 OCTOBER 1926
vehicles, under certain regulations, had the
right to use the King's highway in the same
way as horse vehicles, subject of course, to
reasonable safeguards and provisions. Under
that Act the maximum speed limit was increased from 4 miles to 14 miles per hour, and
the Local Government Board were empowered
to make Regulations prescribing the use and
the construction of motor vehicles. It soon
became evident that the Act was entirely inadequate to meet the rapid development
which took place on the removal of the red
flag. As the result of the rapid development
of motor traffic, especially during the closing
years of the last century, Parliament found
it necessary to take fresh measures in regard
to the regulation of this form of traffic, and,
accordingly, in 1903, the Motor Car Act of
that year was passed, and under this Act we
have, to all intents and purposes, been working ever since. The Act prescribed, amongst
other things, a maximum speed limit of 20
miles, and, as regards what is known as
"heavy vehicles," i.e. vehicles over 2 tons in
weight, it gave power to the Local Government Board to prescribe speeds, an order being
subsequently made for fixing the speed for
this class of vehicle at 12 miles an hour, and
this has been in force since those days.
This Act went a step further, because it
instituted the present system of the licensing
of motor drivers, and may I mention here
that it provided that no one should have a
motor licence to drive a car unless he was at
least 17 years of age, and, as regards motor
bicycles, the individual must be at least 14
years of age. Between 1903 and 1920 motor
traffic developed to such an extent that a demand fell upon the local authorities to improve their roads and make them fit for
motor traffic, a demand which the local
authorities, with the resources at their disposal, found they were unable to cope with,
and, eventually in 1920 a new principle was
introduced in regard to taxation. The main
provisions of these Acts were:---
(1) The taxation of motor vehicles under
various classes;
(2) The formation of the Road Fund, into
which the proceeds of this taxation were
paid;
(3) The
Licensing, Registration and
Identification of Motor Vehicles;
(4) The right of the Ministry of Home
Affairs, after local inquiry, to prohibit or
restrict the use of any motor vehicle on
any particular highway within the area of
a County Council where it is shown that
that vehicle cannot be used on a highway
without either endangering the safety of
the vehicle, or traffic, or where the highway is unsuitable for that class of vehicle.
Following on the cessation of the war, a
new feature presented itself in regard to
motor traffic, and that was the rapid development of chars-a-banes and bus traffic, and it
was found that the existing laws did not meet
the new situation which had arisen. It was
also found that, with two exceptions (Belfast
and, I think, Bangor, who had taken powers
under their own Acts) local authorities had
no power or control over the use of these
chars-a-banes and motor buses in their particular areas, but, worse than that (with the
exception of the two areas I mentioned),
there was no power to inspect these vehicles
which were used for the purpose of carrying
passengers; there was no power vested in
the local authorities to ensure that a motor
bus or char-a-banc, plying inside the area, was
fit for the purpose; there was no power given
to the local authority to fix stands for these
vehicles; and, finally there was no power to
prevent overcrowding, or to control the conduct of the persons employed about these
vehicles.
Following on the representations that were
made to this Government, a Measure was
introduced into this House-- the Char-a-banc
Regulation Act of 1924. This Act gives power
to all town authorities to make by-laws in
regard to (1) the licensing and inspection
of this class of vehicle, (2) the prevention of
overcrowding, the fixing of stands, and (3)
the control of the conduct of the people
employed about the vehicles, but, may I say
in passing, that I regret to say that out of
36 town authorities, only six have passed bylaws. Such is the present situation.
To sum up, our legislative measures
have not kept pace with the development
of motor traffic. May I quote some
figures to show how largely motor traffic
has developed. In 1921 we had 13,350
motor vehicles licensed in Northern Ireland,
and, at the present time, there are no fewer
than 30,000 vehicles licensed.
In passing, may I say that one of the
causes of the development of motor traffic
in Northern Ireland is the fact that local
authorities have responded in such a
public-spirited way to the appeal of
the motorists for good roads, and I
think that the local authorities will be the
first to admit that the Government, in their
administration of the Road Fund, have not
acted ungenerously towards these authorities.
But the improvement of the roads, the
introduction of the cheap car and the development of the motor bus has created a
situation which, in the opinion of the
Government, cannot be met by the existing
statutory provisions. I have already in
dicated the number of accidents that take
place every year, and, unfortunately, I have
reason to believe that the number of
Motor Vehicles Bill-
Second Reading.
HOUSE OF COMMONS
[Sir Dawson Bates.]
accidents during the present year will be
still greater.
This condition of affairs led the Government to the firm conclusion that the time
has now arrived for firm and drastic
measures to be taken to meet the present
situation. A similar condition of affairs has
arisen in other parts of the British Isles,
and the Imperial Government appointed a
special Departmental Committee to inquire
into the whole system of motor traffic and
to make recommendations for its improvement. The Government of Northern Ireland
in the meantime had taken similar steps by
referring the whole matter for the consideration and report of the Roads Advisory Committee of Northern Ireland.
As hon. Members are aware, the Roads
Advisory Committee is a statutory Committee
appointed under the Ministry of Transport
Act of 1919. It comprises representatives of
all interests concerned. We have, therefore, representatives of County and County
Borough Councils, and two representatives
of users of mechanically-propelled vehicles,
one being an hon. Member of this
House, my hon. Friend the Member for
Armagh (Major Shillington), who has had
vast experience in motoring and who represents the Automobile Association and the
Ulster Automobile Club. We have also a
representative of users of horse traffic, and
last, but not least, we have also a representative of the Labour interests. You will
see, therefore, that any representations
which come from such a representative Committee as this must receive the most careful
consideration. The whole subject received
the Committee's careful consideration for
many months, and their findings are of a
unanimous character and are embodied in
the present Bill. I cannot pass from this
subject without expressing the appreciation
of the Government for the great help which
the Committee has given them in framing
the present Measure.
At the same time, having regard to the
very important nature of the recommendations which were made by the Roads Advisory
Committee, it was thought well, while not infringing upon Parliamentary privilege, to consult, as far as possible, other interests which
might be affected by the present Bill. May I
say, as an example, that I had several conferences with the Motor Coach Owners' Association, a body of recent origin, but of growing importance in the country. I received
very valuable suggestions from these gentlemen, and while I will not for one moment
suggest that I see eye to eye with them in the
views which they expressed to me I would,
at the same time, like to express my appreciation of the way they met me on all occasions. But apart altogether from this, having
regard to the importance of the Measure,
and its very far-reaching effects, and in
order to enable every Member of this House
to have an ample opportunity of going into
the Measure in all its bearings. we took the
First Reading at the close of the last
Session, and deferred the Second Reading
until now.
The general effect of the proposals contained in the present Bill is, first, to make
provision for a more comprehensive and
better control of traffic on roads; secondly,
to ensure that motor vehicles, and particularly those classes of vehicles which are
used for the purpose of carrying passengers,
are in a fit and efficient condition and are
not likely to endanger the lives of passengers
using them. The present Bill has been
drafted on these lines, and it comprises three
Parts. The first mainly deals with Motor
Traffic and Motor Offences; Part II deals
with the examination, licensing and the
control of public vehicles, and the licensing
and control of the drivers and conductors of
these vehicles, and Part III is of a supplementary character to give effect to Parts I and
II. I hope the House will bear with me if
I go somewhat carefully into the scope and
effect of Part I.
Before going into it may I say that in framing this Measure we have taken advantage of
the occasion to effect, so far as is possible, a
codification of the law relating to motor
traffic generally, and to incorporate various
existing provisions in this part of the Bill so
as to enable a motorist to understand the
law without referring to old Acts of Parliament? As I have already said, the Motor
Car Act of 1903, under which we are operating
at the present time, contains very valuable
provisions which we do not intend to scrap.
Accordingly, we have selected all the valuable sections of that Act, and these we
propose to re-enact in the present Measure,
but the Act as a whole will be repealed.
Some of the criticism which the Bill received
at the hands of the public following its publication was directed to certain of the old
Clauses in the 1903 Act, and it therefore might be of advantage to hon. Members
to compare several of the Clauses with the
present Bill and they will find, as a result,
that they are identical with many of those
which were in the 1903 Act.
Dealing now with the question of motor
offences, it was the unanimous opinion of the
Roads Advisory Committee and I hope that
opinion will be shared by hon. Members of
this House-that the penal clauses under the
Act of 1903 had proved insufficient in their
scope and character to cope with and suppress the more serious offences in connection
with motor driving which occurred day after
day on our public roads. The Act of 1903
provided a maximum penalty for certain
offences, but the present Bill introduces a new
Second Reading. 1590
Motor Vehicles Bill-
12 OCTOBER 1926
principle by fixing a minimum as well as a
maximum penalty, but only for the more
serious offences.
Dealing with the question of the more
serious offences may I take four of them?:-
(1) Reckless driving;
(2) Drunkenness while in charge of a motor
car;
(3) Driving while under suspension or disqualified from driving;
(4) Driving a heavy char-a-banc or commercial lorry at a speed in excess of the
limit.
With regard to the question of reckless
driving, the Motor Car Act of 1903 prescribed
a maximum penalty of £20–

Mr. DEVLIN: Mine was not a constant

Mr. SPEAKER: I agree with what the

Sir DAWSON BATES: I should be sorry
to say I would not answer a question, but
if the hon. Member will wait I will deal with
that particular point when I come to it.
With regard to the question of reckless
driving, as a result of our experience for
the past number of years, and in view of the
number of accidents which have resulted
from reckless and dangerous driving, I think
hon. Members must have come to the conclusion that the arbitrary form of punishment prescribed under the 1903 Act in no
way meets the offences and has not resulted
in acting as a deterrent to these reckless
individuals. We propose that a person convicted of reckless or dangerous driving will
be liable for a first offence to a penalty of
not less than £5 and a maxmum of £50;
for a second or third offence to a minimum
of £10 and a maximum of £100; and in the
case of a second or subsequent offence the
magistrates are empowered-although they
are not compelled-to send the offender to
prison for a period not exceeding 6 months.
Over and above that, the magistrates are
empowered to suspend an offender's licence
in the case of a first offence, while in the
case of a second or subsequent conviction
the magistrates are compelled, if they convict, to suspend the licence for a period of
not less than three months. These penalties
may be regarded by some as of a drastic
character, but may I emphasise the fact
that these penalties are not directed against
the ordinary careful driver, but they are
directed against the careless driver, and the
driver who is so indifferent to the lives of
his fellow men that he is prepared to
gamble away their lives for the purpose
of making a rapid journey. Hon. Members,
perhaps, will allow me to take an example?
Motor Vehicles Bill-
HOUSE OF COMMONS
Second Reading.
[Sir Dawson Bates]
Can any punishment be too great for an
individual who drives full speed around a
blind corner, on the wrong side of the white
line which is provided for him? That
happens day after day, and the wonder to
me is, when I see some of these drivers, that
there are not more accidents. Again the
local authorities provide warning notices
asking drivers to drive slowly past schools.
I am sorry to say I have myself seen this
warning repeatedly disregarded, and drivers
passing a school at 40 and 50 miles an hour.
If children were to come out suddenly hon.
Members know what would be the result.
Take the example of the driver who wantonly
goes out with a knowledge that his brakes
are inefficient, or in a rainstorm, where he
cannot see a yard before him, rather than
suffer the discomfort of opening his windscreen, continues driving, gambling on the
chances that there will be nobody on the
road.
But there is another reason why we have
to ask this House to impose these penalties.
Hon, Members are aware that, under the Act
of 1903, there is a statutory speed limit of 20
miles per hour for all motor vehicles other
than heavy commercial ones-I refer now
to the ordinary motor-car-but that provision
has been, to all intents and purposes, a dead
letter in this country for many years. At
the time it was passed many cars had only
a maximum speed of 20 miles per hour, but
now the advent of the more efficient car,
with good brakes, in my opinion makes it
futile to maintain this limit. We find to-day
many cases arising where a man may be
driving to the danger of the public, and yet
not exceeding the speed limit of 20 miles an
hour, and, therefore, there is frequent confusion of thought in the minds of magisstrates when such cases occur. After careful
consideration the Government have come to
the conclusion that the best way to protect
human life is to rely upon the offence of
driving to the danger of the public-reckless
driving. But while this is so, it is still open
to the local authorities to apply to the
Ministry and fix a particular speed limit in
their particular areas.
Now we come to the offence of drunkenness
while in charge of a motor-car. Some critics
have found fault because they say that drunkenness while in charge of a motor-car is a
worse offence than driving to the danger of
the public.
Mr. CRAWFORD: Hear, hear.
Sir DAWSON BATES: Personally, I have
some difficulty in saying which is worse-a
man who in cold blood risks human life, or a
man who is foolish enough to take too much
drink, and who gets into the car without a
true appreciation of what he is doing-but
be that as it may, the Government have got
to protect the public, and we do not think it
unreasonable that the penalties imposed for
this particular offence should be similar to
those imposed for the offence of reckless
driving, with the exception that suspension
is compulsory for the first offence. That is
to say, if a man is convicted of drunkenness
in charge of a motor-car the magistrates are
bound to suspend his licence.
With regard to the third offence, that is,
the penalties for driving whilst under suspension, it will be found that under Clause II
we propose that for this offence a person will
be liable, on summary conviction, to imprisonment for a period of not less than one
month and not more than six months. That
is the only case of compulsory imprisonment.
Hon. Members may, at first, think this too
drastic a penalty, but I would remind them
that it would be utterly useless to empower
magistrates to withdraw the licence from a
man on the ground that he is unfit to use a
car and not have the most drastic powers for
enforcing such a Regulation.
Now we come to the last major offenceinfringement of the speed limit for heavy
motor vehicles-in which minimum penalties
are prescribed. Clause V of the Bill practically re-embodies the provision of the
Motor Car Act of 1903, and empowers the
Ministry to make Regulations regarding the
speed of heavy motor vehicles, that is to say,
the chars-a-bancs and commercial lorries of
over 2 tons in weight. Under the existing
statutory provisions, regulations are already
in force prescribing a maximum speed of 12
miles an hour for these vehicles. This matter
has given the Roads Advisory Committee and
myself the greatest possible concern, but,
having regard to the rapid development of
char-a-banc traffic,the enormous improvement
in the design and the construction of these
vehicles, with the added safety to the public,
I am satisfied that the existing maximum
speed limit of 12 miles an hour for an ordinary char-a-banc, fitted wholly with pneumatic
tyres, is unjustifiable and insufficient, and I
propose, following on the passing of this
Measure, to issue a new Regulation, authorising a maximum speed limit of 20 miles an
hour for the ordinary char-a-banc, provided
it is wholly fitted with pneumatic tyres.

refer to lorries?

of the word. Under the law as it now
stands, the taking out of a driver's licence is
a mere formality, involving no more responsibility than the payment of 5s. a year. The
actual form of the present licence as at present issued is such that it is easily transferable, and cases have been consequently reported of the misuse of drivers' licences.
The whole question has received the most
careful consideration at the hands of the
Advisory Committee and the Government,
and also at the hands of the Imperial
Government.
question of the safety of the passengers using
these vehicles, and of other traffic which they
have to pass, demands that they should not
be allowed to travel at more than the speed
at which they will be allowed to travel under

drivers and owners of these vehicles have, in
the past, paid little attention to the speed
limits prescribed for them, and although
every effort is made by the police authorities
to curb this evil, the success of their efforts
has been largely nugatory owing to the ineffective penalties imposed. I have taken the
trouble of taking out some figures, and I find
that during the twelve months ending 31st
July, 1926, no fewer than 574 convictions were
obtained against drivers of chars-a-bancs for
exceeding the prescribed speed limit. In the
majority of these cases the fines imposed were
comparatively trifling. In 25 cases fines of
1s were imposed. In 160 cases, 5s or less was
imposed, and fines of 10s or less were imposed in the case of 160 further convictions.
As I said before, the Government have no
wish and no desire to act in any sense in a
vindictive spirit towards bus owners. Νο
Government has done more than this
Government to encourage the development of,
not alone bus traffic, but general motor
traffic. But if there is any hope of getting
our roads into a proper standard of repair,
the cost of which even now presses hard
upon the ratepayers, and if there is any hope
of reducing the number of road accidents due
to motor vehicles travelling at an excessive
speed, it is necessary to impose the
penalties set out in the Bill. Hon. Members
will find in Clause 5 (2) that for the first
offence the minimum penalty is £1 and the
maximum £10; for the second offence, the
minimum penalty is £2 and the maximum
£20, and for the third and subsequent offence
the minimum £5 and the maximum £50, with
or without imprisonment for a period not
exceeding three months. While the Government is willing to increase the speed limit
to 20 miles, it must be clearly understood that
this privilege is subject to the counterbalancing provisions in this particular Clause
under which breaches of the Regulations will
be visited with the penalties I have referred
to.
I will now turn to the question of the
licensing of drivers, but in dealing with this
matter hon. Members will appreciate that I
am now only dealing with the licensing of
drivers for ordinary vehicles, not buses. I
will deal with the drivers of buses when we
come to the second part of the Bill. We have
re-enacted in this Measure Sections 3, 4 and
5 of the old Motor Car Act of 1903, and in
addition we have added some new provisions
so as to ensure that the driver's licence will
be a more valuable possession in every sense
I am aware that in some countries it has
been thought desirable to impose tests of
physical fitness and ability to drive-(hon.
Members: Hear, hear)-and this aspect of the
question has been most carefully considered.
Some people suggest that no driver should
get a licence until he has gone through a
medical test at the hands of a doctor, but the
result of careful deliberations, not alone in
Northern Ireland, but in Great Britain, is
that whatever advantage such a proposal
might have it would, in the present circumstances, be inexpedient and unduly expensive
to impose such a test in the case of drivers
of ordinary motor cars and of the commercial
lorry I am not thinking now of drivers of
passenger-carrying vehicles- and while this
Bill does not prescribe that an applicant
must be medically examined, it puts the
applicant under an obligation to make a
statutory declaration as to his own physical
fitness to drive a motor car, and also to state
that he is not already disqualified from
obtaining a licence. Hon. Members may say
a statutory declaration means nothing. Any
man who makes a false statutory declaration
involves himself in very serious penalties.
Hon. Members will find this matter dealt
with in Sub-clause II of Clause II. It will
also be seen that the Clause empowers the
Ministry to prescribe the form of the new
licence and the precise particulars which
must be furnished by each applicant.
In
order to prevent the misuse of licences, it is
proposed to prescribe that the licence must
bear the applicant's photograph in the same
manner as a passport does to-day.
Another important feature in Clause II of
the Bill is the proposal to abolish the existing
system under which youths from 14 to 17
years can obtain licences to drive motor
bicycles. From the information before the
Ministry, and I do not think hon. Members
will question its accuracy, it appears that
one of the most fruitful sources of road
accidents is reckless driving on the part of
boys riding motor bicycles, and I hope hon.
Members will agree with me that an immature youth, between 14 and 17 years of age,
without sense of responsibility, should not be
allowed to drive a machine which, in the
Motor Vehicles Bill-
Second Reading.
HOUSE OF COMMONS
[Sir Dawson Bates]
hands of an inexperienced driver, could be
a source of so much danger to the public.
In this connection may I say that, dealing
with the general question of motor bicycles,
I agree with the recommendation of the Roads
Advisory Committee that pillion-riding
should be prohibited--(hon. Members: Hear,
hear) and representations have been made
to me from many quarters to that effect. The
conclusion I have come to is that pillionriding should be put an end to, and I propose to issue an Order prohibiting this
practice. It may be considered by some that
this will be a hardship, but, may I say this,
that the safety of the public as a whole is
more important than the convenience and the
pleasure of a few.
In dealing with the question of licences,
hon. Members will also observe that as regards the drivers of heavy commercial
vehicles, that is, two tons and upwards, no
driver will get a licence unless he is 21 years
of age. Here again, may I say, this may
cause a hardship, but it must be obvious to
anybody who has studied the traffic question
that one of the most fruitful sources of
danger to the public is the employment of
immature youths in the driving of these
heavy vehicles-vehicles that, owing to their
size, these boys, willing and all as they may
be, have not got the physical strength to
control properly.
Now, having dealt with the question of
taking out licences, may I refer now to the
conditions that will have to be observed by
these drivers if they are to be allowed to
retain their licences? The provisions in
this respect will be found in Clause III of
the Bill, which embodies in effect Section 4
of the Motor Car Act of 1903, with certain
provisions that were made under the Roads
Act of 1920, and hon. Members are aware that
at the present time the magistrates are empowered to suspend and endorse licences for
any motor offence. But this Bill goes a step
further. It requires the Courts to suspend
the licences in the case of the more serious
offences. I have already referred to the case
of reckless driving and the question of
drunkenness. While this is so, it is open to
any individual to apply to the Court where
he is convicted for removal of suspension,
and, may I emphasise here, that in every
case where conviction has been recorded
against an individual, and he considers that
he has been harshly treated, there is an
appeal to the County Court Judge sitting
alone.
Then there is another provision in this
case which, I understand, has given rise to a
certain amount of criticism, and that is, that
it is made compulsory on an individual who
is summoned before the Court to produce
his licence. I cannot but think that if the
Bill is to have any effect at all, that is one
of the most important provisions of it, as
it would be quite useless for a Court to
order an endorsement if the licence is not
forthcoming. He can either attend himself
in Court or he can instruct a solicitor or
counsel to produce the licence.
Clause IV is a re-enactment of a similar
Clause under the Motor Car Act of 1903,
under which any motorist is required to stop
in the event of an accident taking place, and
he is also compelled to give his name and
address, if called upon, by any individual
concerned in the accident. I do not think
hon. Members will quarrel with that.
As I have already stated earlier in my
remarks, we propose to give power to the
Ministry to fix the maximum speed limit in
regard to vehicles, and I have already stated
it is the intention of the Government to
increase it for this class of vehicle to 20
miles an hour provided it is fitted with
pneumatic tyres.
or more
Now we come to a matter which has given
my advisers and myself a good deal of
thought-the question of lights on vehicles.
As the law now stands, under the Lights on
Vehicles Act of 1907, all vehicles used on the
road are compelled to carry one
white lights during darkness, while in pursuance of Regulations made under the Act
of 1896, and the Roads Act of 1920, to which
I have already referred, motor-cars are compelled, not alone to carry two white lights
in front, but a red tail light, and it has been
felt for a very considerable time past that
some such provision should be applied to
vehicles other than motor-cars, or rather in
addition to motor-cars, used on the roads.
Hon. Members will observe that we take
power under this Bill to make Regulations
to prescribe the use of a tail light or red
reflector, or a tail light and head light combined-provided that the tail part of it be
visible on all classes of road vehicles. I
think hon. Members who have used motorcars will realise how absolutely necessary it
is, not alone for the safety of the motoring
public but also for the safety of cyclists and
carters, that some precaution of this kind
should be taken.
May I say in connection with the question
of lights, this matter has also given the Roads
Advisory Committee and myself a great deal
of concern. We have been closely in touch
with the Ministry of Transport in England,
who have been engaged in following the
various experiments that have been made
with a view to producing such a device as to
prevent the present danger that exists
owing to the dazzling effect of
strong head lights (hon. Members: Hear,
hear), and if a suitable device is produced,
as I hope it will be before long, the Ministry
will be able to make Regulations under the
powers which it at present has under the
Act of 1896.

We hoped at the time the Act was

Hon. Members will recollect that under

the present time, while there is power for the

Now we come to Part II of the Bill. This
portion of the Bill deals exclusively with
public service vehicles, that is mechanicallypropelled vehicles other than tramcars which
ply for hire or carry passengers for
hire on the public roads. As I have
already said, up to 1924, when the Char-a-banc
Regulation Act was passed by this House,
save in Belfast and Bangor, there was no
general control over this char-a-banc traffic.
But the extraordinary development of char-abane traffic in recent years has created an
entirely new situation. To meet with it, and
following on the representations that were
made by several of the local authorities, the
Act of 1924, to which I have referred, was
passed by this House. The effect of that Act,
as I have already indicated earlier in my
remarks, was to give power to the local
authorities to enable them, first of all, to
issue licences to vehicles that, in their
opinion, were fit to carry passengers;
secondly, to prevent overcrowding; thirdly,
to control the movements of these machines
inside the areas, and, fourthly, to control
the conduct of those engaged in or about
these vehicles.
The Act was mainly an adoptive one, but
I am sorry to say that it has not proved
the success it was hoped. It was hoped at
the time this Act was passed that the powers
which were vested in the local authorities
would have enabled them to have coped in a
comprehensive manner with the char-a-banc
traffic, but I do not think it was fully anticipated at that time that this form of traffic
would have increased so enormously as it
has done and in such a short time. I think
I should state that on the whole the local
authorities who asked for these powers and
obtained them under the Act of 1924 have
not availed themselves to the extent they
might have done of these powers. I find
One defect of the present system is that
if the examination of vehicles is to be carried
out in a proper manner the local authorities
must have at their command the service of
highly skilled officers who should carry out
the necessary technical tests. Hon. Members
will appreciate how difficult it is for small
local authorities with their limited financial
resources to incur the expense necessary for
this very important duty.
But apart altogether from the defects in
the 1924 Act there is absolutely no provision
for the control of char-a-banc traffic in the
rural districts. Taking into consideration
the defects in the Act of 1924, combined
with the enormous development of char-abane traffic and with the entire lack of any
control of this traffic in rural districts, the
Government have come to the conclusion
that it is absolutely necessary in the interests
mainly, may I say, of the travelling community, that there should be a central coordinated system of examination involving
the testing and the licensing of all passengercarrying motor vehicles in Northern Ireland.
A similar system of central control and
regulation has been in operation in the
London metropolitan area for many years
past and has been attended with marked
success, and it is the intention of the
Government, if this House
passes this
Measure, to introduce into Northern Ireland
a similar system of control worked by the
police under the direction of the Ministry
of Home Affairs.
May I point out that at the present time
in Northern Ireland there are no less than
3,900 passenger-carrying motor vehicles. Of
these approximately 3,300 are the ordinary
hackney vehicles with a seating capacity of
not more than six passengers-the remaining
600 being chars-a-bancs of varying seating
capacities. Although it would be impossible,
unless with the expenditure of considerable
time and money to present to this House
accurate statistics showing the number of
passengers which are carried by these
vehicles, at the same time I would not think
it unreasonable to state that these vehicles
carry approximately no less than 20 million
passengers per year. It must be obvious
that in the interests of these passengers
Motor Vehicles Bill-
Second Reading.
HOUSE OF COMMONS
[Sir Dawson Bates]
reasonable precautions should be taken by
the Government, not alone that the vehicles
should be fit for the purpose, but that the
drivers and other persons associated with
them should be under proper control.
There are precedents for the powers which
I ask this House to grant. The history of
the legislation of the Imperial Parliament
for generations past shows the recognition of
the principle that if an individual or a company undertakes to carry passengers for
profit they must conform to the regulations
prescribed by the State for the safety of
these passengers, and this history has shown
that as time goes on Parliament, instead of
lessening these restrictions, has tightened
them.
Take the case of ships. The Board of
Trade exercises the closest possible supervision over the construction, the condition,
and the management of ships. Before a ship
ean le put to sea it must be certified that it is
fit to carry passengers. It must carry a
certificate indicating the limit of the number
of passengers it can carry, and if that
number is exceeded, not only the owners but
the master of the ship are visited with the
most severe penalties. The officers in charge
of that ship must also possess Board of Trade
certificates showing that they possess sufficient knowledge of navigation to control the
movements of the vessel.
Take the history of railways. It is a
matter of common knowledge that the
Ministry of Transport exercises the closest
possible supervision over railways. Their
powers include the supervision of the rolling
stock, the signalling arrangements, the permanent way, and indeed everything that
tends to secure the safety of the travelling
public; and under these regulations a railway
company before they put a driver in charge
ensures that that man not alone is medically
fit to drive the engine, but has also the
knowledge and the experience that would enable him to do so without risk to the passengers whom he is conveying.
The Government, with all these facts before
them and following on the recommendations
of the Roads Advisory Committee, have decided to introduce into this part of the Bill
provisions which will have the effect of taking
away from the local authorities the powers
and the duty of licensing public service motor
vehicles and of establishing a central Government system of licensing of all public service
motor vehicles, and also drivers and conduc
tors, on a similar basis to that which has
existed in the London metropolitan area for
many years past. But, before explaining in
detail the nature of the new arrangements,
I would like to tell this House that I and my
advisers have had several opportunities of
studying on the spot the arrangements which
at present exist in the London metropolitan
area, and I would like to take this opportunity of expressing my very deep appreciation of the help that has been accorded to
me by the late head of the London Traffic
Department-I refer to the late Chief Constable Bassom-and his staff. Chief Constable
Bassom devoted his whole life and energy to
the study of traffic regulations. He was a
man who had a European reputation, and the
extraordinary success of the traffic regulations in London was largely due to him.
Anyone who is interested in the question of
traffic cannot do better than read the very
complete report which he made, and which
was only published after his untimely and
lamented death.
In explaining the new provisions of this art
of the Bill, I would ask hon. Members to absolve me from entering into a detailed explanation clause by clause, and to allow me to give a
general description of the new arrangements
which this part of the Bill proposes to
establish.
In the first place I may say that the new
system will apply to all mechanically propelled vehicles which carry passengers for
hire except tramcars. It will apply to omnibuses, chars-a-banes, taxi-cabs, and the
familiar motor hackney which is met in
every village and town in Northern Ireland.
But may I add that it is not proposed to
apply the Bill to the case of the car which is
let out by private treaty. Hon. Members
are aware that some motor firms keep one or
two of the better type of motor cars for hire
by private treaty by the week or the month
to individuals who do not wish to keep a
motor car of their own. In these cases the
owners of these cars pay the ordinary motor
duty and not the lesser hackney vehicle
licence, and we feel that it is unnecessary
to impose on these owners the necessity of
examining their vehicles, as a class which
can afford to hire this sort of vehicle are in
a position to insist that the vehicle is fit for
their purpose.
Accordingly all vehicles to which I have
referred, except the two classes mentioned,
will, in future, come under Government
supervision. The responsible Department
will be the Ministry of Home Affairs, and
as will be seen by Clause 15, the duty of
inspection will fall upon the police. I would,
however, like to make it quite clear at this
stage, that while it is proposed that the
Ministry should delegate their power of inspection to the police, it is not the intention of the
Government to turn police into inspectors,
but it is their intention to turn expert
inspectors into police. The Government realise that, in view of the importance of the
duties which these men will have to undertake, they must have at their disposal technical inspectors of proved qualification and
worth, and it must be obvious to Members of
this House that we have not, at the present
time, in the ranks of our police, a sufficient
number of individuals who have the necessary technical knowledge.

Mr. DEVLIN: Could you not train them?
You have taught them a lot of things here.
Sir DAWSON BATES: And they will learn
a lot of things more. Hon. Members will
see that under Sub-Clause (2) of Clause 15
the Government take power to increase the

duty. These Inspectors will have, in addition to their technical knowledge, the
authority and influence which members of
the R.U.C. must necessarily have. Hon.
members will see that a great deal of the

Clause 17 of the Bill. May I briefly refer
to these Regulations. First of all, they will
govern the manner in which vehicles are to
be built, furnished, or fitted; they will
govern the actual fitness of the vehicles for
public hire, and for the safety of the travelling public; they will provide for the number of passengers to be carried in any vehicle,
and the space to be allotted to each passenger; they will provide for the class of
vehicle for which conductors are to be provided; and they will provide for such minor
matters as the wearing of badges; the regulation of the conduct of the drivers, conductors
and passengers; the publication of fares and

in a position to satisfy all lawful claims
which may be made against him in respect
of damage, the Ministry is empowered,
through its Inspectors, to issue a licence to
this class of machine.
Mr. MCALLISTER: How is the fee fixed
for the licence?
Sir DAWSON BATES: The fee will be a
sum not exceeding £2 for each vehicle. Hon.
Members will realise that the examination
and testing of these machines will involve
substantial administration charges, and I
think they will appreciate that it is not unreasonable to call upon owners of these
vehicles to meet, so far as possible, the actual
expense involved.
a
As to the question of drivers, hon. Members will observe that Clause 11 introduces
a new principle. It prohibits anyone driving
or operating on motor plying for hire
except a licensed driver and licensed
conductor, and may I state shortly the
principles governing the issue of a licence
to these individuals.
a
An applicant for a licence for driving
must, first of all, be at least 21 years of age.
May I say hear that in London no driver is
allowed to drive any public vehicle unless
he is at least 24 years of age, and I think
hon. Members will agree with me that 21 is
the minimum age at which a driver should
be entrusted with the lives of passengers.
But the applicant must also satisfy the
licensing authority that he is competent to
drive the vehicle of the type for which he
seeks the driver's licence. Hen. Members
will find this provision in Clause 11 (3) of the
Bill, and, briefly, what an applicant must do
when he applies for a licence is this. He
must, first of all, prove his age; he must
provide certificates of character; and he
must provide a certificate of health. I think
this is one of the most important Clauses in
the Bill.
A case came to my knowledge
some time ago of a man who is in hospital
and is being treated for epilepsy. That man
followed the occupation of driving a bus, and
I want hon. Members to realise what the fate
of the passengers would have been if that
man had got a fit when going down a hill.
In addition, the applicant must undergo a
driving test with the actual vehicle in respect
of which he seeks the licence.
In the case of the conductor, the minimum
age is fixed at 18, and here again, as in the
case of the drivers, the applicant will have to
satisfy the licensing authority as to character and general capacity for carrying out
the responsible duties of conductor. Hon.
Members, I do not think, will disagree with
me as to the necessity of ensuring that these
buses should have proper men as conductors.
After all, their duties involve something
more than the mere collection of the fares
from the passengers. It is proposed, in view
of the expense involved of testing and recording, to impose fees of 10s in the case of a
driver, and 5s in the case of a conductor
per year.
Before passing from the question of the
licensing of public vehicles and their drivers,
I think it well to refer to the provisions
regarding the penalties in this connection.
Under Clause 10, Sub-Clause 2, of the Bill, the
owner, the driver and the conductor on any
unlicensed vehicle plying for hire or being
used to carry passengers, will be liable to a
minimum penalty of £1 per day for every day
during the period that vehicle is used. If this
Act is to be of any use whatever, it is absolutely necessary that strict penalties must be
imposed upon individuals who seek to use
vehicles that are not fit for the purpose. For
the same
reason we provide a minimum
penalty of £1 in the case of any licensed
vehicle being driven by an unlicensed driver.
Now we come to one of the most important
provisions in this Measure-the question of
the overcrowding of passenger-carrying motor
vehicles. At the present time the law governing the question of overcrowding in Northern
Ireland is somewhat obscure, but in any
event, the maximum penalty that can be
imposed for overcrowding is £2. According
3E
Motor Vehicles Bill -
