HOUSE OF COMMONS
[Sir Dawson Bates]
to the returns which the Ministry of Home
Affairs have received, no fewer than 305 convictions were obtained against drivers and
owners of chars-a-bancs during the twelve
months ended the 31st July, 1926, for overcrowding, but these convictions have not
succeeded in abating this evil. In the
majority of cases only nominal fines had been
imposed and, accordingly, the evil has grown
rather than diminished. May I quote a case
which occurred in May last. An owner was
prosecuted for allowing overcrowding on his
motor bus. The bus in question was only
licensed to carry 32 passengers, but it was
proved that there was actually 44 persons on
the bus. The magistrate imposed the fine of
15s, a fine which drew the remark from one
of the magistrates that the driver was still
12s to the good, having regard to the fares
which he had received from his extra
passengers.
I would point out to this House that all
motor-carrying vehicles are designed to carry
a defined number of passengers. They pay
licence duty on the basis of the number of
passengers they are supposed to carry, and
I cannot but think that the persisent practice
of overcrowding which is indulged in by
motor owners is one of the greatest evils that
we have to contend with in regard to motor
traffic. Overcrowding conduces to the danger
of the passengers by imposing a strain on the
vehicles which they are not fit to bear. It is
an attempt on the part of the owner to evade
the law by paying less taxation than he is
entitled to pay, but, in addition, this overcrowding adds very considerably to the wear
and tear of the roads. I hope that as a result
of the Regulations which the Government will
make under this Act, to ensure that the buses
will have proper safety doors; that they
will have a clear aisle by which a passenger
can reach the doors in the case of accident.
But all this will be defeated if overcrowding
is permitted.
I saw a bus on fire the other day. I
arrived on the scene shortly after the
passengers had got out. I found that the
safety door at the rear of the car could not
be opened, and I also found that the
passengers had to step over the flames to get
out by the front door. I found that the fire
extinguisher which the bus was supposed to
carry was not in working order. The bus.
however, was fortunately not overcrowded.
But imagine what would have happened in
that bus if the central isle had been choked
and the passengers had not been able to get
out. In taking all these circumstances into
consideration, the Government consider that
the offence of overcrowding should be visited
with very heavy penalties.
In the past it has frequently been the
practice for the owners, when charged with
overcrowding, to plead that their conductors
acted against their orders in allowing extra
passengers to enter the vehicle; while, on the
other hand, the conductors plead that they
are acting in accordance with the express
instructions of the owners. In order to meet
these pleadings it will be observed that the
Bill provides that in the case of overcrowding the penalties should be enforced both
For
against the owner and the conductor.
the first offence, the owner will be liable to
a fine of £1, with an additional fine of 2s 6d
for every person carried in excess of the
prescribed number; for the second offence,
the owner will be liable to a fine of from £1
to £5, with a similar additional fine of 2s 6d
per person over the prescribed number;
while for the third, or subsequent offence,
the initial fine may be as much as £10 but
not less than £1, in addition to the 2s 6d for
each excess passenger. But side by side with
the fines it is proposed to impose on the
owners, the conductors will be liable to fines
of 2s 6d for each excess person carried. In
addition to that, the Courts are required to
endorse the licence of these vehicles, and to
send copies of these convictions to the
Ministry of Home Affairs, who will be empowered to revoke the licence, and remove
the vehicle from the roads.
There is one point in connection with inspection to which I would like briefly to refer. Under Clause 14 any officer duly
authorised will have the right at any time
during the course of a journey to stop the
vehicle if he has any reason to think that the
vehicle is not in a safe condition, and if he
arrives at the conclusion that the vehicle is
unsafe, he can order the driver to take the
vehicle off the road, and the owner, under
these circumstances, will have to make arrangements for the conveyance of his
passengers to their destination by some other
means. Under ordinary circumstances, the
examination of these vehicles from time to
time will be carried out in the various
garages, but hon. Members will realise that
sometimes a machine leaves a garage in a
perfectly sound condition, and only during
the journey develops mechanical defects.
This principle is not a new one. It is in
operation in London with most satisfactory
results. I have seen it myself.
I would like now to clear up one point in
regard to which there is a certain amount of
misunderstanding. It is proposed to remove the powers conferred under the 1924
Act from the local authority in regard to the
inspection and licensing of vehicles, but it
is not intended in any way to affect the
existing powers of local authorities in regard
to the local regulation of motor traffic, and
we
propose that they should still retain
these powers so that in the future, as in the
past, local authorities will have the power of
fixing the stands for chars-a-banes, fixing the
number of vehicles that may stand at any
Motor Vehicles Bill-
12 OCTOBER 1926

Second Reading.
particular stand, and, generally, regulating
char-a-bane traffic.
Now we come to the last-the Third Partof the Bill.
Under Clause 18 all penalties and licences,
fees and duties imposed under this Bill will
be paid into the Exchequer, and by the
Exchequer paid into the Road Fund, and
will, ultimately, accrue to the improvement
of the roads, after payment of the necessary
expenses that will be involved in connection
with the administration of the Act. Up to
the present it has been the practice to pay
out of the Road Fund to the local authorities
a sum to compensate them for the expense
incurred by them in the licensing of these
vehicles. This duty having been removed
from the local authorities, this payment will
in the future cease.
The only other provision in this part of
the Bill to which I think I should draw the
attention of hon. Members is the provision
in Clause 19, which I have already referred
to earlier in my remarks. We propose to
give an individual convicted for a motor
offence the right of appeal to the County
Court Judge sitting alone, and to accord a
similar right to the police.
I would like to apologise to this House for
the time I have occupied in explaining the
provisions of this Bill. It is a Bill of farreaching importance. It may be considered
by some Hon. Members that certain of the
penalties are of a drastic character, but, as
I have already stated, this Measure is not
brought forward in any spirit of vindictiveness against either the motor owner, the
bus owner, or the char-a-banc owner; but the
Government feel that a very serious responsibility rests upon them as custodians of the
public safety, and when one remembers that,
as I have already stated, bus owners, char-abane owners, etc., are carrying upwards of
20 million passengers per annum, without
any control, as compared with about 12
million carried by the railways in a year,
I think the House will agree with me that
the Government is only doing its duty in
asking this House to give them the powers
of control which they ask for in this Bill,
and it is in this spirit I ask the House to
give this Bill a Second Reading. (Hon.
Members: Hear, hear.)
Mr. WILLIAM MCMULLEN: I think the
House will be deeply indebted to the right

but a hazy, nebulous notion as to what the

Possibly that is inevitable in a Measure go
comprehensive as the one that has been submitted to the House this afternoon.
I think it is very gratifying that an

one could not fail to observe the scandal in

This is a very important matter, because

a very important matter, and I hope that
when the Parliamentary Secretary (Mr.
Hanna) comes to reply to any criticisms
offered, he will deal with this aspect of the
watter with the wealth of detail that

HOUSE OF COMMONS
[Mr. W. McMullen]
characterised the speech of the Minister in

I come now to the major point that I wish
to advance in connection with this Bill, and
I claim the attention of the right hon.
Gentleman. As I said earlier, it is a comprehensive Measure, dealing with perhaps
thousands of details, and to me it is a
remarkable state of affairs, having regard to
the number of accidents spoken of by the
right hon. Gentleman-I think something
like 1,300-that no attempt has been made to
improve the efficiency of the operatives of the
buses by ensuring that they are not asked to
work an excessive number of hours. Is it
not a well-recognised thing that a workman
can be efficient for a certain number of hours,
and that if his duties are prolonged beyond
that point his efficiency becomes impaired ?
If we are going to allow the drivers and conductors to be employed for twelve, fourteen,
or sixteen hours a day, they are not for the
last four or six hours of the day in a capable
or efficient state for discharging their duties
satisfactorily.
I have two immediate points of view on
this matter. As the right hon. Gentleman
knows, the Belfast Corporation have now
started to run buses, and, in a limited way,
the buses that are plying for hire outside the
city are in competition with the buses of the
Belfast Corporation. Reasonable conditions
of employment obtain in the Belfast Corporation buses,, inasmuch as a reasonable wage
is paid, and good hours of labour are conceded. Now, how can those good conditions
be maintained on the Corporation buses if
no attempt is going to be made to limit the
number of hours that may be worked by the
operatives in the privately owned buses?
This question can also be examined from
the point of view of the railways. The railways, as everybody knows, are in a parlous
state at the moment, owing to the competition they have experienced from motor
transport. I want to say I am not one of
those people who believe in attempting to
stop the most efficient machine, whatever it
may be.
I believe in having the most
efficient method of doing business, notwithstanding the fact that on one occasion the
hon. Member who shares with
me the
representation of West Belfast (Sir Robert
Lynn) attempted quite erroneously to give
the Belfast public the impression that I
want to destroy all the machines that have
ever been brought into existence. I have
characterised that repeatedly as a stupid
notion, a stupid idea.
I believe that an attempt by the Belfast
Corporation to stop privately owned buses
from coming beyond the tramway terminus
would be as stupid as was the attempt on the
part of the poor, ignorant, unfortunate
operatives towards the end of the eighteenth
century to see an enemy in machinery, to
want to destroy machinery, and to go back
to hand labour. I want to say that I do not
stand for that state of affairs at all. I want
to see the most efficient machine, whatever it
may be. If the buses have got to displace
the railways it may be unfortunate but it is
inevitable. If the Belfast trams become
obsolete as a result of the bus services, it
will be due to the lack of prescience on the
part of the public representatives who a few
years ago could not foresee that the bus was
the thing of the future.
Having said that, I want to make a protest
on the ground that no attempt is being made
to limit the number of hours that may be
worked by the bus operatives. After some
eighty years of organised effort, railway men
have been able to get at least tolerable conditions, but the unfair competition of the
buses from the point of view of the payment
of inadequate wages and the working of
excessive hours is having a damaging effect
amongst the ranks of the railway men. The
result of those conditions is worsening the
conditions of the railway men. It is within
the knowledge of the Members of this House
that within the last three months the Belfast
and County Down Railway Company were in
such a position that it became necessary for
them to submit certain proposals to their
operatives. What were those proposals? The
proposals were that there should be a reversion to pre-war wages and pre-war conditions as an alternative to the Belfast and
County Down Railway closing down.
Does anyone on the opposite Benches stand
for that state of affairs? Do you desire that
the railway men should go back to pre-war
wages and pre-war conditions? You possibly
do not. But you are incidentally assisting to
bring back that state of affairs by not embodying in your Bill a clause making
it obligatory on the bus owners not to employ
their operatives for more than eight hours a
day. I would ask if it is possible to have a
clause of that character inserted in the Bill,
in fairness to the operatives who are engaged
in the Belfast Corporation buses and to the
men who are employed on the railways. As I
have pointed out, after strenuous efforts for
the most of a century the railway men have
now got tolerable conditions, and I think it
would be unfair to the railway men, and to
many others in the community, if those conditions should be jeopardised by not having
a protective clause inserted in this Measure
to limit the number of hours that may be
worked by the bus operatives in the day. I
have no desire to criticise the Measure at
great length, and any other matter I desire
to talk about I will reserve for the Committee
stage. Owing to the comprehensive nature of
the Bill and the defects it contains, possibly

many Amendments will be put forward on

Sir ROBERT LYNN: I am glad that the

Mr. WILLIAM MCMULLEN: You are too

Sir ROBERT LYNN: I hope the few remarks I am going to address to the Minister
of Home Affairs will have the same effect.
May I first congratulate the right hon. Gentleman on the very lucid explanation he has
given of a very long and complicated Bill.
With the general principle of the Bill I think
the House is united in agreement, and any
points we differ on will be matters of detail
that can be easily settled, I hope, in Committee. In the very first Clause of the Bill
I would like to draw the right hon. Gentleman's attention to the paragraph with regard
to reckless driving. We are all opposed to
reckless driving, but the paragraph says a
policeman shall have power to decide the
amount of traffic which is actually there at
the time, "or which may reasonably be
expected to be on the highway." Suppose my
hon. and eloquent Friend, the Member for
West Belfast (Mr. William McMullen) was
billed to speak at Comber. Would a policeman be justified in assuming that there
would be large crowds there, and that therefore a motorist who at a normal time would
be driving at a reasonable speed would at this
particular time be driving recklessly? You
are going to put an enormous responsibility
and an awful power in the hands of the
police. I know that in a good many circles
there is an objection to your linking up the
offence of drunkenness when driving with the
offence of reckless driving. The feeling is
that the two offences ought to be separate,
and that there should be separate penalties
for these offences.
Another point that strikes me is with regard to the minimum fine or penalty that is
to be inflicted. I remember not so very long
ago in this House, when some hon. Members,
amongst them myself, suggested a minimum
penalty, the Members on the Government
Bench were terribly shocked, and they
assured us that such a thing was never
heard of in the British Constitution, and
they had no intention whatever of going in
for such a revolution as that. I do suggest
to the right hon. Gentleman that the precedent he is setting of a minimum penalty is
one that this House should not rashly agree
to. I hold no brief for those who break the
law, but I do think the minimum penalty
you are inserting in this Bill is a very excessive one. The Minister of Home Affairs
says he is carrying on no vendetta against
motorists, but I know there is an impression
abroad that there is a vendetta being carried
on against motorists generally. I am sure
that is the last thing the Minister of Home
Affairs wants, but this particular section of
the Bill will tend to leave that impression.
With regard to the age limit of seventeen,
does the right hon. Gentleman not think
there are other things to be considered in
granting a licence in addition to age? I have
seen boys of fifteen who are remarkably good
drivers. I know quite a number of them,
and, on the other hand, I have known older
people who were never good drivers, and are
never likely to be. I have a friend who took
to motoring and he was a most reckless
driver. He afterwards became a Cabinet
Minister. (Laughter.) He could start his
machine but he could not get it to stop.
That brings me to a point that has been
omitted from this Bill, as it has been omitted
from Bills elsewhere, and that is that those
responsible should make sure not only of the
physical fitness but the driving fitness of
everyone who drives a motor-car. I guarantee
that the bulk of the accidents that take
place are due, not to reckless and fast driving, but to the fact that the people who are
entrusted with motor-cars have never learned
to drive a motor as they should have done.
I hope that in Committee the right hon.
Gentleman will agree to accept Amendments
with the object of ensuring that before a
man is entrusted with a driver's licence he
must prove that he is qualified for his job.
I could not quite follow the Minister of
Home Affairs with regard to local authorities being allowed to impose a speed limit
of their own. He has abolished the speed
limit so far as the ordinary motor is concerned, but any local authority-I presume
he means a county council as well as an
urban council-will have the right to impose
a speed limit that may be not more than ten
or fifteen miles an hour. That would nullify
the abolition of the speed limit.
Sir DAWSON BATES: If they want to
fix a speed limit local authorities will have to
apply for sanction to the Ministry of Home

at the same time, I am sure the hon. Member

should still be retained by the Ministry.
Sir ROBERT LYNN: I think the right

bus, because I know that in the class
of bus we are getting at the present
moment it is not possible at 12 miles
an hour to do the engine justice. It is not
possible because the owner of the bus wants
to get the best service out of the bus, and to
compel the engine to labour at 12 miles an
hour is not the way to get long service out
of the engine of that particular bus. I believe 20 miles per hour will be welcomed, and
I welcome it, because I know it is really a
limit that can be conformed to, and if
violated the driver should be harshly dealt
with.
The other point I want to make is that the
Minister quoted the Act of 1864, the time
when a 4-mile limit was put on, and they
used to go about with a red fiag, because, as
a side issue, he said, it was not the flag I
referred to. I always thought there was only
one colour of red, and I understand it being
a red flag it was the flag I referred to.
Mr. W. McMULLEN: That is logic.
Mr. BEATTIE: That is logical. It would
be no harm if additional lights were adhered
to, that is, what we call in the shipping
world a starboard and a port light, because
I have noticed on one class of vehicle a green
light and a red light, and you can tell from
a good distance what side of the road the
vehicle is travelling on. I would recommend the Government, if it is possible within the lighting clause, to put on port and
starboard lights.

Mr. BEATTIE: Continuing the discussion
on the Second Reading of the Motor Vehicles
(Traffic and Regulation) Bill, may I say that
I do so feeling that certain Clauses of the
Bill are going to be damaging to the motor
trade? I do not want unduly to criticise the
principle of the Bill. The principle the
Minister has in mind is the protection of the
public from the dangers of reckless driving
and from persons who get into such a condition that they are not fit to be on the highway. I feel, however, that the powers the
Minister asks for in order to make this Bill
operative require some little more consideration. There should also be a clearer explanation given to the House, because when
Bills are framed they are framed for a particular purpose, but as years go on that
object is lost sight of with the result that
they operate for some other purpose than
that for which they were framed.
We on
this side of the House have had experience of
a Bill framed for a particular purpose, and
which operated against that purpose.
The first Clause, which I did not touch
upon last night, relates to reckless driving,
and the object of it is to take away the
speed limit which operated in the past. I
notice that Clause 5 implies that speed limits
are going to be re-introduced.
I may be
wrong in my contention, but what that
Clause conveys to me is that power is going
to be given to local authorities to impose a
speed limit on certain vehicles that journey
within their jurisdiction. Arguments will
be used for and against that. We have
Motor Vehicles Bill-
Second Reading.
HOUSE OF COMMONS
[Mr. Beattie]
authorities telling us that the abolition of
speed limit is conducive to the safety of
the public. Then we have other authorities
telling us that it is essential in the interests
of the public to have speed limit. I think
that in the Bill the Minister is really trying
to meet both views.
I paid careful attention to the Bill when
reading it, and I also paid careful attention
to the Minister when he was explaining it
here, but it is very hard for one to grasp the
real situation when the explanation is being
given. A little thought and consideration
sometimes enlighten one, and he feels the
Bill is not just all he thought it was at the
time. There is a revolution in the licences.
The Minister is now asking the House to
abolish the old system of licensing drivers
of motor-cars, as he feels the anomalies under
the old system were so great that there was
danger of the law being evaded. He is now
reverting to the system of passports, whereby
the photograph of the person who is going to
get the licence must be placed on the licence.
I take it that he means the licence will cost
10s and the photograph will cost 1s, and will
be placed on the licence, and will be endorsed
by the authorities.
Sir DAWSON BATES indicated assent.
Mr. BEATTIE: That is to prevent the
transferring of a licence from one person to
another, as was previously done under the
old system. That may be a very good thing,
and it may tend towards preventing a reckless driver, who has misconducted himself,
from being able to drive a car on the highway; but I am not prepared to say it is going
to be so workable as the Minister perhaps
thinks. No law has yet been made that a
pair of horses cannot be driven through, and
I believe that that part of the Bill may be
got over by through certain manoeuvring on
the part of an individual who desires to use
an illegal licence for the driving of a motorcar.
I find that the Minister has answered very
satisfactorily the memorandum from the
Automobile Association complaining about
the Clause in the Bill, which states-
Every person, being the holder of a
licence under this Part of this Act, who is
charged with any offence to which this
section applies, shall bring such licence into
court at the hearing of the charge.
I understand now that it is not necessary
for the person so charged to present the
licence personally, and that his legal representative may do so on his behalf. That is
quite satisfactory to me, and should be to
all concerned.
•
Under Clause 5, it seems to me, powers are
to be invested in the local authorities for
the regulation of the speed of heavy motors
only. I would like to know does Clause 5,
sub-clause (b), include private motor cars
under two tons, or does it only include the
heavy motors over two tons? It says:
To make Regulations as to the speed of
motor cars exceeding two tons unladen.
Is the speed limit to be made by local
authorities only to apply to vehicles of two
tons and over, or is it to apply to all classes
of vehicles below two tons as well?
In another Clause I notice that a person
who now seeks a licence for a public vehicle
will have to prove that he is in a position
to meet any liabilities he may incur.
I think that is a rather harsh Clause from
the point of view of the present owners of
motor buses as they are really working-class
men who set up in a small way and have
established up-to-date_services of transport.
If the Minister gave me the assurance that
this means "covered by insurance" I would
be satisfied with the Clause.
I think the most contentious parts of the
Bill are Clauses 14 and 15. There has been a
general discussion throughout the North of
Ireland that there would be a provision in
the Bill whereby certain people might be
pitchforked into what may be termed sinecure jobs at the expense of the general taxpayers. I notice in one of the Clauses to
which I have referred that allusion is made
to the Royal Ulster Constabulary and special
constables. It may be said that I am speaking without foundation, but I am going to
speak on the best information I have received outside. That phrase "special constables" is open to a very wide construction.
It may mean anything and it may mean
nothing. My suspicions, however, have been
raised by the wording of Clause 15, where the
Minister asks power to extend the limit of
age for the Royal Ulster Constabulary. He
also asks you to give him power to appoint
specials constables. This is a most contentious part of the Bill, and it is going to raise
a certain amount of suspicion-a certain
amount of hard abuse which the Government
will deserve if they pass this. It means that
a special section of the Constabulary will be
selected from a particular group which was
once in operation in this area, the members
of which are over the age to join the Royal
Ulster Constabulary.
The Minister desires this age limit to be
removed so that he can replace members of
the special constabulary under this Bill and
appoint them as mechanical inspectors under
the Vehicles Regulations. I may be wrong
in my prophecy, but I am going to prophecy
now that six district-inspectors of the
special constabulary have already been
selected as inspectors under this Bill, to take

over the mechanical and technical part of
the investigation that will be necessary

I will have to wait until I see if it comes
right. If it is not correct then I ask the

prepared to treat the R.U.C. as it stands?
In that force you have men with a practical

There is another matter I notice, and that

grave hardship, and I think the Minister

at the time.
That is a
Major SHILLINGTON: I rise to congratulate the Government on the handsome
manner in which they propose to deal with
this whole question, as evidenced by the
Bill we are discussing. I think it is quite
necessary that all the rules and regulations
and laws which have already been in force
should be embodied in the same Bill as
those which are going to be made to meet
the existing state of affairs. I would like
to join with other hon. Members in eengratulating the Minister on the very full
and lucid explanation he gave in moving
the Second Reading of this Bill. I am glad
to know that in the Bill he has embodied a
number of recommendations of the Roads
Advisory Committee, and I understand he
will have power under the regulations to be
issued under the Bill to adopt some of the
other recommendations which they have
made. Consequently, I have not very much
criticism to make on the Bill, but there are
one or two points I would like more
information about.
Like other hon. Members I
not
satisfied that it is a wise thing to deal with
the two cases of reckless driving and being
drunk in charge of a motor-car on any highway in the same Clause and with the same
penalties. I think as regards the man who
goes out on a motor-ear in an unfit state no
penalty will be too severe, and if that
Clause could be tightened in Committee I
would be glad to support such tightening
up.
As regards reckless driving, that is
another question altogether. I do not know
whether anybody would undertake to define
what reckless driving is. The Minister in
his remarks yesterday seemed to think one
case of reckless driving was not keeping on
the proper side of the white line when going
round a corner. I agree with that. I have
had some small experience of notoring
across the water, and I find that motorists
keep to their own side of the road when
negotiating a corner. Here you will find two
vehicles going in the same direction, one
attempting to pass the other when going
round a corner. That is a serious state of
affairs.
On the other hand I have had experience
myself of going round a corner where there
is a white line. To the best of my knowledge
there was nothing in front. I have been
on my own side of the road, but when half
way round the corner I have discovered a
large bus either taking up or putting down
passengers. I hope that in the Regulations
which the Minister purposes to issue in connection with this matter he will take into
consideration the advisability of having fixed
stopping places for these buses, because it
is a serious matter when going round a
corner to find one of these large buses not
drawn into the side, but in the centre of
the road. I have known cases where the
vehicles were over the white line. The question of reckless driving must be very much
a matter of opinion. I do not exactly know
what evidence the magistrates will require.
I understand, as regarding the existing speed
limit they require the evidence of two witnesses to show that a man has exceeded a
speed of 20 miles. I do not know whether
the evidence of two witnesses will be wanted
to substantiate a charge of reckless driving.
I would like before this Bill comes to the
Committee stage that some rather better
wording of this clause would be devised.
I come to the question of the driver's
licence. I must say that I cannot agree with
the hon. Member for East Belfast (Mr.
Beattie) in saying that it may be possible not
to compel a driver to produce his licence on
the spot, but to give him time to do so. I
think I am right in saying that the law as
it stands at present compels a man to produce his licence on demand, and I do not
think it has entailed any undue hardships.
I also understand there is the possibility of

Major Shillington]
a new form of licence being introduced. If
that is so it will really be a sort of licence
that can be safely left in the car. There is

As regards that I think the conditions have

and they are able to drive cars under the

There are several other matters I could
draw attention to, but this is scarcely the

Bill comes up in Committee stage. I understand the speed limit for ordinary motorcars is going to be abolished, that is the
twenty miles which was more honoured in
the breach than in the observance. The
local authorities will have power to apply

Of course we realise that there will have
to be a certain section of the Royal Ulster
Constabulary or of the Special Constabulary
-I do not know which it will bewith certain technical knowledge for the
inspection of these public service vehicles
and also for the testing of the drivers of
these public service vehicles. I think the
Government would be wise to get the very
best men they can with the most expert
knowledge possible for the work. I would
like just a little information-the matter may
not have been considered yet-whether it is
proposed to carry out this inspection of these
vehicles and the testing of drivers by
counties, or whether there will be only one
or possibly two stations, say at Belfast and
Londonderry, at which all this inspection
and testing of vehicles and drivers will be

The PARLIAMENTARY SECRETARY OF
THE MINISTRY OF HOME AFFAIRS (Mr.
Hanna): By counties.
Major SHILLINGTON: I am glad to hear
it is to be county by county. Of course that
will mean a slight increase of staff, but it
will be counter-balanced by the convenience
to the public. I must say that I think one
of the most dangerous things at the present

I am afraid the bus companies must realise

recorded on a driver's licence, but I should

There is just one other question to which

traffic. If I read this Bill rightly, I am

Mr. MCALLISTER: As a Member of the
House I would like to thank the Minister of
Home Affairs (Sir Dawson Bates) for the
very exhaustive way in which he introduced
this Bill yesterday. If he erred at all I
would say it was on the side of being too
exhaustive, but of the two alternatives I
think it was very much better and more
acceptable to the House. The alternative,
which is frequently adopted in this House,
is practically to throw the Measure at the
House and to ask individual Members to
digest the Measure for themselves. While
I quite appreciate and while I believe that
the Minister was animated by the laudable
ideas and by the praiseworthy sentiments
which he professed to be the guiding
influences with him on the introduction of
this Bill, on examination and reading of the
Bill, I have come to the conclusion that
there was another object not so highly
praiseworthy to him or to the Government,
and that this Bill when examined line by
line amounts not to a Bill to improve and
direct motor transport in Northern Ireland,
but to all intents and purposes is a supplementary financial Bill introduced, not manfully and courageously as a financial Bill,
but introduced under the guise of a Bill to
improve motor transport facilities in
Northern Ireland.
I base that proposition on the ground that
the only reason in this twentieth century
why medieval legislation such as this
should be introduced must not be for the
purpose of the administration of justice but
for the purpose of raising finance by imposing in practically every paragraph of the
Bill a minimum penalty, which is a retrograde principle of legislation, which is reactionary by every test, which is indefensible, and cannot be defended by any logical
argument. The Minister of Home Affairs
in his exhaustive speech yesterday frequently referred to the nominal fines which
have heretofore been imposed by Petty
Sessions Courts and Quarter Sessions Courts.
We all know from reading the papers and
the reports of these sessions at the present
day that a great proportion of the business
No doubt the Minister of Home Affairs
dealt very exhaustively with Parts I and II
of this Bill yesterday, but if he referred at
all to Part III it was in the most cursory
and passing manner. That is the part of
the Bill which is the reason for its being
introduced into this Parliament. That is the
part of the Bill which deals with the finance,
and by Clause 18 it provides:
(1) All sums received by the Ministry of
Home Affairs or by any officer of the Royal
Ulster Constabulary or by the Council of
any county or county borough by way of
fees for licences granted under Part I or
Part II of this Act, and all penalties and
other sums recovered under or in pursuance of this Act, shall be paid into the
Exchequer of Northern Ireland in such
manner and in accordance with such
directions as may be contained in any
Order made by the Governor of Northern
Ireland in Council under the Roads Act,
1920.
True the next paragraph goes on to say--
(2) There shall be charged on and issued
out of the Consolidated Fund of Northern
Ireland, or the growing produce thereof,
and paid to the Road Fund (Northern Ireland) in accordance with the directions of
the Ministry of Finance, a sum equal to the
proceeds of all sums paid into the said
Exchequer under this section.
That is a very plausible protection for the
motoring public on the face of it, and if it
were not for the knowledge of past history
that we have in this House we might be
satisfied with it. But before the Government
can satisfy us, and the people generally, that
this Bill is not to be passed for the purpose
of raising finance principally-if that is not
so they can satisfy us and disillusion us by
giving an undertaking explicit and unqualified that the Road Fund will not be
further raided for other purposes as it has
been in the past. The Minister of Home
Affairs, according to the report of his speech
this morning, stated that if the fines are not
to be increased it will be impossible to keep
up the roads as they are at the present time.
If the Road Fund had not been raided it
would have been unnecessary to put this

HOUSE OF COMMONS
[Mr. McAllister]
extra imposition on the motorists of Northern
Ireland.
Sir DAWSON BATES: May I interrupt
my hon. Friend for one moment? The point
I made was that the excessive speeds of
these heavy vehicles destroyed the roads and
cast a further burden on the road authorities.
Mr. DEVLIN: But you have put a bigger
tax on them.
Mr. McALLISTER: The fact remains that
we are the most heavily taxed motorists in the
world, and for that we get inferior roads,
and we have this state of affairs because the
Government raided the Road Fund, which
should have been for the upkeep of the roads.
Not only are the Government not content
that at the present time we should be the
most heavily taxed motorists in the world,
but they are putting further taxes on us.
What is the effect of this Bill? For 5s you
can motor from January to December from
Land's End to John o' Groats on first-class
roads. Under this Bill, if it is passed, to go
from Derry to Buncrana will cost one pound
in licence duty. We say we are anxious to
develop tourist traffic in Northern Ireland.
If a tourist comes over here it is going to
cost him his own five shilling licence at
home, it is going to cost him ten shillings
here, and it is going to cost him a further
ten shillings in the Free State. I suggest
that is not the way to develop and encourage
the highly fruitful and productive tourist
traffic that we would all like to see in this
district.
With regard to Clause 1 of the Bill, I
suggest to the Government that when it
comes to the Committee stage it can be very
much simplified. It is unnecessarily involved at the present time. It is bad legislation and draftsmanship, in the first place,
to couple drunkenness with reckless driving,
and, in the second place, to put it in the
hands of a policeman to visualise a hypothetical case, and upon that to give his
evidence in court. The hon. Member for
West Belfast (Sir Robert Lynn) illustrated
a hypothetical case yesterday with regard to
my hon. Friend and colleague, the Member
for West Belfast (Mr. W. McMullen). May I
give the House another hypothetical case
which may arise, and on which a policeman
may have to give his evidence? Assume for a
moment that there is a Labour meeting in
East Belfast, in Ballymacarrett, and that a
motorist knows that that meeting is to take
place at a certain hour. In order to avoid
that meeting he goes by adjoining streets, and
suppose he finds there a mob organised to suppress and destroy the Labour meeting. One
constable may come into court and say that it
was a natural thing to expect in this particular district of Belfast that when there was
a Labour meeting a mob should be organised
to attack it, and that, therefore, the motorist
was not justified in going, as he would have
been justified in going under ordinary
circumstances, at fifteen or sixteen miles per
hour, owing to this organised rowdyism to
break up a legitimate meeting, that he should
have expected that to take place, and that,
therefore, he should be fined. Of course,
another policeman may take another view,
but that is the state of affairs that may be
created under the draftsmanship of Clause 1
of this Bill.
Another thing to which I would like to
draw attention is the doing away with the
speed limit of twenty miles per hour. The
present sytsem of police traps in Northern
Ireland is of the most primitive type. What
takes place as I understand it-I can be corrected if I am wrong-is this: the Government supply a policeman without any special
training with a thirty shilling tin watch to
take the times of the motorists where every
fraction of a second is material and every
yard is material. Now, if you take the case
of ordinary sport, a walking race, a running
race, or a cycle race, where the locomotion
is much slower than motor traffic, the timekeeper is furnished with a highly finished,
high-priced stop watch. Now the professional
motorist and the ordinary working man who
is the owner of a motor lorry or the owner
of a bus are to have their whole livelihood
at stake on the tick of the Government's
thirty shilling watch-that is made in
Germany perhaps. I suggest that is a state
of affairs that should be remedied.
Now with regard to another clause of the
Bill which has already been referred to, the
production of the licence on demand by a
policeman, I would suggest with regard to
that that the Bill be amended to give reasonable time to a person who holds a legitimate
licence and has left it at home to produce it
at a reasonable time. Under what to all
intents and purposes is an omnibus clause
dealing with the question of the suspension
of licences it appears to me that a man who
inadvertently and innocently forgets his
licence may be prosecuted, and it is competent for the court not only to fine him but
to suspend his licence actually because he has
forgotten it and left his licence, properly
granted, at home.
I do trust that when this Bill comes before the Committee it will be scrutinised,
especially with regard to the financial clauses,
by every Member of the House in order to
transform it into a supplementary Finance
Bill, and a Bill to which we may all contribute to make a better Bill for the safety
of the public and the better regulation of
motor traffic throughout Northern Ireland.
Colonel WOODS: I do not intend to make
any speech after the very eloquent speech we

have just heard, but I want to draw the

What effect will it have on the tourist
traffic now we are gradually becoming
more police-ridden than any other community under the sun. We have now the passport instituted in Northern Ireland for
tourists and motorists. It is a passport,
say what you like. It amounts to a passport and it is a passport. Then we have to
pay a 10s licence as against a 5s licence in
Great Britain and, as the last hon. Member
who spoke remarked, it will cost a pound
with the extra inconvenience and annoyance
to tour perhaps for a week in Northern and
Southern Ireland. We cannot say that we
are not more police-ridden, because of all the
places in Great Britain and Ireland Northern
Ireland has had more cases of prosecutions
from police traps, and these police traps are
usually put in places where there is no
danger in speeding. So I am told. I am
not a motorist myself.
Then again we have, as the hon. Member
for Antrim (Mr. McAllister) has said, these
cheap watches. But it does not matter
whether it is a cheap watch or an expensive
one if the man who is reading it has his
mind balanced as well as the watch, because
where it is a limited distance, perhaps a
couple of hundred yards, and his watch is
read a second or two ahead of actual time
it may mean a difference of perhaps five or
ten miles per hour. Well, as time goes on
there will be many more motorists, if this
Bill were not administered in a sense in
which it could be done under the terms of
the Bill. It is very severe and there would
have to be a considerable amount of reasoning put into the reading of it to make it at
all acceptable. We have a policeman, for
instance, being able to place a man in the
position of either being fined £5 or having
to defend himself, which would cost probably just as much, and perhaps more. We
have him in a position to do this, simply
on his own word. Are the police to be allowed to be the judges in every case as to
what dangerous driving is? Is there to be
no definition of that term? Is it going to
be allowed to stand as it is?
Then there is another item in this Bill,
rere lights on motor-cycles. Where are we
going to draw the line? If you follow it to
its logical conclusion every motor, every
cycle, every perambulator, every passenger,
every sheep, goat, and cow would have to
have a rere light and a head light. I think
the idea of having a rere light made compulsory for every moving vehicle or motorist
on the road would be to allow the motorist
to have more or less of an excuse to speed
which otherwise he would not. (Laughter.)
I am sorry you do not seem to follow my
argument. It is not very lucid. I am sure
you will understand that a motorist if he
thinks he must see a rere light on the road
will speed till he sees a rere light. If he
knows that there may be something that has
not got a rere light he will take more care.
Then, again, will dangerous driving or
reckless driving include the destruction of
a pedestrian's clothes through mud-splashing. I think that is a very considerable item,
especially in the badly kept streets of Belfast,
and will it provide for buses and motorists
passing tram cars when they are stationary
and passengers alighting or ascending into
the car.
I understand that this Bill will bring in
a very good thing, that is third party insurance. (An hon. Member: No.) If not, it
should (hon. Members: Hear, hear), because
as my Friends here on the front Bench, the
Socialist Party, pointed out, most of these
bus owners are working men. Supposing
a bus owned by a working man, with very
small capital or none at all, unfortunately
had an accident with perhaps three or four
or six fatalities, who will pay compensation
to these people or their dependants, not
necessarily their relatives? If it were made
compulsory that there should be third party
insurance, people would know that the bus
owner through his insurance would be in a
position to pay compensation where necessary.
Well, I do not know that this particular
Bill is going to do good to anybody except a
few of the foreign legion-I beg your pardon
-the Royal Ulster Constabulary. We have
already a considerable number of men. We
have rather more than anywhere else in the
Kingdom. I have asked the Minister of
Home Affairs would he think it possible for
a man born in Ulster to be able to know
enough to fill any of these jobs. We would
like to have somebody we knew belonged to
the country. I hope the right hon. Gentleman will consider that some Ulstermen might
know enough to be able to inspect the works
of a bus.
I would seriously impress upon the right
hon. Gentleman the effect that this passport
and the extra licence duty is going to have on
the tourist traffic. I am not an orator, but
I wish to impress upon him that particular
fact that it is going to be a source of annoyance and goodness knows we have enoughto the tourist who comes into this country.
(Hon. Members: Hear, hear.) We can do
with a few less, and if every Act and every
Bill brought into this House is going to
make it more annoying I say the sooner we
reverse the procedure in this House the
better.

The fact of the matter is that if you take

600 miles of classified roads would be better off

But it works out in this way. In one county
you have 237 miles of first-class roads, and if

in both counties, the one county with the
237 miles of first-class roads will get a grant

Mr. COOPER: On the whole I agree with
this Bill, although I have great difficulty

(1) If any person—
(a) drives a motor-car on a public
highway recklessly or negligently
Those two things are different offences
and I hold that negligence should not be an
offence at all. If you go before the Petty

motor has touched a cow on the side of the

of cases that is altogether a matter for a

been found to have been guilty of
negligence. I hold, and I belive that

Negligence may occur simply through misjudgment, and such a case should not be

Mr. GEORGE HENDERSON: I think the
Minister of Home Affairs yesterday made out
a very good case as to the urgent necessity
of fresh legislation to deal with the control
and regulation of our motor traffic. The
ever-increasing volume of this traffic, the
numerous and ever-increasing number of
accidents, many of them attended with fatal
results, and the large number of passengers
that are being carried by chars-a-bancs and
other similar vehicles render necessary fresh
legislation, imposing more drastic penalties
on reckless and careless drivers, and ensuring as far as possible the safety of the
travelling public. I am glad the Minister
of Home Affairs is going to raise the speed
limit on vehicles over two tons because the
legal limit of twelve miles imposed on these
vehicles running on pneumatic tyres is
absurd. It was observed by nobody, and
we should try to frame our laws so that they
will be respected by the great majority of
our law-abiding people. I do feel that this
speed limit can be raised even further without undue danger to the public. I hardly
ever travel by motor bus that the speed of
twenty miles an hour is not exceeded and
if the limit is raised to twenty-five miles
it should be rigidly enforced, and I believe
it would be respected by the drivers of buses
and chars-a-bancs.
There is another point, with regard to
the raising of the age limit from 15 to 17. I
do not know that that will entail any very
great harm, although it might do so in the
case of boys in the country who have to go
a long way to school and who ride motorcycles. I think a very much better method of
ensuring the safety of the public would be
that before a licence is issued there should
be some driving test imposed. There should
be a proviso inserted in the Bill that the
Minister of Home Affairs would have power
to issue licences to boys between the ages
of 15 and 17 provided that they could pass
a test for driving. I think that one of the
greatest precautions the Minister could take
against accidents would be to ensure that
all drivers were proficient before they were
granted a licence, because I do feel that a
great many of the accidents that occur are
caused more by inefficient drivers on the
roads than by people who are driving too
fast.
There is another point that I think the
Government should carefully consider, and
that is the fixing of a minimum fine. Supposing a local authority, with the sanction
of the Ministry of Home Affairs, fixed a
speed limit, and supposing a man broke that
speed limit. That is a very easy thing to
do on some very good roads, on which a
motorist might almost unconsciously break
the speed limit. Such a man would be
brought before the magistrates and fined the
minimum fine. I think the Government
should trust to the intelligence of the local
magistrates to impose a suitable fine in such
cases as those. The Bill would not be any
less effective if this minimum fine was removed from it. I agree that the most serious
offence we can think of in connection with
motor driving is being drunk in charge of a
motor car, and that offence should be in a
section by itself. The first section of the
Bill is terribly involved and I hope it will
be improved before it leaves the Committee.

Another point I should like to refer to is

him if his licence was suspended. I think

There is one other thing on which I wish

has been productive of very many accidents.
On the whole I agree with the tenor of the
Bill. It has been said that because the cost

Dr MORRISON: In the first place I want
to congratulate the Government on the introduction of this Bill. It is a rather remarkable fact, and a fact I think that is not
sufficiently known, even in this House, that
in some respects we do not wait for English
legislation to tell us what to do, but that we
are in advance of English legislation. This
Bill is one of those cases in which we are
setting an example not only to the British
Empire, but to the whole of the civilised
world. I could give other instances, in
social legislation, where we are in advance,
and wisely in advance, of the English
system.
I want to say a word or two on the general
questions raised by this Bill, and I speak
with a considerable amount of experience. I
have used a motor bicycle and a motor car,
and all forms of road transport, at all hours
of the day and at all hours of the night, and
in all weathers. I am also in this position
that I happen to be His Majesty's Coroner
for a populons district in County Derry,
and I am brought into contact with those
deplorable accidents that have become so
common. I have no fault to find with the
tone of the criticism that has been expressed
with regard to this Bill. I think it is the
evident desire of every Member of this
House to do what he can to reduce the
appalling number of accidents that are
taking place in our midst, and that often
fall with great force on unoffending people.
I have no desire to interfere with
sport. In a very long and varied life I have
been in as tight corners as any Members of
this House except those who have been in the
war, and to interfere with sport is the very
last thing I would think of doing. But sport
is not to be used to defend and protect
things that are unreasonable. Is it sport for
a big company to engage a man to risk his
life for a big fee, and to cover themselves
by insurance, simply for the sake of advertising the wares they are producing? I call
that commercialism, and commercialism of
a rather low type, and I say this, when commercialism comes into sport, sport suffers.
Many years ago, before motor bicycles and
motor cars were common, I had to treat a
woman who had been run down by a man
on a push bicycle racing down a hill without a lamp. There was a woman with her.
After expressing opinions about recklessness,
I asked her how she escaped. "Oh, said she,
I always walk on the grass." Now, Sir, that
is the position with a great many people.
The public have been driven to the grass for
protection from these people. Members of
the public have been killed on the grass; I
could give you many instances where that
has occurred.
In Coleraine a man was driving his motor
car containing a party who were singing. A
workingman and his wife going home from
their work sought refuge on the grass, but
the motor car ran up on the grass and the
woman was seriously injured. The other
day in Coleraine a man was carried in on a
stretcher to give evidence in a case in which
he had had his leg broken. He saw a motor
cyclist coming along the road, followed by
many others a club, in fact, from Derryand he put a little boy on the bank, and had
one foot on the bank to get up himself when
one of the cyclists who was passing broke his
leg. I myself held an inquest where two
men standing on the footpath were killed by
a motor lorry. The driver turned into the
street at a right angle, and he had practically as much room as there is in this House
in which to turn his lorry and to come on
without any risk of skidding. His lorry,
however, went on to the footpath and killed
those two men who were in a position in
which they thought they were safe.
The majority of motorists are considerate
and careful, but there is a minority who are
not careful, and it is this minority with
whom you have to deal. The ordinary road
user, the quiet, industrious citizen going
about in the discharge of his ordinary work,
is smothered with dust; he is bespattered with
mud; he is blinded with headlights; he is
driven off the road, and in many cases he is
killed or maimed on the grass or the footpath. It has often been a puzzle to me that
the people of this country tolerate the conduct of these persons. It is a puzzle that I
can never explain, except on this ground
Motor Vehicles Bill-
Second Reading.
13 OCTOBER 1926
that Thomas Carlyle was correct when he
said that the British Empire consisted of 36
millions of people--mostly fools. Sir, I am
one of those-(laughter)-who think that
prison doors should be barred on the outside
as securely as they are on the inside.
Punishment to my mind is objectless if it is
not deterrent. As administered by some of
our petty session courts it only excites
ridicule.
Recently in Londonderry a man was
charged with being drunk in charge of a
motor-car. He pleaded guilty. The fine
was 40s. and costs, and no endorsement on
the licence. A few days after that I saw
where in England a man was brought up
for the same offence. He was fined £25, and
his licence was taken from him for a year.
I have come across in 300 inquests many sad
cases of burns and drowning. These, however, in the main were due to some slight
neglect, and in some cases were accidental;
but where innocent people out on their duty
or lawful business are maimed by the reckless driving of people in motor-cars it is a
terrible tragedy. In the main those accidents are due to reckless driving. This conduct is persistently carried on owing to the
inadequate punishment that is inflicted on
them when they are brought before the
magistrates. That is my convinced opinion.
In all these cases, and in all the inquests
that I have held, my opinion is that if
there had been moderate driving, and if
moderate caution had been used, hardly any
of them would have happened.
are
You have had races and speed trials. You
have had them in the County Antrim, where
the public have been shut out of their own
roads. You have had them at Magilligan.
What are they but a glorification of reckless driving that demoralises those engaged
in it? Courage with caution is apt to
secure a prize, but courage with rashness
invites disaster. If you are going to continue these exhibitions I think you
going to do an injury to the country. If
you wish to produce courageous men, it is
not by a system like this that you will do it.
If you want to produce the type that

that in shallow forgetfulness of that great
and precious part of our nature which lies

I want to bring before the House the
appalling suffering that takes place needlessly, not in my district alone, but all over
Ulster, and the necessity for legislation in
is matter. Before I sit down I want to
refer to this question of the minimum fine,
It was raised by the hon. Member for West
Belfast (Sir Robert Lynn), and it has been
referred to by several other Members. Remember that already the principle of a
minimum fixed fine is established in motor
legislation. What great harm can there be
in establishing it in a Measure like this? I
say that you must do one of two things.
You must either have fixed fines, or you
must abolish the Bench as you have done in
regard to illegitimacy cases and offences
under the Licensing Acts, and put the whole
matter into the hands of two Resident Magistrates. I would prefer to have a fixed fine.
In motor taxation, as I said, you have already this fixed fine, and these men who are
pressing objections to this attach more importance to a mere matter of finance than
to the saving of human life. There is in
my district-it has frequently been before
me-a minimum fine in the case of a man
who is caught with a gaff in his hand about
to poach salmon. Does the hon. Member for
West Belfast (Sir Robert Lynn) think the
life of a salmon is anything comparable to
the life of a human being?
Sir ROBERT LYNN: I am sorry to interrupt my hon. Friend, but is he aware that
in that case it is possible for the fine to be
reduced? There is no such provision made
here.
Dr. MORRISON: There is no possibility
of the fine being reduced unless the magistrates make a recommendation which goes
to the Governor, and which in the old days
went to the Lord Lieutenant of Ireland.
Sir ROBERT LYNN: You cannot do that
under this Bill.
Dr. MORRISON: You must not lose a
sense of proportion in this matter. We are
dealing with an appalling condition of things
which hon. Members read of occasionally in
the papers, but they do not know the details
as I have seen them. I saw on Monday a
vigorous, strong, healthy young
man who
for a monetary prize had been used by a
commercial institution to try to advertise
their wares.
He was lying dead with his
face as soft as a sponge, crushed out of all
recognition by his fall. Immediately the
inquest was over I went to see the doctors,
and they had on the table another young
man who was injured in these Magilligan
Races a fortnight previously. He had halfa-dozen bones of his body broken. Two of
the bones were his thigh bones, and there he
was, probably a cripple for life through this
high speeding of motor-cars. He had a persistent high temperature, and he was on the
table under an anesthetic about to be
operated on in the hope that they would
discover suppuration in some of those broken
bones and, perhaps, be able to save his life.
Again and again these cases are coming be

Mr. BLACK: I do not propose now to deal
with any of the details of this Bill, because
I recognise with, I think, all the Members
on both sides of the House, that the Committee stage will be a very long one, and that
there are a great number of questions which
will have to be taken up in detail. There
is one general matter running through the
Bill I would like to mention, and in regard
to which I would like to associate myself
with the observations made by Members on
both sides of the House, that is with regard
to the imposing of a system of minimum
fines. I should have thought that in the
twentieth century this method of legislation
was wholly out of date. The objection is not
merely to taking away the discretion of the
court. The great objection is that where
there is a minimum fine or a fixed fine
prescribed, in a great number of cases the
offences may be of a varying degree of
gravity. I think that if this first clause is
passed into law as it now stands it will be
a classical example of the great evil which
can be brought about by a Government or
legislature trying to take away the discretion
of the courts.
I say this will be a classical example. Just
look at the clause. It deals with two offences,
with driving recklessly and negligently, and
with being drunk in charge of a motor-car.
The offence of being drunk in charge of a
motor-car is at all times and in all circumstances an offence of considerable gravity,
and any Government or any legislature may
well defend the imposition of a minimum
fine for an offence of that nature, and if
the Government had inserted a provision
that an offender should go to jail without
the option of a fine I think it would have
found very many supporters. (Hon. Members: Hear, hear.)
But the clause deals with other offences
than that. It deals with the offence of
driving negligently. The offence of driving
negligently is an offence in which there are
all conceivable degrees of gravity possible.
A man may be guilty of driving negligently,
and he might also deserve penal servitude
for life. On the other hand, a man may
do something negligently that is almost excusable and not deserving of punishment at
gravity and hardly a criminal offence at all,
should be subject to a fine of £5?
If the real reason for imposing this minimum fine is the reason indicated by the hon.
Member for Antrim (Mr. McAllister) that
the Government distrasts the courts who will
have to deal with this offence, then let the
Government take the bold course of coming
before the House and saying they will take
away the trial of these matters from the ordinary magistrates and entrust it, not to two
Resident Magistrates, as was done under the
Licensing Act, because there is nothing more
ridiculous than the way two Resident Magistrates have to be brought together, but to
one Resident Magistrate, a man trained to
weigh evidence and to apportion blame. But
if the Government have not the courage to
do that do not let hon. Members of this
House think of inserting such a fantastic
thing as a fine of £5 for an offence which
is scarcely an offence at all.
There are one or two matters in connection
with the Second part of the Bill as regards
public service vehicles. The great growth
of motor service vehicles is a modern
phenomenon. It has been dealt with slightly
in legislation up to now and will have to
be dealt with again. I am sure the Minister
will not suggest for one moment that this
Bill is the last word on the subject. If
motor vehicles, chars-a-bancs and buses increase in the next few years in the way they
have done in the last few years there is
no doubt that many circumstances will
arise which will necessitate further
legislation. But I think some matters
have already arisen which the Government
might well deal with in this Bill, matters
of no great gravity in a way but which I
think are called for by the great growth in
motor vehicles. One of these is the existing
places where motor vehicles can now stand
and take up positions on the streets of the
towns of Northern Ireland. Already the
streets have become congested, and if there
is the growth during the next five years that
there has been during the last five years the
whole thing will become an impossibility.
One of the greatest nuisances at present
is the jockeying for places and the squeezing
of buses out of their proper places on the
streets. The only places for the buses to
stand at present is the streets, and the cor-
Motor Vehicles Bill-

HOUSE OF COMMONS
[Mr. Black]
porations and urban councils have no power
to provide land or parking places. I think
it would be the proper thing to insert in
this Bill-and it could be done by a short
clause- a provision enabling local authorities with the concurrence and approval of
the Ministry to acquire small portions of
ground and turn them into parking places
for these vehicles. I speak only of public
service vehicles. They might easily cover the

charge for the use of such parking places.
The Ministry might go further and give corporations and urban councils power to
provide parking places for all vehicles and
they could cover the expense by making a
small charge for the parking place and provide a
man to look after the vehicles.
Already apart from the public service
vehicles there is no room on the streets of
Belfast for the provision of the greater
amount of parking places which will undoubtedly be demanded within a few years.
That is not a provision unknown to legislation. In the English Act of 1923 there is
a clause giving the urban councils the precise power I mention. That is a clause which
could be easily taken over and properly
inserted in this Bill.
There is one other matter, too, under this
Bill that the Government proposes-that
the Ministry of Home Affairs should take
over the whole power of the licensing of
vehicles, a power which was formerly
exercised by the local authorities. It is
rather ridiculous that a vehicle which is
covering a journey of a hundred miles
should have a licence in a second town, and
a licence in a third town. Each town should
still be left with power to deal with the
traffic in that town. To a certain extent
that power is preserved, but it is not entirely preserved, and in the city of Belfast
in particular a most alarming situation will
arise unless some Amendment is made in
the Bill. The system of legislation in
Belfast is this, that under the local Acts
the Belfast Corporation have power to
license vehicles and to make by-laws in regard to the vehicles which they license.
Take taxi-cabs, the Corporation have only
power to say that they shall stand at such
and such a place and that the cab stand
shall be such and such a place. The Corporation has only power over the stands for
the vehicles licensed by themselves, and
they have only power to fix minimum fares
for the taxi-cabs which are licensed by
them. Unless you give the Ministry or the
local authorities the power of dealing with
such cases as stands and prescribing fares
the result will be that no one will have any
power to fix the stand for taxicabs in
Belfast, no one will have power to fix
minimum fares for taxicabs, and no one will
have power to deal with drivers if they
charge outrageous fares. That will be a
serious state of affairs, and I would impress
on the Ministry that they should take into
account these matters when drafting any
Amendments which the Government may
submit in Committee stage. I am prepared to
give the Ministry any assistance I can by
submitting to them some Amendments
which I have drafted. That is all I have to
say. I thoroughly approve of the general
principle of the Bill. Some legislation was
necessary. The Government propose
legislate wisely, and one of the wisest things
they have done is the proposed abolition of
the 20 miles speed limit throughout the
Province. (Hon. Members: Hear, hear.)

Mr. P. O'NEILL: After all that has been
heard during the past two days, not alone
from the Benches on which I sit but also
from the Government Benches, I think it
must be apparent that this Bill, like the one
introduced by the Ministry of Agriculture
yesterday, is only good in parts. It will require very serious Amendments when we
come to the next stage. The Minister in
introducing the Bill gave us some figures in
support of it. In his opening statement he
mentioned the number of accidents that
occurred in Northern Ireland during the
last year. There were, he said, 1,300
accidents with 59 deaths. These were not
all attributable, I understand, to negligence
or recklessness on the part of any motor
driver. It would be quite interesting to
know how many of these accidents could or
would likely be avoided had the present
legislation been introduced in the past. In
my opinion many of the accidents that
occur are due to the condition of the roads.
There is no doubt that the road surfaces
have been very greatly improved, but the
dangerous turnings and narrowness of many
of the roads have been the cause of these
accidents. If the Government had gone
about the matter properly all these
dangerous parts of the roads-the narrow
parts of the roads-and the dangerous and
obscure corners, particularly at cross-roads,
might have been improved and a great
many of the accidents could have been
avoided. In addition, the Government
might themselves have employed many
of those people who are getting the dole, as
it is called, and I think that even yet the
Government would be well advised to consider this question of improving the roads.
It is not sufficient to say, as the Minister
has said, that the roads have been put in
fine condition. They are in fine condition
undoubtedly so far as the surface is concerned, but they have not taken the
dangerous parts of the roads away. I think
the Government should consider that
question in the interests of the general
public.

With regard to the Bill, there are one or
two points that have not been mentioned by
any of the speakers. I have been just
wondering why there is not in this Bill legislation for the protection of the railway
companies. Personally, I can speak on this
matter from a less interested point of view
than any other Member of the House. I am
not a shareholder in any railway company,
nor am I interested in any motor-car company, but I think in legislating the Government should be fair to all. Many complaints
have been made in regard to the motor
traffic. Personally, I prefer to travel by
train, because I consider it is more punctual,
more comfortable, and the safest mode of
travelling, but I must admit that I now
travel for exactly half the amount that I
did before the advent of the motor buses.
We should consider the great advantage that
has been to the travelling public of the Six
Counties. No consideration seems to have
been given at all to that question. In fairness to the motor bus people and the motor
carrying people I think any legislation we
should make should not be hard or unjust
on them.
With regard to the question which has
been mentioned by nearly all the speakers
here, the question of the minimum fine, in
my opinion that is one thing that should
be abolished. The question of a minimum
fine should not be in this Bill. I think it
would be much better to bring cases before
two resident magistrates just as in licensing
cases. It was always said in the old times
that the publicans endeavoured to pack the
Bench. In many instances they made great
efforts to get people on the Bench, but it
was only for the purpose of seeing justice
done. A similar state of things would go
on at the present time. People who have
friends on the Bench would endeavour to
get them there in order to see that justice
was done to them, but not to get any particular advantage. At the present time the
licensed trade would not go back to the
old bench of magistrates. They are more
satisfied with the two resident magistrates.
I believe the Government should in this Bill
adopt the course of taking two resident
magistrates in order to try cases, and abolish
the minimum fine. It would be absolutely
fairer in every way, and everybody would
be satisfied and have confidence in it.

donkeys and carts for that matter. I think

anxiety to himself, and, in spite of the previous acquittal, he may be convicted before the
higher court. I suggest that if the Government would accept the suggestion already
made that all cases coming under this section
for reckless driving and drunkenness should
be heard by a Resident Magistrate sitting
alone they might very well do away with both
the minimum penalty and the appeal to a
higher court, and I think both changes would
Improve the Clause. They have, of course,
the precedent of what has been done under
the Licensing Act.
I should like to say something in regard to
drivers' licences. I know the right hon.
Gentleman (Sir Dawson Bates) fairly well,
and I do not think he is likely to go back on
the stand he has taken already, but I hope
he will stick to it that a driver must have
his licence on him. Already cases have been
put forward of where a man gets wet, or
changes his clothes, and forgets his licence.
I am sure cases of that kind are always taken
into consideration by the bench of magistrates who try the case. Such circumstances
are taken into consideration in connection
with the penalty though probably not in connection with the conviction. I, myself, have
been convicted of technical offences before
now and let off without penalty. But it is
not really a very harsh thing to ask a man
to carry his licence with him. A season
ticket holder on the railway has got to carry
his ticket with him, and produce it when
asked to do so, and lots of other people have
got to carry similar documents.
There is one change that I would like to
suggest in connection with the issue of
licences. Firstly, I do not think I ever forgot to carry my licence, because I usually
keep it in my purse and I am not likely to
forget it, being partly Scottish, but where I
do very frequently find myself infringing
the Act is by reason of the fact that I allow
my licence to run out of date. The reason
for that is that the licences are taken out at
all sorts of irregular dates. A man buys a
car to-day, and goes down to-morrow and
takes out a licence on the 14th October.
When the 14th October again comes round
I remember on one occasion finding that I
had been driving my motor-car every day for
about ten months without a licence at all.
That might happen to anyone purely as a
result of omission, and if the licence has not
been asked for and there is no occasion to
refer to it you are quite likely to forget all
about it I would suggest that the driving
licences should be given out in exactly the
same way as are licences for cars, that is at
the first of the year. If a man buys a car
during the course of the year he can take
out a licence for three, six, or nine months
as the case may be at a reduced rate, and
I suggest that the same thing might very
well be done' in connection with driving
licences, and that they should be automatically renewable at the first of the year.
I think that in that way we would do away
with quite a lot of trouble in regard to
failure to renew driving licences.
I would support the plea of the hon.
Member for Antrim (Mr. George Henderson)
to increase still further the speed limit for
chars-a-bancs because personally I think the
limit might very well be increased to 25
miles an hour. I do not think 25 miles an
hour is any greater risk to the travelling
public, and certainly it is no greater risk
to those inside the char-a-bane than if the
limit were 20 miles an hour. I think 25
miles is a limit that could be fixed
and enforced. The 20-mile limit will cer
tainly be exceeded every time the motorist
thinks he can do so with safety.
I understand the Ministry take power to
make regulations with regard to the internal
arrangements of motor-cars and chars-abancs. I think the right hon. Gentleman
yesterday said something about copying the
London regulations. I hope he will not
copy them too closely, because I am afraid
if he does a very large number of men who
are deriving a livelihood from running charsa-banes will be compelled to take their
chars-a-banes off the road, because I understand the London regulations are extremely
severe. They are quite right in one way,
in the provision for emergency exits.
I hope the Ministry will insist upon that.
But I understand they have a number of
other regulations with regard to seating
accommodation, the provision of cushions on
the seats, and so on, and I hope the Ministry
in drafting the regulations will draft them
with some regard to the conditions in force
here. I also hope they will give sufficiently
long warning to the char-a-banc drivers of
what the regulations are to be to enable them
to conform to the regulations in plenty of
time.
Motor Vehicles Bill-
Second Reading.
HOUSE OF COMMONS
[Mr. Johnstone]
I should like again to repeat what was
said by the hon. Member for Derry (Mrs.
Chichester) and that is, that motor accidents
are not always due to the driver. I am a
motor driver myself, and have been for a
great number of years, and I think it is
very largely due to the skill and care and
forethought displayed by motor drivers
generally that ten times the number of
accidents do not happen. (Hon. Members:
Hear, hear.) A great number of people in
Belfast seem to consider that the best way
to cross a road is to start at one corner and

the far corner of the road, and during the

the opposite way to that from which traffic
is likely to come. I beg to support the
