Mr. THOMAS HENDERSON: I wish to
support the Government in the introduction
of this very necessary Bill, but what rather
surprised me was the hard-heartedness of
every Member of this House. I refer to the
question of pillion-riding. I wonder if the
Minister of Home Affairs was 21 years of
age, and had a motor bicycle, would he be
so anxious to do away with pillion-riding.
I was also rather astonished that the hon.
lady Member for Derry allowed this occasion
to pass without challenging the Government
on this question. (Laughter.) Seeing that
the hon. lady Member has not done anything
to defend the ladies who are concerned in
this, I think the Minister should have made
some suggestion to the people who make
motor cycles that they should introduce some
sort of trailer in the event of a young man
wanting to bring a young lady away into the
country. After all it is most essential to do
something for these young ladies. (Laughter.)
I heard the hon. Member for the University
(Dr. Morrison) speaking about the risk men
take for a small prize of no importance.
But what about the young lady that is presomething for these young ladies. (Laughter.)
Yet everyone in this House to-day is prepared to support the Minister of Home Affairs
in his attempt to do away with pillion-riding.
When the question of pillion-riding comes up
in the Committee stage I am going to defend
the modern young lady of to-day.
There is one very important thing about
which the Minister should take more precautions, and that is the question of granting
licences to people for passenger-carrying
vehicles. They should grant no licence to
any individual unless he is in a position to
pay heavy compensation in case of accident.
Take for instance some bus running from
various country districts to the centre of the
city. I know a good number of people who
own that class of vehicle, and if there was an
accident to-morrow they could not pay the
people they have killed one farthing damages.
I think the Minister should see that no person like that is granted a licence at all.
The Minister of Home Affairs has spoken
about reckless driving, but the Minister has
not performed the duty he ought to have
done, and which is a duty the Minister has
got to do, and that is to provide motorists
with proper roads. It is most essential that
the roads should be wide enough, to have
them constructed in such a way as to have
slow and fast traffic. Take the road from
this to Lisburn. The Minister himself has
sat in his office and silently allowed people to
build right almost on the edge of the road.
with the result that in the event of the
Government or urban councils wishing to
widen them they cannot do it. He should
compel the county councils. Even in Belfast
the same thing happens, and it should be the
duty of the Minister to stop these people
from building so near the road that it would
be impossible to widen the roads to the
extent of about 100 feet.
Mr. ANDREWS: That is the law.
Mr. THOMAS HENDERSON: I know the
law was made for landgrabbers. It used to
be the law of the land that no road could be
constructed less than 100 feet. That was
amended in such a way that no road can be
constructed less than 30 feet. The day has
come, and I hope the Minister of Home
Affairs will see to this, that no local authority
will be allowed to construct a road unless it
is 100 feet wide. If he does that there will
be less talk of reckless driving, because there
will be a portion of the road for slow traffic
and a portion for fast traffic.
I sincerely hope that the Minister of Home
Affairs, as he has got a staff of engineers at
his command, will try to do something for
motorists, for apparently every time he comes
to this House there is always some legislation
being brought in to penalise motorists. ]
have noticed that Members are always very
anxious about overcrowding. Why are buses
overcrowded? Because people cannot afford
to pay the huge prices railway companies demand to take them from a country town into
Belfast. If the railway companies would
reduce their fares by about 50 per cent.
instead of being down and out as they are,
which many of the Members on the opposite
side know if they would reduce their fares
by about 50 per cent. they would begin to

prosper. The reason the bus people are prospering so well is because they provide cheap
travelling facilities for the people.
The only thing I am anxious about myself
is that the Minister will see that these people
he grants licences to will be in a position to
pay compensation in the event of an accident

Mr. ELLIOTT: I am only going to occupy
the attention of the House for a very few
minutes. I would say that I congratulate
the Government on bringing in this Bill
dealing with motor traffic. There are one or
two slight alterations I would like to see the

But when the hon. Member for North Belfast, who has just sat down, got up I was
trying to follow his argument, and I was
expecting to hear him going on to urge the
claims of the Belfast City Council to prohibit
buses entering the city area.
Mr. THOMAS HENDERSON: No, no.
Mr. ELLIOTT: However he did not pursue
that argument so far, but he was talking
about buses and roads not being wide enough,

the houses in the country. We want to see

who think that members living in the

As far as pillion-riding is concerned I do
not think the hon. Member who advocated
the claims of pillion-riding will have any

am delighted that the Minister and the
Government are doing away with pillionriding. I think that is one thing that the
majority of people in Northern Ireland will
be very well satisfied to wipe out. I congratulate the right hon. Gentleman who
introduced the Bill on his lucid explanation
of it. I hope some slight alterations will be
made that will make the Bill acceptable to
Members on this side as well as to Members
on the other side of the House
Mr. LEEKE: I agree with the views that
have been expressed by Members of this
House as to the necessity for this Bill. The
continuous and evergrowing volume of traffic
necessitated some action to be taken by the
authorities. I agree also with the remarks
of Members who have spoken to-day when
they say that further legislation must be
introduced when the trade increases. At the
same time there are many irritating clauses
in this Bill which I would ask the Government to consider and remove, to make the
Bill useful and to get the good opinion and
support of motorists themselves.
There is one thing, and that is about the
farmer's lights. Surely the Government
does not seriously intend to insist on farmers
carrying rear lights on vehicles. You must
remember that most of these vehicles are
going at a very slow pace. The motorist
following lights up the road for a hundred
yards, and it is nearly impossible for an
accident to occur in that case. It is only
a way the Government have probably taken
for raising more revenue and putting a tax
on the farmer.
The next point is as regards licences of
motorists. It is very irritating to insist on
motorists carrying their licences
on all
occasions. Some accident could happen
where a man would leave his licence behind,
and it would be ridiculous to insist upon
fining him on that occasion. I think a
broader view should be taken, because the
police and they are not too busy-could
easily find out and verify the statements
made by the driver by taking his number
and name and address, and if he did not
produce the licence in sufficient time I
should say action should be taken. It is not
so, as I have heard some Members here say,
that you have always to carry your railway
ticket. You have not. If you give your
name and address and they verify the fact
that you have a ticket it is passed over. I
appeal to the Minister of Home Affairs to
take that into consideration.
The next question is that it should be
placed in the hands of R.M.'s. I entirely
disagree, because I hold that R.M.'s do not
always give the same justice as is given by
the ordinary magistrates, because these
magistrates understand local conditions
better, and are in a better position to judge
fairly. I think above all things legislation
going to be administered as regards motorists
should remain in the hands of the ordinary
justices.
You are all aware of the great advantage
afforded to the farming community by the
motor omnibus. There is no doubt it is of
the greatest convenience. His produce is
picked up at his door, where originally be
had to drive to the station, and consequently
more profit is left to the farmer.
I would suggest that every encouragement
should be given to these vehicles and that no
unfair restrictions should be placed on
them or anything done that will retard this
growing industry.
Motor Vehicles Bill-
Second Reading.
HOUSE OF COMMONS
[Mr. Leeke]
On the question of the speed limit I hold
that the old limit of twenty miles an hour
was too low because it meant that you were
placing these buses in such a position that
they could not compete with railways.
When you consider the number of stops that
occur in a fifty miles journey you can understand how long it will take a bus to complete
that journey as compared with a railway
train which is not under any restriction as
regards speed. I would also ask the Government to take into consideration the question
of the roads, which was mentioned by the
Member for Antrim (Mr. Crawford). If
motorists have to pay high taxes the least
they can ask for is that local authorities
should receive greater grants SO that
motorists can have the better roads for
which they are paying. That would make
motoring for them more economical and
would tend to develop the trade of the
Province. I hope the Government will consider these questions, and if they administer
the Bill in a broad and reasonable manner
it might confer very great benefits on the
community.
Mr. HANNA: I do not think any person
in my position could complain of the general
tone of the criticisms that have been offered
in regard to this Bill, and I may say it is
a matter of great gratification to the
Government that so many Members of the
House have taken such a keen and lively interest in the Bill. I would like at the earliest
possible moment to assure the House that
the Members of the Government are exceedingly anxious that when the Bill is converted into an Act of Parliament it should
have the unanimous approval and support
of every Member of the House. This is
not really a matter about which we should
be very much in disagreement. The general
principle of the Bill has been admitted by
every hon. Member who has spoken. It is
acknowledged and frankly and openly stated
that the time has now come when it was an
urgent obligation on the Government to take
steps to deal with this problem.
In answer to the hon. Member for East
Belfast (Mr. Gyle) who asked whether or
not it was intended to make any departure
from the ordinary proofs in criminal law in
regard to criminal offences, I want to give
him the assurance that the onus in every
case will be on those who
accuse. The
persons who accuse will, as hitherto, have to
prove their own case. In answer to the
hon. Member for South Belfast (Mr. Black)
who raised the question of parking places,
that will be dealt with more conveniently
and effectively in a Bill that will soon be
introduced in this House in connection with
the roads. In that Bill the greatest consideration will be given to the matters the
hon, and learned Member alluded to.
In regard to the question of the fixing of
stands, I have no doubt that the matter
will be easily accommodated. Already the
Minister of Home Affairs has arranged a
conference with the members of the Belfast
Corporation and I do not think there will
be any difficulty about that question. The
first Clause of the Bill has been discussed
and criticised very generally; in fact it has
been criticised by every hon. Member who
has spoken. The Clause as you find it in
the Bill is an exact repetition of the words
in the old Motor Car Act of 1903. I want to
say that if there is any reasonable apprehension that that first Clause of the Bill
can possibly be interpreted in the sense in
which some hon. Members understand it,
namely, that the penalty mentioned in the
Clause would apply to an act of inadvertence or simple negligence, that is not the
intention of the Government. That has
been the law since 1903, and I venture to
say that no hon. Member can point to a
case where simple negligence has entailed
that penalty. However, the Government are
prepared to have such an alteration made
in that Section of the Bill as will secure
that only those who drive recklessly or
wantonly to the danger of the public will
have this penalty inflicted upon them.
Assuming we have made such alterations
as may be necessary to ensure that, I want
then to ask the House this question: Why
the tears over the fine of £5? If a man
drives recklessly it means that he drives
deliberately and wantonly, and with such
abandon that he is not at all concerned with
such matters as the safety of the lives of the
public and the convenience and comfort of
other people. That is the gentleman we want
to get at. Who says that a fine of £5 is too
much for that man, or that if he is placed
with a drunken person he is out of his
crowd? Now that the House knows what
our intention is I hope it will not spill any
more tears over gentlemen who do these
things recklessly and without any regard for
the safety of other people. I was interested
and a little bit surprised to hear so many
complaints that we had brought the reckless
driver and the drunken driver in charge of
a car into such close touch with each other.
I remember reading the most ancient law code
that exists, where murderers and adulterers
and thieves were all brought in very close
together, and in the last section of that
ancient code, a neighbour's wife and his
servant and his ox and his ass were joined
up, and nobody ever complained about that.
I do not think it really matters whether
they are placed in the position we have
placed them in this Bill or whether you give
them each a section to themselves, but if the
House is anxious that we should put them a
little further apart, I have no doubt we will
be able to accommodate both classes of
individuals.
Motor Vehicles Bill-
Second Reading.
13 OCTOBER 1926
Now I come to this question of a minimum
penalty. This law has been in existence since
1903. Inside the past year, as the Minister
of Home Affairs stated yesterday, offences
against that law have been proven in over
one thousand cases. There have been 1,300
accidents during the past year, 759 people
have been grievously injured, and 59 people
have been killed. It is perfectly obvious
that the fines that have been inflicted in the
past have not helped to put a stop to this
thing. The minimum penalties only apply
in the more serious cases, and I venture to
say that no Member of this House could
conceive circumstances where a grievous
offence has been committed in which the
minimum penalty is not a fitting and suitable
penalty to inflict.
Let me disabuse the mind of any hon.
Member of this House who thinks it is the
intention or desire of the Government to
wage a vendetta against motorists. That is
not the case. The Government is anxious
that every motorist and every member of
the general public should be in entire sympathy with them in regard to this Measure,
but let it be widely known now that
from the moment this Bill is passed, and
passed with the acclamation and consent of
every Member of this House, it will be administered by way of a vendetta against
those who disobey that law. It is essential
that the interests of the great majority of
motorists and of the public generally should
he protected.
With reference to the speed limit in areas,
I would like to inform the House that there
are only two areas in Northern Ireland
where a speed limit applies to-day; that is,
a speed limit as distinct from the ordinary
twenty miles speed limit. One is on the
front at Bangor and the other is in the town
of Carrickfergus. Five applications have
been recently made to the Minister of Home
Affairs for permission to establish speed
limits in other areas. That permission was
refused, and the Government have abolished
all speed limits, and they want this House
and the public to understand that it will be
only after the most careful investigation,
when all the people interested will have a
right to be heard, that any local area will
be allowed to have a speed limit. The intention is to carry out the spirit of this Bill
and to get rid of speed limits as far as
possible.
As the hon. Member for West Belfast (Sir
Robert Lynn) said yesterday, one could conceive motorists driving at 45 miles an hour
without any danger to the public, while in
other areas, such as towns, a speed of ten
or twelve miles an hour might be dangerous.
Look, for instance, at Carrickfergus, with
that narrow street the shape of the letter Z.
We all recognise that until some alteration
is made to that street it would be dangerous
to drive at even a moderate speed through
that town. I give the House the assurance
that it will be only in cases of that kind
that the Ministry of Home Affairs will allow
anything in the nature of a speed limit to
be fixed in any local area.
I have been asked by the hon. Member
for West Belfast (Sir Robert Lynn) to say
something about the cost of this scheme, and
I would ask the House to accept this from
me, that it is too soon to make any pronouncement or to give any detailed figures.
The House will recognise that what we have
set out to do is to bring about a state of the
law that will secure safety for the public
at the lowest possible cost. I have been
advised in regard to this matter-and my
advisers are not without hope-that this
whole scheme will be entirely self-supporting,
and that there will be no cost to the taxpayer. The cost will all come, as the House
thoroughly appreciates, out of the Road
Fund. I hope hon. Members will keep that
in their mind when they come to deal in
Committee with the question of the price of
the licences and the other duties imposed
under this Bill.
The hon. Member for West Belfast asked
yesterday about the Special Constabulary.
There will be no great increase in the
number of police, a very few extra will be
all that will be required to be brought in.
It will be essential that at the head of this
scheme in each county there shall be a
man of technical skill in motor engineering,
and I would like to say that it is the intention of those in authority, when they come
to select individuals for the particular work
that they will have to do under this Bill,
to have regard to the men's knowledge of
motor engineering and their skill and experience, and that no other matter will be
taken into consideration in connection with
the making of the appointments that have
to be made.
Mr. DEVLIN: I do not like to interrupt
the hon. and learned Gentleman, but I would
like to know whether, when these men are
appointed, concurrently with the announcement of their appointment, there will be
given a statement of their qualifications?
Mr. HANNA: I do not know that I can
promise any such thing. That would be a
rather extraordinary step, but I have not the
slightest doubt that when the matter comes
to be debated on the Estimates inquiries will
be made then as to their qualifications. An
hon. Member suggested that in no place in
the world did a policeman stop a bus and
make an examination. I would like the
House to understand thoroughly that no
extra powers are being given to the police

HOUSE OF COMMONS
[Mr. Hanna]
generally. The same powers that the ordin- '
ary police have exercised for the last
twenty-three years will be exercised by them
under this Measure. A few special police

I went to London with the right hon.
Gentleman, the Minister of Home Affairs, to
make inquiries in regard to this matter, and
while we were in Scotland Yard a bus was
brought in. It had been plying for hire in
the streets until a few minutes before the
time we saw it. One of the skilled servants of
Scotland Yard had noticed that the bus was
defective. One of the spokes was cracked
clean through, and he immediately had it
brought in for inspection. When I tell you
that it will be only a matter of eight or ten
of these gentlemen, twelve at the most, for
the whole of the Six Counties, there need be
no fear that the buses will be continually
stopped, and that the people will be put to
very great inconvenience. That such
thing as I have described can happen is a
matter of very great satisfaction to the
general public of London. The General
Omnibus Company, to whom this particular
bus belonged, made no complaint in regard
to the matter at all, because they are their
own insurers, and had there been an accident
on that bus, had it broken down and people
been injured, they would have been liable.
Instead of being worried and annoyed by
any inconvenience that attaches to the periodical examination, they rather welcome it.
a
The hon. Member for East Belfast (Mr.
Beattie) was the first to raise the point about
a driver going out inadvertently without his
licence. He told us in his speech to-day that
it was possible to drive a horse and cart
through most of the law, and he wanted three
days' grace for the gentleman who failed to
carry his licence. There is no change in the
law in this regard, and I have not the
slightest doubt in my mind that if a reputable licensed driver would say to the policeman who stopped him that he had forgotten
his licence, that he had changed his clothes,
or put up any reasonable and fair proposition, he would be allowed to come down to
see the district-inspector, and that would be
an end of the matter. But let me instance
this case. Some hon. Members in this House
are fortunate enough to be the owners of
motor cars, and some of them drive up to
this building, leaving their cars at the front.
Suppose a gentleman got into one of those
cars while the hon. Member was giving of
his wisdom and eloquence to this House, and
as he drove through the gate the policeman
asked him for his licence. Suppose he said,
"I changed my clothes because I got wet,
and I left it at home. I will bring it to
you within three days." What explanation
could we give to the hon, Member? Why,
he would never leave the Home Office until
we had established as many more policemen
as we have now, in order to find the gentleman who had gone away in his car.
No, every honest man who has a licence
will have no difficulty in making his case
good. It is wonderful how the policeman
can just spot the man who has left his licence
at home out of the hundreds of motorists
who are passing by. Remember this, the
policeman has to make a report to his
district-inspector. if he sees some reckless
driving on the road he makes a report to his
district-inspector, who carefully examines
the evidence in every case before any prosecution is directed. That is the first protection that a member of the public has.
The second is this, a policeman comes into
court and he has to prove his case; he has
got to state the facts on which he relies to
establish the guilt of the person he accuses,
and it is the judge, whoever he may be, the
R.M., the ordinary magistrate, or the county
court judge, who determines the matter as
to whether the driver was reckless or whatever the point at issue in the case may be.
I have no sympathy with the man who forgets his licence and who leaves it behind.
If we are to make a success of this Measure,
if we are to succeed in putting down these
irregularities and these offences, it can only
be when all motorists join in assisting us,
when they carry their licences with them
and give us the opportunity of identifying
those who are not really entitled to drive.
The hon. Member also made a suggestion
about different lights on different sides of
the motor car. That will be considered later
on.
The hon. Member for West Belfast (Mr.
William McMullen) raised the question of
third party insurance. If hon. Members
will look at the Bill, they will find on page
11 what the Government propose to do in
this regard. Clause C provides that
no such licence shall be issued unless the
applicant shows to the reasonable satisfaction of the Ministry of Home Affairs
that he will be in a position to satisfy all
lawful claims which may be made against
him in respect to damage to persons or to
property caused by the use upon public
highways of any public service vehicle for
which the licence is sought.
If the owner of a bus, whether a private
individual or a company, can satisfy the
Ministry of Home Affairs that he is in a
position to meet his liabilities, then it will
not be necessary in those circumstances that
the bus should be insured; but if he is not,
then a proper policy from a proper insurance
company will be accepted by the Ministry

ance with the facts. Any person coming
over to Ireland from England or Scotland
will find that his licence is available here,
and similarly a licence granted in Northern
Ireland is available for driving in Great
Britain. I am not at all without hope that
it may be possible that a reciprocal arrangement may be entered into with our nearer
neighbours in regard to this matter.
of Home Affairs as sufficient evidence of the
fact that he will be able to meet such demands as may fall upon him as a result of
his ownership of the machine. But the
Government have not thought fit to introduce a system of compulsory third-party
insurance at the present time. That clause
applies to all passenger-carrying vehicles.
The hon. Member also asked me, when I
came to reply, to say something about the
hours of work. I understand that full
opportunity will be given for discussion of
that matter in the course of a very few days,
but I respectfully submit that it is just outside the scope of this Bill, which is simply
a Bill to deal with the traffic regulations. I
am not in a position to make any pronouncement on that matter, but I have no
doubt it will be considered when it is
raised.
In regard to overcrowding, I just want to
say a few words. When a bus is licensed
to carry a certain number of people it
should be distinctly understood that the law
in that regard must necessarily be obeyed
and respected, because very often a bus is
insured, and insured only so long as it
carries a certain number of passengers. If
that number is exceeded it may be by the
terms of the policy that the insurance is
taken away altogether. You can readily
understand, apart from all the other considerations that have been indicated, when
you take that into account it is absolutely
essential that overcrowding must not be
tolerated or allowed.
A point has been raised by the hon. Member for West Belfast in regard to licence
duty, but what he suggests is not in accord-
I need not delay the House by going any
further into the matters that have been
touched upon. But I do want to say to hon.
Members that it is hoped that every Member
of this House will take a continued interest
in this Measure, and when it reaches
the Committee stage, the Government will be
glad to consider everything that is consistent with the spirit of the Bill as it appears
now, and that will bring about the desired
end, so that when the Bill becomes an Act
it will be something that will have the
approval of every Member of the House and
will represent the unanimous view of the
House in regard to the safety of the public.
(Hon. Members: Hear, hear.)

HOUSE OF COMMONS.

Thursday, 14th October, 1926.
The House met at Three of the clock, Mr.
SPEAKER in the Chair.
Paper Presented to Parliament.

Oral Answers to Questions.
LOAN TO ULSTER FARMERS'
PRODUCE COMPANY.
con-
1. Mr. ELLIOTT asked the Minister of
Finance whether it is a fact that the Government have subsidised the Ulster Farmers'
Produce Company by contributing a
siderable sum to tide them over a period of
financial embarrassment; what amount was
actually contributed; for what purpose was
this money given; and whether, as this is a
purely trading concern, the Government are
prepared to consider applications for financial assistance from other trading concerns
who find themselves similarly embarrassed.
2. Mr. ELLIOTT asked the Minister of
Finance whether in view of the fact that the
Ulster Farmers' Produce Company, in their
balance sheet, as at 27th June, 1925, showed
a loss on the year's trading of £14,532 18s 11d,
and at the same time also showed a balance
owing to the Ulster Bank, Limited, of
£16,265 18s 4d, the action of the Government
in advancing money to that company was
justified.
3. Mr. ELLIOTT asked the Minister of
Finance whether he will state upon whose
recommendation a grant was given to the
Farmers' Produce Company, and the account
in which this transaction appears.
THE MINISTER OF FINANCE (Mr.
Pollock) I propose to take questions 1, 2, and
3 together, as obviously they are connected
with the same subject.
As my hon. Friend has already been informed by letter dated 1st July last, he is in
error in assuming that the Government has
subsidised or given grants to the Ulster Farmers' Produce Society. Following the practice of the British Government in its policy
of assistance to agriculture, whereby the
Imperial Ministry of Agriculture is empowered to make loans to Co-operative enterprises registered under the Industrial and
Provident Societies Acts, our Government
has agreed to make a loan of £15,000 to the
Ulster Farmers' Produce Society on approved
security.
This loan has been made from the Govern
ment Loans Fund under the provisions of
Section 5 of the Exchequer and Financial
Provisions Act, 1923, and the corresponding
Act of 1925. The transaction will duly appear
in the annual account of the Loans Fund;
and I may add that under the terms of these
Statutes, any loss which may be occasioned
to the State as a result of transactions of
this character must be brought to the notice
of Parliament.
These Acts give power to my Ministry to
make loans for the same purposes as the
Department of Agriculture made before the
transfer of services, and as a matter of fact
similar loans have been made by that Department over a long series of years to societies
formed to develop agricultural trading, and
the decision of my Ministry in making the
loan referred to was dictated solely by the
considered policy of the Government of encouraging and assisting agriculture in every
possible way. I am advised that the membership of the Ulster Farmers' Produce Society
is approximately at the present time 3,000,
all of whom are farmers.
As to the alleged antecedent losses of the
trading company out of which the present
Co-operative Society was formed, I am informed that considerable losses had actually
been incurred through exceptional circumstances, which I am satisfied will not recur.
I am certainly prepared at any time to
receive applications from similarly constituted agricultural societies for assistance in
the form of repayable loans.
Mr. ELLIOTT: I beg to give notice that I
will raise this matter on the adjournment,
as I consider the answer unsatisfactory.
ENTERTAINMENT TAX.
4. Mr. DEVLIN asked the Minister of
Finance whether his attention has been called
to a speech delivered by Mr. J. F. Strain,
President of the Northern Branch of the
Irish Rugby Union, on the 17th September,
in which he said the Government is now enforcing the payment of a heavy tax on club
members' subscriptions, and that one club, in
order to save itself from extinction through
the tax, has decided to make no charge for
admission to their matches; and what steps
he proposes to take to remove this tax on
sport.
Mr. POLLOCK: I have read the Press
report of the speech to which the hon.
Member refers. The charging of Entertainments Tax on subscriptions paid by members
Oral Answers.
Oral Answers.
14 OCTOBER 1926
of Sports Clubs is not a new departure. The
practice is being followed which has been in
force both here and in Great Britain since the
Entertainments Duty which was first introduced in 1916, and in fact the Finance (New
Duties) Act, 1916, provides specifically that
where the payment for admission to an entertainment is made by means of a lump sum
paid as a subscription or contribution to any
Club, the Entertainments Duty shall be paid
on the amount of the lump sum.
The Government can see no reason why
these payments made by members, which are
in the nature of a consolidated payment to
view a certain number of games, should be
entitled to exemption from the Tax any more
than payments made by persons at the time
of admission to the field of play.
Mr. DEVLIN: Will the right hon. Gentleman answer the last paragraph of the question-what steps do you propose to take to
remove this tax?
Mr. POLLOCK: I can very easily answer
that. I do not propose to take any steps to
remove the tax.
Mr. DEVLIN: Will the right hon. Gentleman give some explanation as to why there is
a differentiation between the tax that exists
in Great Britain and that in Northern Ircland in view of the oft-repeated boasts of the
right hon. Gentleman and his Government
that the standards in Great Britain and
Northern Ireland are the same?
Mr. POLLOCK: I can also answer that
question very readily. The reason for the
differentiation is because of the much graver
conditions existing in Northern Ireland than
those in Great Britain, and also because of
our extreme necessities as compared with
Great Britain financially.
Mr. GRANT: Arising out of the right hon.
Gentleman's reply, I would like to ask if his
attention has been called to another part of
Mr. Strain's speech in which he said it is not
exactly right to say that the Welsh International Rugby match had been transferred
to Dublin on account of the Entertainment
Tax. I would also like to ask him if it is not
a fact that in connection with the building
of the new Rugby ground at Ravenhill they
received large financial assistance from the
Government of Northern Ireland and yet at
that particular ground they refused to fly the
Union Jack, the flag of the country they received a money grant from?
Mr. POLLOCK: I am not aware fully of
the facts submitted by my hon. Friend, but
I have no doubt he has ample ground for the
statement he has made.
Mr. WILLIAM MCMULLEN: Might I ask
the right hon. Gentleman if this is the considered policy of the Government, and if we
can look to the Government for any change
of policy between now and the introduction
of the Budget in the direction of removing
the Entertainment Tax?
Mr. SPEAKER: I am afraid that question
is not in order because the Government cannot answer any question about their Budget
proposals.
Mr. DEVLIN: Is the right hon. Gentleman aware that if he continues this Entertainment Tax on the present basis he will get
no Entertainment Tax at all?
EXAMINATION OF TYPISTS.
5. Mr. DEVLIN asked the Minister of
Finance under what circumstances he
approved of the regulations respecting
limited competitive examination for the
situations of shorthand-typists and typists
in the Civil Service; whether it was not
understood that these positions were to be
open to all girls in Northern Ireland; and
whether he is of opinion that a limited
competition is the best method of securing
the most competent girls to fill vacancies.
Mr. POLLOCK: When setting up our Civil
Service establishments at the outset it was
decided that a proportion of the posts of
shorthand-typist and typist should be regarded as temporary until such time as it
could be seen from actual experience of the
work what number of permanent officers
would eventually be required.
As a result of this arrangement, a number
of girls who have rendered satisfactory service for considerable periods are still
employed on a temporary footing, and it was
considered that in fairness to them and as a
matter of equity the competition for any
permanent vacancies which at present exist
or which may arise in the immediate future
should be limited to these employees. In
this matter the Government has followed
the practice adopted by the Imperial
Authorities under similar circumstances.
As indicated in the Regulations to which
the hon. Member refers, it is proposed that
after 1st April, 1928, all vacancies in the
grades of typist shall be filled by open
competition.
Mr. DEVLIN: Is this not clearly an attempt to finally establish persons who get
these appointments because of the influence
they are able to exercise on the Government
by their supporters? May I also ask him if
he can justify the Regulation that candidates, who have not already been approved
by the Selection Board, require to obtain
the approval of that Board before presenting
themselves for examination. Will they come
before the Selection Board before they pass
the examination?

Mr. POLLOCK: They will come before the

OUTDOOR RELIEF FOR UNEMPLOYED.

to introduce legislation to enable the

special outdoor relief to relieve the acute
destitution which exists in that neighbourhood, largely due to the slackness in the
linen trade?
The MINISTER OF HOME AFFAIRS (Sir
Dawson Bates): The Ministry of Home
Affairs has been in close touch with the
Cookstown Board of Guardians in connection
with the distress prevailing in that area, and
it has been possible by administrative action
to accord to the Guardians the necessary
powers to meet the situation which has
arisen.
If at any time in the future it becomes
apparent that further powers are necessary,
I will have no hesitation in asking Parlia
ment to accord such powers.
Mr. WILLIAM MCMULLEN: Will the
right hon. Gentleman more specifically tell
us what these powers are? Has he extended

Sir DAWSON BATES: I have extended
Section 3 of the Act of 1923 to that district.
Mr. BEATTIE: Will the right hon. Gentleman tell us what Section 3 covers in a case
of this sort?
Mr. SPEAKER: That is a question more
for debate.

Sir DAWSON BATES: I am sure the

SIR RUSSELL SCOTT'S REPORT.
7. Mr. DEVLIN asked the Prime Minister
when he proposes to lay on the Table the
report of Sir Russell Scott, in relation to
his inquiry as to the economies which could
be effected in the cost of administration in
Northern Ireland.
Mr. POLLOCK: Sir Russell Scott's report
has been received and it is the intention of
the Government to circulate it to Members
at the earliest possible date. The reportwhich is addressed to the Prime Ministerraises questions of much importance, and
the Cabinet has decided that it is right that
the Prime Minister should have an opportunity of studying its recommendations before final decisions are arrived at.
Mr. DEVLIN: Might I ask the right hon.
Gentleman when his report was handed in
to the Cabinet.
Mr. POLLOCK: I am sorry I cannot
answer that question with accuracy, but it
must be some month or six weeks ago.
Mr. DEVLIN: Would the right hon. Gentleman say whether there was any intention
to publish this report until my question was
put down? (Laughter.)
REGULATION OF STREET TRADING.
8. Mr. ELLIOTT asked the Minister of
Commerce whether it is the intention of the
Government to introduce legislation in this
House during the present Session to regulate
street trading on similar lines to that which
has been passed by the Imperial Parliament.
The MINISTER OF COMMERCE (Mr.
Barbour): It is not the intention of the
Government to introduce legislation regulating street trading. If, as I assume, the
Imperial Measure referred to in the question
is the Bermondsey Borough Council (Street
Trading) Act, which was passed in July last,
I would point out that this was not a Government but a private Measure. As the hon.
Member is aware, it is open to any local
authority in Northern Ireland to promote a
Bill on similar lines.

Mr. ARCHDALE: When the Northern

ORDERS OF THE DAY.
Horsebreeding Bill.
Order for Second Reading read.
Motion made, and Question proposed:
"That the Bill be now read a Second Time."
Mr. ARCHDALE: Under the provisions
of the Horsebreeding Act of 1918 there are in
Ireland a number of unlicensed stallions
which, it is pretty clear, are being used for
stud purposes. Unfortunately the difficulty
of securing evidence that these unlicensed
stallions are being used for stud purposes is
so great that it has proved impossible under
the existing Act to remedy the abuse. Under
that Act it has to be proved that an unlicensed stallion has actually been used for
stud purposes. Now in various parts of the
country there are stallions that are carting
and used for various objects like that, and
which are continually being used for stud
purposes and no one can find out from police
knowledge or in any other way.
The main object of the new legislation is
to surmount the difficulty by providing that
stallions cannot be kept without either a
licence or a permit. Permits, which will be
given for very small sums, will be given for
the keeping of unlicensed stallions such as
racehorses, polo ponies, and various other
categories which will be described as
occasion requires.
Horsebreeding Bill-
Second Reading.
HOUSE OF COMMONS
[Mr. Archdale.]
In order to ensure that legal proceedings
will not be instituted merely for technical
offences the Bill contains a provision that
prosecutions are not to be instituted without
the consent of the Ministry. There are no
other new features in the Bill except continuing prosecutions. If a charge is made
that stallions are used for stud purposes
without being licensed there is a continuing
prosecution for each week if we find it advis
able to do such a thing. I beg to move.
Mr. LEEKE: I should like to make a few
remarks on this Bill and to oppose it. I
fully recognise with the Minister of Agriculture the necessity for improving horsebreeding in Ulster. I know that Ulster is
specially adapted for breeding agricultural
horses of the Clydesdale type. At the same
time I should like to point out that there are
some weaknesses in the scheme and also
some weaknesses in this Bill. Whether the
Department of Agriculture rcognise it or not
is another matter. The system they have of
bringing stallions to Northern Ireland for
breeding purposes such as light hunter
stallions is to my mind very weak. They
have brought in the past horses which if put
up in an auction room would not have
brought £50 per head, and yet I understand
the Department bought them at from £200
to, £250 per head. It is a regrettable
squandering of public money. I think a
Department as economical in many ways as
the Department of Agriculture should pay
greater attention to the question of the purchase system and the purchase of horses.
Also the question of judging is to my mind
very weak. The system you have presently
adopted, is sending a purchaser across to
England to purchase these horses-mostly
cast-offs from English studs-and bringing
them across here and you get someone to
take them in the counties and they are
allowed by the system of purchase to pay
for these horses which eventually become
their own property. That is quite all right
So far as it goes. Then in granting
premiums they allow the man who purchased
the horses to stand by the judge when he is
deciding whether these horses are suitable.
Naturally the first thing the official will do
is to recommend the judge to pass the horses
he has purchased in order that his opinion
may be justified. Why not have asked the
Department or county committees of agriculture to advise the judges and allow them
to have stewards, drawn from every area in
which the horses will stand, when the horses
are being judged for premiums.
The next point is regarding young horses.
What about blood stock colts, young colts
running on the grass? What is the Department doing about these horses? Are
they going to give them licences or is there
some reason for refusing and deterring what
is becoming an industry in Ulster? There is
some very good bloodstock raised in Ulster
at present. I think this is a coming industry which should be encouraged and no
undue restrictions should be placed in the
way of development.
There are other things. There are many
existing stallions to which the right hon.
Gentleman has referred. They are working on
farms. They are very old horses and the
only thing left for the owners of these
horses is to shoot them if this Bill is enforced. I think that licences other than for
breeding purposes should be given after due
consideration given to the facts submitted to
the inspectors. It should be taken into consideration whether these horses should not
remain when they cease to be of practical
use except for farm labour.
The Minister of Agriculture must know
that in Northern Ireland there are mountains
where little mountain ponies are raised
which are of great service to the poor man
in Ulster. How are they going to arrange
for licences for these horses? There are
herds of these ponies. What system is going
to be adopted. The Minister has told us that
he cannot find out where these horses are.
How are they going to be found out by this
Bill? It will be much better in cases where
the man is the owner of a stud of young ponies
if he is allowed to continue these ponies without the idea of sending the inspectors to
decide whether or not they should continue,
because, as a rule, inspectors sent are, in
my opinion, very inferior judges of horses.
What are the functions of the Advisory
Committee which, I understand, has been set
up? What do they advise them on? So far
as I can see horsebreeding in Northern Ireland is under the jurisdiction of about three
gentlemen who recommend certain things to
be carried out, and these, I suppose, they
carry out. They are to a great extent interested in horses themselves. The Advisory
Committee should be an independent committee. It should be drawn from the county
agricultural committees of Northern Ireland,
and not drawn from horse dealers and
veterinary surgeons who are financially interested. I hold an independent body should
be set up, and I oppose this Bill on the
grounds I have just stated.

also that it places too much power in the

Order for Second Reading read.
Motion made, and Question proposed:

Sir DAWSON BATES: This Bill is a very
simple one, and is one, I think, that will
require very few words from me. The object
of the Bill is to bring the matter of the protection of animals in Northern Ireland into
line with the law as it exists in Great
Britain. This Bill follows the lines laid
down in four Measures which do not apply
to Northern Ireland. I refer to the Captive
Birds Shooting (Prohibition) Act, 1921, the
Protection of Birds Act, 1925, the Protection
of Animals Act (1911) Amending Act, 1921,
and the Performing Animals Regulation
Act, 1925. We have in this Measure consolidated the principles contained in these
Acts. The first part of the Bill deals with.
the exhibition and training of performing
animals, and the first clause of the Bill provides that anybody who desires to exhibit
or train any performing animal must first
of all get a certificate of registration from
the Inspector-General of the R.U.C. In this
part of the Measure we are differing slightly
from the course followed in Great Britain,
where the certificate is issued by the local
authority. We feel that performing animals
are comparatively rare in this country, and
we think it would not cause any inconvenience to the exhibitor or trainer that he
should go to the central authority of the
Inspector-General. The second clause gives
1681 Protection of Animals Bill-

14 OCTOBER 1926
Second Reading.
jurisdiction to a summary court to make an
order on the production of proper evidence
prohibiting or restricting the performance
of these animals, and the third clause gives
power to the police to inspect any place
where training is going on or where the
animals are being exhibited. Clause 4 sets
out the penalties and offences. I may point
out that the Bill does not apply to the training or exhibition of animals for military,
police, agriculture or sporting purposes.
As regards the second part of the Bill, that
deals with the protection of birds, and we
make it an offence for individuals to use a
tethered live bird as a decoy for the capture
of wild birds and prohibit the use
of birdlime for the capture of wild
birds. I think Clause 8 will particularly
commend itself to those hon. Members
who are fond of birds. It prohibits the
keeping of a bird in a cage of such a size
that the bird cannot stretch its wings. With
regard to the exemptions, the Bill exempts
poultry and any bird that is being conveyed
over land or water for the purpose of exhibition or while it is being conveyed for
the purpose of being exhibited, if the time
during which it is so kept or confined does
not exceed 72 hours.
Clause 9 prohibits the shooting of captive
birds liberated for the purpose. I cannot
but think that this particular Clause will
also appeal to hon. Members. I am glad to
say that the practice of shooting pigeons
which have been confined for a period and
then released for the purpose of shooting
has very nearly disappeared out of Northern
Ireland. It has been stamped out in England
and we propose to follow the same practice
here. I think hon. Members will agree that
that practice cannot in any sense be regarded
as sport.
With regard to the third part of the Bill,
I would like to explain the exact meaning of
it, because Part III is only tagging on a
new Clause to an old Act of Parliament, and
it is rather unintelligible as the Bill stands
unless hon. Members refer to the previous
Act of Parliament. The effect of this Clause
really is to put the law relating to coursing
on all fours with that which exists in England. Under the Protection of Animals Act,
1911, coursing was legalised practically under
all circumstances, subject to the provision
that the hare or other animal that was to be
coursed was not to be released in an exhausted condition. Then followed the Protection of Animals Act, 1921, which I have
explained to the House does not apply to
Northern Ireland. That went a step further
and provided that a captive hare should only
be coursed in a place from which the animal
had a reasonable chance of escape. Although
this Act does not apply to Northern Ireland
the Irish Coursing Club framed their rules
on it and this Act was really in being. I
must say that that is exactly what I would
expect from the Irish Coursing Club.
May I refer to the particular rule, because,
after all, I am only asking the House to make
law the rule adopted by the Irish Coursing
Club? Their rule is this-I only intend to
read the very essential parts of it-
"A coursing park shall not be less than
400 yards long from where the dogs are
slipped to where the hare escapes, and the
breadth of the coursing grounds must be
at least 150 yards. The escape must consist
of a natural bank or planted fence and be
at least fifty yards wide. Canvas shall not
be used in the construction of same, nor
wooden shoots nor boxes."
Anybody who has followed coursing in
Northern Ireland must realise that there are
certain meetings held where these rules are
violated and where, may I say, the greatest
possible cruelty is shown to these animals.
Nothing can be finer than a good coursing
meeting, but at the same time nothing can
be more degrading than some of the meetings
held in Northern Ireland, meetings that do
not carry out the rules provided by the Irish
Coursing Club. I had an opportunity of
reading in the Press an article dealing with
this subject. I do not know whether the
writer had any knowledge that this Bill was
coming before this House, but he puts the
whole subject so simply that I hope hon.
Members will allow me to refer to it. He
says here, and he is apparently an expert on
the subject of coursing,
"It was real sport to watch a stout hare
beat her pursuers over the Raughlin
Meadows after a tight buckle for the lead
and a series of subsequent working interchanges which coursing lovers watch with
greater appreciation than the mere race for
the turn."
Then he goes on-
"On the other hand it was depressing to
see a captive hare, cramped to lameness
through confinement, released only to be
chopped without a chance of getting away
or without giving anything like a test of
the prowess of the pursuing dogs."
I cannot put my views better than those
expressed by the writer of that article. I feel
that this is a Measure with which all sportsmen will agree, and I ask this House to give
it a Second Reading.

But I was wondering exactly what

Having said that I do not know that there

have got no guarantee when those animals

As far as coursing is concerned, I have got
some remarks which I would like to make.
I have had a very considerable connection with
those interested in coursing for many years.
I think that this Clause which was embodied
in the Amending Act to the 1911 Act in 1921
in Great Britain may help not only to
abolish unnecessary cruelty at coursing
meetings but to purify the ancient
sport of coursing. I want to make my attitude towards this sport particularly clear.
As I have said, I have always been closely
associated with those interested in coursing.
I have been very much interested in it myself, and I think the trophies which I have
on my tables can testify to the fact that that
interest has not always been an unsuccessful
one. I want to make it perfectly plain that
I am not speaking to-day in any way as a
faddist. I am not out to abolish, I am out to
improve; and so I think that what I say may
carry a certain amount more weight than it
would if I were looked upon as a crank in
this connection.
I am convinced that the words which are
embodied in this Clause will do a great deal
to help to purify coursing and will do a great
deal to help the Irish Coursing Club, as Eas
been stated by the right hon. Gentleman who
introduced the Bill. As coursing is carried
on at some meetings in Northern Ireland today-of course, I am not referring to all
meetings-it cannot be called sport in any
sense of the word. It is a somewhat lowering
and degrading form of butchery. It is not
even a reasonable test of the quality and
speed and cleverness of a greyhound. I have
known a good many men who wanted to take
up coursing, and who, if they had taken it up,
would have been acquisitions to the coursing
world, but they went to some of the coursing

Second Reading.
[Mrs. Chichester]
meetings in Northern Ireland and were so
disgusted by what they saw that they gave
up all idea of becoming coursers. Quite apart
from the question of cruelty I should like to
see the level of this sport raised to what it
is across the water, and not only to what it
is across the water but to what it is at most
of the meetings in the Irish Free State. As
I said before, by introducing these words into
this Bill I believe we will be helping the
Irish Coursing Club, because their rules are
stricter than the rules of the National
Coursing Club, which is their parent body in
England. Some of the rules have been read
by the Minister who introduced the Bill, but
he did not mention one rule which in my
opinion is a very important one. It is to the
effect that
Any person knowingly running a greyhound at a meeting where the hares
have not been at liberty during
twenty-one days previous thereto shall
be disqualified from running a greyhound at any regular meeting during
the pleasure of the Standing Committee,
and every greyhound the registered property of such person shall in like manner
be disqualified; and any Club using boxed
or defective hares at a meeting shall be
liable to suspension.
That might at first sight not appear to be
relevant, but the point is that unless the
hares have their liberty a considerable
period before coursing takes place they are
in such a condition that there is not a
reasonable chance of escape for them. The
size of the coursing park has already been
read out and what the escape must consist
of. They go on and say further:
The Irish Coursing Club disapprove of
the holding of important stakes on grounds
that shall be less than 600 yards long and
proportionately wide, and that have not all
arrangements up to the required standard.
They ask for a sufficient space to be set apart
at the rere of the slipper for keeping the
hares to be coursed, and they must be allowed their liberty therein. They also state
that under no circumstances shall hares be
transferred from one end of the coursing
ground to the other while coursing is in
progress, and if any club shall attempt to do
so that cluby shall be suspended. They also
say:
The length of the slip must necessarily
vary with the nature of the ground, but
should never be less than from three to
four score yards, and must be maintained
in one uniform length as far as possible
throughout each stake.
It is obvious that if slipping is badly
managed and if the minimum length is not
given there can be no reasonable chance of
escape for the unfortunate animal which is
being coursed. I think hearing these rules
it would be impossible for us to do other
than to realise that this Clause will help to
strengthen the Irish Coursing Club's hands
in dealing with what is obviously an unfortunate state of affairs at some meetings
in Northern Ireland. In Great Britain ali
the meetings are open, and boxed hares are
not used. I have a letter from the secretary
of the National Coursing Club in England in
which he says:
Our object in England is to have good,
strong hares in a natural state.
He says further:
As you know, our object over here is to
provide extra escapes for the hares. I may
further add that no meetings which are
known as enclosed meetings are now in
vogue in this country.
Here, as you know, practically every meeting
is an enclosed meeting, and boxed hares are
used. When reading the article to which the
Minister has referred in a paper with which
the hon. Member for West Belfast (Sir Robert
Lynn) has some connection I could not help
thinking of all that I have heard of the past
glories of this very ancient sport in Ireland,
of the days when Master M'Grath figured here
and when coursing here was equal to, and
even better than, what takes place in Great
Britain. We wish to encourage sport-I am
quite sure we do as long as we can keep unnecessary cruelty out of it-we wish to encourage bigger people in the coursing world
to come over here and revive the past glories
of coursing in Ireland-to revive the past
glories of meetings such as were held at
Holestone, Creagh, and other places. Then
with these rules stricter than those that
obtain in England and with this Bill an Act
with the law behind it, I do hope that cruelty
will be eliminated, and that when public
attention is drawn to the state of affairs
reasonable chances of escape may be provided
and strong hares will be obtainable, and that
prosecutions may, and will, result with a
consequent general improvement in conditions.
I always feel that cruelty is largely due
to thoughtlessness, to want of realisation.
Once we understand there are really very few
of us who would wantonly inflict pain and
continue to do so. It is all very well for
people to speak as the hon. Member for West
Belfast (Mr. William McMullen) spoke to-day
of those who are interested in saving animals
from suffering, and to say as he said, "Are
there not human beings who are suffering
hourly and daily, and what are you doing
to help them?" Some time ago I read a
leading article in the "Morning Post" which
expressed my feelings on this subject so perfectly, and which I think is such an admirable answer to what was said by the hon.
Protection of Animals Bill--
14 OCTOBER 1926
Second Reading.
Member, that having written it down at the
time, as I was so interested, and having
brought it here, I propose to read an extract
from it, if I may be allowed to do so, to hon.
Members. It says:
Any act of cruelty, even any act of
negligence, committed on an animal is as
injurious to the doer as an act of cruelty
or of negligence to a human being; and the
injury is all the more dangerous because
he does not suspect that he is incurring it.
The effect of it is to dull and deaden the
sympathies, to begin or to increase an indifference which is so certain to coarsen the
fibre both of emotion and of spirit, and
therefore infallibly to induce in the cruel
person some measure of hardness or brutality in his dealings also with his fellowmen. Once we realise that cruelty is as
bad for the cruel as for the victim, it
becomes clear that those who work for the
protection of animals against man are
working also for the protection of man
against himself. And since far more cruel
things are done through ignorance and insensibility than through a morbid love of
inflicting pain, the champions of animals
may be discerned as doing for man a very
valuable work of education. When cruelty
to animals has disappeared from earth,
cruelty to man will have disappeared with
it.
Mr. Speaker, if any words of mine can have
the result of bringing home to any individual a realisation of the necessity for
improving the conditions in any coursing
meeting in Northern Ireland, or of saving
any helpless animals, however few, from unnecessary suffering, pain and misery, then
I do believe that a good day's work has been
done in connection with this Bill. In conclusion, I would thank the right hon. Gentleman once more for having introduced this
Measure.
Mr. T. W. McMULLAN: I welcome this
Bill which the Minister of Home Affairs has
introduced. As the last speaker has said, it
is a somewhat belated Measure, but it will
be welcomed by every lover of animals and

had to wait a considerable time for this Bill,
and I am glad that the promise which was

Looking through the Clauses, I was very
much interested in the suggestion of the
hon. Member for West Belfast (Mr. William
McMullen) with reference to Clause 3, Subsection 2. I think myself, in agreement with
him, that there is often cruelty practised
on animals in order to induce them to perform on the stage, and I do not see why a

Regarding Clause 8, under which it is
made obligatory that a bird confined in a

and breadth as to permit it freely to
stretch its wings, it may be due to my want

There is great cruelty in confining a bird in
such a way that it cannot stretch its wings,
and how under any
circumstances the
lengthening of the time of torture should
not be considered as a serious matter, if it
does not exceed 72 hours, passes my comprehension. I think 72 hours of cruelty to any
animal is a very severe and a very unworthy
act, and if Clause 8, Sub-section 2, has the
meaning that I read into it, I would press
for a change, so that cruelty to birds confined to cages should be eliminated as far as
possible.
So far as Clause 11 is concerned, I listened
with great interest to the splendid defence
of coursing to which we have been treated
by the hon. Member for Derry (Mrs.
Chichester). But I have to confess that I
have no sympathy with coursing. I have to

The points that I want to bring before

have been at a coursing meeting once, and
only once, and I would never think of going

that the habits of hares would run largely
on the lines of rabbits. I know this, that
if you have a rabbit hutch with a small
opening, if you start the rabbit back it will
run at once for the hole. If, on the other
hand, you reverse the opening, as I have
seen, it will dash for the place where the
opening used to be, and hit itself so violently
against the hutch that it will probably kill
itself. If that is so in the rabbit, it is probably the same in the case of the hare; it
does not know where it is going. You know
how cattle, especially sheep, will make a
track in a field, and will invariably follow
that track, even in snow. I think that to get
hares, to put them in a box, and to set them
free in a totally new atmosphere, with people
around and all the attendant confusion, does
not give the hares a reasonable opportunity
for escape. Therefore, I always thought
that it was an inhuman sport, and that it
should not be supported.
I listened with very great pleasure to the

I think if

The House should know that wild fowl,

Loans Guarantee [Money].
Considered in Committee under Standing
Order No. 65.
[Mr. MOLES in the Chair.]
Motion made, and Question proposed:
"That it is expedient to amend the Loans
Guarantee Acts (Northern Ireland), 1922-
1926, by increasing from seven million to
rine million pounds the limit on the aggregate capital amount of the loans, the
principal or interest of which may be guaranteed by the Ministry of Finance under the
Loans Guarantee Act (Northern Ireland),
1922; and by extending to the 31st day of
March, 1928, the period within which
guarantees may be given thereunder; and to
charge on the Consolidated Fund of Northern
Ireland any moneys required for fulfilling
any such guarantees."--Governor's Recommendation signified.-(Mr. Pollock.)
The FINANCIAL SECRETARY TO THE
MINISTRY OF FINANCE (Mr. Barbour):
This Resolution is the precursor of a Bill
which proposes to extend the powers of the
existing Loans Guarantee Acts in two
directions-
(a) By extending the limit of the amount
of the guarantees which may be given
from £7,000,000 to £9,000,000, and
(b) By extending the period during which
guarantees may be given by one year,
Without further legislation the powers of
the existing Acts would as regards new
guarantees expire at the end of the current
financial year, but it has been found necessary to bring this Resolution before the
Committee during the present Session on
account of the abnormal activities of the
Ministry of Finance during the past six
months in providing facilities to secure muchneeded employment, and in order that the
further undertakings now under contemplation may not be delayed by the absence
of Parliamentary powers.
In March last, when the limit was increased
from £6,000,000 to, £7,000,000, I informed the
Committee that the actual amount granted
up to that date amounted to £4,430,500. In
deciding at that time to increase the then
existing margin of approximately £1,500,000
to £2,500,000, the Government took into
account the probability of further shipbuilding orders which were in the offing, and I
am glad to be able to say that the hopes
which were then in our minds have to a
certain extent been realised. The present
position will be seen from the printed return which is now in the hands of hon.
Members, and which shows that facilities
amounting to £6,236,500 had been granted
up to 30th September of this year as against
the figure £4,430,900 as reported in March
last. The existing statutory limit is
£7,000,000, and there is further in hand a
balance of £763,500. But it is only right I
should acquaint the Committee of the fact
that negotiations are taking place at the
present time in connection with further
undertakings involving an additional sum
of approximately £1,500,000. Assuming that
these negotiations reach finality, and I have
no grounds for assuming otherwise, the issue
of these further facilities would bring about
excess of three-quarters of a million
pounds over the existing limit of £7,000,000.
I should like in bringing this before the
Committee to take the opportunity of thanking those gentlemen who constituted the
small committee that investigated the various
proposals brought before them, and decided
whether in the interests of protecting the
Exchequer the guarantees can be given.
desire to thank them for their constant care
and the repeated meetings that they have
attended for the consideration of these proposals. I trust the scrutiny they have given
them may result in no charge coming upon
the Exchequer in respect of the actual
guarantees themselves.

now to the first part of the

the maximum amount to a sum of £9,000,000,
that is, an increase of £2,000,000, and in
recommending this important step to the

a serious condition of unemployment would
justify the Government in pledging its credit
to a still larger extent.

From 1930 onwards till 1936 the amount

It will be observed, therefore, that the
Government's contingent liability falls very

Of the additional sum of £2,000,000 now
required approximately £750,000 has already
been earmarked, leaving a balance of approximately £1,250,000 for future developments.
Perhaps the more important part of the
Resolution will be found in the second
part, which proposes an extension of
this legislation for a further period
of one year from March 31st next. The
Government is satisfied, and I am confident
that this Committee will endorse the Government's view, that the employment situation
in the shipbuilding industry is such as to
warrant this further extension of time, not-
.withstanding that the British Government
do not propose to continue these facilities
within the area of Great Britain beyond
31st March next. I need not dwell at length
on the influences which have caused the
Imperial Government to take this step-they
were referred to by Mr. Churchill in his
Budget Speech-save to say that the same
influences do not operate in Ulster in the
same degree. The prosperity of the shipbuilding industry is one of the two hinges
upon which the industrial labour market
in Northern Ireland turns. That industry
would suffer by the withdrawal of these
facilities at a time when every encouragement and assistance the Government can
give is essential, and it is therefore with
confidence that I ask the Committee to pass
this Resolution.
The policy which it recommends has been
endorsed on past occasions by this Committee, and I need hardly emphasise further
the fact that its machinery has proved a
most valuable agent in the alleviation of
unemployment.
I should, perhaps, refer briefly to the new
feature which was introduced in the scheme
last March, and that is the power given to
the Government to make a limited contribution towards the interest charge payable on
guaranteed loans. The necessity for exercising this power has so far arisen only in
one case and the comparatively small grant
involved is the subject of a supplementary
estimate which is down on the Order Paper
for consideration this afternoon. I do not
propose at this stage to enter into the details
of this individual case. I may state, however,
that our efforts in the London market in the
matter of negotiating Government guaranteed loans at a favourable price on behalf of
shipping companies have been attended with
considerable success, showing that the credit
of the Province has been regarded by important London financial groups as being closely
related to that of the British Government.
The power to make interest contributions continues to operate although not specifically reenacted in the Bill which arises from this
Resolution. While theoretically the legislation only contemplates the issue of a guarantee by the Government, it is obviously a
function of my Ministry to assist the applicant in placing the Government's guarantee
to the best possible advantage as regards
price, and consequently it is customary for
my Department to carry out on behalf of the
applicant the entire negotiation with the
lenders. I wish to make this clear, because
in some quarters the impression appears to
exist that the Government itself actually
makes advances. What the Government does
is to guarantee such loan as the borrower may
be able to secure in order to carry out work
in contemplation.
But as regards this interest payment
in respect of any differences of interest
that may arise between the less favourable rate which we are able to secure
in connection with Northern Ireland
Government guaranteed loans and that which
a borrower may be able to get in connection
with a British guaranteed loan, this has only
arisen in one case, and I am glad to say that
the amount of the interest difference which
we shall require to make up is only a comparatively small sum. In this particular case
instead of paying the difference annually
between such rates of interest we have been
able to commute or compound that difference
by making a single payment, which I think
will work out very much more satisfactorily.
I have already stated the fact that the
contingent liability which this Government
undertakes in connection with guaranteeing
these loans is one which I hope will never
materialise if proper care is taken in scrutinising the conditions under which the guarantee is given, and I trust that our estimate
as to the entire solvency of the parties concerned will be well founded during the life of
our guarantee. I beg to move.

CLASS II. No. 10.
LOANS GUARANTEE CONTRIBUTION.
Motion made and Question proposed:
a
"That sum not exceeding £6,870 be
granted to his Majesty for the service of the
year ending on the 31st of March, 1927, to
provide for a contributory payment towards
interest charges under Section 2 (1) (b) of the
Loans Guarantee Act (Northern Ireland),
1926."
Mr. BARBOUR: In moving this Supplementary Estimate, which follows very
appropriately on the discussion we have just
had in connection with the Loans Guarantee
Act, I should recall to hon. Members the
statement which the Minister of Finance
(Mr. Pollock) made in March last when the
question of a State contribution towards
interest charges was under consideration.
My right hon. Friend then stated that
applicants in receipt of our Guarantees
found themselves more or less dependent
upon London instead of local sources for
raising their loans, and hinted that it
was only to be expected that Ulster credit
in the British market should stand fractionally lower than that of the British Government-a circumstance which naturally
involves the shipowner or other applicant
in a slightly increased rate of interest on
borrowings as compared with what would be
the case were the ship to be constructed in
some English or Scottish shipbuilding yard,
and, therefore, to enjoy the benefit of the
British guarantee.
The Government, therefore, asked to be
placed in a position to ensure that a shipowner who is prepared to place his order
in Northern Ireland under the Northern
Ireland guarantee should not have to pay a
higher price for his money on that account,
and the Act passed in March last gave the
Ministry discretion within narrow limits
to contribute to the interest charges, if
such should prove to be necessary, in order
to bridge the gap between the interest
charged on the Imperial Government guaranteed loan and the Northern Ireland
guarantee loan. The necessity for exercising this power has so far arisen in the
case of only one transaction, and it is that
that is the subject of this Supplementary
Estimate. The shipowners were informed
that in the event of the order being obtained
by a Northern Ireland firm the Ministry
would ensure that the loan in question---
one of £650,000, repayable over a period of
twelve years-would be available on the
same terms as if raised under the British
guarantee.
The sum of £6,870, which is now before the
Committee, represents what I may call a
commuted payment in respect of the difference between the interest rate commanded by
the Northern Government guarantee and that
which would have been commanded by a
British Government guarantee in respect of a
similar loan of £650,000. Owing to the fact
that we were prepared to pay a lump sum
down instead of, as I said a few minutes
ago, the difference of interest yearly during
the currency of the loan the amount is considerably less than would have been payable
had we made this annual payment, and the
sum we are now asking for is equal to some
fraction of one-tenth of one per cent. in
the way of interest on the full amount of
the loan. I beg to move.
Question put, and agreed to.

Mr. ELLIOTT: According to the notice
which I gave earlier this afternoon, and because I did not believe that the answers
given to some questions of mine were
explicit enough, I desire to raise a question
which I think is of some importance to the
Government of Northern Ireland, and which
I know is at the same time of a great deal of
importance to some traders in Northern
Ireland. About the year 1923 the Ulster
Farmers' Produce Company came into being.
That was purely a trading company and,
according to their own prospectus,
formed to purchase as a going concern on
the 30th day of June, 1923, the well-known
business of Warden & Stewart, Limited,
carried on for many years as produce
merchants," and so on. The company came
into being in 1923 for the purpose of carrying on this produce business and for getting
a controlling interest. According to the
prospectus
was
"The chief object of the Company is to
secure for farmers a controlling interest in
the sale of their produce, and the profits
accruing therefrom, which at the present
time go into the pockets of private individuals."
So that the company was formed as a purely
limited liability company and trading concern for the purpose of putting the profits,
which were going into the pockets of
private individuals, into the pockets of the
shareholders and directors of this newlyformed trading concern.
Now this Ulster Farmers' Produce Company
did not turn out to be the financial success
that those who promoted it had intended
that it should be, because in the year 1925,
according to the balance sheet which I produce here, at the ordinary general meeting
when the balance sheet was declared, they
found that on the year's trading they had
lost £14,532 18s. 11d., and at the same time
they owed the Ulster Bank the sum of
£16,265, 18s. 4d. In the notice convening that
meeting we read:--
"For the reason stated it will be readily
understood that the year under review has
been one during which the Board have
had grave anxiety and great trouble in
grappling with the ever-recurrent difficulties and problems. In their endeavours
to discharge their duties, and in their
efforts to do the utmost possible on behalf
of the Company, they have each shouldered
heavy responsibilities and individually incurred grave financial risks. So convinced
are they still of the possibilities of the
Company as a help to farmers, of profit to
the shareholders, and of its indispensability to Ulster agriculture generally,
that they have addressed themselves
to the task of reconstructing the
Company in such a way as to afford an
opportunity of securing the necessary
financial help to enable it successfully to
achieve the objects that were in view when
it was originally promoted."
That is from the second annual report of the
Board, and I wish to point out quite clearly
that this Ulster Farmers' Produce Company
has no connection whatever with the Ulster
Farmers' Union. The grant which has been
made to the Ulster Farmers' Union was one
with which I never agreed, because I believe
that it was given by the Ministry of Agriculture for the purpose of ensuring the
sympathy and support of the Ulster Farmers'
Union, so that they could count on the cooperation of those who represent that Union
on any agricultural committees they were on.
The grant was one I did not agree with, but
I must say that it has nothing whatever to
do with the present item that appears in the
question I asked, because we read in the
prospectus of the Company that
in the
"The Company, while working
closest conjunction with the Ulster
Farmers' Union, is a separate and distinct
undertaking, and involves in no way the

The Government propose to support
either by loans or by guarantees Cooperative enterprises controlled by the
agricultural community, organised and
directed mainly to deal with agricultural
produce, the buying of raw materials,
seeds, manure, etc., in order to assist
agriculture generally.
I need not enter into any further details of
the matter, but that is the general policy
of the British Government with respect to
the agricultural interest in Great Britain.
