CLAUSE 10 (Grants of licences for public
service vehicles and penalties for use of unlicensed vehicles).
(1) The Ministry of Home Affairs may
from time to time license to stand or ply
for hire, and to carry passengers for hire,
public service vehicles of such different
classes, to be distinguished in such manner,
as may be prescribed.
Any licence in respect of a public service
vehicle under this section may be granted
upon payment of such fee (not exceeding
two pounds) and on such conditions, be in
such form, be subject to revocation or suspension in such events, and generally be
dealt with, in such manner as may be prescribed:
Provided that-
(a) a licence for a public service vehicle
shall, if not revoked or suspended, be
in force for one year;
(b) the fee to be paid in respect of such
licences shall be uniform in respect of
all public service vehicles of a particular class;
(c) no such licence shall be issued unless
the applicant shows to the reasonable
satisfaction of the Ministry of Home
Affairs that he will be in a position to
satisfy all lawful claims which may be
made against him in respect of damage
to persons or to property caused by the
use upon public highways of any public
service vehicle for which the licence is
sought.
(2) If any unlicensed public service
vehicle is used in standing or plying for
hire or is used to carry passengers for hire,
the owner of such vehicle shall be liable
to a fine of one pound or any greater sum
not exceeding ten pounds for every day
during which such vehicle is so used. The
driver and conductor also shall in every
such case be liable to a like penalty.

The PRIME MINISTER: On the point
that the Clause stand part, I can make a

think this is a very important point. The
Government have considered very carefully,
indeed, the question of enlarging the scope
of the insurance of third party interests,
and for various reasons we thought it would
be wise, in view of the fact that this Bill is
a Measure covering a great deal of ground,
to pause before we went any further in the
realm of compulsory third party insurance
of motor cars generally. There are, as I
daresay hon Members will realise, very
great difficulties in compelling persons of
humble means, owning small cars, to take
out third party insurance policies. Firstly,
the cost of the policy does not depend to any
great degree upon the value of the actual
motor vehicle. It depends upon the third
party risk against which the policy is intended to protect the insuree. In order
to cover certain vehicles, I fear-and my
colleagues agree with me-that the tariff that
might be imposed by the Insurance Companies would raise the cost of insurance
generally throughout the whole realm, on
motor car insurance for that risk.
Secondly, and the very important point
arises, these vehicles may be seldom used.
We will take the case of farmers. Perhaps
on very few occasions in the week, and along
a road to a market town where there is
practically no risk at all, if they were
compelled, under this Bill, to take out a
full third party insurance policy, they would
be paying a premium each year perhaps far
in excess of the licence duty or anything
like it. The risk is comparatively small, and
yet the farming community would be
charged with this very large cost, in addition to the other charges under the Act.
Then again there is the third great objection of launching out in this matter under
this Bill. It is quite obvious to everybody
that the motor industry and motor traffic

CLAUSE 11 (Licensing of drivers and conductors).
(1) No public service vehicle shall stand
or ply for hire or carry passengers for
hire unless the driver holds a licence
granted by the Ministry of Home Affairs,
or (where the vehicle is a vehicle of a class
which is required by regulations to carry
a conductor) the driver and conductor,
respectively, hold such licences.
If any public service vehicle stands or
plies for hire or carries passengers in contravention of this section, the person
driving the vehicle shall be liable to a fine
of one pound or any greater sum not exceeding five pounds, and the owner of the
vehicle shall be liable to a like penalty
unless he proves that the driver or conductor (as the case may require) acted
without his privity or consent.
(2) No conductor shall be employed in
or about a public service vehicle unless
he holds a licence granted by the Ministry
of Home Affairs, and any unlicensed person
employed as such conductor shall be liable
to a penalty of one pound or any greater
sum not exceeding five pounds.
(3) A licence to the driver or conductor
of a public service vehicle may be granted
upon payment of such fee (not exceeding
ten shillings in the case of a driver, and
five shillings in the case of a conductor)
and on such conditions, be in such form,
be subject to revocation or suspension in
such events, and generally be dealt with,
in such manner as may be prescribed:
Provided that-
(a) a driver's or conductor's licence shall,
if not revoked or suspended, be in
force for one year;
(b) a driver's licence shall not be issued
to any person unless he is twenty-one
or more years of age and satisfies the
Ministry of Home Affairs that he is in
all respects fit to discharge the duties,
and is competent to drive a public service vehicle of the type, for which he
requires the driver's licence;
(c) a conductor's licence shall not be
issued to any person unless he is
eighteen or more years of age and
satisfies the Ministry of Home Affairs
that he is capable of discharging the
duties required of him as such conductor.

2 NOVEMBER 1926
HOUSE OF COMMONS.

Tuesday, 2nd November, 1926.
The House met at Three of the clock, Mr.
SPEAKER in the Chair.
Oral Answers to Questions.
ROBERT
MCCULLY-MEDICAL RELIEF
IN NEWTOWNARDS DISTRICT.
1. Mr. KYLE asked the Minister of Home
Affairs whether he has received any communication from the Newtownards Board of
Guardians regarding the action of Dr.
Jamison, jun., in refusing to give medical
relief to a son of Mrs. McCully, Loughview,
Newtownards, and what action he proposed
to take to ensure that the poor in the Newtownards district feceive the treatment to
which they are entitled by law, and whether
he is prepared to hold a sworn inquiry in
this case.
The MINISTER OF HOME AFFAIRS (Sir
Dawson Bates): Representations have been
made to the Ministry of Home Affairs regarding the delay on the part of Dr.
Jamison, jun., in attending Robert McCully.
Preliminary inquiries have been made by
the Ministry's medical inspector into the
case, and as there appears to be some conflict
of statement in the matter the Ministry
propose to hold a sworn inquiry into the
whole case.
DEPOSIT FEE AT LOCAL GOVERNMENT
ELECTIONS.
ex-
2. Mr. KYLE asked the Minister of Home
Affairs whether, in view of the expressed
opinion of the organised workers as
pressed by the Labour Party of Northern
Ireland, in favour of the abolition of the
deposit fee on nomination for election to city
councils, rural councils, county councils and
Poor-Law Guardians, he is prepared to
consider the desirability of making the
necessary statutory changes to effect this
object.
Sir DAWSON BATES: The principle of a
deposit fee on nomination for Local
Government elections was embodied in the
Local Government Act (N.I.), 1922, passed by
the Parliament of Northern Ireland.
The object of this provision was to put a
stop to spurious and bogus nominations in
connection with these elections, which had
been a common practice in the past, and
which involved the ratepayers and bona-fide
candidates in considerable expense.
I am not prepared to consider the question
of introducing legislation amending the law
in the above respect.
Mr. KYLE: Is the right hon. Gentleman
aware that he is not following on parallel
lines with Great Britain in making that
statement, and, in view of the fact that it
has always been the declared intention of the
Government to follow on parallel lines with
Great Britain, would he not pursue that
course in this particular reform?
Sir DAWSON BATES: My hon. Friend
differs from me. The Government do not
consider that this is a reform, and propose to.
carry on as they have been doing under this
Act.
CONDITIONS IN RETAIL DISTRIBUTION
TRADES.
3. Mr. KYLE asked the Minister of Labour
whether, in view of the sweating conditions
obtaining in the Retail Distribution Trades,
he is prepared to take the necessary steps to
have these trades brought within the provisions of the Trade Boards Acts.
The MINISTER OF LABOUR (Mr.
Andrews): No evidence of sweating conditions
in the Retail Distributive Trades in Northern
Ireland having come before my Department,
it is not considered expedient in present circumstances to apply the Trade Boards Act
to these trades.
Should the hon. Member, however, possess
substantial information pointing in the direction of sweating, I shall be obliged if he will
bring it to my notice.
Mr. KYLE: And if I am able to bring the
information to the right hon. Gentleman,
will he give this House an assurance that he
will introduce the Trade Board?
Mr. ANDREWS: I will consider the question carefully when he brings the evidence
before me.
AMALGAMATION OF BELFAST BOARDS.
4. Mr. KYLE asked the Prime Minister
whether he is aware that the Belfast City
Council passed a resolution, at a regular
monthly meeting, that it was desirable
that the Belfast Harbour Trust, Belfast
Water Commissioners, and the Belfast Poor
Law Guardians should be amalgamated with
the City Council, and whether he is prepared
to bring in legislation to this desired end.
Sir DAWSON BATES: I have been asked
by the Prime Minister to reply.
I am not aware that the Belfast Corporation have passed a resolution in the terms
indicated in the hon. Member's question.
I understand that about three years ago
certain Committees of the Corporation had
2099 Oral Answers.

HOUSE OF COMMONS
Oral Answers.
[Sir Dawson Bates]
under consideration the question of bringing
forward a Private Bill, one of the purposes
of which was to transfer to the Corporation
the powers and duties of the Belfast City and
District Water Commissioners.
This particular proposal fell through and
was not proceeded with.
In the above circumstances and having
regard to the fact that the whole question
of local government administration is forming the subject of inquiry by a special
Commission, I am not prepared to consider
the question of any legislation in this respect
at present.
hon.
Mr. KYLE: Would the right
Gentleman tell us when we might hope to
get the report of this Commission?
Sir DAWSON BATES: I have already indicated, in answer to a question put to me by
one of my hon. Friend's colleagues, that the
whole matter is very lengthy, and involves
a great many inquiries, and that I could not
state the specific time when the Report will
come out, but I can assure him at the same
time that the Commission are losing no time
in dealing with this very difficult subject.
REGISTRATION IN HAIRDRESSING
TRADE.
5. Mr. KYLE asked the Prime Minister
whether he is aware that a scheme of registration would meet with the approval of both
employers and employees in the hairdressing
trade, and whether he is prepared to initiate
legislation to give effect to this united request of employers and employees.
Sir DAWSON BATES: I have been asked
to reply.
The Government have received no representations on this matter, and, accordingly,
I am unable to express any opinion or give
any undertaking in connection with the desirability of or necessity for introducing
legislation as suggested.
COST OF LIVING IN NORTHERN
IRELAND.
6. Mr. KYLE asked the Prime Minister
whether, in view of the conflicting opinion
as to the amount of wages necessary to maintain a family, he is prepared to set un a
Commission to ascertain the wage necessary
to provide the basic needs of a family as has
been done in Australia.
Mr. ANDREWS: I have been asked to
reply to this question addressed to the Prime
Minister.
I would like to remind the hon. Member
that an exhaustive inquiry was held recently
in regard to the cost of living in Northern
Ireland, which disclosed the difficulty of obtaining incontrovertible information on a
matter of this kind.
With regard to the Commission appointed
in Australia, to which the hon. Member refers, I would point out that it has been found
impracticable to give effect to its conclusions,
and, in my opinion, therefore, no useful
purpose would, under existing circumstances,
be served by incurring the expense of establishing a similar Commission here.
Mr. KYLE: Does the right hon. Gentleman not consider that it is very useful information to have from the point of view of
the organised worker, and from the point of
view of the organised employer, as to what
the basic wage ought to be in order to provide the necessaries for a man, his wife and
three children in Northern Ireland, and as
he has had the example of Australia, might
he not take that example here and apply it
so that we might get for employers and
employees actual facts beyond dispute as to
the amount of money it would take to enable
a man to keep his family in decency and
comfort in Northern Ireland?
Mr. ANDREWS: Owing to the rise and fall
which takes place in the cost of living the
position is very frequently changing, and,
therefore, the conclusions that might be
arrived at at one particular period would not
be applicable to another particular period.
Again, I may say that the Australian Commission which considered the matter arrived
at certain conclusions, but it was found absolutely impracticable to give effect to them,
because all the available wealth of
Australia would not have enabled the wages
suggested to be paid.

CLAUSE 12 (Penalties for overcrowding of
public service vehicles).
(1) Where a greater number of persons
is carried on a public service vehicle than
the number prescribed for such vehicle, the
owner and also the conductor thereof shall
be guilty of an offence against this section.
and shall be liable on summary conviction
to such penalty as is hereinafter in this
section provided for such offence; and, for
the purposes of this section, the driver of
a vehicle shall be deemed to be its conductor if he is in sole charge thereof.
(2) The penalties for offences against this
section shall be as follows:-
In the case of the owner-
(a) for
a first offence, a
pound;
fine of one
(b) for a second offence, a fine of one
pound or any greater sum not exceeding five pounds;
(c) for a third or subsequent offence, a
fine of one pound or any greater sum
not exceeding ten pounds;
(d) for each offence, an additional fine of
two shillings and sixpence for each
person carried in excess of the prescribed number;
In the case of the conductor, a fine of
two shillings and sixpence for each
person carried in excess of the prescribed number.
(3) Any court before whom a person is
convicted of an offence against this section
shall cause particulars of the conviction to
be endorsed upon the licences issued under
this Part of this Act for the vehicle in
respect of which the offence has been committed and for the conductor of that
vehicle, and shall cause a copy of those
particulars to be sent to the Ministry of
Home Affairs; and that Ministry shall
have power, in the case of a third or subsequent offence against this section, to revoke any such licence for such period as
it may think fit, having regard to the circumstances of the case and to any recommendation of the court below whom the
person was convicted.
(4) Every person, being the holder, as
owner or conductor of a vehicle, of any
licence issued under this Part of this Act,
who is charged with any offence against
this section shall bring such licence into
court at the hearing of the charge and
shall, if so required, produce the same to
the court for the purpose of endorsement,
and, if he fails so to bring or produce
such licence, shall be guilty of an offence
under this Act.

Mr. KYLE: I beg to move in page 13, line
17, after "each" ("for each person") insert
"adult." The reason I want the word "adult"
inserted there is to prevent hardship being
inflicted on the persons who ride in chars-abancs or public vehicles. It is also to prevent
certain things occurring. Supposing
children's party was going off on an excursion on one of these vehicles, such as has
been organised by an hon. Member of this
Committee, it seems to me that this Bill
would prevent a char-a-banc being allowed
to carry more than the number of persons
mentioned in the Schedule. A vehicle that
could carry 32 adults could quite easily carry
50 children, and it is in order to prevent
hardships in that way that I suggest that the
word "adult" should be put in before the word
"person." I do not know that there is any
Motor Vehicles Bill-
Committee.
HOUSE OF COMMONS
[Mr. Kyle]
necessity to press this very much. I am sure
the Minister of Home Affairs will see the
desirability of amending the Measure in this
particular connection. I know it is easy for
him or anybody else to make fun of this
particular Amendment.
Sir DAWSON BATES: No, no.
Mr. KYLE: I know it would be quite easy,
because I can see the difficulties myself.
There is no reason why the position of motor
owners should not be made easy in this
respect. It would prevent hardship being
done in the way I have indicated. The difficulty I see in the matter is that there has
to be some limitation as to the number of
persons to be carried on these motor vehicles.
It would be to the advantage of the Measure
to insert the word "adult" before the word
"person."
Sir DAWSON BATES: I would point out
to my hon. Friend that under Clause 17 of
the Bill power is given to the Ministry to
make regulations describing the type of
vehicle and the number of persons to be
carried. I think it would be a hardship, as
my hon. Friend has pointed out, if two small
children were not allowed to take the place
of one adult. I am sure that the Ministry
when they come to make regulations under
Clause 17 will very carefully consider
the point mentioned by my hon. Friend.
Mr. BEATTIE: I beg to support the
Amendment because if this word "adult" is
not inserted a danger will arise. I have
noticed in these buses children with their
parents, and two of them have been put in as
one person. The bus owners are very sympathetic as regards children travelling with
their parents, and in some cases they do not
make any charge for young "kiddies." The
owners should be protected, because an inspector may come along and seeing a number
of young children he may make a complaint
of overcrowding. I am sure that the
Minister, whether he is prepared to make a
regulation or not, should feel it incumbent
on him to insert the word "adult" in the
Bill. It would afford some source of protection for the bus owner.
Sir ROBERT ANDERSON: I think that
there is probably in the minds of the hon.
Members who have spoken a lack of
appreciation of the meaning they attach
to the word "adult." An adult is a person
over 15 years of age. If you allow a lot of
people below that age into a bus the very
object for which you are passing legislation
will be defeated. If you allow 15 or 20 young
people below 14 years to be crowded into a
bus why the danger would be terrible. There
might be a holocaust and a lot of young lives
lost. If you allow a lot of people from eight
to fourteen years of age to be put into a bus
there would certainly be overcrowding, and
no bus owner should be allowed to let such
a thing take place. What perhaps is operating in the minds of my hon. Friends opposite
is babies or children under four years of age
travelling with their fathers and mothers.
To substitute the word "adult" would
be a dangerous thing. It would leave it open
to any person to put a number of children
from eight to twelve years of age on a bus,
and the risk would be very serious.
Mr. KYLE: I am not desirous of making
it easy for the bus owners to overcrowd their
vehicles, and I join with the hon. Member
(Sir Robert Anderson) in deprecating any
overcrowding on any motor vehicle. It is
obvious to me, however, that where you can
seat five adults in a char-a-bane you could
easily seat seven or eight young people
between the ages of six and thirteen. I have
seen chars-a-bancs going off with crowds of
children of various ages. I think from my
reading of this Measure that a char-a-banc
owner would be prevented from putting more
than 32 persons into a bus, where, in my
opinion, it would be easy to put 40 youngsters. From that point of view I would like
to see the word "adult" inserted there. As the
Bill stands without that word being inserted
the police would be entitled to stop these
chars-a-bancs on account of the number of
passengers being carried, and prosecute the
motor owner by reason of the fact that he
had over and above the scheduled number
of persons in the vehicle. It is simply and
solely for that reason, and for that reason
alone that I desire to see the word "adult"
inserted there.
Mr. CRAWFORD: May I say that I object
to the word "adult" being inserted there for
another reason rather than the one given.
Two persons in a certain town may each
own a bus.
One may be paying a higher
duty than the other, and it would be unfair
for the man paying the lower duty to be
allowed to carry more passengers than the
other. At the same time I have great
sympathy with what the hon. Member (Mr.
Kyle) has said. I think the Minister should
give an assurance that in the regulations to
be made that provision in the case of excursionists should not be rigidly applied to
the exact number of passengers. I hope the
right hon. Gentleman will give that assurance. Personally I would not vote for the
word "adult" being inserted at all.
Sir DAWSON BATES: I drew my hon.
Friend's (Mr. Kyle's) attention to Clause 17.
and if he turns to Sub-clause (c) he will see
that power is given for regulating the number
of passengers who may be carried in any
such vehicle, and the space to be allotted to
each person. My hon. Friend has not
attempted to say what is an adult-whether
an adult is a person of 16, 17 or 18 years of
age, and to put it, as he suggests, in the Bill
would be absolutely impracticable. In the

CLAUSE 13 (Amendment of law as to certain offences in connection with public stage
carriages) ordered to stand part of the Bill.
CLAUSE 14 (Provisions as to vehicles used
to carry passengers whilst unsafe).
Any duly authorised officer shall have
power to stop and examine any public service vehicle whilst plying for hire or
carrying passengers for hire, and, if satisfied that the vehicle does not comply with
the Regulations prescribed for ensuring the
safety of passengers and that danger to the
passengers of the vehicle is likely to ensue,
shall have power to require that the passengers shall leave the vehicle and that
suitable arrangements shall be made by the
owner of the vehicle for the immediate conveyance of the passengers to the places to
which they are entitled to travel on the
vehicle. If the owner of such vehicle fails
to make, to the satisfaction of such officer,
suitable arrangements as aforesaid, he shall
be liable on summary conviction to a fine
not exceeding twenty pounds.

Sir DAWSON BATES: I beg to move in
Clause 14, page 14, lines 23 and 24, to leave
out "to the satisfaction of such officer."
A point was raised during the Second
Reading that this Clause gave too much power
to a policeman where a vehicle broke down
and where the policeman ordered the passengers out and directed the owner of that
machine to convey the passengers to a destination to his satisfaction. There is a great
deal to be said for it and so we propose to
leave out the words "to the satisfaction of
such officer." In future it will be left to the
discretion of the court in regard to all the
circumstances of the case.
Mr. BEATTIE: The Clause reads:
"Suitable arrangements shall be made by
the owner of the vehicle for the immediate
conveyance of the passengers to the places
to which they are entitled to travel on the
vehicle. If the owner of such vehicle fails
to make, to the satisfaction of such officer,
suitable arrangements as aforesaid, he shall
be liable on summary conviction to a fine
not exceeding twenty pounds."
I would like a reasonable arrangement, but I
find it is going to be left out. (Hon. Members:
No, no).
Sir DAWSON BATES: Might I explain to
my hon. Friend? We propose simply to
delete the words "to the satisfaction of such
officer." It still imposes upon the owner of
the machine the necessity of making arrangements for the conveying of the passengers to
their destinations. If the police officer considers he has not made proper arrangements
he can bring the case into court, and it will
be entirely a matter for the court to decide
in all the circumstances whether or not the
arrangements made were suitable and proper.
Sir ROBERT ANDERSON: That covers
the point in an Amendment I have down dealing with the same subject. By the deletion
of these words the Minister has provided for
the necessary arrangements being made, and
that is what I wanted to have done.

This is to make it perfectly clear that the
numerical strength of the Royal Ulster Constabulary is not to be increased beyond the
strength laid down in the Police Act of 1922.
As I pointed out, in reply to the remarks
that were made during the Second Reading,
the intention of the Government was to have
this Act carried out as economically
possible, and the best way to do that is
through the police. At the same time I
think it is right to point out that it may be
necessary to bring in two or three experts,
technical men who have a knowledge of
motoring engineering; but, even if they are
brought in, the total number of men employed in the Royal Ulster Constabularyand those men for the time being will be in
the Royal Ulster Constabulary-must in no
circumstances exceed the number laid down
by the Police Act. If there are any other
questions that hon. Members would like to
ask, I shall be only too glad to answer them.

from this part of the Committee. He has

Therefore you are going to appoint further

I do not believe the hon. Member for Derry
understood that when he withdrew his

Regarding the question raised in regard
to myself, that I had been deceived, and
that the numbers would be increased without
my knowledge, really I think it is a very
simple thing to carry out what the Minister
of Home Affairs has indicated. I think the
Parliamentary Secretary stated
the
Second Reading that a very small number
of men would really be required under this
Bill. I think he said 12 or 15 would probably
be the extra men needed. It is a very simple
thing to do. Instead of filling up the
vacancies that at present exist and that arise
from week to week in the Royal Ulster Constabulary from ordinary recruits, these
ordinary recruits need not be taken and the
men specially wanted under this particular
Bill can be secured. My hon. Friend told
us the qualifications that would be needed
were very simple. I take leave to say that
if he will consider the matter a little more
closely he will see that certain types of men
will be needed if the provisions of this Bill
are to be adequately carried out. It is,
moreover, not an ordinary policeman you
want to examine whether a motor bus or a
char-a-bane from a mechanical point of
view is a safe machine to put out.
The same thing applies to the men who
may have a taxi or a couple of vehicles
plying for hire here. Under the provisions
of this Bill the inspector would have power
to put these machines off the road and
destroy a man's livelihood if he were not
satisfied they were in proper condition to
carry passengers. Therefore, I say the type
of man that will be necessary is a type of
man that you may not have at the moment
in the ranks of the Royal Ulster Constabulary. You may have some of them. I
grant you that at once. I do not know
what their qualifications may be. But 1
think it is absolutely necessary to give the
Minister of Home Affairs power so that he
may take on as men who will be entrusted
with this serious responsibility, men of
efficiency, men that will know their job and
know it well, so that the work that is going
to be done under this Bill will be done in
such a way that the public will
have absolute confidence that these vehicles
that are going to ply for hire and
that they are going to occupy will
be safe for them, and that they are to be
adequately protected as regards the men
that are going to be appointed by the owners
of the buses and the owners of these vehicles
that are going to ply for hire. Also that the
men who are going to examine them and
report and possibly condemn them will be
well qualified for the job. That, I think, is
the reply to the point raised by the hon.
Member for West Belfast (Mr. Devlin).
In regard to the other point about who is
going to be taken on, Englishmen, and so
forth, the numbers that will be required are
so small that I hope that within our own
territory the men that will be needed
will be secured. I have no reason to doubt
that they will.

CLAUSE 16 (Cessation of licensing powers
of certain local authorities).
2 NOVEMBER 1926
Motor Vehicles Bill-

Committee
The Ministry of Home Affairs shall have
power to make regulations (either as
respects all public service vehicles or as
respects public service vehicles of any prescribed class) for all or any of the following
purposes:-
As from the appointed day, the powers
conferred by any general or local Act upon
the council of any county borough or urban
district or the commissioners of any town,
in connection with the licensing of public
service vehicles (by whatever name called)
and their drivers and conductors, including
the power of making and enforcing byelaws for the inspection of such vehicles,
ensuring their fitness for public hire and
preventing overcrowding thereon, shall
cease to be exerciseable; and any licences
issued by any such council or commissioners
in respect of public service vehicles and
their drivers and conductors shall cease to
be operative as from such date or dates as
may be prescribed.
Sir DAWSON BATES: I beg to move, in

with the licensing of public) and to insert

This Amendment and the two following
Amendments are moved in order to make
it perfectly clear that all necessary powers
in connection with the licensing of public
service vehicles shall be transferred to the
Ministry of Home Affairs without at the
same time interfering with statutory or other
provisions which are local in character and
which it is still necessary should be retained
by the local authorities. I beg to move.
Amendment agreed to.
Sir DAWSON BATES: I beg to move, in

Now, in this House we have been discussing
for some time past Bills of infinitesimal
importance. We have been discussing the
Eggs Bill, and the Protection of Animals
Bill, and the Motor Bill, and I think there
were slight soundings here and there in

The right hon. Gentleman did what I have
never known done in any Parliament before.
He selected himself as the Member
Government to discharge the duty of proposing the rejection of this Measure. It is not
customary for a Member of the Government,
and especially a Member of the Government
dealing with Labour problems, to move the
rejection of a Private Member's Bill. Why
did not he leave it to the eloquent, though
ever constantly silent, supporters behind
him? This ought not to have been a Government transaction at all. It should have
been left to the free judgment of the Members
of the House, and I say in the most unqualified terms that I think it was wrong for
the Minister of Labour to have constituted
himself the chief spokesman of the policy
of hostility to a Measure of this character.
But the strange thing about it was that the
right hon. Gentleman, who, as I have said,
is a very humane if not emotional Minister,
and who is genuinely interested in the welfare of the poor, and who was selected to
discharge this duty, is in favour of the Bill
in principle. He does not contradict that.
The right hon. Gentleman is in favour of the
Bill in principle, because here is what he
said about it:
"I quite agree that if a man is asked to
drive a char-a-banc on the streets of a
congested city such as this for the greater
part of eight hours a day he has earned his
daily bread faithfully and well, because he
has undergone admittedly a considerable
mental and physical strain."
And then the right hon. Gentleman went on
with some exaggeration:
"But consider the difference between the
work which that man has performed and
that of some other driver who is asked to
drive a motor char-a-banc in a country
district, say in Fermanagh and Tyrone,
where the vehicles which one meets are few
and far between, and where the traffic
which is available for these chars-abancs to carry is necessarily restricted."
-(Official Report, Vol. 7, No. 24, Cols. 1915,
1916).
But instead of replying to that observation,
or reservation I should say, I will quote the
reply which one of his most loyal followers
delivered with complete promptitude immediately the right hon. Gentleman sat down.
I do not know whether the right hon. Gentleman is a motorist or not-I take it that he
has had some experience-but I think he will
admit, and has admitted in the speech which
he delivered in moving the rejection of this
Bill, that there could be no more laborious
or nerve-racking pursuit in which anyone
could be engaged than in driving or conducting a char-a-bane or motor lorry. He says
that may be true in Belfast but it is not
true in the country districts of Northern
Ireland. What is the reply to that? In
terms more effective than I can use, here is
the answer: The hon. Member for the University (Mr. Johnstone) replying said:
"I must say that I totally disagree with
what the Minister of Labour said on this
point. I think there is just as much care
and just as much foresight required to drive
a motor-car along a country road in Tyrone
or Fermanagh as is necessary in the city of
Belfast, because it is on the country roads
that you are very apt to find someone come
suddenly out of a side road when you are
least expecting it, and you are into an
accident before you know where you are.
Whereas in driving in a large town you are
on the alert all the time. In the country
you are apt to be lulled into a false sense of
security. I think that both from the point
of view of the man himself and of the travelling public there should be a restriction of
the number of hours he is allowed to drive."
-(Official Report, Vol. 7, No. 24, Col. 1926).

Now what does the Measure propose to do?
It proposes to restrict the working hours of
a man engaged in this most laborious and,
as I say, never-racking pursuit, to limit his
working day to eight hours, forty-eight hours

Mr. MCALLISTER: I beg to
19, to leave out the first sub-Section. I am
opposed to this sub-Clause because it introduces a highly obnoxious principle.
Sir DAWSON BATES: Perhaps my hon.
Friend will tell the Committee which sub-
Section he refers to. In the Amendment it
says "page 19, sub-section (1).”
Mr. MCALLISTER: Page 19, line 1. I am
opposed-
The CHAIRMAN: It is sub-Section (2) I
take it?
Mr. MCALLISTER: Yes. I am opposed
to this sub-Section, because it introduces a
highly obnoxious system of legislation. We
find that it is a principle of justice and a
tradition of the law that a man is presumed
to be innocent until he is proved guilty.
Recently legislation has been introduced in
this House in which the onus of proof is very
frequently cast on the defendant. I suggest
that is surely a bad principle on which to
base a code of legislation, such as the motor
law or any other penal legislation. Instead
of a man being presumed innocent until he
is proved guilty under this Clause a man
will be presumed to be guilty until he proves
his innocence.
I can imagine the dilemma of a judge of
long experience in the criminal courts- the
dilemma in which he will find himself if he
has to deal with this particular sub-Clause
as it stands at present. His whole training
has taught him to presume the innocence of
the defendant until his guilt is proved. 1
can imagine his dilemma when a man comes
before him on a serious and grave issue.
There is a conflict of testimony and serious
and grave doubt as to which way to give his
decision. By this Section he is compelled to
convict a man whom he believes possibly to
be innocent, although he is not in a position.
as very often occurs, to give proof of his innocence. Those of us engaged in the law are
in a position to appreciate the difficulty in
which we often find ourselves. We know, we
are perfectly convinced that a person is innocent, but it is another thing to prove or to
get evidence to establish that position. On
these grounds I am opposed strongly to this
principle of legislation in casting the onus
of proof on the defendant in a criminal
charge, which should not be put upon his
shoulders.
Sir DAWSON BATES: My hon. Friend has
suggested that this is a new principle. I
may point out to him that this is simply
taken from the old Act, an Act in operation
for the last 23 years. Up to the present time
I have never heard anybody question it or
say that it is anything but proper. My hon.
Friend will readily understand that the facts
of the case must be within the knowledge of
the defendant. I can imagine a case where
an individual having his engine passed at a
full test, subsequently goes and puts in a new
engine and represents that that is the engine
that has been tested. Surely that is not a
Clause that will work any injustice. It has
never worked any injustice in the past, and
I trust will not work any injustice in the
future.
Mr. GYLE: On the Second Reading of this
Bill I raised this question. I was assured
that there was nothing in the Bill that threw
the onus of proving his innocence on anyone
that would be brought up for a default under
the Bill. I was specifically assured that
there was nothing in the Bill of that nature.
I had in my mind that I saw it somewhere,
but at the moment I was not able to point
out the Clause. I know it will create a grave
injustice, because I know that under another
Bill it has created grave injustice where the
onus of proof is thrown on the defendant. I
hope the Government will see their way to
make it perfectly clear that the defendant
will not be compelled to prove his innocence
but rather that the plaintiff must prove that
the man is guilty.
Mr. MCALLISTER: In reference to the
reply of the Minister of Home Affairs one
situation that I can see may occur under this
Bill is this. Take the position of a large
merchant in the City of Belfast. He has a
large number of motor cars. He has to rely
for his information on subordinate officials
in his business. He does not know how to
arrive at the horse-power of his car. He does
not know the dimension of the engine bore or
stroke. If an employee gives him wrong information I suggest this sub-Clause will
penalise him substantially by calling upon
him to discharge the onus. It would be unjust and unfair in the circumstances.
Amendment negatived.
Clause ordered to stand part of the Bill.

motor car had paid him a shilling to take
them to that place of worship, he would not
have been fined at all, but this man declined
to perjure himself, with the result that he
was fined £30.
In a similar case another man was prosecuted, and the evidence of the constable was
that the man was driving along with his wife

The Ministry of Home Affairs may make
regulations prescribing all or any of the
following methods for the prevention of
mud-splashing by vehicles to which this
Act applies:-

The following new Clause stood on the
Order Paper in the name of Dr. Morrison:
NEW CLAUSE (Penalty for obstruction).
Any person who places a stationary
object on a public road in such a position
as to interfere with the access to, or the
use in its full width of, such road by a
motor propelled vehicle used for the carriage of persons for hire or otherwise,
except under a special permit from the
Ministry of Home Affairs, shall be liable,
on summary conviction, to a fine of five
pounds.
Clause not moved.
NEW CLAUSE (Penalty for drunkenness
while in charge of a motor car).
2. (1) If any person is drunk while in
charge on any highway or other public
place of a motor car, he shall be liable on
summary conviction to a fine of five pounds
or any greater sum not exceeding fifty
pounds; or in the case of a second or subsequent conviction to a fine of ten pounds
or any greater sum not exceeding one hundred pounds, or in the discretion of the
Court to imprisonment for a period not
exceeding six months, or to both such fine
and imprisonment.
(2) Any police constable may apprehend
without warrant the person in charge of
any car who commits an offence under this
Section within his view, if such person
refuses to give his name and address or
produce his licence on demand, or if the
motor car does not bear the identification
mark or sign required in pursuance of the
Roads Act, 1920.

or urban district and the commissioners of
any town shall have power to make bylaws as respects public service vehicles
used in standing or plying for hire, or
used to carry passengers for hire, within
their county borough, urban district or

district"), for all or any of the following

vehicles of any particular class, that is to

standing or plying for hire on specified
streets or portions of streets, or in any
specified area in the district, or from
carrying passengers from any depot or
stand in any such street or area, either
generally or during particular hours;

Mr. DEVLIN: It would be certainly more
interesting than the statement I am about to
make. At any rate I told them that if I had
known there were any politics in Bangor I
would not have come there at all. At all
events this deputation waited upon the
Urban Council to ask them to prevent the
people of Bangor from using the buses to the
extent to which they were using them. One
would have imagined that as representatives
of Bangor they would have been in open revolt against such a proposal as to hamper or
put obstacles in the way of motor traffic
down to Bangor, because, in the first place,
Bangor is a very uninteresting place
intellectually, and it would have been so fine
a thing to bring the people of Belfast to
Bangor. It would have tempered a certain
amount of the dour ignorance of Bangor
with a good deal of the intellectual brightness of the Belfast citizens. But what do
they do? The Urban Council thank the
deputation, tell them that they are in complete and absolute sympathy with them, and
that they see their point of view-while it
was their business not to see the point of
view of any interested party at all but the
point of view of the public-and the whole
thing resolved itself into a mutual admiration society that had gone mad while they
paid each other compliments and told each
other what splendid fellows they were being
by hampering and putting obstacles in the
way of these motor chars-a-bancs carrying
poor people in the summer time to Bangor.
Therefore, I say, whether they be members
of the Belfast Corporation, of which my hon.
Friend (Mr. Thomas Henderson) used to be
always in the minority, but of which he now
is a member of the almost triumphant
majority-because I noticed that those
private and confidential communications
were turned down by the rest of the
corporators. Was it these gentlemen who
were turned down who made this suggestion
to the Ministry? Was it on the face of their
own prima facie representations that you
accepted these suggestions? These are all
illuminating facts of which 1 think the
Committee ought to be put in possession, but
we were left in a state of absolute ignorance.
Then the hon. Gentleman (Mr. Thomas
Henderson) here, in one of those fine inspirations of his, comes forward with a suggestion,
a suggestion that calls forth a concession.
Mr. HANNA: A guarantee.
Mr. DEVLIN: Which is more than a concession. A concession from the Government
is a questionable commodity, but a guarantee
publicly given is a sure fact. The hon.
Member not only succeeds in getting a
concession but he succeeds in securing a
guarantee, a guarantee not only given by
the hon, and learned Gentleman (Mr.
Hanna), who is a very able but very modest
member of the Ministry, but a guarantee
given in the presence of the Prime Minister
which binds the whole Cabinet.
Now I say that all these things of which
I have complained have been entirely due
to the fact that the Minister did not explain the new Motor Bill when it was
introduced. He calls this and these others
new Clauses. If they are new Clauses why
are they not explained to us? On the
strength of your first Bill you got a Second
Reading and you come along now with this
Bill and do not offer a word of explanation.
I say that these are methods not worthy
of this Committee, and the oftener we make
our protest against them the better it will
be for the carrying out of our legislative
work.

Marketing of Eggs Bill.
Considered in Committee.
[Mr. MOLES in the Chair].
CLAUSE 1 (Power of Ministry of Agriculture to refuse to grant licences to wholesale
dealers in eggs in certain cases).
(1) The Ministry of Agriculture (in this
Act referred to as "the Ministry") may,
if it thinks fit, refuse to grant a licence
under section one of the Marketing of Eggs
Act (Northern Ireland), 1924 (in this Act
referred to as "the principal Act")-
(a) to a person who fails to satisfy the
Ministry that he has provided premises
and equipment which appear to the
Ministry to be suitable for the conduct
of his business as a wholesale dealer in
eggs, or who proposes to use for the
conduct of the business of wholesale
dealer in eggs premises previously used
for that purpose by a person whose
licence under section one of the principal Act has been suspended or revoked;
or
The MINISTER OF AGRICULTURE (Mr.
Archdale): I beg to move, in Clause 1, page
1. line 14, to leave out from the word "or"
("or who proposes to use") to the word "revoked" ("suspended or revoked").
The Amendment to this first Clause which
I propose to move is to relieve the minds of
some hon. Members and of a considerable
number of egg dealers who thought it might
be used for other purposes than the Ministry
intended. We have no other intention than
to prevent people turning their businesses
over to others members of the family and
working under an assumed name. We are
quite prepared to leave out that part of the
Section which displeases them.
Mr. ELLIOTT: I would just like to say
how much I appreciate the action of the
right hon. Gentleman in deleting the words
which appear in this Amendment. Some of
my Parliamentary colleagues on this side of
the Committee and I appealed to the right
hon. Gentleman to summon a conference at
which this matter could be discussed, and I
am very glad to say that the right hon.
Gentleman acceded to our request. The conference was held, and some of the matters
which were quite obscure, so far as we were
concerned, were cleared up. We suggested
to him that this Clause was too drastic, and
so he very kindly consented to propose the
Amendment which now appears on the
Paper. I heartily support the Amendment,
and I beg to thank the right hon. Gentleman for his kindness in meeting us so far.
Amendment agreed to.
Question proposed: "That the Clause, as
amended, stand part of the Bill."
Mr. GEORGE HENDERSON: I have an
Amendment on the Paper to leave out the
entire Clause.
The CHAIRMAN: I have put the Question
in the necessary technical form, and the hon.
Member can speak against it.
Mr. GEORGE HENDERSON: The Minister in deleting the greater part of this
Clause has in some degree modified my
objections, but I fail to see why this Clause
is necessary at all, considering the powers
that the Ministry have under the principal
Act. The present Bill says:-
(1) The Ministry of Agriculture (in this
Act referred to as "the Ministry") may, if
it thinks fit, refuse to grant a licence under
section one of the Marketing of Eggs Act
(Northern Ireland), 1924 (in this Act
referred to as "the principal Act")-
(a) to a person who fails to satisfy the
Ministry that he has provided premises
and equipment which appear to the Ministry to be suitable for the conduct of his
business as a wholesale dealer in eggs,
I think the Ministry have ample powers
under the Act as it stands to deal with any
such cases. The original Act reads as
follows:-
(1) The Ministry of Agriculture for
Northern Ireland (in this Act referred to
as "the Ministry") shall grant a licence to
carry on business in Northern Ireland as
a wholesale dealer in eggs to any person
applying for such licence who complies or
undertakes to comply to such conditions in
relation to the preparation for sale and
the consignment of eggs as may be prescribed from time to time by the Ministry,
with respect to any class of such business,
in order to secure-
And so on. I think the Ministry have ample
powers, because they have powers to prescribe
under what conditions these men will retain
their licences. I remember being very much
interested in a lecture by Professor Williams
on "A1 Milk." He threw on the screen a
photograph of the cowshed in which he
started to produce "A1 Milk," and I venture
to say that if any official of the Department
had been sent down to inspect that cowshed
2175 Marketing of Eggs Bill- HOUSE OF COMMONS

Committee.
Mr. G. Henderson]
he would not have granted Professor
Williams a permit or a licence to produce
the "A1 Milk' in that cowshed. But
Professor Williams said this "We delivered
the stuff, and the Department had to give
us a certificate.”
What the Department of Agriculture
should be interested in is this: Are these
men delivering the stuff? I say it is probably
an advantage to have a big suite of buildings
and costly plant for the purpose of handling
the eggs, but if that is made a condition
it may injure to some extent what I regard
as essential, that is, competitive buying.
I do hold that there is nothing to hinder an
egg merchant in very humble buildings from
producing good stuff, splendid stuff, and 1
do feel that the Department have ample
powers under the old Act to deal with these
licences and with the revoking of them.
I wish to say that, while I differ in some
respects from the Ministry of Agriculture
in regard to this Bill, I am quite sure that
their object is to improve the egg products
that we put on the market, but there is
just the danger that the Ministry may drive
theory too far. I think this Bill is driving
theory a bit too far. I feel that the
Clause is entirely unnecessary, unless the
Minister can convince me that he has not
sufficient powers under the old Act to regulate these licences.
Mr. PATRICK O'NEILL: I wish to say
that to a very large extent I am in agreement
with the hon. Member for Antrim (Mr.
George Henderson). I believe that a Bill of
this nature is not absolutely necessary for the
inarketing of eggs, and that sufficient power
is already in the hands of the Ministry. 1
have been wondering whether, if there were
as many egg dealers in this Committee as
motor drivers, we
would have had far
greater changes in the Bill. It is not that
on the Motor Bill I think Members acted
as they did for personal reasons, but because
they had a far better grasp of the subject
under discussion. I think the Marketing of
Eggs Bill is one that is not thoroughly
understood by all the Members of this
Committee, and I think that those who do
understand it, that is, the egg merchants
through the country who have objected very
strongly to many of the Clauses of the Bill
are in a better position to judge as to the
requirements in that respect than any of
the Members of this Committee. I think
the Minister of Agriculture in introducing
this Bill did not give us sufficient information as to the necessity for it. On these
grounds I desire to support the rejection of
this Clause, which has been moved by the
hon. Member for Antrim (Mr. George
Henderson).
Mr. ARCHDALE: I really apologise to the
hon. Member for not giving a little more information about the Clause, but the Amendment coming in prevented me from doing so.
This Clause is only securing the Ministry's
satisfaction regarding the place of business
before the licence is granted. We have
already given over 1,900 egg merchants licences for their business premises. These were
all inspected after we had granted the licences, and this is only providing for the inspection of the premises before we grant the
licences. We are not going to be any more
severe or any stricter than we were before,
and we hope we will not put any more men
out of business.
We
As regards the necessity for this Bill, of
which my hon. Friend the Member for Down
(Mr. Patrick O'Neill) was speaking, we have
got to compete against nearly every foreign
country-Denmark, Belgium, France, Canada,
and New Zealand-and every one of these
countries is watching the egg and butter
trade far more strictly than we are. Their
rules are far more severe in every case. Last
year, 1925, there were 22,000,000 great hundreds of eggs imported into England.
have got to contend with that enormous import, and that is the reason why prices keep
low, but I am glad to say that our prices are
the highest of those obtained for any eggs
that come into the United Kingdom. (Hon.
Members: Hear, hear.) Our prices are low,
but we have got to contend with all these
eggs from other countries, and our prices per
great 100 are the highest in England at the
present time. We hope to get a great deal
more money into the trade in a short time.
We have got 1,000,000 more poultry between
May, 1925, and May, 1926. We exported
100,000 more great 100's of eggs last year than
we did the year before, so altogether, with
the continued export and the increase in the
number of poultry, we hope to have a very
considerable increase. The only differences
in this Egg Bill from the old one are relating
to breaches of the rules, purchase by weight,
and the sale of stale and dirty eggs. I think
it is only fair to the egg merchants that other
people who sell eggs should be obliged to have
their eggs looked at. Country people came
into market with dirty eggs in the old times,
and retailers who were not licensed could go
out there, purchase these eggs, and give a
lower price for them than the exporters who
were obliged to have clean eggs.
The CHAIRMAN: I am afraid the right
hon. Gentleman is getting considerably beyond this particular Clause, though I am
sure the Committee appreciates the point he
is making.
Mr. ARCHDALE: I beg your pardon, and
I certainly bow to your ruling. This Clause,
of course, only refers to business premises,
and I hope the two hon. Members who have

objected to it will be satisfied with my

wanted an assurance from the Minister that
this Bill would not be used to squeeze out a

to this Clause, I beg leave of the Committee to withdraw my Amendment.

CLAUSE 4 (Extension of Power to make
Rules).
Question proposed: "That the Clause stand
part of the Bill."
Mr. GEORGE HENDERSON: I think
this Clause does not come under the definition given by, the Ministry of Agriculture in
regard to this Bill, that it was only tightening up the Regulations and making further
provision for seeing that they were carried
out. This Clause seems to me to introduce
an entirely new policy. Clause 4 says:
"The Ministry may, by rules made under
the principal Act, provide that persons purchasing eggs for resale by retail shall
comply with conditions which are the same
as, or similar to, the conditions from time
to time prescribed in relation to licensed
wholesale dealers."
I contend that that is an entirely new principle to the principal Act and I object to it
because I feel that it will be putting unnecessary restrictions on people buying eggs
for resale on the home market. The Minister
of Agriculture in his very lucid statement
said that the object of this Bill was to supervise the English market where our eggs
were competing against eggs from all nations,
to put them out in the most attractive and
very best manner. This Clause does not deal
at all with that but with the buying of eggs
for resale in the home market. Does the
Minister of Agriculture want power to insist
that these men, probably shopkeepers from
Belfast city and other towns going to country
markets to buy eggs for resale, would be
compelled to test these eggs or to grade these
eggs, or does he want power to make it a
condition that they cannot use the same boxes
for conveying these eggs twice?
The Regulations dealing with the wholesale
merchants preclude them from using the
same standard egg boxes on a second occasion. Does the Minister of Agriculture want
power to make a condition like that with
regard to men going to buy eggs for resale
in the home market? These men can take
their boxes with them, and it would save
them a good deal of expense, and they are a
big factor, I would say, in competing with
the wholesale men for eggs and keeping the
prices stable. I do think it will be admitted
by the Minister of Agriculture, and probably
by the Committee generally, that with unrestricted competitive buying for eggs there
is no commodity where there is so small a
margin between the price gained in the
market and the price paid by the consumer.
I do not think it can be alleged with any
accuracy that there is really profiteering in
any sense in eggs, because the margin between the prices gained and what the consumer pays is comparatively low, and one of
the great factors in helping to produce this
is the competition at present between the
men buying for resale in the home market
and the shippers.
If the Ministry of Agriculture do not want
to inflict any of these restrictions, because
these are restrictions that apply to the whole
traders, I think there is no need for this
Clause in the Bill. It is to their interests
to get the most attractive stuff they can,
and now that this Bill is putting, and I believe rightly putting, some responsibilty on
the producer-because I have no sympathy
with any person who wilfully markets stale
eggs or keeps them until they are stale- I do
not see why the Ministry should want to
impose these restrictions on the home trade.
I think they will probably attain their object
by other Clauses in the Bill. I feel that this
Clause as it stands puts powers into the hands
of the Ministry to interfere with that part of
the trade which is supplying the home consumer. Of course the Minister of Agriculture
may say that they do not intend to do this,
that, and the other thing, but really the
power should not be given in the Bill.

Mr. PATRICK O'NEILL: I am in agreement with the hon. and gallant Member for
Armagh, who has just spoken, and with the

Mr. DAVISON: I attended the conference
referred to by the Minister of Agriculture,
and I went to it inclined to take a view
against this compulsory buying of eggs by
weight. But, listening to the arguments
there, I was convinced that this buying by
weight could be nothing but beneficial to
the farmer or the producer. I heard the
views put forward both by the buyers and
the producers or sellers of eggs. This is no
new thing. It has been working for years
in some districts to the satisfaction of the
farmer and the producer. There is, and can
be, I understand, no difficulty in the carrying
out of this Measure. It has often been said
that the farmer could not tell what the
weight of his eggs is, but the hon. Member
for Antrim (Mr. G. Henderson) has told us
Committee.
Marketing of Eggs Bill-

HOUSE OF COMMONS
[Mr. Davison]
that the Ulster farmer or producer is a
very shrewd man. I know he is, and that
he will be quite able to find out what the
weight of his eggs is and to see that he gets
full value.

The present system of buying eggs by the
dozen from the farmer offers more opportunity for fraud on the part of the buyer
than this method which the Government now
propose to substitute, because the farmer
does not necessarily get an equal price for
every dozen eggs he sells. The dealer might
tell him, Well, these eggs are 15-lb. eggs
and 16-lb eggs," when in reality they would
be 17-lb. eggs, and the farmer would not
know. It was merely the dealer's opinion of
the eggs he was getting from the farmer, and
in a mixed lot of eggs it would be very difficult to say what would be correct. When a
farmer is selling by weight the farmer knows
how many pounds he is selling, and the price
he should get, and he cannot be defrauded.
If he has any suspicion he is not getting
credit for full weight he can have it checked
from time to time, and if he finds the dealer
he is dealing with is not honest he can go
to some other dealer.
The hon. Member for Antrim (Mr. G.
Henderson) has referred to the means of
checking the weight and of the necessity of
going to a weighbridge. The ordinary farmer
has not got so many eggs as to make it
necessary to go to a weighbridge to get them
weighed. There cannot be very much in that
point. With regard to this Amendment as
a whole, it would reduce this Clause to a
nullity, because it would leave the buyer and
the seller of eggs in exactly the same position
as they were before the Act came into
operation. At the present time anyone can
buy eggs by weight or sell eggs by weight,
but there is no compulsion. If you add the
words suggested by the Amendment you are
left in exactly the same position, and you
might as well be without the Clause. For
those reasons I intend to support the Clause.
Mr. MILLER: I am not convinced by the
arguments of the hon. Member for Antrim
(Mr. G. Henderson). Like my hon. and learned
colleague for Armagh (Mr. Davison) I was
invited to a conference a few days ago. I
understood it was merely a conference among
what I might call agricultural members,
those who were naturally interested in egg
production, but to my astonishment when I
went into the room I found there were egg
buyers, egg shippers, egg collectors, egg
inspectors, egg eaters, and egg producers-I
do not mean hens. (Laughter.) What struck
me very forcibly in that connection was that
my friends and I went in, with a bias in
favour of counting. Two men got up. One
was an old man, I think he said he was 40
or 50 years in the trade, and after a good
deal of searching in his pockets he produced
various pieces of paper from which he tried
to convince us he was on the royal road to
the workhouse, and that in a few more years
he would be down and out. He bought his
eggs by the dozen, and in two years he calculated he would be down and out.
When he was finished another man got up.
He was rather an amateur. He said he had
been buying eggs for years by weight, and
that the people he bought them from were
well satisfied with the price they got. He
was making money by leaps and bounds. It
seems to me that when you have two systems
one of which is going to lead you to the poorhouse, while the other is going to make you
rich, you will not have very much difficulty
in choosing between the two. The Minister
of Agriculture has put it forward that he
brought this in to deal with the case of the
small eggs. A short time ago a man came to
me and said he had been defending the
Minister of Agriculture at public meetings,
and being a man with rather a delicate conscience he wondered whether he was doing
the right thing or not. He said, "Just before
I left home I ordered my man to take a
barrowful of eggs and dig a hole in the
manure heap and bury them." I asked what
was wrong, and wondered if the Minister of
Agriculture was going to start some way of
making artificial manure out of eggs. I said,
"Were they bad?" He said they were perfectly good. I asked, "Why do you bury
them?" and he said "I offered them to four
merchants and none of them would buy
them as they were too small."
Eventually he had to throw them out. He
ate all he could. I was going to say he was
like the Americans who eat all they can and can
all they can't. He gave them to the labourers
and to anyone round about who wanted
them, but still like the widow's cruse they
kept increasing until eventually he had to
take them out and bury them. I said "It is
a terrible thing that you have to bury those
eggs." It struck me there was something
wrong in an Act that prevented good eggs,
even if they were a bit small, being sold.
When I saw this Bill I said the Minister of
Agriculture is on the right track, because a
small egg will have a chance as well as a
large one. I might say that this man also
told me he was not cute enough because a
lady who lived near the sea-it was in County
Antrim, I think-said she had no difficulty in
getting rid of small eggs as the landladies were
tumbling over each other to get the small eggs
as they got sixteen for the price of twelve.
They said if one is going to serve a rasher and
two eggs, it does not much matter whether
they are sixteen pounders or seventeen
pounders.
I have yet to be convinced that the fairest
way is not selling eggs by weight. In fact,

I am more convinced than ever that it is.
But at the same time I would like to join
with my hon, and gallant Friend the Member
for Armagh (Major Shillington), in asking
the Minister, as it is the fashion in Acts of
of Parliament to have different sections
coming into operation at different times and
having appointed days for this and for that,
to follow the fashion and fix the appointed
day for this Clause to come in six months or
a year after the rest of the Bill. That will
give the hens time. I am told that when the
Government some time ago asked the hens
would they kindly lay more eggs, no matter
what size they were, the hens obligingly said
they would, and they began to lay two or
three in the day but they were smaller eggs.
Now the Minister wants them to produce big
eggs, and he should give them, and especially
the young chickens coming out in the spring,
time to realise what he wants.
I would like to join with my hon. and
gallant Friend in asking that this should be
put off for a year. There is another reason
why it should be put off for a little time.
There has been a good deal of talk about the
checking of balances and paying £5 to £10
for the balances. The difficulty was that
some of these spring balances weighed only
the half pounds, and therefore the poor
farmer's wife coming into the market could
not tell where less than a half pound came
in. The delay would give the makers of
those balances time to produce an article
that could be used all over the country which
would give the weight to within an ounce
or two. For these reasons I would ask
the Minister of Agriculture if he would consider on the Report Stage the advisability of
putting off this Clause for six months or a
year.
Mr. DEVLIN: I have no desire whatever
to interfere in any way with so exhilarating

much to have been there, because I understand that at that conference an eminent

They went to that conference with firm and

the two hon. Gentlemen.
I would like to know from the Government

by weight or by the dozen, whichever way
they choose. This Clause, I take it, will

From whom did the Minister get the demand
for this change? I have not heard from anyone here to-day- unless the converted who
have come here in all meekness to tell the

was-that this demand was made upon the

business in Fermanagh or Tyrone or whatever other inspiring county it was held in.
I am
am here for the purpose of acquiring

very excellent Members of Parliament, have

That is what I would like the right hon.

Let him in imagination constitute this

There has been only one practical suggestion offered from the other side, and that
was from the hon. and gallant Member for

They support the Government not because
the Government, are good, but very often
because the Government are bad. What I
want to say is this, appeals have been made
by the hon. Gentleman who comes fresh from

Mr. CRAWFORD: I am concerned simply
with the desirability of the farmers getting
the best price for their eggs. I took the
opportunity of consulting a considerable
number of them, and I think that nine out
of ten are strongly in favour of selling eggs
by weight. They informed me they can
very nearly tell whether there would be
seven or eight eggs to a pound. They said
that in the long run it would be a very
great benefit to them to have their eggs sold
by weight instead of by the dozen as heretofore. Seeing that I represent an agricultural constituency, and that I have ascertained the opinion of quite a number of
persons who are very strongly in favour of
selling eggs by weight, I am determined to
support this Bill.
Mr. MCALLISTER: I must say that I do
not follow the logic of the suggestion made
by the hon. and gallant Member for Armagh
(Major Shillington) that the operation of
this Clause should be postponed for six
months, because if the Clause is bad now it
will be equally bad six months hence; if it is
going to do harm to-day it will equally do
harm six months later. With regard to the
conference, I am very sorry that the hon.
and gallant Member for Armagh did not detail to us the evidence upon which he was
converted, because I was anxious to hear the
concrete facts that changed his opinion from
the time he entered the conference until he
left it. It appears to me that if the selling
of eggs by weight is going to be so beneficial
to the farming community as is represented
by the Ministry, the farmers are quite com.
petent to discern that fact for themselves,
and as the better way is bound to prevail no
compulsion would be necessary at all.
We have heard testimonies to the shrewdness of the Ulster farmer, and they are
justified. If he finds that he will improvė
his position by selling his eggs by weight instead of by numbers he will undoubtedly
adopt that method. I think it is a dangerous
thing to bring in a Clause like this which
practically revolutionises the whole method
of selling eggs in Northern Ireland. The
egg industry is a very important part of the
business of the small farmers, and I do think
that before asking us to vote the Ministry
should have put a substantial case before
the Committee, and given us clear concrete
and positive reasons, as to why this important trade should be revolutionised.
Mr. McBRIDE: I rise in support of this
Clause, because I do not see that there can be
any hardship imposed in the selling of eggs
by weight. Eggs have been bought by
weight throughout County Down for a considerable time, and everybody seems to be
satisfied with that method. To come to the
ordinary working man, if all eggs were
sold by weight not only in the market but
over the counter it would prevent a practice
that I have seen myself, of people going into
a shop and picking out the large eggs and
buying them from the shopkeeper, while the
poor people who come along have to be
content with the small eggs and to pay the
same price. If eggs were sold by weight
everybody would get a fair deal. Nobody
would be robbed. So far as the Irish farmer
is concerned he would get into touch with
the new method very quickly. I have great
pleasure in supporting the Clause.
Mr. ARCHDALE: I would like to say a
few words in reply to my hon. Friends. Eggs
have been sold by weight nearly all over the
Northern Province for the last ten years,
and in a great many places in the Counties
of Antrim and Down selling by weight has
been carried on for ten years. In the
creameries they are buying by weight. The
reason for bringing in this provision is that
it helps not only the producer but the egg
trade. Nineteen-twentieths of them are very
keen to have this proposal passed. The
producer gets the benefit. If a man brings
in a basket of eggs and sells them at so much
a dozen he gets as good a price for the small
eggs, to which the hon. Member for Fermanagh and Tyrone (Mr. Miller) referred,
as he does for the large ones, and that is not
fair.
The man who buys them, of course,
separates them into grades. They have to be
sold in grades. We are obliged to grade
them correctly, so as to get the top price
which we have attained. Eggs are bought
by weight in England, and we cannot retain
the position we have gained there after much
endeavour unless we prepare the eggs
properly. There is no great difficulty in
handling the eggs by weight, and as regards
weighing, of which the hon. Member for

Ministry's inspector meets him on the road,
if this Clause is put in operation in the way
in which it might be it might hold up the
shipment of those eggs so that he misses the
market, and it might mean very serious loss
to a man whose eggs were perfectly in order.
I would like some assurance before supporting this Clause that it will not operate in
such a way against a man when he is trying
legitimately to do his business in a proper
way, and put him to a great deal of in-

possess. Clause 6 of the principal Act reads

and then to take for the purpose of examination samples of eggs. I think that is ample
power for the Ministry of Agriculture to

might lead to undue and serious interference

Ministry are not satisfied with the powers of

--could they not institute the same surprise

Mr. PATRICK O'NEILL: I want to say

the inspector might stop these consignments

would not have minded so much.
No one
objects, I am sure, to the inspection. It is

Mr. ARCHDALE:
I would just like to
say that this Clause was put in because it
ought to have been in the first Bill, but

has now given us permission to have it. This
power of inspection is in force in every
country that exports eggs to Great Britain,
and the reason we put it in is that our
inspectors many times have looked at eggs in
the place of business, in the store, and the
merchant has given a promise to re-handle
those eggs properly before forwarding them,
and we found that they were sent forward
without being re-handled as promised. This
gives us power at the steamer, or anywhere
else like that, to examine the eggs to see
whether they are in a fit condition to go to

Fermanagh (Mr. Elliott) that the power will
not be used in any way to delay a consignment catching the train or the steamer. It
never was our intention to do any such thing.
but it is most important that we should have
power to see that the eggs after they leave
the merchant's store are in a proper and fit
condition to go to the market in Great
Britain.
Mr. LEEKE: There is just one point
regarding inspection which I certainly think

eggs consigned out of this country are booked

pass the Government inspector. Who will
pay the new freight, or will the railway

the through rate or will they have to be

point and should be looked into. If it is

I should like to repeat that I have made

Mr. ELLIOTT: After the explanation that

Mr. CRAWFORD: I have exactly the same

CLAUSE 1 (Licences and permits for
ownership or keeping of stallions).
Any person who, after the appointed day,
owns, keeps or has control of a stallion of
three years old and upwards calculated
from 1st January in the year of his birth
shall be liable on conviction to a fine of
five pounds, unless the stallion is licensed,
or a permit has been granted in respect
thereof, under the provisions of this Act:
and any person who has been convicted of
owning, keeping or having control of a
stallion contrary to the provisions of this
Act, shall, if since such conviction he owns,
keeps or has control of such stallion contrary to the provisions of this Act, be
guilty of a continuing offence and be liable
on conviction to a further penalty of forty
shillings for each week or part of a week
during which he is guilty of the continuing
offence.

CLAUSE 9 (Burden of proof).
In any proceedings under this Act for
owning, keeping or having control of a
stallion without a licence or permit, the
burden of proof that a licence or permit
in respect of the stallion was in force, and
(where the age of the stallion is in question)
the burden of proof of the age of the
stallion, shall lie on the person charged;
and until the contrary is proved it shall be
assumed that neither a licence nor a permit
was in force on the day on which the
offence was alleged to have been committed,
and (if the age is in question) that on that
day the stallion was a stallion of the prescribed age.

Motion made, and Question proposed:
"That it is expedient to amend Section one
of the Housing Act (Northern Ireland), 1923,
by enabling the Ministry of Home Affairs
to make grants in respect of the construction
of houses, when the same are completed on
or before the first day of April, 1928, being

of Northern Ireland, or the growing produce
thereof, by virtue of Section three of the
said Act. - (Governor's Recommendation
signified.)-(Mr. Barbour.)
-
The FINANCIAL SECRETARY (Mr.
Barbour): The proposed extension for a
further year of the period during which
grants will be paid in respect of certain
types of houses will automatically throw
an additional charge on the Exchequer, and,
accordingly, it is necessary to take this
Money Resolution before the Bill can proceed
further. It will be convenient, perhaps, if
I inform the Committee what our actual
liabilities have been in the past up to the
commencement of this financial year, and
what the estimated liabilities will be for the
subsequent two years up to the 31st March,
1928. Up to the 31st March last the actual
number of houses completed in respect of
which subsidy was payable and the amount
of subsidies paid are as follow:
Amount of Houses built and
Subsidy receiving Subsidy
2,043

Private Builders £131,160
Local Authorities 22,920
As regards the liabilities in respect of subsidies subsequent to the 31st March last,
provision was made in the Estimates for
subsidies in respect of the completion within
the year of 2,000 houses by private builders
and 1,000 by Local Authorities. The latest
information goes to show that in the case of
'private builders the number has been underestimated, and may be raised to 2,500, while
in the case of Local Authorities some 800
houses, or 200 less than the Estimate, may
be built.
As regards the year commencing 1st April
next, an approximate figure only can be given
and it has been estimated that perhaps 1,500
houses may be built by private builders and
800 by Local Authorities within that period.
The estimated figures for the two years,
therefore, would be a total of 4,000 houses
built by private builders and 1,600 by Local
Authorities, and the grants would approximate to £400,000. This figure assumes that
an average amount of £70 subsidy per house
will be paid.
I would remind hon. Members that the
grants are paid out in the first instance from
the Exchequer, which will be recouped over
a period of years in respect of these advances
by means of the terminable annuity which
will continue to be charged on the Vote for
Grants to Local Authorities, etc., in accordance with the provisions of the Housing Acts.
I beg to move.

The Parliamentary Secretary gave a figure
