The demand for a recognised annual holiday during which wages should continue to
be paid has been urged for many years by
Labour organisations, but so far the claim
has not been conceded over the greater part
of industry. In some countries. I am informed, such provision has been laid down by
law, but there is no legal enactment in
Britain, France, U.S.A., Germany, or in
most of the important industrial countries
As a result of the strong pressure trade
unions were able to exert in the post-war
period in the direction of extending the
leisure time of the workers, a number of
organisations did succeed in obtaining agreements which embodied the grant of an
annual holiday with pay. In most cases
where holidays with pay were gained the
agreements covered only individual firms, or
certain localities, or special grades. In one
case, that of the printing trade, the agree
ment covers the entire body of workers, of
all grades in all localities. On the railways
all workers except the shopmen have an
agreement giving an annual holiday with
pay, while municipal and co-operative employees have in very many cases gained the
same concession. In the boot and shoe industry the workers have recognised holidays
with pay but under an arrangement with
the employers they contribute half of the
holiday pay. They get fifteen days holidays
in the year. In addition to those I have
mentioned there are literally hundreds
of other sections of workpeople in Great
Britain who get these holidays with pay.
I have here, if anyone cares to examine it,
a full list of the agreements in Great Britain
under which the workpeople get holidays with
pay. In Northern Ireland in a number of
trades or sections of trades, holidays with
pay is the rule.
Broadly speaking, all
salaried workers get holidays with pay in
contradistinction to the wage earners. It
seems to me on this, as it has been on other
questions before the House, that this is an
instance again of "to him that hath shall be
given." The salaried workers who in the
main can make provision for their holidays
are paid for those holidays, but the wage
earner-the textile worker and the shipyard
worker-as a rule do not receive sufficient
wages to enable them to save enough money
to permit their enjoying their holidays. It
is true, as I say, that all salaried workers
get holidays with pay in contradistinction to
the wage earners. That the same treatment

That this question has received careful consideration by Government experts is
evidenced by the interim report of the Committee on Adult Education issued in March,
1918 (Cd. 9107), in which it is stated:
That wage earners should be entitled by

not only urged the importance of periods of
rest, but of facilities being given to enable

putting these recommendations into force
can be remedied by this Government if they

workers, to assist the shop assistants, instead of always bolstering up the privileged

fair play to the bottom dog, to the underpaid worker, I ask this House to express
their opinion this afternoon that the underpaid workers should get their holidays with
pay to enable them to be fit and well to carry
on their work for the period of time they
have got to earn their living.

induce local inventors to do something towards a solution of this problem?
dealt with in that Measure. With regard to
the point raised by my hon. Friend the
Member for East Belfast (Mr. Beattie) with
regard to mud-splashing, I think there is a
certain amount of misunderstanding in regard to this matter. In the 1896 Act power
is given to make Regulations dealing with
mud-splashing, and to make a Regulation
that devices should be used to prevent mudsplashing. Therefore, it is entirely unnecessary to introduce that matter into the
present Bill.
I may point out that so far back as 1919
the Local Government Board, acting under
powers conferred upon them by the 1896 Act,
did make a Regulation and prescribed that
heavy vehicles should all be provided with
anti-mud-splashing devices, but the practical
operation of the Regulation showed it was
impossible to enforce the law. In other
words, there was no suitable device. While
I admit quite frankly it is a hardship on
pedestrians that they should have their
clothes splashed with mud I think it
would be a greater hardship on motor
owners that they should be asked by law
to do a thing that is not possible, and that
if they did not carry out an impossible task
they should be fined.
We are still going into this matter and are
still studying it very carefully along with
the Ministry of Transport in England. They
have conducted a very elaborate set of experiments. They invited the inventors of
these anti-mud-splashers to come before
them and show the merits of their different
appliances. No fewer than thirty-two inventions were brought forward, and they
were all tested. I might tell the House what
the final finding of the Committee in charge
of the matter was. They say:
The judges, after careful consideration,
do not recommend any award in either
class.
They were divided into three classes.
They have come to the decision because,
in their opinion, the devices failed in the
first essential of a mud-splash guard; that
is to say, no device reduced the amount of
mud splashed to a negligible quantity.
As I said earlier, if any individual can produce a suitable device I can assure him it
will be welcomed not only here but in England, where the Ministry of Transport, like
ourselves, have come to the conclusion that
until a suitable device is introduced it would
be unfair to the motoring public to enforce a
Regulation of this character.

Mr. DEVLIN: I want to join in the protest made by the hon. Gentleman against
this expenditure. In the speeches that have
been delivered here in the House statements
were made in which we were represented as
callous and inhuman representatives who
have no regard for the comfort of an
important Force charged with the defence of
public order. I think that that was a most
unfair interpretation to put upon our
attitude in regard to this Vote. There is no
one I know of who is not anxious to see the
police properly housed. As long as these men
are charged with an important, responsible
and very irksome, and sometimes very irritating work to do, it is the duty of everyone
to show them the greatest consideration and
to treat them well.
But our objection takes another form
altogether. We think for the reasons stated
on the last occasion, which we repeat here,
that £800,000 is a very large sum of money
to spend, not in the erection of barracks
alone, but in the improvement. The right hon.
Gentleman, the Prime Minister, stated on
the last occasion that this was a legacy that
was left to the Northern Government by the
Imperial Government, notwithstanding his
representations and his protestations that
this responsibility was forced upon the
Northern Government. Well, I have never
heard during all the debates on the Irish
Police Votes in the British Parliament
where any Member ever raised any question
of the comfort and convenience of the Irish
Police Force, or stated that they were badly
housed. I have no doubt that, during certain periods in our Irish history, the police
served the Imperial Government well, and I
have never known an instance of any representative, the most sympathetic to the Police
Force, ever raising his voice in protest
against the way they were treated or the way
they were housed. And it came to me as a
complete revelation that the police barracks
of the country were in the deplorable condition described by the right hon. Gentleman,
the Prime Minister.
But, as my hon. Friend has stated, it
seems to me strange that since the Northern
Government were able to make such a powerful impression on the British Government in
regard to all other matters, they were not
able to secure funds substantial enough to

ought to be properly housed, whether policemen or peasants, at the same time I think
some of the expenditure on police accommodation is of a very indefensible character.

To revert again to the argument that
has been submitted by the hon. Member for
West Belfast, that the Imperial Government
should be attacked in many ways because of
their neglect in handing over the police
barracks in such a condition, let me remind
him that the Colwyn Committee, who were
arbitrators in this matter, approached it
from the point of view of placing the citizens
of Northern Ireland exactly in the same
position as the citizens of Great Britain,
and as the citizens of Great Britain
locally provide their own police and provide
their own police barracks, the Colwyn Committee naturally argued why should
Northern Ireland be placed in a privileged
position as compared with the citizens of
Great Britain. Now I stated when this case
was being argued before, that it was a most
difficult argument to meet, because in these
matters we have fought our corner exactly
upon the basis that the citizens of Northern
Ireland were entitled to the same conditions
and the same privileges in every way as the
citizens of Great Britain. And as I say,
when we come to discuss this question we
cannot have it both ways. Be that as it may
the Colwyn Committee, a purely arbitration
committee, settled that we were entitled to
provide our own police barracks and to provide them in our own way. I cannot see the
argument in respect of housing, that if this
£800,000 were only devoted to housing, and
so on. This £800,000 is devoted to housing.
It is doing what hon. Members opposite are
always clamouring for, it is to house
3,000 people and possibly their families.
Therefore, it is doing exactly what we are
doing in other cases. We are providing, or
helping to provide, houses for the general
community by allowing subsidies, and here
we are simply providing, not luxurious, but
necessary accommodation for the police of
Northern Ireland. I am greatly surprised
that hon. Members opposite, who are so
clamant on the subject of decent accommodation for the ordinary citizens of the country,
should raise a clamour because the policemen in Northern Ireland are being placed in
a position of common decency and nothing
more.

Mr. KYLE: I want to move that this
Clause be deleted. I cannot see why the
Comptroller and Auditor-General should be
put in any different position to any other
person in the land. It is not lawful to give
an unstamped receipt for an amount
of more than £2, and the receipt
does not hold unless there is
2d
stamp on it. I cannot see at all why
the Minister of Finance wants to make a
differentiation in this particular case. Why,
if he is going to put this thing through the
Committee here, should an ordinary person
be compelled to put a 2d stamp on a receipt?
It seems to me that he is going in direct
violation of the law, as it stands to-day, in
regard to the stamping of receipts, and I am
surprised that a man of his probity, and with
his ideas of financial matters, should desire
to make it legal that a receipt should not
bear a 2d stamp. For that reason I desire to
see this Clause deleted.
Mr. POLLOCK: It is not intended by this
Clause to empower the Comptroller and
Auditor-General to make documents legal
that are in fact illegal. If my hon. Friend
will read the Clause carefully he will see
that all that is contemplated by it is that if
the Comptroller and Auditor-General re
ceives a document receipted without a stamp,
he can use it as a voucher in his accounts.
It does not preclude him from taking steps
against the offender if he considers it necessary to do so. I am not here to say whether
he will or will not communicate with the
person who received the money, and who has
neglected or deliberately omitted to impose
a stamp. I am not here to say whether any
or what action will be taken in respect of
that omission. I am sure that the Comptroller
and Auditor-General can be trusted to see
that the law is enforced, but there are cases
in which he must necessarily be permitted to
exercise his descretion.
I mentioned a few minutes ago, to some
friends here, a case which is an example
of what may take place. A person residing
in the French Riviera, in Mentone or Monte
Carlo, returned a receipt with a French
receipt stamp on it. I am quite sure that he
could not get a British twopenny receipt stamp
where he was residing, and very foolishly he
assumed that a receipt stamp issued by the
French Treasury was a proper stamp to affix
to the document. Suppose the Comptroller
and Auditor-General had begun corresponddence with that gentleman, how much would
it have cost all over twopence? And he could
not enforce the law, even if he wanted to do
so. Curious cases arise, and the only object
of this Clause is to ensure that the Comptroller and Auditor-General, in his discretion, may use in the Public Accounts Committee a document without the stamp affixed
to it, for the purpose of showing that the
money was legitimately paid and legitimately
acknowledged.
Amendment, by leave, withdrawn.
Clause ordered to stand part of the Bill,

Mr. PATRICK O'NEILL: I notice that the

General. I have not any doubt at all that

It would be a very extraordinary thing if

""
Local Government (War Service
Payments) Bill.
Order for Second Reading read.
Motion made and Question proposed:
That the Bill be read a Second time."
Sir DAWSON BATES: I am sure that
every hon, Member of the House will appreciate the short Bill which I have the privi
lege to submit. The object of the Measure,
as its heading states, is to remove doubts as
to the powers which were conferred upon
Local Authorities by Section 1 of the Local
Government (Emergency Provisions) Act,
1916. Hon. Members, doubtless, are aware
that during the late War many local authorities undertook to make payments in respect
of salary or wages to local officers and employees, or their dependents, who took service
in His Majesty's Forces. In the case of the
undertakings given at the commencement of
the War, these were not supported by statutory sanction, and ultimately the Imperial
Parliament passed the Local Government
(Emergency Provisions) Act, 1916, enabling
the fulfilment of such undertakings, and
gave specific powers to local authorities to
grant leave of absence to any officer or servant for so long a period as might be necessary to enable him to serve in His Majesty's
Forces. In addition, power was given to
authorities to make payments to officers and
employees or their dependents, of portions
of their salaries or wages, and in the event
of the death of an officer or employee whilst
serving with the Forces, to make payments to
his widow or other dependents.
During the period of the War, the salaries
or wages of officers or workmen of local
authorities were, like persons in general employment, increased at different times to
meet the increased cost of living, by means
of bonuses and in some cases by an actual
permanent increase; but local authorities, in
making their contributions in respect of men
in His Majesty's Forces, had only regard to the
salaries and wages the men were in receipt
of at the time they joined up, without reference to the bonuses or increases which
had been made to those who had continued
in the actual service of local authorities.
It will be thus seen that the effect of
paying employees who joined up early in the
War on the basis of the remuneration which
they received at the time of joining up, and
of ignoring bonuses or additions was that employees who joined up later received a larger
amount by reason of the additions made by
way of bonus or increment.
Some time after the termination of the
War, the question was raised as to whether
salary or wages payable to men on War
service included the appropriate bonus which
would have been payable to them had they
remained at home, and it was decided in
the House of Lords in the Sutton case, a
decision with which many hon. Members are
familiar, that salary or wages included
bonus, and, accordingly, men who joined up
were entitled to increases that took place
during the period they were engaged in the
War. The important feature of the Sutton
case was that the appellant was a Government official when he joined up, and that in
effect there was a continuity of services
whilst in the Army. In a subsequent case
(the Druce case) which went to the House of
Lords, Druce failed on the ground that
there was no continuity of service, and that
when he had joined the Forces, in effect, ho
severed his connection with his employers.
Mr. BEATTIE: What about the Harbour
Board?
Sir DAWSON BATES: We are not dealing
with the Harbour Commissioners at the
moment. This decision, coupled with the
statutory limitations of time within which
payment should be made, has raised difficulties in the way of local authorities in
making them without statutory sanction.
Some local authorities have taken the risk
and made payments of agreed amounts of
bonuses to their ex-Service officials, but it
was found in the case of others that the
amounts involved were so large that it was
desirable to obtain Parliamentary sanction,
and it is for this purpose the Bill is presented
to you. It is a one-Clause Bill which is to
enable local authorities to pay or agree to
pay to their ex-Service officials, or their dependants, such proportion of the bonus and increment of salary as they may decide, and at
the same time to remove any difficulties
which might arise by reason of the Statute
of Limitations. It will be noticed, in order to
expedite the payments, it is proposed that
they should be made by local authorities
before the 31st March, 1928, the end of the
financial year.
Mr. DEVLIN: My only objection to the
Bill is that it is a permissive Bill. I want
to say at the very outset that I am very glad
this Bill, such as it is, is introduced, but I
think it ought to have been made a
compulsory Bill-a Bill compelling local
authorities to carry out the voluntary
promises which they gave to these men when
they consented to go to the War. I cannot
understand how it is that the Belfast

Corporation not only propose to keep their

Mr. POLLOCK: And they lived at home.
Mr. DEVLIN: I do not know whether they

Colonel WOODS: I am very glad to hear
the hon. Member for West Belfast (Mr.
Devlin) expressing himself in such terms in
favour of the Bill. The history of this Bill
should be known to hon. Members. When
the men came home after the War, this
question of the bonus was raised by exemployees and re-employed men of the
Belfast Corporation. The Corporation
thought it was a tremendous amount of
money to give away for nothing after the
men had fought, and so after a lot of haggling and bargaining they came to an arrangement by which the men were to accept 60
per cent. of the amount they were entitled
to. Then a number of years went on and
the plea was made that they could not do
this without an Act of Parliament. Hence
this Bill has been brought in. The persons
responsible in the Corporation have been
unjustly accusing this Government in this
particular case. I am very glad to see it
brought up now. I did not like to hear the
right hon. Gentleman (Mr. Pollock), who has
just left, say that the men who joined from
the Harbour Commissioners lived at home.
They did not. I knew several of them in
France. That was not a worthy thing to
say.
There is another thing I would like to say
before I sit down. I would like to thank the
Prime Minister for the interest he displayed
at Question time in the matter of the
Sailors' and Soldiers' Land Trust. I hope
that his great influence will be brought to
bear on the Press and on the Members of the
Imperial House in the matter of having the
rents made reasonable. I am very glad to
hear his sentiments, and I hope his influence
will be brought to bear in this connection.
Mr. WILLIAM MCMULLEN: I do not
think we can offer any objection to a
Measure of this kind being introduced by
the right hon. Gentleman (Sir Dawson
Bates). I would like to have some information as to the position of a person to whom
the Statute of Limitations does not apply.
I understand the position in the main
is that for the majority of the men who have
claimed against the Corporation, the Statute
of Limitations prevents these men from
making a legal claim against the Corporation
without legislation being passed in this
House. Some of the men were demobilised in
1919, and two years ago made a claim against
the Belfast Corporation under the resolution
passed in the Belfast Corporation
to be
entitled. I do not think the Statute of Limitations applies to these men. I would like
to have a statement from the right hon.
Gentleman as to whether this Bill would
preclude these men taking action against
the Corporation for the purpose of recovering
the full amount. The only objection I have
to the Bill is that it does not give the men
what they are justly entitled to. I think a
promise is a promise. If the Belfast Corporation gave an undertaking to give to the men
who went to fight in France or Mesopotamia
or other places certain benefits, or if they
did not return then their dependants
would get the benefits, I think a
promise so given should be treated as sacrosanct. I do not think it is good enough for
the Corporation to come now, six or seven
years after the war has concluded, and tell
the people the amount we undertook is too
large. You come to a compromise under
which you get 60 per cent. of what you are
entitled to. That is the objection I have
to the Bill. It does not go far enough. The
Government do not see the wisdom of compelling the Corporation to fulfil their obligations in the letter and in the spirit of the
resolution passed at the time when they
wanted the men to go to the front. Under
the Bill they only get 60 per cent. instead
of 100 per cent. I would like the right hon.
Gentleman to define the persons to whom
the Statute of Limitations does not apply
and to say whether it will prejudice any
claim they may make.

tations, that is, by laying aside for six

he is debarred by something of that nature
his right is not taken away at all. If the
employees of the Harbour Commissioners
referred to by the hon Member for West
Belfast (Mr. Devlin) conceived they had
any such right against the Harbour Commissioners-I do not say whether they had
or not, it would need careful scrutiny of

would imagine before the expiration of six
years, they would have sought to enforce

This Bill does not in any way take away
from the rights they have. What this Bill
does is this: under some resolutions which
were passed it was doubtful whether people
were entitled only to half the original wages
or whether they were entitled to get
half the bonus and half the addition
which would have been made in the
normal course to the employees. There
were a series of cases that went to the highest
courts. One case particularly, the case of
a Post Office servant, went to the House of
Lords, and the House of Lords held in that
case under the contract under which he
went out, that is under the promise made to
him by his employers, the Post Office, he
was entitled not only to half the original
wages, but to half the normal increase
which he would have got if he had
mained in the Post Office and not joined the
army. On that decision there was a general
impression among the men of the local
authorities that that was a case of general
application, and that every man, no matter
what the terms of his contract, was entitled
not only to half the original wages, but to
half the additions as well. And it was when
that impression was abroad that this settlement was negotiated with the Eelfast Corporation. I think the hon. Member for West
Belfast, who has just sat down, ought to
congratulate himself very much and the
gentlemen who negotiated this settlement
on behalf of these men with the Corporation
because they struck when the iron was hot
and they got this 60 per cent. bargain.
re-
Mr. W. MCMULLEN: The hon. Member
will allow the point that the members of the
Belfast Corporation were quite cognisant of
the fact that they had passed a resolution,
and why did they not of their own volition
put that question into operation without
waiting on any case going before the House
of Lords before giving effect to the resolution
which they were quite conscious they had
passed?
Mr. BLACK: I am afraid the hon. Member rather misunderstands me. The real
point at issue between these men and the
Belfast Corporation was whether in fact the
resolution which the Corporation passed
only applied to existing wages or applied
also to future wages. But after this case of
the Post Office servant was decided, members
got active and they negotiated this settlement, which in the light of what has happened since is a wise settlement; for since
that case went to the House of Lords other
cases came before the court, particularly the
Druce case, and also went to the House of
Lords, the whole tendency of decisions in
recent cases is to be very jealous about holding that a promise for wages included
future increases. The whole tendency in
recent cases was that a promise for half
wages only referred to half the man's wages
when he joined the army. And although I
have not in mind at the present time the
exact wording of the Belfast Corporation's
resolution, I fancy it would be more than
arguable on behalf of the Belfast Corporation
if they sought to contest the case at the
present time, that from the resolution they
come rather under recent decisions than
under the Post Office case. Accordingly I
hink the men made a wise settlement with
the Corporation. And one of the provisions
of this Bill is to say that the men having
made this settlement, if any ratepayers
sought to have it held that the resolution
did not in fact cover this, the Corporation
will be protected and that they will be enabled to pay without their payment being
challenged by the auditor or by the high
courts. It gives power to make the payment.
This is a Bill entirely in the interests of
the people claiming these payments, and I
think it is a Bill which should commend
itself to the House.

Oral Answers to Questions.
BANN DRAINAGE.
an
Mrs. CHICHESTER (by private notice)
asked the Minister of Finance if he will
make a statement as to what procedure he is
adopting regarding the Bann Drainage Report-and when this House will have
opportunity for its discussion? Will he also
state-in view of Paragraph 6 of the Departmental Report-Page 29, whether further investigations has taken place as to the
necessity of still further lowering the summer
level of Lough Neagh? Can he state now
what percentage of the total cost the Government are prepared to contribute if the
scheme outlined in the Report is proceeded
with? Also, if the scheme is eventually un-
Neagh
dertaken-will the present Lough
Drainage Authorities be superseded, and the
present Drainage Rate levied by those Authorities be abolished.
a
The MINISTER OF FINANCE (Mr.
Pollock): This question implies rather
lengthy answer, which I hope you will overlook.
On account of the major issues involved in
the Report on Bann Drainage I have thought
it desirable to refer the matter to the Drainage Advisory Committee which is meeting on
the 19th instant, and will then settle the
procedure which it will adopt in considering
the Report. I am informed, however, that
at their first meeting the Committee decided
that it would be open to members of the
Committee to consult the bodies whom they
represented, save in such cases as the Committee itself decided to the contrary.
The Government is prepared at any time to
give facilities for a discussion of this subject,
but the hon. Member will, I am sure, realise
that it would be desirable that a discussion
should not take place until after the Advisory
Committee has reported in order that the
Committee may be in no way prejudiced in
arriving at its conclusions.
The possibility of affording relief from
flooding by the abolition of navigation has
been before me on several occasions, but I
am advised that although the summer level
of Lough Neagh could be reduced by this
means yet flooding would occur to practically
the same extent as at present and would be
delayed for only a few hours. It is thus
evident that the maintenance of navigation
the Upper Bann has a practically
negligible effect on the drainage problem.
on
The question of Finance is dealt with
exhaustively by the Report of the Departmental Committee which examined this
aspect of the matter, and I am able to state
that the Government is prepared to meet
50 per cent. of the cost of these works provided that it receives definite assurances that
the remaining 50 per cent. will be forthcoming.
Should this scheme eventually proceed it is
impossible for me at this early stage to state
what form the Bill that will be required to
give effect to it will take. I am unable,
therefore, at this juncture to make any
statement in regard to the position of the
existing drainage authorities.
Major SHILLINGTON: Arising out of
that answer, may I ask the right hon.
Gentleman if he will give representation to
Portadown Urban District Council on this
Advisory Committee? I see the scheme
evidently contemplates the striking of a
special rate on the urban district of Portadown in addition to that part of the rate
levied in connection with the counties, and
I would be glad if he would consider that.
I think it is county representation on the
Advisory Committee at the present time.
Mr. POLLOCK: At the moment I cannot
recall all the representatives of the different
interests on this Committee, but on the face
of it I do not see any special objection to
the introduction of a representative from
Portadown on the assumption that Portadown will be vitally interested and will
perhaps have to bear a larger percentage of
the levy than some of the other districts
further removed from the place itself.
ULSTER FARMERS' PRODUCE SOCIETY.
Mr. BEATTIE (by private notice) asked
the Minister of Finance whether his attention has been drawn to Kemp's Gazette
dated 8th November, 1926, wherein it is
shown that the Ministry of Finance for
Northern Ireland has taken a bill of sale
for £15,000 from the Ulster Farmers' Produce Society (Warden & Stewart, Ltd.), of
motor lorries, motor cars, baling machine,
waggons, etc.; whether this is all the
security which the Ministry of Finance
holds for the repayment of this £15,000,
and will he further state who are the personal guarantors, and how much each guarantor guaranteed to the Ministry.
Mr. POLLOCK: The reply to the question
is as follows:
Oral Answers.
Oral Answers.
10 NOVEMBER 1926
I am of course aware that my Ministry
has taken the Bill of Sale to which the hon.
Member refers, but it is by no means the
sole security for this loan. In addition to
the Bill there is firstly a mortgage on the
immovable assets of the Society by means
of an equitable deposit of Title Deeds, and
secondly, joint, and several personal seeurities for a sum of £5,000. I do not consider that it would be fair to the guarantors
for me to disclose their names publicly, but
they are all men of substance.
Mr. BEATTIE: May I ask the right hon.
Gentleman whether he would be prepared,
without mentioning names, to state how
much each of the guarantors is personally
responsible for?
The PRIME MINISTER: They are jointly
and severally responsible.
Mr. ELLIOTT: Arising out of the reply
of the right hon. Gentleman I would like to
ask if he has discovered since he replied to
some questions I put to him concerning this
company, that this company does not
consist of 3,000 farmers, that the total
number of shareholders is less than 1,500, and
many of these are not farmers at all; and if
he has been misled in this matter whether
he will take immediate steps to have this
money recalled?
Mr. POLLOCK: I have not the knowledge
before me to deal with the statements of my
hon. Friend (Mr. Elliott) behind me. The
information that I have received is exactly
that which I stated in this House, but I will
make some inquiries, although they may
not-they cannot-affect the result.
LABOUR EXCHANGE, CORPORATION
STREET.
Mr. BEATTIE (by private notice) asked
the Minister of Labour what immediate
steps he is prepared to take to relieve the
congestion at the new Labour Exchange in
Corporation Street; is the Minister aware
that through all the rain this morning a
queue of four deep, extending from Corporation Street to York Street, had to
remain outside and were soaked to the skin;
is the Minister aware of the hardship imposed by the closing of the Exchange between the hours of 1 and 2 p.m. to those
persons who have found employment
earlier in the day, seeing that this hour was
used for the withdrawal of books; is the
Minister prepared to re-open the Exchange
during this hour, or is it the intention of
the Minister to use this Exchange to inflict
further hardships on the men and women
who are compelled to go there to register.
The MINISTER OF LABOUR (Mr.
Andrews): I regret very much to say that
this morning there was a considerable
amount of congestion at the men's side of
the new Employment Exchange. I am informed that this was due largely to the fact
that all the claimants who should have
signed the register to-day apparently wished
to do so at the earliest possible moment.
Arrangements are being made for these
men to attend next Wednesday at stated
intervals when, I hope, there will be no
further difficulty. This morning all the
traffic was cleared by 1-15 p.m., and I am
glad to acknowledge the valuable assistance
given to the staff in this direction by the
hon. Member (Mr. Beattie) himself, Trade
Union officials and some members of the
Local Employment Committee who were
present. I am also glad to be able to state
that since the opening of the Employment
Exchange the payment of unemployment
benefit to claimants has not been interfered
with.
With regard to the second part of the
question, the Exchange is open between 1
and 2 p.m. for the purpose referred to.
Mr. BEATTIE: I wish to give notice that
I will raise this question on the Adjournment, with the object, perhaps, of assisting
the Minister in regard to the present
procedure.
TEMPORARY WARDERS-QUESTION OF
PERMANENCY.
Colonel WOODS (by private notice) asked
the Minister of Home Affairs whether he
will sympathetically consider the position of
temporary warders, all of whom are ex-
Servicemen, with a view to appointing them
to the permanent staff, as they have already
been temporarily employed for periods
varying from three to five years.
The MINISTER OF HOME AFFAIRS (Sir
Dawson Bates): The answer is in the
affirmative.

Mr. BEATTIE: Then the Government coal
is not landed. We have an Emergency
Powers Act, and I am certainly going to
claim that through that Act the Government
should take drastic action against the per
sons who are putting into their pockets the
profits that are being made per ton on coal.
Other foreign coal-Silesian, and Dutch.
and other coal-is reduced in price, but the
American coal is increasing in price. From
four to five weeks ago it was being bought at
from 45s. to 50s. per ton, and still we were
charged 90s. per ton in Belfast. What is
the use of giving the Controller power to
control the coal and then have the Controller himself allowing the merchants, or
importers, or whoever it may be to take a
profit of 33s. per ton on the coal? It was
brought home to me this morning. After I
had stood with the elements beating on me
for three hours and had seen thousands of
unemployed men soaked to the skin standing
there, men who were not able to purchase
a bag of coal, and who would have to go home
and endeavour to get their clothes dried as
best as they could, I said that if it were
possible I would try to bring before the
notice of the Government that coal which
is landed in Belfast to-day at 60s. per ton,
plus 3s., is being sold at 96s. I say that
profit is unreasonable and that it is not fair
to the Ulster community to allow them to be
charged 96s. for coal that is purchased at
this price.
On the last occasion when I asked the
Ministry of Commerce about this matter I
was in touch with certain coal interests, and
I stated that if a day or two longer had been
allowed I would have had the purchasing
prices of coal in America at that time. At
that time it was 50s. and we were selling it
at 90s. To-day we are giving 60s. per ton
and the controlled price is 96s. Surely with
the present position of affairs in Northern
Ireland, with so much unemployment and
destitution, and with winter on us very
severely, the Government are not going to
allow any coal importers or any bellmen between them to make a profit of 33s. per ton.
This is the last day on which the Government intend to meet for some time-until
November 23rd-and I think we could not
do better to-day than devise some ways and
means to bring to book those persons who
have made fortunes out of the unemployed
workers during the past six months.
I have always said that I did not object to
reasonable profit, that any man who gives his
services is entitled to be paid, but I could not
sit in this House and see 33s over and above
the purchasing price being charged at the
present time. I make this protest to the
Minister and I ask him to have investigations
made to get the purchase price of American
coal to-day, to-morrow, and the following
days, to keep in close touch with them, to
base his price on reasonable profits to the
importers and to the bellmen, to make that
the controlled price, and see that that price
is charged faithfully to the consuming public.
To-day we are not getting a fair crack of the
whip. We are being fleeced high up and low
down. We have a Controller and an Emergency Powers Act and I do think these are
not being worked together in the interests
of the coal consumer. I know that questions
may be put to hide the real position, but 1
am certain, and definite, and very emphatic
on the figures I am using to-day as being
correct figures for the coal that is now being
landed in Belfast. I am giving the figure for
American coal to-day as 72s 6d. I am very
definite on that, and I ask the Government
before retiring for a holiday to do as I ask,
find a reasonable price and see that that
price is carried into operation by both bellmen and coal importers.

over that cold-stored butter, and, of course,

Owing to the new seed we have produced
you can get twenty-five per cent. more from

In anything the hon. Member (Mr. George
Henderson) can do to help us we will be only
too glad to work with him. If he can get
all the farmers in the country to co-operate
he will be a clever man, because there is a

difficulty in all our co-operative societies
and creameries is that someone gets a little
jealous of his neighbour and he leaves the

opposite that if coal can be imported into
Belfast it should be got into the hands of
those people, particularly the poor people,
at as low a price as can possibly be secured.
From the infinite variety of sources from
which this coal comes and from the number
of importers there is generally difficulty in
arriving at a particular price on a particular day. The House must assume there will
be these difficulties and these varieties. No
human being can undertake that they will
not arise. If you take the price of coal in
Belfast, it is so horribly and disgracefully
high that one might almost be disposed to
say it is at least so high that the poor people
must be suffering great privation. But yet,
if we compare the prices of coal in Belfast
with the prices obtaining elsewhere, we find
that we are on a lower scale than any of the
corresponding places.
It is a horrible fact that poor people
should have to pay £4 16s 0d a ton for coal,
but to assume, as hon. Members opposite
assume, that the Government is supine and
indifferent is, I think, a gross insult to the
Government. The Government are as
keenly concerned as any other body-indeed
they are far more anxious-to see that the
people of Belfast get coal at the cheapest
possible price. It was for that reason that
the Government went into the market, in
order to checkmate, if that were possible,
the operations of the natural play of commercial forces, because if a man buys an
article, it does not matter how cheaply he
buys it, he wants to get the market price.
He is not concerned with philanthropy; he
is in business not for amusement, and not
for his health. And if he happens to make
20s per ton of profit on a particular cargo,
on an operation of three months' duration,
you must bear in mind the risks he is running. Possibly when the turn comes there
will be a drop some day of 30s a ton, and if
he is committed to 20,000 tons of coal where
does he stand?
This will show to the House that this
problem cannot be so easily disposed of as
my hon. Friends dispose of it in their
speeches, when they say that the Government
must ensure that the price is so and so. The
Government have bought and own a large
quantity of coal to-day, and the moment it
arrives it will be in the hands of the consumers at a price which will ensure the
Government no profit, except such profit as
will secure the Government against any loss
upon the average purchases they have made.
The price of coal rose a month or six
weeks ago. The Government prices vary from

not seeking employment. In my opinion

from the Minister of Labour, nor are we
likely to get any statement until this Parliament meets in February next. Poverty,
destitution, unemployment, slumdom, the condition of the poor, these are the really vital
elements that count now in the politics of
the nation. We have got rid of the passions
of politics and of the catch-cries and shibboleths that attracted and occupied the attention of the public for so long. The people
are now regarding politics as a thing that
concerns their inmost lives, their bread and
butter and their existence, and as something that should help them to meet the
grim realities of the situation. I would
have imagined it would have been the
function of educated and experienced men,
first of all, themselves to give a lead and
then to seek the co-operation of other gentlemen, and get the best minds of the community to consider the whole question as it
affects the people we represent.
These are considerations that as far as I
can see have never been before the Government, and if they have been before the
Government we have not heard any explanation from them. We are now at the end
of this Session, hurried along at a ruthless
pace, a few Bills passed of practically no
significance, including a Motor Bill, a Protection of Animals Bill. an Egg Bill, and
other Measures, all, in my judgment, of infinitesimal importance as compared with the
big things of life that we have to contend
with, and yet not once have we given one
afternoon to the discussion of the most vital
thing that touches the life of the whole community, and that is the existence of the
poor in our midst.

Pork is sold in the country, dead-weight, at

thing might be said about eggs. In Belfast
they are at least 6d a dozen more than they

said, I was not able to find out the retail

radically wrong with that state of affairs,
We do not grow "Kaiser Heels" in my constituency, but we do grow good potatoes.
If this Inquiry is set up I would like it to
be wide enough in its scope to be able to find
out exactly who the profiteers are, because
I think it is unfair that the workers of
Belfast and other industrial areas should be
asked to pay more than 100 per cent. more

produce. There is too much profit being
made and the middle-men's profits must be
cut down if the farmers are to produce
at a remunerative price and if the

reasonable price.
I understand that milk is being bought in

should set up a Committee of Inquiry to find
out where this profiteering is, and I am quite

seen that it is not the farmers who are
profiteering but the men who are merely
handling agricultural produce.

Mr. BEATTIE: I take this opportunity of
bringing to the attention of the House a
question that requires immediate remedy to
remove certain hardships that are being imposed at the present time on the unemployed
men and women in the City of Belfast. I do
not bring this forward in any vindictive
spirit, nor yet am I going to mention any
special person on whom to put the blame. I
want to say that everything has been done
by the officials to try to alleviate the hardship and sufferings that have been caused by
the congestion at the Labour Exchange. I
want to take this opportunity of trying to
give some little assistance so that we in this
House may be able to alleviate the hardship
that I personally saw caused by the unforeseen circumstances of the weather conditions
and so forth. This morning I happened to
be at the new Exchange representing unemployed workers at the various courts, men
and women. The morning turned out to be
very wet, but at ten o'clock when I was at
Frederick Street I noticed a very long line
extending right from the Exchange up York
Street, and also on the far side of the street
there was a line of persons waiting to get into
the Exchange. With the old Exchange and
several sub-Exchanges at our disposal that
certainly did not happen. On the new Exchange being opened and all the sub-Exchanges
being brought in there in or about the same
time things took place which, in my judg.
ment, could have been avoided. It is with
that view I am going to ask the Minister
to try to revert back to part of the old
system until such time as the new Exchange gets properly into working order, and
is able to deal with the percentage of unemployment that we have in the City of Belfast
at the present day.
Unemployed men and unemployed women
cannot afford to buy coal to-day to any great
amount owing to the high price. Unemployed people cannot afford to buy clothes.
Their clothing is of the scantiest nature.
The majority of unemployed persons owing
to the long time they have been out of work
are now only in possession of one suit of
clothes to cover their nakedness, and that
also applies to the women section. The depression in trade which has caused people to
be out of employment so long has made them
so poverty stricken that the result is that
they have not very many garments to put on
them if anything should happen to the garments they are wearing. This morning I
saw men drenched to the skin. One old man

would point out to the hon. Member that on

The hon. Member, I am sure, will appreciate that in changing over from half a
dozen Exchanges in the city to two, it was a
very considerable undertaking. The records,
all documents, and the staffs had all got to
be transferred. We could have pursued
either of two courses. One would have been
to take a week to do the work, and the
consequence would have been that the
benefit of those claimants drawing unemployment benefit would not have been paid
for that week. We were anxious not to
impose that serious hardship upon our unemployed people and, therefore, we took the
course of making sure, above everything
else, that no one would be kept waiting for
one single moment for the benefit to
which he was entitled and which we
were anxious that he should receive.
1 am glad to say that that aim of ours has
been fully fulfilled. The staff have worked
with praiseworthy energy and devotion to
duty, and I am glad of this opportunity of
paying my tribute to them for the almost
superhuman efforts which they have made
to enable the change over to be made with
as little inconvenience to claimants as possible.
The hon. Member (Mr. Beattie) has indicated that we intend to do the whole work
associated with the payment of Unemployment benefit in this Central Exchange. That
is our ultimate aim, but realising that we
are dealing with abnormal conditions at the
present time, and that we will have to deal
with a very much smaller number of claimants later on, we have purposely kept on the
Frederick Street Exchange to help over what
I hope is a temporary period. The matter
has been most carefully gone into from that
standpoint. Again, two large waiting-rooms
are not quite completed, but the roofs are
upon them. At the moment they are not
closed in at the ends. I regret, therefore,
that they are draughtier than they ought to
bę. I am quite willing to give an undertaking to the House that if the waiting-rooms
which we propose to provide are not sufficient to meet the demand made upon
them they will be enlarged as was originally
intended. The contraction of one of the
waiting-rooms was simply done because when
we took over the building of the Exchange
the total sum was much larger than we felt
justified in expending. I am glad to be able
to assure hon. Members that this Exchange
is, in my opinion, one of the finest, if not the
finest, in the United Kingdom.
I am sure every hon. Member will appreciate that there are always initial difficulties in connection with a change over of this
character. These difficulties will be got over,
and I really am surprised that the hon.
Member thought it necessary not only to
ask this question but to raise the matter on
the Adjournment as well, especially as he
received in answer to the question the assurance that everything would be done that
is possible to see that the regrettable incident
of to-day will not be repeated. The hon.
Member raised the question of the Exchange
being paid for by the Imperial Government.
I need not go very fully into that, because
the House knows quite well that over and
over again we have voted money for the
building of this Exchange. I am sure he
will accept the assurance of my right
hon. Friend, the Minister of Finance,
and myself, that it is a burden which

23 NOVEMBER 1926
HOUSE OF COMMONS.

Tuesday, 23rd November, 1926.
The House met at Three of the Clock, Mr.
SPEAKER in the Chair.
Oral Answers to Questions.
CIVIL SERVICE COMMITTEE.
1. Mr. KYLE asked the Minister of
Finance whether he can state the date on
which the Civil Service Committee last met;
when it will meet again; and whether there
is a good deal of delay in attending to
applications by Civil Servants to retire with
the permission of this Committee.
The MINISTER OF FINANCE (Mr.
Pollock): I may preface my reply to the
hon. Member's question by stating that the
Civil Service Committee is in no way under
my jurisdiction. I am informed that it last
met on the 3rd of the present month, and
that a date has not yet been fixed for the
next meeting. The dates are arranged
according as business arises for its consideration.
I am advised that there has been no
avoidable delay on the part of the Committee in considering applications by Civil
Servants to retire with the permission of
the Committee.
Mr. KYLE: Might I ask the right hon.
Gentleman who is responsible if the Ministry
of Finance is not?
Mr. POLLOCK: The Ministry of Finance
is represented upon the Civil Service Committee, and perhaps it will enlighten my hon.
Friend if I give him the names of those who
are constituent members. The members of
the Committee are:
Sir Alfred Denis, K.C.B., appointed by the
Lord Chief Justice of England;
Viscount Cross, appointed by the Treasury;
Colonel Johnston, appointed by the Secretary of State;
Sir Ernest Clark, K.C.B., appointed by the
Government of Northern Ireland;
S. Sloan, Esq., appointed by the transferred
officers.
Perhaps I had better give the names of the
secretaries in case the Hon. Member (Mr.
Kyle) chooses to address them or
one of
them. One of them is Mr. Gatliff, who is
appointed by the Treasury, and the other
Mr. Dunbar, who is appointed by this
Government.
Mr. KYLE: To whom is this Committee
responsible?
Mr. SPEAKER: I think it is very likely
a Committee to which the hon. Member (Mr.
Kyle) can address himself. There are many
Committees over which the Government
have no control.
Mr. DEVLIN: Then what power have hon.
Members of this House in dealing with these
matters?
Mr. POLLOCK : I doubt very much
whether hon. Members have any power, because this Committee is appointed under the
Government of Ireland Act, and, therefore,
being a statutory Committee it is not possible to get outside the limits of its powers.
Any officer who desires permission to retire
under the eighth Schedule of that Act must
show to the satisfaction of the Committee
that the duties he is required to perform
are not analogous to those he had been performing before his transfer or involve an
unreasonable addition to those duties. This
in fact is an appeal tribunal for the protection of Civil Servants who had been in the
employment of the Imperial service and who
joined us, and their rights are secured by
the conditions under the statute to which
I have referred, and by appeal to the
Committee.
Mr. CRAWFORD: Might I ask the right
hon. Gentleman is there any appeal from
the decisions of this Civil Service Committee?
Mr. POLLOCK: I do not quite follow my
hon. Friend. Appeal by whom? If he means
by the Civil Servant there is no appeal. It
is the final tribunal which settles his whole
status.
MILK SUPPLY:
2. Mr. KYLE asked the Minister of Home
Affairs whether in view of the large number
of cases of milk adulteration reported in the
papers, and more serious still, the spread of
tuberculosis due to infected milk, he is prepared to take adequate steps to ensure a
clean milk supply in Northern Ireland.
The MINISTER OF HOME AFFAIRS
(Sir Dawson Bates): With regard to the
question of milk adulteration, the local
authorities in Northern Ireland already have
ample powers under the Sale of Food and
Drugs Acts to deal with adulteration, and
the fact that there has been such a large
number of prosecutions shows that they are
exercising their powers in this respect.
With regard to the second part of the
question, the local authorities have also
wide powers under the Dairies and Cowsheds Order of 1908, enabling them to take
2359 Oral Answers.

HOUSE OF COMMONS
Oral Answers.
[Sir Dawson Bates]
due and proper steps to ensure that milk
shall be pure and free from contamination.
The Order in question makes particular
provision for the steps to be taken to prevent infection from tuberculosis.
It is understood that the Local Government Commission has given special consideration to the question of a pure milk supply,
and pending the receipt of their report and
of any recommendations in this respect, it is
proposed to defer consideration of the question of conferring further powers on local
authorities in the above respect.
Mr. KYLE: Is the right hon. Gentleman
aware that in certain districts-Portadown
for example-according to the Press reports
they say that the high infantile mortality
is largely due to the defective milk supply,
and in view of that does he not think for
the sake of the health of the Six Counties,
he should get legislation on the lines suggested by the Tyrone and Fermanagh Agricultural Organisation Society?
Sir DAWSON BATES: I am not aware
of the report to which my hon. Friend refers,
but I would be glad to receive it from him
and to go into it.
WILLIAM GREER-SCHOOL
ATTENDANCE PROSECUTION.
3. Mr. DEVLIN asked the Minister of
Home Affairs whether, in November, 1923,
William Greer, of 53 Argyle Street, Belfast,
handed over the two children of his deceased
wife to her sister, who, as legal guardian,
was afterwards paid the War Office pension
of 7s for the children; whether the children
were not sent regularly to school, and their
guardian, who has since died, when
questioned by the school attendance officer,
gave the name of Greer as father of the
children; whether, in August last, Greer
heard that the police in the Shankill Road
district were looking for him, and that he
had been fined 19s at the Summons Court for
failing to send the children to school;
whether he was not served with the summons, and did not know anything about the
matter until long afterwards; whether hearing that there was a warrant out for his
arrest, he surrendered at the Shankill Road
barracks on the 19th August, and, although
he did his best to explain matters, was taken
into custody, and conveyed to Crumlin Road
barracks, where he served a sentence of 14
days, being released on the 1st of September;
and what steps the Minister proposes to take
to quash the conviction against Greer, and
to compensate him for the illegal imprisonment which he suffered.
Sir DAWSON BATES: I have no information which would enable me to answer the
first part of the question.
The facts of the case, so far as the police
are concerned, are as follows:-
On the 23rd March, 1926, William Greer
was prosecuted on the complaint of the Lord
Mayor, Aldermen and Citizens of Belfast for
failing to send his children to school, and
was fined 19s, or in default 14 days'
imprisonment.
As the defendant did not appear, I have no
doubt that the Court required proof of the
service of the summons in the usual way
before hearing the case.
On the 3rd April a warrant was received by
the police, who called at Greer's address but
failed to find him.
On the 19th August he surrendered himself
to the police, and stated that he had no
money to pay the fine, and wished to go to
prison.
Greer did not state that he was not the
guardian of the children, nor that he was unaware of the summons having been issued.
He was lodged in Belfast Prison on the
day of his surrender in compliance with the
Warrant of the Court.
No memorial or appeal has been received
from Greer or from any other person on his
behalf.
If he is of opinion that he has been illeg
ally imprisoned, it is open to him to seek
redress in the Courts in the usual manner.
ENGINEER OF BELFAST PRISON.
4. Mr. BEATTIE asked the Minister of
Home Affairs whether it is a fact that an
Engineer has been appointed from the Board
of Works for the Belfast Prison; whether, in
future he will consider the advisability of
giving officers on the prison staff an opportunity of filling such and similar posts the
same as was done when the Prison Service
was directly controlled by the Imperial
Government.
Sir DAWSON BATES: As I explained in
the answer which I gave to a question
addressed to me by the hon. Member for
North Belfast (Mr. Kyle) on the 4th instant,
a foreman of works has been transferred
from the staff of the Works Branch of the
Ministry of Finance to the Prisons Service.
With regard to the second paragraph of
the question, the normal practice which I
have adopted is to fill all posts in the Prisons
Service from the existing staff, provided

there are candidates having the requisite
qualifications. In the present instance the
post required qualifications of a special

PURCHASE OF LURGAN SHOW
GROUNDS
The following question stood on the Paper
in the name of Mr. William McMullen :
5. To ask the Minister of Home Affairs
whether it is a fact that the Lurgan
Urban Council have concluded an agreement with the Lurgan Agricultural Society
to purchase the Lurgan Show Grounds, at
a cost of £1,750, for the purpose of holding
fairs; whether such purchase is contrary
to the wishes of the inhabitants who desire
to continue the use of the main thoroughfare for this purpose, or alternatively,
desire the development of the new street
sanctioned by the Ministry twelve months
ago, from Carnegie Street or Hill Street;
whether he will take steps to ascertain the
wishes of the inhabitants of Lurgan before
sanctioning the purchase of the Lurgan
Show Grounds; and whether he will state
what is now the Council's intention regarding the projected new street.
Mr. SPEAKER: Before the right hon.
Gentleman (Sir Dawson Bates) answers this
question I should like to ask him whether
it is a matter over which he has any power.
We have got to be very careful in this House
not to infringe upon, discuss, or ask questions about matters which are under the
control of elected bodies, whether urban
councils or county councils.
Sir DAWSON BATES: I think it is a
matter within my control.
Mr. SPEAKER: All right.
Sir DAWSON BATES: It is understood
that tentative negotiations are in progress
Fetween the Lurgan Urban District Council
and the Lurgan Agricultural Society for the
purchase of the Show Grounds for the purpose of fairs and markets in the district, but
nothing definite in this respect has yet been
decided, and no application for sanction to
the arrangement has yet been received by
the Ministry of Home Affairs.
If and when an application for sanction to
the proposal is received, the Ministry, before
confirming it or otherwise, will take all
necessary steps to inquire into the merits of
the proposal.
As regards the new street, in connection
with which a loan was sanctioned by the
Ministry in October, 1925, it is understood
that the Council are desirous of proceeding
with the work as soon as possible, but have,

the land.
SPAHLINGER TREATMENT FOR
CONSUMPTION.
6. Mr. WILLIAM MCMULLEN asked the
Minister of Home Affairs whether he is
aware that the most eminent medical men
of the leading countries of Europe have
given it as their considered opinion that
the Spahlinger treatment for consumption
is a most satisfactory one; whether such
opinion is based on observation of permanent cures affected in advanced cases of
this disease which did not prove amenable
to other alleged cures; and whether it is
a fact that this treatment is not available in
Northern Ireland and other countries owing
to the fact that Monsieur Spahlinger has not
sufficient money to place it on the market
in a manner to protect the treatment and
the public against spurious and deleterious
imitations; and, if so, whether he will state
what financial assistance the Government is
prepared to give, so that the treatment may
be made available for all sufferers from
this dread disease in Northern Ireland.
Sir DAWSON
of
BATES: The work
Professor Spahlinger in connection with the
treatment of tuberculosis has engaged the
attention for some years past of the Government of Northern Ireland as well as of other
Governments.
In the early part of last year the Government, in conjunction with the Belfast
Corporation, arranged for a special mission
of Northern Ireland experts to visit Geneva,
with the object of studying this special form
of treatment on the spot.
The result of this investigation bears out
the opinion of many medical experts, and
goes to show that the Spahlinger treatment
undoubtedly possesses distinct possibilities.
However, it is not possible for a considered
opinion on the scientific soundness of
Professor Spahlinger's methods to be given
unless and until he is prepared to have the
complete technique and details of the preparation of his serum and vaccine submitted to scientific investigations.
Repeated representations have been made
to him with this object in view, and financial
undertakings have been promised to him in
the event of his agreeing to follow out this
course and of the results being considered
satisfactory.
It is understood that the Imperial Government is prepared to incur considerable

the event of the negotiations coming to a

CHARGES FOR CONVEYANCE OF FARM
PRODUCE.
8. Mr. ELLIOTT asked the Minister of
Agriculture whether it is a fact that the
steamship companies have advanced their
charges for conveying farm produce, principally potatoes, from Northern Ireland to
the cross-Channel markets; and, as this advance in freight is causing a serious reduction in the price the farmer will receive for
his produce, whether the Minister will interview the steamship companies concerned with
a view to having the rates again revised,
So as to enable the farmers of Northern
Ireland to put their produce in the cross-
Channel markets at remunerative, and, at
the same time, competitive prices.
The MINISTER OF AGRICULTURE (Mr.
Archdale): I am not aware of any general
increase of this nature. Following the outbreak last year of Black Scab in South Derry
the carrying companies, at the instance of
the Ministry, put into force temporarily a
number of specially reduced rates for the
conveyance of potatoes from stations serving
the scheduled areas to cross-Channel centres.
Generally these special rates are being continued, but so far as carriage to Bristol
Channel ports is concerned, it was
practicable to have the rates renewed for
this season. I am happy to say, however,
that the companies have now met the
Ministry to a considerable extent by agreeing
to a scale of charges a little higher than last
not
year's special rates. The new rates apply
from the 22nd instant until the 15th June
next.
PERMIT TO SHIP POTATOES. MESSRS.
R. MCKEE & SONS.
9. Mr. WILLIAM MCMULLEN asked the
Minister of Agriculture whether it is a fact
that his Department refused to issue a permit
to the firm of Robert McKee & Sons, Merchants,
Kilkeel, to ship 32 tons of potatoes to Liverpool on or about the 5th April, 1926, because
it was alleged that the aforementioned firm
owed the Department a sum of twenty-four
shillings and sixpence; whether the firm in
question denied owing the money and refused
to pay, as a result of which a cargo of
potatoes shipped by them was held up at
Whitehaven, and the firm put to the expense
of £82 to have the cargo released; whether
his Department subsequently acknowledged
that the firm did not owe the money, and
refunded the amount which the firm had
been compelled to pay before the cargo was
released; and, if this is the case, whether
his Department will take steps to compensate
the firm for the expense to which they were
put, and if the Minister will state whether
it is the policy of his Department to take
direct action to hold up cargoes while the
constitutional procedure of the law courts
is open to them for the recovery of any
alleged debt.
Mr. ARCHDALE: The Ministry did refuse
to give Messrs. McKee a certificate as indicated in the first part of the question.
The firm denied owing the amount stated
to be due, but produced no evidence that
the account was incorrect. Instead Messrs.
McKee illegally shipped the consignment
without the certificate required under the
Black Scab in Potatoes (N.I.) No. 2 Order,
1923. This illegality was no mere technical
breach of the Order, but was an infringement calculated to jeopardise the potato
export trade of Northern Ireland. The
Ministry has no evidence, as to the loss,
if any, incurred by Messrs. McKee, but if
there was any such loss it was entirely due
to the firm's own illegal action as stated,
and, consequently, no question of compensation by the Ministry arises.
It should be stated that, notwithstanding
the aforesaid serious breach of the law, the
Ministry immediately on receiving urgent
representations from Messrs. McKee sent an
inspector to Whitehaven to facilitate the
release of the cargo, Messrs. McKee at the
same time having paid the amount stated
to be outstanding, and also having agreed
to pay the reasonable expenses of the
inspector.
The Ministry is advised that the cargo
was duly released on the second day after

its arrival at Whitehaven. Subsequently
Messrs. McKee represented to the Ministry
that they had been put to expense and
trouble by the delay at Whitehaven, and

In the circumstances the Ministry decided
(1) not to institute legal proceedings against
the firm for their infringement of the Order,
and (2) to waive the claim for the expenses

With regard to the last point in the

by merchants at regular intervals, instead

practice of refusing further credit when

PRICE OF COAL.
10. Mr. KYLE asked the Minister of
Commerce whether he is aware that there
has been a reported decrease in the price
of coal at the pit-head to 50s per ton, and
could he state on what basis he allows merchants to charge 96s per ton in Belfast.
The MINISTER OF COMMERCE (Mr.
Barbour): I presume the hon. Member has
in mind pit-head prices in Great Britain.
It is, I understand, a fact that certain coal
in Great Britain is being sold at the pit-head
at prices as low and even lower than that
mentioned in the question. As the hon.
Member will appreciate, however, coal is not
yet being produced in Great Britain in
quantities sufficient to warrant the shipment
to Northern Ireland of substantial supplies,
and difficulties are being experienced in securing permits even in respect of supplies
for
Conpublic utility undertakings.
sequently, the price of 96s per ton, indicated
by my Ministry as a reasonable maximum
retail price for coal delivered direct by merchants to household consumers within the
city of Belfast, has been arrived at after
taking into consideration the c.i.f. prices of
Continental coal purchased some time ago
and now arriving in Belfast. As the hon.
Member may have observed, not only have
there been during the current month considerable fluctuations in price quotations in
the Continental market, but freight prices
have also shown a tendency to alter in an
upward direction. The advance of 6s per
ton in the reasonable maximum price notified
by my Ministry on 9th instant was, therefore, occasioned by advances in initial price
and increasing difficulty in securing the
necessary freight. A close watch is being
kept on the position, but, so far, it has not
been practicable to arrange a modification in
the price of ordinary black coal. It is likely,
however, that prices of brown coal will show
a downward tendency in the immediate
future.

NEW LABOUR EXCHANGE IN
CORPORATION STREET.
Mr.
MCMULLEN (by private notice)
asked whether it is a fact that no attendant
is employed at the men's Rota Committee
since the opening of the new Labour Exchange in Corporation Street; whether this
is responsible for the facilities previously
accorded to Trade Union officials and publie
representatives being withdrawn; whether
any consultation took place between the
aforementioned representatives and the
Ministry previous to their withdrawal, and
if not, will he state by whose authority it
was done, also whether the attendants' hours
of employment have been reduced by four
per week while uniformed policemen do duty
inside the Exchange, and whether an
unctuous appeal to the employers to give
employment is likely to be efficacious, while
the Exchange is understaffed, and 30,000 unemployed signing the register in Belfast.
Oral Answers.

Oral Answers.
23 NOVEMBER 1926
(Mr.
The MINISTER OF LABOUR
Andrews): There is an attendant who
is responsible for controlling the traffic at
both the men's and women's Rota Rooms,
and, in addition, there is a porter at each
door on the ground floor directing claimants
to the Rota Rooms.
Trade Union officials have been asked to
attend 15 minutes before the commencement
of the Rota meetings in order that they
themselves may not be unduly delayed and
that the work of the Rotas may be facilitated.
The concentration of work in the new Employment Exchange has enabled the Department to effect some economy in the cost of
the staff, including messengers and cleaners,
and the effect of this saving on the numbers
employed has been minimised by making
slight variations of the hours of work.
There is no policeman on duty outside the
building engaged on traffic control.
The Department has always itself followed
the policy which it has appealed to employers to adopt in the employment of their
staffs.
Mr. KYLE: The Minister has stated that
there is an attendant at the men's side and
at women's side at this Labour Exchange.
I have been a constant attender there, and
that is not so. There is no attendant at
the men's side at all.
Mr. WM. MCMULLEN: I would like to
ask the right hon. Gentleman how his
appeal to employers to employ ex-Servicemen is going to be efficacious if he does not
set
good example.
a
He has set
bad example by not properly staffing
this Exchange, and it is leading to serious
inconvenience to trade union officials.
a
Mr. ANDREWS: The hon. Member is
aware that this Exchange was only opened

not understaffed. When we have had some
experience of the matter and if I find that
it is understaffed I shall not hesitate to give
instructions to have the staff increased. I do
not think that at the moment it is understaffed.
POLICEMEN AT LABOUR EXCHANGES.
Mr. WILLIAM MCMULLEN (by Private
Notice) asked the Minister of Home Affairs
whether he will state when it became part
of a policeman's duties to do duty inside a
Labour Exchange, and whether the members of the Royal Ulster Constabulary are to
be used to keep disabled ex-Servicemen out
of employment.
Sir DAWSON BATES: I have authorised,
on the representations of the Ministry of
Labour, the arrangement under which a
policeman is stationed in a few of the larger
Labour Exchanges when payment of Unemployment Benefit is being made.
This arrangement is one of long standing,
and is solely for the safeguarding of the
public moneys at the Exchanges.
With regard to the latter portion of the
question, I am not aware that the discharge
of this duty by members of the Royal Ulster
Constabulary in any way prevents disabled
ex-Servicemen from obtaining employment.

The following motion stood on the Paper
in the name of the Prime Minister:
That this House, at its rising this day, do
adjourn until Tuesday, 30th November, at a
quarter before Twelve o'clock, and that only
formal business relating to the Royal Assent
to Bills agreed to by both Houses of Parliament and the Prorogation of Parliament be
taken on that day.
The PRIME MINISTER: I beg to move
the Motion standing in my name, leaving out
the latter part, which, I understand, is unnecessary. The Motion is:
That this House, at its rising this day,
do adjourn until Tuesday, 30th November,
at a quarter before Twelve o'clock.

The people will ask who are the Members
of the Senate? What is the Senate?
Senate is a body that amends our Bills after
we draft them. First of all, we consider the
policy. Then when we fashion out our policy
in the form of Parliamentary ideas We
transfer them to the draftsman. Our ideas
are incorporated in a Bill, and we bring it

Reading and a Second Reading. Then public
discussions take place, and we watch the

body so wise that it proceeds to propose
Amendments.

sharp, for Woodburn and Beltoi. Each man

TEACHERS' PENSIONS.
2. Mr. BEATTIE asked the Minister of
Finance whether he proposes to introduce a
Statutory Order to raise the pensions of all
retired public elementary teachers whose
pensions are less than fifty pounds a year
to that standard, in view of the large number
who have less.
The
MINISTER OF FINANCE (Mr.
Pollock): The reply to the hon. Member is
in the negative, as his proposal would have
the effect of placing a teacher who retired
after curtailed service or commuted a part
of his pension on the same footing as one
who served the full period of forty years
and did not commute. The effect of the
Pensions (Increase) Acts and the Old Age
Pensions Acts, taken together, is already to
give very considerable concessions to a large
number of pensioned teachers.

DISPENSARY RELIEF.
4. Mr. BEATTIE asked the Minister of
Home Affairs, whether he is aware that upon
the occasion of confinement many dispensary
medical officers charge fees to persons who
are entitled to receive gratuitous medical
attendance, and what steps does he propose
to take to bring this practice to an end.
The PARLIAMENTARY SECRETARY OF
THE MINISTRY OF HOME AFFAIRS (Mr.
Hanna): The right hon. Gentleman (Sir
Dawson Bates) has asked me to reply.
Dispensary medical officers are required to
attend without fee or payment all persons
duly and properly entitled to dispensary
relief, and I am not aware of any cases of
breaches of the regulations in this respect.
If the hon. Member is aware of any such
cases I shall be obliged if he will bring them
under my notice, when I shall have due
inquiry made.
