Debate on Address.

Unemployment.
But humbly regret that no proposals have
been made in the gracious Speech to ensure
that all those who are willing to work
should get work to do, or failing that,
should be provided with maintenance by
the State.
(Hon. Members: Hear, hear.) There is no
doubt that this question is one in which
there is a terrible lot of dishonesty. Even
yesterday while my Friend, the hon. Member,
the Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Kyle), was
making his speech here, he nearly got into
hysterics over the fact of this thing being
mentioned in the King's Speech. He seemed
to be under the impression that there was a
possibility, as he said himself, of the "pubs"
being opened on Sunday. I do not know
whether he considered this in itself to be
such a great iniquity, or whether he probably
thought that if such did occur he might lose
the love of his audience at the Custom House
steps.
But that is not the only thing we have
heard mentioned with regard to the Licensing
Act. Only yesterday in this House one of the
Ministers told me that the Government had
accepted a lease of this building in which we
are sitting, with a special stipulation clause
that no alcoholic liquors could be consumed
in it under any conceivable circumstances,
and that even if we were to drink the health
of the King, it must be done in ginger pop.
Now, was there ever such hypocrisy or dishonesty known? Do you ask us to believe
that all the Members of this House are teetotallers? If that is so I suggest that many
of them could take an action against their
countenances for libel and obtain very heavy
damages. I hope that in the new lease for
the building of the Parliament at Stormont
no such clause is inserted, because if there is
I can foresee very great difficulty and even
trouble. We were told by the Minister of
Finance yesterday that this "Home of Rest"
in the country would be inhabited by 700
Government officials. If that is so I am sure
these men are very likely to complain that
they are unable to obtain reasonable refreshments there while the other 400 who live in
the city will be able to go to the licensed
houses.
I think it is about time the Government
looked on this matter in a more straightforward and more honest way and were determined
not to be led or directed or dictated to by a
few faddists. They should consider the population as a whole. This, in my opinion, would
be much more satisfactory. If the Government in these matters are prepared to consider the advice which I have given here, I
believe that my coming here may be of some
service, but if on the other hand they are
only prepared to go on as they have been
doing-ignoring the claims and wishes of
those I represent-then I am afraid that it
may be said that I can serve no useful
purpose by being here. (Hon. Members:
Hear, hear).

could give yesterday were 61,598, That marks
a very serious state of affairs, and I regret
to say that the Government are not giving
the attention to this problem that is desired.
I stated more than once in this House that I
do not think the problem is going to be
solved by the methods the Government have
adopted. Whether you agree with our point
of view or not we believe we have put sensible
and concrete proposals before this House
that would mitigate to a considerable extent
the unemployment problem as it confronts us
at present.
One suggestion I remember putting forward was that the Minister of Labour should
take steps to ascertain the number of youths
engaged in industry, and also the number
of people over 65 years of age engaged in
industry. The view of the Government-it
is only a passing phrase-is that we are
coming into a more prosperous time in the
near future than we are experiencing at
the present moment. The Government have
not taken the step I suggested. If they
have taken any step of that nature or
character it has not been adumbrated so far
as the King's Speech is concerned. If the
Government are serious about this question,
if they want to achieve a solution of the
problem then some step of this character
should be taken, because up to the moment
the Government have only been tinkering
with the problem.
Last year I attempted to show what effect
machine production would have
on the
problem, and I was told by a number
of people that I wanted to revert to
the Stone Age. I have not the slightest
objection to the introduction of improved
machinery. I hold that machinery should
be utilised for the purpose of lightening the
burden of people, but not penalising the
people. I regret that any improvement in
machinery is used for the purpose of making
the position of the people worse. I pointed
out the effect of the conversion of ships
from coal burning to oil fuel. We have
gone a stage beyond that. We have now
introduced the Diesel engine which has
resulted in the disemployment of a large
number of people. The only way to solve
the problem is to tackle it on orthodox lines
or otherwise. We are simply to go on and
continue paying thousands of pounds each
week by way of unemployment benefit without getting any nearer to the solution than
at the present time.
Now, I may may be told that it is very
difficult for this Government to grapple
with the problem in the way I suggest inasmuch as the Government has not really got
the power. I will probably be told that in
order to try to get a solution of this problem
it should be dealt with internationally. As
we here have not got control over foreign
services it would be a difficult matter for
the Government to tackle. If that point of
view is put forward the implication of that
statement is that this Government should
attempt to get these powers they have not
got. We are paying four millions as an
Imperial contribution. The Premier has
told us that is being paid for certain purposes, to provide a Navy and to get the
benefit of consular services throughout the
world. In order to get a solution of this
problem it may be necessary for this Parliament to take that whole state of affairs into
consideration, because our territory is too
small, and the chances are we are much too
poor to continue an Imperial contribution
of that kind. Possibly the situation might
be palliated if we had control of international affairs and attempted to develop
greater trade between this country and some
of our Dominions or even foreign countries.
I regret to say we have not got those
powers. It leaves the Government in a difficult position, also anyone who attempts to
tackle this problem, and wants to give concrete proposals. I know I have been told
that my proposals mean Socialism, and that
the spokesmen for the Government are not
prepared to follow me on those lines. If
the hon. Member for the University (Dr.
Morrison) intends to follow me in this debate I suppose we will be given a rehash
of that old hoary subject of the evils trade
unionism has worked throughout Northern
Ireland. The hon. Member forgets that he
belongs to the most powerful organisation in
the world-an organisation that is responsible for excommunicating Dr. Axham for
attending to administer anesthetics to the
patients of Dr. Barker in London.
Dr. MORRISON: Quite right.
Mr. W. McMULLEN: The hon. Member
will tell us about some little petty-fogging
thing that has happened in the backwoods
of Ulster. We will be told that the responsibility that exists in Northern Ireland is
due to the iniquities of some trade union
official.
But the matter cuts much deeper than
that. We are not attempting to tackle agriculture in the way we should, and that will
probably be the basis of our activities for
the future. The way in which we tackle
agriculture will probably either make or
mar Northern Ireland. (Hon. Members:
Hear, hear.) If we judge by the King's

We are told that the figures have been

the present time. I suggest that
these numbers have not been reduced

trade or as a result of numbers of people

disallowing benefit to a large number of
people who were receiving it. We have got
a most extraordinary state of affairs. We
have the Parliamentary Secretary (Mr.
Gordon) going to the Shankill Road and
making a speech, in which he says it is a
slander on the working classes to say they
are not genuinely seeking work, while his
own Department are disqualifying people on
these grounds. We cannot accept both statements. If one is right the other is wrong.
Perhaps the hon. Member next time he intends to make speeches will make speeches
that are really true and are a reflex of the
activities of the Department he represents.
I want to suggest that that speech was not.
A large number of people have been disallowed benefit. That is how the figures
have been reduced.
I come to the main point of the Amendment. I will probably be told it is an outlandish idea that could only originate in
the brains of the three people who occupy the
front Opposition Bench-that no other people
of loyal Ulster would be able to conceive
such an outlandish idea as this. We ask
that work should be provided for them, or
that the State should maintain the people.
I have no doubt the hon. Member (Dr.
Morrison) who represents the University
will suggest this is an outlandish idea-that
it is wild, extravagant, and fantastic, and
could only come from an irresponsible
person like myself. But we find that larger
and larger numbers of people who do not
accept our full point of view are being forced
to the conclusion that if the employing
class of the country cannot provide employment the State should give them some sort
of maintenance. I happen to have a letter
to-day from a fairly unexpected quartera quarter that formerly was looked upon
as a citadel of Unionism and Protestantism
-from the people of the Shankill Road. One
of these people asked that the Government
of Northern Ireland should reinstate all
contributors to the Unemployment Fund
who have been signed off the register within
the last twelve months. I suggest that is
tantamount to the plea I am putting forward. If they are restored to the unemployment register it is the duty of the
Government to provide some sort of maintenance for these people who have been
struck off the unemployment register.
Does any right hon. or hon. Gentleman contemplate the position a person unemployed
is placed in? Did anyone for a moment ever
stop or hesitate to think about the awful
suspense people are in who are in receipt
of unemployment benefit at the present time?
I am daily in contact with these people. I
am at the Labour Exchange practically every
day in the week. I know the fears and
apprehensions of these people, coming before
the courts and committees, very often unsympathetic, where it is a crime to be idle
for two years, and where it is becoming a
greater crime. Can you imagine the harrowing suspense and inental agony of waiting
day after day for the whole source of income
to be cut off, and for them and their families
to be forced to go to the poorhouse? I suggest it is a desperate state of affairs
altogether.
heavy
The Minister of Labour has a
responsibility on his shoulders, a responsibility that some of us would not care to
undertake an exceptionally heavy responsibility, and from his own point of view he
may be attempting to discharge that responsibility as satisfactorily as he possibly can.
But I do say with all the emphasis I can
command it is unsatisfactory that simply
because a person is unemployed for two
years it should be looked upon as a crime,
and that these people. as a consequence
should have their income cut off, and their
only fault is they are unemployed for two
years.
I do not want to weary the House. I
have explained our point of view very fully
before. In attempting to do it again it is
only a recapitulation of things I have stated
on former occasions. (Hon. Members: Hear,
hear.) I may point out that unless a change
has taken place in the mentality of the
people who occupy the Front Benches their
reply will be a rehash of old replies and
shibboleths that we have got from the Front
Bench since we came into this House. I
hold that until such time as production is
Debate on Address-
Unemployment.
HOUSE OF COMMONS
[Mr. W. McMullen]
for use instead of for profit there is absolutely no solution to the question of unemployment. You may attempt to dispute
that. You may say it is very far fetched.
I challenge you to suggest any other remedy
for the problem of unemployment except
that production should be for use instead of
for profit.
If I wanted to examine the thing closely
I might point out that scarcely a commodity
produced at the present time is produced
for use. All commodities are produced for
the purpose of making a profit. Foodstuffs
are not grown for the purpose of satisfying
the pangs of hunger of the people. Foodstuffs are produced for the purpose of making
a profit. We have seen in this country when
there has been an abundant crop of potatoes
or an abundant crop of corn, and at the
same time we have seen many people in
Belfast going hungry. If these foodstuffs
were produced for the purpose of satisfying
the natural appetites of the people they
would be utilised for that purpose. But
they are being produced for the purpose of
providing a profit. As long as that is being
done we hold it is absolutely impossible to
find a solution of this problem. Well, I
do not expect the Government will look upon
it from our point of view, or that they will
attempt to tackle the economic interests of
their supporters, who are really standing
between the people and this problem. We
say it is a serious enough matter for the
Government taking a different point of view.
It is no longer a question of an employer
having a right over the management of his
own affairs. Up to the time that our economic troubles became acute it might be
argued that the employer could be allowed
to manage his industry in exactly the way
he liked. I would point out that the situation
is radically different at the present time.
We, as ratepayers, have got to bear the
burden as a result of the mismanagement
on the part of the employer class in this
country. If the shipyards and linen
merchants and those responsible do not
attempt to bring the management of their
industries up to date it probably means that
we are incapable of competing in many respects with employers in different other
countries throughout the world. The inevitable consequence is that large numbers of
people are unemployed. With employment being denied we ratepayers have got
to come to the assistance of the Unemployment Fund, and if we have got to pay the
piper we have a right to call the tune.
Inasmuch as we are paying or will have got
to pay to a very considerable extent
should be allowed a voice so far as this question is concerned.
we
It was suggested by the hon. Member for
West Belfast (Mr. Devlin) that it might be
much better instead of a number of discussions taking place in this House on the
question of unemployment the matter should
be referred to some people for the purpose
of considering the whole thing very carefully, and possibly bringing in a report on
the question. That has been done up to a
point some months ago without any practical,
satisfactory results, but I think an attempt
should be made along those lines again for
the purpose of finding out if we can get a
number of people to come together to try
to take stock of our whole situation, to take
stock of the agricultural position, to take
stock of the industrial situation, and we
should endeavour to get some people as members of the commission or committee who have
got views that are not absolutely orthodox
for the purpose of putting their point of
view, so that we may attempt to get a
solution of this very acute chronic situation
that we are in at the present time.
If we continue along the lines that we are
going on, and if I am here to move a similar
Amendment this time twelve months, my
position will probably be that I shall have to
record a still greater increase in the numbers
of unemployed.
The MINISTER OF LABOUR (Mr.

:
Mr. W. McMULLEN: I hope not myself,
but when I cast my mind back to 1923 I see
there were 37,000 people unemployed; in
April, 1925, we had 48,600 people unemployed,
and coming to to-day, taking the figures
given by the Prime Minister yesterday, we
have 61,000 people unemployed with no hope
of employment. Some of the right hon.
Members who occupy the front Government
bench are optimistic concerning the whole
question. The only remedy the Minister of
Labour was able to propound on a previous
occasion was that if we had the grit, vision,
and determination of our forefathers all
would be well. I happened to have an
opportunity quite recently of addressing a
meeting on the Shankill Road, formerly a
quarter in which I would scarcely be allowed
to speak, and I told the people there that
the right hon. Gentleman, the Minister of
Labour, suggested that if we had the courage,
vision, and determination of our forefathers
we could find a satisfactory remedy to the
question of unemployment. They laughed
hilariously at the idea that all we required
to have was vision, grit, and determination.
God knows, it was exemplified during the
sectarian troubles in Belfast that we had all
the courage and determination that were
required, and it will surely not be suggested
that our vision is more obscure or dimmer
than that of our forefathers or our fathers

If
we have got courage, determination, and
vision some of us have got the remedy--
(Hon. Members: Hear, hear)-and if hon.
Gentlemen are not prepared to take steps

This Government, like many Governments
in the past, are not wise during a crisis but
will get wise when the crisis develops and
gets over-mature and the people ripe for
action, but they will be too late. Like all
Governments who pass through crises they
will be too late when the time comes because
the people who share our point of view-we
may not be here will occupy the benches the
gentlemen on the Government side occupysome of them fast asleep at the moment
(Laughter). When that day arrives a solution will be found to this acute and chronic
problem of unemployment. I beg to move.
Sir ROBERT LYNN: To a great deal of
what the hon. Member (Mr. W. McMullen)
has said I am sure no Member of
this House would take any exception. We
who are strongly opposed to Socialism are
agreed that the Socialists are as anxious as
we are to try to find a settlement, but personally, I have always felt that they are
going about it the wrong way. Take my hon.
Friend. His first suggestion-indeed practically the only suggestion he made is that
the people should be withdrawn from work
at the age of sixty-five. I wondered as he
was making that statement in what position
the Minister of Labour would then find himself if everyone over sixty-five was suddenly
withdrawn from labour. In the second place,
he pointed out how the introduction of
machinery had accentuated unemployment,
but then, forgetting what he had said in
the earlier part of his speech, he proceeded
in the latter part to point out that the real
cause of the trouble, and in this I agree with
him to a large extent, is that our machinery
is not sufficiently up-to-date. He cannot
have it both ways.
I suggest that some practical help should
be given to the Minister of Labour in trying
to solve this question of unemployment. It
is not a question that is going to be solved
by one section of the House or by one party,
but by the united efforts of everyone in the
House. Personally, for five years I have
made suggestions here with regard to unemployment, and even at the risk of wearying
the House I will repeat them. I have said
the present is a most suitable time for the
Government to take over the principal roads
in the country and re-make them. In the
memory of even the youngest of us a revolution has come over transport. Whether
people like it or whether they do not the
whole system of transport has been revolutionised within the last twenty-five years.
We know that the majority of our roads are
absolutely unsuited to the heavy traffic they
have to carry. Sooner or later the Government will be called upon to take on the task
of re-making all these principal roads. Could
there be any more suitable time for doing
that work than the present? Why, nearly
every one at least of the men folk who are
unemployed-could with very little training
be utilised for making these roads so that
they could carry the heaviest traffic. History
teaches us and our own experience teaches us
that good roads lead to prosperity in every
country where good roads have been introduced. Then there is another point. This
Province of ours suffers from flooding, and
there is an enormous amount of work that
will have to be undertaken by public bodies
because private bodies cannot do it.
Mr. KYLE: Hear, hear.
Sir ROBERT LYNN: I admit there are a
lot of things that public bodies have to do
because private concerns have not got the
capital to do it. Drainage is surely one of
the most essential. It is quite true we passed
a Drainage Act last Session, but the effect
of that Act was to accentuate rather than
remove the difficulty. Then--I am sorry the
Minister of Agriculture is not here-there is
a splendid field for work in the matter of
forestry. I know something has been done
in that respect, but I would like to know
whether more could not be done and whether
this is not the proper time to do it, because
I am sure there is not a Member of this
House who does not feel it would be better
to provide work for these people than to give
them I know the Minister of Labour objects
to "dole" and I do not like the word myselfto give them unemployment insurance. The
longer you keep people from work the less
fit they are for work. I am sure even the
three Socialist Members will agree with me
in this that they would much prefer to see
the people working than getting unemployment insurance.
Mr. KYLE: Hear, hear.
Sir ROBERT LYNN: I do urge these three
points on the Minister of Labour, and I would
like as a humble back-bencher to pay my
tribute to the excellent work he has done.
He has worked enthusiastically and he has
done all that one man can do, but this House
and this Government should back him in trying to make better roads, trying to bring in
a large scheme of drainage, and going in for
forestry. If the House and the Government

Mr. KYLE: Hear, hear.
Dr. MORRISON: He said, "If the Member
for West Belfast makes a speech I will make
a bet you will reply." I think very highly
of the hon. Member for West Belfast who
puts his case forcibly and strongly, and he
has made a clear distinction as to the esteem
in which he holds this House as compared
with another house to which he goes, namely
the Belfast Board of Guardians. I think that
when he comes in here he recognises that he
is in association with honest men and, in

comports himself in a way which is a credit
to the assembly to which I am very pleased
to belong.
He referred to the medical profession in
his speech, and he said I belong to the closest
trade union in the world. In a certain respect
that is true. I do not know if his memory
or that of some of the other Members of
this House goes back far enough to remember
a gentleman who came round through the
North of Ireland posing as a painless extractor of teeth. I was told that after he
had gone through Belfast the dental hospitals
in the city were engaged for months repairing
broken fragments of the jaws that remained
after he had extracted those teeth. I heard
also of a man who was operated upon by this
skilful manipulator who had an abscess
followed by gangrene and he lost half his
tongue and had great difficulty in speaking
afterwards. Assume for a moment that the
like of that happened to the hon. Member
for West Belfast (Mr. W. McMullen).
Mr. KYLE: Or to the hon. Member for
the University (Dr. Morrison.)
Dr. MORRISON: Assuming that the deserving army of unemployed had only such a
champion as he would be under those circumstances, I think that instead of protesting against our conduct he would congratulate us upon the attitude we take as
a medical profession. So far as I can see the
attitude of the medical profession is designed to protect the public, and the attitude of the hon. Member for West Belfast
is to victimise the public, or a large section
of the public. Our object is to eliminate
shams. I do not want to say that my hon.
Friend is a sham, but a man who chiefly
employs himself in exploiting the misfortunes of the public is sometimes thought
by numerous people to be more or less deserving of having that appellation applied to
him.
The medical profession insists on a trade
mark. It insists that everything should be
genuine and that there should be no shams.
We take advantage of our position to make a
law that even the member who is himself
qualified is not allowed to sign a certificate
for a man who is unqualified, because there
is the danger of his exploiting the public
and imposing on them. Consequently, if I
myself wrote a certificate or covered a man
who was not qualified I would be guilty of
infamous conduct and my name would be
expunged from the Register. This loose,
silly talk about making a victim of that
English doctor who assisted a bone-setter is
the purest nonsense that ever was listened to.
I pass from that, Mr. Speaker, as I see you
are getting somewhat restless. I make the
mistake of following the man
who precedes me. I sometimes think that when
another hon. Member is allowed to travel
over a wide field without limitation from
Mr. Speaker I should have similar indulgence.
Mr. SPEAKER: I am afraid I must explain my attitude. I think the hon.
Member for West Belfast (Mr. William
McMullen) who introduced this Amendment
merely referred to the medical profession as
being the greatest trade union of all

hon.
Mr. DEVLIN: I am quite sure that
whether the hon. Gentleman (Dr. Morrison)
is effective or not we are always delighted to
hear him, and I congratulate the medical
profession upon the tremendous asset he is
to them in defending them when no one has
attacked them. He has ventured to speak of
quacks, and I forget what the other appellations were that he applied to some of the
most distingushed servants of humanity. Sir
Herbert Barker I think is the name of one
whom he rather stigmatised in language
which I think was unworthy of the hon.
Gentleman. For the great services he has

was honoured with the greatest distinction

nobler or no more unselfish profession than
the medical profession, at the same time I
must dissent from his description of Sir
Herbert Barker and those associated with
him in that work, whether medical men or
otherwise.
I rise for the purpose of supporting this
Amendment in the hope that the discussion
may be productive of some good to our
Northern Province. I stated yesterday, and
I repeat it to-day, that I have been somewhat disappointed at the resourcelessness
which has been manifested by the present
Government in dealing with this question of
unemployment. I would have expected that
after the stress that was laid upon the subject in the King's Speech something practical
would have been stated as to the intentions
of the Government, that they would have
been able to inform the House, and through
the House to inform the people of Ulster as
to whether we are going on as we have been
going on in the past or whether the Government had in their minds some new and fresh
proposals to solve this problem.
As I said yesterday, I would be the last to
withhold from the Minister of Labour (Mr.
Andrews) the credit which he deserves for
his unceasing labours and for his untiring
work and his deep and unselfish interest in
the Department over which he presides, but,
if he will allow me to say so without detracting from any credit which is due to him,
I think the function of the Minister of
Labour, and the function of his colleagues in
the Cabinet, is to see if there is any other
way out of these economic and industrial

You have made a large claim-it is a matter

-that you have passed a great education
Measure. In the sphere of secular education
I venture to say that very few people have
any complaint to make about it. You are
expending large sums of money on primary

girls when they reach the age of adolescence,
when they are coming out from the schools.
There is no prospect of employment for them.
We know that to retain these boys and girls
at school to the age of fourteen or fifteen
years involves tremendous sacrifices on the
part of the parents of these children, and
when they are well educated, at least when
they are well equipped as far as primary
education can equip them, they find themselves at a loose end. There is no employment for them, and up to the present very
few politicians and no statesmen, or even
humanitarians, have realised the vital importance of this question not only to these
boys and girls themselves but to the future
of the State. It is bad enough to have large
numbers of adults standing in idleness with
no prospect of work, but to look forward with
anything like hopefulness or serenity to a
future in which the boys and girls leave the
schools in order to become idlers is a
situation that I think ought to cause grave
concern to those who control the State. You
have an opportunity that no other Government have and I speak now in the most
friendly spirit-because this is a very
small area. You control six counties.
It is very compact. You are able to come
into close touch with the conditions, and
therefore in dealing with these things you

the first things that the Government ought
to do is to appoint either a Commission or
a Committee to try to devise some means by
which this most important, and, as I think,
most vital, problem should be dealt with.

remember taking part in what was known

May I ask the right hon. Gentleman (Mr.

As the hon. Member has suggested, I in
my capacity of Minister have had a direct
touch, and perhaps I may say direct responsibility largely for the investigations that
have taken place in regard to the value of
a drainage system for the Six Counties. The
necessity of it is obvious. For the last
three years the weather conditions have
been of such a character that the land
has been largely soured and great areas
have been rendered unfit for suitable and
productive cultivation. That has all been
admitted. While that is so it must not be
aboverlooked that the conditions
normal. My hoa. Friend (Mr. Devlin)
favours that word both in regard to industry
and in regard to agriculture. We must not
allow our views on a subject of this kind to
be perturbed unnecessarily by the exceedingly
abnormal conditions of two or three years,
but the information derived from those abnormal conditions has been sufficient to
justify the view that it will be an advantage
that greater attention should be paid in
respect of arterial drainage-that is the relief
of the land generally-and the relief of the
land from soured and water-logged conditions
which I am sorry to say habitually obtain,
apart altogether from the extraordinary
conditions that have developed because of the
weather circumstances of the past two or
three years.
The question is what have we done? The
hon. Member's curiosity is quite laudable and
quite justifiable. I should like to satisfy
him. We passed the Measure last year to
which the hon. Member (Mr. Devlin) has
referred. That Measure imposed on public
authorities the responsibility of supervising
the condition of the land under their control
and the enforcement of certain work upon
the farmers themselves so that watercourses
and drains that were clogged and various
other difficulties should be removed prior to
any preparation for the relief which it is
hoped will be received for the promotion of
main drainage in the Six Counties. That
brings me to the Bann, which is the outlet of
practically the whole eastern part of the Six
Counties. I gave an undertaking when the
Measure was submitted that is now an Act of
Parliament from last Session that we would
prosecute scientific investigation of the
conditions of the Bann in order that it
might be discovered whether modern
scientific and engineering knowledge could
solve the problem that for a period of 150
years has been attempted and was discovered
or thought to be insoluble. Our engineers
have been working from that time to this
moment on this subject assiduously and I can
give the assurance to the House that within
a few days, perhaps, or at any rate within
two or three weeks, we shall have the full
report and recommendations of these
engineers as to how the Bann problem can
be tackled.
Any conferences or conversations I have had
with the engineers on the subject rather point
to the fact that in their opinion the problem
is not insoluble, that, at any rate, it can
be greatly ameliorated, if not absolutely and
thoroughly cured to the extent that perhaps
some of us wish it to be cured; but, at any
rate, as I say, a great remedial measure can
be undertaken on the Bann, and I am living
in hopes-I do not wish to give positive
assurance that the financial side of the
question may come within the ambit of our
means. Beyond that I cannot go, and I hope
that assurance will satisfy not only the hon.
Member (Mr. Devlin), but also Members of
the House who have exhibited such an interest in this great and important subject.

come after us, seeing that forests
trees cannot be raised in a week or a year,

Mr. ANDREWS: As regards the Amendment I look upon it as most important. It
sets out that all those who cannot find work

hon. Members who have spoken to this
Amendment have not tried to tell us what

who earn somewhere between 50s and 60s per
week to receive that amount when unemployed? Or again are the labourers to be

week? Or is maintenance to be paid at a
flat rate?
Now I venture to suggest that the way we
provide through our Unemployment Insurance Acts for our unemployed people is
fairer than any of these methods, because
in the first place it pays benefit in relation
to the need of the person claiming benefit,
and in the second place it provides that only
those receive benefit who are entitled to it.
Now the Amendment itself does not propose
to pay benefit or maintenance, whichever you
like to call it, to everyone. It says that it
shall be paid to those who cannot obtain
work and who are willing to accept it. Well
that means that benefit is not given to all
comers, and that you are bound to have
local employment committees and courts of
referees just as at present to decide who
shall get it and who shall not get it.
Again is it proposed to pay maintenance to
those who may not be available for work?

Again, someone has referred to the question of artificial silk, and suggested that the
machinery of our mills which could not be

the first place the situation of our linen

place because the machinery which is entirely suitable for flax spinning would be
totally unsuitable for silk manufacture.
Mr. DEVLIN: Would the right hon.
Gentleman say how it is that an English

Mr. ANDREWS: The answer to that question is this. The firm that came over from
England, and which we welcome, has gone

And then again we have done what we

My own Department has also done what it

done. I would like to point out that in
Belfast and Derry juvenile unemployed and

And then it should not be forgotten that

The PRIME MINISTER:
Hear, hear.
Mr. ANDREWS: There is nothing I detest
more than make-believe or holding out
to people false hopes which are bound to lead
to disappointment. I hate window-dressing.
I have said before in this House, and I
repeat it to-day, that we in this little area
of ours cannot hope to be able to do better
as a Government for our unemployed people
than the great wealthy country of Great
Britain does for its unemployed people. Our
struggle for these five years has been to keep

and is at the present time considering, many

in step with Great Britain. We have pledged

May I say in conclusion that I am rather
surprised that my hon. Friend the Member
for West Belfast (Mr. Devlin) has raised the
question of forming committees to explore
this problem of unemployment? He was one
of those who suggested the Unemployment
Conference should be held, and it was held.
The personnel of that Conference has never
been criticised. It was composed of employers, it was composed of workers' representatives, it was composed of hon. Members
opposite as well as those behind me, and
included the hon. Member for West Belfast
himself. That Conference very earnestly
tackled the whole problem. We formed ourselves into various committees. There was a
Shipbuilding Committee, a Linen Trade
Committee, a Building Trade Committee, and
a General Purposes Committee, and my hon.
Friend (Mr. Devlin) was actually the vicechairman of the General Purposes Committee. Those committees all worked. The
Parliamentary Secretary (Mr. Gordon) and
myself attended every meeting of the main
Conference. It is true we did not attend the
committee meetings, and the reason was this,
that we felt it was right that we should
leave the committees untrammelled in any
way to explore the problem from their
standpoint and from the fact that they were
experts in connection with the particular
matter into which they were asked to
inquire.
Those committees reported to the main
Conference, and their reports were earnestly
considered and were published. I have never
heard those reports criticised. I have heard
them favourably commented on in many
directions. If those reports did not unearth
anything very new, at any rate they proved
that it was extraordinarily difficult to do
anything beyond what the Government had
already been doing to mitigate this serious,
tragic difficulty that we have faced all these
years. Now, that Conference is still in
being, and if the hon. Gentleman desires it
should have another meeting I am quite
willing.
The Development Commission is also still
sitting. It is exploring various problems
with which we are faced. It has considered,
Mr. BEATTIE: I rise to support the
Amendment, and I do 80
because of
the necessity of such an Amendment
being put into operation immediately.
I was rather surprised at the innocence
the Minister of Labour has shown
in regard to what it really means. I am
sure that with the knowledge at his command he has got a greater conception of the
interpretation of the Amendment than he
allows this House to understand. Several
points in his remarks were worth noting.
He gave us three ideals-peace, stability, and
security. The last is the most important to
the class I represent here, because I claim,
and rightly claim, it is the lack of security
that is the cause of so much discontent and
grumbling and differences of opinion. If the
Government can give security to the workers
that is all they ask. They ask for security
of a kind that will give them the same treatment and the same social standard whilst
out of employment as they would enjoy when
in employment.
I would like to draw the Minister's attention to this. Sometimes I have been very
severe in regard to the Ministry, not to the
Minister as a person. When the Minister
has had as close contact with the masses of
the people who have no security whatsoever
as I have had perhaps the attitude he adopts
to-day will be discarded. Here is the case of
a man who claimed to get security in the
Six Counties:
Dear Sir-I am writing to ask you if you
could get me a job on the relief work, as
the wife and I and family are on the verge
of starvation. I have tried everywhere to
get a job, but no use, and if I cannot get
unemployment money I must get something. For God's sake do your best and
do something for me.
That is a man who was constantly in employment up to the year 1921. Owing to the
upheaval at that particular time he was
thrown out of employment. He was never
able to return to employment, he never had
the opportunity. The Government of
Northern Ireland never provided work for
him although he is quite willing to work
to-day. He is struck off unemployment
benefit because he has not fulfilled the conditions in the past two years.
Here is the case of a widow who has two
sons, and who, owing to the insecurity, has
Unemployment.

HOUSE OF COMMONS
[Mr. Beattie]
had to turn out and get a job in the Belfast
Ropework Company to support her two ablebodied sons. They are willing to work but
cannot get it, and owing to the tightening
up of the new regulations in regard to extended benefit are denied the right to benefit,
and the widow, who is up in years, has had
to turn to the Belfast Ropework Company
and take employment. That is security of a
kind I am not inclined to agree with.
There is another man, the father of six
children, who lives in Kilroot. He happens
to have the same name as the hon. Member
for County Down (Mr. Patrick O'Neill), who
made his maiden speech to-day. He was in
constant employment in the shipbuilding industry up to August, 1920, when he was
compelled through circumstances to leave.
He was working in Govan shipyards till
1922. He drew unemployment benefit from
1922 to January, 1923, when he joined up in
the Free State army. He came back in
April, 1924, and after he had been restored
to benefit his case was brought under review, and he was finally turned down as not
meeting the conditions set out by the
Ministry. He has six children, and his wife
and he are now on the verge of starvation.
If that is security I am rather surprised.
The masses, so far as I can see by past legislation have no security whatever. They
have free access to the roads, but I read in
a story recently that the reason the masses
were allowed to use the roads to go to their
work was that if they did not get them free
they would not go over them, and the
employing classes would have to go and do
the work themselves.
We have 61,000 unemployed workers in the
Six Counties. This number is ever increasing. It is not decreasing, because, while you
show a decrease this month against the
month of January, I want to challenge the
Minister and tell him to-day that we stand
at a higher figure of unemployment than we
did in January. Not on his register, quite
naturally, because he has made a provision
that he is going to reduce the register under
his control. Then the regulations, against
which I protested in this House on the last
occasion, have been the means of turning off
thousands of heads of families, and young
men and young women who have no provision for their upkeep other than their
parents. I heard the hon. Member for the
University (Dr. Morrison) say he would put
a test.
We have already challenged the
Minister to give us a test, a test for work.
All you have got to do is to offer a job to
any man and you will find out whether you
will be disappointed by his refusal, I do
not say they are all of the one brand. There
are black sheep in every squad, but the
majority of these 61,000 are genuine seekers
for work. I am sorry the hon. Member for
the University (Dr. Morrison) is not here.
Mr. WILLIAM MCMULLEN: He is.
Mr. BEATTIE: I did not see him behind
me. I am glad to see him on this side of
the House because I believe that the day is
not far distant when he will be sitting along
with me and my two colleagues. I know of
a case in which the test was put to an applicant for work. He got instructions from the
Bridge End Exchange to go out to a farmer
named Henry, away out at Craigantlet, a distance of about six miles from the city. He took
the position and walked the six miles out to
the farm in the morning. When he arrived
the farmer told him he had got to work about
nine hours a day and the wages would be
twelve shillings a week with three meals a
day. That was a married man with a family.
He took the challenge and followed that employment for three weeks, doing the six
miles in the morning and six at night, living
on twelve shillings a week with three meals
a day and keeping his wife and family. That
is one of the men whom the Minister has
now turned down from extended benefit.
We have also hundreds of other genuine
cases, cases that I personally took up and
brought to the Ministry only to find that
there was no redress from the decisions
arrived at. I have been told that Local
Employment Committees have been set up
and that representatives of the workers are
on those committees. If you will bear with
me for a moment or two I will tell you how
those committees act. I happen to be a
member of one. The members that now act
on the Rota Committees, in regard to
extended benefit, have no more power than
the ordinary individual who walks the
streets of Belfast. They can give a decision,
but that decision is not taken into account
when it goes into the scrutineers' quarters.
The scrutineers' quarters are in the various
Exchanges. There is no claim passed through
the Rota Committee now which is allowed
direct. It passes through the manager's
hands, and another new thing that has been
introduced-one of the methods of tightening
up the regulations-is that when vou are
overdrawn to the extent of, I think, 120 or
125 stamps -a man who reaches the age of
say twenty or twenty-two--if you are overdrawn these stamps by that amount the axe
goes on the table. For people from twentytwo upwards I believe another margin of the
overdrawn account is allowed. I believe
there are about three scales, and if they have
overdrawn their accounts to those extents I
hear-I only take it from hearsay the
decision of the officials in the Department is
to disallow any claims presented to them.

Mr. ANDREWS indicated dissent.
Mr. BEATTIE: If I am wrong I got the
information from a member of your committee. I prided myself on having got the
age of self-dependent persons reduced from
twenty-five to twenty-two during the last
Session, but I have now received a circular
letter informing me that the age of selfdependent persons has been increased from
twenty-two to twenty-five. I regret this
increase in the age. It means that a man
who has a son of twenty-five years of age,
and who has £2 8s per week, is going to have
to keep his son and his wife on that amount,
because his son will be denied the 18s of
extended benefit. 38s for the man and
woman, with 10s for the son is 48s. That is
the maximum, and anything over that would
prevent him from receiving benefit. I regret
that that provision has been added.
I would also like to refer to one more of
the Minister's remarks. He said that the
Government were assisting Sir Samuel Kelly
in the development of the coal industry. I
personally would have been more satisfied if
he had said that they were going to restore
the Bill discarded by the last Government,
namely the Bill for the development of the
hydro-electrical scheine. Electricity is the
coming force, and we should have an eye to
that condition of affairs, so that we may be
in a position to take up electrical development when the time arrives. I believe that
the sooner the Government restores that Bill
the better it will be for Northern Ireland.
The Minister referred to several schemes
to which I was going to refer, but seeing
that they have been dealt with already, I
do not intend to say anything about them
at the present moment. I would just like
to tell the Minister that we are drifting
every day towards a state of affairs which,
once it matures, will be very hard to check.
You claim that you want to work on parallel
lines with Great Britain. We claim the
same, but if your conditions for extended
benefit are going to be on parallel lines with
those in Great Britain, you are doing a
grave injustice to the working-class people
of Northern Ireland, because you must remember that the regulations drawn up in
Great Britain have been drawn up knowing
that if they cut off benefit from a particular
class of applicant, then he is provided for
under the Poor Law. That does not prevail
here, and I say that if you should relax the
regulations and allow people either to have
extended benefit, or else bring pressure to
bear on your comrades in the Government
to compel the Guardians to do as the various
Boards in Great Britain do, grant outdoor
relief to all those who are denied the right
to extended benefit. Something has got to
be done. I live right in the heart of my
constituency, and I seem to be the only representative here who has the whole cares
and worries of that division on his shoulders.
Perhaps my hon. Friend (Mr. Gyle) on my
left will not allow me to say that, but I
come in close contact with these people. I
meet them at my own door, morning, noon,
and night, and their hardships are unbearable. I can assure the House that I feel it
myself when I take up a case, write to the
Ministry, find that I am denied the right to
reconsideration, and then have to inform
the claimant of the result. I can assure
you that it is small wonder that they seem
ready for an explosion almost at any time.
I would appeal to the Minister to consider
fairly and justly the relaxation of the regulations. That would be maintenance in a
way. It would not be maintenance in the
sense of the Amendment, but it would be
maintenance in a way, and it would be such
as would give some little comfort in the
homes of these people. It will not give all
that is needed or required, but it would be
a palliative, and we on these Benches are
prepared to take a palliative, knowing perfectly well that that is about all we will
get. I would ask the Minister to put the
full facts before a committee, and I believe
that if the conditions of affairs in England
and Scotland were placed before that committee, and also the condition of affairs in
Northern Ireland, they would ask to have the
regulations relaxed. Your auditor-or whoever it may be that is coming over-will
surely consider the position of the
Guardians in refusing out-door relief. I desire to support the Amendment in its entirety, but at the same time I would ask the
Minister to give what I have said in regard
to securing equal treatment under the new
regulations his sympathetic consideration.
Mr. KYLE: I want to support the
Amendment which has been so eloquently put
forward by my colleague, the hon. Member
for West Belfast (Mr. William McMullen).
This Amendment states specificially the
Socialist demand on behalf of the working
classes. That is that the State should provide work, or, failing work, that the State
should provide maintenance for the people.
That in a nutshell is the position which the
Socialist Party in Northern Ireland, or the
Socialist Party in any part of Great Britain
and Ireland, will put forward to the upholders of the capitalist system to-day. We
have heard very eloquent speeches this
afternoon from the hon. Member for West
Belfast (Sir Robert Lynn) who sits behind
us, and from the Minister of Labour (Mr.
Andrews). Both these speeches were admirable, but neither of them attempted to deal
with the fundamentals of this particular
Unemployment.
Debate on Address-

HOUSE OF COMMONS
[Mr. Kyle]
Amendment. It is all very well to say that
we should have the roads mended. Undoubtedly we should have the roads mended
and kept in repair. It is all very well to say
that we should have inquiries made into the
possibility of developing the sugar beet industry. That is very necessary and very
useful. It is all very well for the Minister
of Labour to say that he has supplied the
community of the Six Counties with something round about 9,000 houses. That may
be very necessary and very useful. It is all
very well to have inquiries made into why
there is this volume of unemployment. All
these inquiries are useful and necessary.
I would say to the Minister, in reply to
the question which he asked of these Benches,
as to how we were to determine what that
maintenance should be, that he should here
and now declare his willingness to set up a
Commission in Northern Ireland consisting
of representatives of all parties in this House
to inquire fully into what would be necessary to keep a man, his wife, and three
children, so that that Commission might
determine accurately the amount of money
that it would take to buy the necessaries of
life for the ordinary or normal family, and
that then that should be the standard of
maintenance that he, as Minister of Labour,
should give to the people for whom the State
cannot provide work.
My colleague, the hon. Member for East
Belfast (Mr. Beattie) has dealt with the
problem of security. I would like to add a
word or two to what he has stated in regard
to the problem. If there is one thing more
than another that we of the working classes
need and desire, it is security, and the State
has recognised that up to a point. Within
the last twenty years there has been a tremendous development of the social services,
development along the lines of National
Health Insurance, Unemployment Insurance,
and in various other ways. The State is
endeavouring in its own way to get security
for the great mass of the working people. We
want to see that further extended. We want
still further to increase the security which
we of the working classes have. That
security to the huge number of the unemployed at the present day in the Six Counties
may seem a myth, yet it is more than there
was twenty years ago, more than there was
ten years ago.
The Socialist party want that security developed, because after all it is the working
classes who produce all the wealth of the
community. It is not that the workers cannot produce enough to keep the people fed,
clothed and housed. The workers
can
produce the food, the workers can produce
the clothes, the workers can produce the
machines, and they can produce the goods
with the machines. It is because, as the
Member for West Belfast (Mr. William
McMullen), stated, that the primary object
of industry to-day is to enable people to make
a profit, instead of to supply the people
with the things that they require, that the
State should be organised, and so provide the
people who are the community, with the
necessaries of life. I have yet to hear that
denied. It is the State's duty to look after the
people whom it governs. Surely that is one
of the first things that the State should conceive to be its duty, namely, to see that the
inhabitants of the State are fed, clothed and
housed. Those are three essential things. It
is for that reason that I support this Amendment.
The acceptance of this Amendment would
mean a fundamental change in society.
There is no doubt about that. It would mean
an entirely different outlook. It would mean
the acecptance of that principle which the
hon. Member for West Belfast (Mr. William
McMullen) laid down, that things should be
produced primarily not for profit. The passing of this Amendment would mean a
tremendous change, because we see from the
Press that the interests which supply capital
to the various industries have made more
profits during the past three years than they
did in the three previous years when industry was good. The banks are paying 18,
20 and 25 per cent. interest to their shareholders, in the last three years of the most
unexampled depression. The putting into
operation of this Amendment would mean
the alteration of all that. It is not, as I
have stated, that the workers cannot produce
the goods, because we have it on the
evidence of some of our leading scientists
that one man with machinery can produce
enough woollen goods to do 300 people for one
year. One man with machinery can produce
enough cotton goods to do 250 people for a
year. Five men with the aid of machinery
can produce enough out of the ground to
supply 1,000 people with food for a year. It
is because of this capitalist system, which
is a curse, not only to the working people,
but a curse to many of the employers, and
it is because of this outlook of the employing
class, speaking generally, that we are in this
impasse, and that we are in the deplorable
position in which we find ourselves to-day.
Make no mistake about it, capitalism itself
is breaking up. The hon. Member for West
Belfast (Sir Robert Lynn) is away. I am
sorry for that, because he is rather keen on
this particular question. In fact, he brought
in the name of Karl Marx. Karl Marx was
not always right, but he was not very far

wrong in his magnificent work on Capital,

climate of ours need clothes to wear—

Mr. KYLE: I bow to your ruling, but I.
was trying to point out the implication of

Perhaps when the vote comes to be taken

being imposed in Northern Ireland at the

Mr. T. HENDERSON: I did not intend
to take part in the debate on this Amendment, but for the life of me I cannot see how

I agree with the hon. Member for West

I cannot allow this occasion to pass without

I must say on behalf of the unemployed

Position of Leaseholders.
Mr. MCALLISTER: I beg to move as an
Amendment to the Address, at end to add
the words:-
But humbly regret that no mention in
the gracious Speech of intention to initiate
legislation to enable leaseholders, during
the currency of their leases, to have their
leases renewed, or to purchase the landlord's interest on just and equitable terms.
In rising to propose this Amendment I
feel I am moving an Amendment which will
commend itself to 95 per cent. of the people
of Northern Ireland and that it is in the
form of a highly constructive Amendment,
and, if accepted by the Government, it will
promote the collective and individual
interests of all the people in Northern
Ireland. Shortly stated the position of a
leaseholder in Northern Ireland up to the
present time is this: He takes a lease at a
stated ground rent, and he is compelled at
high cost to build a house or other building
on that land, and at the expiration of that
lease if he is in the hands of an extortionate
or unconscionable landlord-a landlord
without any sense of moral responsibility in
his business dealings, he is entirely at his
mercy. He has to accept his terms or surrender and allow his property to be confiscated.
About twenty years ago the Irish
Nationalist Party in the Imperial House of
Commons introduced a measure which would
have remedied the grievance which I propose
should now be remedied and the measure was
of such a meritorious character that it was
adopted by the English Government of the
day. It passed through the British House of
Commons, but by ingenious manoeuvring the
Tory landlord party in the English House of
Lords secured the insertion of an ingenious
amendment making it inapplicable to
building leases and the whole intention and
the whole benefit of that beneficent legislation was destroyed.

We all know, particularly those who are
coming into daily contact with these leases,
that 95 per sent. of the leases granted in
Northern Ireland are what are termed building leases. The House of Lords introduced
an Amendment to the Bill as it then stood
excluding these building leases, that is, leases
with a covenant to build, from the scope of
that Measure. They realised at that time
what they were doing, because Lord
Lansdowne rather gave the show away by
stating that every lease of any value in
Ireland was in the nature of a building lease.
Therefore, this Act was of no material effect.
The official Unionist Party from Ulster
impeded and opposed and stopped by every
means in their power the passage of that
beneficent legislation.
Immediately before the last General
Election for Northern Ireland, my colleagues,
the Unionist candidates for Antrim, were
about to address and hold a meeting in Portrush, and by special request they were asked
to meet a deputation of the Unionist leaseholders in Portrush, and the present Parliamentary Secretary to the Ministry of Home
Affairs was delegated to speak. He professed
to speak for and on behalf of his colleagues,
and he stated in reply to that deputation that
they had a most meritorious case and
expressed his sympathy with them. At least,
from letters I have received from North
Antrim, all who were present at that meeting went away under the impression that
they had more than sympathy and that action
would be taken in order to mitigate the
wrongs which the present system of tenure
inflicts upon them. I may say in passing
that I have had many letters from those who
voted for my Unionist colleagues at that
election and were present at that deputation.
They have come to their senses and have
seen the error of their ways and will never
be guilty of the same mistake again.
I wish to point out a few concrete cases
which have come to my personal knowledge
Position of Leaseholders. 88

HOUSE OF COMMONS
[Mr. McAllister]
after only a few minutes' inquiry. I know
of one man who holds two houses in a town
in Northern Ireland. The present rent of
those two houses is £4 19s 6d.
Mr. POLLOCK: Ground rent?
Mr. MCALLISTER: Ground rent. His
lease is about to expire. I should say the
houses were built entirely by him and his
predecesors in title. The landlord did not
contribute a brick, did not pay for an inch
of cement in the entire structures, and his
demand now is that he should receive a fine
of £200 and a rent of £20 before he will renew the lease. I know of another instance
under the same landlord. I may say that
landlords own whole towns in Northern Ireland, and in many instances are ruining the
towns. I do not speak in regard to all landlords, because there are just landlords in
Northern Ireland as well as unjust. This
particular landlord in a case which came
under my personal notice let land whereon
six houses were built. The rent for the
whole six houses was £7 15s. The lease was
about to expire, and an offer he made, along
with several alternative offers, was that he
would let one of these six houses at a fine of
£200 and a new rent of £15 for the one house,
'where the original rent for the whole six
houses was £7 15s. Not only so, but he gave
the tenant seven days to accept or refuse that
offer. Further, there was a covenant in his
lease whereby the tenant was bound to keep
the premises in repair. He said to the tenant, "If you do not accept my terms at the
end of the lease I will confiscate your property and I will sue you for £1,000 damages
for failure to keep the property which you
built yourself in order." That is a case
which has come under my own personal
notice.
I know another case in another town, and
this is a town in which I suppose I did not
get ten votes at the last election. Leases are
about to expire practically throughout the
whole town, and one landlord holds in his
hand the prosperity or the absolute ruin of
that town. In one instance brought before
my notice the only terms upon which the
landlord will renew his lease is at thirty
times the present poor-law valuation. Within the last few years the tenant has spent
£1,500 in creating and erecting and renovating the place. There are many more instances like that, but I have only a few moments
to quote these few concrete cases. Men like
myself engaged in my profession are coming
across these cases continually and daily, and
are in a position to realize the great injustice of this wholesale confiscation that some
of the landlords are guilty of at the present
time.
I came into this Parliament with the intention of offering constructive criticism, and
if this is not constructive criticism I do not
know what constructive criticism is. This is
an Amendment which if accepted will improve the collective and individual interests
of the people. Take the case of a thrifty
artisan who denies himself throughout his
whole life every luxury, only spending his
money on the necessaries of life. He expends
his whole funded income on building a house,
say, at £400 and the lease expires at the end
of ten years and the landlord puts a pistol
to his head and says, "Instead of £4 rent you
now pay £20." I suggest this is a state of
affairs that in a civilized community at this
hour of the day a just Government with the
interests of the people at heart cannot allow
to continue for another moment. I have
great pleasure now on behalf of the leaseholders of every section and creed and class
and party in Northern Ireland in moving
this Amendment and urging upon the
Government the necessity for removing one
of the greatest injustices which exist in
Northern Ireland to-day.
Mr. McGUCKIN: I have the greatest
possible pleasure in seconding the Amendment that has been moved. May I say that
in doing so it occurs to me, having listened

McAllister) because this is a relief Measure?
It is the removal of an injustice to the leaseholders of Northern Ireland. As far as I
could understand it is a Government
Measure. It was a Government promise, at
any rate. It was a Government promise
which has not been redeemed, and because
it was a Government promise and has not

this undoubted grievance that deputation

Amendment.
The injustice to the leaseholders requires
very few words. We all know the case of
the hard-working tenant, the man who holds

That was in the year 1906 or thereabouts-
I cannot give you the exact date. No doubt
my other hon. Friends have been longer
in this House than I have; my experience of it is limited at the moment, but
in the limited time at my disposal I have
been wonderfully surprised to learn of the
interest taken by the Government, on their
own statement, in the toilers and the democratic people of Northern Ireland. Casting
our minds back to the year 1906, one wonders
when this sudden interest was born. One
wonders further, now in the year 1926, when

one wonders how this undoubted grievance
romained unremedied. It was a simple

What was the cause of it? Who is to
blame? I would like to hear an answer to

Amendment arises because those questions

sure, for us to suppose that the same spirit
--shall I call it?-of landlordism which perneated the minds of the Tory Benches in

Northern Ireland. Surely that cannot be so.
If it is not so, I wonder what the reason is
why we have heard nothing in the Speech as
to this alleviating Measure. I have little
further to add on the question of this Amendment. I challenge anybody to deny that it
is a grave injustice to the toilers and the
workers, to the lessees of their holdings, that
the law in its present condition should remain. I ask for some explanation of why
these points, having been brought to the

The ATTORNEY-GENERAL (Mr. Babington): This Amendment, which has been so
clearly moved and seconded, is an Amendment which goes a great deal further than
the House has been led to believe, either by
the hon. Member for Antrim (Mr. McAllister)
or the hon. Member for Derry (Mr. McGuckin) who has spoken in support of it. If
the Government were to accept this Amendment to the Address it would cut right across
all the law of the land as it at present
exists. As the House is probably aware, the
relations between landlord and tenant, at
any rate so far as holdings other than agricultural are concerned, have been governed
for centuries by the law of contract. That
law has left both landlord and tenant perfectly free to contract with each other upon

and when the House considers that those

Therefore, I might point out to the House
in the first place that this question which
has been raised in this method, by way of
an Amendment to the Address, is one of
supreme importance when you come to consider the ultimate bearing that it has on
the life of the community. As I have said,
the relationship between landlord and tenant
has been governed for centuries by our law
of contract, and one would think to listen
to some of the remarks that have been made
in the introduction of this Amendment that
this grievance, which is now being voiced,
is one which is peculiar to Ulster. But
that is not so. The law of Northern
Ireland with reference to the relationship of
landlord and tenant, allowing for some small
differences, is exactly the same as the law
of Great Britain as a whole, or Great Britain
and Northern Ireland as it is now, and the
tenant in England or Scotland or Wales,
business premises

or urban
premises, or indeed any premises-for they
have not got the relief given in this country

any difference that may arise, and any injustice that may be done, is an injustice
which arises from individual cases between
individual landlords and individual tenants.
Many Members of this House who have
seen that most fascinating play of Mr. George
Bernard Shaw's "John Bull's Other Island,"
will remember the protest of the motor
driver when the Irish tenant was complaining that the land that he had torn from the
hillside with his own hands had been taken
from him by his landlord. He replied that
his father had set up in a drapery business
in London, had expended a large sum of
money in developing that business, and had
produced a very valuable business indeed,
and after he had reached the summit of
success he was turned out in the street by
a harsh landlord without a penny of compensation, and had no redress at law. Therefore this proposition is one that is not
peculiar to our country. It is peculiar to
the law of contract as it applies all over the
United Kingdom of Great Britain and Northern Ireland, and it is most necessary that
this House should look into the matter very
carefully before they allow themselves to be
committed to anything in the nature of

of the commercial life of this country. I am
rather surprised that this point has been

injustice that is undoubtedly done in individual cases as between landlord and tenant.
But individual injustice is done in almost
every branch of life as between individual
members of the community, whether it be
between landlord or tenant or whether it be
between two commercial men who contract
together in respect of any commodity,
whether it be houses or whether it be land.

Mr. BABINGTON: My recollection of the
Town Tenants Act was this, that it only
gives the tenant a right to compensation for
disturbance in cases where the premises
were used for business purposes, or a right
to compensation for improvements where
those improvements were made before the
passing of the Act. It goes on further to
give a right to compensation for improvements after the passing of the Act in cases
where those improvements were made with
the knowledge of the landlord, and there are
provisions in the Act enabling questions of
dispute as to whether the improvements
were to be made or not to be decided by the
County Court Judge. But I submit those
provisions of this Act are not on the same
footing as the Amendment now before the
House, because this is an Amendment to
give absolute security and tenure and also to
give them the right, or perhaps it may be in
the alternative to purchase out their premises
and become the owners of the premises which
they formerly had as tenants.
May I point this out to the House? That
as a general proposition a tenant who takes
land and builds a house upon a contract
which only gives him a tenure of say from
50 to 60 years, which was the common
tenure in some of the smaller towns in
Northern Ireland, did so with his eyes open.
He knew what he was doing. Conditions of
course changed between the time at which
he entered into that contract and the time
when the lease falls in. It is to be
regretted that so many tenants in Northern
Ireland build upon those conditions. You
find across the water that tenants will not
build on those conditions, and I have been

build upon anything less than a fee simple.
A Scottish tenant would not even build on a
999 years' lease, which is regarded in this

with this difficulty in Northern Ireland,
namely, that a lot of these tenants have built

The PRIME MINISTER: To-morrow if
time permits some of the Supplementary
Estimates will be taken, but the main
business will be the Financial Resolution in
regard to the Unemployment Insurance
Agreement Measure, which, as hon. Members
are aware, is a Measure complementary to
legislation at present under consideration at
Westminster. This legislation is of an extremely urgent character, and it is proposed
that both stages of the Financial Resolution
be taken to-morrow, the Second Reading of
the Bill on Tuesday next, 16th instant, and
the remaining stages on Thursday, the 18th
instant. In addition to this Unemployment
Measure the Second Reading of the Housing
Bill will be taken on Tuesday and also the
Loans Guarantee Financial Resolution. On
Thursday, the 18th, the consideration of the
Unemployment Insurance Bill will be supplemented by the Second Reading of the
Loans Guarantee Bill, the Second Reading of
the Administrative Provisions Bill, and the
consideration, of the Supplementary Estimates. It is proposed to adjourn from
Tuesday, the 16th instant, until Thursday,
the 18th instant, Wednesday, of course as
hon. Members are aware, being St. Patrick's
Day.

CASE OF MR. THOMAS O'DOHERTY,
SCHOOL TEACHER.
1. Mr. DEVLIN asked the Minister of Home
Affairs whether Thomas O'Doherty, a public
elementary school teacher, presently undergoing a third year's course at Queen's University, was arrested on the 23rd January,
1926, at the Donegall Pass Barracks, Belfast,
on the charge of stealing a bicycle from the
Students' Union, on the 19th January;
whether on the 25th and 26th of the same
month the police in charge of the case received written and oral statements from Mr.
R. N. Greer, a fellow student; Mr. William
Parr, Registrar of Stranmillis Training
College, and Professor Lloyd, M.A., of the
same college, proving conclusively that Mr.
O'Doherty was at the training college at the
time at which the bicycle was supposed to
have been stolen, and at the time he was
supposed to have been seen riding the cycle
in the University grounds; whether the
police suppressed this evidence, and whether
Mr. O'Doherty, after being twice before the
Magistrate at the Belfast Police Court, was
committed for trial on 1st February on the
charge; whether at the Commission on the
24th February Lord Justice Andrews, after
hearing only part of the evidence for the defence, stopped the case, and instructed the
jury to return a verdict of not guilty;
whether the Minister can say what action
he proposes to take against the police connected with the case, and what compensation
he is prepared to offer Mr. O'Doherty for the
treatment he was subjected to.
The ATTORNEY-GENERAL (Mr. Babington): As this matter relates to prosecutions
for which I am responsible, I have been
asked to reply to the question. The reply
is as follows:-
In this case Mr. Thomas O'Doherty was
returned for trial on the evidence of three
witnesses, one of whom identified him as the
man who removed the bicycle; the other two
identified him as the man who subsequently
disposed of it in their shop.
There was nothing irregular in the proceedings or in the conduct of the police, and
no evidence was suppressed.
Under these circumstances no claim for
compensation can be entertained.
Mr. DEVLIN: Can the right hon. and
learned Gentleman say whether the magistrate who tried this case stopped the case
and said there was no evidence against this
man upon which he could be convicted? Is
the right hon. and learned Gentleman aware
that three distinguished members of the
Teachers' Training College came forward
and gave evidence that it was impossible for
this man to have committed the offence as
he was in the college at the time it was
committed?
Mr. BABINGTON: The facts with reference to the action of the learned judge who
tried the case are as follow: The witnesses
for the Crown were produced and maintained
their evidence as to the identification of the
accused. The Crown case proceeded to a
close, and was not stopped by the learned
judge and, therefore, it must be taken that
on the case, as presented by the Crown, there
was, at any rate, a charge which had to be
answered. After the Crown case had closed
five witnesses were called on behalf of the
defence, and at the end of the evidence of
the last of these five witnesses the learned
judge stated that having regard to the
standing of these witnesses and the volume
of evidence for the defence it would not be
safe for the jury to convict, as there might
have been a mistake, and, accordingly, he
directed the jury to find a verdict of not
guilty. The case was not stopped; it was
allowed to proceed until a sufficient volume
of evidence had been called by the defence
to warrant the learned judge in saying that
the matter was in doubt, and that, therefore,
the accused was entitled to be discharged.
Mr. DEVLIN: Is it not a fact that the
police were in possession of the statement
of these three distinguished men, and that
the police kept this evidence of these men
back when the trial took place in the police
court? I should like to ask the Attorney-
General, as, I take it, he directs prosecutions, or at least controls them, whether
this information was put in his possession
before he sent the case to the assizes.
Mr. BABINGTON: The supplementary
question which the hon. Member has just
asked me is based on a misapprehension as
to the way in which criminal prosecutions
are carried out under our law. When the
accused is brought before a magistrate on
an indictable offence the magistrate has no
jurisdiction to try the case. His only
jurisdiction is to say whether or not there
is a prima facie case on the evidence of the
Crown against the accused, and, though
that evidence may be contradicted by
evidence upon the other side, if he is satisfied that a prima facie case stands and
Oral Answer.
11 MARCH 1926
Debate on Address.
Mr. SPEAKER: Order, order.
requires investigation he is bound to return
it for trial. The matter then comes before
the law officers upon the evidence of the
Crown witnesses, and again if there is a
prima facie case a prosecution is directed.
It then comes before the grand jury, and
again if a prima facie case is established a
true bill is found. It then comes before a
petty jury and a judge for the purpose of
trying the issue that has been raised between
the respective parties.
In this particular case the police behaved
with perfect propriety. They had the
positive identification of the accused by a
messenger, who was attached to the
University, and who swore that he saw the
accused riding this particular bicycle out of
the University on 19th January, at some
time after three o'clock. They had also the
evidence of Mr. Andrews, junior, who said
that at 4-30 on that afternoon the accused
presented the bicycle to him for sale, and
they had the evidence of Mr. Andrews,
senior, the last witness's father, who said
he purchased the bicycle from the accused
at some time about 5-30, and upon that
evidence the police charged the accused before the magistrate. The police had in their
possession when the accused was brought
before the justice a copy of the statement
by Mr. Greer, who, I think, is also in the
University, accounting, or purporting to
account, for the movements of the accused
at some of the material times. The police
with perfect propriety produced that
document to the magistrate, but were told
that as there was a prima facie case that
document should be preserved for use, if
necessary, when the matter was investigated
by the petty jury.
The accused was represented by counsel
and a solicitor, and his counsel, who
has very considerable experience in these
matters, could if he had so wished, or if he
thought he could displace the prima facie
case, have produced not only this Mr. Greer
but the two other witnesses whose names are
mentioned in the question. They were not
produced, and accordingly the prima facie
case stood. There was absolutely no alternative but for the matter to come before a
petty jury for investigation.
Mr. SPEAKER: I am afraid this is really
developing into a debate. I certainly should
not have allowed it but for the fact that
there is only one question on the Paper.
Mr. DEVLIN: Arising out of that may I

witnesses were not distinctly clear-
Mr. DEVLIN: Therefore I wish to

ment. (Mr. Cooper.)
Which Amendment was at end, to add
the words:-But humbly regret that no
mention is made in the gracious Speech of
