Amendment again proposed.
Position of Leaseholders.
Mr. BABINGTON: When our proceedings
were interrupted last night under Standing
Orders I had almost concluded what I had
to say with reference to this Amendment.
I think I had pointed out to the House that
so far as this Amendment is concerned it
raises issues of very great magnitude, indeed
a great deal more serious and fundamental
than was suggested by the proposer of the
Amendment.
This question as to the renewal of leases
by landlords is one which has always been
D
Position of Leaseholders. 100
Debate on Address-
HOUSE OF COMMONS
[Mr. Babington]
carried out under the ordinary law of contract. Of course, it is quite obvious that
renewals are made upon reasonable terms
by landlords, or terms which are considered
reasonable by tenants. In other cases unreasonable demands are made, and the
reasonableness or otherwise of those demands
must be defined by the value of the premises
at the fall of the lease. We are all perfectly
well aware of the fact that in a big number
of cases the value of the premises has appreciated to a very great extent during the
currency of the term, and when the lease
falls in the reasonableness or otherwise of
the demands of the landlord must be determined by the value of the premises in the
open market, whether that value be determined by reference to rent or whether it be
determined by reference to the capital value
of the premises.
It happens every day, and it is not very
long since I had a case of this sort before
me in the City of Belfast in one of the main
thoroughfares. The tenant had held premises at a rent of £600 per annum, and
when the lease fell in the demand his landlord made from him, and which the landlord
was able to get in the open market, was a
rent of £2,500 per annum, so greatly had the
value of premises in the central part of the city
increased during the currency of that lease.
The House will readily understand that if
the interests of the tenants, and it is impossible to distinguish between them, are converted into perpetuity, either by giving them
perpetual tenure or by some system of purchase by which the interest of the landlord
is transferred to the tenant, the whole basis
on which dealing and trafficking in houses
and house property is carried on will be
completely done away with, and a new system
will have to be evolved in its place.
It can easily be seen that there is a very
great distinction between the case of land
and the case of houses and house property,
because in the case of land the tenants are
occupying tenants, and such a thing as a
lease of agricultural land in this country is
very rare, indeed. Therefore, when the
tenants were converted into peasant proprietors the lands continued to be dealt with
on the basis of an absolute interest from that
time on, but in the case of houses that
cannot be so, because there are a great
number of people who set up in business
who require terms. They do not know
whether their business is going to succeed
or not, they have not the financial backing
behind them to take perpetuity or to purchase the absolute interest in the premises,
and they have to go into the market and
lease premises. In the same way
great number of householders are not in a
position to purchase the fee-simple of their
a
dwellings, and they have to take them on
lease.
If any interference such as this Amendment suggests was to be sanctioned by Parliament the only effect of it would be that
those persons who became perpetuity holders
under any Act that might be passed to that
effect would in their turn become landlords
of other tenants. It is impossible to devise
any new form of tenure by which the
business instincts of the people could be
satisfied without upsetting the whole of the
commercial relations of the community.
Therefore, I suggest that so far as this
Amendment is concerned it has not been
properly thought out. It has been dictated
by the fact that there are, unfortunately, in
some cases landlords who are unreasonable,
but it does not necessarily follow that because some landlords are unreasonable the
whole system. of land tenure is one that
ought to be done away with and scrapped.
There is no country in the world, so far
as I am aware, that has ever been able to
devise a satisfactory system for the tenure
of land other than the one based upon freedom of contract in the open market. The
same rules, with slight modifications, apply
in the great communities in America, and
also on the Continent, and until some better
system is devised it is quite impossible for
the Government to undertake to interfere
with landlord tenure and to destroy the
basis upon which all commercial contracts
have been carried out for the last few
hundred years. I have nothing more to say
on this Amendment. I can only say on
behalf of the Government it is quite impossible to undertake a vast and sweeping
reform of this sort upon the very short and
flimsy evidence that has been produced here
of one or two exceptional cases of hardship,
which if they were looked into carefully
with all the relevant facts might prove easily
susceptible of explanation.

May I say in the first place I am sorry

what the law on the subject really is, but
there are other aspects of this question that
have got to be considered. I know the case
that the hon. Member for Antrim (Mr.

Considering the modest character of the proposal which has been submitted by my hou.
Friend, the Member for Antrim (Mr.
McAllister), I think if we are to judge the
speech of the right hon. and learned Gentleman it is an indication of the brilliant contributions he will make to our subsequent
debates. The right hon. and learned Gentleman is a very useful member of this Government. He was badly needled in this House.
He will surround or cover with legal camouflage the real and vital questions which are
submitted, because I fail to find in his
speech a single attempt to deal with the
merits of the proposal submitted by my hon.
Friend.
He gave us an elaborate disquisition upon
the law of contract, but he ought to know
as well as I do that the preservation of contracts means the sterility of progress. Contracts have always been broken by successive
Governments. There was a contract between
landlord and tenant in Ireland, but the
public resentment was so great against the
whole landlord system that even a landlord
Government was compelled to transform our
landlord system and create a system of
peasant proprietorship, so that really I am
not moved in the least by the right hon. and
learned Gentleman's somewhat ornate description of the value of contracts. What is
the simple proposition that my hon. Friend
submits? It is that no man who has built

from him, in the creation of the wealth of
which he was the main factor.
My own view is that these increased values
should go neither to the tenant nor to the
landlord. I think they should go to the
community. It is a perfectly monstrous
thing in any great community like the city
of Belfast, or Manchester, or Liverpool,
where in the public interest public taxes
are paid and development brought about not
by landlord or tenant, but by the whole
community, that the increment should go
to any individual landlord or tenant irrespective of the community who have created
that interest. I am supporting this Amendment
for the simple reason that I want to remove
the injustices that have been done to the
hard-working, thrifty, progressive citizens in

and learned Gentleman has stated that my
hon. Friend has brought this question forword and that it is not worthy of consideration of this House, because it deals only
with odd cases. I know myself there are

The tenants of those houses are afraid to

he is entitled to do. Therefore, I say it is
a bigger question than the right hon. and
learned Gentleman asserts it is. It is a

here. The right hon. and learned Gentlemian stated that no such suggested legislation

Surely, if the British Parliament, from

which you follow, and which you say it is

side of the House. It is a very reasonable
and feasible Amendment which is going to
do justice to the people of Ulster and to
assist and encourage them in the development of their property. A number of years
ago a man who has done absolutely nothing
to develop or to make Belfast what it is at
the present time purchased property in
Royal Avenue. The tenant of that property
had to leave it because the rent of the shop
and premises was raised from £100 up to
almost £500. When the rents for these business premises in the centre of the city are
raised, who has to pay them? The working
people have to pay for them when they go
to purchase their goods. Therefore, I think
the Government in all fairness to those
people who are trying to develop Ulster,
which we all love very dearly, ought to take
into consideration this very important
Amendment that affects the backbone of
Ulster, if I may say so. They would only
be doing a justice that has been kept back
for a long period. If hon. Members opposite
accept the Amendment they will be lauded
to the skies by many of their most loyal
supporters. I have great pleasure in supporting the Amendment, and I sincerely
trust that the Government if they do not
accept the Amendment will give the hon.
Member for Antrim (Mr. McAllister) an
undertaking that they will set up a Select
Committee.
Mr. GYLE: The very eloquent maiden
speech that was delivered by the Attorney-
General certainly placed the matter in a
very clear light from the legal standpoint,
but one of the illustrations that he gave
from George Bernard Shaw seemed to me
from a layman's standpoint to give his whole
case away. (Hon. Members: Hear, hear.)
He told us about a farmer who had scooped
out on the hillside a farm and who complained to an Englishman regarding the
rent that he was being charged and the
Englishman said that that was nothing because his father had built up the business
and the landlord had taken it away without
any compensation. (Hon. Members: Hear,
hear.) That is exactly our case. That is
the case we put before the Government. I
did not intend to speak on this Amendment
because unfortunately for myself I am in the
position of having a lease expiring at a very
early date. I am entirely in the hands of
a landlord on whom I cannot bring any
reason to bear. He has got an exaggerated
idea of the value of his property, and unfortunately we have no law to compel him
to listen to reason. So I find myself in
exactly the same position as some of
those unfortunate people who reside in
North Antrim.
I would impress on the Government the
fact that during the last election I was
visited by many business men who impressed
upon me the necessity to have a Town
Tenants' Act passed into law at a very early
date. I know the case of a block of property
in the centre of the city--I mentioned this
before-which a landlord purchased. The
rent prior to that was something like £32 per
annum, but he raised it to £200 a year.
Does the Government say that the action of
a man who purchases a block of property and
puts a burden on the tenants of £200 a year
and thus drives some of them out of business is just, right, or fair? Is that justice
between man and man or justice between
tenant and landlord? I fail to see it. I
know that the Government may not be able
at the moment to accept the Amendment.
I would rather be inclined to agree with my
Friend the hon. Member for West Belfast
and impress on the Government the necessity
of setting up a Select Committee of this
House to go into this matter. I agree that
that is the proper way in which all legislation should be approached. A Royal Commission or Select Committee should be set
up so that we would understand and know
exactly the trend that legislation would take.
We would know what effect it would have
and that justice would be done between man
and man. I have therefore great pleasure
in supporting the suggestion made to the
Government by the hon. Member for West
Belfast that a Select Committee or Royal
Commission be set up in connection with
this matter so that we may do something
or other for the unfortunate tenants whose
leases are now running out.
Mr. JOHNSTONE: I had not intended to
intervene in this debate, but on account of
Position of Leaseholders. 110

what the hon. Member for Antrim (Mr.
Crawford) has said I feel I must say something because I happen not only to be one of
those unfortunate people whom the hon.
Member wishes to protect but I happen also

think I am not so bad as that. I arrived

say is this that I think there is a good deal
to be said on both sides of this question.
After all, the tenant who takes a piece of
land from a landlord and erects a house on
it is making a bargain with his landlord.
He may make a good bargain or he may make
a bad bargain. He may make an exceptionally bad bargain, and then everybody says
he has been badly treated. We are all liable
to make bad bargains. I do not suppose
there is a single Member of this House who
bas not made a bad bargain.
It should be said that Parliament has
always been in favour of protecting men who
are put in a position which an unconscionably bad bargain has forced upon them. Innumerable Acts have been passed by various
legislatures to protect borrowers from money
lenders, and I do not see why the Government
should not consider the question of protecting
the tenant from a landlord who is trying
through an unconscionably bad bargain to
extort from him a perfectly extortionate
rent for the land which he has to give up
at the end of his term of tenancy. He has
taken his tenancy for 10, 15, 20, 50, 99 or 999
years in the expectation that he was going to
make something out of the tenancy, otherwise he did not deserve to be in business
at all. But there should be a limit to the
extortion which his landlord is able to exercise over him at the end of that tenancy. The
same procedure has been recognised in a
number of other cases. It has been recognised in connection with the carrying on of
business. A man must get reasonable compensation for the amount of business he is losing.
At the present time you have passed laws
which prevent the ordinary landlord of an
ordinary house from getting an extortionate
rent out of his tenant, and I do not see why
the Government should not consider the question of setting up a Committee as has been
suggested to consider in what way the tenant
could be protected from being treated in an
extortionate way by the landlord.
The PRIME MINISTER (Sir James Craig):
I suppose there is no Member of the House
who has learned more during the debate
yesterday and to-day on this subject that I
have myself. I happen to know practically
nothing whatever about the law that regulates these matters, and the specific cases
brought to our notice yesterday by the hon.
Member for Antrim (Mr. McAllister) were
also unfamiliar to me. I heard nothing whatever about them. I have listened to the debate and I have heard debates in the Imperial Parliament on this subject on many
occasions. All I can say is that it is one of
the most difficult problems that any person
can undertake, because the moment you touch
the sanctity of contract, whether that contract is entered into between one rich man
and another rich man or between two poor
men-the moment the State steps in and says
under certain circumstances the sanctity of
that particular contract is not to hold good
then you do really strike in my opinion a
very heavy blow at the stability and credit
of the community.
I do not believe there is the parallel some
hon. Members would lead us to believe between the old Land Acts or the modern Land
Acts and the cases of these leaseholders. The
hon. Member for North Belfast (Mr. T.
Henderson) mentioned how this subject
hit men SO hard in the city of
Belfast and similar towns. I was always
brought up in the belief that the city
of Belfast had reached its present magnificent
state of development, with its fine buildings
and fine streets, through the fact that we
existed here on a short lease system which
enabled, from time to time, older property
to be swept away and better houses and better
thoroughfares erected in their place. I was
always brought up in that belief. It strikes
me that one of the great difficulties with
regard to the whole matter is this, that it is
so involved and covers such an enormous
amount of ground that it would be foolish
of the House to think that even in a couple
of days one could discuss all the ins and outs
of the matter.
I think the hon. Member for West Belfast
(Mr. Devlin) made a suggestion which, perhaps, appealed to me more than any others.
He said that the Prime Minister in Great
Britain proposed to deal in some way with
this very thorny subject and he also paid
me the compliment of saying that I was a
strong supporter of the Prime Minister of
Great Britain, and that I endeavoured all I
could to follow in his worthy footsteps. That
is perfectly true. I know of no man more
desirous of smoothing out the difficulties of
all these complicated problems, and therefore I can say to the House that if legislation
is passed in the Imperial Parliament dealing
with this matter in any way we as a Government will very carefully consider how it can
be made applicable to Northern Ireland.
I think it would be useless to set up a
Select Committee because we would only at
the end of that have no further information
on the subject than we have to-day. Besides,
Select Committees are very expensive. I am

Mr. KYLE: I beg to move the Amendment
whch stands in my name-at the end, to add
the words:
But humbly regret that no proposals
have been made in the gracious Speech to
amend the Rent and Mortgage Interest Restrictions Act (Northern Ireland), 1925, in
view of the prevailing discontent with that
measure in Northern Ireland.
When the Rent and Mortgage Interest Restriction Act was passing through this House,
many Amendments were proposed from the
Benches on this side asking for various reforms. The Government's invariable reply
was that if hardships arose the matter would
perhaps then be considered. It is because
hardships have arisen in regard to the Rent
and Mortgage Interest Restriction Act that
we are expressing regret that no proposals
have been adumbrated in the King's Speech
to alleviate those undoubted grievances which
presently exist under that Act.
It was pointed out when the Act was passing through this House that it was giving the
rent agents too much power, and I suppose
we have got to console ourselves now when
we have seen for the first time in this
Session that the Government party are a
landlord party, and that not only are they
a landlord party but a rent and estate agent
party also. I am strengthened in that belief
by the very interesting function which took
place a few weeks ago, when the Minister of
Home Affairs was present in the city of
Belfast at a gathering of these people who
were rejoicing with one another. I say,

The MINISTER OF HOME AFFAIRS
(Sir Dawson Bates): Listening to the hon.
Member for North Belfast (Mr. Kyle), one
would think the Rent Restriction Acts had
ceased to exist. I would remind my hon.
Friend that last year we passed a Measure
continuing rent restriction for a considerable period. We went far further than the
British Government did, because under their
Act control ceases in 1927. Under our Act
houses of a valuation of less than £26 are
continued under control until 1930. But in
addition to that, my hon. Friend does not
give the Government credit for one important provision we brought in under our Act
when we reduced the 25 per cent. payable
for repairs to 15 per cent. I think he has
only quoted one specific case where he stated
injustice has been done under these Acts.
One case has been mentioned-in Montrose
Street. From what I know of that locality
all those houses are of £8 valuation or under,
and I can assure my hon. Friend that if
he refers to the Act he will find that in the
case of houses of £8 and under, whether it
becomes vacant or not, the landlord cannot
contract to raise the rent beyond that payable under the Rent Restriction Acts.
Mr. KYLE: May I ask does the right hon.
Gentleman doubt my word? Is he denying
that the landlord is charging 25s for a house
that was let at 10s 5d; because I can get
him proof?
Sir DAWSON BATES: I hope my hon.
Friend does not think for a moment that
I doubt his word. I am only quoting the
law. I accept his word that the landlord
has increased the rent, but I can assure him
it is entirely illegal. I am sure if the tenant
in the case takes legal advice he will find
the opinion I have expressed entirely con-

HOUSE OF COMMONS
[Sir Dawson Bates]
firmed. He asks what is the Government
going to do for the protection of these men.
They have the courts. If there is an infringement of the law any man has a right
to go to the courts. I am certain the hon.
Member, when he has this information from
me, will see that that tenant is made right
with regard to the avaricious landlord.
Mr. KYLE: If it is possible.
Sir DAWSON BATES: With regard to
the future, I think anyone will agree
that action as regards rent restriction must
be hand in hand with the problem of providing houses. That is the attitude the.
Government took up when they extended the
period of control until 1930. Alongside with
that we have passed several Housing Acts,
and with the result of these Housing Acts
I am more than satisfied. I find that in the
urban areas, since March, 1924, no less than
5,500 odd houses have either been commenced
or completed in that period. Perhaps I am
not such a pessimist as my hon. Friend, but
I am in hopes that when 1930 comes Belfast
will to a large extent have reduced the
abnormal shortage which exists. And it
may be that when that time arrives, if the
shortage is not reduced in 1930, it will be a
matter for those in power to consider
whether or not there is a necessity for the
continuance of that Act. But do not forget
this: When I consider this question I always
take the view-and I think the vast majority
of people who have studied the question take
the view-that if one wants to remove the
house shortage one must depend on private
enterprise. There is nothing that checks
private enterprise more than insecurity for
the future.
And for these reasons, when
these Acts were passed, the Government
wished to reassure builders as to how they
stand with regard to the future.
I hope, as I said before, when 1930 comes
--I hope my hon. Friend will be here to
see how matters stand then-I hope the
shortage will be reduced to such an extent
that there will be vacant houses, and that
the tenants of some of those old houses will
be placed in decent houses. For these
reasons the Government cannot accept this
Amendment.

that he could inform him it was illegal. I

I think that is the Act.
Sir DAWSON BATES: I do not deny that.
Mr. BEATTIE: I understood you to tell
my colleague that in the house in Dunluce
Avenue which does exceed £8 the landlord

The Act that the Government passed last

to give the landlord the right to increase
the value of his house during the time when
you should not be asking for an increase.
Then as to the 15 per cent. for repairs
which this Government graciously granted to
the landlords and for the abolition of which
I asked, there has been no better results
from that than from previous Acts. I find
to-day in several houses I have. been in, to

altogether. It is absolutely no good because

To go over and reiterate my objections to

House on that Act last Session. I am not
going to bore the House by repeating that
speech. But I ask the Government to agree

and I am told on very reliable authority that
no reductions had taken place in rent as the

this House last year. I dare say the right
hon. Gentleman and his Parliamentary Secretary (Mr. Hanna), who is now preparing his
notes intellectually to slaughter everyone who
puts up a case from these benches, will prob
ably tell us they have no responsibility in
this matter. hold they have responsibility
in the matter, because the Minister of Home
Affairs made a very strong point when introducing this Act that it was going to
benefit many people who were finding great
difficulty in paying their rent at that time.
We find after the Act has been on the Statute
Book for nearly twelve months they have not
got the benefit of the 10 per cent. reduction
on the net rent of the houses. We have.
the right to expect that the right hon. Gentleman and his Department should have made
the provisions of that last Act passed in this
House much clearer to the people than they
seem to have been made.
I will probably be told that responsibility
does not rest with the Department, but I
hold there is a large measure of responsibility, because I believe a state of affairs
exists very extensively over the whole North
of Ireland that the people have not got the
benefit of the 10 per cent. reduction that the
last Act gave. I do not know what steps the
Ministry have taken to explain the whole
matter. The particular place I refer to is
Newry. You will agree that Newry is a large
provincial town, perhaps one of the largest
outside Belfast and Londonderry.
Mr. LEEKE: Portrush?
Mr. W. MCMULLEN: Portrush is not so
important as Newry, notwithstanding the
controversy about Portrush. Newry is a
more important place than Portrush. I believe I am justified in assuming that if the
people of Newry do not know anything about
the provisions of the Act passed here there
seems to be fairly complete ignorance of its
provisions throughout the whole Province.
That, perhaps it will be argued, is not absolutely relevant to the matter under discussion.
To go back to the reasons why an Amendment should be made to the recent Rent
Restriction Act, great hardship has been inflicted on people where the valuation of their
houses is more than £20. Rents have been
enormously increased and people who occupy
business premises have been penalised in a
way they should not be penalised. Instance
after instance could be given of extortions
that have been made by landlords on people
who occupy business premises in the centre
of the city. These could be multiplied indefinitely by people who occupy business
premises on the outskirts of the city. All
these things taken together justify us in
asking for an amendment of the Rent Restrictions Act. I hope the right hon. Gentleman and his Parliamentary Secretary will
not take up the attitude they usually take
up towards this question by giving us a
blank and absolute refusal, but that they
will lend a ready ear to the splendid case
made from these benches for an alteration
or amendment of the Act. If they turn to
the question with anything like an impartial
mind I have not the slightest doubt the
Government will come to the conclusion that
an Amendment is absolutely essential and
that during the present Session we will get
that Amendment to a most unsatisfactory
Act.
Mr. HANNA: I quite agree with the hon.
Member (Mr. W. McMullen) that a good deal
of misunderstanding exists with regard to
this Act of Parliament. I think that has
been very fully exemplified by the speeches
of those who have spoken on the other side
of the House and particularly by the speech
of the hon. Member for North Belfast (Mr.
T. Henderson). It is idle to suggest that any
man who says he is the owner of a house,
and it is the only house he holds, can go
right off to the county court judge and demand possession of that house. That is not
the law. What he would have to do would
be to serve a six months' notice on the
tenant that he required the house for himself, and only those single house owners who
purchased their houses before 1st May, 1923,
could possibly claim the benefit of this Section. Then he must prove to the satisfaction
of the judge that he requires the house for
himself, and if he makes false representation
to the judge, and if he succeeds in getting
a decree, and if afterwards he proposes to let
the house at an exorbitant rent or sell it
he is subject to the penalties of the law pro-
Ivided in the Act.
If, on the other hand, he wants the house
for his mother-in-law whom he likes-if
there is such a thing in the world-he has
got to determine the tenancy in the ordinary
way and he has got to prove that he requires
the house for himself or for some of his
friends for a residence, and he must at the
same time be prepared to offer alternative
accommodation to that tenant. He must find
another house for the tenant reasonably
equivalent to the house he wants possession
of in all respects as to situation, rent and
accommodation. When hon. Gentlemen in
this House suggest that the law is that a man
can go down and get his house at once, is it
any wonder that people in Newry are mystified as to the meaning of the Act?
Mr. THOMAS HENDERSON: That has
taken place.

Mr. LEEKE: I feel disappointed that
greater provision has not been made for
agriculture. This, as we all know, is one of
the most important industries in Northern
Ireland, and the only thing that I can see
is the foreshadowing of legislation for the
inspection of the potato crop, which will be
exported. That is a very questionable
method of assisting agriculture, because it
has been tried in the past, and has not been
a success. However, on this occasion it may
improve, and if so it will certainly facilitate
the trade of Ulster.
As the House knows, the farmers presently
are faced with pre-war prices for their produce and with war expenses for carrying out
their business, and a grant should be made in
order to enable them to carry on their
business in a manner that would help unemployment in this country. There has recently been passed-at least within the lifetime of the last Parliament-an Education
Act, part of the expense of which was thrown
upon the farmers. This is the first time the
farmers have been asked to shoulder
burden like that, and I do not think it
is fair. I hold that that should have been,
as it has always been in the past, a completely national charge, and not added to
the burden of taxation, which is retarding
and handicapping the development of the
agricultural industry in this country.

I would like to back the hon. Member's

Mr. MCALLISTER rose.

Mr. MCALLISTER: No. As a Nationalist
representative I would be false to my
position, to those whom I represent, and to
this House, if I did not enter my protest
against the fact that no cogent proof, no
tangible promise, is included in the King's
Speech that the disadvantages and injustices
under which we labour are about to be readjusted: We appreciate and we reciprocate
the expressions of goodwill and concord that
have been so frequently uttered by the Prime
Minister, and his hopes that a better spirit
and more cordial relations will prevail between the different sections of the community. But I would suggest to him that
if those hopes are to fructify, if they are
not mere picturesque phrases, he should take
immediate steps to transform them into
practical shape. Let us see that we are
entitled to draw natural and logical inferences from those expressions of opinion. I
would suggest to him that he should take
immediate steps to show that those gestures
of goodwill are not gestures made by Mintsters with empty hands, but gestures made
by Ministers equipped and ready to deliver
the goods to us in the shape of fair and
equitable and just treatment to the minority,
equal status in the State, equal representation in public and local boards, and in all
the Departments of the State.

We seek no favours. We are only here
for the rights which our population of onethird of this State entitles us to, and I
suggest to the Government as a business
proposition that if the industries of Ulster
are to prosper, if they wish to develop the
full resources of the area, they can only
do that by the co-operation of the whole
community, and not by the efforts of twothirds alone. If you do not deal out to the
minority equal rights of citizenship, which
is the price of their co-operation, you cannot
develop the full resources of the State. 1
know that you are spending £10,000 in advertising the linen industry in America.
hope that that will bear fruit, and that it
will be repaid to you manifold, but in all
seriousness I suggest to the Government that
the best propaganda they could have in
America, at home, and elsewhere, is the articulate voice and sympathetic co-operation of
a justly governed and satisfied minority.
That you can have in overflowing measure if
you deal out to us equal rights and equal
citizenship in this State. The Government
must realise that, if we are not to receive
equal rights of citizenship, human nature
forbids us contributing our full quota, and
our full co-operation to restore the prosperity
and progress of Ulster. I do not want to
develop that point any more. We are reluctant to raise this issue, but if we are to
perform useful service here we must insist
on having some tangible proof that we are
going to receive justice from the Government
of this country.
I do not want to take up the time of the
House, but there is another item that I
would like to mention. One thing that has
struck me, particularly since I came into
this House, is the unaccountable haste with
which legislation is introduced and passed
through all its stages, without giving the
Members an opportunity of considering the
probable results and consequences of that
legislation, without giving Members an opportunity of obtaining the opinion of the electorate upon it, and without giving the
electorate an opportunity of investigating
how that legislation is going to affect them
and without giving them an opportunity of
voicing their opinion on the proposed legislation. Now I suggest that the Government
take into consideration the relative position
of Members of the Government and private
Members who sit on these benches. When
you introduce legislation here you come fully
equipped with all the relevant data handed
to you in tabloid form by an efficient staff of

such concern for the interests of those who
have suffered hardships undoubtedly in the
past two or three years Not only has
relief of rates been given to a very great
extent, but we have lent money at such rates
of interest as to be practically negligible for
the purpose of replacing stock lost through
disease, and also, which is equally important,
in my judgment almost more important,
there has been the provision of seed potatoes
at about half the natural commercial value
of this article.
It must be remembered that potatoes have
suffered greatly in the North of Ireland from
a disease known as the scab, and it must be
obvious to anyone who has discussed this
subject that this disease is developed by
impure and improper seed. The Department
has arranged for immune varieties of seed
to be provided to farmers at, as I say, very
low cost in order that the whole country may
be relieved of this pest. It must be clearly
understood that our great market for the
surplus of our potato crop is Great Britain
and Great Britain will not accept the
potatoes coming from the North of Ireland
under the conditions under which we have
been raising them. All these things are being
taken into account by the Ministry of Agriculture. I repeat there is no country that I
am aware of which has shown more concern
for the interests of that industry than
Northern Ireland.
My hon. Friend (Mr. Crawford) behind me
put forward the rather empirical suggestion
that the period of extension of the land
annuities should be largely increased, and
the rate consequently lowered, alleging as he
did that a parallel case was that of the
licensed trade. There is no parallel between
the two cases.
In the case of the licensed
trade the doubling of the term of repayment
by the publicans costs the Government or the
country nothing, but if the period of 68
years which is accorded to the farmers
for the redemption of the cost of their farms
were extended in the sense suggested by my
hon. Friend it would mean an enormously
heavy charge upon the Province and would
automatically reduce our revenue So
seriously that the money thus lost would not
be available for the ordinary services of the
country. Therefore, a suggestion of that
kind, I am afraid, cannot be received
favourably by the Government. If there
was no other difficulty in the way, this is a
reserved service, and anything of that kind,
even if it was conceivable, would have to be
introduced by the Imperial Government.
We ourselves have no authority to deal with
the provisions of the Land Act, and
particularly with the provisions of the
previous Land Acts which were entirely
carried out by the Imperial Government.
The hon. Member for Derry (Mr. Leeke)
referred to education as a national charge.
Education in Northern Ireland is at present
a national charge. The extremely simple and
negligible rate which the county authorities
have imposed and which the Government
have indeed supplemented cannot bear with
any hardship on the farmers, and if the
education of the children of the farmers is
not a subject about which they are So
greatly concerned that they cannot afford
twopence or threepence additional on the
rates imposed by the county councils, they
have very little concern for the interests of
their children. Let me make a comparison.
We speak of the burdens we have to bear
already, and they are great no doubt at the
present time. Our taxation is on the same

basis, or practically the same basis, as that

The farmers have to pay 50 per cent. of the

that was that the White Paper, on which the
financial proposals of the Bill were framed,
did not deal with that subject or make any

were entirely ignorant ourselves of the whole
thing. Labour matters were transferred to
Northern Ireland, and the liability consequent upon that fell on the Northern Government.
This Measure, having become a transferred
service, the Treasury, in dealing with the
subject, not only admitted that there was
no fund in existence-no surplus in existence
in order that we might start our operations
in regard to this insurance matter, but as
a matter of fact the British Fund having
been at the time in the condition of a deficit
to the extent of some millions we were
charged with a proportionate amount, which
on calculation came to £160,000. We, therefore, started an insurance enterprise, not
with any capital behind it, not with a surplus that had been derived from the previous
operation of the Fund, but actually there
was a deficit of £160,000. That amount has
been paid by Northern Ireland to the Unemployment Fund of Great Britain.
Following that, we were met with a very
unexampled condition of depression, and consequent increase of unemployment, so that
this deficit of £160,000 began to creep up and
creep up until at the end of the last financial
year it amounted to two and a half million
pounds approximately. It was at this point
that it was quite obvious that the situation
rendered it necessary that the Government should take some steps to resolve our liability, and indeed by statute the
responsibility was laid upon my shoulders
so long as I occupied the position of Minister
of Finance to take such steps as would bring
the Fund into a condition of solvency.
matter was then taken up with the British
Government, and the grievances under which
we laboured were presented to the Government on the other side. Discussions began
between the two bodies the British
Government and ourselves-with the result

Anderson, to examine the whole question.
The
This Committee reported to a Cabinet
Committee appointed by the British Cabinet,
of which the Lord Chancellor was chairman,
and out of its negotiations and as a result
of its deliberations an agreement was
reached, which is embodied in the White
Paper, which I have had circulated to hon-
Members, and which, I hope, has been read,
On the assumption that it has been read
I need not enter into all the details beyond
stating a bare outline. It provides that as
from the 1st October, 1925, the responsibility
for the maintenance of the Unemployment
Insurance Fund in a condition of solvency
shall be undertaken as to 75 per cent.
liability on the part of the Imperial Govern-1
ment, with 25 per cent. left upon our
own shoulders. That, in essence, is the
nature of the arrangement that has been
made. The details and method of calculation are of a somewhat complex character
such as it would be difficult for me to enter
into and explain fully. The White Paper
contains the whole of the Agreement that has
been made between the Chancellor of the Exchequer and myself officially and it also very
clearly sets out by way of memorandum the
whole of the conditions under which that
Agreement was reached and the results that
are expected to accrue. It shows that for
the six months from the 1st October until
the end of our. financial year it is estimated
that the responsibility of the British Government will be a certain sum, £600,000 odd, and
our liability will be proportionately £800,000
odd.
Under the Agreement also the British
Government undertakes to pay fully 75 per
cent. of the deficit that has accrued on the
1st October; that is to say, assuming that the
liability on that date is £3,600,000 it must be
carried by the provision of yearly interest,
and the British Government is undertaking
to provide 75 per cent. of that interest-that
is to say upon the accumulated deficit. 1
do not pretend that this is an arrangement
that I in my position of Finance Minister
would have preferred. I thought, and I still
think, that under the conditions in which
the transference of an autonomous authority
was made to us that the merging of the two
funds into a General National Fund would
and should have been the natural and proper
solution of this matter. I am glad to see
that reference was made in the Imperial
Parliament only yesterday to this fact, and
the opinion was offered that possibly that
might have been the best solution of the
problem. But be that as it may, we were
very glad indeed to be able to arrive at this
solution because it relieved the Northern
Parliament, the Northern Government, and
the people of Northern Ireland, of a burden
which it was quite impossible for them with
their limited area to bear. Under these circumstances, therefore, I think the House
will agree that the arrangement that has
been made is the best that could be made,
the Bill when it is presented will probably
receive the approval of the whole House. I

CASE OF MR. THOMAS O'DOHERTY,
SCHOOL TEACHER.

Mr. DEVLIN: I must apologise to the
House for raising a question that perhaps
may be regarded by most Members as of
very little importance, but I think it would
be well even in the midst of the tremendously
important issues which have been discussed
during the last few days if we should sometimes remember that the jealous guardianship
of the spirit of justice is one of the first
functions of a constitutional assembly. I
ventured to put a question to the Minister
of Home Affairs to-day with reference to a
recent event that took place in our city and
I think the best and simplest way for me
to deal with this question is to recite the
facts, briefly as they were stated in the Press,
School-teacher's Case. 152
School-teacher's Case.
HOUSE OF COMMONS
[Mr. Devlin]
an
On 19th January a bicycle was stolen from
the basement of the Students' Union at
Queen's University. On the 23rd of the same
month two detectives called at the house
where Mr. O'Doherty, a teacher, lodged and
questioned him about some stolen property.
He denied that he knew anything about such
property and was asked to go to Donegall
Pass Police Barracks to take part in an
identification parade. He did so. The parade
was held, and I understand from information
conveyed to me that that parade was
absolute farce. Two of the men who were
called-I think it was two men-Mr. Andrews
and his son, stated they thought they saw
this man before. Mr. O'Doherty was arrested
and charged with the larceny of the bicycle
and removed to the police headquarters where
he remained until the following Monday,
when he was brought before the magistrates.
He was remanded until the subsequent Monday, when he was committed for trial to the
Commission. The Resident Magistrate said a
prima facie case had been made out.
On Wednesday, as I have said already, the
trial of Mr. O'Doherty started at the Commission, and before it was finished the judge
directed the jury to acquit this young man.
His Lordship stated a message boy who was
the chief witness for the Crown had made an
honest mistake. The only direct evidence
against Mr. O'Doherty was the evidence of
this message boy. There was no doubt two
other men were brought in to identify this
man but they were very circumspect and they
were not at all sure, and thev certainly were
not very distinct that that was the man.
Under these circumstances one might not
have any reason to complain if it were not
for the subsequent facts. And what are the
facts? It was stated that at the time this
larceny took place Mr. O'Doherty was in the
company of Mr. William Parr, registrar of
Stranmillis Training College, and Mr. R. N.
Greer, a student of the College, half a mile
from the scene of the larceny of the bicycle.
and that at twenty minutes past three
Professor Lloyd, M.A., entered the room of
the College and found them there.
My ailegation against the Government, or
against whoever is responsible for the conduct of these prosecutions, is that all these
statements were in the hands of the police
and that this evidence was suppressed. I
want to know whether counsel or whoever
appeared for the prosecution had the evidence
of these three honoured members of the community and eminent men in the College that
Mr. O'Doherty was in their company at the
time this larceny took place and that it was
impossible for him to have stolen the bicycle,
and why the police suppressed this evidence
and did not bring it before the magistrates.
What I think ought to have been done is that
the police themselves should have consulted
the Attorney-General, or whoever authorises
these prosecutions, and told him they had
this evidence in their possession, and have
the case instantly dismissed instead of keeping this young fellow in prison having a
stigma put upon him on the eve of a great
career of public usefulness in a position of
responsibility where a charge of this character was destined materially to damage his
prospects. At the same time the charge was
allowed to hang over his head and the only
evidence was the evidence of these people.
The case went on, and, as I have said,
the judge, Lord Justice Andrews, ordered it
to be stopped and said there was no evidence
against him except the evidence of this boy.
and clearly that was a mistake. No doubt
a small matter of this sort may seem of
very little importance, but the character and
the position of a young student in a Teachers'
College is of some importance to the conmunity. What would have happened if this
Mr. O'Doherty at the time he was engaged
in conversation with these professors and
representative men in the College had gone
out to take a long walk and had been away
at the time this incident occurred? Nothing
would have saved him from a conviction and
the ruin of a life-long stigma enduringly
placed upon his character. Yet all that evidence was withheld by the police and never
produced in the lower court. It was not
brought forward although they had it in their
possession until the case came before the
Commission.
Mr. O'Doherty had been freed by the action
of the judge and jury from the stigma or
crime, and I think that considering his posi.
tion and the wrong that has been done him
and the torture to which he has been subjected by this curiously tortuous policy by
which he was prosecuted he is entitled to
a public apology and compensation at the
hands of the Government. Therefore I think
it my duty to raise it here. It may have no
effect, but I take it that it will make the
police and those in charge of the administration of justice more careful in the future
before they bring citizens before a Police
Court. force them into an Assize Court, and
have a charge of this character levelled
against them. Although a man may be subsequently declared innocent one knows that
when these charges are made and carried so
far as in this case they are very often a
stigma for life. I have, therefore, felt it my
duty, in view of what I regard as the unsatisfactory answer of the Attorney-General.
to bring this matter before the House.

The hon. Member (Mr. Devlin) who has
raised this question has said, in the first
place, that the parade was a farce. I have
investigated that, and I can assure the House
that that is not so. The parade was carried
through in the ordinary way. The accused
was identified, in the first place, by Mr.
Andrews, senior, who, when he was first
faced with the men on parade, was not sure,
and made a mistake as to the identity of
the prisoner, but afterwards said he was
certain of the prisoner. His son, to whom
the bicycle was brought in the first instance,
made no mistake, and was absolutely certain
as to the identity of the prisoner, and the
boy, who had seen the bicycle being driven
out of the University, was absolutely clear
and unshaken until the end, and none of
these witnesses, so far as the identification
goes, was shaken on cross-examination.
Therefore, so far as the prima facie case
was concerned, the case was complete against
the accused until it was displaced by the
evidence for the defence.
Now, what statements were in the hands
of the police? They had the evidence of
these three witnesses. They had the bicycle
which had been stolen. They had also a
statement from a Mr. Greer, which was taken
by the police, I understand, at the instigation of the accused, and which threw some
doubt upon this question of identification.
But that was not a matter which the police
had any authority or right to try. That was
a matter for the magistrate alone in the
first instance, and the statement was not
suppressed, but was produced to the magistrate in court. As I said before, the accused
was represented by very able counsel, who
elected, in the accused's interests, I take
it, not to call these three witnesses, and

HOUSE OF COMMONS
[Mr. Babington]
submitted upon the evidence upon which the
prima facie case is established. The accused
was then returned for trial in the ordinary
way.

It is suggested here that, so far as the
Attorney-General is concerned, the statement
for the defence should have been submitted
along with all the other statements, and
that then I should have said there should
be no prosecution. I would like to inform
the House that, so far as this prosecution
is concerned, and so far as m
as my duty as
Attorney-General is concerned, it would have
made no difference to the question as to
whether a prosecution should go on or should
not go on if all this evidence which was
ultimately produced had been submitted to
me. If there is a clear statement by competent witnesses, unshaken upon their own
testimony, but only contradicted by other
witnesses, I have to direct a prosecution,
because that is a question of evidence, which
has to be submitted to a petty jury, who
have to believe one side or the other, according as the witnesses present themselves to
the jury in court. Therefore, this prosecution could not have been stayed, no matter
what evidence had been laid before me, and
the case rightly went to trial, and was duly
disposed of by the learned judge before whom
it came.
As I said before and I want. to emphasise
this point, because a lot of importance seems
to have been attached to this particular case
-when the case came before the learned
judge and petty jury, it is quite plain that
the evidence of the three Crown witnesses
stood, because if there had been a flaw in
it, or if it had broken down in crossexamination, the learned judge would have
withdrawn the case from the jury before the
defence was gone into; but that was not done.
It was not until four or five witnesses had
been called for the defence that the learned
judge saw, that there was such a conflict of
ovidence as between the witnesses for the
prosecution and the witnesses for the defence
that there might possibly have been some
mistake.
Mr. DEVLIN: That is a scandalous way
in which to present the situation. The right
hon. and learned Gentleman has no right
whatever to say that in the mind of the judge
there was conflicting evidence, because the
judge distinctly stated that there might have
been a doubt in the case. The right hon.
Gentleman is acting as a further Crown
prosecutor in this case.
Mr. BABINGTON: I am not acting as a
further Crown prosecutor. If anything
arises out of this it is not due to any action
upon my part. The hon. Member who raised
this question said that the learned judge
said there was
The
clearly a mistake.
learned judge did not say that. What the
learned judge said was that having regard
to the evidence for the defence there.
might have been a mistake, and, therefore,
there was a doubt in the case, and it would
not be safe for the jury to convict upon that
evidence. That is the way the matter stood.
The learned judge directed the jury that
under the circumstances of the case it was
safer for them to return a verdict of not
guilty, and accordingly that was done.
I do not know whether any wrong has been
done. The accused has now been acquitted.
He is in no different position from any other
accused brought before the Court on insufficient evidence and acquitted. The only
really serious matter in this case which I'
wish now to contradict in the clearest and
most emphatic manner-the only thing which
distinguishes it from the case of any other
accused person acquitted on a criminal
charge is the fact that there has been an
allegation made against the police of, first
of all, having held a parade which was a
farce, and, secondly, of having suppressed
ovidence which was in their hands. I say
to the House that in neither of these charges
is there any degree of substance whatever,
and that this particular prosecution was
conducted with perfect propriety.

COLERAINE INQUIRY — ARBITRATOR'S
FEES.
1. Sir ROBERT ANDERSON asked the
Minister of Finance whether it is a fact
that, in connection with an inquiry at
Coleraine into the price of land for the
erection of 48 labourers' cottages, the
arbitrator's fees amounted to £72 98 0d, and
if so what action he proposes to take in the
matter.
The MINISTER OF FINANCE (Mr.
Pollock): The amount of the fees is correctly cited by the hon. Member; they are
collected by the arbitrator, not for himself,
but on behalf of the Ministry of Finance,
and are paid into the Exchequer as Stamp
Duty on the award.
The Stamp Duty is fixed so as to approxi
mate closely in its yield to the amount
which the Ministry has itself to pay, to the
arbitrator. In deference to views put forward to the Ministry by a local authority
last year the scale was revised as recently
as 21st August, 1925, in a manner which
appeared to be more equitable, both to the
local authorities and the State. The Order
embodying the scale will be found amongst
the published Statutory Rules and Orders,
and I am sending a copy to the hon.
Member. I see no grounds for revising the
Order afresh. It must be borne in mind
that up to the year 1919 Rural Councils were
frequently put to the expense of High Court
appeals against the amount of compensation
assessed, whereas now there is no appeal,
save on matters of law. This represents a
very considerable saving.
The arbitrator's personal fees, which are
payable by the Ministry of Finance, will
amount to slightly less than the figure
quoted. The basis on which they are paid
was fixed after prolonged discussion between
my Ministry and the Surveyors' Institution,
and is lower than the corresponding scale
in force in Great Britain.

DISSOLUTION OF LOCAL AUTHORITIES.
4. Dr. MORRISON (for Mr. MILLER)
asked the Minister of Home Affairs if he will
state how many public boards or councils
have been superseded during the past five
years, and what, in the view of the Ministry,
was the result as regards economy, efficiency,
co-ordinance with the Ministry, efficacy of
appointments, and matters in general.
The MINISTER OF HOME AFFAIRS (Sir
Dawson Bates): In the latter end of the year
1921, and the beginning of the year 1922, the
Ministry dissolved 21 local authorities in
Northern Ireland, including 1 County Council, 4 Urban District Councils, 1 Town Commissioner, 7 Boards of Guardians, and 8
Rural District Councils.
The urban authorities in question were reconstituted in January, 1923, and the rural
and county authorities in May, 1924.
As the hon. Member is aware, the circumstances under which it was found necessary
to dissolve these local authorities and to
appoint Commissioners to discharge their
duties were of an exceptional character, and
the period of dissolution was too short to
enable the Ministry to constitute a comparison of a reliable character.
At the same time, the Ministry is satisfied
that during the short period of office the Commissioners on the whole discharged their
duties with economy and efficiency, and in
due accord with the Statutes and Regulations
governing the services for which they were
responsible.

widow's
The MINISTER OF LABOUR
Andrews): An application for a

employed in his own garden.

KING'S SPEECH.
The Governor's Answer to the
Address.
The PRIME MINISTER (at the Bar) reported the Answer to the Address from His
Grace the Governor of Northern Ireland as
followeth :-
I have received with great satisfaction the
expression of your thanks for the Speech
with which I opened the present Session of
Parliament.
165 Insurance Agreement Bill-

16 MARCH 1926
Second Reading.
ORDERS OF THE DAY.
Unemployment Insurance (Agreement) Bill.
Order for Second Reading read.
Motion made and Question proposed: "That
the Bill be now read a Second time."
Mr. ANDREWS: The Bill which I have
the honour to ask the House to give a Second
Reading to to-day is in my opinion one of
the most important measures which this
House has ever been asked to consider.
After all, it is a Bill to ratify an Agreement
entered into between His Majesty's Imperial
Government and our Government for the
purposes of establishing a mutual re-insurance scheme in order to ensure that insured
persons throughout Great Britain and Northern Ireland shall receive for equal contributions equal benefits.
It has been suggested in this House and
outside it that this Government should never
have accepted any responsibility for dealing
with unemployment insurance. I would like
to make it perfectly clear that we had no
option, that it was laid down in the Act of
1920 that this insurance matter as well as
other labour matters would be a transferred
service. Hon. Members are aware of the fact
that our Parliament was opened by His
Majesty in June, 1921. As early as September
of the same year I brought the position as
regards unemployment insurance before my
colleagues and notwithstanding the fact that
we did not take over our powers until
January of the following year my colleagues
and I made frequent representations to the
appropriate Departments in Great Britain,
laying before them the injustice which had,
unintentionally no doubt, been done to us
through the White Paper which in setting
out the financial relations between Great
Britain and Northern Ireland had not made
any allowance for the probable liability we
would be faced with as regards this Fund.
Owing to the persistent exertions and the
influence of our Prime Minister early in
that year we received a sum of approximately
£477,000 in order to meet the transferred
deficit from the British Fund of £160,000 plus
the increased debt which we incurred up to
the end of the financial year. I may say that
we never accepted that payment as a final
solution of the problem, and since then we
have with considerable persistency and
earnestness been pressing successive British
Governments to right this wrong. It was not
until August last that we were able to arrive
at a settlement of the matter as set out in
the Schedule to this Bill. I do not feel that
it is necessary that I should take up the time
of the House to-day in going through, clause
by clause, the various provisions in the Bill
itself or in the Agreement in the Schedule
to which I have referred. I think it will
suffice if I make a general statement which
would put hon. Members in possession of
the real effect of the Agreement to which I
have referred.
The debit balance on our Fund at the 30th
September last, viz., £3,614,000, less the sum
of £183,000, which is the proportionate part
for Northern Ireland of the British Fund's
deficit of £7,935,000, calculated on an insured
population basis, shall be placed to a suspense account-that is the first part of the
Agreement-while the parity figure of
£183,000 shall be placed to the debit side of
the current account-that is the second part
of the Agreement.
It is proposed that the Unemployment
Fund of Great Britain and the Unemployment Fund of Northern Ireland will be
maintained in a state of parity in respect of
the period from the 1st October, 1925, to the
31st March, 1926, and for the four succeeding
years. This state of parity will be maintained by the payment of additional Exchequer grants, called the equalisation payments,
from Northern Ireland
revenues to the
Northern Ireland current account of the
Unemployment Fund.
יד
The burden so placed upon the Northern
Ireland Exchequer will be relieved by a payment from the Imperial Exchequer amounting to approximately 75 per cent. of the sum
required to equalise the respective burdens
upon a population basis. The remainder of
the equalisation payment will remain a net
charge on the Exchequer of Northern Ireland. I may add, however, that if at any
time the liability of the Imperial Exchequer
exceeds £1,000,000 in any one year the Im-.
perial Government will be free, without
breach of agreement, to re-open the question on its merits. It is estimated that
the payment from the Impeel
chequer will be this year, calculated in the
manner prescribed by Article 3 of the
Agreement, about £680,000, leaving about
£335,000 to be found by the Northern Ireland
Government beyond its normal contribution.
Now, hon. Members may ask what is to become of the £3,431,000 placed to the Suspense
Account. The interest will be dealt. with and
borne by the two Exchequers in exactly the
same way as the equalisation payment, and
only the future can disclose what will be
the fate of the capital debt. Hon. Members
will fully appreciate the great advantage
that this Agreement is to us-
The PRIME MINISTER: Hear, hear.
Mr. ANDREWS- -when I say that the
debt per insured person with us was £14, and
when measured in exactly the same way the
Insurance Agreement Bill-
Second Reading. 168
HOUSE OF COMMONS
[Mr. Andrews]
redebt was only 15s per head of the population
of Great Britain. It will be interesting for
the House to know that three proposals were
niade for dealing with this important
natter. The first was our proposal, namely,
that the two Funds should be
amalgamated. For the time being,
at any rate, that proposal was not
acceptable to His Majesty's Government,
and the Agreement which is contained in the
Schedule attached to the Bill itself was
arrived at after prolonged negotiations and
very earnest efforts on both sides. It is perfectly evident to prominent statesmen in
Great Britain, I think, that if the burden
which this Agreement imposes upon us is
beyond our capacity to bear the only solution
of the problem will be that of re-amalgamation.
A third proposal was, however, put forward
by the Socialist Party in Westminster, and.
I think I am stating it quite fairly when
I say that that proposal was that we should
continue to borrow to the full extent of our
capability to do so, and when we had exhausted our own strength that the British
Treasury would come to our aid as moneylenders to allow us to get further into debt,
the dead-weight of which would in the end
have submerged us.
The PRIME MINISTER: Hear, hear.
con-

has put forward the view that after all the

acting in the interests of their own
stituents. They may have thought so, but
I doubt it very much, taking the long view.
But even supposing for argument's sake that
I grant that, what would have been the
position if the Unionists at Westminster had
taken the same short-sighted, selfish,

We would not have to-day been considering

such great advantages upon our industrial
classes in Northern Ireland." On the contrary, we would have been left in the very

Willing to wound, and yet afraid to strike,
Just hint a fault and hesitate dislike.

e that equal social

is an
honourable Agreement, honourably
entered into, and it must be honourably
carried out
The PRIME MINISTER: Hear, hear.
Mr. ANDREWS- -as if it were not it
would crumble to pieces, and would become

unemployment insurance at Westminster.

nade to me and my colleagues to depart from
.parallel legislation with the Imperial Par

In other words 73,557 houses were being
erected in England and Wales-of course I
refer to subsidy houses-as compared with
3,303 houses being erected in Northern
Ireland under similar circumstances, the relative proportion of houses being 24 for
England and Wales to 1 in Northern Ireland,
which compares very favourably with the
relative population figures which approximate 30 to 1.
The policy of the Government, which has
been consistently followed and which has
been embodied in the various Acts passed by
this House, has been to encourage private
enterprise as much as possible; to reduce
unnecessary hampering restrictions, and at
the same time to work in the closest cooperation and harmony with the local
authorities, offering them the same inducements as we hold out to private builders.
181 Government Contracts-
Employment of Ex-Servicemen. 182
16 MARCH 1926
I would like to take this opportunity of
paying a tribute to the whole-hearted support
which the Government has received from the
various local authorities. They have given
grants ranging from £25 to £40, and in a
very large number of cases they have
arranged to remit rates for a period ranging
from 5 years to 10 years.
Representations have been made to me by
some of the Urban Authorities, advocating
the extension of the maximum limit from
950 superficial feet to 1,400 superficial feet.
The Government, after careful consideration, have been unable to accede to this
request. They feel that if the maximum
limit was extended, it would act as an encouragement to private builders to confine
their attention to houses of the villa type,
a type which always commands a ready scale,
and by this means the policy of the Government to provide houses which would be
within the resources of the working classes
would be neutralised and defeated.
It being Half-past Four of the Clock,
further Proceeding was postponed, without
Question put, pursuant to Standing Order
No. 2.
Government Contracts.
EMPLOYMENT OF EX-SERVICEMEN.
Colonel WOODS: I beg to move: That,
in the opinion of this House, it is the duty
of the Government in all Government contracts to make provision for the employment
to the fullest possible extent of disabled.ex-
Servicemen, and to this end to confine such
contracts to employers enrolled on the King's
National Roll."
This Motion, I know, will meet with the
sympathy of every Member of this House.
It contains nothing new. It is only brought
up for the purpose of showing public bodies
what their duty in this matter really is. 1
will not take up the time of the House by
enlarging upon the subject. It is one well
known to every Member. I am simply asking
for the unanimous vote of the House on this
Motion. There may be someone who may
object to the wording or phrasing of the
Motion, but it is surely one that has more
decision about it than the one passed two
years ago in this House, that really meant
nothing at all. If such a Motion as this is
passed it will strenghen the hands of the
Government in dealing with contracts.
Major SHILLINGTON: I would like to
second the Motion moved by the hon. Member
for West Belfast (Colonel Woods). I think
that the time has come now when the
Government should put down its foot and
not receive contracts from any firm unless
that firm is on the King's National Roll of
Honour. There was a resolution passed two
years ago, to which my attention has been
drawn, but I do not think it goes quite far
enough. I understand this matter was under
discussion quite recently in the Imperial
House, and a resolution was passed there
something on the lines now suggested. I know
arguments will be put forward by the Government that they do not see their way to accept
the resolution, and that the resolution
already passed has resulted in large numbers
of firms being added to the National Roll.
I quite admit that during the last few years
the number of firms enrolled on the Roll
has tremendously increased, but that is
largely accounted for by the fact that up to
1921 and 1922 we had no local Employment
Committees here, and the Roll was not prominently brought before the public. It
was worked by a sub-committee of the
Selection Committee of the Appointments and
Training Branch of the Ministry of Labour.
Since the local Employment Committees and
Roll Committees were. set up the matter has
been working satisfactorily, and the Ministry
of Labour has been able to bring the Roll
under the notice of employers.
The number of firms enrolled has increased
from 100 or 200 to 900. Unfortunately, while
that is true, it is also quite true that the
numbers of disabled ex-Servicemen now unemployed are considerably greater than years
ago. I understand that throughout the North
of Ireland we have some 1,800 or 1,900 disabled
ex-Servicemen, and of that number 1,200 or
1,300 are in the city of Belfast. I think,
seeing that it is seven years and more since
the Armistice, it is really necessary that
there should be some benefit shown to firms
to induce them to employ a certain percentage of disabled ex-Servicemen. The giving of
contracts should be considerably tightened.
They should only be given to firms on the
National Roll, and I hope the Government
will see their way to accept this Resolution
proposed by the hon. Member for West
Belfast (Colonel Woods).

was no difference of opinion whatever between the Government and those Members

Incidentally, I had almost a feeling of resentment as I listened to my hon, and gallant
Friend (Major Shillington) who hoped that

I say that I felt something in the nature

Preference is always given in the giving of

-unless there are some circumstances which

when I proceed for a few minutes with the

I think it will be agreed that it was very

I gave an instance of a type of contract

that circumstances will result at times, all

The instance I gave then may well be repeated because it is so typical of something
that may possibly arise that hon. Members
should be fully seized of the nature of it.
It was a case where ex-Servicemen's
houses were being built in Londonderry.
Tenders were taken out with the object of
proceeding with that work. It was found
that there were tenders from those who were
on the King's Roll and one tender from a
firm who were outside that category, but the
difference between the two lowest-the one
firm on the King's Roll and the other outside the King's Roll-was so great that it
enabled 13 additional ex-Servicemen's houses
to be built. Would any Member of this
House suggest for a moment that the rules
which we have laid down in cases like that
should be adhered to. It is very seldom that
cases like that turn up, but there are instances where there are exceptional circumstances, and these exceptional circumstances
are provided for in the British Resolution.
The wording in the British Resolution is
"Except under exceptional circumstances."
Our wording is "all other things being
equal." I cannot myself see that there is

You simply compel the Government in their

1,200 ex-Servicemen-
Major SHILLINGTON: Disabled.
Mr. KYLE-disabled ex-Servicemen have

That being the case, it seems to me they
are doing their best to forget them to-day
to the extent that there are so many idle in

One can understand the arguments that
might be put up by the right hon. Gentleman, the Minister of Finance, and one can
understand, of course, how Governments
always want to have saving clauses. They
want to protect themselves against every
possible eventuality, but in protecting themselves they are leaving themselves open to the
charge I am making against them this afternoon of making it easy for employers to
forget their promises to the ex-Servicemen.
I happen to be in the position that I have

to refuse to do justice to the disabled ex-

the Motion.

Sir DAWSON BATES: When the debate
was suspended I was giving the reasons that
led the Government to refuse to accede to
the request of certain of the local authorities that the maximum should be increased.
I think it is well to point out in this connection that during the last month the Belfast Corporation arrived at the conclusion
that it would be desirable in connection with
their future housing schemes to embark on
a somewhat smaller and cheaper house than
those hitherto erected, in order to meet the
requirements of the comparatively poorly
paid workers.
I have already had a conference with the
representatives of the Corporation with a
view to arriving at an arrangement which
would involve the erecting of a certain
number of houses with a minimum of 550
superficial feet. Since that time I have
observed a good deal of unfounded criticism
in regard to the erection of this type of house.
It has been suggested, if one can believe all
one sees, that the Government's policy really
is to create slums instead of do away with
them. I emphatically deny that. What we
aim at is a cheap, self-contained, well-built,
and healthy house even though it may be
small.
There is no use in building for the artisan
classes houses which have to be let at a
rent which they cannot afford to pay. If
these type of houses are erected the artisan
classes cannot afford to pay the rent, and
then the houses are let to people to whom
they never were intended to be let. On the
other hand if the artisan classes do take
them they sub-let them at exorbitant rents
and so the evil of over-crowding
perpetuated, and that is a thing the Government are most anxious to stop. I may point
out that the smallest of these houses will
contain a kitchen, scullery, and all
accessories of that character, and at least
two bedrooms. I refer to the class of houses
of 550 superficial feet.
Mr. BEATTIE: Two bedrooms?
is

I hope the House will pass this Measure so
as to enable the progress of building to be
continued for another year. I beg to move.

we are going to go back a generation practically if we permit these houses to be erected
in Belfast. It is all very well for the right
hon. Gentleman (Sir Dawson Bates) to say it
is in order that these houses can be let at a
rent which the workman can pay. We have
pointed out time after time that the way
the workman can pay is not by reducing the
rent for the house but by giving him decent
Housing Bill—

wages, and obviously that is a much fairer

I am sure there is not in Belfast or out of
it a public man, or a party, or any people
who are interested at all in housing but will
condemn the proposal to erect these small
houses. I had thought we had got to a
higher standard. I had thought that the
Government had realised that it was the
proper thing that the working classes should
be housed in better houses than they were a
generation ago. That will not be the case it
the Minister of Home Affairs does not think
fit to reconsider the decision at which he has
apparently arrived, that is to grant a subsidy of £280 a house to houses of the nature
which the Belfast Corporation are talking
about building-and I did not catch in its
entirety his remark as to whether or not he
had determined to give this subsidy of £80
per house to the Belfast Corporation for
these buildings that they propose to put up.
I call them buildings for you could not call
them houses. There are several associations
of women who are interested in housing in
Belfast. There is one-the Women's Advisory Council-which I understand is not a
party organisation. I think the Minister of
Labour (Mr. Andrews) addressed a meeting
of it one day, so that if that is the case it is
hardly to be looked upon as a blood red
revolutionary party. They have, I understand, condemned in no uncertain measure,
the proposal which the Belfast Corporation
has before it to erect these houses.
The right hon. Gentleman (Sir Dawson
Bates) might have said that he hoped or
believed that in another year we are going
to have a sufficiency of houses, that the
housing grant will be no longer given after
this year for which he proposes to extend
the Housing Act. We know quite well, and
he knows quite well, that next year he will
be met again with the request to extend
these Housing Acts for a further period, to
extend the subsidy for a further period, because he knows as well as the head is on
his body that it is not possible to get all the
houses that are required built inside one
year. Further than that, it should be the
Government's aim, when the Corporation of
Belfast has failed to house adequately the
people of Belfast, to be responsible as a
Government for the erection of houses. We
have a precedent for that, and Conservatives
always dearly love a precedent. We want
them to accept the precedent of the Conservative Government on the other side,
namely, to build the houses themselves, so
that the people may be housed in a more
adequate way than they have been housed
hitherto.
Sir DAWSON BATES: May I interrupt

Mr. KYLE: If the proposal is as laid

the social services becoming better as far

Sir DAWSON BATES: We are not.
Mr. KYLE: That is what the right hon.
Gentleman is doing.
Sir DAWSON BATES: What I pointed

Mr. KYLE: In other words they are

Sir DAWSON BATES: They did.
Mr. KYLE: They did not, and that

I am glad that the right hon. Gentleman
(Sir Dawson Bates) has seen his way to prolong the subsidy for another year.
I am
quite sure that before that year is up he

Mr. T. W. MCMULLAN: I had not the

If a man owns a house to-day, or builds a
