I think that beyond that suggestion which
the Minister has turned down-for very
adequate reasons I am sure as he sees them
-that the limit should be increased beyond
950 feet, say up to 1,200 feet. I have the
feeling that if houses could be built with an
accommodation of 1,200 superficial feet the
class which is competing for workmen's
houses would automatically be taken away
from that competition, and be able to
occupy this other class of house. I have
talked this matter over with the surveyor
for a local authority, and he tells me that
a house of 1,200 feet could be built for about
£750, and that it could be let at a rent of,
say, £45 a year. If such houses could be
produced and be let-not sold, but let-at a
rent of £45 a year by public authorities it
would really help in the end the working
men very greatly, because it would take
away this competition for workingmen's
houses which at present exists. Of course,
I quite see the arguments against it. It is
a big question, but it might be worth the
reconsideration of the Government.
Another point that occurred to me was
that this is Government money, this is taxpayers' money, which goes into the subsidising of these houses. I am told that a great
deal of the material used in the houses
which are built under these subsidies is not
home production. I am told that French
slates, French cement, and many other
things are introduced in these building contracts. They may not be in the houses that
are built by public authorities, but they
certainly are in a great many houses that
are built by private enterprise. I think the
Government should have the power, seeing
that they are giving away the taxpayers'
money, to have inserted in the contracts a

these houses.
I thought I would like to say a few words
on the Housing Acts. I know my own constituents in Bangor, County Down, would
like to see the 1,200 superficial feet introduced into the Act, and, looking at it with
whatever intelligence I have got, I can see
a great deal of reason for the raising of that

which are supposed to be built for working
men, but which are practically open to

I was strongly opposed in the Belfast

There are labouring people with nine, ten,

Quite recently we had a housing scandal in

You have heard of the cost of these houses,

Mr. WILLIAM MCMULLEN: I think the

Imagine the state of affairs in the case of

a worker in a mill, factory or shipyard with

is not going to be asked to live in a house
of 550 superficial feet. Very few of the

poor unfortunate people, working for small
wages, will be compelled to live in them.
This is a serious matter. People, no matter
how humble their occupation, have the right
to a decent abode. They are not going to
get it if you are going to encourage the local
authorities to build houses of 550 superficial
feet. I would protest with all the emphasis
and vehemence at my command against any
such iniquitous proposal. If any houses of
this kind are built I would suggest that the

to live in one of them for twelve months,
and then probably he would come to the
conclusion that such a house was not fit for
human habitation, and we would have the
subsidy withdrawn.
I hope that sufficient has been said from
these Benches to show the iniquity of these
proposals, and to induce the right hon.
Gentleman to reconsider the matter. I have
no doubt that if he does give it any further
thought, he will come to the conclusion that
it is not a fit and proper state of affairs at
all. I will tell you what should be done in
my opinion. You speak about a conference
on unemployment. I have often felt that
some sort of a conference should be called
for the purpose of discussing our housing
arrangements in Belfast and other places.
What attempt is being made to destroy the
slum quarters of Belfast? An attempt was
made in the ward that I represent in the
Corporation. Two streets were widened, new
houses were built, and the situation was improved generally so far as those two streets
were concerned, but whoever was responsible
for that stopped operations. I think a sensible proposal would be to call together
representative men for the purpose of considering this housing question, the building
of sufficient houses, the knocking down of
the old and dilapidated houses, and the
erection of decent houses in their place, and
so carrying out that policy until such time
as we had decent housing accommodation in
the centre of the city instead of the haphazard methods we are following. As the
hon. Member for North Belfast (Mr. Thomas
Henderson) has pointed out, it is absurd to
build workmen's houses at Whitewell, where
a workman has to pay a threepenny tramfare to get to the centre of the city, and
three pence back again. If a conference
were called, and proper thought and consideration were given to the whole question,
we could improve the housing conditions in
the centre of the city. I hope that something of that kind will be done to
improve the conditions under which
people are living in the centre of the city,
and let us have better housing conditions than we have at present, instead
of a proposal of this kind to build tworoomed houses. I think that the right hon.
Gentleman, who proposes such a Measure,
and his Parliamentary Secretary should be
compelled to live in such houses for twelve

would compel them to live in them for

Mrs. CHICHESTER: May I just say that
I hope the right hon. Gentleman, who has

It is not a question of size. Size is not

I trust very much that the right hon.

Mr. DEVLIN: I cannot quite follow the
point of the observations of the hon. Member
(Mrs. Chichester) who has just sat down.
She was rather critical of the protest made

houses.
Mrs. CHICHESTER: I did not question it.
Mr. DEVLIN: She did not tell us whether
that was an admirable housing condition or
not. She stated that she spoke on behalf of
rural Ireland. The hon. Member (Mrs.
Chichester) must know that if there is one
section of the community more than another
that ought to value decent housing conditions it is the people who live in rural
Ireland. I myself am very proud to belong
to a party which forced a Labourers'
Housing Act through Parliament-an Act
which was responsible for the creation of
some 60,000 labourers' cottages. It seems a
curious reflection, but I remember that that
Act was passed in spite of the protest and
votes of those who support the hon. Lady
(Mrs. Chichester) in this House. Then as
now those who constitute what I call the
reactionary classes in this country, thought
any place good enough for the working
classes to live in, but, fortunately, the social
conscience of the toiling masses of the people
has been so roused that they are not prepared to accept with the placidity of the
hon. Member the conditions that previously
prevailed.
In my judgment next to the question of
unemployment the most pressing of all problems and the most human of all problems is
the question of housing. (Hon. Members:
Hear, hear.) A proper adjustment of our
housing question means the adjustment of
countless other questions-health, comfort,
ease of mind. All these things are dependent upon the occupation of decent
sanitary dwellings for the workers, and
when we consider that people spend about
three-fourths of their lives in their homes it
is vital that these homes should be made as
attractive as possible for those who inhabit
them. What sort of life do you expect
people to live who occupy a house with two
bedrooms and a kitchen? My hon. Friend
(Mr. William McMullen), referred to some of
the houses he has seen in the ward which he
represents, and which constituted for many
years part of my constituency. I was round
those districts, and I went into some of these
houses. I found that it is almost impossible
for an ordinary adult to crush himself into
the bedrooms of these houses-and these are
Corporation houses built before the war.
They were most discreditable, and now instead of trying to improve these conditions
you are going to spend public money in perpetuation of these evils. That is what you
are doing.
For my own part I would not give a farthing of a subsidy to any builder unless a
builder who is erecting decent healthy houses
at a rent which the people can pay. We
know ourselves that most of the houses being
built now are, as the hon. Member for Down
has said, mostly built not for the class
whom the State intended the houses for, but
are built for what is known as the better
class. Nearly all these houses for which
subsidies have been granted are houses
which we know are not for letting but for
sale. You are actually subsidising commercial enterprise. You are giving people
Government money to make money out of it
for themselves. That is what you are really
doing. It was never intended by those who
approved the subsidy for houses that that
class should benefit by that step. It was intended, as I understand it, that since
economic conditions made it impossible to
build houses at rents which the people could
pay that the subsidy would be given to
enable them to let houses to the working
classes at rents which they could pay. That,
I think, is in the minds of many hon. Mem.
bers. I wonder is it in the minds of the
Government? Was that the Government's
intention? Or is it a general proposition
that you are to give subsidies to everybody
who builds houses? If that is so it is opposed
to all sound economics.
I am sure no one is prouder than the hon.
Member for Derry (Mrs. Chichester) to see
labourers' cottages scattered all over the
Province and all over Ireland, but let me
point out to the House that the same spirit
of mentality prevails here as prevailed in
the days when these labourers' cottages were
being built. I remember-and I do not
think the right hon. Gentleman, the Prime
Minister can contradict me-that a certain
proportion of the funds for building these
cottages was given to the whole of Ireland, and the Unionist and the Tory
Councils in Ulster would not use the
money. It was used in the South of Ireland
with the result that they had a larger proportion of houses in the South than you have
in Northern Ireland, and that was simply
because you have a strange mentality, as I
said before. You cannot understand why
there should be an uplifting ambition
amongst the working classes to live a cleaner
and healthier life.

Therefore, I think that this Parliament

this:
Let the Government do anything,
however reprehensible, and we will never
say anything about it." You cannot have
the unity of Ireland if you vote for decent
houses for the people. You will not destroy

houses to the people. This is not a political

at the root of the health, comfort, and
welfare of the people, and the health, comfort and welfare of the people are the foundations of the stability of the State.
I would have imagined that hon. Gentlemen
on the other side would have risen up here
to back the proposals of the hon. Gentleman
(Mr. Wm. McMullen). Why should you always leave it to Socialists and to other evildoers like myself to be always the apostles
of good causes? If you had sufficient common sense, even in your own interest you
would say that it would be well not to be
forced into it by either of these hon. Gentlemen sitting before me or those who sit here
with me, but you would do it as a mere
matter of policy, apart altogether from the
question of humanity. When the hon. and
learned Gentleman (Mr. Hanna) who, I see,
has taken laborious and pretentious
notes of the various
delispeeches
vered, rises, I want him to answer this question: Can he justify compelling a family of
two, not of 19, such as my hon. Friend (Mr.
T. Henderson), has proudly boasted of as an
ancestral asset, to live under these conditions?
If you are going to rear up a healthy manhood and womanhood in the future of Ulster
the whole thing is entirely wrong. I agree
with the hon. Gentleman (Mr. William
McMullen) that it would be a good policy to
start off in accepting his suggestion as one of
a series of suggestions, and that is to set
up a Committee to explore this whole question. In my judgment it would pay the State
and the Government to have a special
Department dealing with housing. Housing
should not be in the hands of the Home
Office at all. I do not say that the right
hon. Gentleman (Sir Dawson Bates) is not
as sympathetic as it is possible for him to
be, but owing to the serious multitudinarian

the House to deal with this whole question
of housing and try to solve it upon lines

Motion
made and Question proposed:

The MINISTER OF COMMERCE (Mr.
Barbour): Hon. Members will see that the
net amount of this Estimate is £32,185, and
is made up of the items amounting to
£33,315 included under the first five Subheads which hon. Members will see on page
3 of the little pamphlet of Supplementary
Estimates less the Section 2 Receipts of
£1,130 which are brought to account under
Sub-head S.-Receipts Appropriated in Aid.
The gross expenditure provided in Section 8
represents additional services carried out on
repayment terms on behalf of Northern
Ireland Departments and this sum, namely,
£5,980, is off-set by receipts which are paid
in from the various Departmental Votes.
Dealing with Section 1, there is provided
a sum of £29,500, which represents expenditure incurred this year over and above the
sum originally provided for work at
Stormont. This points to a welcome acceleration in the carrying out of the works.
I should remind hon. Members that, although under the accounting arrangements
which govern the service it is necessary for
this money to be voted by the Parliament
of Northern Ireland in the first instance,
recoupment is subsequently effected from the
Imperial Government under whose control
the works are being carried out, but under
the procedure prescribed by the Act recoupment is not made directly through this Vote
but payment is made direct to the Exchequer
of Northern Ireland.
Turning to Section 2, the first item of
£700 will interest hon. Members as this provides for the expenses of surveying the River
Bann in connection with the drainage investigation. The actual work of survey has
now been completed, and it is hoped that the
Report of the engineers will be in the hands
of the Government in the course of a very
few days. The second item provides for
payment of rates for Hillsborough Castle,
which is a liability of the Northern Government. The Imperial Government undertook
the purchase and initial renovation expenses
in consideration of the Government
Northern Ireland assuming liability for
maintenance, and of course the Government
of Northern Ireland is liable for the rates.
of
The third item of £1,100 for insurance
represents, as explained in the note, arrears
of premiums payable in respect of the year
1924-25.
Section 3 provides for three new services.
The purchase of Hampton House is for use as
a Men's Hostel in connection with the Stranmillis Training College Scheme. When the
Supplementary Estimates. 214
Supply-
16 MARCH 1926
original estimate for the current year was
presented, a sum was provided for the, erection of a new hostel, but it is now proposed
to adopt Hampton House for this purpose on
grounds of economy. The building will provide living accommodation, it is estimated,
for a maximum of 80 students. Their instruction will, of course, be carried out at
the Training College itself. The temporary
hostel at present in existence is a hired
building and only accommodates a portion of
the male students, the remaining living in
lodgings or their homes. It will be given
up as soon as the adaptation of the new building has been completed. This charge of
£4,850 will be finally met from what we know
as the Colwyn or Imperial grant of £400,000.
Subhead "N" provides for two new services: An unemployment relief scheme at
Ardglass Harbour, which contemplates the
reclamation of a plot of ground to be subsequently leased to herring curers. This estimate provides merely for the cost of the
requisite material, and provision for wages,
estimated at £420, in connecton with the
work has been included in the Supplementary Estimate for Harbour and Commercial Services. The total cost of this reclamation, therefore, amounts to £840.
As regards the additional laboratory at
Stormont, this is for veterinary research,
and hon. Members will see that a token
vote of £10 only is asked for in this connection. It is in order that Parliamentary
approval may be given for this work, the
expenditure on which will not mature for
payment until the coming financial year.
The necessity for the laboratory arises from
the transfer as from 1st April next to
Northern Ireland of the veterinary services
formerly carried out as a Council of Ireland
Service by an Imperial Department. The
work has so far been carried out in a
laboratory in Queen's University, but it is
considered desirable that the entire work of
animal research should be concentrated at
Stormont now that the Northern Government will shortly have control over the entire field of operations and a small laboratory
at present exists at Stormont.
The next three items in Subheads P, Q,
and R provide for works expenditure in
consequence of the taking of the census.
The items included in the credit Subhead
are self-explanatory and require no further
explanation. I beg to move.

to do it.
The Prime Minister was, no doubt, very
amusing the other day. Of course it would
take well with his supine followers, but his
explanation did not affect me in the least
degree. He said "Look what they are doing
in Australia." I forget the place where they
are building, but it is a long way from any
centre of population. What is really the
fact? That this is a Federal Parliament
they are building out in Australia. There
are four State Parliaments and there is a
Federal Parliament, and the real reason
why this Federal Parliament House is being
built is this-because I know Australia well,
and I remember following the controversy
that took place in regard to the new capital
-that, Melbourne being jealous of Sydney
and Sydney jealous of Melbourne, neither of
the two would consent to the other being
made the capital, and, therefore, they de
cided to build the Federal Parliament House
in some neutral place. There is no analogy
whatever between this case and the case of
Northern Ireland. This Parliament covers
an area almost as small as
a county in
Australia, and yet we are building a Parliament House away out five miles from the
city, a most unbusiness-like transaction from
a purely business point of view and a most
inconvenient arrangement from a Parliamentary point of view.
This House has never been consulted about
it. We have never been told how far this
enterprise has developed, or who is building,
or what it is going to cost, or who is responsible for it. The first opportunity .we
have for securing information is when
quietly, now fifteen minutes after the normal
time for the adjournment, we get this paper
with £29,500 placed upon it. I will take a
division upon that, first of all as a protest
against it being raised here at all at this
stage of our proceedings, and, secondly,
against the Government having deliberately
refused to give us any information upon this
point.

The hon. Member, to go to the next point,
has said that hon. Members were never consulted with regard to the site chosen for
our new Parliamentary institutions. The
fault is entirely his own. He and his colleagues remained out of this House. We
could not wait until he and the others made

deciding.
Mr. DEVLIN: There was no hurry.
The PRIME MINISTER: Ah, there was

Mr. DEVLIN: Then you would not need

The PRIME MINISTER: We would need

in time Ulster constituencies will return
Members who propose to attend to their

hear.) At all events, we are bound to have
some permanent place in which to carry on
our deliberations. The question of the site
had to be settled long, long ago, and in my
opinion, after five years, the best site that
could possibly have been selected was chosen
for our Parliamentary Institutions, and also
for housing our Civil Servants. Belfast itself
is growing all the time, and what appears
to be the outskirts of the city to-day will
probably be more or less the centre of the
city in a generation. Therefore, above all
else, we have at a comparatively reasonable
cost sufficient elbow room to expand at any
time. We have also upon the site one of the
best model farms in connection with our Egg
Testing Station, and our chicken runs, and
my right hon. Friend, the Minister of Agriculture, has his flax and other experimental
buildings, which he carries on at our very
door. Consequently we are able to utilise
every bit of that estate of 250 acres for

buildings. I hope that with this explanation

CLASS V. No. 2.
AGRICULTURAL SERVICES.
Motion made, and Question proposed:
"That a supplementary sum not exceeding
£10 be granted to His Majesty for the services
of the year ending 31st March, 1926, to defray
the expenses of the Ministry of Agriculture
in respect of Agricultural Education and Research, Improvement of Live Stock, Agricultural Development, Agricultural Statistics
and Afforestation, including sundry Grants
in Aid and certain capital expenditure under
14 and 15 Geo. V., c. 13, s. 1 (N.I.)."
The MINISTER OF AGRICULTURE (Mr.
Archdale): This Supplementary Estimate is
to bring to the notice of Parliament certain
sums which could not have been foreseen
when the 1925-26 Estimates were introduced.
We have been able to find the amount required from savings on our main Estimate,
so that the Supplementary Estimate simply
provides for a token figure of £10. A1 refers
to Agricultural Research and Faculty of
Agriculture. As mentioned by the Minister
of Commerce (Mr. Barbour), we found it
necessary since we have to take over the administration of veterinary diseases on the
1st April, to erect a laboratory at Stormont.
We have one there already, but we want
this new one so that we can carry on necessary post-mortem work, and deal with milk
samples submitted in connection with the
Bovine Tuberculosis Order.
The next item is Agricultural Education.
Following on the provisions of the Education
Act a Superannuation Scheme has been
framed, applicable to agricultural teachers
in Northern Ireland. Under this scheme
contributions to the Technical Teachers'
Superannuation Fund, Northern Ireland, are
to be made by the employers of agricultural
teachers. The next item is the building
grant to the Royal Ulster Agricultural
Society. For the last number of years the
Royal Ulster Agricultural Society has given
us a large space in the Londonderry Hall at
Balmoral in order to show the Ministry's
exhibit. They did not charge any rent for
it, and they were most helpful to us. Owing,
however, to the increasing exhibits in cattle,
poultry, etc., they find it is impossible for
us to continue exhibiting in that hall. They
have, therefore, arranged to erect a building
on a prominent site in their grounds for
our exhibits. It has been found that nothing
so much interests the farmers at these shows
as the Ministry's exhibit. They have been
crowded from morning till night. We have
found also in the Ministry that there is
nothing better to educate the farmers than
this exhibit, where they can see the effect
of all research work before their eyes.
As I have said, the society is erecting a
large shed for our permanent use. It will
cost about £5,000, We will pay £2,000
towards it, as the society's finances would
not enable them to pay the whole cost. We
think it will prove a tremendous benefit to
those engaged in farming to have this big
shed at Balmoral for continual use, and I
think it is very generous of the Royal Ulster
Society to pay their large proportion (£3,000)
as they have arranged to do. (Hon. Members:
Hear, hear.).
As to G2 (Seed Supply Schemes), the first
two items, A1 and A2, were before the
Committee last year, and were agreed to. As
there are two new schemes adopted (B1 and
B2), we thought it advisable to bring them
here, so that the Committee would know
exactly how much money was spent on these
subjects. Owing to a big outbreak of black
scab amongst potatoes in the Londonderry
area a considerable area had to be scheduled.
The farmers had been in the habit of growing non-immune varieties of potatoes for the
Belfast and Dublin markets. On the scheduling of the district the sale of these
varieties was immediately stopped. Owing to
the low prices obtained for what they did
grow, their sale in the ordinary market being
stopped, we provided a considerable quantity
of immune seed, which we wanted to get
grown in these districts, and sold it to them
at the price of their own seed. That involved
a loss of £3 108 per ton to provide the
farmers in that scheduled area with immune

varieties, which they had not been able to
get before. They only grew skerries before,
and they were in great demand in Belfast
and Dublin.
B (2) refers to the great want there is
in the country for a white immune potato
to replace the varieties that have been grown
by farmers in Northern Ireland, and as
the only new immune variety thought suitable cost £60 a ton, no farmer in the country
would be able to grow that. We bought two

in the autumn when the seed is lifted, so

dear for the farmers to buy. We bought
this seed and arranged to give it as I have
said. That means a sum of £125. We anticipate a good receipt from B1 (Seed for
Planting) because we have already got £500.
We sold the seed at the rate of ordinary
notatoes to these people at their own places.

in this respect. (Hon. Members: Hear,
hear.) But as I said at the outset I am
anxious to take this opportunity presented
by this grant which we are passing to express my appreciation for all the Department
has done. It is very hard for Governments
to be held responsible for damage which is
caused by the hand of God. It is very hard
for Governments to have to step in and
assist financially when their finances are
more limited than their compassion. I
would like to say now it is a very serious
thing for the afflicted farmer whose rates-
I need not repeat once more in this House
-are intolerable, whose rates are at present
so heavy, and whose rates if the hon.
Members opposite got their way would be
increased enormously, if as he stated in a
previous discussion outdoor relief were compulsorily forced upon the guardians in rural
areas, and consequently the rates would rise
enormously. It is a serious thing for these
men whose rates as I say are already intolerable and whose incomes are negligible,
who toil unceasingly with very little to
show as a result, and whose income in many
cases is smaller weekly than the income of
the unemployed who are drawing the dole.
I want to impress that fact upon the House,
because I want them to realise if they do
not realise it how these struggling farmers
are striving to exist on a far smaller sum
than is drawn by some of these unemployed.
I wish to say it is very hard for the people
in the condition I have described to reason
clearly. It is very hard for them to recognise that the Government has to take
certain precautions in order to safeguard the
potato trade, or is treating them fairly in
imposing restrictions which they think
penalise them. I do think it is right and
proper here to-day when this opportunity
has occurred that I as one of the repre-
Supplementary Estimates. 230
Supply-

sentatives of these people, knowing something of what the Department has done to
help them and knowing something of the

I felt it really was incumbent on me as

been a very great help to these people. I
only wish I could move that it might be increased. I am one of those who believe that
you do not do enough for the agricultural
community, and that you cannot do too much
to help them, because I want to emphasise
the fact that apart from hardships they
should be considered, because they are the
backbone of Ulster. They are the men who
made Ulster what she is. They are the men
on whom we will have to rely to keep Ulster
as she is. Calamity has overtaken them certainly in the area to which I am referring
through no fault of their own. It was up to
the Minister of Agriculture to go to their
assistance, and I am glad to say the Ministry
has responded and the demands have been
recognised to the extent of this £1,375. I
would like to say that I hope this will not
be the last concession, and that, perhaps, in

Mr. ARCHDALE: I would just like to say

from around that particular district come.
People from all over Ulster come to
Balmoral, and there is no place where we can
get so many men together to get the benefit
of the exhibit as we can there. We certainly will continue to do our best to help
other local shows, and since we began we
have always done so.
Mr. BEATTIE: Will the right hon.
Gentleman explain the reason for that overplus stated there? I am looking at F3 and
I find that the revised estimate is £2,000. I

Mr. ARCHDALE: That was granted to

The CHAIRMAN: Perhaps I might explain the procedure in regard to these Estimates and Supplementary Estimates. There
are presented following the Budget statement
original Estimates-that is the technical

that is has either over- or under-estimated.

CLASS IV. No. 2.
EDUCATIONAL SERVICES.
Motion made and Question proposed:
"That a supplementary sum not exceeding
£10 be granted to His Majesty to complete
the sum necessary to defray the charge
which will come in course of payment during
the year ending on the 31st March, 1926, to
provide for Educational Services, including
Grants in Aid of the Teachers' Pension
Fund, Northern Ireland (10 and 11 Geo. V,
c. 67; 12 and 13 Geo. V, c. 13 (N. I.), and
Grants under 18 and 14 Geo. V, c. 21 (N.I.),
and certain capital expenditure under 14 and
15 Geo. V, c. 13, s. 1 (N.I.).
The PARLIAMENTARY SECRETARY OF
THE MINISTRY OF EDUCATION (Mr.
Robb): The Committee will find details of
this Estimate on page 11 of the Supplementary Estimates. It arises in this way:
Although the sums already voted by Parliament for Educational Services in the current
financial year will be sufficient to cover all
expenditure which will become chargeable to
that year, it is considered necessary to present this "token" Supplementary Estimate
in order that the specific authority of Parliament may be obtained for certain payments
for which no express provision was made in
the Estimates previously submitted. We
have the money in hands, but we have not
got Parliamentary authority to pay it out.
The first item is the provision of Hampton
House. That, of course, has been bought by
the Government for the purpose of a men's
hostel in connection with the Training
College at Stranmillis. The present hostel
for men students a rented house at Royal
Terrace has accommodation for only 27
students, with the result that 45 students
are obliged to live either at home or in
lodgings; those not provided with hostel
accommodation receiving an allowance in lieu
of board and lodging. This arrangement is
not satisfactory, and it is very desirable
that all the men students should live in the
hostel.
The other two items are contributions to
be paid by the State to two.teachers' pensions
funds-one for secondary and the other for
technical teachers. The statutory orders
under which those payments fall to be made
come into operation at 1st April this year,
so that those two sums could not be provided
for in the original Estimate. The orders
have not come into operation during the year,
and these are sums which under those orders
will receive sanction during the current
financial year. I beg to move.
Question put, and agreed to.

Loans Guarantee (Money).
Order for Committee read.
Considered in Committee under Standing
Order No. 65.
[Mr. MOLES in the Chair].
Motion made and Question proposed:
That it is expedient to amend the Loans
Guarantee Acts (Northern Ireland), 1922-

I. By increasing from six million pounds to
seven million pounds the limit on the aggre
gate capital amount of the loans, the prinpal or interest of which may be guaranteed
by the Ministry of Finance thereunder; and
by extending to the 31st day of March, 1927,
the period within which guarantees may
Loans Guarantee
Committee.
16 MARCH 1926
be given under the Loans Guarantee Act
(Northern Ireland), 1922; and to charge on
the Consolidated Fund of Northern Ireland
any moneys required for fulfilling any such
guarantees.
II. By authorising the Ministry of
Finance, in any case where the principal or
interest of a loan has been guaranteed by
the said Ministry to pay an amount not exceeding one-tenth of the interest payable in
respect of so much of the loan as is proposed
to be raised for expenditure in Northern
Ireland, or, alternatively to pay a capital
sum, not in excess of the value of such
interest payment; and to charge on moneys
provided by Parliament any sums required
for the said purpose. (Governor's Recommendation signified)-(Mr. Pollock.)
Mr. POLLOCK: This Money Resolution
which I am now about to submit to the
Committee is the foundation of a Bill which
will be presented in due course, probably in
a day or two. As the Committee is no doubt
aware, Parliamentary sanction was given up
to a limit of £6,000,000, empowering the
Ministry of Finance to guarantee certain
sums on behalf of those who undertook to
make capital expenditure in Northern Ireland. Up to the present, of that £6,000,000
we have exhausted a sum of something over
£4,000,000, leaving approximately a balance
of £2,000,000 unexhausted. For reasons I
will explain in a minute or two I think it is
necessary we should come to ask for an additional £1,000,000 in order that the money at
our disposal, or rather that the guarantees
which will be at our disposal, will amount
to a sum of £3,000,000.
In asking the Committee to increase the
existing margin to £3,000,000 the Government
have taken into account the possibility of a
greater demand on the part of ship-owning
interests for tonnage during the coming year.
I am in hopes that that expectation will be
realised, and there are indications at the
present time that ship-owners are beginning
more and more to discover the necessity for
keeping pace with modern development in
regard to shipbuilding. For this reason 1
feel that it is necessary we should have this
amount of £3,000,000 to enable us to guarantee up to that extent should the necessity
arise. Undoubtedly, the provision of these
guarantees has had a very substantial bearing upon the provision of labour in Northern
Ireland. At the present moment there are
something like 8,000 men who are employed
in work being carried on under these guarantees, and I think I am not going too far in
stating that the probability is that if such
Government encouragement had not been in
existence a number of these men would today be unemployed.
The second part of the Resolution which
appears on the Paper deals with a different
department of the same subject. Up to the
present, as have informed the Committee,
we have guaranteed ship-owners and shipbuilders up to approximately £4,000,000.
This money has been advanced by lenders
of various kinds, bankers and others, at the
same rate as the British Government's Guarantees, working under the Trades Facilities
Act, have been able to secure. But in case
some exceptional circumstances might arise
when the Government may find it necessary
to bridge any small difference that might
accrue by reason of the Northern Ireland
guarantee not being exactly of the same
standard as the British guarantee we think
it necessary that some provision of this kind
should be made.
Undoubtedly, British security stands at
the top of the world, and whether the
Northern Ireland security, good as we know
it to be, will be able to secure continuously
the same rate as the British Government
is something I am not prepared at the present moment to argue, because it may be
possible that owing to some exceptional
circumstances, where we may probably desire
to guarantee some operation, we might have
to pay some small trifle under the rate of
the British guarantee. The difference cannot
be very great, but I think it is right that
the Ministry of Finance should have the
power to negotiate on these lines if the
contingency should arise.
The Committee is fully aware of the present depression in shipbuilding, and of the
necessity that exists, especially in Northern
Ireland, to provide labour for those men,
who, unfortunately, are walking about the
streets through no fault of their own, and
it is because of this that I am asking the
Committee now to give the Ministry of
Finance the necessary authority to negotiate
under the conditions I have just outlined.
I beg to move.
Question put, and agreed to.
Resolution reported, and agreed to.
Bill ordered to be brought in by the
Minister of Finance, Mr. Milne Barbour,
and Captain Dixon.

THE ENTERTAINMENT TAX.
1. Colonel WOODS asked the Minister of
Finance whether he contemplates reducing
the entertainment tax to an amount at
least equal to that imposed by the Imperial
Government.
The Minister of Finance (Mr. Pollock):
This matter continues to receive my careful
consideration, but clearly the honourable
Member will not expect me to anticipate
my Budget statement.
EX-SERVICEMEN IN CIVIL SERVICE.
2. Colonel WOODS asked the Minister of
Finance whether he contemplates allowing
temporary civil servants to qualify by
examination for permanent positions in the
Civil Service as has been done in Great
Britain.
Mr. POLLOCK: The position in regard
to the employment of ex-Servicemen in the
Civil Service in Northern Ireland is
materially different from that which exists
in Great Britain. On the constitution of
our various Departments a large number
of ex-Servicemen were employed as temporary clerks, and approximately 65 per
cent. of the clerical appointments made
have been filled by ex-Servicemen, who were
admitted to established posts without
examination. The treatment accorded to
ex-Servicemen in the Northern Ireland
Civil Service will bear favourable comparison with that extended to them in the
Imperial Civil Service, and, indeed, it is
believed with any other Government
Service in the world.
Further, all temporary appointments of
a clerical and subordinate character are
reserved for qualified and suitable ex-
Service candidates, and it has been
arranged that a percentage of future
clerical vacancies in each Department will
be reserved for ex-Service temporary clerks.
Mr. R. J. ADGEY.-IMPORTATION OF
FIREARMS.
3. Colonel WOODS asked the Minister of
Home Affairs whether it is according to the
facts that certain firearms are being, or
have been, imported from the Continent, or
America, by the Chairman of the Police
Committee, of the Belfast Corporation,
trading under the name of Robert J. Adgey,
of 97 Peter's Hill, Belfast, and distributed
or sold throughout Northern Ireland without official permits accompanying the same;
and whether other firms, handling similar
goods, enjoy similar privileges.
The MINISTER OF HOME AFFAIRS
(Sir Dawson Bates): The answer to the
first part of the Question is in the
affirmative. Official permits have been obtained by Mr. Adgey in all cases where such
are required by the Regulations. All firms
handling similar goods enjoy exactly the
same privileges.
SPECIAL-CONSTABLE WILLIAM
PRESTON.
4. Mr. BEATTIE asked the Minister of
Home Affairs whether he can state the
specific reasons for not allowing 5086 Special-
Constable William Preston, 23 Platoon,
entrance into the R.U.C., seeing that he
passed the test on November, 1925, and was
qualified to enter the said Force.
Sir DAWSON BATES: While it is a
fact that Special-Constable William Preston
complied with the minimum requirements
for admission to the Force, the number of
candidates with much higher qualifications
was far in excess of the number of
vacancies.
Mr. BEATTIE: I would like to ask
whether, in view of this constable's valuable
services and high recommendations, the
Minister of Home Affairs would be prepared
to reconsider the question of his entry into
the R.U.C.?
Sir DAWSON BATES: The qualifications
of each candidate are considered, and those
with the best qualifications are admitted
first.

VACANT
Housing in Belfast.
DWELLINGS.-RECORDS
WATER COMMISSIONERS.
OF
6. Mr. WILLIAM MCMULLEN asked the
Minister of Home Affairs whether he is
aware that at a meeting of the Belfast City
and District Water Commissioners, held on
the 11th March, 1926, the Finance Committee
reported that during the month of February
2,481 streets were inspected; that it was
ascertained that 357 dwelling-houses were
vacant, and whether he would state if he
conceives it to be in the public interest to
have dwelling-houses vacant while so many
citizens urgently require houses, and what
steps he proposes to take to remedy this
state of affairs.
Sir DAWSON BATES: I am aware that
according to the report furnished to the
Finance Committee of the Belfast City and
District Water Commissioners on the date
in question 2,481 streets had been inspected
during the month of February by the Inspectors of the Commissioners, and that it
was ascertained that 357 dwelling-houses
were vacant at the time.
I also understand that from the corresponding report made to the Commissioners
in December last, the number of vacant
dwelling-houses was 400, while from the report made in July last the number was 475,
and also that the number in April last was
487.
It will thus be observed that according to
the official records of the Water Commissioners there has been a substantial decrease during the last year or so of the
number of vacant houses in the city.
Further, it should be borne in mind that
new houses are being completed in Belfast
at a rate of, approximately, 100 a month,
and it is only natural that in these cases
there may be some delay in the occupation
of them.
Accordingly, the circumstances do not
appear to me to warrant any action on the
part of the Government, even if it were
possible to take such action usefully.
Mr. W. MCMULLEN: Will the right
hon. Gentleman state, in answer to the
Mr. SPEAKER: That is a matter for

Mr. SPEAKER: I think that is so. I

NUMBER OF HOUSES IN THE CITY.
7. Mr. W. McMULLEN asked the Minister

that there were 80,093 houses and 154 under
construction in the City of Belfast in that

Restriction Bill on the 13th May, 1925, that
there
were approximately 82,000 in the

1911 and 1923 has since been maintained,
reduced, or increased, and if he will state

houses in the city at the present time.
Sir DAWSON BATES: I am aware that
the Census returns for 1911 disclosed the
fact that on the appointed date in 1911 there
was a total of 80,247 houses in the City of
Belfast, including 75,172 inhabited houses;
4,921 uninhabited houses, and 154 houses in
process of erection.
The statement made by me on the 13th
May, 1925, during the debate on the Rent
Restriction Bill that there were, approximately, 82,000 in the city in the year 1923,
was based on evidence tendered to the Departmental Committee on Rent Restriction,
and this information has been verified from
the records of the Belfast Corporation,
from which records it would appear that
the actual number of houses in the city on
the 31st December, 1922 was 82,220.
The rate of building between 1911 and
1923 cannot be usefully taken as a
criterion of housing progress, having regard to the fact that building operations
were practically suspended during and immediately after the war.

REPORT OF LOCAL GOVERNMENT
COMMISSION.
8. Mr. W. MCMULLEN asked the Minister
of Home Affairs when it is expected that
the final report of the Poor-Law Commission
will be issued.
Sir DAWSON BATES: In reply to a
former question asked by the hon. Member
on the 14th December last, I stated that it
was understood from the Chairman of the
Commission that he hoped to be in a
position to issue the Report by the end of
the present month.
The Commission has been sitting constantly since then, and considerable progress, it is understood, has been made
towards arriving at the necessary decisions,
which will form the basis of their recommendations.
It is understood, however, that owing to
the many difficulties and complexities of
the various problems that have confronted
the Commission, it will not be possible for
them to issue their Report for some time
yet.
MONEY FOR ERECTION OF PARLIA-
MENT BUILDINGS.
9. Mr. DEVLIN asked the Prime Minister
whether he is prepared to appoint a deputation, consisting of representatives of all
parties in the House, to interview Mr.
Churchill, and ask him to consent to the
diversion of half the cost of the new Parliament buildings at Stormont Castle to the
erection of workers' houses in Belfast and
other parts of Northern Ireland, where the
shortage of dwellings is most acute.
The PRIME MINISTER (Sir James Craig) :
No, Sir. The British Government have no
statutory power to divert any of the money
destined to the erection of Parliamentary
buildings. The Joint Exchequer Board only
approve of such a scale of expenditure as is
deemed necessary to meet the Imperial
statutory obligation under the Act of 1920 to
provide Northern Ireland with her Parliamentary and administrative buildings, together with the necessary equipment, and I
am satisfied that the expenditure proposed
has been reduced to the minimum. Further,
I would point out that the building of
houses is a matter primarily for local
authorities and private enterprise, to which,
however, this House is voting contributions
from time to time which compare favourably
with grants by the Imperial Government to
local authorities in Great Britain. The
British Government could not be reasonably
asked or expected to give an additional
grant towards housing in Northern Ireland
which they are not in a position to make
towards housing in Great Britain. In this
regard we are already assured under the
Colwyn Committee of sufficient money to
provide equal subsidies and to maintain
equal conditions with Great Britain.
Mr. DEVLIN: Does the right hon. Gentleman not think that, if a request of the
character indicated in my question were put
to the Chancellor of the Exchequer, Parliament would sanction a change in the
arrangement so as to enable Parliament to
have a smaller House and the poor people
larger ones?
The PRIME MINISTER: As a matter of
fact, I do not think the House to be erected
at Stormont would be considered by anybody
as larger than is absolutely necessary for the
purposes for which it is intended.

remuneration, and the conditions of service; to report-

[Mr. Pollock]
(a) whether the general organisation is
on sound lines;
(b) whether there is a redundancy of
staff;
(c) whether the standards of remuneration and conditions of service are
reasonable;
and to make recommendations."
The Government think it best to give Sir
Russell Scott the greatest possible latitude
in conducting his inquiry, so that it will be
left to him to decide what evidence he will
take and the procedure which he will adopt.
In regard to the last portion of the hon.
Member's question, it would not be possible
to postpone the introduction of the Estimates
until Sir Russell Scott has reported, but this
procedure will, in any case, cause no delay in
giving effect to any recommendations which
Sir Russell Scott may put forward. Members
will, therefore, have an opportunity, when
the Estimates are introduced, of making any
suggestions in regard to possible economies.
Mr. DEVLIN: Will the right hon. Gentleman answer that portion of the Question
which asks whether Sir Russell Scott will
investigate the present method of appointment and promotion? Will that be included
in the terms of reference?
Mr. POLLOCK: Yes, I presume that all
relevant circumstances connected with the
conditions of the Civil Service in Northern
Ireland will be taken into account. That is
contemplated.
Mr. DEVLIN: What form will this inquiry take? Will Sir Russell Scott sit and
receive evidence from outsiders?
Mr. POLLOCK: It is entirely within the
province of Sir Russell Scott to determine
the best method of arriving at what the
Government has in view. It is not for us to
dictate to him where he will sit or how he
will occupy his time. That is entirely a
matter of his own volition.
NEW ROADWAY AT STORMONT.
11. Mr. BEATTIE asked the Prime
Minister whether he can state the reason
for the delay in starting to make the new
roadway from the new Parliament House
to the main road.
Mr. POLLOCK: I propose to take this
Question. At the end of January last the
Joint Exchequer Board approved the proposal of the Northern Ireland Government
that the cost of construction of this road
should he met from Imperial Funds under
Section 34 of the Government of Ireland Act,
1920.
The necessary surveys were put in hand
forthwith and cross and longitudinal sections
prepared and transmitted to II.M. Office of
Works.
The Imperial Government gave an undertaking that advertisements for tenders would
be issued as soon as the specifications and
Bills of Quantities had been prepared, and
I anticipate that these advertisements will
bo issued shortly.
Continual representations are being made
to the Imperial Government as to the necessity for an early commencement of the work,
which will give much needed employment
to many unskilled labourers.
Mr. BEATTIE: In view of the abnormal
distress that is being caused by unemployment and the simplicity of the work is the
Minister not prepared to proceed at once
with the making of this new roadway so as
to relieve the distress in the city?
Mr. POLLOCK: It is not within our
province to undertake this work, but constant pressure is being brought to bear on the
British authorities in regard to the matter.
It cannot be expedited any more than it is
being carried out at the present time.
ERECTION OF NEW PARLIAMENT
HOUSE.
12. Mr. BEATTIE asked the Prime
Minister whether he can state what date
building operations are going to commence (n
the erection of Parliament House.
Mr. POLLOCK: I have been asked to
reply to this Question. The hon. Member
will no doubt recollect that the plans which
were originally decided upon for the new
Parliament and Departmental buildings at
Stormont were, for reasons
of economy,
amended to a very considerable extent. This
has resulted in unavoidable delay, but work
under the foundations contract is approaching completion and a contract has already
been made for the supply and delivery on the
site of the stone and granite required to
bring the building to the first floor level.
The development of the drawings and details for the complete super-structure is
being proceeded with at present, and strong
representations have been made to the Office
of Works as to the necessity for pressing on
with the work with the utmost possible expedition.
Mr. DEVLIN: Can the right hon. Gentleman inform the House--because we have
never had any information on this point—
what exactly is the responsibility of the
Imperial Government in regard to the erection of this building? We have never been
told that. Does it mean that the British
Government proposed to pay but are not

MIDLAND RAILWAY-EXPELLED
WORKERS.
13. Mr. McMULLEN asked the Prime
Minister whether he is aware that a number
of men were expelled from their employment
in the Midland Railway during the recent
seotarian troubles in the city on account of
their religion, some of whom had given up
a life-time service to the Company, and had
almost qualified for pensions, and whether
now that we are enjoying uninterrupted
peace he will use his good offices to have
these men restored to their former positions.
The MINISTER OF LABOUR (Mr.
Andrews): I have been asked by my right
hon. Friend, the Prime Minister, to reply.
This is a matter, I am informed, which
was not brought about by any action of the
Company, and it can only be settled between
the Company and their employees; it is not
one in which the Government is in a position
to interfere.
I understand that the question is a particularly difficult one at the present time,
having regard to the regrettable retrenchments which the Company is forced to make
owing to the continuous fall in its receipts.
Mr. W. McMULLEN: I would like to inquire whether a move of this character
would not do more to promote peace throughout the Province than any number of
speeches from right hon. Gentlemen opposite?
14. Mr. McMULLEN asked the Minister of
Home Affairs whether he will state when it
is expected that the Report of the Commissioner appointed to inquire into the activities
of the Housing Department of the Belfast
Corporation will be issued.
Sir DAWSON BATES: It is expected that
the Report in question will be issued in the
course of the next few days.
Mr. W. McMULLEN: Would the right hon.
Gentleman be prepared to put a date-week
or month?
Sir DAWSON BATES: I have already said
the next few days.
Mr. W. McMULLEN: Your days are somewhat long. I want to find out the length of
them.
SCALE OF FAMILY INCOME.
15. Mr. BEATTIE asked the Minister of
Labour, in view of the abnormal distress
caused by the introduction of the Hardship
Rule on family income, whether he is prepared to reconsider the whole question, and
reduce the self-dependent age to 21 years.
Mr. ANDREWS: The direction by my
Department to Local Employment Committees on this subject is to the effect that
extended benefit will ordinarily be withheld
from single persons who are not more than
25 years of age if a Rota Committee is satisfied that there are relatives to whom the
claimant can reasonably look for support,
and that the family incomings are such that
hardship would not result if a grant of extended benefit were not made.
This direction is to the same effect as the
direction of the Imperial Ministry to Committees in Great Britain, and, having regard
to the Government's policy of parallel
administration, I cannot agree to alter it.
Mr. BEATTIE: As to the last part of the
answer, is the Minister prepared now to
appoint a Committee to reconsider the question of the scale of family income, and have
it on parallel lines with Great Britain?
Mr. ANDREWS: I am of opinion that the
scale of family income taken as a whole is
about in step with the scale in Great Britain.
If the hon. Member can produce evidence to
the contrary I am prepared to consider the
matter.
Mr. BEATTIE: In view of the evidence I
have produced, and as the cost of living is
ten points higher here than in Great Britain,
is the Minister still determined to keep the
family income at the starvation rate he has
now said?

APPLICANTS DISALLOWED BENEFIT.
17. Mr. BEATTIE asked the Minister of
Labour whether he can state the number of
applicants who have been disallowed benefit
from all causes since the 1st October, 1925,
up to and including Saturday, the 12th of

Labour whether he can state the total

genuinely seeking work from the 1st October,

ROMAN CATHOLIC EX-SERVICEMEN IN
ASSISTED SCHEMES.
19. Colonel WOODS asked the Minister of
Labour whether he can state what steps
have been, or are being, taken by the
Government to protect the interests of
Roman Catholic ex-Servicemen in Government assisted schemes, and to ensure that in
such schemes they will receive equal treatment to that given to Protestant ex-Servicemen, and also to increase the percentage of
all ex-Servicemen to be employed upon all
Government assisted schemes.
Mr. ANDREWS: I can assure the hon. and
gallant Member that steps are taken by the
Government to protect the interests of both
Protestant and Roman Catholic ex-Servicemen on Government assisted schemes. Outside Belfast preference is given to ex-Servicemen irrespective of their religion, and inside
Belfast, where employment is given to
Roman Catholics in the proportion of onethird, the question is being carefully
watched by the Belfast Local Employment
Committee. I may add that the priority conditions at present in force in Belfast were
drawn up at the outset by a Committee upon
which all sections of the community were represented including representatives of ex-
Servicemen.
Colonel WOODS: May I ask the right hon.
Gentleman if he intends to increase the percentage of ex-Servicemen employed on
Government assisted schemes, as in England,
it is 75 per cent., and in Ulster it is somewhat less than 60 per cent?
Mr. ANDREWS: The position in Great
Britain and here is different because there
I am glad to say it has not been found
necessary to discriminate as between Protestant and Catholic. At the time these
relief schemes were started it was considered
by a Committee representative of all classes
and creeds in the community that there
should be a discrimination, and on the whole
it has worked satisfactorily. As I have said
the Local Employment Committee is keeping
watch on the position as it may change from
time to time.

EIGHT-HOUR DAY IN MOTOR
TRANSPORT.
20. Mr. W. MCMULLEN asked the Minister
Labour whether he is aware that
at a recent meeting of the Belfast and
District Branches of the National Union of
Railwaymen, a resolution was passed asking,
Oral Answers.
Oral Answers.
18 MARCH 1926
inter alia, that the Government should
make the eight-hour day applicable to the
motor omnibus and mechanical transport industry, and that the drivers employed in
this industry should be subjected to a
medical and eyesight test similar to enginedrivers on the railway, and whether he proposes to take any action in the matter.
Mr. ANDREWS: I have received a copy of
the resolution referred to. I understand
that my right hon. Friend, the Minister of
Home Affairs, intends to introduce at an
early date a Bill to secure the more effective

HANDLING GOODS AT THE DOCKS.
21. Mr. W. MCMULLEN asked the Minister
of Labour whether he has recently framed new
regulations under the Factory and Workshop
Act, 1901, for the processes of loading, unloading, and handling goods at the docks
and wharfs of Northern Ireland, and if so,
will he state when it is intended to introduce
such regulations.
Mr. ANDREWS: The answer to the first.
part of the question is in the affirmative.
New draft regulations, similar to those recently adopted in Great Britain, have been
published in Northern Ireland and certain
minor objections have been lodged. These
are at present under consideration by my
Department and can, I think, be satisfactorily met without formal inquiry. As
soon as these matters have been adjusted the
new code will be brought into operation.
MARKETING AND EXPORT OF EGGS.
22. Mr. W. McMULLEN asked the Minister
of Agriculture whether he is aware
that British public opinion is not informed
as to the improved way in which Irish eggs
are now marketed and exported, and whether,
in conjunction with the Minister of Agriculture for the Irish Free State, he will take
steps to inform the British public of these
improvements.
The MINISTER OF AGRICULTURE (Mr.
Archdale): Every effort has been made by the
Ministry, since the passing of the Marketing
of Eggs Act, to inform the trading community and the general public in Great
Britain as to the provisions of the Act. To
this end the daily Press and the appropriate
trade journals have been freely used. Explanatory matter has been furnished to
various associations of traders in Great
Britain and to individual merchants, and
the Ministry's principal marketing inspector
has been in constant touch with British
merchants interested in egg distribution.
Where feasible I shall be happy to cooperate with the Minister of Agriculture for
the Irish Free State in promoting the general
interests of the Irish poultry industry.

Adjournment of the House.
Motion made, and Question proposed:
That this House, at its rising this day, do
adjourn until Tuesday next.-(Captain
Dixon.)
Mr. DEVLIN: I rise for the purpose of
entering a protest against the methods by
which the business of this House is carried
on. We are suffering in this Parliament
from the impatience of Ministers to rush
Bills through the House. We are in the
habit of getting the Second Reading of a
Bill one day and a day or two after the
Committee stage is announced; in fact, the
Committee Stage of the Housing Bill is on
the Paper for to-day and the Second Reading was only passed on Tuesday. Yesterday
was a holiday for the Ministers, but not
for everybody.
Mr. POLLOCK: No.
Mr. DEVLIN. It was not a holiday for
some of the Ministers, because I see they
were making St. Patrick's Day speeches too.
Mr. POLLOCK: And others.
Mr. DEVLIN: Yes, I said others, some of
them good and some of them bad St.
Patrick's Day speeches. It is easy for the
Ministers to be ready for the Committee
Stages of these Bills, because they have very
efficient Civil Servants and they. have legal
advisers. They can get all their Committee
work done for them, whereas those of us
who have no Civil Servants behind us and
are not able to secure any legal Parliamentary assistance from draughtsmen or
others have to sit down and study these
Bills. First of all we have got to study the
Bills themselves and then we have to draft
the Amendments, and very often we get
only a day or two in which to do the work.
The result of this hurried legislation is
that we have already had to introduce other
Bills to improve the Bills already passed
owing to the imperfections contained in
them due to the hurried way in which they
were passed. I do not know whether it is
-It see you are getting impatient, Mr.
Speaker.
Mr. SPEAKER: It occurred to me that
the hon. Gentleman's arguments are rather
directed towards the delay of business which
this Motion proposes, because it proposes the
House shall not sit again until Tuesday
next.
Mr. DEVLIN: I was only taking advantage of it. I thought the proper time
to have done it, as the hon. Member for
North Belfast (Mr. Kyle) proposed to do it,
was upon the previous Motion, but you
ruled that would not be in order.
Mr. SPEAKER: It was not in order.
Mr. DEVLIN: Therefore, we could not
discuss it then, and I thought on the present
Motion would be a good time to raise it.
I do put it to the Prime Minister that this
is not an overworked assembly. We only
work here about three months in the year,
and, as I have already stated, three days
in the week and three hours in the day.
Yet these Bills are flung at us. In fact,
last night one of the Bills was flung after
me as I went out-someone flung a Bill at me
and that was the first I knew about it.
That is a most unsatisfactory way of carrying on the business of a Parliament, and it
is especially indefensible since nearly all
the Members of the Government are business men. I hope the reason we have so much
industrial depression and that our
mercial condition is in such an unfortunately
tragic and pathetic position to-day is not
that the business men are controlling their
businesses by the same methods as
they are now conducting their Parlia
mentary affairs. I put it to the Prime
Minister that when a Bill passes its Second
Reading we ought to get at least a week before it is put down for the Committee Stage,
in order that we should understand the
character of the proposed legislation and also
the best methods by which we can amend
that legislation if it is possible to do so.
com.
The PRIME MINISTER: I am afraid I
will be just as much out of order as the hon.
Member (Mr. Devlin), but it may shorten

Bills to which the hon. Member referred. If
I take them as they are on the Order Paper
he will follow me. The Unemployment Insurance Bill is a Bill with which everybody has
been thoroughly familiar for some time past.
As he knows, it is merely confirming the
Agreement entered into and to which it
would be impossible to allow any Amendment whatever. We must carry out the
Agreement or throw it over, and, of course,
it is in the interests of the working classes,
and all classes, in Ulster that this Bill
should go through. The other one is the
Housing Bill, which is merely a continuing
Bill and which has proved so useful to the
community here. The same remark applies
to the Loans Guarantee Bill, which is a Bill
merely continuing the present practice which
has helped our industries so much.
It is the practice of the Government to give
as long a period as possible between the
Second Reading and the Committee Stage,
but hon. Members will realise that there are
certain Measures which must be got through
before 31st March, otherwise the benefits that
are conferred on the people here would not
fall into the present financial year, which
ends on 31st March. Therefore, if we do ask
hon. Members to sit a little longer these
days in order to get the business through it

Loans Guarantee Bill.
Order for Second Reading read.
Motion made, and Question proposed:
“That the Bill be now read a Second time."
Mr. POLLOCK: This Bill, of which I propose to move the Second Reading, is really
in effect a continuation Bill also. It has
been so often moved by me in this House
that those who have been Members for some
time are perfectly familiar with the subject,
but, in view of the fact that we have some
new Members who have recently taken their
seats. I think that courtesy demands perhaps,
that I should give a little more extended examination of the proposals of the Bill.
I had thought that perhaps it might
expedite matters and suit the convenience
of the House if I read a few lines of the
statement which I made when the original
Measure, or principal Act as it is called, was
before this House. On that occasion I fully
explained not only the aims and objects of
the Measure, but also the method of procedure. Let me state again that
It is a Measure intended to authorise the
Government to guarantee loans to public
bodies, to corporations, and to other persons, provided that there is sufficient
security behind the borrowers to warrant
the Government in undertaking the liability of guaranteeing the lenders against
any possible loss.
་
There is a clear difference, it must be remembered, between lending money and
guaranteeing the payment of money, and the
Bill, of which I am now moving the Second
Reading, is intended simply to guarantee
and not to lend. In regard to the procedure
under the Measure, it may be as well to repeat that a small advisory Committee has
been established of three persons of financial
experience, intelligence and independence,
whose duty it is to determine on the evidence
which is submitted to them whether the conditions or circumstances of the applicants
conform to the intentions of the Act.
The two primary considerations involved
are, first, that the security offered is sufficient to warrant the Government in undertaking the liability, and, second, that the
amount of employment provided under the
scheme is commensurate with the Government guarantee.
This Committee, of which I have spoken,
will have the assistance of technical persons,
such as accountants and professional men of
knowledge and experience, to advise them
on the matter, while, of course, the veto of
the Ministry of Finance is always retained.
One of the very important objects in cou
nection with the Government guarantee is to
enable those who propose to expend money
on capital enterprises to secure that money
at a lower rate of interest than would be
possible under their own personal securities.
Of course the main concern of our Government in prosecuting the Measures under this
Bill is that unemployment may be relieved,
and that labour may be provided for numbers
of those who otherwise would not be engaged
in work, and I am sure I may state that any
sacrifice which the Government and Parliament may undertake in regard to this is
fully justified. A leaflet has been circulated,
I believe, giving the particulars of those
guarantees into which the Government has
entered, and it will be found that we have
utilised the Measure to the extent of
slightly over four million pounds. Assuming
that the British Government have given
guarantees to something like the same extent,
and that the owners themselves have provided considerable capital in connection with
these undertakings, it is not an unfair assumption that there has been provided
through the machinery of this Act work of
the value of ten million pounds. It is also
not unfair to assume that if these guarantees
had not been provided a great part, if not
the whole of the work that I have just Dow
mentioned, would not have been undertaken,
and therefore the conditions. of unemployment would have been much more acute than
they are to-day. From that point of view
alone, I am sure hon. Members on both sides
of the House will admit that the Act which
we passed as early as 1922 has been fully
justified in its operation.
The Act of last year gave Parliamentary
authority to the Government to issue
guarantees to the extent of six millions, and
one of the objects of the present Bill is to
increase that amount by one million. That
is to say, that the Government in the aggregate should be empowered to give guarantees
to those persons who are desirous of borrow.
ing money under the circumstances that I
have outlined up to a maximum of seven
million pounds. That will leave a margin of
three million pounds to be operated upon in
case of necessity. I think I am justified in
asking the House to take the precaution of
adding this additional million to the surplus
which I have indicated, because there are
some signs, not perhaps very definite or
very manifest, of an improvement in trade,
and we have ourselves tentative indications
of shipowners in Great Britain undertaking
a programme in regard to the provision of
additional tonnage. For that reason therefore, I think it is necessary to provide that
three million pounds should be at the disposal of the Government for the purpose of
giving guarantees up to that amount, if
necessary.
The second clause in the Bill, which I may
touch upon very lightly, introduces another

This will, therefore, let the House understand that the limit imposed upon the
Government, or the Ministry of Finance, in
regard to these guarantees is that any gap
which may be filled shall not exceed one-tenth

that such a contingency may not arise, but
as the amounts have now become very considerable it is in my judgment, and in the
judgment of the Government, better to provide for such a contingency, if it should come
to pass, and as the limitation is very rigid

who were formerly employed by Messrs.
Dinsmore. If they will not do that let them
start a company or resuscitate the company
that was there, and get the factory started
for the production of woollen goods. I think
the Government will have to widen very
considerably this question of loans guarantees. They will have to make it more easy
for companies to borrow money, and get the
cheap credit which the right hon. Gentleman
(Mr. Pollock) has said is on a par with
London. He thinks it is as good as London,
and we would like to agree with him on that
score. The figures of unemployment are
growing so heavily--they were 37,000 two
years ago, and are 61,000 to-day-that unless
the Government can back more companies
or start such themselves one cannot help
but view with alarm this growing volume
of unemployment.
We do say that it is desirable that the
State should in times of peril like this step
in with these facilities for cheaper credit.
It was to make that point with regard to
the woollen mills outside Ballymena that I
rose. Further, I feel very strongly that as
we are giving guarantees to shipowners we
should have some say as to the conditions

The PARLIAMENTARY SECRETARY
OF THE MINISTRY OF LABOUR (Mr.
Gordon): It is difficult with any degree of
accuracy to estimate the real expenditure
by a Department, more especially a Department such as the Ministry of Labour. This
Supplementary Estimate is a result of the
prolonged and unprecedented unemployment,
and also of the social legislation that has
been brought in during the past twelve
months. I think it only right that I should
explain as briefly as possible to the Committee the necessity for introducing this
Supplementary Estimate. If hon. Members
will look at A (Salaries, Wages and Allowances) on page 8 of the Estimates they will
observe that there is £18,000 down for the
purpose of the employment of additional
temporary clerks. When we introduced the
Widows', Orphans', and Old Age Contributory Pensions Act we had to take on some
temporary officers, and at the same time we
had to employ a certain proportion of the
headquarters' staff for the purpose of carrying out the preliminary work in connection
with that Act. Those two things represent
a sum of £18,000.
D1 (Printing), £1,300, also reflects the
heavy unemployment obtaining. There has
also been some very heavy printing in connection with the introduction of the new
Contributory Pensions Scheme. In order
that reduced rates might be obtained it was
necessary to secure as large quantities of
stocks as possible, but a corresponding reduction in the Vote for 1926-27 will be
effected. As to postage, telegrams and telephones (£1,500), this is largely the result of
work in connection with the Widows',
Orphans', and Old Age Contributory Pensions Act. It will be remembered that some
of my hon. Friends on the Opposition side
suggested that the Ministry of Labour should
endeavour to make it as easy 88 possible for widows claiming widows' and
orphans' pensions by obtaining certificates of birth and marriage, and other
matters connected with the claim.
As a
result of the Ministry of Labour undertaking this responsibility we estimate for
£165. You will see that on page 9 £1,200 is
required as payment to officers in respect
of cost of administration of unemployment
insurance.
Some of the trade unions have been unable
to pay the unemployment benefit out of
their own funds for some considerable period,
and as a result could not enter into a contract with the Ministry of Labour whereby
they would use the funds of the Ministry
for the purpose of paying unemployment
benefit to their members through their trade
unions. These are known as association
claims. Consequently, some of these societies
are in a better position to-day than they
were formerly, and have made an arrangement
with us whereby they are paying unemployment benefit to their members through their
trade unions and not directly through the
local employment exchanges. This means
extra cost on the Department, and we are
asking the Committee to vote £1,200.
Then there is the sum of £1,000 for the
manufacture of health, pensions, and unemployment insurance stamps and other
matters. There is also the audit of approved
societies and insurance committees. I might
let the Committee know that the National
Health Insurance Audit Department charged
this Ministry to 31st March, 1925, on the basis
of 289,000 insured persons, of which 90,000
were members of international societies
whose accounts were audited in Great Britain.
The Audit Department since then has discovered that these provisional figures should
have been 344,000 and 120,000 respectively.
This Supplementary Estimate is therefore on
account of the increased cost of the Audit
Department, which is an agency service
carrying out work in connection with our
Health Insurance Department.

en-
Mr. KYLE: As we have ended our work a
little early I want to draw the attention of
the House to a question I had on the Paper
asking the Minister of Home Affairs (Sir
Dawson Bates) if he is prepared to issue a
synopsis of the report that was given by
District-Inspector Allen in regard to the
Whan versus Walker case. I have
deavoured on two or three occasions to get
this report from the right hon. Gentleman.
To-day I have asked for a synopsis of the
report as I believe that if this report was
either acted upon by the Home Office or
made known to the people who are interested
in the case of this Mrs. Whan it would be
sufficient to prove that this woman is innocent, and that she has been the victim of
circumstances unparalleled in this city or in
the Six Counties.
The case goes back to the year 1922 when
this woman was arrested on the charge of
sending poisoned chocolates to a Mr. Walker,
who resides in the Braniel, Castlereagh.
That case was disposed of, and immediately
following that this woman was again
arrested along with her son on a charge of
assaulting Mrs. Walker, despite the fact that
her son had never seen Mrs. Walker in his
life before. Following on that this woman
was again arrested and charged with assaulting Mrs. Walker in High Street, Belfast.
and, despite the fact that there was no independent witness to give evidence, she was
again brought to book for this alleged
offence.
It seems to me that there is a conspiracy
against this woman, and it is in the interests
of justice that we ask for the publication
of this District-Inspector's Report. This
District-Inspector was in the Imperial Secret
Service for a long period-about twenty
years I understand-and he was put on by
the responsible authorities to investigate
this case.
In the course of his investigations a pocket book, which was supposed
to have dropped from the pocket of a son or
son-in-law of Mrs. Whan was discovered. He
investigated the source from which that
pocket book came, and we understand that
that source is marked in the report which
we are asking should be published.
Out of that pocket book there were two
letters taken. One of these letters was supposed to have come from Mrs. Whan's sonin-law, a young man named James Ferguson
Courtney. It purported to have been delivered through the usual post channels and
bore evidence of having passed through the
General Post Office at Belfast. But, as it
transpired afterwards, it was never posted
in the usual course of posting, nor was it
ever delivered by a postman or anyone else
to Mr. James Ferguson Courtney, nor to anyone at his address or elsewhere. The second
one purported to be a reply from the same
gentleman to Mrs. Whan. It was duly
stamped and ready for posting but not
closed.
Sir DAWSON BATES: Might I ask my
hon. Friend what he is reading from?
Mr. KYLE: I am reading from the affidavit of Mrs. Whan. If there is any other
information the right hon. Gentleman wants
I will be pleased to give it to him. If he is
going to issue this report and so clear his
Department from the charge which I am
trying to level at them now, of deliberately
withholding this report to cover up their own
incapacity, to cover up a scandal connected
with the administration of his Department,
if I can assist him in any way I will do so
with pleasure. This District-Inspector Allen
