Sir DAWSON BATES: The whole question
is whether or not the police report, made
as a result of the investigation of an alleged
crime, is to be published. In my opinion
nothing would be more disastrous to the
proper administration of the law than that
a police report, which has been sent in to
the authorities, should be published. Now
in this case the facts appear to be, shortly,
as follow:-
:-
In April, 1922, Mrs. Whan was charged, as
a result of a private prosecution, with sending
chocolates to Mr. Walker. Informations
were refused. In the following month a
further private prosecution was brought by
Mr. Walker, alleging an assault. As a result of the investigation of the Court on
that occasion Mrs. Whan received sentence
of two months' imprisonment.
On August 23 following proceedings were
again taken-by the public prosecutoragainst Mrs. Whan for sending threatening
letters. That case was returned to the
Assizes after due investigation by the
Attorney-General, and the case came before
the late Lord Chief Justice and a jury, and,
as a result, Mrs. Whan received sentence of
six months' imprisonment. Further charges
were subsequently made in 1923 in regard
to further threatening letters, and, as a
result, District-Inspector Allen was authorised to make a report in regard to that
case and the other cases that had gone before.
It was
That report was duly received.
submitted to the former Attorney-General,
and, having investigated the whole facts of
the case, the Attorney-General decided that
there was no case to bring criminal proceedings against either Mrs. Whan or against
Walker. That was in 1923.
At the end of two years Mrs. Whan
appears to have arrived at the conclusion
that she had been badly treated in respect
of the matters on which she had been found
guilty by a competent Court and jury.
Accordingly she brought an action against
Mrs. Walker, claiming damages for false
imprisonment. The case came before the
Court, and on an application on the part
of the defendant that the case should be
remitted to the county court judge the Court
went into the whole case and granted the
application, and the case was remitted to
the county court judge. That was in 1925. I
understand that since that time Mrs. Whan
has abandoned her case.
These are the facts, which I have gone into
very fully. I think nothing would be more

HOUSE OF COMMONS.

Tuesday, 23rd March, 1926.
The House met at Three of the Clock, Mr.

Oral Answers to Questions.
COST OF LIVING IN NORTHERN
IRELAND.
1. Mr. KYLE (for Mr. Beattie) asked the
Minister of Labour whether in view of the
statement made by him that he does not
consider the cost of living higher in Northern Ireland than in England, and as this is
in direct conflict with the prevailing opinion
in Northern Ireland, he would be prepared
to set up
a committee to consider the
question of the cost of living in Northern
Ireland.
The MINISTER OF LABOUR (Mr.
Andrews): A committee under the chairmanship of my hon. and learned Friend,
the Parliamentary Secretary of the Ministry
of Education (Mr. Robb) investigated this
whole question, and, after exhaustive
evidence had been taken, reported in
September, 1923, that they had no reason to
think that there was any large difference
between the cost of living in Northern
Ireland as compared with that in Great
Britain.
Since this report was presented my
Department has kept in close touch with
the course of prices in this area, and, while
there are variations in the prices of particular commodities- some being cheaper
and some dearer-all the evidence points to
the fact that the cost of living is not
greater here than in Great Britain. I am
of opinion, therefore, that no useful purpose
would be served in incurring the expense of
setting up another committee to consider the
question.
Mr. KYLE: In view of the fact that
bread, milk, and coal-three very essential
things to working-class life are all dearer
here than they are in England, would the
Minister not see his way to reconsider that
statement, especially in view of what has
taken place since that inquiry, and that
these prices are higher to-day than they
were then?
Mr. ANDREWS: I have really nothing
to add to what I have already stated.
SALE OF IMPORTED BUTTER.
2. Mr. McBRIDE asked the Minister of
Agriculture whether he is aware that
foreign butter is sold in shops wrapped with
Irish creamery labels, and will he make
inquiry if such is the case.
The MINISTER OF AGRICULTURE
(Mr. Archdale): For some time past very
close attention has been given by the
Ministry to the question of the descriptions
applied to butter sold in Northern Ireland.
In consultation with the Ministry, the
Ulster Agricultural Organisation Society
convened a committee representative of the
Ulster creameries (some of whom during the
scarce season import butter to supplement
their own manufacture and thus keep up
their trade connection with their regular
customers). The recommendations of that
committee in which the Ministry concurred
were to the effect that in order to secure
uniform observance of the terms of the
Merchandise Marks Acts, creameries should
arrange to show on wrappers containing
imported butter the following description-
"Finest Imported Creamery Butter,
Empire Produce;"
or
"Finest Imported Creamery Butter,
Foreign Produce."
Following the issue of a circular to the
creameries intimating that the Ministry
would be satisfied with an arrangement of
this kind, public notice was given by the
Ministry through the medium of the Press
to all persons dealing in imported butter
of their legal obligations in the matter of
descriptions under the Merchandise Marks
Acts, and advising merchants and retailers
to safeguard themselves by having wrappers
containing imported butter conspicuously
marked on the lines set out in the intimation to the creameries.
The Ministry is satisfied that the action
taken has been productive of good results,
and inquiries are at present being pursued
on behalf of the Ministry in connection with
complaints as to non-observance. The Ministry
will not hesitate to take legal action in any
case where the facts warrant such a course,
especially as every section of the butter
trade must now be aware that, under the
Merchandise Marks Act, 1887, the application of a false trade description to goods
renders the
person concerned liable to
prosecution.

more for the benefit of the people. I beg to

The MINISTER OF HOME AFFAIRS (Sir
Dawson Bates): The Government cannot
accept the Amendment which has been moved
by my hon. Friend (Mr. Devlin.) May I say
that I take exception to his figures when he
says that we are 10,000 houses short. I think
he exaggerates the situation. Apart altogether from that, I think it is far more satisfactory that this Bill should be only
continued for another year, when the whole
situation can be reviewed in the light of the
facts as we will know them then. One has
to have regard to further considerations such
as technical considerations and finance, and
in the circumstances I can see no object in
continuing the Bill beyond 1927 unless the
situation should necessitate such a step.

Now, I would like just to put a few of the
facts concerning the country before the House.
This Bill is framed for the purpose of relieving the housing shortage. That housing
shortage is very acute in rural areas, especially as to the sort of houses that could be or
would be occupied by the agricultural
labourer. I believe that this Bill has as it
stands, or as it has stood up to now, to a
certain extent-perhaps indirectly-helped
the housing shortage, and I believe that
gradually it might relieve the housing shortage in the country still further. But, unfortunately, the tendency at the present
moment is to erect houses averaging perhaps
roughly 700 feet and upwards. Well, now, it
is quite obvious that houses of that size, even
in the country where perhaps it is
possible to erect them at slightly less cost
than in towns could not be built at a cost
which would make it possible for the agricultural labourer to inhabit them. It is
quite impossible for the builders to erect
them at a cost which would make it possible
for rents to be charged which the average
rural worker could pay. At the present
moment in my district the utmost that any

week, and I believe that that is the rent
which is being paid for the ex-Servicemen's
cottages, and I know that they are finding it

of 18 6d to 28. Now, it is quite obvious
that it would be impossible to build
houses of these larger sizes which could

Why do some of us feel so intensely upon

by these labourers' cottages without venturing to look into them, to watch those who
inhabit them, and to try to understand what
is the effect of these improved housing conditions in rural Ireland. I find it
mirrored in the faces of the people

the subject very feelingly indeed. They said
thev thought it would be a good thing to
build a certain number of these houses.
They are not going to substitute these houses
for the larger houses. They will be built
pari passu. The richer people among the
working classes can take the larger houses;
the married people with four, five, six or
seven children can go for the larger houses.
But do let us consider those who are poorer
and who have no children, and who cannot
afford anything but an odd room here and
there, and that with great difficulty, at the
present time. I would like to see all the
inhabitants of the Six Counties properly
housed. My right hon. Friend (Sir Dawson
Bates) has got certain latitude in the matter,
and he is able to say, "Yes, I think that for
a certain part of the town, or for a certain
part of the country, the superficial area can
be reduced," and thus permit a few of these
houses to be erected. That is all it means.
We are not going to thrust these houses on
the local authorities; they will be able to
judge whether they will provide such houses
or not. The local authorities are not going
to make married people with families live
in these houses. There is no compulsion the
whole way through. Supposing after
year's time it was found that people were
not taking these houses, naturally no builders
would build them. If they found such houses
an uneconomic proposition they would stop
building them and would build a larger type
of house. In the meantime, what the Government are most anxious to do is to meet the
requirements of the working people, whether
they are very poor or moderately rich.

Mr. KYLE: I was desirous of inserting an
Amendment to Clause 2 of this Bill. I would

.1
"that the Government shall have the

receiving a loan."
The Amendment goes on to define what
the duties would be of the director who
would be appointed by the Government. 1
hold that if companies are to receive Government credits the Government itself should
be directly interested in the management of
that concern. They should have a director
on the board of directors, and his principal
duty, I take it, in addition to seeing that
the affairs of the company were carried out
properly, would be to see that the conditions
of the employees were on a fair and reasonable basis. That was the purport of the
Amendment I wanted to see inserted in this
Bill. I think it is only a fair and reasonable thing. It has been exemplified in the
South African Government, which has
adopted this principle in a Measure that was
before their House quite recently. They
have adopted the principle that when they
are lending money to a mining company in
South Africa there shall be a director appointed by the Government on the board
of
directors of that mining company. The
duties of that director are not defined as I
have defined them; nevertheless, the Government have accepted the principle.
This principle has, I think, been debated,
not only in Great Britain and South Africa,
but in many countries. Where Government
money is being used in the interests of
private companies there should be a representative on the board of directors. I want
to see our Government adopting and accepting that principle. I hold it is invaluable.
Although we are providing credits for private
companies we have got no say as to how
those credits are going to be used. It seems
to me that it is getting back to the old
principle of no taxation without representation.

we give credit to a company for £1,000,000

HOUSE OF COMMONS
[Mr. Pollock]
Measure. But I think it would be convenient
if even at the risk of taking up the time of
the House for a few minutes, that I should
enter at some greater detail into the circumstances which led up to the Measure which
I am now presenting to the House.
Those who carry their minds back to the
period when the Government of Ireland Bill
was under consideration and became
an Act of Parliament will recall that provision was made for the establishment of a
body which was described as the Council of
Ireland. The function of that body, as described in the Measure, was to administer the
services common to both areas, that is,
Northern and Southern Ireland. It was contemplated of course at that time that
Southern Ireland would conform to
the terms of that Measure, as
have done here in the North, and
if that had happened the establishment
of the Council of Ireland would, no doubt,
have been of very considerable service. But
as Southern Ireland refused to accept the
terms of that Measure, it became necessary
for the Imperial Government to substitute
some administration that would take the
place of the Council of Ireland so far as
Northern Ireland was concerned.
we
The services to which the Council of Ireland
had to direct its attention, presuming it had
come into existence, were diseases of animals,
fisheries, and railways. The Imperial
Government then took over So far as
Northern Ireland was concerned the
functions which it was intended the Council
of Ireland should carry out, and appointed
an Imperial officer in Belfast, with a staff, to
administer the services to which I have referred. We had the advantage here of the
presence of a gentleman of long experience
in administrative work, of great military record, and altogether a most efficient servant.
(Hon. Members: Hear, hear.) And I should
like to express not only as a personal matter,
but on behalf of the Government our great
appreciation of the attitude of Mr. Tallents
towards all the matters with which he was
brought into contact. Not only did he do his
duty as an Imperial servant, watching
Imperial interests, but he entered sympathetically into any matters concerned with
our difficulties here in Northern Ireland with
a sympathy which I am bound to recognise.
Following the operation to which I have
referred, and which was to have have had
existence for five years, the Boundary question intervened. When a settlement of that
matter was reached there was embodied
therein an arrangement by which the powers
of the Imperial Parliament in respect of
the old Council of Ireland services should
be transferred to us here. The wording of
that part of the Agreement which followed
upon that arrangement was a provision as
follows:-
The Governments of the Irish Free State
and of Northern Ireland shall meet together
as and when necessary for the purpose of
considering matters of common interest
arising out of or connected with the exercise and administration of such powers.
I have no doubt that this provision will be
of considerable value both to Northern Ireland and to Southern Ireland, assuming that
Southern Ireland approaches the different
subjects in the same spirit as we desire to
do on our own part. Up to the present, of
course, there has been no definite gesture
made from one side or the other in respect
of these matters.
In the meantime it is necessary that we
ourselves here in this Parliament should by
the Measure which I am now introducing
take or give the necessary powers to administer the services that formerly came
under the control of the Imperial Government--the services known as the Council of
Ireland services. It probably would have
been possible that His Majesty's Privy Council by Order in Council could have transferred these services without the necessity
for legislation in this Parliament. But in
view of the fact that we have been legislating
in local matters for some years, the feeling
was that we were in a position to deal with
these things more satisfactorily than by
Order in Council or by adaptation of the
law. It was thought right that the Measure
I am now submitting should be presented to
this Parliament, and that is being done with
the full accord of the British Government,
so that there is no difference of opinion
in respect of the procedure as regards that.
But some of the provisions of the Bill
go further than mere adaptation. These are
necessary in order that the financial provisions of the existing Acts may be brought
into line with the changes of law that have
already been made in this House. I am referring at the present moment to the method
of financing services under the Government
Loans Fund which was passed here some
time ago. Provision was made for the supply
of money to the different objects which come
within the ambit of that Act, and power is
therefore taken in the present Bill to enable
loans, for example, for fishery purposes to
be made from that fund instead of from the
Endowment Fund of the Department of
Agriculture or from voted money as the
case may be.
Similarly the whole section of the Bill
headed Contagious Diseases of Animals presents in a clear and easily understood forni
the financial provisions of the various
Diseases of Animals Acts. Briefly, it may
be stated that these diseases fall into two
categories, and these categories correspond to
two separate accounts within the Cattle
Diseases Fund. One class of disease is that
317 Administrative Provisions Bill- 23 MARCH 1926

Second Reading.
relating to cattle, pleuro-pneumonia, foot and
mouth disease and swine fever. Generally
speaking the responsibility for paying compensation in respect of destruction of cattle
suffering from these diseases is regarded as
a State liability. On the other hand, all
other cattle diseases are regarded as matters
of local interest, and all the expenses are met
by means of a special rate struck by the local
authorities for the purpose of meeting these
liabilities.
There is, however, one disease which recent
legislation regards as inore in the nature of
a State liability, that is to say, cattle tuberculosis, and in regard to this provision is
made by which the entire cost of compensation for cattle slaughter in such instances
is met from State funds or moneys voted
by this Parliament. I feel that hon.
Members will agree that liability under this
head should be a State charge. It has in
fact been so since last year, as a result of an
Act passed in the British House of Commons
which extended to Northern Ireland.
The only other matter in the Bill to which
I think I should call attention is the allocation of these services in respect of fisheries
and railways. It is intended that our
Ministry of Commerce should have control of
these matters. In one case of the question
relating to diseases of animals, that will
naturally revert to our Ministry of Agriculture, therefore these two Ministries will
assume responsibility in respect of matters
with which the Council of Ireland would in
the alternative have been concerned.
There
is only one other matter now before I move
and that is the question concerned in Sections
7 and 8 of the Bill, that is where licences
for rod fishing are made available without
any extra payments between Southern Ireland and Northern Ireland, in other words
to make a reciprocal arrangement whereby
licences for rod fishing given in one of the
areas will be made available in the other
area.
The latter provision is necessary by reason
of the fact that within the last few months
some of the inland fishing districts which
operate on both sides of the border have been
re-arranged by agreement between the Irish
Free State and the British Government, in
order that each Board of Conservators may
be completely within the jurisdiction of one
Government. Full effect has not yet been
given to this change, and the clause in the
Bill provides for necessary facilities for
completing such arrangements.
This is the general purport of the Measure
which I am now moving, and as hon.
Members will, I am sure, realise that it is
entirely uncontroversial and that it is necessary it should pass this House before the
first of the month, the date on which the
transfer is made, I hope the House will give
it a Second Reading if possible without any
undue delay.

Members: Hear, hear). One had only to

if ever, foot and mouth disease comes to our
part of the country-we are all glad to see
it is not and has not been-if this fell
disease comes amongst our cattle here the
disaster would not be so great as it will be
if ever it does come without any provision
being made by the farmers themselves paying an insurance premium in regard to
their cattle.
In regard to the fisheries which the right
hon. Gentleman has referred to, an arrange.
ment has been entered into between the
Irish Free State and the Imperial Government, whose responsibility in this matter
we now take over. I would like further to
suggest that I cannot see very much necessity for the latter paragraph in Clause 8 of
the Bill, which says:
Provided that the holder of a licence in
respect of which a reduced licence duty is
charged shall not be entitled in respect
of such licence to vote at any meeting held
for the election of conservators.
I think that might very well be eliminated
from the Bill unless there is some very
cogent reason for its being inserted. As the
right hon. Gentleman himself has said,
there is nothing controversial in regard to
this Measure. I think it is enlarging the
scope and power and functions of the
Northern Government, a thing we on these
benches always have desired. I think we all
welcome this Bill with open arms, and we
hope that it is the precursor of a still
further enlargement of powers of our Parlia
ment, and that some day we may hope to be
able to manage our own affairs in entirety.

MINISTRY OF HOME AFFAIRS.
Motion made, and Question proposed:
That a supplementary sum not exceeding
Two Thousand Two Hundred and Eightynine Pounds be granted to His Majesty for
the service of the year ending the 31st March,
nineteen hundred and twenty-six, to defray

Sir DAWSON BATES: In moving this
Supplementary Estimate I may point out
that the items are largely self-explanatory.
One item-£2,130-is the amount of unforseen
expenditure in connection with the Housing
Inquiry. I hope the Commissioner will be in
a position to report within the next few days.
Another item is in connection with the Local
Government Commission that is going into
the whole question of public health. Owing
to the complexity of the various matters it
has been found impossible for the Commission to report so far, but I hope also we
will be in possession of their report ere long.
From the £379 a sum of £350 is a re-vote in
connection with sending a special commission
to the Continent to investigate and report
upon certain methods of treating tuberculosis. That is all that is necessary to be
said in connection with this matter, and I
beg to move.
Mr. KYLE: I see the right hon. Gentleman
the Minister of Home Affairs, has mentioned
the sum of £2,130, being, I suppose, the
Government's share of the expenses of the
Housing Inquiry which sat for a considerable
period in the City Hall. I found out the
number of sittings which this Inquiry held.
There was a preliminary sitting on 15th
September, and there were subsequent meetings which began on 5th October and
ended on 18th January. There was a
total of 35 sittings, that is, if you take the
preliminary sitting as one, so that the cost.
to the Parliament of Northern Ireland is £60
per sitting. We have not yet been favoured
with the report of the Housing Commissioner,
so, I suppose, we cannot very well go into
that particular question, but I was afraid we
might not have an opportunity at any other
stage of going into this Housing Inquiry
report, so far as we are responsible for it.
It is because I feared we might not at a later
stage get an opportunity of discussing the
proceedings of the Inquiry, which we partly
pay for, that I have taken this opportunity
to-day.
I think everybody will agree that the
Housing Inquiry was necessary, and, therefore, there is no question of our quarrelling
with the Government over the establishment
of the Commission, but we do think that the
cost to the Government and Parliament of
Northern Ireland is excessive, in that we
should pay to one or two people who were
responsible no less a sum than £60 for each
sitting. This sum of £2,130, which we are
asked to vote this afternoon, I expect, will
only be about one-third or one-quarter of
the total expenses of this inquiry. It goes
to show how expensive it is to have
tremely capable Commissioners appointed.
Nevertheless, it seems to me to be an exorbitant sum of money to be demanded for
their services without knowing to what
detail they had to go or the amount of their
work. All we do know is that the sittings
covered a period of four months, and that
we vote the sum of £2,130 for those services.

If it had been bricklayers who asked for

I could imagine, though I could not describe,

As I said a moment or so ago, the Housing
Inquiry was necessary, because I think, reading the reports that appeared in the Press,
it has been clearly demonstrated that so far
as private enterprise is concerned in regard
to the building of houses they have delibe
rately and with malice aforethought robbed
the community. There is one firm in particular who, according to the evidence submitted at the Housing Inquiry, deliberately
robbed the public, robbed the citizens of
Belfast. I say that deliberately. And that
is in the name of private enterprise. That
is all being used by some strange twist of
people's minds into an argument against
direct labour for housing, because the Corporation of Belfast and the Housing Committee of the Belfast Corporation are
composed of business men. There is only
one Labour representative out of fifteen on
that Housing Committee. All these business
men, who are out to serve the interests of
the community, forsooth, could not stop
private companies from robbing the Belfast
Corporation, and thereby robbing the people,
both by supplying rotten material in regard
to timber and in regard to slates. In all
these regards this Inquiry, to my mind, has
been an indictment of private enterprise and
an indictment of the morality of private
enterprise.
Where it has been possible, through the
slack administration of the Belfast Corporation to rob the public of an extra £100,
these business men never thought twice
about doing it, and it is, I think, nothing
short of a scandal that the people who are
responsible for this deliberate defrauding
should be able to hold up their heads in the
City of Belfast to-day. I do want to say
that this sum of £2,130, representing £60
a sitting, is, in my opinion, too much for

That a supplementary sum not exceeding
Five Thousand Pounds be granted to His
Majesty for the service cf the year ending

The PARLIAMENTARY SECRETARY
OF THE MINISTRY OF LABOUR (Mr.
Gordon): I would like to make perfectly
plain to the Committee the reasons for introducing this Votc. The amount of sickness
was greater than was anticipated and
budgeted for in the original Estimates, and
consequently the increased unemployment
meant that great numbers who were not entitled to benefit were retained in insurance
under the Prolongation of Insurance Act,
1921, as extended by the Expiring Laws Continuance Act. As a result of the prolonged
unemployment, the physical standard of
these people was considerably lowered, and
undoubtedly many of them have been thrown
upon the funds of the Health Insurance
Societies. May I explain what the amount
is required for? As Members of this Committee are aware, the State gives a statutory
grant of two-ninths of sickness, disablement,
maternity benefit and administrative expenses, and it has been found that the sickness exceeded our former Estimate, and
consequently we are called upon by the
Approved Societies to make good our statutory grant of two-ninths of all benefits.
Accordingly I beg to move.
Mr. KYLE: In regard to this question, one
would have liked to have heard the Parliamentary Secretary tell us why there should
be this discrepancy in the budgeting on the
former occasion. He says it is in consequence of the increased number of sick
people. Might it not be that it is in consequence of the great volume of unemploy.
ment, and of the action of his Ministry in
denying unemployment benefit to a considerable number of people. The female members
of the population are very often ill, as has
been pointed out by the hon. Gentleman
(Mr. Gordon). They are in such a state of
health that nearly any doctor will certify
them as being unfit to carry on their work.
The result is that when the hon. Gentleman's Department puts these people off unemployment benefit they immediately go to
the doctor and get a line which entitles them
to draw National Health Insurance. I think
if the hon. Gentleman had stated that, he
would have pointed out a grave sore in regard to the general health of the people of
Belfast. I do not know so much about the
country districts in this respect, but I do
know that a very considerable number of the
textile workers in Belfast do not enjoy anything like robust health. It is in consequence, I take it, of that fact that the hon.
Gentleman is asking for this additional sum
of £5,000.
Mr. WILLIAM MCMULLEN: I am rather
surprised that a Supplementary Estimate of
this kind should come before the Committee.

position as to whether unemployment is decreasing or whether the numbers are reduced

Health Insurance. I hope the moral will not
be lost on the right hon. Gentleman, the
Minister of Labour. After all, if he does not

National Health Insurance. I suggest that
it would be better to relax the regulations,

Five Thousand Five Hundred Pounds be

Mr. POLLOCK: The majority of hon.
Members of this Committee are familiar
with the procedure in respect of the Vote
which I am about to present. It was my
custom, in the earlier days of the Parliament, to enter into this matter with some
considerable detail, but as time proceeded,
and as the White Paper which is issued conveys
full information in regard to the different
items of the Vote, I curtailed my remarks
last year, and the year before, to a simple
explanation of the salient features of the
Vote. It is, of course, intended to provide
for the continuity of the services until hon.
Members have had an opportunity of entering into and criticising as much as they
think just, the different Estimates, when they

will be submitted. Towards that end, therefore, this White Paper has been issued,
showing that we require £2,005,500 for presumably three months' expenditure upon the
different services of the Province.
I think, perhaps, it would be convenient if
I bring out some of the prominent features,
by taking the classes of the Estimates categorically. Class I, which deals with the
Houses of Parliament, Cabinet Offices, and so
on, shows an increase of £657. This is a
comparatively small increase and arises because of the addition of Senators' expenses,
and also a reduction in the returns from
Private Bills which we expect will accrue.
It does not require any further comment, I
think, than this explanation of the small
increase.
When I come to Class II, the Ministry of
Finance, of course, I am on larger ground.
I think I should explain that the small increase in the Ministry of Finance itselfthat is, in the Department of £6,000 odd,
results from the decision to take a census in
the coming year. We estimate that the expenses of the census will be anything from
£5,000 to £7,000. Public Works and Buildings show an increase of £25,000 or thereabouts, but that has not very much interest
to us as a Parliament, because that money
is repaid by the Imperial authorities. Old
Age Pensions show an increase of about
£150,000, and hon. Members will realise the
cause for that increase. It is due, not only
to the removal of the thrift disqualification,
but also to the estimate made of the additional cost arising from the Widows,'
Orphans' and Old Age Contributory Pensions
Act, which was recently passed in this House.
I come now to the Ministry of Home
Affairs, in which there is a very happy decrease in all departments. The Royal Irish
Constabulary, it will be noticed, is down
some £35,000.
Mr. KYLE: Ulster:
Mr. POLLOCK: The Royal Ulster Constabulary, thank you. I was so long accustomed
to the old form that it is hard to get away
from it. There is £35,000 of a decrease in
the Royal Ulster Constabulary. In the
Special Constabulary there is a very dramatic decrease from £1,220,000 to £164,000.
Hon. Members will realise without any difficulty the explanation of that very large decrease, namely, the disbandment of the Special
Constabulary and the winding up of all

The other items do not call for any comment.
Prisons are down £16,000, which I am sure

I come now to Class V. The Educational
Services show a reduction of over £100,000,
and this is largely the result of the reduction
in teachers' salaries which took place in

time in respect of Diseases of Animals
administration. The Committee will under
stand that although this is a charge brought
into our Estimate it is simply a transfer from

Authorities and deducted from our residuary
share, that is to say, instead of the Imperial
Authorities paying it we ourselves deal with
the matter direct. There is also an
additional sum of about £20,000 provided in

Class VII (Ministry of Commerce)
shows a reduction on the Estimates in the

presumably, apply to the coming year, and

Ministry of Commerce estimate is reduced by

The net result of the two parallel columns
is that there is a reduction in the expenditure
of £667,732. I think, considering the
circumstances with which we have been
faced in the past, these estimates are not
at all discreditable to those who have control of the administration of the various Departments. I am sure I express the hope of

to be reckoned with this time next year we
shall be able to emerge from it with decreased expenditure arising from the

but the procedure usually followed is, that
when the Estimate proper is introduced in

The MINISTER OF COMMERCE (Mr.
Barbour): The object of the first of these
financial resolutions is to enable the Ministry
of Commerce with the approval of the
Ministry of Finance to place on the annual
Estimates any sums necessary for the pur.
pose of assisting any light railways, either
by means of a capital sum or by an annual
payment. Similar provision is contained in
the Light Railways (Ireland) Act, but it is
necessary to re-enact this, being a financial
provision in the present Bill. So far as can
be foreseen the section will never operate in
connection with any new undertaking, but it
is necessary to make provision to continue
the grants which were agreed by the
Imperial Treasury at the inception of the
Clogher Valley Light Railway. The annual
provision to be made is in respect of a sum
not exceeding 2 per cent. of the dividends
guaranteed by the local authority on the
capital locally subscribed at the time that
that railway was laid down.
The second financial resolution which I beg
to move will enable the Ministry of Commerce to make grants from voted money for
the purpose of assisting fisheries. This power
was previously inherent in the Department
335 Administrative Provisions (Money), HOUSE OF COMMONS Administrative Provisions Bill. 336
[Mr. Barbour]
of Agriculture and Technical Instruction,
and generally speaking the grants were confined to grants in aid of the fund of boards
of conservators of inland fisheries. These
grants were to assist them in the protection
of such fisheries which are a valuable asset
to Northern Ireland, not only from the point
of view of its export trade, but also by reason
of the attraction that well stocked fisheries
prove to the more sporting class of visitors
to this area.
.
of
The third resolution which I beg to move
relates to payment out of voted money in
respect of cattle slaughtered in the case of
the existence or suspected existence
tuberculosis. Until last year the compensation paid for cattle slaughtered by
local authorities on these grounds was as
respects one half borne directly on the rates
and as respects the other half payment was
made from the general account of the Cattle
Diseases Fund. This fund is built up from
a cattle diseases rate struck by county and
borough councils, the proceeds of which were
paid over to this State fund. In the year
1925, however, the Imperial Government considered that this was placing an undue
burden on local authorities. more particularly in view of the national interest involved in the suppression of tuberculosis,
which as hon. Members are aware, is at
times occasioned by germs being carried from
the cow. Accordingly an Act was passed
which extended both to Great Britain and
Northern Ireland by.
Which
the local
authority was relieved from any direct liability, one-fourth was charged to the central
fund and the remaining three-fourths was
provided from moneys voted by Parliament.
The present resolution proposes to continue
this system, which I am sure will have the
support of all hon. Members.

The fourth and last of the financial resolutions which I beg to move deals with the
State grant on accounts of compensation to
be paid by reason of the slaughter of animals
suffering from certain diseases. In moving
the preceding resolution I touched on the
finance of the general account of the Cattle
Diseases Fund, which in the main is provided
from a rate struck by the local authorities
themselves. There is, however, a special
account of the fund for which the State
accepts almost total liability. This account
provides for the payment of compensation in
the case of cattle slaughtered by the State
on account of pleuro-pneumonia, foot and
mouth disease or swine fever. The suppres-.
sion of these diseases is regarded as a matter
of such national concern that the entire responsibility is undertaken by the State. This
resolution proposes that there shall be voted
annually to finance this special account a
sum of money not exceeding £8,000 in any
one year. This maximum is Northern Ireland's proportion of the maximum in the
Diseases of Animals Act, 1894, for all Ireland
of £20,000. I need hardly say that the
amount voted each year within this maximum is usually based on the experience of
former years. If any outbreak of these
diseases on a large scale took place in Northern Ireland it would, of course, be necessary
to seek the sanction of the House to provide
a sum in excess of the statutory maximum
proposed to be fixed by this resolution. I
beg to move.
Question put, and agreed to.

Pharmacy (Temporary Provisions)
Bill (S.)
Order for Second Reading read.
Motion made, and Question proposed:
"That the Bill be now read a Second time."
The MINISTER OF HOME AFFAIRS (Sir
Dawson Bates): The Bill before the House is
intended to amend the Act which was passed
last year in two small but at the same time
important details. The last section of the
Act makes provision for the fixing of an
appointed day to bring into operation those
parts of the Act which deal with examinations and the issue of annual licences. These
licences, according to certain provisions of
the Act, had to be issued on or before the 1st
of January. In consequence, it was necessary
to fix the appointed day before that date so
that there might be legal authority for
collecting licence fees.
When this appointed day was fixed, all the
Act came at once into operation, including,
of course, the sections which deal with the
holding of examinations. This empowered
our Pharmaceutical Society to set up their
own examinations, but it also debarred them
from recognising those of the Southern
Society.
I had hoped that the first meeting of the
Council of the new Society could have been
held during the summer, shortly after the
passing of the Act, but owing to difficulties
which a new Society such as this had to face.
that was found quite impossible. The result
was that since the appointed day there have
been no means by which students could take
the examination and qualify for membership of the Society, and the Bill now provides for the recognition of the examinations
of the Southern Society up to 30th September
of the present year. I think to do anything
else would impose a hardship during the
interregnum between the formation of our new
Society and the setting up of the examinations under the Society. Of course, hon.
Members realise that that only lasts to 30th
September of the present year.
Another connection in which we propose to
amend the present Act is under Section 19,
sub-Section 2 of the Act, which provides for
the executors of a deceased chemist who was
registered under the Act carrying on the
business, subject to the usual control and
having a proper manager, but unfortunately
no provision was made in the case of a
business being carried on by the executors of
or
a chemist who died prior to the passing of
the Act, and therefore would not be a
registered chemist. We propose to rectify this
by providing for the business of a
chemist or druggist who dies before
within nine months of the passing of
this Act being carried on, provided
they have a qualified manager. Hon. Members will appreciate that it would be very
hard in certain cases if the executors through
a technical fault could not carry on the
business on behalf of the relatives of a deceased chemist. Those are really the only
two points in the Bill. I beg to move.
Mr. WILLIAM MCMULLEN: The way in
which measures relating to the Pharmacy
Bill have been dealt with by the right hon.
Gentleman would seem to me to be fairly
extraordinary. In May last year a Bill was
introduced which he described then as a
piece of perfect legislation. We have become used to the right hon. Gentleman and
his Parliamentary Secretary refusing to
alter even a comma in any Bill introduced
in this House. During the passage of this
Measure through the House the right hon.
Gentleman moved Amendments which occupy
about twenty columns of Hansard, and now
before the ink is properly dry on the Act
passed in May last we are asked to pass
further Amendments. I am of the opinion that
even if this amended legislation is passed
this afternoon it will be necessary before
very long to come to the House again and
ask for further legislation. I do not recollect
that the right hon. Gentleman and others
who spoke from the Government benches
made any attempt to tell us exactly how
pharmaceutical chemists in Northern Ireland were placed under this new arrangement. I understand they are placed in a
very disadvantageous position, and that there
are no reciprocal arrangements between the
Pharmaceutical Societies in Great Britain
and the Free State with that in Northern
Ireland, so that the activities and the operations of pharmaceutical chemists who
qualify in Northern Ireland are very much
circumscribed.
It is not possible, I understand, for a pharmaceutical chemist who qualifies in Northern
Ireland to obtain employment in the Free
State. I understand a similar state of affairs
exists in Great Britain, so far as anyone who
qualifies in Northern Ireland is concerned.
I am told on exceptionally reliable authority
those are the circumstances, and if that is
so it is not a satisfactory arrangement at all.
The Government should have taken this
aspect of the matter into consideration before now. I do not think it could be argued
that a person who qualifies in Northern Ireland is not as satisfactory a pharmaceutical
chemist as anyone who qualifies either in
the Irish Free State or in Great Britain,
Pharmacy Bill--
Second Reading.
24 MARCH 1926
because the examination is exceptionally difficult, at least it is as difficult as that in any
other part of the world I have any information from. The right hon. Gentleman when
speaking to some of the Amendments in May
last stated:
This will ensure that in future those who
wish to sell poisons by retail or dispense
prescriptions will have to undergo a
lengthy practical training and pass the
severe examination required for the certificate of pharmaceutical chemist.
The point is this, if that statement is correct
how is it a person who qualifies as a pharmaceutical chemist in Northern Ireland when
he goes to Great Britain before his membership is recognised has to serve 4,000 hours?
Sir DAWSON BATES: We hope he will
be.
Mr. W. McMULLEN: Your hopes are one
thing, but the actual facts are another.
That person at the moment is expected to
serve 4,000 hours, or two years, before he is
allowed to qualify and serve as a pharmaceutical chemist in Great Britain. Why that
should operate against a person who qualifies
in Northern Ireland is somewhat difficult to
understand as I am told a person who comes
from New Zealand will be allowed to practise
as a pharmaceutical chemist in Great Britain
on payment of a fee of fifteen guineas. It
seems a remarkable thing that a person who
qualifies in Northern Ireland should be discriminated against. Those are the points I
would like the right hon. Gentleman to take
into consideration, because it leaves a person
who qualifies in Northern Ireland in an unsatisfactory position. It means that under
the present arrangement if he becomes unemployed he has no possibilities or opportunities of obtaining employment either in
the Free State or in Great Britain, and that
is not a very satisfactory state of affairs for
a person who has passed a very stiff examination in Northern Ireland.
I think we have got the right to request
that before legislation of this kind is introduced in Northern Ireland some regard
should be had to these matters. The right
hon. Gentleman assured us on the last occasion that as a result of consultations with
members of the Pharmaceutical Chemists'
body he succeeded in having perfect legislation, and now he comes and asks us to
amend that legislation. I suggest he should
go and have consultations with those people
again and give them amended legislation
along the lines I have suggested. If he does
so, as far a the occupants of these benches
are concerned, we will facilitate him.
The PARLIAMENTARY SECRETARY OF
THE MINISTRY OF HOME AFFAIRS (Mr.
Hanna): I do not know if the hon. Gentleman (Mr. William McMullen) is complaining
that the Government have taken steps to set
up a Council here to secure that only people
who are properly qualified to deal in pharmaceutical matters should be allowed to do so,
or if he is complaining of the length of
service we expect or the amount of skill they
must have. It is the intention of the Government in conjunction with representatives of
the Society that those people who served
their apprenticeships here and passed their
examinations should, be able to take their
place in any part of the world as skilled
pharmacists. It would be impossible for this
House, as the hon. Gentleman must know, to
pass a law that England and the Free State
should recognise our chemists immediately
they have passed their examination.
This amending Measure has been brought
in not without consultation with the members of the Northern Pharmacy Council,
but at their express request, and in strict
conjunction with them. They are anxious
for it. I understand an old arrangement
existed between the Pharmaceutical Society
in Ireland with the similar Society in
England that chemists in the one country
were recognised in the other, and we are not
without hopes that having secured that only
fit and proper person are admitted with
the passing of this amending Bill reciprocal
arrangements will again be made between
the Councils so that the chemists of the one
country will be recognised in the other.

as the hon. Gentleman (Mr. William

are introduced, the ill-digested information
on which they are based, the bad draughtsmanship due to the ill-considered methods
of the Ministers, put this House to tremendous inconvenience and trouble in considering these matters. There would be a cry of

Municipal Corporations Bill.
Order for Second Reading read.
Motion made, and Question proposed:
"That the Bill be now read a Second time."
Sir DAWSON BATES: The object of this
Bill is to amend the law relating to the
granting of charters of incorporation as
boroughs to urban districts so as to bring
it into line with existing conditions. At the
present time, if the inhabitants of one of
the large urban districts' desire that their
urban district should be constituted into a
borough with all the rights and privileges
attaching to that status, the procedure is
somewhat complicated and indefinite., Prior
to the transfer of the services under, the
Government of Ireland Act, 1920, a petition
for incorporation had to be presented to
His Majesty, in whom was vested the authority to grant a charter, acting, of course,
on the advice of the Privy Council. It is
understood that the functions of His Majesty
in this respect have become delegated to the
Governor of Northern Ireland, but it appears
that there is some doubt as to whether the
Governor should act on the advice of the
Privy Council of Northern Ireland or the
Privy Council of Great Britain.
We propose under this Bill to regularise
the situation and to establish the position
of the Northern Ireland Privy Council as
the body on whose advice the Governor will
act, following any petition which his Grace
may receive from any urban authority asking
for a charter of incorporation. Under this
Bill we propose to amend Section 14 of the
Municipal Corporations (Ireland) Act, 1840,
by repealing that section and substituting
section enabling his Grace the
Governor, acting on the advice of the Privy
a new
Municipal Corporations Bill-
Second Reading.
24 MARCH 1926
Council of Northern Ireland, to grant a
charter of incorporation to the inhabitants
of any urban district with a population of
not less than 10,000 inhabitants. We also
propose to preserve the rights which still

put down on a piece of paper, to get 2,500

expressly forbidden to do, I think it would be
a step in the right direction. One can see,
one saw recently-

25 MARCH 1926
HOUSE OF COMMONS.

Thursday, 25th March, 1926.
The House met at Three of the Clock, Mr.
SPEAKER in the Chair.
Oral Answers to Questions.
EX-SERGT. P. DONOHOE'S GRATUITY.
1. Mr. KYLE asked the Minister of Home
Affairs if he would expedite the payment of
a gratuity to Mr. P. Donohoe, Ex-Sergeant,
R.U. (S.)C., who was rendered unfit for
further service by an injury received while
on duty on the 30th May, 1925.
The MINISTER OF HOME AFFAIRS
(Sir Dawson Bates): The delay which has
taken place in the settlement of this case
has arisen from the fact that my Department was not aware until quite recently
that Mr. Donohoe was in receipt of a
pension as an ex-member of the Royal Irish
Constabulary. Under the Special Constabulary Pensions Amending Order, 1924, the
amount of such pension or gratuity may be
taken into consideration in the assessment
of any pension, allowance, or gratuity payable to Mr. Donohoe in respect of his
service in the Special Constabulary, and the
extent to which this factor will be taken
into account, is at present receiving my
sympathetic consideration.
I hope that the matter will be settled
within the next few days, and I regret the
delay which has unavoidably arisen.
Mr. W. MCMULLEN: I would like to
ask the right hon. Gentleman whether it is
legal to disburse outdoor relief by way of
money in Northern Ireland.
Sir DAWSON BATES: I do not quite
follow.
Mr. W. McMULLEN: Is it legal to give
outdoor relief in money instead of goods?
Sir DAWSON BATES: I am not aware
of anything against it. I think what has
taken place is perfectly legal.
Mr. BEATTIE: I think a clearer explanation is necessary. I would like to know
from the Minister is it the practice in
Northern Ireland in the case of the majo
rity of Guardians to give outdoor relief in
money instead of in kind.
Sir DAWSON BATES: The hon. Member
is a Guardian himself, and is familiar with
the practice. It sometimes happens that
relief is given in money. It is usually
given in kind.
Mr. KYLE: I can give the right hon.
Gentleman an example in connection with
what has taken place at Antrim Poor-Law
Guardians where a person, who is receiving
outdoor relief, has to go to the shop of a
member of the County Council.
Sir DAWSON BATES: Unless the member of the County Council is also a member
of the Board of Guardians I am not aware
that he is doing anything illegal. I think
it is unusual but not illegal.
OUTDOOR RELIEF IN ANTRIM.
2. Mr. KYLE asked the Minister of Home
Affairs whether he is aware that the Antrim
Poor-Law Guardians in giving outdoor
relief insist that applicants for relief are
compelled to make their purchases at a
shop which is owned by a member of the
County Council.
Sir DAWSON BATES: So far as the
Ministry of Home Affairs is aware, poor
relief as dispensed by Antrim Board of
Guardians is generally paid in money, but
sometimes in kind.
No stipulation of any kind is made or
could be made by the Guardians as to where
the recipients shall spend the money or obtain the goods.
as
It may be added for the hon. Member's
information that a County Councillor,
such, has no connection with a Board of
Guardians, unless he should also happen to
have been elected as a Guardian.
LABOURERS' COTTAGES IN BALLYMENA
RURAL DISTRICT.
3. Mr. KYLE asked the Minister of Home
Affairs whether any application has been
made by the Ballymena Rural District
Council to his Department for the erection
of labourers' cottages in that area; whether
any of these houses have been erected, and
whether it is
a fact that no choice is
given to the applicants as to the suitability
of the sites.
Sir DAWSON BATES: The Ballymena
Rural District Council have formulated a
scheme under the Labourers Acts, providing
for the erection of 175 cottages, and a local
Inquiry in connection with the scheme is
being held on the 15th proximo.
None of the houses have yet been erected,
and cannot be started until the Ministry's
confirming Order has been issued as a result
of the Inquiry.
It is not a fact that no choice is given
to the applicants as to the suitability of the
sites. The rural district councils in Northern

[Sir Dawson Bates]
Ireland generally endeavour to meet the

INSPECTION OF MEAT.
4. Mr. KYLE asked the Minister of Home
Affairs whether he is aware that in the
Urban District of Ballymena provision has
been made for the inspection of all meat
intended to be sold within the urban area
for human consumption, and for prohibiting
the sale of meat except after inspection,
while in the adjoining rural district no such
provision exists, and if he will consider the
advisability of introducing a Bill to confer
legislative powers on rural district councils
similar to those already conferred on the
urban district councils, so as to bring about
a state of uniformity in both town and
country in the matter of ensuring for the
public a sound and wholesome meat supply.
Sir DAWSON BATES: Suitable arrangements exist already under which rural district councils can be invested with powers
enabling them to exercise control over
slaughter houses and meat supply generally
in their districts.
These powers have not been generally
availed of by rural district councils, and the
whole question of ensuring uniformity of
inspection in connection with food and milk
supplies is at present, I understand, engaging
the attention of the Local Government Commission.
Pending the receipt and consideration of
that Report, I am not at present in a position
to give any undertaking in regard to the
introduction of new legislation on the subject.
Mr. KYLE: May I ask the right hon.
Gentleman whether he would expedite the
work in that connection in view of the recent
outbreak of disease in the country areas in
particular? It is thought that this, perhaps,
has something to do with it. Would he
expedite the Local Government Inquiry, and
would he see that the rural districts put
these by-laws into force?
Sir DAWSON BATES: I can assure my
hon. Friend that the Local Government Commission, which is presided over by the hon.
Member of the University, is fully alive to
this matter.
WORKING OF RENT RESTRICTION ACT,
1925.
5. Mr. KYLE asked the Minister of Home
Affairs whether he is aware that certain
grave hardships have arisen as the result of
the Rent and Mortgage Interest Restriction
Act, 1925, and whether he will ascertain the
conditions under which the occupants of
certain houses are being forced to leave their
houses despite the fact that they have paid
their rent in full for the past number of
years, and cannot find any alternative accommodation.
Sir DAWSON BATES: I presume that the
hon. Member refers to the limited number of
case where one-house owners, who became
landlords from the 1st May, 1923, have recovered their houses under Section 4 of the
Act of 1925. This question was fully debated
in Parliament, which, in passing the Bill,
decided that greater hardship would be imposed by depriving the one house owner of
the right to obtain their houses for their own
occupation.
Mr. KYLE: Would the right hon. Gentleman consent to the appointment of a small
committee to determine in these cases
whether greater hardship is being done to the
tenant of the house than to the owner of
the house.
Sir DAWSON BATES: No, sir.
CASE OF
EX-SERGEANT JOHN MelLDOON.
6. Mr. KYLE asked the Minister of Home
Affairs whether he will state the reasons why
John McIldoon, an ex-sergeant on the Special
Constabulary, has been refused the same
treatment as the members of the Specials of
the "A" Force, and whether he is now prepared to grant this man his just dues and
remove the slur cast on his character and
conduct.
Sir DAWSON BATES: With regard to the
first part of the hon. Member's question, 'it
may be pointed out that the member of the
Force named, although enrolled as a member
of the "A" Class Special Constabulary, was
employed as an instructor for the "B" Class
Special Constabulary. These instructors are
attached entirely to the "B" Class and no
question of their disbandment has as yet
been raised.
With regard to the latter part of the question I may add that the member of the Force
concerned was given one month's notice of
the termination of his contract in December
last on the ground that he was not up to the
standard of efficiency. As I have already
said, no question of disbandment arose in
this case, whoh was dealt with in the
ordinary course.

10. Mr. KYLE asked the Minister of

his officials as a rendezvous for the entertainment of their friends, and what action
he proposes to take to end this practice.
The MINISTER OF LABOUR (Mr.
Andrews): I have made inquiries into the
matter and the facts do not support the
suggestion contained in the hon. Member's
question. On the contrary, the live register
has unfortunately risen at Newcastle recently due to certain pay-offs at the Silent
Valley and elsewhere, and I am informed
that the staff has been voluntarily working
overtime recently in the office and this has
no doubt given rise to the report which
the hon. Member has received.
Mr. KYLE: Is the right hon. Gentleman
aware that certain residents in Newcastle
Mr. ANDREWS: As far as I know there
is no justification for the complaints which

PAYING OFF OF SHIPS' CREWS.
11. Mr. W. MCMULLEN asked the Minister
of Labour whether he is aware that
ships making Belfast their final port of
discharge do not pay off their crews in
Belfast, but proceed to British ports, and
whether, having regard to the numbers of
unemployed seamen in Belfast who require
to travel to Great Britain in search of employment, he will take steps to have such
ships paid off in Belfast.
Mr. ANDREWS: I understand that, for
reasons of accuracy, it is the practice for
Shipping Companies to pay off the crew of a
vessel at the port where she will remain
longest-tied up, discharging, loading or repairing, as the case may be and I have no
authority to interfere with this practice.
I believe, however, that Northern Ireland
owned ships whose final port of discharge
is Belfast generally pay off their crews at
this port.
Mr. W. McMULLEN: Is the right hon.
Gentleman aware that the number of ships
owned and registered in Northern Ireland
is very limited, and would he be prepared
to make representations to the Board of
Trade in this connection?
Mr. ANDREWS: I have already answered
the hon. Member's question quite fully.
I have no power to interfere in connection
with the matter.
SUGAR BEET AND ELECTRICITY
REPORTS.
12. Mr. DEVLIN asked the Minister of
Commerce when the reports on Sugar Beet
and Electricity will be issued by the Commission on the Natural and Industrial Resources of Northern Ireland.
The MINISTER OF COMMERCE (Mr.
Barbour): I understand that the Commission has now settled the drafts of its
Reports on both subjects, and that final
copies are being prepared for signature
and presentation. The question of their
publication will be considered by the Cabinet
immediately they are received.

Mr. DEVLIN: In the discussion that took
place on the Address, some of us on these
Benches ventured to raise a number of
matters which we deemed to be of sufficient
public importance to bring before the
Government. I was somewhat surprised that
we really got no reply from the Government
Benches to many of the questions which
we raised on that occasion. Therefore, this
is the opportunity which presents itself for
Members like myself to, in some cases, repeat the statements we made, and in others
to bring before the House other aspects of
the question dealt with by us at the time.
Now, in the first place, I desire to register
my protest against the seeming neglect of
the Government in regard to the problem
of unemployment. It is quite true that the
right hon. Gentleman, the Minister of Labour
(Mr. Andrews) has repeatedly told us about
the work he was doing for the unemployed,
and the methods by which he was dealing
with unemployment grants, and we have
always said, at least I have, that in that
matter he has displayed considerable sympathy, though I do not admit, nor am I
prepared to admit now, that he is free, or
that his Department is free from that
criticism which I propose to apply to the
administration of the unemployment grants.
One of the claims that have been made
repeatedly in this House, and outside this
House, by the Prime Minister, is that the
treatment of unemployed in Northern Ireland is carried out precisely on the same
lines and in the same spirit of justice and
generosity as that which exists in Great
Britain. I desire to say that that is not so.
(Hon. Members: Hear, hear.) When we consider what we regard as a very satisfactory bargain that the Government has
arrived at with the Imperial Government
in relation to the finances of unemployment
we are entitled, speaking here for the poorest
and lowliest of the population, to make a
claim for treatment at least equal to the
treatment meted out to the unemployed in
Great Britain.
It may be perfectly true that the amount
of the unemployment allowance given by the
Government is similar to that which is paid
to the unemployed in Great Britain, but
there has always been an attempt made here.
not so much by a policy of rhetorical obscurantism but rather by a complete and absolute
silence on the part of the Government to
keep this aspect of the situation entirely
away from the public, and that is that the
unemployed in Great Britain have their unemployment grant considerably augmented
by contributions from Boards of Guardians.
In the financial adjustments I therefore say
that Northern Ireland does not pay the same
amount to the unemployed as they do in
Great Britain, and that the ratepayers in
Northern Ireland have not to bear similar
burdens.
What is the reason why unemployment has
been so deeply and profoundly felt in
Northern Ireland? It is because an in-

Govan,
I will give you a case in point.
which is a comparatively small community,
at least small compared with Belfast, depends
entirely on shipbuilding, and their case is
very much like the case of Belfast as far as
the sufferings which come to them from unemployment in connection with the depression in the shipbuilding industry are concerned. I have figures here showing that the
Govan Parish Council, which is a body
equivalent in powers and administration and
authority to the Belfast Board of Guardians,
paid out in 1925 £237,295 more in outdoor
relief than it did in 1921. 1 am not talking
about Poplar; I am talking about Govan.
The Belfast Guardians in 1925 only paid out
in outdoor relief £14,178, or about £7,000
more than in 1922.
I think the Minister of Finance would be
able to adjust for himself these figures and
to see what a tremendous contribution a
community like the community in Govan
must have paid in order to enable the poor
to bear the burden imposed on them by
unemployment in the shipbuilding industry.
If that generosity, if we choose to put it
that way, has been shown where only one
industry has been struck, then how much
more limited or how much more penurious
has been the spirit shown towards the unemployed here, where you have the linen industry struck as well? When we contemplate
the number of women who have been out of
employment in consequence of depression in
the linen industry you can easily see that
the burden which Govan has borne has been
a tremendously larger burden than that
borne in the City of Belfast.
I want to come to the question of the
Ministry of Labour. The Ministry of Labour
in stopping extended benefit to so many men
and women have acted, in my judgment, in
an indefensible way. You say to these people
they must get a spell of work and stamp
their cards a certain number of weeks before
they get benefit. The Minister knows from
his own official statistics that it is impossible
for these people to get a spell of work. I
should like to ask him how many people have
been deprived of benefit on the ground that
they were not looking for work, because, as
the right hon. Gentleman knows, and as he
has often complained to me, I have showered
his Department with communications which
I have received from persons who have been
denied unemployment benefit, and the ground
on which the unemployment benefit has been
refused to them is that they were not looking
for work. Who decides that they are not
looking for work? What is the test that is
applied? I know myself that this test could
not have been effectively applied in many cases
that have come to my own personal knowledge. I have one case in my mind of one
of the decentest and most respectable men in
Belfast, who has haunted my own door-he
is only one of many but I take an interest
in them all-and who had trudged for months
in the search for work and could not get it.
Only the other day through the kindness of
an hon. Member of this House I got him
employment, and that man is moved by
almost inexpressible gratitude to the person
who secured him employment. That was one
of the men who was turned down because he
was not looking for employment. I say that
there must be some clearer explanation
given by the right hon. Gentleman (Mr.
Andrews) in regard to the methods and the
tests that are applied when these people are
refused benefit, and of the grounds upon
which they are refused, before we can regard
the present system of administration as
satisfactory.
I come now to another question which I
raised here on the Address, and to which I
draw the attention of the Prime Minister,
because this is a matter about which I feel
most profoundly and one to which I think
he will give most sympathetic consideration.
That is the question of the position of the
boys and girls leaving our primary schools.
The question is: What is to become of the
adolescent population who are coming out
into the world after they have completed
such education as they have got? I understand that 12,000 boys and girls leave our
primary schools every year in Northern
Ireland, 6,000 in Belfast and 6,000 in the remainder of the Six Counties. I live quite
close to the Technical Institute here and
some evenings I watch the pupils going into
and coming out of that Institute. I watch
their ingress and egress with pride, because I am very happy to see so many of
our young men and women taking advantage of that magnificent institution.
But has it ever struck Ministers or those
who are responsible for the strength and
stability of the State and its future
what is to become, first of all, of the boys
and girls when they leave school, and,
secondly, of those more efficiently equipped
youths when they come from our great
Technical Institute? I have got no answer
to that. I think it is more than an
economic or industrial question. It is a
State question, it is a human question to

The worst of this Government is that
they have the mentality of the old politicians. They are thinking in the past.
They think that if you say a word against
the present Government you shake and destroy the glory of the Empire. That is the
attitude they take up, with the result that
every suggestion that comes from these
Benches is turned down. If it comes from
me, according to the Attorney-General (Mr.

an enemy of Ulster. I understand that is
how he stigmatised me in St. Jude's Church
the other night. I hope he will so stigmatise me here in the Presbyterian General
Assembly, because the stigmatisation is the
more sacrosanct the more sacred the institution in which it is delivered. If it comes
from me it comes from an enemy of Ulster.
If it comes from any of the hon. Gentlemen

I think the Government ought to approach

merits how far they ought to receive the
the consideration of the Government.
Let me go further. I have in this regard, and in many other regards, to protest
against the mentality of the Government in
relation to all other parties but their own
in this House. For all practical purposes
you might as well write your decrees in
Stormont Castle, call them Bills, bring
them down here, and get them sanctioned,
if not approved, so far as our opinion in
legislation or administration is concerned.
I do not believe since we came into this
House you have ever accepted a single suggestion we made. I do not believe you have
ever accepted an Amendment we proposed.
We may be very ignorant and no doubt we
bear the brand of our cult-but at the
same time it is quite possible that even the
most ignorant may make a suggestion
worthy of consideration, but we have never
made any. I must point out to the right
hon. Gentleman (Sir James Craig) that
when he invites us into this House and
makes what he calls, and what others call,
a generous gesture, I would like to know
what we are invited into this House for.
You could just get on the same way without us for all the influence we have been
able to exercise since we came in. I could
understand that attitude if you were dealing with politics or with matters of
sectarian concern, but not on questions of
industry, on questions of humanity, on
questions like shipbuilding, questions like
the linen industry, or housing. On
questions like unemployment and the treatment of those who are unemployed we are
far more competent to form a judgment and
to give advice than anyone on the Government Benches, because we live amongst the
people and the people are constantly coming to us. The Government in my judgment suffer from one defect. They are too
much detached from the people, and do not
know what the people are thinking or what
they are doing. Therefore, I trust that in
what I have said I have been able to give
you some free information which will be much
more useful to you than the legal advice
given by many of the somnolent guides and
officials whom you have.
I come now to the question of housing.
That is another matter on which we have
been treated with absolute contempt. We
have raised in this House, and out of it,
the vital importance of building houses for
the class of the community who want houses,
that is the working class: The Prime
Minister the other day, when dealing with
this matter, said-I must confess it was a
very innocent observation for him to make-
"Oh these two-roomed houses" because I
still prefer to call them two-roomed houses
-"are only occupied by a man and his wife
without children; those who have children
can get larger houses." The right hon.
Gentleman (Sir James Craig) with his knowledge of Belfast must be well aware that
the people who go to these two-roomed
houses are the people who are worst paid,
that the men with large families are very
often the worst paid. If there is only a
man and his wife they are
very often
better able to pay for a costly house than
the poor man who is badly paid with a
large family. In this regard I am glad to

Two rooms! Why not give a larger grant

of the notices in the windows and of the

Dr. MORRISON: I should like to say a
word or two in reply to what has fallen from
the hon. Member for West Belfast (Mr.
Devlin). To begin, I may say I listened to
him with great interest, and with a number

I am sure that is so, and I know he has
done very valuable work in this respect, with
a great deal of which I agree, but I, too,
in my small way have been doing a little
with the same object in view, and I am sure

But in this matter of unemployment insurance I believe there is room for a considerable difference of opinion. I congratulated
the hon. Member in the lobby this morning.
When coming to the House to-day I travelled
with some people from County Antrim and
we had a very interesting conversation as

hon. Member. I said 1. thought it was

a
people who differed from thein; and 1 Hoped

He tells you what he has done for pensions

ment insurance out of the rates.
The chief objection to the hon. Member's
proposition is this: Why should unemploy
ment insurance be treated differently from
other subjects for which provision is made
by the Imperial Parliament and by general
agreement amongst all politicians? Why, for
instance, should unemployment insurance be
treated differently from workmen's accident
compensation? Why should it be treated
differently from national health insurance?
Government legislation in the Imperial
House affecting this House has definitely
decided and clearly defined the lines on which
certain things should be done for the working man, and why should unemployment
insurance be shifted into another range or
another area from national health insurance?
If you start this system of supplementing
unemployment benefit from the rates here
you will add a burden which will be crushing on all ratepayers, and many of the
working class themselves pay rates.
It is a well-known fact that the whole
matter of granting outdoor relief resides with
the decision of the Board of Guardians itself.
If you have a Labour Board of Guardians
naturally they will view the claims of Labour
in a different aspect than a. Board of
Guardians composed of capitalists or farmers.

turned down because of a complaint that

thought it unfair that he should be struck off
the dole. There was one thing in his story
that he did not venture to tell me about,
and it was that last year he was for six
months on the dole. He was a tailor, and he
said he had been turned down through an
anonymous complaint. I said that that was
a very unreasonable thing, and that I would
go to the Ministry about it. I went to the
Ministry and I found out the whole story.
They had all the files before them. The case
had been looked into very particularly, and
the decision of the Ministry with all this
evidence before them was that the man was
instructed to go before the Employment Committee and tell his story. The Ministry said,
"Here you have a Committee appointed to
deal with these things. It takes it out of the
hands of the Ministry, and if the Committee
say such a man is entitled to unemployment
benefit they will not over-rule the decision
of the Committee." The man went to the
Committee. I do not know what evidence
they had, but I know it was composed of men
of all sections, and they decided the man was
not entitled to the dole and that he had made
no genuine effort to obtain work.
I was
talking over this matter with a business man,
and he said to me, "That man is not,
perhaps, so deserving as you think, because I
have a number of tailors, and I have not
enough work to go round them all, but I
have work that will be paid at a lower rate.
Remember, there is no absence of work.
There is work for what are called ready-made
clothes that would be paid at a lower rate,
but I understand their trade union will not
allow them to do that work, and the consequence is I have to send my work to London
and get my ready-mades made by cheaper
labour there, because in the towns in rural
Ulster-and in Belfast for anything I know
"the men are not allowed to work at that
lower rate." So far as I am concerned, I
would not have very much sympathy for any
man who refused to accept a reduction
the standard wages of 5s. or 7s. 6d. a week in
times of commercial depression. That is the
position I take up with regard to that matter.
