With regard to this question of two-roomed
houses, of which I have heard so much, I am
entirely in agreement with the views put
forward by the Prime Minister when this
subject was under discussion in the House.
I have been engaged all my lifetime working
for the poor, and doing what I could for
them. I think nobody has done more as a
dispensary doctor than I did for the district
over which I was medical officer. I got the
forms and had them filled up, I condemned
the houses in which they were living, and
I had new houses built. We have double the
number of houses in that dispensary district
than are to be found in any other dispensary
district in the Coleraine Union. I speak
therefore, with authority on this matter,
with more authority, perhaps, than that
of the hon. Member for West Belfast (Mr.
Devlin). He spoke of the great improvement
in the social position of the workers who
Occupy these houses. I agree with him,
wholly agree with him. He spoke of the
bright houses, and the healthy, cheerful
children. Again I agree with him. I could
have told him how we, in our own district,
got up an association and offered prizes for
the way in which these cottages were kept.
We had rambler roses climbing up the sides
of the houses, as a result of the prizes offered
to encourage the workers to beautify their
houses and set an example to the others. It
is beyond all question that that has done
an immense amount of good. If you house a
man well, you alter his whole social position.
If we had in the country what you call here
two-roomed houses-houses with good kitchens
and two bedrooms-many of the labourers
who are compelled to live in the old cottages
would be glad and delighted. They would be
thankful to God that they had places where
they could sit under their own vine and
under their own fig tree, none daring to make
them afraid. They would not be under the
farmer; they would be sitting there free of
the farmer. They could sell their labour in
the best market, as many of them do, and
they could hold up their heads in the same
way as the farmers are now able to hold
up their heads when they meet the landlords.
I take advantage of this occasion to appeal
to the Minister of Home Affairs to see that
every facility will be given in the country
for the erection of these houses, and I could
easily understand that in Belfast it would
be an immense advantage to people to have
such cheap houses rather than to go on
living in some of the slums in which they
are compelled to reside. I had no intention
of speaking to-day, but these are, subjects
that affect me very deeply, and in which I
am deeply interested. My viewpoint is
different from that of some of the Members
opposite, and I hope I am right. At any
rate, I can easily understand that people
may differ from me, and that both of us may
have the same object in view.

What happens when a claim is submitted?
The hon. Member for the University (Dr.
Morrison) said a few moments ago that

asure him as well as other hon. Members

Claims are being submitted to the Local
Employment Committees. The Committee
hear the case. So that hon. Members may

which decides these cases is composed of an
employer, a worker and a clerk. The employer and worker, at least, decide the cases,
and the clerk registers the decision of the.
Committee. The employer and worker after
having heard the applicant before them go

Mr. LEEKE: I was intending to point out

In regard to fisheries, in the past it has

This in the past was largely availed of,

of Government in Ireland was changed the

business.

harbours. I come from County Derry, which

with by the Government, and, as I have

The hon. Member for the University (Dr.
Morrison), in expressing his views of the
conversation which he had with people in
the train about Armoy, said that the hon.
Member for West Belfast (Mr. Devlin) was
rather inclined to put taxation on the
farmers. I think of all the people who have

strongly than hon. Members from these
Benches. We have always held that the
charges that have been put upon the farmers are far too heavy, and that every encouragement should be given to keep down
local taxation instead of allowing it to
increase. If the farmers have to pay high
rates and taxes it naturally follows that
they cannot very well employ large numbers
of hands. It is only by keeping expenses
down and by the Government assisting them
with grants that they are able to carry on
their industry, and at the same time employ
and give the agricultural labourer the
standard of subsistence to which he is
entitled, or give him those facilities which
are essential to his life and comfort and
which make him an effective workman.
If the Government could see their way to
carry out my idea in regard to the fisheries
I would suggest that they should appoint a
small Committee to go into the matter of
the whole fishing industry in Northern Ireland, and to accept suggestions from people
who are interested in it regarding the manner in which it should be governed and developed in the future. I respectfully submit
to the House that this should be promptly
and effectively dealt with, as I hold it would
be one of the first ways in which unemployment could be reduced in the Northern area.
I know that there are fishermen at present
anxiously awaiting some move by the
Government by which they will be able to
purchase new boats and new gear in order
to engage in this attractive industry which
lies off our coasts, and which is at present
exploited by English and Scottish trawling
companies.
Again, some of the most important salmon
rivers in the country are flowing through
the Northern area, and some Commission
should be set up to go into that and see how
they could be utilised to the fullest advantage and make this, which will be one of
the most important industries, so useful that
it will relieve both inland and deep sea
fishing. The inland fisheries of Ulster have
not been developed to the extent that they
should, and lesser still have the deep sea
fisheries. There are, as I say, hundreds of
miles of fisheries lying without a harbour or
refuge of any kind by which a fishing boat
or trawler can run alongside and discharge
a catch so as to reach the British market
in time to be sold in that fresh condition
which would attract customers. I hope the
Government will take note of all these points
and that they will take steps to have this
industry developed to its utmost limits and
so assist the fishermen in a prolific and fruitful field for absorbing unemployment. I
respectfully submit that to the House.

Mr. WILLIAM MCMULLEN: I am quoting for a six-county Ulster, not a ninecounty Ulster at all.
Mr. LAVERY: In 1840?
Mr. WILLIAM MCMULLEN: In 1841. In
that year the population of Ulster was
1,648,945, and if anyone takes the trouble to
find out the population of Belfast or any
of our industrial or working centres, you
will find that in most of our industrial
centres the population has increased very
considerably. In Belfast the population has
increased by about 600 per cent., and in
nearly all our industrial or urban areas it
has increased very considerably. We find
that the decrease is in the countryside, and
absolutely no attention at all is being paid
to the countryside to-day. I hold that if
our industrial undertakings are going to be
depressed for some time to come-and there
is all likelihood of that-then the Government should give whatever attention they
possibly can to agriculture.

•
Take the number of holdings into consideration. If the Minister of Agriculture
(Mr. Archdale) would attempt to have more
people placed on the land we might go a long
way towards solving the problem of unemployment. We have got 16,756 holdings of
from thirty to fifty acres. Now, if it were
possible to settle either two or three more
people on each of those holdings we would
absorb-I see the hon. and learned Member
(Mr. Hanna) laughs. This is a very serious
matter, and when I pass on to another point
he will possibly find that there is some room
for them.. I suggest that if you had a
different method of agriculture-the hon. and
learned Member, if he has not done so,
could study the agricultural conditions in
countries on the Continent, and he will find
that we have not got the same density of
population in the Six Counties, or even in
England and Wales. There they have 639
people to the square mile as against 618 in
Great Britain. That does not indicate that
we have got a surplus population. It shows
that there is tremendous room for development. The hon. and learned Member is
inclined to laugh. If it was possible to
settle two or three people on each of the
holdings of from 15 acres to 30 acres-and
the number is 29,156 in Northern Irelandwe would possibly be able to absorb all the
unemployment we have got in Northern
Ireland at the present time.
There is a considerable acreage of land
in Northern Ireland not under cultivation.
Forty-one per cent. of the land is not cultivated, but is in pasture. The acreage under
cultivation is 1,300,000 out of over 3,000,000,
and that shows a tremendous scope for development there. I suppose the Minister of
Agriculture will be at Stormont Castle
attending to his hen run, which is probably
of far more importance to him than being
in this House to hear what the Members
have got to say. If the Government, seeing
they have got no industrial policy, would
try to hammer out an agricultural policy,
it would mean something, because the alternative is to go on doling out the thousands
of pounds they are doling out. As 1 have
frequently pointed out in this House, they
have no solution for the problem. We are
asked repeatedly for a remedy for that
problem. We have got ideas on the subject,
but if we come to present those ideas we are
very much forced to accept the extremist
point of view that Parliamentary institutions
are absolutely futile. It is not possible to
get the heads of Departments to act whether
the ideas are sensible or not. I am not
addressing the Department of the Minister
of Labour at the moment; I am more concerned with the Ministry of Agriculture. I
do not see anyone representing that Department on the Government Benches, in fact,
very few of the agricultural representatives
are here this afternoon. We get no suggestions from those people as to how agriculture
should be dealt with. It is left to someone
from these Benches, who does not know a
great deal about it-

What policy has the Government to deal
with the problem of unemployment? They
have no policy at all. They have no conception of the way in which they should deal
with the problem. Suggestion after suggestion has been made by Members sitting in
these Benches-I think we could fairly claim
a monopoly of suggestions as far as this
House is concerned-that some attempt
should be made to find the number of youths
and juveniles in our industries at the present time and also the number of people of
65 years of age in them. There should be
some attempt made at one end of the scale
to give juveniles and youths a better education than they get at the present time, and
there should be an attempt to take our aged
of 65 and over 70 out of industry, in order
to give our young and middle-aged, male
and female, population an opportunity of
performing useful service. I will be told
that will cost money. I have been told
before that it would cost money, but I believe it would be a much better alternative
than paying approximately £53,000 per week
in unemployment benefit indiscriminately.
We may temporarily relieve the situation
until such time as the Government may be
able to prepare even some partial solution
of this question.
There are a great many proposals that
could be placed before the House. Most of
them have been put before it by previous
speakers, and I have no desire to recapitulate
any of the arguments that have been adduced
by those people further than to attempt to
get the Government to concentrate on the
question of agriculture, because I think it
would be accepted as orthodox economics that
our imports are paid for by our exports, and
I find that last year our imports exceeded
our exports.
Mr. POLLOCK: By how much?
Mr. W. MCMULLEN: I do not know

quite easily. If I attempted to open the

land-borne traffic there is an adverse trade

and if we cannot sell our linen? We cannot
go on indefinitely having an adverse trade

a much more bankrupt state than we are at
present unless we make some attempt to
develop our home market. These are orthodox economics, they are not Socialist economics. They are not outlandish. They aren

Mr. ANDREWS: I am rather sorry that
the hon. Member for West Belfast (Mr.
Devlin), who raised this debate, is not in
his seat at the moment. Evidently he believes
in the principle of having his fling and
running away, and consequently living to
fight another day.. When he raised this important question I did hope he would put
forward some concrete suggestion to which
the Government could give effect in order to
help to mitigate this unemployment tragedy
which has been going on in our midst now
for more than five years.
that
The only suggestion he put forward, which
I think is worth mentioning, was
another Commission should be established
in order to investigate the whole problem.
He was a member of the Conference which
was brought together by the Lord Mayor
and myself, so that we might explore this
problem from every standpoint, and we spent
many days extended over many weeks and
months. The hon. Member for West Belfast
was actually the Vice-Chairman of one of
the most important Committees, the General
Purposes Committee. We established sub-committees of that Conference of men engaged in
the different industries—shipbuilding, linen,
and the building trade-and they investigated
their own particular side of the problem
Reports were presented by them and the
reports were published. I do not say that
those representatives were able to suggest
anything new that the Government could
do in order to deal with this problem, in
fact, I think those reports one and all
proved the truth of what I have frequently
said in this House, that this problem cannot be solved by any Government. It can
only be solved when trade gets going again
through its natural channels and when the
state of Europe permits that being an
accomplished fact. No Government can
compel people to order ships who do not
require ships or to order linen who do not
want it. Really all that a Government can
do is to endeavour to mitigate the evil, and
that I say this Government has done to the
greatest extent in its power. We have done
it at least in equal measure to what any
other Government has done, and we are
spending about £4,000,000 per annum and
doing everything possible to help our unemployed. I deplore the fact that Members
of the Opposition should come here and
raise these debates with the greatest of
frequency, and at the same time not be able
to make a single practical suggestion towards the solution of the problem.
There is another course that some hon.
Members of the Opposition pursue which,
I think, is also to be deplored. They endeavour to paint the picture blacker than
it is. For instance, the hon. Member for
North Belfast (Mr. Kyle) quoted some
figures. He said that about 50 per cent. of
the claims recommended by our rota committee were being turned down by headquarters. As a matter of fact only about 3
per cent. are being turned down. And I
want to assure the House that headquarters
are absolutely impartial in connection with
this matter. The claims that have been
turned down by the local employment committees at times have been referred back
to the local employment committees with the
suggestion that the claims should be granted,
and the claims which have been passed by
the local employment committees are only
turned down when the Department is of the
opinion that the local employment committee or the rota committee has neglected
to take into consideration some statutory
provision or regulation which they ought to
have done. But such statements as that to

I am justified in saying that the position is

A great deal has been made to-day out of
the fact that our regulations are supposed
to be harsh and unfair, and I have been
appealed to again and again by hon. Members
opposite to relax them. Hon. Members know
as well as I do that I cannot relax them. If
I did, I would be doing the greatest disservice to our unemployed people in Northern
Ireland that it would be possible for any man
to do. And I will tell you why. The Unemployment Agreement with Great Britain
which the Opposition here have approved was
only made possible, as the Prime Minister
and the Minister of Finance know, owing to
the fact that since this Parliament was
established we have kept in step with Great
Britain, both in legislation and in administration. I was frequently heckled by
Ministers and officials across the water as to
whether we did or whether we did not keep
in step with Great Britain, and it was only
because I was able to assure those in
authority in Great Britain that I was doing
so that this Agreement was made possible.
And if I were now to relax the regulations
it would simply mean the tearing up of this
Agreement, and we would be drifting whether
we liked it or not up against the proposition
of having to raise the contributions here and
lower the benefits as compared with Great

necessary works-the works which will be

Member for West Belfast (Mr. Devlin), who
sits behind me, was vice-Chairman. He says
that after the reports of that committee had
been issued nothing new came forward. It
was not the fault of the Committee. It was
the fault of the agenda to which they were
tied down and the scope to which their
activities were confined.
Mr. ANDREWS: On a point of order, I
really must correct my hon. Friend (Mr.
Beattie). I am sorry to interrupt, but it is
necessary that I should let the public know
what the position is. In no way were the
Committee tied down. The Committee had
power to go over as wide an area as ever
they liked, and to cover the whole field of
unemployment from every standpoint.
Mr. BEATTIE: I accept the statement of
the Minister. I took it from the various
statements made of ways and means whereby
the problem of unemployment could have
been attacked. I think the hon. Member for
West Belfast (Mr. Devlin) put other points
of view before the Government, but the
Government refused to accept them, in the
light in which he presented them. It was
from that point of view that I made the
statement. I wanted to say that the Committee had at its command representatives
of all classes, and several schemes of relief
could have been brought about which the
Minister's own Committee had also been discussing. These schemes were not brought
forth, why I do not know, but perhaps whoever replies for the Government may be able
to tell us.
One of the schemes was the widening of
the Upper Newtownards Road, to make the
footpath safe for travellers who have to use
it against the heavy motor traffic that goes
along that road. That was one of the suggestions put forward at the Minister's Committee. It was stated that both the Belmont
and Knock Roads were unsafe for people to
walk on the footpath, and that actually one
part of the road had no footpath at all.
That would have employed from three to
four hundred men and would have been at
least a palliative. If the Minister had
accepted the suggestion from the Committee
it would have given a short spell of employment to some of the unfortunate people who
are so long out of employment, and who are
denied the right to unemployment benefit.
The next point to which I would like to
draw the Minister's attention is the administration of the regulations. I suppose I am
one of the Members who just knows sufficient to warrant him in attacking the
Minister of Labour's Department on occasions when I think fit. The Minister states
that three per cent. have been turned down
as against the statement of the hon. Member
for North Belfast (Mr. Kyle) of fifty per cent.
I do not believe that they eventually went as
far as fifty per cent (hon. Members: Hear,
hear)--but if they have only gone the length
of three per cent. then that three per cent.
must have come to my door, without at all
taking into consideration the number of
claims to which hon. Members sitting alongside and behind me attend. I believe I must
have attended to three per cent. of the claims
turned down. Therefore. I feel justified in
saying that a very large percentage of the
claims that are recommended by the Rota
Committees are disallowed when they go to
headquarters on the grounds, as set out in
the regulations, either of family income, or
of not having sufficient employment within
the past two years, or of not genuinely seeking work.
I know from my personal experience that
the hon. Member for West Belfast (Mr.
William McMullen), who sits beside me, is
right when he states that the 6,000 people
who are off the register have not really found
employment. Some may have found employment, but the 6,000 have not, and I do not
believe that the Parliamentary Secretary to
the Ministry of Labour (Mr. Gordon) has
any authority for saying that 6,000 persons
have found employment within the last three
months. My contention, so far as the reduction of the register is concerned, is that
1,600 Specials had to come on to unemployment insurance, and so the regulations were
put into operation and the rod was laid on
fast and furious for a period of two months,
weeding out all the applicants it was possible
to weed out and throwing them on the streets
with the idea that these 1,600 men were to
come on to the register on the 1st March.
Perhaps the Minister may say that that is a
wild idea, but it is my opinion, and I am
right in holding the opinion that the
Ministry made the regulations more severe
in the first two months of this year than was
necessary, with the result that a lot of
people are in semi-starvation at the present
time and living on charity from one day to
the other.
The next thing to which I would like to
draw the attention of the Government is
housing and their failure to tackle the question in a reasonable way. Housing has been
under discussion by the Government, and,
while from their speeches they seem to be
anxious to solve it, they have never made
a real effort to solve the housing problem.
If the Government were serious about the
problem at all they would have set up a
Consolidated Fund Bill--
Second Reading.
25 MARCH 1926
committee with the object of building themselves the houses necessary to house the
people. It is part of the Government's duty
to see the people fed, and I think they were
neglectful as representatives of the people in
not setting up a housing scheme of their
own and in getting the labour put into
operation with so many people unemployed.
The Minister of Home Affairs (Sir Dawson
Bates) spoke about a bath. I would like to
tell the Government that working-class
people require to be washed just the same
as the Government. There is only one difference, namely that the working-class people
would not require any whitewashing the
same as the Government. We may be gross
and crude, but the hon. Member for West
Belfast (Mr. William McMullen), I think,
expressed it when he said it is a grand little
class to belong to.
1 want to say quite candidly that the lack
of sincerity on the part of the Government
since I became a Member of this House in
regard to the requirements of the working
classes of the Six Counties has been deplorable. I regret that they have not tried to
put their house in order and to establish
themselves as a Government to which the
people would look up and of whom they could
say, "They have done their best for us."
All I can say is that if this is the best
the Government now in office can do for the
people of the Six Counties, then the sooner
the people realise that and say "You are unfit to hold office in the Six Counties. We will
have to displace you and put the Members
of the Opposition in your place," the better,
because, even if we did not put all we would
like to into practice, we would have the sincerity. You were sincere enough in your
talk, but when it came to putting it into
practical operation it did not materialise,
and the people had to suffer because the
Government were thinking more of economy
than of the peoples' needs.
Before sitting down I would like to say
that I endorse all the remarks passed by my
hon. Friends on the Front Bench and behind
me. The sooner the Government realise their
fault in neglecting the wants of the people
and drop their policy of coming here one
day, and no sooner are they here than they
are thinking about what time they can get
away, the sooner they get into good practical
working order the better for them and for
the people. I endorse all the remarks that
have been made from this side of the House.
Mr. THOMAS HENDERSON: I have listened with a good deal of attention to the
speeches delivered from both sides of the
House to-day regarding many important
questions concerning the lives of the people
of Ulster. I am satisfied after listening to
the speeches from this side of the Houseand with a great many of them I quite
agree that had the Government any plans
for solving the unemployment problem they
would readily put them into operation. I
regret, along with many other hon. Members
on this side of the House, the absence of
the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Archdale)
this afternoon. I think his presence was
most important in view of the statements
that have been made from the Government
Benches regarding emigration. If the
Canadian Government and the Australian
Government can bring people from this
country, place them on the land out there,
give them the land, give them implements
to till the land, give them homes to go into,
surely to goodness the question of adopting
some regulations so that the Ulster people
might be put on the land here instead of
being obliged to go to foreign lands is worthy
of consideration by the Government. I think
the Minister of Agriculture should have been
here to let hon. Members know whether
emigration is a good thing or a bad thing
for Ulster. Personally, I believe that, with
hundreds of thousands of acres lying undeveloped in Ulster, emigration is a bad thing
for Ulster, and that if this Ulster land were
developed it would be a good thing for Ulster.
Regarding the road construction schemes,
about which many of us on the Opposition
Benches have spoken, report has it that the
London Omnibus Company have purchased
many of our local firms here. If that is so,
the people from London will make you hurry
up and give employment in the reconstruction of your roads. Going out on one of
the country roads, I found that the Ulster
Government apparently has no control over
the urban districts. I think the time has
arrived now when the Minister of Home
Affairs should have a frontage line on all'
our main arterial roads, that is for the
future development of Ulster. Motor
omnibuses and other motor vehicles have
come to stay, and it is absolutely necessary
that the Minister of Home Affairs should be
the responsible authority in the reconstruction of the roads for future development.
Many of our main roads are a disgrace.
Belfast is the capital of Ulster now, and it is
essential that the main roads throughout
the length and breadth of the Province
should be made 60 feet wide and should be
constructed in such a way as to be able to
carry the heavy traffic of the future. The
Minister of Home Affairs should get in touch
with the various urban districts and the
authorities in the small towns and get them
to arrange to have a frontage line. If you
go along any of these roads you will find
new houses are being built, and they are
making the roads so narrow that when
Ulster develops in the future these people
will have to be paid heavy compensation
in order that the roads should be widened.

The hon. Member for East Belfast (Mr.

Mr. BEATTIE: Take it from them.
Mr. T. HENDERSON: I would not like

be utilised for the benefit of the Ulster

Government to extend the docks.
Mr. ANDREWS: No, no.
Mr. T. HENDERSON: It is to the

methods of solving this very important
question, as apparently the old methods are

this question, to throw some of the responsibility on the Opposition side by setting up
a Commission and inviting Members of the

sit on that Conference, that is the captains

Mr. T. W. MCMULLAN: And lost them.
Mr. T. HENDERSON: Very few of them

compelled to go there and explain why
they have not come to the Government's

very little respect for the captains of the
linen industry. They have let it lapse in
such a way that it will never recover. It
does not matter whether this Government
gives grants to the linen industry. It is
my honest belief the linen industry will

opinion is that the reason there is so much

I have often sent hundreds of people to

happiness to the homes of those people.
I would suggest to the Government now

HOUSE OF COMMONS
[Mr. Speaker]
The amendments which an instruction
proposes to sanction must be such as
would further the general purpose and
intention of the House in the appointment
of the Committee. The object of an
instruction is, therefore, to endow a Committee with power whereby the Committee
can perfect and complete the legislation
defined by the contents of the Bill, or

HOUSE OF COMMONS.

Tuesday, 30th March, 1926.
The House met at Twelve of the Clock, Mr.
SPEAKER in the Chair.
Oral Answers to Questions.
APPOINTMENTS TO STAFF OF CROWN
AND PEACE, BELFAST.
1. Mrs. CHICHESTER asked the Minister
of Finance whether any appointments have
been made to the staff of the Clerk of the
Crown and Peace, Belfast, since the passing
of the County Officers and Courts Act
(Northern Ireland), 1925; if so, whether such
appointments were made in accordance with
the terms of that Act, and whether the persons appointed were ex-Servicemen.
The MINISTER OF COMMERCE (Mr.
Barbour): My right hon. Friend (Mr. Pollock)
has asked me to take this question for him.
No definite appointments have been made
to the staff of the Clerk of the Crown and
Peace, Belfast, since the passing of the
County Officers and Courts Act (Northern
Ireland), 1925, save of those officers who,
under the terms of the Act, were entitled
to permanent establishment. Some permanent posts are still unfilled, and under
Regulations shortly to be issued will be
staffed by candidates recruited by examination. In the meantime, in order not to
hamper the work of the office, it was found
necessary to make temporary appointments
to these posts, and assent was given to the
transfer from the personal staff employed
by the Clerk of the Crown and Peace, in his
capacity as Registration Officer of Voters'
Lists of two officers who were not ex-Servicemen. The last two temporary appointees
have, however, been ex-Servicemen candidates.
As stated, however, these appointments are
purely temporary, pending examination
candidates becoming available.
CONVICTIONS AGAINST LICENSED
TRADERS.
2. Mr. CRAWFORD asked the Minister of
Home Affairs whether he will state the
number of convictions against licensed
traders for the years 1924 and 1925 respectively, and also the number of cases in which
their licences were endorsed.
The MINISTER OF HOME AFFAIRS (Sir
Dawson Bates): The number of convictions
in 1924 was 234, as against 196 in 1925.
Licences were endorsed in 27 cases in 1924,
and in 14 cases in 1925.
་
NEWTOWNARDS CAMP.
3. Major SHILLINGTON asked the Minister
of Home Affairs under what terms the camp
at Newtownards is in the occupation of the
Northern Government; also, how many men
are quartered there at the present time.
Sir DAWSON BATES: The camp at Newtownards is held by the
he Ministry under a
yearly agreement dated 30th November, 1925,
from the War Department at an annual
rent of £1,080, subject to six months' notice
on either side.
The Ministry has to pay all rates and taxes,
to insure the premises, and to keep them in
good condition and repair.
The number of men quartered at Newtownards camp at present is 143 of all ranks,
including 20 members of the Special Constabulary.

The MINISTER OF LABOUR (Mr.

ORDERS OF THE DAY.
Mines (Working Facilities, Support
etc.) Bill.
Order for Second Reading read.
Motion made and Question proposed:
"That the Bill be now read a Second Time."
The MINISTER OF COMMERCE (Mr.
Barbour): The primary object of this
Bill is to enable rights to work
minerals to be granted in cases where
there is a likelihood that they may
be left permanently unworked, either
through legal disability, or through the concurrence of two or more persons being required and not being obtainable, or, further,
by reason of the minerals being owned in
such small parcels that they cannot be
properly or conveniently worked by themselves. In order further to facilitate the
working of minerals power is also taken in
the Bill to grant ancillary rights, such as
way leaves and the right to a water supply.
A surface owner may claim protection for
his interests in respect of damage to any
buildings or works belonging to him by
reason of the working of minerals under his
land, or compensation in the event of its
being held that the importance of the getting
of minerals is paramount.
The power to grant rights to work minerals
or ancillary rights, or to impose restrictions
upon the working of minerals is vested in
the Ministry of Commerce acting upon the
findings of a tribunal which is set up by
Clause 11 of the Bill. With respect to the
personnel of this tribunal I should explain
that in Great Britain, where a similar Bill
received legislative sanction in the year 1923,
the Railway and Canal Commissioners constitute the tribunal. Their services are not,
however, available for this particular duty
in Northern Ireland, and it becomes
necessary, therefore, to set up a new body in
Northern Ireland.
The members of the tribunal in Northern
Ireland will number three, one being a
practising barrister of at least ten years'
standing, one a member of the Panel of
Official Arbitrators, and one an officer of the
Ministry of Commerce. In cases where there
may be dissatisfaction with the findings of
the tribunal as to the amount of compensation, provision is made for an appeal to the
County Court; and it is provided that in
hearing such appeals the County Court shall
have the assistance of a specially qualified
assessor.
Hon. Members may remember that the
Commission on the Natural and Industrial
Resources of Northern Ireland recommended
the application to Northern Ireland of a
Measure on the lines of that now before the
House. Other representations to the same
effect have been made to my Ministry, and,
while I do not desire to suggest that undue
obstruction to the development of minerals
has occurred in the past, I do think that the
existence of the powers outlined in Part 1 of
this Bill will tend to foster the development
of the mineral resources of our Province.
Part II of the Bill concerns coal mining
only, and repeals two sections of the Mining
Industry Act, 1920. The first is Section 4,
which required the Board of Trade to appoint
Pit and District Committees and Regional
and National Boards. As hon. Members will
appreciate, local conditions in Northern Ireland render a provision of this kind unnecessary in our Province. Section 20 of
that Act established a Fund, for the
improvement of social conditions of colliery
workers, to be administered by a Committee
and a body of Assessors officially appointed.
Mines Bill-
Second Reading.
HOUSE OF COMMONS
[Mr. Barbour]
The income of this Fund is derived from a
levy upon the coal owners of one penny per
ton of the output of coal mines. The life of
the Fund was limited by the Act of 1920
to five years, which period expired in
March, 1926. While such a Fund may be
desirable and of value to the workers in Great
Britain where the coal mining industry has
attained very large proportions, there
appeared to be little justification for putting
it into operation in Northern Ireland during the past two years. We have only one
coal mine, and during the past two years

CLASS III. No. 5-PRISONS.
Motion made and Question proposed:
"That
a sum not exceeding £39,863 be
granted to His Majesty to complete the sum
necessary to defray the charge which will
come in course of payment during the year
ending 31st March, 1927, to defray the expenses of prisons and the maintenance of
criminal lunatics confined in district and
central criminal asylums (17 and 18 Vic.,
c. 76; 34 and 35 Vic., c. 112. s. 6; 40 and 41
Vic., c. 49; 47 and 48 Vic., c. 36; 61 and 62
Vic., c. 60; 1 Edw. VII., c. 17. s. 3; 8 Edw.

Geo. V., c. 13, s. 1 (N.I.). Note.-£15,000 has

Supply-
Committee.
HOUSE OF COMMONS
Sir DAWSON BATES: This Estimate
possesses at all events one satisfactory
feature, that is, it represents a saving of
over £15,000 as compared with last year.
Last year the Estimate was for £70,365,
while this year it is £54,863.
This decrease is due to a variety of reasons.
It is partly due to the fact that we have
fewer convicts and fewer prisoners. That
everyone in this House will agree is satisfactory. Last year owing to there being no
accommodation for convicts in Northern Ireland we had to maintain a considerable
number of convicts in English and Scottish
prisons at very considerable expense. Since
that time we have been able to fit up part of
Belfast gaol as a convict prison, and we have
been able to bring back all our convicts who
were formerly in England and Scotland, and
following the reduction of prisoners we have
been able to make certain re-arrangements with a view to further economy. We
have reduced Derry Prison to the status of
a local prison or bridewell now, and instead
of having a governor there
have
we
warder in charge. This enabled us to transfer the Governor of Derry Prison to Armagh,
to take the place of the Superintendent who
had resigned. This, of course, effected
considerable economy.
a
a
This new arrangement has also enabled us
to transfer a number of warders to Belfast
Prison, and the result is we have been able
to deal with these new prisoners from
England and Scotland practically without
any increase to the general staff.
Hon. Members will observe in looking
through the Estimate that in addition we
have been able to make a considerable reduction in the total number of our staff.
re-
Now with regard to food, the Committee
will observe that there again there has been
a saving of no less than £2 ຄ. head
in the food of the prisoners. This
duction is mainly due to perhaps better contracts and reduced prices. I would like to
point out that the rations of the prisoners
compare very favourably with those provided
in England and Scotland.
We have made arrangements for the erection of 16 houses for the use of married
warders within the Belfast Prison grounds,
but of course outside the prison walls. It
will be very much more satisfactory to have
these warders close at hand, and in addition
it will enable us to effect a considerable
saving in the allowances for these warders
for quarters when they had to find them.
With regard to motor transport last year
a system of motor transport for the conveyance of female prisoners to Armagh from
Belfast was instituted by means of a prison
van. The system proved both economical and
satisfactory as it saved escort, and it is
undesirable to have these women taken by
train. Now to meet an objection that was
raised we have decided to have this van running daily, so as to enable us to discharge
these female prisoners in Belfast rather
than Armagh, where they have to find their
own way home by train.
I think hon. Members will agree that
while the main object of imprisonment is
that it will act as a deterrent, at the same
time, where possible, we should do something on the reformative side of prison
treatment, I feel that this applies particularly in the case of first offenders and
youthful criminals, and every effort is made
to keep this aspect of the question before
our prison officials, and I am glad to say
that they entered into the spirit of it and
are fully alive to the necessity of helping.
I would like to refer to the activities of
the Prisoners' Aid Societies operating in
Northern Ireland, which are run entirely
as voluntary institutions. A small grant
is made to them out of Government funds
towards the expenses, and the gratuities,
which are earned by prisoners, are paid to
the prisoners through these societies.
Mr. CRAWFORD: Might I ask the right
hon. Gentleman to speak a little louder.
He is speaking the other way, and we cannot hear him here.
Mr. DEVLIN: All the criminals are on

Sir DAWSON BATES: I was referring

societies to help them in their work, and
that the money earned by the prisoners
is paid to them
through these societies. Of course, at the same time, the
societies are largely dependent upon voluntary subscriptions. The officials are
entirely voluntary. They do their best.
They meet the prisoner outside and do
their best to find employment for them, and
try to help them to settle in a better walk
in life. I would like to take this opportunity of expressing my appreciation of the
valuable services which they render to the
community in taking up this work.
I would also like to express my appreciation
of the valuable help we have received from
the Toc. H. Society. They have arranged
for the holding of a monthly concert for
the prisoners, and also for weekly lectures
of an instructive and interesting character.
These lectures are greatly appreciated by
the prisoners, and the Governor of Belfast.
Prison reports that they have improved the

think the greatest possible affliction that can

13 APRIL 1926
Industrial Assurance.
The following Notice of Motion stood on
the Paper in the name of Dr. Morrison:-
"That, in the opinion of this House, the
Industrial Assurance (Northern Ireland) Act,
1924, has not been instrumental in abolishing or effectually controlling the abuses
which existed previous to the passing of that
Act; and this House calls upon the Government to appoint a Select Committee to investigate and report upon the whole question
of Industrial Assurance in
Northern
Ireland."
Mr. SPEAKER: Before the hon. Member
proceeds, I take it that he has got a seconder
for the Motion?
Mr. DEVLIN: If nobody else seconds the
Motion, I will do so.
Dr. MORRISON: I beg to move. This
matter, so far as I know, is non-controversial. Every Member of this House has
the same object in view as I have, and whatever decision we come to will be a decision
to try to secure that justice shall prevail
in Northern Ireland. The Second Reading
of our Industrial Assurance Act took place
on 8th October, 1924, and those who turn
up the Official Report, Volume 4, No. 15,
will find that the Minister of Agriculture
on that occasion informed the House that
the average of the sums assured was about
£10, and that the payments made were
about 21d. per week. The total amount contributed under this system in the United
Kingdom was £37,000,000 a year. Then he
made what was, to me, a striking statement, that for every shilling paid by these
people, sevenpence was returned to them, and
fivepence went to the Companies.
In ten
years 9,000,000 policies were issued by one
company, and of that number 6,400,000
lapsed.
Mr. KYLE: For the purposes of accuracy,
would the hon. Gentleman enlighten me by
repeating those figures. We understood him
to say that for every shilling paid ninepence went to the contributor.
Dr. MORRISON: Fivepence was collared
by the companies, and sevenpence went to
the people who were paying their 24d. a
week. In the case of one company, 6,400,000
policies lapsed out of a total of 9,300,000.
In ten companies 5,000,000 policies lapsed in
1913, and 4,000,000 of those were effected in
1912 and 1913. These facts are taken from
Lord Parmoor's Commission which was instituted by the British Government, and its
report on this matter was unanimous.
Now the Industrial Assurance Act was
passed in the British House in 1923, and it
was passed in this House in 1924. The second
Section of the Act provides that the Minister
of Commerce shall appoint an officer who is
called the Industrial Assurance Commissioner for Northern Ireland, and I think
he also acts as Registrar of Friendly
Societies. Section 44 enacts that the Commissioner shall make a report to the Minister
with comments on the valuations of these
societies, their returns, or on other matters
brought before him, and that this report is
to be laid before the Parliament of Northern
Ireland by the Minister. That is what I
want to comment on in this case. I want all
these tables submitted in some form whereby
we can analyse them and see whether or not
justice has been done.
The most remarkable thing I have noticed
in connection with industrial assurance is
the growth of these societies. Twenty-five
years ago these societies were practically nonexistent, or at least they did a very small
business, and now the turnover that they
have is something amazing. I have the report here of one of these societies issued in.
the local Press in my neighbourhood. It has
total funds of £38,000,000, an increase of
5,000,000 for the year, and it has twelve
officers in Coleraine. If you multiply those
twelve officers by five or six other societies
you have in every district in Ulster this band
of men running into the houses of the poor
and inducing these people to insure, and,
therefore, it is our policy to see that justice
is done to them.
I have here a report taken from the "Whig"
of another of these societies. Of new policies
issued in 1925 there were 723,873 assuring a
sum of £12,745,440. The premium revenue on
existing policies was £3,945,035. The increase of revenue over the previous year was
£199,636. The income from investments
after Income Tax had been paid was
£444,659. I do not know what amount of
total wealth that represents, but there must
be a huge capital sum invested when they
have an income of almost half a million
annually. The number of policies in force in
this society is 5,762,579, and the sum assured
represents the vast figure of £73,321,250. Now
that does not refer to general insurance at
all. It is described in the report of that
society as the "industrial branch," that is.
for sums of £10.
In the report of that annual meeting the
Chairman said:

Quite a lot has recently been heard
about the Locarno spirit. We had our
Locarno some years ago, and I am proud
to say that the best I can wish for the
new Locarnos is that they will produce
results as beneficial to all concerned as
have the efforts of our company and its
staff in this direction."

HOUSE OF COMMONS
[Dr. Morrison]

We do not often hear high moral principles
enunciated at business, annual, or general
meetings. That is the sort of stuff that we
hear occasionally coming across the Atlantic
from Washington. This high-toned morality
is familiar to us, and this unctuous rectitude
is fortunately not very common here.
would like to point out in this connection
that the chairman of this company, who
takes such a high moral tone, is, if this
report of Lord Parmoor's Commission is
correct, at the head of a company whose
officials are putting their hands into the
pockets of 5,762,579 poor people every year
and taking from them £3,954,035. It works
out that they are taking 80,000,000 shillings
from these poor people, and for every shilling, as I stated at the beginning, all they
are paying back to these people is 7d, they
themselves retaining 5d.
Now, I am able to allege from my own
experience and that is the experience of a
dispensary doctor, whose work in his neighbourhood lies amongst the poor, and who
knows the conditions probably better, or as
well as anybody in this House that in connection with these industrial assurance
societies there is a very large amount of
fraud and of exploiting of the poor. The
poor who join the assurance societies belong
to what I call the "submerged tenth." They
are the most helpless and, I maintain, the
most deserving people in the community.
They are down and out, and in many cases
-indeed in practically all cases-they suffer
from sickness or some other visitation of
Providence. They are not in any trade
union, and so have no trade union leaders
to defend them. They are not able to defend
themselves, and they are at the mercy of
anybody who comes round telling a plausible
story and offering them something that will
enable them to provide for the burial of
their relatives or of themselves.
I once heard a Labour Member of this
House raising this question of where the
poor died. I think he could not have raised
a more important question. Some of my
people, after the flax mills were done scutching, used to go across to Scotland. Some of
them, as frequently happened, took ill and
died, and then their friends had to face a
very serious problem, and that was how
were they to bury their dead in a strange
place like that; either that or bring the
body home. The question was not an easy
one. They had no money, and I suppose
the friends and relatives raised what they
could. I am told-and this is speaking of
pre-war days-that it cost from £7 to £10
to bury a dead person in Glasgow, and that
was a matter of very serious moment to
these people. I myself had to bury an aged
servant, and the cost to me was £11 for a
modest funeral. I put it to the House that
there should be some provision by which
people who die after coming from a strange
I place into an industrial centre such as this
for a moderate sum, such as can be had
in the country, would be able to get a place
to bury their dead. The very last time I
came to this House I saw a motor hearse
coming down Donegall Place and turning
into Royal Avenue. There were four people
carrying the coffin. They were taking the
coffin away, and, as a last tribute of respect,
they were carrying it. They stopped in
Royal Avenue to put the coffin into the
hearse to take it away, perhaps, to some
remote portion of County Derry. It contained, probably, some person who had come
into Belfast, and had died there. We have
plenty of privileges in the country, but I
am afraid it is impossible for a poor person
to get buried here, and naturally all poor
people, who know that death is coming with
sure and certain steps, know that provision
must be made to get a coffin and a grave,
and that leaves them at the mercy of these
people who go about.
What I maintain happens is that the agent
gets the applicant to sign a form. That was
the old system in operation in my day.
These people put their names to the bottom
of a form and undertake to pay 2d or 3d
per week, and then the agent fills in the
rest of the paper. One of the peculiarities
of these societies is that the agent makes a
weekly report. He must have new business,
and that forces him, perhaps, to do things
for the sake of retaining his position that
otherwise he would not do. Now, when the
name is signed and the report filled in, when
the state of health is filled in, and all these
things are done for the people, and death
takes place, the society repudiate the age
or they repudiate the state of health. I
know that the agent in many cases would
be willing that the policy should be paid in
full, but when death occurs these reports
and all particulars have to be sent to the
head office, inquiries are made, and then
it is found that the age is inaccurate. The
man in the head office asks for the length of
the disease. The agent knows that the
patient may have been suffering for twenty
years from that disease, but the head office
raises the question, and the result is that
difficulties like this are raised, and that
hundreds of these cases are paid a reduced
sum, while hundreds of them never get a
penny.
On the Third Reading of this Bill I said
that three things were necessary to protect
the poor. Unfortunately those recommendations could not be added to the Bill at that
particular stage, but I said that three things
were essential to protect the poor. The
first was that for every lapsed policy there

should be returned to the insured person
half of the premiums that he had paid.
Then, with regard to the age, my recommendation was that if the age is accepted at the
time the policy is issued no powers should
be allowed to these people to raise the
question of age when the policy matures.
I stated further that when the agent accepted
the age of the insured without a certificate
he should be barred from raising that question when the policy matures. It is very
easy for the agent to get the age. You can
get a certificate which costs 3s 7d. This
House could make it easier than that because
it has already provided a means in another
direction of getting a certificate at a cost of
sixpence. That power could be extended to
these people for the purpose of life assurance.
None of these suggestions of mine were accepted, and the Bill went through.

This Commissioner who has been appointed
will be paid by this House. It is his business to make a report of some nature.
think it is the desire of a great number of
people in this House that we should have a
detailed report from the Commissioner as to
four particular things. I would like to know
how many policies have lapsed during 1925?
How many matured policies were paid short
and how much were they paid short? How
many were disputed on the ground of fraud
as to health and age? As the Act provides
for the policy holder getting protection in
the Recorder's Court or free of cost under
the Insurance Commission how many have
sought protection at these tribunals and
with what result? I think that if the Commissioner would secure from these societies
a return covering these points we would be
able to judge whether or not these poor
people are being treated fairly, decently and
honestly. What I maintain is that very few
of these cases come into court. These people
are helpless. In many cases they have no
means of fighting their claims. They may
have become insured for £10, and they will
take £3 or £5 in settlement. I maintain
that that is unjust, and seriously unjust,
and that this House should set its face
against it and stamp it out, and see that
justice is done to these poor people.
One of the recommendations made with
regard to benefiting the position of these
people was that they should get a free paid
up policy, and it was stated that if the
details on the application forms were not
filled in by the individual but by the agent
the forms were not valid. Who is to prove
all this? I maintain that if you create difficulties like that the injustice will go on and
on. As I have said, very few of these cases
ever appear, but I have clipped one out of
the paper.
It is the report of a trial that
took place in Co. Tyrone last year. It is
typical of the way these people are induced
to sign some form that is not correct; in fact,
a form that can be legally described as a
fraud. By means of that fraud, however, a
rich company is able to get rid of its liability
and pocket the premiums that have been
paid by these poor people. This is the case:
Before Judge Linehan, at Dungannon
Quarter Sessions, Catherine Quinn, Creenagh, Dungannon, brought an action against
the Britannic Assurance Company, Ltd.,
for the amount of a policy on the life of her
mother, Sarah Quinn, deceased. Her sister,
Susan Quinn, brought a similar action
against the same Company on foot of
another policy. The respective amounts
were £9 and £9.
Mr. Corr appeared for plaintiffs, and
Mr. Skeffington for defendants.
Catherine Quinn said she insured her
mother about fifteen months before her
death. She paid the premiums till her
mother's death when the defendants refused to pay.
After the insurance a nice
gentleman-(laughter) came round and
looked at her mother, and said she looked
well. There was no objection till her
mother died.
Before the policy was effected or completed
the inspector had to come round and inquire
into it. He came round and saw this woman
and said her mother looked very nice. He
was quite pleasant and amiable, and no difficulties were raised until the mother died, and
then they objected to the policy on the
ground that it was granted under fraudulent
misrepresentation. It appeared that the
mother was 13 years older than they had
stated. When she died the company refused to pay. So far as I can see they
pocketed the fifteen months of contributions in both cases and refused to pay. Mr.
Corr, an honest man, probably thought that
as other societies settled these cases and gave
a trifle to close people's mouths, if he took
them into court they might be ashamed of
themselves and settle with the parties. I
know that when you have written your name
to a fraudulent statement it cannot be expected to hold in law, but my point is that
these people were enticed to do this thing.
The insurance agent induced them to do it
and they put their names to this document,
which stated the facts wrongly, at his request. He assured them that they would
make it all right. Mr. Corr thought to

The defendants closed down part of

surance in certain districts which the company were determined to put down, hence

I maintain that this wholesale fraud of
which this gentleman speaks is brought about
not by the poor people direct, but by the
agent of the society who induces them to
put their names to these documents and then
fills them in. At any rate serious injustice
is done on a vast and huge scale to I think
the most deserving of our community. It is
the duty of this House to see that a correct
and full report is given of everything that
is carried on in Northern Ireland under our
Insurance Commission.
I do not intend to move that a Committee
should be appointed. My only object was to
ventilate this question and let the people
know what is going on. I consider, and my
experience during a somewhat lengthened
life has taught me, that the best solvent
for abuses is public opinion. If you get the
attention of the public concentrated on any
abuse you will find that it will be shifted
by the force of public opinion. I maintain
that this injustice has been going on and that
it is time, now that we in Northern Ireland
have got the control of this matter in our
own hands, we should insist on a detailed
report on these matters being put before us
so that the House would be in a position
to criticise them, and direct public attention
to them with the object of having the abuses
abolished. I beg to move.
Mr. KYLE: Apparently the hon. Gentleman (Dr. Morrison) has made no arrangements for anyone to second the Resolution.
I have great pleasure in doing so. He has
made an admirable case for the appointment
of a Select Committee to investigate the
whole question and report. The figures he
has given are, I am sure, sufficient to alarm
any person who takes any interest in the life
and welfare of the working people. He
states that out of every shilling collected
only sevenpence is returned to the contributors or agents, and fivepence out of every
shilling is pocketed by the companies either
for administration or for profits. I do know
that according to the Press reports we see
from time to time of the annual meetings of
these various insurance societies the profits
paid to the shareholders are tremendous.
Twenty and thirty per cent. are not unusual.
It means that a great many people pay into
these societies for a period of time, and then
for some reason or another their policies
lapse and all the money they have paid in
is lost.
I think that the hon. Member (Dr.
Morrison) has made a good case for the
appointment of a Select Committee. We of
the working class know what takes place.
An agent comes along and asks you to insure
either yourself or those dependent on you in
order that they may be buried decently.
Most of us desire that to take place. The
result is that we become insured and pay the
premiums, and then the breadwinner gets out
of work. He may be out of work for a considerable period, with the result that the
premiums go behind. Though he may have
been a member for a considerable number
of years, yet when his contributions get behind a certain amount or a certain length
of time the insurance company lapse the
policy, and all the money paid on behalf of
the man's wife and children and himself is
lost.
The hon. Member (Dr. Morrison) only
wants a Select Committee to report on this
question. If the Government see fit to agree
to this Committee and to its reporting on the
question I think this House will perhaps take
more definite steps towards ending this particular scandal than even the hon. Member
who proposed this very laudable Motion
might care to support. It seems to me that
the only logical outcome of any Committee or
of any report that may be submitted will be
the adoption of some national scheme of
assurance. No doubt there is a tremendous
field open for the Government to take up the
question of industrial assurance. It would
mean that the people would have the security
of the State behind them. If there was a
national scheme the people who pay in would
get some recompense for their money if they
happened to be out of work and were not able
to pay the premiums. It is for these reasons
that I want to support the hon. Member for
the University on this question. I think
he said quite truthfully that the growth of
these societies during the last 20 years has
been phenomenal. In my own lifetime they
have increased out of all knowing.
Dr. MORRISON: It is a gold mine.
Mr. KYLE: It is perfect gold mine for
the shareholders of these societies. There
is no doubt about it, it is a tremendous hardship to ordinary people to pay in without
much knowledge of the policies they sign.
They have probably the best intentions in
the world of paying the premiums and are
unable to continue them after a few years.
The amount of profits made by various
societies-take for example the Prudential-is
tremendous. The profits they make each year
are made principally on the nennies and twopences of working-class members whose
policies have lapsed. I do think it is a great
scandal that this thing should be allowed to
go on without adequate steps being taken by
the Government to protect the ordinary
citizens. I have, therefore, great pleasure in
seconding the Motion proposed by the hon.
Member for the University.

assurance although they say it was

system.
As to the first, that is transfer to the

That probably is the reason why no legislation was attempted in that direction at that
time as regards the method of carrying on
the business prior to the passing of these
Acts on both sides of the Channel.
There is no doubt that at that time many
Companies and Societies of repute were conducting their business fairly and with a
reasonable regard to the interests of their
policy holders. There is no doubt, however,
that side by side with this there was a great
volume of business conducted without any
real desire to safeguard the interests of the
policy holders. The public conscience was so
stirred in the matter that in May, 1919, the
Board of Trade set up a representative Committee under the Chairmanship of Lord
Parmoor to inquire into the whole business.
The Committee found that the employment
of these men, this army of collectors, was a
very costly business, and that in the majority
of cases they enjoyed quite extravagant remuneration as considered in relation to the
premium income of the companies.
business was, and is, conducted by Joint

as much as 30 per cent., while on the average

The
Hon. Members will understand that the
position of the collector was one for which
there was considerable competition, and that
the privilege of making a particular collection was readily marketable. The Committee found that as much as £200 to £300
would be paid for the privilege of collecting
£10 per week, and of that £10 so collected
it was not unusual for the agent to receive
£2 10s as his remuneration. There also

secure and keep securing a large number of
new customers. The result was that an intensive campaign for new business was being
continually carried on. Mothers were

Again, the mover said-I took a note at the
time and I hope it is accurate-that the
agent gets the applicant to sign the form
and then fills in the necessary particulars
himself. That is almost in contravention of
the Act, and if the agent does fill in any
particulars the company cannot afterwards
question the accuracy of the details so filled
in. That was very important, and a safeguard was introduced into our Act which
certainly should have done away with abuses
of that kind. Then in the matter of lapsed
policies very considerable protection is given,
that is to say, a new paid-up policy must be
issued under certain conditions in exchange
for the lapsed policy, and the premiums will
not be lost altogether after 7th June, 1928,
in cases where five years' premiums have
been paid, owing to the requirement that
free paid-up policies must be given on the
forfeiture of any policies. I may say that
the reason for the postponing of this benefit
of giving these free paid-up policies in exchange for lapsed policies till June, 1928, is
that it is necessary to give the weaker companies and societies time to make provision
to meet the stipulated benefits. In view of the
fact that the report on the first year's working of our Act will be presented to this
House in a short time, my hon. Friend (Dr.
Morrison), may think that he has been a
little anxious and prematurely zealous on behalf of those in whom he takes such interest
and may allow this matter to stand over till
he receives this report.

the public who are interested in this question should get the information contained in
the Report at a cheaper figure than it is
published at now.
One is glad to welcome the advent of
economy on the Government benches. One
is always glad to welcome economy in Government administration, but on this occasion,
to spend £600 on a cheaper issue of this
Report might mean a great deal more economy
in the administration of our affairs in the
future, than has been evident up to now.'
What I mean by that is this. If the people
of Belfast, by reason of the fact that the

read the Report and the Commissioner's
statement regarding the mal-administration
that has taken place in the provision of
houses for the people, it may induce them to
take a very keen interest in the affairs of
the City Council and of the Government,
By getting this Report for 6d they may take
such an interest in public affairs that they
will see economy is brought about, not only
in civic, but in Government affairs.
Members opposite are quite aware that
there is a tremendous interest being taken
in this Report, and a very considerable

Mr. DEVLIN: The Government have regarded this whole business as a very important matter. They so regarded it when they
appointed a Special Commissioner,
understand, at the request of the City Corporation. The result of it has been a very
costly inquiry. A tremendous sum has been
spent on legal expenses, partly by the
Northern Government, partly by the City
Corporation, and partly by persons interested
in the explorations of the Commission.
Having regard to that tremendous expense-
I think £3,000 odd it cost the Government
and the City Council-£100 a day-and also
to the cost of the Inquiry to the individuals
concerned, I cannot for the life of me understand why the Government want to confine
the knowledge of the result of the Inquiry to
a very limited number of people.
This Inquiry was of the greatest possible
interest and concern to the working classes
of the community. We have been discussing
here almost day after day the question of
housing. It is the biggest and most vital
concern of the common people, and therefore I think it is all-important, if we are to
have sound and honest civic administration,
that the report of this Commissioner should
reach the home of nearly everyone who is
interested in housing, and that is practically
every citizen in the community. What
workingman can afford to buy a copy of this
report at 5/-? I do not see why the Government, when they were not making it a document easily accessible to the masses of the
people, should have gone to any expense at
all, because the people who pay 5/- for a
document of that sort could easily have paid
£1 for it. They could have allowed any.ne
who liked to print it, and anyone who was
very much interested to go and buy it at £1.
If the purpose of publishing it at all is to
allow the findings to pierce their way into
the homes of the people, who are preeminently the parties concerned, then it
ought to be published at a price that would
make it easily accessible to all these people.
The right hon. Gentleman (Mr. Pollock)
says, why should the taxpayers of our
Northern Province pay for this report when
it does not concern them? It does concern
them. An hon. Gentleman suggested that
the cost of the report should be 3d. I would
suggest that it should be sold for a penny in
the country, for the benefit of the people of
Limavady. No doubt they will have a report
of their own, and I would like to know how
many people in County Derry will buy that
report if you are going to charge the same
price for it. Then the right hon. Gentleman
says you can read the report in the newspapers. A great many people do not read
newspapers at all. At all events, when you
buy a newspaper you put it to one side
if you are busy, and you do not see it
again, but when a report is published in a
Blue Book or in pamphlet form you put
it to the one side that is, if you
have any civic pride and after you have
ceased to be shocked and you want to settle
down into a condition of mental inquiry,
you lift the document again. Therefore, 1
do not think there is any point at all in the
assertion of the right hon. Gentleman that
if anyone wanted to read this Report he
could do so in the newspapers. The newspaper report is an abbreviated report, although it is a very long report. The papers
gave very considerable space to it. Notwithstanding that, I do not think the people
would be satisfied with having it in that
form; they would want to have it in
pamphlet form, such as has been published
here at a cost of 5s.
I press this matter from the point of
view that the Government regarded it as
so important that they spent £3,000 upon
the Inquiry; secondly, that if they thought
it worth while to publish the Report at any
price they ought to have published it at a
price that would make it accessible to the
people; and, finally, it is all-important that
when an inquiry of this sort takes place
the people should have in some substantial
and permanent form a record of the deliberations of the Inquiry, and the judgment
of Mr. Megaw who conducted the Inquiry.

As I say, the matter is very important. I
believe that many of our constitutional institutions are hanging in the balance. There
is a tendency to suppress municipal authorities, not only in Ireland, but elsewhere. I
an all the time for the maintenance of whatever democratic principles in the constitution we have. I do not believe in
autocracies, and I do not believe in handing
over to autocrats control of the people's
affairs. I think the only way to prevent
Bolshevism or Mussolini-ism is to preserve
the purity of our civic administration, to
exercise a keen watchfulness on the part of
ali concerned in our civic and public administration, and to give every encouragement
to the common people to take a practical and
continuous interest in the manner in which
their vital affairs are carried on.
Therefore I would again say to
right hon. Gentleman that since
sound governmental

he ought to find
it equally sound economics-because it is
equally sound business-to spend a further
sum in spreading amongst the
common
people the knowledge of what has been done
under the administration of the City Council in relation to housing matters.
The housing question, as I have said, is
one of the biggest and most vital of all our
public concerns. I do not want to repeat
what I have said so often in this House and
elsewhere, that I believe bad housing is the
cause of nearly all our vices and our
miseries, that if you have decent, clean and
sanitary houses and comfortable homes for
the people, you have the best safeguard
against criminality and disease and all the
evils incidental to bad housing conditions.
But if you are going to let the people feel
that their housing interests are to be played
fast and loose with, either by elected representatives or any other authorities, then I
am afraid that you will cause such a spirit
of mistrust amongst the people themselves
that they will cease to have faith in public
men or in democratic and constitutional
government. As one who believes in every
safeguard for the preservation of our constitutional rights, I think the more a document
of that sort is scattered widespread amongst
the people the better it will be in the public
interests.
Mr. WILLIAM MCMULLEN: The Government have attempted to make great play out
of the fact that the Press of Belfast have
given considerable space to this Report. I
know a large number of people have come
to borrow the copy of the Report that I was
fortunate enough to get from the Belfast
Corporation who have absolutely no faith in
the Belfast Press giving them the truth of
the whole matter. (A laugh.) The right
hon. Gentleman (Mr. Pollock) laughs. I d
distinctly remember that one of the most
important points in connection with the
whole inquiry was suppressed by one of the
leading papers in Belfast. I refer to the aspect of the matter in which the late Mr.
Crotty of Messrs. Crotty & Aicken, was
acting in a dual capacity as valuer for the
Corporation and agent for the vendors. A:
a matter of fact, on returning from a visit
to Dublin, I bought two Belfast papers, one
an evening paper, and one a morning paper.
One of those papers made no mention of the
fact that Mr. Crotty had acted in a dual
capacity. As a result, I have heard that
matter discussed in many parts of Belfast,
and there has also been comment on the
attitude that the Belfast Press have adopted
since the Report was issued. I have heard
it stated repeatedly that, with the exception
of one paper, no lead has been given in the
Press of Belfast to the public as to what
should be done to the people who have been
adjudged guilty of mal-practices and maladministration in the Corporation.
I should point out, as has been pointed out
before, that there is a great desire on the
part of the people to have the full Report,
so that the salient features and important
points in the Report should not be kept
back from the people. There is a great
suspicion in the minds of the people that
the Press of Belfast is not giving them the
whole truth, and the people are anxious to
ascertain the full findings of the Commission
that was appointed. In view of the many
things that will come up in the Estimates
as we go along, I do not think it is a strong
argument for the Government to say it
would not be good economy, on their part,
to publish this Report, even at a loss of £600.
because, after all, it would not be a loss. I
hold that money spent in educating the
public is not lost at all. As we go through
the Estimates, we will probably be able to
point out to the Government that larger
sums are being spent for a much less useful
purpose, than the amount it would cost the
Government to issue this Report at a nominal
price. For these reasons, I would like the
Government to reconsider this matter. They
are possibly adopting this attitude out of
consideration for the people who have been
impeached. I cannot understand any other
reason for their attitude. The argument of
economy does not strike me as being sound
at all. There may be a desire on the part
of the Government to save the people impugned in the Report. Powerful influences
are being brought to bear at the moment
with the object of trying to save some of the
people who have been adjudged culpable up
to the moment. If the Government cannot
give us a more satisfactory reason for refus-

Mr. KYLE: Could the Prime Minister tell

The PRIME MINISTER: The business of
this week will be devoted entirely to the
taking of certain estimates for the services
for 1926-1927. On Wednesday, the 14th inst.,
the Estimates for Old Age Pensions, Unemployment Grants, County Court Officers,
and Miscellaneous Legal Charges, and
Stationery and Printing will be taken, and
on Thursday, the 15th inst., Houses of Parliament, Cabinet Offices, Widows', Orphans',
and Old Age Contributory Pensions, and
Record Office.

is concerned the current year has been
normal. So far as the volume of business
is concerned the year compares favourably
with the preceding year. I do not think
the Estimates call for any further comment
from me.
