sum of £2,900 for fees for Crown prosecutions
to people apart from the Attorney-General.
I would like the Prime Minister to say
whether he believes this is in the interests
of Ulster. I would like to know exactly what
Ulster is. A man whom they executed in
Ireland said that Ireland was not of the
chemical properties that constituted Ireland,
but was of the men, women and children.
I would like to know whether the Prime
Minister's conception of Ulster is the
chemical properties of which it is constituted
or the men, women and children?
The CHAIRMAN: I think the hon.
Member ought not to pursue that. It must
be apparent that I could not permit a
scientific excursion into the region of
chemistry on a Vote of this kind.
Mr. WM. McMULLEN: No one will
possibly know better than yourself that
whatever my abilities I certainly could not
give a scientific disquisition on chemistry or
kindred subjects. For that reason I have
no intention of embarking on such a dissertation as you suggest. I want to confine
myself to this Estimate that is under consideration. I would like to know, and I
think I have a right to ask in view of the
amount of destitution and unemployment
that exists in Northern Ireland at the
present time how right hon. Gentlemen view
this question. If Ulster means the men,
women, and children that constitute this
part of the country, and the Prime Minister
and those associated with him have got the
love of Ulster-meaning the people-that
they profess to have in the daily Press, I
would like to know if it is playing the part
of the big brother and protecting the weak
members of the community to say that one
gentleman should have £3,500 and then to
pay to members of the legal fraternity £2,900
outside the duties which the right hon. and
learned Gentleman (Mr. Babington) performs
as Attorney-General. It is scarcely good
enough to sit quietly on the Government
benches without giving a reasonable explanation or justification-if there is any-for
what in my judgment is an extravagant expenditure, and I certainly will give very
whole-hearted support to the Amendment to
reduce this Vote by the amount suggested.
I perhaps would allow the matter to pass in
ordinary circumstances, but we are living
under very extraordinary circumstances, and
I do not think a Vote of this kind is justified at the present time.
Mr. LEEKE: In rising to support this
Amendment I should like to ask for some
information about this item of £150 for
defence of public officials. I should like to
know if in that sum is included the defence
of cases which the police may bring up before
the County or Petty Sessions Courts. I think
it is ridiculous that public officials like
police, chancing their arms in cases in which
there is really no evidence such as excessive
motor speeds or breaking the licensing lawsshould bring defendants before the Courts,
and then if the case goes against the police
it turns out that the defendant has to pay
the costs of the public officials. I think that
is ridiculous and that where a case goes
against the police the Crown should pay the
expenses and not the defendant. It is most
unfair that there should be any encouragement given by the Government to public
officials, who are anxious in most cases to
bring themselves before the authorities in
order to get promotion, to chance their arm,
as I said, and place themselves before their
superiors by some case in which they are
beaten. If they are beaten then I hold that
the Crown should pay the costs. It is ridiculous, and it encourages officials to bring cases
for which there are not substantial grounds,
and it is a waste of public money caused by
the action of public officials. I hold that
every discouragement should be shown by the
Government in order to check that practice
and to save public money, and where judges
and magistrates think it necessary they
should be able to give a decision against the
costs being paid by the defendants, and the
costs should be charged to the Crown. That
would discourage officials from bringing
ridiculous cases.
The ATTORNEY-GENERAL: The hon.
Member for West Belfast (Mr. William
McMullen) has described this Estimate as
scandalous, but, fortunately, he added that
he did so without having any real knowledge
upon the subject. He need not have added
the addendum that he made to his criticism
of the Estimate because I think the Committee will have gathered that fact from his
criticism without his having admitted it
himself. Everybody who knows anything
about the way in which justice is administered in this country knows that it is quite
impossible for the Law Officers of the Crown
to conduct all the numbers of prosecutions
which have to be brought during the course
of a year and which are reflected in these
Estimates. Every prosecution that is brought
has to be laid before the Attorney-General,
in the first instance, all the evidence has to
be read, and if there is anything that has to
Supply-
Committee.
14 APRIL 1926
be cleared up or that remains in doubt, it has
to be cleared up one way or the other before
a prosecution is directed, and in numbers of
cases which come before the Attorney-General
prosecutions are refused on the ground that
the evidence is not satisfactory or
on the
ground that in law the person who is accused
is not guilty of the offence charged against
him.
In addition to that the Attorney-General
has to be on hand during the whole year
for the purpose of advising not only the
Government themselves but all the various
Government Departments upon matters
which arise from day to day, some of them
legal questions, some of them constitutional
questions. These have to be decided as
quickly as possible in order that the business of the community may proceed, and
everybody knows quite well that at the
present time there is a vast amount of work
which has to be done in the Legal Department in Northern Ireland, owing to the
fact that the constitution is new, and that
every day matters of great constitutional
importance are arising owing to the conflict
between the law as adapted to this country
and the law of the United Kingdom in
general. These matters have to be dealt
with immediately as they arise, and the
Attorney-General has to be on hand to deal
with them.
So far as the actual physical prosecutions
and the conduct of all the numerous prosecutions that occur either at the Criminal
Assizes in Belfast, or at the numerous Assizes which take place twice a year in the
country, and the Winter Assizes, are concerned, those have always been conducted
by regularly-appointed Crown Prosecutors,
and I may say for the information of the
Committee that those Crown Prosecutors
are paid at a very much lower rate than
that at which the ordinary private practitioner is paid. That sum of £2,900, which
has been the subject of criticism, and which
appears in the Estimate as "Fees to Counsel," includes not only the fees to counsel
in respect of all the Crown prosecutions at
the Belfast Criminal Assizes, at the Winter
Assizes, and at the County Assizes in July
and March, but it also includes the other
fees that are paid to counsel in respect of
civil business in which the Crown is a
litigant, just as any other person who appears before the Court.
I beg to state here on behalf of the Legal
Department and of the Government that,
whatever may be said about any other Department of the Crown, this Department is
administered as economically as it possibly
could be. There is no private citizen, there
is no firm of solicitors in this country that
could administer the amount of business

that is administered by the Legal Department at anything like the figure that appears in this Estimate. When you take
into account the amount of money that has
to be paid to assistants, the fees that are
expected and paid-and legitimately paidby ordinary litigants these are moderate
and moderate in the extreme.
One or two other criticisms have been
passed upon this Estimate. The hon. Member for Down (Mr. P. O'Neill) has asked
for an explanation of the difference between
the salaries, as set out in the schedule of
the Estimate, and the actual Estimate which
the Committee is asked to pass. Those
variations are accounted for by the war
bonus which these officials have been receiving under statute. Some of them have
been reduced, but these war bonuses have
been continued since the salaries were
raised in that way during the war, and the
differences some of them are not very
great are accounted for by those bonuses.
It has also been pointed out by the hon.
Member that there is an increase in these
fees to counsel of £300 this year. It is
quite impossible to have a fixed amount for
those fees paid to counsel, because the
Crown in one year may be involved in very
heavy civil litigation, which may necessitate the expenditure of a larger sum than
in other years, and, in addition to that,
the number of prosecutions which occur
for criminal offences is a matter over which
neither the Government nor the Law Officers
of the Crown have any control, and it is
only at the end of the year that it is possible to say what expenditure is necessary
in that respect.
In regard to the point that has been
raised with reference to the Under Sheriffs
and the fees payable to the Sheriff of
Belfast being only £150, whereas the fees payable to the Under Sheriff for Londonderry
County and City are £300, that is a matter
which is settled by statute. I am not at the
present moment exactly aware of what other
remuneration the Under Sheriffs receive,
but I know that they do receive a considerable amount of remuneration from other
sources. Without having that information
it is impossible to draw any comparison between either Tyrone and Belfast or be-
Wetween other counties and Belfast, but the
Committee may take it that, so far as these
salaries are concerned, they are statutory
salaries, and until they are altered by legislation in this House they must appear in
the Estimates in the form and shape in
which they appear in the statute under
which they have to be paid.
I do not think there is anything further
in respect of this Estimate to which I need
refer. One of the hon. Members-I think it

As to the basis of cost of publications that
entered a good deal into the discussion
carried on yesterday it is the desire of the
Government in the matter of Government
publications that great regard should be given
to the ability of the persons interested in that
publication to pay the price demanded for
its issue. The cost of issuing any Government publication is borne by the Department
from which it originates, but then the
Stationery Department takes over the supply
at what is fixed as the market or sale price,
and any loss-the difference between the cost
of producing the publication and the amount
which we hope to realise eventually by the
sale or disposal-has to be borne by the Department from which the publication originates. I may say for the information of
hon. Members that even a publication of this
sort, the Estimates, costs about 10s. to produce, but as hon. Members will see the sale
price of this to the ordinary public is 4s.,
it being considered desirable and a justifiable
thing in the public interest that the Government should bear that difference in the cost
of the publication. This is a matter of
very great public interest throughout the
whole Six Counties.
I should like to assure the hon. Member
for Down (Mr. O'Neill) who raised the
question as to whether the printing was done
by contract or otherwise that I am in complete sympathy with him in the matter, and
that we did get competitive tenders for all
the printing work. We are always particularly anxious to receive competitive bids
from stationers and printers throughout the
Six Counties. Being a representative of a
county myself I can assure him I am particularly jealous on that point, to see that no
one should be at a disadvantage in tendering

I can assure hon. Members that every care

realise that the amount asked for under
this Estimate is to provide the sums

the different Acts are entitled to receive.
The administrative expenditure incurred

Supply-

formed part of the Old Age Pensions

other Votes for the Ministry of Finance are

Secondly, the Estimate now provides for
the first time for the cost of Old Age
Pensions which are payable by virtue of the
Widows', Orphans' and Old Age Contributory Pensions Act of 1925. This new expenditure is shown separately in Sub-head
B, page 38, from the normal Pension charge
under Sub-head A.
The net increase of £153,000 in the Estimate is a consequence of the passing of
legislation in this House during last year.
Of the total increase, £114,000 is due to the
Old Age Pensions Act (Northern Ireland),
1925, and £39,000 to the Widows', Orphans'
and Old Age Contributory Pensions Act
(Northern Ireland), 1925. In point of fact,
the increased charge under the Old Age
Pension Act of 1925 is greater by about
£127,000, but owing to the facts that the
amount provided for the payment of pensions
in the past year was somewhat overestimated, and that a certain number of
pensioners, estimated at 500, who receive
pensions at less than the maximum rates
will have their pensions increased to the
maximum rates under the Widows',
Orphans' and Old Age Contributory Pension
Act and transferred to Sub-head B,' the
actual increased charge in the Estimate
under Sub-head A is reduced to the figure
mentioned above, namely, £114,000.
Hon. Members will remember that it was
stated in the White Paper issued when the
Bill for the modification of the statutory
condition as to means was introduced last
Session that an addition is expected of
approximately 5,500 pensioners-some at
modified rates-through the operation of that
Measure, while it is probable that the
majority of the 3,500 persons who, prior to
1st April this year, were in receipt of reduced pensions only, will now have their
pensions increased to the maximum rate.
Sub-head B.-Pensions (Insured Persons)—
provides for a nine months' charge only as
the Service begins on 2nd July, 1926, in respect of Old Age Pensions payable under
the Contributory Old Age Pensions Scheme.
I should, perhaps, remind hon. Members
that Contributory Pensions are paid to
persons over 70 from voted moneys irrespective of the statutory conditions as to
means, residence
or nationality of the
pensioners under the Old Age Pensions Acts
-otherwise the provisions of the Old Age
Pensions Acts apply to these pensioners.
It is estimated that as from the commencing date, 1,500 new pensioners will draw
pensions under the Act, and, in addition,
500 persons who, under the ordinary Old Age
Pensions Acts (Sub-head A) draw pensions
at less than the 10s rate, will now be transferred to Sub-head B, and will have their
pensions brought up to the maximum rate
of 10s a week.
The cost of administering the Contributory
Old Age Pensions Scheme is a liability of the
Ministry of Labour and consequently the
administrative costs, including the payments
made to Imperial Agent Departments, are defrayed from the Vote for the administrative
expenses of the Ministry of Labour. Such
costs are finally chargeable against the
Pensions Account, and a payment is, therefore, made from the Pensions Account to the
credit of the Ministry of Labour Vote. That,
of course, refers to pensions paid to insured
persons, because the responsibility for administration under the ordinary Old Age
Pension Act rests with the Ministry of
Finance. I beg to move.

but a misapprehension exists as to the

Supply-
Committee.
HOUSE OF COMMONS
Mr. KYLE: An entrance fee.
Mr. POLLOCK: If you like. This amounts
in the aggregate to a very large sum of
money, to a good many thousands of pounds,
and the Government by law and by custom
which has existed from time immemorial
have been in the habit of giving them a

order that they may assist in the education
of their members.
In regard to the £500 grant in aid to the
Inn of Court, this is following also a practice that has existed from time immemorial.
A considerable sum of money was granted
by the Imperial Government to the Inns of
Court in Dublin, and when the separation
took place and an Inn of Court was established here it was only following the practice
that had been adopted. It must be borne
in mind that the purpose of this £500, which
is spoken of here as a grant in aid, is not
necessarily for barristers. It is for the
judges and all members of the Court in
order that they may have their law reports,
their reference books, and all kinds of
literature for the purpose of assisting in
the administration of the law. Therefore,
this £500, which is called a grant in aid,
is not really a grant in aid for barristers
at the Bar, but a grant for the purpose of
assisting in the administration of the
general law of the land in the different
Courts.
Mr. BEATTIE: Might I ask just on a

that Inn of Court in Dublin, to which the

of Court. I would like to know whether that

The ATTORNEY-GENERAL: This question is one which agitated the legal profession
in Northern Ireland for a considerable time
before a solution was found for it. As the
Committee are aware, prior to the Act of
1920 the legal profession in Ireland was one
and undivided and all the members of the
profession graduated in the King's Inns in
Dublin. That had not always been so, because in more remote times members of the
legal profession in Ireland had to eat their
dinners and take their terms out in London;
but from the time the jurisdiction was conferred upon the King's Inns we trained our
own lawyers at home. The King's Inns
Library when it was set up was one of the
libraries which originally had the privilego
of getting a copy of every book that was
published, and consequently they had a
magnificent library. That privilege was afterwards compounded, and a sum of money was
paid each year by the Imperial Government
to the King's Inns for the purpose of maintaining their library. That was done as a
public matter. It was not done as a private
matter, and the library that was bought out
of those funds was not a private library.
One of the hon. Members opposite has said
why do not the lawyers out of their large
fees pay for their own libraries. I may inform the Committee that they do. There is
no lawyer in Northern Ireland in decent
practice who has not got a library of his own
-in most cases a great deal more valuable
than the amount of money that is to be found
in this Estimate-because, unfortunately, the
law has now reached such a stage of complication that a library for even private use
runs into somewhere about £1,000. But in
addition to that there must of necessity be
some public library, to which students have
access and to which young members of the
profession have access in order to consult
authorities which they are not able to purchase for themselves. That is done in order
to keep up the profession of the law,
and to keep up the knowledge of the
community in law, and the benefit
of that is reflected in public matters,
because when a member of the public hires a
barrister he expects to get somebody who
knows what he is talking about, and unless
some proper library is established where
people can learn their business and where
they can have access to the authorities it is
quite impossible that the knowledge of the
law should be at all adequate.
I think the Committee will realise that
nowadays this question of the law is one of
the largest and most important matters in
the State. If the Committee will only think
it over they will realise that there is hardly
an action that a man takes from the time he
gets up in the morning until he goes to bed
at night which is not governed by law. His
house is ruled by law; he is protected in his
bed by the criminal law; he is protected,
again, as he walks to his business in the
morning by the criminal law; he is protected
also by the law of negligence; if he is a workman, when he gets into the workshop in the
morning to do his work he is protected by
the Factory Acts and by the Workmen's
Compensation Acts, and if anything goes
wrong with him during the course of his business he has the Pension Acts, which have
to be construed, and to which he is entitled
to resort for compensation. In the same way
his employer is governed by law from morning till night. He has the company laws
with which he has to comply, and a hundred
and one other statutes which rule his conduct of his life and business from the time
he goes into business until the day he leaves
it.
If some hon. Members of the Committee
would only devote a little time to finding out
Supply-
Committee.
14 APRIL 1926
the amount of material that has now been
accumulated on the legal side of the community, the amount of authorities that have
to be consulted, the number of statutes that
have to be read in order to deal with even
the simplest proposition they would realise
that this study of the law is a matter of most
immense importance. When we, through no
fault of our own-we members of the legal
profession in Northern Ireland-severed our
connection with King's Inns it became necessary for us, in order to educate the members
of our own profession in Northern Ireland,
to set up some form of library to which the
young people could have access and to which
the practising barrister could also have access
for the purpose of discharging his duty to the
public.
It has been suggested here-it is not the
first time I have heard it suggested-that we
voluntarily severed our connection with the
King's Inns in Dublin. The way in which that
occurred was this: It was perfectly obvious
that originally we could not set up any form of
body which could adequately deal with legal
education in Northern Ireland. The root of
the jurisdiction and the right of the barrister
to practise depends originally upon the
authority of his Majesty's judges, who say
who is to practise in their Courts. The right
of audience depends upon the authority of the
judges, and as it depended upon the authority
of the judges from time to time they delegated that power to the Inn of Court across
the water. That precedent was followed in
this country, and they then said that any
student whose credentials had been inquired
into, who had partaken the necessary terms,
who had passed the necessary examination,
and who had been certified by the Benchers
as being fit to have audience in Court-they
then said they would grant audience to those
members. But if you will think over it for a
moment you will see that it is quite obvious
that that could not obtain in Northern Ireland so long as the jurisdiction to authorise
the members of the profession to practise was
in the hands of the King's Inns in Dublin,
because, while the authority to certify a
barrister as having passed the necessary
examination would be vested in the body in
Dublin, the authority to say whether that
individual should practise or not would
remain with our judges here, and they would
have no power or control over the body in
Dublin which certified the individual
having the right to practise.
as
Consequently it was absolutely essential
that we should set up some body in Northern
Ireland which should undertake the legal
education here and which should be subject
to the authority of the judges of our own
Courts and not subject to the authority of
the judges of the Free State. It became absolutely essential for us to set up a body of
our own, and as a result of our doing that
we lost our interest in the library which had
been accumulated for so many years in the
King's Inns in Dublin, and we had nothing
corresponding to it to take its place in this
Province. It is also, I think, pretty obvious
that this being a public matter it would be
quite impossible to start that library by
private enterprise, but I have no doubt that
in course of time owing to private enterprise
we shall be able considerably to augment it.
Consequently, by this grant which appears
on the Estimate we have got a sum of money
which will give us at any rate the very minimum of a nucleus for a library for the Inn
of Court of Northern Ireland. It will enable
us to place at the disposal of our students
some means of making themselves acquainted
with these matters of law and legal decision
and statute law, which it is necessary they
should become familiar with before they are
fitted to transact any business before the
Courts. Accordingly, I submit to the Committee with some confidence that this is, after
all, a public matter, one which is absolutely
necessary not only in the interests of the
profession but in the interests of the public,
and that it is most reasonable and proper expenditure to be made by the Government in
regard to the position in which the profession
finds itself.

nection with the administration of the law

mate has been drawn. I should like to draw

THE LAND ACT-APPOINTED DAY.
1. Mr. DEVLIN asked the Minister of
Finance whether he will represent to the
Imperial Government the necessity of expediting the appointed day under the Northern Ireland Land Act, so that it may be
fixed generally not later than the first day
of May.
The MINISTER OF FINANCE (Mr. Pollock): I assume that the hon. Member is
referring to the fixing of appointed days for
the vesting of estates in the Land Purchase
Commission. It will be realised that it
would be impossible without an inordinate increase of staff for dates to be arranged
instanter.
I am satisfied that the Commission are
proceeding with the administration of the

circumstances I do not consider it necessary
to make representation to the Imperial
Government in the sense suggested by the
hon. Member.

DEPORTATION ORDERS.
5. Mr. O'NEILL asked the Minister of
Home Affairs whether he will state the
number of persons on whom he has served
deportation orders in Northern Ireland, and
when he proposes to withdraw these orders.
Sir DAWSON BATES: Fifteen Orders
under Regulation 23A made under the Civil
Authorities (Special Powers) Act (Northern
Ireland), 1922, prohibiting entry to or
residence in certain specified areas in
Northern Ireland, have been served which
are still in force.
Of the fifteen persons affected by these
Orders, 6 are not ordinarily resident in any
part of Northern Ireland.
These Orders are kept constantly under
review, and are withdrawn when their
continuance is no longer considered
necessary. It is not possible to state when
withdrawal can be made in any particular
case.

efficient ways and manners that any Chairman of Ways and Means could do, £1,500 is
too high a figure for the salary of the Chairman of Ways and Means for the Six Counties.
We have been told in the past that the
working-class people had to go step by step
with Great Britain. If we are going to ask
the under-dog to go step by step with Great
Britain we are bound to ask the heads and
officials of the House also to consider the
people whom they govern and for whom they
legislate. We are legislating for a million
and a quarter people, and, while I recognise
that it is just as easy to legislate for five
millions as for a million and a quarter, still
the million and a quarter are not so able
to bear the expense as the five millions are.
Therefore, under that head I think £1,500
is really too much for the Chairman of Ways
and Means.
The next point I come to is in regard to
the Members of the Senate. We are asked
to vote a sum of £940 this rear as against
£400 last year, plus an addition on page 4,
of £100. I do not object to the Senators,
who are not being paid, being given railway
fares, but I would ask the Minister what
class fares are given. Is it first class, or
second class, or third class. This seems an
enormous amount for all the meetings the
Senate holds.
We come down to the Members of the
House of Commons and we find here a reduction. I presume that is on account of
one of the Members on the Government
Benches having been elevated to a higher
position with, I expect, attached to it a
salary of £1,200 or £1,500.
Then we come to "B" (Salaries, wages and
allowances). We find there that there has
been an increase all over, and that there
has been a reduction of the staff. You will
notice from the figures that although we
have got rid of one superfluous member of
the staff, in the person of a messenger at 258
a week, we have instituted instead a second
clerk assistant to the House of Commons at
a salary of £684. That is, we have taken
away one messenger at 258 a week, and we
have substituted a second clerk assistant to
the House at £684. You carried on for four
years, I understand, without this second
clerk assistant, and if you carried on during
those trying years, which you contend were
the hardest, in the life of your Government
then I say you should this year be able to
Supply-
Committee.
15 APRIL 1926
carry on without that extra appointment.
For that reason, I think this appointment
should be reconsidered, thus saving the
amount of money allocated to this particular office.
Other items of the Estimate are in reference to the Sergeant-at-Arms and Black
Rod. While, perhaps, one does not like to
reiterate the opinions expressed by the Opposition time and again, and by some Members
of the Government who had the courage of
their convictions that these positions are too
highly paid, we do believe that one man
should be capable of carrying out the
duties. The Government should be prepared
to economise as much as possible in the upkeep of this Parliament, because economy is
called for by the people of the Six Counties,
and a Commission has been called for by
Members of this House, although the
Government defeated the aims and objects
of the mover of that Amendment. If you do
not economise I believe the continuation of
your Parliament of Northern Ireland will be
shorter than you expect, because I am fully
satisfied that the economic conditions of
the Six Counties will not warrant your
spending money on the Houses of Parliament to the extent set out in this Estimate
which we are asked to pass to-day. If you
are to retain your Parliament intact for the
term of your life and for generations to
come you have got to cut down your Estimate for the Houses of Parliament. The
Minister who set out this Estimate has, I
say, increased every Department and to-day
there is a net increase of £1,269 on last year's
figure. I claim that this is uncalled for. No
increase in work has been put on the staff,
and surely no extra calls have been made on
this House. I believe the calls in the past
were the heaviest and that future calls will
be less, and so less money should be spent
on the Houses of Parliament. Therefore, I
move that a reduction of £1,000 should be
made in this Estimate.

Mr. DEVLIN: Then I am satisfied with

I am here as one of those who represent

of the religion of those who constitute over
35 per cent. of the population. One would

One would have thought that the first

to the Catholic minority whom you invited

Catholic in the Senate

Mr. DEVLIN: With me it is not a question of who is to blame. The question is
that I decline as a representative of 35 per

I am now giving my reasons. After the

this Parliament was entitled to select a

The candidate was a man against whom nothing could be said. He was not a wild
politician. He was not a politician
at all. We selected a leading merchant
honoured by all members of the
community in order that he might be

was appointed. A more indefensible action I

order to protect themselves from attacks of

We have no place in the administration of

city.
Mr. POLLOCK: No.
Mr. DEVLIN: I can give the right hon.

Catholic on the Bench, not a single Judge
in Ulster-
Mr. POLLOCK: Yes, you have.
Mr. DEVLIN-though we constitute 35 per

the very last not to rejoice in that new spirit

The CHAIRMAN: Perhaps the hon.
Member will help me in a little difficulty.
I fully appreciate the line of argument he
is forced to follow. His objection to the
payment of the Senate at all is that his
party is not represented in the Senate.
Obviously a good deal must be allowed by
way of analogy and illustration, but it is
equally obvious that we must not permit
the specific question before us to drift into
something that is only remotely related to
it.
Mr. DEVLIN: In Southern Ireland,
against whose Government on religious
grounds you made so violent a protest that
you got a Parliament of your own, they
proceeded to give nearly half the seats in
the Senato to Protestants. I rejoice at that
and I am very glad to be able to do it,
because a generous act of toleration cannot
be overdone. The result is that the
Protestants were won over, and the Southern
Government have secured the support of the
overwhelming mass of the Protestant population in the South of Ireland. We did not
ask for half the Senate. We did not ask for
a third of the Senate. All we asked for in
the first instance was one Member and you
refused to give it. Therefore, from the point
of view of voting any money for the Senate
I could not conscientiously do so.
I hate to introduce these matters in the
House, but I must remember that I am here
as one of the representatives of the Catholic
minority, and I would be unworthy of my
position and lacking in courage if I did not
come here, no matter whom it pleased or
whom it displeased, and say what I have to
say. You will always have these sectarian
questions raised until you realise that we are
something more than the blacks in South
America. In South America the blacks have
no rights; they have to obey the laws.
They are told that they are allowed to live,
and that is precisely what we are allowed
to do. The only function we are allowed to
discharge is to come here and represent the
people who sent us and try, although we
succeed, to redress the people's
never
grievances.
I understand a compliment was paid to the
right hon. Gentleman, the Prime Minister,
for the gesture of good-will he made towards
the Southern Parliament. Would he make
a gesture of good-will towards the North?
It is not the Southern people who have to
live under this regime; it is the Northerners.
The Southern people have to bear no responsibility, but we have. We have to obey the
laws and we are subject to their administration. We have to bear civic and public
responsibilities, and we are entitled, not
merely to fair play, but to some slight mead
of justice and tolerant treatment at the hands
of the Government. Therefore I say that
every time a Vote of this character is proposed in this House when I can discuss it.
and protest against the treatment we receive
I will take the opportunity of doing so.
With regard to the general question of
economy I am sorry the Member for West
Belfast (Sir Robert Lynn) is not here to
discuss the retrenchment part of these Estimates. It is really a pity that Members of
Parliament will not come to the House and
try to practice what they preach, because
this is the place to do it. I do not go to
the house-tops to attack the Government or
do it in the newspapers. I come here and
attack them face to face, where they can
meet my impeachments if they can, and
where they can deal face to face with the
questions we put forward and the protests
we make. I think it would be desirable
that other Members having other views
should come to the House and discuss them.
I can only say that the carrying on of this
Government is a very costly experiment.
According to the speech of the Prime
Minister it is going to be a permanent and
enduring factor in the life of the community,
and I quite agree that if the masses of the
people are to be asked to make retrenchments they ought to be shown an example
by the Government itself. I do not, therefore. propose to enter into any of the subjects raised by the hon. Member for East
Belfast (Mr. Beattie), but I take advantage
of the opportunity to make the protest I
have just made.
The PRIME MINISTER: As the hon.

the case.
There was a General Election in
1921 and there were twelve Roman Catholics
returned to this Parliament. Those twelve
representatives had the power in their own
hands, without an ad misericordiam appeal
to Members on this side of the House, to
return, I think three certain, and possibly
four Members to the Senate. (Hon. Members:
Hear, hear.) Those twelve Roman Catholics-
I use the term because the hon. Member
for West Belfast (Mr. Devlin) has introduced

this religious side of the question, and not

repudiated this Parliament, they stayed out

ment was not here to stay, and it was not

Mr. DEVLIN: For all Ireland.
The PRIME MINISTER: There is Home
Rule for all Ireland. Nobody denies it. It
is true there are two Parliaments instead of
one, but it is we on this side of the House
who are endeavouring to carry on. Home
Rule largely because these twelve Roman
Catholic Members kept out of the House and
refused to do their duty as representatives of
the people. Now, forsooth, the Leader of
that Party (Mr. Devlin) comes here to-day
and complains that we do not do what they
themselves would not do when they had the
opportunity. That is my first point.
There was another election to this House
last year, and again twelve Roman Catholics
were returned-I am speaking from memory.
Again only a minority of them have come
here to represent their own views. Whose
fault is that? It is not the fault of the
Senate and it is not the fault of hon.
Members sitting on this side of the House,
but it is a repetition of the fault for which
the Roman Catholics were responsible in
1921. that they did not come here and take
full advantage of their voting strength and
put into the Senate those representatives
they desired. Such a travesty of argument
I have never heard before, even from the
hon. Member.

Southern Protestants had not the power to
secure any seats in the Senate the Southern
Government gave them half the seats.
The PRIME MINISTER: I can answer
that very satisfactorily, indeed. Ulstermen
in the South of Ireland, like loyal men, threw
themselves into the task of helping the
Government of the day to govern the country.
They entered heartily into overy branch of
civic life. Throughout the length and
breadth of Southern Ireland they said,
"There is a Government in power. It is our
duty to support and sustain that Government,
and make it workable." The hon. Member's
followers throughout Northern Ireland did
nothing of the kind. They repudiated and insulted this Parliament, and then, having
changed their tactics-and I am delighted
they have done so and come in here to do
their duty-they blame our party for the
faults they themselves have committed. I do
not think it would be fair of me to transgress
any longer on the patience of the House, but
I can only say that I am prepared to meet.
the hon. Member at any time on any platform to justify the action this Government
has taken since its establishment.

is really very little to be said. There is a
slight saving this year, I think of £112 as
will appear on page 6. So far as the
personnel is concerned, it is exactly the

When this Measure of social reform was
passed in this House we had great hopes and
aims, and I am very glad to be in a position
to say that those hopes and aims have all
been realised. It was a great Measure of
social reform. It has brought brightness,
consolation, and hope into the homes of
many of our people where previously there
was little but despair and distress. It has
been said that this Parliament of ours is
extravagant, that the Government has really
not justified its existence, because it has done
nothing for our industrial classes. This Act
was passed by this House, and personally I
feel that if we had done nothing else since
our Parliament was established but pass this
great Measure, considering the advantages

which it confers upon 80 many of our

Mr. KYLE: The Minister of Labour said.
it had been stated the Government is extravagant. We have never really charged the

other way-that they have not treated Le

see the
Government treat them. While it is true

very considerably alleviated the hardships
that these women and children had to
undergo, yet there are a great many drawbacks in the scheme itself, as was outlined
at the time the Measure was going through
the House. While that payment of £42,000
does represent an increased measure of happiness in the homes of the people concerned
there are cases of, I might almost say, unsympathetic administration by the right 1cn.
Gentleman's department. I can give you the
case of a woman whose husband had been
lying in bed for a period of nine years prior
to his death. That woman has not received
a pension, despite the fact that her husband'
was an insured person.
Mr. ANDREWS: Was he drawing benefit?
Mr. KYLE: He drew disablement benefit
after he had exhausted his ordinary health
insurance. Up to now that woman has not
got her pension. The Widows' and Orphans'
scheme which the Minister has asked this
Estimate for is undoubtedly what he has
described it, a Measure of social reform,
but I do think that the faults of the Measure
are becoming more and more apparent to
the public and also to the widows and
orphans who thought that the Measure was
going to mean considerably more to them.
I do not want to belittle in any way the
pleasure and happiness that the £42,000 bas
given to the people who get it, but there are
a very considerable number of widows who
are not entitled to the benefits under the
scheme and whom we would desire to see
included. They might be included if the
Minister would adminster the law in the
sympathetic way that one would think the
right hon. Gentleman would do. There are
cases of hardships, and there are cases where
it is difficult to get evidence of the husband's
death, and equally difficult to find out
whether or not the husband had been in an
insured position for two years preceding his
death. All these regulations make it extremely difficult for us in some instances, of
which the right hon. Gentleman's department has had notice, to welcome the Measure
in the way we would like if it had been a
real pension scheme instead of what it is, an
insurance scheme. I do say, however, that
despite these limitations the scheme itself
has brought a considerable amount of satisfaction to a very considerable number of
people, and I do earnestly entreat the
Minister of Labour to give sympathetic consideration to the claims that come beiole
his department from time to time. Where
the regulations do not debar people altogether, I think he might infuse into this
Measure a little more of the milk of human
kindness. If he infuses some of the generosity that one would associate with the right
hon. Gentleman in administering such an
important Measure as this, the widows and
orphans of the Six Counties will have reason
to bless him.
Mr. DEVLIN: I just desire to say a word
or two on the Estimate which the right

With him I rejoice that so many of the

The provisions of this Act only apply to the
widows and orphans of insured persons, but

Of course, that is not so
We are, I see, to pass an Economy Bill.
I do not know what it is. It is a very

If it proposes to save large sums of money,

Now, I was a strong supporter of this Act.

Yes, I constantly was pressing for the

from

the Minister of Labour was informed of the

This always reminds me how easy it is to

Mr. MILLER: I would like to put a
conundrum to the right hon. Gentleman (Mr.
Andrews), and it is: When is an orphan
not an orphan?" A case was brought to my
notice some time ago and I thought the
party was very badly treated. The case was
that of a widow whose husband had been a
delicate man. He died and left the widow
and two small children. The widow remarried in August last. She put in a claim
for pension for the children but not for herself, because she could not get it. The pension
was refused, and the matter was brought to
my notice.
I went to the Ministry about
it, and I was told that if she had not been
married until after the 4th January she
would have been entitled to a pension of
18s a week, but that immediately on her
marriage she would lose the 10s, while the
pensions for the children would continue. But
as she had married before January the
children were left out in the cold. That is
the way the matter stands at present. The
man she married is a soldier, serving his
King and country in Egypt, and she is doubly
a widow, or rather a grass widow. There are
probably many cases of that sort, and 1
would ask the right hon. Gentleman to give
them his earnest consideration.
Mr. BEATTIE: I wish to take this opportunity to call attention to exceptional circumstances that have come under my notice.
Our Act as it stands requires further legislation in order to make the whole of it
operative. Section 44 is lying dormant at
the present time; it cannot become operative
until this House passes a Legitimising Bill.
I may be wrong, but I have received replies
from the authorities to that effect. Section
44 applies to illegitimate children. A husband
dying leaves a woman with a child, which
is called an illegitimate child. That widow
is not qualified for the pension. I had one
case brought under my notice of a naval
man, who was the father of a child. He
went to sea, and coming home at the end
of twelve months he married the girl. But
he died four months after the marriage. The
widow applied for a widow's and orphan's
pension, but owing to Section 44 not being
rendered operative by a further Legitimising
Bill her application was refused.
I would also like to bring before the notice
of the Minister the case of widows who
claimed the pension prior to the 4th January,
1926. A widow who became a widow prior
to the 4th of January, 1926, will be in receipt
of the pension until her youngest child
attains the age of 14, or, if the child is
attending a continuation school, the age of
16. But her pension will cease when the
child reaches the age of 14 years and 6
months, and she will not be entitled to any
further pension until she becomes 65 years
of age. A lady whose husband died on the
4th January, 1926, or afterwards, and who
is left in a similar position, receives the
pension throughout her life if she does not
re-marry. Is there any way of remedying
that great hardship, which is causing a
good deal of dissatisfaction? I have had
cases brought to my notice in which one
husband died last year and another husband
this year. One has the pension for a limited
period only, and the other has continuity
of pension. I do not know whether it would
be possible to make the Act retrospective in
order to cover those who have been left
widows since 1922, when the depression in
trade set in. In Scotland a widow who ha
had a child previous to her marriage could
obtain the pension for the child. but in
Northern Ireland she could not do that
owing to the absence of a Legitimising Bill.
It has been contended by some Members of
the Government that we are opposing the
Estimates for political reasons. I want to
repudiate that statement.
The CHAIRMAN: I think the hon.
Member had better defer his statement of
the reasons for reducing an Estimate until
he reaches an Estimate on which he makes

doing that in this case.
Mr. BEATTIE: I would like to increase
the amount of money mentioned in this
Estimate. This is a Vote on which I think

and to remove the anomalies, some of which

Another case that I want to bring to the
notice of the Minister is that of the insured
contributor who had 52 stamps to his credit.
His normal occupation was that of a cobbler.
A cobbler is a person employed by shoemakers. who takes the cobbling work home.
I understand that in past years the big warehouses that carried on boot repairing gave
out cobblers' work, but did not class the
cobblers as employees of the firm,
and took no responsibility for paying
health insurance stamps. A cobbler
is now classified as a master shoemaker, and owing to that fact his widow is
not entitled to a widow's pension. The case
I want to refer to is that of a cobbler who
had 52 stamps to his credit, and who was
two years on the sick list before he died.
His widow has been denied the right to a
pension, and she has five little "kiddies" depending upon her. At the present moment
she is carrying on the cobbling business
herself. I called in to see her, and told her
that if it had been possible for me to bring

against me, because the normal occupation

owing to the increase of work in the office

on Record Office work, and he has been relieved to a corresponding extent of some of

has also been necessary to advance the status

instead of receiving a salary on a scale of
£60-£250, plus an allowance of £50 a year,
is placed on the scale of £300, rising by £15
to £400.
There is no other expenditure item to
which attention may be called in the Estimate, but in general it may be stated that
the Office continues to stimulate public
attention, as is evidenced in the collection
and recovery of various types of Ulster records and in a number of very valuable

if hon. Members would bear with me just a

It appears that a member of the family-
Arthur Dobbs-was Governor of North
Carolina between 1754 and 1765, and had
collected information relative to exploration
to discover the North-West Passage into the
Pacific from the Arctic Ocean. The earliest
of these documents was the journal of Henry
Kelsey, covering the period between 1683 and
1722. Kelsey had spent a whole life in
exploration, and was probably the first
Englishman to penetrate from the Hudson
Bay coast to the prairie country of Western
Canada. It was not known that a copy of
this journal was in existence, and the Hudson
Bay Company, in London, as soon as they
heard, sent over members of their staff to
copy the journal in extenso. In addition,
inquiries have been received from Canada
as to the possibility of making manuscript
or printed copies for use in the Dominion.
It may also be mentioned that the Dobbs'
papers include an account of the Quebec
campaign of 1757, evidently by an eye-witness.
This, by the way, gives a different version
of the death scene of General Wolffe from
that which appears in the histories.
Mr. KYLE: Tell us about it.
Mr. BARBOUR: It is available in the
Record Office.
Coming to that part of the Department's work which deals with the replacement of destroyed records-it may be
n:entioned that about 1,400 papers of this
kind have 80 far been received. So in
addition to the mere receiving and recording
of the less interesting legal papers it is
hoped that this may be the means of building matters of considerable historical and
sentimental interest relating to the historical
life of our Province. I beg to move.
Mr. BEATTIE: I am not going to move a
reduction, because I believe the Office is
necessary. But I would like to know, seeing
it is a Record Office Vote, can we in that
Office in any way get at the assets of the
Northern Government. Do you keep
record of the buildings purchased either by
Imperial money or Northern Ireland money?
Can we get at what the assets of the Northern
Government are?
Question put, and agreed to.

Mines (Working Facilities,
Support, &c.) Money.
Considered in Committee under Standing
Order No. 65.
Motion made, and Question proposed:
"That for the purpose of any Act of the
present Session to make provision for facilitating the working of minerals, and for
in posing restrictions on the working of
minerals required for the support of buildings and works, and to amend the law with
respect to Mines, and for purposes connected
therewith, it is expedient to authorise the payment out of moneys provided by Parliament,
subject to Rules made under any such Act,
of the salaries or remuneration and the expenses of the Tribunal appointed to hold
inquiries and determine compensation, and
of the Assessors appointed to sit with the
County Court when hearing appeals, for the
purposes of any such Act."-(Governor's
Recommendation signified.)-(Mr. Barbour.)
Mr. BARBOUR: This is the Mines (Working Facilities, Support, etc.) Money Resolution. The Bill provides for the establishment
of a tribunal consisting of રી practising
barrister, a member of the Panel of Official
Arbitrators appointed under the Acquisition
of Lands (Assessment of Compensation) Act,
1919, and one officer of the Ministry of Commerce. The rate of remuneration to be paid
to these members, and generally the incidental expenses which may be incurred in
connection with any sittings of the tribunal,
will be laid down in accordance with the
provisions of the Bill by Rules to be made by
the Ministry of Commerce with the approval
of the Ministry of Finance. The officer of
the Ministry of Commerce to serve on this
tribunal will be an existing officer of the
Ministry, and consequently no additional
expense will be incurred under this head.
We are, therefore. concerned only with the
fees which may be payable to a barrister and
to a member of the Panel of Official Arbitrators, together with any small incidental
expenses which may arise, and a possible expense in the event of appeals from the
tribunal's awards being made to the County
Court. The Bill in this case provides that
when hearing an appeal under this section
the County Court shall have the assistance
of a specially qualified assessor, who will be
selected from a list of persons of experience
in mining matters to be framed by the
Ministry of Commerce.
I am sure hon. Members will appreciate
that this Bill must be a provisional Measure
to a very great extent. We think it right
that the Government of Northern Ireland
should be in a position of readiness should
the desire originate on the part of anyone to
prosecute the development of minerals within
our borders and it would be a great pity if
any barrier should be found to exist for
which legislative provision had not been
made. The meetings of this tribunal will
only be called very rarely, but it is not
possible to give any idea of what expense may
be involved in providing for this tribunal,
but in any case it is bound to be very light
indeed. I beg to move.

CASE OF MRS. WHAN.

Affairs whether it is a fact that the case of
Mrs. Whan has now been taken out of the
hands of District-Inspector Allen and put
into the hands of the Detective Department,
and whether it is a fact that Mrs. Whan's

Written Answers.
BALLINAMALLARD POLICE BARRACK.
Mr. COOPER asked the Minister of Home
Affairs whether he can state the cause of the
delay in building a police barrack in Ballinamallard, and if he is aware that many complaints have been made owing to the village
being left so long without police protection.
I regret to say
Sir DAWSON BATES:
that the scheme for the reconstruction of
police barracks and for the erection of new
barracks, including one proposed to be bullt
in Ballinamallard, has been delayed for
some months mainly on account of the fact
that if the scheme had been carried out in
its entirety the cost, it is now ascertained,
would have been very much in excess of the
original Estimates.
It has been found necessary, therefore, to
revise the various plans of reconstruction
and erection so as to bring the total cost
within the financial resources at the Government's disposal.
With regard to the latter part of the hon.
Member's question, I may point out that
Ballinamallard is constantly visited by
police from Irvinestown, and I am not aware
of any complaints having been made in the
manner suggested.

The whole question of the reconstruction
and building programme is at present receiving my earnest attention, and I hope
that operations will be resumed at a very
early date.

Pensions Bill-

20 APRIL 1926
ORDERS OF THE DAY.
Pensions (Increase) Bill.
Order for Second Reading read.
Motion made, and Question proposed:
"That the Bill be now read a Second time."
The MINISTER OF FINANCE (Mr. Pollock): I rise to move the Second Reading of
this comparatively small Measure consisting
of five Clauses. Although in itself not so
very important, still I think it will be necessary that I should offer some explanation
of its incidence and of the interests which it
affects. In order that this may
be
thoroughly understood I would remind the
House that the Imperial Parliament passed
two separate Acts in connection with the
increase of pensions to the different Services.
Both these Acts deal with pensioners whose
pensions were in force prior to August, 1914.
It will be realised that the pensions were on
a very low scale in the period prior to the war
because of the low rates of remuneration
which were generally accorded in comparison
with those of later dates. Accordingly, in
order that grievances might be removed and
justice done to those poor pensioners the
British Government passed an Act in the
year 1920, granting certain increases to the
pensions then in existence, but as time went
on it was found that this increase did not
conform fully with the rise in the cost of
living, and in 1924 an amending Act was
passed directed to increasing further the
pensions to which I have referred.
The pensioners affected include on the one
hand Civil Service and police pensioners and
other pensioners paid from State funds, or
quasi-State funds, and, on the other hand,
pensioners of local authorities.
The pensions paid by the last-named, that is, the
local authorities, were only to be increased
by consultation with the Treasury, and although decisions were reached between the
Treasury and the local authorities these pensions were not mandatory, and it was left
to the local authorities to use their own judgment in regard to the standard of pensions
they gave to those who had been in their
employment. The amending Act of 1924, as
I have said, brought into operation larger
increases than the 1920 Act, and if hon.
Members will consult the Bill itself they will
see that they conform with the increases
mentioned in the sub-section of Clause 2.
Turning for a moment to the relationship
between these two Acts passed by the
Imperial Government to ourselves, I need
hardly remind hon. Members that the Act
of 1920 was passed before the transfer to
Northern Ireland of any of the functions
under the Government of Ireland Act, and
they, therefore, applied to such pensions as
were at that date being paid from Imperial
T
funds to Royal Irish Constabulary pensioners
and the Civil Service pensioners retired
from Irish Departments. A proportion of
the pensions belonging to Northern Ireland
were collected, and are being collected from
us through a deduction from our residuary
share of taxes.
When the 1924 Act was passed the situation was a little different because at that
time this Parliament was functioning, and
the situation arose that some of these
pensioners became legally entitled to claim
upon the British Government for the increases that were granted in that Act, but
our Ministry of Finance established the
position with the British Treasury that it
was not competent for the British Government, without consultation with this
Government, to impose any additional
burden upon the Government of Northern
Ireland through the machinery of this Act.
Therefore, when it came to us we agreed that
while in equity and in justice it was quite
right that we should bear our portion of that
burden we established the position with the
British Treasury that it was not competent,
as I have said, for the British Parliament to
pass any Measure of that kind without our
concurrence, and it is to conform with the
arrangement that this Bill is required. In
other words it regularises, if I may put it in
that way, the arrangement as between the
British Government and ourselves. I need
only say now that the main increase will
take place in connection with the Royal
Irish Constabulary pensioners. It will add
about £6,000 per annum, which, of course,
will
be gradually diminishing as the
pensioners disappear from Northern
Ireland expenditure.
Clause 2 of the Bill makes corresponding
provision for those pensioners whose
pensions are directly paid from Northern Ire
land funds or revenues-namely, National
School Teachers and Petty Sessions Clerks.
The Government feel that as we have kept
pace with British social legislation and
have conceded the propriety of a charge in
connection with the R.I.C. and other
pensioners to whom I have already alluded,
it would be inequitable and illogical not to
treat similarly the pensioned teachers and
Petty Sessions clerks. It is, therefore, proposed that further increases be made on the
same basis as is provided in sub-Sections A,
B, and C of the second Clause of the
Measure. If reference is made to this particular part of the Clause hon. Members will
be able to understand the exact character of
the increases that are suggested.
The first sub-section to the proviso to
Clause 2 is somewhat involved, and perhaps
requires a little explanation to make it
simple, but it is both simple and equitable
when it is understood. It insures that no
Pensions Bill-
Supply.
HOUSE OF COMMONS.
[Mr. Pollock]
pension shall be increased beyond the
pension that would be awarded to શ
pensioner retiring to-day with શ similar
length of service, who has cost of living
bonus reckoned as a pensionable emolument.
An example will explain. Suppose a prewar pensioner retiring on a salary of £140
receives a pension of £70.
Under the proposals embodied in the Bill he will, if otherwise qualified, receive a total pension of
£105, that is to say, £70 and 50 per cent.
added, making it £105. If, however, a Petty
Sessions Clerk who retired on the 1st April
of this year on a similar salary, but with
cost of living bonus added only receives a
pension of £100, the pre-war pensioner will
get not £105 but £100. I am sure that the
House will agree that it would be wrong
that anyone should be in receipt of a larger
sum under the new arrangement than a
clerk retiring at the present time under
identical conditions.
The second sub-Section to the proviso deals
with a different matter. Under Clause 70,
sub-Section 3, of our own Education Act it
provides that the Ministry of Finance may
grant to any then existing pensioned teacher
such increase beyond that authorised by the
Pensions (Increase) Act of 1920 as would
bring his pension to an annual sum not exceeding £50. The object of this sub-section
is that the provision made in our
Education Act of 1923 for the pensions of
retiring teachers will not be prejudiced; in
fact, that the bargain, if you like to put it
that way, that was then made with, the
teachers shall be maintained. That is, in
short, the object of the sub-Section.
own
Now I come to Clause 3, which is very
simple, and I am sure that it will be held
by hon. Members to be very equitable; that
is to say, there was a provision which was
made originally that pensioners must reside
within the area of the British Isles, otherwise the pensioner would forfeit his pension.
Under this Clause that embargo is removed,
because, as we can readily realise, it may
happen that the relatives of the pensioner
may have gone abroad, and it is an unfair
thing to refuse to pay a man his legitimate
pension simply because he desires to reside
with his family at a distance.
Clause 4 of the Bill, which is really the
last Clause, gives the Ministry of Finance
power to apply the provisions respecting
increased pension percentages to the
pensions payable by local authorities.
Power is given to local authorities still
to preserve the right of these authorities
to regulate the terms and amounts
of the pensions given to their retiring
servants. I can only say in regard
to that that it seems to be only fair.
Those who have close and intimate knowledge of all the circumstances of their
servants and the question of whether they
have or have not earned a particular pension
-it seems only reasonable to assume-really
understand these matters to a greater degree
than the central authority. Therefore, instead of making this provision mandatory
with local authorities, it is a permissive
increase, and is left to their own judgment
to decide. These are the main features of
the Bill, and I beg to move.
Question put, and agreed to.
Bill committed to a Committee of the
Whole House for to-morrow.

Mr. ARCHDALE: Of the total increase
of £14,972, which this Estimate shows, page
112, £13,313 is due to the transfer to the
Ministry as from the 1st April last of the
administration of the Diseases of Animals
Acts. This Service was previously administered by the Imperial Government. The
inclusion of provision in the Northern Ireland Estimates for the Service does not, however, imply a new charge on our revenue.
Under the old arrangement we were still
liable for the cost of the Service, which was
recovered from us in the form of a deduction
from the Northern Ireland residuary share
of reserved taxes. In future we will adminster the Service ourselves and meet the
cost direct.
The real increase, therefore, is only
£1,559, which is entirely due to automatic
inerements of salary to staff and to certain
additions of personnel necessary by the progressive extension of the Ministry's activities.
Sub-head A-Salaries, Wages and Allowances-This has been divided into eight Sections so as to give a clearer idea of the salary
cost of the various branches in which the
head-quarters establishment is grouped.
The total increase of £13,990 in the salaries
Estimate is to the extent of £11,376 due to the
transfer to the Ministry of the staff previously employed in the Imperial Secretary's
Department for Discases of Animals work.
The total staff taken over numbers 43, including 13 veterinary inspectors engaged at
ports or on general duties, 21 ship inspectors,
cattle brander, disinfector, and an outdoor
clerical staff of 7 persons. With the exception
of one veterinary inspector, who has been
allocated to the Animals' Diseases Station at
Stormont for the purpose of research work,
and whose salary is included in the Agricultural Services Estimate, the salaries of all the
staff transferred are shown on this Estimate.
The real increase in salary costs is represented by a sum of £2,515, partly due to
automatic increments of salary and partly to
a slight increase of staff to keep pace with
the expansion of the Ministry's work, particularly with regard to the marketing of
eggs, live stock schemes and the suppression
of black scab in potatoes.
Sub-head B-Travelling and Subsistence
Expenses--provides for the travelling
expenses of administrative staff and headquarters' inspection staff, and would have
shown a reduction but for the necessity of
providing for the travelling expenses of the
newly-transferred staff of Veterinary
Inspectors.

Sub-heads D1 and D2-Printing

ago, before the names of trade unions were

serve on his committees and one thing and
another, but he never pays any attention at
all to the interests and desires of the people
who produce all the wealth of the community,
namely, the agricultural labourers and the

ask us to vote a sum of £64,000, a net increase

that £11,376 is due to the Diseases of Animals

Mr. P. O'NEILL: I beg to second the
Amendment proposed by the Leader of the

of this Vote. As a matter of fact, I think

what I say. In the matter of the planting
and growing of potatoes, one of the most important industries in the Six Counties-as a

the net result? There is no market for
these potatoes to-day, and they cannot even
give them away.

County Down.

Potatoes are not the only thing. Take the
case of flax. You have advised them to grow
flax, and if there is one industry on farming
lines that should pay it is flax. But still
it is not an economic proposition at all, as
the farmer knows. Why, I cannot understand. The linen industry has practically
a monopoly, but still the growing of flax has
not been a paying proposition to the farmer.
I do not see why you should advise them to
grow flax, because I daresay that in seventy,
eighty, or ninety per cent, of cases there has
been a loss on it. I think it is a great
mistake, yet that is how you expect the
farmers to live. How do you justify the
service at all? Would you get the farmers
to say that the Ministry of Agriculture
could not be done without? If you ask the

to them, and 100 per cent. in some districts
will say that it has been an absolute disservice to them, and particularly in the

under the Black Scab Order that they really
do not know what to turn their hands to.
Thousands of tons of potatoes to-day in Down
could be got for the taking of them away.
I do not see how under these circumstances
the Ministry can at all justify its existence,
and I certainly believe that I am quite
justified in seconding the reduction of this

market for potatoes, I would prefer potato
growing to sugar beet, although if the sugar
beet industry should be started in Northern
Ireland I would recommend the farmers to
give it every support, in order to ensure its
success, if that is possible. I do not feel
competent to say it would be successful;
there are others much better able to judge
of that matter than I am. We have to be
guided by our experts. I am sure the
Government will meet this demand in the
sympathetic way that they meet every demand, if it is found possible to make a
success of the sugar beet industry in this
country.
It is strange to hear some of the criticisms that have been levelled against the
Minister in this Committee. I have been
keeping in very close touch with his actions
in regard to horse breeding and cattle
breeding, flax growing and potato growing,
and also eggs, and I know that we will
never have a more sympathetic Minister
of Agriculture in Northern Ireland than we
have at present. (Hon. Members: Hear,
hear.) He is at all times willing and ready
to be advised by those who know the subject, and he takes every means of ventilating among the agricultural community what
he intends to do before he does it, of finding
out the pros and cons of the case, and
whether it will be for the benefit of the
farmers that something should take place.
He acts with caution and sympathy. I find
that he does not rush to prosecute farmers
who have inadvertently overstepped the
regulations. He gives them fair and reasonable notice that they are doing wrong before he launches a prosecution.
The farming community to-day are on perfectly good terms with the Ministry of Agriculture. I think my hon. Friend, the
Member for Derry (Mr. Leeke), is bound to
admit that. If he thinks of the spirit that
existed amongst the farmers of the County
Down when the old Department of Agriculture held sway, and of the friendly spirit
that exists between the Ministry of Agriculture and its officials and the farmers today, he will find that a very different state
of affairs now exists. (Hon. Members: Hear,
hear.) I know that the farmers have been
very badly hit. I know that the efforts made
to get assistance for the farmers were sympa.
thetically considered by the Minister of
Finance and the Minister of Agriculture, and
I am sure they are prepared to adopt
any reasonable suggestion, if it is backed by
common-sense, that the Members on the
Opposition or on this side of the Committee
offer to relieve the difficulties that exist today. But I have heard no suggestion from
the Opposition as to what can be done in
regard to the potato crop. I would recommend the farmers of County Down to grow
a variety of potatoes that they can get a
market for, and not Lochar. They have
known for years that they can get no market
for Lochar, but if they do plant Lochar they
have this advantge they get double the crop,
and they are as well off in the long run as if
they grow another variety.
I think the Minister is perfectly right in
making compulsory the growing of immune
varieties. If they find fault with the Minister
because they are not allowed to grow nonimmune varieties I think they would have
something worse to say of him if he allowed
them to do so. I have great pleasure in
supporting the Minister in connection with
this Estimate.

these people are being exploited, and for that
reason I think it is the duty of the Minister

I come next to the Chemical and Animal
Nutrition Division. Experiments in feeding
minerals to pigs, poultry, milch cows and
calves are being carried out with
interesting results, and in some cases

series of experiments with balanced rations
is in operation. Most of the loss and mortality
in livestock is due to malnutrition and
through this cause farmers are annually
losing thousands of pounds.
As to the Seed Testing and Plant Disease
Division, let me give figures to show the
increase. In 1925, 2,703 samples of seeds
were tested, an increase of 30 per cent. on
the previous year, and five times the number
received in the 1923 seed testing year-the
year we began.
The Committee will be interested to know
that Northern Ireland produces annually
about 30,000 tons of rye grass seed. Our
Province is the chief world centre for rye
grass seed production, and exports 20,000 to
25,000 tons annually. The Division is paying a good deal of attention to the investigation of potato diseases and diseases of
fruit trees.
The egg laying competitions conducted by
the Poultry Division continue to be popular
and every year entries have to be turned
down. At present 71 pens of six pullets
each are complete. I would like to call the
attention of the Committee to the fact that
in England the average number of eggs per
pullet of the National Utility Poultry
Society is 161.55; United States, 164.4;
Canada, 172.2; and Northern Ireland, 181.86.
(Hon. Members: Hear, hear.) Our egg laying competitions are doing some good.
The Animal Diseases Division has only
been functioning for a comparatively short
period, but already 1,000 cases chiefly of an
advisory character have been dealt with.
The laboratory at Queen's University has
been given up since 1st April, and all investigations are now made at the Stormont
laboratory. At present the Division is cona
Plant breeding is still being pursued, and
we have now quite a number of new promising varieties of flax, oats, etc., but it
will be some time before we have these in
bulk for distribution.
The Animal and Crop Husbandry
Division is a new feature of the Ministry's
work and will centre largely at the Hillsborough Research Station.
As to the building grant to Queen's
University (A2), the erection of the building
which provides lecture rooms and laboratories for the purpose of the Agricultural
Faculty at the Queen's University is now
proceeding apace, and its completion before
the end of the current financial year is expected. Provision is made for payment to
the University of £30,000 as the balance of
the total grant in aid of £34,500 allocated
by the Government in accordance with the
Government Loans and Exchequer Provisions (Northern Ireland) Act, 1925. This
expenditure will, as heretofore, be repaid
from the special grant of £400,000 awarded

of £30,000 includes a re-vote of the unexpended portion of last year's provision of
£18,000.
As to the Hillsborough Research Station
and Experimental Farm (A3), it is proposed
to establish an Animal Nutrition, &c., Research and Experimental Station under the
control and management of a Board of
Trustees representing the Ulster Farmer's
Union, the Ulster Agricultural Organisation
Society, the Ministry of Agriculture and the
Faculty of Agriculture of Queen's University. The Board will act in co-operation
with the Ministry and with the Agricultural
Faculty at Queen's.
To finance such a station a total sum of
£100,000 will be needed, viz., £40,000 for
capital, and £60,000 as an endowment, to
produce an income of £3,000 per annum,
which is calculated to be the annual cost
of running the institution when fully
established.
As to the capital required, the Government
agreed to give a direct State contribution of
£20,000 in the form of £10,000 cash together
with lands and buildings at Hillsborough,
Co. Down, the balance of £20,000 being provided on behalf of the farmers by diverting
that amount from the supplemental grant
of £128,644 in relief of rates.

provided by the farmers by five annual instalments of £12,000 each from the supple-

During the financial year which has just

been made in the Estimates.
As to Agricultural Education, this subhead shows a decrease of £6,300 as compared
with last year, when it was necessary to
provide for considerable capital expenditure
on the erection of farm buildings and cottages at the North-West Institute, Strabane.
This work as well as the works of extension
and improvement at Greenmount Agricultural College, Antrim, is now practically
completed, a few outstanding charges only
remaining to be met. Provision for upkeep
of the Ulster Dairy School is slightly higher
in view of the progressive increase in the
number of pupils in residence. There are
now 47 pupils in residence-it is full-and
there were only 32 in 1922-23. The upkeep
of the North-West Institute is also estimated
at a higher figure to allow for development
of operations following the completion of the
new farm buildings. That Institute is also
full. There are now 20 pupils, and there
were only 10 in 1922-23. At Greenmount
we have got 36 pupils. We hope that the
number will gradually reach 50.
The Estimate for the improvement of live
stock (C1) shows an increase of £400 over the
Estimate for last year. This increase is,
however, more than counter-balanced by a
corresponding increase in the Estimate of
departmental receipts accruing from resales of stud animals. Additional provision is made for grants to milk recording
associations to cope with the rapid increase
in the number of associations. The extra
funds are provided out of the special Development Grant of £54,000. It may interest the Committee if I give the figures of
the various years:-In 1921, there were six
associations, and 1,244 cows under test; in
1926, there are 53 associations and 10,360
cows under test.
In conection with the Live Stock Breeding Acts (C2), the increase of £50 for cost
of special inspectors for licences is due to
the large number of special inspections
of bulls required. The expenditure included under this heal is more than
covered by receipts which may be estimated
at about £1,000 a year. We have now 6,639
licensed bulls in Northern Ireland. When
we began this work a great many were complaining that we would not have bulls in the
country. As a matter of fact the number is
practically the same as in 1923-24.
The Estimate for the Animal Quarantine
Station remains at the same figure (£500)
as the original Estimate for last year. Two
consignments of valuable breeding animals

through this station. Unfortunately, the
prevalence of foot-and-mouth diseasesin
England and Wales renders it necessary to
continue to prohibit importations of cattle
in the ordinary way.

The CHAIRMAN: No; I have very carefully indeed considered the point put by
the hon. Member. I have considered what
position we would be in if I yielded to the
argument of the hon. Member. It would
open to the Opposition at any time to quit
the House, and on that ground to suspend
the business. Equally if the hon. Member
were pressing some point of paramount importance it would be open for the whole of
the Members on the Government Benches
to quit the House, and that that should be
advanced as a reason for the suspension of
public business. That is an argument that
could not be held.

your ruling in the matter. I would like you
to read the Standing Order which prevents

The CHAIRMAN: "If Mr. Speaker or

House, shall be of opinion that a motion
for the adjournment of a debate, or of the
House, during any debate, or that the
Chairman do report progress, or do leave
the Chair, is an abuse of the rules of the
House, he may forthwith put the question
thereupon from the Chair, or he may decline to propose the question thereupon to
the House."
