Mr. W. McMULLEN: I desire to move a
reduction in this Estimate of £1,000. I do
so for the purpose of asking the right hon.
Gentleman who has just spoken, whether
there is such an animal in Northern Ireland
as an agricultural labourer. I have heard
animals of all classes discussed on this and
the previous Estimate, but he appears to be
oblivious of the fact that such people as
agricultural labourers exist in Northern
Ireland.
I am at loss to understand on an occasion
of this character, when two very important
Estimates have been submitted to the
House, why no effort has been made by the
right hon. Gentleman to discuss the problem of unemployment. I had occasion previously to call the Government's attention
to this aspect of the matter. You were
absent in Dublin, I understand, on that day
for a purpose which you believed to be of
more importance than the question discussed before the House on that occasion.
Of course it is for yourself to determine
whether the business which took you to
Dublin. But, as I say, I cannot understand
question we were discussing. I have come
to the conclusion that the subject under discussion was of tremendously greater importance than the object of your visit to
Dublin. But, as I say, I cannot understand
how it is that you have not attempted to
deal with the problem of unemployment.
I have observed in reading the Press that
a large number of people are unemployed in
all our small provincial towns throughout
the North of Ireland. Most of these people
are in receipt of unemployment benefit. We
have repeatedly stated from these Benches
that it is not a satisfactory state of affairs
by any means to have people continually
drawing benefit week after week without
any attempt being made to deal with the
problem of unemployment. The hon.
Member for North Belfast mentioned what
appears to me to be very important, the
large number of people who are leaving
week after week for Canada and the United
States of America. You were inclined to
laugh and to treat the whole matter in a
very jocular way. It may appear to you to
be a matter for mirth. To other people it
is quite a serious problem. Two or three
days ago I observed a family of seven, the
father and mother and five children who
were emigrating to the United States of
America. Now it appears to me to be absolutely a tragic thing. I attempt to put
myself into the position of that father who
is forced to take his family from Northern
Ireland away to seek a home in the wilds
and prairies of Canada, and if it is possible
for the Government by any means, even at
the risk or expense of making in roads upon
the vested interests of Northern Ireland, it
is the duty of this Government to try to
establish more people on the land than there
are on it at the present time.

Now some people may be inclined to

attempt was being made on our part to

the soil who have got no previous knowledge
of agriculture. It is not a question of that
kind at all, because, that would be a state
of affairs not too -satisfactory-(hon.
Members: Hear, hear)-although perhaps
these people were turned into almost anything during the course of the late war.
They have been made machine-gun men and
airmen. They were trained and equipped
for any particular purpose for carrying on
the war. When the purpose is peace and a
suggestion is made of any kind at all then
it is impossible to do it. If you want men
of Northern Ireland to take the life of a
German or an Austrian lack of knowledge
is no drawback and money is no obstacle.
But when it becomes a question of trying
to solve the problem of unemployment the
difficulties are insuperable and the Government are not capable of dealing with them.

Of course I do not know as much about
agriculture as possibly the hon. Member for
the University (Dr. Morrison), or the hon.
Member for County Down (Mr. O'Neill),
who appears to know so much about the
problem of agriculture. It appears to me
not so difficult a question at all, provided
you are prepared to tackle it in the right
spirit. I made a remark on the question of
agriculture one day previously which caused
much merriment.
Mr. MARK: You are always amusing.
Mr. W. McMULLEN: I am very glad I
serve some purpose, even if it is only to
amuse. Even that is a legitimate purpose to
serve. Some people are even less useful than
to be amusing. Even if I only amuse I
serve some function. But I am speaking of
the number of people settled on the soil
here in comparison with other countries. 1
think the Government publication gives the
figures as 239 people to the square mile as
compared with about 618 for Great Britain.
I suggest that this is a very serious state of
affairs-that there should be only 239 per
square mile in Northern Ireland as against
638 in Great Britain. That should give the
right hon. Gentleman some food for thought.
I think you have got 41 per cent. of the land
of Northern Ireland under hay, and you
have 12 per cent. of the land under grass.
Now can some development not take place
there? Can some attempt not be made for
the purpose of planting a large number of
people on the soil of Northern Ireland. If
you did that by taking the very large holdings you have in Northern Ireland and
possibly starting on them without encroaching on the land preserved by the supporters
of the Government-if you attempted to induce these people with their large estates
to employ more labour than they employ
at the present time, you probably would be
able to absorb a very considerable percentage of the unemployed in Northern Ireland
at the present moment.
You have got, further, to take into consideration the purchasing power you would
give to these people. Their purchasing
powers at the present time are very, very
low. In most of the towns it is only for a
very short period they are allowed to draw
unemployment benefit. At a later stage I am
hoping to give the Parliamentary Secretary
to the Ministry of Labour (Mr. Gordon)
some information on that subject as to how
unemployed workers in these small urban
areas and in the country districts are being
treated. Their purchasing power is exceptionally low, and if it were possible to
place these people in employment, to give
them more purchasing power than they have
at the present time, you would relieve probably the unemployment in the cities to a
very considerable extent. Would not that be
a much more satisfactory state of affairs? It
might cause the right hon. Gentleman (Mr.
Archdale) to think. After all, that is not
a terribly difficult process, and if any remarks I can make will induce the right hon.
Gentleman to think, and to think along
those lines because I should probably point
out that in a great many of the things the
right hon. Gentleman has tackled he has
proved very progressive and some of the things
he has done mark a tremendous amount of
progress as compared with the state of agriculture in Northern Ireland ten years ago.
But while the right hon. Gentleman (Mr.
Archdale) is quite prepared to think in terms
of hens, of cows, of horses, and of cattle of

all kinds, he cannot give any consideration

people who occupy these benches until you

the agricultural labourer and to make some
attempt to put these people on the land.
The countryside is being depopulated. I
pointed out on the last occasion on which
I spoke on this subject that the population
of Northern Ireland from 1841 up to the
present time had decreased in round figures
about 370,000, and that during the same
years the population of Belfast has increased
from about 70,000 to about 470,000. Nearly
every urban area in Northern Ireland has
increased its population too, while the
countryside is depopulated. Some steps
should be taken for the purpose of keeping
the agricultural labourers in the countryside instead of allowing them to flood into
the cities to overcrowd an already overcrowded market, and some attempt should
be made also to stem the tide of emigration.
The life blood of Northern Ireland is being
drained. What you are losing Canada,
Australia, and other countries are gaining.
I hope that in future when the right hon.
Gentleman (Mr. Archdale) comes to this
Committee he will at least have developed
so far that we will get some mention from
him of the agricultural labourer.

I have listened to the denunciation of and

as I can judge from going through the

Dr. MORRISON:
In any event, may
I be allowed to say that I think this
one of the lapses, one of those
samples of loose rhetoric that we
sometimes hear from the hon. Member for
West Belfast? I wanted to say a few words
with regard to the scientific aspect of the
work carried on by the Ministry. I am
interested, living as I did all my life on
the land, mixing with agricultural people,
and seeing the mortalities that occur
amongst cows from milk fever, amongst
horses from lockjaw, in every sphere and
amongst every type of animal death upon
death, to the great loss and detriment of
the farmer and to the detriment of the
State in general. Early in the formation of
this Parliament I went to the Ministry and
put my views before them as a practical
man, who had first-hand knowledge of what
was needed, and I am prepared to tell the
Committee now that they acted on those
suggestions of mine, that they have taken
the necessary steps to make use of all the
discoveries that science has made for the
prevention of disease, and that this policy
which has been developed in connection with
the University is part of the work they
have carried out to prevent disease.
Last year I got from the Ministry of
Agriculture a list, a rough estimate of all
the animals that had died in Ireland, of
horses, cattle, and sheep, from operations
and other causes, and the steps that were
being taken to prevent such losses. If I
would be inclined to say anything about the
Ministry it would be that, instead of lacking
initiative, the Minister and perhaps some of
his principal clerks have, even for me,
rather much initiative, but you cannot have
too much of a good thing. What I wanted
to get up to talk about was this grant to the
farming societies, this grant to the Farmers'
Union and the Agricultural Organisation
Society. The Agricultural Organisation
Society has, very strong claims. As I understand it, there is £1,000 given, and of this
£700 goes to the Ulster Farmers' Union for
the educational work carried on by them,
and the Organisation Society gets £300 out
of the £1,000. Now that is not enough; it
is not a fair division, and I would suggest
to the Minister that it should be divided
in the proportion of £500 to each. Originally
the Organisation Society got £1,200 in
1923-1924. The Farmers' Union have got
three grants of £1,000 each, and now, of
this grant of £1,000, £700 goes to the
Farmers' Union and only £300 to the
Organisation Society.

I am told that it is impossible to keep
an organiser on the road for the sum of
£300, and, while the farmers themselves
through this Organisation give £600 to help
to educate their brethren living and working
on the land, they cannot keep their
organisers going about lecturing and trying
to educate the farmer unless they get a
little extension of their grant. I would like
to point out that it is a co-operative society,
which I know will meet with the approval
of hon. Members on the opposite side of the
Committee, It stands for co-operation, for
self-help, for enabling a man to make an
effort for his own benefit and for the benefit
of those who are going about begging and
craving for work; it is to make two blades
of grass grow where only one grew before.
That is exactly what this Organisation is
doing, and, therefore, I think the limit
should be increased in this matter.
With regard to emigration and this
subject which the hon. Member for West
Belfast (Mr. William McMullen) brings up
so frequently, I think that in discussing
agricultural questions it is rather out of
place. We know that agricultural labourers
are excluded from unemployment benefit,
and it is a bad thing. It is a bad thing
for a man to be an agricultural labourer,
but the reason for that is, as hon. Members
on the opposite side of the Committee know,
because there is no outlook for them by
reason of the fact that the Labour Party,
of which hon. Members opposite are such
distinguished members, have kept their
brethren in agricultural Ulster and in the
country badly fed, badly paid, and badly
clad in order that in the cities they might
have plenty.
Living in the country as a dispensary
doctor I have come in contact with a large
number of people, and I have recommended
them to emigrate. I said, "
There is no
chance for a working man or for a farmer
here. Go to the Colonies, not to the United
States. Keep under your own flag."
I got
in touch with the Commissioners of different
countries like Australia and New Zealand,
and I know to-day hundreds of men who
followed my advice, with whom I have kept
in touch ever since, and who are grateful
for the advice I gave them. What we want
in this country is not the limiting of
emigration and the congregating of the
people in slums in Belfast and other
places, but the encouraging of our people
to go out to free countries where they have
a chance, and where their arrival will be
good for the nation and for the countries to
which they go as it will be a help to this
country.

When on the previous Vote I referred to

informed they are the Arran Victory and

there is any greater demand in the English

When the Minister replies I would like to

potatoes is to be sent to, the conditions under

in regard to the best use of their land and
the best use of the labour on the land.
The workers' union is exactly the same. It
is a body of men who want to get the best
terms for their labour, and who want to
render faithful and efficient service. 1
think the right hon. Gentleman should be
chary about putting down £1,000 for the
Ulster Farmers' Union. He would not have
dreamt of asking the Government for a
grant of £1,000 to enable us to help the
agricultural labourers. I assure the right
hon. Gentleman that the agricultural
labourers need organisation as much, if not
more, than the Farmers' Union. They need
education. I think it is very strange that
the Government should back up the enemy
of the agricultural labourer, and subsidise
them with £1,000.
Agricultural wages is a tremendously important matter. According to the figures
supplied by the right hon. Gentleman, some
of these agricultural labourers are getting
only 22s 6d a week. It is no wonder trade
is depressed, for at such a rate of remuneration these people cannot buy things. The
agricultural labourers are just as important
as the farmers, and, therefore, they should
be considered, educated and subsidised,
rather than the farmers. From that point
of view, I think there is a good deal of
reason for grumbling at the fact that the
right hon. Gentleman has not a representative worker on this committee. I am quite
certain that there are as good men among
the agricultural labourers as there are
among the farmers. If the Minister took
the trouble to seek for them, he would get
men to represent the workers on the various
committees that act under his Ministry;
but, apparently, as I said a few moments
ago, the right hon. Gentleman is living
twenty or fifty years ago when trade
unionism was not very well known. If hẹ
would only cast his eyes across the water,
and pay attention to what the Prime
Minister and the Minister of Labour say
occasionally about Northern Ireland going
on parallel lines with Great Britain, he
would see that the Ministry of Agriculture
in England asks the unions to submit the
names of representatives for seats on these
committees. I suggest that the right hon.
Gentleman should adopt the same course,
as it apparently meets with satisfaction
when it applies to the Ministry of Labour
or other Departments of the Government.

was abused in some way, and as one of the

of the inquiry are. I cannot compliment

he appointed to conduct the inquiry. Mr.
Beattie, who is a King's Counsel, tried to
make little of me in drawing attention to

injuries. Mr. Beattic is a man who is most
anxious for Parliamentary honours, and
after his conduct at that inquiry there is
one thing I am convinced of, and that is
that he will not be a useful asset to this
House.
I

The MINISTER OF COMMERCE (Mr.
Barbour): I beg to move in Clause 6, page
6, line 2 (" may determine to be entitled
thereto ") at the end to add:
"Provided that in case such compensation
is payable in respect of a holding subject
to a land purchase annuity, the tribunal or
county court shall determine whether the
security for the payment of the annuity
is prejudicially affected, and, if so, what
amount of the annuity ought to be redeemed in view of the prejudice to the
security, and thereupon the applicant shall
cause the amount of the annuity so determined to be redeemed, and the redemption
price until paid shall be a charge on the
compensation to be paid by him."
Hon. Members will be aware that under
the Land Purchase Act the minerals were
vested in the Land Commission, and, consequently, this clause has been inserted in
order to protect their position under this
Act. It is in order to provide that any
security for the payment of the annuity
should not be prejudiced by the granting of
any right to work minerals or any diversion
of them. The amendment has been agreed
to by the Ministry of Finance.
Mr. KYLE: I think I would like the
Minister to explain how this would affect
farmers who hold the land or are buying out
the land. Does this mean that tenant farmers themselves will not have any right to
the minerals, but that they will be vested in
the Land Commission?
Mr. BARBOUR: Hon. Members should
remember in considering this Bill that it
is only to provide means for working
minerals where satisfactory arrangements
cannot be arrived at between any parties who
may be interested in working the minerals.
It is intended to facilitate and encourage the
working of minerals. Consequently, the
farmer who owns the surface and wishes to
work the minerals will have to satisfy the
Land Commission that the security for the
annuity is not prejudiced in any way. Any
application from the farmer will receive
most favourable consideration.
Amendment agreed to.

the coal mining industry in Great Britain

It was before the passing of the 1920 Act and

As a matter of fact the Act in which these

[Mr. Kyle]
as we have now before us. It is because of

Mr. BARBOUR: The effect of this Amendment and what the Government desires to receive is absolution for not having applied to
whatever extent might have been necessary
the Clauses of this Act. I could really
amplify what I have already said to almost
a wearying extent to the Members of the
Committee if I went fully into the very
elaborate machinery to which we would have
had to resort in order to give effect to the
Act as it stood during that period. The
Mining Industry Act of 1920 provided that
the Advisory Committee on coal and the
coal industry should consist of a chairman
and twenty-four other persons, of whom
four should be representative of owners of
coal mines; four should be representative
of workers in or about coal mines; three
should be representative of employers in
other industries; three should be representative of workers in other industries; one
should be a mining engineer; two should be
agents or managers or under-managers of
coal mines, holding first-class certificates;
one should be a coal exporter; one should
be a coal factor
or coal merchant; one
should be a person with experience of commerce other than the production or distribution of coal; one should be a person with
experience in co-operative trading; and three
should be persons with expert knowledge of
medical or other science. To apply that
Act as it stood would have been almost impossible, but, so far as the future is concerned, I think the hon. Member for North
Belfast (Mr. Kyle) may regard us as sympathetic to the coal miners. At the present
stage when the coal mining is in such a very
early state of development we should have
liked, anyway, to have consulted the views
of the owner of the mine before entering
into any commitments. I would respectfully
suggest that this is a matter which might
stand over until we know how best the
interests of the people who work in the coal
mines can be protected, and until we have
gathered knowledge of the extent of the
industry and the likelihood of coal, or other
mining, in Northern Ireland progressing.
Mr. KYLE: Would the right hon. Gentleman (Mr. Barbour) consent then to postpone
the Committee Stage of this Bill until he
prepares a form of words that would meet
our requirements?
The PRIME MINISTER (Sir James Craig):
I think my right hon. Friend (Mr. Barbour)
has interpreted the desire of the Government
that we should carefully keep watch upon
this matter, and if the development of coal
mining in Northern Ireland is such as to
involve a very large number of persons we
will see to it when the time comes that the
miners in Northern Ireland are placed in a
somewhat analagous position to those in
England or in Scotland. In this Bill, which
is of a different character, it is not proposed
to include the Clause to which the hon.
Member (Mr. Kyle) refers, but he can rest
assured, as I say, that if there are a large
number of people employed in the coal
mining industry in Northern Ireland, and,
if that industry develops to any large extent,
my right hon. Friend (Mr. Barbour) will
bring in a short Bill to establish the principle of which the hon. Member (Mr. Kyle)
is speaking to-day.
Mr. DEVLIN: I would suggest that we
should allow this Bill to pass. I am very
glad to know that the representations made
by the hon. Member for North Belfast (Mr.
Kyle) have had the desired effect. He did
not, as far as I gathered, put forward any
suggestion that the elaborate machinery recited by the right hon. Gentleman (Mr.
Barbour) should be set up here. What he
simply asked was that precisely similar
labour conditions should exist in Northern
Ireland to what exist in the mining districts
of Great Britain. I am very glad that the
Prime Minister has given that promise-a
definite promise and I would, therefore,
suggest that we should allow this Bill to
pass.

(Barbour): In moving this Vote I think

sudden death of Northern Ireland's first
Comptroller and Auditor-General, Mr.
Huggett--an officer whose position has necessarily brought him into 'close touch
with those Members of this Committee who
have served on the Committee of Public
Accounts. The Comptroller and Auditor-
General is, in fact, the arbiter who indicates
to that Committee whether the money
voted by this Committee for supply
services is properly and economically spent,
and who suggests to them possible lines of
criticism in dealing with the annual
Appropriation Accounts. Coming to us at

Huggett brought to bear on the accounts
of our Public Departments ripe experience,
indefatigable zeal, and wide knowledge of
the technique of accounting not only in
the region of Government finance, but also
of commercial procedure. He has reported
on the accounts of our Department for the
first four financial years-his last report,
that on the accounts for the year 1924-25,
having been completed but a few weeks
before his death at a time when he was
struggling against that illnesss
suddenly carried him away. He was indeed a faithful servant of the public and
of this House. (Hon. Members: Hear,
hear.)

Sir ROBERT ANDERSON: Before touching upon the subject of the Amendment which
has been submitted to the Committee by the
hon. Member (Mr. Kyle), may I be permitted
as one who was associated with the late Mr.
Huggett as Chairman of the Public Accounts
Committee, just to say a word in regard to
the splendid services he rendered to this
Government during the period he was associated with it. I do not think I ever had
to do with a higher-minded public servant
that the late Mr. Huggett. He was a man
of the greatest courage, a man who had in
the very fibre of his being all the best
traditions of the Civil Service, who in whatever work he did did it with the greatest
efficiency, the greatest ability and with a
single eye to promote the interests of the
Government he was associated with. Mr.
Huggett came to his duties at a very difficult
period in the history of this Government,
just when the foundations were about to be
laid, and I think no Government and no
country could have been better served at
that particular stage than by the late Mr.
Huggett. I am sure I am only voicing the
feelings of every Member of the Committee
when I say we all deeply regret his passing
hence, but we are glad-some of us-that we
had the proud privilege to be associated with
him in the work of the Department that he
carried on with such conspicuous ability.
(Hon. Members: Hear, hear.)
Now in regard to the Amendment before
the Committee I think my hon. Friend (Mr.
Kyle) was especially dealing with this particular Department that has to do with audit
matters and the Comptroller and Auditor-
General's work. I know from personal knowledge that the late Comptroller and Auditor-
General worked night and day in order to
get through the work he had to perform,
and on several occasions he mentioned to me
that the work of the staff that he had available, while possessed of the greatest efficiency,
could be more efficiently and better carried
on if extra assistance could be given to it.
I think it is one of the Departments in
connection with the work of the Government
with which we should not deal with a parsimonious hand. Anyone who has studied
those very admirable reports that the Comptroller and Auditor-General has submitted
to the House from time to time will see the
great importance of the work that has got
to be done. They deal with every Department of the Government's work, they go into
every detail down to the expenditure of every
penny of public money. I think we should
for the sake of a few hundred pounds extra
see that there is a proper staff to do this
work, and do it well. It would be money
that would be spent to the advantage of
Parliament and the country as a whole.
Mr. DEVLIN: I am sorry I have to
disagree with my hon. Friend (Mr. Kyle), who
moved a reduction of this Vote, because, in
my judgment, the expenditure is perfectly
justified. (Hon. Members: Hear, hear.) I
take this opportunity of associating myself
with the generous eulogy which has been
delivered by the right hon. Gentleman the
Minister of Commerce (Mr. Barbour), and
the touching and eloquent references made
by the hon. Member for Derry (Sir Robert
Anderson) in relation to the late Mr. Huggett.
I desire to associate myself with these
tributes to the memory of a great, fearless,
and competent public servant. I have not
much direct experience or intimate association with Civil Servants, though I try, as
a public representative, to observe the
methods by which they perform their duties,
but I must say this, that a more faithful
watchdog of the public interests and a more
competent official in the discharge of the
exceedingly delicate duties he had to perform I never met. (Hon. Members: Hear,
hear.) The hon. Member for Derry (Sir Robert
Anderson) has spoken of him as a Government servant. He regarded himself as more
than a Government servant. He was a great
defender of the public interests, and I
confess that my relationship with him was
of this character, that his one great passion
was to inspire Members of Parliament with
a spirit of watchfulness over public accounts
and public expenditure. He sought their
co-operation that there might be a close and
watchful interest manifested in all that concerns the workings of our financial system.
He was
a simple, modest man, of great
personal charm in addition to his fine
qualities as a public servant, and I am sure
Ulster and the public service are poorer by
his death. I desire to join with those who
have spoken in paying this tribute to his
memory, and extending to his relatives our
profound sympathy.
Mr. BEATTIE: I would like to associate
myself with the remarks made by the
Minister of Commerce, the Chairman of the
Public Accounts Committee, and the last
speaker, regarding the late Mr. Huggett. I

Motion made, and Question proposed:
"That a sum not exceeding £603,736 be
granted to His Majesty to complete the sum
necessary to defray the charge which will

ending on the 31st day of March, 1927, to

Geo. V., c. 13, s. 1 (N.I.).” (Note.-£200,000
has been voted on account.)
The MINISTER OF HOME AFFAIRS
(Sir Dawson Bates): In submitting this Estimate, I think it is due to the officers and
men of the Royal Ulster Constabulary, that
Morrison, Hugh Smith
Mulholland, Captain The Hon. Henry
George HOL

TELLER FOR THE NOES—
Capt. Dixon.
I should, at the outset, express the appreciation of the Government for the valuable
services they have rendered during the past
year. One of the most important adjuncts
to a State is the existence of an efficient
Police Force, and one in which all classes
of the community have reposed their confidence. I venture to say, and I am sure hon.
Members, even on the Opposition Benches
will admit, that in the Royal Ulster Constabulary we have a Force which commands
the respect of all classes of the community.
If you want an efficient Police Force, you
must, first of all, have men whose character
will bear the closest investigation; men of
educational attainments; men of good
physique; and men with the proper temper
and tact to deal suitably with the people
with whom they come in contact. The fact
that we have such an efficient Force to-day
is due to the great care that has been taken
in the selection of the men. The Govern-
Supply-
Committee.
21 APRIL 1926
ment are most anxious to attract to the
Force the best type of man, and we offer
every encouragement to the best type to come
forward. I would remind hon. Members
that 50 per cent, of the promotions to the
commissioned ranks are given to the rank
and file, so that it is open to any constable
who joins the Police Force to look forward
to the time when he may become a District-
Inspector, or a County Inspector, or possibly
the Inspector-General himself.
Turning to the Estimate itself, one of the
most satisfactory features about it is that it
represents a saving of £35,000. Whether or
not my hon. Friend, who sits opposite (Mr.
Kyle) will use the converse argument he
used on the occasion of the last Vote, and
offer no opposition to this Vote on account
of the fact that it shows a decrease I cannot
say, but I suggest that he should. Dealing
with some of the most important Sub-heads,
hon. Members will find under the Sub-head
of "Pay" that there is an increase of £11,000.
This is due partly to the fact that last year
the pay was slightly under-estimated, and
secondly it is due to the normal operation of
increments. Hon. Members will apperciate
that the longer the man remains in a Police
Force the bigger the amount of his pay up
to a certain period. In connection with this
Sub-head hon. Members will see that in
accordance with the undertaking which I
gave this House, the temporary service of
Weights and Measures which was rendered
necessary at the time of the disbandment of
the old Royal Irish Constabulary has been
discontinued, these temporary Inspectors'
places being taken by members of the Royal
Ulster Constabulary, seventeen of whom, I
am glad to say, have passed a very stiff examination which is provided for the purpose
by the Board of Trade. The Inspector-
General, by a re-arrangement of the districts,
has been enabled to reduce the number of
men employed on this particular duty to 12,
and I am in hopes that it may be possible to
continue the number employed at that
number.
With regard to Rent Allowances, hon.
Members will see that there is a slight increase in regard to that, but here again this
arises from the fact that there are more men
qualified to get these allowances because they
are married. With regard to Clothing, hon.
Members will see that we have been able to
effect a saving of no less રી sum than
£13,500. That is due to the fact that last
year, in order to give more employment, and
in order that we should have a reserve stock
of clothing, we placed larger orders than
were absolutely necessary for the Force,
and this year we only provided for
15,000 yards. As regards Transport, here
again we have been able to effect a reduction
of 50 per cent. in the amount for Transport.
Dealing with Appropriations in Aid, hon.
Members will observe an Appropriation in
Aid for the first time of £6,000. This represents the cost of the police service in the
administration of the Road Acts. The
advent of motor cars has of course placed a
considerable additional burden on the police.
For instance, they have to look after the
control of motor traffic, and make sure
motorists pay the licences, and we feel it
only right that this sum should be paid out
of the Road Fund.
With regard to the Appropriation in Aid
for the use of extra police, hon. Members
will see that it is more than last year. This
is due to the fact that we
had the "A"
Special Constabulary and our own Royal
Ulster Constabulary was not up to full
strength, and the local authorities concerned
got those extra police free.
•
My hon. Friend the Member for West
Belfast (Mr. Wm. McMullen) raised the
question the other day of the accommo
dation for prisoners while under arrest in
the police court. He complained that the
washing accommodation is not such as it
should be. I have gone into this matter
personally, and there is a great deal in his
complaint. I am taking this matter up,
and I hope I may be able to arrive at a
satisfactory solution as I agree with him
that prisoners awaiting trial should, at all
events, have the opportunity of making
themselves as respectable as they can in
appearance. Reverting to the Sub-head
dealing with Rents, I might point out that
we have not yet been able to arrange for
the establishment of a depot, but in the
meantime we are carrying on with the
camp at Newtownards which we rent from
the military authorities. A sum of money
has been appropriated to provide a depot,
but we thought it would be better to wait
until things became more stabilised when
we might be able to build more cheaply
than at present, and we considered that
the present arrangement, which enables
the police to come to Newtownards for
their refresher courses was the most satisfactory for the present.
With regard to barracks, considerable
progress has been made both in the reconstruction and erection of barracks, but
we have had a great many difficulties to
meet in regard to sites. However, I hope
that during the course of the present year
considerably more progress will be made
as the Government is most anxious that
the members of the Royal Ulster Constabulary should be properly housed. Hon.
Members know that the condition of the
barracks was simply deplorable when we
took them over and we are doing our best
to rectify them. I think these are the main
points of the Estimate, but I shall be very

Mr. WILLIAM MCMULLEN:
tremely satisfactory to know that the right

I have always thought it an extremely unsatisfactory state of affairs that people,.many

was brought there. It was due to the stupid.
ity of those splendid fellows in the Force

Now it has been said by the previous
speaker that the amount paid for the Royal
Ulster Constabulary is a very good form of
insurance, but the hon. Member who leads
the Opposition told us that it cost 13s. 4d.
per head of the population. He might have
tried to reduce that to a little finer fraction,
and told the Committee that that only meant
less than one halfpenny per head per day for
the entire population, so that if you calculate
on that basis the amount does not seem very
extravagant to maintain law and order and
the protection of interests that are vital to
us throughout the territory over which this
Constabulary exercises jurisdiction.
Mr. KYLE: Can you tell us anywhere it
costs more?
Sir ROBERT ANDERSON: The items in
which I am especially interested are not the
larger items that appear here by way of
wages. I want just to emphasise the report
of the Public Accounts Committee, which I
think most hon. Members of this Committee
have been reading-if not they should have
read it-or of which they possibly have seen
extracts in the public Press. That Committee spent very considerable time last year
--and I think they are likely to spend some
time this year again-in investigating certain
matters. Last year we found a condition of
affairs in regard to what some people might
possibly consider minor matters, but when
they are all added together they amount to
a considerable sum, and the principle that is
involved is a very vital one, while the underlying idea of efficiency and economy has also
to be considered.
First of all, I am glad to see that the
Ministry have succeeded in bringing down the
charges for telegrams and postage. They had
Supply-
Committee.
21 APRIL 1926
reached an inordinate height, in fact in considering them I was surprised to find that the
authorities in control of the police in the
different parts of the country allowed telegrams to be sent for the merest trifles, such
as requirements for whitewash brushes and
things of that kind, amounting to a very
considerable sum. I rather fancy that some
of them must have been under the impression that we had our own postal service
and that these things were no charge whatever. We must bear in mind that the Post
Office is a reserved service and that the
charges must fall upon ourselves in connection with matters of this kind. There was
room for a very considerable saving from the
figures presented to us by the Comptroller
and Auditor-General last year, and I am glad
that very effective steps have been taken to
reduce these Estimates, though I am not at
all sure that there is not room for still
further considerable reduction under this
particular head.
Then there is the question of travelling
expenses, transport charges, and subsistence
allowances. Under these three headings
there is room still, I think, for considerable
saving to be effected. During the difficult
and trying times through which the Constabulary passed undoubtedly they had to
use transport very freely. They had to use
the best possible means of locomotion irrespective of expense, and one could not
criticise them for so doing because they were
effectively dealing with law breakers, trying
to restore order throughout the country, and
to secure peace and good government. But
now that we have reached a state of comparative quietude it would be well for the heads
of the Constabulary in association with the
responsible officers of the Ministry to see that
the most rigid rules are laid down by which
these transport charges could be reduced and
subsistence allowances and things of that
kind brought down to a minimum. I see by
the Comptroller's recent report, which the
Public Accounts Committee have yet to consider, and to which I presume it would not
be in order to refer to-day, that these matters
are again dealt with, so that we may take it
that there is still room for improvement in
these directions.
I must say I can only corroborate what
everybody in this Committee, whether on
these or on the Opposition benches, has said
that we are all proud of the Royal Ulster
Constabulary. They are a splendid body of
men, desirous of doing their best for the
community, and I have never heard a single
complaint that they do not do their duty
irrespective of creed, class, or religion. I
think they have behind them, and no work
of the Constabulary can ever be effectively
carried out unless they have behind them the
moral support and strength of the community as a whole. I believe they have that
behind them to-day. They have got that
support, and they have won from the community recognition of the fact that they are
doing their utmost to help forward the best
interests of the people over whom they are
placed in control. Those are the only observations I have got to place before the Committee. I am glad that there is a reduction,
but I would once again point out that in
some of the smaller items there is still room
I believe for substantial economy without
destroying in any way the good work which
the Constabulary have been doing, and which
I hope they will continue to do in the
interests of Ulster for many years to come.
(Hon. Members: Hear, hear).

with the remarks of previous speakers who

see the time come when we can get back again
to the strength of the police force which we

for so heavily officered or so heavily manned

are one or two items to which I would like
to draw attention, not in any sense of criticism, but merely for the purpose of making
recommendations or suggestions to the
Government. One particular item about
which I am very keen is under sub-head Eclothing-and the next is under sub-head
F-arms, ammunition, and accoutrements.
The clothing is not supplied by Northern
Ireland firms, or the blankets, as far as
I am informed.
Mr. POLLOCK: I am afraid you are wrong
there.
Colonel WOODS: I hope so. I will be
very glad if I am incorrect. The clothing
used by the men on point duty-these white
waterproofs-is extremely useless for this
particular purpose, because, as the right
hon. Gentleman (Sir Dawson Bates) himself
will notice, they are wearing at the armholes and at the sides where there is constant bending of the arm. The rubber is
worn away, as the material will not stand
the strain. I would suggest that the authorities should use the old flexible material,
which is used for the ordinary overcoats,
with white arms or sleeves, as are used in
London and across the water.

HOUSE OF COMMONS
[Colonel Woods]
The other item to which I wish to refer
is that of £1,250 for accoutrements. There,
again, I would ask the attention of the right
hon. Gentleman (Sir Dawson Bates) to the
pointsmen who are still carrying revolversor holsters, at least-batons, and ammunition
pouches without any shoulder support. These
when they get their overcoats on constitute
a considerable weight. The right hon.
Gentleman checked me once when I said
that the weight was somewhere about
thirteen pounds, but I think it is somewhere
between nine and thirteen, and when the
coat gets wet the strain of this heavy weight
on their waists all the time the men are
moving their arms about is very fatiguing
and uncomfortable, and, in my opinion, it
is quite unnecessary. It only requires a
little thought or consideration from the right
hon. Gentleman to correct that particular
complaint.
Some attention has been directed to locomotion and boot allowances. I find after
comparison of these two items that there
are thirteen men in the force who have got
neither boot nor motor-car allowance. I
should like to know who these gentlemen
are, and why there are only thirteen of
them who have no need of one or other of
these allowances. Do they go about in their
bare feet? The other matters on which I
would have liked to touch have been very
thoroughly dealt with by previous speakers.
The hon. Member for Antrim (Mr. Crawford), who found fault with the charges for
postage and telephones, suggested that the
telephones should not be used when postage
would do. Local telephone calls only cost
11d, while a postage stamp costs 1d.
Sir ROBERT ANDERSON: Long distance
calls cost more.
Colonel WOODS: Yes, of course, but I take
it that most of these telephone calls are
local. I would like to see a reduction of this
force, and the time will come when it will
not be necessary to keep up such an enormous force as we have now, when you take
into consideration that we have a splendid
volunteer force as well. It is strange to think
that where one policeman was sufficient once
there are about four now. I hope the time
will soon come when it will be possible to
reduce this force to normal dimensions.
Major SHILLINGTON: I should like to
congratulate the Ministry on the fact of
their being able to introduce an Estimate
which shows a small reduction as compared
with that of the previous year, and also to
join in the compliments that have been
paid by previous speakers to the members
of the Royal Ulster Constabulary. There is

I am given to understand that at the present time applicants for enrolment in the

classes solely and only in relation to their
height, that men of five feet eleven inches
and upwards are put into class one, and
that if a man does not reach five feet eleven
-if he is, say, only 5 feet 10 inches-he
is put into class two. My contention is that
you would be just as likely, and much more
likely in some cases, to get a more efficient
man of 5 feet 10 inches than you would be
if the man were 5 feet 11 inches, and
height should not be the only question
to be taken into consideration. (Hon.
Members: Hear, hear.)
The Minister referred to the promotions to
commissioned rank in the Force, and I think
he said that fifty per cent. of those promotions go to men who rise from the ranks.
I would like to know what arrangements
are being made in regard to the filling of
vacancies in respect of the other fifty per
cent. Have the Government any scheme for
the training of cadets, or any system
whereby some of our promising young
Ulstermen who have done well, say, at the
University can get into the Royal Ulster
Constabulary? I do not know of any such
arrangement at the moment, but I would be
glad to hear if anything of that sort is
contemplated.
I would like again to refer to the question
of the camp at Newtownards. The Minister
very kindly answered a question which I
put to him a few weeks ago and gave me
to understand that that camp is costing the
Government £1,080 a year altogether, and
that the Government have to pay the rates
and taxes on that camp and insure it.
They have to pay that for what is really
a camp of sufficient size to accommodate
two military battalions. I understand that
there are two camps, but now that there are
never likely to be more than 200 men of the
Royal Ulster Constabulary there at the
present time there are only something like
150 would not it be possible to get the

and also elections. The elections do not
come very often, and, therefore, I think the
bulk is due for police attendance and the
preservation of the peace at political demonstrations. Surely we have reached this stage
in Northern Ireland when we can have our
political demonstrations without interference
from those who differ from us. I have
witnessed processions of all classes of Irishmen in Dublin and in Cork, and I have
enjoyed them. They can do the thing more
artistically in Dublin than in Belfast. We
have now in this Parliament amongst the
private Members representatives of both
sections, and I do not see why we should
not be able to suggest to those who look to
us as political leaders for guidance that
these demonstrations should be arranged in
such a way and in such territory that it
would not irritate anybody, and where no
interference would take place, and where the
presence of police would be unnecessary.
In connection with Sub-head D-Travelling
Expenses-I would very much like to know
whether the Royal Ulster Constabulary are
still carrying out the same old arrangement
which held good in the Royal Irish Constabulary under which a constable who produced a
bicycle to his superior officer was immediately put down for a cycling allowance
of so much a month, so much a quarter, or
so much a year as the case might be. I
understand that that man's superior officer
never had any authority to inspect that
bicycle from time to time, and it might
have done duty for any number of constables in the same barracks. I think it
would be much better if the Government
would provide so many bicycles for each
barracks at their own expense and do away
with that allowance altogether, and I would
like to know what proportion of this
£3,800 for travelling expenses is really due
to this cycling allowance.
I would like also to emphasise the points
that have been raised already by hon.
Members who are Members of the Committee
on Public Accounts in regard to the questions that were referred to them. I think
there is room for great saving yet in regard

like to say that I think it would be desirable,
as regards those motors that are used on
Government service, that a record should

would see that the uses to which these motorcars are put are proper uses.

Mr. BLACK: There is one matter not
touched on in this Estimate which seems to
me very striking, and that is the archaic
manner in which remuneration to both
officers and men is set out here. The first
we have under Sub-head A-pay, and the
second under Sub-head B--allowances.
the allowances were only allowances
special officers and men for special duties on
special occasions one could understand that
they may be set out separately. Take the
men. You have boot allowance for 2,930 men
at £3 188. each, and medical allowance for
2,950 officers and men at £1 7s. Or look at
the officers. You will find that the Inspector-
General, the Commissioners, the County
Inspectors and the District-Inspectors are
given rent allowance. The Deputy Inspector-General the County Inspectors, and
the District Inspectors are also given locomotion allowances. These form really part
of the salary or remuneration. Instead of
setting them out separately surely it would
be more satisfactory if boot allowance,
medical allowance and other allowances
were added on to the pay of the men so that
they would get a certain fixed amount equal
to the additional perquisites. If the rent
allowance, locomotion allowance and other
things were added to the ordinary salaries
of the superior officers we would be able to
see at a glance the real remuneration of the
sergeant or constable and also the real remuneration of the Inspector-General, County
Inspectors, and District Inspectors, per
annum. As it is now one has to go through
quite a number of things to try to find out
what the salary is or what wages are being
paid to the members of the Constabulary.
I know in no other Estimates, so far as I
have been able to see, is there this splitting
or setting out as allowances what is in
reality pay. In other services they do not
allow for a certain amount of salary and a
certain amount of medical allowances. Give
a man his salary and let him find his own
doctor and his own boots and his own locomotion. It would be more satisfactory and
businesslike than the present arrangement.
We would see what we were voting as remuneration both to officers and men.
There is one other matter I would like to
mention, and that is just to rub in what has
been stated already by the Member for
Derry (Sir Robert Anderson). The Public
Accounts
Committee were startled and
shocked by some things they came across
in the Constabulary accounts. I see that the

appointed-will keep a very vigilant eye on

With regard to that item, I see a very
striking and surprising thing in this Estimate. At the end of Sub-head B there is
set out a number of drivers to whom it is
proposed to pay an allowance of 2s. per day.
That is, I presume, because they have
qualified themselves as drivers. The item
sets out the number of drivers who got
this allowance in 1925-26 and the number
estimated for in 1926-27. The curious thing
is that there were only 40 in 1925-26, while
the estimate shows that 55 are to be paid

have a further reduction possibly next year.
I hope that there will be an assurance from

the year in regard to this Estimate, whi: .

The hon. Member for East Belfast (Mr.
Beattie) asked some questions about the subsistence allowance. That allowance is provided for where any member of the Force is
absent from the station on duty, and a
special scale is set out of the amounts that
are paid. If they are away for eight hours,
and under twelve hours, constables and sergeants are allowed 3s 6d, head constables 4s,
and officers 5s, and if they are away for
twelve hours and over, they are allowed 5s,
6s and 7s respectively. Then there are a
number of regulations which are all set out
in the Statutory Rules and Orders of Northern Ireland under the Constabulary Act.
Those matters are provided for, and that
scale is rigidly enforced. Vouchers must
always be supplied by any members of the
Force applying for subsistence allowance,
and all travelling expenses require to be
audited.
The hon. Member (Mr. Beattie) pointed out
that he had reason to believe that in connection with the motor cars belonging to
certain officers the men were engaged in
doing repairs to those private cars. If that
is so, we have no knowledge of it. It is
improper and not right, and we would be
very glad of any information which would
help to put a stop to anything of that kind.
Let me, at this stage, say in connection
with the report of the Public Accounts Committee that every word of it has been carefully studied, not only by the Minister of
Home Affairs, and by those associated with
him, but by all the officers in charge of the
Constabulary, and that the greatest regard
will be paid to every recommendation the
Committee have made. We want to take the
fullest advantage of their most careful deliberations to see that there will be no abuses
of any kind in connection with the Constabulary.
The hon. Member for West Belfast (Mr.
W. McMullen) asked about the locomotion

As regards the question raised by the hon.
Member for Down (Mr. O'Neill) with respect
to clothing, in 1924-25 the Police Force was
by no means at full strength, and I think
that is largely the cause of the amount at
that time being less than in the subsequent
year. As to the question of women police,
mentioned by the Member for Antrim (Mr.
Crawford), I am aware that the British
Government have increased the number of
women police. The Northern Government
are looking into this matter very carefully,
and if the experiment proves a success in
England, the Government will take into consideration the advisability of appointing
more women police.

Mr. THOMAS HENDERSON: At yesterday's sitting of the House, I said I would
ask the Minister of Home Affairs, at the
adjournment of the House to-day, a question
regarding the result of the Inquiry that took
place recently in the Union Infirmary. I
may say that I have seen the result of the
Inquiry, and that I am quite satisfied.
only want to take this opportunity of thanking the Minister of Home Affairs for the
very prompt manner in which he took up
this matter. I am quite satisfied that, as a
result of the Inquiry, proper attention will
be given in future to patients who are in
the unfortunate position of having to be
taken to the Mental Hospital. I believe that
good has been done as a result of the Inquiry,
and I wish to compliment the Minister and
the gentleman who conducted the Inquiry.
But I cannot allow this occasion to pass
without referring to a statement made by Mr.
Beattie, K.C., who represented the Poor-law
Guardians at the Inquiry. He said that I
had told falsehoods and made mis-statements,
and that I had not the courtesy to attend
the Inquiry and prove my statements. The
statement that I gave to the Minister of
Home Affairs was the statement given to
me by the deceased gentleman, who was an
inmate of Purdysburn Mental Hospital.
Therefore, I only took down the statement
of the patient, and handed it to the Minister
of Home Affairs. The Superintendent, or the
head of the Purdysburn Mental Hospital, I
understand, had previously sent a letter to
the Minister of Home Affairs, so that I was
not the first one to call attention to the
injury that this poor man had received. I
want to take exception to the methods
adopted by a member of the Bar in attacking
me and in trying to intimidate Members of
this House.
Mr. SPEAKER: I understand the hon.
Member is making a personal explanation
in connection with some adverse comments
upon his actions, but he is not entitled in
this House to go further than that, and to
make reflections upon members of outside
bodies such as the Bar.
Mr. T. HENDERSON: I will content myself, then, with sincerely thanking the
Minister of Home Affairs for the great
improvements that will be brought about as
a result of the Inquiry.
BUSINESS OF THE HOUSE.
Mr. KYLE: May I ask the Prime Minister
for a statement on the business of the
House?
The PRIME MINISTER: To-morrow it is
proposed to take the Mines (Working
Facilities, Support, etc.) Bill, as amended;
the Pensions (Increase) Bill, Committee;
and the Economy (Exchequer Relief) Bill,

On Tuesday, it is proposed to take the

Commercial Services, Ministry of Finance,
Public Works and Buildings, Special Constabulary, and Ministry of Home Affairs.
On Wednesday, the Committee stage of the
Economy Bill, and on Thursday the Jury
Bill.

HOUSE OF COMMONS.

Thursday, 22nd April, 1926.
The House met at Three of the Clock, Mr.
SPEAKER in the Chair.
Oral Answers to Questions.
BALLYMENA ARTIFICIAL SILK
FACTORY.
1. Mr. DEVLIN asked the Minister of
Commerce whether his attention has been
called to the statement in the Imperial
House of Commons by the President of the
Board of Trade, to the effect that ten artificial silk factories have been started in
England since the 1st of July, 1925; whether
he can say when the factory near Ballymena
will start production; whether other factories are to be established in Northern
Ireland; and what steps, if any, the heads of
the linen industry are taking to adapt some
of the linen factories to the production of
the new material.
The MINISTER OF COMMERCE (Mr.
Barbour): The answer to the first part of
the question is in the affirmative. With regard to the factory established near Ballymena the Company issued their prospectus
in February this year, in which it was
stated that the property, works and water
rights had been acquired, the machinery was
in course of manufacture, and that the
Company expected to be in a position to
commence delivery to customers during the
month of September. So far as my information goes, no concrete proposals for the
establishment of other factories in Northern
Ireland have hitherto been made, although
I am aware that negotiations towards this
end are proceeding. While I have no doubt
that the linen industry is carefully watching
the development of the uses of this new
textile, I have no information which would
suggest that steps have been taken by any
linen manufacturer to adapt an existing
linen factory to the production of artificial
silk.
Mr. DEVLIN: Is the right hon. Gentleman aware that within the last few days the
President of the Board of Trade has made
further statements in the Imperial Parliament to the effect that the value of artificial
silk manufactured in the United Kingdom
and exported during the first quarter of 1926
has increased by 82 per cent., and does the
right hon. Gentleman not think this new
industry offers a magnificent opportunity to
the heads of the linen trade to open up a new
branch and find an outlet for their own
enterprise and work for their operatives?
Mr. BARBOUR: I have noted the reference that has been made to the wonderful
development that has taken place in this
new fibre. My personal opinion is that there
would be considerable difficulty in adapting
the linen machinery in any way to the preparation of this fibre, but I am sure the
heads of the linen industry are watching the
course of these developments, and if they
can see that it can with advantage be adapted
to any of the fabrics which, they make at
present, they will not neglect such an opportunity.
Colonel WOODS: Is the right hon. Gentleman aware that in Dunfermline the linen
machinery has been adapted to the manufacture of artificial silk fibre?
Mr. BARBOUR: I am not aware of it.
Mr. DEVLIN: I have a number of other
supplementary questions. Shall I send them
to the right hon. Gentleman?
Mr. BARBOUR: I shall be glad to receive
them.
CHAIRMAN OF NORTH ANTRIM
REGIONAL EDUCATION COMMITTEE.
2. Mr. BEATTIE asked the Parliamentary
Secretary to the Ministry of Education
whether the Chairman of the North Antrim
Regional Education Committee holds the
offices of sanitary sub-officer under the Ballymoney Rural District Council, relieving
officer under the Ballymoney Board of
Guardians, and Infant Life Protection
officer; whether it is legal for him to hold
these offices, and, if not, why he is permitted
to do so.
The PARLIAMENTARY SECRETARY OF
THE MINISTRY OF EDUCATION (Mr.
Robb): The Ministry has been informed
that Mr. Hanna, who has been appointed
Chairman of the North Antrim Regional
Education Committee, holds the other offices
to which reference is made in the hon. Member's question.
The attention of the Antrim County
Council as the education authority for the
county, the Regional Education Committee,
the Ballymoney Urban Council, and the
Ballymoney Rural Council was called to the
matter in order that these bodies might
have an opportunity of considering it, and
in the event of their being advised that an
irregularity had occurred, of taking such
action as might be competent for them.
Oral Answers.
Oral Answers.
22 APRIL 1926
The Ministry also communicated with Mr.
Hanna, but that gentleman has informed the
Ministry that he had been advised that his
position is unassailable.
In these circumstances the Ministry did
not consider that it developed upon it to interfere any further in this matter as it was
not in any way responsible for the appointment of Mr. Hanna as a member of this
Regional Education Committee.
LOCAL GOVERNMENT OFFICERS ON
REGIONAL COMMITTEES.
3. Mr. BEATTIE asked the Parliamentary
Secretary to the Ministry of Education
whether he can state what Local Government
officers were appointed members of Regional
Education Committees in Northern Ireland,
and were then required to resign; and
whether other Local Government Officers
were appointed members of Regional Education Committees in Northern Ireland and not
required to resign, and for what reason was
this distinction made.
Mr. ROBB: The only case which has come
under the notice of the Ministry of Education where a member of a Regional Education
Committee when appointed to that position
held an office of profit under a local Council
or Board in the area under the control of
the Committee is that of Mr. Hanna, member of the North Antrim Regional Education
Committee referred to in the preceding
Question.
A member of the Ballymena Regional
Education Committee was appointed by that
Committee as its solicitor on condition that
he resigned his membership of the Regional
Committee, and he duly complied with this
condition.
The Ministry has no knowledge of any
other cases of this kind.
ULSTER OFFICERS IN "B" SPECIAL
CONSTABULARY.
4. Colonel WOODS asked the Minister of
Home Affairs whether he will consider the
advisabality of augmenting the number of
Ulster officers and Ulster non-commissioned
officers, clerks, and instructors employed in
the "B" Special Constabulary, which is recruited and regarded as essentially territorial in its constitution.
The MINISTER OF HOME AFFAIRS
(Sir Dawson Bates): As I pointed out to the
hon. and gallant Member in reply to a
question put by him on the 20th instant, out
of the total staff attached to the Force of
"B" Special Constabulary over 90 per cent.
are Ulstermen.
In selecting the full-time personnel of the
reorganised "B" Force, preference is given
to members of the Special Constabulary and,
other things being equal, to those who are
Ulstermen.
SIR RUSSELL SCOTT'S INVESTIGATION.
5. Mr. DEVLIN asked the Prime Minister
whether Sir Russell Scott had started his
investigation into the Northern Ireland
Civil Service, and, if so, why no public
announcement was made to this effect;
whether he will state what method Sir
Russell Scott has adopted to get at the facts,
and whether Members of this House will be
given an opportunity to place their views
before him.
The MINISTER OF FINANCE (Mr.
Pollock): I have been asked to take this
reply.
Sir Russell Scott assisted by two other
Treasury officials, started his inquiry in Belfast on the 7th April, and concluded his
examination of the work of the various Departments on the 13th instant. The method
he adopted was to begin with a personal
investigation on the spot into the work and
staff of each department, and he is now coordinating the results thus obtained with
additional statistics and reports which are
being supplied at his request. The conduct
of his investigations was left entirely to the
discretion of Sir Russell Scott, who
apparently did not consider it necessary to
make any public announcement of his
inquiry.
Mr. DEVLIN: Does the right hon. Gentleman think that this method of inquiry will
satisfy the public, and did he convey to Sir
Russell Scott that representations had been
made in this House that the inquiry should
he of a public character and that all persons
interested in his investigations should have
an opportunity of taking part in them?
Mr. POLLOCK: Yes. Sir Russell Scott
was informed that reference had been made
in this House in something like the terms
the hon. Gentleman has now suggested, but
the gentleman in question did not think it
necessary to do other than conduct the investigations in regard to the matters which
he was called upon to undertake without
consulting any outside authority.
Mr. DEVLIN: Does the right hon. Gentleman not think it a scandalous performance
on the part of this English official to come
over here and investigate the accounts of the
Ulster Government and the Ulster Province
without giving a single member of the
public an opportunity of taking part in his
investigations or appearing before him?

NORTHERN IRELAND CIVIL SERVICE.
Mr. SPEAKER: Order. The hon. Gentleman (Mr. Devlin) can talk about the
scandalous conduct of the Ulster Government,
but I do not think he is entitled to talk about
the scandalous conduct of
an official of
another Government, who undertook a duty
without restrictive terms of reference and to
whom complete liberty of action was allowed.
Mr. DEVLIN: With all respect, this man
comes over here to interfere in our business.
Mr. POLLOCK: No.
Mr. DEVLIN: Yes, he does.
Mr. POLLOCK: Might I intervene? Sir
Russell Scott was invited to come here by the
Government to undertake a specific work.
Mr. SPEAKER: The position is, as I understand it, that this British Civil Servant was
invited to come here, and so far as his actions
are concerned I do not think it falls to the
lot of this House to depreciate them, though,
of course, this House can criticise the Government for having invited him.
Mr. DEVLIN: Again with all respect, the
Minister has stated that this man came over
here and interfered in our business, that he
set up his own court, carried on his own
inquiry, pursued his own explorations and
treated with contempt the citizens of Ulster
and all those who were interested in——
Mr. SPEAKER: Order, order.
Mr. DEVLIN: I will discuss the matter in
a minute or two. When we come to the
Economy Bill I will say more about the whole
performance.
Mr. SPEAKER: The hon. Member is entirely outside the purview of what comes
within the province of this House in what
he says.
He can criticise the Government
for having adopted this way of bringing
about economies, but he is not entitled to
cast aspersions on the gentleman whom they
asked to come here, and who is the servant
of another Government.
Mr. DEVLIN: I would like to know what
business a servant of another Government
has to come here and interfere in our business and then to be immune from the criticism of this House. It is the most extraordinary position I ever heard of.
Mr. SPEAKER: As I say, that is a matter
entirely for the Government of Northern
Ireland as to whether this was a proper
method to adopt, but the hon. Member is
not entitled to reflect upon the conduct of
the gentleman who came here.
Mr. DEVLIN: I never heard of such an
extraordinary thing. I will discuss the
matter on the Economy Bill.
6. Mr. DEVLIN asked the Prime Minister
whether he is prepared to appoint a Select
Committee, consisting of representatives of
every section in the House of Commons, to
inquire into the method of appointment to
and promotion in the Northern Ireland Civil
Service, the number of officials dismissed
during the past six months, and the reason
assigned for their dismissal, and the number
appointed during the same period.
Mr. POLLOCK: I have been asked to reply
tc this question. The reply is in the negative.
I may say, however, for the hon. Member's
information, that the only officials whose
services have been dispensed with are those
who had been engaged in a purely temporary
capacity, and whose employment has been
terminated because their services were no
longer required.
Mr. DEVLIN: In order to remove more
than a suspicion-a sound fundamental belief
on the part of a large number of the public
that these appointments are made for purely
political reasons and given to camp followers
of his as against the appointment of efficient
officials, and to avert and prevent a continuance of this form of criticism, will the
right hon. Gentleman agree to the appointment of a Select Committee of the House
to investigate the matter?
Mr. POLLOCK: I am not prepared to concede the statement of the hon. Member, and
I cannot agree to the suggestion he has made
that a Select Committee should be appointed
for the purpose he has indicated.
Mr. BEATTIE: Will the Minister not be
prepared to accept the suggestion made by
the hon. Member for West Belfast (Mr.
Devlin), owing to the statements made in
this House in regard to these appointments?
I am sure he will get some very good information from Members of this House as to
how the appointments are made to the
various Ministries of the Northern Government. I would suggest that the Minister
should accept the suggestion.
