Economy Bill--
Second Reading.
22 APRIL 1926
Bill Presented.
JURY LAWS AMENDMENT BILL,
"to amend the Laws relating to Juries in
Northern Ireland," presented by Sir Dawson
Bates; supported by Mr. Hanna; to be read
a Second time upon Thursday, and to be
printed. (Bill 9.)
ORDERS OF THE DAY.
Economy (Exchequer Relief) Bill.
Order for Second Reading read.
Mr. POLLOCK: I rise to move the Second
Reading of the Economy (Exchequer Relief)
Bill. I have caused to be circulated a
memorandum explaining the provisions of
the Bill, which will, I hope, serve to remove
any obscurities which the inevitable legislation by reference necessarily entails.
This is a very important Measure, not
alone because of the material issues involved,
but because it seeks by its provisions to
emphasise the fundamental truth that the
financial stability of the State transcends
every other consideration. It is the foundation of all progress, all prosperity. The
State differs in no respect from the individual; once destroy a man's financial credit
and catastrophe ensues. So it is with the
State. Many States, great and small, in
their departure from this law have brought
upon themselves calamitous results.
It is, therefore, to maintain the traditional
unimpeachable structure of British credit
that the Chancellor of the Exchequer some
weeks ago submitted the Economy Bill, which
has been the subject of so much discussion
at Westminster. In two of the most important features of this Measure we are very
directly interested for very definite and
cogent reasons. First, under our present
constitutional arrangements our whole financial system is so interwoven with that of
Britain it would pass the wit of man to keep
them separate. Second, our own financial
necessities are so great, I am searching in
every quarter and in every Department of
our national machinery for any saving that
can be effected.
The provisions of the Bill fall naturally
into two main divisions; firstly, the amendment of the law in regard to the State's
contribution to the Contributory Insurance
Schemes, and secondly, the readjustment to
a small extent of the State's financial relations with local authorities. I propose to
place before the House, as briefly and concisely as possible, the main principles
underlying the Bill, and to explain at the
same time the motives which have led the
Government to contemplate the various
changes which are now proposed.
I would
ask Members in raising any points to recollect that detailed explanation will be given
on each clause in Committee, and an opportunity will then arise of that close scrutiny
of detail which is not appropriate to a
Second Reading.
I turn now to the clauses dealing with the
two Contributory Insurance Schemes, and
in order to explain them fully it is necessary
for me to ask the House to carry their
thoughts to what is commonly termed the
Colwyn Award, with which this matter is
so closely interwoven. The House will recollect that in devising a formula for the
determination of our contribution towards
Imperial services, the Colywn Committee
first constructed a standard year-1923-1924and then proceeded to enunciate principles
for the guidance of the Joint Exchequer
Board in determining the manner in which
any deviations from the expenditure and revenue in that standard year were to be dealt
with. Stated in broad outline, and without
certain
necessary correctives, if Great
Britain increased her local expenditure-in
the main, expenditure on social servicesabove the expenditure of the standard year,
Northern Ireland was to be allowed a corresponding increase, if warranted by the
circumstances. On the other hand, if Great
Britain's local expenditure actually decreased, the Joint Exchequer Board are to
presume that a corresponding decrease in
our local expenditure is called for, and if
such does not take place the costs of maintaining the service at the old level must be
found by Northern Ireland from her own
resources.
It immediately follows, therefore, that if
the Imperial Government takes steps, which
result in a diminution of their local expenditure, and we, for our part, decide to maintain the particular services involved at the
old standard we have to bear the excess
cost ourselves. These considerations have,
as the House will at once realise, a most important bearing on our whole financial situation and policy, and unless we are in such
affluent circumstances that we can afford to
disregard the effects of the Colwyn Report,
and to bear entirely unaided the cost of maintaining local services here at a higher level
than in Great Britain it follows that we
must, of necessity, carry into effect here any
reductions in expenditure which are made
across the water.
This, therefore, is the position which has
confronted the Government since it became
known that the Imperial Government had
decided to make certain reductions in its
State contributions toward the contributory
insurance schemes. The first eight clauses
of this Bill provide for changes in the
administration of these services in Northern
Ireland, which are identical with those now
Economy Bill-
Second Reading.
HOUSE OF COMMONS
[Mr. Pollock]
being carried into effect in Great Britain,
and if Members will refer to the last page of
the White Paper which has been circulated
with the Bill they will notice that the total
savings which it is estimated will result
from these clauses amount to nearly £170,000.
Suppose that we had decided not to reduce
the State Grant toward National Health Insurance or the Exchequer contribution toward
Unemployment Insurance, we would have
been required to find that £170,000 entirely
out of our own resources; it would not have
entered in any way at all into the calculation of the contribution, and under the
arrangement we would have received no
allowance for it whatever. I do not need to
emphasise the fact that we cannot afford to
pay this £170,000, and it follows, therefore,
without argument, that we have no choice in
the matter, but must of necessity legislate
on parallel lines with Great Britain.
That is the financial effect viewed in the
light of the Colwyn Award. But we can
view it from a less material standpoint.
Take Health Insurance for example. The
whole scheme in Northern Ireland is absolutely interlocked with the British Scheme;
we have large societies operating in both
areas, and both providing similar benefits,
and we have a Joint Central Committee on
which we are represented, controlling
common Central Funds. It would, therefore, be wholly impracticable to dissociate
ourselves from, and to do anything else
but follow suit with Great Britain.
Then take Unemployment Insurance. There
is here too a reason why it is incumbent
upon us to follow Great Britain in regard
to the changes which are now being made.
The terms of what is generally known to us
as the Cave Award are no doubt still fresh
in the minds of every hon. Member of this
House. They are embodied in the agreement
made between the Chancellor of the Exchequer and myself and ratified by this
House in the early part of the Session, and
the full scope of that agreement, with its
consequential substantial contribution by the
British Exchequer to our Unemployment
Relief Fund, can only be obtained if we continue to follow any measures taken by the
Imperial Government. We are, therefore,
from a common-sense point of view bound to
reduce our State contribution to the Fund
to the extent of the reduction made in
Great Britain. Of the general effect of this
reduction I will deal at greater length when
I come to consider the clauses of the Bill.
I think I have now been able to show the
necessity of following Great Britain in regard
to these Insurance Services, but at the same
time it is desirable that I should show that
in so doing we are not acting inequitably
toward the insured population of Northern
Ireland, a very important factor in the discussion of this Measure. Ever since its inception in 1911 the National Health Insurance Scheme has been attended by the most
remarkable and phenomenal measure of
success; approved Societies have been able
to build up large reserve Funds, and one
factor which has assisted them in so doing
has been the rise in the rate of interest
which can be earned. I do not propose to
enter into this factor, but I may mention
that the present accumulated funds of these
Societies are the tremendous sum of
£65,000,000. One of the first factors or causes
of the exceptional success in respect of the
accumulation of these reserves is that when
the Insurance Fund was started in 1911 the
rate of interest on investments was only calculated at something like 3 per cent, or 3}
per cent., while from the financial development that ensued the value of money increased so much that these Societies were
enabled to invest their money at from 4, per
cent. to 5 per cent., and we have the Chancellor of the Exchequer's authority for
stating that this one factor alone increased
the volume of their surplus by £2,000,000 a
year.
Moreover, the Widows' and Orphans' Contributory Pensions Act of last year has, in
addition to placing a very considerable new
charge on the State, provided a large
measure of relief to Approved Societies inasmuch as from January, 1928, additional
sickness and disablement benefits will not
have to be provided for insured persons between the ages of 65 and 70. We have, therefore, at the present time a very remarkable
contrast between the financial position of the
State and the financial position of these approved societies. Here we see these great
societies rolling in-I do not want to use extravagant adjectives, but I think ordinarily
we would describe them as almost colossally
wealthy.
On the one hand there is undoubted
stringency, and continual examination and
re-examination of expenditure in order to see
whether reductions can be effected; while on
the other hand we have a very satisfactory
condition of wealth and prosperity. I maintain that the time has now come when the
State should make some small reduction in
the annual sums granted to approved
Societies, which are based on the benefits distributed by such Societies, and provision on
this behalf is accordingly made in the Bill.
There is nothing inequitable in this. That
is the whole issue. It will not affect contributors in any way whatever, and the sole
effect which it will have will be to
slow up to some extent the rate at
which approved societies are accumu
lating surpluses. And if we did not
make this reduction what would be the
Second Reading.

Economy Bill-
22 APRIL 1926
result? The formula of the Colwyn Award
would relentlessly operate, as I have already
explained, and we would be forced to find
the money from our already too depleted
pockets.
I have already touched upon the provisions
in the Bill affecting the Unemployment
Fund, namely, a reduction in the Exchequer
contribution from 8d. to 6d. If we stood
alone and discussed our Unemployment Insurance Fund purely from our own point of
view I have not any doubt at all that if we
attempted to reduce the contribution from
8d. to 6d. we would bring our fund into a
very parlous condition, but in discussing this
matter we have to recall the whole circumstances under which the Fund is at present
operating. Let me say at once that this proposal-the reduction from 8d. to 6d.-does
not affect in the slightest degree the position
of our Unemployment Fund vis-a-vis the
corresponding British Fund. Under the Unemployment Insurance Agreement the
finances of our Unemployment Fund here are
definitely linked up with those of the British
Unemployment Fund, and to a very considerable degree have become associated with our
Exchequer, obtaining large issues therefrom,
not by way of repayable loan as in the past,
but by direct out and out payments.
Let me in a few words attempt to explain
the position. It is of such an involved
character-the calculation between the two
Governments-that I think it may be said
in the words of the Chancellor of the Exchequer that it is expressed in language only
intelligible to those who are masters of this
intricate and highly specialised subject.
Therefore, the explanation that I propose to
offer will be made as clear as I am able to
do in the simple language that I would
naturally employ. The two Funds are to be
maintained on a parity-at present a parity
deficit-proportionate to our insured populations. To achieve this parity, we under
present conditions must make large
additional contribution from our Exchequer,

Now see how this operates under the

Sir ROBERT ANDERSON: May I ask the

deemed to subscribe her total population proportion of all expenditure on Unemployment
Insurance, which includes the State Grant.
But, under the Colwyn Report she is only
allowed in cash her actual expenditure on
State grant, with the result that she has
to make up the difference between this expenditure and the amount she is deemed to
spend under the Cave Award. Naturally,
the more the figures of each item are
reduced proportionately, the more the
difference diminishes. In this case the net
effect is £41,000 on the latest Estimates.
This is a real immediate saving to the Exchequer, which, if the 8d. contribution stood
would have had to be found from our own
pockets. I almost despair of making myself
clear on this point-it is one for mathematicians rather than for debate, but I can
assure the House that the facts are as I have
stated them.
I have dealt sufficiently with two important parts of the Bill which relate to
our relations as between Great Britain and
ourselves. I now come to the second main
division of the Bill, namely, that part from
Clause 9 onwards, which touches upon the
fringe of the subject of our financial relations with local authorities. When assistance was first given to local authorities,
chiefly for the relief of rates, it was by way
of the assignment of some definite source of
revenue for that purpose. This system has
since undergone very (considerable modifi-,
cations, and for a number of years the
tendency has been to replace it by some
system of definite grants, Accordingly,
Parliament has on numerous occasions provided by statute for the payment of grants
to local authorities for a great variety of
purposes, amongst which of course we have
Housing, then grants for various purposes
connected with Public Health; and more recently grants for educational services. There
still exist, however, one or two relics of the
early system, and I think it is clear that

the equities of the case-certainly the simplicities of the case-demand at the present
time some re-adjustment of these financial

I think my point can best be illustrated
by reference to some of the specific provisions of the Bill. Take Clause 9, for instance. Existing legislation provides that
after certain of the expenses of collecting
Dogs Licence Duty have been met, and
an appropriate transfer made to the Petty
Sessions Fund, the balance of the proceeds
of the duty is to be handed over to local
authorities in relief of local rates. Since
this was originally enacted years ago many
other forms of State assistance to local
authorities have been created, and the
Government feels that to a very large extent,
if not indeed entirely, the purposes for
which the proceeds of this Licence Duty were
originally handed over to local authorities
are now met by grants from the Exchequer
in aid of particular services. It is proposed
therefore, that first of all
recognise as a legitimate charge on the
Dogs' Fund the expenses of the Royal Ulster
Constabulary in connection with the collection of the Duty, as well as the other
expenses already charged thereto, and that
after allowing for these expenses one-third of
the surplus should be paid into the Exchequer, leaving two-thirds to be handed
over to the local authority. While logically
under the circumstances I have mentioned
the Exchequer might have appropriated the
whole sum, it was felt that it would be unfair
to local authorities to require them to forego
the full amount immediately. I have suggested, therefore, that they should receive
two-thirds.
we
should
Now I come to a clause that has been
the subject of some discussion and takes us
back to a somewhat remote past, this is
Clause 10 It has always been recognised that
the Valuation Department performs a dual
service. It not only carries out valuations
which govern the collection of local rates,
but it is also an important piece of machinery
in connection with the assessment of Income
Tax and Licence Duty. Some 50 years ago
it was agreed in principle that local authorities should contribute toward the cost of
the Valuation Office, and their payments
were fixed at a sum which then amounted to
one half of the cost of the Department. Now
it must be remembered that this arrangement was made very shortly after the great
valuation of Ireland made by Griffiths, and
consequently there was at that time very
little real work carried out by the Valuation
Department. It followed then that the cost
was on a very low basis and the local authorities, having agreed to pay half or rather to
pay an amount which then represented half,
escaped with practically a nominal sum.
Since then conditions in this Department as
well as in every other department of life
have changed very materially. The costs
have increased to a very large extent relatively in the last ten years. There has
been a very large increase in salaries and
travelling expenses.
We feel, therefore, that the time has now
come-in fact I am of opinion that it was
reached many years ago--when we should
make some adjustments in the annual payments. The Bill proposes, therefore, to amend
the contributions of counties and county
boroughs in order to bring the total annual
payment up to approximately one-half of the
present cost of the service. That is simply
on the same principle that has been adopted
50 years ago, when the amount was originally
settled.
It is interesting to note that the income
which local authorities obtain as a result of
valuation approximates to the sum of
£2,500,000 per annum, whilst the Exchequer in Income Tax and Licence
Duty receives something less than £300,000.
That is to say, the Valuation Office is maintained as to nine-tenths for the local authorities practically, and one-tenth for the State.
As I have, therefore, been hunting around-I
quite frankly admit it-(laughter)-for something that could relieve the pressure, I did
think it was fair that the local authorities
should bear a proportion-not necessarily the
proportion involved in the relative
importance of the work carried out for them,
but that they should at any rate bear the
proportion that was originally arranged 50
years ago, that is to say, one-half. The arguments are overwhelmingly in favour so far
as the equities are concerned. I do not think
if it were submitted to any tribunal that
there would be any difficulty in coming to
that decision.
Since this Bill was introduced I have received various representations from various
parts of the country through our representatives-not that this is an unfair claim, I do
not think anyone has made such a contention
-but that in view of the very heavy burden
on the local authorities at the present time,
it would be an additional burden upon them
-although the cost would not be very heavy,
but it would be an additional burden upon
the rates if the Government carried out the
intentions of the clause I have been discussing. The Government sympathises with
the argument, although still contending for
the propriety of the claim that has been
made, and the Government, having concern
for the interests of the ratepayers equally
with their concern for the State, have
arranged, in deference to the representations,
to amend this clause in such a way as will
meet the views of the local authorities at the
present time.

amount of pains he must have taken to get

I congratulate him on his memorable

Clause 11 of the Bill does not require any
great explanation. At the present time we
are bound by statute to pay annually the sum
of £42,881 to Road Authorities in aid of expenditure on roads and bridges. This grant
dates from a period long before the establishment of the Road Fund, which is now specifically earmarked for the purpose of constructing and maintaining the roads, and is, under
present circumstances, an anomaly.
Members will no doubt agree that this expenditure should now fall on the same plane
as other expenditure of the same nature,
and emerge from the Road Fund to the local
authorities, and the clause proposes to make
arrangements to this end. It is only a
question of transferring the method of issue.
Summing up the effects of Parts 3, 4 and 5
of the Bill, if we deduct £5,000 surrendered
by the cancellation of Clause 10 it will result
in a saving to the Exchequer to the extent of
something like £43,000. I have no hesitation
in saying that this transfer of burden is
amply justified, for the credit of a State
transcends every other consideration. May
I cite a parallel? Government property is
exempt from rating, but Government pay a
bounty in lieu of rates which closely approximates to the ordinary rating. The Government has not stereotyped its contribution. As
the rates have increased of recent years, so
the contribution has increased. The Government has automatically increased its contribution, therefore applying the same argument we did not think it was unfair-that
the local authorities should recognise the
change that has taken place as the Government has done in the matter of the Road
Fund.
The additional burden which will be imposed as a result of this legislation is
negligible, and though it will not be welcomed, I would remind local authorities that
they escape here many burdens wihch corresponding bodies in Great Britain have to
shoulder.
I have now explained generally the reasons
which have prompted the Government to introduce this Bill, and I have also briefly
scanned the provisions of the Measure in
order to some extent to assist the House in
grasping the main features of the various
proposals and the probable effects of each
particular clause. I do not think, therefore, I
need expand the arguments any further than
I have done, and I simply beg to move the
Second Reading of the Bill. (Hon. Members:
Hear, hear.)

The right hon. Gentleman has stated that

reserves, and now the State, jealous of the
amounts the societies have accumulated,

Mr. KYLE: That is the interpretation I

here to-day. While we may let you have the

Where is the economy, except at the expense

Economy Bill. It is a confiscatory Bill, a

that no body of employers could have had
the unblushing audacity to bring a Measure
of this kind before this House, simply and
solely because it is being proposed in Great
Britain. If Britain does a foolish thing, and
proposes to rob its insurance societies, I do
not think it is right that Northern Ireland
should do the same, and I think that the
public of the Six Counties should be and will
be bitterly opposed to the proposals in this
Measure.
The right hon. Gentleman has made a very
plausible case. He gave as one of the reasons
why these societies should be robbed the fact
that the interest on some of the funds has
increased since the time the money was invested. Surely that applies to practically
every investment that has been made. If
you are going to take into account the fact
that the rate of interest has changed from
the time the money was invested, you should
also take into account the same fact when
it applies to other things. When people lent
money to the State during the war money
was not worth as much as it is now, with the
result that people to-day are getting more
than they bargained for when they lent their
money to the State. If it is right to
economise in this way, or to take this money
in this way, then I hold that it would be right
for any Chancellor to reduce the interest on
the National Debt. It is just the same proposal
made in a different way. The only redeeming
feature about the whole Measure is that it
will give some future Government a precedent for submitting some confiscatory proposals at a later stage. That is the only
valuable point about the Measure. I beg to
move.

who make no claim to have more than the
ordinary knowledge of the man in the street
about finance. As I say, this Bill is an
outrageous attempt to rob the poor of their
savings. It is an insult to the spirit of
thrift which they have shown.
It is an
indication that if they manage their affairs
with capacity and with care they will be
penalised for it when the exigencies of
Government finance demand it. I, therefore,
second the rejection of this Bill, and I hope
it will not be passed by the House.
Sir ROBERT ANDERSON: I think it
would be well for the House to follow the
example of the Minister of Finance in the
very calm, dignified, and argumentative statement which he submitted to us on this very
important Bill which we are now about to
consider. After all the main proposals of
the Bill are perfectly understandable, and I
do not think any difficulty should arise in
connection with the points about which the
hon. Member for West Belfast (Mr. Devlin)
has spoken with such fire, with such eloquence, and with such heat. It is well for
the House to bear in mind the position in
which we stand with Great Britain from a
financial standpoint. (Hon. Members: Hear,
hear.) Let us never forget that the main
taxing and collecting authority, after all, is
the Imperial Government, and that we are
bound up in our financial relationship with
the basis laid down in the Colwyn Committee's Report, which I presume the hon.
Member for West Belfast (Mr. Devlin) has
read and inwardly digested.
Mr. DEVLIN: Three times.
Sir ROBERT ANDERSON: And understands I hope thoroughly and completely.
Mr. DEVLIN: I have read it three times
and I do not understand it yet.
Sir ROBERT ANDERSON: He quite
candidly admits that he does not understand
the financial position laid down there, and I
can quite understand that because I think
the speech he has just delivered to the House
confirms what he has so candidly admitted
just now.
Mr. KYLE: We know that we are being
robbed.
Sir ROBERT ANDERSON: The first thing
we have to consider here to-day is our future
financial position as a Government. The
Minister of Finance (Mr. Pollock) has laid
down very clearly and beyond the possibility
of a doubt that if we do not follow step by
step with Great Britain in connection with
the matters that are defined in this Bill
then we have got to face the music ourselves,
and will our hon. Friends on the Opposition
Benches tell us, if we have got to face
£300,000 or £100,000 of additional charges,
where that money is to come from?
Mr. BEATTIE: Where it is.
Sir ROBERT ANDERSON: Will they tell
us where it is to come from and how we are
going to finance our Unemployment Fund, in
which, after all, they ought to be very
seriously interested? (Hon. Members: Hear,
hear.) Let us not forget that we have still
to bear up to twenty-five per cent. of the
interest charges and the deficit that is likely
to arise yearly in connection with that fund.
I trust and I hope that the House will prefer,
and I trust that the country will also confirm the Minister of Finance in the attitude
he has taken in regard to this great question,
and that is that it is far better to try to
find a way out by the solution which he has
presented to the House to-day than to proceed to borrow money-(Hon. Members:
Hear, hear)-and thus inflict a permanent
debt upon the Six Counties.
Economy Bill-
Second Reading.
HOUSE OF COMMONS
Mr. KYLE: You are going to take it off
the poor. There is no doubt about that.
Sir ROBERT ANDERSON: I think it
would be disastrous to the best interests, to
the industrial interests and to the interests
of the working classes themselves, if we as
a Government placed ourselves in the position
that we had to go and borrow a huge pile of
money to meet our financial obligations. It
is much better to begin at once to square our
accounts every year, to maintain the credit
of the Province, because by doing that you are
doing something that is going to help every
class and every interest in the community.
(Hon. Members: Hear, hear.) That is what
I wished to say on the general financial
question with which the Minister of Finance
is trying heroically to deal in the Measure
which he has submitted to the House.
In connection with health insurance and
unemployment insurance, surely my hon.
Friends on the Opposition Benches must know
full well that in the arrangements recently
inade regarding this matter in conference
with the British authorities we were compelled practically to follow step by step in
these social matters, otherwise the consequences will be very serious indeed, as I
have already pointed out. In 1911 when
the National Health Insurance
was first
introduced it was introduced
experiment, and it was fixed
certain financial basis. The system had
got to be tried and worked out in order
to see exactly what the results would be.
Here let me say, once and for all, so far as
I am concerned in regard to legislation of this
and a similar character that what Parliaments have done Parliaments can undo.
Mr. KYLE: Hear, hear.
as
an
upon a
Parliaments
Sir ROBERT ANDERSON:
can alter Measures from time to time, and
the Leader of the Opposition would be the
first to say if certain things were wrong that
Parliament should reconsider them in the
light of new facts, in the light of fresh information and in the light of the working
of the scheme which Parliament itself
originally brought into being. What is the
effect to-day? Through circumstances that
nobody could foresee the National Health Insurance Societies have a huge surplus of
something like £60,000,000. It was never contemplated by Parliament they should build
up such a huge surplus, and that surplus is
steadily on the increase. This Measure
which was brought in and passed by the
Imperial Parliament, and which we now
follow, does not propose to do what the hon.
Member for West Belfast (Mr. Devlin) has
indicated. It does not propose to take one
penny piece of that surplus that already
exists in connection with these Societies. It
is theirs for them to appropriate in whatever
way they like, but the State steps in now and
says that in view of this huge accumulated
surplus they have got it is not necessary
for the State to give them such large contribution as hitherto.
There is nothing unreasonable in a proposal of that kind, especially when we bear
in mind the difficult financial position which
the country is in and is likely to pass through
during the coming years. Further, why have
these Health Societies accumulated such a
great surplus? It has not always been through
frugal management. I am sure a great deal
could be attributed to that, but from information that sometimes comes to me I think
these Societies should have been a little more
generous and should have given to their
members greater assistance and help than
they have been doing. If that had taken
place then the surplus would not have been
as large as it is to-day.
The same argument that I have used in
regard to national health applies with equal
force and strength to the question of unemployment insurance. Here, again, there is
a modification proposed and neither the
actuaries nor those who have criticised the
proposals submitted to the British House or
to this Parliament have made the statement
that the withdrawal or reduction of the contribution provided from Parliament would
make any of the societies bankrupt or would
lessen the benefits they would confer upon
the insured persons or upon the unemployed.
They have never made that argument, and.
bearing those facts in mind, Parliament is
now proceeding to review them in the light
of fresh facts and in the light of
ascertained knowledge, and I think that a
change can take place without doing any
injury to the interests concerned, and that at
the same time in making these reductions they
are strengthening the credit of the State and
preventing additional taxation, both direct
and indirect, being put on the people. As
far as I am concerned I am quite prepared
to support the Measure submitted by the
Government through its Finance Minister
this afternoon.
We come now to another part of the Bill.
I have dealt with the two main proposals,
which are the only two proposals that have
been taken exception to by the Leader of the
Opposition in the Amendment which he has
submitted to the House. The Minister of
Finance in his very lucid explanation in regard to the Clause dealing with local authorities has, if I may be permitted to say it,
taken a statesmanlike and wise course in
indicating that when the Committee Stage is
reached Clause 10 will be withdrawn. I think
I would be prepared to cross swords with the
Minister of Finance on some of his stateinents with regard to the question of the
contribution by local authorities. I could,

that would have arisen at many local and

I do not think we need worry about licenco

difficult times and the Minister of Finance
has so far during his association with this
Government steered us so safely and securely,
every year having a balance on the right side,
Studying closely and carefully our financial
position it is evident that we have had
difficult times during the last three or four

be certain financial obligations which this
Government may have to undertake in the
coming years, I think the Minister of Finance
may have more difficulties in making matters
right during the next three or four years.
But I sincerely hope everything will go well
and that the Measure he has now placed
before the House, while doing injury to no
interest, will consolidate our position, will
maintain the splendid position in which we
stand before the world to-day and SO
strengthen the credit of Ulster that we will
be able to go forward and help in the best

likely to find them. Is there lead in Slieve

are.
In regard to Clause 9 of the Bill which

reason it has been annulled is that on

is being raised at present they could not
afford to pay a levy. I hope that what the
Minister said as to the possibility of much
larger quantities of coal being raised in the

gentleman who had the courage to undertake
the development of an industry such as
Sir Samuel Kelly has undertaken to develop
at Coalisland will be successful in his efforts,
because I think he deserves every credit for

they are a success I do not see why this
little levy for welfare purposes should not
have been retained, but if the undertaking is
a failure I am sure that no one in this House
would claim that the levy should be put into

that the Bill should be introduced? I think
that information should be made known
to us.

HOUSE OF COMMONS.

Tuesday, 27th April, 1926.
The House met at Three of the Clock, Mr.
SPEAKER in the Chair.
Private Business.
re-
LOCAL BILLS-STANDING ORDERS.
The CHAIRMAN OF WAYS AND
MEANS (Mr. Moles): I beg to move the
Amendments to the Standing Orders
lative to Local Bills, which stand in my
name upon the Order Paper. Standing
Order No. 38 enumerates the places in
London at which the promoters of Local
Bills are required to deposit copies of those
Bills, and the effect of the first of the pro
posed Amendments is to take out the Irish
Office, which no longer exists, and to add to
the list the War Office. It also requires the
promoters to lodge a copy with the Home
Office in place of the copy which was previously deposited with the Imperial Secretary, that office now no longer existing. A
new Order which appears on the Paper together with an Appendix is to require more
detailed information from local authorities
and joint boards where permanent works
are intended to be undertaken by them.
The information which these Estimates will
give is essential to the Ministry under
whose authority it may be necessary to
raise the desired loan. I may add for the
information of the House that this Standing
Order has been included in the Standing
Orders recently passed at Westminster, and
it is merely keeping our Standing Orders
in line with those of Great Britain. With
the permission of the House there are a few
corrections I desire to make in the new
Standing Order as set out on the Paper.
In line 2, after "(C)" it is necessary to insert the words 'proposed to be carried
out," and in the last line but one of the
third paragraph, after the word "statement,' "the word should be " of " instead of
"for," this being a purely typographical
error. Then in the Appendix at the top of
page 3 the word "wire" should be "ware."
I beg to move.

ORDER No. 38 (Deposit of Bills at
Public Departments).
On or before the twenty-first day of
December a printed copy shall be deposited:
(1) of every Local Bill at the Ministries of Finance, Home Affairs, Labour,
Education, Agriculture, and Commerce
in Belfast.
Local Bills-Standing Orders. 706
(2) of every Local Bill at the Office of
His Majesty's Treasury, at the General
Post Office, at the Home Office, at the
Irish Office, so long as it shall continue
to exist, and at the Office of Woods in
London.
(3) of every Local Bill affecting any
dock, harbour navigation, pier or port.
foreshore or tidal lands, at the Office of
the Board of Trade in London.
(4) of every Local Bill affecting any
railway at the Ministry of Transport in
London.
Amendments made:
Order No. 38 (2), leave out "at the Home
Office, at the Irish Office, shall continue to
exist, and "
After "Woods " insert "at the War
Office and in duplicate at the Home Office
in London."
After Order No. 43 (Estimates to be deposited at the Ministry of Home Affairs)
insert the following new Order:
"On or before the thirty-first day of
December, copies of the estimates of expense of any work or purpose described in
the appendix marked (C) proposed to
be carried out by any municipal corporation, district council, joint board or joint
committee, or other local authority, shall
be deposited at the office of the Clerk of
the Parliaments, the Ministry of Finance,
and the Ministry of Home Affairs.
"The estimates shall be in the form set
forth in the appendix marked (C) or as
near thereto as circumstances may permit, and no other estimates shall be required from the promoters.
"If any moneys are required to be borrowed to meet any excess of expenditure
previously authorised by Parliament, or
any Government Department, there shall
be deposited with the said estimates a
statement of the purposes and reasons for
the borrowing.
"Together with the said estimates
there shall be deposited a statement showing the full particulars with respect to
the district of the local authority, that is
to say: (a) area of the district; (b) population according to the last census; (c)
rateable and assessable value according to
the last valuation list; (d) rates made in
the district during the last preceding
financial year; (e) the sum of the balances
of outstanding loans contracted by the
local authority; and (f) the amount of the
outstanding loans to which the limitation
of Section 238 of the Public Health

Questions for Oral Answers.
CANDIDATES FOR ROYAL ULSTER
CONSTABULARY.
1. Major SHILLINGTON asked the
Minister of Home Affairs whether he can
state how many candidates are at present
on the waiting list, in the different grades,
for the Royal Ulster Constabulary, and
whether in the grading of these applicants
preference is given to men with Army service or services in the Special Constabulary,
and what is the average height required in
each grade.
27 APRIL 1926
Oral Answers.

Oral Answers.
Sir DAWSON BATES: I wish my hon.
Friend had been more precise in stating what
he is asking for, but so far as possible the
quota will be kept up.
The MINISTER OF HOME AFFAIRS (Sir
Dawson Bates): With reference to the first
part of the hon. and gallant Member's
question, the number of candidates at present
the waiting list for the Royal Ulster
Constabulary is 159. They are graded as
follows:-
on
1st Class
2nd Class
3rd Class

..........


The reply to the second part of the question in the affirmative.
With regard to the last part of the question, the height standard for the 1st Class
list is 5 ft. 11 in., for the 2nd Class list
5 ft. 10 in., and candidates of a lower height
standard are placed in the third category,
but this arrangement is subject in all cases
to the proviso that a man who possesses
special educational or other qualifications
may be graded to a category above that for
which he would be qualified on the ground
of height alone.
Mr. PATRICK O'NEILL: Arising out of
that question may I ask the right hon.
Gentleman if in the further recruitment of
this force the undertaking or agreement
made by the Prime Minister as to the
religious basis of the force will be carried
out fairly?
Sir DAWSON BATES: I may remind my
hon. Friend that the recommendation of the
Police Committee was that one-third of the
force should be Roman Catholics. The
Government have so far as possible tried to
carry that into effect, but, unfortunately,
the Roman Catholics did not come forward
and the police force had to be filled up.
Mr. DEVLIN: But will the arrangement
be carried out in case applications are made
by them?
Sir DAWSON BATES: The whole question is whether or not the candidate is suitable for the police force and has the necessary qualifications.
Mr. PATRICK O'NEILL: But if they are
suitable will the quota of Roman Catholics
be kept up?
Sir DAWSON BATES: As far as possible, but I would remind the hon. Gentleman that the police force originally had to
be filled up owing to the fact that the Roman
Catholics did not come forward.
Mr. DEVLIN: Now that the force is
filled up and that the Catholics have not
got the numbers which, according to the
arrangement, they were entitled to, will the
right hon. Gentleman consider the advisability of trying to meet that situation by
giving favourable consideration to those
applicants who may now apply?
Colonel WOODS: Might I ask the right
hon. Gentleman are there any vacancies
existing at present, and if so how many?
Sir DAWSON BATES: I really could not
tell. There may be about three or four, but
not more.
Mr. McBRIDE: Might I ask the Minister
of Home Affairs has the height required for
the Royal Ulster Constabulary been increased
from 5 feet 8 inches to 5 feet 11 inches since
the disbandment of the Special Constabulary
in December last, and if it is a fact that a
candidate who has passed all the examinations but is just below 5 feet 11 inches is
only graded in the second class while an
applicant with little or no distinction is
graded first class if he is over 5 feet 11 inches
in height?
Sir DAWSON BATES: I am afraid my
hon. Friend could not have been listening
to the answer I gave earlier. 1 have explained that the men are all graded, and
those who are 5 feet 11 inches are placed in
the first category, and until that list is exhausted no appointments are made out of
the second category. Of course I would remind my hon. Friend that height is not
the main thing. The main question that
arises is whether or not a man is likely to
become a suitable policeman and possesses
the necessary qualifications.
BANN DRAINAGE.-ENGINEER'S
REPORT.
Major SHILLINGTON asked the Minister
of Finance whether he has received the report
from the engineers who have been investigating the flooding of the Lough Neagh and
River Bann areas; whether this report, when
ready, will be made public, and whether the
Government have considered what action
they will take in connection with this matter.
The MINISTER OF FINANCE (Mr.
Pollock): I have received the report. Having
regard to the importance and difficulty of
the question, my hon. and gallant Friend
will appreciate that the Report needs careful
consideration, and this it is receiving. It is
not in a form suitable for publication in its
entirety, but, without making any promise
at the moment, the Government will consider how far, consistently with the public
interest, it would be possible to make public
later the more important parts of the Report.
Mr. COOPER: Arising out of that question, may I ask the Minister of Finance if
anything has been done about the drainage
of Upper Lough Erne?
711 Economy (Exchequer Relief)—

HOUSE OF COMMONS
Committee.
Mr. POLLOCK: No, sir. The position in
regard to Lough Erne is somewhat different.
As my hon. Friend (Mr. Cooper) knows, both
sides of the country are concerned in that
very difficult problem, and until a solution
is found in respect of that difficulty nothing
has or can be done.
POSSESSION OF ARMS BY "C" FORCE.
Major SHILLINGTON (by private notice)
asked the Attorney-General if he can inform
the House whether any provision is being
made with reference to arms in the possession
of members of the "C" Force consequent
on their disbandment.
The ATTORNEY-GENERAL (Mr. Babington): The Government proposes to deal with
the matter under the existing Firearms Act,
and for that purpose to amend the Act, so
as to allow two forms of permit to be granted
--one to have arms, and another to have
and carry arms. These permits will be
granted by the County Inspector as heretofore, but the Government propose to give a
right of appeal from any decision of a
County Inspector refusing a permit to a
Resident Magistrate. All ex-members of the
"C" Special Constabulary will be eligible to
apply like other civilians.

ORDERS OF THE DAY.
Economy (Exchequer Relief) [Money]
Considered in Committee under Standing
Order No. 65.
(Mr. MOLES in the Chair.)
Motion made, and Question proposed:
"That for the purpose of any Act of the
present Session to make provision for re
ducing in respect of certain Services the
charges on Public Funds, and for increasing, by means of a payment into the Exchequer of Northern Ireland of certain
sums and otherwise, the funds available for
meeting such charges, and to amend accordingly the law relating to National Health
Insurance and certain other matters, and
for purposes related or incidental thereto,
it is expedient to authorise payment out of
moneys provided by Parliament, as a contribution towards any additional benefits
payable out of the Navy, Army and Air
Force Insurance Fund by virtue of any Act
passed in the present Session of the Parliament of the United Kingdom, such sums
as the National Health Insurance Joint
Committee may periodically ascertain to be
required for such contribution, having regard to the number of persons entitled to
benefits out of the said Fund, and actually
resident in Northern Ireland." (Governor's
Recommendation signified.-Mr. Barbour.)
The FINANCIAL SECRETARY (Mr.
Barbour): I think it will be the wish of
the Committee that I should explain the
exact effect of the Resolution, which is now
under consideration. This Government has
already accepted the principle that any
benefits which may be given by legislation
of the Imperial Parliament to British members of the armed forces of the Crown
should also be extended (where corresponding legislation comes within our powers) to
those soldiers, sailors and air men who enlist from our Province. I might refer in
passing to the provisions of Section 9 of our
Finance Act of 1924, in which we extended
to serving Ulstermen certain concessions
which had been made by the British Parlia
ment in regard to Death Duties. The proposals in the Resolution now before the Committee seek to give to those of our men who
have served in the Forces, and who are
subsequently discharged, the same benefits
which men from other parts of the United
Kingdom will receive under the new
British legislation in regard to National
Health Insurance.
In order to explain the Resolution I must
outline briefly the existing conditions under
which men of the Forces receive benefits
under the National Health Insurance
Acts. These men pay no contributions
whatever to this scheme. Contributions are
paid on their behalf from the Service Votes,
and after provision has been made for the
necessary credits to approved societies in
the small number of cases where the Service
man belongs to such a society the residue is
transferred to the Navy, Army and Air
Force Insurance Fund. During the period
of service no benefits are payable out of this
Fund except maternity benefit, because in
the ordinary way these men, while in the
service, receive hospital treatment, etc., according to the terms of their engagement.
A value is, however, placed on these entitlements, and the usual State contributions
713 Economy (Exchequer Relief)-
Committee.

27 APRIL 1926
paid in respect of them into the Service
Fund. To this Northern Ireland is already contributing in respect of persons
enlisted from Northern Ireland. When
men are discharged they may, if they are
physically fit, enter approved societies as
fully paid-up members, and an appropriate
credit is given to the society from the
Fund, but men whose health is impaired by
their service and who cannot for this reason join approved societies, continue their
membership of the Navy, Army and Air
Force Fund, which, under the law as it
stands, can only provide ordinary Health
Insurance benefits for them.
The Resolution, which I now beg to move,
proposes that there shall in future be paid
to these men from the Fund the additional
benefits to which the ordinary members of
approved societies have become accustomed,
such as additional cash benefits, dental
treatment, and SO forth. The British
Government have included in their Economy
Bill a clause which enables this Fund to
provide these additional benefits, and they
will be provided, not only for discharged
Servicemen resident in Great Britain, but
also for those resident in Northern Ireland.
By paying these additional benefits the
Fund at the same time involves the Exchequer in an increased charge, viz., the
one-seventh State contribution towards the
cost of the benefits. It is, however, not
feasible for the British Government to impose that charge on our Exchequer here; it
must be done of our own volition. The
equities of the case are clear, and it
is, therefore, with a view to accepting this
charge that I move the present Resolution.
There are approximately 500 men involved,
and the cost to the State will, as far as
we can assume, be in the region of £100 per
annum. I beg to move.
Mr. KYLE: I want to oppose this Money
Resolution. It has got to do with the
Economy Bill which will shortly be before
the Committee, and this Resolution strikes
at the very root of State stability. The State
made a promise, and for trivial reasons
which have been given here and also in the
House of Commons in England they are
breaking that pledge and promise. This
is money going to be saved by the State. I
think when it is brought home to members
of the Government and to the public that
the £217,000 proposed to be saved by the State
is coming from the poor, the sick, the
maimed, the afflicted and even the unem
ployed, any self-respecting man should oppose
such a Measure. Pledges were given, and
before this arrangement existing between
the State and the approved societies was
broken there should have been consultations
with the approved societies. I want to ask
the right hon. Gentleman has such consultation taken place between the approved
societies and the Government? When did
these consultations take place and what was
the result of them?
On the 22nd July, 1925 Mr. Neville
Chamberlain, the present Minister in Britain,
in reply to Sir Robert Horne, said:
I am very glad to hear my right hon.
Friend disclaim any idea of raiding the
surpluses. That, in my view, would certainly be interpreted, and I think with
some justification, as a breach of pledges
which have been given to approved societies.
It has been expected that the reward of
efficiency of administration on their part
would be the power to use their surpluses
in order to give additional benefits to their
members. And to say to those who have
exercised efficiency in their administration
in the hope of obtaining these additional
benefits, "We are going to take away that
which you have by your thrift and your
care accumulated," would, it seems to me,
be an unjustifiable procedure.
That was the statement made by Mr.
Neville Chamberlain last year, and this same
Minister is proposing to raid this Fund and
we are proposing to follow suit. Those of
us on these Benches are opposed to saving
by the State at the expense of the poor.
It means that the poor are going to be
denied the additional benefits they would
get if the State maintained their contribution of two-ninths instead of one-seventh.
I cannot follow the right hon. Gentleman
in his treatment of the soldiers, sailors and
airmen, but if the fund is going to be saved
to the State it seems to me that these
soldiers, sailors and airmen, who have got no
voice and are precluded from making any
objection by reason of the fact that they
are serving in His Majesty's forces, are going
to be denied what might be additional benefits if the State subscribed their quota.
The MINISTER OF LABOUR (Mr. Andrews) indicated dissent.
Mr. KYLE: That is what is happening on
The other side. The State is not going to
pay the same contribution in the future as
in the past, and the men are going to be
denied the benefits which that money would
have been paid for. For these reasons I
think that every person who believes that
the State's word should be kept should
oppose this Money Resolution, and also the
Economy Bill in its entirety. As I say, we
are entitled to oppose this Measure by every
means in our power. Let us try to get the
people of Northern Ireland to realise what
the Government is doing. The State are
now taking up the cudgels in this way by
depleting the funds of these approved
societies by reducing their contribution to
two-ninths instead of one-seventh.
715 Economy (Exchequer Relief)— HOUSE OF COMMONS

Committee.
The CHAIRMAN: I am afraid we are
entering upon a Second Reading debate the
second time-(hon. Members: Hear, hear)-
whereas the simple question before the Committee is whether or not the Resolution we
are now asked to pass ought to be or ought
That
not to be accepted by the Committee.
somewhat narrows, though it still leaves a
wide field.
Mr. DEVLIN: I do not know within what
limits the Committee are to discuss this
matter, but for my own part I think it is
our business, profoundly and vitally opposed
as we are to this Measure, that we should
take every advantage of expressing our views
and pointing out to the public and those
interested the grave wrong that is being done
to the working classes of the community.
Now, what is really being done in connection with this Measure. The Government,
as my hon. Friend (Mr. Kyle) has said, are
pledged in honour to make certain contributions to the National Health Fund.
The employees are pledged in honour and
law and so are the employers. This is not a
Bill to readjust the payment. It is not a
Bill to estimate fairly what reductions ought
to be made by each party concerned in the
transactions, but you come forward now still
to place the burden upon the shoulders of
the employers and employed, and to sneak
out of your own responsibility in regard to
a matter so much concerning the health and
welfare of the toiling masses of the people.
Apart altogether from the broad opposition which I have to this Measure, I have
particular reasons for objecting to it in
Ulster. We have no medical benefits in
Ulster. The medical service is not available
for the insured persons in the Six Counties,
and while it is quite true that in England at
the instigation of the Chancellor of the Exchequer compulsorily insured persons are to
be deprived of £2,800,000 a year in addition
to the charge placed upon them of £1,900,000
per annum in respect of medical benefit, the
insured persons there have medical benefit,
and the sickness experience, I am told,
though increasing there is nothing like so
heavy as it is in Northern Ireland. The net
result of the legislation in England will be to
place many societies in deficiency, and in
Northern Ireland, if this Bill is placed on
the Statute Book it will mean that the contributions will not be able to maintain the
sickness experience. I, therefore, think that
legislation of this character is to be
seriously deprecated, apart altogether from
the question of economy.
The Government, as I have said, have come
along here and they propose to lessen the contribution they are to pay at a time when
there is a clamant demand on the part of the
people of Northern Ireland for medical benefits. These benefits have been denied to
Ulster and, consequently, proportionately
you are taking away more from the working
classes of this country than is being taken
away from the working classes of Great
Britain, because the State makes a certain
contribution to medical benefits in England,
and it makes no contribution to medical
benefits here in Northern Ireland.
The CHAIRMAN: I am very reluctant, as
my hon. Friend appreciates, to intervene, but
I am afraid we are getting away from the
specific question. Also, the aspect of the case
he is now discussing is not to be found in the
Bill, the Committee Stage of which will be
taken an order or two down the Paper.
Mr. DEVLIN: I will not be here to-morrow
and I want to say what I have to say to-day.
The CHAIRMAN: If my hon. Friend can
get it within this Resolution that is all I am
concerned with. I am not in the least objecting to his saying it, except as a matter of
order.
They

Mr. DEVLIN: I want to warn the Government that they are doing a grave injustice
to the people of Northern Ireland.
are not moving step by step with
Britain, they are moving a step forward
against the people just as they did in the
case of the old-age pensions. For that

Mr. ANDREWS: Mr. Moles, in accordance
with your ruling, with which I am in entire

by hon. Members opposite. This Money Resolution simply gives the Government power
to put a charge upon the State which the
State has not borne up to the present. Those
persons who remain, owing to their having
certain disabilities, upon this Army, Navy
and Air Force Fund have up to the present
been denied the advantage of extended
benefits. It is now proposed to place those

position if after their period of service they
remain insured persons, as other insured persons associated with our various approved
societies. Therefore, I cannot see how hon.
Members opposite are holding the view that
we are by means of this Money Resolution
robbing the insured persons, the approved

from Government funds both as regards the

other occasions upon which I shall probably
have opportunities of putting my views before
the Committee as regards the general charges
717 Economy (Exchequer Relief)—

27 APRIL 1926
Committee.
which have been levelled against the Government in connection with the Bill itself, which
at this stage we are not justified, in my
opinion, in considering.
Mr. KYLE: Would the right hon. Gentleman or some other right hon. Gentleman on
the Government Front Bench, tell us whether
they had any consultation with the National

Mr. ANDREWS: I intended to deal with

Mr. KYLE: At least on the other side of
the water they have been ashamed of their
Measure, but on this side of the water they

Mr. WILLIAM MCMULLEN: This Resolution as set out on the Order Paper is not
very clear, and I do not think the matter

one-seventh, as is being done in this Bill.
The CHAIRMAN: I am afraid that if

Motion made, and Question proposed:
"That the surplus moneys remaining in
the Dogs Act Account, established for the
purposes of the Dogs Regulation (Ireland)
Acts, 1865 and 1919, after all statutory deductions have been made, shall, as to onethird, be paid into the Exchequer of

Mr. POLLOCK: On the Second Reading of
the Economy Bill I explained in some detail
those provisions of the Bill which will have
the effect of transferring to the Exchequer
one-third of the surplus remaining in the
Fund after making the necessary provision
for administration. I am now asking the
Committee to confirm, to approve, a
Resolution authorising this change.
This will not, I am happy to say, involve
us in the perplexities attached to the money
resolution which my right hon. Friend the
Financial Secretary has just disposed of.
The facts in regard to this Resolution are
perfectly straightforward. We estimate that

MINISTRY OF HOME AFFAIRS.
Motion made, and Question proposed:
"That a sum not exceeding £43,605 be
granted to His Majesty to complete the sum
necessary to defray the charge which will
come in course of payment during the year
ending on the 31st March, 1927, to defray
the salaries and expenses of the Ministry of
Home Affairs (15 and 16 Geo. V., c. 3, s. 4
(N.I.) )."-(Note-£16,000 has been voted on
Account.)
Sir DAWSON BATES: The Estimate
which I have the honour to submit for the
consideration of the Committee shows a
saving of £5,719 over that of last year.
The Committee will observe that with regard to inspectors there is an increase of
four. Two of these inspectors are appointed to deal with the increased work under
the Housing of the Working Classes Act.
When it is realised that houses
are increasing and being completed at something
like 200 a month, and having regard to the
increase in the number of labourers' cottages, I think hon. Members will agree that
it is a right measure that these inspectors
should be appointed.
ap-
The Committee will also observe that provision is made for the appointment of a
pharmacy inspector. The duty of this
officer is to see that the terms of the Act
are fully complied with. The officer
pointed is an ex-Service man with very high
qualifications. I should explain that this
item will not be a permanent burden on
this Vote. Hon. Members will recollect that
under the Pharmacy and Poisons Act, 1925.
it is provided that during the working of
the Act for the first two years the entire
amount of the fees collected for licences
should be handed over to the Society so as
to enable that Society, which had not funds
of its own, to get thoroughly on its legs.
At the end of the first two years the Government can claim half of the fees which,
having regard to the amount collected, would
amount to something like £480, which will
in future go to appropriation-in-aid.
Then it will become necessary to appoint
an assistant temporary inspector to keep upto-date investigations in connection with oldage pension appeal cases. I may point out
that for the year ended 31st March, 1925, we
had no less than 2,460 cases to deal with,
while for the year ending 31st March, 1926,
there were 2,688 cases decided. There were
arrears to the extent of over 500. I think
it is obvious to hon. Members that it is very
unfair and undesirable that poor people who
are claiming pensions should have their
claims held up owing to the fact that it is
impossible to get through the work. The
inspectors are part time men and are paid
a fixed fee for each day employed.
With regard to the administrative staff
we have been able to effect considerable
savings. I think before the end of the year
we will be able to effect still further savings
having regard to the disbandment of the
Special Constabulary.
I think it would be interesting, in view
of the charge which is sometimes made
against the Government that we are not fully
alive to the claims of the ex-Servicemen,
if I was to point out that out of a total of
84 new appointments-i.e., by new appointments I mean those other than transferred
officials-no fewer than 78 are ex-Servicemen,
and of the balance of 6, four were too young
to serve, and two were over age.
With a view to further economy, while it
became necessary for the appointment of a
medical officer to inspect school children
under the Education Authority, we have
been able to make an arrangement under
which one of our medical officers, who has
had less work to do owing to the disbandment
of the Special Constabulary, will be employed
on this particular work. It was first thought
that it was necessary to appoint an additional
inspector, but we have been able to make this
very satisfactory arrangement. These are
the only particular items which I think
necessary to explain to the House. I need
not point out that I shall only be too glad
to answer any point that may be raised by
hon. Members.

HOUSE OF COMMONS
[Mr. Beattie]
The sooner you set up a select committee
for the revision of salaries of Ministers who
only take their spare time to these offices
the better. Perhaps a favourable committee
was appointed on the occasion when these
salaries were set out. Perhaps they believed
in that day that great services were required
and great financial sacrifices on behalf of
Ulster. But there are no such great services
attached to this Ministry, nor yet is there
financial sacrifice on the part of the person
who holds the office. Therefore, I ask that
a special committee be appointed to investigate the salaries paid to this Minister and
other Ministers, with a view to reducing
them and bringing them to something like
parallel lines with Great Britain, according
to the number of the population they hold
authority over. You ask the working classes
to go step by step with Great Britain. If
you reduce your pay down accordingly to
the numbers you represent, I believe you
will have a very small amount; just sufficient
to warrant the office being retained and no
more. I have great pleasure in moving a
reduction of £1,000.

Only the other Sunday a lady came here
from Dublin having taken advantage of a
cheap excursion to Belfast. She was
arrested, and taken to the police barracks.
She sent for me because she knew I would
always come to the aid of persons in difficulty whether guilty or not. There was no
charge against her. She simply had her
name upon this list. As a matter of fact
the police treated her with great courtesy.
I raise no objection to the manner in which
she was treated, and neither did she. She
was kept there two or three hours, and I had
to sit the whole time there myself. I was
asked to be responsible for her for the rest
of the day. Of course, I accepted the responsibility under duress. No sooner did I
do that than they let her free, and then she
went her way and I went mine. She went to
the station that evening and took the train
back to Dublin.
What is the meaning of all that senseless
proceeding? I cannot understand it at all.
At any rate, I do not care who the people
are, guilty or guiltless, if their liberty is to
be taken from them they ought to be told
the reason why. If they are criminals they
ought to be indicted for their crimes. If

these deportations, and that they will erase
from the list the names of respectable
citizens and put an end to this senseless
procedure.

With regard to the political prisoners as

I think a continuance of this policy
when there is peace prevalent in
all parts of the Province is a
bad policy. A spirit of mercy apart altogether from the spirit of justice is a spirit
that never loses anything, and it would be
far better to make a clean sweep of this
whole question and clear out every political
prisoner under the control of the Northern
Government, stop these deportation orders,

Gentleman will be able to give us an assurance on this point.

Mr. BARBOUR: In introducing the Estimates of the Expenditure of the Ministry
of Commerce for the present financial year
I
should like to refer briefly to the
numerous and various activities which have

One branch of the Ministry is concerned
with the administration of numerous duties
relating to the registration and control of
Limited Companies, Insurance Companies;
the administration of the Industrial
Assurance Act; the control of Electricity
and Gas Undertakings, as well as the control
and inspection of Mines and Quarries, and

Turning to the Estimates, I am glad to
be able to inform the Committee that in
spite of the extra work which has been
thrown on the Ministry by the transfer
of Council of Ireland Services, the total
amount now sought is less by £1,124 than
the amount submitted to this House last
year.
In the Salaries, Wages and Allowances
sub-head there are some changes. There
is a slight increased expenditure as a result
of the extra staff required by the Ministry
to deal with the additional duties thrown
upon the Department by the administration
of the Industrial Assurance Act, and the
transfer of the Council of Ireland Services.
The absorption of new Services has necessitated the following proposed re-arrangement of staff:-The addition of one higher
executive officer, one junior executive officer,
three clerks, and one fishery officer, and the
elimination of one assistant principal and
one higher clerical officer, a gross increase
of £1,241.
In the second place the provision of
£1,350 made last year for the expenses of the
Development Commission is this year reduced to the nominal sum of £25, the Commission having now concluded its activities.
In Travelling and Subsistence Expenses,
it has been necessary to make an increased
provision to the extent of £200, owing to the
assumption of new duties by the Department.
According to information which has been
supplied to my Ministry by the late Imperial
Secretary, travelling expenses in respect of
Fishery Services may be estimated at £150.
The remaining £50 is on account of consultants in respect of Railway Services.
The Works Services shown under Subheads C1, C2, C3 and C4 are ordinary establishment and maintenance costs, showing a
decrease in each of the items.
The net decrease of £95 shown in respect
of the three Printing and Stationery Services, D1, D2 and D3 would have been greater
had it not been for increased requirements
in respect of the new Services.
Only one further item in this part of the
Estimate calls, I think, for comment,
namely, the increase of £300 in respect of
fees to Consultants (Sub-head F.). Until
this year the Ministry has found it necessary
to make provision for only two outside consultants, namely, the Inspector of Mines and
Quarries and the consultant to the Electricity Commissioners. In the present Estimates
provision has been made for securing outside advice in respect of railways. The staff
of the Ministry of Transport in England
includes a number of technical inspectors
who carry out many duties in connection
with the maintenance of the safety of passengers and of railway workers. There has
not yet been time to judge accurately what
the volume of these duties will be in connection with the railways of Northern Ireland,
and it has been deemed advisable, therefore,
to make some provision in the Ministry's
Estimates for obtaining the advice of an
outside engineer in respect of such matters.
There is, however, the possibility that one of
the technical officers of the Ministry of
Finance may be able to undertake any inspections in this connection, in which case
the cost will, of course, be proportionately
reduced. I beg to move.

761 Labour Situation in Derry.

27 APRIL 1926
Labour Situation in Derry.
Adjournment.
LABOUR SITUATION IN DERRY.
Motion made and Question proposed:
"That this House do now adjourn."-
(Captain Dixon).
Mr. LEEKE: I wish to draw the attention
of
the House to the position of the
unemployed in Derry City. They are at
present going through a very bad time owing
to being deprived of the unemployment
grant. Hon. Members will have seen from
the Press that a huge procession marched
through Derry recently on a deputation to
the Board of Guardians, with a view to
getting some subsistence, which would place
them and their families in a position that
they would not starve. It is a very serious
situation in which they are left owing to
some legal technicality which deprives them
of the right to draw unemployment benefit.
I would appeal to the Minister of Labour to
take into consideration the case of these unfortunate people, and establish some machinery or some method so that possibly something will be done to relieve them from the
serious plight in which they are placed at
the moment. I recognise how difficult it is
at times for the Minister of Labour to deal
with cases such as this, but I think of all
the cases at present existing in Northern
Ireland this is the most extreme.
The local ratepayers are, I know, groaning under excessive taxation, and it is very
difficult for the Guardians to immediately
hand out sufficient money to meet these
deserving and necessitous cases. I think
it is the Government's duty to see that no
one starves, and it would be a slur on this
Government if it happens that in Derry
City anyone dies from starvation. The
Minister of Labour presides over the Department of the Government which is
primarily charged with the duty of seeing
that the unemployed are paid benefit. I
pay this tribute to him-I recognise how
sympathetic he is towards Labour in Ulster,
and I know if it is possible for him to do so
he would immediately and promptly take
some effective measure that would help
these unfortunate people in the position in
which they are placed to-day. There are,
I understand, 700 of them altogether. I
think that surely some temporary measure of
relief could be passed through this House.
I am not sufficiently acquainted with the
legislative machinery to know how quickly
it could be done. I think it could be done
in a day-have a temporary measure passed
that would deal with these cases-and I
think it is the duty of the Government to
take immediate steps to have it carried out.
I see where a local contribution was
given by Lady Anderson in Derry-a very
prompt action for which I think a tribute
should be paid her. In the meantime, the
Government must feel it is their duty to
have these cases dealt with immediately. I
think the Minister of Labour will surely
take some steps to co-operate at least with
the local authorities with a view to having
these cases met. There is a real danger in
allowing people to march in procession
through the streets hungry. That is what
breeds Bolshevism and all other revolutions,
which, we believe, are so dangerous to the
community and to the peace of Ulster.
Surely it is the Government's duty to see
that nothing is done which will cause any
trouble in the labour world. I would appeal
to the Minister of Labour here to-day to
take the Derry case immediately, and deal
with it promptly and effectively, and to relieve the present existing distress in that
area. I would also ask him to go carefully
into the various industries which are presently languishing in Derry City, and to see
if relief works could not be established.
Let him take the matter up with the
Corporation and Guardians and other public
bodies to see if relief works could not be
established with the view of absorbing this
huge number of unemployed presently existing in that city. It is deplorable to see
the corners crowded with men who are
anxious and able-I know the ability of the
Derry labourer-and honest in their desire
to obtain work. I think it is the duty of
the Government or of the Ministry of
Labour to see that work is placed in their
way. If it is I think it will be immediately
availed of.
Mr. BEATTIE: I rise to support the
appeal made by the hon. Member for Derry.
I do so whole-heartedly. I ask the Government first and foremost to study the result
of the Derry position. The Derry position
is no worse than the Belfast position, and
the cause of the result in Derry is also the
cause of the result in Belfast and the Six
Counties.
The cause
can really be put
down to one thing, and, that is, this parity
arrangement with Great Britain, walking
step by step. I am going to ask the Minister or the Government to take away from
the Minister of Labour the power that he
has at his command of putting any regulations into Derry City or elsewhere on parallel lines with Great Britain. The conditions
in Derry are not similar by any means to
the conditions in Great Britain, nor yet are
they similar in Belfast.
The Derry unemployed to-day are
suffering at the hands of the Minister
of Labour, because the Minister of
Labour, through the agreement made
by the Government of walking step by
step with Great Britain is insisting upon
regulations being adhered to by these
various committees and executive officers that
it is impossible to apply to Northern Ireland,
763 Labour Situation in Derry.
HOUSE OF COMMONS Labour Situation in Derry. 764
[Mr. Beattie]
Seven hundred men have been struck off in
Derry, presumably for not having a reasonable period of employment in the past two
years. Now can that regulation be applied
as a practical proposition in Derry City? A
reasonable period of employment in the past
two years is what is required. It is one of
the regulations hitting the Northern men
very severely. They are being denied the
right to live-not the right to exist, because
if they were getting existence it would be so
much the better. They are actually being
denied the right to live because they cannot
find a reasonable period of employment in
the past two years.
If the Government were doing honestly and
fairly by the people of the Six Counties, they
would tell the British Exchequer it is an
utter impossibility to go along parallel lines
with Great Britain under the Agreement as
they have drawn it up to the detriment of
the working-classes. If you fail to do that,
your duty lies in another way. Your duty
is to bring in an emergency Bill, and if the
Prime Minister is a man of his word-but
those who are well fed and well housed do
not think of those who are not well fed-if
the Prime Minister is a man of his word.
that the social standing of the people will
not be lessened one iota as compared with
that of the people of Great Britain, he will
present to this House at the earliest possible
moment, an Emergency Powers Bill compelling the Guardians in the various districts, to grant outdoor relief to the
unemployed as they do across the water.
The PRIME MINISTER: That would be
very undemocratic.
Mr. BEATTIE: It would be giving the
working-classes some little subsistence to
which they are entitled under the Northern
Government. The point that I make is this;
that under the present administration, the
poor-law authorities in Northern Ireland are
composed of men of the same calibre and
same type as the Government of Northern
Ireland is composed of. They absolutely refuse to comply with the appeals and representations of the working-classes to the
various Boards.
I myself have appealed on many occasions
and I have done things to try to bring them
round to the way I think to assist unemployment which I should not have done. And if
the Government and if the guardians say
"We will not carry on on parallel lines with
Great Britain," and if the Government say
"We will not bring in an Emergency Powers
Bill to compel them to pay outdoor relief,"
the result will be what the Government are
asking for. The result will be starvation
and poverty in the Six Counties, and I am
sure it will not retaliate on the shoulders of
the Opposition, as it will retaliate against
the Members of the Government.
I join in the appeal made by the Member
for Derry that the Minister of Labour should
be curtailed in his powers in regard to 10gulations for extended benefit, and that the
workers of Ireland should get equal
opportunity of getting the right to live, by
allowances from the extended benefit fund.
Therefore I have great pleasure in supporting the appeal.
Mr. ANDREWS: I appreciate very much
the hon. Member for Derry's courtesy in

Now there are only four ways, so far as I

which they have no sale. The next way in

In Derry we have had a large number of

have obtained employment. Again, the
Government have promised to subsidise in

cost of which is somewhere in the neighbourhood of £330,000, and the grant from the
Government to that scheme is £55,822,
approximately. It is expected that on that
scheme when it is started-I hope in

The other way in which the Government
can approach the matter is through the pay-
