Government should not do something.
I say, with great regret, that unfortunately
this question is not confined to Derry. The
same state of affairs exists in Belfast. It
is as well that right hon. Gentlemen opposite
should know the situation. I have come to
the House repeatedly in a fair way, as I hope
now to do it in a fair way, to make an appeal
to right hon. Gentlemen to try to arrive at
an understanding of what the situation is.
Right hon. Gentlemen-I do not know
whether they know it or not-are sitting on
a safety valve, and it may explode at any
moment. I addressed a demonstration before
I came to the House this morning of, at
least, 1,000 people. Why did those people,
decent people, congregate at the back of the
City Hall in Belfast? Because the regulations of the right hon. Gentleman have become more stringent recently. I want to
submit this for the consideration of the
House. Do hon. Gentlemen opposite suggest
that it has been possible for people to secure
what they conceive to be a reasonable amount
of employment within the past two years?
I know men who have walked the boots off
their feet in making an earnest effort to
obtain employment, and they cannot possibly
get it. When they have been unemployed for
two years their benefit is discontinued.
Perhaps the most pitiable cases are those
who are single. I have seen cases of spinsters
advanced in years, absolutely friendless and
moneyless, and those decent respectable
people, who have spent all their lives in
industry, cannot get employment and cannot get unemployment benefit; and under
your obsolete poor-law they are not supposed
to exist. The poor-law has no knowledge of
a person who is single. Perhaps the Prime
Minister is not aware of that. I submit this
to the Prime Minister and ask for an impartial decision and judgment upon it;
is it fair that a person who has lived
an
honourable life in industry until
he has become 50 years of age, and
who cannot get employment or unemployment
benefit, should be offered the hospitality of
the Union Workhouse? It appears to me to
be a scandalous state of affairs altogether.
I appeal to the right hon. Gentleman, not
in any party spirit, but in the interests of
the people of Ulster, to reconsider the whole
thing. I know that the Prime Minister has
got great influence with the British Government, and surely it is not beyond his power
to point out to them that the situation here
is entirely different to the situation in Great
Britain. We have two main industries, and
if there is a slump in those two main industries what opportunity is there for the
people to obtain employment? In Great
Britain many other opportunities offer; the
industries there are numerous and diverse.
Here we are limited, circumscribed, to about
two industries, and then the poor unfortunate
people who have been unemployed for two
years are denied their unemployment benefit.
There is this benefit. Our Unemployment
Fund is in a better position than it was six
months ago, when it was about four and a
quarter millions in debt. The British
Government have liquidated three-quarters
of that, or 75 per cent. One would have
imagined that when the British Government
came to our assistance the regulations would
have been relaxed; instead of that they have
been tightened. It is more difficult to
qualify for a continuation of unemployment
benefit than it has been in the past. I do
not want to approach this question in an
embittered way at all.
Mr. ANDREWS: I am sorry to interrupt
the hon. Member, but I do not think it
would be right that our people should have
the impression, which would be quite inaccurate, that the British Government have
agreed to be responsible for the liquidation
of the debt of three and a half millions. All
that the British Government have agreed to
is that three-fourths of the interest shall be
brought in as part of the equalisation
arrangement, which is a very different thing.
Mr. W. McMULLEN: That was not clearly
explained to the House, because I know
crowds of people, besides myself, who hold
the opinion that I have expressed. That, of
course, may be wrong, and I accept the right
hon. Gentleman's correction on that point.
But I would ask that, in the unprecedented
situation in which we find ourselves, no
attempt should be made to justify what is
being done on the ground of what is being
done in Great Britain.
no
Our problem is different. We are not
attempting to belittle the difficulty in which
the Government are placed. There is one
question that faces the Government, that of
the persons who cannot obtain employment
and who cannot get unemployment benefit.
Are those people to starve? That is
question that wants answering, and
amount of prevarication or evasion will
satisfy the people. It is a direct question,
and it merits a direct answer. That is the
question I put up to the Government, and I
appeal to them, not in any party spirit, but
on humanitarian grounds, to do something
to relieve the starvation and hardship that
exist amongst the people at the present time.
I make an appeal in that spirit to the
Prime Minister, and to the right hon. Gentleman in charge of the Department.

Motion made, and Question proposed,

at the present fraction. How could it be
argued that the existing benefits will not be
interfered with, or that an extension of
benefits would still be possible, or that the

point the Minister of Health in Great
Britain, Mr. Neville Chamberlain, one of the
villains of the piece who are responsible for
this Economy Measure, said as reported in
Hansard, when dealing with a proposal to
reduce the amount of the contribution payable by the other contracting parties-
If you reduce the contribution you must
add to the number of societies that will
be deficient, and decrease the number of
societies that have surpluses. I find that
the surpluses were only accumulating at
the rate of five millions a year, but is it
certain that we can count upon the repetition of the surpluses which were accumulating down to the end of 1923. I beg the
House not to take this as by any means
certain. I beg them to understand that
there are some rather disquieting features
on which we have information, which
render it very unlikely that in future quinquennials the surpluses will be anything
like what they were.
In regard to that, some very interesting
statements appear in the evidence of the
Deputy Government Actuary before the
Royal Commission--

I think a grave warning like that from the

margin" which the Government now

Think of the amounts received by contributors and how they have depreciated since
the 1911 Act became law. A man received
15s; the cost of living has now reduced that
to 8s 9d. A woman received 12s; the cost of
living has now reduced that to 7s. That
section of the community which is the most
hardly hit, the people who are not able to
work, the people who are not able to do anything for themselves, were in receipt of disablement benefit of 7s 6d a week from the
approved societies; that has been reduced
since 1911 to something like 4s 4d because of
the increase in the cost of living. This class
of the community are going to be still
further depressed as a result of this Clause
and this Measure. They are the most helpless class in the community. The State
should be deciding to increase this amount,
to double the present figure, and this could
be done if the present contribution of the

to keep a man who has been disabled from one
cause or another. When you bear in mind

of 4s 4d surely the time has arrived when instead of the State reducing its contributions
as is proposed in this Clause, they should at
least be maintained if not increased, so that
the disablement benefit might also be increased in favour of the most helpless
section of the community.
In past years there has been a considerable amount of talk as to what was to be
done with the surpluses of the various

to this clause becoming part of the Bill.
these people will be left absolutely stranded

I have, because I hold it is a most reprehensible Measure. This clause is one of the
most reprehensible clauses in a most reprehensible Measure.
Words cannot give expression to the
feelings of any person who has any experience at all of dealing with National Health Insurance benefits to the people who are affected.

ment that the State contributions should only

which I think we are sometimes liable to
forget when discussing matters of this

a different position entirely when discussing
a matter of this kind from what the Members
of the Imperial Parliament are, and if we
concentrate our thoughts upon that particular
point I think a good deal of unnecessary
discussion will be avoided.
To me the question in connection with this
matter at the moment is a financial one.
There has been no reply to the argument
that has been advanced by the Minister of
Finance (Mr. Pollock), and others as to where
the £117,000 is to come from to meet the
deficiency that will arise as far as we are
concerned if we do not adopt exactly similar
measures to those which have been adopted
by the Imperial Parliament. (Hon. Members:
Hear, hear.) That really is the crux of the
whole position. We have in connection with
a matter of this kind to consider ways and
means most carefully. The £117,000 stands,
according to the financial basis on which we
are working at the moment, until four years
hence when the Exchequer Board under the
Act of 1920 may reconsider the whole position.
In the meantime we have no alternative but
to move step by step in matters of this kind
with the legislation of the Imperial Parliament. Otherwise we will find ourselves up

are
We cannot take the view that we
limited by the necessity of adhering to any
particular principles on which the scheme
was originally set up or by any statement
which was made at the time of the inception
of the scheme, or any explanation, or any
defence of the provisions contained in the
original Bill. On the contrary we hold
that the National Health Insurance scheme
was in the nature of
a great, novel
experiment in the field of social welfare,
And it must now be open to Parliament,
untrammelled and unfettered, to review the
whole scheme in the light of thirteen years'
experience of its working, and to make
such changes, however drastic, as that
experience may have shown to be desirable.
Therefore, I take it that the Royal Commission came to the conclusion that there
is no breach of any pledge when the Government of the day, whether here or in Westminster, came to the conclusion that it is
desirable, owing to altered conditions, or for
other reasons, to depart from the original
scheme.
In this connection I would like to point
out that this is not the first time that the
original Act has been departed from. The
benefits have been changed, the contributions have been changed, and on a previous
occasion the statutory contribution has been
changed by the father of the Act himself,
Mr. Lloyd George. In the first instance, the
statutory contribution for men was twoninths, and for women, one-fourth. In 1920,
Mr. George was responsible for changing
the fourth to two-ninths, so there is no
foundation, in my opinion, for saying that
there was a pledge given so definite, so distinct, and so clear that it fettered and trammelled future Governments to such an extent
that under no circumstances could they
depart therefrom.
I would like to point out, in conclusion,
that I feel the insured persons are in no
danger. After the first valuation the surpluses showed £1 per insured person in
Northern Ireland, and, after the second
valuation, which has only been recently completed, the surpluses showed £3 per insured
person in Northern Ireland, so that they are
growing, and the most that can be said against
this Measure is that it interferes to some extent with the rate of progression of those reserves, and that it may in that way interfere
with an advantage which insured persons
would otherwise obtain. But that really only
affects additional benefits, and, as has been
said by my right hon. Friend, the Minister
of Finance, this is a State scheme. There

necessary that I should say any more than
this, that hon. Members opposite are fre
quently professing to be economists, and yet
on every occasion when economy is suggested
they are opposed to it.

The MINISTER OF COMMERCE (Mr.

Clause, I cannot help coming to the conclusion that hon. Members do not altogether

This Clause is provided for those men who

forces of the Crown, and have come back

disability which they have derived from the
War, will not be accepted as an insurable
risk by any Approved Society, and, therefore.
are obliged to fall back on such benefits as

Force Insurance Fund. When this Fund
was started no provision was made for any
additional benefits being extended, but now,
when so many of the Approved Societies are
enabled to give additional benefits to those
first contemplated under the National Health
Insurance Act, it was felt that it was only
justice that this one fund to which these men

in the Bill in respect of which the Government is prepared to accept an extra charge

Mr. ANDREWS: Might I point out that

the reduction of the State contribution people

NEW SCHOOL AT LISBELLAW.
3. Mr. MILLER (for Mr. Cooper) asked the
Parliamentary Secretary to the Ministry of
Education whether he can state what is the
delay in building the new school at Lisbellaw.
The MINISTER OF FINANCE (Mr. Pollock): I propose to reply to this question.
I understand that the delay in completing
the school in question has been caused by the
difficulty experienced by the manager and
his contractor in getting delivery of bricks up
to the standard which had been agreed between the manager, his contractor and the
Government architect. Efforts are being
made, with the assistance of my Ministry, to
find a way out of the difficulty.
Oral Answers to Questions.
MEMBERS OF PARLIAMENT IN
AMERICA.
1. Colonel WOODS asked the Minister of
Commerce whether any Member of this
House is employed by the Northern Government in America; if so, in what capacity;
and whether the whole or any part of his
remuneration is chargeable against public
funds.
The MINISTER OF COMMERCE (Mr.
Barbour): The answer to the first part of
the question is in the negative. The remainder of the question, therefore, does not
arise.
NORTH ANTRIM REGIONAL EDUCATION
COMMITTEE.
2. Mr. KYLE asked the Parliamentary
Secretary to the Ministry of Education
whether he would state if the North Antrim
Regional Education Committee has purchased
a garden in which to erect huts for school
purposes; what price was paid for the garden;
and what was done with the bulbs, flowers
and vegetables in the garden.
The PARLIAMENTARY SECRETARY
TO THE MINISTRY OF EDUCATION (Mr.
Robb): The North Antrim Regional Education Committee recently bought a plot for
the erection of temporary huts to relieve
existing congestion in the Ballymoney Model
Schools; the price paid was £300. The
Ministry has no information as to what was
done with the bulbs, flowers and vegetables
in the plot.
Mr. KYLE: Is the Ministry satisfied that
the plot they bought is worth £300?
Mr. ROBB: Yes, Sir.
HOURS OF TEMPORARY CIVIL
SERVANTS.
4. Colonel WOODS asked the Minister of
Finance whether he proposes to make the
working hours of the temporary civil servants uniform with those of the transferred
civil servants employed by the Northern
Government.
Mr. POLLOCK: Under the conditions of
their engagements the working hours of
temporary civil servants are 44 a week
(inclusive of luncheon interval) or 8 hours
a day on ordinary week-days and an attendance of 4 hours on Saturdays. It is not
proposed to modify this arrangement, which
is also in force, as regards new entrants appointed to established posts since this Government was established. Transferred officers
came here with certain rights; amongst
others their terms of service in most cases
comprised a 42-hour week, the same as is still
in force in the Imperial Service. I am happy
to say, however, that almost without exception they have voluntarily, and, in some
cases, continuously, much exceeded this
limit without any increased cost to the Exchequer. The few anomalies that have occurred owing to the different conditions of
service of the two classes are of trifling importance, and I fear, inevitable in the
circumstances, and they will automatically
disappear in course of time.
HOUSING IN BALLYMONEY.
5. Mr. KYLE asked the Minister of Home
Affairs whether he can state if the Ballymoney Urban District Council purchased a
field wherein to erect houses; what is the
area, and what was the price paid for the
field; from whom was it bought; what did the
levelling of the ground cost; what did the
building of the houses cost; how many houses
were built, and what is the rent of each?
Oral Answers.
Oral Answers.
29 APRIL 1926
The MINISTER OF HOME AFFAIRS (Sir
Dawson Bates): The Ballymoney Urban District Council purchased a field some years
ago, for the purpose of a housing scheme,
from Lord Antrim. The area of the field in
question is 6.74 acres, and the purchase price
was £500, together with a sum of £50 paid by
way of compensation for disturbance.
The estimated cost of the development of
the land, i.e., for the provision of roads,
sewers, etc., was £719 14s 6d.
Twenty-two houses in all were built on the
site of three types of varying sizes and
character.
The contract price for the erection of the
houses was £9,530, or on the average £433 per
house.
The houses are at present let at rents of
10s, 11s 6d, and 12s 6d a week, respectively,
according to the class.
POLICE BARRACKS AT BALLYMONEY.
6. Mr. BEATTIE asked the Minister of
Home Affairs whether he can state the cost
of the Police Barracks at Ballymoney, the
total cost of lighting the same, and the total
number of Royal Ulster Constabulary living
in the barracks.
Sir DAWSON BATES: The R.U.C. Barracks at Ballymoney are the property of the
Government.
The premises were reconstructed last year,
and the cost of adaptations and alterations
amounted to £5,210, exclusive of the cost of
lighting. The cost of lighting the premises,
including the provision of generating plant,
switchboard and batteries was £332.
The fixed strength of the Station is:-
1 District-Inspector,
1 Head-Constable,
2 Sergeants, and
9 Constables.
Of these, 1 head-constable, 2 sergeants, and
5 constables reside in the barracks. The
head-constable occupies the only married
quarters provided.
Mr. BEATTIE: I would like to further ask
the Minister if it is a fact that the lighting
in this barrack was supplied by the Ballymoney Lighting Company for £7 18 9d per
annum, and that the present system of lighting, which has already cost the Government
£352, is going to cost the Government approximately £100 per year. In view of this statement is the right hon. Gentleman prepared
to re-consider the whole position with regard
to the lighting of these barracks and the
building of palatial buildings for so few men?
Sir DAWSON BATES: I cannot admit the
accuracy of my hon. Friend's statement, but
if he wishes for any further information in
regard to the question of the lighting and the
construction of these barracks, and will put
down a Question, the Minister of Finance
will give him all the information he asks for.
Mr. BEATTIE: The accuracy of my statement will be confirmed by the Ballymoney
Lighting Company.
CLOGHER VALLEY RAILWAY
COMPANY.
7. Mr. MILLER (for Mr. Cooper) asked
the Prime Minister whether the Government
has received representations from the Clogher
Valley Railway Company asking for financial
assistance, and, if so, what action the
Government propose to take in the matter.
Mr. BARBOUR: I have been asked by my
right hon. Friend to deal with this Question.
The reply to the first part of the Question
is in the affirmative. As to the second point,
the Government liability in respect of the
working of the Clogher Valley Railway for
the financial year 1926-27 will not, it is estimated, fall much short of £5,000. In these
circumstances and having regard to the
present financial stringency, the hon. Member
will appreciate the Government's difficulty
in acceding to the request of the Company
for further financial assistance.

Economy (Exchequer Relief) Bill.
Considered in Committee. (Progress, 28th

CLAUSE 8 (Amendment of s. 3 of Unemployment Insurance Act (Northern Ireland),
1925).
Debate resumed on Question, "That the
Clause stand part of the Bill."
Question again proposed."
Mr. BEATTIE: In continuation of the debate on this Clause, I may say I think the
Committee has reason to understand the
position so far as this Clause is concerned, as
it affects one of the most important issues in
the Six Counties at the present time, that is,
the Unemployment Fund. I know the
Minister of Finance is desirous of seeing
financial stability. I would also be desirous
of seeing it, but I would not be prepared to
make the sacrifice the Minister of Finance
is prepared to make. The sacrifice for stability in my opinion is too great to make on
this occasion. The reduction of the State
contribution to the Unemployment Fund
means perhaps more than some hon. Members opposite realise. I maintain that any
reduction of the contribution means a further
extension of disallowances.
We have an arrangement here brought into
operation between Great Britain and
Northern Ireland. That arrangement, I presume from the Minister's reply to questions
put from these benches, means step by step,
and that failing that we are going to lose our
arrangement with the British Exchequer.
We can lose money, which is very valuable,
I know, to the Government of Northern Ireland at the present moment, but there is
nothing more valuable to any State than
human life. I believe the existence of human
life is at stake in regard to this Clause because of the percentage of unemployed we
have in Northern Ireland. If it was decreas
ing I would be hopeful, but I think that on
the whole, if anything, it is increasing.
Economy Bill-
Committee.
29 APRIL 1926
Mr. ANDREWS indicated dissent.
Mr. BEATTIE: I believe a decrease has
taken place on the register of unemployed
according to the figures of the Minister of
Labour, but is the decrease any intimation to
hon. Members that all the persons who are
not signing the register for unemployment
benefit are really in employment? I maintain that those persons who have been disallowed benefit under this agreement with
Great Britain have not all really found
employment. The majority who were struck
off the register are walking about the streets
of Belfast in starvation. It may be argued
that our fund will not be any the worse off
or any the poorer, and that the insured contributors will not suffer through this Clause.
Mr. POLLOCK: Hear, hear.
Mr. BEATTIE: If it can be argued that
though this is going to take place the Fund
will stand in the same position as it previously did when 6d was paid, I certainly
will be an attentive listener to the propounder of that argument.
Mr. POLLOCK: What about the million
and a half?
are
Mr. BEATTIE: I will say this that while
you are making for security you are going
into a state of bankruptcy. You are making
no security under this Clause for the people
whom it most affects. You say you
walking side by side with Great Britain in
all things of importance to this Government,
but, we, on this side of the Committee, know
that step by step is not being kept in all
things. In this thing, which is a most important thing to the Government at the
present moment, I think that a deviation
should also take place. You grant certain
powers to the Minister owing to your arrangement with Great Britain. Great
Britain reduced the contribution, and the
Minister of Finance for Northern Ireland
also comes along to reduce the contribution.
In my opinion the reduction of this contribution means the throwing off the register
of anything from 5,000 to 10,000 people.
The Minister is declaring his line of action
without hiding behind a bushel, and without
undue reservation as to what the circumstances of the present case are, and he
is using his iron rod and declaring in
fact of all opposition that the arrangement made between Great Britain and
ourselves must be adhered to. Men,
women and children are suffering to-day
owing to that arrangement, because if a
man in the Six Counties to-day cannot show
more than eight weeks' work in the past two
years the Minister of Labour is determined
he shall receive no more extended benefit.
Mr. ANDREWS: That is not so.
Mr. BEATTIE: When you make a statement in repudiation it seems quite natural
that it is not so, but as one who has had large
experience, and is intimate with the work,
I say it is correct. As to the point made last
night by my colleague, and the point made
by the hon. Member for North Belfast, I
will not retract or retrace them because I
might be subject to severe criticism elsewhere, but it is very hard at the moment to
think out the lines best suited to meet the
Government in their very simple arguments.
If 6d was paid and if they give 6d now to
take its place I cannot see how this reduction
in the State's contribution is going to make
the Fund any better for the unemployed
worker, but I would say that, as hon. Gentlemen opposite are aware, when pledges are
given, no matter whether they are verbal or
in writing, they should be kept. Pledges by
the State to contribute so much to this Fund
were given, but the State is coming now at
this late hour of the day and asking this
Fund to sacrifice to the State a certain
amount. They are not asking the employer
or employee to reduce his contribution.
I would be more inclined to accept a reduction from the employer and the worker than
from the State, because I believe the State
has broad shoulders.
This Clause really means to take from the
weakest and give to the strongest. A sum of
£117,000 is involved. It could be very easily
saved, I believe, in this Northern Parliament, and is not such a large amount when
you consider the amounts that have been

cautious-in criticising the Government along

British Government are the only people who

Sir ROBERT ANDERSON: I desire to state
in a sentence or two why I am going to
vote for this particular Clause of the Bill
now being considered by the Committee.
Naturally, when I read this Bill at the outset
it did not make much appeal to me in regard
to several of its Clauses dealing with local
authorities, and I was inclined to think that
possibly the Government might have been a
little more sparing in connection with the
various matters they were dealing with, and
which the local authorities and the local
rates were very much interested in. But
there is one particular aspect of this Measuro
which makes an irresistible appeal to mc,
and that is one that has not been stated in
this Committee very often. It has been
mentioned by the Minister of Finance this
afternoon, and I think our Friends on the
Opposition Benches will appreciate-I hope
they will-this particular view-point.
The Minister of Finance, as I gather, is
aiming at a balanced Budget, and his diffi
culty arises from one particular cause and
from one particular cause only, as far as I
can appreciate the situation, and that is
the fact that he has got to find something
like half a million pounds in order to make
up the deficiency in connection with unemployment. (Hon. Members: Hear, hear.)
That weighs with me immensely in connection with this whole Bill. It simply comes
to this. The position this House is in to-day,
and the position the taxpayers of Northern
Ireland happen to be in, is due to the fact
that the Government, whatevor sins it may
be blamed for from time to time, can never
in my judgment, be blamed for lack of
sympathy in the matter of assisting the unemployed.
They pledged the credit of Northern
Ireland to the tune of over three million
pounds, not knowing exactly where it was
to come from, or what the future was to be.
That was a great act of faith, and I think
it was an act that should receive more
appreciation than it has done from those
who are chiefly interested. Then we reach
a stage when we are not adding to the

In the course of time as valuations on new

of valuation necessarily enlarged the maintenance of the establishment cost considerably more money. Up to now no claim has

seem to me that it was only suitable that
those who received the benefit of the estab-

The ATTORNEY-GENERAL (Mr. Babington): I might explain to the Committee the

draw money for road purposes. The first

is paid unconditionally to county councils.
Under the Roads Act, 1920, there are certain
sums paid to the county councils

by that Act. In the first place, there
are paid to them under Section 3
certain costs of administering the fund and
certain overhead charges for management,

a first charge on the Road Fund. They then
are entitled to a portion of certain sums
out of the money that remains after the
payment of these sums which are paid unconditionally, and those funds that are paid

undoubtedly subject to conditions.
What this Bill is intended to do is this,

Duties Grant, is to be on the same footing

1920, which are subject to no conditions.

of making the fund, which was formerly

be paid out of the Road Fund, but it will
be paid unconditionally and not condition-

the Minister of Finance (Mr. Pollock), that
this money which was being raised by motor
taxation would go to the Road Fund in
relief of rates.
I think it is a very peculiar time for the
Government to try to withdraw money from
the relief of rates. It is a very funny way
for this Government to try to balance their
Budget at the expense of the ratepayers of
the Six Counties, because the ratepayers are
the most overburdened people in the Six
Counties at the present moment, and a
great many of them are among the poorest
people in the Six Counties. If that is the
only way the Government can balance their
Budget, I think it is a poor way to do so.
We have heard a good deal to-day about how
we are off in comparison with the ratepayers in England, and the British taxpayers,
but the Government have not told us that in
England the Government pay 75 per cent.
in aid of the rates on agricultural land,
whereas the Ulster Government last year
only paid 52 per cent., and even then they
are reducing that this year by £32,000. I do not
wish to repeat myself, but, even with the corrections of the Prime Minister and the Minister of Finance, I cannot see any other effect
that this Clause has than that it takes from
the local authorities a grant of £43,000,
which they have enjoyed since 1888, to help
to balance the Budget. I say the Government are putting that burden
upon the
people least able to bear it, and I ask the
Committee to reject this Clause.
Question put, "That the Clause stand part
of the Bill."

he was a first-class Mines Inspector. He is
now responsible for the inspection of no less
than 315 quarries and 15 metalliferous mines
in Northern Ireland, a figure which is constantly increasing. The primary object of
his work is to secure proper protection of
the men engaged in the quarries and of the
general public. The Mines Inspector acts as
Inspector of Factories for the Ministry of
Labour in so far as mines are concerned. A
report of his work is laid before this House
annually, and the report for 1925 will be
available at an early date.
The sum of £300 is provided for the Consultant to the Electricity Commissioners for
Northern Ireland. This Consultant advises
the Commissioners on all technical points
which come before them for consideration.
Among these may be mentioned :-
Applications for consent to the erection
of new generating stations or to the extension of existing generating stations;
Applications for consent to the erection of
overhead lines;
Applications by Corporation for consent to
the borrowing of moneys for the carrying
out of extensions for electricity schemes;
Applications for statutory powers to
supply specific premises outside the statutory area of supply.
I should like to impress upon the Committee that this work demands the services
of a first-class consulting technical engineer.

A sum of £300 has been provided for fees
to consultants in respect of railway matters.
As the Committee is aware my Department
is practically without experience in matters
of railway administration, and is, therefore,
unable to gauge at the outset the extent to
which the services of railway consultants
may be required. The Ministry of Transport in London employs a large staff of
technical engineers, but I do not contemplate
any necessity for setting up a similar
technical establishment within the Ministry
of Commerce.

The balance of £100 in this Estimate is
ear-marked for what I may call technical
contingencies in which it may be necessary
for my Department to employ expert consultants, and in particular for the necessary service of inspection at the Coalisland mine,
which is carried out periodically by qualified
inspectors of the Mines Department of Great

my Ministry. The inspection of coal mines
is specialised work, and subject to special
statutory requirements. It follows that a
coal mines' inspector must be properly qualified for the purpose of exercising these special
duties, which do not fall within the scope
of the duties of an inspector of mines and

be mentioned such fortuitous circumstances
as boiler explosions, in connection with enquiries into which it may be necessary to
summon expert assistance.
A question was asked by the hon. Member

honourable Friend enquired whether the
duties of this officer embraced matters connected with inland fisheries, and I wish to
tell him that his duties do include the inland
fisheries.

With regard to grants in respect of agriculture, we are continuing the stereotyped

HOUSE OF COMMONS
[Sir Dawson Bates]
With regard to the housing grants, the first
of these is A1. Hon. Members will recollect
that under the Act of 1919, the Government
undertook to pay an annual sum of 25s for
every 20s of rent collected. That Act was
availed of to a very small extent owing to
the high cost of building materials, and of
course, has long since expired.
With regard to A3, hon. Members will recollect that two years ago an arrangement
was entered into between the Government
and the Belfast Corporation in respect of
houses which they built under the 1919 Act.
459 houses were built, and the Corporation
were entitled to get a grant of 25s in respect
of every £ collected, and accordingly the
Government decided to commute that sum
for a cash payment of £127,500, and the
sum appears under A3, represents the interest
on that amount. I might point out that this
arrangement was subsequently embodied in
an Act of Parliament of this House.
A4 and A5 deal with the subsidies to local
authorities and private owners, and I might
point out that in connection with the houses
erected under our Housing Acts, a grant is
made of £60, subsequently increased to £80.
I find that as regards the houses erected by
local authorities that up to date, no fewer
than 1,936 houses had been approved for
erection by local authorities, and of these
877 houses have been completed up to date,
and grants have been paid in respect of 348.
I think it right to point out that the disparity between the 877 completed houses and
the grants that have been paid in respect of
the 348 is largely due to the fact that owing
to certain events which happened in connection with the Belfast Corporation the
Ministry have thought it necessary to make
the most exhaustive investigations of the
houses before paying any grants.
With regard to private builders, I find
that since 1st March, 1924, 3,829 houses have
been approved of for erection, and 2,320 have
been certified as completed, and grants have
been made in respect of 2,167. If hon.
Members will look at the chart which has
been hung up in this House they will see
that the progress in building operations has
been extremely satisfactory.
With regard to "B," that is the grants
which are made in respect of labourers'
cottages, it will interest the Committee if
I tell them that between the years 1883 and
the outbreak of the war, only 6,118
houses of this character were completed in Northern Ireland, and that
since the passing of our Labourers
Act of 1923, proposals have been
put forward by rural district councils, involving no fewer than 1,796 new cottages, and
schemes have been actually approved of
involving 425. Indeed, just before leaving
my office to-day, I find that a new scheme
has been presented to the Ministry, involving
no fewer than 234 houses.
With regard to the grants from C to S
these are all stereotyped, and fixed by Act
of Parliament. I have already dealt with
the temporary grant in relief of rates on
agricultural land, and the remaining grants,
I think, largely speak for themselves. It
will be observed that the grant in aid of
the Belleek Road no longer appears, as I am
glad to say that this bridge is nearing completion, and I hope it will be finished by
June next. I think these remarks cover
practically all the points in this Vote, and
I beg to move.

who are constantly in their places listening
to the speeches of right hon. Gentlemen, and
sometimes to their own---which are sometimes
much more interesting than those of the
right hon. Gentleman (laughter)-it is left to
the Opposition to keep a House practically for
the Government while these matters of the
gravest concern and large public expenditure
are being considered.
I hope the people of Ulster will read of the
proceedings that have taken place here, and
that they will realise that this vast sum of
money has been forced through the House,
that the followers of the Government have
gone home-a place in which I have no doubt
they will be just as usefully employed as they
are here--and that you have reduced the agricultural grant by £32,000. Did you tell them
you had reduced that grant by £32,000 before
you let them go home, or will they awaken
in the morning-after they have caught their
trains to find that, while they were wending their ways to County Down or over the
Midland or Great Northern Railway, the
Government, or their supporters who are
here, were actually robbing agriculture of
£32,000? That will be a revelation to them
in the morning when they read it in the
paper.

HOUSE OF COMMONS
[Mr. Devlin]
It is the method of dealing with these Estimates against which I venture to protest.
We should have had a whole day for the discussion of this-probably two days-and, as
the hon. Gentleman (Mr. William McMullen)
below me has said, why should these things
be rushed? This is not a very busy Parliament. We, as he has stated, only meet about
three months in the year, and we ought to
find time for the consideration of these
matters. It would be a very useful pursuit for
the Members of Parliament to find time to
come here to consider and discuss these Votes
and to analyse and dissect them as custodians
and sentinels of the public interest. That
should be our duty here, and there is plenty
of time in which to do it. But, instead of
that, we have had this discussion here this
rather unsatisfactory discussion-in a
practically empty House, with all the heads of
the Government gone away-I think a Member of the Government peeped in just now,
but when the most of the Members of the
Government have gone, all their agricultural
supporters gone, and no one left here but the
Minister of Home Affairs (Sir Dawson Bates),
his assistant, and the despised Opposition. If
it were not for this Oppostion we would never
know anything about the mystery of this
proposal to take away a grant of £32,00 at a
serious time for agriculture.
Here, let me say that at a time when the
linen industry is in a bad way, and when the
shipbuilding industry is in a bad way, and
when the possibilities are that our people
must go back to the land-because after all,
however industries may disappear, the grass
will continue to grow, and we must ultimately fall back upon agriculture-it is at
this moment, when everything should be done
to cultivate and foster our agricultural
strength, and to assist the farmers in the
difficult tasks they have to perform, that the
Government, at eight o'clock at night, proceed to rob them of £32,000, just as you were
robbing the workers in the earlier part of the
day by this Economy Bill. It has been a good
day's work, and I put the Government in the
political dock for their criminal conduct towards these two great interests, the interests
of the working classes, who were robbed by
the Economy Bill, and the interests of the
agriculturists who are being robbed by this
Vote.

RETIRED PUBLIC ELEMENTARY
TEACHERS.
1. Mr. GEORGE HENDERSON asked the
Minister of Finance whether he can state
how many of the Public Elementary Teachers
of Northern Ireland, who retired before the
31st March, 1901, are still alive, and whether
he will state the amount of the pension
granted to each on the occasion of retirement, and the increase in each case allowed
under the Pension (Increase) Act, 1920.
The MINISTER OF FINANCE (Mr.
Pollock): The number of Public Elementary
School Teachers who retired from schools in
Northern Ireland on or before 31st March,
1901, and are still alive is 32. It is,
obviously, outside the scope of an oral reply
to give the figures relating to each case, but
I may state that the total of the original
pensions amounted to £832 0s 8d. The total
of pensions now in force is £1,403 19s 8d, an
increase of £571 19s 0d, or 69 per cent. on the
original pensions. Of this increase £314
15s 4d was directly due to the Pensions (Increase) Act, 1920, and £189 12s 8d to the
amendment of that Act by the Education
Act (Northern Ireland), 1923. In conclusion,
I might point out that under the Pensions
(Increase) Bill, which has been before this
House, an additional increase is given, which
will take effect from 1st April, 1926.
I am sending to the hon. Member a detailed statement showing the particulars in
connection with each case.

can make any statement on the subject.
It
The PRIME MINISTER (Sir James
Craig): The Bill to which the hon. Member
refers is a Private Member's Measure.
has not been the subject of negotiations
between the Governments of Great Britain
and Northern Ireland, nor have any representations--official or unofficial-been invited
by or tendered to the promoters by or on
behalf of this Government. I have not seen
a copy of the Bill.

authority he made the statement that he was

Mr. SPEAKER: I do not think it would be
within the province of the Government to
inquire from individual Members of the

Mr. DEVLIN: If this Gentleman or any

capacity makes a statement reflecting upon
this Government and committing them to a

of it, is it not the right of this Parliament to

Mr. SPEAKER: I have no doubt if such a

that so far as the Government is concerned

is at present on the Statute Book:-
any existing enactment by which any

imposed on account of religious belief or
on a member of any religious order as such
shall, as from the appointed day, cease to

That Clause is in the Act of 1920, and therefore whether the Northern Government, the

The PRIME MINISTER: That is my

THE GENERAL STRIKE.-PRICE OF

Mr. KYLE: I wish to ask the following
question, of which I have given the right
hon. Gentleman, the Minister of Home
Affairs, private notice:-
To ask the Minister of Home Affairs if
he is aware that the coal merchants in
Belfast have increased their prices for coal,
and what steps the Government are going
to take to prevent this exploitation of the
needs of the people in the necessities of life.
The MINISTER OF COMMERCE (Mr.
Barbour): I have been asked by my right
hon. Friend to take this question.
The answer to the first portion of the hon.
Member's question is in the negative. My
Ministry has been, and is, in close touch
with the Coal Merchants' Association, who
assure me that they have not increased
coal prices in Belfast. The price at which
bags of coal are being sold by coal merchants
is, and will, I understand, continue to be,
the same as has been in force for the past
Division No. 50.

month. Any increase in selling prices would,

Jury Laws Bill-

HOUSE OF COMMONS
[Sir Dawson Bates]
At the outset, I propose to explain some of
the reasons which have led the Government
to bring in this Measure. The Jury Law has
remained unaltered since the Act of 1876,
with the important exception of the Sex
Disqualification Act which was passed in
1919. The 1876 Act under which we are working at the present time, dealt with the qualification of Jurors, and provided a procedure
for summoning them, but I need hardly
point out to this House that the conditions
to-day are very different to those prevailing
fifty years ago, and as a result the Act has
become, to a large extent, obsolete and outof-date, and I think this will appear clear
to the House when I come to deal with the
details of the Measure.
For many years past there has been a
growing discontent with the burden of the
jury service. This discontent is, I believe,
largely due to the inequalities which prevail
at the moment. These inequalities partly
arise owing to change of conditions, notably
the passing of the Land Acts under which
tenant farmers become the owners of the
freehold, and this I will refer to afterwards,
but it is also very largely due to the difficulties in procedure prescribed under the present law. As a result, many people are
escaping jury service who are in a much
better position to bear the loss of time and
the expense involved than others who are
called upon to serve. For example, a person
whose name appears on the list may be never
called upon to serve, while his neighbour,
who may own a farm of a very much smaller
valuation, and be in a very much poorer
financial position, may be called at frequent
intervals, and this anomaly may, and does,
result from the mere accident of the initial
letters of their names.
But there is another reason. I am sorry
to say that there are a large number of
cases of evasion of this important duty of
citizenship, with the result that an increased
burden is thrown upon those who are prepared faithfully to discharge their duty.
In the country, the existing qualifications
produce an unnecessarily large number of
jurors, while in the city, the reverse is the
case. In the country, as the result of the
present qualifications, many people
called upon to serve who can ill afford the
time and the expense, when, as a matter of
fact, there is really no necessity for them
to be summoned.
are
In the cities the number of jurors is too
small and, consequently, they have to be
summoned at frequent intervals, and the
burden there is very severely felt, and as regards Belfast this condition of affairs is more
acutely felt since the transfer of the
Judiciary to Northern Ireland, where the
jurors of Belfast are called upon to serve
in cases which come from all over the Six
Counties.
a
The Government, since they came into
being, have been urged to undertake
Measure of Jury Reform, but, knowing the
difficulties surrounding the question, they decided before embarking on legislation, to explore the matter thoroughly from all angles,
as they felt that even if there should be delay
it would tend towards having a more satisfactory Measure, and accordingly, the
Government appointed a Commission, with
Lord Justice Andrews as Chairman, to inquire into the whole matter. That Committee was very representative, not alone of
the legal profession but also of the laymen,
and while I refer to this matter, I would
like to take this opportunity of expressing
the thanks of the Government to Lord Justice
Andrews and his Committee for the very
exhaustive and valuable report, which forms
the basis of the present Measure now before
the House. The Committee made a large
number of recommendations, some of which
we could not see our
way to adopt for
reasons which I will explain hereafter, but
I think it will be agreed that we have included in the Bill most of the important
recommendations.
There is one matter which I wish to make
clear, before going into a detailed explanation of the Bill. Hon. Members are aware
that under the Government of Ireland Act,
1920, matters relating to the Supreme Court
are reserved, and the Committee made recommendations which fall into three categories namely:-
(1) Those which were clearly outside the
competence of this Parliament;
(2) Those which were clearly within our
competence; and
(3) Those about which there is some
doubt as to whether they are within our
competence or not.
We have, therefore, excluded those falling
within the first category, from the Bill, but
I shall refer to them later on, and we are
now dealing with the second and third
classes, so far as we have been able to
accept the recommendations. We have
adopted this course after consultation with
the Imperial Home Secretary.
Coming now to the provisions of the Bill, I
think it would be convenient if I was, first,
to state shortly the existing law, governing
the qualification for jury service, and then
to indicate the changes which we propose
making; afterwards I will deal with the rules
of procedure which we propose to make.
The qualifications for jury service are
contained in Section 2 of the Act of 1876, and
that Section provides that every man between

21 and 65 residing in any county, and having
the necessary qualifications, is liable to serve
on all juries, whether civil or criminal, and
the qualifications are:-
(1) he should have a clear annual income.
of £10 from freehold lands;
(2) that he should have a clear annual
income of £20 from leasehold lands;
(3) that he should either in his own
name, or a member of a firm, be rated-
(a) in respect of lands and tenements
of a net annual valuation of £40;
or
(b) £10 in respect of a dwelling-house,
except in the case of Belfast and Derry,
where the vaulation should be £20.
(4) that he should be a director of any
Incorporated Company.
(5) that he should be a member of a
Board of Harbour Commissioners.
Now, with regard to the first two qualifications, namely, a clear annual income of £10
free from freehold lands, or an annual income of £20 from leasehold lands, it will be
obvious to hon. Members how difficult it is
to ascertain how much a man derives as
annual income from either freehold or leasehold land. Some registration authorities, I
understand, assume that because a valuation
is of £10, the individual must necessarily
have an income of £10 out of it. Others have
not accepted this view, and I think that it is
unsatisfactory that there is no certain measure of qualification, but apart altogether
from this disadvantage, the tenure of land in
Northern Ireland has altered very materially
since the Act of 1876 was passed. In the old
days a £10 freeholder was very often a man
of substance, and a man well able to bear
the burden of jury service, but by the
operation of the Land Purchase Acts, the
number of freeholders has increased enormously, and, at the present moment, a
farmer who has bought out his farm with a
£10 valuation may be called upon to leave his
farm with nobody in charge, and go and serve
on a jury, while his neighbour, who may be
a judicial tenant, with a valuation up to
£40, and who is in a very much better
financial position, escapes altogether.
With regard to urban areas other than
the county boroughs of Belfast and Derry,
as I said before, the rating qualification is
£10. Fifty years ago that amount brought
in a fairly substantial class of householder,
but since that time the standard of valuation has risen, and the result is that this
valuation captures many men to whom jury
service is a real hardship.
As I have already stated, the number of
jurors produced under the existing Jury Acts
is. apart from the county boroughs, excessive, and our object is to simplify the qualification, and to fix it at such a figure as
will produce the required number of jurors,
and, at the same time, not impose a hardship upon those least able to hear it. Lord
Justice Andrews' Committee recommended
the abolition of the freeholder, and the leaseholder qualification, and the substitution of
a simple rating qualification, and in this Bill
At
we have adopted this recommendation.
the same time, and having regard to the
fuller statistics at our disposal than were
available for the Committee, we have come
to the conclusion that the rating qualifications which were recommended by Lord Justice Andrews' Committee, would be too high
to produce sufficient jurors, and, accordingly,
we have decided that the qualifications should
remain as at present in county boroughs,
namely, £20; that in the case of counties it
should be fixed at £20 for urban districts
and towns; and at £16 for other parts of
the counties, and hon. Members will find
these particulars set out in the First
Schedule at page 14.
I believe the adoption of these qualifications will produce a sufficient number of
jurors, and, at the same time, relieve the
man of small means, especially those dependent upon their daily wages, or others, such
as farmers and shopkeepers, who have no
assistants to work for them in their absence.
I might point out here that under Section
2 of the 1876 Act, it is provided that if a
person is qualified within the Borough but
lives within 12 miles of the Borough Courthouse in the county, he is to serve in the
Borough and not in the County. Unfortunately, the Section is somewhat obscure.
It is doubtful whether this Section applies
to all jurors, or only those who are qualified
by reasons of being a Director of a Company
or Harbour Commissionera. In practice, a
narrow interpretation is put upon this
Section with the result that the present
Section is not of very much use. I think
this might be regarded as another example
of how modern conditions have rendered the
old Acts obsolete. The great growth of
travelling facilities has caused an increasing
number of business men to reside outside
the city, and, as a result, their services are
lost to the city, and I think hon. Members
will agree that it is only right that those
men, whose interests are mainly bound up
in the city, should bear their share of jury
service in the Borough. On the recommendation of the Jury Commission, we propose
to extend the distance from 12 miles to 25
miles, and we propose to make it quite clear
that this will apply to all jurors qualified
in the city who reside outside the city within that area.
There is just one other matter in this Clause
to which I would like to draw the attention of

this House. It has been found that there

DEVLIN: Could the right hon.

Sir DAWSON BATES: My hon. Friend

Mr. DEVLIN: Does the right hon. Gentleman ask a body of sensible men to believe

Sir DAWSON BATES: My hon. Friend is
a bachelor, and I do not think he

in this Bill, in order to stop what

that the husband in such cases is to be

The second Clause of the Bill deals with
the preparation of the lists of special juries,
and makes very little change in the existing
law, save that it reduces the qualification
for a special juror in some of the counties.
We propose to fix it at the figures set out
in the Second Schedule, page 14. I might
point out that special jurors are required
for the trial of actions in which the parties
require a special jury, and they are also
required for the purpose of forming grand
juries at quarter sessions, and we have found
that, as a result of the present qualifications,
we have got an insufficient number of special
jurors in certain of the counties. The changes
we propose follow the recommendation of
Lord Justice Andrews' Committee.
Now we come to the very important question-the question of exemptions-and these
are dealt with in Clause 3, and if hon.
Members will turn to the Third Schedule on
page 15 they will find the exemptions. In
putting forward these exemptions I have been
mainly guided by this principle that no
citizen is entitled as a matter of privilege
to claim exemption-(hon. Members: Hear,
hear) and that there should only be exemption in order to meet the convenience of the
public, or in the interests of the State, and
for no other reason can exemption be justified.
The First Schedule to the old Act
of 1876 contains a list of exemptions, and we
propose to re-enact this list with some very
important exceptions. In this matter we
have followed the recommendations of the
Committee, and we propose to abolish the
exemption that has hitherto been given to
civil engineers and pharmaceutical chemists,
with this important exception that in the
case of a "one-owner" shop, who has no
qualified assistants, he should be exempt.
I think you will agree with me that it is in
the public interest that shops of this kind
should be left in the hands of qualified
individuals.
But I come now to what is a more farreaching change. Under the Act of 1876,
all persons holding any public office under
His Majesty's Government or in any public
Department, or any local authority, and
paid from rates or taxes, are exempt from
jury service. That is the present law.
Mr. DEVLIN: Why?
Sir DAWSON BATES: My hon. Friend
will get ample opportunity later on to explain what a good Measure this Bill is.
Mr. DEVLIN: But the right hon. Gentleman is explaining this Bill-and it is his
Bill, not mine-and I would like him to
explain why these exemptions were granted
in the past.
Sir DAWSON BATES: If my hon.
Friend will only have patience I will
try to explain these matters to him.
Lord Justice Andrews' Committee recommended that this exception should be entirely
abolished. There is 110 such general
exemption in England, and generally speaking civil servants and officials of local
authorities have to take their share in jury
service, and we think that the reasons for
the exemption given in 1876 do not exist today. I think in the absence of cogent
reasons why these officials should be exempt,
the public naturally resent that these
officials should escape the burden of jury
service, and thereby throw a greater burden
on others. The Committee do not recommend any exceptions, but we have found it
necessary to insert certain exceptions from
the general rule. We have tried to make
these exceptions as few as possible, having
regard to the principle which I have laid
down, but there are certain classes which we
consider should be exempt, such as officers
of the Army, the Navy, the Air Force, members of the Constabulary and Prison Officials.
These are exempt in England and we propose
to exempt them here. So far as regards our
own Civil Service, we have only exempted
from jury service the permanent Head and
Deputy of each Ministry, and hon. Members
will appreciate that they can only mean
three at the most in each Ministry. We have

also exempted the Comptroller and Auditor

These officials-they are very few in

whose cases may previously have been

With regard to Imperial Departments in
Northern Ireland, we have thought it right
to exempt the heads of these Departments
who may be in charge of the Head Office in
Northern Ireland. We also exempt officers
of the Post Office, and officers in the
employment of the Commissioners of
Customs and Inland Revenue. and, with
regard to these categories, we might, point
out that they are already exempt by Imperial Statutes, and the reason why we have
reinserted their names in this Bill is for the
purpose of having a comprehensive Schedule
which will be easy of reference. I think hon.
Members will agree that there is an overwhelming case for exempting these officials
on the grounds of public convenience, as
hon. Members will realize the enormous
inconvenience that might be caused to
the public by the taking away of
postmaster or postmistress, and apart altogether from this, a great deal of expense will be caused to the public service
in having to send down substitutes for these
officials, many of whom carry on duty singly.
With regard to officers of local authorities,
we propose to exempt, for obvious reasons,
all officials who have statutory duties to
perform in connection with the preparation
of jurors' lists, and this would exempt such
officials as town clerks. county secretaries,
and rate collectors.
Clause 4 provides that grand jurors should
be selected in Belfast in the same way as
grand jurors are selected in the counties.
I confess that I approach the explanation
of the next Clause of the Bill with a certain
amount of diffidence, and I fear that it will
be difficult to explain this very technical
matter clearly. It deals with the method
to be adopted by the sheriff in selecting the
names for his panel, and I will try to explain how the selection takes place at
present, and how we propose to alter it in
the future, because, as I said before. it is
very largely due to the existing procedure
that so many inequalities exist in the
present system.
I shall assume that the sheritt is starting
his book for the first time, as we provide
that he should do in the first lists prepared
under this Act. The names are arranged in
alphabetical order on the same principle as
our words are arranged in a dictionary.
The sheriff begins at the letter "A," and
takes the first name. He then goes to the
letter "B" and takes the first name, and so
on through the letters of the alphabet, coming back to the letter "A" and taking the
second name there, and so on through the
letters of the alphabet, he proceeds in this
way until he has obtained a sufficient
number of names. When he comes to strike
his second panel he goes to the letter next
after the letter from which the last name
on the previous panel was taken, and he
proceeds as before.
Now, hon. Members are probably saying
that there is very little difficulty about that,
but the difficulty now comes in when the
sheriff starts a subsequent panel, and it acts
in different ways in towns and county, and
I will tell the House how it arises. Section
19 of the Jury Act of 1871, which prescribes
the rotation in which the sheriff is to summon
the jurors, had the object in view that no
one was to serve more than once in three
years, and, accordingly, this Act, in order
to ensure this condition of affairs, laid it
down that in making up subsequent panels
after the first, the sheriff should proceed in
like manner as before, "taking the names
of the persons not already summoned during
the current or next two preceding years,
so far as may be necessary until the entire
book has been exhausted, and then he is to
start again.
Coming back to the book, no difficulty probably arises in regard to the second panel,
and if the book contained sufficient names for
the panels for three years without repetition
and no more, no difficulty would arise at
subsequent panels. In the cities, however,
the lists do not contain the requisite number,
with the result that when the book becomes
exhausted in any year, the Sheriff, on account
of the words I have emphasised, cannot go
to the name of a person who served at the
remotest date, but must go to the first name
on the list, with the result that the persons
whose names come early in the letters of
the alphabet, such as the names beginning
with letters "AB" or "MA" are summoned
much more frequently than those beginning
with "AO" and "MO." The people whose
names come under the short letters, such as
"I" or "U" are at a great disadvantage as
compared with those down in the long letters
such as "A," "G," or "M."
In the counties it operates somewhat
differently. It does not cause anyone to be
summoned more than once in three years,
but it prevents the people low down in the
long letters ever being called at all. I am
afraid that this system can only be clearly
understood by seeing the system in actual

operation on the Jurors' List, and if any

After hearing evidence of those
practical knowledge of the system, the Committee recommend that the words:-
Taking the names of the persons not
already summoned during the current or
next two preceding years
should be repealed. This will mean that the
sheriff, instead of going back to the beginning of the book after three years, will go
right through it from beginning to end, and
thus every person on the list will take his
share of service. Where the book contains
less than a three years' supply, the names will
be gone through, and the Sheriff can take
in those who have failed to serve before going
to those who have already served.
The next Clause-Clause 6-makes improvements in the machinery for the revision of
the lists. Under the provisions of this
Clause, on the first list prepared by the local
officers after the passing of the Act the name
of every person who appears to be qualified,
apart from any question of exemption, will
be included, and each case will be ruled on
by the County Court Judge or Revising
Barrister revising the list. Where a claim
for exemption is proved to his satisfaction,
either on the grounds of Statute, ill-health,
or for any other cause, he will strike the
name off the list, and he will mark it
"permanent," or "temporary," as the case
may be. If marked permanent the
name will not appear on future lists, but if
marked "temporary" it will appear again as
soon as there is reason to believe that the
temporary disqualification, say on the ground
of ill-health, has disappeared, notice being
given to the person concerned of the intention to re-insert his name on the list.
This system should prevent the list being
cumbered with persons who are really


exempt, and should prevent a great deal of
inconvenience and annoyance to the public.
I fear that the task of revising the first list
will be a rather lengthy process for the Revising Barrister, but, at the same time, I am
convinced that a great deal of the success
of the Act will depend upon the thoroughness
with which the list is revised, and, as regards future lists, this will give less trouble
to the Revising Barristers in the future.
With regard to Clause 7, this Clause speaks
for itself. In the cities,, the jurors' lists
were prepared by wards, but this has really
served no practical purpose, and indeed has
caused inconvenience, and accordingly, we
have provided that in the future, there will
be one general jury list for the whole city.
As regards counties, the unit hitherto has
been baronies, but this is entirely obsolete,
and we propose that the list should be, in
the future, prepared according to the Local
Government areas now in existence.
Clause 8 also speaks for itself, and I would
like to draw the attention of the House to
the fact that for administrative convenience,
we propose to divide the letter "M" into
two-names beginning with "Mac" or any
abbreviation being treated as a separate
letter.
Clause 9 removes a small anomaly which
was created by the Local Government Act
of 1898, in connection with the expense of
preparing the lists. Hon. Members will remember that the lists are prepared by the
Secretaries of County Councils, and by the
Clerks of Unions, where the Clerk is an
existing officer. The Act of 1898, to which I
have referred, provides that the expenses incurred by the county council in the preparation of the lists should be borne as a
county-at-large charge. On the other hand
the urban district councils have to pay for
the expense of preparing the lists so far as
the urban district councils are concerned,
and the result is that the urban district
councils have both to pay their own expense,
and also their share of the county-at-large
charge. This Clause will exempt urbau
authorities from any county-at-large chargo
so far as regards their own area.
Clause 10 provides for the payment of the
officials who undertake their work, on the
average of the previous three years, and this
is in accordance with the recommendation of
the Lord Justice Andrews' Committee.
Clause 11 gives power to the Presiding Judge
to divide the panel into two or more sections,
and will enable him to excuse from attendance on any specified days during the
sittings of the Court, the names of the jurors
whose names appear in any one or more of
these sections into which the panel may
have been divided. This provision is one entirely in the interests of the jurors, and will
meet a long-felt want.
The second part of Clause 11 confers
powers on judges similar to those which they
have in England, under which a judge, after
a very heavy trial-for example, a murder
trial-will be empowered to excuse the jurors
who have served, from further service for
a period of years, and I cannot but think
that this should appeal to the House as an
eminently fair provision.
The third Sub-Clause of Clause 11 provides
machinery for the judge to deal with cases
where incapacity to serve has either escaped
the notice of the Revising Barrister, or has
arisen since the revision. At the present
time if a man who is otherwise disqualified

appears on the jury panel, while the judge
may on that occasion excuse him from attendance at a particular Assize, he has no
power to strike his name off the jury panel,
with the result that he will be called on the
following Assizes. We propose to give the
judge power to direct the sheriff to pass over
such name during the curreny of the list,
and we provide machinery that the circumstance will be brought before the notice of
the Revising Barrister at the next revision.
With regard to the fourth Sub-Clause of
Clause 11, this deals with the question of
medical certificates. At the present time I
do not think there can be any doubt, but
that sometimes medical certificates are given
to jurors on very slight grounds, and with
comparatively little cause, and the result
is the judges are placed sometimes in a very
difficult position when the panel is called.
Under this Sub-Clause we provide that a
juror is only to be excused on the ground of
ill-health on the production of a proper
medical certificate, the form of which is set
out in the schedule. It is quite true that
Lord Justice Andrews' Committee recommend that the medical doctor should provide
an affidavit. We fear, however, that this.
would impose a hardship on the jurors, and
we cannot but think that the matter will be
rectified by the proposals in the present Bill.
Clause 12 has for its object the tightening
of the machinery for the imposition of fines
on defaulting jurors, and we propose that the
fine should be imposed by the judge unless
some reasonable cause is shown for the nonattendance, and that immediately after a fine
has been imposed that notice shall be immediately given to the defaulter, and subseqeuntly enforced, unless the fine is remitted by the judge for cause shown. We think
that if this Clause is strictly enforced it will
do away with an abuse which has been undoubtedly a legitimate cause for grievance on
the part of jurors in their endeavour to do
their duty.
Clause 13 only applies to juries in civil
cases. It has been customary up to the present to pay a common jury £1 1s 0d-that is
for the whole jury-and we propose that in
lieu of that, each member of the jury shall
receive a sum of 5s. This remuneration, of
course, will be borne by the litigants.
As regards special juries, it is provided by
an old Irish Act that each juryman in the
special jury was to receive £1 18 0d, but it
is also customary to pay this only where a
jury had found a verdict, or where the action
had been settled after the jury had been
sworn, and the effect of this Measure will be
to make the custom legal. It is also proposed that in the case of a new jury that
each juryman shall receive an additional
sum of £1 1s 0d. These amounts, of course,
as I have said before, will be paid by the
litigants.
Clause 14 provides that the judge trying
a civil case, may direct that the jury ought
not to disperse during the luncheon interval,
and he may order that lunch should be provided for the jury at the expense of the litigants. This will save the time of the Court
and the time of the jurymen, and will also
save expense.
We provide under Clause 15 that unless
a Coroner deems it necessary, it should not
be essential in the interests of justice for a
Coroner's jury to view the body.
Clause 12.-The provision giving the
Government power to bring the different
parts of the Act into force at different
dates will enable us to put in force the
portions of it which are essential for the
preparation of next year's lists on the new
basis, even though the arrangements, about
which I am in correspondence with the
Imperial Home Secretary, may not have
matured by that date, as there is no doubt
as to our competence to deal with these particular matters.
I fear I have made considerable demands
on the patience of this House, but before
sitting down I would like to refer briefly to
the recommendations which were made, and
which we have not been able to deal with.
These recommendations fall into two
categories:-
(1) Those matters which are within our
competence to deal with;
(2) Those which partly come within our
competence and partly outside it.
Now, with regard to the first of these categories, i.e., those which are within our competence, the proposals are five in number:-
(1) The abolition of grand juries at quarter
sessions;
(2) The payment of the expenses of certain
jurors in crime cases;
(3) The payment of certain expenses of the
sub-sheriff;
(4) The exemption of women jurors;
(5) The enactment of an income qualification by persons who are not rated.
With regard to the abolition of Grand
Juries, I might point out that the Committee
recommended that the Grand Juries at Assizes
and at the Belfast City Commission should
remain, partly on the ground that some of
the cases that are tried at these tribunals
are more serious than those tried at Quarter
Sessions, and partly that it is desirable that
every precaution should be taken to see that
prisoners were not put on their trial without
adequate justification, but I would point out
to this House that serious criminal cases are

bring about this change.
The Committee also recommended the payment of expenses in criminal cases where the
juror was brought over a distance of 10 miles.
It is suggested by the Committee that these
expenses should be paid out of the fines on
jurors. It is quite clear, however, that the
fines on jurors would not provide sufficient
funds to anything like meet such an expense;
indeed, in some counties, there might be no
fines at all. But apart altogether from this
aspect of the question, this proposal would
introduce an entirely new principle of farreaching effect. Jury service, especially in
criminal cases, has from the very earliest
time been regarded as a duty of citizenship,
which ought to be discharged by the citizen
without payment. After all, while citizenship
has its privileges, it has also got its duties,
but the criminal law is designed, not merely
for the punishment of criminals, but also for
the protection of law-abiding citizens, so that
they may pursue their daily avocations in
peace and have security of life and property.
The duty of jury service is a part of the
return which they make for this security.
Under the proposals contained in this Bill
jury service should approximate to a maximum of once in 3 years, and in some counties,
the interval of service may be even 4 or 5 or
possibly 6 years, and it does not seem to me
that it would be a great hardship if a man
should be called upon to attend at Quarter
Sessions, or at Assizes, once in 3 years or
sometimes even less, but apart altogether
from this, the provisions of the Bill will
exempt from jury service a great many individuals who are at present on the lists, and
who are less able to bear the cost of
attending.
This recommendation of the Committee
would not apply to Belfast, and I would remind
this House that the additional power which
we have given the Courts to divide the
panel into sections will in itself lessen the
actual time in which a juror will have to
attend. We have considered the whole
question very carefully, and we are strongly
of opinion that it would introduce a principle
that has never been hitherto adopted in
Great Britain and that is opposed to the
whole theory of jury service.
With regard to the recommendation that
under sheriffs should be relieved of the
expense of printing jury panels, jury summonses, and ballot cards, the Government
feel that all these matters were taken into
consideration when the salaries of the
sheriffs were fixed in 1920. The position of
these officers was enormously improved by
the Sheriffs Act of 1920, and the Government
do not see that there is any case for an
alteration in the existing system.
The Committee recommended that the law
should be amended so as to enable women to
be excused from service without the necessity of having to give a special reason for
their application for exemption, but we are
unable to accept this recommendation, which
appears to be wholly opposed to the principle
of the Sex Disqualification Removal Act of
1919. After all, women who are qualified to
serve as jurors have received the full rights
of citizenship, and I cannot but think that
they must also undertake the duties and
responsibilities attaching to their citizenship.
Now we come to a recommendation of the
Committee where it is recommended that persons in receipt of an income of £250 a year
and upwards, who are not rated, should be
liable for jury service. The Government
agree that there is much to be said for the
equity of such a proposal, but I think on reflection it will be seen that the administrative difficulties would make it impossible for
the Government to accept the proposal. Hon.
Members have only to reflect on the inquisitorial attitude of the income tax people in
regard to this, in order to see the undesirability of having a similar body inquiring as
to whether they are financially qualified to
serve on a jury. Apart altogether from this
point of view, the expense involved in setting
up such machinery renders the proposal unacceptable.
Now we come to the second class of recommendations which are partly within our
province, and partly without it, and they
are:-
(1) The reduction in the number of common jurors in civil cases from 12
to 6.
(2) The reduction
in
the number of
challenges where persons are jointly
charged.
(3) The alteration in the form of oath.
These matters, no doubt, are within our competence, so far as they relate to trials at
Quarter Sessions, but they are clearly outside our competence so far as they relate to
High Court trials. Trials of civil cases at
Jury Laws Bill-
