Second Reading.
Quarter Sessions with juries are of extremely
rare occurrence, but so far as the Supreme
Court is concerned, I may say that the Imperial Government would not be prepared to
consider legislation on these lines, and
the same remark applies to legislation
with regard to the right of challenge
and a form of oath. I might explain that
with regard to the right of challenge where
prisoners are jointly charged with felony,
each prisoner is entitled to 20 challenges, and
the Committee recommended that in noncapital cases the right of challenge should be
limited to 20 among all prisoners jointly
charged with an offence, unless the judge
otherwise ordered. It will, of course, be
obvious to hon. Members that where there
are a number of prisoners jointly charged at
an Assizes, the Sheriff must necessarily
summon a large number of jurors in case
all the challenges are exercised, but I think
we have met this point to some extent by the
provision in Clause 11 which enables the
Judge to divide the panel into sections, and
to require the attendance only of those jurors
who are required at the moment. I regret
that we cannot go further than this, but we
are precluded by the decision of the Imperial
Government.
Mr. DEVLIN: What about challenges for
the Crown? Is that continued?
Sir DAWSON BATES: That was not the
subject of a recommendation by the Committee. That is a matter entirely for the Imperial Government and not for this Government. The Committee also made an important
recommendation with regard to the trial of
actions by a judge without a jury, a matter
which is outside our competence.
They
based their recommendation on certain provisions of the Administration of Justice Act
of 1920, which was in force in England at the
time the Commission sat, but we find on inquiry these sections did not work satisfactorily, and they have been actually repealed by an Act passed in the Imperial
House last year. We are, however, discussing the matter with the Imperial Home
Secretary, and I hope it will be possible to
arrange for a provision being inserted in an
English Bill, whereby complicated civil cases
which depend on the prolonged examination
of expert witnesses, and documents
accounts should be tried by a judge without
a jury, but this, however, is a matter outside
our competence, and can only be carried by
arrangement with the Imperial Government.
or
I have thought it right, even at the risk of
wearying this House to explain this Bill at
considerable length, because, as I said earlier
in my remarks, the subject is a somewhat
difficult one, and I also hope that by going
into the Bill at considerable length, I would
remove a good deal of misunderstandings
that appear to exist in regard to the contents
of the Bill, and perhaps save a certain
amount of unnecessary discussion. We have
endeavoured, so far as possible, to make the
Bill self-contained, and to avoid legislation by
reference. It was impossible to have a com.
plete codification of the existing Acts, but I
think the Bill, as it now stands, will be a
fairly complete guide to the Jury Law as we
propose it shall be in its amended form.
We have dealt very fully with the two most
important recommendations made by the
Committee, viz:-
The alteration in the qualification of
jurors; and the inequality of the incidence
of jury service.
We have attempted to stop evasion, and
we have, I am glad to say, immensely improved the administrative precedure of the
preparation of the jury lists, and I have no
doubt as time goes on, it will be found that,
as a result of this Bill, the whole system of
jury service will have been immensely improved, and the burdens, which have hitherto
pressed sorely upon a large body of people
will have been removed. I beg to move.
Mr. KYLE: I want to congratulate the
right hon. Gentleman, the Minister of Home
Affairs, on his very able speech this afternoon. He has dealt in a very masterful way
with this most complicated subject. I think
that this House does owe him a deep debt
of gratitude for the pains he has taken to
make clear this very complicated Measure.
However, in his explanation he raised one
complication in the minds of some of us
when he said that certain matters were outside the competence of this House. I thought
that we had now our own Judiciary and our
own Inn of Court. We in the North of
Ireland having our own Judiciary, having
our own Inn of Court, and having our own
officials, thought we were competent to deal
with all matters relating to the law. I would
like the right hon. Gentleman, or his Under-
Secretary, to explain exactly what he means
by saying that certain things are outside our
competence. I was under the impression that
the Imperial Government had little or nothing, as a matter of fact, to do with us in
regard to the administration of the law in
Northern Ireland.
This Bill seems to be an advance in the
right direction towards a wider responsibility
amongst the citizens of Northern Ireland,
though I must say that the principal thought
that strikes one on examining the Measure
is for what purpose was the Committee under Lord Justice Andrews set up. Evidently
not much attention has been given to the
conclusions of that Committee. We had
reason to believe, in view of the delay that
has taken place since this Measure was first

HOUSE OF COMMONS

spoken of, certain changes as to service on

certain recommendations of the Committee,
and look at the Measure in the light of those
recommendations. The right hon. Gentleman
has stated that under Clause 13 there is a
change in the payment of common juries in
civil cases from 1s. 9d. to 5s. The Committee
recommended that 10s 6d should be paid to
jurymen serving on a common jury in civil
trials. One wants to know why the Home
Office took the pains to establish this Committee if this and other reforms recommended by the Committee were not accepted.
There is another matter which the Committee recommended and which I think
everybody interested in law at all is very
keen to see established, and that is the
abolition of grand juries. I would like to
hear some of the lawyers in this House saying
what they think about grand juries. The
Committee recommended the abolition of
grand juries in County Courts and that the
Judge should be given the power to enter "No
Bill" on an indictment. It seems to me that
this very desirable reform is entirely lost
sight of by the Minister of Home Affairs, and
that no attention has been paid to it.
Nor, again, has any attention been given
to the recommendation to alter the number
of the common jury from twelve to six. The
right hon. Gentleman, though he did explain
what took place on certain occasions in the
Law Courts, did not assure hon. Members of
this House that there was any cogent reason
for refusing to accept the recommendation
of the Committee, which proposed to alter
the number from twelve to six, and which,
one would like to point out, would not have
meant any further expense on the litigants
who are going to pay the common jury.
Nor, again, has any regard been paid to
the expressed wish of the Committee that
there ought to be an allowance for travelling
and subsistence in the case of jurors coming
from outside the ton miles radius. One wants
to know why that recommendation has not
been thought important enough to be considered by the Minister of Home Affairs. It
seems to me that apparently all that have
been considered fully have been the interests
of existing officers in altering their remuneration for preparing the jury lists.
I would say that most people would welcome the abolition of exemption in .the case
of civil servants, and the other exemptions
which the right hon. Gentleman has put
before the House, and which it would take
one to have before one in order to ascertain
exactly who are the people who are going to
be exempt. I think in the public interest
it is desirable that a great many exemptions
that held formerly should be abolished, to
the end that there may be a greater number
of people interested-directly interested-in
the administration of the law in our Six
Counties.
In conclusion, I do think it is the duty of
the Parliamentary Secretary (Mr. Hanna) to
explain more fully to this House why certain
matters to which the Minister of Home
Affairs has referred are outside the competence of this House. Are we masters in our
own domain so far as the administration of
the law is concerned, or are we not? It
seemed to me that we were, but now the right
hon. Gentleman (Sir Dawson Bates) is casting
very grave doubts upon our competence to
deal with our own law affairs, and I do think
he owes an explanation to the House in connection with that very important matter.

I am opposed to increased taxation as a

I regret with other hon. Members on this

very serious affair for him. If he is in the

the service of commercial travellers, the

Another class for whom restrictions are
suggested in the Bill are pharmaceutical
chemists. Pharmaceutical chemists have
heretofore been exempted, but now the suggestion is that those only will be exempted
who are duly registered, who are the proprietors of a business and have in their
employ no duly qualified person or persons
to assist them. Under recent legislation in
connection with the Dangerous Drugs Act the
proprietor of a pharmacy has serious responsibilities. He is responsible for the safe
custody of all drugs coming within the
Dangerous Drugs Act, and he is responsible
under heavy penalty. Certain potent drugs
are only used in emergency cases, and by
Act of Parliament the proprietor must keep
in his possession the key of the poisons lock.
I would submit that, even though a pharmaceutical chemist should have a qualified
assistant, he is not permitted by law to delegate his authority on potent drugs to any
assistant, whether qualified or otherwise.
In a case of life and death it might be a very
serious thing if the head of the firm, the
responsible proprietor who must carry the
key, should be absent from his business, and
I would appeal to the Minister to take this
matter into his serious consideration.
a
Chemists and druggists and registered
druggists are not exempted, and yet they
come under the same restriction in the
Dangerous Drugs Act. In quite a number of
towns in the North of Ireland there are no
pharmacies, and as
rule in those little
towns, poisons are distributed through the
only registered druggist. The registered
druggist cannot have a qualified assistant, so
under circumstances of that sort he is the
only one who can supply poisons or medicines
containing poisons. One of the poisons used
most frequently in these country places is
laudanum, and that is used in connection
with sicknesses of horses. I can quite
imagine that a farmer coming a very considerable distance into one of these small
towns to get medicine for a horse that was
in a dangerous condition would be very much
upset if, owing to the absence of the druggist
on jury service, it was impossible for him to
get relief for that animal on that day, or,
perhaps, two or three days subsequently. In
the meantime he might lose his horse. I
would appeal to the Minister that chemists
and druggists and registered druggists should
be treated in the same way as pharmaceutical
chemists.
In a short time these bodies will be one.
We have a new Pharmaceutical Society, and
it is only a question of a year or two until
they all amalgamate as pharmaceutical
chemists. I think it would be a matter of
anticipatory courtesy, apart from this
question I have raised, that the same treatment should be meted out to chemists and
druggists and registered druggists as is meted
out to pharmacists.

There is one other matter I want to refer
to, and it is this. You are proposing in this
Bill to extend the area of service for jurors
in the High Courts in the City of Belfast to
a radius of twenty-five miles. Is that not so?
Sir DAWSON BATES indicated assent.
Mr. G. HENDERSON: I think that radius
is much too wide, but this is really more a
Committee point than a Second Reading
point. It is a great injustice to bring men
a distance of twenty-five miles to serve on
juries in the High Courts. I understand
that sometimes these courts will last as long
as six weeks. It is a great hardship to bring
a man twenty-five miles. It is all very well
to talk about the service jurors do in the
city. The city man can get a tram and go
to the Courthouse, and if he is not called he
can go home and attend to his business, but
if you bring a man twenty-five miles to serve
in the High Courts in the City of Belfast he
cannot go home in the next half hour and
start his work again. I think the area should
not be enlarged, or if it is enlarged it should
be a very much smaller area than is proposed.
The other point I want to touch upon is
this. It is certainly a pity the Government
in this Bill have not seen their way to adopt
the recommendation of Lord Justice Andrews'
Committee, and to pay jurors who travel
over ten miles at least their out-of-pocket
expenses. The Home Minister in justifying
the Government in not adopting that recommendation said it would clearly be a new
principle. I think after fifty years it would
not be an unpardonable sin if one new principle was introduced into this Bill to do
away with an injustice that has prevailed for
fifty years. Of course, the right hon. Gentleman put this on a very high level and
wanted to talk about the privileges of citizenship, but when you summon, at a distance of
25 miles, to serve as a juryman a small farmer
who has not the money to pay his expenses,
it is very hard for him to raise his patriotism
to that pitch. I do hope that before this Bill
goes through this House the Government will
see its way to change its attitude in this
one respect, and will pay jurors who are
summoned a distance of over ten miles at
least their out-of-pocket expenses.
I have known of my own experience-and
I suppose I am not the oldest man in this
House, although I am creeping up-men summoned to serve on juries in the City of
Belfast, and because they had not the money
to pay their railway fares they tramped
seventeen or eighteen miles to the Court and
back again at night. If you try that you
will find your patriotism evaporates before
you get to the end of the thirty-four miles.
Therefore, I do appeal to the Government to
introduce at least one new feature into this
thing, which has not been revised for fifty
years, and pay these men at least their outof-pocket expenses.
Dr. MORRISON: One or two suggestions
have been made in regard to changes and
alterations that I would like to comment
upon. The first is the proposal to abolish
the grand jury. I have always thought it was a
wise thing that the person placed in the dock
should have the protection of a jury, and it
is a further benefit for him to have the protection of a grand jury. I can easily understand a case happening where there was a
prejudice against a particular man or
against his religion, or his principles, that
may influence a decision, and the decision
would be injurious to him. Therefore, I
think that the more protection a man can get
the greater is the advantage. I do not believe
that substituting a judge for the grand jury
would meet the case. My experience of
judges, and I speak with a certain amount
of trepidation as there are prospective judges
in this House-
Mr. DEVLIN: They are in the smokeroom.
Dr. MORRISON: My experience of judges
is rather unfortunate, because I think that
everyone in connection with the Crown, from
the Crown prosecutor up to the judge, when
he sees a man in the dock at the instance
of the Crown assumes that he is guilty. It
is a principle of British law that until a
man is proved guilty he is assumed to be
innocent, and the Crown, in my opinion, is
biased by force of habit in the other
direction. On that ground, therefore, I
would object to the abolition of the grand
juries.
Secondly, the grand jury is a very old
institution. It discharges not only its
functions for finding bills, but also social
functions. It brings people together. It
enables me, for instance, as I happen to be
a grand juror, to meet my hon. Friend, the

member of that august and influential body,
and I think the same spirit should animate
the common juror. He is performing very
important duties, and he should feel it is a
privilege for him to occupy that position.
The injustice that was done-and in my
opinion it was a very serious injustice-to
the small farmer will be remedied by this
Measure, notwithstanding the fact that since
land purchase became practically uniform
over Northern Ireland, indeed over all Ireland, and since the farmer became the
owner in fee, it was his duty to serve as a
juror if he was summoned. Some men who
could not afford to bear the expense were
summoned at very serious inconvenience, as
I know from very small farmers in my own
district. That, I think, will be abolished by
this Bill.
Then there is the question which I think
is a vital one, namely payment of jurors. I
remember ten years ago trying to start a
party to bring about reforms in connection
with injustices and grievances that were common to the whole country, and to do it by a
non-political body. One of the things that I
had down in the programme was the payment
of jurors. We had a big meeting in Coleraine, the whole question was discussed, and
subsequently I had conversations with men
occupying high positions on the Bench, and
they told me of the enormous diffculties that
presented themselves the moment you attempted to alter the jury law. They told me
that to pay jurors in Ireland would involve
an expenditure of something like £17,000 a
year.
This is an age of economy, and, seeing that
we have set free the small farmers, to whom
an injustice had been done, and upon whom a
heavy task had been laid, is it a wise thing
for us to adopt this principle of the payment
of jurors? You have, for instance, in the
County Insurance Committee, dealing with
the question of tuberculosis, members paid
for their services.
If you
extend that
principle to jurors, you have also the same
right to extend it to members of boards of
guardians and to members of rural district
councils. You are extending a principle that,
I think, will certainly involve the country
in extra expense and in extra taxation. I
think that the principle is a bad one, and

that it should not be adopted by us.
Economy, in my opinion, is the first and most
important lesson that we have to learn in
Northern Ireland to-day, and if we violate
this principle in the matter of the payment
of jurors I think we will be making a mistake.
Mr. DEVLIN: I would like to start by
congratulating the right hon. Gentleman, the
Minister of Home Affairs, on his remarkably
lengthy, and, as far as he went, extremely
lucid speech, because for length I have not
heard anything like it since Gladstone introduced his Home Rule Bill in 1886. In fact,
the next greatest speech I ever heard before
this one was the speech of Mr. Lloyd George
introducing his famous Budget. Then the
Imperial Parliament had to adjourn for two
hours to give him a rest, and I was thinking,
having regard to the length of the right hon.
Gentleman's speech, in all consideration and
humanity, of suggesting a rest for him. The
lucidity of the speech was remarkable in this,
that it was not made so much for the purpose
of making clear what was in the Bill, as trying to obscure what was not in the Bill.
That is the only justification that I can
understand for the rally which the hon.
Member for the University (Dr. Morrison)
has made to the assistance of the Government. He has delivered a fine old Tory
speech worthy of half a century ago. He has
told us about "old friends, old times, old
manners, old books, old wine," and he wants
to show us that the only safety for existence
rests in the preservation of antique institutions. The hon. Gentleman who has just
sat down has asked why should a juror not
discharge the duty he is called upon to discharge without payment, just as a member
of a rural district council. My answer to
that is this, that in the one case it is compulsory, and that in the other case it is not.
A man can serve upon a rural council when
the meeting place is very near his own home
if he likes, but in this case a man is compelled to come a long distance, very often
under not very attractive conditions, and to
give his time and his attention to public
work without being paid for it.
But I do not understand the principle
the hon. Gentleman has laid down, that there
should be no payment for public service.
Has he not accepted it as a Member of Parliament? Is it not accepted by the Ministers?
Is it not the rule and law in the matter that
judges are paid, and if you pay Cabinet
Ministers and pay Members of Parliament
and pay judges, and pay lawyers to prosecute,
and pay lawyers to defend, simply because
you are using their professional capacity and
their time, what justification have you for
denying payment to a juror, who is in an
infinitely worse position to give his time and

his services, and who, as in the case of my

All these things are things that the ordinary juror has to do, but he is the one class
of citizen less capable of doing it than any
other, and then the hon. Gentleman answers
it by saying there is nothing in the world
so fine as good old wine. The hon. Gentleman attacked the judges in his usual style
and charm. He almost went as far as I ever
went in his references to judges and Crown
prosecutors and other permanent and enduring corner-stones of the State. He told us he
did not like to speak frankly, as he was in
the midst of potential judges. He was not
in anything of the sort; all the potential
judges were in the smokeroom, and my own
view is that the hon. Gentleman took an
unfair advantage of his legal colleagues in
the Government party by making that sweeping declaration against the sacrosanctity of
those whom he calls prospective judges.
This Jury Bill was proclaimed as one of
the chief marks of the excellence of the
present Government. It was to be one of
their star Measures, and it must have been
so regarded by the Home Secretary when, as
I have said, he gave so much of his own time
and study, and occupied so much of ours, in
explaining it. What single abuse does it remove? In what way does it simplify the jury
system? In the first place, you would hardly
ever have heard of the necessity for changing
the jury laws if it had not been for the
clamant demand of those who are legally
jurors for payment for their services. That
is really what caused so much controversy in
the newspapers, the injustice that is done to
jurors in this way. You are going to add to
the number of jurors, but you would not
have had to do so to such an extent if you
had accepted the recommendation of Lord
Justice Andrews' Committee to make a jury
of six instead of twelve. You are extending
the distance which jurors must travel to
25 miles of the City of Belfast. The right
hon. Gentleman may just contradict me as I
go along, because I want to meet anything
he has to say.
But of all the extraordinary things I ever
heard in order to justify this Measure and
this was the argument about which he got
so intensely indignant when I ventured most
modestly and moderately to interrupt him—
I never heard anything to equal the proposed
change in the law to prevent men transferring their property to their wives if they
otherwise would be compelled to act on a
jury. Was there ever such a preposterous
statement made, not only by any Minister,
but by any sensible man, that because I am
not a juror at present I am transferring all
my property to my wife in order to prevent
my being put upon the jurors' list? Surely
the right hon. Gentleman was not serious
when he put forward that proposition.
I suppose that on this matter I disagree
with everybody, but I am going to state my
point of view. Lord Justice Andrews' Committee recommended the abolition of grand
juries in the case of Quarter Sessions. For
my part, I am in favour of the abolition of
grand juries everywhere. I do not believe
in them at all. I did not know what their
functions were until I heard it described by
my honourable, humorous, and delightfully
frank Friend who sits opposite (Dr.
Morrison). He told us what the function of
the grand jury was. I thought he was describing not a trial, but a social saturnalia,
from the description he gave. He said that
the grand jury was a gathering of good old
Tories, assembled not in a Court of Justice
but round the festive board in which they
drank their wine and paid mutual compliments. They shook each other by the hand,
and roused old memories; they fostered good
feeling and developed old friendships, and
concluded by singing "Auld Lang Syne." I
think that is not an exaggerated description
of the grand jury given by the hon. Gentleman. But was there ever such a farce as to
preserve an institution for the purpose so recited by the hon. Gentleman?
I know what the grand juries were for. They
were political institutions in the old daysa collection of seasoned Tories brought into
Court to be addressed by a Tory judge who
was an ex-politician, and who, having no
further opportunities of making political
speeches, used to make them to the grand
juries. That was the grand jury, as I understand it, of the old days; that is what my
hon. Friend wants to perpetuate still. I
am opposed to that altogether. I agree with
Lord Justice Andrews' Report that they
should be abolished at the Quarter Sessions.
I go further, and say they should be abolished
altogether. In the first place, they take up
the people's time. Here were litigants, common jurors, busy lawyers, all sitting in court
until the grand jurors marched forth from
the festive board, after the High Sheriff had
proposed the toast of the judges and told
them what magnificent men they were. They
replied, and told the High Sheriff what a
grand character he was, and then further
speeches were delivered by civic and Ulster
statesmen upon what grand administrators
they were, and meantime the scales of justice
were unmoved.
These affairs went on in a practical community like Ulster, where we are supposed
to do our business on business lines. I say,
I therefore, that the grand jury should have

Mr. DEVLIN: If I might interrupt the

think it was quite right to make these

Mr. CRAWFORD: I think it would be a

muneration has always been demanded by

W. McMullan) that commercial travellers
ought to be exempt, and a case might be
Such remade also for the managers of business
houses, who are called away from their

I do not see why teachers should be
exempted. If a teacher is taken out of a

There are other persons, who, from lunacy,

expression, and I wonder who is to be the
judge of these things?
On the whole I would be in favour of
voting for the Second Reading of this Bill.
But I earnestly hope that the Government
will see their way to make some concessions
in the Committee Stage. The most important
one, so far as my opinion is concerned,
would be that jurors should be paid, at least,

am all for economy. (Laughter.) Members
may laugh, but economy is not cheese paring.
Economy is good management. The thing
could be managed so that the poorer section
would receive some help. Why should they

to a Court of Law and you will find the
lawyers are paid, win or lose. Everybody is
paid except the poor jurors, who can
hardly afford the expense of travelling from

Mr. MILLER: There is one point I
would like to make in answer to the Minister of Home Affairs. The right hon. Gentleman has given us a great lecture on the

present it is not. One man has nothing to

Mr. GYLE: As one who has served on both
common and grand juries, I feel that the

abolished. I was sorry, indeed, to find that

farce from beginning to end. We go upstairs
with the various Bills, and when you get upstairs you find that there is scarcely a grand
juryman who knows what the first procedure is. Then you ask someone who has
happened to be there before to take the
chair. A general conversation ensues around
the table, and the Bills are passed down and
marked "True Bill." That has been my experience, and I have served on grand juries
on several occasions.
With regard to the commercial travellers,
I quite agree that there is a considerable
amount of hardship existing regarding them.
Often and often we know that the traveller
makes up his journeys perhaps for a month
or even six weeks ahead. I would suggest
that if you cannot see your way to exempt
the commercial traveller that at least he
should get six months' notice before he is
going to be called on for service. He only
receives 21 days' notice at the present time.
I suggest he should get six months'
notice. He would then be in a position to
go down to the Sub-Sheriff and arrange with
him whether it would be convenient for him
to attend at the particular time he was summoned for, or whether an arrangement could
be made whereby he could attend a subsequent time. These are little things, but
they are important to many men who have
to find time to attend on juries.
There is another thing in connection with
the juries. I think there should only be
a sufficient number of men summoned to
take up the likely business for one week
at a time. I have found myself summoned
on a jury and have often had to attend
every day for three weeks, and yet was never
called on to serve on a single jury. Over
and over again that has occurred. Why it
has occurred I do not know, but I do find
that on many occasions a juryman has been
summoned say on Monday. He goes away
after being discharged on Tuesday, and when
he came back on Wednesday he was again
summoned to serve, and so on right through
the whole time the Court was sitting. I
think some arrangement should be come to
whereby alternate weeks could be taken, and
the matter so arranged that we would not be
summoned to attend for three weeks in succession when perhaps only one week was
necessary.
I hope that there will be some amendments put forward in connection with this
Bill. I am sure it would be competent for
this House to arrange for six jurymen instead
of twelve. We all know the old saying, that
the best committee of any is a committee of
three and two do not attend. That is
usually the best committee you will find to
do work. When you have twelve men acting
on a jury you find one or two dominating
the others. The other ten men are not
thinking anything about the case. They are
rather wondering how soon the verdict is
going to be brought in so that they can get
off to attend to their business. I do hope
that if it is not competent to do this
in this Bill the Government will impress on
the Imperial Government that six jurymen
are quite competent to deal with all cases
except those cases where men are brought up
on trial for their lives. In other cases six
men are, I think, quite competent to deal
with them. As I say, I hope that this
Government, if it is not competent to carry
out this reform, will impress on the Imperial Government that in the very near
future something of that sort will be done.
Mr. LEEKE: I would like to join with

jurors
as are absolutely necessary to have the work

The hon. Member (Mr. Leeke) opposite says

and the hon. Member for Tyrone and Fermanagh (Mr. Miller) says that they are

have ever taken part in any Criminal Court
in any capacity, that our judges are particularly hard to persuade of the guilt of a prisoner
-(hon. Members: Hear, hear)-and I do not
think it would be right that that statement
should go without contradiction.
The hon. Member (Mr. McAllister) who
shares with me the honour of representing
County Antrim, and who sits opposite, raised
the point that the Government have dealt
unfairly with the Clerks of the Crown and
Peace in connection with their remuneration.
As this is a very technical matter, perhaps
the House will bear with me if I stick very
closely to my note in connection with it.
The hon. Member's suggestion was that we
were making an onslaught upon the emoluments paid hitherto to the Clerks of the
Crown and Peace. We do no such thing.
The Clerks of the Crown and Peace will be
paid under this Bill all that they were entitled to be paid, and the amount that they
have always been paid. Under the Jury
Acts, 1871 to 1876, the Lord Lieutenant w was
empowered to fix scales of remuneration for
the officers who had duties under the Jury
Acts, including Clerks of the Peace. At
Jury Laws Bill—
Second Reading.
HOUSE OF COMMONS
.
[Mr. Hanna]
that time Clerks of the Peace and Clerks of
the Crown were paid mainly by fees, but by
the County Officers and Courts (Ireland) Act,
1877, the offices of Clerks of the Crown and
Peace were amalgamated so far as new
entrants were concerned. These amalgamations took place as vacancies occurred, and
were completed in all counties in Northern
Ireland many years ago.
The Act provided that, after the union of
offices, the Clerks of the Crown and Peace
were to receive a consolidated salary payable
by the Treasury, and Section 21 provided
that all fees, which were then payable in respect of their duties to Clerks of the Crown
and Peace, should be paid into the Treasury,
but that they should be allowed to keep such
part of the fees as would cover their actual
out-of-pocket expenses of doing the work.
The revision of Jurors' Lists is specially referred to. The intention of the Act is clear
that Clerks of the Crown and Peace were to
receive no personal profit other than their
salaries. The remuneration of Clerks of the
Crown and Peace, that is, as between the
Clerk of the Crown and Peace and the
County Council, has been fixed by various
Orders in Council, the last of which are
dated 26th November, 1919, and 5th November, 1920. The scale is £20 up to 500 names
on the general list of jurors, and 8d for every
additional name, and £5 up to 500 names, and
2d for each additional name, for all names
appearing on the Special Jurors' Book.
An Order in Council dated 2nd February,
1920, provides that this remuneration, which
is collected by the Clerk of the Crown and
Peace from the County Council, is to be
divided into two moieties-one, representing
the profit, is to be paid into the Treasury,
and the other, representing the amount of
the out-of-pocket expenses incurred in the
preparation of the lists, is to be retained by
the Clerk of the Crown and Peace. This
Order in Council merely continues an arrangement which has been in force for many
years, and is based on the assumption that
it actually cost the Clerk of the Crown and
Peace one-half of the remuneration in outof-pocket expenses.
The Clerk of the Crown and Peace does not
require assistance throughout the year for
the purpose of the Jury Lists. His work
thereon does not begin until he receives the
lists from the county secretaries on the 1st
August, and is completed as soon as he sends
the lists to the Sheriff some time in December.
So far as the present Bill is concerned the
amount received by the Clerk of the Crown
and Peace for expenses will be increased for
the first year at any rate in Belfast, but will
probably decrease after that; it will only decrease in so far as the number of names is
reduced, and in the case of the Clerk of the
Crown and Peace, as distinct from that of
the county secretaries and the rate collectors,
his work will decrease in arithmetical proportion to the number of names. It is,
therefore, obvious that he will not require
the same amount of clerical assistance in
future as in the past, and that, therefore,
he ought not to receive the same amount for
expenses.
If the Clerk of the Crown and Peace argues
that he is losing any profit to himself, the
answer is that he should never have received
such profit, and that it was never intended
that he should do so. If, on the other hand,
he argues that 50 per cent. of the remuneration, which he receives from the county
council, will not cover his expenses, he will
have an overwhelming case for obtaining a
revision of the 50 per cent. basis in his
favour, provided he proves his case by the
production of proper vouchers.
The hon. Member for County Antrim (Mr.
George Henderson) was rather confused when
he suggested that the Bill extended the area
from which jurors were chosen. The twentyfive miles referred to in the Clause of the
Bill which was then in his mind is the area
within which those members of the public,
who have a rated valuation in the City of
Belfast, may be brought to serve in the City
of Belfast.
I do not know that there is really any
other matter I should mention, except to
point out, as I might have done earlier, but
will do now, that the hardships that were
inflicted in the old days on people in very
humble circumstances will all disappear now.
It will now be impossible for a juror's summons to be served upon any man who would
not have the means to pay his train fare or
'bus fare to the court, because no man whose
valuation is less than £16 will be called upon
to perform any service as a juror. It is the
sincere hope of the Government that many
reliefs will be experienced by the general body
of jurors in the country, and I respectfully
take this opportunity of stating to the House
that in my humble belief they have made
great progress along the road to that desired
end.

Then take Part V of the Bill-grants in aid
of local expenditure. In this part of the
Bill the Government are taking not £4,000

of rates which they have enjoyed since the

Fund, according to pledges given in this

would have been far more honest to have

This is done at a time when the Prime
Minister has stated in this House that the
Government are anxious to keep down rates
to their lowest level. It is done but a short
time after a very heavy additional burden
has been placed upon the agricultural industry by the Widows', Orphans' and Old
Age Pensions scheme passed last year. I am
not going into the merits or demerits of that,
because I believe it is a fine scheme in a
great many directions, but what is the
effect of it? I say that at the very lowest
estimate that Act put an additional burden
upon the agricultural industry of from
£170,000 to £180,000 a year. And yet, at this
time, the Government have seen fit to come
and take a grant that has been used up to the
present time in relief of local rates in order
to balance their Budget. And they call that
economy. I think it is deplorable, with the
rates as they are at present, crushing down
men who cannot afford to pay them, that the
Government should put such a proposal before this House and ask us to pass it.
Then, again, they come here and tell us
that they want to relieve agriculture, which
is our chief industry and the very basis of
all our prosperity, and yet, instead of giving
agriculture a little more relief, in order to
balance their Budget they are putting additional burdens on the industry. And that is
done at a time when they are taking from
the direct grant in relief of rates on agricultural land the sum of £32,000. I said in
this House last year, when the Widows,'
Orphans' and Old Age Contributory Pensions
Bill was before the House, that in my

ORDERS OF THE DAY.
Emergency Powers Bill.
Order for Second Reading read.
Motion made and Question proposed: That
the Bill be now read a Second time.
Mr. BARBOUR: Hon. Members will recollect that in the course of an answer to a
question by the hon. Member for North
Belfast on the subject of coal supplies, I
announced the Government's intention of
seeking powers to protect the interests of the
community, especially of those who, through
lack of financial means, are least able to face
the hardships which an upheaval, such as is
occurring across the Channel, brings in its
train. The peculiar feature of the present
position is that the difficulties which face us
do not arise through any industrial dispute
or disagreement within our own borders,
where, I am glad to say, amicable relations
continue. Unfortunately, however, our
sources of supply of coal and certain imported foodstuffs have, for the time being, been
seriously interrupted, and although the
general public throughout Northern Ireland
has taken the position calmly and risen to
the occasion, there has been a tendency on
the part of some to endeavour to secure as
large stocks of supplies as possible, regardless,
of the interests of the general community.
There are in our midst a number whose
means of subsistence are not such as to enable
theme to take thought for the morrow by
laying in adequate stocks of fuel and food
while these were freely available. These less
fortunate members of the community must
be protected, not only against any difficulty
in securing their daily needs, which would
be likely to arise from panic purchases on an
unnecessarily large scale by those who can
afford to do so, but also so far as this is
practicable by means of regulation against
any unwarranted increase in prices of
essential commodities.
Now, turning to the Bill, which is in the
hands of hon. Members, I need make no
apology for the brief time given for consideration. If action on the lines I have
indicated is to be taken, it must be taken
now. (Hon. Members: Hear, hear.) It is
axiomatic that only the existence of very
exceptional circumstances would justify the
Government asking for powers to intervene
in the general commercial life of the community.
In 1920 the Imperial Parliament enacted a
Measure entitled the Emergency Powers Act,
to deal with a situation somewhat similar
to that which faces us to-day. That Act we
have adapted to local conditions. Stated
briefly, the Bill empowers the Governor,
when satisfied that a state of emergency has
arisen, to issue a proclamation that such
emergency exists, and, thereafter, to make
regulations for securing the essentials of
life to the community and for regulating the
supply and distribution of food and other
necessities.
979 Emergency Powers Bill- HOUSE OF COMMONS

Second Reading.
[Mr. Barbour]
Before sitting down I should like to take
advantage of this opportunity of appealing to
the people of Ulster to take to heart the plea of
the Prime Minister of Great Britain, that the
community at large should bear with fortitude and resolution any inconveniences
which they may be called upon to face, and
so facilitate and support the efforts that the
Government is making to safeguard the
supply of the essentials of life for all classes
of the community. I beg to move.
Mr. KYLE: This Measure has been introduced in much haste, and even the right hon.
Gentleman himself says that the Bill under
the circumstances is note required for
Northern Ireland, that is to say the conditions here are normal. We all hope and
trust that they may remain normal in the
industrial field (Hon. Members: Hear,
hear.) The right hon. Gentleman has
stated that the Bill is based on the Emergency Powers Act, 1920. It is because he has
left out two of the most important Clauses
in the Emergency Powers Act, 1920, that I
took the step I did a few moments ago, in
giving my opinion and the opinion of the
Opposition that this Measure should not be
rushed through this House this afternoon.
In the Emergency Powers Act, 1920, there
are two provisions which are not mentioned
at all in this Bill, and unless the right hon.
Gentleman is prepared to put these two provisions in, I shall give this Bill all the
opposition I possibly can. These are two
vital provisions. One of them is:
Provided that nothing in this Act shall
be construed to authorise the making of
any regulations imposing any form of compulsory military service or industrial conscription.
The other proviso, which is more important
than that is:
Provided that no such regulation shall
make it an offence for any person or persons to take part in a strike or peacefully
persuade any other person or persons to
take part in a strike.
These two Clauses are in the Emergency
Powers Act, 1920, which was passed by the
Imperial Parliament, and on which the
right hon. Gentleman is basing this Bill.
If the right hon. Gentleman can get up in
his place and say he is prepared to put these
two provisions in, it may modify considerably
the amount of opposition which will come
from these Benches. It is desirable that the
people of the Six Counties should remain
calm. It is also desirable that the Government should have control of the essential
foodstuffs. It is essential that they should
have control of the coal supplies. I am not
wanting to minimise in any way the im
.
portance of any of these factors in the
general situation. All I am concerned about
is that if the occasion arises, which heaven
forbid, we in the trade union movement in
Northern Ireland have got to take our stand
along with our comrades and brethren in
Great Britain in this huge industrial strike.
Now I want to see that the interests of the
trade unionists in Northern Ireland are
protected. We would be very much indebted
if some Member of the Government can say
whether or not they are prepared to put in
these two provisos. Limp and all as they
are, they do maintain some of the liberties
of the subject, and it is because I believe
that these two provisos should be in this
Bill that I want an assurance from the
Government that they are prepared to accept
Amendments along these lines. I have stated
that we are not opposed to the Government
getting control of the food supplies,
or the coal supplies, or anything
that would help to see that the people
are given the essentials of life. It is
essential at the present time with any
Government in power, to see after the supply
and distribution of food and water, and fuel
and light amongst the common people. It is
in order solely to see that the interests of
the trades unionists are protected that I am
offering this opposition to the Emergency
Powers Bill.
The PRIME MINISTER: The intention of
the Government in introducing this Bill was
to limit it as far as possible to the points
actually mentioned in the Measure. It was
not intended to go further afield for all sorts
of restrictions or references to other Acts
or anything of that sort. So far as the first
point referred to by the hon. Member is concerned, we have no power, even if we desired, to conscript in any way under the
Act of 1920. Therefore, it would not have
been within our ambit or powers to include
any section dealing with enlistment as suggested by the hon. Member. With regard to
the other point, of course, that is somewhat
different. There are slightly different conditions in Great Britain to what there are
here. I am as hopeful as anybody can be
that no untoward difficulties will arise in
Northern Ireland. Our sole object in this
Bill is to have the necessary powers in our
hands to prevent any panic or greed, or any.
thing of that sort interfering with the
general public-large masses of the public,
and especially poor people, being deprived of
their fair share of food, coal and the other
amenities of life. I think that the hon.
Member will see that it is impossible for
us to cover everything or all exceptions, and
I do not think he need have any fear that
there is any ulterior motive behind the Bill.
except what appears on the face of it,

CLAUSE 2 (Emergency Regulations).
(1) Where a proclamation of emergency
has been made, and so long as the proclamation is in force, it shall be lawful
for the said Governor, by Order in the
Privy Council of Northern Ireland, to
make regulations for securing the essentials
of life to the community, and those regulations may confer or impose on any Minister
or Ministry of Northern Ireland, officer of
the Government of Northern Ireland (including any police officer or constable),
local authority, or other person acting on
behalf of the said Government, such powers
and duties as the said Governor may deem
necessary for the preservation of the peace,
for securing and regulating the supply and
distribution of food, water, fuel, light, and
other necessties, for maintaining the means
of transit or locomotion, and for any other
purposes essential to the public safety and
the life of the community, and may make
such provisons incidental to the powers
aforesaid, as may appear to the said Governor to be required for making the exercise
of those powers effective.

Turning now to the detailed provisions in
this Estimate, hon. Members will remember
that we are concerned with three classes of
expenditure. The first is under Section 34
of the 1920 Act, and covers all expenditure
for which the Imperial authority is liable,
namely, the provision of a Parliament House,
administrative buildings, and otherwise.
The second comprises those works which are
of a general character and do not concern
the Imperial Government, and the third
applies to those specific works carried out on
behalf of Northern Ireland Departments.
If we turn now to Sub-head "D" hon.
Members will doubtless remember that it was
originally the intention to erect at Stormont
a suite of three Government buildings
consisting of a central building for
Parliamentary purposes, with two wing
buildings, for the accommodation of departmental staffs. In view, however, of the
necessity for the utmost economy, a suggestion was made by the Imperial Government
that both the Parliament buildings and the
departmental staffs should be accomodated
under one roof, and the acceptance of this
suggestion was made conditional on the
speeding up of the work which had been, in
our view, very unnecessarily delayed. After
protracted negotiations, an agreement was
arrived at in regard to the accommodation
which was to be provided. The building
plans have been approved, so that everything
is now in order for the rapid prosecution of
the building. The Joint Exchequer Board,
which is the tribunal, as hon. Members
The work of the strengthening and altering of the foundations, which were originally
put in for the central building, is now well
in hand, and a contract has been placed for
the working of the stone. Drawings and a
specification are being prepared for the
insertion of all the work of the basement,
the ground floor, and the building, three feet
above ground level. Therefore, it may be
said that the work is proceeding as expeditiously as possible, and it is hoped that its
prosecution will not only be proceeded with
but will be continuously carried out.
In addition, at Stormont, the Imperial
Government have agreed to construct a main
road, which we now understand is to be a
processional road, to give a more direct
entrance to the Stormont buildings than that
which already exists.
Mr. BEATTIE:
A processional road?
Mr. POLLOCK: Yes, a processional road
to distinguish it from the other avenues
which are already in existence, but which
are more circuitous and also limited in point
of breadth. The construction of this road
will be commenced in the very near future
and will, it is hoped, give employment to a
considerable number of men almost immediately. In addition to this the Joint Exchequer
Board has given authority for the expenditure of £10,000 for the purpose of re-conditioning the avenues at Stormont generally—
these other circuitous avenues to which I
have referred and I am glad to state that
work has been started on the main drive
from the Newtownards Road to Stormont
Castle. This road, as many hon. Members
are doubtless aware, was in a very bad condition, and at some points was actually
dangerous. Not only is some work being
given there, but we will have the advantage,
at any rate until the new road is provided,
that a suitable entrance to Stormont will
be in existence.

Section III summarises the main works
activities carried out by the Ministry of
Finance on behalf of other Departments of
our own Government. They are really
domestic works services. Each item will be
found charged in the appropriate Departmental Vote, so that hon. Members will probably be familiar with them. In this
connection, I should explain, for the benefit
of those Members who are not familiar with
our Estimates system, why a second opportunity is afforded to hon. Members to express
their views upon this expenditure. There is
a dual responsibility in connection with
work services.
(1) The responsibility of the requisitioning
Department for its requisition; and
(2) The responsibility of the Ministry of
Finance for the technical performance
of the work.
Our object in adopting this formula is to
ensure that our system does place responsibility for these Services upon the proper
shoulders, even though it entails the submission to Parliament on two separate occasions
of each item of expenditure. Sub-head "M"

Member (Mr. Patrick O'Neill) also referred,
we are quite alive to the fact that the building must be maintained, just as this building
has got to be maintained, but I apprehend
that as time goes on the cost of cleaning,
sweeping, and painting the Parliamentary
Buildings, will not be greater than in the
case of a building of the same character
erected on any other site. But, generally, in
regard to the expenditure upon these great
works for which the Imperial Government are
responsible, the matter does not lie within our
hands, and therefore, I wish to repeat that,
though the expenditure is very large, it is
being undertaken from Imperial funds, and
we have no responsibility for it in any way.
In regard to the question which the hon.
Member for West Belfast (Mr. Devlin) rather
stressed, that is the unsuitability of the site,
I was under the impression that the hon.
Member objected rather to a site in any
part of Northern Ireland territory, that his
inclination was towards a site which was very
much further removed from the centre of
things here (hon. Members: Hear, hear)—
even than Stormont, so that, as far as convenience or inconvenience is concerned, I
do not think the site of the Parliament
Building affects him very much. But I
should like to remove from his mind any
misapprehension in regard to the question
of locality, so far as the arrangements of
business men in Belfast are concerned. In
the Law Courts, which will be erected-and
I hope they will be very shortly begun—in
a central part of the city, there will be very
large accommodation for the departmental
staffs of those Departments with which the
people ordinarily come in contact, and only
those Departments which are not very much
concerned with, or in contact with the
people will be located in the Stormont buildings, so that all that apprehension about inconvenience to merchants, solicitors, and all
those other people who naturally come in
contact with Government Departments may
be put aside once and for all. There will be
no difficulty on that head.
With regard to the question of motor
engines, to which the hon. Member (Mr.
Beattie), who is not present at the moment,
referred, I can give him this assurance
that if the engines which are at present
stored at Sprucefield are suitable for the
lighting of police barracks, certainly they
will be used. But it is quite natural that the
Government should be influenced by the
Supply-
Committee.

To refer again to the origin of the leasing

about the delay in respect of the building of

I do not think there is any further

CLASS III. No. 3.
SPECIAL CONSTABULARY.
Motion made, and Question proposed:
"That a sum not exceeding £64,281 be
granted to His Majesty to complete the sum
necessary to defray the charge which will
come in course of payment during the year
ending on the 31st day of March, 1927, to
defray the Salaries and Expenses of the
Special Constabulary (12 and 13 Geo. V., c 8.
(N.I.)). (Note.-£100,000 has been voted on
account.)
Sir DAWSON BATES: I may point out
that following the settlement of the Boundary question and the final arrangement
arrived at, with the British Government
giving their assent to the sum of £1,200,000
to cover the cost of the Special Constabulary
to the end of the financial year and also the
cost of disbandment, we proceeded at once
to take steps to reduce the number of
Special Constabulary. The first two forces
dealt with were the "A" Special Force and
the "C 1" Special Force. The terms of disbandment were that each was to receive two
months' pay and allowance as a bonus.
Since December there has been a steady
process of disbandment, but hon. Members
will appreciate that a Force of this size cannot be disbanded all at once. Barracks had
to be evacuated, and the stores brought into
the depot and checked, and during that process, until each barrack is actually evacuated, there must be a certain number of men
in charge. The operations have, I am glad
to say, proceeded with great smoothness
during the past few months, with the result
that out of a total in Class "A" of 3,600,
only a little over 400 remained at the beginning of the current year.
Hon. Members will appreciate that in
dealing with the personnel of Class "A" it
is necessary to have men at Sprucefield,
where we have very valuable stores, which
have to be arranged with a view to their
sale at a subsequent date. The same remark
applies to Princes' Dock where the bulk of
the motor cars are being stored prior to their
sale. Many of these cars have been sold,
and we hope to be able to evacuate Princes'
Dock early in June. Then, again, we have to
keep a number of Special Constabulary at
Rosscor, looking after the ferry until the
bridge there is completed, but I hope that
the road and the bridge will be completed
by June.
Mr. BEATTIE: What about Ballyvarley?
Sir DAWSON BATES: My hon. Friend will
get an opportunity of discussing this Vote
afterwards.
Mr. BEATTIE: I wanted to know about
Ballyvarley Bridge.
Sir DAWSON BATES: Perhaps my hon.
Friend has discovered where it is.

Mr. DEVLIN: Hear, hear.
Sir DAWSON BATES: My answer is that
there is nothing that tends to the peace of
the community more than the fact that you
have a number of trained men ready to
answer a call if it should come. If at any
time, in any district, a disturbance should
break out we are now in a position to call
out whatever number of men is necessary.
Hon. Members will realise that we work with
a minimum of regular police, and so have
not a big reserve. If these "B" men are
called out for whole-time work they will
receive the ordinary pay of the "A" Special
Constabulary. They will also receive the
indemnity which every policeman has in
respect of injuries which he may receive, and,
in the case of death, the relatives will have
that indemnity. Hon. Members will observe
that there is a cash provision for a bonus of
£80,000 to the "B" Force. I might point out
that this comprises a bonus for the March
Quarter of last year, at £10, which is estimated at £45,000. The balance of £35,000 is,
roughly, three-quarters of the full annual
We are still going to retain Special Constabulary of the "A" class at a strength of
250 for the year. On 1st April, we had 374,
and we are asked to estimate for a strength
of 250 for the whole year. Of course, that
number includes 60 "A" Specials who are
doing duty under the Customs regulations
and their cost is recovered from the Imperial
Government. I understand these 60 men
might be necessary to assist the customs,
but it cannot be stated that 250 are necessary
for the year. If it is going to be implied
that 250 men are necessary as a guard for the
valuable materials that we have stored in
our depots, I think we are going to have a
very costly guard. When the winding-up
took place the Government should have
wound the Force up completely, and no

year for a force which has now become nonexistent except for 250 men.
I understand that in the reduction of the
Force, those who were left over have been
very unfairly dealt with. I understand
that men with long experience, and officers
with families depending upon them, are being
dispensed with, and that younger men who
have only the experience they gained during
their term in the Specials are being retained.
I know for a fact that that has actually
happened in platoon offices. I believe that
in other offices preference will similarly be
given where influence is used. If it is going
to be a question of retaining a position in
the remaining 250 by influence, I am opposed
to any number being retained. I think at
this late hour of the day we should abolish
the 250, with the exception of the 60 men
required for Customs work.
In regard to the "B" Force, I do not
think that any case has been put up for

to put them on the dole. These men are
already on the dole. The only thing they
have been useful for in the past twelve
months has been guarding the homes of some
of the Members of the Government at night.

Mr. DEVLIN: In the previous discussion
that took place on the police Vote I did not
intervene, because I quite recognise that the
first duty of the State is to have an adequate
Police Force, and a Police Force that is not
only adequate in the public interest and for
the service of the State, but a Police Force
that would be decently and even generously
treated by the Government. But I rise to
oppose this Vote on principle. On the last
occasion on which I discussed the "B"
Specials, I objected to them upon this funda
mental ground. I objected to policemen who
are not policemen. It is not a Police Force;
it is a class apart. They are private individuals given a bonus by the State for the
purpose of having some superior rights over
other members of the State. You may take
a street or road in which there are fifty
people living, and two or three individuals
in that street or road are specially selected
to have some superior right over the rest of
the community. I, as a democrat, object
entirely to the setting up of a class section
amongst the members of the community.
This Committee has not withheld from the
Government any claim the Government may
make for adequate financial support for the
maintenance of an ordinary Police Force.
There is no such Force in England. There
is no such Force in Southern Ireland. There
is no such Force in any democratically
organised community that I know of in
Europe. And why it should exist in Northern Ireland I do not know. I am sorry the
right hon. Gentleman, when submitting this
Estimate did not give the Committee some
reasons for its existence. My hon. Friend,
the Member for North Belfast (Mr. Kyle),
has stated that this is merely giving a grant
to your own political supporters. I think
that is the general view held by everybody.
Why should you select any particular and
specific members of the community, and give
them authority as policemen without being
policemen ? That is what you have done.
What is really the fact? You have in this
most extraordinary Force, 500 officers and 40
men. Who was the genius who conceived
that system-500 officers and 40 men? The
40 men were the wise men in the Unionist
Clubs, and the 500 officers were the English
garrison brought over to Ulster. I believe
these 500 officers are nearly all Englishmen,
and they were brought over here to rule 40
Irish men. That is the explanation. It shows
once again the advantages that England can
always have over even Northern Ireland.
Now, perhaps the right hon. Gentleman
(Sir Dawson Bates) will tell us why this
entirely useless expenditure is continued.
First of all, let him deal with the principle
involved, namely, that there should be no
policemen in the State unless they are policemen. You have been given all the financial
power you need to employ an adequate police
force. The right hon. Gentleman, the Prime
Minister, has repeatedly said in this House
and out of it, that there is now peace in the
North of Ireland. We all agree that there

towns on the border when the police were
all shut up in their barracks. Now, I think
it is the duty of this House to see that that
peace continues. (Hon. Members: Hear,
hear). The people who are able to see that
that peace will continue are the members of
the B force. I would like to ask the Government to consider the question of their pay.
I think they ought to get more than £3 a
year, and I think the number of officers
should be reduced so as to allow the men
who did the work in those troublesome times
to get a little more pay for the ensuring of
peace now.
Mr. WILLIAM MCMULLEN: I want to
join with those who have stated this afternoon that there is no justification for this
Vote. The hon. Member (Mr. Cooper) who
has last spoken suggests that some compensation should be given to the people who
brought about the peace. He seems to forget
that the people who brought about the
alleged peace were the people who have been
disbanded some months ago. (Hon. Members: No, no.) Yes. Those people were
largely employed in a full-time capacity-the A
class and others and I say that, apart from
the 500 officers who have been criticised here,
the larger part of this Estimate appears to be
making provision for 15,000 men at £3 a man.
That appears to me to be a ridiculous proposition altogether. I do not agree with the
right hon. Gentleman that this force will perform the function he suggests, because if he
is right I think the way to keep absolute and
perfect peace would be to enrol every
citizen as a special constable. Pay us all £3
and then you will have a safe and absolute
guarantee that there will be no such thing as
disorder or lawlessness. If your principle is
sound why not extend it? You are confiring
your principle to 15,000 people. If your
argument is sound that it is a proper way to
ensure peace, the best way is to enrol the
whole of us as special constables. Let every
member of the Province at any rate every
male citizen, and even every female, who
hope to be loyal citizens of Ulster-be enrolled as special constables, and then you
will be guaranteed that perfect peace which
the whole of us very much desire.
My strong objection to this is based, first
of all, on the fact that I do not consider this
special police force to be necessary. We can
find money in this Province, small and all as
it is, and limited and all as our finances are,
to indulge in luxuries of this kind, but when
the money is required for any essential service we are told that our Province is too poor
to afford it. As the hon. Member for West
Belfast (Mr. Devlin) has pointed out, we
propose to reduce the State contribution to
Unemployment and National Health Insurance, and I have been forced to the conclusion that the amount we are saving under
those heads in the Economy Bill approximates to the amount we are going to spend
as far as this force is concerned. It appears
to me to be an entirely unjustifiable state of
affairs, because I do not believe that this
force is necessary.
Under another item in this Estimate you
will be forced to spend £10,210 as rent of
houses hired for barracks and compensation
in respect of commandeered premises paid
directly by the Ministry of Home Affairs.
That is another item of £10,210 which is quite
unnecessary, because you first of all keep the
force intact, and then you appear to find it
necessary to have barracks for these people
and to spend an additional amount of £10,210.
Of course, it does not serve much purpose to
attempt to pick out items and to criticise
those items, because to me the whole thing is
absurd, and the details are quite as absurd
as having 500 officers and forty men. The
whole thing is perfectly ridiculous.
This charge was formerly borne by a grant
from the Imperial Parliament. Now it would
appear to be a permanent charge upon our
own finances. The right hon. Gentleman
(Sir Dawson Bates) did not make that point
perfectly clear, but I take it that the Government intend this to be an annual charge upon
our finances. He did not give any indication
that at any future date the Government
would contemplate the disbandment of these
people. Now, we are surely not going to continue to live in such a state of affairs that
we will require this force in addition to the
very large and efficient police force that we
have got. As was pointed out this afternoon

years, and that during the past four years
practically every Post Office official in Northern Ireland, who attained 60 years of age,

from one to two years; whether he can state
the number of (a) head postmasters, (b)
salaried officials, and (c) other ranks (indoor
and outdoor) who are at present, serving or

beyond the age limit of 60; and whether he
will undertake to make representations to

Post Office officials compulsorily retired at 60

the Post Office is a reserved service, the
establishment, regulations of which
common throughout the United Kingdom. It
will accordingly be readily appreciated that
it is not within my, province to interfere in
these arrangements which are a purely
domestic matter of the Service concerned.
I, therefore, regret that I am unable to give
the undertaking referred to in the last part
of the question.
Mr. DEVLIN: Is it a rule of the Northern
Government that they do not interfere in any
degree with the administration of the Post
Office? Have the Northern Government
nothing whatever to do with the Post Office?
Mr. BARBOUR: We are consulted in
certain matters entirely at the discretion of
the Post Office, in which case, of course,
express any opinion that seems to us desirable.

LOWER BANN DRAINAGE RATE.
2. Mrs. CHICHESTER asked the Minister
of Finance whether he will state what
Authority is at the present responsible for
the drainage of the Lower Bann, and if that
Authority is the Lough Neagh Drainage
Board; whether the Trustees are bound to
apply the maintenance rates which they levy
to the drainage of the area subject to these
rates; and, if this is not the case, whether
he will state specifically the works in the
Lower Bann which they are bound to maintain, and on which the Drainage Rate is at
present expended.
The MINISTER OF FINANCE (Mr.
Pollock): Since the passing of the Drainage
Act of 1925-that is our Drainage Act-each
County Council is the Authority responsible
for the drainage of lands within its area.
The Lough Neagh Drainage Trustees are,
however, responsible for the maintenance of
certain portions of the channel of the
Lower Bann
as
as well
certain other
works and watercourses in and surrounding Lough Neagh and the Lower Bann,
which are specified in the Award of
the Commissioners of Public Works dated
the 4th day of April, 1859, and of which I
have lent the hon. Member a copy. The
Trustees cannot apply the maintenance rates
levied by them to general drainage purposes
within the area subject to these rates, but
only to the maintenance of the works, etc.,
specified in the Award of the Commissioners
of Public Works which I have mentioned.
Mrs. CHICHESTER: Arising out of that,
is the right hon. Gentleman aware that in
a recent test case in regard to this Drainage
Rate the solicitor for the Lough Neagh Drainage Trustees definitely stated, with regard
particularly to the question of the Glenstall
River, which is mentioned in the Award to
which the right hon. Gentleman has referred,
that the Lower Bann Navigation Trustees
had no jurisdiction over that area, and in
fact had no control over that area at all
quite apart from the one to which I have referred?
Mr. POLLOCK: I am not cognisant of the
particular case to which my hon. Friend behind me has referred, but it would appear
to me that it is not competent either for
me or for the Government to interpret an
Act of Parliament. That lies within the
domain of the Courts, and if the perso
person who
is aggrieved in this case will present it to
the Courts in the ordinary way, I have no
doubt that a legal interpretation of the
Award of the Commissioners of Public Works
will be given. I cannot go any further than
that, I think.

BELFAST UNION-BOOT CONTRACT.
3. Mr. BEATTIE asked the Minister of
Home Affairs whether it is the fact that he
has refused to sanction a local boot manufacturer's estimate for supplying boots and
shoes for the ensuing twelve months to the
Belfast Board of Guardians.
The MINISTER OF HOME
IE AFFAIRS (Sir
Dawson Bates): The Belfast Board of Guardians at their meeting on the 23rd ult., resolved to accept a tender for the supply of
boots, shoes and clogs from Messrs. Williamson, of Belfast, although the tender in question was not the lowest tender received by
them.
The action of the Guardians in this respect
is not subject to the sanction of the Ministry,
The Ministry has no power at this stage to
intervene in the matter.
The Guardians have been, accordingly, informed to this effect, and also that it is a
case in which the Guardians should act on
their own responsibility and be prepared to
justify their action to the Auditor in the
event of any question being raised.
Mr. BEATTIE: In view of the state of
unemployment among boot and shoe operatives in this city, and the danger that the
Guardians see ahead of a surcharge being
made, could the Minister not give instructions to the Board that the conditions they
have set forth and their reasons for giving
the contract to a local employer are such that
he in his wisdom should sanction the contract as agreed upon by the majority of the
Belfast Board of Guardians?
Sir DAWSON BATES: I am not satisfied
that the granting of this contract to Messrs.
Williamson would relieve unemployment,
but I would like to point out that the hon.
Member (Mr. Beattie) does not quite appreciate the position of the auditor. The
auditor is there for the purpose of protecting
the ratepayers against improper or imprudent contracts, and it is a matter entirely for
the Guardians to justify the granting of such
a contract when the matter comes before the
auditor at the annual audit.
Mr. WILLIAM MCMULLEN: Is the right
hon. Gentleman aware that the reason that
determined the Guardians to give the contract locally was that they received a letter
from the local branch of the National Boot
and Shoe Operatives indicating that unless
the work was placed locally it would mean
that about twelve men would be unemployed
after a period of about three months?
•
Sir DAWSON BATES: From the information at my disposal I am absolutely satisfied
that the information which my hon. Friend
(Mr. William McMullen) has is entirely incorrect.

Mr. BEATTIE (by Private Notice) asked
the Minister of Commerce whether he is
aware that, despite the definite assurance of
the Coal Merchants' Association that coal
prices had not been advanced in Belfast,
there have been instances where merchants
have in the present week charged bellmen
prices in excess of those charged in the preceding week; whether he is aware that such
advances in price range between 1s. 4d. and
6s. per ton; and what steps ho proposes to
take in the matter.
Mr. BARBOUR: It has been intimated to
my Department that in certain cases merchants have advanced the prices at which
coal is charged to bellmen. From inquiries
made, however, I am satisfied that such cases
are exceptional, and that the great majority
of the transactions have been carried through
at the regulated prices. As regards the last
part of the question, I would inform the hon.
Member that I propose to issue
ue immediately
a direction definitely restricting coal deliveries, and fixing maximum prices at which coal
may be sold by merchants.

Turning now to the inland fisheries we are
faced with a number of problems, perhaps
the most urgent of which is a demand from
several sources for legislation dealing with
the pollution of fishery waters by flax water.
Hon. Members may know that a Committee
appointed by the Secretary of State for Home
Affairs, and my right hon. Friend, the
Minister of Agriculture, recently investigated
this question and made several recommendations for legislative changes. The report of
that Committee has still to be acted upon.
In order that fishery interests may have an
opportunity of keeping in touch with the
legislative or other contemplated changes, I
propose to establish a small Advisory Council
representative of such interests.
In regard to the administration of railways, hon. Members will, I am sure, appreciate that this is a most complicated matter.
If I may cite an example-each railway company in Northern Ireland is under obligation to furnish to my Ministry, as successors
to the Ministry of Transport, very detailed
statistics, and representations have been
made that a curtailment of such statistics
might be made with advantage, not only to
the railway companies but to the community
in general. This point I am having very
carefully investigated.
If hon. Members will now turn to the details of the Estimate they will note that the
first Sub-head in which a change occurs is
A2, Works Services. Practically the whole
increase, which amounts to £994, is in respect
of new works or works of special maintenance at Ardglass Harbour. These include
the completion of the work of cleaning and
repairing the old dock purchased in 1925-6.
The amount, £230, included for this item is
the balance of the provision already approved
Hon. Members will, no doubt, recollect
that a Supplementary Estimate was presented
last month in respect of certain unemployment relief work at Ardglass. The half of
the cost relating to materials, etc., was included in last year's figures for this Subhead, the balance, consisting of wages cost,
being accounted for under a separate Subhead A3, which is now, of course, deleted.
In Sub-head B is included the last instalment of the grant of £9,000 to Kilkeel Harbour, authorised in 1923-24. The work has
now been completed at a somewhat smaller
cost than originally anticipated, and the
amount shown, £1,441, represents the Ministry's share of the final liability of 20 per
cent. of the contract price, which, in accordance with custom, has been retained for
twelve months after the completion of the
work. In the same Sub-head the item of £10
included in respect of reconstruction works
at Coleraine Harbour refers to a service in
which my Ministry is co-operating with the
Ministry of Labour. The works are expected
to cost upwards of £60,000, and the Ministry
of Labour has consented to make, from the
Unemployment Grants Vote, a grant amounting to 75 per cent. of the wages expended in
respect of unemployment workmen specially
engaged for the work in accordance with the
usual conditions governing Relief Scheme
Grants. The Ministry of Labour grant is
limited to a maximum of £20,000, but should
the assistance given by way of unemployment
grant be less than £20,000, the Ministry of
Commerce has undertaken to contribute
either the difference between that sum and
the amount advanced by the Unemployment
Relief Grant or a sum of £3,000, whichever
is the less. The Ministry of Commerce will
not become liable for its share of the grant,
if any, until the work is completed, probably
next year, and, therefore only an Estimate
is now included.
The next Sub-head in which there is any
notable change is Sub-head D. The utilisation of mechanical devices for the tabulation

Notwithstanding the substantial amounts
involved I need not detain the Committee by
an extended explanation of Sub-heads G1,
G2, and G3. These Sub-heads formed the subject of portions of last year's Estimates and
Supplementary Estimates, at which time they

Very careful consideration has been given
to the results secured by the Ulster Tourist
Development Association, and to the tangible
and intangible return obtained for the grant
made last year towards the funds of the Association. So satisfactory do these results
appear that it has been decided to contribute
