I now come to an entirely new Sub-head
which up to the present has been borne on
the Northern Ireland Services Vote of the
Imperial Government, viz., Fisheries Grants
and Allied Payments. I shall deal first with
the last four items covered by this Sub-head
by saying that the grants to hatcheries,
grants in respect of marine motor engineering classes, special inquiries and experiments
and miscellaneous expenses are provided for
to the same or to a smaller extent as in
last year's Imperial Estimates, and that, in
the opinion of the late Imperial Secretary,
who has heretofore e administered these Services, the provision made is adequate and
reasonable.
The other item, namely, Contributions to
Conservators, calls for fuller explanation as
it exceeds by £415 the corresponding Imperial
Estimate last year. As the Committee is no
doubt aware,
the inland fisheries of Northern
Ireland are at present supervised by four
Boards of Conservators, three of which have
been accustomed to receive necessary financial assistance from the Government. Without this financial assistance they would not
be able to carry on their work and the inland
fisheries would suffer severely. In recent
years there have been several important
changes in the area and an increasing need
for vigilance; consequently the exponses of
some of the Boards have been very greatly
increased. Recognising this, the Imperial
Government has granted considerably increased sums to these Boards, and as a result
of territorial changes which took place during
the last financial year, further increases and
changes in amounts of financial assistance
were under consideration. In view of the
pending transfer of the Fisheries Services no
decisions upon these grant questions were
made by the Imperial Government. The
sums, therefore, included in the Estimate
before the House are those recommended by
the transferring Department.
Sub-head L and M may require some explanation, relating as they do to Services
which have not formerly appeared on this
Vote. Sub-head L was formerly borne on
the Vote of the Ministry of Home Affairs,
but now it appears on the Vote under consideration, as it was felt desirable to include
in one Vote all railway expenditure from
public funds. The Government is under a
statutory liability to pay to the County
Councils of Tyrone and Fermanagh a certain
proportion of the rates raised in those two
counties in respect of the baronial guarantee
to the Clogher Valley Railway Company.
Sub-head M is transferred from the Imperial Estimates. Under the Clogher Valley
Railway Act a baronial guarantee was given
of 5 per cent. on the paid-up ordinary capital
of the Company. The Government guaranteed a repayment to the County Councils
of part of any payments under the baronial
guarantee up to a maximum of 2 per cent.
on the capital. The Clogher Valley Railway
Company has never been able to pay its own
dividends, and the Government has each year
been called upon to pay the full amount of
its guarantee, viz., £2,467.

The final expense Sub-head with which I
must deal is that relating to the Ulster Publicity Branch. The Committee are doubtless
familiar with the valuable work which has
been carried on during the last four years
by the Ulster Association. That Association
is being wound up on 30th instant, and the
Government feel that the very valuable
machinery created by the Ulster Association
for the dissemination of commercial and agricultural information should not be allowed
to disappear. As hon. Members are aware, it
is the practice for overseas parts of the
Empire to maintain offices in London where
information relative to the respective
Dominion can be readily obtained. While
there is no proposal to set up any elaborate
Government Office in London, the Government, having regard to the fact that during
the past two years many inquiries relative
to Ulster have been dealt with by the London
Office of the Ulster Association, think it
would be of service to Northern Ireland

With regard to the Revenue Sub-head O,
I need make no observations beyond remarking that the receipts in 1925-6 were very much
greater than anticipated, owing almost entirely to the substantial development during
the year of the Ardglass Herring Industry,
which resulted in increased harbour dues
and an increased revenue from the letting of
curing plots. It is hoped and anticipated
that last year's good season will be repeated
and improved upon, not only in 1926-7, but
also progressively in future years, and that
it will be possible to draw correspondingly
increased relief from this Sub-head. In this
connection I would direct the Committee's
attention to the item "Branding Receipts,
£80." This is the first occasion on which this
item has appeared in respect of Northern
Ireland, either in the Imperial Estimates
or in these Estimates, and is an indication of
the extent to which herring curers appreciate
and take advantage of the new Crown Brand
for Northern Ireland. I beg to move.
Mr. LEEKE: I beg to move a reduction of
the Vote by £100. I should like further information from the Minister of Commerce regarding this Advisory Council which is being
set up. I agree that it is a very wise step
and one which will materially assist the fishing industry in Ulster, but is this Advisory
Council to be a senior body and a controlling
authority over the Boards of Conservators in
Ulster or is it not? I have always held that
the constitution of the Boards of Conservators in Ulster has not been such as to
assist and encourage the fishing industry.
The Conservators are largely drawn from
agricultural areas and inland districts, and
very few of them that I have known have
been associated to any extent with deep-sea
fishing or fishing in outside waters.
I desire also to point out another matter,
and I am sure the Minister of Finance will
be pleased to hear this. I can make a suggestion here to-day that will assist the Ulster
fishing industry immediately, without taking
a penny from the national finances; on the
contrary, it will be a paying matter. (Hon.
Members: Hear, hear.) I refer to the dor-
Another matter I would like to mention
is the question of the herring industry. This
has been a very neglected industry in
Northern Ireland. I think that along the
Ulster coast are to be found the best fishing
beds; at least, they are as good as any along
the English or Scotch coasts or other parts
of Ireland. These are largely fished and
exploited by Englishmen and Scotsmen. I
make no objection to English capitalists
coming here and investing money, but it is
a pity that the same thing could not be done
by Ulster firms instead of English and Scotch
firms. I do not see any reason why they
should not come here, but I do not see why
Uister should not be able to encourage its
own workers and develop the fishing industry themselves. These English and
Scotch firms come here, and then take the
fish direct to English and Scotch ports, where
they are handled. As a matter of fact, they
are then shipped back to Belfast, and to the
Belfast people-fish actually caught at their
own doors.
There are about 500 tons of fish caught and
sold locally, and about 4,000 tons imported,
so far as I can gather from the figures I
have obtained. That is a state of affairs
that should not exist, and it is clearly the
duty of the Minister of Commerce to look
into it. I am sure that this Advisory Council
will take steps to make Ulster a very important fishing centre. One of the greatest
disadvantages we labour under at present is
the matter of harbour accommodation. Right
round the coast of Ulster are many useless
harbours, owing to the fact that they are
silted up or have not been properly attended
to within the last few years. I do not see
why the Government, at little expense, could
not engage a dredger to have these harbours
cleaned out. Besides being useful for
fishing purposes, they would be effective
in the development of commerce, and bringing supplies to the small towns round
Ulster.
There is a type of pier I would like to
draw attention to, namely, the fishing pier.
A special class of fishing pier is largely used
about the Hebrides, in the North of Scotland. These piers could be erected in small
villages, and they would largely assist in
the development of the fishing industry,

[Mr. Leeke]
because, owing to the want of harbour accommodation, herring curing has not been developed to a great extent in this area. They
would also be of great assistance in absorbing
a lot of the unemployed who are to be found
round the coast of Ulster. We have heard a
great deal of talk lately about getting people
out of the cities and back to the land. If
you get them back to the coast it would also
materially assist the industry, and be a great
national benefit. (Hon. Members: Hear.
hear.)
I would also like to draw the attention
of the Minister of Commerce to the question
of hatcheries. The salmon fishing depends
largely on whether the hatcheries are sufficiently encouraged or not. I notice that the
contributions to Conservators of fishery districts for services rendered in connection with
fisheries amount to £815. That, to my mind,
is rather small. I think other items could be
cut down, and an increase made there. Only
men who have a thorough knowledge of the
fishery industry should be appointed on these
Boards. If the grant to hatcheries was increased that would increase the supply of
salmon. Two of the most important branches
in Northern Ireland are the salmon and
herring industries. If these were properly
encouraged it would be of great assistance
to the commercial life of the community.
I think it is ridiculous that we in Ulster
have to buy our own fish back from English
and Scotch people. If the English and
Scotch people can carry on this industry
we cannot complain, except on the ground
that if the Government neglects to encourage
the Ulster people they should be blamed.
Some adequate steps should be taken to have
this industry properly developed. There is
then the question of Coleraine Harbour, and
the £10,000 grant which the Minister of
Commerce has mentioned.
Mr. POLLOCK: £20,000.
Mr. LEEKE: £20,000. Pardon me. Has
the Coleraine authority accepted that?
Mr. BARBOUR: It is still under conconsideration.
Mr. LEEKE: Is it not a fact that that
is due to the unfair conditions which the
Government have asked the Coleraine people
to agree to? The people are anxious and willing to agree if the conditions are such that
they could accept them without placing an

for the discussion of any Estimate.

The CHAIRMAN: I am in this position.
At the setting up of this Parliament we had
to lay down certain procedure that would
govern our debates. We did adopt by special
Resolution the whole of the procedure of
the Imperial Parliament, with the necessary
local adaptations. I am governed in my conduct in the Chair because these rules are
there, and it is my business to see that they
are observed. I am sure my hon. Friend
appreciates my difficulty. Nobody believes
more in full and free discussion than I do.
Mr. DEVLIN: I must confess that on the
few occasions on which I provoked the
Government into frankness it was in many
instances to their advantage. I think the
Government, instead of trying to closure this
method of controversy, ought to be very glad
to have an opportunity, before their constituents and before the people, of clarifying the
situation, and letting us know where we stand
in these matters.
The CHAIRMAN: I may say with confidence to the Committee that I would not
allow the Prime Minister or any other
Minister to interfere with the due and proper
rights of the Opposition to discussion. (Hon.
Members: Hear, hear.) My business is rather
to protect the minority. The Government
can protect itself.
Mr. DEVLIN: I am not sure of that.
The CHAIRMAN: At least it is their business, not mine. But while the rules are there
my business is to see that the spirit, and, if
necessary, the letter of them is observed. It
is entirely with that object in view I made
the observations which I have made.

Frankly, I want to say to the Committee that

and organisations the money of the taxpayers.
Mr. GEORGE HENDERSON: Hear, hear.
Mr. DEVLIN: We have no control over

That was the Ulster Association, and

sufficient number of our natives in fishing.
Repeated attempts have been made to encourage them to adopt this vocation, but so
far the natural resources round about our
coast have not been taken advantage of by
our own natives to the same extent that they
have been by the drifters and other fishermen, who follow the fish round the coast of
the United Kingdom.
I am informed that the total for all deep
sea fishing vessels (first-class) is 61, and the
number of men employed 246. The in-shore
fishing boats are used to a greater extent than
the deep sea drifters. There are 161 motor
boats, employing 382 men, and there are 325
yawls, employing 450 men. While this shows
that fishing is carried on round the North
of Ireland, I think it also shows that it is
not carried on to anything like the extent
we would wish to see it. As I said in my
remarks in introducing the Estimate, I believe that the fishing industry is capable of
development, and it will be the object of my
Ministry to study in what way this can be
done. I think why so much of the fish caught
near our shores is not landed here and used
for the supply of the home market, as might
naturally be expected, is because better markets exist on the other side of the channel.
Drifters are more apt to make their way to
Fleetwood and Holyhead, where a more
ready market exists for the fish that they
catch over here.
I may state of the work done by the Imperial Government, that very considerable
progress has been made in establishing the
fishing industry at Ardglass, where there has
been a sale of fish on a freer scale than exists
in any other fishery harbour in Northern
Ireland. It may interest hon. Members to
know that the total value of salmon exported
from Northern Ireland in 1925 was £92,000,
and the value of pollan used locally and exported, was estimated at about £12,000. The
total value of eels exported was about £20,000.
The total value of inland fish was about
£132,000, and the total value of inland and
sea fishing in Northern Ireland would aggregate close on £250,000. That will give the
Committee some idea as to the present value
of the industry as a whole, and to what extent the expenditure of public money may be
justified in trying to develop this industry
still further.
As regards the provision of harbours, hon.
Members will know that there are only two
Royal harbours, namely Donaghadee and
Ardglass, which are supported as Government
enterprises. The development of harbours
has been regarded more as a local matter, and
I think my colleagues on the Belfast Harbour
Commissioners have always taken a certain
amount of satisfaction from the knowledge
that there has never been any Government
money spent on Belfast harbour. It is entirely done by local enterprise, with money
raised by themselves. So far as the smaller
harbours round about our coast are concerned, these have been regarded more as
the care of the County Councils, but grants
have been made from time to time from
Government sources in order to relieve the
County Councils in carrying on these works.
The harbours take advantage of the natural
estuaries, but in some of them the expense
of development would be very great indeed.
At Ardglass, that has been developed as far
as the nature of the soil there permits. It is a
rock bottom. There are no natural outlying
rocks or islands to protect it from wind
blowing directly into the harbour, and as
hon. Members will appreciate, a rock-bottom
anchorage is not very secure.
So far as Killough is concerned, it undoubtedly is a very fine natural inclosure, but
it also faces directly out to the sea, and for
any value that would eventually emerge at
Killough it would mean unhappily a large
amount of money to be spent in it. The
natural anchorage or safety that is afforded
there is very limited. It is a tidal harbour,
and so to give sufficient depth of water for
boats coming in and able to emerge at all
states of the tide, dredging would have to be
done. There is the natural inclosure of two
or three acres, but it would be a very great
expense, and there are not so many local
advantages there for a fishing port. These
small ports on the coast of County Down are
all dependent more or less on imports of
coal and the export of agriculture produce,
such as potatoes, and also granite blocks,
taking advantage of the natural resources of
the County Down. They are all in the same
condition; they are ports which can only be
entered or left round about high tide.
As regards the harbours of County Antrim,
in which, naturally, I am greatly interested,
I share in every way the sympathy expressed
by my colleague in Antrim County Council
with the Rathlin Islanders. They are very
often completely cut off from communication
with the shore. But the position with reference to the harbour facilities and communication with the harbour at Church Bay is the
responsibility of the County Council. I am
told that the pier at Ballycastle was
originally built by private enterprise. I
have already received a deputation from the
County Council with respect to improving the
facilities, both on the island and on the
mainland. I hold to the opinion that this
is a matter in which co-operation between the
county council and possibly my Ministry-if
the Minister of Finance can see his way to
give assistance in the matter-will be the
means by which this difficulty might be
solved.

two sub-heads in this Estimate. One deals
with the statutory contribution to the Unemployment Fund, and the other deals with
the equalisation payment.
Hon. Members will appreciate the importance of our re-insurance arrangement with
the Imperial Government when they observe
that in the last financial year for a period of
six months the fund received under this agreement no less a sum than £1,025,000, and this
year it is estimated that the Unemployment
Fund will receive by this arrangement the
sum of £1,365,000. On many occasions 1
have dealt with the grievances, and on
great many occasions I have travelled over
the whole field of the unemployment grant,
and I really feel that there is nothing new
that I can tell the Committee in connection
with either on this occasion. I beg to move.

Mr. KYLE: I desire to move a reduction
of £1,000 in this Vote, in order to draw attention to the very harsh measures adopted
by the right hon. Gentleman's Department in
dealing with applicants for Unemployment
Insurance benefit. In consequence of the
equalisation arrangement that has been
made, the Minister of Labour has felt compelled to issue instructions to his Departmen to be more harsh than it used to be.
Some months ago the Minister of Labour
gave an assurance to this House that ex-
Servicemen were not to be harshly treated.
Since then a number of disabled ex-Servicemen have come to me, and others have written to me, to inform me that the right hon.
Gentleman's Department had turned down
their application for Unemployment Insurance. Each one of those men had been under
training in one of the departments set up
for the training of disabled ex-Servicemen.
They had been discharged from that training, they had not been able to find employment, and now they have been denied
unemployment benefit.
It is felt very widely in Belfast that this
action is taken in consequence of the agreement that has been entered into between the
English Government and our own Government. A huge number of people have been
turned down during the past six months,
particularly since this equalisation arrangement was made. That strengthens the
conviction of a great many people that it
is in consequence of the arrangement
that
was entered into between the
Imperial and the Northern Exchequers that
the huge number has been very considerably
augmented during the past few months. It
is because of that that I move a reduction of
this Vote by £1,000. I do so for the purpose
of calling attention to what one might call
the scandalous treatment of the unemployed
by the right hon. Gentleman's Department.
We have been assured repeatedly in this
House and outside of this House that the
Ministry would give sympathetic consideration to the findings of the committees
that were set up to deal with the claims for
unemployment insurance benefit. During
the past three of four months the findings
of those local committees have been set aside
day after day, and I want to challenge the
statement made by the Minister of Labour
in this House some little time ago, when he
said that something like only 3 to 5 per cent
of the claims that were admitted by the
local employment committees were turned
down by his Department. The percentage,
in my opinion, is very much higher, because
I believe that, as one individual myself, I
have at least 3 per cent of the total number
of applicants for benefit coming to the office
in which I work, to inform me that they
have been turned down by the headquarters
of the Ministry of Labour. I know that my
two colleagues who sit on this Bench are
inundated with applications from men who
have been turned down, despite the fact that
the committee had recommended their claim.
I have seen cases myself, and have been even
the committee which recommended
certain applicants for benefit, only to find
out afterwards that the headquarters of the
Minister of Labour have, turned down the
applicants.
on
It is to make a protest, however weak and
inadequate, against such treatment of the
unemployed that I speak here to-day. The
situation, apparently, is not getting any
easier; in fact one might say it is getting
much more difficult. What are the facts?
In the Frederick Labour Exchange there is
a department to which men go who want a
job on what is called relief work. When
those men go there, they are asked how long
they have been out of work, and if they say
"two years" the gentleman in charge of the
Department will say "We are only at the
three year men yet." That is to say, you
have got to be at least three years out of
work before you are entitled to go on the
rota for relief work
#
Then, if a man has not been employed for
two years, the Ministry turns his application for benefit down, on the ground that he'
has not had a reasonable period of employment during the past two years. And yet
their own Department in Frederick Street
would be able to tell the Minister the fact
Committee.

that it is not possible for hundreds, if not
thousands, of men to get work, men, too,
who are keen, anxious, willing and able to
work. I The headquarters of the Ministry,
at 7 Upper Queen Street, turn these people
down, and one must blame the right hon.
Gentleman for that; he is responsible for the
work of his Department. Despite his
sauvity, and despite the good-natured way he
has of putting people off, the Minister of
Labour is the villain of the piece, so far as

It is appalling to think of the men who
are not able to get work. The Minister's
Department says "Unless you have been out
three years you have not a chance," and then
the headquarters say, "Because you cannot
prove a reasonable period of employment
during the past two years, you are denied

there is the offence that I have already
mentioned, the treatment of disabled ex-
Servicemen. I do not know how the right
hon. Gentleman sleeps in his bed at night.
It is ghastly to have even to speak to these
people, and to try to tell them what the regulations are, and that we are responsible for
the regulations that are depriving so many
people of the means of subsistence during a
period in which they cannot get work. As I
say, I do not know how the right hon. Gentleman has an easy conscience, and how he can
sleep in his bed at night.
Regarding the workers who attend at
Amelia Street, I advise any Member who
thinks that we on these Benches use strong
language to go to Amelia Street himself, and
to see things as they are, from half-past
eight o'clock in the morning until half-past
three in the afternoon, to see the never ending stream of humanity there, and to ask
himself, "How would you like that your girl,
your wife, or your mother, would be put to

In connection with unemployment in the
linen trade, the right hon. Gentleman knows
quite well that it has been practically
impossible for a great many pecple to get
employment during the past two years. He
knows that better perhaps than I do, better
probably than any other Member of this
House, and yet again the same barrier is
raised. Those people are turned down not,

hundreds. Some people go so far as to say
thousands.
Mr. WILLIAM MCMULLEN: So it is.
The Estimate will show you that.
Mr. KYLE: By thousands these people are
turned off, because they cannot get what is
not there. They could not get employment
during the last two years. The right hon.
Gentleman (Mr. Andrews) knows quite well
that it has been impossible, but I think he
does not realise how serious a matter this is
to the textile workers of Belfast, who have
not been able to get work and are denied unemployment benefit. They cannot pay their
rents, they cannot get bread, they cannot get
anything. Surely it is a very drastic step

have been put in force with such severity as

Mr. BEATTIE: I wish to support the reduc
tion of this Vote as a protest against the
arrangements attached to this agreement.
In doing so, I do not want to use any words
that would be likely to cast any reflection on
any individual, but I feel so strongly on this
matter that I am afraid I would be apt to
lose my temper if I went into it too closely.
With the knowledge I have of the arrangement come to between this Government and
Great Britain, and of the regulations put
into operation by the Minister of Labour
(Mr. Andrews), I feel that a grave injustico
has been done to the class to which I belong,
and that is one of the sections of the shipbuilding and engineering workers. What do
we find among shipyard workers to-day? We
find men who have had forty years' continuous employment in the shipyards struck
off benefit, because they cannot show a
reasonable period of employment within the
past two years. What I am going to quote
is no hearsay, but actual fact. I have had
men coming to me to seek my advice and
assistance, and to see if it was possible to
get them re-established under extended
benefit. These are men of sixty-three and
sixty-four, aye, and sixty-five years of age,
very healthy and physically fit to carry on
the work if they could find it. I want to
tell the Minister that it is age, and age alone,
that applies to men of that description.
I know the case of one man, under whom I
served my time, a man of sixty-four years of
age, who had paid into unemployment insurance from the commencement, and who, in
1921, through no fault of his own, was thrown
out of work. He endeavoured to get work
throughout the small engineering shops, and
at last he took a job as labourer. His age will
be up in a year, and he was ousted always
by the younger men. He was denied the
right to get a job, and continued on in benefit
until the recent regulations were brought in,
when he was immediately struck off benefit.
That man has a delicate wife and family.
The family certainly are grown up, but two
of the daughters are also unemployed. I
went to that man's home, and I told him that
it was useless for me to take up his case with
the Minister of Labour, because the regula
Supply-
Committee.
HOUSE OF COMMONS
[Mr. Beattie]
tions were such that he would not be restored to extended benefit until he could show
a spell of employment, to show that he had
got a reasonable period within the past two
years. I remember that man very well being
in comfortable circumstances. To-day he is
sitting at home with the gas out off, with no
fire in the grate, and when he applied to the
Belfast Board of Guardians, after being
denied by the Minister of Labour, he was
denied the right to outdoor relief, because
some members of the Board thought he had
not made a reasonable effort to get employment, owing to his being so long out of work.
That is one of the cases that are within my
own knowledge. Sometimes I hesitate to repeat them, because I would rather be going
the right way to remedy them, only the
Government is too strong for me in this instance.
I could cite another instance of an ex-
Serviceman, who is in receipt of a pension
of 23s 9d per week. He was through the
whole war, and left half of his head in France
we may say. He came back and got a spell
of extended benefit, when he was suddenly
denied the right to any further extension,
and he applied to the Board of Guardians.
This man has a wife and a family of six,
under fourteen, and the Belfast Board of
Guardians denied that man's right to outdoor relief because he had not been genuinely
seeking work, and the Minister of Labour
turned him down for not having the necessary period of work inside the last two years.
My objection to all this is that it is hitting
the poorer classes so heavily that there is
bound to be something worse come out of it
than what has actually taken place up to the
present. If the Minister of Labour (Mr.
Andrews) had come to this Committee and
had said "I am going to put into operation regulations that will hit the working
classes very hard. I am compelled to do so
by the agreement with Great Britain, but I
am going to ask the Government to see that
other public boards make provision for the
nien who will no longer receive benefit under
the regulations," if the Minister of Labour
had done that I would have said he was making provision for the men to whom he was
going to disallow benefit, and I would have
said he was sincere in his effort to bring solvency to the Unemployment Fund in Northern Ireland without casting any hardship on
any class of the community. But that was
not done. The arrangement is brought into
operation; the hardship is imposed, and the
people cannot defend themselves one way or
the other.
Perhaps the Minister may argue that not
so many have been turned off, but I would
say that upwards of 10,000 people and their
dependants have been turned off extended
benefit since the 1st January, and I believe
I am moderate in my estimate when I say
that, because I have come in touch with them
in very large numbers. Every night I leave
this House the string is waiting at my door,
and their appeals are such that I must stand
and listen to them, knowing perfectly well
that I am helpless to assist them, either
through the Poor Law Guardians or through
the Ministry of Labour. The Board of
Guardians are now going to juggle with the
lives of the people similarly to what the
Minister of Labour has juggled with the
lives of the people, and the people are being
allowed to sink between these two Boards,
and no real effort is being made by either
one of them to assist the people to provide
the necessaries of life, and to try to keep
their homes intact during the times of trade
depression,
The hon. Member for North Belfast (Mr.
Kyle) referred to the green card system, and
said that a man needed to be out three years.
That system might be all right if you qualified according to the number of your family,
It might be all right for a married man
with three or four of a family, but you also
have hard cases of single persons, who, if
they receive the old-age pension, will not receive green cards. You have single men and
women who are as hard, hit as any member
of the community, and who will never have
an opportunity of receiving a green card
through the Ministry.
I had a textile worker with me to-day, who
had eleven weeks' work in the past two
years, a widow with four of a family.
Her claim was allowed at the court by me
representing her, but when she went to headquarters she was disallowed, and now she is
thrown on the palms of her hands with four
kiddies, and no provision for her, because,
as I said before, the Board of Guardians have
made no provision. They do not read the
Poor Law Act in the same way as we do,
that it is an Act to relieve destitution.
f
As I said before, we could raise a big discussion from these Benches round this agreement. We have repeatedly stated our determination to see some justice done to the
unemployed workers, because, in the depression that has existed since 1920 up to now,
there are certain members of the community
who have not had a reasonable opportunity
to get into employment at any time. As far
as the regulations are concerned, I think
the Minister of Labour would be justified,
even at this late hour of the day, in approaching once again the Imperial Authorities with
the object of being allowed to deviate from
that position of step by step for the reason
that owing to the condition of industry in
Northern Ireland the scope at the command
of the unemployed workers is not equal to
that at the command of the unemployed
Committee.

workers in Great Britain. The areas are

I must go back a little, because the interruption rather altered the sequence of my
remarks. The point is made by hon. Members opposite, that the position is not getting
better because the reduction in the number

the position had improved on the 1st January

To-day it has fallen again, and although the
figure is still high it is a considerable improvement on the year, because it is now
down to 25.7 per cent., as against 40.2 per
cent. a year ago.
As regards the shipbuilding industry, again
we have an improvement, although I admit it
is not very large, but it is in the right
direction. A year ago there were 35.7 per
cent. of our shipyard workers unemployed,
and to-day the figure is 33.3 per cent. May
I point out at this stage, to prove that we are
not the only community suffering through
this regrettable industrial depression, that
the shipyard workers in Great Britain, who
are unemployed reach a per centage of 36.9,
or 3.6 more than here. I want to be quite
frank with the Committee. I regret to say
that in the building trade the percentage has
risen during the last twelve months by per
cent., but that is due to the regrettable holdup in the building operations of the City
Council. Again we have to take into consideration another fact. During this period
which I am covering 3,000 Specials have been
disbanded, and these have either been absorbed into industry, as I think about half of
them have, or else they are registered
amongst our unemployed. And so I feel that
I am entitled to say the position has improved considerably during the last few
months, but I am a little uneasy about the
immediate future, due to the fact that
as far as the spinning end of
the linen trade is concerned, the
exchanges in France and Belgium
still going in the wrong direction.
makes it almost impossible for the home

Then again, we are already feeling the
effects of this unfortunate dispute across the
channel. Already dock workers are becoming
unemployed, and certain concerns have been
obliged to stop entirely, or go on short time.
While there are anxieties lying ahead, I
think we should rejoice that during the past
year the movement has been in the right
direction. I think it was the hon. Member
for East Belfast (Mr. Beattie), wondered
how it was that I could sleep in my bed at
night. I quite admit that this problem gives
me very great anxiety. It is a heavier public
burden than I ever carried in my life, or
ever expected to have to carry, but at the
same time I have the satisfaction of feeling
that my colleagues in the Government and
myself, and also those who sit behind me, have
done everything possible for us to do to
mitigate the sufferings of our unemployed in
these sad industrial days.
I think it was the hon. Member for East
Belfast (Mr. Beattie) who also said that I

As I have said before, the Guardians are the

Mr. POLLOCK: The following arrangements have been made provisionally for next

On Tuesday, it is proposed to take the Committee stage of the Jury Laws Amendment
Bill; and, in addition, the following Estimates will be placed on the Paper :-Class
IV., No. 2, National Health Insurance; Class
II., No. 1, Ministry of Finance. The other
Estimates that follow in succession will be:-
:-

As regards the remainder of the week,
further progress will be made with the Jury
Laws Amendment Bill, and it is proposed
to take the Second Reading of the Teachers'
Superannuation Bill and the Unemployment
Insurance Bill.
I should perhaps mention, with regard to
the Teachers' Superannuation Bill, that it
will be circulated over the week-end. It is
purely an administrative Measure, which
repeals the Teachers' Pension Act of 1879,
and makes altered provision for the method
of financing pensions, in order to meet the
altered circumstances arising out of the
Education Act and the Award of the Colwyn
Committee. It makes no alteration in the
rules for the payment of pensions, and I,
therefore, take it that it is a non-contentious
Measure. Following that, there is the Estimate for the Ministry of Education.
The Ancient Monuments Bill and the
Queen's University of Belfast Bill are now
under consideration in another place, and
it is expected that these Measures, will be
available for discussion in this House, possibly towards the end of next week.

BELFAST CORPORATION CLERKSHIPS.
1. Mr. DEVLIN asked the Parliamentary
Secretary of the Ministry of Education
whether the Belfast Corporation Committee
published an advertisement in the local
papers, on the 24th of March, inviting applications for the position of male junior clerk;
whether 38 applications were made, and the
candidates subjected to an examination;
whether one candidate scored 401 marks, the
second 384 marks, and the third 364 marks;
whether these three, with a fourth, were interviewed by the Committee, which afterwards recommended for appointment the
third candidate in order of merit; whether
the Corporation, at the meeting on the 3rd
instant, refused to confirm the recommendation of the Committee, and referred the
matter back for consideration; whether the
Chairman of the Committee stated at the
close of the debate that the Committee would
simply re-affirm its previous decision, and
whether the Minister can say what steps he
intends to take to ensure that all candidates
for such positions shall receive equal treatment, and that the implied contract in the
advertisement that the first candidate in
order of merit shall be selected will be
carried out.
The PARLIAMENTARY SECRETARY OF
THE MINISTRY OF EDUCATION (Mr.
Robb): The Belfast Education Committee
has notified the Ministry of the appointment
of Mr. Frederick Baxter as a junior clerk,
and a further intimation has been received
that when the appointment came up for confirmation by the Corporation the matter was
referred back by that body to the Education
Committee for reconsideration. The Ministry is, however, not in a position to verify
the other statements in the first part of the
hon. Member's question.
The Education Act prescribes that the
approval of the Ministry is necessary only
as regards the number and remuneration of
officers of education authorities.
The appointment in question arose owing to a
vacancy in the staff already authorised, and
as no change is involved, either in the number or remuneration of the officers of the
Committee, the Ministry is not called upon
to interfere with the discretion of the
Committee as to the person selected for the
appointment.

EXAMINATIONS FOR CHEMISTS'
APPRENTICES.
2. Mr. GEORGE HENDERSON asked the
Minister of Home Affairs whether it is the
fact that four examinations have been conducted by the Free State Pharmaceutical
Commission for Chemists' Apprentices in
Northern Ireland since the 1st November
last, practically all candidates being allowed
to qualify; whether he will state the number
of candidates who have presented themselves
at such examinations for the past six months,
the number who have passed, and the number who presented themselves for the
previous twelve months, and proved successful; whether he will take steps to have the
examinations for Chemists' Apprentices conducted in future in Northern Ireland under
Government supervision, and what is the
reason for the prolonged delay in making
arrangements for the holding of these
examinations in Northern Ireland. ⠀⠀⠀
The MINISTER OF HOME AFFAIRS (Sir
Dawson Bates): I understand that two examinations for Chemists' Apprentices have
been held in Dublin by the Pharmaceutical
Society of Ireland since the 1st of November
last, but as these were not under the control
of this Government there is no information
available as regards the number of candidates
who presented themselves.
I am informed by the Pharmaceutical
Society of Northern Ireland that these
examinations were held under the supervision of Sir William Moore, M.D., who was
appointed Visitor by the Privy Council of
Ireland in 1903; that they have proved an
adequate and satisfactory test, and that
there is no reason whatsoever to suppose
that they were not properly and fairly conducted.
As the hon. Member is, perhaps, aware,
regulations regarding examinations have
lately been made by the Pharmaceutical
Society of Northern Ireland, and it is ex-

Committee.
pected that examinations will be held in
June. In any case, the examinations of the
Pharmaceutical Society of Ireland cannot be
recognised after the 30th of September next.
This date was fixed by the Pharmacy (Temporary Provisions) Act, which was recently
passed, and my speech on the Second Reading
of the Bill contains the reasons for the

NATIONAL STRIKE AND UNEMPLOY-
MENT BENEFIT.
Mr. DEVLIN (by Private Notice) asked
the Minister of Labour whether he can give
any figures relating to the number of additional claimants for the unemployment
benefit arising out of the national strike, and
whether the Minister will consider the
question of granting extended benefit for a
period of six weeks to all unemployed
workers, signing on up to the first day of
May, as the prospect of these workers securing employment has been destroyed owing to
the industrial trouble.
The MINISTER OF LABOUR (Mr.
Andrews): It is estimated that the number
of persons in Northern Ireland who, up to
the present, have lost their employment,
either wholly or partly, as a result of the
situation in Great Britain, is approximately
5,500.
As regards the second part of the question,
the hon. Member will understand that here,
as in Great Britain, each claim to extended
benefit is considered in the light of the individual circumstances, and regard will,
naturally, be paid to the opportunities which
the claimant has had for employment during
the period which has elapsed since his claim
was last under review, and to the extent to
which these opportunities may have been
affected by the position resulting from the
situation in Great Britain during the past
week.

Hon. Members will see that this Amendment creates no additional or new
expenditure on the part of Parliament. Why
I wish to move this Amendment is to
prevent differentiation between local officers
and Clerks of the Crown and Peace. Under
the Clause as it stands at the moment
local officers are to have their remuneration
protected by securing to them a sum not less
than the average for the three years therein
specified. I suggest to the Committee that in
all fairness and equity Clerks of the Crown
I base this Amendment to a great extent on
the fact that by the 1920 Act these men are
expressly provided for. It is specifically
stated that Parliament has no power to reduce their remuneration or emoluments. I
suggest to the Committee that if you reduce
the expenses that these officers were entitled
to by the 1920 Act, and cast upon them new
duties and burdens as this Bill does, and if
you put them to expense to which they were
not put by the 1920 Act, you thereby reduce
their remuneration. I suggest to the Committee with perfect confidence that if you
pass this Measure without adopting the
Amendment, I suggest you are running contrary to the Act of 1920, which you have no
power to do. It would seem common sense
and logic and elementary law that where the
1920 Act is in conflict with any Measure
passed by this Committee the 1920 Act must
prevail. From my recollection-I speak
subject to correction if I am wrong-I am
perfectly certain there is a clause in the 1920
Act which specifically states that where any
Measure passed by this Parliament is in conflict with the 1920 Act, the 1920 Act must prevail. I suggest that this Bill without this
Amendment is a Measure that is in conflict
with the 1920 Act and which there is no power
to pass. As the Committee is aware this money
is contributed by the local authorities, and, as
the Parliamentary Secretary of the Ministry
of Home Affairs (Mr. Hanna) has stated, a
moiety of that sum is allocated to the
Ministry, and the other moiety is retained
by the Clerk of the Crown and Peace as expenditure. I do not want to detain the Committee, but I think it is perfectly obvious
that unless this Amendment is adopted a
wrong will be done to these men, an illegal
act will be done, and an injustice inflicted
upon them, and you will drive them, if they
so choose to adopt the remedy, to take an
action against the proper authority to have
their positions as defined by the 1920 Act.

Sir DAWSON BATES: The Government
cannot except this Amendment. My hon.
Friend (Mr. McAllister), notwithstanding the

to understand the position that the Clerks
of the Crown and Peace occupy at the present time. In the old days, prior to the Act

of 1877, Clerks of the Crown and Peace were
remunerated by receiving certain fees from

it was provided that for the future their
salaries should be fixed at a certain figure,
and in addition that these Clerks of the
Crown and Peace were to draw and receive
from the local authorities the various fees
and emoluments which they formerly received, and which they put into their own

they received these sums of money, after

Friend (Mr. McAllister) to understand this

to retain the actual out-of-pocket expenses

said, were consolidated.
It was also provided that from time to
time an Order in Council should be made

clearly set out that they were only to retain
for their own use the actual out-of-pocket
expenses. Accordingly an Order in Council

Peace should be retained as for his actual
outlay, and the other fifty per cent. should
be paid into the Treasury. Subsequently a

The ATTORNEY-GENERAL (Mr. Babington): In answer to the question put by my
hon. Friend (Mr. Cooper) I might say that
the method is quite simple. The actual outof-pocket expenses under the last Order in
Council are not, in fact, ever totted up.
What happened was this: Prior to the amalgamation of the two offices of Clerk of the
Peace and Clerk of the Crown all the money
that was derived from the county councils
in respect of the revision of the jurors' lists
went straight into the pockets of the Clerk of
the Peace, whether it was for remuneration

offices were amalgamated he got a joint
salary which covered that work, but an
Order in Council was made saying that fifty
per cent. of the receipts from the county
council should be paid into the Treasury.
That is represented in his remuneration and
is part of his joint salary for the two offices,
but the other fifty per cent. is expressly
named in the Order in Council as being for
the expenses of the Clerk of the Crown and
Peace. That fifty per cent. is for expenses,
whether his expenses be more or whether
his expenses be less, and they are not calculated and no account of them is rendered.

Major SHILLINGTON: I beg to move in
page 11, line 10, to leave out "seven" ("of
seven days from") and insert "fourteen."
The object of this Amendment, as of all
Amendments, is to prevent any hardship
arising. It is to extend the time from seven
days to fourteen days for the person on whom
the penalty was imposed to have the case
considered by the persons who imposed the
penalty. Seven days might be too short.
The person might be away from home or ill
or something of that sort. It is generally
thought it would be better to increase it to
14 days. I hope the Government will see
their way to accept this Amendment.
Sir DAWSON BATES: The Government
are prepared to accept the Amendment.
Amendment agreed to.
Clause, as amended, ordered to stand part
of the Bill.

a day or half a day or two days
Mr. HANNA: You would love it.

The CHAIRMAN: Having had an opportunity of considering the hon. Member's
Amendment I have come to the conclusion
that it must be dealt with as a new Clause,
as it deals with a matter of principle. I will
therefore deal with it when we come to the

Clause ordered to stand part of the Bill.
CLAUSES 14 (Detention of jurors in civil
trials during interval for refreshment), 15
(Duties of jurors upon Coroner's inquest),
and 16 (Short title, construction, bringing of
Act into operation, and repeal), ordered to
stand part of the Bill.
The CHAIRMAN: We now come to the
new Clauses. We will take them before we
proceed to discuss the Schedules.
NEW CLAUSE (Jurors' Travelling Expenses).
(1) The Council of any County may make
provisions for the payment of the reasonable travelling expenses of any persons
summoned to serve as common jurors in
such county at any Assizes, Court of
Quarter Sessions or Civil Bill Court
therein, and duly attending, pursuant to
such summons, subject to such limitations
as to distance, amount, mode of payment
or vouching, or otherwise subject to such
conditions as the council making such provision sees fit to impose, but subject always
to the provisions of this Section hereinafter
set forth. Provided always that it shall
not be obligatory upon any Council of a
County to make any such provision as is
herein before authorised.
(2) Provisions for such payments by the
Council of any County deciding to make
such provision shall be made by means of
a scheme adopted by such Council to come
into operation at such time as is provided
therein, but no such scheme shall come into
operation until same has been submitted
to, and has been approved of, by the
Ministry of Home Affairs.
(3) All moneys required for the payments
authorised by this Section may be raised
by means of the poor rate.
Brought up and read a First time.
Mr. JOHNSTONE: I beg to move, "That
the Clause be now read a Second time." We
have put down this New Clause because we
feel there is a very great feeling throughout
the country, and I think also in Parliament,
that there is a good deal of inequality at
the present time in the way in which jurors
are treated. Serving on a jury is a privilege
dear to the heart of every Ulsterman as it
is to every British citizen, but, unfortun-
If you take County Antrim, for instance,
a juror who is serving at the County Antrim
Assizes and lives at Lisburn is not put to
anything like the same inconvenience as a
juror who lives at Ballycastle and who has
to travel a considerable distance. We should
like as far as possible to equalise, more or
less, the position of jurors as regards this
public service. It is impossible, of course,
to save the time or the amount of trouble
of jurors who live at a long distance, but it
is possible at any rate to pay them out-ofpocket expenses, and we are proposing that
in those counties where the feeling exists
among the people generally that out-of-pocket
expenses should be paid to jurors who live
at a long distance, so as in some way to
recoup them for the extra time and trouble
they have, the county council should be permitted to make Regulations so that they can
pay jurors coming from outside a certain
radius such travelling expenses as they consider right.
We propose that this should be done on a
scale and according to a plan which will be
arranged after consultation, or in consultation, with the Home Office, and which would
presumably, as far as possible, be uniform
all over Northern Ireland.
We have also left this matter entirely at
the discretion of the county councils. There
may be counties where such a possibility as
I have suggested does not exist, or where the
majority of the inhabitants of the county
are not of the opinion that jurors disabilities
should be in any way relieved. In those
counties it is optional upon the part of the
county councils to make provision for the
payment of jurors' expenses. We have also
put down a proviso that the money for this
particular purpose should be raised by
means of the poor rate. It was suggested in
the report of the Committee on Jury Service that this should be met by fines, and
by insisting upon the fines for non-attendance being paid. There is, however, I understand, some difficulty in establishing a principle such as that, because the fines do not
go into a fund belonging to the county council, and it is the county council that we
suggest should foot this bill.
With the permission of the Committee I
will move this Clause, not in the form in
which it appears here, but with the following
addition. After Section 1 I should like, with
the permission of the Committee, and, of
course, my seconder, to add the words:-

Committee.

[Mr. Johnstone]
Subject to these powers being confirmed by
any Act of Parliament of the United
Kingdom.
The reason I wish to add those words is,
that I understand there is a question
whether such a provision as we have put
down here may not be ultra vires, whether
this Parliament has power to permit the
county councils to make such provision for
the payment of jurors. I add those words
because I understand that a Jury Bill is
likely to come before the Parliament of the
United Kingdom inside a very short time,
and it will enable the responsible authorities to go into the matter as to whether
this new Clause is ultra vires or whether
it is not. If it does prove to be ultra vires
a new Clause can be inserted in the Jury Bill
at Westminster so as to remove the disability. I beg to move.
Mr. GEORGE HENDERSON: I think

this as
an additional charge on the ratepayers through the county councils, who do

The CHAIRMAN: If the hon. Member
does that, he had better take care. What
may happen is, he may reserve himself beyond the point of redemption. If this new
Clause be carried, it definitely establishes a

Mr. GEORGE HENDERSON: As I have
said, although I approach this Bill with
some fear, I feel I am voicing the opinions
of a great many people whom I represent.
As long as I remember, local authorities and
other representative bodies all over the Six
Counties have been passing resolutions asking that at least out-of-pocket expenses
should be paid by the Crown to jurors when
they are summoned. I think the Government in refusing to adopt the very modest
recommendation of Lord Justice Andrews'
Committee on this point have treated the
jurors in a way that they should not do,
because they have ignored this big body of
public opinion, which is almost universal,
that at least the out-of-pocket expenses
of jurors should be paid.
The only new thing in this Bill in connection with the payment of jurors is, I think,
in Clause 13, and that is, in the High Courts
where a juror acts on a jury, and where there
is a verdict come to, or where the case is
settled after the jury has been sworn, the
juror gets a sum of 5s. That is the sole
provision that the Government, I think, contemplate with regard to jurors' expenses.
The Home Secretary in dealing with this
Clause said that one of the reasons why it
was not adopted by the Government was that
it introduced an entirely new principle. I
think it has been said before that it would
not do any harm to introduce something new
after fifty years. If these men have been
labouring under an injustice for fifty years,
there is no reason why we should perpetrate
it for fifty years more.
The Clause that I intend to put before the
Committee goes a little further. It has been
suggested that in criminal cases jurors who
are summoned on a panel, and who have to
travel 10 miles or upwards, should receive
their out-of-pocket expenses, and a reasonable
subsistence allowance if their duty as jurors
keeps them over night from home. I was
going to suggest in the Clause that I intend
to move that that distance of ten miles
should be reduced to five. I cannot see why
the Crown in dealing with this matter should
differentiate between jurors who are summoned and not called and jurors who are
summoned and who act upon a jury, because
each has to bear the same disabilities. Each
has to leave his home to come to the court
and to incur expenses. Whether he is called
or not called I think the disabilities are the
same. Therefore, I say that this Bill which
differentiates between a juryman who is
summoned and called and a juryman who is
summoned and not called is not doing evenhanded justice to the jurors.

The Member for the University (Mr.
Johnstone) raised a very pertinent question
when he said that Lord Justice Andrews'
Committee suggested that these expenses
should be paid as far as possible out of fines.
It is said that the county councils have not
control over these fines; it is the Crown that
has control over them. I am speaking, of
course, not as a lawyer, but as a farmer, and
so am open to correction if I make a mistake,
but I do feel that the Government should face
this question courageously, and that they
should take some account of the opinion that
is practically universal over the Six County
area that jurors should at least be paid their
out-of-pocket expenses, and that these should
be a Government charge.
I do not see, as the hon. Member for the
University has proposed, how this Committee is going to impose this charge on the
county councils, and I do not see why they
should try to impose this charge on the
county councils. Of course the Government
may accept the Clause. I expect they will,
because it will take them out of a very bad
hole, and it will enable them to say to jurors,
"Why we are going to let the county councils
pay you, and if they do not, then look to
them." They should treat this question in
a businesslike way, and should recognise that
these men have a long standing grievance.
We are only asking that they should be paid
actual travelling expenses and any other
expenses that they incur. I cannot
vote for this Clause inasmuch as it
establishes the principle that these expenses
should be paid by the county councils, and
even then it is optional. The only possible
way to remove these inequalities and this injustice is for the Government to make provision for the out-of-pocket expenses
jurors, whether engaged in civil or criminal
cases, to make it a Government charge, and
not to attempt to put it upon the county
councils.
of
Sir ROBERT ANDERSON: I regret extremely that the Government have not seen.
fit to accept what, I think, was the unanimous finding of the Committee presided over
by Lord Justice Andrews in connection with
this matter that the Committee is discussing
now. I am sure they feel that they might
be dipping too largely into the public purse
to undertake a duty of this character. I
speak as one who has always held the opinion
that jurors, being an integral part of the administration of the law, should at least in
criminal cases be paid their out-of-pocket
expenses. Every other functionary in connection with the administration of the law is
paid the judge who presides, the prosecuting
counsel or solicitor, the very man who serves
the summons upon the unfortunate juryman.
They are all remunerated for their services,
and the administration of the law does not
suffer in the slightest degree.
.
I know the argument is sometimes put
forward that a juryman stands in such an
independent position that you will get purer
administration of the law if there is no remuneration paid to him whatever. Now
there has been a grievance in connection
with this matter for a long number of years.
For, instance, I will give you a case in point.
I will take the county, Derry, that I am
familiar with. Take the men who have to
travel from Moneymore and Magherafelt
into the City of Derry, some of them poor
struggling men. They have to spend nights
and days there, away from their homes, and
away from their work. I think, seeing that
they perform such a useful function the
least that the State should do, when it pays
in other directions to those who administer
the law, is to pay these men their out-ofpocket expenses. The Government do not
propose to do that, and I am sorry they
have not seen their way to do it, but I think
the time is coming when the principle will
be recognised.
I do not mind whether this practice of not
paying the jurors has been in existence 100
years or 50 years, we have to deal with
modern conditions, and we have to deal with
a great many changes that have taken place
in regard to matters of this kind in other
public relations. I quite recognise that the
Government in this Bill have tried to lessen
the burden that has been inflicted upon the
poorer classes of jurors to a considerable
extent I am frank enough to say thatdoing away with the £10 leasehold and freehold qualifications and raising the rateable
value. I think they will in future possibly
be drawing the bulk of their jurors from a
class which is better able to bear the burden
than those who have borne it hitherto. That
is a step forward, and I gladly welcome it
and frankly acknowledge it.
Seeing the Government have failed, the
proposal is to leave it optional and give the
county councils the power to do it. The view
I take of this matter is this. I do not like
to see local authorities, such as county
councils that have been elected for other purposes altogether, brought in in connection
with the administration of the law of the
land. (Hon. Members: Hear, hear). I
think it is a bad precedent to establish, and
one that may have far-reaching consequences.
If jurors are to be paid they must be paid
from some funds provided by Parliament,
and that will remove matters entirely from
the county councils, who have a great deal
to do in connection with expenditure in other
directions. This Clause says to them that
under the administration of the law of the
land, and especially the criminal law in
which these jurors are going to be called
upon to take a useful part, they are to find
the funds-from what? From the poor rate.
Jury Laws Bill-

HOUSE OF COMMONS
[Sir Robert Anderson]
I am entirely opposed to this particular
Clause, unless some good reasons are advanced during the discussion. It is going to
establish a precedent here that will take
away from all future Governments that may

of the land.

that he will swear the necessary jurors and

Mr. DEVLIN: It is customary when an

perhaps like the hon. Member (Mr. Miller)

I will have a word to say in a moment or

there is an irresistible case for their payment.
There are two methods by which this payment would be brought about. One is by the

I do not like this Amendment of the hon.

Mr. HANNA: Will the Opposition come

Robert Anderson), told us that he was absolutely opposed to this unless it was paid by
the Government. I can remember that on
other occasions when we on this side of the
Committee brought forward resolutions advocating Government expenditure, he simply
denied the right of the Government to agree
to it on the ground that the Government
could not afford it-not on the ground that
it was not something that was right. I find
him working one way on this Bill and working in a different way on other matters.
My hon. Friend (Mr. George Henderson)
argued in a similar strain. I think something must be done for the poor unfortunate
jurors who, as an hon. Member stated, are
asked to travel from Magherafelt to the
City of Derry. These men cannot afford it.
They are asked to pay something or another
which is beyond their means. I think it
would be an exceedingly small charge that
would be put on county councils to meet
this matter. I do not see how hon. Members
can go back to their constituents if they are
not prepared to see justice done to these men
who are asked to leave their homes and do
work for which they are unpaid. I hope that
we will not be asked to vote on this question.
I hope the Government will accept the
Clause, because I think it is a very small
thing, indeed, we are asking them to do. I
think the county councils should take this
matter upon themselves and see that it is
properly carried out. I daresay 2d or 3d in
the on the rates would cover it. Of course
we are not in a position to know what it will
really cost. If this new Clause is accepted it
is up to the county councils to find out
exactly how much it would mean. I hope
the Government will accept this Clause.
The PRIME MINISTER: I have listened
to this debate with great interest, and perhaps the Committee will bear with me if I
make a few observations. In the first
instance, the hon. Member for Antrim (Mr.
Crawford), who makes the suggestion that
the cost of this should fall upon our funds,
is making a proposition that we could not
carry out. The difficulty with this Bill is a
very real one. Where it touches High Court
matters we really have very little jurisdiction, and the consequence is that it is a
rather complicated matter. Some of the hon.
Members behind us have put down this
Amendment, believing that at all events it
would establish the principle in an Act of
Parliament that justice was to be done to
those jurors who were called a long distance
to attend Assizes. Now the question arises
here whether this Clause, if it were inserted
in the Bill, would really be of very great
value or not. That is the question we have
to decide here now. The Clause if inserted
in the Bill must have the few words that
the hon. Member for the University (Mr.
Johnstone) read out to the Committee placed
in the forefront; that is to say, subject to
provision being conferred by any Act of
Parliament in the United Kingdom. In other
words, it is very doubtful in my opinion-
I do not hesitate to say so to the Committee
-whether the Imperial Parliament at Westminster would for a moment give more
favourable terms to this area than they are
prepared to give to the rest of the United
Kingdom. Therefore, I fear the Clause in
that regard is of very little value indeed.
The second consideration has been dealt

with very fully by the hon. Member for
Derry (Sir Robert Anderson) and the hon.

view they take up is this, that the

their shoulders the responsibility on
to the county authorities of whether
payment to jurors is to be made or

storin in the county councils that it would
be very much better on the whole to avoid.
I take it that is the sum and substance of
the hon. Member's suggestion. I quite agree
that it is most undesirable to place county
councils in a more difficult position than is
necessary, and if elections throughout the
counties are to be conducted on whether a
person is going to promise that he will pay
jurors or not, it would not be for the good
of Ulster as a whole. There are very much
more important and serious matters engaging the attention of county authorities than
the mere payment of jurors.
Then coming down to practical politics, I
think myself that as sensible people, entitled
to do the best they can in the matter, it
would be advisable if my hon. Friends were
to withdraw the Amendment altogether, in
view of what has happened to-day. If they
withdraw the Amendment it means, of
course, that there is no possibility in this
Bill, and probably not for some time to come,
as the hon. Member for West Belfast (Mr.
Devlin) has said, of dealing with the question of the payment of jurors. Therefore,
we do undoubtedly postpone that possibility,
but at the same time common sense seems
to direct that the Amendment be dropped
altogether, and leave the Bill as it was
originally drafted. In that way we will
avoid it probably being turned down by the
Imperial Parliament not sanctioning the
effectiveness of the Clause later on, and at
the same time probably be satisfying the
great majority of the county councils when
we do not shift the responsibility from the
Government on to each individual county
council. Perhaps my hon. Friends would see
fit to withdraw the Amendment and leave
over to another time the consideration in a
more competent way of the whole question
of the payment of jurors.
Mr. DEVLIN: I do not quite follow what

The PRIME MINISTER: With regard to
High Court matters, which is a reserved
service, it is necessary not only for us to

of the Crown and Peace and so forth. When

themselves must embody in their Bill those
matters that affect the High Court. Consequently, we are dependent upon them passing
their Act before this Bill can have full effect.
It is in order to prevent them not giving
the power to do this very thing we are

Amendment.

NEW CLAUSE (Grand Juries at Courts
of Quarter Sessions).

Book in respect of any indictment at such
Court of Quarter Sessions."

Mr. COOPER: I merely want to say that I

First of all the case has been dealt with by

decided whether he thinks there is a case or
not. Very often the Crown will not recognise
what a Grand Jury does, because if the
Grand Jury throws out a Bill the Crown
comes in and says the Bill must go up.
Therefore, what is the Grand Jury for?
People are brought in from all over the
country, and the judge tells them he thinks
they will have no difficulty in finding a true
Bill, and the jury come in and say there is
a true Bill, and then they go home. They
take up considerable time of the solicitors
who are waiting in that court, and I, as a
practitioner in the County Court for twenty
years and I do not think I have ever missed
a Quarter Sessions-would dearly love to see
the Grand Jury abolished altogether.

NEW CLAUSE (Temporary Appointment
of additional Judge in connection with Revision of Jurors' Lists for Belfast and
Antrim).
(1) If the Governor of Northern Ireland
is satisfied that the Recorder of Belfast is
unable by reason of the duties imposed
upon him by the Juries Acts or this Act
in connection with the revision of jurors'
lists, to transact the business of his courts
with proper dispatch, the said Governor
may appoint the judge of the county court
of any other county or county borough, or
a practising barrister of not less than ten
years' standing, to act as additional judge
of the first-mentioned courts or any of them,
during such period or periods of time in the
years nineteen hundred and twenty-six and
nineteen hundred and twenty-seven as the
said Governor may direct, and subject to
any conditions which the said Governor may
impose. Any additional judge so appointed
shall have all the powers, jurisdiction and
privileges, and may perform any of the
duties, of the Recorder of Belfast whether
under the Juries Acts or this Act or otherwise.
In this section the expression "Recorder
of Belfast" means the Recorder of Belfast
and County Court Judge and Chairman of
Antrim.
(2) There shall be paid out of moneys
provided by Parliament to any additional
judge appointed under this section such
remuneration and expenses as
may be
determined by the Minister of Home
Affairs with the consent of the Ministry of
Finance.

Sir DAWSON BATES: I beg to move,
"That the Clause be now read a Second
time." As I explained on the Second Reading debate, a great deal of work will be
thrown upon the Revising Barrister or the
Recorder on the first revision of the jury list,
because on that occasion the name of everybody who appears to be eligible to serve will
appear on the list, regardless of whether or
not they are entitled to exemption. When
the list is
gone through, the Revising
Barrister will go carefully into every name
and mark against those names whether the
person is entitled to serve or whether he is
permanently or temporarily disqualified.
After that list is gone through in the first
year, the subsequent list will be very much
smaller for the reason that any name marked
on the first occasion as permanently disqualified will be struck off and will not come
before the Revising Barrister again, and those
temporarily disqualified on the first revision
will not appear on the list unless due notice
is given to the particular person interested.
While on the first occasion the revision will
take a very considerably longer time than it
has done on former occasions, subsequent revisions will occupy much less time and will
not entail more than one or two day's work
on the part of the Revising Barrister.
Having regard to the enormous amount of
work the Recorder does-last year he barely
found time to do the revision-it seems to
the Government that it will be impossible
for him to find time to revise the first list
without assistance. It is expected it will
take nine or ten days to revise the first list,
and I think it is very undesirable that the
ordinary work of the Recorder should be
interfered with, and that litigants should

Mr. DEVLIN: I have once again to enter

ought to have been in the Bill when it was

come up for Second Reading. It has become
the habitual practice of the Government, and

a Bill, have it read once, then a Second time,
when there is a discussion, and then, on the

Bill. It may be said that these are matters

The CHAIRMAN: The only new Clause

that it is exposed to two objections, either of
which is fatal. The first is that it proposes
that this House should legislate in respect
of a matter which is not within its province,
namely the High Court. The second objection is that it proposes to increase the charge
upon the Crown, which is not open to a
private Member. On both these grounds the
hon. Member's new Clause is not in order.
Mr. GEORGE HENDERSON: From your
ruling on a previous Amendment, I thought

The CHAIRMAN: If the hon. Member will

that if he reserved certain principles to a
later period he might reserve himself beyond the point of redemption. This is
exactly what I had in my mind. I might
further point out that the principle involved
in the other Amendment was that it gave permission to certain public bodies to do certain things. In this particular case it is
not even permissive, and if it were permissive, the two objections which I
have enumerated, first, that it proposes legislation which is not within the province of this House, and
secondly, it proposes to increase the charge
upon the Crown. Upon both these grounds
his Amendment would fail. He did not quite
correctly gather what I ruled,
Mr. GEORGE HENDERSON: I do not
dispute your ruling, but I feel I am representing a principle which has the support

included in this Bill.
The CHAIRMAN: I could not, of course,

that whatever he wants to discuss must be
within our rules of procedure. I have indicated to him two respects in which his new
Clause is not within our rules of procedure.
The first is that it proposes that we should
legislate on a matter about which we can
make no legislation. The second is a purely
personal one, that he proposes to increase the
public charge, which is beyond the province
of a private Member. These are the two
points, and I think when the hon. Member

Mr. T. W. McMULLAN: I beg to move in
the Third Schedule, page 16, after line 7, to
insert "Commercial Travellers."
This is another class for which I would
appeal. I have been asked by the Minister
of Home Affairs to define what I really mean
by a commercial traveller. I would say that
a commercial traveller may be defined as an
employee of a manufacturer or trader, whose
entire occupation is soliciting orders for his
employer. It seems to me that if a commercial traveller is occupied at a considerable
distance from Belfast-as so many of them
are-with all his interests in that particular
district, if he is on commission and is
called upon to serve on a jury in Belfast, he
has to lose his entire commission for the
time he is serving. If, on the other hand,
he is on a salary his firm has to suffer considerable loss, and in these times of bad
business I do not think even the Minister of
Home Affairs would wish to inflict such a
loss.
Only on Saturday last, a commercial traveller told me that during last year he was
called on a civil jury in the High Court.
He was brought backwards and forwards
regularly to the Court for five weeks, and,
though he had to answer his name, he was
only called on one jury in that time. Now
that traveller's journey was in County
Tyrone and County Derry, and through
going and coming in order to answer his
name-not to do public service---he told me
that he found it very difficult indeed, during
that time, to get any business transacted.
That meant that five weeks of that man's
time were lost to his firm. It would require
the wit of the Parliamentary Secretary
(Mr. Hanna) to define where any amusement
was to be found for the firm that employed
that particular man. I know in my own
business we have often had considerable inconvenience through calls upon our commercial travellers for jury service. I do not
want to go into this matter too much, but
I appeal to the Minister of Home Affairs to
give it his serious consideration. I do not
want him merely to turn down this suggestion, because I believe a man like that ought
to get off. Commercial travellers are men
who are loyal, upright, good citizens, and
who deserve consideration.

The PARLIAMENTARY SECRETARY TO
THE MINISTRY OF LABOUR (Mr. Gordon):
The Estimate which I desire to bring before
the Committee this evening will be found
on page 3 of the Revised Estimates, and it
amounts to a total sum of £135,000. Some
time ago the Committee voted £45,000, leaving
£90,000 to be allocated. Without unnecessarily wearying the Committee, I would like
to explain as briefly as possible what it is
this money is required for. I will refer to
it under three heads-Benefits, Administration, and Medical Certification.
I would like to inform the Committee that
in 1924 the Approved Societies of Northern
Ireland paid in sickness benefit something
like £440,500, and in 1925 that had risen to
£155,100. For the year 1926-27, owing to the
increased surplus shown by the recent valuation of the Societies, increased benefits will
be given during the next five years to the
members of the various Approved Societies.
Consequently, that would have meant an increased contribution from the State, but our
future contribution to the Approved Societies will be on the new basis of calculation.
The reason I am introducing this question
of the new basis of calculation is not for the
purpose of rousing the fighting abilities of
the Opposition, but to remind them of the
fact that the State's contribution has been
reduced from two-ninths to one-seventh in
the case of men, and to one-fifth in the case
of women. The amount the Government propose to give towards Sickness, Disablement,
Maternity, and Sanatorium Benefit, including
the additional benefits I have referred to, is
£118,500.
We now come to the Administrative
Expenses. As hon. Members are aware, the
Administrative Expenses include salaries,
rent, expenses of Insurance Committees,
expenses of Sick Visitors, and the expenses of
running the Deposit Contributors' Fund. The
combined Administrative Expenses of the
Approved Societies is something like £77,000,
and towards these expenses the Government
propose to make a grant on the new basis of
contribution of £11,000.
