In 1922-23-I am going to trouble the House
with a very few more figures the number of
individual students was 17,331 and the
number of class entries was 37,621.
The Report for 1925-26 will show over 20,000
individual students and nearly 45,000 class
entries. We have now 97 centres of technical
instruction where in 1922-23 we had eighty,
which in itself was a very respectable figure.
The spread of technical instruction has
meant an increase in the number of teachers.
Over five hundred and fifty teachers are now
of
engaged in the schools and classes
technical instruction; and, of these, two
hundred and thirty are in full time employment.
The position of the teachers in our
technical schools and classes was not satisfactory when the Ministry first assumed its
responsibilities. They certainly had the
advantage of an addition to their pre-War
salaries, in the shape of a bonus which
varied with the movement of the cost of
living. But still there was no fixed general
salary scale; nor was there a really suitable
scheme of superannuation.
With the sanction of the Ministry of
Finance, we have now set up salary scales
for these teachers, upon the same lines as
those already adopted for the secondary
schools. We again have a basic minimum
commencing salary, payable by the local
authorities or managers of the technical
schools; and, with that, fixed annual increments, which are paid by grant from the
Ministry. Moreover, the Ministry of
Finance, after consultation with the Ministry
of Education, has recently laid before Parliament a scheme of superannuation for agricultural and technical school teachers, which
closely follows that adopted for teachers in
secondary schools.
Before I leave the subject of technical
instruction, I should like just to say one
word upon
the direction in which the
Ministry is moving in this field. We recognise the vital importance, not only to the
future welfare of technical instruction, but
to the welfare of our skilled industries, that
there should be a lively and intimate connection between our technical schools and
our industries.
a
Presidental
Lord Londonderry, in
Address to the Association of Technical Institutions at its meeting in London, early
in March last, urged upon the Association
the necessity of establishing a satisfactory
system of apprenticeship in skilled industries in order to ensure the proper recruitment of the ranks of our skilled
workers. He pointed out the way in which
technical schools could assist this work.
"What profit," he asked, "is there in a
scheme of technical education, however perfect, which is not generally recognised as an
integral part of our industrial training."
With that view the Ministry and, I have
no doubt, the country at large are in full
agreement. To this end, we have been giving
a certain number of trade scholarshipseighty annually, to be precise which are
awarded to apprentices in certain skilled
trades at the conclusion of the second year
of their apprenticeship. They are tenable
at the Belfast College of Technology, where
the scholars pass through a specially trained
course in their particular trade, a course
which is a blend of theoretical and practical
instruction. I am happy to be able to report that employers have welcomed the institution of these scholarships, and that
generally they recognise the scholarship
period as part of an apprentice's years of
indenture. The expenditure on these
scholarships will be found under Sub-head
D2, of Vote II, which announced to £3,000.
Before I pass to our local education
authorities I ought, I feel, to say something
of the Queen's University, to which we make
annual payment of thirty-six thousand
pounds under statute. It is true the University is a self-governing body, in the
guidance of which the State can exact no
share as a condition of this expenditure.
That is a good thing educationally, and one
which we do not, in the least, wish to see
changed. But we are always glad to assist
the University, which, in its turn, has shown
itself very ready to assist the Ministry in its
difficulties, particularly in the matter of our
arrangements for the training of teachers.
The Committee will remember that a short
Act was passed recently, enabling local
authorities to contribute from the rates to
the funds of the University. We are aware
that a beginning has been made, and that
some of these authorities are now taking
advantage of their powers under this Act.
It requires no word from me to commend
the services of the University to the community, and I feel I shall not be alone in
expressing the hope that the University may
receive a really adequate measure of assistance from these local bodies.
I have left as my last topic what is, probably, of most interest, namely, the progress of the local administration of education in the counties and the county boroughs.
The Education Act of 1923 is now in full
operation everywhere. The Education Committees of Belfast and Londonderry are at
the close of the second year of their existence. In the counties, the Regional Education Committees have been in charge of their
areas for the past twelve months. We are
already able to speak of the working of the
new system, though naturally we shall be
able to say more about it in another year
or so.

I think we may claim to have revived, if
not actually to have created, a healthy public
interest in education in Northern Ireland. In
the days of a highly centralised system, when
the public voice had so narrow a channel
for expression, public interest was naturally
never very widespread, and, in any event,
could never be very vocal.
From the
But that has all been changed.
day when the proposals of the Government
first appeared, when it was seen that educational administration would be shared between the Ministry of Education and the
organs of local government, the columns of
our newspapers have been full of the topic
of Education.
Now that the Act of 1923 is in operation,
the doings and sayings of the various local
authorities are fully reported and are eagerly
read. The Press has done much to encourage
this healthy interest, and to it much of the
credit belongs. But the Press itself is largely
a reflection of public opinion-
Mr. DEVLIN: I do not know.
Mr. ROBB -and the extent of public
interest may be fairly measured by the
amount of space devoted to a subject in the
newspapers. We welcome this activity, and
in spite of the fact that the Ministry is often
a subject of criticism, we regard that as a
sign of health in the body politic. We had
far rather be criticised than forgotten.
As hon. Members are no doubt aware, three
of the counties are divided into several
regional areas; the County of Antrim has
five; the County of Londonderry has three,
and the County of Tyrone has five. Each
region is under its committee, responsible to
the county council-the education authority
in all the counties, whether divided or notfor general educational administration within
the area allotted to it.
Three counties, the Counties of Armagh,
Down, and Fermanagh, are being administered
as a single region each. That is to say, there
is one regional committee in each of these
counties which, under a scheme approved by
the Ministry, administers the whole county
the area allotted to it.
The difference between these two kinds of
local administration is really one of form,
rather than of substance, because, in order
to secure the full local representation and
control required by the Act, the schemes
under which the three single-region counties,
if I may call them so, are operating, all provide for the appointment of various local
sub-committees, upon which devolves the performance of the duties of administration in
the locality which they represent.
There is, of course, this important
difference, that, whereas in the single county
areas the regional education rate is a flat
rate over the whole county, in the other
counties, the counties divided into several
regions, the rate is struck for that part of the
county only which is comprised within each
region. Finance, of course, must play a very
important part in every scheme of administration; and we shall watch closely the
operation of the system in each county, in
order to secure the most economical-under
which head I include the most efficientmethod of working. The Ministry has an
open mind in regard to the mode of applying
the Act in particular counties, a mind which
is governed chiefly by the two considerations
which I have just named.
Of all the problems confronting our local
education authorities there are five, which,
in my opinion, overshadow the rest; first,
there is the problem of securing efficient elementary school accommodation; second, is
that of enforcing school attendance; third,
comes the provision of opportunities for
further education, whether at secondary
schools or at continuation and technical
schools; fourth, the establishment of an
effective system of medical inspection and
treatment; and last, we have that bugbear of
all administrations, the problem of finance.
That there are other problems I know too
well; but they are either minor problems by
comparison, or problems which have an
interest more or less peculiar to one or two
areas or localities within areas. But the five
which I have mentioned are of universal
application, though they do not, of course,
exert an equal pressure over all. I propose
to do no more than touch upon these to-day.
In Belfast the problem of elementary
school accommodation stands by itself. It is
a problem, not of to-day, nor of yesterday,
but of many years' standing, and it is a
problem which has arisen largely owing to
the rapid rate of the growth of the population. Schools, not so long ago ample enough
and within the reach of green fields, are now
overbuilt, cramped and overcrowded. There
are, I know, old schools, schools long out of
date, which in a normal state of things
would require replacement or reconstruction.
That is the case everywhere, and we must
always be prepared for a policy of systematic
and periodic rebuilding.
But the trouble in Belfast is that even our
newest schools, those of comparatively recent
date, which are otherwise quite admirable
school buildings, are in a great number of
cases planned on altogether too small a
scale.
I cannot speak too highly of the way in
which the local education authority in Belfast has faced its difficulties and taken the

In the City of Londonderry, and in the
county areas generally, the problem of
school accommodation takes rather a different shape. Here, too, there are, unfortunately,
some old and inefficient school buildings
which require replacement or reconstruction.
But, as a rule, the school buildings are
reasonably efficient. It is rather a question
of deciding upon the best use to be made of
the existing accommodation. It will then be

are
Single-teacher schools are, in the nature of
things, the least economical form of school
accommodation, and educationally the least
efficient. While we recognize that these
schools must always persist in sparsely populated and remote rural districts, we
aware that there are many such small schools
now which, by judicious amalgamation or
by a well-placed new building, could be
superseded, to the benefit of pupils and
teachers and to the advantage of the public
purse.
In pursuing a policy of amalgamating
schools wherever possible, local education
authorities may rest assured that they will
receive the full support of the Ministry.
They will, doubtless, be confronted with
obstacles with which the Ministry itself has
long been familiar, but, armed with an intimate knowledge of local conditions and with
the added weight which their representative
capacity gives them, they will probably find
themselves better able to deal with these
difficulties than any central authority could
hope to do. In any event, their battle is the
battle of the Ministry, as indeed it is that of
the taxpayer at large, and, as I say, they can
rely upon our assistance.
Before any general line of action can be
taken by the local authorities it will be necessary for them to formulate schemes, after a full
review of existing facilities. Such a course
has hitherto been rendered difficult, if not
actually impossible, owing to the delay of
transfers, pending the settlement of doubts
as to the effect of transfer upon the facilities
for religious instruction. These doubts have
now been removed, and conditions satisfactory to all parties appear to have been decided upon. The Ministry knows that the
detail arangements are liable to make the
actual transfer a long proceeding, but we
hope, now that the path seems clear, managers will without delay intimate to the
authorities everywhere in what relation they
desire their schools to stand as part of the
local school supply.
I have already spoken of school attendance.
The figures I gave make it clear that this
part of the Act is being everywhere effectively administered. I have also alluded to
local responsibility regarding secondary education and continuation and technical
schools and classes. On that I will say no
more now.
Medical inspection and treatment of elementary school children has, I am glad to
say, been recognized by all our local authorities as a matter of first importance. Belfast
already has a very complete scheme in course
of operation. The other authorities have
taken preliminary steps and are all at one
stage or other of the establishment of a form
of medical service under the Education Act.
There is no doubt that ultimately the whole
of our elementary school population will be
brought under proper medical supervision.
Here, perhaps, more than in any other part
of their activities, local authorities will be
breaking new ground in Northern Ireland.
Progress undoubtedly depends upon the measure of co-operation which the parents
accord them in this work, and the Ministry
feels sure that the authorities will not look
in vain to the public for sympathy in their
efforts to secure for the Province the full
benefits which will be derived from a school
medical service organized upon a sound and
economical basis. I may say, in the same
connection, that the Belfast Education
Authority has already had a scheme in operation for the feeding of necessitous children.
The Estimates of the Ministry show that
out of a total contemplated expenditure of
£1,942,145 we are looking to the local education authorities to raise £67,500 from the
rates. Hon. Members will get this last
figure from the sum of £135,000, which they
will find under Sub-head F of Vote II, that
amount representing the Ministry's grant to
local education authorities of two pounds for
every pound raised by the education rates.
We know that there is an outcry against
the burden of the rates, but this cannot be
based upon the burden imposed by educational expenditure. Let me make a brief
comparison of the incidence of this expenditure upon the common purse and upon the
local rates. A penny rate in the pound is
estimated roughly to produce £20,000 over
the whole Province. Expressed in terms of
rating, therefore, our total educational
expenditure comes to just over the equivalent
of a rate of eight shillings and a penny. Of
this, the State finds seven and ninepence
three farthings, while the local authorities
find the rest-say, threepence farthing.

That is the position to-day. My right hon.
Friend, the Minister of Finance, has no

We are, undoubtedly, faced by an expansion of our educational services. We have
economised to the utmost to assist in meeting
that expansion. This year shows a net decrease in the Ministry's Estimates of one
hundred and nine thousand, four hundred
and nineteen pounds. I find it difficult to
suggest any direction in which the Ministry's
Estimates can be further reduced if we are
adequately to perform the task given us, and
it seems to follow that the cost of expansion
must be met locally. Before the Act of 1923,
local authorities used to rate for technical
instruction, up to a maximum of twopence
in the pound. There was, perhaps, an
average rate struck, throughout the Province, of a penny farthing. As I showed,
the average local rate comes to threepence
farthing, and that means that the local
authorities have, so far, only paid twopence
of new money for the benefits which they
receive under the Act.
By the Education Act, in the words of
Canning, "We call the new world into existence to redress the balance of the old."
We created local education authorities to
assist the State in the supreme task of
assuring the future of our children. I refuse to believe that these authorities will
answer us with words which were also used
by the great Canning, though in quite
another connection-" I give thee sixpence !
I will see thee damned first!" I beg to
move.

Although some people might complain that
it was a very lengthened statement, I think
those of us who remained in the House to
listen to it will quite recognise that he
amply justified the time which he occupied in
the delivery of a most impressive and interesting statement. (Hon. Members: Hear,
hear.) I rise to join with my hon, Friend (Mr.
O'Neill) in a protest against the manner in
which the voluntary schools are treated.
We understood that when the Act of 1920
was passed-that is the Act which established
this Parliament-no religious denomination
would suffer thereby.
Now the Catholics of Northern Ireland do
suffer by the operation of this Measure, because they are in a worse position now under
this Parliament than they were under the
Imperial regime. Under the old system they
were entitled to a grant of two-thirds for
their schools-for Catholic schools-as indeed
a two-thirds grant was given to all schools
under the national system in those days.
Under the new arrangement they are not entitled to any grant towards the building of
schools, and, considering the financial difficulties to which the hon. and learned Gentleman (Mr. Robb) referred, it seems to me
rather an indefensible policy that, while you
are finding it difficult to raise money to build
schools, you refuse to assist those who are
ready to raise a substantial portion of the
building fund themselves. That has always
been done in the case of Catholic schools.
They have raised one-third of the building
fund themselves, and the State has given
them a two-thirds grant.
Now it may be said that under this new
system, since there is a rate in aid, the
public are entitled to representation in the
government of the schools, but what do you
get out of the rates? I was quite astonished
to hear the figures read by the hon. and
learned Gentleman (Mr. Robb). He said that
if there was a rate struck for education it
would amount to 8s 1d in the pound. But of
the total amount spent on education 7s 94d is
paid by the State. In other words about
3d is voted by the local authorities, and
yet because of the introduction of this principle of making the local authorities partly
responsible for the building of schools, you
take away two-thirds of the grant from the
voluntary schools.
This Act was passed in 1923. There was an
Amending Act passed in 1925 to meet the
objections raised, not by the Catholic school
managers or the Catholic authorities, but by
the Presbyterians, who are always a most
militant body when they are looking for
anything, as the hon. Member for Antrim
(Mr. Crawford) well knows. (Laughter.)
They raised a row and they got an Amending
Bill, but I want to know how many of the
schools have been transferred in the intermediate period between the passage of that
Amending Act and now. I should also like
to know how many schools have been transferred altogether-Catholic and Protestant
schools--because I take it that an Education
Act when it is passed is for the purpose of
creating, if not perfection, at least an improved system, something that will appeal
in a more widespread way to the general desires of the people.
I would like to know whether all this talk
about these educational reforms and the
passage of these two Measures have justified
themselves in what has occurred from then
till now. For my part I think it would be a
far wiser policy for the Government to give
to voluntary schools the grant of two-thirds
for building which was formerly given under
the National Board. If you want the public
satisfied, and if you want to maintain the
position which our schools occupied before
this Act was passed, then you ought to do
that. Probably if we had been as vocal as
the Presbyterians were we might have got
our wrongs righted long since. In my judgment there ought to be great consideration
shown to the Catholic body in Ulster, which
constitutes thirty-five per cent. of the population, on the fact that, although holding so
strongly on these questions, although holding
very deeply and profoundly conscientious
convictions, they have given no trouble to
the Government in relation to education,
neither in relation to the education nor in
the administration of that Act. I think that
will be admitted by the hon. and learned
Gentleman opposite and by his staff.
And this I must say in regard to his staff—
and I must say it in regard to Lord London-

derry, who was the Minister of Education for

a
hon. and learned Gentleman (Mr. Robb)—
who, one would think, was a model
utilitarian from the method in which he

called the fetish of practical utility, and that
he also told us that he did not regard as
sacrosanct the commercial value of education.
I was delighted to hear so idealistic
sentiment secretively issuing from the mass
of oratory with which he dealt with the
Estimate. Therefore, I trust that I will find
a sympathetic listener in the hon. and
learned Gentleman. I think it was wrong to
attempt to take away the privileges, very
much enjoyed by the pupils, by the parents,
and by the teachers, that were given in our
elementary schools in regard to the teaching
of the Irish language. No teacher has been
compelled to teach Irish. The work has been
done voluntarily. Therefore, I think that
where the pupil wanted to learn Irish, where
the parents wanted their children taught
Irish, and where the teachers were willing
to teach Irish, they should have had an opportunity of doing so. After all, although you
are Ulstermen, you must have some respect
for the language which is regarded as the
native language of Ireland-I was going to
say of your native land, but it is also the
language of a considerable portion of your
native Ulster. It is spoken in Donegal, in
the Glens of Antrim, and in many other parts
of Ulster, but even so, as a mere matter of
sentiment, if the people want to learn the
Irish language or have their children
taught the Irish language they ought to have
the privilege of having it taught in the
schools.
Now, as I said, you passed an Amending
Act to please a certain section of the community. It did not please them and it did
not satisfy them. I do not say they are insatiable, although once a notorious-I will
not say a notorious, but a well-known judge,
who is one of themselves, asked a witness
what his religion was, and he said "I am
a Presbyterian," and the judge said "That
is not a religion; it is an appetite."
(Laughter.) I believe that, notwithstanding
what that judge said, they were not insatiable, but, although you have made these concessions to them, they are unsatisfied still.
And yet you have never made the slightest
concession to the Catholic minority. One
would have imagined that when you got all
the power into your own hands-because, as I
have before stated in this House, you went
to England and told them that you were a
minority and did not want to put yourselves
under the heel of a Catholic majority-and
that is how you got your Parliament-and
when, on the strength of your being a
minority, a very vocal minority, a very
violent minority, and a very revolutionary
minority, and as a result of your violence
you got this Parliament, one would have
thought that, in the light of your
experience of your propaganda, and of
your success both as propagandists and
as revolutionaries, you would have given some
consideration to the rights of the minoritylarger in Ulster than you were in the whole
of Ireland-in respect of educational matters.
I trust, however, that the new Minister
(Viscount Charlemont), who, I hope, comes
with a virgin mind, free from all the fetid
atmosphere of these religious and bitter
controversies, will apply himself to the task
of devising some scheme whereby justice may
be done to the Catholic voluntary schools.
Before I deal with one or two other matters I want to come to the question of the
Irish language. I was very glad that the

I think it is a great mistake to be forcing too

much food on little children-a physical mistake. It is a mistake to compel the teachers
to try to impart education to children on toc
many subjects. I think it would be better

well as
to purely scientific and trained

Mr. MCALLISTER: In the first place I
should like to join in the congratulations to
the hon. and learned Member for the very
lucid, comprehensive and interesting way in
which he introduced his Estimate and on the
interesting way in which he covered the
whole field of education. I hope it will be
taken as a precedent by Ministers when they
are introducing their Estimates that there
should be such detail and such earnest
endeavour to communicate to the Committee
all the information they have at their disposal. I am very grateful to the Parliamentary Secretary for the manner in which
he introduced this Estimate.
I do not intend to cover in detail the
ground which has been gone over by my two
colleagues, but I do think, and I suggest,
that the Education Act is bound to be defective where you have a large body comprising 34.8 per cent. of the people admittedly
placed in a worse position than they were
before the passing of this Act for the simple
reason that their conscience forbids them to
adopt certain matters in that Act. I think
that is a grievance which should undoubtedly
appeal to the Government and to all fairminded men in the Committee and to fairminded people in the country. The hon. and
learned Gentleman when introducing this
Estimate stated, I think, in substance, that
the greatest handicap for the development of
education in Northern Ireland at the
moment was school building. But here is a
Clause vitally affecting the very part of the
administration which he states is in the most
retrograde position at the present time. It
is admittedly the greatest handicap to
education.
He must admit that their Act has forbidden the largest denomination for which
the Act is administered from receiving the
two-thirds grant they were hitherto entitled
to receive under the former regime. As the
hon. Member for West Belfast (Mr. Devlin)
has said, our claim is put forward in a
moderate way, and I would appeal to the best
instincts of the Government, of the Ministry,
and of the Members of the Committee to see
that that undoubted grievance is adjusted.
My colleague, the hon. Member for West
Belfast, has referred to the courtesy and
efficiency of the staff of the Ministry, and I
should like to add my testimony to his. I
have found that these gentlemen when
approached in a case of an individual
grievance, have been, so far as I can see,
animated with the highest possible motives.
They discharge their duty honestly and
conscientiously, and endeavour to meet and
accommodate representations made by Members where they are satisfied genuine
grievances exist. I have great pleasure in
adding my testimony to that of my colleague
in that respect.
I would ask the Government to take into
consideration that 35 per cent. of the people
are admittedly placed in a worse position
from an educational point of view than they
were before this Act was passed. I ask them
to meet the conscientious objections of those
for whom we speak.

Mr. KYLE: I also congratulate the Parliamentary Secretary on his speech in introducing this Estimate. He did, I think for
the first time since I came into this House,
deal with the policy the Government intended to pursue following the policy laid
down since the Act was passed. It is on that
question I would like to say a word or two.
The hon. and learned Gentleman, in his very
admirable speech has referred to the elementary school as being the commencement of
the educational services of the community. It seems to me his Department has
entirely overlooked some criticisim levelled at
the Education Estimates last year in regard
to the fact that the Government had not
seen their way to establish crèches or nursery schools in Belfast or Derry City. It
is admitted, on the other side, that these
nursery schools, where they have been in
operation, have performed great service to
the community in looking after the children
of the working-class mothers who have to
work in the factories.
In addition to looking after the children
of these working-class mothers they have
added to the-decorum, I was going to sayto the good manners of the children. They
have taught the children good manners, particularly where these nursery schools have
been established for a period of years, and
I think it would be a very good thing if the

to make inquiries as to the possibility of the

one form of criticism I would like to offer to
the hon. and learned Gentleman.
I do also want to say how much I agree
with the hon. and learned Gentleman when
he criticises those people who write to the
Press and always seem to have the viewpoint of wanting to know does it pay. I
quite agree with him that this is not the first
question so far as education is concerned.
I also agree that in the secondary schools that
he spoke of the elimination of profit-making
has been a very good feature in the sense
that the Ministry has taken over those secondary schools.
There is, however, one matter in regard to
secondary schools which, I think, should receive the Ministry's attention. These
secondary schools are governed by a Board of
Governors, and it is alleged-I do not know
how much truth there is in it-that these
Boards of Governors advertise for teachers
in secondary schools, but that as they already
have the posts filled those advertisements are
mere blinds. Would it not be possible for
the Ministry to devise some other method
of appointing the secondary teachers in these
schools than to leave it to the Board of
Governors who do it to-day? Seeing the
Ministry itself is interested financially, I
think it would be in the best interests of the
teachers themselves that there should be
some committee of the Ministry along with
representatives of the assistant masters and
mistresses-I am not aware whether that is
the organisation that looks after the secondary
teachers but whatever organisation looks
after them-in order to allay suspicion in
the minds of those people who have been denied appointments. Maybe they would
have a complete answer. I do not know,
but I have heard this stated quite freely,
and have had instances given to me where it
was alleged that the Board of Governors for
some reason known to themselves refused
very capable and competent men as secondary
teachers. It is felt that this would be a
better way of governing the secondary schools
than the method at present in operation.

rightly the Government should be twitted
with a breach of faith in that connection,
because when the arrangement was entered

was come to that it was final and that the
salaries of those teachers were settled irres-

Mr. WILLIAM MCMULLEN: Hear, hear.
Mr. KYLE: I stated not only here but outside this place that the 1923 Education Act
was a charter for education in the Six
Counties; that it was very desirable and did
provide the machinery which, however imperfect it might be at the moment, gives the

I want to subscribe most heartily to the
doctrine of the widest possible education for
all, and when I say widest I mean widest.
I do not mean that the elementary school
should be used only for turning out a good
shipyard worker or a good textile worker. I
do not mean that the technical school should
be used only for the purpose of turning out

Mr. WILLIAM MCMULLEN: I would like
to say just a word or two before the Parliamentary Secretary replies. I listened with

To me it was extremely and intensely
interesting, and I could have gone on listening to him for a considerable time longer. I
think most of the points that would
naturally come to one's mind have been

I am keenly interested in the position of

being largely lost at the present time. I am

learned Gentleman (Mr. Robb) to concentrate
his attention on this problem, because it
seems to me to be an extremely and an
exceptionally important one. If we had a
normal industrial situation boys of fourteen
years of age would probably find an outlet
in our mills and factories and shipyards, but
owing to the abnormal industrial itantion
boys and girls on leaving school find it
impossible to obtain employment. Those
boys and girls are running about the strets,
largely wasting their time, and unfortunately
the education that they have got at the clementary school is wasted too.
I do not know whether the hon. and
learned Gentleman (Mr. Robb) appreciates
this point or not, but it has been my
experience that when boys leave the elementary schools there is a gap in their education. For the next four or five years they
take very little interest in education, and
they generally lose any little they have been
taught. It is only when they approximate
to the age of 20 that boys who are bright and
intelligent come to appreciate the value of
education. That gives a period of from 14
to 20 years of age during which there is a
gap in the education of youth. In the midst
of our present industrial depression it might
be possible to keep our boys and girls at
school say until 16 years of age. I would not
make any arbitrary suggestion as to how
that should be done, but I believe the problem should be taken into consideration by the
Ministry of Education in conjunction with
other Government Departments. .It is
perhaps apropos that just at this moment
the Minister of Labour sits on your right
hand, because I think the Department of the
hon. and learned Gentleman (Mr. Robb) and
the Department of the right hon. Gentleman
(Mr. Andrews) could collaborate on this.
question with very good results.

I am pleased that no attempt has been

think all impartial persons will agree that
education deserves a large Vote. Some of the
things that have taken place, even within
the last few years, could not possibly have
taken place in an educated community. It

is more necessary than it is in Northern
Ireland, and I would be prepared to spend

present time on education. If any attempt

A remarkable development has taken place
J
in the question of education within recent
years. Probably if we had had an assembly
of this kind ten or fifteen years ago, we
would have had a good deal of opposition to
the feeding of necessitous school children.
Now there is scarcely anyone who is opposed
to the feeding of necessitous school children.
All the arguments that were adduced against
the idea of feeding necessitous school children have been exploded, and we have now
decided to see that the children get the
necessaries of life in order that they may be
able to assimilate the education that is imparted in the day schools. We do that even
if parents are not carrying out their parental
duty of seeing that their children are properly fed, or if they are not in a position to
do so. That marks a very great advance.
From very many points of view our educational system is up to date and is in advance
of a good many places that I have been in.
I think if the hon. Gentleman would give
his attention to the two points raised by the
hon. Member for North Belfast (Mr. Kyle) and
myself, we could congratulate ourselves on
having educational services that would compare favourably with any other educational
services that I know of.

The hon. Member for West Belfast, who

Ministry. No alternative programme that

Ministry is not prepared to sanction every
programme. Hon. Members will understand
that there might be lazy people who would
like to teach a little less than we would expect them to teach, but any teacher, or manager who submits an alternative programme
will have that alternative programme sympathetically considered by the Ministry.

that, having regard to the very responsible

be as economical in the apportionment of
those salaries as possible. Their judgment as
to what they should do was entirely free and
unfettered. They had no instructions as to
how the salaries were to be given, nor had
any Minister, with one exception, approached
them on the matter at all. The only
recommendation they got was that exception,
and that came from the Prime Minister himself, and the suggestion of the Prime Minister
was a very characteristic one-and it is a
suggestion to which men in receipt of salaries
are not often prone-and it was that his
salary should be made as low as possible as
he did not want a burden on the finances of
our young Parliament.
In settling the salary of the Prime Minister
we had to keep this wish to some extent before us, and I think I am speaking the minds
of my colleagues on that Committee when I
say that, though we settled the salary of the
Prime Minister at £3.200, we did not think it
Supply Committee-
-Cabinet Offices.
HOUSE OF COMMONS
[Mr. T. W. McMullan]
represented his value to Ulster. We put that
at a very much higher figure-(hon. Members: Hear, hear)-but we had to fix something according to his wishes as far as we
could, and hence the salary we framed for
him. But at the time we arranged that
salary we had no data to go upon as to the
possible expense for hospitality and entertaining to which the Prime Minister would
be subjected, nor had we any knowledge, nor
had he any knowledge, that later on he would
be called upon to take the responsibility of
the great establishment at Stormont Castle.
I am satisfied, and I think most hon. Members of this Committee will feel satisfied that
we were wrong in our conclusions as to this
salary and the allowance which should be
paid to the Prime Minister. Events have
proved that hospitalities have been forced
upon him far beyond what the payment given
would be sufficient to meet. I think the
suggestion made to-day is a fair and a reasonable suggestion, and the amount will not
more than cover the expense to which our
Prime Minister is put in maintaining the
great position whch he has to maintain as
head of our Northern Government. I have
great pleasure in supporting the Vote.
Sir ROBERT ANDERSON: I do not look
upon the proposal now before the Committee
as a proposal for an increase of salary at all.
Mr. POLLOCK: Hear, hear.
Sir ROBERT ANDERSON: I do not think
it is fair to put it in that category.
Mr. POLLOCK: Hear, hear.
Sir ROBERT ANDERSON: I was hoping
that a proposal of this character, considering
the facts, which must be known to all hon.
Members of this Committee, would have gone
through without any opposition and practically unanimously. I do not intend to labour
the many points referred to by some of the
previous speakers, but I think we must all
be familiar with the very heavy outlay that
must exist in connection with the Prime
Minister's residence. It is a very delicate
matter to refer to, and I was hoping that in
the most generous and magnanimous manner
possible this amount would be voted here today. My hon. Friends in the Opposition, I
am. sure, are looking forward to the time
when they will sit on this side of the House.
I am sure the Leader of the Opposition (Mr.
Kyle) will look forward to the time when he
will be in occupation of Stormont. I think
it is fair and reasonable to fix some figure
that will be a precedent for the time when a
very poor man who has ability, character,
standing, and efficiency, may occupy the
supreme position in Ulster. We would bе
all glad to put him in a position to maintain the good name of Ulster, and to be able
to extend generous hospitality-to all who
called with him. I think if we look upon the
question in that broad, generous way we
would not refuse to allow this small sum
that is proposed to-day to go through. We
are not voting this sum to the man at all.
We are really voting the money to whoever
may be the occupant of the position of Prime
Minister in connection with our Parliament
here. We may have a man who may not require it, or we may have the other type of
man I have indicated, and then assistance of
this character will be needed.
I am sure that no matter on which side of
the Committee we sit we will all have sufficient pride in our Province to see to it that
even the man without any money will be
in a position to maintain the good name and
hospitality of the Province over which he
may be called upon to preside. On those
grounds I support the proposal now before
the Committee, and I sincerely trust it will
go through without any controversy, and
that our Opposition Friends will see that
after all on this occasion the money is not
going into the pocket of the Prime Minister,
but to the office. I am sure that we on this
side, and those who are on the Opposition,
consider that he has adorned the position,
and has rendered splendid service to the
whole country, irrespective of creed or class.
The con-

cern of the hon. Gentleman (Sir Robert

My namesake, the hon. Member for Down

of the Prime Minister greater than they did.
If they are going to reconsider the situation
there are other aspects that require consideration.
We possibly would not offer any hostility

of people in Northern Ireland at the present
time without a meal in the house. Under

those circumstances are we justified in voting

I do not accept the standpoint of the hon.

opposite. We are told we are a community,
the community of Ulster that Ulster counts.
I have mentioned before that Ulster to me
means men, women and children. We are being
repeatedly told that our finances are limited.
If the Ulster loaf is only a certain size, and
everyone requires to get a slice of that loaf,
the larger the slice the Prime Minister gets
the smaller the slice someone at the opposite
end of the scale gets. If the Prime Minister
is going to be the big brother of Ulster, he
will surely have some concern for the smaller
members of the family. In ordinary circumstances if there is a weak member of a
family the collective love and care of the
other members of the family would be bestowed upon the member of the family who
is weak. It should not be a question of the
person who is the big brother usurping or
abusing his position for the purpose of doing
injury to the person who is at the bottom of
the social scale. That is precisely what is
happening here.
I am sure
my hon. Friend (Sir Robert

Mr. POLLOCK: No.

Mr. POLLOCK: I rise at this juncture
because the hon. Member (Mr W. McMullen)

which he was not a listener. He rather suggested that something irregular was done
when the Hospitality Vote was before the

HOUSE OF COMMONS
[Mr. Pollock]
Committee yesterday. I took the opportunity of bringing before the Committee a matter which was entirely germane to the matter of that Vote. Now, I wish to remove some
apprehensions that appear to be in the mind
of the hon. Member who has just sat down
in regard to the objects of the Vote.
I stated that as a result of my observations
from this time last year when the Hospitality Vote was presented by my right hon.
Friend (Mr. Barbour), who sits beside me,
that I had considerable uneasiness that the
Hospitality Fund did not fulfil the functions
for which it was originally intended. Let us
bear in mind what the hon. Member for
Derry (Sir Robert Anderson) has emphasised
-that this is not a question of increasing
the Prime Minister's salary. It is a question
of re-imbursing him for expenditure in the
public interest, because I know to my own
knowledge that he has to entertain many
people, not people of our own Province alone,
but individuals coming from the other side,
entirely in the interests of the Province.
The hon. Member who has just addressed
the Committee used some fantastic figures in
saying the Prime Minister had £80 a week.
That is fantastic nonsense. If you take the
Prime Minister's salary as it appears in the
Estimate book at £3,200 and deduct incometax and super-tax, I question if his income
from it is £30 a week, and to speak of £30 a
week as sufficient to maintain the position
he does in the interest of the Province is
quite absurd.
Comparisons have been made by hon. Members between salaries on the other side of the
water and those obtaining here. I am not
now discussing the general question of
salaries, but I am adhering to the particular
case under discussion. It is on record that
Mr. Clynes, Minister without portfolio in the
Labour Government, has placed it on record
that the £5,000 a year that he received was
totally insufficient to support him living in
11 Downing Street. It is perfectly ridiculous
and fantastic to compare the expenditure in
11 Downing Street with the expenditure
necessary in our Province by one in the
position of Prime Minister, because the expenditure in this case is made entirely in the
interests and for the benefit of the Province of Ulster. Mr. Clynes had no obligation to undertake any hospitality more than
any ordinary person.
Mr. John Burns, the famous Minister,
stated that £500 a year was enough for any
man, but when he came into office he very
graciously accepted £2,000, and he was quite
willing when he was raised a step in the
ladder to accept £5,000 a year. I did not
consider it was too much for him, but I
place it alongside the statement of the hon.
Member (Mr. Beattie) that £500 a year or
£1,000 a year is enough for any man in any
position.
Mr. BEATTIE: I said £1,000.
Mr. POLLOCK: The point is this that the
Hospitality Fund, as I stated yesterday, does
not cover the particular expenses to which
the Prime Minister is subject. It does
cover special visitations of distinguished
people or distinguished bodies. The allegation
that it was secret fund in any way or that
it is not open and visible to anyone who is
curious on the subject can be refuted by
this statement. When the accounts for this
Hospitality Fund have been fully checked,
and found to be accurate, then I am expected
to give a certificate that they are correct, and
they are passed on to two superior officers of the
Ministry of Finance and subjected to further
examination, and ultimately they go to the
Comptroller and Auditor-General. The
statement that the money which is spent is
not devoted to the object for which it is
intended is perfectly absurd and has no
foundation in fact. During the five years in
which the Prime Minister has carried on
here, I know that he has spent very large
sums over and above the amount that he has
received in respect of his office as Prime
Minister. He has never made any complaint.
I have had no conversation with him on the
subject. As I said yesterday this has not
been inspired by him. I am simply making
this appeal to the House on the ground of the
injustice of putting the Prime Minister to
expenditure which is altogether in the interests of the Province.
Mr. BEATTIE: The Minister did not explain that the spending of this money was
subject to the supervision of the Comptroller
and Auditor-General.

certificate was necessary that the amount

this State consists of only six counties, it
seems to me, and to a great many other
people, that the extent of the hospitality and
the salaries that are being paid is absurd.
The right hon. Gentleman said something
about Mr. Clynes drawing £5,000 a year as
Leader of the Imperial House. He said there
was no comparison between Mr. Clynes and
the Prime Minister. It is quite true that
there is no comparison between the Leader
of the Imperial House of Commons and the
Leader of a Six County Parliament. I do not
know anything about the hospitality that has
to be given by our Prime Minister.
I am
sure that, like every other member of the
Irish race, he would want to give hospitality
in a generous way. I am not gainsaying
that. But I do think that the whole
business of the Cabinet, even the
whole business of this Parliament,
is on too grand a scale for the importance of
the work that is done. I think the Committee
that was established, and that we heard
something about to-day, might be reappointed to consider this question from that
particular angle. I do not know that my
colleagues, or I, or anybody would wish the
hospitality of the North of Ireland to be anything less or more than it is elsewhere, but
it is a significant fact that the Prime
Minister of Northern Ireland has £3,200 a
year, and that the President of the Irish Free
State has £2,500. It is also a significant fact
that the Cabinet Ministers in the North of
Ireland, governing a Province of Six Counties, have each a salary of £2,000 a year,
while the Ministers responsible for Departments in the Irish Free State have £1,600
each.
That is something, of course, that the Committee referred to, had under their purview
at the time they fixed these salaries, but
again I might suggest that it would be an
admirable thing for that Committee to reconsider the various salaries that they laid
down as fit and proper in their opinion. We
have had the evidence of one very important
Member of that Committee, who said that
they had no data to go on. Now that they
have data to go on, they might reconsider
the matter. While they are doing that they
might also pay attention to another item,
that is, the employment of piece-work Senators. I give them that to go on with.
Mr. LLOYD-CAMPBELL: I want to voice
my support of the proposal that is before
the Committee. I was a Member of the
Committee that drew up these salaries, and
perhaps, as my colleague in the representation of North Belfast (Mr. Kyle) has sug-.
gested, it would be better if that Committee
were to meet again and reconsider their

Mr. GEORGE HENDERSON: The hon.

Mr. DEVLIN: Everybody knows that you

Mr. CRAWFORD: A few words will serve
to indicate the purpose I had in my mind
when I put down these three Amendments.
In page 3, lines 1, 2, and 3, it says that certain
people, though they are not actually resident
in the city of Belfast, but live in the country

The PARLIAMENTARY SECRETARY OF
THE MINISTRY OF HOME AFFAIRS (Mr.
Hanna): No. They will have to serve in

Mr. CRAWFORD: Then again, the Bill says
that this twenty-five miles is to be measured
from the courthouse in the city. So far as I
know miles on the road are not measured from
the courthouse, but from somewhere in the
centre of the city, and that being so makes
the thing a little more difficult. I do not see,
unless you take a pair of compasses and
measure all round from the courthouse how
you are going to arrive at this distance.
The words in the Clause are
"being resident within twenty-five statute
miles of the courthouse thereof,"
and I suggest that we should strike out these
words and so allow any person who has property in the city of Belfast, and who lives
even thirty miles away from the city to
serve. I do not think it would do any harm.
Then, again, I think it would be a great
advantage it it could be arranged in any
way that not so many jurors are summoned
to Quarter Sessions. I have myself seen
sixty men summoned and some of them
brought from as far as thirty or thirty-five
miles, and when they arrived they found that
there was only one small case to be tried. I
think it would be a wise thing if the number
of jurors summoned to Quarter Sessions
could be limited to some number, even say
fifty-two, so that, even if you had two
prisoners and all the rights of challenge were
exercised, there would still be a sufficient
number of jurors to try the cases. I see the
Parliamentary Secretary to the Ministry of
Home Affairs (Mr. Hanna) shakes his head
as much as to say that that could not be
done, but time and again I have seen jurors
submitted to the greatest injustice by being
hauled up to Quarter Sessions when there
was practically no business to be transacted.
These men had to pay their own railway
fares backwards and forwards and lose their
day, and sometimes, just to suit the convenience of some highly paid official, who
could have been there earlier in the day,
they had to wait for some considerable time
before they could get away. The result was
that they missed the train that would take
them home and had to spend an evening in
Ballymena. I think if the number summoned was limited to some number like
fifty-two it would enable jurors not to be
summoned so frequently. It would do no
harm in the cause of justice, but would be
an immense advantage all round.
Another thing I would like to see is that
if it is discovered, say, three days before
the Court was held that the cases are very
few in number, or that the prisoners could
be remanded to a later Court without any
injustice being done, the jurors should be
notified of the fact, and not brought in
there on a wild-goose chase. I am suggesting
these things in the interests of jurors and
of common sense, and I do hope that the

Mr. DEVLIN: I rise to move the rejection
of this Measure. For years there has been
a clamant demand on the part of the inconvenienced and busy public to have some
relief through the passage of some adequate
measure of jury reform. We thought that
when the right hon. Gentleman (Sir Dawson
Bates) came along with this Measure, and
in view of the prolonged and somewhat
obscure oration he delivered in introducing
it, we were at least to have the charter of
the juryman's freedom. But, instead of that,
we have a ragged and unsatisfactory Measure
presented. It does not touch upon the most
vital things which inspired all the demands
for jury reform. In fact, it is another
example of the hasty legislation which distinguishes this House. One of the proofs
of that is that the right hon. Gentleman
(Sir Dawson Bates) has come along again
with a number of Amendments to his own
Bill. I do not know any man alive who
should be so experienced in the somewhat
tangled task of improving his original
measures by imperfect changes in the form
of new Clauses.
I wish I had the experience of the hon.
Member for Antrim (Mr. Crawford), so that
I could point out in his most experienced
and efficient way the evils under which jurymen suffer. It was rather a pity that he
missed his train the other night--no, that
he got his train, that was it. (Laughter.)
The worst of the hon. Gentleman is that
he misses his train at the wrong time.
(Laughter.) He remained here to-night to
propose his Amendments, that would have
been a magnificient improvement on this
Bill, and he would have moved them earlier
if it had not been for the inspiring cause
that was bringing him hurriedly back to
Ballymena.
What are the two things that are most
objectionable in this Jury Bill? The first
is that the citizens-mostly business menare compelled at great inconvenience to
themselves and at considerable loss to their
businesses, to attend as jurors without remuneration. We heard from the hon. and
learned Gentleman, the Parliamentary Secretary of the Ministry of Home Affairs (Mr.
Hanna), who sometimes shakes his head-
(Laughter)-when pearls of wisdom are
falling from the lips of his colleague (Mr.
Crawford), the very high moral doctrine
that public service should be given without
any financial requital. Now, that was all
very well when the jury system was first
introduced, but we have moved forward
since then, and I know very little public
service that is given free. There is much
excellent private philanthropy and humane
work done, but I know of very little public
service rendered now unless people are paid
for it.
While the principle that service is intended to be paid for is universally adopted
and in operation I do not see why this
particular class of people should be dragged
from their businesses and from their homes
and compelled to discharge public duties in
the public interests any more than
any other section of the people. They
are brought there to sit in court sometimes
for three or four days to await the convenience of judges and all the rest of the
organisation of justice. They are put to a
great inconvenience and, therefore, I say they
ought to be paid. If you do not pay them a
salary-and you pay everybody who renders
public service a salary-then you ought at
least to have agreed to pay their out-of-pocket
expenses. The idea not only of not paying
them for their loss of time but of compelling
them to pay their own train fares and soinetimes the cost of remaining overnight in
large towns, having come in from country
places, without any compensation whatever
is in my opinion unjustifiable, and how any
Jury Reform Bill can be introduced and
passed without dealing with this gross wrong
to the interests of those who give public services is a matter which must be justified
before I at all events could vote for this Bill.
In the second place, I thought that this
Bill would contain proposals to abolish
Grand Juries, but it did not propose to do
anything of the sort. Even the Home Secretary (Sir Dawson Bates) was more reactionary than the hon. Member for North
Belfast (Mr. Lloyd Campbell), a thing I
never hoped to see in my day and generation.
It required the hon. Member for North Belfast, who certainly does not march very
rapidly along the lines of democratic progress, to come forward and to propose a sort
of intermediate motion to abolish the Grand
Juries at Quarter Sessions. Then when the
judgment of the House was taken it went in
favour of that Motion and against the
Government, and I am quite certain that if
a proposal had been made from the opposite
benches in favour of the abolition
of the Grand Jury at Assizes it would
also have been abolished, and then this
Bill would have done the only good thing

What was

Mr. GEORGE HENDERSON: I beg to
second the Motion for the rejection of this
Bill. Like the hon. Member for West

has some foundation after we listened to the

My main objection to the Bill, as I have
said, is in connection with what it leaves

burning question all over Ireland with regard to the jury system was that jurors
were dragged from their homes, that they
had to pay their own travelling expenses,
and, as the hon. Member for West Belfast
(Mr. Devlin) said, if they had to stay over
night they had to pay their hotel expenses.
I do not know that there is any question
more hoary in Northern Ireland except probably the question of the Bann drainage, because as long as I can remember it has been
agitating the minds of public boards, and
there is hardly a prominent politician who
came over to Northern Ireland but gave
pledges in regard to jurors.
I was very much disappointed the Government could not see their way to accept the
very modest proposals recommended by Lord
Justice Andrews' Committee. They dealt
Here
with this question of remuneration.
is what they say, and they express it so well
that I will read it to the Committee:-
We are, however, of opinion that there
is a limitation to the duty which the citizen
owes to the State in this regard; and we
agree with the evidence of all the witnesses
examined on the subject before us, that
he ought not to be expected, in addition
to giving his time and his services, to bear
substantial out-of-pocket expenses in attending the Court.-
I want the Government to listen to this sentence particularly-
This is a liability which ought to be discharged by the State, which obtains his
services free.
What do they recommend? They recommend that jurors summoned by the Crown
who had to travel ten miles or upwards
should have their out-of-pocket expenses
paid and also a reasonable subsistence
allowance if compelled to stay overnight. I
say that more reasonable or more modest
proposals could not have been inserted or
recommended by any Committee to meet this
question which has been agitating the minds
of this Province for the last 30 or 40 years.
I do not believe there is any question affecting our internal politics that has a greater
weight of public opinion behind it in this
Six County area than the payment to jurors
of at least their out-of-pocket expenses. I
know the Minister of Home Affairs gave us
one reason on the Second Reading why he
did not adopt this suggestion of Lord Justice
Andrews' Committee. It was that it would
introduce a new principle. If we do not
introduce new principles at least once in
fifty years we would be apt to get behind.
Why should this Committee perpetuate an
injustice lasting for fifty years? It should
have been removed long ago, and this Bill
should remove it now.
The Minister of Home Affairs told us
about the privileges and duties of citizenship, but I venture to recite him a case I
know of my own experience, and I shall
repeat it now. It is the case of a poor, small
farmer being summoned to attend the courts
in Belfast. He lived seventeen or eighteen
miles from the city, and because he could
not afford to pay his travelling expenses he
had to tramp there and back. This is not
a recent occurrence, but in my own experience it has happened. I venture to predict
that if any Member of this Committee tried
that experiment his sense of citizenship
and patriotism would evaporate before he
had passed the thirtieth milestone.

The Prime Minister said in this respect
that if the Government had accepted this
very modest recommendation and included
in this Measure an allowance for the payment
of jurors' expenses, the Imperial Parliament,
who has some authority with regard to the
High Court, would have thought we were
travelling too fast, and would have put the
rein on us. I do not think that is a proposition the Government should really put
up. We claim we are a very progressive
community. Why should we not try to lead
in some cases? If this injustice is kept on
in England that is no reason why we should
tolerate it here. That is no reason why we
should not give a lead to our friends across
the water. The Prime Minister said they
would object if the jurors were more
generously treated here than in England. I
think this Bill is really doing that, because
the provision it makes for the payment of
jurors is that in civil cases, where a jury
gives a verdict, they shall receive 5s. That
is treating our jurors more generously than
in England.
Mr. DEVLIN: They will go to the devil
on the 5s.
Mr. GEORGE HENDERSON: It is establishing that principle. I do not see myself
why a juror who is summoned, and has to
attend the court-he is put to the same
disadvantage, and is taken from his business
whether he is sworn on the jury or not,
and if he is not there to answer his name
he will be fined-should have any difference
made between him and the juryman who is
empanelled and gets his 5s.
There is one other matter I wish to refer
to. Under the First Schedule, we would
really have better jurors for the county
areas had we put the rated qualification
the same in the country districts as in the
city and urban districts. I do not see why
it should be lower in the country districts
than the urban. For these reasons I have
no option but to oppose the Third Reading
of the Bill.
Mr. HANNA: Before dealing with the
arguments of the two hon. Members who
have moved and seconded the rejection of
the Measure, may I be permitted to say a
word or two in answer to the observations
of the hon. Gentleman (Mr. Crawford) who
sits behind me? On this point of the distance of 25 miles, it does not follow that a
man who lives at a greater distance than
25 miles from Belfast avoids the obligation
of serving as a juror. He will then be
summoned to perform and do jury service
in the county in which he resides. It is
absolutely essential that we should have

I am glad to say that as a result of what
we are doing by this Bill we will have

serve more than, we hope, once in four years.
On the second point which the hon. Gentleman raised as to the panel of 52 jurors, if
it happened that two prisoners were indicted
jointly for a felony those two prisoners could
refuse to join in their challenges and they
would each be entitled to challenge twenty
jurors without giving any reason, and as
many other jurors as they could give reason
for. If we had adopted the suggestion
of the hon. Gentleman only to bring
a panel of 52 jurors to the Quarter
Sessions it would simply mean that in
a case such as I have instanced if the
right of challenge was exercised to its utmost
limit you could not have a jury, and the 52
men brought from their homes at terrific
expense would have to come back again the
next day with 52 more. That is a state of
affairs we cannot contemplate, and, therefore,
we cannot reduce the panel to 52. I can
promise the hon. Member and the Committee
generally that the utmost care will be taken
not to summon more jurors on any panel
than is absolutely necessary for the due administration of justice with the least inconvenience to the jurors themselves.
As to the other point the hon. Member
made, that in the event of their being only
one or two prisoners to be tried, it would
be quite all right to send word to the jurors
to say they need not come this time as there
were only two or three prisoners to be dealt
with and they would be let out on bail, I
cannot understand the hon. Member. It is
the first duty of the State that pretends to
have any regard for the freedom of the
citizen to place that citizen on his trial at
the earliest possible moment. It is impossible to say to him, "We have kept
you in jail for a month now. It is
not worth while bringing jurors to try you.
We will open the jail doors and admit you
to bail." That is impossible, and I am sure
the hon. Member who has experience of the
administration of the criminal law in his
capacity as magistrate understands how
necessary it is to deal with prisoners at
the time the law says they ought to be dealt
with. I am very glad there is machinery
for dealing with another class of person
where we do not need jurors, and I hope
to be associated with my hon. Friend in the
exercise of that privilege to its fullest, whereever and whenever it is required.
I am always terribly moved when I hear
sad stories, and the hon. Member for County
Antrim (Mr. G. Henderson) knows my weakness in that regard. He moved me terribly
when he told me about that poor, small,
trudging farmer walking back and forward.
If the hon. Member had his way to-day and
Jury Laws Bill—
Third Reading.
HOUSE OF COMMONS
[Mr. Hanna]
if the House accepted his Motion to reject
the Bill that small farmer would be tramping yet.
Mr. GEORGE HENDERSON: He should
get his expenses.
Mr. HANNA: By this Bill we secure that
that very small farmer will never have to
start out on any such march. If we adopted
the hon. Member's suggestion and rejected
this Bill we would still compel the £10 man
to start his walk to the courts. But we have
changed all this and yet we are told we have
done nothing.
Mr. GEORGE HENDERSON: May I ask
the hon. and learned Gentleman does he
count the man with £16 valuation a large
farmer?
Mr. HANNA: I count him a very substantial farmer, a very useful citizen, and a
man competent to render great assistance to us in the discharge of the administration of justice. I do not know any farmer
in the County of Antrim with a £16 valuation who will have to walk to any court upon
which he will be called to serve. If he lives
in the County of Antrim and if he has to
walk at all it will be only once in five years.
To-day again we heard this complaint about
the payment of jurors. The hon. Member
for West Belfast (Mr. Devlin) stated that
public service ought to be paid for. I quite
agree, if a
man undertakes service for
another. If hon. Members come here, to
perform services as Members of this House,
then I think we are reasonably entitled to
such remuneration as we get. But whose
work is it that a juror is doing in a criminal
case? He is there for his own protection.
He is there as part and parcel of the
machinery of the court, and in my humble
opinion
Mr. DEVLIN: May I ask is all the other
machinery not greased financially?
Mr. HANNA: Other members of the
Court are there performing, over and above
that, the calls that the State makes upon
them. Is it not perfectly clear that it is
the bounden duty of every man who values
his own liberty to take very great care that
those who encroach upon it are placed where
they will not be able to do those things?
I take the liberty, humbly and very respectfully, of disagreeing with the recommendation that jurors should be paid in criminal
cases. I am now simply giving expression to
my own view. I have always felt that it is
a duty that is incumbent upon every man
to serve upon a jury in a criminal case. I
can appreciate the arguments that have been
used in regard to it, but I do think it would
be impossible for us and I think the House
will agree with me-to pay jurors attending
at the High Court and at the Assizes. We
are not competent to do it.
Even if the Government had come to the
conclusion to admit the principle that jurors
might be paid, would it not be distinctly unfair to pay jurors who have got to attend
at Quarter Sessions, because it would then
lie in the luck of the ballot, as it were, as
to whether they should be paid or not,
irrespective of any principle. I hope it will
be a long time before the Government will
be charged with any want of principle
running through important Measures such
as the one we are dealing with here to-day.
I do not know that I have anything more to
say in regard to the Bill than this, that I do
think it is a good Bill, that it will bring
about a great deal of satisfaction amongst
our people, that it will relieve very humble
people of any inconvenience and of any expense, and that it will secure that those who
are called upon to do jury service will be
put to the very least inconvenience that is
possible. I do hope that this House will
give the Bill its Third Reading now.
Question put, "That the word 'now' stand
part of the Question."

COTTIER HOUSES IN
BALLYMONEY
RURAL DISTRICT.
1. Mr. KYLE asked the Minister of Home
Affairs whether he will state in how many
cottier houses in Ballymoney Rural District
there is only one bedroom; how many of
these cottier houses were condemned as
insanitary by the Medical Officer of Health,
and how many cottages does the Council propose to build.
2. Mr. KYLE asked the Minister of Home
Affairs whether he will state how many
cottier houses in Ballymoney Rural District
have no chimneys, the smoke coming out by
the door; has the sanitary sub-officer
reported on them, and what action the
Council took in the matter.
3. Mr. KYLE asked the Minister of Home
Affairs whether he will state if in the hamlet
of Balnamore, in Ballymoney Rural District,
the sanitary accommodation consists of one
out-office for each street; if each street has a
public cess-pool in front of five residences;
how many reports on the sanitary state of
the hamlet were made to the Rural District
Council by their sanitary officer during the
six years ended the 31st March, 1926; and
what action the Ministry proposes to take in
view of the danger to the public health in
that district.
The MINISTER OF HOME AFFAIRS
(Sir Dawson Bates): I propose to embody
in one reply the answers to the three
questions put down by the hon. Member on
the subject of the housing conditions in the
Ballymoney Rural District.
The information at the disposal of the
Ministry in this connection does not indicate
the number of rural labourers' houses with
only one bedroom or without chimneys, but in
this connection I think it well to state that
the Ballymoney Rural District Council have
formulated a new scheme for the erection of
96 labourers' cottages, which in addition to
the 379 cottages already provided in this
district, will make a total of 475 cottages
provided for rural workers in the Ballymoney Rural District.
A public inquiry will be held at Ballymoney
by the Ministry's Inspector on the 26th
instant, into the Council's scheme, and the
Inquiry will deal generally with the housing
conditions in the district.
It may, however, be added that it is the
duty of the Council's Sanitary Officer to
report to the Council any unsanitary housing
conditions that come under his notice, and
the Ministry notes that during the last 4
years no fewer than 61 such reports were
submitted to and considered by the Council.
The Ministry has no definite information
as to whether these reports specifically relate
to the classes of houses referred to by the
hon. Member, and it can only be presumed,
pending the holaing of the local inquiry referred to, that the scheme now pending is to
a considerable extent the result of the Council's consideration of these reports.
As regards the case of the village of Balnamore, the Ministry notes that an adverse report was made to the Council in February
last by the local Medical Officer of Health as
to the sanitary condition of certain houses
in the village, and that the Council has taken
appropriate steps to have remedied the insanitary conditions referred to.
The Ministry's functions do not arise in
such cases unless and until formal complaint
is made as to default on the part of the
local authority concerned.

MINISTRY OF LABOUR.
