The PARLIAMENTARY SECRETARY
OF THE MINISTRY OF LABOUR (Mr.
Supply Committee-
17 MAY 1926
Ministry of Labour.
Gordon): I think it will be more convenient
in introducing the annual Estimate of the
administrative expenses of the Ministry of
Labour to give a general view of the extensive activities of the Department which are
performed in Great Britain by the Home
Office and the Ministry of Health as well as
by the British Ministry of Labour. To facilitate the performance of these duties the
work of the Ministry here is organised, as
you will observe from the Estimate, in four
Departments, and I should like to explain
briefly the scope of each in order to show
that they are run on economic lines, performing good work and giving a good return for
the expenditure involved.
The first department with which I propose
to deal is called Industrial Relations, which
will be found on page 88 of the Estimates.
The foundation for all our economic wellbeing is the promotion and maintenance of
industrial peace by fostering cordial relations
between employers and their workers. I am
glad to say that our record of good relations
between employer and employee continues
unimpaired, and at no time was it more in
evidence than during the general strike when
both sides showed anxiety and earnestness to
do nothing which would imperil those relations.
In 1925 there were only 52 disputes involving a stoppage of work, and the number
of working days lost in consequence was the
lowest on record since this Government was
established, only 3,900 workpeople being
affected as compared with 14,800 in 1924. It
is our earnest hope that this record will continue throughout the ensuing year.
This Department is also responsible for the
administration of the Trade Board system,
which covers 4,800 firms. About 6,900 factories and workshops are subject to the provisions of the Factory and Workshop Code
and the Truck Acts. These firms, employing,
roughly, 250,000 workpeople, are
inspected periodically. 2,800 premises were
year,
inspected during the
and active
steps taken to secure the protection
of those engaged in industry, and although
we show an increase in the number of
officials, this has been caused by an internal
reorganisation of the Department which will,
I trust, assist still further the working
of the Trade Board system and will concentrate in this Department the supervision of
compliance with the whole body of statutes
administered by the Ministry.
The Employment and Insurance Department of the Ministry administers the three
great insurance schemes-National Health,
under which 340,000 persons are insured;
Unemployment Insurance, covering 266,000
insured persons, and Contributory Pensions
covering 347.000. The National Health Insurance Vote has already been taken, so that I
need not detain the Committee further on the
subject. The Contributory Pensions Act, as
hon. Members are aware, came into operation
on the 4th January last and pensions and
allowances have already been awarded to
approximately 3,500 widows and over 9,500 dependent children.
still
Applications are
being received at the rate of about 40 per
week, and as from the 2nd July next old-age
pensions at the age of 70 will become payable
to insured persons without the fulfilment of
tests as to means, etc., and we have strengthened this section to deal with these
claims, as will be seen from the Estimates.
new
The Unemployment Insurance administration has been fully debated on Vote 3 of
the Ministry, and I should like on this
occasion to refer to some of the other
activities of the Ministry in this connection.
The work of the Employment Exchanges, of
which there are 20, with 22 branches, contiues to receive the greatest assistance from
those public-spirited gentlemen and ladies
who give freely of their time to serve on the
Local Employment Committees and their subcommittees. There are 17 Local Employment
Committees at work and 57 sub-committees.
Their help is extended in many directions,
but I will just mention a few.
Last year
26,247 vacancies were filled through the
operation of the Employment Exchanges.
This is a record and compares with a figure
of 14,727 for 1922, the year when we first assumed control.
The King's National Roll in connection
with the employment of disabled ex-Servicemen has grown from 124 firms employing
1,371 disabled men in January, 1923, to 950
firms employing 4,984 disabled men. The
Committees have also assisted the Department
greatly in the organisation of instructional
classes for unemployed women and juveniles.
With the valuable and generous co-operation
of the local Technical Education authorities
44 classes for unemployed women have been
completed at several centres throughout
Northern Ireland, and 19 are now in progress. Over 1,000 women have been covered
by this scheme of training.
As regards unemployed juveniles, educational classes for 542 have been held last
winter in Belfast and for 243 in Londonderry,
while manual instruction has been given in
9 centres to about 230 juveniles. The
Ministry is greatly indebted to the Local Employment Committees and Technical Education authorities for their assistance in this
promising movement, and it is hoped that it
will be developed further this year.
The total capital value of the Relief
Schemes that have been approved to date is
just over £4,250,000, in respect of which the
Department has sanctioned grants amounting to £1,070,000. By this means 685 under-
Supply Committee-
Ministry of Labour.
HOUSE OF COMMONS
[Mr. Gordon]
takings of permanent public utility have been
put in hand, which have provided almost
23,000 spells of work for our unemployed. At
the present moment 88 schemes are in hand,
on which about 2,000 men are receiving
direct employment, in addition to the persons
who are indirectly engaged in providing the
necessary materials.
The last two Departments of the Ministry
to which I wish to refer briefly are the Inspectorate and Finance Departments. As the
Committee is no doubt aware, instead of having separate staffs of inspectors to secure
compliance with each code of statutes as was
the practice heretofore, and is still the case
in Great Britain, we have placed all the inspection duties imposed on the Ministry by
Parliament in the hands of a combined inspectorate, so that as far as possible when
any premises are inspected in connection with
one code of legislation the inspector sees at
the same time how compliance stands as regards all the other statutes for which the
Ministry is responsible. This is obviously
as convenient as it is an economical arrangement, and I am glad to say that the extent
of compliance with the standards laid down
by Parliament is steadily improving.
The Finance Department of the Ministry
is naturally a very important one, as it is responsible, in addition to general financial and
establishment duties, for all the accounting
arrangements in connection with the disbursement of an annual sum of approximately
£4,000,000, of which by far the greater part
is paid in small amounts. In addition, a considerable proportion of the income of the Department is received in the form of individual contributions under the Insurance
Schemes, which have all to be credited
directly or indirectly to individual accounts.
For instance, under the Health and Unemployment Insurance schemes about 950,000 insurance books and cards have to be examined
each year in order to allocate the credits between the various approved societies and insured persons. In connection with both these
schemes our financial relations are
so interwoven with those of the corresponding
schemes in Great Britain that our system of
accounting must be uniform in the interests
of our own insured contributors.
A sum of £14,589 is included in the Estimate
for the Finance Department for the cost of
such services as registry, typing staff,
messengers, cleaners and establishment
services generally, which are common to the
whole Ministry. Eliminating this figure,
and also the cost of the agency
service-£1,058-in connection with the
re-establishment in civil life of disabled ex-Servicemen, for which the Imperial
Ministry of Labour pay us, the estimated cost
of the financial and accounting work of the
Department for the current year is £25,719,
or no more than slightly over one-half pe
cent. of the sum to be disbursed.
I have thought it desirable to give this
general review of the work of the Department because its very wide ramifications
may not be generally appreciated. The Estimate for this year provides for the first time
for the administration for a full year of the
new contributory pensions scheme, and the
administration of any new social service, of
course, necessarily involves additional cost.
It has been our constant endeavour, however,
to see that strict economy in administrative
expense is observed, and Sub-head A of this
Estimate, which is for the cost of the staff,
and includes the principle administrative
cost, shows a decrease of £3,322 over last
year's Estimate.
The Estimate provides for a gross administrative expenditure in 1926-27 of £252,433, but
this figure includes a sum of £20,150 for
capital expenditure on the new Belfast Employment Exchange. The net expenditure
figure, before credit is taken for the receipts
appropriated-in-aid under Sub-head V, is
£232,283, and this is no more than 5.8 per cent.
of the sum for the disbursement of which
it is estimated the Department will be responsible during the current year.
view, this is a very reasonable administration
charge for the many wide-reaching social services administered by this Department. The
receipts from the various funds and other

in reduction of the administrative expenses
are shown to be £119,155, so that the net
amount which Parliament is being asked to
vote this year is £133,278, or £12,592 less than
last year.

from the Belfast Board of Guardians.
is the decision of the Guardians:-
:-
Here
The responsibility for providing for the
genuinely unemployed is a national obligation, and has been so recognised by the
legislation of recent years, which has
made provision for this purpose, and a
huge staff of officials has been brought
into existence under the direct control of
the State.
That is to say, you have all the machinery
for providing for the genuinely unemployed.
The Minister of Labour limits the meaning
of "genuinely unemployed." You may be
genuinely unemployed for two years, but
when that period has elapsed the Minister
tells you it is a crime to be unemployed.
If you have not had a reasonable period
of employment within the two years, off you
go; you have really committed a crime under
the regulations that exist. The Poor-law
people say that
the Poor-law Acts were never intended to
provide for the compulsorily unemployed
under existing circumstances, and to
attempt to do so even in part would necessitate a large additional staff, which,
with the increased cost of relief, would inflict upon the ratepayers of Belfast a
burden which would be unfair to the working classes, and disastrous to the industries
and businesses of the city, and would only
result in further unemployment.
In justice to the bona-fide workers of this
city we protest against the present system,
which results in transferring in rapidly
increasing numbers unemployed insured
persons from State benefit, and putting the
responsibility on outdoor relief, which is
unfair and demoralising to those desiring
work and unable to find it, and inflicts
upon the Guardians an unreasonable
burden and an impossible responsibility.
We, therefore, call upon the Government,
with their specially organised State Department, to make arrangements, and if
necessary further provisions, so that all respectable deserving citizens who are insured persons, honestly endeavouring and
genuinely seeking employment and unable
to find it, will not be driven to seek Poorlaw relief.
In face of that unanimous decision of the
Board of Guardians, you must face the fact
that they are throwing the onus on to the
Minister of Labour. They charge the
Minister of Labour with pauperising the decent industrial classes of the city and Six
Counties. He is charged with putting the
taint of pauperism on those who are out of
work through no fault of their own after a
period of two years. The Guardians also say
that the Poor-law Acts were never intended
to provide outdoor relief under existing conditions. That is where I say the juggling
comes in, and the poor fellow who is thrown
in the air from one party to another is
dropped between the two, with the result
that life has become intolerable to him.
Then you have the Derry Board of Guardians.

There is another matter which I wish to
raise. I am bombarded week in, week out,
about the way people obtain Government
positions, especially in the Ministry of
Labour. I am asked what influence is at
the back of any person who gets a salaried
position for which he is not qualified, and
to which he has no right? I have asked

a back door, and I want that back door
closed against all who are not competent to
enter in by the front door, whether they
are the sons and daughters of Members of
Parliament or not. If my son is not qualifiied to go in by the front door, I do not
want him to get in by the back door.
The back door is badly abused, and I hope
to see it barred right and tight. If a girl
is not qualified to pass the entrance examination, she can be put in as a temporary
clerk into one of the Exchanges. She may
only remain there for one week, and may
then be transferred to the Minister's Department without undergoing an examination.
When she gets into the Minister's Department she may get a permanent position over
the heads of highly qualified girls who cannot obtain the position because of the way
priority is given. They should be admitted
on merit, but the appointments are not made
on merit. That back door must be closed.
You must give consideration to merit, and
to merit alone, and not have these inferior
people going in to abuse the unemployed,
people who are not competent to administer
the regulations.
This is a grand opportunity to place all

ployment regulations, while highly qualified

From the point of view of the interest displayed in this most important Estimate, I
do not know whether it is worth while persevering, or whether the marked attention
of the Minister and his Parliamentary

answering communications sent by Members
of this Committee, and by trades union
officials, to the Ministry in regard to people's
benefits. It takes about ten days in order
to extract an answer from this Department
of the Ministry of Labour. Will the right
hon. Gentleman try to take into consideration the position of the person denied unemployment benefit. When it is the case
of a father, responsible for a wife and a
number of children, I think the Minister
should take into consideration the awful
position of harrowing suspense and anxiety
that the head of the family is in. I have
known these people, after they have been
turned down at the headquarters of the
Ministry of Labour, to be in at my office
morning after morning to ascertain if any
reply had come back to my letter, from the
Minister of Labour. It has been my painful duty, for about eight or nine mornings
in succession, to tell these people I have
not had a reply. I have seen me, at the end
of three weeks, writing to the Department
to find out whether they intended to reply
or not. It is not fair for these people to
be kept in suspense. Perhaps the person
has hesitated about seeking for outdoor
relief, so that the delay really means the
punishing and penalising of a family more
severely than if they were told at once the
claim was disallowed. I hope some attention will be paid to this matter. The
Minister has got a fairly adequate staff, judging by the amount paid in salaries. When representations are made on behalf of an
applicant, we ought to expect a reply in a
lesser period than a week. I would give any
reasonable amount of time for the purposes
of inquiries being made on the subject-I
know it takes some time to do that. A delay
of ten days, however, is too long, and it
should be very much shortened.

The question of local committees has been
referred to, and I could not understand the
interjection of the right hon. Gentleman
(Mr. Andrews) who suggests that what the
hon. Member for West Belfast (Mr. Devlin)
suggested was taking place was not correct.
We know that morning after morning
applicants come before the local committees.
When the members of the Court have made
their decision the clerk of the Court will
attach a typewritten sheet to indicate that
in his opinion the applicant should not be
paid benefit without the matter being referred
to headquarters and very closely scrutinised.
I suggest that that is tantamount to a person
being disallowed benefit. I have gone
through some papers-I should not tell the
hon. Gentleman that-and I have observed
that five out of every seven claims are turned
down, due to the attachment of this
particular typewritten statement to the
person's policy. The whole thing is a
complete travesty. I would not take part on
these Courts, because it is an insult to the
intelligence of any person to be invited by
the Minister of Labour to function on a
local committee, and then when you have
exercised your judgment to the best of your
ability and you make a decision, having had
the whole facts before you, the clerk in the
employment of the Ministry of Labour is
asked to veto the decision that we may have
arrived at or call the judgment in question.
It is a complete farce to expect employers or
workmen's representatives to come there and
waste their time. It is doing no more than
wasting their time if the decision arrived at
by the collective wisdom and judgment of
that Court goes for nothing on the word of
the clerk of the Court.
In addition to that we have got some person
in headquarters vetoing the decisions of the
Rota Committees, a person who has not
necessarily got the industrial experience that
is essential to form a capable judgment on
all these very vital and important questions
affecting the positions and the lives of the
unfortunate applicants for unemployment
benefit. In my view this whole question
needs to be reviewed and a different attitude
taken up, unless it is the deliberate policy of
the Ministry to follow this line for the purpose of disqualifying as large a number of
people as they possibly can. A good many
people are convinced at the moment that it
is the deliberate policy of the Ministry to
disallow any person if they can get the
slightest pretext for doing so. I know a
very large number of people whose minds
the Minister would have the greatest difficulty in disabusing on that particular point,
because the facts to them are exceptionally
obvious.
In connection with the Courts of Referees,
large sums of money are being spent, and I
think from the Ministry's point of view that
money is very well earned. I will grant the
fact that the employees of Frederick Street,
Amelia Street, and the different Exchanges
with which I have come in contact seem to
be sympathetic and to favour the applicant
as far as the regulations will permit them.

could absorb quite a lot of labour, doing

probably also would be of great advantage to
the Province, because you could then have a
suitable berth or landing place for
à direct mail service to England. That,
in my opinion, would be worth consideration by the Ministry of Labour. It
would create a great lot of employment, and
there are various other ways in which I
think the Ministry could undertake work of
great public advantage which would also
ease the situation considerably, because you
cannot possibly go on as you have been going
on, that is, simply paying a slight dole, a
dole that is not at all sufficient for the needs
of the people who are out of employment, the
needs of a family, as we have heard
mentioned to-day, who have only a matter of
a few shillings a week to keep two or three
or four alive. I therefore hope the Ministry
and the Government will give this matter
very serious consideration, and in the
shortest possible time undertake some of
these works in order to abate this great
catastrophe of the shortage of employment at
the present day.

Now the hon. Member also asked me a
question about the number of widows who
were turned down. As regards pre-Act
widows the total number is 1,655, and the
post-Act widows is 24, making 1,679 rejected
claims altogether. It was perfectly evident
to those who were charged with the responsibility of investigating these claims that
many of them would have to be turned down,
because the widows, who were pre-Act
widows but had no children, sent forward
their claims in large numbers for pensions.
Of course the provisions of the Act do not
permit of these pre-Act widows who have no
children receiving pensions, and, therefore,
it was inevitable that these claims would be
turned down.
The Committee will remember that while
post-Act widows were entitled to receive
benefits whether they had children or not,
pre-Act widows were not treated in the same
way, and for this reason: post-Act widows
receive pensions because of contributions
which have been paid by their husbands to
entitle them to these pensions, but in the
case of pre-Act widows they are more or less
receiving the pensions they obtain not on the
contributory basis but as a compassionate
grant. And thus there was discrimination
between those who had children and those
widows who had not, because it was considered that those widows who had children
were not in a position to earn their daily
bread, while those who were free to earn
their daily bread not having the care of
children imposed upon them could reasonably be expected to continue to do so.
The hon. Member for North Belfast (Mr.
Kyle) also asked me as to how the matter
stood as between the Free State and ourselves as regards having some reciprocity
arrangement to cover those persons who,
while living in the Free State, are employed
in Northern Ireland and vice versa. The
problem not only affects the Irish Governments but it also affects the Imperial Government as well. It is a most difficult one. All
I can say in that respect is that the officials
of our various Departments with the approval of their Ministers are continuing to see
if a way out of an admitted difficulty can be
found. Of course the trouble is that if the
rates of benefit and the conditions of benefit
and the contributions were the same in the
two areas very little difficulty would present
itself. But, as a matter of fact, while our
conditions and rates of benefit and rates
of contribution in Great Britain and in this
part of the United Kingdom are the same,
in the Free State while the contributions are
higher the rates of benefit are lower and the
conditions for the receipt of benefit less
favourable to the unemployed persons. You
see where the conditions are not the same
it is extraordinarily difficult to make arrangements which will be fair to the two
areas and to the inhabitants of the two
areas. But one is not without hope that with
the spirit of good-will on all sides an arrangement may be come to of a satisfactory
character.
The hon. Member went on to refer to the

in which my hon. Friend, the Parliamentary

touched the outside fringe of the problem,
and although everything was done to adver-

The question of Trade Boards was also
referred to, at considerable length, by my
hon. Friend. He criticised severely one of
the Chairmen of our Trade Boards, and I
must say it is the first complaint I have received in reference to either of these Gentlemen, who I have always found discharged
their difficult duties with great impartiality,
and with great fairness. Trade Board
administration is a most difficult matter,
and it cannot be carried on satisfactorily
without a great deal of good-will on the part
of all parties. The Chairman's duty is extraordinarily difficult. You get the workers
ranged on one side, and you get the employers ranged on the other side, and I
have always personally impressed upon these
gentlemen that, in the discharge of their
difficult and responsible duties, they should
endeavour to act as conciliators, rather than
arbitrators. That, I believe, they are
earnestly trying to do, but when you get
both sides very determined not to give an
inch, it sometimes becomes necessary for the
chairman to come down on one side or the
other, and probably create a certain amount
of ill-will towards himself. I must say that I
deprecate attacks being made upon these
men, who are called upon to deal with an
extraordinarily difficult problem, because I
feel they are entitled to the support of all
who desire to see happy relations existing
between capital and labour in Northern
Ireland.

The King's National Roll of Honour has
been referred to by several hon. Members.
It was mentioned by the hon. and gallant

I must say it is true that there are about
1,300 disabled ex-Servicemen still unemployed

Again, the question of ex-Servicemen on

As regards the staffs in the Labour Exchanges themselves they are practically all

I now go on to deal with a very difficult
matter, and that is whether the responsibility for dealing with poverty begins and
ends with the Government, or whether the
Guardians here are entitled to accept the
same responsibility for dealing with distress
which the Guardians in Great Britan undertake. This is a matter which I feel I ought
to be quite frank about. For many years I
have accepted some blame because having a
difficult duty to discharge myself I have
always been anxious not to make another
man's duty, which I knew to be difficult,
more difficult because of any words I uttered.
It is quite true that at the meeting of the
Belfast Board of Guardians on Tuesday of
last week, to which the hon. Member for East
Belfast (Mr. Beattie) has referred, state-
-ments were made by members of the Board
with which I am in entire disagreement.
Judging by the newspaper reports of these
speeches, it seems to me that the Guardians'
position is this; that we, the Government,
should be responsible for dealing with unemployment and paying benefit in exactly
the same way that the Imperial Government
does. That responsibility we are not prepared to shirk, but the Guardians go on, and
they say it is the duty of the Government
here to accept a responsibility beyond this,
and which no other Government anywhere in
the world has ever accepted before. Now, I
do not hold in my keeping the conscience of
the Guardians, nor do I hold their purse.
They have stautory duties to perform, as I
have statutory duties to perform, but I
cannot see that they are performing their
statutory duties when they ask that the
Government should take upon itself the entire
responsibility of dealing with destitution and
poverty in Northern Ireland no matter from
what cause it arises.

are longest out of employment, and the

Mr. DEVLIN: But, may I interrupt the
right hon. Gentleman-
Mr. ANDREWS: I was only going to
finish. The point is this, if the man can

Mr. ANDREWS: I can say in this connection that if the man can show the Department that he is genuinely seeking work he

That is common ground. The difficulty is to give effect to those desirable aims,
because it is absolutely impossible with our
two main industries in such a depressed

Firearms (Amendment) Bill.
Order for Second reading read.
siderable body of loyal law-abiding persons
who have co-operated in the public interest
with the Government in its efforts to maintain law and order, who voluntarily came
forward to help the Government in the hour
of need, and who enrolled themselves as members of the various classes of the Special
Constabulary. So long as these men were
members of the Special Constabulary they
were entitled as such to have arms in their

Motion made and Question proposed:
"That the Bill be now read a Second time."
Sir DAWSON BATES: The Bill now before
the House is a very short and simple
Measure, and may almost be regarded as
self-explanatory. The object of the Bill is to
enable a differentiation to be made in the
cases of persons who require authority to
have and carry arms, from the cases of
persons who only require to keep arms on
their premises.
I might point out at the outset that under
the existing Firearms Act only one Firearm
Certificate can be given. This certificate
entitles the holder to have in his possession
use, and also carry, a firearm, but under the
law as it now stands this can only be granted
under very strict limitations, amongst others
that the applicant has good reason for requiring such a certificate, but there are many cases
in which persons may legitimately desire to
retain arms on their premises who would not
be in a position to offer a good reason for
carrying arms, and the result is that such
persons, in view of the existing very narrow
statutory restictions upon the grant of firearms certificates, could not under the present
law be permitted to keep firearms at all, and
would, therefore, in the absence of such a
certificate be compelled to surrender weapons
which, in many cases may have been bought
out of their own money to assist the State in
the maintenance of law and order, or which
may have very high sentimental value to the
owners.
It is, no doubt, highly desirable that the
carrying of arms should be restricted as
much as possible, and it is probably due to
this fact that the Firearms Act which was
passed in 1920 limited the grant of firearms
certificates to the extent that I have
mentioned. We do not propose to alter in
any way the present restrictions upon the
grant of such certificates entitling persons to
carry arms, but it has been felt for some time
past that there should be some means of
enabling a qualified permit to be given which
will permit persons to have arms in their
possession, in their houses, without giving
them permission to carry them.
As I said before, there is a very con-
It will be appreciated by the House that
the present law governing the issue of Firearm Certificates which is within such strict
limitations would not enable the authorities
to grant certificates to carry arms in those
cases. At the same time there is no reason
why these law-abiding citizens should not be
allowed to retain their own arms while not
being permitted to carry them. Accordingly,
under Section 1, it is provided that a permit may be granted to an individual to have
arms, if in the opinion of the authorities
such permit can be granted without any
danger to the public. Such permit while, as
I said before, it will enable an individual to
have a firearm in his dwelling-house, will
not permit him to carry it outside unless he
procures a certificate under the 1920 Act.
We propose for this limited certificate to
charge a nominal fee of 2s 6d on the first
issue, and 1s on each annual renewal.
Under sub-section (5) we take power to
enable arms surrendered, seized, or found,
to be readily disposed of. There is at the
present time no specific power to deal with
surrendered arms where the owner cannot
be given a Firearm Certificate, and where
the owner will not make any arrangements
for the disposal of the arms, or where arms
are found where the owner is unknown. In
some cases also arms are seized, and where a
case may not be considered, in the view of the
Attorney-General, of sufficient importance to
prosecute, the matter can be dealt with under
this Section by an order for the destruction
of the weapons. This Section, of course, in
no way interferes with the powers of the
Court in respect of orders for the disposal of
arms.
At the present time there is no right of
appeal from the decision of the Police, and
we propose that an appeal should be given to
the Ministry of Home Affairs where an
applicant is not satisfied with the decision
that may have been taken by the police
authorities in refusing a permit. I beg to
move.
Firearms Bill-
Second Reading.
HOUSE OF COMMONS-
Mr. WM. MCMULLEN: I want to oppose
this Bill, and I do so on the ground that I
do not think it is very desirable that people
should be in possession of firearms. I have
always proceeded on the maxim that, where
there are firearms these weapons, at some
stage or other, are going to be used, and it
is always the safest course for a community
to adopt not to allow the citizens to have
arms, and then you have a guarantee that
there is going to be no trouble. The chief
objection I have to this Measure is that
there is not equitable discrimination in so
far as the people who make applications for
The
permits for firearms are concerned.
Member for East Belfast (Mr. Beattie) had
occasion to draw the attention of the House
to a case that happened in East Belfast, and
I must say we were profoundly dissatisfied
with the way in which it was handled by
the right hon. Gentleman's Department.
We have no guarantee that under this Bill,
or under any Act, it is going to be fairly
or equitably done in the future. We cannot
close our eyes to the existing state of affairs
in Northern Ireland, or to the things that
have taken place here for some number of
years past. A particular section of the community was singled out. They were called
Special Constabulary and they were armed.
We want peace so far as this particular
portion of Ireland is concerned. We do not
want to see a recrudescence of what took
place four years ago. I am inclined to think
that the Ministry will discriminate against
people of Labour sympathies, or people who,
it might be alleged, had any tendency to
revolutionary ideas. A discrimination might
be used also against people whose religion
was not acceptable to the right. hon. Gentleman's Department.
I regret to have to say that, but the facts
we have come up against, up to the present,
compel us to say frankly and candidly that
greater consideration has been given to
people of a particular political point of
view, and of a particular religious persuasion, than to people of other political
views and religious persuasions. From that
point of view, and from the other point of
view mentioned, I think it is not a very
desirable state of affairs to allow that large
section of the community to have-
Sir DAWSON BATES: To carry arms.
Mr. WM. MCMULLEN: To have or to
carry arms, or to have them in their houses,
it does not matter. If a person wants to be
a law-abiding citizen there is no necessity for
him to have firearms. If there are other members of the community who are not lawabiding, we have a responsible and adequate
Government which is capable of dealing with
these people. Under these circumstances
why anyone, outside the ordinary Police
Force, should be permitted to carry firearms,
is more than I can comprehend. If it is for
sporting purposes, I have not a great deal
of objection to offer. But I believe it is not
for sporting purposes. It refers more to
persons who want to be in possession of revolvers.
The PARLIAMENTARY SECRETARY OF
THE MINISTRY OF HOME AFFAIRS (Mr.

Sir DAWSON BATES: I may make it

Mr. WM. MCMULLEN: I think practical

This Bill will probably have the effect of

Mr. DEVLIN: I move the rejection of
this Bill. I listened to the speech of the
right hon. Gentleman, and really for the
life of me I could not understand why he
introduced this Bill at all. He offered no
justification for it, and I fail to see what
justification there is for it. In the first
place, I agree with the hon. Gentleman (Mr.
William McMullen) who has just sat down,
that no one outside the forces of the Crown
ought to be allowed to carry revolvers and
ammunition. If this were a Bill to give
authority for the issue of licences for sporting guns I would raise no objection at all,
but what does the right hon. Gentleman
mean by giving licences to people to carry
revolvers? What does a private citizen want
with a revolver? I notice a sort of interrogatory look of exclamation on the face of the
Parliamentary Secretary of the Ministry of
Home Affairs (Mr. Hanna), and when he
comes to reply I hope he will do what the
right hon. Gentleman (Sir Dawson Bates)
has not done, and that is to give some
explanation as to what civilians-private
citizens-want either with revolvers or
ammunition.
We have known the mischief that has been
created in a community by private people
being allowed to go about armed. In fact
the Government had to introduce special
legislation, including flogging, in order to put
down the performances of armed civilians, and
I do not see what reason-what possible reason-there is for introducing a Bill of this
character. I suppose I will be told that it
is for the purpose of defence, that these people
need these revolvers to defend themselves
and their property. I have given all the reasons. I am a sort of devil's advocate on this
question. I am giving all the reasons for the
introduction of this Measure, which the
Government, who have fathered the Measure,
have not given for themselves. No doubt
it may be said that this is to enable these
citizens to defend their homes and so on, but
the estimates prove that we are spending
sufficient money upon the defence of the public without constituting private individuals
guardians either of their own or of the
public interest.
The great cause of the War-if I may be
allowed to enlarge upon this subject-in my
judgment the whole cause of the European
War was that the world was too well armed.

If there had been fewer arms, if there had

Mr. DEVLIN: You do not know. I would

Mr. BEATTIE: I want to pass a few
comments on this Bill. I see it as an amending Bill to the principal Act.
Mr. SPEAKER: Does the hon. Member

Mr. BEATTIE: I will second the rejection, because I do not believe in firearms at
all, though I have tried to have a licence
granted to one of my electors. It is only
bringing the danger nearer home to give permission for firearms to be kept by a person

got possession of firearms, of rifles, and revolvers, and ammunition. It did not require
an Act of Parliament to keep them, and
there was
an Act of Parliament on the
Statute Book then forbidding them to have
them. What is the use of an Act of Parliament if you are not going to put it into
operation? In this Bill, which is an amending Bill to the 1920 Act, the Government want
the people who were armed in 1921 and 1922

I am not prepared to accept the Minister

We had a statement made here recently

Mr. GYLE: I rise to support the rejection

I remember with fear and trembling on

never required one. As my hon. Friend has

perhaps I should say a few words upon this

which was passed by the Imperial Government, in order to get back to sanity, as far

be trusted with them. (Hon. Members:
Hear, hear.) And the difficulty that has confronted the Government is to see that these

Now under that Act of 1920, when a person is found with arms for which he has no
certificate he is liable to be prosecuted. But
the House will understand that there are,
unfortunately-and with many of the observations that fell from the Benches opposite
I am in thorough agreement-at the present

down. It is only from time to time that

under the Act of 1920 are granted upon discrimination, which is not just. I know
nothing about that, for I have nothing to
say in the administration of the Act itself,
until criminal prosecutions are brought.
But I should think, from what I can see,
that it is very unlikely that there is any
unfair discrimination, either as against persons of any particular class of the community
or otherwise.
I can assure hon. Members of this, that
when the matter reaches the hands of the
police, and through them reaches my hands,
there is no discrimination. Anybody who
has been following the newspapers latelyand there has been a considerable number
of prosecutions under the Firearms Act, 1920
-can easily satisfy himself that there has
not been any discrimination. Any person
who has been discovered without a certificate, in possession of arms, has been prosecuted, no matter what section of the community or what political party he belongs to.
Where do we stand at the present time?
As I said there is, undoubtedly, a very large
quantity of arms in the hands of persons
who cannot be trusted with them, and the
hon. Member for East Belfast (Mr. Beattie)
appears to think that this Act is designed to enable further persons to become possessed of arms. But I can assure
him that this is not so. This Act is designed
with exactly the opposite intention because,
just as people who have arms which they
wish to make an illegal use of will not disclose these arms or apply to the authorities
for a proper certificate, so persons, who may
be trusted with arms and who are reputable
citizens, are also afraid to apply for a certificate under the Firearms Act, 1920, because
they are afraid they may not get it. And
the result of that is this; these arms continue to be in the country, and people continue to evade the law, continue to evade
taking out certificates or permits. And the
Government has come to the conclusion,
after investigating the administration of this
Firearms Act, 1920, that it would be much
better in addition to having a certificate
enabling a man to have and carry arms which
is the certificate he gets under the Act of
1920 to have another certificate, namely, a
certificate or permit, as it is called, to have
arms, that is to have them in the house.
What the Government hope and what the
police authorities hope and what I hope
is this: if this Bill becomes an
Act of Parliament that a great number
of persons who would not be granted
a full certificate under the Act of 1920 will
come in and take out this permit in order to
have arms in their own house without
having liberty to carry them, and I hope and
I believe that the result of this Bill when it
becomes an Act of Parliament, will be that
a great quantity of arms which are at present
in the country will be located by the police.
The owners of them will come in and ask for
a permit under this Bill which is now before
the House, and I think there will be no
difficulty in their doing that, because the
House will readily understand that there are
a great many men who will be granted a permit to have a revolver or some weapon in his
house who would not be granted liberty to
carry it. These people will come in and ask
for permits. If they are people who can be
reasonably trusted to have a weapon in their
house, then they will be granted their permit. I hope in the course of some monthsat any rate in the course of some twelve
months-we will be able to schedule a very
large number of arms which are in the
country under these permits granted under
this Bill. If that be so, this Bill will be all
to the good.
The Government have no intention of
issuing indiscriminate permits under this
Bill. It is not designed for that purpose. It
is really designed for the purpose of locating
arms at present in the country by giving this
mure limited firearms permit than that
which is given by the Act of 1920, and also
giving further notice to all and sundry that
if they do not come in and take out either
a full certificate under the Act of 1920, or a
limited permit under this Bill, that they are
liable to be prosecuted, and will be prosecuted so far as it is possible for the police to
discover these arms. Now, I do not believe
that under this Bill we will locate all the
arms, unfortunately, which are in the hands
of private individuals in Northern Ireland,
because no matter what Act of Parliament
you pass a large number of people will still

should not be in the hands of the police.
After all, a police officer, however broadminded and tolerant he may be, has certain
prejudices regarding people, and he generally
acts on the advice of his subordinates. In a
country district a policeman might say to
himself, "this man attends Orange meetings,
and I do not know whether it would be safe
to give him a licence." I think the civil
magistrates would be the proper authority.
Most of them have been appointed by the

the persons to whom it would be safe to issue

Mr.
BARBOUR: As this Bill, which
originated in another place, has already received very detailed attention there, it may
not be necessary to give more than an outline of its main provisions, with which hon.
Members are probably already fairly
familiar. In brief, it may be said that this
Bill brings the law relating to Ancient Monuments to the level of that attained in Great
Britain by the Ancient Monuments Act of
1913, which did not apply to Ireland. In one
or two minor points where experience has
disclosed the defects in the British Act, we
have taken the opportunity to improve
Pollock, Rt. Hon. Hugh MacDowell
Robb, John Hanna
TELLER FOR THE NOES-
Captain Dixon.
machinery. The Bill is divided into four
parts. The first deals with the guardianship
of ancient monuments and gives power to the
Ministry of Finance to accept such guardianship from the owner, and having accepted
such guardianship to maintain the monument. The Ministry, I may state here, is
already in possession or guardianship of some
24 ancient monuments in Northern Ireland
whose charge it took over from the Board of
Works, Dublin, on the setting up of Northern
Ireland.
Part 2 deals with the acquisition of monuments, and gives power to accept complete
possession by purchase, gift, devise
bequest.
or
Ancient Monuments Bill- HOUSE OF COMMONS.
Second Reading.
[Mr. Barbour]
Part 3 deals with protection. This is
arranged in various grades.
As
Clause 5 permits the Ministry to make a
list of monuments, the preservation of which
is deemed of national importance. The inclusion of a monument in such list has the
effect of preventing the owner from taking
action likely to affect the monument
seriously, without giving notice to the Ministry of Finance. It does not prevent him
from taking such action, but merely ensures
that the Ministry shall be notified.
wilful vandals are probably not numerous,
it is expected that this provision for a notification will open up communications between the owner and the Ministry, and allow
opportunity of dissuasion from any injudicious action. However, if this course is not
likely to be of avail, and the monument is
of sufficient importance, the Ministry may
make a Preservation Order placing the
monument under its protection.
(Clause 6) When such Order comes into
force, alteration cannot be effected without
the Ministry's consent. In order to prevent
any fears of wanton interference with the
property of individuals under this clause, we
have inserted a provision in Clause 6 (3)
that Preservation Orders made by the
Ministry must be laid before Parliament
and may be voided by a simple vote of
either House.
Under Clause 7 it is provided that if while
a Preservation Order is in force the Monument, owing to the neglect of the person in
charge, is liable to fall into decay the
Ministry may take over the guardianship.
Provision is made by clause 9 for the payment of compensation for any act involving
interference with private rights of property
under any provision of the Act and the
assessment will proceed on the lines familiar
in the case of acquisition of lands for public
purposes under the Acquisition of Land
(Assessment of Compensation) Act.
Part 4 of the Act contains a number of
miscellaneous provisions. These include the
power to receive voluntary contributions for
the maintenance of any special monument
(Clause 10).
Power is also given to County Councils, including the Councils of County Boroughs, to
accept guardianship or ownership of monuments.
Under Clause 13 an Advisory Committee is
set up containing representatives of the leading learned bodies associated with the study
of antiquities in Northern Ireland. This
body will advise the Ministry generally in
the administration of the Act.
Clause 18 is intended to ensure the
reporting of the finding of archæological
bodies to the Advisory Committee, the intention being that local museums shall have
an opportunity to arrange purchase in such
cases.
It is expected that this system will ensure
that the finder of such object will be better
informed as to the value of his find and so be
able to secure a fair price, and that the
circumstances of the finding, which are very
important for the advancement of knowledge,
will be duly recorded.
Clause 18 (4) embodies a working arrangement which has been entered into with the
British Treasury enabling the application of
Clause 18 to objects which come within the
category of treasure trove, provided that the
Crown rights have been waived. Generally
speaking, hon. Members will, I hope, agree
that this Bill will enable the Government to
take more effective steps than have hitherto
been possible for the preservation of the
more outstanding monuments of the past in
our Province. As the law stands at present,
the owner is absolutely under no restraint in
Ireland, which in this respect has fallen, it
may be said, below the standard of the whole
civilized world.
The Bill generally gives the State power
to intervene, always giving compensation
for any interference with the rights of private property and providing for the supervision of Parliament. I beg to move.

It is a historical matter. A remarkable state
of affairs is that though this gentleman was
born, executed, and buried within a distance
of one hundred yards from High Street, the
citizens of Belfast know practically nothing
about that. A large number of people who
have got connections with Ireland are very
much interested in the period associated
with the United Irishmen. I believe it would
add to the attraction of the Province if the
Government could see their way to take these
matters up and act in a spirit of impartiality. I notice that in Government publications they are not manifesting that spirit of
impartiality.
I had an opportunity recently of reading
the foreword in the Ulster Year Book, and I
took the trouble one Sunday evening to confirm or contradict the historical statements
contained in that foreword. I took down
Protestant authors for the purpose. I took
down the work of a gentleman who has written
a history of the Irish Presbyterian Churchthe Rev. Mr. Reid. I took down the references
written by Protestant clergymen in connection with the United Irishmen period, the
battles of Ballynahinch and Ednavaddy in
County Antrim, and I want to say that the
foreword I have referred to was written in a
spirit of partiality and did not necessarily
represent the facts. I think many of these
things could be dealt with with great benefit
to the Province, because those incidents lose
all their bitterness when a number of years
have passed away. They simply become a
question of historical moment or historical
importance. I would like to see this Province rich in folk lore and historical associations, and for that reason I welcome the
Measure. If I have any regret at all it is
that the Bill does not go far enough to enable the Government to do some of those
things of which I have spoken. (Hon. Members: Hear, hear.)

ORDERS OF THE DAY.
THE BUDGET.
Statement by the Minister of Finance.
Motion made and question proposed:
"That this House approves the proposals of
the Government for meeting the financial
requirements of the year."-(Mr. Pollock).
The MINISTER OF FINANCE (Mr. Pollock who was received with general cheers):
During the financial year which has recently
ended, several events of outstanding
financial interest to our State deserve more
than a mere passing comment.
UNEMPLOYMENT INSURANCE.
The first and unquestionably the most
important of these matters arose in connection with the critical position of our Local
Unemployment Insurance Fund. The difficulties of that problem have been the subject
of so much discussion in this House and
elsewhere that it is unnecessary to recapitulate them in detail. It is sufficient to say
that the burden of the accumulated deficit
of the Fund had become so heavy at the
period of the presentation of my Budget a
year ago that I foresaw that unless some
arrangement could be made with Britain it
would be impossible to continue the payment
of benefits, or at any rate the benefits would
be greatly restricted.
As the result of protracted negotiations
with the British Government, I am happy
to say that this calamity has been averted.
The terms of the arrangement have been
repeated so often here that I need not restate them except to say that, notwithstanding the important relief which has resulted
from the arrangement, we are still left with
a serious financial responsibility if we are
to maintain our Fund in a state of equality
with the British Insurance Fund.
ISSUE OF ULSTER LOAN.
Another matter to which I think we are
entitled to make special reference is the
issue of our first Ulster Loan. Its objects
were mainly to provide the necessary funds
to lend to Local Authorities for various
works of public utility, and it is an encouraging feature of the issue that such a
large proportion was taken up by local interests, as well as in the London market.
This is a very encouraging evidence of the
confidence in the security and credit of the
Ulster Government.
ULSTER SAVINGS CERTIFICATES.
I wish also to touch upon the Ulster
Savings Certificates. The continued success
of the isues of these Certificates offers eloquent testimony to the thrifty habits of our
people. At the end of the year £2,183,000
had been invested by about 25,000 people.
The repayments that have been made since
the isue was started have amounted to
£350,000, so that it will be seen that the
scheme is really something in the nature of
a small Government Savings Bank system
which is being carried on in the interests of
people of small means in the community.
On the expiration of the current issue,
which will probably be about the month of
August, I have decided to continue the issue
of these Certificates but without the British
guarantee. The success of our first loan, to
which I have referred a moment or two ago,
proves that the security of our own Government is perfectly ample and unimpeachable,
and I have come to the conclusion that the
balance of the British Government security
unexhausted to the amount of something
over one million should not be used for purposes of short-term securities, but should
more properly be held in reserve for any
financial contingency that may arise where
long-dated loans may be desirable. I am
sure the House will appreciate the reasons
which have actuated me in continuing the
Finance Minister's Statement. 1372
The Budget-
HOUSE OF COMMONS.
[Mr. Pollock]
Certificates under the full guarantee of the
Northern Government.
LOANS GUARANTEE.
con-
Advantage still continues to be taken of
these facilities, which have already been of
great assistance to several industries, notably
in the case of shipbuilding, where it is estimated that approximately 8,000 men
tinue to be employed under these Acts. Between four and five million has been already
guaranteed, and in order to make provision
for any applications that may arise, this
House has passed a recent Act increasing
the maximum to £7,000,000. The rates of
interest on loans under our guarantee compare favourably with the British rates, and
I need hardly assure the House how allimportant the future of this scheme is in
the interests not only of the industries of
our Province but of unemployment.
DOUBLE TAXATION.
Announcement has already been made by
the Chancellor of the Exchequer and the
Minister of Finance of the Free State that
an arrangement has been reached whereby
deductions of double Income Tax will be
obviated. This will be of great advantage
to many people in Northern Ireland where
our investors laboured under a distinct
grievance. For some time past we have
urged upon the British authorities the hardship resulting from the old system. The
are
agreement and I am happy to say it has
now become an accomplished fact-gives
complete relief from Free State Tax, either
by repayment or by cancellation of assessment to people who
domiciled in
Northern Ireland. In the case of persons
domiciled or resident both in Northern Ireland and the Free State the agreement
provides an equitable method of assessment
which will avoid causing hardship.
TRADE BALANCE.
I come now for a moment to our trading
conditions. It is a truism in economics to
assert that in these modern and utilitarian
days the financial stability of a State must
in the end depend on the character and
volume of its trading.
No country can continue ad infinitum to
buy and use more goods than it can pay for,
just as in the case of an individual, and as
the payment must be made in the form of
other goods it follows that a densely populated country like Britain must either work
to produce goods for payment or ultimately
starve.
It will be of interest, therefore, to examine
how our small State-as a unit distinct from
the Kingdom-fares in this respect.
From the figures that have been carefully
collected and compiled by the Department
over which my right hon. Friend (Mr.
Barbour) beside me presides, I find that the
imports into the Six Counties for the last
calendar year-I say calendar year as
distinct from our financial year-amounted
to round about £60,000,000 whilst the value
of the exports was £59,500,000-a curious
approximation of equality—showing
apparent debit balance of £500,000.
an
But when account is taken of invisible
items-items such as the investments
Northern Ireland people have in Great
Britain and other matters which I need not
enter into I am satisfied that there is a
final balance in our favour. (Hon. Members:
Hear, hear.) I am making no comparison
with other countries on this subject, but it
appears to me from this factor that given
favourable trade conditions we can face the
future with confidence. (Hon. Members:
Hear, hear.)
I come now to the expenditure of last year
and a statement of the revenue of the Province available to meet it. First, in regard
to Expenditure, it will be remembered that
full details of transferred expenditure are
given in the Estimates which were investigated item by item by the Committee of this
House. The Reserved Expenditure has
similarly been carefully examined by the
Members of the Imperial House of Commons, and, therefore, it will only be
necessary to summarise the figures rather
than go into minute detail and to make
those deductions which are necessary in
order to enable us to appreciate their sig.
nificance.

EXPENDITURE, 1925-26.
The total expenditure of the Province
over which our local Parliament has
control amounted during last year to
£8,357,000, of which sum the amount spent

previous Estimates submitted in respect of

the actual requirements of the Government were £489,000 less than the Estimate. That is, the actual expenditure
during the year was the sums I have

only half of the sum voted for Unemployment Relief Grant was required or was
actually spent, and also a reduction of
approximately £100,000 in the cost of education. These are the sums that account for
the variations between Estimates and Expenditure.
The balance of our Transferred Expenditure is represented by what are known as
Consolidated Fund Services which amounted

RESERVED EXPENDITURE.
Having dealt with the expenditure over
which we have control in this House, 1
come to what is known as Reserved Expenditure, that is that which is made by the
Imperial Parliament in the conduct of the
services in Northern Ireland over which
they and not we have control.
The expenditure controlled and incurred
by the Imperial authority amounted last
year to £1,719,000, which is £37,000 less than
the original estimate. This expenditure
includes the Post Office service, the cost of
collecting the different reserved taxes-that
is Customs and Excise and Income Tax, and
so on; Pensions of the Royal Irish Constabulary, which still continue to be a heavy item
of the expenses in which we are involved;
Judges and Supreme Court, Land Purchase
Commission, Civil Superannuation—that is
the superannuation of those Civil Servants
who have retired from the Imperial Service
but who carried on work in Ireland for
Ulster; and minor items of a miscellaneous
character. These comprise the expenditure
which the British Government have made
on our behalf.
The total of transferred and reserved
expenditure is, therefore, £10,076,000.
TRANSFERRED REVENUE.
Having dealt shortly with the expenditure which we made last year through both
avenues I come now to the question of
revenue which was collected in order to
meet that expenditure.
Now let us see how the revenue has come
in. The receipts of revenue over which
we have local control totalled last

There is not anything of special significance in regard to the different items of
revenue except perhaps in regard to the
returns of Entertainment Duty and Motor
Vehicles taxation. These, I may mention,
continue to show a satisfactory increase.
Four years ago the Entertainment Duty
amounted to £81,000. Last year the yield
was £105,000. As hon. Members know I
have had considerable pressure brought
upon me to remove this duty-(Hon. Members; Hear, hear)-but in view of its
importance to the revenue I have, after careful and prolonged investigation, come to the
conclusion that any relaxation of the charges
cannot safely be contemplated at the present
time. (Hon. Members: Hear, hear.)
With regard to the Motor Vehicles Duty,
it is significant that in a period of three
years the revenue from this Bource has
risen from £204,000 to £335,000. This is a
very remarkable increase and is a particularly interesting evidence of the approach
of the motor age.
RESERVED REVENUE.
Having dealt with this revenue which we
impose and collect, I now come to a very
important section, that is the reserved
revenue which is imposed and which is
collected by the Imperial Government. These
comprise Customs and Excise, and the Inland
Revenue Taxes. These sources of revenue
yielded a total of £7,588,000 against an estimate
of £7,825,000. In addition to these, Post Office
receipts amounted to £810,000 against an
estimate of £815,000, which, I might mention,
was subsequently revised to £810,000 owing
to the continued depression of trade. The
Post Office found the condition of trade had
reduced the returns, and curiously enough
their revised Estimate which was made some
months after the start of the financial
year was exactly corresponding with the outcome of £810,000, showing the great accuracy
of these highly-trained and specialised
officers in carrying out their duties.
In these figures there will be found some
food for thought, and I therefore feel
tempted to pause here for a few moments
and examine them in some detail as I feel
they will be found of considerable interest
to the House and, possibly, to the community.
CUSTOMS AND EXCISE.
I take first Customs and Excise as to the
duty upon spirits. The Estimate for the year
for spirits amounted to £1,480,000; the actual
yield showed a deficit of £188,000, that is,
£188,000 less than the estimate made by the
Customs and Excise people. It may offer
some comfort to those whose laudable desire
for the restriction of the use of alcoholic
liquor has frequently found expression in
this House if I offer some comparative
figures of the consumption as apart from
revenue of spirits during the last decade.
The actual consumption of spirits, which
include whisky, brandy, gin, and rum, etc.,
amounted in 1925-26 to 350,000 gallons. This
shows an average of .27 or, roughly, onequarter of a gallon per head of the population-two pints, I suppose that is. In the
year 1914 the consumption in Northern Ireland of strong spirit was .72, or, roughly, threequarters of a gallon per head, so that since
the outbreak of the Great War the quantity
of spirits consumed in Ulster has diminished
by two-thirds. Whether that decrease in
consumption marks a change in the drinking
habits of the people, or is the result of what
some people claim to be the very excessive
rate of duty on spirits, is something which
must be left to individual opinion.
Mr. CRAWFORD: Hear, hear.
Finance Minister's Statement. 1376
The Budget-
HOUSE OF COMMONS.
Mr. POLLOCK: I cannot dogmatise upon
the subject. The facts are there, that there
has been a most extraordinary decrease in
the use of spirits by the people of Northern
Ireland in ten years. There is another item
that perhaps may be of interest, and that is
the consumption of spirits in Northern Ireland is almost exactly half of the quantity
consumed in Scotland, and practically equal
to the English rate of consumption. The
yield of the duty on. spirits in Northern Ireland last year was almost exactly £1 per
head of the population.
Now I come to beer. In regard to beer, the
Estimate a year ago was £890,000, and in
this article of drink there is also a deficit of
£63,000. The receipts of the year indicate a
consumption of 7,443,000 gallons, which is
equivalent to 5.8 gallons, not far from 6
gallons per head of the population. By contrast the consumption of beer in Britain is
18 gallons per head against barely 6 gallons
in our Province. I do not know whether
that may be considered a virtue on the part
of our people, but that fact remains that we
only consume one-third the quantity of beer
that our fellow citizens can get through in
Great Britain.
Tobacco, with a yield of £920,000, shows a
deficit of £24,000 on the Estimate. The consumption of this article in Northern Ireland
is about 2 million pounds in weight, equal
to 1 pounds per head of the population.
I do not profess to any great theoretical
knowledge of economics, but I took the
trouble of finding out roughly how much
actual expenditure of money this revenue
from spirits, beer and tobacco represents,
and I think I am not far wrong in saying
it is about £3 15s per head of our population. That is to say that, taking the average,
the people of Northern Ireland-men, women
and children-spend £3 15s each in respect
of spirits, beer and tobacco.
The use of tea has remained practically
unchanged, the consumption representing
8,700,000 pounds, which is not far from 7
pounds per head of the people. On the
other hand, sugar is slightly increased by a
sum of £14,000, the consumption of this
article equalling 68 pounds per head.
INLAND REVENUE.
Now, having left Customs and Excise, I
come to Inland Revenue, which comprise under
that head all forms of income tax and super
tax. The returns under this head show a
very serious falling-off, and especially in
Income Tax which is £280,000 less, but this
has been offset by unexpected increases in
Corporation Profits Tax, and also in arrears
of E.P.D., as it was called, Excess Profits
Duty, so that the total return from this
Department has varied to the extent of an
increase of £81,000. I might mention that
the assessment of certain concerns to Excess
Profit Duty necessitated consequential rebates of Income Tax, so that the drop
in the yield of the latter tax is due to this
cause and gives no reason for apprehension.
This explanation I have offered shows
that Income Tax in reality is being maintained at the normal standard, which under
the very depressed industrial and commercial condition of the country at the present
time is something, I think, for which we
may congratulate ourselves. (Hon. Members:
Hear, hear). We need not expect to get
much further revenue from E.P.D. or Corporation Profits Duty, as these are expiring
taxes, and we are only relying upon the
remnants for any small revenue which may
come in.
In addition to the transferred and reserved
revenues through the Imperial Government
there are items of non-tax revenue amounting to £986,000. Included in this amount is
that very considerable item, the Land
Purchase Annuities, amounting to £665,000.
and, of course, hon. Members know this does
not vary from year to year more than a few
pounds. It is significant-and I hope hon.
Members who represent the farming community will take note of this-that the arrears
of these annuities at 31st March only
amounted to £9,000, or about 1 per cent. of
the total. (Hon. Members: Hear, hear.)
Whether this close payment may be regarded
as an evidence of the condition of the farming community, I am not prepared to dogmatise on the subject, but at any rate from
the point of view of revenue it can be regarded as eminently satisfactory.
POST OFFICE.
I have already given the House the figures
for the Post Office. I will repeat them; they
are:-

Last year I can recall I was able to remark
upon the very welcome fall in the deficit
on the Post Office. I am sure hon. Members
can appreciate that there is no better indexat anyrate it is one important and valuable
index of the condition of trade, and, therefore, the deficit I have spoken of, £53,000,
must be to some extent regarded as a reflex
of the depressed condition of our principal
industries. Nevertheless, I am pleased to
think that even this sum of £53,000, large
as it is, is much less than the deficits which
were being experienced some few years back.
Therefore, while we deplore the fact that the
Finance Minister's Statement. 1378
The Budget-
18 MAY 1926
deficit is £53,000, we may keep up our hearts
and take courage, and probably when commercial and industrial conditions return to
normal we shall be able to wipe off the
deficit and possibly return to the conditions
that exist in Great Britain.
The White Papers, which explain the financial relations between Northern Ireland and
Great Britain, show that the Treasury experts put the deficit for 1919-20, which was
the year of transfer, at £95,000. Actually in
our first year of separate existence the deficit amounted to no less than £104,000.
OTHER REVENUE.
We received from Church Temporalities
£18,000, while from dividends on our Capital
Fund Investments and interest on advances
to the Unemployment Insurance Fund, the
return was £303,000. And finally, we received
as a grant-in-aid from the Imperial Government a sum of £1,134,000 as a grant for
Special Constabulary. The result of all this,
the revenue on the one side and the expenditure on the other, is that we made a contribution to the Imperial Service of a sum of
£2,600,000. Adding up all these figures, the
resulting balance as between the revenue and
expenditure for last year is a surplus of
£50,081.
With such a favourable balance, under the
conditions, I mean, small though it may be,
some may ask me "Why have you made such
an outcry as you have been doing on the necessity for economy, and why have you been
making such searches for new sources of revenue?"
But I would remind hon. Members that
had it not been for the contribution of
£685,000 from the Imperial Treasury as a
grant-in-aid towards the equalisation of the
Unemployment Insurance Fund we should
have been faced with a heavy deficit indeed,
and we must also bear in mind in discussing
these matters that were it not for the continuing assistance from the same source, we
should, undoubtedly, have been compelled to
discontinue or drastically reduce Unemployment Insurance Benefit for this year.
As I have said earlier, this calamity has
been averted, but the people of this Province
have little idea of the anxious days and
nights spent by the Members of the Government before agreement was reached in respect of this great problem.
1926-27.
I now leave the last year behind and come
forward to this year that lies ahead. Last
year was certainly not free from anxiety. I
pass on to offer a forecast to the House of the
expenditure which is expected to be necessary to carry on the services of the State
during the year upon which we have recently
entered, and also of the revenue which will
be necessary to meet the expenditure.
ESTIMATES OF TRANSFERRED EXPENDITURE.
The book of Estimates which has been gone
through with meticulous care, if I may so, by
the Members of this House, contains full information in regard to the different headings
under which the expenditure is expected to
be made, and I do not propose, therefore, to
enter upon a detailed explanation of variations in comparison with last year.
CONSOLIDATED FUND SERVICES.
The first principal items of expenditure
come under the head of Consolidated Fund
Services. These amount to £642,000, which is
£38,000 less than the expenditure in last year,
1925-26. The decrease is due to the fact that
we do not anticipate such heavy temporary
borrowings this year. These services consist
of the salaries of the Speakers of the Senate
and House of Commons, the Comptroller and
Auditor-General, etc., also interest on temporary borrowings and the Sinking Fund
charges, which have been established for the
various purposes set out in detail in the
Finance Accounts. No country can be expected to progress or show signs of progress
unless it makes full provision by a Sinking
Fund for the debt which is in existence.
There are still some expenses to be met
arising out of the last General Election, and
a small provision is made for any byelection which may be necessary during the
year.

GRANTS.

Local Authorities Grants, amounting to a

Unemployment Relief Grants.

grants towards their local expenditure in respect of their Education Committee work
have a tendency to increase from year to

SOCIAL AND EDUCATION SERVICES.
Under the head of Social and Educational
Services we have-
Old Age Pensions, amounting to over
£1,000,000:
National Health Insurance;
Unemployment Insurance;
Widows &c. Pensions; and
Education, apart from the Grants to
which I have just referred.
These services amount to £4,722,000, showing a very substantial increase on the Estimates as compared with last year of about
£650,000. This large increase is due to the
provision which has had to be made as a
result of the modification of the Thrift Disqualification Clauses of the Old Age Pensions
Acts, the new Widows' and Orphans' Pensions, but, as the House will no doubt appreciate, chiefly to the heavy burden of unemployment.
POLICE, PRISONS AND LAW.
When we come to the Section which covers
Police, Prisons and Law we reach a total
expenditure of about £1,072,000.
In comparison with last year, these Estimates
show a decrease of not far from £1,000,000,
and the House will readily understand that
this arises from the disbandment of the
Special Constabulary Force. There still remains a special expenditure for this service
which, as the House will recall, relates to
the winding up of the "A" Specials as well
as the continuing expenditure for the "B"
Force, which is being reorganised upon a
definite future basis.
EXPENDITURE UNDER SECTION 34.
It is expected that under Section 34 of
the Government of Ireland Act the expenditure on public buildings, for which the
Imperial Authority is responsible, will
aggregate close on £200,000. I can only
regret that the amount is not larger, because if it had been larger the presumption
is that the construction of these works
would have proceeded with greater expedition.
Mr. DEVLIN: Could the right hon.
Gentleman
say what these buildings
include?
Mr. POLLOCK: Yes, there is no difficulty
in answering my hon. Friend's question.
The public buildings include the work that
will be carried on at the Parliament Buildings, a part of the work that will be undertaken at the Law Courts, and any smaller
matters for which the Imperial Government
is responsible. The administrative offices are
chiefly comprised in the Parliament Buildings.
Although the outlay is made by us we
secure repayment from the Imperial
Authority, and of course are dependent
upon the Treasury for the Estimate which
we present. Although the amount is estimated at £200,000, we hope that the prosecution of these great works will be
expedited sufficiently to warrant a much
heavier outlay.
COSTS OF ADMINISTRATION.
The cost of administering the general
services of the Province locally, apart from
those which I have just detailed, I estimate
at about £530,000. Included in this sum,
however, there are items for works and
buildings, travelling expenses, stationery
and printing charges, and a number of
miscellaneous sub-heads of great variety.
Some purely temporary services are also included, such as the taking of the Census,
which is non-recurrent, but without going
into great detail, I may say that the real
administrative costs, viz., the salaries of
our public servants, impose a charge on our
revenue of something just over half that sum;
that is to say, about 3 per cent. of our total
expenditure. I am advised that this outlay
compares favourably from the point of view
of economy with services in other States, so
far as any calculations are comparable.
These figures that I have given amount, as
I have said, to £7,547,000, being the total
expected expenditure on supply services
under our own control.

The Estimate of the expenditure on this

REVENUE DEPARTMENTS.
Under the head of revenue collection is
the cost of Customs and Excise Duties, In-.
land Revenue Taxes, &c., and the Estimate
for these services is £174,000, which is a
slight increase of £3,000 over last year's
expenditure. This is really part of a
general rise in the cost of revenue collection
which is common to Great Britain.
LAND PURCHASE COMMISSION.
The Estimate for this service is £266,000,
an increase of £22,000 over the actual outlay of last year. This service is still
carried on by the Imperial authorities, and
is not under our control. This increase is
due entirely to the passing of the recent
Land Purchase Act, which will, when fully
matured, transform the vast majority of
Unbought Tenants into freehold land owners.
R.I.C. PENSIONS.
This very heavy liability varies little from
the expenditure of last year. The amount
involved is £246,500, a decrease of £2,500.
This charge is a statutory obligation which
we are bound to meet, and the consolation
that we have in providing pensions for these
retired servants is that the amount will
gradually decrease as the years pass by, and
ultimately lapse. How long it will be before
that time arrives I have no idea. The
Pensions Increase Measure, which this House
passed last week, has necessitated a slight
increase in this provision over the sum which
would otherwise have been necessary; that
is to say, increasing the pensions of those
old servants, whose salaries were small when
the pensions were generally determined, and
whose pensions were not in keeping with the
present cost of living.
CIVIL SUPERANNUATION.
Under this head there is a liability this
year of £53,000. This is to provide for the
pensions of Civil Servants who have retired
in the past, and are still living, and for
whose pensions we are liable.
JUDICIARY AND SUPREME COURT.
Under this head is included the Consolidated Fund expenditure on the salaries and
pensions of Judges, etc., and the ordinary
cost of the Supreme Court. The total
amounts to £85,000, and as it varies only
slightly from year to year, calls for no
particular comment.
MINOR SERVICES.
These include a proportion of the costs of
the following Imperial Departments :-
Home Office,
Treasury,
Paymaster-General,
Exchequer and Audit Department,
Civil Service Commission,
Government Chemist,
National Debt Office;
and also for Works, Stationery, and other
services performed for the Reserved Departments. Although provision is not now made
under this head for the Council of Ireland
Services, the reduction which is implied has been offset by temporary increases
in works services, of which the principal
items are the re-building of the Custom
House, which threatened to fall; alterations
to Belfast Post Office, and the erection of
a new post office at Strabane. The cost of
all these minor services is estimated at
£78,000.
The total, therefore, of all these Departments of expenditure, both reserved and
transferred, is £9,967,000.
I have thought it necessary to give rather
fuller explanations of this reserved expenditure, in order that the House may be advised
exactly of the nature of the charges.
REVENUE.

Or shall we say roughly, for the purpose of
