-(Mr. Barbour.)
:
Dr. MORRISON (who was received with
cheers) I would like to say a word or two in
regard to this Bill. It has been my misfortune to be absent from the House and not to
have an opportunity of intervening in the
discussion on it, a circumstance which I very
much regretted. I read a summary of the
speech of the hon. Member for West Belfast
(Mr. William McMullen) in yesterday's
paper, and, while it was very short, I have no
doubt that there were a good deal of
his suggestions with which I agree and also
many matters with which I would have disagreed had I been present. He made reference to Goldsmith, and I am sure he deplored what I consider is to the shame of
Ireland, that this most distinguished literary
man has had no recognition from his fellowcountrymen-practically no recognition. I
know that there is a statute to his memory
in front of Trinity College, and that that
ancient seat of learning took advantage of the
fact that he had been studying medicine there
for one or two years to claim him as one of
their students. It is a fact, however, that his
home is being used as a cattle shed, and that
there is no lasting memorial to the work of
this distinguished Irishman, who was associated with some of the ablest men of his day
in the literary clubs in London. He was an
associate of Burke, of Sir Joshua Reynolds, of
Dr. Johnson, and of Boswell, the most select
club probably in the world, and the most distinguished men, perhaps, in the British
Empire at that time, and the fact that he
lies now in an unknown grave in London is
a terrible calamity for the credit of this
island of ours. I think no better purpose
could be served if this Bill would allow the
right hon. Gentleman (Mr. Pollock) who is
Minister of Finance, and who has in future
to deal with these questions, to make arrangements with the Free State by which some
national memorial could be erected in
memory of this distinguished Irishman.
1469 Ancient Monuments Bill-

19 MAY 1926
Third Reading.
Mr. POLLOCK: Where?
Dr. MORRISON: That is a matter for discussion and agreement. He is an honour to
Ireland North and South, and every rightthinking man would claim to have the privilege of perpetuating his memory. The hon.
Member (Mr. William McMullen) referred to
modern history-in fact the hon. Gentleman
is a modernist. I think he referred to the
monuments to Dr. Cooke and Dr. Hanna.
This Bill is intended to deal with ancient
monuments, and I would like to refer briefly
not to the memories and monuments of men
whom some of us remember-because I myself
remember Dr. Hugh Hanna-but to events
that took place probably 1,500 years ago. It
is those things which I think this Bill is intended to look after and to perpetuate. I
have the privilege of living in the Bann
Valley, which in my opinion, and in the
opinion of others well qualified to judge, is
the garden of Ulster. Through the Bann
Valley runs the River Bann.
Mr. DEVLIN: Hear, hear. (Laughter.)
Dr. MORRISON: I am glad to think that
the hon. Member for West Belfast (Mr.
Devlin) has improved his geography, because
when the Drainage Bill was under discussion it seemed to me that he wanted
a lesson or two.
Be that as it may, the Bann was formerly
the main avenue by which the enemies of
Ulster found access to the heart of the
Province. Anything that was worth raiding
on the banks of the Bann, and from the
Lough, they raided. In my own dispensary
district there was an abbey at the southern
end of the Bann-the abbey of Agivey. This
was raided by the Norsemen in the tenth
century, and in order to protect many valuables from these marauders a gold cup was
carried away by one of the monks and
buried in a field. In 1833 this valuable cup
was discovered, and it appears that it was
manufactured in the fifth century-1,500 years
ago. It is now preserved and kept for safety
in the safe of the parish church. I think
that that cup should be kept in the National
Museum of Ireland or in the Ulster National
Museum.
Further north was the monastery or abbey
of Macosquin. There is an ancient burying
ground there, and it was used by Protestants
as a burying-ground until it ceased to function. It is a very old ground, and the
Protestants of Ulster buried there since 1620
-the date of the Plantation. I have been in
it frequently. It was the site of an old abbey
-the abbey of Macosquin. A remarkable
thing in connection with the abbey or graveyard is a beautiful Celtic cross, which was
probably produced in the eighth century. It
was used as a pillar attached to the gate leading into the graveyard. The humiliating
position in which it was placed was recognised, and a voluntary effort on the part of
those who were interested in relics like that
enabled sufficient money to be produced to
take it from that dishonourable position in
which it was placed and erect it in the centre
of the graveyard, where it is now admired
and will be preserved by coming generations.
In a corner of that graveyard there is an
old baptismal font, probably 1,500 years old,
and there is an old pathway to it by which
members of the faith to which this
monument originally belonged go to
respect it and to treat it with the
reverence which they customarily show to
anything associated with their religion. This
graveyard is now in the hands of the district
council, and while they take care of it I think
it should be a national duty to preserve
things like that that are priceless and perpetuate them for the use of coming generations. (Hon. Members: Hear, hear). You
have the Tourists' Association, of which I
have heard something during the discussions
on some of the Estimates. When people
come from Portrush and Portstewart they
drive to the Salmon Leap, the Cutts at Castleroe, but if these things were properly advertised they would go along past Castleroe to
this old abbey at Agivey, and the abbey or
graveyard of Macosquin. These are old
historic places with scenery equal to any
scenery that can be seen in County Wicklow,
where you have such delightful places as the
Vale of Avoca, Glendalough, and the Powerscourt demesne.
If these things were placed before the
public in a handbook they would find them
more interesting than anything they could
find in Scotland or England. If we preserved
the valuable things we possess in Ireland we
would have not only beautiful landscapes
but most interesting relics which we could
inspect and admire at our leisure when we
are on holidays. In connection with ancient
monuments I should like to refer to Dunluce
Castle. The history of Dunluce is interesting
to those who have read it. It is especially
interesting to me, because the district in
which I live on the opposite border from
Dunluce-was perpetually raided by the
McQuillans, who had already occupied the
Route territory. The McQuillans and
O'Cahans were constantly cattle-raiding and
burning, but ultimately the McDonalds
superseded the McQuillans. I do not know
anything more interesting than the story of
Sorley Boy McDonald, who was then head
of the clan. He was sitting in this ancient
castle of Dunluce when an envoy from Queen
Elizabeth came to him with a document in which she recognised and
confirmed him in his estates. When
his secretary read this document to
him Sorley Boy McDonald asked for the
document and pushed it on the point of his

sword into the fire, at the same time saying

It is a most interesting thing to look back
on the crumbling ruins of that castle and to
think that this Bill may be the means of

know who originated this Bill. I see associated with it the name of a noble Lord from
the other House. I think if he has had any

I am glad to have had the opportunity of

Mr. DEVLIN: I am quite sure the House
will rejoice to have the hon. Member
(Dr. Morrison) back again in his place.
(Hon. Members: Hear, hear.) We have
had
week
very busy and interesting
a
discussing Parliamentary proposals of
the Government, dealing with almost every
aspect of our public and social life, and 1
am quite certain that nothing could have
inspired the hon. Gentleman to remain away
from Parliament during that most prolific
period, if it were not for the fact that in
the solitude of his home on the banks of
the Bann, he was engaged in the archæological, historical and antiquarian studies, of
which he has given us so complete and
masterly a result in the speech which he
has just delivered.
He has told us of the need for a monument
to Oliver Goldsmith in Ulster. I thought
he had forgotten, but he did not-the hon.
Member never forgets any real historical
fact that there is a monument to Oliver
Goldsmith in front of Trinity College, in
Dublin, and, therefore, the only point of
his reference to Oliver Goldsmith was that
we ought to erect a monument to him here
in Ulster. If the hon. Gentleman introduces
a Bill to carry that suggestion into effect
I will gladly join with him in carrying it
through this House, and, of course, after
what he has said about the Senate, there
will be no difficulty there.
Now, I was delighted to hear this high
and splendid note of patriotism sounded by
the hon. Gentleman. It is a fitting thing,
I think, that in Ulster there ought to be
some tribute to the many fine and conspicuous and brilliant figures in the life
of this nation. Oliver Goldsmith was not
only a poet of great charm, but he was also
to some extent a great social figure. I am
not quite sure whether the hon. Gentleman
(Dr. Morrison) agreed with him in his
dealings with social questions. I do not
know if he remembers one of the poems of
Oliver Goldsmith, in which he said-
Princes and lords may flourish and may
fade,
A breath can make them as a breath has
made,
But a bold peasantry their country's pride
When once destroyed can never be supplied.
I think that is as appropriate to our present
conditions as it was when these words were
written over a century ago.
I would like to see a monument raised in
this city to Wolfe Tone. We are now all
making our suggestions. He was the first of
the great revolutionaries. From the Cave
Hill he proclaimed the eternal principle of
independence and of equality and fraternity,
and I take it that we owe our Parliament to
the declaration of the principles of Wolfe
Tone, and that if we are comparatively free
to-day we owe that to that great Protestant
revolutionary. Of course it took a century
of education and a series of political vicissitudes to get us to emulate Wolfe Tone. He
tried to rouse the people in a spirit of revolution. He did not succeed. The only successful revolutionary I know is the present
Lord Carson. He was able by the organisation of a revolution to secure us
this Parliament. Although he did not

secure
us the liberty which Wolfe
Tone fought for at all events he secured us
such a measure of liberty as we have got, and
it would be in the nature of things considering it was revolutionary methods that won
our Parliament that there ought to be erected
in Belfast on the Cave Hill a great monument to Wolfe Tone who was the first of the
revolutionaries.
I am glad that this Bill proposes also to
maintain and to keep perfect as far as possible
Greyabbey. Greyabbey is to us known as the
place in which was born the Rev. Mr. Porter,
.the great Presbyterian Minister. He fought
in 1798 against foreign aggression, and his
name has been immortalised for the courage
and self-sacrifice with which he went out to
fight against the imposition of foreign rule.
All these monuments have been associated
or less with recurrent risings or
revolutions in support of the great
principle of the right of the people
to control the destinies of their native
land. I am very glad that this Bill
has been proposed, because in addition to the
preservation of these historic monuments
it shows the birth of a spirit of genuine
patriotism upon the part of the Government

Mr. KYLE: On this very important Measure, I would like again to draw the attention
of the House to the disabilities from which
certain widows suffer under the Widows',
Orphans' and Old Age Contributory Pensions
Act. Despite the fact that their husbands
contributed for a great many years under
the National Health Insurance Acts, certain
widows are being deprived of widows'
pensions. I wish to ask the Minister of
Zabour if he could not see his way to take
some of the £50,000 of a surplus that we
heard about yesterday for the purpose of
enabling some of these widows who are living
in very distressing circumstances to get pensions. I would like him to extend the Act,
so that they will suffer less than they are
suffering at the present time.
I want to instance the case of a widow
in Belfast, to which I drew the attention
of the right hon. Gentleman (Mr. Andrews)
some time ago. The right hon. Gentleman in
accordance with the regulations has denied
the woman's right to a pension. According
to the regulations he is acting fairly. That
is, according to the regulations as they exist
at present this woman cannot get a widows'
pension. But, as her husband had contributed
for a very considerable time to the National
Health Insurance scheme, I want to press the
right hon. Gentleman as to whether it was
the intention of the legislature to exclude
applicants like her from the benefits of the
Act.
I would also like the Minister to tell us
whether in any circumstances an applicant
for benefit has the right of appeal, and what
machinery he has set up so that appeals can
be heard. In the Act itself there is some
mention of suggested machinery. I want to
ask the right hon. Gentleman has he set up
that machinery yet for the purpose of dealing with appeals from applicants who are
dissatisfied with the decision of the Ministry
in regard to their pensions.
There is another matter that I want to
press upon the attention of the Minister of
Labour. That is the question I raised the
SA
Despite all these assurances nothing has
yet been done, and twelve months have
elapsed. One is prepared to admit that there
are certain difficulties in the way, but surely
those difficulties are not so insuperable that
the Minister of Labour of Northern Ireland
cannot get over them. In view of the sympathetic way that this matter has been dealt
with in the Dail and in this House by the
right hon. Gentleman (Mr. Andrews), the
people affected-I am thinking particularly
of the people at Belleek-have been looking
forward for the past twelve months to some
arrangement being entered into, to the end
that those who live in the Free State and
who work in Northern Ireland might get
unemployment benefit. If they could only
get the unemployment insurance benefit for
which they and their employers have contributed stamps it would be a step in the
right direction.
I do not ask that these people should get
extended benefit. I am only asking that they
should get benefit in respect of the contributions that they and their employers have
made. I would like the right hon. Gentleman to tell us what is the trouble in this
matter, and whether any of us could help
him to overcome the difficulties. Twelve
months is not a very long period in the life
of a nation, but it is a fair length of time in
the life of a human being, and these people

Mr. JOHNSTONE: I rise largely for the
purpose of gaining information. Last
October I brought before this House the case
of young unemployed persons, and I must
Appropriation Bill—

[Mr. Johnstone]
say that both the Minister of Finance and
the Minister of Labour were very sympathetic. The Minister of Finance, who
takes a very considerable interest in this
matter, went so far as to say that the Government were already making inquiries and
were making up their minds as to what they
were going to do.
I was very glad to hear in the course of
the debate on the Vote for the Ministry of
Labour this week that a number of these
unemployed young men were now being
taught something in the Municipal College
of Technology, but I do not consider that
that is a fit and adequate substitute for the
scheme which I know both the Minister of
Finance and the Minister of Labour have
already been considering, and which I hope
they are still considering, with a view to
introducing it at an early date. After all,
the attendance of a young man who is unemployed at technical classes for one.or two
hours in the day is a very poor substitute for
a real day's work.
These young men-they are not really
young men; most of them are merely boys
from the age of 16 on-even if they have to
attend a technical class for an hour or two
during the day, are not learning habits of
regularity and unremitting industry at the
most important time of their lives, and at a
time when it is vitally necessary that they
should acquire those habits.
No man or nation is of very much good to
the world unless he or it has acquired habits
of regular hard work. The time to acquire
those habits is when the boy is becoming a
man. If he does not acquire those habits
at that time, if he is taught that he is going
to receive a few shillings a week, just sufficient to keep him above the borders of starvation, and that there is no necessity for
him to work to receive that money, he is
never going to turn into a useful citizen.
We have heard over and over again from
the Minister of Labour that we are moving
step by step with England. In this matter
we are not moving step by step with England. The Minister of Labour and the Minister of Finance know perfectly well-better
than I do the conditions in England. They
know that in England these boys, instead of
receiving unemployment benefit, are being
put into training schools where they are acquiring training in a large number of useful
arts and crafts, with a view to their being
sent to the Colonies, where they will have a
chance of becoming good citizens of the
Empire.
I know the Minister of Labour and the
Minister of Finance are both taking a very
great interest in this matter, and I rise in
the hope that I may get some assurance from
them that similar advantages will be given
to the unemployed boys and young men of
Northern Ireland.

the right hon. Gentleman the Minister of

The House will remember that ever since this

have no particular representation.
single word has been uttered in defence of

National Health Insurance. It went through

entitled to.

a certificate from a doctor, and he strikes

I heard the right hon. Gentleman, the
Minister of Finance, saying that this
National Health Insurance Bill was pheno
menally successful, and he told us the societies had something like £65,000,000 profit—
which should have gone to the workers. If
that is the intention of the Act, I say it is
phenomenally unsuccessful. What I want
to point out is this: The Minister, in
deference to suggestions I made to him, has
so altered the conditions that these arbitration courts are held in provincial towns
to accommodate the people. I maintain that
that is not enough. There should be some cheap
easy court of appeal by which, if there is a
difference between the family doctor and the
doctor who is acting for the society, some
other person should come in to say the family
doctor is right or the company doctor is
right. And it was with the object of raising
that point and urging how necessary it was
that it should be done that I have come here.
When we passed the Industrial Insurance
Act we gave the person who was insured to
the extent of £10 the right of appeal to a
cheap court to have his case determined.
Why should not the person who is insured
under the National Health Insurance Act,
with a disability which may last for 10, 15,
or 20 years involving a very large sum
greater than £10, have the right of going to
the county court and having the case determined, if this is provided in the interests of
the poor, and that is probably why it was
included in the Bill? They do not want
litigation because the poor are not able to
provide the money. If it is done in these
cases and done with the unanimous consent
of the House why should the same opportunity not be provided for cases of dispute?
I have brought these cases where injustice
was done before the Minister and he has
done everything he can up to a certain point.
I now make this appeal to him that he will
provide some cheap or certain way of doing
justice and deciding a matter like this and
seeing that justice is done to many of these
people who are utterly unable to carry on
any legal proceedings or to know where they
should go in case justice is denied them.

There is another matter upon which I was
not able to speak owing to illness. It has
reference to the Special Constabulary.
When the "A" Force was disbanded I do
not think enough appreciation was expressed
of their services, but that was not their
fault, or the fault of this House. It was the
fault of strangers. For instance, the trouble
that arose in the Special Constabulary was
not engineered by Ulstermen but by one of
these strangers from across the Channel who
are always thought more of than the local
men. He was a Welshman, I believe. When
you look over the Estimate for the Special
Constabulary you will find there a very
curious thing. The number of men is
diminished from 20,000 to 15,000, yet the staff
has increased not only in numbers but in
expense. You will find there is an increase
of £9,670 for the administration of that
Force while the decrease as far as the men
are concerned is £188,700. The Estimate
looks very nice and it might appear to those
who glance at it casually that this is not
quite right, but under administration you
will find £22,000 put in for the training of
the men. That is not for a material object.
They are not going to have it. Therefore,
the £22,000 they had last year is reckoned
as a decrease this year. It is simply not
taken at all.
I do not want the House to think I am
harping unduly on one string, but it appears
to me to be a fact proved again and again
that a man has only to be an Ulsterman in
order to have damned his opportunities of
ever getting promotion under the Government. Distinguished Ulster officers have
been discharged from the Special Constabulary and men with not nearly so good
records from across the water have been kept
on. That needs a lot of explaining. It
might be convenient to the Government or
to their particular party to keep these
gentlemen employed, but it is not fair.
In answer to the question to-day about
instructors-that is not a very highly paid
job it was pointed out there were eighteen
instructors in Tyrone and Fermanagh and
one was an Ulsterman. Is there anything
wrong with the ex-Servicemen from Tyrone
and Fermanagh? Have they less brains
than those people from across the water?
Do they not know anything? There is an
ex-sergeant of the Tyrone regiment, who
fought with particular distinction during the
war. He is a Lewis gun instructor. He
cannot get employment with the "B"
Special Constabulary. There are no instructors in Tyrone and Fermanagh who know
anything about the Lewis gun. I have that
from an absolute authority.
The belief is held in the Special Constabulary-and I would like to see that
belief dissipated-that you need not expect
anything if you are an Ulsterman, therefore,
you will not be disappointed. I would like
to know why it is the policy in the Government to down every Ulsterman unless he
has some particular influence with either
Members of the Government or the Government as a whole. Why should they have to
take a back seat to those who come across
the pond simply to make a living out of
Ulster? That is a question to which I
would like an answer, because again and
again that has been proved, or appears to
have been proved.
There is another point about which I want
to ask the Minister of Finance. When the
new chief of the Civil Service in Northern
Ireland was appointed the reason given for
his appointment was that he would be able

Mr. LEEKE: I should like to take this
opportunity of drawing the attention of the
House to the unemployment that exists in
Derry City. If you carry your minds back
a
few months you will remember the
strenuous efforts which were made by the
Government to retain Derry City under the
flag of Northern Ireland. (Hon. Members:
Hear, hear.) Evidence was given then by
the leading people in the city, who were sup
porters of the Government, that Derry City's
economic life depended upon their remaining
in Northern Ireland. They have managed
to retain it, and the result to-day is that
Derry City is seething with unemployment
and its industries are lying paralysed. I
would like to read to this House a letter 1
received this forenoon. It is from the Unemployed Workers' Council, and is as
follows:
We have decided to organise a march of
the unemployed of Derry to Belfast to interview the Minister of Labour with a view to
having a rate of outdoor relief struck at
once.
For this purpose we intend to set out on
Monday, May 24th, hoping to arrive in
Belfast on the 26th.
We earnestly desire that you arrange
with your colleagues representing Derry
City and County to meet us in Belfast on
above date, also that you arrange a meeting
with the Minister and our deputation, and
that you act as spokesman on our behalf
along with Mr. Sam Kyle, M.P.
Thanking you in anticipation, and sincerely trusting the above arrangements will
not cause any inconvenience. I hope to
hear from you at your earliest.
I am, yours faithfully,
Patrick McCauley.
I think that unless people were on the verge
of starvation they would not start on such a
desperate journey as marching from Derry
City to Belfast under existing circumstances.
While a great deal has been done I must
say to a certain extent there has been some
effort to assist the large industries of Belfast, Derry City has been surely and steadily
ignored. I do not see why this should be.
After all, Derry City and County represent a
part of Northern Ireland, and they should
receive the same consideration as other parts
of Ireland, the same, at any rate, as Belfast
City. Even some of the provincial towns
have received some assistance, but there is
none for this area. I think Derry City at
the present time is in a worse position with
regard to unemployment than any other part
of Northern Ireland. You must remember
that this serious condition of affairs affects not
only the unemployed, the workers, but
equally affects the capitalists of the City of
Derry. If they are not getting some encouragement and assistance the same as other
areas like the City of Belfast and other
merchants, they cannot be expected to compete in industry, and so the Government
should take some serious steps to deal and
grapple with this problem.
These people have approached the Derry
Board of Guardians, who have said that they
do not feel that they could at the present
time accept the responsibility of granting
outdoor relief to these people. Financially
they say they are unable to do it. The
Government say that they have no legal
standing to do it. Therefore, what is everybody's business is nobody's business, and
these people are allowed to starve between
these two bodies. That, after all, is surely a
serious refusal on the part of the Government to do its duty. They should at least-I
appeal to the Minister of Labour (Mr.
Andrews)-get into consultation with the
Derry local authorities to see if they cannot
give some grant, and if the local authorities
cannot give some grant something should be
done to deal with this problem.
I do not know what reply I shall get from
my Unionist colleagues from Derry City and
County as to whether they are prepared to
meet this deputation or not, or whether they
are sympathetic enough to meet and deal
with this problem when the deputation arrives. I shall consult with one of them
later, but at any rate, I should like to know
from the Minister of Labour now if any
practical steps have been taken to deal with
the problem of unemployment in this area.

word or two on the matter of unemployment
in Derry City. If the hon. Member (Mr.

City compares very favourably, in fact,

in Derry City. Everything has been done up
to the present, I think, that could reasonably
be required from the Corporation of Derry.
One-third of the members of that body are
elected to represent Labour, and do represent
Labour very efficiently and well.
I had from the Minister of Labour to-day
a pledge that any further schemes that may
be submitted by the Corporation of Derry
will be immediately and most sympathetically considered. I have had interviews
with the Minister in the past-not this year,
but during the last Parliament-over various
schemes for Derry City. I always found the

he has met any request ever made to him,
as far as Derry is concerned, in a most

Mr. W. MCMULLEN: You cannot give
any suggestions at all. Now what I have

before I say that I want to say to the hon.
Member who is now occupying the last Government Bench (Mr. Shillington), that we

Some Members on this side of the House-1
think the hon. Member for West Belfast
(Mr. Devlin), who sits behind, my two

and converge on Belfast to demand that
something should be done.
Now I will take the responsibility of
extending an invitation to the hon. Gentleman to come and address that demonstration
on Saturday and give the demonstration
the benefit of his views. I hope the hon.
Gentleman will accept the invitation because I believe he will be welcome there.
Anyone will be welcome who will contribute
some direct suggestion that is going to
alleviate the hardship and suffering that
exists among these people. I have not the
slightest bit of doubt, because I get letters
frequently from people who live in the
smaller urban centres in the midst of
rural districts making suggestions, that
there should be a more equitable distribution of the land in Northern Ireland. It
should not be beyond the ability of the
Government to effect some redress of that
kind, because it is pointed out by Government information that there are about 129
or 150 very large estates in Northern Ireland. I have asked the right hon. Gentleman several times to give us some idea of
the extent of these estates.
The amount of information given in
Government books is very limited. We are
told I am speaking from memory-that
there are about 129 or 150 large estates.
They are over 500 acres-but we are not
told how much they are in excess of 500.
Some of them might be 15,000 acres. I think
there is one of the hon. Gentlemen connected with the Government who either

himself or his father-has an estate of

cur quota in any way to the solution of this

Mr. POLLOCK: Is it park land?
Mr. W. McMULLEN: I did not say park.
I said estate. It is information I am looking
for. I am not making any dogmatic statement. I am asking for information, and I cannot get it in Government publications. I am
anxious to have the information. It would
probably obviate my making some fatuous
suggestions at times if I had the information
I want. I know the hon. Member who so
ably deputises for the Minister of Home
Affairs in his absence agrees that I make
many fatuous suggestions at times. But I
know he can appreciate the fact that the
making of fatuous suggestions is not confined
to this side of the House. I think the hon.
Member himself has erred on one or two
occasions in that respect.
I would like some information particularly
on this question of agriculture, because I
admit I am not an authority on the question.
Perhaps the hon. Member would discard
those papers he has got pertaining to affairs
of State, the internal affairs of State, and
give us some information about this very important problem of agriculture. He can
scarcely represent an agricultural constituency without knowing something about
agriculture. It is the base of our whole prosperity so far as Northern Ireland is concerned. We are an agricultural State. We
should have far more discussions on agriculture than on unemployment benefit.
(Hon. Members: Hear, hear.) I think the
right hon. Gentleman (Mr. Andrews) gets far
more than his share of the attacks that come
from this side of the House. Probably in
future more attacks will be directed towards
the Minister of Agriculture.
I am sure the very able Parliamentary
Secretary of the Ministry of Labour has
trodden along these lines so far as this problem is concerned, because he is closely
associated with this matter in industrial life
and represents an agricultural constituency.
When he is travelling down to Portrush and
other parts of County Antrim, I am sure
his mind very often wanders over the problem of agriculture in its relation to unemployment. We would also like to have the
benefit of his views on this question. I hope
as the result of my intervention in the debate
we will be given the benefit of the views of
someone who understands the problem of
agriculture.
There is only one other matter I want to
speak about. I believe it has been briefly
referred to by my colleague the hon. Member
for North Belfast (Mr. Kyle). It is in connection with widows' and orphans' pensions.
I would like to know from the Minister of
Labour or his Parliamentary Secretary
whether it is contemplated in the near future
to extend this Act, because there is a fairly
large number of widows and orphans not
covered by the Act on the Statute Book at
the present time. This would be a very desirable reform if it could be effected, and I
hope if it is not practicable or possible at
the moment, the thing will be kept very
clearly in mind, and at the earliest opportunity we may have a chance of discussing
an Amending Bill in this House for the purpose of covering a larger number of widows
than are covered at the present time.

Mr. HANNA: In the absence of the right

enough appreciation of the "A" Force of
police had been given expression to. I think
that that statement is scarcely accurate, because from practically every side of the
House testimony has been borne to the activities of all the branches of the Police Force
in restoring law and order in our midst.
Then the hon. and gallant Member went on
to draw attention to the Estimate, and rather
suggested where he did not state it that the
Estimate was not accurate, and he indicated
that in his opinion far greater expense was
contemplated in the next year than in the
past. In the last Estimate the higher
officers' salaries in connection with the "A"
and "B" Forces were set out and charged
as against the "A" Force. The "A" Force
has now been almost entirely disbanded, and
the salaries of these officers who perform
duties in connection with both branches of
the Force are now set out and charged as
1501, Appropriation Bill-

19 MAY 1926
Second Reading.
against the "B" Force. That answers very
largely the point made by the hon. and
gallant Gentleman.
Colonel WOODS: But it is an increase.
Mr. HANNA: No, there is no increase. As
a matter of fact, there has been a very substantial decrease, and for this reason County
Commandants whose salaries were approximately about £900 have now been reduced
to £450-
Colonel WOODS: With an addition of
£150.
Mr. HANNA-and there have been very
substantial reductions in the salaries of the
Area Commandants, and, indeed, in all
branches. The hon, and gallant Gentleman now
reminds me there has been an addition of
£150, but it is perfectly clear that that sum
allowed for a motor-car will be a distinct
saving to the Government. If these officers
had the use of Government cars and were
paid according to mileage the sum of money
required would be very substantially more.
Not only that, but they would require to
have a skilled driver whose salary would be
roughly about £200 a year in itself.
The hon. and gallant Gentlemen then suggested in connection with disbandment that
it was the policy of the Government to down
every Ulsterman who had not got any influence. That is not the fact. I am informed
and believe that the system of disbandment
has been that when a branch is disbanded
all ranks go, but that when a branch is cut
down volunteers under the new terms who
are recommended for detention get the first
chance, and that the selection is made regardless of any question of nationality. I
am further informed that all have suffered
equally in this regard.
In regard to the matter which the hon.
and gallant Gentleman raised in his speech
as well as in the question asked in the
House as to the number of sergeant
instructors in the counties of Tyrone and
Fermanagh, I can only repeat what the
right hon. Gentleman the Minister of Home
Affairs said in that regard. These sergeant
instructors were appointed on the recommendation of the County Commandants in
those two counties. Both Commandants are
Ulstermen and are local men. I would not
attempt to try to inform the hon. and gallant Member on a matter of which he has
had great experience, but I do understandand I think perhaps he will agree with me—
that every man who has been a soldier is
not qualified to be an instructor. I understand an instructor requires to have particular skill and aptitude for the work he
has got to perform. I have no doubt the
County Commandants were greatly influenced by the requirements necessary on
that occasion, and I have no doubt they
consulted and considered that sentiment
that suggests an Ulsterman should get
preference. I think that as far as the Government is concerned no complaints have
been made by either the officers or the men
themselves in regard to those instructors.
Indeed, we have evidence from time to time
that the most cordial and happy relations
exist amongst them.
Colonel WOODS: May I ask the hon. and
learned Gentleman a question? From what
he says is it a fact that only one man out of
the two counties is fit to be an instructor
in the "B" Specials?
Mr. HANNA: No, I did not say that.
What I do say, and what has been said, is
that only one man has been appointed. There
may be many more who may be perfectly
competent. I am not in a position to judge,
and I do not know. I only do say this, that
the most cordial relationship has existed between those instructors and the men, and
that we hear no complaints about them
in that regard, and that they entirely
satisfied the County Commandants who
recommended them.

One other point, and then I hope I shall
be able to resume my seat. The hon. and
gallant Gentleman tells us he was advised

to give instruction in the Lewis gun. I do

the advices and information which I myself
have got in my capacity as Parliamentary

I think I have now dealt with all the points.
Mr. DEVLIN: May I ask the hon. and

Mr. HANNA: No. I am not aware that

The MINISTER OF AGRICULTURE (Mr.

Appropriation Bill-
Second Reading.
HOUSE OF COMMONS.
[Mr. Archdale]
read the Report of the Ministry of Agriculture for the last year? If he has not got a
copy I shall be most happy to send him one.
In it he will see described the schemes we
are trying to carry out to improve the position of agriculture, and which if they were
carried out would take some more men on
the land. Farmers cannot be expected to
take more men on the land than they require.
Unless agriculture is prosperous they cannot
take more men on the land. Then a man
taken on the land must be fit to do hard
work and must also have a knowledge of
agricultural matters. As I said, our schemes
are all plainly set out in the Report for last
year, and I hope the hon. Member will be
good enough to look at the Report.
Last year in Northern Ireland I am glad
to say there was a small increase in tillage.
That, doubtless, will please the hon. Member,
though he stated there was some remark of
mine in Hansard that not an additional acre
could be put under tillage. I could not quite
catch what he said, but I hope there will be
a great increase in tillage in the future, as
agriculture cannot prosper with only grass
and grazing.
Mr. BEATTIE: I would like to ask the
Minister of Agriculture a question. I take
him to mean that any man who is employed
upon the land must be physically fit. To me
that would mean that a city man who has
been out of work for two years and six
months and has been living in a state of
semi-starvation would not be a fit and proper
person to send to the country to do agricultural labour.
Mr. ARCHDALE : I take it a farmer
would not be very keen to take a man who
was not able to do proper work. In the
country many old men are feeble, but are
kept on by farmers who employ them purely
from motives of charity. Great numbers of
old-age pensioners are working on farms and
getting fair pay and a good living. But you
cannot compel any man to go to the country
and you cannot compel any farmer to take
a man who is not fit to work.
Mr. DEVLIN: Would the right hon.
Gentleman tell us what he is doing to develop

Mr. ARCHDALE: We have got a considerable number of unemployed men engaged in

Mr. DEVLIN: Would not this be a proper

Mr. ARCHDALE: With the permission of

That is the great difficulty about absorbing

Oral Answers to Questions.
NUMBER OF WINE LICENCES
GRANTED.
1. Mr. CRAWFORD asked the Minister of
Home Affairs whether he will state the
number of Wine Licences granted by the
Excise Authorities in Northern Ireland
since the Intoxicating Liquor Act of 1923
came into operation.
OF
FINANCE (Mr.
The MINISTER
Pollock): I propose to take this question on
behalf of my right hon. Friend. Since the
passing of the Intoxicating Liquor Act, 1923,
10 new licences for the sale of wine for offconsumption have been issued by the
Customs and Excise Department, of which 8
are at present in force.
CONVICTIONS FOR ILLICIT
DISTILLATION.
2. Mr. CRAWFORD asked the Minister of
Home Affairs whether he can state the
number of convictions for illicit distillation
during the last three years, and also the
number of persons sent to prison during the
same period for this offence.
The MINISTER OF HOME AFFAIRS (Sir
Dawson Bates): In answer to the question
of the hon. Member, I beg to state that the
number of convictions for illicit distillation
during the last three years is 195, and the
number of persons sent to prison during the
same period for this offence is 63.
Mr. DEVLIN: Is not the cause of all this
illicit distillation the high duty on whisky?
RURAL AND COUNTY COUNCIL
WORKERS' HOURS OF LABOUR.
3. Mr. KYLE asked the Prime Minister
whether he will state when the Government
intends to introduce a Bill to regulate the
hours of labour of workers employed by
rural district councils and county councils.
The following question also stood in the
name of Mr. Kyle:
WHITLEY JOINT INDUSTRIAL COUNCIL.
4. Mr. KYLE to ask the Prime Minister
whether it is the intention of the Government to set up a Whitley Joint Industrial
Council to govern the conditions of employment of workers employed in the nontrading departments of the rural district
councils and county councils.
Sir DAWSON BATES: I have been asked
by the Prime Minister to reply. I propose
to embody in the one reply the answers to
the two questions put down by the hon.
Member.
The establishment of the councils is a
matter for consultation and decision as
between the local authorities and their employees, and the same consideration applies
to the question of the hours of labour of
workers employed by the local authorities.
Mr. KYLE: Is the right hon. Gentleman
aware that the time of the working week of
these workers is 56 hours, whereas in the
shipyards and textile trades the hours are
47 and 48? In view of that fact is he not
prepared to ask the county councils to set
up this Whitley Council to regulate the hours
of the workers who work for the county
councils?
Sir DAWSON BATES: The principle of
the Whitley Council is an entirely voluntary
one. It is a matter between the employers
and the employees.
Mr. KYLE: I am quite aware that the
Whitley Councils are voluntary associations.
It is because I know that that I am asking
the right hon. Gentleman to ask the county
councils and rural councils to be so good as
to volunteer to set up the Whitley Council
to regulate the wages and hours of their
employees.
Sir DAWSON BATES: I am afraid my
hon. Friend does not understand the
position that I occupy in relation to the
local authorities. It is a matter entirely in
their own discretion. I do not propose to
interfere with it.
Mr. KYLE: The right hon. Gentleman
seems to think that I do not understand
his position. Well, it is quite obvious that
no one in this House can understand his
position as well as himself. I do understand
the position of the road workers and the
other workers who are employed by the
county councils and rural councils. I merely
asked the right hon. Gentleman if he would
be so good as to ask the county councils to
set up the Whitley Council, and he says no.

ORDERS OF THE DAY.
Queen's University Bill [S.]
Motion made, and Question proposed:
"That the Bill be now read the Third time."
Dr. MORRISON: I have not had an opportunity until to-day of speaking on this
Measure, and I would like to say a word or
two with regard to it. There have been some
letters complaining of the fact that the
library and the museum were not available
for the public. So far as I know, the Senate
and everybody connected with the University
would be keenly desirous of creating an
interest in the University amongst the people
of Belfast and the Six Counties, and if any
plan could be devised that would secure that
object it would be welcomed by the governing
body of the University. Some Amendments
were put down to the Bill by the Labour
Party and they were ruled out of order. I
think that was due to a misunderstanding as
to the powers of the University. We are
protected in the University in this way that
no legislation can take place without the
sanction of Convocation. We should clearly
Queen's University Bill-

20 MAY 1926
Third Reading.

.
of
understand that Convocation consists
every graduate of the University who has
entered his form and paid his fee. It is the
broadest constitution in the world; nothing
can be broader than it.
Mr. KYLE: It is, within limits.
Dr. MORRISON: Every member has the
right to vote on this important question.
After Convocation has decided the changes
that were necessary to give representation to
the county councils nothing further could be
introduced into the Bill without a further
meeting of Convocation. I think that if
Labour desires to be represented in the University nobody would take serious objection
to it. I have heard a Member of the Labour
Party say in this House that he thought the
time was coming when his party would cross
the floor and the Government would disappear.
Mr. KYLE: Merely change, not disappear.
Dr. MORRISON: The Government would
retire to the other side into the cold shades
of the Opposition.
Mr. KYLE: That is better.
Dr. MORRISON: I think there is a possibility, but not a probability, that that might
happen, and if it did happen I imagine the
University would confer an honorary degree
upon the leader of the Labour Party.
The MINISTER OF LABOUR (Mr.
Andrews): Hear, hear.
Dr. MORRISON: I quite imagine that my
hon. Friend (Mr. Kyle) opposite would be
introduced by me and that the noble Marquess, who is Chancellor of the University,
would robe him. But, on the other hand,
there is the possibility that he or his party
may never cross the floor of the House. Indeed, when he was making his speech I
thought of the celebrated answer which the
second Charles gave to his brother James
when he told him, "James, there is no possibility of the British people ever killing me
to make you king."
What we have done is that we want to give
representation to the county councils, and
we want the county councils to recognise the
great fact that the University is their own.
It is for the education of their boys and girls.
It is a thing everybody in Ulster should be
proud of, and we should look upon it as a
privilege and not a duty to contribute. In
my days in the University I think I paid
more attention to sport than to study, but,
be that as it may, I was in the first Rugby
fifteen. (Hon. Members: Hear, hear). The
House is only beginning to discover the versatility of my attainments. (Laughter).
Probably as a result of that the Secretary
of the University, the late Mr. Finnegan,
whose unexpected death produced such depression and regret amongst all sections in
Belfast, asked me to go out to see the football
field and the cricket field.
We used to play in the grounds of the University, but those grounds were exhausted by
being built upon to provide further accom.
modation for the students. I went out to
see this field, which is remote from the
University, on the Ravenhill Road. It was a
splendid field but there was no pavilion. 1
put it to the Labour representatives across
the House that Labour is able to have
splendid pavilions in the football clubs with
which they are associated. They have legitimate and proper accommodation for their
players in their clubs, but here you have.
boys and girls who are going to have control
of very serious matters in Ulster, and they
have a cricket field and a football field, but
no pavilion. I think that is in itself a matter
greatly to be deplored, and if they had ample
funds in the University a grant would be
made to meet that end. I come to this question of the contribution to the University.
It is admitted, I think, by everyone who has
studied the facts that Queen's gets a smaller
contribution from public bodies than any
other university in Great Britain.
Mr. KYLE: Look at the county council, a
representative of which is sitting beside you.
Dr. MORRISON: I will deal with that.
When the congestion, and the numbers, and
the expense of running the University came
before the Senate they looked around for
help, and they naturally followed the example of the older universities in England
and went to the county councils. Now this
Bill is simply for the purpose of giving the
county councils representation on the Senate,
a fit and proper proposal which meets with
the approval of not only Dr. Livingstone,
the Vice-Chancellor, but of all the Senate
and of all the University members. I regret
to find that in two counties-one of them I
am ashamed to say is my own-no grant was
made. I represent not the University
specially. I represent the country graduates
of the University, and what I say on this

Mr. JOHNSTONE: Before the House proceeds to vote on this matter I should like
to say a few words in regard to this Bill.
I possess, I think, the unique distinction
in this House of being a member of those
three bodies whose actions have been so
much discussed in connection with this
Measure. I am a member of the Senate, I
am also a member of the Academic Council,
and I am a member of Convocation, and I
was present at the meetings when this Bill
was considered, and at the meetings when
this Bill was accepted. A great many criticisms of this Bill have been offered since it
came before the Senate and before this
House. There is only one of those criticisms
which was offered when it was passing
through one of those three bodies of which
I have just spoken, and which alone, I may
say, has the right to say what the changes
in the constitution are going to be.
I should like to clear the air a little in
regard to what I think are misconceptions
regarding the relative positions of Queen's
University and this Parliament. This Parliament has absolutely no power whatever to
interfere with Queen's University, except on
the original proposition of the University
itself. The University has to make up its
mind what changes it wishes, and then it
must have them passed in a Bill by this
House and by the Senate. It is open for
the House of Commons and the Senate, or
for either, to refuse to pass that Bill, in
which case the position reverts to what it
was before.
This is not a Bill to give Queen's University
£36,000, because that £36,000 is part of the
deed under which this Parliament sits, and
this Parliament could not refuse that £36,000
to Queen's University. If it refuses that
£36,000 it breaks the Act by which it sits.
So let there be no misconception or misunderstanding. That £36,000 is not a grant
from this Parliament, and, as a matter of
fact, I should like to take this opportunity
of saying that £36,000 is not even a fair
estimate of the amount that comes to the
funds of Northern Ireland's University. The
exact grant towards Queen's University is
£26,000. The £10,000 which makes up the
£36,000 is something over which this Parliament or this Government have no control
whatever, because it is part of the residuary
estate of the old Royal University, which
comes to Queen's University automatically,
and which the Government have no power
whatever to divert from that object.
£10,000 is handed to the Government of
Northern Ireland, and they in turn hand
it Over to the University, and if the
University were not to get that £10,000 it
would not come into the funds of Northern
Ireland. Therefore, I would like the
The
positions of the University and this Parliament to be perfectly clear.

Having said so much in regard to the

The principal criticism offered against this

giving us money, or at least some of whom

anxious for money-it is, perhaps, the most

not giving this

The object with which this representation is
being given is that of extending, as far as
we possibly can, the interest in the University, of extending, widening, and deepening
interest in the University, and of making
the people of Northern Ireland feel that
Queen's University is the University of
Northern Ireland-(hon. Members: Hear,
hear) is the University which Northern

That is the principle which was advanced

three bodies I speak of. When I say that

When that Vice-Chancellor retired owing

May I say that I think the University
authorities ought also to consider the desirability of giving Labour representation.
Everyone who follows the development of our
modern life and the development of modern
culture is well aware that the passion for
learning exists as largely amongst the working classes as amongst any other section of
the community. We cannot all divorce ourselves from prejudice. Nobody knows that
better than I do. And really there ought to
be a desire upon the part of the University
authorities to allay the spirit of suspicion
that exists that the powerful intellectual
forces in a place like Ulster are not inclined
to allow for these prejudices, natural passions, and ambitions which exist in the mind
of the working classes in regard to the principle of higher education. There are many
working men and many representatives of
Labour who are men of culture.
I have been reading some of the speeches
at great intellectual assemblies, and I do
not know any speeches more instinct with
culture and great intellectual power than the
speeches of Mr. Ramsey McDonald. There
are other speakers who are ornaments to
those assemblies and who enrich the discussions with the powerful contributions they
make to the culture and progress of English
public life. That, perhaps, may not be very
manifest in the narrower area over here, out
it ought to be the function of the University
to encourage intellectual development and to

the University authorities I venture to submit to them that apart altogether from the

Mr. BEATTIE: I take this opportunity in
the time at our disposal to say one or two
things in regard to the position of certain
classes of the community. They are not as
secure as I would desire. To-day we have
agreed to the adjournment of the House
until the 1st June, and we have also made
preparation on that day to allow no general
discussion to take place, which will mean
that it will be the 12th October before Members on this side of the House will have an
opportunity of endeavouring to bring the
pressure that is necessary to bear on the
Government to do something for those who
can at the present moment do nothing for
themselves. I might draw the House's
attention to the question with which I am
so familiar-that is the question of unemployment. It may be boring-I am sure it
is-to some Members of the Government,
but I can assure them that the boredom
they have got to suffer by my speaking here
is nothing like the pangs of hunger the
unemployed workers have to suffer owing
to the depressed conditions of labour and
their being denied benefit under the Unemployment Insurance Act. We have been
told, even in this House we have been told
repeatedly, that the Opposition repeat
their speeches. There is only one way of
presenting the unemployment question, and
that is by telling the facts in regard to the
regulations. I have endeavoured on several
occasions to make that perfectly understandable to every Member of the House, but I
have not been able to get the Minister and
his colleagues to make any alteration.
There is the case of a man, one of my constituents, who a fortnight ago was allowed
twelve weeks' benefit by a Rota Committee.
That committee was composed of representatives of the employers, of the workers,
and of the Ministry. But the headquarters
of the Ministry were not quite satisfied with
the man's history, they were not quite satisfied with the decision of that composite
body, and they sent the man's case to another court, with a footnote of so damning
a character on the application that the committee had no option but to disallow the
claim. There is a case in which one court
allowed the man twelve weeks' benefit, and
the other court disallowed his claim owing
to the request of the headquarters of the
Ministry of Labour.
We have heard it stated here that only
2.7 of the claims that pass through the Rota
Committees are disallowed. If I did not
know the Minister as well as I do, I would
take it that his figures were wrong. But I
would like to know how those figures are
compiled. I would be prepared to challenge
that figure of 2.7 owing to the number of cases
that have come under my own observation
of claims being disallowed by headquarters
after being passed by the Rota Committees.
I am quite satisfied in my own mind that in
every case in which a Rota Committee
grants the application of a man who has
been more than two years out of employment, as soon as the headquarters receive
the claim they either disallow it or refer it
to another committee within twelve days
from the date of the decision of the first
committee. That is quite clear, and that is
a fact.
The regulation in regard to the two years
is hitting the unemployed so hardly that
I take the opportunity presented by the
Third Reading of this Bill to present their
case once again to the Minister. It is all
very well endeavouring to keep a fund in a
state of solvency, but the sacrifice is rather
great, because there are 10,000 people who
have no income whatever. You have the
Boards of Guardians all over the Six
Counties refusing to meet their obligations,
and the Government are condoning the
offence by standing idly by and allowing
them to adjudicate in the manner to which
I have referred.
It has been repeatedly stated that the
poor-law does not give sufficient power to
that authority to administer outdoor relief
on the same scale or conditions as prevail
in Great Britain. If that is so, I ask the
Government, who have got legal advice at
their command, to make a definite statement defining the duties of the Guardians,
and how far the Guardians can go under
Section 13 of the Poor-law Act of 1898. If
they make that statement adverse to the administration of the poor-law guardians, I
will say they have acted in the manner I
have expected, that is, if they tell the
Guardians in a direct fashion that they have
sufficient law to see that no man, woman
or child is allowed to starve, owing to the
state of unemployment and the refusal to
pay unemployment benefit.
I would also like to refer to the Widows',
Orphans' and Old Age Contributory
Pensions Act. Great hardships have been
created under the Act which was placed on

pleaded once before that the date should be
made retrospective, but of course the
Minister of Finance told us that a money
resolution would be required to meet the
liability. Last night three widows came to
me. Their husbands had died between
Christmas and the New Year. They have

The hon. Member raised individual cases,
which are always very difficult for a Minister
to deal with without having specific notice
beforehand that they are going to be raised.
A specific case of hardship in a population
of a million and a quarter or more is bound
to crop up. The worst of it is that these
isolated cases, when they are given the prominence of discussion in this House, rather
create a false impression outside. I am
quite sure that there is not a single case
of real hardship in Northern Ireland that
cannot be met by the proper authority.
I would have all the Ulster people know
that my right hon. Friend here (Mr.
Andrews) is limited by statute as to what
he can do and what he cannot do. I wish
to make that perfectly clear. The second
point that I would like to make is that if
my right hon. Friend was to take the easy
road towards popularity it would be possible
for him to endear himself to the hearts of
all who are unemployed to-day, but
on the other hand he would gravely
prejudice the unemployed of the future.
Appropriation Bill-
Third Reading.
HOUSE OF COMMONS.

[The Prime Minister]
Although we are bound in writing and by
Act of Parliament to honour the agreement
that was so recently entered into on the subject of unemployment, although we are bound
by all that one State can bind itself to
another to honourably fulfil the obligations
inside that document, still my right hon.
Friend (Mr. Andrews) cannot be accused because he carries out faithfully that agreement that he has not got as soft a heart as
any man in Ulster. But, as I say, if he were
out to play for cheap popularity he could
say "Let everybody have relief from Government funds, let everybody who comes along,
no matter whether they fall inside the ambit
of the regulations of the Act or not, receive
unemployment benefit." I can imagine those
at the street corners deserting the hon.
Member (Mr. Beattie) and saying "You are
no use, I am off to Andrews around the corner
who will do more for me. Of course, any
Minister in his responsible position could
immediately curry popular favour. What
are the stern facts of the case? A breach of
the agreement that we reached would have
meant a loss of £680,000 this last half year
and £1,000,000 this year.
Mr. DEVLIN:
It is our money.
The PRIME MINISTER: It is not our
own money. That again is a false impression.
That means it is our own money if we repudiate citizenship with Great Britain,
which I will never be a party to.
Mr. DEVLIN: We have repudiated it.
The PRIME MINISTER: No, we have
not.
Mr. DEVLIN: May I ask the right hon.
Gentleman whether the arrangement when
the 1920 Act was passed was that we were to
pay £8,000,000 and if we did not pay
£8,000,000 or an amount subsequently to be
agreed on you broke the contract?
The PRIME MINISTER: No, that is not
true. The facts of the case are that when
the White Paper was drawn up on which
the Act of 1920 was based the whole of Great
Britain and ourselves were in a state of trade
boom, and the receipts into the Exchequer
were such as to justify the then Government,
or the Treasury officials at all events, anticipating that Ireland as a whole should pay
a contribution of some £18,000,000 a year to
Great Britain. When the South ceased to
function under the Act of 1920 and we set up
our own Parliamentary institutions we were
saddled with what was considered a fair proportion or some £8,000,000 per annum, but
the £8,000,000 was qualified by this, that if in
any year the Joint Exchequer Board fixed
upon a lesser or larger amount that amount
would be paid by Northern Ireland as its
fair share of the contribution towards the
War debt, the maintenance of the Army, the
Navy and the Air Force, and other national
services, in which services we equally benefit
with Great Britain. (Hon. Members: Hear,
hear.) It is not as though we were cut off
in any way and could not benefit from these
services. It is towards that upkeep that the
contribution is fixed by the Joint Exchequer
Board.
However, this is rather drifting from the
point I was endeavouring to make with regard to the position in which we find ourselves to-day. The cold hard facts that each
and all of us have to face are these: By a
loose or wrong administration of the Unemployment Acts in Northern Ireland you run
grave risk of losing the contribution from
Great Britain, which in any year might
amount to as much as £1,000,000 sterling.
Mr. DEVLIN: Why? Could the right
hon. Gentleman say why we would lose it?
Mr. POLLOCK: We could not get it.
The PRIME MINISTER: The reason that
we would lose it would be because the agreement states distinctly that the Act passed in
the Imperial Parliament holds good just so
long as Northern Ireland goes along pari
passu with Great Britain in its administration of the Act, and no longer, and if at any
time
Mr. DEVLIN: I do not like to interrupt
the right hon. Gentleman so often, but on

same advantages as the unemployed in Gt.
Britain? Is he aware that the boards of
guardians

When the then Leader of the Ulster Party
accepted Home Rule in 1920 for Ulster, it
was on the distinct understanding and under
solemn pledges that not a man, whether he
be a workman or any other person inside the
Ulster area, was to be penalised in any way
by the acceptance of self-government for
Northern Ireland. We have to see that that
is carried out, and we will see that it is
carried out. What are the facts of the case?
It would appear by the debates each time
they are started in this House, that the
Government of Northern Ireland, and therefore, as I say, the people, were doing nothing
to aid the unemployed and the poor in our
midst. In fact, I think that the hon. Member opposite at one time accused us of doing
nothing for the people. I think he said so
in so many plain words, but I also think he
regretted it afterwards. He did not exactly
mean what he said. What are the real facts
of the case? I have had figures taken out
of the Estimates this year for the poor, the
distressed and the needy, the widows and
orphans, and old age pensions, and they
amount altogether to the large sum of
£5,256,000. I will not say the Government is
finding it. I do not wish to have any credit
given to the Government, but the people of
Northern Ireland-the taxpayers-are finding
that large sum of money in order to help the
distressed in our midst. I say that is not a
bad record. (Hon. Members: Hear, hear.)
It is covered by the Unemployment Insurance Act, it is covered by unemployment
grants to help works to aid the unemployed,
and it is covered by old-age pensions, widows
and orphans' pensions, and other categories,
amounting to the grand total of £5,256,000.
How then can it be said that the Government
are not doing all that is humanly possible
and within their limited financial powersin order to keep our Budget balanced
from year to year-how can it be said they
are not doing everything that can be done in
order to help the unemployed? We have in
vited the local authorities to put up schemes,
because I think all parties have agreed that
it is much better for men to receive pay for
work than to receive the dole for doing
nothing. That is agreed by all sides of the
House. (Hon. Members: Hear, hear.) What
is my right hon. Friend (Mr. Andrews)
doing? He is doing what I think no other
Government has ever done. He busies himself by going about endeavouring to attract
local authorities to come along, and he says:
"Will you not do something in order to
help us to give grants that we may be able
to take up the unemployed." No one has
ever worked harder than he has during the
five years he has been Minister of Labour.
I know he does not wish to get the credit
for it. He has an able staff who are most
anxious to do what they can.
There is a separate question altogether
raised by hon. Members, and that is the
question of the duties of boards of guardians.
I myself have listened to the debates, I have
studied the question, and I have never yet
been able to penetrate the mentality or
psychology of the Socialist Members opposite.
I always understood that Labour Members
or Socialist Members were extra democraticthat they believed in democracy. I think the
hon. Member (Mr. Kyle) was begging to-day
that a member of the Labour Party ought
to be put on the Senate of the Queen's University. That is very laudable indeed, and
I do not object at all, but why was he so
very anxious that Labour should be represented there? I should imagine if he
analysed his own feelings and his own mind
he would arrive at the conclusion that it
was because it was a democratic age that
some representative of Labour should be
seated there giving his advice along with
others of that august body. If that is what
is at the back of his mind I cannot see how
he can reconcile that with asking the
Government to bludgeon their way into a
democratic assembly of elected poor-law
guardians and tell them what their duty is.
Mr. BEATTIE: My object was to explain
the power that the guardians have. The
point I placed before the Prime Minister
was that they have not sufficient power.
The PRIME MINISTER: I am not going
to enter into a long argument with the hon.
Member, because I understand that he has

of guardians, and I have not. But is he
quite sure that the boards of guardians
have exhausted all the powers they possess?

[The Prime Minister]
Government is used for walking into these
popularly-elected bodies and telling them how
to manage their business. Let us do away
with them altogether if we do not like them,
but while they are the machinery in this
country for carrying out definite purposes, I
say we should allow those men in the city
of Belfast and in the city of Derry and in
the counties who are discharging that duty,

shoulders and who have to stand very harsh
and severe criticism-I say we should allow
them to carry out the powers they discharge
to the best of their ability and to the satisfaction of those who returned them for that
purpose.
I remember not very long ago in London
some board of guardians-1 do not remember
in which of the areas it was-spent a great
deal of money in helping the poor, and if I
remember rightly it was the Socialists who
objected strongly to the Government on the
other side going in and interfering in any
way. I rather imagine it was-
Mr. DEVLIN: Was it Poplar?
The PRIME MINISTER: I know it was
one of those boards of guardians that went
along the road which, I presume, the hon.
boards
Member opposite would like
of
guardians here to go along. But what hap
pened? The Minister of Health, I think it

at the suggestion that the Government
should go down and interfere with the freely

Mr. BEATTIE: I think the Prime Minister is not doing justice to my point. That
is quite the reverse of what I asked the Prime
Minister to do. I said that if they had not
got sufficient powers I want the Government
to give them the powers so that they could
give equal social service under the poor-law
here as in Great Britain.
Mr. SPEAKER: With regard to this question, I think I should state what appears to
me to be the Parliamentary position. I think
the hon. Member for East Belfast (Mr.
Beattie) is quite right in saying that what
he wishes to do is to ask the Government
what powers the Guardians have. That is
quite in order, of course. Then, although
it would not be strictly in order on this discussion, he wants to ask them if those powers
are not sufficient to increase them by legis
lation. It is only on those two grounds in
my view that these discussions with regard
to boards of guardians are in order in this
House. It is clearly not within our competence to discuss the internal administration
of popularly elected assemblies. The only
thing in order in this House is the question
as to what powers they have got and, not on
this occasion but on another, the question of
increasing those powers.
The PRIME MINISTER: I am obliged to
you, Mr. Speaker, for your ruling, because
that is exactly the view I take myself,
namely, that if the local bodies have exhausted the whole of their powers and there
is still great need in the community then, and
then only, would the matter come before the
Government. But the old statutory obligation still rests upon each locality to look
after the needy in their midst, and what I am
endeavouring to explain to the House is that
so far as the Government are concerned, no
stone has been left unturned by any Department to take up as many as possible of these
poor fellows that are out of work through no
fault of their own. It does no good to create
dissatisfaction outside by making it appear
that there are some powers in reserve that
the Government are not exercising which
could help the lamentable condition of affairs
as it exists to-day. But my right hon. Friend
(Mr. Andrews) and I see, at any rate, a little
break in the clouds. We have in view several
schemes which we are endeavouring to
mature. I do not say they will reach more
than the fringe of the difficulty confronting
us, but, at all events, there is no opportunity
lost where we can see a chance of improvising
work and doing something that will give
these people employment. The House and
the country may rest assured that neither
my right hon. Friend nor any of his colleagues will fail them. (Hon. Members:
Hear, hear).

Rumours have it that the proposed scheme

I have seen it stated several times in

engineers to the Lower Bann Navigation
Trust, that at the time of the last drainage.
scheme the Board of Works left a considerable number of coffer dams at the bottom
of the Lower Bann. These now form

many times, and it is very obvious that anything that is left in the river which prevents

Then I am informed on very good authority
that the mouth of the Agivey River is completely silted up, that the discharge from the
Glenstall River forms a ditch practically
the whole way across the river at this point,
that one of the arches over the river on the
Derry side is also completely silted up, and
that the new race at Castleroe is completely
dammed up. I mention these matters because it seems to me that some of them
might be dealt with now, and so relieve the
people whose lands are flooded in this particular area. I am also told that the fishery
cribs at Castleroe are of great assistance to
the discharge of floods, and in this connection I would like to read what has been
written to me by one of the farmers who
live in that neighbourhood, and who suffer
greatly from the floods. It seems that the
lessees of the salmon fishing board up these
cribs until the season opens for taking
salmon, which is sometime about the first
of May. He goes on to say-
"You can imagine what this means
during two of the principal spring months
when miles and miles of land are covered
with water as at present."
He goes on to ask if I could find out, either
by question in this House or otherwise, if
the lessees have powers to do this, and he
points out that this should be a matter
which concerns the drainage trustees, but
that they obviously take no interest or have
no power in the matter, since they have
allowed the stream at the King's Gap to be
encroached upon to the extent of twelve feet,
which practically barricades the whole river.
I realise that these are very small matters,
but the right hon. Gentleman (Mr. Pollock)
in turn must, after all, realise that this is a
small community, and that these farmers
look to the Government to help them in their
small difficulties, just as they would look,
perhaps, to their mothers or their fathers.
They look on this Government as a paternal
one. It is very near to them, and they come
to it for assistance. They would like to have
an answer to these things. I know quite
well the right hon. Gentleman cannot give
me an answer on these particular matters
to-day, but perhaps he may be able to help
in the future, and I could communicate any
information he could give me to these
farmers.
I would like, just before sitting down, to
refer, although indirectly, to what has
already been said on the question of unemployment, to unemployment as it affects this
particular question, or as this particular
question affects unemployment. I want to
know would not it be possible to deal with
this whole matter of the drainage of the
Bann boldly, to take up the scheme-if it is
a big one take it up whole or take it up
piecemeal-and then to erect huts-I am now
talking of the Lower Bann entirely, and not
dealing with the question of the Upper Bann
-and bring down some of the unemployed
from Derry City and from Coleraine, and
put them on to these works which I have suggested, and on to other works which have
been suggested. It would help the farmers.
and would do an enormous amount of good
to the agricultural industry in that part of
the world
We have started a drainage scheme in the
same part of the world for the smaller rivers.
This scheme is shortly to be carried out, and
I very much hope that it will be started
this summer. The County Council propose
coming very shortly to the Ministry of
Labour, I think, for a loan in this connection,
and I hope we will be able to employ a considerable number of men in this way in
these drainage works on the Culnady River.
But that is very small in comparison with
this larger scheme, and if the Government
could only hasten this big scheme and employ these men on Government work I am
sure it would be of enormous benefit to the
whole of the community.
Anyhow before closing I want to beg of
them that another year will not be allowed
to pass without something being done for
the relief of this drainage. The farmers to
whom I am referring suffer all the disadvantages that the whole agricultural community suffers at the present time, and in
addition they have this terrible flooding and
this drainage rate, which they have to pay,
and for which they receive nothing. Yesterday on another Bill we heard a great deal
about the glories of the Bann Valley; we
even heard of the raids that had taken place
across the Bann, raids by the O'Cahans and
the McQuillans, with fire and the sword. I
would like to say that, in my belief, no
raid carried out by these redoubtable
warriors could have possibly created more
havoc in that part than the inroads of the
Bann in flood, nor could they possibly have
had more lasting or more disastrous results.
Once more I would ask the Minister to say
if he will take this opportunity of lifting,
at any rate, a corner of the veil, giving us a
glimpse into the possibilities regarding this
scheme, and so allow those interested in the
subject as I am to go away with a few
crumbs of comfort.

I quite agree that there is a difficulty in
bringing people back to the land. I sometimes hear it argued, not in this House
but elsewhere, that the unemployed should
be brought to the land. I know the difficulty of bringing citizens of a big industrial community to work on the land. (Hon.
Members: Hear, hear.) Some people think
working on the land is like walking up and
down High Street. I think working on the
land requires some skill, it
quires a great deal of training, it

and it requires many things that people do
not seem to pay any attention to. (Hon.

a thing which could be very well done
by a large number of working people. It
is of an entirely different character. I believe in afforestation for another reason.
I think one of the tragedies of the War was
the cutting down of trees in Ireland, and
indeed in all countries. I remember attending in America a great Arbour day celebration which was the first initiated by
President Roosevelt. It compelled every person who cut down a tree to plant three trees
instead until vast tracts of land were covered by most valuable trees. And that has
gone on. We do not do that here. Vandals
as well as financiers came over to this
country, bought estates and cut down and
sold the trees, and made off with the booty.
Nothing was done. Not only were we robbed
of a great rich possession in our woods but
we were robbed of the beauty-
