It will be observed, therefore, that the
Government's contingent liability falls very
considerably after the year 1929.
Of the additional sum of £2,000,000 now
required approximately £750,000 has already
been earmarked, leaving a balance of approximately £1,250,000 for future developments.
Perhaps the more important part of the
Resolution will be found in the second
part, which proposes an extension of
this legislation for a further period
of one year from March 31st next. The
Government is satisfied, and I am confident
that this Committee will endorse the Government's view, that the employment situation
in the shipbuilding industry is such as to
warrant this further extension of time, notwithstanding that the British Government
do not propose to continue these facilities
within the area of Great Britain beyond
31st March next. I need not dwell at length
on the influences which have caused the
Imperial Government to take this step-they
were referred to by Mr. Churchill in his
Budget Speech-save to say that the same
influences do not operate in Ulster in the
same degree. The prosperity of the shipbuilding industry is one of the two hinges
upon which the industrial labour market
in Northern Ireland turns. That industry
would suffer by the withdrawal of these
facilities at a time when every encourageinent and assistance the Government can
give is essential, and it is therefore with
confidence that I ask the Committee to pass
this Resolution.
The policy which it recommends has been
endorsed on past occasions by this Committee, and I need hardly emphasise further
the fact that its machinery has proved a
most valuable agent in the alleviation of
unemployment.
I should, perhaps, refer briefly to the new
feature which was introduced in the scheme
last March, and that is the power given to
the Government to make a limited contribution towards the interest charge payable on
guaranteed loans. The necessity for exercising this power has so far arisen only in
one case and the comparatively small grant
involved is the subject of a supplementary
estimate which is down on the Order Paper
for consideration this afternoon. I do not
propose at this stage to enter.into the details
of this individual case. I may state, however,
that our efforts in the London market in the
matter of negotiating Government guaranteed loans at a favourable price on behalf of
shipping companies have been attended with
considerable success, showing that the credit
of the Province has been regarded by important London financial groups as being closely
related to that of the British Government.
The power to make interest contributions continues to operate although not specifically reenacted in the Bill which arises from this
Resolution. While theoretically the legislation only contemplates the issue of a guarantee by the Government, it is obviously a
function of my Ministry to assist the applicant in placing the Government's guarantee
to the best possible advantage as regards
price, and consequently it is customary for
my Department to carry out on behalf of the
applicant the entire negotiation with the
lenders. I wish to make this clear, because
in some quarters the impression appears to
exist that the Government itself actually
makes advances. What the Government does
is to guarantee such loan as the borrower may
be able to secure in order to carry out work
in contemplation.
"
But as regards this interest payment
in respect of any differences of interest
that may arise between the less favourable rate which we are able to secure
in connection with Northern Ireland
Government guaranteed loans and that which
a borrower may be able to get in connection
with a British guaranteed loan, this has only
arisen in one case, and I am glad to say that
the amount of the interest difference which
we shall require to make up is only a comparatively small sum. In this particular case
instead of paying the difference annually
between such rates of interest we have been
able to commute or compound that difference
by making a single payment, which I think
will work out very much more satisfactorily.
I have already stated the fact that the
contingent liability which this Government
undertakes in connection with guaranteeing
these loans is one which I hope will never
materialise if proper care is taken in scrutinising the conditions under which the guarantee is given, and I trust that our estimate
as to the entire solvency of the parties concerned will be well founded during the life of
our guarantee. I beg to move.

Question put, and agreed to.

SUPPLY.
Supplementary Estimates, 1926-27.
Considered in Committee.
Mr. MOLES in the Chair.
CLASS II. No. 10.
LOANS GUARANTEE CONTRIBUTION.
Motion made and Question proposed:
"That a sum not exceeding £6,870 be
granted to his Majesty for the service of the
year ending on the 31st of March, 1927, to
provide for a contributory payment towards
interest charges under Section 2 (1) (b) of the
Loans Guarantee Act (Northern Ireland),
1926."
Mr. BARBOUR: In moving this Supplementary Estimate, which follows very
appropriately on the discussion we have just
had in connection with the Loans Guarantee
Act, I should recall to hon. Members the
statement which the Minister. of Finance
(Mr. Pollock) made in March last when the
question of a State contribution towards
interest charges was under consideration.
My right hon. Friend then stated that
applicants in receipt of Our Guarantees
found themselves more or less dependent
upon London instead of local sources for
raising their loans, and hinted that it
was only to be expected that Ulster credit
in the British market should stand fractionally lower than that of the British Government-a circumstance which naturally
involves the shipowner or other applicant
in a slightly increased rate of interest on
borrowings as compared with what would be
the case were the ship to be constructed in
some English or Scottish shipbuilding yard,
and, therefore, to enjoy the benefit of the
British guarantee.
The Government, therefore, asked to be
placed in a position to ensure that a shipowner who is prepared to place his order
in Northern Ireland under the Northern
Ireland guarantee should not have to pay a
higher price for his money on that account,
and the Act passed in March last gave the
Ministry discretion within narrow limits
to contribute to the interest charges, if
such should prove to be necessary, in order
to bridge the gap between the interest
charged on the Imperial Government guaranteed loan and the Northern Ireland
guarantee loan. The necessity for exercising this power has so far arisen in the
case of only one transaction, and it is that
that is the subject of this Supplementary
Estimate. The shipowners were informed
that in the event of the order being obtained
by a Northern Ireland firm the Ministry
would ensure that the loan in question--
one of £650,000, repayable over a period of
twelve years-would be available on the
same terms as if raised under the British
guarantee.
a
The sum of £6,870, which is now before the
Committee, represents what I may call a
commuted payment in respect of the difference between the interest rate commanded by
the Northern Government guarantee and that
which would have been commanded by a
British Government guarantee in respect of
similar loan of £650,000. Owing to the fact
that we were prepared to pay a lump sum
down instead of, as I said a few minutes
ago, the difference of interest yearly during
the currency of the loan the amount is considerably less than would have been payable
had we made this annual payment, and the
sum we are now asking for is equal to some
fraction of one-tenth of one per cent. in
the way of interest on the full amount of
the loan. I beg to move.
Question put, and agreed to.

Mr. ELLIOTT: According to the notice
which I gave earlier this afternoon, and because I did not believe that the answers
given to some questions of mine
explicit enough, I desire to raise a question
which I think is of some importance to the
Government of Northern Ireland, and which
I know is at the same time of a great deal of
importance to some traders in Northern
Ireland. About the year 1923 the Ulster
Farmers' Produce Company came into being.
That was purely a trading company and,
according to their own prospectus, was
formed to purchase as a going concern on
the 30th day of June, 1923, the well-known
business of Warden & Stewart, Limited,
carried on for many years as produce
merchants," and so on. The company came
into being in 1923 for the purpose of carrying on this produce business and for getting
a controlling interest. According to the
prospectus
""
"The chief object of the Company is to
secure for farmers a controlling interest in
the sale of their produce, and the profits
accruing therefrom, which at the present
time go into the pockets of private individuals."
So that the company was formed as a purely
limited liability company and trading concern for the purpose of putting the profits,
which were going into the pockets of
private individuals, into the pockets of the
shareholders and directors of this newlyformed trading concern.
Now this Ulster Farmers' Produce Company
did not turn out to be the financial success
that those who promoted it had intended
that it should be, because in the year 1925,
according to the balance sheet which I produce here, at the ordinary general meeting
when the balance sheet was declared, they
found that on the year's trading they had
lost £14,532 18s. 11d., and at the same time
they owed the Ulster Bank the sum of
£16,265, 18s. 4d. In the notice convening that
meeting we read:-
"For the reason stated it will be readily
understood that the year under review has
been one during which the Board have
had grave anxiety and great trouble in
grappling with the ever-recurrent difficulties and problems. In their endeavours
to discharge their duties, and in their
efforts to do the utmost possible on behalf
of the Company, they have each shouldered
heavy responsibilities and individually incurred grave financial risks. So convinced
are they still of the possibilities of the
Company as a help to farmers, of profit to
the shareholders, and of its indispens
ability to Ulster agriculture generally,
that they have addressed themselves
to the task of reconstructing the
Company in such a way as to afford an
opportunity of securing the necessary
financial help to enable it successfully to
achieve the objects that were in view when
it was originally promoted."
That is from the second annual report of the
Board, and I wish to point out quite clearly

on any agricultural committees they were on.

If this had been a grant to benefit the farmers
of Northern Ireland I certainly would have
been the last person to get up in this House
to oppose it.

Mr. POLLOCK: It comprised plant, machinery, freehold and leasehold property.
Those were the assets that were returned to

Admittedly against that they disclosed liabilities. This has got nothing whatever to do
with the co-operative society, beyond the fact

balance between debit and credit of roughly

the necessity for helping and assisting agriculture, we may take risks. We are taking
risks every day in order to help all sorts of
enterprises in the community. We are taking
risks, although they may be negligible, with
the shipowners in whose interests my right
hon. Friend (Mr. Barbour) submitted a Money

practical measures to ascertain that those
risks are not of a very heavy character or
indeed likely to mature at all.
Therefore we said to those who were concerned in this matter that in addition to
the transfer of the assets of the society we
would require a personal guarantee for a
sufficient sum to make the loan a perfectly
secure operation. That was given, and in
view of the position as I have outlined it,
and in view of the claims that agriculture
has upon the Government, we came to the
conclusion that it was a suitable risk, and
also that in the interests of farming and
in the interests of agriculture the existence
of a Co-operative Society and such a large
number of farmers was of great advantage
to the farming community, because it enabled them to check the prices that were
submitted to them by ordinary traders in
regard to the value of the materials which
they used in the progress of their industry.
Those are the whole facts of the case, and
there is not any mystery about it at all.
All this outside talk about individual interest and interfering with ordinary traders
and all that sort of thing is entirely apart

them that assistance by lending them a sum

Sir ROBERT LYNN: I disagree with the
hon. Member who has just sat down on one
point and one only. That is that there is

to present, can present it in a more striking

was justified in giving this loan. What are
the facts? To get down to the simple bare
facts: A private limited liability company
was set up with capital and ordinary shareholders and directors, and they start to
trade in agricultural produce, just as any
company might trade in linen or ships or
something else; and as a result of their
trading as a private company they lost
£14,000 or £15,000, whatever the sum was.
Then they found themselves like many other
people-in straits. They began to ask how
they were going to get out of it. They
began to bethink themselves of the kindly
maternal Government that takes us all out
of our troubles and creates a Utopia. Then
they discover there were Acts of Parliament
that would prevent them from getting this
loan, being a private limited liability company, and they simply change their name.
They change nothing else and the Government comes along and loans them this
money.

Sir ROBERT LYNN: I would like to know

Tuesday, 19th October, 1926.

CASE OF MR. C. H. CLENDINNING.

for the systematic persecution of Mr. C. H.
Clendinning by the police force in Belfast.

Dawson Bates): No persecution of Mr. C.
H. Clendinning by the police of Belfast has
taken place. After numerous cautions,
summonses have been issued against him for
causing obstruction on the thoroughfare.
As the cases are sub judice, it would obviously be undesirable to discuss the matter
further pending the hearing of the summonses.

PORK INDUSTRY IN NORTHERN
IRELAND.
5. Mr. CRAWFORD (for Mr. Elliott) asked
the Minister of Agriculture whether any
steps have been taken, or are likely to be
taken, by the Ministry, to stabilise the Pork
industry in Northern Ireland.
The MINISTER OF AGRICULTURE (Mr.
Archdale): I assume that my hon. Friend is
concerned with the prices paid to farmers
Loans Guarantee (Money). 1736
Oral Answers.
HOUSE OF COMMONS

[Mr. Archdale]
for pork. In recent years the question of
pork prices in Ulster markets has received
almost constant attention from the Ministry.
Admittedly the fluctuations from time to
time have been acute and occasionally quite
unexpected. At conferences summoned by
the Ministry the whole question of stabilisation has been fully gone into by representatives of the Ulster Farmers' Union, the
Ulster Agricultural Organisation Society,
and the bacon-curing interest. While the
Ministry would welcome an arrangement
whereby an advance indication of probable
prices would be available for the farming
community, it is clear that there would be
serious difficulties in putting any such
arangement into force as a voluntary measure. Official machinery for the fixing of
prices is clearly out of the question. It is
not a feasible proposition since-apart from
fluctuations resulting from local conditions
-consideration would have to be given to
world variations in prices which could not
be foreshadowed with any degree of accuracy.
The Ministry notes that in recent months
there has been in several districts a tendency to sell fat pigs by live weight and that
in some quarters serious consideration has
been given to the question of catering for
the fresh pork market in Great Britain.
These two factors, no doubt, tend towards
the stabilisation of pork prices.
BONDS TO MOTOR OWNERS.
ACTION BY FREE STATE.
6. Colonel WOODS asked the Minister of
Commerce whether he is aware that the
Free State authorities are now refusing to
issue or renew bonds to motor owners in
Northern Ireland doing business in the
Free State, and whether he has any knowledge of the cause of this action.
The MINISTER OF COMMERCE (Mr.
Barbour): I am informed that the Free State
Revenue Commissioners have recently refused to issue or renew bonds in respect of
motor vehicles registered in Northern Ireland and occasionally used in Free State
territory for business purposes. The Commissioners have apparently taken this action
on the ground that, although registered outside Free State territory, the vehicles in
question, being used in the Free State for
commercial purposes, are subject 'to payment
of Customs duty.
THE COAL SITUATION.
Mr. DEVLIN (by private notice) asked the

the prohibitive prices to the poor, and the

shortage and to the profiteering going on,
he can now state what steps he has taken to
safeguard the interests of the people in respect of the coal supplies.
Mr. BARBOUR: As I propose to make a
full statement to the House to-morrow on the
coal position, I would ask the hon. Member
to allow me to defer an answer to his question till then.

Mr. POLLOCK: I think it is somewhat
unfair to the Government to assume or even
to suggest that it has or is likely to enter into
a transaction of an indefensible character,
such as my hon. Friend (Mr. Devlin) suggested. My hon. Friend asked for the names
of the small Committee that has been
appointed. I should say that in the procedure which we have adopted we have followed
exactly the Imperial method. The Imperial
Government instituted a system for two
purposes: one for the encouragement of the
production of new and modern tonnage,
mainly in order that labour might be provided. The Imperial Government established
what is known as the Trades Facilities Commission. That Committee consisted of three
gentleman prominent in business circles in
London. They scrutinised every application
that was made under the Act, and they either
refused it or accepted it. As our interests
were greater and our labour conditions much
more disastrous we followed exactly the same
course as that adopted by the British Government, and we passed an Act which is known
as the Loans Guarantee Act, which
powered the Government to set up a Committee and proceed as I have indicated. The
names of these gentleman who have undertaken most useful and valuable work to
which my right hon. Friend (Mr. Barbour)
gave testimony, when submitting the Money
Resolution, are-Mr. Stirling, managing
director of the York Street Spinning Co.;
Mr. James Mackie, head of one of the largest
engineering concerns in the country, and also
interested in almost all the departments of
the linen trade in the province; and, from the
bankers' point of view, Mr. Hardy, exmanager of the Provincial Bank. These are
the three gentleman who scrutinise the applications that come before them, and in no
case has their judgment been interfered with
by the Government. It is entirely for them
to say whether
an application is sound
or otherwise. Numbers of applications they
have turned down. One principal object that
the borrowers have in view in coming to the
Government is to secure lower rate
of interest than would ordinarily accrue to
them by borrowing in the ordinary way.
If they had to make public issues the prob
a
ability is that the rates of interest would be
higher than can be secured by a Government
guarantee. That is one advantage. Another
is that it enables them to carry out a complete shipbuilding programme that otherwise
perhaps the present fluid state of their
finances would not be sufficient to meet.

But my hon. Friend (Mr. Devlin) need not
be under any apprehension as to the character of the security, and I do not know of
any method we could adopt that would enlighten him to any greater extent than we
have done. We submit and lay upon the
Table here every transaction, and it is open
to him or to any hon. Member, from the
information which is given, to table any
Resolution here, or to offer any comment
upon the transactions as they appear. But
when I indicate that firms like the Royal
Mail Steampacket Company, the Union
Castle Line, the British African Line, Messrs.
Furness Withy-and these are all firms who
have millions of loose money, or rather not
millions of loose money, for that is unfortunately uncommon in these days, but
millions of property-firms like the Glen
Line, the Atlantic Transport Line, and

generally joined together in security with
the shipbuilders, and there is also the security of the particular ships to which the loans
apply, it will be seen that there is no conceivable loophole shall I say?-in regard to
the character of the security. With every
respect to my hon. Friend (Mr. Devlin) 1
think he must assume that the Government

the outcome of these things whether the
Government have exercised due prudence or
otherwise in the conduct of their business.

But the main feature, the main justification, is that our shipyards would have been
closed had it not been for the operation of
this guarantee, just as many of the shipyards
in Britain are closed because the shipowners
are not prepared under present conditions to
come forward and to continue their shipbuilding programmes. Also I am bound to
say that, although we are suffering from a
condition of unemployment unexampled in
the history of the country, still our yards
here are in a better position than any of the
yards of the Kingdom with one or two exceptions, and I say here most emphatically and
advisedly that had it not been for the operation of this method of financing the various
concerns which we are now discussing, I
have no doubt at all that both our shipyards

thousands of men would have been walking
the streets.
I can give the assurance to the House that
the security is perfectly ample. The hon.

Motor Vehicles (Traffic and Regulations) [Money]..
Considered in Committee under Standing
Order No. 65.
[Mr. MOLES in the Chair.]
Motion made, and Question proposed:
"That for the purpose of any Act of the
present Session to make further provision
with respect to the use of mechanically-propelled vehicles on public highways, and with
respect to the licensing and regulation of
certain classes of such vehicles and their
drivers and conductors, and for other purposes related or incidental to the matter
aforesaid, it is expedient to charge on and
issue out of the Consolidated Fund of
Northern Ireland, or the growing produce
thereof, and pay to the Road Fund (Northern
Ireland) in accordance with the directions
of the Ministry of Finance, a sum equal to
the proceeds of all sums paid to the Exchequer of Northern Ireland in respect of fees
for licences granted, and in respect of
penalties and other sums recovered, under
or in pursuance of such Act."-(Governor's
Recommendation signified.)-(Mr. Barbour.)
Mr. BARBOUR: Hon. Members will see
from the text of the Resolution which
appears in the Order Paper that no new
feature is proposed. The Resolution follows
the procedure already laid down by the
Roads Act, 1920. This procedure, namely,
the passing of moneys to the Road Fund via
the Exchequer instead of paying them direct
into the Road Fund, gives statutory effect to
the principle embodied in the Exchequer and
Audit Act that all revenue is to be paid to
the Exchequer. The Road Licence Duty is a
Revenue Tax, the same as any other, and not
a special tax, levied specifically for the purpose of financing the Road Fund, although
in practice the proceeds of the tax are
applied to road purposes. Similarly, the
proceeds from penalties which go to the
Road Fund would normally go to the Petty
Sessions Fund or the Exchequer: that is to
say, towards the cost of the administration
of justice. The charge on public moneys,
which necessitates the passing of this Resolution, is merely a formal one seeing that the
amount which will be payable out of the
Consolidated Fund to the Road Fund in any
year will have previously been paid into the
Consolidated Fund in the forms of fees for
licences and penalties and other sums recovered under the provisions of the Act.
Although the Resolution is of a formal
character, it may be of interest to Members
to know generally what amounts are likely
to be paid into and issued from the Consolidated Fund under this section. An
account of the Road Fund showing the
receipts and payments is furnished each

Mr. BARBOUR: I was just coming to that.
As regards the amounts payable by way of

there will be an increase or a decrease. While
the amounts of the various penalties are
proposed to be considerably increased under
the Bill, which fact of itself would have the
effect of increasing considerably the aggregate sum accruing to the Exchequer, it is
hoped that, on the other hand, this will have
the necessary deterrent effect in regard to
the number of offences. Accordingly, the
penalties which may be inflicted will result
in larger individual sums, but possibly not

1751 Malone Training School Bill—
Second Reading. 1752
HOUSE OF COMMONS
Malone Training School Bill.
Order for Second reading read.
Sir DAWSON BATES: The object of this
Bill is two-fold. It involves (1) the taking
over of the Malone Training School (formerly
the Malone Reformatory) by the Government, under circumstances which I will
mention afterwards; and (2) the provision of
accommodation for Borstal boys in Northern
Ireland, for whom, at the present time, there
is no accommodation.
Under the reformatory system in Northern
Ireland the liability for providing reformatory treatment is placed upon the County
Councils and County Borough Councils, and
the Government is authorised by Statute to
make a contribution towards the cost. For
many years past reformatories have been conducted, and are still being conducted, by
charitable organisations, supported partly
by private subscriptions, and partly by
payments made by the local authorities
for the maintenance of the inmates,
and supplemented by Government grants.
Before any organisation can start a Reformatory a licence has to be obtained from the
Ministry of Home Affairs, and these institutions are inspected from time to time by
the Inspectors of the Ministry. So far as
local authorities are concerned, they discharge their obligations by making arrangements with these certified schools for the
reception of the children which may be committed from their areas in a Reformatory
School. It is not, therefore, proposed to
interfere with the existing system, or to interfere with the existing institutions which,
for many years past, have carried on, and
are still carrying on, such good work.
Difficulties have, however, arisen in connection with the Malone Reformatory. This
institution was founded so far back as 1860,
when a number of public-spirited citizens
banded themselves together to provide a Reformatory for Protestant boys. The present
magnificent buildings were erected, and since
that time the founders and their successors
have carried on a social work, the value
which it is almost impossible to exaggerate.
I would remind hon. Members that all the
children who have been sent to this Reformatory are children who had committed
offences, and who have given evidence of a
tendency to drift into a life of crime. The
Reformatory has given a chance to many
thousands of boys who would otherwise have
run a grave risk of becoming confirmed
criminals, and the records of this institution
alone show that 85 per cent. of those who
were committed to it have become good
citizens.
But the situation has somewhat changed.
At one time the numbers of this institution
were as high as 130, while at the present
time there are only 32 boys at the school.
If one could say that this decrease in
numbers was due to the improvement of the
morals of the boys in our community it
would be a matter for sincere congratulation,
but, unfortunately, such is not the case. In
the old days the cost of maintenance of a
boy in one of these institutions was comparatively small, but, with the increased
cost of living, managers of schools were
forced to ask the local authorities for an increased contribution for the maintenance of
the inmates, and accordingly the magistrates, with a view partly to keeping down
the rates, and partly in the mistaken idea
that they were ruining the boy's chances in
life by committing him to a Reformatory,
became more and more reluctant to send
boys to these schools. Then the Probation
Act came into force, which encouraged magistrates to take what I think was a mistaken
course. I agree that no more useful and
necessary Act was ever passed, provided the
powers under it were properly exercised; but
when one hears of cases of boys being put
on probation seven or eight times, I think
it must be obvious to everyone that, at all
events, the Act is not being properly utilised.
In all these circumstances, therefore, the
number of committals became, by degrees,
fewer and fewer, and the results as regards
Malone Reformatory was that the numbers
have fallen from 130 to 32, and, in consequence, the committee of management found
themselves unable to carry on the institution
as an economical proposition with this
number of boys. In these circumstances,
after very careful consideration, the committee of the institution decided that there
was no other course but to close down the
school. As a result of my representation,
the committee very kindly agreed to postpone the carrying out of their decision until
the Government were in a position to make
other arrangements, for, in the event of the
school closing down, there would have been
no provision whatever for Protestant boys
committed to a Reformatory in Northern
Ireland.
For some time past the Government have
also had under consideration the question
of the maintenance of Borstal boys in
Northern Ireland. As hon. Members are
aware, at the time the Government of Ireland
Act of 1920 was passed, there was no such
institution in Northern Ireland. Up to that
time it was customary to send Borstal boys
from Northern Ireland to Clonmel, and in
1920, when we took over, there were no fewer
than 52 boys from Northern Ireland there.
These particular boys have long since been
released, and since we took over no further
boys were committed to Clonmel. In the
meantime the only course open to the Government, pending the establishment of a Borstal
1753 Malone Training School Bill-
19 OCTOBER 1926
Second Reading. 1754
Institution in Northern Ireland was to make
arrangements for the accommodation of these
boys in England, and in this connection I
would like to express my indebtedness to
the Imperial Home Secretary for the
facilities he placed at my disposal. We have
at the present time 31 boys undergoing treatment there, and the number shows રી.
tendency to increase.
There are many objections to sending
Borstal boys from Northern Ireland to
England. One is that the maintenance
charges are high, amounting to no less than
£110 per annum, and the travelling expenses
are heavy; but there is a further objection
which, I think, will appeal to everyone in
this House. It cuts the boys completely off
from their parents, as, of course, the distance is so great that it is impossible for
parents in the position of life which most
of them are in to incur the expenditure of
going over to England to visit their children,
and it certainly does add very much to the
pain which these parents must feel when
their children are convicted when in addition
they realise that they will not see them
perhaps for 3 years.
We are faced then with the problem of
having to find accommodation for Reformatory boys, and also for Borstal boys. The
Government went into the matter very
closely, with a view to seeing whether or
not some arrangement could be made under
which the Malone Training School could be
utilised for both purposes, and as a result,
after negotiations, to which I will refer
later, the trustees of the Malone Institution
have agreed to hand over their premises to
the Government free of cost. It is intended
to treat both Borstal and Reformatory boys
in this institution, and in this connection I
have consulted a number of experts on the
subject who have had considerable experience of this work both here and in Scotland,
and I am advised that there is no difficulty
in treating these boys in a combined institution provided there is adequate supervision
and proper segregation, and I am quite
satisfied that we will be able to make adequate arrangements. I might explain to
this House that the modern system of the
treatment of Reformatory boys, and also
the treatment of Borstal boys, is more on
the principle of a school than a prison.
Practical experience has shown that by far
the best results are obtained by this method,
and now that the treatment for both these
classes is the same, there is not the same
objection which has hitherto obtained to
combining the treatment in the same
building.
Hon. Members will be interested to know
that as regards Reformatory boys in
Northern Ireland, no less a number thau
85 per cent. of the boys discharged kept
straight, and I think these figures are very
satisfactory, and I also think that if they were
more fully known by magistrates the same
reluctance to commit these boys to such
institutions would not exist. I also find
that as regards the Borstal Institution the
results here again are of a satisfactory
character. No less than 71 per cent. of
those who have been convicted for the first
time afterwards turned over a new leaf, but
in the case of those who had been previously
convicted the results have not been so satisfactory. Only 55 per cent. of them have
been successfully treated. I might remind
the House that the ages at which a boy can
be committed to a reformatory run between
12 and 16, although it is seldom that boys
so young as 12 are in fact committed. As
regards Borstal boys, the ages run between
16 and 21, and they may be kept for a
maximum of 3 years, so that hon. Members
will see that the ages, to a large extent,
overlap.
Hon. Members will find
an agreement,
which is set out in full in the Bill, which
has been entered into between the Government and the trustees of the institution.
This is, of course, subject to the sanction
of Parliament. If the Bill is thus approved,
the effect will be that the property of the
Malone Training School will pass to the
Ministry of Home Affairs, and the Ministry
will carry on, as I have already indicated,
a combined Borstal Institution and Reformatory School. The agreement also provides
that any of the existing officials who are not
taken into the employment of the Government will be compensated as may be deemed
fair by the Ministry of Home Affairs and
the Ministry of Finance, after consultation
with the Committee, for the loss of their
employment. I may say that it is the intention of the Government to appoint the
present manager of the Malone Training
School to be manager of the new institution.
This gentleman has proved himself a most
efficient manager, and has devoted himself
to the work of reclaiming these boys who
have come under his care in a very unselfish
way, and without hope of any financial
reward. I cannot speak too highly of the
principal of this institution and I think it is
very fortunate that the Government can look
forward to the new institution being carried
on under his management.
The cost of carrying on the combined institution will be, in the first instance,
a charge on the Government funds, but local
authorities will remain liable to make contributions in respect of boys committed for
Reformatory treatment from their own particular areas. We are satisfied that this
proposed arrangement will be an economical
1755 Malone Training School Bill- HOUSE OF COMMONS

Second Reading.
[Sir Dawson Bates]
one. We are paying, as I have already said,
£110 per head in England in respect of
Borstal boys, while the present cost of maintaining a boy at the Malone Training School
is about 30s. weekly. We do not propose to
alter the existing law in regard to Reformatories except so far as Malone Training
School is concerned. The existing Reformatories will remain exactly on the same
footing as they are at present. This proproposed institution is, to a certain extent, a
new experiment, but I think it will afford a
satisfactory solution to what has been રી
difficult problem.
In conclusion, I trust that the courts will,
in future, show less hesitation in sending
boys to the Reformatory who really ought to
be there. When I say that, I do not for one
moment suggest that a boy who has made a
first slip should be sent to such an institution, for I feel that the proper persons to
control the boy are his own parents. At the
same time, if a boy either has not got the
parents, or if his parents are indifferent to
his welfare, I think the State should step in
and see that the boy gets the chance in life.
which his parents do not give him. I beg to
move.

Industrial Assurance (Juvenile
Societies) Bill.
Order for Second Reading read.
Motion made, and Question proposed:
"That the Bill be now read a Second time.
Mr. BARBOUR: The object of this short
Measure is to amend slightly the provisions
of the Industrial Assurance Act (Northern
Ireland), 1924, in relation to certain juvenile
assurance business carried on by Friendly
Societies. It has been the practice of some
of the Friendly Societies to recruit juvenile
members. Such juvenile members are insured for funeral and other benefits, and
as time goes on are granted full membership
on the attainment of a certain age. In the
case of certain Friendly Societies subsidiary
societies or branches are specially formed
for juvenile membership, and in other cases
branches of the societies enrol both juvenile
and adult members. This class of assurance
does not come within the purview of the
Industrial Assurance Act (Northern Ireland),
1924, unless and until collectors are employed
to receive the premiums.
Some of these societies have, in fact,
elected to employ collectors to collect the
premiums of the juvenile members, the
ordinary method of payment at lodge meetings not being found convenient in the case
of children. This practice was recognised
when the Act of 1924 was framed, and provision was made in Section II whereby the
Industrial Assurance Commissioner was empowered to grant a certificate of exemption
from the provisions of the Act to juvenile
societies whose membership was limited to
persons under 18 years of age. The section.
has, however, in practice proved to be not
quite sufficiently elastic, since it makes no
provision for branches whose membership.
includes both juvenile and non-juvenile
members, even where the employment of
collectors is limited to the collection of
the contributions of juvenile members.
As hon. Members are aware, Friendly
Societies with their headquarters in Great
Britain are entitled to carry on business in
Northern Ireland. Thus it happens that a
considerable part of the Friendly Society
activities in our area is in the hands of
branches or societies connected with bodies.
whose headquarters are across the Channel.
It is, therefore, desirable that we here
should work in close co-operation with the
Imperial authorities in legislation affecting
such societies, and, in fact, in the preparation of the Measure now before hon.
Members my Ministry has kept in close
touch with the Industrial Assurance Commissioner's Department in London. A Bill
on similar lines has already been introduced
into the House of Lords.
The text of the substituted Section II does
not require much explanation. It provides
that the parent Act shall not apply to a
juvenile society as defined, notwithstanding
that premiums of the juvenile members are
received by collectors if and so long as the
premiums of any adult members are not
received by collectors. I beg to move.

1759 Expiring Laws Continuance Bill-

HOUSE OF COMMONS
Second Reading.
Expiring Laws Continuance Bill.
Order for Second Reading read.
Motion made, and Question proposed,
"That the Bill be now read a Second time."
The ATTORNEY-GENERAL (Mr. Babington): This Bill is for the purpose of continuing certain temporary measures, some of
which deal with matters which are within
the control of this Parliament. Others deal
with matters which have been legislated for
in the Imperial Parliament but are still
within our control. They were originally
either experimental or liable to revision and
only for a definite limited time. They have
to be continued from year to year, and a
single day only is fixed for their continuance,
namely, 31st December, 1927. The Bill has
been framed so as to fit in with the corresponding provisions of the Imperial statute
which deals with matters which relate to
Northern Ireland in so far as the Imperial
Government has got power to legislate for
Northern Ireland.
This present Bill supplements the provisions of the Imperial Act by dealing with
these enactments relating to subjects with
respect to which this Parliament has power
to legislate, so that the two Measures taken
together will be exhaustive and provide for
the continuance of all necessary temporary
Measures. Hon. Members will find the
Measures themselves in the Schedule to
the Act. In the first part are set out
those statutes which were passed by the
Imperial Government, and in the second
part are set out those Measures which
were passed by this House. These include, as
hon. Members will see, a lot of matters which
are not perhaps of very much importance,
but some of them, such as the Courts
(Emergency Powers) Act, 1914, which is still
in force with regard to a number of Orders
which were made under it, must necessarily
be continued. Then there is the Harbours,
Docks and Piers (Temporary Increase of
Charges) Act. These authorities had no
statutory power prior to the war when
heavier charges were imposed on them, and
a temporary measure was passed giving them
power with certain limitations to make
certain charges. This is continued for the
present. The other Acts in the second part
of the Schedule are the Local Government
(Emergency Powers) Act, 1921, the Civil
Authorities (Special Powers) Act, 1922, the
National Health Insurance Act, 1924, and the
Canals (Continuance of Charging Powers)
Act, 1925. The Government consider that
these existing temporary measures should
continue. I beg to move.
Mr. WM. MCMULLEN: I am rather surprised that in introducing this Measure the
Attorney-General did not think fit to make
some
reference to the Civil Authorities
(Special Powers) Act. It leaves one in a
difficult position. I do not desire to move
the rejection of the Bill, because I appreciate
fully that if I attempted to move the rejection of this Bill on account of my objection
to this particular Act of 1922 not being repealed, I would probably be doing a thing
that would result in the holding up of a
great many desirable Measures that are
contained in this Bill. I have no desire to
do that. I thought some reference should
have been made to the Civil Authorities
(Special Powers) Act. Anyone who takes the
trouble to read the debates-
Mr. SPEAKER: May I interrupt? The
long established practice in the Imperial
Parliament, which of course we follow, with
regard to this particular Bill which comes
up every year, has been that the discussion
on the different enactments which are continued should take place in Committee Stage
when it is open to any hon. Member to move
to leave out a particular enactment in a
particular schedule. It has always been held
that it shall not be discussed on the Second
Reading, which is merely taken as an
affirmation of the principle that certain
temporary laws shall be continued, and that
is all.
Mr. WM. MCMULLEN: I have no desire at
this stage to go into the merits of this
question. As a matter of fact I did not
intend to go into the merits at all. Anything
I have got to say on the particular Act to
which I referred I will say in the Committee
Stage. I thought, however, the best thing
would be to mention the matter so that the
Government themselves would see the wisdom
of amending this Bill when it comes to the
Committee Stage. I think it will be agreed
by anyone who pays attention to this question
at all that that was an Act put on the statute
book purely for an emergency. Fortunately
that emergency has passed, and I would ask
the right hon. Gentleman to consider the
advisability of removing this Act from the
Bill now before the House. If the Government do that it will save my colleagues and
myself the trouble of moving the rejection
of that particular Act.
Mr. KYLE: I bow to your ruling that
matters may not be discussed at this stage.
but one would have thought when the
Attorney-General asked us to give a Second
Reading to this Measure and mentioned
certain Acts which he declared the Covernment wanted a continuance of, that the
Government would have given some definite
and cogent reason as to why these Acts should
be continued. There is not only the Act referred to by my colleague (Mr. Wm.
McMullen), but there is the Local Government (Emergency Powers) Act, 1921. What
reason have they for desiring to continue the

powers they then got in this year 1926 in
face of the assertion made by Members of the
Government and speakers on the Government
side that there is now no state of emergency
so far as Northern Ireland is concerned?
In the whole of Great Britain and
Ireland there is no more peaceful and
law-abiding place than Belfast and the
North of Ireland. Employees here have
always lain down with the employers. Employees have given way to the employers in
the reduction of their wages, and there is no

all this, the Government wants the continuation of those Acts of Parliament which
are reprehensible from a democratic point of
view. I would feel almost disposed to oppose

these two Acts which no democratic Government ought to desire to have continued an
instant longer than absolutely essential in the
interests of the community in which we
reside.

AGRICULTURAL SERVICES.
Motion made and Question proposed:
"That a supplementary sum not exceeding
£1,350 be granted to his Majesty for the ser-
Ivice of the year ending 31st March, 1927, to
defray the expenses of the Ministry of Agriculture in respect of Agricultural Education
and Research, Improvement of Live Stock,
Agricultural Development, Agricultural Statistics, Afforestation, and Diseases of Animals, including sundry Grants in Aid and
certain Capital Expenditure under 14 and 15
Geo. V, c. 13, s. 1 (N.I.), and 15 and 16 Geo.
V, c. 17, s. 13 (1) (N.I.), (16 Geo. V, c. 4
(N.I.))."
The MINISTER OF AGRICULTURE (Mr.
Archdale): The Supplementary Estimate
which I am now bringing before the Committee is in addition to the original estimate
in respect of Agricultural and Research
Grants-in-Aid. This Supplementary Estimate
is necessitated by important changes which
have been made since, but we have been
able, by certain savings and by receipts from
Grants-in-Aid, to reduce the amount to the
sum of £1,350. We saved £1,400 out of Receipts Appropriated in Aid, this being due
to the fact that owing to the outbreak of
foot and mouth disease in England we could
not spend as much as we had intended on the
purchase of bulls in England. With regard
to the item "Replacement of Live Stock,'
it will be remembered that in most counties
وو
there was a tremendous loss of cattle and
sheep by fluke in consequence of the weather,
and the Government agreed to pay 3 per cent.
of the interest on loans advanced to farmers
on the security of their farms and two solvent trustees. The banks were to charge 5
per cent., of which the Government agreed
to pay 3 per cent. and the farmers were to
pay the remaining 2 per cent. The loan was
to terminate on 31st December, 1926, but the
Ministry of Agriculture realized that no man
could replace his stock in that time or gather
the money to replace his stock, SO my
Ministry got the Ministry of Finance to agree
that the loans should be extended, one-third
to be repaid on 31st December this year, onethird to be repaid on 31st December next
year, and one-third on 31st December, 1928.
Therefore a further sum representing our
share of the interest will have to be paid to
the banks, and that is the sum which we
estimate to be £750,
The next item in the Supplementary
estimate is the building grant to the Royal
Ulster Agricultural Society in respect of the
annex we put up at Balmoral. I think that
any Member of the Committee or any member of the public who was at the show last
year will agree that that building added
enormously to the benefits of the show we
held there for the farmers. It was crowded
from the beginning to the end of the show
and the farmers who went there were able
to see what could be done and were able
to appreciate for themselves the benefits of
the research work, and of the various experiments we had been making. In addition
to the other exhibits there were exhibits of
baby beef and the fattening of pigs.
We
found it was not suitable to have animals in
the same building as butter and other agricultural produce, so we decided to build an
annex in conjunction with the Royal Ulster
Agricultural Society. We estimated that the
total cost of the whole scheme would be
about £8,000: The Government gave a grant
of £2,000 and we are now asking for another
£1,500, making £3,500 in all, and the
remainder will be found by the Royal Ulster
Agricultural Society.
The particulars of the next item in the
Supplementary Estimate, "Unemployment
Relief Scheme" (Forestry)" are pretty clearly
set out in the Estimate. We are increasing
our forestry acreage faster than we had intended in order to provide more employment,
We are engaging extra labourers and we hope
in a short time to get more land and thus
increase the acreage still further. The next
item refers to the purchase of new areas for
afforestation, but as all the schemes we had
in hand are not yet finished we only put
down a sum of £100. We have, however,
three areas in view that we are trying to
purchase for a reasonable sum. By the end
of next year, at the present rate of planting,

I now turn to the second item in the
Supplementary Estimate, which relates to
the purchase of coal. In dealing with this
sub-head it may not be out of place if at
the outset I review briefly the history of
the Government's activities in the matter
of ensuring coal supplies throughout
Northern Ireland during the stoppage at
the mines. As hon. Members are doubtless
aware, for some months prior to the beginning of the strike, on or about the 1st May,
it was obvious that the strike so long talked
of would materialise, and steps were taken
to impress upon public utility undertakings,
public institutions and industrial concerns
generally, the need for laying in substantial
stocks.
In many cases this advice was followed,
with the result that in the early days of
the strike the Ministry, through its Emergency Organisation, was able to maintain
coal supplies at a satisfactory standard,
though transfers of coal from the well-
Supplementary Estimates. 1780
Supply-
HOUSE OF COMMONS

[Mr. Barbour]
stocked concern to its less fortunate neighbour were found necessary in certain cases.
Details of the Emergency Organisation and
of the Rationing Orders have already appeared in the public Press. Stated briefly,
the organisation comprises five county controllers, who work in close touch with my
Ministry on the one hand, and with subcontrollers in the various urban centres on
the other. The object of the organisation
is to maintain essential services during the
period of the emergency.
When the general strike came to an end
on 12th May and no settlement of the coal
strike was in view, the question of direct
purchase of coal by the Government was
fully considered. It was ascertained, however, that private enterprise could be relied
upon to bring in coal in adequate quantities,
and so long as the summer weather continued this arrangement was found to work
satisfactorily.
Mr. KYLE: As long as coal was not
needed.
Mr. BARBOUR: In fact it may be said
that the arrangements made have resulted
in
satisfactory supplies being available
not only for the private consumer but
for industry almost up to the present
time, with the exception of a short
interruption of supplies caused by shipping delays due to the severe weather in the
Atlantic. The activities of my Ministry
have been mainly directed towards encouraging the importation of foreign coal
and safeguarding the position of those
poorer members of the community who rely
to a great extent on gas for their means of
cooking and heating. With this end in view
the Ministry has been, and is, keeping in
close touch with gas undertakings throughout Northern Ireland, and I am glad to say
that the outlook as to the adequacy of fuel
stocks at such undertakings for some time
to come is reassuring.
To our thinking it seemed eminently desirable that all large consumers of coal
should always maintain their stocks at a
standard adequate to meet requirements for
a period of four or five weeks ahead,
especially since even were the strike to collapse forthwith, several weeks must elapse
ere normal supplies of British coal would be
available. As it may be hazarded that
prices in the British market are likely to
fall but slowly, we felt justified in urging
the adoption of a policy of forward buying
by large consumers. The general position
has been materially relieved by the commendable policy adopted throughout by our
two largest heating and lighting undertakings, namely, the Belfast gas undertaking and the Belfast electricity undertaking, both of which have contracted for
sufficient supplies to enable them to carry
on until about the end of the year.
Hon. Members may have noticed in the
papers that the gas undertaking has contracted for delivery of no less than 10.000
tons of foreign coal between now and the
end of the year. While such is the case in
these undertakings, unfortunately large consumers generally were not prepared to
adopt our suggestions that they should
enter into forward contracts. There is little
doubt, I think, that there was a feeling
throughout industry that a collapse of the
miners' strike might be expected towards
the end of September, a factor which
undoubtedly led to a certain amount of
hand-to-mouth buying by large consumers.
With the arrival of the colder weather and
the abolition of summer time the demand for
fuel increased very considerably. Added to
this factor was the increasing difficulty of
obtaining coal from the Continent. So long
as coal from that source was available the
risk of the merchant in importing large quantities was not so marked as in the case of
importation from America, where a minimum period of six weeks might elapse
between the date of contract and the date
of delivery in this country. Moreover, purchases of foreign coal, whether American or
Continental, required immediate cash payments, an important factor to be taken into
consideration by the importer. It was clear,
therefore, that from the merchant's point of
view unless large consumers would enter
upon forward contracts there was a decided
risk that were he to bring in large quantities of foreign coal under contract for forward deliveries at a high price, he might
suffer loss when normal supplies of British
coal became available.


It was in view of these difficulties that the
Government decided to supplement private
efforts by entering the market and making
purchases of coal direct from America, since
we believed at that time that the task of purchasing supplies for the whole of Northern
Ireland was likely to prove of too great
magnitude for private enterprise, having regard to the risk of loss attached to forward
purchases, which the Government fully
appreciate.
Supplementary Estimates. 1782
Supply-
20-OCTOBER 1926.
The Estimate now before the House is, as
hon. Members will appreciate, largely conjectural, as it is impossible to form any
estimate of what loss, if any, will accrue to
the Government by reason of embarking upon
this scheme.
The note on the Estimate explains the procedure adopted. Purchases of American coal
are made by an agent on the authority of my
Ministry. The financing of the transactions
is undertaken by the agent. The coal is to be
sold to merchants throughout Northern Ireland and prices will be determined by my
Ministry after taking into account purchase
price, freight, and all expenses prior to the
sale to the merchants. The prices at which
the coal will be available to consumers will
be settled by the Ministry in consultation
with the coal merchants. The loss, if any, to
the Government will naturally arise out of
such stocks which may remain on hand after
supplies become available from the usual
channels.
There has been a good deal of talk and
maybe misapprehension in the Press and elsewhere as to the action of the Imperial
Government in placing an embargo upon the
transhipment of coal from British ports. In
this connection it may not be generally appreciated that the situation in Great Britain
generally has throughout the whole duration
of the strike been more serious than that with
which we were faced in Northern Ireland.
Factories have been closed down for lack of
fuel and households have been subjected to
actual privations. To give an idea of the
emergency arrangements in Great Britain I
should like to put hon. Members in possession
of the rationing orders which were made at an
carly stage after the outbreak of the general
strike.
So far as actual household consumption is
concerned, domestic consumers were only entitled to 1 cwt. of coal per fortnight without
a permit, provided their stock did not exceed
5 cwts. Only in very exceptional circumstances could a permit for greater quantities
be obtained.
For industrial purposes under the Coal
Emergency Directions, consumption of coal
by industries must not exceed 50 per cent. of
the consumption during the corresponding
period of the previous year without a permit
issued by the Local Authority.
As regards gas and electricity for power,
this was not allowed to exceed 50 per cent. of
the consumption during the corresponding
period of the previous year without a
written permit from the Local Authority.
Street lighting, whether from electricity or
gas, was to be reduced to a minimum.
During the summer months the British
Government allowed re-export of foreign
coal to Northern Ireland, but in September
a warning was given to all importers of
foreign coal that permits for re-export would
not be issued. The Northern Government,
immediately this state of affairs was brought
to its notice, took action, with the result
that the Imperial authorities agreed to allow
the transhipment of a certain limited
quantity of foreign coal from English and
Scottish ports to Northern Ireland. The
present position is therefore this. that
while the output of British coal is steadily
increasing, it is not yet keeping pace with
the increase in demand and the falling off
in the importation of foreign coal. According to a Press report the weekly output is
now about 1,000,000 tons, as contrasted with
some 200,000 tons about a month ago. For
the information of hon. Members I may
state that the normal amount of coal brought
to the surface in England and Scotland
under ordinary conditions amounts to 5
million tons per week, and, speaking very
roughly, just to give hon. Members some
idea of the position, I believe that the disposal of this coal is divided into thirds.
One-third is exported, one-third is used in
pig-iron and steel and manufacturing industries generally, and the remaining one-third
is available for domestic consumption and for
public utility undertakings. So you will see
that, even with the increased amount raised
last week, we are still very far short of the
actual consumption in England and Scotland. The situation in Great Britain is,
however, improving, but until there is a
more marked increase in the number of men
returning to the pits we cannot expect substantial supplies of coal from across the
Channel. At the same time my Ministry is
keeping in close touch with the Imperial
Mines Department.
There is another and રી very important
aspect of this question which has been referred to during the last day or two, and
that, of course, is the question of profiteering
in the coal trade. Undoubtedly at the present time coal prices are high, and very high
prices are justified owing to the cost of importation. I say high prices as compared
with the prices that we ordinarily expect.
Mr. BEATTIE: One shilling a stone!
Mr. BARBOUR: Those prices under present
conditions are unfortunately rendered very
much higher in consequence of the very small
quantities in which coal is being distributed.
Not only is this due to the original price,
but I think in some of the processes of distribution higher prices are being charged
than are possibly justified. This is due;
I think, to the operations of a new class
of coal vendors, who are actually buying
Supplementary Estimates. 1784
Supply-
HOUSE OF COMMONS

[Mr. Barbour]
coal from the bellmen who used to distribute
it, and are breaking it up into smaller quantities and charging what seems to be an
excessive price for those very small supplies.
One of our great difficulties in fixing
prices of foreign coal is that there is
a tendency for the market on the Continent
to change in an adverse direction from week
to week. Fortunately so far as the city
of Belfast is concerned houcholders can, despite the great increase in the price of coal,
obtain gas at prices which at this juncture
cannot be regarded as otherwise than very
satisfactory. I was interested to note from
a Press report the other day that no less
than 35,000 houses in Belfast have gas
meters installed, and that as an indication
of the substitution of gas in lieu of coal for
heating and lighting a test has shown an
increase of 25 per cent. in consumption of
gas as contrasted with consumption at the
corresponding date last year. I have already
referred to the policy of the gas undertaking in covering their requirements by
large forward purchases, and I am glad to
take this opportunity of expressing my
appreciation of its activities, not only in
providing heating and lighting at such an
exceptionally cheap rate, but also for its
unfailing assistance to my Ministry in helping less fortunately placed undertakings.
In investigating complaints as to excessive
charges for coal my Ministry have been
keeping in touch with prices charged in
Great Britain. It is a matter of satisfaction to note that having regard to the
heavier freight from Continental ports to
Northern Ireland ports the prices in Great
Britain vary but little from those obtaining
in Northern Ireland. As hon. Members may
have noticed, the prices charged in England
and Scotland have formed the subject of
investigation by the Imperial Authorities,
the result of which has been a decision
against the proposal that coal should be
strictly controlled in price. Personally I am
disposed to consider that if, as I propose
should be done, adequate publicity is
given to a reasonable price standard for coal,
the public will thereby be in a position to
assist the Government in preventing abuses.
Before I conclude I should like to make an
appeal for the exercise of the greatest
economy in the use of fuel, whether in the
home, in industry, or in the public service
undertakings. My right hon. Friend, the
Minister of Home Affairs, has already requested Local Authorities to take steps to
reduce street lighting to a minimum and to
take other measures likely to reduce the
consumption of coal. I am glad to say that
such steps are being adopted generally, but
at the same time I should like to supplement my right hon. Friend's request by
taking this opportunity of impressing upon
Local Authorities who have not yet taken
action, the need for taking immediate steps
to conserve our stocks.
are
It is necessary that we should face the
fact that the present position in regard to
coal supplies is undoubtedly one of gravity.
When, however, we consider that we
now in the twenty-fifth week of the coal
stoppage and that whereas we formerly
drew our coal supplies from a base of 100
miles or so away, and now we must look
to ports thousands of miles away for
our supplies, it is a remarkable tribute
to the system adopted that we here in
Northern Ireland have thus far come
so successfully through the emergency. As
regards the future, the success of the
measures we have adopted will to a great
extent depend upon the sympathetic Cooperation of our citizens throughout
Northern Ireland in assisting the Govern
ment by curtailing fuel consumption to a
minimum. Provided the greatest economy is
exercised I am hopeful that we shall come
through the present emergency, not, it is true,
without considerable inconvenience and privation, but without any grave interruption
in the maintenance of the really essential
requirements of the community.

them how they suffer. I say if anything
ever justified Socialism or prompt and
immediate Government action it is this
situation here. The Government would have
been perfectly justified in taking over the
coal and rationing it, and selling it to the
poor people at a price at which they would
be able to buy it.
Now I come to another question. It is,
perhaps, of infinitesimal importance compared with the larger and wider issue, and
that is the question of supplying coal to the
schools. I understand that half a ton of
coal has been given to the transferred
schools, but the schools that have not been
transferred have got no coal at all. While
you have an Education Act in operation
compelling the children to go to school you
have them in these schools shivering with
the cold, coming out of cold homes and
suffering in a way children ought not to
suffer. I want to know has nothing been
done to see that the schools are supplied with
coal, not only the provided schools but the
non-provided schools in Northern Ireland.
The concluding part of the right hon.
Gentleman's speech was an appeal to the
people. Does he think that appeal is necessary? People cannot afford to pay the price
asked for coal at the present moment. In
addition to that, I heard of a case the other
day of a bellman who had two tons of coal
on one of his lorries. He was stopped, and
SL
all the coal the bellman was carrying was
bought by a wealthy man in the city. It

nothing else-to which they are subjected in

The PRIME MINISTER: I did not intend
to intervene in the debate, had it not been
that since my return from abroad a certain:
number of serious cases of profiteering in
coal have been brought to my notice, and I
have consulted with the Minister of Com-.
merce since I arrived in the House. We have
talked over the matter and with his concurrence I propose to say a few words to the
House on the subject of coal and its distribution, and how far the Government can
intervene in the matter.
First of all, everyone will exonerate the
Government from having caused, in any way,
Supplemental Estimates. 1808
Supply-
HOUSE OF COMMONS.

[The Prime Minister]
the shortage of coal that has arisen, not only
here but in Great Britain generally. You
cannot blame us in any way for that. The
question then arises how far can the Government intervene and help in a difficult
situation. I think that my right hon. Friend
beside me here (Mr. Barbour) will testify to
the fact that the coal merchants in Ulster
have worked in the most harmonious way
possible with his Ministry in this crisis.
(Hon. Members; Hear, hear). And it is
largely owing to their wide experience in the
industry that Ulster has so far tided over a
great difficulty with so little hardship. 1
am in a position to say that the situtaion is
much graver in many parts of Great Britain
than it is here. There is no doubt whatever
about that. It is due, I think, to the House
to realise and to recognise the work that has
been done by my right hon. Friend the
Minister of Commerce and his officials in
this difficult time. The Government will
see that a large supply of coal is available.
I am sure that no hon. Member wishes to
make political capital out of a matter
which might have serious consequences if
either my right hon. Friend or I
were to
reveal to the House the steps that have been
taken by the Government still further to
ensure an ample supply of coal to the people
during the winter months that lie ahead. 1
can assure the whole of the people that everything that can be done has been done and is
being done in order to ensure that there shall
be no shortage of a serious character in the
forthcoming months.
As to the regulation of prices, it is obvious
to everybody that the control of prices is
far beyond the power of my right hon.
Friend or the Government as a whole. As a
result of the demand for coal throughout the
whole world there are queues of boats waiting their turn in the ports of the continent
in order to get whatever supplies they can,
and to steam out to other ports as well as
to here. Therefore there is great difficulty
in actually getting the coal from other
countries. That naturally means that there
is great competition; it also follows that the
price rises, and over that we here can have
no control whatever.
But what I think the House and what I
think the people of the country are entitled
to is to know what happens after the coal
arrives in our ports, and when it comes to
be distributed throughout the Six Counties.
I think that is a legitimate question to ask,
and the steps that my right hon. Friend
(Mr. Barbour) proposes to take are that he
will have published in the papers what the
Ministry of Commerce considers is a fair
price for the time being for coal inside the
Ulster area, so that all may know whether
or not they are being charged an exorbitant
price, either by the wholesaler or by the
retailer who goes through the streets. The
publication of these prices by my right hon.
Friend and his advisers, who are in the coal
industry, will be of great assistance to everybody, and will probably stop some of the
rather loose charges that are being made
here and there to the disturbance of the
people as a whole.
Mr. WILLIAM MCMULLEN: Will the
Prime Minister allow me to ask him this
question? I am sorry to interrupt the right
hon. Gentleman, but it is an important point
and I think it should be brought out. Will
the right hon. Gentleman, the Minister of
Commerce, take any steps to find out the cost
of the coal, either on the Continent or in
America, to the wholesalers, in order to insure that there is no wholesale profiteering
so far as the wholesalers or importers are
concerned? The point made by the Prime
Minister up to the moment affects the situation when the coal arrives in Belfast, and
my point might be overlooked. The wholesaler might be charging an exorbitant price
to the retailers, and in that way wholesale
profiteering could take place if steps are not
taken by the Government to find out the
amount of money that the importer is paying either in America or on the Continent for
the coal.
The PRIME MINISTER: Of course what
I intended to convey was that the control the
Government have over the purchase of coal
ensures that the Government know what
price is being paid for the coal, the freightage and so on, right up to the port of Belfast, or whatever port it may arrive at in
Northern Ireland. When the prices are
published in the Press, daily or as often as
is found necessary by the Ministry, they will
be a guide for the people as to what they
should pay and what they should not pay for
coal.

question of the retailers, that is to say, those

those who buy a sack and then retail it in

the community.

any cases whatever, in high or low degree,

of coal, then the full power that we possess

Then, if they are controlling the supplies, why not control the prices? Surely

HOUSE OF COMMONS.

Thursday, 21st October, 1926.
The House met at Three of the clock, Mr.
SPEAKER in the Chair.
Oral Answers to Questions.
PERSONS DISALLOWED UNEMPLOY-
MENT BENEFIT.
1. Mr. WILLIAM MCMULLEN asked the
Minister of Labour whether he will state how
many of the 35,445 persons who were disallowed Unemployment Insurance benefit
under Sections 1, 2, 3, 4 and 5 of the notification form are still unemployed and without
benefit.
The MINISTER OF LABOUR (Mr.
Andrews): As I pointed out in my reply on
Tuesday last the figure of 35,445 refers to
applications which have been rejected and
not to the number of individuals affected,
which is very much smaller.
I have no means of ascertaining the exact
number of persons in the classes referred to,
who are still unemployed, and without
benefit, but I have no doubt that the majority
are either now employed or receiving benefit
following further spells of insurable work.
INSURANCE OF AGRICULTURAL
LABOURERS.
2. Mr. KYLE asked the Minister of Labour
whether he has seen the report of the Com-
Imittee set up to investigate the conditions of
agricultural labourers in regard to Unemployment Insurance, and whether, in view of
the fact that a majority report has been
issued in favour of the application of the
Unemployment Insurance Acts to agricultural labourers, he is prepared to bring in
an Amending Bill to include agricultural
labourers in Northern Ireland.
The
Mr. ANDREWS: The reports of this
Committee are receiving attention.
Committee have unanimously recommended
that no scheme of Unemployment Insurance
for agricultural labourers should be established in Scotland, and, as regards England
and Wales, they have suggested, by a
majority of one member only, a scheme distinct from the existing Unemployment
Insurance scheme with separate rates of
contributions, benefits and administration.
The hon. Member is aware that as these
Reports have been addressed to the Imperial
Ministers of Agriculture and Labour, who
jointly set up the Committee, it would, for
obvious reasons, not be fitting for me to express my views on the subject in this House
until they have had an opportunity of indicating to the Imperial Parliament the
action they propose to take.
Mr. KYLE: Is the right hon. Gentleman
prepared to make that Report available for
hon. Members of this House? I would like
to know, in view of the fact that Scotland.
which the right hon. Gentleman mentioned.
asked permission-that is the farm labourers
and farmers both-not to be reviewed under
this particular Committee, but that the
workers in England and Wales asked to be
reviewed, and now that the majority of the
Committee have reported in favour of it,
whether the right hon. Gentleman will place
upon the Table of this House a copy of that
Report, so that it may be available for hon.
Members here.
Mr. ANDREWS: As this Report is not
addressed to me. but to the Imperial
Ministers. I do not think I would be justified
in promising to place the Report on the
Table of this House as the hon. Member
(Mr. Kyle) suggests.
Mr. KYLE: Seeing that the Report will
be available for Members of Parliament on
the other side of the water, would the right
hon. Gentleman not make it available for
hon. Members on this side by laying it upon
the Table of the House?

Mr. SPEAKER: I do not think the right
hon. Gentleman (Mr. Andrews) could lay
upon the Table of this House a Report to
another Government. Of course, the Report
is available at the Stationery Office on purchase, like all other Government publications.
BELFAST MAIL SERVICE.
3. Colonel WOODS asked the Minister of
Commerce whether he can state if steps have
been taken to accelerate the delivery of crosschannel mails arriving in Belfast via Fleetwood, and mails posted
ed before 9 a.m. in
Belfast.
The MINISTER OF COMMERCE (Mr.
Barbour): As the hon. and gallant Member
is aware, the Post Office is a reserved service,
and I would, therefore, suggest that the
question is one which should more properly
be addressed to the Postmaster-General
through the medium of the Imperial House.
The hon. and gallant Member will doubtless
appreciate my embarrassment in replying to
questions relating to a reserved service. In
the present instance, however, I feel entitled
to state that proposals for an earlier delivery
of the Fleetwood mails have been submitted
by the Postmaster-Surveyor to the Belfast

Corporation and the important trade
associations. I am not quite clear what the

Surveyor I am sure that he will readily
obtain the information he desires as well as

Mr. DEVLIN: Might I ask the right hon.
Gentleman what precisely is the relationship
between this House and the Imperial Parliament in regard to Post Office affairs? In regard to the postal service in the Six Counties
have we any authority over it, or is the
