TEACHERS' INCREMENTS.
4. Mr. BEATTIE asked the Parliamentary Secretary to the Ministry of Education
whether he can state the numbers of teachers
in Northern Ireland who received no increment in the years respectively ended the 31st
March, 1924, and the 31st March, 1925, and
the 31st March, 1926; and also the numbers
that did receive increments in these years.
The PARLIAMENTARY SECRETARY
OF THE MINISTER OF EDUCATION
(Mr. Robb): It is presumed that the question
relates to the principal teachers and
ordinary assistant teachers employed in the
public elementary schools in Northern
Ireland, as it is in schools of this type only
that the teachers are paid their salaries
directly by the Ministry of Education.
There are no statistics available from
which the information asked for in the
question could be supplied and the compilation of a return giving the detailed particulars requested for each of the five years
specified would be so laborious that its
preparation would interfere seriously with
the performance of the ordinary duties of
the clerical staff of the Ministry,
It may be stated generally, however, that
there are about 4,300 principal and ordinary
assistant teachers employed in the public
elementary schools. When allowance is made
for the very large number of teachers
(upwards of 2,100) who have already attained
to the maximum salary of the normal scales,
and for teachers (about 400) who, being still
recognised on probation only, are not yet
eligible for increments of salary, the total
number of teachers to whom normal salary
scale increments could be awarded in any
year if their service reached the necessary
degree of efficiency is estimated to be about
1,800, of whom it is estimated that about
1,600 receive these increments and about
200 are not awarded increments because their
work in the schools falls below the required
standard.
GOVERNMENT POSITION ON HOUSING
PROBLEMS.
5. Mr. DEVLIN asked the Minister of
Home Affairs whether he can make a statement explaining the position of the Government in reference to the housing problem:
whether the Ministry had sent a circular to
rural councils informing them that housing
schemes should be strictly confined to urgent
cases, and whether this new policy applies
also to Belfast.
The MINISTER OF HOME AFFAIRS (Sir
Dawson Bates): As regards the first part of
the question, I must ask the hon. Member to
await the Second Reading of the Housing
Bill, which is at present before Parliament.
The circular to which the hon. Member
refers relates wholly to the provision ot
labourers' cottages by rural district councils,
and does not affect the housing situation in
Belfast.
Owing to the unprecedented number of
schemes, which are at present being considered by rural district councils for the provision of labourers' cottages, the Ministry
considered it essential to warn the councils
that their new schemes should be strictly
limited to cases of urgent necessity.
EXEMPTION FROM VACCINATION.
6. Mr. WILLIAM MCMULLEN asked the
Minister of Home Affairs whether it is a fact
that under the laws of Great Britain in relation to vaccination, a parent can claim
exemption for his children from vaccination,
and, if so, whether he is prepared to initiate
legislation of a similar character in Northern Ireland.
Sir DAWSON BATES: It is a fact that
the law in England in regard to vaccination
differs from the law in Northern Ireland,
and that in the former case a parent can
claim exemption.

Oral Answers.

[Sir Dawson Bates]
Whether the existence of exemption in
England has been a contributing factor or
no, it is a fact that in recent years there
have been considerable outbreaks of smallpox in England, and the absolute immunity
from this disease in Northern Ireland is, no
doubt, due to the compulsory arrangement
that exists here.
In all the circumstances I am not prepared
to introduce legislation on the lines suggested
by the hon. Member. (Hon. Members:
Hear, hear.)
Mr. WILLIAM MCMULLEN: Would the
right hon. Gentleman say why? I would also
like to ask him if he believes that it is fair
to make an implication of the character that
is contained in the answer to the question
when he admits himself that he has not got
reliable information as to whether these outbreaks can be attributable to nonvaccination?
Sir DAWSON BATES: I have only tried
to point out that in Northern Ireland the
community is practically immune, while the
contrary is the case in England.
Mr. WILLIAM MCMULLEN: Does the
right hon. Gentleman suggest that that is
due to the fact that there is no exemption
under the vaccination laws?
Sir DAWSON BATES: I can only draw the
same conclusion as anybody else draws.

in contemplation the provision of a free park

Urban District in Northern Ireland has the

Sir DAWSON BATES: There is no official

Ballymoney, nor is there any information
before the Ministry regarding the proposal
of the Urban District Council to provide a
park in the Urban District.
Several Urban Districts in Northern Ireland have public parks.

was threshed out at the time the Rents

CONTROL OF STREET COLLECTIONS.
11. Mr. KYLE asked the Minister of Home
Affairs by whose authority the regulations
controlling street collections have been put
into force against the collections taken at
street corner political meetings; whether he
19 aware that these regulations are being
used to prohibit collections at meetings held
under the auspices of the Independent Labour
Party, despite the fact that this body was
merely doing what it has done for many
years;
and whether he is aware that
collections at street corner meetings in Great
Britain are legal; and what action he is prepared to take to remove this injustice.
Sir DAWSON BATES: As regards the first
part of the question, the procedure adopted
with regard to breaches of the Regulations
governing street collections is the same as
that used in
dealing with other minor
breaches of the law. Prosecutions are
usually instituted on the authority of the
police officer in charge of the district, but in
cases of doubt, the matter is referred to the
Attorney-General for his directions.
With reference to the second part of the
question, the Regulations are enforced
against all persons making street collections,
irrespective of the objects for which such
collections are made.
I have no information as to the general
practice in Great Britain. Regulations vary
in different police districts, and it is possible
that collections at open-air meetings are per-
Imitted in certain districts.
The Regulations now in force in Northern
Ireland were made by O.I.G., R.U.C., in
December, 1923, in substitution of Regulations previously made by the Inspector-
General Royal Irish Constabulary, and in no
way differed in any material respect. They
require that a permit shall be obtained for
all street collections other than those made
at open-air religious meetings, and I do not
consider that any alteration is called for.
These Regulations are made in the interests
and for the protection of the public. They
are designed to ensure that such collections
are only taken up by responsible persons for
a legitimate object, and that all money so
subscribed is applied to the purpose for
which it is obtained. They also ensure that
the expenses of the organisers do not absorb
an undue proportion of the proceeds.
Mr. KYLE: In view of the fact that the
right hon. Gentleman is not prepared to
waive these Regulations, we will refer to this
matter on the adjournment.

ORDERS OF THE DAY.
Loans Guarantee (No. 2) Bill.
Order for Second Reading read.
Mr. POLLOCK: This is a one-clause
Measure and follows naturally the Money
Resolution which was discussed at considerable length a few days ago and introduced
by my right hon. Friend (Mr. Barbour) who
sits beside me. Under normal conditions I
would have been content to have simply
drawn attention to it seeing that this
Measure, which was introduced first in 1922,
has been discussed at such length and on so
many occasions not only by my right hon.
Friend who sits beside me, but also by the
Minister of Labour. As the principles of this
Measure were discussed at such length I
should feel almost ashamed to have occupied
the time of the House by entering at very
great length into all the features of the Bill.
But my hon. Friend the Member for West
Belfast (Mr. Devlin) in addition to the long
list of grievances which he has piled up
against the Government has added yet another in complaining that Ministers in presenting Bills to this House have not been
sufficiently discursive to satisfy his omnivorous thirst for knowledge, and therefore-
Mr. DEVLIN: I beg the right hon. Gentleman's pardon. I am quite sure he is enjoying himself. I did not complain that they
were not sufficiently discursive. I said they
were too discursive. But their discursiveness
was cloaked under rhetorical sentences in
order that we should not understand what
the proposals were. (Laughter).
Mr. POLLOCK: I certainly understood my
hon. Friend's complaint was that Ministers
3M
1827 Loans Guarantee Bill-

HOUSE OF COMMONS
Second Reading.

[Mr. Pollock]
were
not sufficiently explanatory-I have
used the word discursive-not sufficiently discursive in presenting the Bills for which they
were responsible. As I say, therefore, I feel
that I must re-traverse the field that has been
so often travelled over and enter with more
detail than I would otherwise have done into
the reasons which dictated the passing of the
Measure both in Great Britain and in
Northern Ireland in respect of the guaranteeing of borrowed money.
When the condition of labour became so
serious in Great Britain the British Government, in its quest for expedients to assist
conditions as they then were, introduced a
Measure known as the Trades Facilities Act.
This Measure was intended to guarantee
persons or bodies of persons who would enter
into and make capital expenditure and who required to borrow money for such expenditure.
The guarantees offered by the British Government were very wide. The first assumption
of course was that there should be absolute
security. Assuming absolute security, the
operations of this Act extended far and wide,
even to the Dominions provided the
materials were manufactured in Britain. As
our conditions of labour were, if anything,
more serious than those in Great Britain,
we decided in the year 1922 that we should
ask Parliamentary sanction for carrying out
the same programme of guarantees which the
British Government had undertaken through
the Trades Facilities Act. In order to
differentiate and to distinguish our Measure
from that of Great Britain we called it the
Loans Guarantee Act, but in effect it duplicated the British Measure.
The machinery of the Measure consisted in
the appointment of a small business-like
committee composed of three most outstanding commercial and banking men in Great
Britain. We followed that practice,
and we also, having received Parliamentary
authority, established a small committee of
three outstanding men in our community.
Their business was to scrutinise the security
that was offered by those who proposed to
borrow money, and also to see whether the
objects for which the money was to be
borrowed were such as came within the provisions of the Act. It was found in practice
that the scrutiny of these gentlemen was
severe in this respect at any rate. It was
their duty to see that the taxpayers' money
was not jeopardised, and therefore they were
very careful to see that those persons who
desired to borrow money should be able to
offer substantial security. We followed the
same practice here.
The British Government has under their
Measure guaranteed various persons and
bodies of persons sums aggregating about
£70,000,000. We made in the operation of
our Measure an arrangement with the
British Government that in the case of
capital expenditure that was made partially
in Great Britain and partially in Northern
Ireland, the British Government would
take care of and guarantee the amount expended in Great Britain while we on Our
side would undertake to guarantee the expenditure made locally.
May I give a concrete case of how that
operates and perhaps that will convey to the
minds of hon. Members opposite who, up to
the present, seem to have rather a vague
idea as to the modus operandi of this
Measure. Let me take the case of the City
of Derry Waterworks. That community desired to establish waterworks costing between
three and four hundred thousand pounds.
As metal pipes formed a very material part
of the expenditure-to convey the water
from the reservoir to the city, some six
or seven miles-it was clear that a considerable part of the expenditure would be made
in Great Britain, where these pipes were
manufactured. We arranged, then, with the
British Government that they should take
care of that part of the expenditure made
in Great Britain-guaranteeing, I meanand we on our side were willing to guarantee
the amount of labour and material that was
used in Northern Ireland. Therefore, the city
of Derry in borrowing that amount had the
British part guaranteed in Britain and the
local part guaranteed here.
Now that gives hon. Members, I think, a
fairly clear idea of how the Measure operates.
(Hon. Members: Hear, hear.) As the greater
number of guarantees we have given here relate to shipbuilding perhaps I should state
that the average proportion in which the cost
of ships is guaranteed is one-third by the
British Government and two-thirds by ourselves. That is because two-thirds of the expenditure is made here and one-third is made
in Great Britain. Now it has been asked by
hon. Members on the other side why do these
people whom we guarantee not borrow the
money themselves on their Own standing. In the first place they are enabled to
borrow more cheaply because of the Government's guarantee. In the second place, and
most important, they were not prepared to
go on with the work-in the great majority
of cases at any rate, probably in alland the inducement we are offering enabled
them to come to the conclusion that their
shipbuilding programme should be expedited
as we would guarantee borrowing. They
made the expenditure I have indicated.
Of course our whole object was that these
splendid artisans in our shipyards should not
be turned out on the streets and their whole
life's work practically brought to an end
if our shipyards were closed by there being
no work to be done. I make this statement
Loans Guarantee Bill-
Second Reading.
21 OCTOBER 1926

here without any fear of contradiction, that
had it not been-indeed I have made the statement over and over again-had it not been
for the operation of the Measure which I am
now submitting our whole shipbuilding works
would have come to a standstill, because
there was no inducement for shipowners to
continue their programme. The condition of
trade throughout the world was so bad that
tonnage requirements were very low. The
great concerns the Union Castle and Royal
Mail lines had no special object in prosecuting their shipbuilding programme unless
they got some facilities that were a sufficient
inducement to go on. It was therefore because of these facts that our Government,
following the example of the British Government, thought it necessary to do what we
have done in connection with this matter.
I have mentioned that the British Government is guaranteeing the cost of various
undertakings aggregating seventy millions of
money. Our commitments up to 30th September of this year are about six millions and a
quarter, and with the negotiations that are
going on now and, if I may use a nautical
phrase, with the shipbuilding programme
that we see in the offing, it is quite obvious
that we shall require from this Parliament a
larger authority than that which already
exists. It is because of that I am now here
with this Measure and asking the House to
pass its Second Reading as we require two
millions additional in order to provide for
those proposals which we anticipate will be
brought before us in a very short time. On
the basis of our present commitments, the
Government's liability decreasing as these repayments from time to time are made, our
liability under our guarantees amounts to six
millions. Next year, assuming that no increase is made in the meantime, these payments will be reduced to £5,400,000. The
following year there will be a reduction to
£4,800,000 by the repayments. In 1929 the
commitments will come to £4,400,000, and in
the following year they will be reduced to
£1,400,000. I give these figures in order that
the House may know that these are not long
term loans.
Sir ROBERT ANDERSON: What length
are they?
Mr. POLLOCK: From five years up to ten
years, and in one case in my recollection
twelve years.
Sir ROBERT ANDERSON: That is the
maximum?
Mr. POLLOCK: That is about the maximum.
Sir ROBERT ANDERSON: Thank you.

Mr. POLLOCK: I pass from that and propose to deal with the questions that have
been addressed to me. The hon. Member for
Down (Mr. P. O'Neill) asked me categorically
to reply to three separate questions. One was
in relation to the proposed guarantee to the
municipal body in the city of Derry. Under
the terms of the Loans Guarantee Act any
public body proposing to make capital expenditure which has for its object the employment of labour can take advantage of this
Measure, and assuming that the security is
adequate, and that is important, the Government is prepared to guarantee moneys
borrowed for the purpose I have indicated.
That is my reply to the first question of my
hon. Friend.
The next question was directed to the
guarantee that was entered into in order that
the firm of Dinsmore might be placed in a
position to buy its works, the length of the
term in this case being fourteen years. The
hon. Member for Derry (Sir R. Anderson)
asked me the length of the term, but it was
not then within my recollection because there
are so many things before me that I cannot
be expected at the moment to remember the
exact period. But let me inform my hon.
Friend, and also the hon. Member for
West Belfast (Mr. Devlin) that the length
of the guarantee depends on the length of
the borrowing. Bankers object to long loans.
The business of a banker is to turn over his
money as quickly as possible, and when
money is borrowed from a banker the general
rule is that the term is a short one. On the
other hand, when Insurance Companies are
the lenders, they desired lengthened terms
rather than short terms because they do not
want to be troubled from time to time with
renewing their investments. In the case of
these people the loan is generally for a longer
period, and as a matter of fact I believe that
these long loans to which attention has been
drawn are financed by Insurance Companies.
I see
that Insurance Companies have
financed, to the extent of £1,450,000, schemes
in which we are interested, and the length of
the term in those cases depends entirely on
the arrangement existing between the person
who borrows and the concern or person who
lends. That explains why there is such a
differentiation in the terms. At the same
time it is our object to limit our guarantee
to as short a term as possible and we like
guarantees that are quickly liquidated. All
these matters are taken into account when
we are dealing with persons who are
applicants.

and Institution. - (Governor's Recommendation signified.)—(Mr. Barbour.)
Mr. BARBOUR: There are two clauses in
the Money Resolution. Clause (a) provides
that any existing pensions payable by the
Committee of Management of the Reformatory School to ex-employees shall be continued, and shall be provided from voted
moneys annually. The charge under this
head will be approximately £26 per annum,
and is in respect of one ex-employee.
Clause (b) relates to the future expenditure
on the Training School when the premises
have been transferred to the Government
under the Act. These expenses will comprise the pay and allowances of the staff,
the maintenance charges of the buildings
and the farm, and the expenses of feeding
and clothing the Borstal or Reformatory
inmates actually in the institution or who
may be committed thereto in the future.
As regards committals to the school under
that part of the Children's Act which deals
with reformatories, the expenses will be
partially offset by the statutory contributions required to be made by the Local
Authorities in the case of youthful offenders

committed from their areas at rates to be
determined by the Ministry of Home Affairs
and the Ministry of Finance under subsection (3) of Clause 3 of the Bill.
Hitherto reformatories in Northern Ireland have been maintained by private
enterprise, towards whose costs both the
State and the Local Authority make contributions in supplement of private funds.
This only applies to boys sent to Malone
Reformatory and will not affect the position
so far as other existing institutions are
concerned. The Malone Reformatory for
boys was until recently financed on this
basis, but latterly as a provisional arrangement in order to ensure its existence almost
the entire cost has had to be equally shared
by the State and the Belfast Corporation.
In the current Estimates the State share
amounts to a total of about £1,100, being
at the rate of 12s a week per head. The
effect of the school becoming a State-owned
school will be that in future, should this
Bill become law, the expenditure will be
payable in the first instance from Government funds and a contribution received from
the Local Authorities. The rate of contribution still remains to be determined.
The expenses of maintaining the Borstal
inmates are entirely defrayable from State
funds. As hon. Members will have observed
in the Estimates which have been presented
cach year, an arrangement has been made
with the English Prisons Board under which
they receive Northern Ireland Borstal
offenders. In our Prisons Estimate for the
current year there is included a sum of
£4,400, representing the cost of 40 inmates
in England, which works out at a cost of
£110 per head--the sum paid by us to the
English Board. It is proposed in due course
to arrange for the transfer of these Borstal
boys to the new institution in Northern
Ireland.
The cost to the Committee of Management
of the Reformatory School has latterly been
in the region of 30s per head per week,
which includes staff charges and all other
overhead charges, together with the cost of
feeding, clothing and upkeep generally.
The effect of having the Borstal boys in the
same institution will reduce the total upkeep
charges per head, although as a set-off
additional staff will be necessary. One may,
therefore, reasonably expect that the gross
cost of the new institution will be less than
the combined amounts at present being spent
by the Committee of the Reformatory School
and by the Exchequer in payments to the
English Prisons Board.
There are certain trust funds, as set out
in the Fourth Schedule to the Bill-the interest on which has been utilised in the past
towards the upkeep of the institution-and
these will accrue to the Government in so
far as they are not required for the payment

Enactments of the Parliament of Northern

Mr. KYLE: I beg to move, in the Schedule,
Part II, to leave out "The Local Government
(Emergency Powers) Act, 1921 [N.I.]." The
whole Act.
I think it is necessary to go back to the
year 1921 to draw the attention of the
Government to the situation as it was when
the Government felt it necessary to bring in
the Local Government (Emergency Powers)
Act. At that time there was disturbance in
the country, and the Government felt it
necessary to introduce a Measure to deal with
those local authorities who did not exercise
their duties in a lawful way. The Government stepped in and superseded any such
local authority by appointing a Commissioner. This Measure made provision
for the appointment of a Commissioner,
and for the payment of the Commissioner when he was engaged on those
duties. That was done where the Ministry
was satisfied that the local authority had refused or failed to fulfil the duties that the
local authority was set up to carry out. In
the discussion that took place in this House
at that time, the right hon. Gentleman, the
Minister of Home Affairs, stated in the
Second Reading of the Bill :—
I venture to hope, and I say this with
all sincerity, that this emergency arrange
ment will be of the shortest possible
duration, and I look forward to early resumption of their responsibilities by the
local authorities. It is proposed to limit
the duration of the Bill to one year, and I
shall move an Amendment for that purpose at a later stage.

The right hon. Gentleman did move that
Amendment at a later stage, and the Bill as
passed was applicable for only one year. But
each succeeding year that Bill has been renewed under this particular Measure that is
now before the House, the Expiring Laws
Continuance Bill. That statement of the
right hon. Gentleman seems to imply that
if the local authorities resumed their
activities he would not desire to have the
powers conferred upon him in this Act. It
is from that point of view that I desire the
Committee to say that it is in the best interests of Northern Ireland that the Bill
shall not operate any longer. As a matter
of fact all the local authorities which the
Government suspended in that year, and from
that year, have now resumed their normal
work as local authorities. The Government
have stated from time to time in this House
and outside it, and it is a thing we all
appreciate very much, that the utmost peace
prevails in the Six Counties so far as the
administration of the law and the working
of the local authorities are concerned. There
fore I beg to move the Amendment, the
Expiring Laws Bill-
Committee.

exercised improperly. The

Expiring Laws Bill- HOUSE OF COMMONS
Mr. WILLIAM MCMULLEN: I beg to
move in the Schedule, Part II, to leave out
"12 and 13 Geo. 5, c. 5, The Civil Authorities
(Special Powers) Act (Northern Ireland),
1922. The whole Act."
I do not think it can be gainsaid that this
was an Act that was obviously and undisputably intended for an emergency.
It was
pointed out by the gentleman who introduced
the Second Reading, Mr. Megaw, that what
the Government were doing was embodying
the essential features of the Restoration of
Order in Ireland Act into the Special Powers
Act. Now that Restoration of Order in Ireland Act was designed for a definite and
specific purpose, and the essential features of
that Act were re-enacted in the Special
Powers Act. I think it will be conceded that
that Act was placed upon the Statute Book
for a definite and specific purpose.
As in the case of the previous Act, the
duration of this Act was for one year, and I
notice that during the course of the debate
on the Second Reading the then Attorney-
General, Mr. Best, resisted the suggestion
that the Act should be put upon the Statute
Book for a longer period than one year. We
have got to try to cast our minds back to
see why this Act became necessary. I think
the general state of lawlessness that prevailed
in the Province at that moment is indelibly
impressed on most people's memories.
The authorities were more or less powerless
and the rule of the gun was probably more
efficacious than the law of the country or any
decision of the courts. I notice that at the
same time coroners' inquests were abolished.
Sir DAWSON BATES indicated dissent.
Mr. WILLIAM MCMULLEN: I notice that
in the course of the debate there was a suggestion that that should be done, and I was
of opinion that the Government had defended
that proposal and had made it a feature of
the Act. Probably that was not done, but
there was a suggestion at the time, and the
hon. Member for the University (Dr. Morrison), being himself a coroner, was very
much opposed to that proposal. Rifles and
bombs were being freely used at this particular period and the Measure was clearly
intended to deal with that state of lawlessness that prevailed in the Province. Surely
at a time like the present, some four or five
years afterwards, when peace reigns right
throughout the Province, no case can be made
out for the continuation of this Act.
The year previous to the introduction of
this Act something like 110 murders were
committed, and it was pointed out during the
course of the discussion in March, 1922, that
some ninety murders had been committed up
to that moment, and that it was anticipated
that at the rate murders were being committed at that time the figure of 110 murders,
which had been committed during 1921, would
be eclipsed before the end of March, 1922.
Now surely it will not be suggested that a
Measure that was placed upon the Statute
Book to cope with a situation of that character is required at the present moment. It
might be argued that it does no harm to
allow an Act of this character to remain on
the Statute Book. The right hon. Gentleman,
the Minister of Home Affairs, advanced that
argument when we were discussing the
previous Question before the Committee, but
I do not think he can suggest that no one has
suffered under this Act, even if it were true
that no person or no authority had suffered
under the previous Act, because I had occasion in this House some months ago to raise
the question of twenty young men who were
taken from their homes in the early hours
of the morning and lodged in Crumlin Road
Jail, and afterwards in Derry Jail. These
people, as far as my recollection goes, were
not brought to trial but were kept in prison
until the Attorney-General thought fit to
release them. On a subsequent occasion a
young man, the secretary of an innocuous
and harmless organisation, was arrested on a
Saturday morning and confined in Belfast
Jail for the period of one week and no charge
was brought against him. After a week's
detention to enable the Attorney-General to
make the necessary inquiries that young man
was released.
No attention or consideration was given to
this aspect of the matter the amount of
hardship that is inflicted upon a home when
a young man is summarily dragged out of
that home in the early hours of the morning,
wrenched from his friends, and confined in
any of the jails in which the right hon.
Gentleman might think fit to place him. I
do not think it right that powers of this
kind should be vested in the hands of the
right hon. Gentleman (Sir Dawson Bates).
I do not look upon the Attorney-General (Mr.
Babington) as being a politician in the same
way as I look upon the right hon. Gentleman (Sir Dawson Bates) as being a
politician. I think the Attorney-General
would take a fairly detached and broadminded view of this question, but the right
hon. Gentleman (Sir Dawson Bates) is purely
a political partisan. I regret to say that he
looks at all these questions through political
spectacles. (Hon. Members: No.) I am
rather inclined to think that he does.
However, I do not think powers of this
character should be reposed in the hands of
the right hon. Gentleman or even in the hands
of the Attorney-General. We have got our
Law Courts, and why powers of this kind
should be retained by the Minister of Home
Affairs or by the Attorney-General is more
than I know. If a person has committed an
overt act, or an act of any kind, the Courts

Mr. DEVLIN: I rise for the purpose of
supporting the proposal of my hon. Friend,
and I am somewhat surprised, I may say,
that this Bill is included in the Expiring
Laws Continuance Bill, because I should have
imagined that at this stage of Northern life
there should be no necessity to continue these
Bills upon the Statute Book. What is the
vital principle involved? The Government
in a time of public emergency felt it necessary
to ask for special emergency powers, and one
of those powers was to arrest persons and
hold them in prison and not bring them to
trial, but keep them there as long as the
Government liked. In my judgment that is
the negation of the principles of British
justice and human justice. It may have been
justified in times of great public excitement,
though I do not know that it was just as
completely justified as the Government
believed. But now, when all these passions
have been subsided and the bitterness has
disappeared, I think it is a most unconstitutional thing for the Government to retain
these powers when the necessity for their
existence has disappeared.
My hon. Friend below me (Mr. W.
McMullen) has stated that he differentiates
between the Home Secretary and Attorney-
General, that one is a politician and the
other is not. I believe they are both
politicians. That is why they are now talking together and not listening. (Laughter.)
Both right hon. Gentlemen are politicians.
One is a prominent politician who lately
has engaged in an orgy of oratory all
over the city. The other right hon.
Gentleman feels that silence in this
crisis in our fortunes in Ulster is a
larger tribute to the power of Unionism
in Ulster. At all events they are both
politicians, and in my opinion there can be
nothing more fatal to the spirit of justice
than to leave matters of this sort in the
hands of politicians. If the right hon.
Gentleman, the Attorney-General, were a
lawyer only I am quite convinced he would
agree with me that Magna Charta-that is the
great principle of holding every man innocent until he is proved guilty-would be quite
sufficient for Northern Ireland as it is quite
sufficient for every other part of Great
Britain. But we live in a peculiar community here, and that principle universally
accepted by all British peoples does not
apply here.

The ATTORNEY-GENERAL: This Civil
Authorities Special Powers Act was placed
upon the Statute Book in 1922, as hon. Members opposite have said, in a period of great
emergency. It was designed for the purpose
of securing order out of chaos, and I think
most Members of the House will agree that
so far as that goes it has served its object.
(Hon. Members: Hear, hear.) But it was
also designed for the purpose of preserving
and maintaining that order which was produced as
a result of this Act after the
catastrophe of 1921 and 1922. And the only
question that this Committee has to address
itself to now is as to whether the time has
come beyond all question when this Act
should be allowed to lapse. And unless it can
be pointed out that some great injustice is
being done by the continuance of this Act
upon the Statute Book, I would suggest that
it is absolutely necessary that it should be
continued until it is certain beyond all
question that peace is not only been with
us but that it has been ensured for the
future.
There are a considerable number of matters
which are dealt with in this Civil Authorities Special Powers Act at the present timenot matters that have been referred to by the
hon. Members on the other side of the House,
namely, arrests and matters of that description, but there are a lot of subsidiary matters which hon. Members who read the Regulations made under this Statute well know
are matters which may turn up from day
to day at any time, even in a peaceful or
moderately peaceful community.
At the present time there are in existence some 25 or 30
Orders of various descriptions, not Regutions that were passed by the Ministry of
Home Affairs under this Statute.
It is said we are an absolutely peaceful
community. I am thankful to be able to
say from the point of view of the administration of the criminal law, that that is so.
But unfortunately all our people are not
necessarily perfect, and if the law has been
vindicated it is necessary in the interests of
the preservation of that law and the preservation of that state of peace that we have at
present, that every possible machinery should
be available by the Crown in the case of
persons who, though at present they have
not given any trouble through any overt act,
have still not repented in spirit from the
positions that they took up in 1921 and 1922.
And it is absolutely necessary that this Act
should be maintained on the Statute Book for
a further period. I agree with what the
right hon. Gentleman, the Minister of Home
Affairs, has said. It is not intended, and the
Government would not like to suggest, that
this Statute should be kept on the Statute
Book indefinitely. But it is merely a question of degree as to whether the time has now
come when it should be removed, and the
Government is not able to say that is so, and
consequently this Statute should still be
continued in this Expiring Laws Continuance
Act.
Mr. W. McMULLEN: There is just one
aspect of the matter which might induce the
Government to change their mind on this
subject. I think the point has been made by

Mr. BEATTIE: I would not have got up
to speak on this Bill if it had not been for
the Attorney-General using the expression
that the people for whom the Bill was intended had not up to date repented in spirit.
I would like to know what is the broader
meaning of the Attorney-General's words.
In my opinion the Government do not seem
to think that they as a political party are
too safe with the people of Ulster, but they
wish the Emergency Regulations to remain
so that they can get their political opponents
at any time and put them into jail. Let us
see where we are." You will never get a
political opponent of the Northern Government to repent in spirit. You can take his
body and put it in prison, but you cannot
subdue the spirit within that body. I would
certainly feel more safe as a political opponent of the Government if we had a wider
interpretation of the statement made by the
Attorney-General and were shown that there
is the same freedom for political opponents
inside the Six Counties as there is for those
political opinions in other countries
throughout the world.
To-day that cannot be said. I brought
several cases of great hardship on certain
householders through this Act being in operation before the Home Secretary, and the
Home Secretary felt the authorities under
this Act were justified in going to a particular home two nights in the week and
rousing the children, the wife and the
husband from their beds in order to search
for some person who was not in that locality.
If those are the powers the Government ask
for the right to go to any person's home at
any time to search for some person who is
not in that district-I am opposed to those
powers being vested in my political opponents. I am prepared to accept the law. I
am prepared to accept the judgment of the
legal men who have to administer the law,
but I am not prepared to sit idly or quietly
by and be judged by my political opponents.
Suppose something in connection with me
was brought forward and the Home Secretary
and the Chief Whip were sitting in consultation in the Home Office deciding what they
were to do with my body, what hope would I
have of ever being freed from the surroundings of the prison? None whatever. I want
to say quite candidly that the Act is absolutely and solely for the subduing and incarcerating of the political opponents of the
Unionist Party. From that point of view I
am out to oppose it and to ask the Government to bring in the same Regulations as prevail in every country in the world, and so
give freedom to all political parties in Ulster.
You have orders against the political opponents of the Government, and from that point
of I view I am out to oppose it, and I will go
into the lobby against the Government for
using the Government machine to suppress
political opinion.
Mr. MCALLISTER: I am sure it is a
matter of congratulation for all parties in
the Committee that a spirit of tranquillity
and peace prevails in Northern Ireland at the
present moment, and I think the joint efforts
of every section in the Committee should be
towards consolidating and solidifying that
position. But the fact remains that a large
section of the political opponents of the
Government of Northern Ireland at the
moment believe that this Bill is directed
against their liberties and security. If you
want to consolidate your own position and
the position of successful government in

curtailed without his right to trial by a
properly-constituted tribunal. You have
tribunals here in Northern Ireland to which
you can safely leave the liberties, and the
safeguards, and the interests of your political

no brief for Mr. Cook or Mr. Smith. Indeed,
I am rather inclined to think they are bad
leaders, but still the fact remains that our
industries are in a very serious position,
not only here but across the water. I would
like to suggest to the Government that they
should use their influence to try to bring
an end to the strike, and so relieve the
position that we are in to-day in Ulster
through the ineptitude of the Government
of Northern Ireland in not seeing that there
were proper supplies of coal available.
Mr. KYLE: We on these Benches want to
indict the Government because they did not
take sufficient steps to ensure that everybody
in the Six Counties should get coal. They
did ask for emergency powers. They got
those emergency powers, but they did not
take sufficient steps to deal with the situation. In other words, they were dilatory in
dealing with the coal position. I think it
was amply demonstrated yesterday that the
Government have been dilatory. It is quite
true that they appointed gentlemen to act
als Coal Controllers, but those gentlemen
did not act in the public interests, so far
as the people of Northern Ireland are concerned. I do not want to say one word
about the Coal Controllers, or any other
persons who cannot speak for themselves. I
would rather indict the Government; it is
much pleasanter to do that.
We are justified in indicting the Minister
of Commerce, however pleasant he may be,
for not taking steps to ensure that there
should be coal for the people of the Six
Counties. It is all very well to appoint
gentlemen to look after this question, but
apparently they only looked after it for those
people who can pay an exorbitant price for
the coal. It is from that point of view we
say, and I think the public will agree, that
up to now we have not seen any sign of
any purchase of coal by the Government.
It was only yesterday that we heard it stated
that a Government agent was going to purchase coal. The Minister of Labour says
they have bought coal. We have not yet
seen it advertised, and we have not seen it
made available for the people of this Province. It is from that point of view that
we say the Government are worthy of condemnation for the dilatory way in which
they have handled the coal situation.
There are other matters mentioned in this
Estimate, and one is the unemployment
relief works at the Royal Harbour of Ardglass. I do not want to minimise the
importance of the coal question by introducing other matters, but I want to ask the
right hon. Gentleman, who is responsible
for this Supplementary Estimate, if he is
doing something by putting up this sea-wall
at Ardglass Harbour, which will be a deterrent to the taking over of Killough Harbour,
as has been advocated by the merchants and
other people at Killough? Is he doing something that will make it more difficult for
the Government to take over Killough
Harbour, and to make it the harbour for
that particular district, so that fishing boats
can come in there no matter from what
direction the wind is blowing? The people of
Killough in getting together a number of
people who are interested in the development of their harbour have been doing good
work, not only for themselves, but for the
Six Counties, and I hope that the Government is not doing something that will make
it impossible for the Killough people to get
their harbour put into proper condition, and
to solve the difficulties of the fishing fleet
of the north-east coast of this country.
The hon. Member for North Belfast
(Mr. Grant) has thought fit to say that we
moved a reduction of £1,000 in this Vote
yesterday to the end that the people of
Belfast and the Six Counties could not get

The Vote is for £2,000 that the Government
think they might lose in this connection, but
that has absolutely nothing to do with the
purchase of coal.
The hon. Member for North Belfast (Mr.
Grant), who has had very much longer experience of Parliament than some of us on
this side, instead of trying to mislead us,
should try to lead us in this particular con-

WAYS AND MEANS.
Finance (Stamp Duty).
Considered in Committee.
Mr. MOLES in the Chair.
Motion made and Question proposed:
"That it is expedient to amend the law
relating to Stamp Duty in certain cases, and
to re-enact, with amendments, the enactments charging Stamp Duty upon certain
instruments and provide for the application
of the proceeds thereof."
Mr. POLLOCK: The Money Resolution
which I am about to submit to the Committee
is the natural and necessary forerunner to
the Finance Bill which will be introduced
later. The Bill itself is entirely concerned
with stamp revenue and contains three main
provisions. May I say at once that it is not
contemplated that it will make any change
in taxation?
The first of these provisions is designed
to exempt certain Grants or Letters Patent
issued under the Great Seal of Northern
Ireland from the Stamp Duty on such documents which is made statutory by the Stamp
Act of 1891. The limits within which such
exemption may be granted are naturally very
narrow. If I may offer an example it will
perhaps convey to the Committee more
clearly what I am about to argue.
I may
mention that there are Letters Patent issued
to the Lords Justices for the Government of
Northern Ireland in the temporary absence
of His Grace the Governor and the Letters
Patent empowering the Controller of the
Stationery Office to exercise the rights and
privileges in connection with Crown copyright in Northern Ireland. Technically the
Stamp Duty of £30 in such cases is payable
by the parties themselves, but it has always
been the practice of the Imperial Government in the past to bear that burden as the
documents in question were relating to
matters of public interest and for public.
duties. When one Exchequer only was involved in this manner it meant merely a
transfer of money from one pocket to
another, that is to say the stamping authorities imposed the tax which was paid from
the Civil Contingencies Fund. This Fund
was later recouped from the Exchequer
by means of voted money. But when
two Exchequers are involved the matter
becomes very tortuous and very involved,
and it implies that the Imperial
Government becomes responsible in Northern
Ireland for the payment of these duties.
Clearly this is inequitable as the Imperial
Government is merely making a certain appointment for the convenience of administration in Northern Ireland. Hence the proposal to exempt these instruments from duty.
The other provisions of the Bill deal with
the Stamp Duties to be charged on admissions of persons as students at the newlyestablished Inn of Court of Northern
Ireland and as Members of the Northern
Ireland Bar. It is proposed to re-enact the
rates of duty imposed in respect of the
King's Inns in Dublin under the Stamp Act
of 1891, and also to introduce an exemption
in respect of the barrister's fee with a view
to obviating hardship which would otherwise result from the establishment of the
Northern Ireland Inn of Court. The
exemption is in favour of those persons
called to the Northern Irish Bar who have
entered the King's Inns in Dublin at an
earlier period, and who, having paid their
fee for the King's Inn in Dublin, are not from

Provision is also made for the payment

This is not a new departure, for Sections
20 and 28 of the Stamp Act of 1891 provided
for somewhat similar payments to
the
Society of King's Inns in Dublin. Under
our last Finance Act, the Committee may
remember, on account of the severance of
Northern Ireland, or rather of the severance
of the Northern Ireland Bar from that of
the King's Inns in Dublin we stopped the
payment of the contribution that was
annually made to the Inns of Court in
Dublin. It is proposed now to relate this
grant to the duties payable by the barristers'
profession here, that is to say they will
receive a corresponding contribution to that
which was made to the King's Inn in Dublin
out of the fees which are recovered from.
students and barristers. The justification,
of course, for such a payment out of public
moneys arises from the fact that the
barristers are carrying out what in fact is
a public duty in addition to their Own
personal occupations. Therefore, the Measure
is designed to give a working minimum
grant to the Inn of Court with an appropriate maximum beyond which no contribution will be made. That is to say, the
contribution to the Inn of Court here will
correspond in some measure with
original contribution made to the Inns of
Court in Dublin. I beg to move.

CONTROL OF STREET COLLECTIONS.
Motion made and Question proposed:
"That this House do now adjourn."
--(Captain Dixon).
Mr. KYLE: As I indicated earlier this
afternoon I want to raise the question of
the Regulations the Ministry of Home Affairs
has put into operation prohibiting collections at political meetings held in Belfast
and outside Belfast. I asked the question
to-day under what authority the Minister
was acting in prohibiting collections at street
corner political meetings and he has referred
me to Regulations passed in Dublin in the
year 1918, which have since been taken over.
by the Government of Northern Ireland
under the Government of Ireland Act, 1920,
and put into operation by the Inspector-
General in the year 1923. If any Member on
the opposite side, or on this side either,
would care to read these Regulations he
would see immediately what these Regulations were intended to cover. These Regulations were intended to cover and regulate
what we call flag days, street collections for
this, that, and the other purpose. I think
most people will agree, whether on this side
or the other side, that these Regulations or
some Regulations were necessary. I quite
agree that it is a highly desirable thing that
there should be Regulations preventing unauthorised persons from taking collections.
(Hon. Members: Hear, hear.) But that is.
an entirely different thing from what the
Minister has done in regard to taking collections at ordinary propaganda meetings.
The Independent Labour Party and the
Labour Party hold meetings from time to
time in Belfast and outside Belfast, and at
these meetings a number of people are congregated and the chairman announces that a
collection will be taken up. No one is com-
.pelled to give. No force of any sort, kind or
descripton is used. Merely the announceinent is made that a collection will be taken.
There is no question here of interfering with
these Regulations in so far as these Regulations state that when a collection is made.
persons must stand within say 20 or 100 yards
of each other along the streets. These meetings are held at a given spot and collections
are asked for from the people congregated
there, and I defy the Minister or anybody
else on the Government side to say that these
Regulations were ever intended to govern
meetings of the character for which we have
asked for permission to take collections and
have been refused.
In Great Britain collections of this nature
are taken every day and every week by the
Independent Labour Party and the Labour
Party on the other side of the water, and it
is only here, where the boast is that we walk
step by step with Great Britain and on
'parallel lines with Great Britain, that the
authorities have taken the action which they
have taken so far as this matter is concerned.
It may be asked by the Minister why have
applications for permits not been made.
Applications have been made for permits by
some of our local Labour Parties. In regard
to South Belfast, the Labour Party made an
application and I have a letter here signed
by some gentleman for the Commissioner to
say that he cannot see his way to grant a
permit for a street collection. Now in the

4. Mr. Kyle asked the Minister of Home

an
Sir DAWSON BATES: The facts of the
incident referred to in the Question are
briefly as follows:-
On the date in question a crowd-numbering some 2,000 persons-attended at the Workhouse while a meeting of the Guardians was
in progress. A large force of police was on
duty in the road outside and, at the request
of an official of the workhouse, a few police
were stationed in the vicinity of the Boardroom.
During the course of the Guardians' meeting two Members of this House who are also
members of the Board of Guardians, refused
I am advised that the Chairman of a Local
Authority has a common law power to direct
the removal (if necessary by force) of any
member who refuses to obey his ruling, or
prevents the business of the meeting from
proceeding. Both the hon. Members were
afforded an opportunity of leaving voluntarily
before force was used.
I subsequently received complaints from
both these Members as to the conduct of the
police, alleging that they had been needlessly
assaulted, and that insulting language had
been used. This was entirely denied by thi
police concerned in the removal.
Both the hon. Members were informed of
the result of my inquiries, the names of the
police concerned in their removal were given
to them, and they were offered an opportunit
of identifying the police in question. It was
also pointed out that if the police had in
any way exceeded their duty, it was open to
theso Members to obtain redress in the courts
where the evidence of all parties would be
heard and the whole matter sifted by an
independent tribunal.
I regret that this course was not adopted,
but it is still open to either of the hon. Members to do so should they consider that the
circumstances justify it.
Mr. KYLE: Arising out of that answer—
and I must thank the right hon. Gentleman
for obtaining the statement-I would like to
ask is it his opinion that officers of the
Crown, police officers, have the right to
assault a member after he has been taken
out of the Boardroom? I am not now disputing the right of the police to remove a
member, but immediately he is outside the
room, is it the right hon. Gentleman's
opinion that the police have the right to
assault any person who may be put out?
Sir DAWSON BATES: The police have no
right to assault anybody at any time. As I
pointed out to the hon. Member, if he feels
that the police exceeded their duty he has
of course the law available. I might remind
my hon. Friend that the police are not above
the law. They are like all other citizens.
They are bound by the ordinary law.

BALLYMONEY LIGHT AND POWER
COMPANY.
5. Mr. KYLE asked the Minister of Home
Affairs whether he will state the names of
the Urban District Councillors of Ballymoney who are shareholders in the Ballymoney Light and Power Company, Limited,
or paid officials of that company, which has
contracts from the Council for lighting the
streets of the town and the Town Hall; and
whether he approves of contractors to a
public body being members of that body.
Sir DAWSON BATES: The Ministry
has no information as to whether any members of the Urban District Council of Ballymoney are shareholders in the Ballymoney
Light and Power Company, Limited, or are
paid officials of that Company.

to inquire into or to determine questions as
to the eligibility of members of local authorities.

himself or his partner interested in any

September, 1926; in how many of these re
ports was no action taken; how many were
made the subject of prosecution; and what

Sir DAWSON BATES: According to information furnished to the Ministry it would
appear that during the year in question, the
Sanitary Sub-Officer of the Ballymoney Rural
District Council reported 47 cases, and in
connection with these the Council gave
directions that in 45 cases notices should be
given for the abatement of the nuisances
complained of. It was not found necessary

THE INTOXICATING LIQUOR ACT, 1923.
9. Mr. GYLE asked the Prime Minister
whether it is the intention of the Government to introduce at an early date the Bill
mentioned in the King's Speech to amend
the Intoxicating Liquor Act, 1923.
The PRIME MINISTER (Sir James Craig):
The purpose of the proposed Bill is merely to
clear up matters in doubt regarding the
interpretation of the Act of 1923 and its
bearing on the administration of the Liquor
Laws generally. In view of the fact that
questions on this difficult code are still
arising, and have to be carefully considered
by the Ministry of Home Affairs, the
Government has decided to postpone the
introduction of this small Bill till next year.
(Hon. Members: Hear, hear).
Mr. DEVLIN: Will the right hon. Gentleman consider the desirability when proposing
legislation next year to take into consideration the unsatisfactory working of the last
Act and to see whether some of the causes
of the things complained of could bo
rectified?
Mr. GYLE: Will the Prime Minister also
take into consideration the fact that he repeatedly promised members of the trade that
he would attempt to remove the disabilities
imposed by the 1923 Act, or, to use his own
words, that where the shoe pinches he would
have it removed.
The PRIME MINISTER: With regard to
the question by the hon. Member for West
Belfast (Mr. Devlin), the Act so far has been
of inestimable advantage to the Ulster people
--(hon. Members: Hear, hear)-and the
pledge. I have given to the Ulster people will
be kept, that is to say, there will be no
further legislation dealing with the matter
during my time. With regard to the hon.
Member (Mr. Gyle), who sits below the gangway, the only pledge that I have ever given
to anyone in Ulster with regard to this
Amending Bill was that where it was discovered in the courts that there were difficulties in interpreting the law as it was passed
by this House, those rough angles would be
smoothed over by an Amending Bill. The
difficulty about doing it this Session, my
right hon. Friend informs me, is that some
of those difficulties are still arising, and the
Government think, on the. whole, it would be
better to wait for a few months longer in
order that all the difficulties experienced by
the courts in interpreting the law should be
cleared up in one Bill instead of, perhaps,
their having to introduce another one next
year.

THE CANAVAN CASE AT CARRICKMORE
PETTY SESSIONS.
10. Mr. DEVLIN asked the Minister of
Home Affairs whether he can state the circumstances which induced the Minister to
order the discharge from the industrial
school at Omagh of Canavan's four children;
whether the father was summoned at the instance of the Omagh Regional Committee for
failing to comply with a school attendance
order in respect of the children; whether the
case was heard at Carrickmore Petty Sessions; whether the school attendance officer
stated in evidence that the house in which
the family resided was like a cattle shed and
unfit for human habitation (there being no
windows and only one bed consisting of hay,
with a blanket thrown over it); that there
was no food for the children, and the father
was unable to find employment; whether the
mother was blind, and had to be led about
by one of the children, while none of the
little ones had sufficient clothing to appear
in public; whether the magistrates ordered
the father to be imprisoned for one month,
and committed the four children to the industrial school; and what steps the Minister
proposes to take to relieve the magistrates
responsible for that conviction and sentence
of their judicial powers.
Sir DAWSON BATES: Patrick Canavan
was prosecuted before the magistrates at
Carrickmore P.S. on the 29th September, by
the Omagh Regional Committee, for failing
to comply with an order made by the Committee requiring him to send his four children to school. The prosecution was brought
under the provisions of Section 33 of the
Education Act, 1923.
The evidence, as reported in the Press, disclosed that this family was living in conditions such as are described in the hon.
Member's question, but it should be made
clear that before any prosecution was instituted, arrangements were made to provide
the childern with clothing to enable them to
attend school.
After hearing the evidence, the magistrates
convicted the defendant and ordered him to
pay a fine of 33s and 7s costs, and in default
of payment, to be imprisoned for one month.
They also ordered that the four children be
sent to industrial schools.
I was advised that, having regard to the
terms of the Section, the order sending the
children to the industrial schools was made
without jurisdiction, and was, therefore, of
no effect. Under those circumstances, I had
no option but to order their discharge. May
I say that I took this course with great regret, as it is obvious that they would have
been much better in the schools, where they
would have been properly taken care of than
under the care of their parents who are,
evidently, unable to look after them?
The magistrates who adjudicated made a
bona-fide mistake as to their jurisdiction, and
no action on my part is necessary or desirable.
Mr. DEVLIN: Does the right hon. Gentle
man think that a month in prison is a fair
sentence to impose on this poor man against
whom, obviously, no complaint was made except his extreme poverty? Does he think a
month in jail was not too great a sentence to
give in a case of that sort?
Mr. SPEAKER: I am afraid the hon.
Member cannot expect the right hon. Gentle
man to give his personal opinion.
Mr. DEVLIN: With all respect, he exercised his right to release this man, didn't he?
Sir DAWSON BATES indicated assent.
Mr. DEVLIN: Yes, he exercised his right
to release this man. Therefore, he does not
think the sentence was justified, for which
humanity I am profoundly thankful. But is
it fit and proper that persons like these
magistrates should be allowed to deal with a
case of this sort and so outrage the spirit of
humanity as to send this poor man to jail?
Mr. SPEAKER: That has already been
answered in the latter part of the reply.

ARRANGEMENTS WITH FREE STATE.

Labour (Northern Ireland) to the Ministry

he will state whether he is prepared to conclude arrangements or not,
Loans Guarantee Bill. 1890
Oral Answers.
26 OCTOBER 1926
(Mr.
The MINISTER OF LABOUR
Andrews): As the hon. Member is aware, the
Free State Government has thought it desirable to discontinue reciprocal arrangements with Great Britain and to diverge
from the common social legislation that
formerly obtained throughout the United
Kingdom, and the standards now prevailing
in the Free State are lower than those here.
In consequence, it is no longer possible to
secure for persons moving between the Free
State area and the United Kingdom the continuous enjoyment of the uniform benefits
which formerly existed.
I am ready to consider any practical proposal which the Free State Authorities can
put forward to minimise as far as possible
the effect of their divergent policy not only as
regards unemployment insurance but other
social services, but unfortunately they have
been unable to do so either at the conference
to which the hon. Member refers or at any
other time.
Mr. W. McMULLEN: I would like to ask
the right hon. Gentleman whether he believes there would be any insuperable difficulty in effecting a simple arrangement
whereby a Northern worker temporarily employed in the Free State could have the value
of his contributions whilst employed in the
Free State transferred to his credit in the
Northern Ireland fund.
Mr. ANDREWS: The practical difficulty
is this, that the contribution in Northern
Ireland does not possess the same value as,
in other words it possesses much greater
value than, the contribution in the Free
State. It is an extraordinarily difficult thing
to devise a method by which this difficulty
can be got over. What I have to be careful
about is that nothing is done which will be
unfair to the people of Northern Ireland.
Mr. W. McMULLEN: I would like to ask
the right hon. Gentleman could he not
arrange for a reciprocal transfer of contributions. That seems a simple proposition.
Mr. ANDREWS: For the reasons I have
already explained it is extraordinarily difficult to do anything of the kind. There are
other services to be considered besides these
unemployment services, and if the matter
can be settled it can only be settled at one
time in connection with a great many other
matters.
Mr. W. McMULLEN: I would like to ask
finally whether the right hon. Gentleman is
prepared to go into this matter even more
fully with representatives of the Free State
Government for the purpose of removing this
unnecessary hardship that is being inflicted
on many workers on each side of the Border?
Mr. ANDREWS: I did not create the difficulty, and I think it is for the Free State
Government to submit to me proposals to
get over it which I might consider fair and
right and in the interest of the people of
Northern Ireland.

Mr. DEVLIN: Not for the first time have

first complaint that we have made with
regard to the Government's action relating to
these Measures. It is done on every occasion
when a Bill is produced, and what they do
is this. They introduce a Bill and they want
to see what the people think about it. When
the people think badly about it they then
begin to think are the people worth thinking
about-what precisely is the class of people
who oppose these Bills, whether they are
electoral or political in value. If they are
politically or electorally of any value then
a stock of Amendments is placed on
the Paper in order to satiate the appetite
of their followers for concessions in
relation to the particular Measure
which is introduced. That, perhaps,
applies more fully to the other Bill-on
which I propose to speak at greater length
when that Bill comes before the Committee.
But I do think that the right hon. Gentleman
is entitled to tell us what is the meaning of
these Amendments, why they are introduced.
what is the particular character of the influence brought to bear on him, and why he
has been moved to change the whole Bill
which we passed on the Second Reading by
submitting the series of Amendments to
which I have referred?
The PRIME MINISTER: My right hon.
Friend (Sir Dawson Bates) has agreed with

the whole public of Ulster would have a

ing the Minister and advising the Govern.
ment as to any Amendments that they

Therefore, we cannot be charged in these
cases with having done anything unconstitutional, and surely my right hon.
Friend (Sir Dawson Bates) is far wiser to
put in the few words that are required in this

what you are proposing, and if all the outside public are not satisfied with it something

animals.

After your
explanation it is scarcely necessary for me

animals come from Great Britain and are

But the particular point I want to make
s that I know that cruelty is practised as
far as the performance of animals is concerned, and I am desirous of stopping what
I believe to be cruel and reprehensible
practices. I see no reason why a police

person, should not have the right, if he believes cruelty is being practised at the
Hippodrome, say, or other music hall, of

Sir DAWSON BATES: My hon. Friend in
moving this Amendment rather suggested
that the police would have no knowledge of
animals performing when they come to the
city, but I would remind my hon. Friend that
under the Bill every man who wishes to perform his animals has to register with the
police, and, therefore, it is within the knowledge of the police the time the first performance is to take place. As the Bill now stands
it is open to a constable or other authorised
person to go behind the stage right up to the
time the animals go on to the stage to perform.
After that he must come to the front and
there see the animals perform. Practically
the animals are in front of him all the time
except for the period during which the constable is actually going from behind the stage
to the front. I am sure my hon. Friend will
agree with me that it would be very unfair
to these performers that all the little tricks
which I know they indulge in should be
known to the ordinary outside public. I am
sure my hon. Friend has seen rabbits taken
out of a hat, or supposed to be taken out of a
hat-
Mr. DEVLIN: Only at elections.
Sir DAWSON BATES: I am sure my hon.
Friend will agree with me that it would be
very unfair and would serve no useful purpose in preventing cruelty to say that a constable should have the right to go behind
and to remain behind all the time the

Mr. DEVLIN: I regret that I cannot

(Sir Dawson Bates). In the first place I

for theatrical purposes are unkind. (Hon.

class of people who render such service to
charity-(Hon. Members: Hear, hear)-or
who are moved by રી higher spirit of
humanity than those engaged in the

the medical profession I do not believe there
is any class of the community who give such
loyal and gratuitous services for great public
causes as the members of the theatrical profession, and while I can quite understand
and sympathise with the humanitarian idea
that is at the back of the mind of the hon.
Gentleman, I could not possibly, even by
innuendo, lend myself to any charge that
they were inspired by any other feeling than
that which I have indicated.
Then to put it on a lower ground, what interest would it be to these people who have
these birds, dogs, or animals, to be unkind to
them? The healthy condition of these
animals is the greatest asset which their
owners have. The animals cannot perform
their functions, whatever they may be, on
the stage, unless they are healthy and well
preserved. The efficiency of those birds and
animals on the stage depends entirely upon
the kindness and thought that is given to
them to preserve their lives and their health
and their utility. Cruelty to those animals
could not possibly lend itself to the efficient
discharge of their duties.
Finally, I object altogether to a policeman
following everybody around. One day he
may be following a politician, he may put
him into prison without any trial according
to law. Another day he is following a flag;
one day it may be your flag, and another
day it may be their flag. Another day he is
going to take charge of all motorists. I have

to the House with a feeling that it has been
one of the contentious matters for a number
of years throughout the North of Ireland.
I do so also with the feeling that this is
a question that could have been very well
dealt with inside the Motor Vehicles (Traffic
and Regulation) Bill, but for some unknown
reason the Government did not think it
worth while to touch the question of the
human element inside that Bill.

I say that they have dealt with everything else that was necessary, but
left the most important and most
essential thing out of the Bill. That was
the human element.
Now the Measure which is presented to
the House, and of which every Member is
in possession, is to regulate the hours,
limiting them to 48 hours per week, for all
public service vehicles in the North of Ireland. That Bill, I think, though it is only
a small Bill in its way, is very large in its

As the mentality of the right hon. Gentleman is such that he thinks the alternative
must be given to the railway workers of
going back to pre-war, I am rather afraid
The Bill means one of two things. If the
Government votes against this Bill they are
voting for lengthening the hours of the big
bulk of the railway workers of the North of
Ireland. That alternative is placed before
the workers of the railway companies. If
you vote in favour of the Bill, which I hope

(Mr. Devlin)-if you vote in favour of this

Let us take the Bill as it stands. Provision is made for a 48-hour week. That is
the total number of hours to be worked.
Then there is also provision made for breakdowns or emergencies. I think that is very
reasonable. If you look over Section 3, you
will find the principle in Sub-section (1)
which governs the whole of Section 3, governing the overtime to be applied. I know Members may say that if a man is journeying to
Newry, and if he gets to Newry and his eight
hours are up what is the man to do. Is another driver to go on? Nothing of the sort.
If the bus is stationed in Belfast, if that is
its home destination for the driver it is a
case of emergency. The bus has got to be
brought in. It cannnot be left in the street.
That would constitute a case of emergency.
It is not lawful for them to leave it on the
street over night.
The Bill also sets out what an employee is.
It is not necessary to go over the
wide field of what an employee is.
Every Member of the House, I am sure, is
aware of what an employee is. But Section
4 sets out the penalties for any offence under
Section 1. These penalties are not too severe.
They compare favourably with the penalties
set out in the motor regulations. Section 4,
too, sets up the machinery. Now, some hon.
Members of this House have had experience
of this machinery. I have been one of them.
I know how this machinery works. I know
how suitable it is to the present regulation of
the hours or to a violation of the Act if
accepted by this House. I have no fear in
my mind that the machinery will not meet
the requirements both of the employing class
and of the employees. Now, the Bill itself is,
as I said at the beginning, something that
the human element is in. It is not very
often we get that element in any Bill brought
forward in this House. This Session I have
heard of nothing only horse-breeding, motor
traffic, the protection of animals, the marketing of eggs and other things like that. Those
do not affect the human element at all. The

a refresher and have many advantages that
the driver has not got.

the
What were the findings of
inquiry? While it was not plainly stated
that it was due to industrial fatigue of the
railway employees, men in signal boxes from
sixteen to eighteen hours per day guiding
the destinies of trains which come along at
so many per hour on the great railways in
England, the result, through these inquiries
and the focussing of public opinion of the

behind them, and there has been established
an eight hours' day for the railwaymen of
Great Britain and Ireland.
Let us see where we stand to-day. The
Minister of Home Affairs says that the
number of accidents on the railways is decreasing, but, on the other hand, the number
due to motor traffic-there were 1,300 last
year, or 25 per week-is increasing, and the
total number of accidents in Northern Ire
land this year will be greater than it was
last year.
There is only one cause, and
there is only one cure. The cause is the
overworking of the men in these public
services. The cure is the same cure as has
been applied all over the world to every
servant in a responsible position, namely,
to lessen his hours of work to such a number
that he will have sufficient leisure to get
himself ready for the next day's work. I
would like to say that during my lifetimeit has not been a very long one up to nowduring the working part of it I had very
long hours. I got up at five in the morning,
and I got home at six at night. I know the
difference between 48 hours and 54 hours.
I know the state of physical fitness I was in
when I was working 54 hours and when I
was working 48 hours. My physical fitness
was reduced every day as the week went on.
I hope you will accept that statement. The
drudgery from Monday morning to Saturday
got worse instead of better, but when I got
a rest over the week-end I felt a fit man
going to my work on Monday and starting
afresh at my daily toil.
There is an old Greek saying to the effect
that in order to live well one must first of
all live. Life in the real sense of the word
is impossible without an income sufficient
to maintain physical and mental efficiency.
To ensure such an income to every worker
is one of the main points of the Labour
Party's policy. There is, however, another
essential factor in the conditions required
for an efficient physical and mental life.
That is leisure. Long hours of work are
inimical to the full development of mind
and body, apart from their bad economical
