effects under the existing social system. To
argue this proposition at length would be
pushing at an open door. The case for a
working day of not longer on an average
than eight hours has already been admitted
in a large number of industries, and a 48
hours or less working week has been secured
in the United Kingdom by law or voluntary
agreement between employers and employed
in occupations employing more than ten
million workers, including, I would say,
shipbuilding, engineering, textile, railways,
buses, tramways, docks, structural undertakings and transport.
For many decades the eight-hour working
day has been in the forefront of the programme of the organised workers throughout the world, and so insistent has been the
international demand for its establishment
by law that the Peace Conference at Paris
thought it advisable to include it as an item
in the International Treaty of Versailles.
It may not be carried out, as the Minister
of Finance has stated, but in the United
Kingdom there are over ten million workers
to-day enjoying the benefits of a shorter
working week. I could tell you the reason
why it may not be carried out, but I am
rather afraid of treading on the border line,
and Mr. Speaker pulling me up because I
would have to enter into the international
question, and take you from Paris to
Washington and back again to Britain, and
show you the reason why the ratification of
the Washington Convention did not take
place. It was no fault of the worker. It
was the fault of the Government who dishonoured themselves in not ratifying that
agreement.
From its inception the Labour Party has
never ceased to advocate a Measure for the
fixing by law of eight hours as a maximum
working day. In doing this it has taken over
the task which its pioneers began and carried
on persistently in the face of the Opposition
of the other two parties who cordially agreed
that legislation limiting working hours of
adult workers was economically unsound and
socially undesirable. The description of the
proposed eight-hour law as being an iron rod
driven into the delicate machinery of industry given by a leading Liberal statesman
is characteristic of the Liberal and Conservative attitude on this question. Now,
after many years of propaganda in its favour
the Labour Party has behind it, the great
bulk of public opinion. We have behind us
here in Northern Ireland, as is shown by the
Paper which each Member of this House has
got, 5,000 railway workers whose standard of
life stands in jeopardy of being reduced by
the railway companies, and we have upwards
of a thousand public service drivers and conductors. Although the Press has not given
this Bill the publicity that the Motor Bill
I have already mentioned that about ten
millions of workers in the United Kingdom now normally working forty-eight
hours or less per week are under the terms
of legal enactments or collective agreements.
From this fact it has been argued that it is
unnecessary to enforce a shorter working day
by further legislation. Voluntary effort
through trade union action it is urged will
secure this object without recourse to the
State. But the case for a legal eight hour
day is exactly the same as that for a legal
minimum wage. Below the level of the wellorganised workers are those who cannot combine effectively for the purpose of securing
a reduction in working hours. For them
there is no hope except in State action.
Moreover, the powerful trade unions that
have gained the shorter working day for their
members are aware
from past experience
that collective agreements may be modified
to the workers' disadvantage. They know
that when trade is slack, when commercial
and industrial depressions take place, the
tendency among employers is to demand
either reductions in wages or longer working hours, or both. This has been exemplified during recent years after the short boom
in trade which followed the Armistice.
We have seen numerous and, unfortunately,
successful assaults upon the worker's
standard of life, even in occupations which
were not suffering from depression and in
which profits were still high. Therefore, the
trade unionists, taught by experience, desire
to have the advantage of greater leisure buttressed by legislation which at the same time
should apply to workers in a less favourable
position. This is the contention of the trade
unionists both in Great Britain and throughout Ireland. They have won shorter hours
and their experience has told them that the
law is the only safeguard against the
standard of life of the workers being reduced.
Collective agreements sometimes are all right
but there is no safeguard of the standard of
life which the workers claim they should
have.
We claim that labour should not be regarded merely as a commodity or article of
commerce, nor as simply being the raw
material out of which profits may be made.
To a certain class of mentality prevalent
among the comfortable classes social stability
and orderly progress can only be ensured by

and opportunities for the wise use of it the
common people will in time make this land
a land in which the great majority of its

sympathetic consideration of the Government

under existing conditions to apply uniform
conditions to these varying circumstances it
would be found that on many of these routes
chars-a-bancs would no longer be able to continue to ply, with the result that there would
be considerable public inconvenience and
unemployment would result therefrom.
It is quite true that a great many of our
workers in the United Kingdom enjoy an
eight-hours day. I accept the hon. Member's
figures when he says nine or ten millions.
The State has, for many years, considered
that it was desirable that hours for women,
for children and for young persons, should
be regulated by Statute, because it was felt,
and readily felt, that as young persons and
women and children were not, as a rule,
organised to the degree that adult males are,
it was the duty of the State to protect
those who were not in a position to protect
themselves. But I venture to suggest that we
would do an injury to the manhood of Northern Ireland if we took away from them their
self-reliance. We have always found that a
man was capable, as a rule, of looking after
himself, and most of those workers who are
males and who enjoy an eight-hour day
enjoy it not as a result of the action of the
Government at all, but by agreement with
their employers. (Hon. Members: Hear, hear.)
I only know of two instances where, during
the war, the Imperial Government interfered
for the purpose of regulating the hours of
labour for men. One was in connection with
the railways, and the other was in connection
with the mines. I would like to say this in
no controversial spirit that the result of the
ignoring of economical conditions in connection with legislation affecting mines has
had-I will not overstate it-some influence
in bringing about the disastrous trouble with
which we are faced at the present time.
As regards the railways, the workers on
our railways enjoy their eight-hour day at
the present time through agreement with
their employers, not under statute at all. I
venture to suggest that what the railwaymen are capable of doing through their
organisations, those engaged in the motor
transport service could gradually bring
about. But to come along and say that

Now I remember on one occasion there was
some criticism because this House gave to
the Governor in Council powers of a limited
character, namely, to keep unemployment
insurance in step with Great Britain. But
what do I find here? I appreciate the confidence which the Opposition evidently have
in me, because they propose to give me power
--unrestricted power-off my own bat, to use
a sporting expression-to decree who shall be
brought within the scope of this Measure.
Mr. BEATTIE: Have you not that power
under the Unemployment Acts?
Mr. ANDREWS: That means, if I am correctly advised, and I think I am, that I
actually could conscript the hon. Member for
East Belfast (Mr. Beattie) himself, and decide
that he should become a driver or a conductor or perhaps a misconductor-of one of
these motor vehicles.
Mr. BEATTIE: You are the classification
agent. That is all you are.
Mr. ANDREWS: The classification agent?
I do not think, to be quite frank, that such
wide powers should be given to any man, no
matter who he is, and I therefore feel that
it was probably unintentional that this power
should be conferred upon me by this Bill.
But now, for a moment, let us look at Clause
3. This changes the unit or standard of
time allowed by Clause 1 of the Bill from
one week to one day, and yet it has not defined the permissible number of hours per
day, apart from overtime. If I remember
correctly, the hon. Member (Mr. Beattie) in
his speech said that the object of this Bill
was to prevent any man from being unduly
oppressed by having to work on a single day
an unreasonable number of hours, but I
maintain that under this Bill it would be
quite permissible for a worker to be asked
to drive a car for sixteen hours a day for the
first three days of the week, which is certainly not the intention of the hon. Member
for East Belfast (Mr. Beattie), as I gathered
from the speech he has just made.
Again when we come to deal with the
question of overtime we get into equally great
difficulty, because it is quite true that overtime is permitted in case of emergency or
breakdown, but it can only be brought about,
even in this case, by the consent of the
employer and the trade union. Supposing
that there is no trade union in connection
with some particular service, who is to give
the permission then? There is nobody to
give the permission and, therefore, the overtime cannot be worked. Thus a bus travelling, we will say, from Ballymena to Antrim
may break down; overtime cannot be worked,
and the result might be that the passengers,
the driver, and the conductor would have
either to billet themselves in their char-a-banc
all night, or they would have to arrange to
get some other vehicles to come to take them
to their destination while the machine, which
had temporarily broken down, and which a
very short time might rectify, lay on the
roadside. A more absurd position than that
I think could scarcely be imagined.
Then again I come to the provision
dealing with what is to take place in case
there is any misunderstanding or dispute.
It is dealt with in sub-Clause (2) of Clanse
4. Here we have a Munitions Tribunal to
deal with offences. Now, at the present
time no Munitions Tribunal exists, and,
therefore, I take it that the suggestion is
that in time of peace the Munitions Tribunal should be resurrected and re-christened upon the understanding that a rose by
any other name would smell as sweet.
I could go on criticising every Clause in
the Bill, but I think it is quite unnecessary. I think I have shown, if I may say
so, that this is an unworkable measure,
that it does not even carry out the intentions of the hon. Member (Mr. Beattie) who
has introduced it. I am absolutely satisfied
that it would lead to unrest, to public inconvenience (Hon Members: Hear, hear.)-
to litigation, and probably to industrial
strife. I think it is not in harmony with
the traditions associated with the legislative efforts of this honourable House.
Therefore, for these reasons, and for
others too numerous to mention, I feel it
to be my duty to move that it be read a
Second time upon this day six months.

BUILDING OF PARLIAMENT HOUSE
AND LAW COURTS.
Motion made and Question proposed: That
this House do now adjourn."-(Captain

Mr. THOMAS HENDERSON: A short
time ago I raised a question in connection
with the building of Parliament House and
also the building of the Law Courts, and,
seeing that the Prime Minister is with us
this evening, and seeing further that we are
almost on the verge of Christmas, I would
like some information from him as to when
the work is going to begin in such a manner
as will give employment to the unemployed
of Belfast and of Ulster generally. I want to
say that I am not at all satisfied. The Prime
Minister has made statements repeatedly in
regard to the progress that has taken place,
and this House was also told that in the very
near future the building of the Law Courts
would be started. Up to the present time,
notwithstanding the fact that there are
citizens in Ulster and in Belfast, in parti
cular, where these Courts are going to be
built, on the verge of starvation, no intimation has been conveyed, either through the
Press or to Members of this House, that the
work is going to be started immediately.
would like some information as to when Parlia
ment House is going to be built and also
when the Law Courts are going to be started.
The PRIME MINISTER: I only wish that
the hon. Member had used the customary
channels to acquaint me with the fact that
he was going to raise this question this afternoon. Had he done so I would have been in
a better position to reply to him. As it is
I must just tell the House what I happen to
know at first hand. The delay in proceeding
with Parliament House and the Law Courts
is very regrettable. It has been occasioned
by many reasons which it is outside the
powers of the Northern Government to
influence in any way, because, as the hon.
Member (Mr. Thomas Henderson), and the
House are aware, the buildings in connection
with both these sides of our life here are
supplied at the entire cost of the British
Exchequer and do not fall upon our Own
Votes. Therefore, the control that we have
upon the actual buildings is very much less
than it would be had we the matter entirely
in our own hands. But I may tell the hon.
Member that the British Government very
kindly agreed to bear the cost of the main
avenue leading from the Newtownards Road
up to where the House will eventually stand,
and that contract, which is a very costly one,
is in progress of being carried out at the
moment. My right hon. Friend (Mr. Andrews)
informs me that somewhere between
80 and 100 men have been taken on by Messrs.
Grainger Brothers, who are the contractors,

ALLEGED POLICE ASSAULT ON
BELFAST GUARDIAN.
Mr. KYLE: Notice has been given that
we would raise the question of an assault
made upon an hon. Member of this House
upon the adjournment. I want to protest
very emphatically against the action of the
Minister of Home Affairs (Sir Dawson Bates)
in saying that he is not prepared to take any
disciplinary action in regard to the sergeant
and constable who went out of their way to
assault a Member of this House. I do not
contend, nor does anybody here contend, that
when a member is being removed from a
publicly elected body the police ought to go
out of their way to assault that person after
he leaves the room. I daresay it would be
the duty of somebody or other-I do not
know exactly whose-if Mr. Speaker ordered
some Member to leave the House and he did
not do so-
I suppose somebody would come and
take him away, though I do not suppose he
would wait for that. (Laughter) But, having
removed him from the House, I cannot see
at all that the police have any jurisdiction
over him after he leaves the room. It is
because this has taken place, because this
assault took place outside the Boardroom that
I wish to press the importance of this case.
I saw quite recently where in Great Britain
a man had interrupted the proceedings of a
meeting and had disobeyed the Chair, and the
police came and took him away out of the
meeting. I noticed that on that occasion the
police refused to act us the police acted here
on the 15th June, and I would not like to
think that it was because of a difference in
political opinion that this action took place.
The action of this sergeant certainly gives
one furiously to think. One could, perhaps,
overlook the action of a constable who might
want to curry favour with his chief, but one
cannot overlook the action of a sergeant who
goes out of his way to use provocative
language that one would not care to use in
every day rough and tumble conversation
much less in this House.
There is no use in the Minister of Home
Affairs saying that the Member in question
has the right to take legal action against this
constable. I think it is the right hon. Gentleman's duty, as the responsible Minister in
this part of the country, to see that the
citizens, quite apart from Members of this
House, are protected, and I do not think he
doubts the bona fides of the Member who has
stated to him what actually took place on that
day outside the Boardroom. From that point
of view, I would insist that some disciplinary action should be taken against people
who forgot themselves so far as to commit
an assault for which there was no occasion,
and to use language unbecoming a public
servant.
Mr. BEATTIE: I do not want to take up
very much time, but as a public representative, and as one who represents a big constituency in this House, and part of the same
constituency in the Poor-Law Board, 1 feel
that a grave injustice was done to me on the
15th June. I do not complain of interruptions
or of rough handling, cr of anything that is
done within the bounds of common decency,
but I do complain of the conduct of two
gentlemen, one called Sergeant Taylor, of
Donegall Pass Barracks, and the other
Constable Looney, who conducted themselves
in a manner that was likely to incite to riot.
Remember, there was no incitement to riot
in the Boardroom, and I do not complain of
anything that happened inside the Boardroom.
But when I reached the landing on the top
of the stairs, and as I was putting on my hat
and coat, this sergeant of the Constabulary
came behind me and struck me with his fist
on the back of the head, telling the
constables at the same time to put me down
the stairs. The constables then twisted my
arms, and Constable Looney, who was on my
left, struck me on the side, and used an
expression which I have conveyed to the
Minister, and which I am not going to repeat
here. They dragged me down the stairs, and
the servants of the hospital and the
infirmary, and the applicants for outdoor
relief who were standing there, said it was
an utter shame and scandal for any officers
of the force to treat any individual in the
way they treated me.
I myself went to the gate, and at the
instigation of District-Inspector Lewis I
appealed to the mob not to take action on
their own initiative. I knew that in the mob
on that particular day there was a certain
number of firearms, and that the lives of the
sergeant and the constable would have been
in danger if I had pointed them out to the
crowd. I protected those individuals from

I went, and they pitched me on to the road.
I ask the Minister of Home Affairs to take
some disciplinary action in the case of
Sergeant Taylor and Constable Looney. With
the other two policemen I have no fault to
find; they were acting under the instructions
of the sergeant. The sergeant was the man
who started it; Looney carried it on. That
is a truthful statement in regard to the incident as it happened, and I leave it to the
Government to say if I was properly treated
on that occasion.

SPEAKER in the Chair.

under the Standing Order, Sittings of the

ORDERS OF THE DAY.

SUPPLEMENTARY ESTIMATES, 1926-27.
Considered in Committee.
(Mr. MOLES in the Chair).
Class IV. No. 4.
UNEMPLOYMENT GRANTS.
Motion made, and Question proposed:
"That a Supplementary Sum, not exceeding
£10, be granted to His Majesty, to complete
the sum necessary to defray the charge
which will come in course of payment during
the year ending on the 31st March, 1927, for
grants to Local Authorities, etc., in Northern
Ireland, for assistance in carrying out
approved schemes to relieve Unemployment,
and for expenses in connection with training
unemployed persons for Oversea Settlement."
The MINISTER OF LABOUR (Mr.
Andrews): Under the provisions of the
Empire Settlement Act of 1922, the Imperial
Government have arranged schemes with the
Governments of the different Dominions for
the settlement of approved emigrants from
the United Kingdom, and for the provision
in conjunction with the Dominions of financial assistance. The financial facilities consist of very much reduced fares to most of
the Dominions, including Australia, Canada,
and New Zealand, and a great many young
men from the United Kingdom have taken
advantage of these facilities and have gone
to make their homes, for the time at any
rate, within the Einpire in those Dominions.
The matter is a difficult one. The Imperial
Government found, however, that there were
many young men willing and anxious to go
to the Dominions who were not able to do
so because of the fact that they did not
possess the necessary farming knowledge,
and so the Imperial Government decided to
establish in Great Britain two training
centres, where those young men could receive the requisite amount of farming
experience and knowledge, so as to be acceptable to the Dominions and to the Dominion
authorities.
As we have had the same difficulty here,
we felt that it was the duty of the Government to establish a similar training centre
in Northern Ireland, and we were fortunate
in being able to obtain at Richhill a farm
of 200 acres of good and suitable land, with
desirable buildings upon it, for the purpose.
The idea is that those young men in Northern
Ireland who desire to go to the Dominions
should have the same opportunities brought
within their reach here that their fellowcountrymen in Great Britain now enjoy.
I would like hon. Members to appreciate
that there is no pressure of any kind whatever being put upon those young men. They
will be taken into this training establishment at Richhill, where there will be instructors, and where they will see the work
done and help to carry it out in a proper
manner upon the spot. I am sure that hon.
Members will appreciate that it is desirable
that those young men should have their
wishes gratified, and that they should become
qualified for life in the Dominions if they
so desire.
I would like to explain to the House that
the cost of this scheme will be borne, for this
year at any rate, upon the Unemployment
Grants Vote, and that this Supplementary
Estimate of £10 is simply asked for to-day
to give Parliament an opportunity of expressing its views in connection with the general
principle. May I say that I quite share the
views of many that it is most unfortunate
that these young men cannot find useful employment here, and that they are obliged to
break their home and family ties by going
across the seas. But we cannot always have
things as we would like to have them, and
we have got to look at facts as they are.
We have a surplus male population at the
present time, and from the returns with
which I have been furnished, not once but
many times, I am inclined to fear that even
if trade were normal again, unless very unexpected developments took place in connection with our industrial life, we would
still have a surplus male population. Therefore I think that what we have got to direct
our attention to to-day is this: Are these
young men to live on here getting employment
intermittently as ordinary labourers, or are
they to be given a chance to make good in
other parts of the world within the Empire?
I think that between these two choices no
one who really desires the welfare of these
Supplementary Estimates. 1952
Supply-
HOUSE OF COMMONS
[Mr. Andrews]
young men will have any doubt as to the
course which we as a Government and as a
Parliament ought to pursue.
We ought not, as I have said, to put any
pressure upon these young men to leave
Northern Ireland, but on the other hand if
they desire to go I think we ought to bring
within their reach the facilities to which
I have referred. I may say that it is intended that this training farm should be
worked upon business lines, that these
trainees will help to cultivate the ground,
will help to do the ploughing work, look
after the horses and cattle, do the milking
work, do some repair work to fences, and
cut timber, in other words, do everything
which it is possible for them to do in order
to acquire the knowledge which the Dominion
authorities demand that they should possess
before they would accept them as emigrants.
It is for these reasons that I have confidence
in bringing this Vote before the Committee.
It has often been said by hon. Members that
it is the duty of the Government to do everything humanly possible to help our unemployed. We as a Government are doing
everything we can for those who desire to
remain at home, and by this new activity
I think I may say we are doing all that we
feel is desirable to help those who desire to
seek employment elsewhere to obtain it. I
beg to move.
Mr. KYLE: I want to say in connection
with this Supplementary Estimate that we
on these benches dissociate ourselves from
the statement that emigration is going to be
a cure for unemployment. We do not want
to say we are opposed to young men being
trained for agricultural purposes.
We want
to see them trained to follow agriculture just
as we want to see them trained in technical
schools to follow their trades. But in this
thing it seems to me the Colonies are going
to derive all the benefit from this training
scheme. Lord Selborne said the value of an
agricultural labourer to the community was
£100 a year. If that is so, and I have no
reason to doubt it, there should be some
arrangement made with the Colonies that
they should bear the cost of the training of
the men who are going out to enrich their particular countries. If that arrangement has
not been made it ought to be made as expeditiously as possible. There ought also
to be facilities at this particular training
place at Richhill to train men to follow
agriculture in our own land. It seems to
me to be not an altogether desirable thing
that we should equip an institution to train
people to work in other lands. It would be
much better business to train those same
people to work in our own land so that we
may reap the benefit of their labour so far
as the land is concerned. I do not want to
oppose this Estimate, but I do want definitely
to dissociate myself from the statement
alleged to have been made by the Prime
Minister that emigration is a cure for unemployment, or even a partial cure.
Mr. JOHNSTONE: I would like to speak
to this Vote and to say how heartily I welcome the statement that has been made by
the right hon. Gentleman, the Minister of
Labour. This is an instalment of what I
hope will ultimately become a much wider
scheme for getting hold of the young unemployed persons. I preached over and over
again in this House against the fact that up
to the present time, or up to the time this
scheme was initiated, there has been no provision for getting hold of the young unemployed men between the ages of sixteen
and twenty. Those are the years during
which it is vitally
ortant a young man
should learn to work. If he does not learn to
work then he is going to be a loafer for the
rest of his life, a danger to the public and a
perpetual drag on the community.
I am
very glad that this scheme has been put
into force. I should like to know from the
Minister of Labour at what age he proposes
to take those young men under his charge.
Mr. ANDREWS: Nineteen,
Mr. JOHNSTONE: Nineteen. I think that
is too late. If you leave a boy unemployed
from the time he leaves school till he is
nineteen you are not going to make very much
of him after that. I do not quite follow the
logic of those who say that because these
young men are being trained to go out to the
Colonies we are therefore not doing anything
to help employment at home. Surely if there
is no work at home for those young people,
and if there is work in the Colonies it is
much better that we should send our labour
out there. Hon. Members have spoken in
this House very often as if emigration was
some unheard of thing only suggested now in
a time of unemployment. Emigration has
been going on continuously from this country
as long as I can remember, and I am sure as
long as a great many people who are a great
deal older than I am can remember. It has
been going on from every country in
Europe. It has been going on from England,
from Germany, from Italy, and from the
Scandinavian countries. There has been a
constant stream of emigrants to the new
countries beyond the sea. I do not think it
is likely to stop, because there are opportunities there which are not to be found at
home, and there are chances there for men
to make good which they would not have in
the congested districts at home.
I do not see why we should put any stop
to that. I think every one of us is proud of
what the people who emigrated from Ulster
to America have already done and of what

some fuller information than has been given

point I would like some fuller information.
I cannot say I can give this scheme an
unqualified blessing, because, as I pointed
out in this House some time ago, there has
been a tremendous decrease in the rural
population from the year 1841 to the present
time. It is all very well to encourage the
people to emigrate and settle in some part
of the Dominions, but where is the objection
to trying to settle some of those people at
home? The argument has been put up
before that our territory is limited, and I
think the right hon. Gentleman the Minister
of Agriculture told us on one occasion it
was scarcely possible to settle one more
person on the land in Northern Ireland than
are on it at the present time. We have
repeatedly in this House asked for the reestablishment of the Wages Boards. That
would be an important start so far as preventing depopulation was concerned, and
would tend to getting a larger number of
people settled than are at the moment.
I think the Government should give the
question of the re-establishment of the Wages
Boards some fuller and more sympathetic
consideration than they have done up to the
present. What would be the position?
Supposing our agricultural labourers were
in receipt of higher wages than they have
at the present time that would be reflected
on our industrial situation inasmuch as
those people would effect much larger purchases out of the towns and cities, and we
would find thereby a gradual reduction so
far as unemployment is concerned.
The Department of the right hon. Gentleman the Minister of Agriculture issued a
very interesting book recently giving agricultural statistics. I regret I have not had
a full opportunity of going into that question up to the moment owing to the fact
that Parliament has been sitting, but from
a cursory glance at that book I find that
the acreage under tillage has decreased very
considerably since the termination of the
European war. It is all very well to say
you cannot do these things, but the fact
remains that you were able to do them
during the course of the war. And if you
were able to do them for war purposes why
cannot you do them for peace purposes?
There has been a considerable reduction in
the acreage under tillage, and we have had
no comment upon that fact in this House
at all.

If they have no knowledge of the work they

ginning. Let them have a certain amount

it is simply the beginning of a very much
larger and better scheme.

The PRIME MINISTER (Sir James Craig):

without first having taken some training in

However, this is a very modest suggestion.
The suggestion simply is that for about three
months any of those young men who desire
to break into a new life abroad in our

above all some lectures warning them what
is necessary when they arrive at their new
destinations. Anyone who has travelled in

In speaking to Mr. Massey, when he was

which are now bearing his name. (Hon.

In Canada more recently I met Ulster

Member for West Belfast (Mr. Devlin) will

It only shows that it would be, on the part

pursuit so that when you arrive either in
New Zealand, Australia, or Canada you will
have something at any rate of an assurance
that you know how to start off in life."
Now, some hon. Members said we should
begin to train our young people at home in
farm work before we start to train people
for the Dominions. We have been doing
that for a considerable time past. We have
at Greenmount in County Antrim, at
Strabane and at Cookstown training schools
for those desirous of extending their knowledge in farming and again settling on the
soil. That has not been neglected by any
means. That has been going on for some
time and this in no way clashes with that
scheme or would be allowed in the slightest
degree to interfere with it.
May I say that there is really a much
wider aspect of the question still. The
Colonies and Dominions are just as much
part and parcel of the British Empire as we
here in Ulster are. (Hon. Members: Hear,
hear.) The spirit of those people is evinced
by the great demonstrations made by the
various Prime Ministers of the Dominions
while in conference at the present time and
shows that they are all loyal to the British
Crown and Constitution. Now it is intensely important to Great Britain and to
Ulster also that there should be a close connection with, and a steady influx of good
British blood and capital into, the Dominions,
because if the country at home does not pay
careful attention to those outlying parts of
the Empire there is always the chance that
by foreign blood-and in Canada by
American blood-they may be getting the
whole country into mortgage to the American
people. American people may come into
Canada to such an extent that it would be
difficult for the British left there to maintain
those traditions that have brought us to the
proud position we in to-day as an
Empire.

Therefore, I do say if we are sending out
from time to time a small number-we can
only spare a small number, I agree, from
the Ulster area-we should send them out
somewhat prepared for the duties they are
going to take up. Let me just point to one
moral alone. The tariff in America on our
linen goods is something between 40 and 60
per cent. In the adjoining nation of Canada,
or the adjoining Dominion of Canada, the
rate of import duty on our linens is only 25 per
cent., and we as part of the Empire have a
rebate of 10 per cent., which reduces the
actual duty paid to something like 15 per
cent. for the entry of linen goods into
Canada as against. from 40 to 60 per cent.
into America.
We should therefore use all our endeavours
to keep Canada thoroughly British, and
Canada will repay us, I believe, because I
think that there is a growing understanding
on the part of the outlying parts of the
Empire that if they require and desire help
from the mother country they on their part
would be generous and would make a
gesture of assistance to the home country
that is bearing so much of a burden.

I have yet failed to find that everything
has been done that might have been done to
grapple with the problem of unemployment
especially in rural Ireland. We are quite
conscious of the causes of unemployment in
the city of Belfast and perhaps in towns
like Lurgan, Portadown, Ballymena and

There have been no schemes for the purpose of keeping the rural population from
going not only to Canada but into the towns

I want to say this, that if the Government
and the House would carefully look into this
annual report of agricultural statistics issued
by the Department of Agriculture they would
find grave cause for reflection, because they
would see that there is a steady decrease in
tillage farming at home. Tillage farming,
according to this report, reached its lowest
ebb of pre-war times in 1914. Then with the
exigencies of the war it went up in 1918,
and there was an increase of 219,000 acres.
That was just about the same level of our
tillage land in 1882. Then we decreased 107,000
acres in the middle of 1919, and there was
a further decrease of 45,000 acres in 1920,
and in 1921 63,000 acres were lost to employment. That decrease is still going on. The
House will probably remember that I discussed this question on the motion for the
adjournment. The Chancellor of the
Exchequer had told us there was an adverse
trade balance in this country last year of
half a million, and I expressed this opinion
that if our dairying industry were properly
organised and properly educated and
properly run and encouraged that half
million pounds could be wiped out. I think
that statement has been amply borne out
by the recent report of the Development
Commission, which says we were only exporting one-third of the butter at the present
time that we did twelve years ago.
I think these facts should give the Government serious cause for reflection. It should
give not only the Government but every
man who desires the welfare of this area
grave cause for reflection. I believe the
time has come when the Government should
appoint a commission to inquire into the
cause of the decline in the tillage area in
this country and to inquire into the cause
of the great decline in the exports of the
dairying industry, and to make a report how
best these things could be encouraged and
developed. I do feel that we are running the
risk of not going to get full value for the
money we are spending in this connection,
and I feel that the money could be better
spent along lines that would encourage our

industry.

country, which is and must remain the
primary industry of the country, and which
will help to ease to some extent the terrible
question of unemployment.

The greatest problem that statesmen of today have got to face, and I think the greatest

There is one thing that strikes me in

The old system of landlordism has practi
cally come to an end. In another thirty or

will be in a position of considerable advantage compared with the agriculturists in
England and Scotland, who cannot lay claim

fore, I cannot see why agriculture in this

lure of the cities has a great deal to do with

The FINANCIAL SECRETARY TO THE
MINISTRY OF FINANCE (Mr. Barbour):
As the Bill proposed to be introduced in
consequence of this Money Resolution is
purely a Money Bill this Resolution must be
disposed of before the Bill giving effect to
these proposals can be introduced.
The first part of the Resolution is in
general terms and defines the scope of the
proposed legislation which I shall briefly
summarise. In order, however, that the
Committee may understand what is
necessarily a somewhat technical subject, it
is necessary that I should touch upon the
provisions of the Government Loans Exchequer Provisions Act, which became law
in October of last year. This Act authorised
the establishment of a Government Loans
Fund somewhat on the lines of the British
Local Loans Fund, and the issue therefrom
of loans for various purposes, the more
important being, firstly, loans to Local
Authorities for Health, Housing, and other
social and sanitary services, to farmers for
certain agricultural purposes; to civil servants for housing purposes; and, secondly,
loans to the Exchequer to enable it to
finance (a) the subsidies paid to builders
under the Housing Acts; (b) the cost of Police
Barrack reconstruction; (c) advances
the Claims Fund.
to
Prior to October, 1925, moneys had been
advanced for these various purposes from the
Exchequer out of temporary borrowings
totalling approximately one million pounds.
and as it was estimated that fresh advances,
amounting to approximately one million
pounds, would be required for issue during
the period up to 31st March next, it became
necessary to issue Ulster Loans Stock for two
million pounds, half of which was, of course,
required to repay to the Exchequer the
moneys which had been temporarily
advanced in the three preceding years.
Fresh advances have proved heavier than
was then anticipated, mainly by reason of
the activities of Local Authorities, and,
accordingly, it is necessary to seek further
funds at an earlier date than was previously
thought likely.
No new principle is involved, and the purposes for which the money will be utilised
remain as before. I need not, therefore,
enter more fully into this question at the
present stage save to remind hon. Members
that the Fund will be recouped over a period
of years in respect of these advances by the
repayment of principal and interest from
the borrowers and by means of the terminable annuities which have been charged on
Votes by Acts of Parliament in respect of
the subsidies for housing and the capital
outlay on barrack reconstruction.
The Resolution specifically provides for an
increase in the amount that may be advanced
from the Fund in connection with the provision or improvement of buildings for the
accommodation of the Royal Ulster Constabulary. The limit imposed by the
Exchequer and Financial Provisions Act of
1924 was £375,000, but this amount was
largely in the nature of guesswork and
actual experience has shown that the scheme
will require an expenditure of approximately
£800,000. It is intended that advances to an
amount not exceeding this figure will be
spread over ten years. The terminable
annuity which has been charged on the Vote
for the Royal Ulster Constabulary for repayment of these advances will be correspondingly increased.
The Bill will contain other provisions
bearing upon the issue of loans from the
Government Loans Fund, but these do not
call for comment, being mainly intended to
define more clearly the Government's lending powers.
201401
The last part of the Resolution contains
certain provisions in respect of the post of
Comptroller and Auditor-General. Their
effect is to alter the salary of that officer
from a fixed one of £1,350 to the same scale
as that of a Secretary to a Minister, viz.,
£1,200, rising by the operation of increments
to £1,500. It is considered that this revised
scale is more in keeping with general
practice and as the occupant of the post will
lose by the change in the initial years, the
additional expense involved is inconsiderable.
It is further proposed to fix the age of
retirement of the Comptroller and Auditor-
General at sixty-five instead of tenure at
pleasure as heretofore, and paragraph (c) of
the Resolution is intended to make it clear
that the holder of the post comes under the
ordinary Superannuation Acts, save that
his pension is payable from the Consolidated
Fund. I may say that the present holder
of the post has been consulted in regard to
these proposed changes and has agreed to
these provisions being applied to himself. I
beg to move.
Question put, and agreed to.
Resolution reported and agreed to.
Bill ordered to be brought in by the
Minister of Finance, Mr. Barbour, and

Horse Breeding Bill.

CLAUSE I (Licences and permits for
ownership or keeping of stallions).
Any person who, after the appointed day,
owns, keeps or has control of a stallion
of a prescribed age shall be liable on conviction to a fine of ten pounds, unless the
stallion is licensed, or a permit has been
granted in respect thereof, under the
provisions of this Act; and any person who
has been convicted of owning, keeping or
having control of a stallion contrary to the
provisions of this Act, or has been convicted before the appointed day of an
offence against sections one and fourteen
of the Horse Breeding Act, 1918, in respect
of a stallion shall, if since such conviction
he owns, keeps or has control of such
stallion contrary to the provisions of this
Act, be guilty of a continuing offence and
be liable on conviction to a further
penalty of forty shillings for each week or
part of a week during which he is guilty
of the continuing offence.
Debate resumed on Amendment-(26th
October)-in Clause 1, page 3, line 7, to leave
out the word "of" (a fine of ten pounds) and
to insert instead thereof the words, "not
exceeding."
Mr. GEORGE HENDERSON: I will not
detain the Committee very long on this
Amendment, which was discussed yesterday.
The Clause as it stands fixes a minimum fine,
and as I said yesterday, I think this is a
case, if there is any case at all, which should
be left to the discretion of the magistrates
to hear the evidence and decide the amount
of the fine. As the Clause stands the magistrates have no option but to impose the fixed
fine, and I think it comes very badly from
the Minister of Agriculture to suggest, as he
did yesterday, that the Benches in Ulster
cannot be depended upon to hear a very
simple case like this and decide it on the
evidence. The magistrates are largely
appointed from the political party represented by the right hon. Gentleman, and I
think they can be depended upon to hear a
simple case like this and decide it on the
evidence. I think it is a dangerous system to
put a minimum fine in Bills. I beg to move
accordingly.
Mr. MARK: I would like to ask the
Minister of Agriculture to give this Amendment the consideration which I think it
deserves. If you will read the Bill-
Notice taken that 10 Members were not
present; Committee counted, and 10 Members
being present,
Mr. MARK: You will see that any person
who after the appointed day owns, keeps, or
has a stallion of the prescribed age is liable
on conviction to a fine of £10. The appointed
day, according to the Bill, is 1st January
next, but according to the last Section of the
Bill the Minister of Agriculture may determine a day earlier than 1st January next.
The appointed day might be 1st December,
and I do not think the people in the rural
districts of Northern Ireland can be made
to understand this Bill. Some little mountain man might have a stallion hauling turf
from the bog, and to have him through ignorance of this Bill, which will only be about
a month old when it comes into effect, to be
liable to a fine of £10, is, I think, preposterous. I think it could be very well left in
the hands of the magistrates as suggested by
the hon. Member. Had it been a case where
a man had done a glaring wrong or broken
through some provisions of the Bill I would
not have asked the Minister, but here is a
case, where through mere ignorance or mere
forgetfulness, a man may offend, and to have
him salted in a fine of £10, where he might
not have £10 in the world, is very harsh. I
have no doubt the Minister will meet the case
sympathetically. I do not like these minimum fines, and if the Minister would see his
way to say he would consider this matter on
the Report stage, I think it would meet the
requirements of the case, and possibly the
hon. Member would see his way not to press
the matter to a division.
Mr. ARCHDALE: A minimum fine is no

to feel it very greatly I think I would like to
consider it till the Report stage comes up
and see if anything can be done to meet his

The MINISTER OF HOME AFFAIRS
(Sir Dawson Bates): The effect of this Bill
is to extend for a further year-that is until
March, 1928 the operation of the Housing
Acts in Northern Ireland. Hon. Members
are aware that under these Acts a subsidy is
granted from Government funds to private
builders or urban authorities in respect of
houses built by them and which comply with
certain prescribed conditions. The amount
of the subsidy is £60 per house, which is increased to the sum of £80 if the house is
completed within six months from date of
commencement.
Housing Bill-
Second Reading.
HOUSE OF COMMONS
[Sir Dawson Bates)
The conditions briefly are that the houses
must be either of the kitchen or small
parlour type, with a maximum superficial
area of 950 square feet, and a minimum of
600 square feet, but in special conditions the
minimum is reduced to 550 square feet in
urban areas and 500 in rural districts. The
houses must be built in a workmanlike
manner and in accordance with the rules
laid down by the Ministry.
The Acts, as hon, Members are aware, also
enable local authorities to supplement the
Government grant by a further subsidy out
of the rates not exceeding £10 per house, or,
if they so desire, they can lend £100, free of
interest. In addition, power is given to the
local authorities to exempt houses from the
payment of rates for a period not exceeding
ten years, and I am glad to say a great many
-in fact the majority-of the local authorities have availed themselves of these powers.
I am glad to say that the progress of the
housing operations since the. Acts came into
force has been very satisfactory, but, while
this is so, the Government do not suggest
for one moment that these Acts have entirely
solved the housing problem, but at all events
the success of the operation of the Acts
justifies the Government in coming to the
House and asking for an extension of the
Acts for another year.
The statistics in regard to the housing
operations' under the Acts, which the Minis-"
try keep, show a gradual increase in the
number of houses. These statistics are reproduced in a chart, and I think there is
one in the Dining-room of this House, which,
I am sure, has been perused with interest by
hon. Members. I find that, up to date, the
number of houses so far approved for erec
tion by private enterprise amounts to 4,773;
and of these 2,977 have been completed. As
regards urban authorities and the rural
districts, I find the number approved ofand, of course, hon. Members will appreciate
that this does not include labourers' cottages
-amounts to 1,960, of which 1,046 are completed, and, of course, a large number of
those are in rural areas.
Just to show how there has been a steady
flow of the building of this type of house. I
may say that I find that last month no less
than 150 houses have been approved for
erection by private owners. When I mention
that figure I do not refer to those built by
local authorities, but to those built, or proposed to be built, by private owners. I think
these statistics compare very favourably with
the progress of housing operations in England, and when I say that, I would like to
express my appreciation of the way in which
local authorities have co-operated by making
these grants, and also by exempting houses
from rates. I find in that connection that
no less than twenty-two urban districts are

supplementing the grant of £80 from the
Government, and eleven of these authorities
are exempting these houses from rates, while
no less than eight rural districts have given
grants and sixteen have exempted the houses
from rates for periods varying from five to
ten years.dtow
undoubtedly ther
In addition to all this a very large number
of local authorities have put into operation
the Small Dwellings Acquisition Acts, under
which individuals can purchase houses and
pay the interest and the capital by instalments spread over a period of years, and
operation of the Small
Dwellings Acts, coupled with the Housing
Acts, has done much to help on the progress
of building in Northern Ireland. (Hon.
Members: Hear, hear). I find that £11,115
was sanctioned last year in connection with
loans by rural districts, and no less a sum
than £322,000 was sanctioned as loans in
urban districts, and hon. Members will
appreciate that when I refer to the fact that
there are many other houses that do not
come within the operation of the Small
Dwellings Acquisition Acts, which applies
only to houses up to £1,200 in value.
Government's policy is, as I have already
indicated, to encourage private enterprise
and to secure as quickly as possible suitable
houses for the working classes, and I think
I am justified in saying that this policy has
been very successful up to the present. I
beg to move.

Oral Answers to Questions.
BLACKWATER BRIDGE.
1. Colonel WOODS asked the Minister of
Home Affairs whether he is aware of the extremely dangerous condition of the bridge at
Bracadysart, on the Cookstown-Draperstown
Road, and whether he can state the approximate date when it will be rendered safe for
the public.
The MINISTER OF HOME AFFAIRS (Sir
Dawson Bates): It is presumed that the hon.
and gallant Member refers to the Blackwater
Bridge, in Brackagh townland, of Londonderry
County. This bridge is on a third class road,
and was maliciously damaged in July, 1922.
It has since been bridged over with timber,
and is passable for traffic.
It is understood that a proposal for its repair will be brought before the road
authority at the forthcoming quarterly meeting in January next.
Colonel WOODS: May I ask the right hon.
Gentleman is he aware that a very serious
accident took place there inside the last
three weeks?
Sir DAWSON BATES: No, sir. I am not.
IMPORT OF YARNS.
2. Mr. KYLE asked the Minister of Commerce whether he can state the value and
the number of bundles of yarns imported

GUARDIANSHIP OF CHILDREN.
4. Mr. KYLE asked the Prime Minister
whether he has considered the advisability of
bringing in a Measure under which equal
guardianship of children may be secured for
both parents, and whether it is the intention
of the Government to introduce legislation on
this subject on the same lines as that now in
force in Great Britain.
The ATTORNEY-GENERAL: The Prime
Minister has asked me to take this question.
The Government have considered the advisability of applying the English legislation to
Northern Ireland, and have come to the conclusion that it would be both unwise and
impracticable to do so at present. This conclusion has only been arrived at after careful
consideration of the law in both countries,
and the reasons cannot be stated within the
limits of an answer to the question.

ORDERS OF THE DAY.
Motor Vehicles (Traffic and
Regulation) Bill.
Considered in Committee.
[Mr. MOLES in the Chair.]
CLAUSE 1 (Reckless driving and drunkenness while in charge of motor-car).
(1) If any person-
(a) drives a motor-car on a public highway recklessly or negligently, or at a
speed or in a manner which is dangerous to the public, having regard to
all the circumstances of the case, including the nature, condition and use
of the highway, and to the amount
of traffic which actually is at the time,
or which might reasonably be expected
to be, on the highway; or
(b) is drunk while in charge on any highway or other public place of a motorcar;
that person shall be liable on summary
conviction to a fine of five pounds or any
greater sum not exceeding fifty pounds, or,
in the case of a second or subsequent conviction to a fine of ten pounds or any
greater sum not exceeding one hundred
pounds, or in the discretion of the court to
imprisonment for a period not exceeding
six months, or to both such fine and imprisonment.
(2) Any police constable may apprehend
without warrant the driver, or person in
charge, of any car who commits an offence
28 OCTOBER 1926

Committee.

under this section within his view, if such
driver or person refuses to give his name
and address or (being the driver) to produce his licence on demand, or if the motorcar does not bear the identification mark or
sign required in pursuance of the Roads
Act, 1920.
(3) If the driver, or person in charge, of
any motor-car who commits an offence
under this section refuses to give his name
or address, or gives a false name or address,
he shall be guilty of an offence under this
Act, and it shall be the duty of the owner
of the car, if required, to give any information which it is within his power to give,
and which may lead to the identification
and apprehension of the driver or other
person by whom the offence has been committed, and if the owner fails to do so he
also shall be guilty of an offence under this
Act.

The CHAIRMAN: In view of the number
and complexity of the Amendments on the
Order Paper on this Bill I propose to make

number of the Amendments put down in

there are Amendments which are the same
in part, but different in some minor details.
It will devolve on me in my position in some
circumstances to make a selection of the
Amendments, and I purpose to do that,
leaving the Committee always in possession
of the more important matters. The first
two Amendments may be taken as typical,
one being in the name of the hon. Member
for Derry (Sir Robert Anderson), who proposes to leave out the words "or negligently,"
and the other in the name of the Minister
in charge of the Bill, who proposes to leave
out "negligently," but to insert other words.
The practice in such cases is to take the
Amendment which proposes to omit words
in order to insert words prior to the Amendment which merely intends to omit the same
words. I, therefore, call on the Minister
of Home Affairs to move his Amendment.

Sir DAWSON BATES: As there was રી
general misconception of the meaning of the
Clause as it originally stood in the Bill, may
I point out that the Clause as originally
drafted was simply a repetition of the old
section which appears in the 1903 Act, which

Motor Vehicles Bill-
Committee.
HOUSE OF COMMONS

[Sir Dawson Bates.]
as originally drafted, and which was made
clear to the Committee, is in effect that
where the word negligence appears that
means criminal negligence as opposed to
common law negligence. It does not apply
to misjudgment on the part of a driver, or
a technical offence or the case of a driver
who goes round on the wrong side of the
police. What we want to try and arrive at
is a Clause which will clearly show that what
the Government want to get at is the driver
who recklessly and wantonly drives to the
danger of the public.
I am glad to think that that class of
driver is very much in the minority among
motor drivers. (Hon. Members: Hear, hear).
I think that the vast majority of motor
drivers drive carefully not alone in their
own interests but in the interests of the
public. Still as we all know there is a small
minority of motor drivers who are totally
indifferent to human life and who drive recklessly and wantonly, indifferent to anybody,
even to themselves. I think hon. Members
have only to turn to the papers, as I said
on the Second Reading, to see the terrible
toll that is extracted. Only the other day
a case came to my notice where a man was
convicted for the fourth time, and his record
was that he had two persons killed to his
credit, or discredit, and one person injured.
That is the individual we want to get at in
framing this new Bill. I would like to ask
this House not to be diverted by false motives
of sentiment. The Government do not wish
to persecute anyone. I say the Government
and this House too have a very serious responsibility when one realises the enormous
loss of life which takes place annually.
Since this Bill was introduced, or shortly
before that, I had an opportunity of meeting
further motor organisations. and I would
like to say this that I found there was a great
deal of misconception as to the real effect of
this Bill. I have had very satisfactory talks
with them, and just in the same way as the
motor traders and the bus owners so the
ordinary private car owners have met me in
the most fair and frank manner. They realise, as I think most hon. Members realise,
that something must be done, and I think
they also realise that the Government are
trying to bring in a really effective and good
Measure. I therefore beg to move the Amendment standing in my name, to leave out
"negligently" and insert "wantonly." I do
not know whether it would be possible also to
move the second Amendment at the same
time.
The CHAIRMAN: No, it would not.
Colonel WOODS: Might I ask the right
non. Gentleman to state exactly who is to be
the judge of whether a driver is driving
wantonly or with negligence. He does not
say. It says further on in the Bill that the
whole power is given to the constable.
Sir DAWSON BATES: No, no.
The CHAIRMAN:
I think the hon. and
gallant Member misses the point. What the
Amendment proposes is to omit the word
"negligently," and there can therefore arise
no question as to who is to interpret negligence. Perhaps the hon. and gallant Member
wishes to ask who is to be the interpreter of
the word "wantonly."
Colonel WOODS: Yes, I would like an
answer given to that. The right hon.
Gentleman referred to the case of 8
man who might have a number of
accidents to his credit, or discredit. That
might very easily happen in the case of any.
one. A man might be merely unfortunate
without necessarily being careless or negligent, or driving to the danger of the public,
and I would like the Minister to give some
further explanation to clear that point up.
Sir DAWSON BATES: I am glad the hon.
and gallant Member has raised this point. I
would like to take this opportunity of removing any misapprehension that may exist in
the mind of the public that a policeman's
word is one whit more valuable than the
word of any ordinary respectable citizen.
If a policeman brings a case he must show
why he has formed the opinion that the man
was driving wantonly. May I again quote
an instance of what I mean. Suppose a
policeman brings forward a case that a man
is driving at a speed of thirty or forty miles
an hour round a blind corner, and that he
was going at such a speed that he had to
go outside the white line and met a person
who was coming in the opposite direction.
Those are all circumstances that the policeman must establish to the Court, and the
Court is the body which will say whether the
man was wantonly or negligently driving,
not the policeman.
As regards the man who had killed two
individuals, the case I had in my mind was
that of a man who had been twice convicted
of drunkenness and once of negligence, and
on the fourth occasion he is again charged
with reckless driving. That is the type of
case we really want to get at and not the
case of an error of judgment or a technical
error.
Mr. P. O'NEILL: I should like to know
what necessity there is to insert the word
"wantonly." Is the word "recklessly" not
sufficient?
Sir DAWSON BATES: Might I explain
that we want to try to help the magistrates
in interpreting this Clause. The magistrates
are laymen and there has arisen a great deal
of confusion in their minds in the past as
to the interpretation of the word "negligent."
We want to make it clear that before a man
can be convicted he must be guilty of both
wanton and negligent driving. not common
law negligence but criminal negligence.

which I think meets the case amply.
Amendment agreed to.

these offences are only committed by a very
small minority of the motoring public? The
extraordinary thing is that this class commit
such an offence over and over again. The
vast majority of people who motor do so without committing an offence. Yet we do see
road hogs-I think that is the best description
I can give them-who are absolutely indifferent to human life or property, and they
commit these offences again and again. One
of the most interesting things that have been
brought to my notice in connection with this
Bill when going through the statistics is to
find that these individuals come back again
and again like the criminals for whom my
right hon. and learned Friend the Attorney-
General is responsible. (Laughter).
I want to emphasise this because there has
been a great deal of misunderstanding when
dealing with this question of minimum
penalties. This will not do any harm to
ordinary motoring, but I do think it will do
a lot to put an end to this reckless and wanton
driving which at the present time is causing
so much loss of human life. I quoted some
figures on the Second Reading, but as I said
then I have reason to believe that when the
figures for the present year are added up
there will be a very large addition in the
number of deaths and injuries. That is the
condition of affairs that this Committee has
to take into consideration, and I do implore
hon. Members to realise their responsibility.
Are we as a Committee to sit by here and see
this continued loss of life going on without
taking any step to stop it?
One has only to look at the fines inflicted
upon these individuals to see how utterly,
inadequate they are, fines of 5s or of 10s.
The principle of a minimum penalty is not
a new one. There are dozens of cases I could
quote where the principle has been established, and only lately in the Imperial House
of Commons the principle has been established in the Criminal Justice Bill, where if

a man is convicted of drunkenness in charge

Mr. MCALLISTER: I am entirely against
the principle of introducing into this Committee in the Measure which has been introduced at the present time the principle of a
minimum fine. I am against it because it is
reactionary, is oppressive, is inequitable, and
is contrary to the traditions of legislation to
which we have been accustomed up to the
present time. In my judgment there is no
justification for it in the administration of
the law. In the first place, you withhold
from the various courts the discretion which
they should have, you usurp their functions,
and in this Committee you pre-judge all the
various cases which are bound to be brought
in the future under this Bill. Without
facilities for apportioning the exact extent
of blame in each case, you now propose to
affix a penalty. The fact remains that in
the original Bill--not this new Bill which is
now before the Committee-you fix a minimum
fine of £5 and now you fix it at £1, so that
on your own admission by pre-judging these
cases in a fine of £5 the public might be
inflicted in £4 unjustly.
Reflections have more or less been cast upon
the courts that have had to try motor cases
up to the present, particularly the petty
sessions courts. I have a great respect and
a most profound liking for the petty sessions
courts. In my experience these courts perform their duties in a most satisfactory
and commonsense way, and I have rarely
known of a miscarriage of justice taking
place. With regard to the small and
nominal fines to which the Home Secretary
referred in introducing the Bill, I think the
explanation is a very simple one, and reflects
the highest credit on the foresight and
justice and actual views of these petty
sessions courts, because the explanation is
that in the vast majority of cases in the
past few years the prosecutions have been
in respect of heavy motor vehicles and buses
exceeding the twelve miles speed limit. Anyone knows that is an absolutely absurd
proposition, and the magistrates taking that
logical and reasonable view saw the absurdity
of it and inflicted a nominal fine.
These petty sessions courts, which have
been the subject of the strictures of the
Home Secretary, have anticipated the introduction of this Measure by four or five years.
I think in all views of the case their administration of the motor laws has been justified,
has been equitable and just, and has met
the ends of justice in every way. I object
entirely on principle, and I think every
lawyer with any experience objects, and is
entirely opposed to this principle of a minimum fine. You place the courts in a very
serious dilemma, because you prevent them
from apportioning the blame and fixing the
penalty accordingly. What may be a severe
penalty to the driver of a hired motor-car
may be a small penalty to a merchant prince
who drives his own car.
Before I sit down may I say that the
Opposition have been criticised from time

the Order Paper we see thirty or forty

They will, at all events, agree that we have
tried to change this very oppressive and
unjustifiable Measure into what I hope will
be a highly efficient and workable Measure.
I should like to say that we on these benches
are glad, apart from all personal feelings,
that our views have been forced upon the
Government, and that they have been driven
to accept and put into practice the criticism
we made on the Second Reading of this Bill.
I do suggest to the Government it would
have been a better tribute to the prestige
of this House, would have been

Sir ROBERT ANDERSON: I must confess

might be necessary for such a thing to be

Certain charges are before benches of magistrates and very often a very paltry fine is
imposed for what, after all, is a very serious

instances-I do not say as a general rule,

Under this Bill I would have a minimum
fine for a man who is drunk in charge of a
motor-car, and who is likely to do himself
and his passengers grave injury, and who is
also likely to do other folk who are occupying the highway serious injury. I would
also have a minimum penalty for any
motorist who recklessly or wantonly takes
charge of a vehicle in the same way and is
a danger to himself and to the community.
I think there should be a minimum fine for
those two offences, and then leave it to the
discretion of the magistrates what larger
sums they would impose taking all the circumstances of the case into consideration.
For those two classes of offenders I believe
there should be nobody who has the slightest
scrap of sympathy. Personally I have not
the slightest scrap of sympathy for them,
and I think there ought be a minimum fine
imposed when that offence is committed.
In regard to this particular Clause the
only complaint I have now is that the
Minister has reduced the minimum to one
pound, which does seem to be a very paltry
penalty for a man who recklessly drives
what, after all, if not properly handled is a
very dangerous machine on the highway. So
that I do not think anyone can reasonably
complain of the reduction in this case from
five pounds to one pound. Then there is a
third class of offence for which I would have
a minimum fine, that is for the man who has
been convicted, whose licence has been taken
from him, and who again deliberately goes
upon the highway and drives his vehicle.

The ATTORNEY-GENERAL: It appears to
be the opinion of most Members of this

to the public from reckless motoring has

intervention is necessary to protect pedestrains and others using the roads in a lawful
But having regard to the large number of

I think the Committee will agree that one of
the objects of this Bill which is aimed at by
the Government, namely, to tighten up the
motoring regulations, is a matter which is
really essential and calls for Government intervention at the earliest possible moment.
And the question is, I submit, how is it to
be tightened up. This Bill really creates no
new offences. It is merely dealing in a new
manner with offences that have been committed up to the present.
The way in which these matters will come
before the Bench of magistrates in future
will be quite different from the way in which
they come before them now, because the
speed limit-and I would ask the Members
of the Committee not to forget this-is being
abolished under this Bill. Therefore, the
only form of offence which will remain is
the offence of driving to the danger of the
public in a wanton and reckless manner.
The speed limit having been abolished,
allowing motorists to drive at such a speed
as they may think right having regard to all
the circumstances, I do not think that

being harshly dealt with when the penalties
for wanton and reckless driving to the danger
of the public are hardened up.

But what happened? And I ask the Committee to remember this. When he made

hung upon his words. We find to-day in

has only five Members on his own side of

I do not think that is fair to the followers
of the right hon. Gentleman, who in all good
faith came here a week ago and who were
told what was in the mind of the right hon.
Gentleman in his Bill. After he gets them

progress and power, he comes here and
changes and transforms this whole Measure.
Why did he do this? What is the meaning
of this radical change? During the discussion of this Bill on the Second Reading
many Members from different parts of the
House offered very important criticisms.
Most of their criticisms were of a character
so impressive that they have now become
or will become incorporated in the new
Measure which he has proposed to-day. In
his speech, and in the equally powerful
though somewhat briefer speech of his learned
assistant in the Home Office (Mr. Hanna),
there never was, after what was said from
these Benches and from the Benches opposite,
the slightest indication that they would be
prepared to accept the Amendments suggested
in the speeches delivered both from here and
the other side.
In the meantime the motor forces were
mobilised. All the motor organisations were
set at work. Pronouncements were delivered
that no more Unionist electors would be
driven by over-inflicted motor cars when
political emergencies demanded. Threats
were held out to the Government, and to
give an idea of the horrors that were in
store for them a meeting was to be held
in the Presbyterian Assembly rooms-an
indignation meeting-at which I was to be
the chief orator. It seems to me that my
suggestions can have no effect in this Presbyterian Assembly to which I am constitutionally elected to declare my opinions, but I
frighten the Government when I go to the
Presbyterian Assembly in Grosvenor Road.
Then the whole operations began, and these
motor men met and frightened the right
hon. Gentleman. They brought him to heel,
or rather he brought them to the Home
Office, which is the same thing. They had
a conference, and he listened to what they
had to say; and what did they say? They
only said what many Members on this side
of the House and what many Members on
the other side said. They only made the
same suggestions made here by the elected
representatives of the people.
But the right hon. Gentleman gets up and
says to them, "I will give you everything you
ask for." The threat of not driving the
voters to the poll at the next election was
so completely impressive that he at once
succumbed to the potential results of his
wicked action in the House when he introduced the Bill in the historic speech to which
I have referred. In my opinion that is only
part and parcel of the policy carried on by
this Government, to which every Member of
the House, let him belong to whatever party
he may, ought to enter a protest. (Hon.
Members: Hear, hear). I have not much
respect for this House myself. I do not think
it is much of a Parliament at all. The best
proof of that is that nobody attends it.
When there is anything important such as
the Second Reading of an old Bill in fresh
form, the Government's supporters do not
think it worth while to come here. While
I am in this Parliament I will stand for its
dignity and power. (Hon. Members: Hear,
hear).
The Government have repeatedly succumbed to influences outside with the result
that when Members of this House come forward with Amendments or propositions to
improve a Measure their Amendments are
treated with contempt, while outsiders who
have no substantial right to have their
opinions conceded, unless it is part of our
controversy in the House, can become masters
of the situation and of the Government. There
is a moral to be drawn, too from this thing.
The motor organisations in most of their
claims, not in all of them, have my sympathy. The moral of this thing is that the
motor organisation is a powerful and wealthy
organisation. They can influence the Government. But what does the lesson teach?
When the Government are doing something
which a large and influential section of the
people do not like these people can so mobilise their forces and bring such influence to
bear that they can compel the Government
to change their whole Measure.
And I commend this to those who attend
football matches. I am sorry the Chancellor
of the Exchequer is not here so that he

I need not delay the House by going any
further into the matters that have been
touched upon. But I do want to say to
hon. Members that it is hoped that every
Member of this House will take a continued interest in this Measure, and that,
when it reaches the Committee stage, the
Government will be glad to consider everything that is consistent with the spirit of
the Bill as it appears now, and that will
bring about the desired end, so that when
the Bill becomes an Act it will be some
thing that will have the approval of every
Member of the House and will represent
the unanimous view of the House in regard
to the safety of the public. (Official
Reports, vol. 7, No. 21, col. 1666.)
The Bill was introduced at very considerable length by the Minister of Home Affairs,
because it was a matter of great and grave
importance. It was a matter that affected
the general public so intimately that every
Member of this Committee, no matter on
which side he sat, deemed it his duty to take
an interest in it. On behalf of the Government I invited every Member to maintain
that interest and let us have the benefit of

these Amendments to the Bill are the result
of the care and study given by those who
have charge of the Bill, the recommendations made by Members of this Committee
in their Second Reading speeches, and of the
representations made to the Ministry. I
may say that I am indebted to some hon.

be an evil day if the practice which the hon.
Member (Mr. Devlin) so eloquently protested

which the procedure adopted in this Committee is intended to bring about.

There is no radical change in this Bill.
There is no change of principle in the Bill
from beginning to end. It is a perfectly
clear and simple Measure, and I cannot, for
the life of me, understand how there could
have been so much confusion about it. It
is true that we have had a long discussion
on the First Clause. That is all to the good,
and I would have the Committee understand
now that, even after we have finished with
this Clause in Committee, we will welcome a
continued interest in the Clause on the part
of all Members of the Committee until it
finally leaves the House, always in the hope
that, as our only concern is the safety of the
general public, when the Bill is given the
full force of an Act of Parliament it will be
the unanimous product of this Committee.
