NOVEMBER 1926

The MINISTER OF COMMERCE (Mr.
Barbour): I may say that I have had very
short notice of this question, and I am sorry
to disappoint the hon. Member in not being
able to deal with it as he or I might desire.
I have noticed Press reports of the incidents
referred to by the hon. Member. From
inquiries made, however, I am satisfied that
the fires were not of a serious nature, and
were indeed such as occasionally arise during
the normal process of gas manufacture
where different grades of coal are being used.
I understand that the particular cargo, the
use of which gave rise to the difficulties reported in the Press, is now exhausted.
Mr. DEVLIN: May I ask the right hon.
Gentleman has he called the attention of the
authorities at the gas works to the fact that
they refused to make any statement as to
the cause of these fires, and that they refused to give the public any information?
Does he regard it as a trivial matter that
three officers were seriously injured, one
being in a critical condition? In view of
the fact that this incident to which I have
referred occurred after the first two fires, I
would like to know what was done to prevent the third fire from taking place?
Mr. BARBOUR: As I said at the beginning, unfortunately I have had little time to
look into this matter, but so far as any instructions having been given as to information being withheld, that has not so far
come within my knowledge.
Mr. DEVLIN: Is it not the custom in
cases of this sort that the Ministry of Commerce would make inquiries in the interests
of public safety when they find from the
newspapers incidents of this character occurring? I may say also that I do not know
what the right hon. Gentleman regards as
notice. I handed him this question two
days ago.

ORDERS OF THE DAY.
Exchequer and Financial Provisions Bill.
Order for Second Reading read.
Motion made, and Question proposed:
"That the Bill be read a Second time."
Mr. BARBOUR: I may state for the information of hon. Members that the main
proposals of the Bill now submitted hinge
on the Government Loans Fund, which was
established by the Government Loans Fund
and Financial Provisions Act of 1925.
Powers to make various classes of advances
described in the Schedule to that Act were
already in existence, some by transference
to the Ministry of Finance from certain
Imperial Departments, such as, for instance,
Public Works Commissioners, or by powers
conferred by this Parliament, such as Loans
to Education Authorities. The necessity for
the 1925 Act arose from the necessity of
raising, by means of long-dated borrowings
moneys required from time to time for loans
to Local Authorities and to others, the repayment period extending, in some cases, to
as much as 60 years. In setting up our
system the British practice was followed
generally, but one new feature was introduced, which enabled the Exchequer itself
to borrow from the Fund to facilitate certain
capital expenditure already authorised in
Northern Ireland statutes, such as housing
subsidies and police barracks reconstruction
expenditure, and I may say that in the Bill,
which I am now submitting in connection
with the last item, there are included definite
proposals increasing the limit of the expenditure to be authorised under this head, to
which I shall refer later on.
Hon. Members will remember that under
the 1925 Act Ulster Loans Stock was created,
of which £2,000,000 was issued in due course,
and the proceeds utilised to the extent of
£1,118,000 in repaying to the Exchequer the
outstanding principal of Loans made from
the Exchequer during the 3 years prior to
the establishment of the Government Loans
Fund. The balance of £900,000 was to provide
money for fresh advances which would probably be required in the period from the
passing of that Act up to 31st March next.
We now come to the proposals contained in
the Bill before the Committee. Under Clause
1 it is proposed that the Ministry of Finance
be empowered to raise by the issue of Ulster
Loans Stock a sum of £4,250,000 in all, and
consequentially to lend up to that amount
for the various services financed from the
Fund. That is to say, the £900,000 margin
under the 1925 Act is on the verge of becoming exhausted, and authority is required
to advance during the next 2 years, i.e.,
in the period up to 31st March, 1929, a further
sum of, approximately, £2,250,000. Hon.
Members may remember that the Act of 1925
contemplated the introduction of an Annual
Bill to provide for such extensions of lending
power, and in time to come it is hoped that
this method will be the normal procedure.
We are, however, still dealing with the abnormal initial years when it is extremely
difficult to estimate, even for a period extending over 21 years, the calls which will
be made by local authorities and the Exchequer on the Fund. In these circumstances
administrative convenience has suggested a
further extension of the first special initial
Exchequer Bill-
Second Reading.
HOUSE OF COMMONS
[Mr. Barbour]
period rather than an extension providing
for a year's requirements only. It would be
idle for me to pretend that this figure of
£2,250,000 is an accurate forecast of the requirements of the Fund over this period; we
have, however, judged to the best of our
ability the demands that are likely to be
made upon it.
1 Clause 2 consolidates in a convenient form,
with certain amendments, the existing
enactments relating to the various classes of
loans. No new feature of importance has
been introduced, but the opportunity has
been taken to consolidate and clarify the
powers of the Ministry of Finance as regards
its lending operations. It will be appreciated
that for the first year of our existence while
we were feeling our way our lending powers
were obtained piecemeal from this House
according as new demands arose. Consequently, as a glance at the Second Schedule
of the Bill will show, our powers are scattered through various Northern Ireland Acts,
no less than nine in all. The present Bill
embodies in the First Schedule a comprehensive list of lending purposes. The various
classes of loans are now described under three
categories:-Local Loans, comprising loans
made to local authorities on the security of
the rates, Land and Works Loans, which
generally comprise the smaller lending operations formerly vested in the Commissioners
of Public Works, Dublin, and also include
the power granted to the Ministry by legislation of this Parliament to lend to civil
servants for housing purposes, and thirdly,
Development Loans, which generally provide
for the making of loans for any purposes
for which previously the Department of
Agriculture, the Forestry Commission,
the
Development Commission and the Intermediate Education Board had power to lend.
The new consolidated authority does not
depart from the spirit and intention of the
original authorities. If anything, it tightens
control.
While
on the subject of the various
classes of loans, it may be convenient if at
this stage I refer to the enactments
specifically repealed in the Second Schedule.
Most of them are repeals of the Sections
which are now replaced by the First
Schedule, but there are, however, two provisions which deal with loan services to
which I should perhaps draw the attention
of the House. The first relates to Civil Service Housing Loans, which under the
Finance Act of 1923 are subject to a time
limit, namely, 31st March, 1928. This limitation was introduced as a result of representations made in this House, but the
Government feel that it should now be removed. The provisions have been of great
benefit to civil servants generally, at first to
officers transferred from Dublin, who were
unable to find houses to rent, and now in an
increased degree to those ex-Service men who
have been recruited locally. Moreover, the
transfer of Government Offices to Stormont
must inevitably compel a proportion of Civil
Servants now residing outside Belfast or at
the furthest point of Belfast from Stormont
to obtain houses in the vicinity of the new
offices. I may perhaps add as a general
observation that the security for these loans
is of an ample character.
The second relates to Section 2 of the
National School Teachers' Residences (Ir
land) Act, 1875, and in this connection it is
proposed to remove the £250 limit beyond
which under that Act a loan cannot be
made.
Clause 3: Power is taken in Clause 3 to
increase the amount that may be spent on
police barrack reconstruction to £800,000,
the amount fixed at present being £375,000.
I stated in connection with the Money
Resolution that the earlier figure of £375,000
was in the nature of guesswork. As a re
sult of a survey undertaken in 1923 of the
then existing accommodation it was found
necessary to erect new barracks in about
90 cases, and to reconstruct existing barracks
in about 115 cases. Forty cases were selected
in which to commence operations, but it
soon became apparent from the contract
prices and tenders received that on the basis
of the improved accommodation, which had
been agreed as necessary, the provision of
the original sum of £375,000 would be inadequate for carrying out the scheme as
originally contemplated. Steps have been
taken to reduce the cost of the scheme to a
minimum, consistent with efficiency, and
more particularly by the introduction of
new type of standard barrack, but even 50,
the cost of carrying out the scheme on the
lines proposed will, it is estimated, entail
an expenditure of about £800,000. It is in
tended that this scheme shall be carried out
over a period of ten years, and on this basis
average annual issues of £100,000 will be
required from the Exchequer.

Mr, KYLE: The only point of criticism
I want to level at this particular Measure
is the proposal outlined in Clause 3 to
which the Minister has referred. It seems
to me if the object is to make arrangements
for the provision of something like 90 new
barracks and the reconditioning of 115,
costing on the average about £4,000 each, it
is doing something that this House should
not approve of, because it seems to me if
we are going to do that-erect 90 new barracks and recondition 115 already existing
ones-we are making provision for a police
force which is out of all proportion to what
should be required for the governing of
1,250,000 people. To spend or to propose to
spend £800,000 on police barracks-roughly
about 17s 6d. per head of the population-is
something that should give us all pause
before we agree to it. The original sum of
£375,000 was large enough, but to expend
£800,000 is a thing I do not think men in
their senses would agree to. It may have
been necessary to have had a huge police
force during the three years 1921 to 1923,
but at the present time to make arrangements for the housing of all these policemen
who are now in the force is something that
a future House of Commons will not agree.
to, and I think maybe the present Government itself will not agree to the maintenance of such a huge police force at such a
cost for such a small community as ours.
That is the only criticism I have to level
at that particular Clause.
Then there is Clause 4 where it seems an
unlawful practice is going to be agreed to by
the Ministry. It is a very funny position for
the responsible Minister of Northern
Ireland to agree that an unlawful practice
should be established, and that he should
make an unlawful practice lawful by passing
a Clause in an Act of Parliament. I am glad
to be able to congratulate the Ministry on
the success of their loan, the Ulster loan.
But speaking generally in regard to the provisions made by this House I do not see
that it is going to put us-as I feared and as
I stated in this House-it is going to cost
Ulster people more to raise their own money
than it did to borrow the money from the
fund raised in Great Britain.
Mr. O'NEILL: With regard to section 5 of
this Act I should like to hear from the
Minister on whose recommendation it has
been decided that the salary of the Comptroller and Auditor-General should be increased by the amount he now asks. Has
this been in the report of Sir Russell Scott,
or was it the Ministry themselves? In the
debates on all the Estimates I think the
general trend of opinion was that the salaries
of officials were quite large enough in this
Parliament, and at this stage of this Session
to introduce in this Bill an addition to any
salary is a thing that I at least take exception to, and I am sure there are other
Members in the House who will also do the
same.
I thought the time had arrived when there
should have been some curtailment of the
salaries of officials, considering that you are
preparing for a reduction in the population
of the area which you govern. It was said
the other day that there were more people in
your area than you could employ, and you
have made preparations for their removal by
putting them into a training school for
three months so that they could be exported.
In that condition of affairs it is not at all
in keeping with the proper government of
the country that the salaries of officials
should be increased. For that reason I certainly object to this increase under Section
5 of this Act.
With regard to the matter which the hon.
Member (Mr. Kyle) who sits immediately
in front of me raises-the cost of the police
barracks which has been increased by over
100 per cent.-I do not think it is at all
necessary. I think the Government might
have in that instance at least been more
economical. I believe that many of the
barracks would have done without spending
the amount they are spending on them, or
at any rate with much less cost than they
propose. If the Government were anxious,
as a Government should be, to go in for
economy this is a very bad way of economising. I do not see that there is any necessity
as a matter of fact for this increase with
regard to police barracks from £375,000 to
£800,000. That is a very large item, and if
we do not raise these matters when they are
introduced in a Bill I do not know at what
stage you are going to put a stop to this
thing. I do not really see how you can go

portions of this particular Bill.

The MINISTER OF FINANCE (Mr.
Pollock): I should like to take the points
raised on the three Clauses under discussion
categorically. As regards the police barracks
I am sorry to say we have great cause of
complaint against the Imperial authorities
for handing over to us police barracks in
such a disgraceful condition that it really
implied this, that the great mass of them
were not fit for human beings to live in.
And although our efforts were directed
naturally at the time of the transfer to the
responsibility that should have rested on the
Imperial Government-that these and other
buildings should be transferred to us in
such a condition that we could reasonably
expect them to be suitable for the purpose
for which they were intended-as I have said
to our great regret the Imperial authorities
refused to recognise any liability in respect
of police barracks, and justified their action
because of the conditions under which police
barracks are provided in Great Britain,
where it is well known the local authorities
are responsible for all the police arrangements.
It was very difficult of course to traverse
an argument of that kind, because if we
claim to occupy a place analagous to that of
our fellow-citizens in Great Britain in other
matters, how could we claim an advantage
over them in regard to police barracks? But
I would remind the House that while this
Estimate of £800,000 is submitted in the Exchequer and Financial Provisions Bill it does
not necessarily follow that that amount will
be spent. I would remind the House that
the improvements contemplated in police
barracks will extend over a period of 10
years and there will be very ample time not
only for this Parliament but for the succeeding Parliament to scrutinise the work as it
is continued. That is my reply to my hon.
Friends who sit opposite in respect of the
police barracks, and I am quite sure they
will admit that under the circumstances
we are proceeding judiciously. As far as the
question of economy is concerned there is no
one in this House feels the responsibility or
more necessity for economy than I do be
cause of the liabilities that have been thrown
upon the Government for matters into the
nature of which I need not enter now, but
which will make it somewhat difficult to
balance our accounts this year.
As regards the second point raised, that
is about the receipt stamps, that is really
too small a matter to warrant any great
discussion. The explanation is that the
Comptroller and Auditor-General must
satisfy himself that all vouchers presented
by the Departments in support of payments
fulfil the requirements of the law, but where,
by inadvertence or otherwise, a person receiving money and signing a receipt is under
the impression that a Governmental receipt
requires no stamp it would be obviously the
reverse of economy to enter into any great
correspondence with regard to the nonimposition of a twopenny stamp, a course
which in the end would probably cost a
great deal more than the stamp itself. This
simply gives the Comptroller and Auditor-
General power, when he sees there has been
a bona-fide mistake made, to accept the
voucher as a true and accurate voucher of
payment. That is all that is implied, and
really there is nothing in it to raise any
apprehension whatever or to introduce anything in the nature of looseness in the
arrangement.
The third point raised was in regard to
the salary of the Comptroller and Auditor-
General. I should explain to the House that
when the first Comptroller and Auditor-
General was appointed he had served a long
period with the Imperial authorities, and
had become a pensionable officer, or rather
had reached the age at which automatically
he could claim a very considerable pension.
When arrangements were made with him we
were under the impression that that pension
would go towards his payment as Comp

the lecture on economy that was delivered by

and is one of the most highly paid officers.
in the whole service. I think the Comptroller
and Auditor-General in Great Britain receives something like £3,000 or £3,500 a year,
because this officer is responsible to Parliament and to Parliament alone. The idea
I had in my mind in settling his salary at

the salaries of other highly-placed officers of
Mr. DEVLIN: I think the reply of the
right hon. Gentleman is extremely unsatisfactory. It is quite a novel position for him
to occupy to stand up in this House and
defend extravagance. It almost strikes me
that, while he is inclined to be very economical in all things that affect the general
masses of the public, there is no Minister
who lends himself so completely to what in
my judgment is indefensible expenditure.
Take the case of these police barracks. Does
the right hon. Gentleman think that at a
time like this, when there is a clamant demand for houses for the poorer people, when
there is poverty, and even destitution, prevailing throughout the Province, and when
people are complaining, and complaining
bitterly, that the Government can justify
such a striking increase in the cost of the
improvement and maintenance of police
barracks in this Northern Province? There
is no artisan or labourer who does not feel
the need for better housing. There is no
section of the working classes which does not
make constant demands for improved housing
conditions, and always the answer to this,
and to all the claims we make in the direc
tion I suggest, is "We cannot afford it. We
cannot afford it." Yet he can afford to expend, not £375,000 on police barracks, but
he wants the House now to sanction the
increase of that outlay to £800,000. A more
extraordinary condition of things I have
never heard of, that at a time like this
entirely unneedful expenditure is taken on
the shoulders of the State while, as I say,
extreme poverty, destitution, and bad housing prevail all over the Province. In
addition to that I want to know what is the
necessity for this increased expenditure on
the maintenance of police barracks in Ulster.
Mr. POLLOCK: To give them decent
accommodation.
Mr. DEVLIN: I would like to do a tour
with the right hon. Gentleman and see how
much this pathetic story he has told us about
the indecent conditions under which the
police live is justified. I only know them by
passing along the roads, and I think they
are very comfortably housed. I remember
when I was on the Public Accounts Committee I could not attend it very often, but I
should have liked to attend it, because you
would not expect humour in a Committee of
that sort, but it was the most extraordinarily
funny Committee ever I was on. We actually
shrieked with laughter. My hon. Friend the
Member for Antrim (Mr. Crawford), I believe, is still shrieking with laughter at some
of the expenditure we discussed on that
Committee. I remember one item which
amounted, I think, to £3,000-a little over
Exchequer Bill-
Second Reading.
HOUSE OF COMMONS
[Mr. Devlin]
£3,000 for telegrams and stationery in connection with money to be spent on the whitewashing of police barracks. When I heard
this I said to the Committee, "I cannot
understand this for the life of me, because
I could whitewash the whole Government for
£3,000." Imagine £3,000 for telegrams about
whitewashing. It reminds me very much of
a conversation I once had with a young naval
officer crossing to Holyhead. He was giving
me an example of the red tape that was
carried on at the Admiralty, and he said,
Do you know that at one time on our ship
we wanted twenty bags of sawdust, and it
cost the Admiralty £1,200, because we could
only give the order in Devonport, and we
had to bring the ship into Devonport before
we could get that sawdust?" That spirit of
sawdust and telegrams for whitewashing
seems to have permeated the conduct of our
affairs in Northern Ireland. That gives the
House an idea of the amount of money that is
spent on these things. I deny entirely-I do
not care what the right hon. Gentleman (Mr.
Pollock) says-any necessity whatever for
this expenditure, not only of £375,000 but of
the £800,000 which the right hon. Gentleman
is asking for. Then, in addition to that, the
population, as my hon. Friend the Member
for Down (Mr. Patrick O'Neill) has stated,
is decreasing in Ulster. This money is being
mostly used, I take it, in rural Ulster.
Mr. POLLOCK: Everywhere.
Mr. DEVLIN: But especially in rural
Ulster, because the police barracks in the
city were very good. The British Government took very good care to see their shop
windows well looked after, and, therefore,
they took good care of the police barracks
in the city. But this is mostly in rural
districts, and to spend this enormous sum
in improving police barracks, or in making
them more convenient for the police, is, in
my opinion, a most unjustifiable proceeding,
and I was glad the right hon. Gentleman did
not attempt to defend it.
As I say, the population is decreasing
in Northern Ireland, especially in rural
Northern Ireland, and you do not need the
same number of police. You ought to reduce
the number of police, and you ought not to
have any need for so many police barracks,
and, therefore, your expenditure should
decrease, and you should be able to spend
this money in some productive pursuit in
the Northern Province. You are spending
£16,000 for a college in which to train
emigrants to go out to Canada. If that
college is as I take it it is to deal with
potential citizens of mighty lands beyond
the seas, then you are getting rid of more
population, so that, in face of the everdecreasing population,, and the clamant
needs of the people, the workers in the community who have to toil long and constantly,
for better houses, I think there is an amount
of brazenness about the Government in
coming forward and making a proposal of
this character.
I just want to say a word about the increase of salary to the Comptroller and
Auditor-General. Last year there was a
motion made to reduce the salary of Mr.
Huggett. I voted against that. I am in
favour of real economy, but I believe that
the best officials ought to be paid the highest
salaries, and I know myself of the services
which Mr. Huggett rendered. He was the
most perfect watchdog of the public interests
and finances I have ever known. He
examined the accounts meticulously, and he
drew the attention of the members of the
Committee to anything he saw wrong. He
even came into personal contact with the
members of that Committee, and pointed out
the needs for economy, and upon that point
my hon. Friend (Mr. Beattie), who represented Labour, and myself, were absolutely
behind Mr. Huggett. I am not so enthusiastic,
therefore, about the question of this increase
of salary. I believe that a competent official
responsible for such important public work
ought to be well paid, but I think on the
other questions which have been raised by
my hon. Friends, and considering the constant refusal of the right hon. Gentleman
(Mr. Pollock) to vote sums of money for
what are essential public needs, in view of
the fact that we asked him to create the
same standards of taxation here in the
Northern Province as those that exist in
Great Britain, and his constant refusal to
de so he has constantly refused to do that;
he has imposed taxes on Northern Ireland
which are not imposed in England-in view
of all these circumstances I venture to join
in the protest which has been made by my
hon. Friends.

The PRIME MINISTER: I would not have
intervened in this debate but for the fact that
the question of the housing of the Royal
Ulster Constabularly had been attacked by
the hon. Member opposite (Mr. Devlin).
When the separation between Great Britain
and ourselves in regard to our financial
relations was effected, we-my right hon.
Friend, the Minister of Finance, and Ihoped that the British Government in
handing over the old R.I.C. barracks would at
the same time make a very generous allowance
to us in view of the deplorable condition of
the buildings. I do not know whether hon.
Members in this House have had an oppor
tunity such as I have had of investigating
the condition of some of the police barracks
that were bequeathed to us when the separation took place. I venture to say that no
language could overstress the evil conditions
Exchequer Bill-
Second Reading.
4 NOVEMBER 1926
of certainly a large number of those barracks.
I have seen with my own eyes dwellings in
which the men were required to live that
were utterly unfit for human habitation. I
do not think that that language is too
strong. What was to be done to remedy
this indefensible situation became an acute
question with my colleagues and myself.
We made a very strong appeal to the
Imperial Government, and my right hon.
Friend (Mr. Pollock) and Sir Ernest Clark
both appeared before the Colwyn Committee
and made the strongest representations that
a large sum of money should be allocated
in the final settlement in order to enable us
to put these buildings into something like
decent repair. After months and months of
arguing the case, and putting before the
Committee the strongest possible evidence
as to the realities of the situation, I am
sorry to say that our request for assistance
in this particular direction was turned down
by the Colwyn Committee.
Mr. DEVLIN: Shame
The PRIME MINISTER: I quite agree
with the hon. Member that it was a shame.
Then the practical question immediately
arose, what was to be done? The only thing
that could be done was, first of all, to put
into sanitary condition those barracks in
which it was possible to do so, and in the
second place to build afresh on a new and
a standard style where the existing barracks
were absolutely unfit for further use. That,
of course, entails a large amount of money,
but I venture to say that the whole House,
and I think the whole of Ulster, would
insist on the guardians of our peace and
order inside the Ulster area being properly
housed. (Hon. Members: Hear, hear.).
as we
The first thing necessary to ensure a contented police force-such a force
require in Ulster-is to see that the men are
properly housed. What is it we are asking? This is 1926; we are not living in the
back ages. The Government and this
Parliament have voted large sums of money
to help to improve the housing conditions of
the poor. Are we to do that and neglect
those who guard the lives and property of
the poor as well as of the rich? I say no.
In spite of the vehemence and anger which
have been exhibited by the hon. Member for
West Belfast-
Mr. DEVLIN: I am not angry; you are.
You only think I am angry.
The PRIME MINISTER: At any rate
in spite of the strong language that has been
used in this regard by the hon. Member,
I think it is only fitting that this House
should vote the sums of money necessary
for this purpose. I may say to the House
that the Ministry of Finance has cut down
very severely the original Estimate that was
prepared, in order to ensure that there
should be no feeling amongst the people
that money was being wasted in this
direction. This is a Cabinet matter-it has
been considered by the Cabinet-and it was
decided that, while the limit of expenditure
must be strictly defined, essential matters.
such as sanitation, water and lighting, must
be assured in all the police barracks throughout the Ulster area. I fear it is going to
take us longer to carry out those renovations than we would have liked, but it is
necessarily slow work.
We have got to get our Estimates, we have
to buy land, sometimes we have to bore for
water, and we have to make arrangements
with the local authorities regarding lighting
and heating; but I can assure the House
that rapidity will be observed in getting
those fine men placed in proper habitations.
I have the greatest respect for the Force
itself, and I know they will be patient-as
they must be during the considerable
period that must elapse before we are able
to say to them that we are satisfied that all
is well in regard to the police barracks in
the Northern area. I do trust that the
House will generously vote the
money
necessary for this purpose, being assured by
my right hon. Friend (Mr. Pollock) that not
a single shilling will be wasted in doing
what we think right and proper in this
matter.

Further, there is not a Member of the Opposition who is not desirous of seeing all the

dealing with the expenditure of £7,000 or

up big palatial buildings, with installations

liness and personal comfort of the men, and

munity that we were looked after in suck

condition. They have neglected to carry out
that duty. It is the duty of the Minister
of Finance to make proper representations
to them, and if they refuse to meet their
just demands, which the Government contend are just, let them withhold the amount
from the Imperial contribution and save the
taxpayers this horrible imposition which
you suggest should be put on the already
overtaxed people.
With regard to the salary of the Comp
troller General, I do not take so much
exception to the amount of the increase. I
think we are justified in paying for the best
possible man who can be secured for that
position. After all he has the protection
that we have in dealing with these accounts.
I for one would not be opposed to the increase in that salary at all.
Mr. POLLOCK: May I intervene at this
juncture? I am concerned at the publication
of figures which are misleading, and I would
like to remove a misapprehension which
seems to exist in regard to the figures. The
£800,000 referred to in the Bill will reach
its maximum, if the money is spent, at the
end of ten years. In the meantime, the Vote
for the R.U.C. includes a sum of money
which will extinguish the expenditure in a
period of twenty-five years, so that the
£800,000, to which reference has been made
as the cost of the R.U.C., so far as this year
is concerned, also provides for the extinction
money of the cost of the barracks which
has been criticised by the hon. Member (Mr.
McAllister). I am particularly anxious that
that information should be conveyed not only
to the House but to the public.
Mr. GEORGE HENDERSON: I just want
to ask one question about the third Section
of the First Schedule under the heading of
"Development loans." Under this loans are
available for the development and improvement of agricultural land and live stock and
of land suited for forestry, for the purchase
of agricultural machinery, implements and
equipment, and the purchase of agricultural
buildings. I would like the Minister to give
some information with regard to the extent
to which these loans have been applied for
and granted. What are the terms of repayment of loans granted to farmers to improve
their farms and live stock?
Mr. POLLOCK: The purpose of this Bill
is only to provide the necessary powers to
make these advances or loans to which my
hon. Friend refers. It gives no return of the
amount or numbers of the loans, and the
hon. Member would require to give some
notice in order that definite figures may be
furnished.
Mr. GEORGE
HENDERSON: I just
wanted to raise the question. It is not
generally known amongst the agricultural
community that such loans are available. If
these loans are granted at a reasonable rate
of interest with long terms of repaymentit would be of great benefit to the agricultural community.
Mr. POLLOCK: They have existed for the
last fifty years.

HOUSE OF COMMONS.

Tuesday, 9th November, 1926.
The House met at Three of the clock, Mr.
SPEAKER in the Chair.
Oral Answers to Questions.
IRISH LINEN TRADE.
1. Mr. DEVLIN asked the Minister of Commerce whether his attention has been called
to the statement that the improvement in the
linen trade, which was hoped for at the beginning of the year, has not come; whether
the prospects in the United States are decidedly bad; and whether he can say if there
are now any signs of an improvement in the
industry; what are the methods adopted in
connection with the advertising campaign, to
which the Government contributed a large
sum, and what effect, if any, it has had in
improving the trade.
The MINISTER OF COMMERCE (Mr.
Barbour): Whilst my attention has not been
called, specifically to the statement which
forms the subject of the first part of the
hon. Member's question, I have noticed in
certain American newspapers statements expressing an extremely unhopeful view of the
prospects of the Irish linen trade in the
United States market. There is nothing in
the present situation to warrant extreme
pessimism of this kind. Recovery from the
conditions of industrial and economic dislocation of the post-war years must of necessity be slow. There is no doubt that the textile industries have been passing through a
period of extreme depression, but they are
not unique in this, and I would remind the
hon. Member that the American textile industry has itself shared in these unfortunate
conditions. The benefit of the gradual monetary stabilisation on the Continent of Europe
should eventually make itself felt, and the
feeling in the Belfast linen industry, as I
know it, is one of hope, I think I may indeed
say one of confidence, that we have passed
the trough of the depression.
With regard to the latter part of the question, the general arrangements for the Publicity campaign in the United States are in
the hands of a special Committee in New
York, which is composed of men conversant
with every phase of the linen trade, many of
them in fact the direct representatives of
Ulster linen houses. Amongst the activities
of this Committee may be included: The
issue of monthly trade magazines to linen
retailers throughout the length and breadth
of the United States, and the insertion of advertisements in specially selected publications appealing not only to the trade but also
to the individual consumer. There is a further circulation of booklets, window and
counter cards, mats and special literature.
Window displays are being organized and
publicity for linen is being secured in the
editorial columns of newspapers and magazines. In addition to this a portion of the
Publicity Fund will be devoted to educational
work in schools and colleges, women's clubs,
and art exhibitions.
The active launching of the Publicity Campaign only took place in the beginning of
September last, and whilst it is too early to
look for concrete results from the publicity
efforts, it is satisfactory to note that the
reception accorded to the campaign is decidedly encouraging. Moreover, the hon. Member may have noticed that despite the generally adverse conditions arising out of the
dispute in the mining industry there has
been during the past two months a distinct
improvement in the unemployment figures
relating to the linen industry.

LICENSING PROSECUTIONS AT
LURGAN.
The following Question stood on the Order
Paper in the name of Mr. Grant:
To ask the Minister of Home Affairs
whether his attention has been drawn to a
report in the "Northern Whig," of 20th
October, dealing with three licensing prosecutions heard before Mr. G. McElroy,
R.M., and Major Dickie, R.M., at Lurgan;
whether in a case against Thomas Mulholland for shebeening the police evidence went
to show that whisky, porter, "Red Biddy
and empty bottles were found on the
premises, yet the magistrates granted a
dismiss; whether in a second case against
Richard Burphy, for having failed to enter
in his delivery book details of porter received
by him at Tandragee, the magistrates imposed a nominal fine of ten shillings, while
the case against the vanman for aiding and
abetting was dismissed; whether in a third
case two men, named McCourt and McGribben, were let off on payment of a fine of five
shillings for selling intoxicating liquor without a licence; and whether, in the view of the
right hon. Gentleman, the magistrates
adjudicated with undue leniency, and not in
accordance with the evidence.
Mr. SPEAKER: Perhaps I should say before calling on the hon. Member that I have
looked into the matter with which this
question deals, and, although it is a fact that
it would not be in order to question any sentence or decision given by a judge of the
High Court or of any County Court, or of
any other Superior Court, at the same time
I think that does not apply to Resident
Magistrates, or to the ordinary members of
the Bench. Therefore, I rule that the
question is allowable.
Mr. GRANT: I now put the question.
Sir DAWSON BATES: In the first case
referred to against Thomas Mulholland, one
half-pint of whisky and three bottles of
Tawny Wine (which, I am credibly informed, is sometimes known as "Red Biddy")
were found on the premises in addition to
three empty porter bottles. The charge was
one of keeping intoxicating liquor for sale
In the second case a delivery van belonging
to Mr. Brophy was found to contain one
dozen of stout, for which there was no invoice. The court evidently did not consider
that the case was an aggravated one, and
imposed a penalty on Mr. Brophy of ten
shillings. The case against the vanman was
withdrawn on the conviction of Mr. Brophy.
In the third. case Peter Gribben and
Edward McCourt were summoned with others
for selling beer without a licence on the
occasion of a sports meeting. There was
some doubt as to who was responsible for
having the liquor there, and after a prolonged hearing, the court convicted the
above-mentioned men, and fined them 5s
each, with 8s 8d costs.
I have no reason to question the decision
of the two experienced Resident Magistrates,
who heard these cases, and had the whole of
the evidence before them.
Mr. GRANT: Arising out of the right hon.
Gentleman's reply, I would like to ask him
if he is aware that the Attorney-General for
Northern Ireland, in this House, on October
28th, said that
anyone who peruses the records of the fines
that are imposed in a great number of
cases for matters, which are really serious,
will see that at present a lot of those fines
are purely illusory. (Official Report, Vol.
7, No. 25, col. 2034).
That being so, will the right hon. Gentleman
consider the advisability of fixing minimum
fines in these licensing cases?
Sir DAWSON BATES: I am not aware
that the Resident Magistrates did not regard
these as serious cases, and I think their
decision was entirely correct.
Mr. DEVLIN: Would the right hon.
Gentleman consider the advisability, under
the Poisons Act, of taking steps to deal with
this atrocious sale of what is known as "Red
Biddy," a form of poison sold as wine, which
is working widespread and universal demoralisation amongst the whole of the people
of the Province?
Sir DAWSON BATES: I am not aware of
that. I have not the same experience of
"Red Biddy as the hon. Gentleman.

MINING AREAS IN ANTRIM.
5. Mr. KYLE asked the Minister of Labour
whether he is aware that acute hardship
exists in the mining areas in Antrim, owing
to the refusal of his Department to pay
unemployment benefit to the miners who are
unable to obtain remunerative employment,
and that the wages paid to the men engaged
in the mines are less than thirty shillings
per week; and what action he is prepared
to take to see that Unemployment Insurance
benefit and adequate wages are paid to these
men.
The MINISTER OF LABOUR (Mr. Andrews): The claims to unemployment benefit
of workers in the iron-mining industry in
County Antrim have been refused by my
Department only where the statutory conditions were not fulfilled: and the hon.
Member will, I think, agree that their claims
have been sympathetically dealt with when
I say that the men have received from the
Fund, on an average, 500 days' benefit in
excess of what their contributions entitled
them to. I have no power to reinstate any
person to Unemployment Benefit who does
not satisfy the prescribed conditions.
As regards the wages paid in the industry,
I am informed that the men work in intermittent spells and that it is a common prac
tice for them to follow farming or other
employment in addition to mining. I am informed that they are paid on a piece-work
basis which yields in a normal week from
32s 6d to 48s according to the time which the
men devote to work in the mines.
offered to those men who have been longest
unemployed and have the greatest responsi
bilities as regards wife and dependent children. The system has been repeatedly
reviewed and has met with the approval of
representatives of Trade Union organisations,
and I am satisfied that it is the most equi
table to all concerned. My hon. Friend's
suggestion would mean that in many instances work would be given to single men,
while married men would consequently be
deprived of it. I would be glad, however,
to discuss the matter with the hon. Member

9 NOVEMBER 1926
Motion made, and Question proposed:
That, notwithstanding any Standing Order or
Custom of the House, the remaining stages
of the Local Government (War Service
Payments) Bill, and the Finance (Stamp
Duty) Bill, may be taken at this day's sitting.
-(The Prime Minister).
Mr. DEVLIN: It is the business of the
independent Members of this House to raise
a protest against the action of the Government in forcing this legislation through without discussion. I can very well understand
that the Government might be inspired to
take up this attitude if they had passed
through a period of prolonged Parliamentary
work on their part and considerable obstruction on the part of the Opposition. I do not
think the Prime Minister or any Member of
the Government has any legitimate reason
to complain as to the attitude of the
Opposition towards the Bills which the
Government have presented, nor do I think
they will assert that there has been any unnecessary time occupied in the criticism of
the Measures which have been introduced by
the Government. Therefore, I cannot understand the mentality of the Government at
the end of a Parliamentary Session of three
weeks in submitting a Motion of this character, which practically means that they
want to carry these Measures through by a
rather indefensible form of closure.
When Parliament met less than a month
ago we expected to find that as a result of
quiet, careful, and considerate attention to
the problems which they proposed to solve
by Parliamentary action the Government
would have brought forward their Measures
in complete and perfect form. As they had,
through the period of their vacation, nearly
three months to consider these proposals, I
would have imagined, as I have said, they
would have brought forward their Measures
in perfect Parliamentary form. Instead. of
that, there has not been a single Bill introduced by the Government that has not been
So imperfect, as the Government have
admitted, that no sooner was the Second
Reading passed than we were face to face
with a series of Amendments put upon the
Paper by the Government-that is, to their
own Measures. Anyone must come to the
conclusion, therefore, that these Bills and
the proposals that have been submitted have
been very ill-considered, because if they were
well considered there would be no need for
the Government to introduce the pages of
advertisements-(laughter)-excuse me, I
have been recently at the Advertising Clubpages of Amendments to their own Measures.
I would have thought that a Government
with any sense of self-respect would have
considered and hesitated before they would
have made an admission of the character
indicated in the method of procedure they
have adopted. They, first of all, occupied the
time of the House in the Second Reading of
a Bill which they themselves proposed. Then
they proceeded to occupy the time of the
Committee in dealing with a series of Amendtuents which, if they were all linked together,
would constitute a Bill. In that way the
Government have practically occupied the
whole time of the House during the last
three weeks. That is bad enough. But then
we have the Prime Minister or the Chief
Whip coming forward on several occasions
this Session and moving the suspension of
the 6-30 p.m. rule, which meant that those
Members like myself and my colleagues on
these Benches, who give constant and active
attendance in this House, are compelled to sit
here beyond the Parliamentary hour in order
to let the followers of the right hon. Gentleman home by an early train. Of course, 1
am in a better position to judge than the
right hon. Gentleman, because I watch the
departure of these Gentlemen-a regular
scamper of the Parliamentary followers of
the right hon. Gentleman to catch their
trains.
The result is that we are kept here discussing these questions in the absence of
those Gentlemen who should discuss them
during the normal hours, from 3 p.m. to 6-30
p.m., which is not a very long Parliamentary
day for any of us considering that we meet
only three months in the year. We would
first of all have the advantage of discussing
these questions in an atmosphere of mental
clarity, and in the second place we would be
able to get contributions, no doubt
magnificent contributions of wisdom and
worth, from the followers of the right hon.
Gentleman who depart every day to their
various scenes of intellectual activity. I
object entirely to this method of legislation.
In the first place, it shows a great contempt
for Parliament. Here we have a Parliament
of our own. I quite admit it is a Parliament nobody wanted. The right hon. Gentleman (the Prime Minister) did not want it,
and we did not want it. It is a Parliament
set up without the sanction of anybody,
forced upon us by the British Government
without asking our leave. The right hon.
Gentleman has stated in several of his
speeches that he accepted it because it was
imposed upon him. I accepted it because it
was imposed upon me at a later stage.

broadening out the scope of the debate is

HOUSE OF COMMONS

that I think we ought really to know where

Minister and the Government as an outrage
upon the dignity and status of this Parliament. Now that I am in this Parliament I
want to preserve its dignity, not that it nas
much dignity, but such as it has we want to

-for this extraordinary method of passing

leave and the rest of us will be compelled
to remain to a late hour in the evening.
Upon several grounds I object to this and
I intend to vote against it. I object to it on
the ground that there should be no rushed
legislation. I object to it on the ground that
such time as we have has been occupied by
the Government in amending their own
legislation, because, as I have stated before,
they never accept any Amendments of ours.
As a matter of fact, the series of Amendments which they placed upon the Paper in
relation to one of their most important Bills
was a series of Amendments that was put
down, or was about to be put down, by
Members of the Opposition and which were

body. These are two reasons. The third is
that I think the people will come to the conclusion that there is no need for this Parliament at all. You can come here and rush
your legislation through in whatever form
you like and determine whether it is legislation that requires discussion or whether
you will introduce a Bill to amend it. As
these are the methods which the Government
have adopted all through this Session and
all through last Session I cannot, for one,
sanction the procedure which has been suggested by the Motion of the right hon.
Gentleman, and I will vote against it.
The PRIME MINISTER: I am always

Mr. BEATTIE: On the Third Reading of
this Bill I would like to make one further
appeal to the Minister before the Bill becomes
a statutory Measure. I feel that the Bill
does not meet the requirements of the com
munity of the Six Counties, and when I say
that I mean the trading and travelling
public. I feel that this is an opportun
moment for the Government to hesitate
and consider the amount of damage done to
property and goods of the people of the Sir
Counties by what we generally term in the
city mud-splashing. Mud-splashing is &
thing that every person endeavours to avoid
if possible, but there are times when it is
absolutely impossible to get out of the wa

of the heavy motor traffic. Now it has been
brought to my notice by the Minister of
Home Affairs that there has been nothing
yet put on the market that would eliminate
the mud-splashing from heavy lorries. Well
to a certain extent I would agree with the
Minister in that statement. But I do not
think that it is a proposition outside the
genius of man. I believe it is a practical
proposition and if properly attended to an
invention could be brought out preventing to
a very large degree the great annoyance now
caused by heavy motor lorries.
We
We
I might say, as a Member of the Board
of Guardians, that in that Board we had
not the brains or the genius to invent a
separate lighting and heating scheme,
wanted something drawn up to save the ratepayers' money, and to give the best service
to the institute we could possibly get.
found we were wanting in intelligence, as
far as invention was concerned, and we decided to send out a prospectus asking the
trading public to send in schemes whereby
the best central lighting scheme would be
applied to the Belfast Union. We had
schemes from all over Great Britain. We
had them from throughout Ireland. We had
somewhere about 32 schemes to choose from
before proceeding with the best scheme. We
decided to give a prize of 100 guineas, and
that 100 guineas has been the means of
bringing in to the ratepayers of Belfast a
scheme, which has not yet been set upon to
work out, but it has been the means of
bringing in a scheme whereby the ratepayers
in future will be saved thousands of pounds
per annum through the saving of coal by the
better central lighting and heating scheme
in the Belfast Union. Now I contend that
100 guineas has been well spent, because to
take the wild-cat ideas of architects before
they give the thing serious consideration
sometimes leads public authorities into very
large expense. So we took the most modern
way of doing it. We admitted we had not
got the intelligence, and we sought what the
trading public could do in setting out
schemes and we offered 100 guineas.
My point is here that we in Northern
Ireland have roads that are altogether
different from those in Great Britain. That
cannot be denied. Great Britain has good
roads, and I believe our best road here to-day
-and I say this with little hesitation-would
only come about equal to the second grade
road in Great Britain.. We have the
journeys round the coast, and, perhaps, some
hon. Member, when he was spending his
holidays down at the coast, happened to be
trapped on a wet day, just on a road where
he could not take shelter from a mudsplashing char-a-banc, and if he had that
experience I am afraid he would not be in a
very nice state of mind when the char-a-banc
passed. On a country road, meeting one of
these buses, you are liable to be covered from
head to foot in the class of weather that
causes this annoyance.
Going on to the scheme I suggested on the
Committee stage, that we should endeavour
to assist our local people who have got the
inventive mind, and we have in the Six
Counties certain men of great ability and
genius for invention. It cannot be denied
that during the war men from Ulster brought
inventions forward, with the result that they
were accepted, and did good service for the
time they were required. We have men of
the same class and type of mind in Ulster
to-day. We have a very simple proposition.
It may seem a very hard one to solve. but
I think it is simple to the man whose mind
is concentrated on that class of work, because
the demonstrations in London have proven
to me that if a committee of neutrals had
been set up, without too much consideration
being given to the cost of upkeep, we would
have had a system of protection from mudsplashing to-day in Great Britain. We
would have had a device attached to lorries
protecting the travelling public from mudsplashing. Now, there is a scheme that I
am going to refer to now. I notice the
Minister is reading the Report.
Sir DAWSON BATES: I have read it.
Mr. BEATTIE: Then you will be conversant with this. There is Scheme 32. It
is an Englishman's idea, and we have an
Irishman's idea also, and, being an Irishman, I want to see Irish ability coming
forward. I am going to say an Irish invention is responsible for the protection of
the body as far as clothes are concerned.
The only fault I find with the Irish invention is that it does not keep the lower
reaches of the legs free from splashes, but it
certainly does keep the head and body free,
as was shown on the screen which the demonstrators had erected for the purpose. We
have the 32 inventions, which were the nearest
to perfection demonstrated on that occasion.
I believe it is possible for other men, with
the knowledge gained by inventions recently
put on the market and rejected, to bring out
a perfect device in the North of Ireland. If
we can bring a device of this kind to per
fection, we can capture the whole trade of
Great Britain and Ireland, because we can
get the patent rights if the scheme is brought
to perfection, and it will create in the North
of Ireland an industry that does not exist at
present. From that point of view alone, and
from the point of view of giving employment
to the people who are walking our streets, I
think the Government should consider the
question of spending some money with the
object of encouraging genius to give us the
assistance that we require to deal with this
problem of preventing mud-splashing.

HOUSE OF COMMONS
[Mr. Beattie]
I want to give you two or three concrete
facts of damage to business premises caused
by mud-splashing. I have already told you
what happened to myself, and I would now
like to make a point on behalf of business
premises. We will take the city streets on
any slushy, wet morning. If you go round
any of the streets in which the footpaths are
not too broad, you will find mud splashes on
the windows of premises and on the goods
exposed at and around the door. That state
of affairs is rather disappointing to business
men who have sent their employees out to
clean their windows and to decorate
the outside of their shops. It really
means that the employees have been
wasting their time, for as soon as the
work is done a lorry may come along and
make a target of the window and the goods
at the door, splattering mud on the window
and destroying any goods that are exposed
outside the door.
A draper did not foresee one morning the
class of weather that was coming. He hung
out about £50 worth of goods outside his
door. The rain came on. Of course he had
his screen out to protect the goods from the
rain, but the rain left the streets in a bad
way, and then a lorry heavily laden with
potatoes came along, and the man concerned
tells me that the £50 worth of goods displayed
outside the door was depreciated to the extent of £20. The damage was done to shirts,
suits of clothes, dust coats, and women's
wear. That sort of thing is very annoying
from a business point of view.
It is very annoying to go up Donegall Street
on a wet morning, and to find that when a
lorry is passing you have to run into a doorway to avoid the mud-splashing. I would
also like, while on this subject, to call the
attention of the Belfast Tramways Committee
to the splashing caused by shifting points on
the track. I want to suggest to the Minister
that he should make regulations to deal with
this problem, and give a lead by opening a
competition for the best device for preventing mud-splashing. I will take the test of
the Automobile Association as the test necessary for the competitors. The competition
could be open, or it could be confined, whatever the Minister thinks fit. If he thinks he
can get good brains in Great Britain, let him
have an open competition; if he thinks he
can find the brains locally, let him confine
the competition. I believe in confining the
competition to our own manufacturers, and
in giving them an opportunity of bringing
out a successful invention.
The best device, as I said before, has
eliminated the risk to wearing apparel above
the lower portion of the body. There is a
device in the book for attaining that object.
That scheme would do me very weil, because
it throws mud only eighteen inches from the
wheel. The mud has not the opportunity of
getting up owing to the device attached to the
wheel, and in consequence the pedestrian's
body is protected. There were twelve points
attached to the competition in Great Britain,
Every one of those, with the exception of two,
is necessary. One exception is the matter of
cost. I am not very much concerned about
the initial cost, if I am going to protect the
people and their property. I think the ques
tion of cost should not be considered until
protection is provided for the people. The
other exception is appearance. Do you think
a pedestrian who has had a mud bath is
more objectionable in appearance than a
motor lorry with an ugly guard? I would
prefer the ugly guard on the lorry, no matter
what its shape or make, to the splattering of
the pedestrian on the footpath.
I make my appeal to the Minister on the
ground of protection for the public, I make
it on the ground of protection for business
premises, and I also make it on the ground
that the travelling public have the right
to walk the streets without being mudsplashed from head to foot. I tell the
Minister that this omission from the Bill is
going to cause very much grumbling and dissatisfaction throughout Northern Ireland,
and I ask him to accept my suggestion in
regard to setting up a competition, whereby
he can secure the assistance of the best brains
in the North of Ireland in bringing about a
scheme of protection that will be suitable to
all concerned. I make this appeal to the
Minister of Home Affairs.

Dr. MORRISON: I would like to say a
word or two on what I believe to be a more
important question than has been raised by
any of the speakers who have addressed you
on this matter to-day. The rate of mortality
due to reckless driving has impressed the
public, and has impressed this House.
would be inclined to say that second only
to reckless driving in danger to motorists,
and consequently to the public, is the danger
from obstructions placed on the road. In the
country we do not worry about an occasional
spark from a passing motor, but when we
know that road metal and other obstructions
are placed on the roadway to the danger of
the men driving motors I think it is time
to make a complaint. I would just like to
give you an illustration. Two young fellows
a few years ago came down to Portrush
driving a motor cycle and sidecar. They
went out from Portrush to Bushmills and
coming home at night ran into a heap of
road metal that projected four feet on to the
roadway. Their motor bicycle was thrown
over and both young fellows were killed. I
think I heard the hon. Member for West
Belfast (Mr. Devlin) describe all these Bills
as twopence ha'penny things that nobody
wanted. Here is a case of two young fellows
from his own constituency who came down
to Portrush and met their death through no
fault or cause of their own. This Bill and
the suggestions I made are introduced to prevent such things.
I venture to say that Members of the
House, if they cast their memories back,
will remember the man who went from
Jerusalem to Jericho, and fell amongst
thieves. Three individuals passed him. The
first to pass him on the other side was a
priest, the second was a Levite, and the
third was a good Samaritan. I suggest, in
the case of these two young fellows from
Belfast, that the good Samaritan is the Home
Secretary, who is trying to make provision to
safeguard the public. The hon. Member for
West Belfast (Mr. Devlin) has, therefore, the
option of deciding whether he is the Levite
or the priest. He is certainly not the good
Samaritan. What we did in that case was
to pass a resolution. I held the inquest in
this case, and we said the accident was due
to placing, four feet across the road, an
obstruction which overturned the motor
bicycle, and we called on the county authorities to have the roadways freed from these
obstructions.
That is the second occasion on which
juries, over which I presided, called
upon the county authorities to take steps
to prevent these obstructions on the side of
the road. One was where a man was killed
through his neck being broken, and this was
the second. Another case was that of a
skilled driver, who came from Belfast to
take up a job in Portrush. The very first
day he was at work, and when coming back
from his dinner, he was run down on the
public road and killed. I think myself that
the accident was probably due to obstacles
on the road. All over Ulster you will see
the persistent, vicious habit of placing road
metal and other things on the side of the
road, at corners-most dangerous placesand at bridges. You will find heaps of
stones two feet out on each side of the road.
People accustomed to motoring know that
sometimes a foot will enable a motorist to
come safely through and avoid a collision
that might have ended fatally, or produced
a calamity such as those we read about so
much,
I introduced two Amendments in this Bill

make provision to deal with these things. I

Mr. KYLE: I beg to move, "That, in the
opinion of this House, it is desirable that
every employee throughout Northern Ireland shall receive at least one week's
holiday, with pay, in each year."
In moving this Motion I want to draw the
attention of the House to the urgent importance of this particular question, and, if
I can, also to draw the attention of the House
to the present position of the men working
in the shipyards, engineering establishments,
mills and factories, and the women workers
who are working in the warehouses and the
mills and factories. When these people are
told in the middle of July, or at Christmas,
or at Easter that their mills or the shipyards are going to be closed down it is for
them not so much a holiday as a period of
enforced idleness. As a matter of fact,
during these past two years deputations of
trade unionists have waited upon the shipyard employers to the end that they might
see their way
to reduce the period of
holidays in the middle of the year owing to
the fact that the wages of the workers are so
small that they cannot save any money to
enable them to enjoy a holiday.
I want the House to express their opinion
this afternoon as to whether or not it is
desirable in the public interest that employees throughout the Six Counties should
get holidays with pay. Of course, everybody
Everyagrees that a holiday is necessary.
body realises the necessity for a period of

family ties and housework in addition. On

holidays themselves have the effect of

the subsequent curtailment of the necessaries of life to himself and his family
makes the health of the community come into

The death rate of the total population is
considerably higher in Northern Ireland
than it is in England and Wales. In 1920
the death rate in Northern Ireland was 16.6,
in England and Wales 12.4; in 1921 it was
15.2 in Northern Ireland, and 12.1 in England and Wales; in 1922 it was 15.4 in
Northern Ireland, and 12.8 in England and
Wales; in 1923 it was 14.7 in Northern

1924 the death rate in Northern Ireland had
gone up to 15.9. Surely it is evident that
it is very necessary that we should do much
before we can raise the standard of health
to anything like a moderately decent level.
If Great Britain has, as some statesman
declared, a C3 population, what on earth
must ours be classified as? Surely it behoves

not be so difficult to carry into effect, as in
some of the larger countries, Measures for
the improvement of the health of the

I think it right to take this opportunity
to correct a very wrong impression which
people have regarding the amount of time
lost through one cause and another in the
industrial field. We hear it stated very often
that the strikes that take place from time to
time are the greatest drawback to the development of industry. What are the facts
in this connection? The fact is that there
were 8,000,000 working days lost during the
year 1925 as a result of industrial disputes.
That is a very large figure, but when you
take into consideration that there were
12,000,000 workers, it means roughly that twothirds of a day per worker was lost in industrial disputes in the year 1925. According
to the evidence of the chief medical officer
in Britain, Sir George Newman, no fewer
than 150,000,000 days were lost through sickness in 1925, which shows how much more
important is the health of the community
than even this question which occupies so
much attention both in the Press and in
private conversation. In addition to that
there were in 1925 375,000,000 days lost
through unemployment. That is. of course,
in Britain. I wanted to take the opportunity
of correcting the 1ather false impression
which people have that all the time that is
lost is lost through trade disputes, when the
actual fact is that there is considerably more
time lost owing to sickness and ill-health
than to any other preventible cause. As
attempt should be made to remedy that cause
by this House to-day passing this Motion.

induce local inventors to do something towards a solution of this problem?
dealt with in that Measure. With regard to
the point raised by my hon. Friend the
Member for East Belfast (Mr. Beattie) with
regard to mud-splashing, I think there is a
certain amount of misunderstanding in regard to this matter. In the 1896 Act power
is given to make Regulations dealing with
mud-splashing, and to make a Regulation
that devices should be used to prevent mudsplashing. Therefore, it is entirely unnecessary to introduce that matter into the
present Bill.
I may point out that so far back as 1919
the Local Government Board, acting under
powers conferred upon them by the 1896 Act,
did make a Regulation and prescribed that
heavy vehicles should all be provided with
anti-mud-splashing devices, but the practical
operation of the Regulation showed it was
impossible to enforce the law. In other
words, there was no suitable device. While
I admit quite frankly it is a hardship on
pedestrians that they should have their
clothes splashed with mud I think it
would be a greater hardship on motor
owners that they should be asked by law
to do a thing that is not possible, and that
if they did not carry out an impossible task
they should be fined.
We are still going into this matter and are
still studying it very carefully along with
the Ministry of Transport in England. They
have conducted a very elaborate set of experiments. They invited the inventors of
these anti-mud-splashers to come before
them and show the merits of their different
appliances. No fewer than thirty-two inventions were brought forward, and they
were all tested. I might tell the House what
the final finding of the Committee in charge
of the matter was. They say:
The judges, after careful consideration,
do not recommend any award in either
class.
They were divided into three classes.
They have come to the decision because,
in their opinion, the devices failed in the
first essential of a mud-splash guard; that
is to say, no device reduced the amount of
mud splashed to a negligible quantity.
As I said earlier, if any individual can produce a suitable device I can assure him it
will be welcomed not only here but in England, where the Ministry of Transport, like
ourselves, have come to the conclusion that
until a suitable device is introduced it would
be unfair to the motoring public to enforce a
Regulation of this character.

three times the number of human beings
Mr. POLLOCK: Probably occasionally
more. To revert again to the argument that

should be attacked in many ways because of
their neglect in handing over the police

and as the citizens of Great Britain
locally provide their own police and provide
their own police barracks, the Colwyn Committee naturally argued why should
Northern Ireland be placed in a privileged
position as compared with the citizens of
Great Britain. Now I stated when this case
was being argued before, that it was a most
difficult argument to meet, because in these
matters we have fought our corner exactly
upon the basis that the citizens of Northern
Ireland were entitled to the same conditions
and the same privileges in every way as the
citizens of Great Britain. And as I say,
when we come to discuss this question we
cannot have it both ways. Be that as it may
the Colwyn Committee, a purely arbitration
committee, settled that we were entitled to
provide our own police barracks and to provide them in our own way. I cannot see the
argument in respect of housing, that if this
£800,000 were only devoted to housing, and
so on. This £800,000 is devoted to housing.
It is doing what hon. Members opposite are
always clamouring for, it is to house
3,000 people and possibly their families.
Therefore, it is doing exactly what we are
doing in other cases. We are providing, or
helping to provide, houses for the general
community by allowing subsidies, and here
we are simply providing, not luxurious, but
necessary accommodation for the police of
Northern Ireland. I am greatly surprised
that hon. Members opposite, who are
clamant on the subject of decent accommodation for the ordinary citizens of the country,
should raise a clamour because the policemen in Northern Ireland are being placed in
a position of common decency and nothing
more.

Mr. KYLE: I want to move that this
Clause be deleted. I cannot see why the
Comptroller and Auditor-General should be
put in any different position to any other
person in the land. It is not lawful to give
an unstamped receipt for an amount
of
more than £2, and the receipt
does not hold unless there is રી 2d
stamp on it. I cannot see at all why
the Minister of Finance wants to make a
differentiation in this particular case. Why,
if he is going to put this thing through the
Committee here, should an ordinary person
be compelled to put a 2d stamp on a receipt?
It seems to me that he is going in direct
violation of the law, as it stands to-day, in
regard to the stamping of receipts, and I am
surprised that a man of his probity, and with
his ideas of financial matters, should desire
to make it legal that a receipt should not
bear a 2d stamp. For that reason I desire to
see this Clause deleted.
Mr. POLLOCK: It is not intended by this
Clause to empower the Comptroller and
Auditor-General to make documents legal
that are in fact illegal. If my hon. Friend
will read the Clause carefully he will see
that all that is contemplated by it is that if
the Comptroller and Auditor-General re
ceives a document receipted without a stamp,
he can use it as a voucher in his accounts.
It does not preclude him from taking steps
against the offender if he considers it necessary to do so. I am not here to say whether
he will or will not communicate with the
person who received the money, and who has
neglected or deliberately omitted to impose
a stamp. I am not here to say whether any
or what action will be taken in respect of
that omission. I am sure that the Comptroller
and Auditor-General can be trusted to see
that the law is enforced, but there are cases
in which he must necessarily be permitted to
exercise his descretion.
I mentioned a few minutes ago, to some
friends here, a case which is an example
of what may take place. A person residing
in the French Riviera, in Mentone or Monte
Carlo, returned a receipt with a French
receipt stamp on it. I am quite sure that he
could not get a British twopenny receipt stamp
where he was residing, and very foolishly he
assumed that a receipt stamp issued by the
French Treasury was a proper stamp to affix
to the document. Suppose the Comptroller
and Auditor-General had begun corresponddence with that gentleman, how much would
it have cost all over twopence? And he could
not enforce the law, even if he wanted to do
so. Curious cases arise, and the only object
of this Clause is to ensure that the Comptroller and Auditor-General, in his discretion, may use in the Public Accounts Committee a document without the stamp affixed
to it, for the purpose of showing that the
money was legitimately paid and legitimately
acknowledged.
Amendment, by leave, withdrawn.

Local Government (War Service
Payments) Bill.
Order for Second Reading read.
Motion made and Question proposed:
"That the Bill be read a Second time."

Sir DAWSON BATES: I am sure that
every hon, Member of the House will appreciate the short Bill which I have the privilege to submit. The object of the Measure,
as its heading states, is to remove doubts as
to the powers which were conferred upon
Local Authorities by Section 1 of the Local
Government (Emergency Provisions) Act,
1916. Hon. Members, doubtless, are aware
that during the late War many local authorities undertook to make payments in respect
of salary or wages to local officers and employees, or their dependents, who took service
in His Majesty's Forces. In the case of the
undertakings given at the commencement of
the War, these were not supported by statutory sanction, and ultimately the Imperial
Parliament passed the Local Government
(Emergency Provisions) Act, 1916, enabling
the fulfilment of such undertakings, and
gave specific powers to local authorities to
grant leave of absence to any officer or servant for so long a period as might be necessary to enable him to serve in His Majesty's
Forces. In addition, power was given to
authorities to make payments to officers and
employees or their dependents, of portions
of their salaries or wages, and in the event
of the death of an officer or employee whilst
serving with the Forces, to make payments to
his widow or other dependents.
During the period of the War, the salaries
Οι wages of officers or workmen of local
authorities were, like persons in general employment, increased at different times to
meet the increased cost of living, by means
of bonuses and in some cases by an actual
permanent increase; but local authorities, in
making their contributions in respect of men
in His Majesty's Forces, had only regard to the
salaries and wages the men were in receipt
of at the time they joined up, without reference to the bonuses or increases which
had been made to those who had continued
in the actual service of local authorities.
It will be thus seen that the effect of
paying employees who joined up early in the
War on the basis of the remuneration which
they received at the time of joining up, and
of ignoring bonuses or additions was that employees who joined up later received a larger
amount by reason of the additions made by
way of bonus or increment.
Some time after the termination of the
War, the question was raised as to whether
salary or wages payable to men on War
service included the appropriate bonus which
would have been payable to them had they
remained at home, and it was decided in
the House of Lords in the Sutton case, a
decision with which many hon. Members are
familiar, that salary or wages included
bonus, and, accordingly, men who joined up
were entitled to increases that took place
during the period they were engaged in the
War. The important feature of the Sutton
case was that the appellant was a Government official when he joined up, and that in
effect there was a continuity of services
whilst in the Army. In a subsequent case
(the Druce case) which went to the House of
Lords, Druce failed on the ground that
there was no continuity of service, and that
when he had joined the Forces, in effect, he
severed his connection with his employers.
Mr. BEATTIE: What about the Harbour
Board?
Sir DAWSON BATES: We are not dealing
with the Harbour Commissioners at tho
moment. This decision, coupled with the
statutory limitations of time within which
payment should be made, has raised difficulties in the way of local authorities in
making them without statutory sanction.
Some local authorities have taken the risk
and made payments of agreed amounts of
bonuses to their ex-Service officials, but it
was found in the case of others that the
amounts involved were so large that it was
desirable to obtain Parliamentary sanction,
and it is for this purpose the Bill is presented
to you. It is a one-Clause Bill which is to
enable local authorities to pay or agree to
pay to their ex-Service officials, or their dependants, such proportion of the bonus and increment of salary as they may decide, and at
the same time to remove any difficulties
which might arise by reason of the Statute
of Limitations. It will be noticed, in order to
expedite the payments, it is proposed that
they should be made by local authorities
before the 31st March, 1928, the end of the
financial year.

they consented to go to the War, I cannot
understand how it is that the Belfast
